| **Lighthouse** | Automated audits for performance, accessibility, SEO | Quality checks |
| **Device toolbar** | Emulates screen sizes, touch and network throttling | Responsive testing |

Firefox and Safari have equivalent panels with slightly different names, such as *Inspector* and *Debugger* in Firefox.

**Debugging techniques**

- **Breakpoints:** line breakpoints, *conditional* breakpoints (pause only when an expression is true), *logpoints* (log without changing code), DOM-change breakpoints, fetch/XHR breakpoints and event-listener breakpoints.
- **Stepping:** step over, into and out of functions, while watching variables and the call stack.
- **The `debugger` statement:** pauses execution at that line whenever DevTools is open.
- **Network tools:** disable the cache, throttle to slow connections, block requests, and copy a request as `fetch` or cURL to replay it.

**Example: Console API beyond `console.log`**

```javascript
const users = [{ id: 1, name: 'Ada' }, { id: 2, name: 'Linus' }];
console.table(users);                      // shows the array as a sortable table

console.time('sort');                      // start a named timer
const nums = Array.from({ length: 1e6 }, () => Math.random());
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);
console.timeEnd('sort');                   // "sort: 182.4 ms"

console.group('Order #42');                // collapsible, indented group
console.log('items: 3');
console.warn('shipping address missing');  // yellow warning with a stack trace
console.groupEnd();

console.assert(nums.length === 1e6, 'Length changed!'); // logs only when the condition is false
console.trace('How did we get here?');                  // prints the current call stack
```

**Example: Console-only helpers** (the DevTools Command Line API, not standard JavaScript; they only work when typed into the Console)

```javascript
$0                                 // the element currently selected in the Elements panel
$('nav a')                         // shorthand for document.querySelector (if the page hasn't defined $)
$$('img:not([alt])')               // querySelectorAll returned as a real array: images missing alt text
copy(JSON.stringify(users))        // copy any value to the clipboard
monitorEvents(window, 'resize')    // Chromium: log every resize event
getEventListeners($0)              // Chromium: list the listeners attached to the selected element
```

**Example: pausing in code**

```javascript
function applyDiscount(cart) {
  for (const item of cart.items) {
    if (item.price < 0) debugger; // pauses only for suspicious data, and only when DevTools is open
    item.final = item.price * (1 - cart.discount);
  }
}
```

Remove `debugger` statements before shipping. Most linters flag them.

**Key Takeaways**

- DevTools let you inspect the DOM, styles, network traffic, storage, performance and memory of a live page.
- Use the Network panel to debug APIs and the Performance panel to diagnose slowness.
- Breakpoints, especially conditional breakpoints and logpoints, are more effective than scattered `console.log` calls.
- The Console API (`table`, `time`, `group`, `assert`, `trace`) and Command Line helpers (`$0`, `$$`, `copy`) speed up investigation.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On any website, use the Network panel to find the largest resource and the slowest request. Reload with "Slow 4G" throttling and note how the load time changes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a loop over 1000 objects that has a bug for one specific item. Find it using a conditional breakpoint instead of `console.log`, then do the same with a logpoint.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A user reports that a page feels slow. Walk me through how you would use DevTools to diagnose the problem." *Hint:* separate loading performance (Network, Lighthouse) from runtime performance (Performance panel, long tasks, layout thrashing), and reproduce the user's device conditions with throttling.

#### Feature Detection and Polyfills

Your users run many browsers and versions. You might want to check *which browser* the visitor is using and branch on that, but this **user-agent (UA) sniffing** is fragile: UA strings are long, inconsistent and deliberately misleading (almost every browser claims to be "Mozilla"), browsers are reducing the information they contain, and a browser that gains a feature later still gets the fallback.

**Feature detection** asks the right question instead: *does this browser support the feature I need?* You test for the API itself and then use it, or choose a fallback.

**Analogy:** instead of checking a guest's nationality to guess which languages they speak (UA sniffing), you simply ask, "Do you speak Italian?" (feature detection).

Feature detection supports two related strategies:

| Strategy | Starting point | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **Progressive enhancement** | A working basic version for everyone | Add better features where they are supported |
| **Graceful degradation** | The full-featured version | Make sure it still works acceptably when features are missing |

**Polyfills.** A **polyfill** (a term coined by Remy Sharp in 2009) is code that implements a missing *API* using features the browser already has, so your code can use the modern API everywhere. A **ponyfill** provides the same function without modifying global objects.

Polyfills can only add APIs. **New syntax cannot be polyfilled**, because an older engine fails while *parsing* code it doesn't understand, before any polyfill can run. Syntax needs **transpilation** at build time.

| Need | Example | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| Missing API (function, object, method) | `Array.prototype.at`, `structuredClone`, `fetch` | Polyfill (core-js, or a hand-written one) |
| Unsupported syntax | `?.`, `??`, `class` fields, arrow functions | Transpiler (Babel, TypeScript, esbuild, SWC) |
| Missing CSS feature | `display: grid`, container queries | `@supports` with a fallback layout |

```javascript
// Source code (ES2020)
const city = user?.address?.city;

// Transpiled for older engines: same behaviour, older syntax
var _user$address;
var city = user === null || user === void 0
  ? void 0
  : (_user$address = user.address) === null || _user$address === void 0
    ? void 0
    : _user$address.city;
```

**Example: feature detection in JavaScript and CSS**

```javascript
// Check that the API exists before using it
if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {
  lazyLoadImagesWithObserver();  // modern path
} else {
  loadAllImagesNow();            // simpler fallback that still works
}

// Check CSS support from JavaScript
if (CSS.supports('selector(:has(a))')) {
  document.documentElement.classList.add('has-support');
}

// Some features exist but can still fail (Safari private mode, quotas, disabled storage)
function storageAvailable() {
  try {
    const key = '__test__';
    localStorage.setItem(key, key);
    localStorage.removeItem(key);
    return true;
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}
```

```css
/* Baseline layout that works everywhere */
.gallery {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
}

/* Enhanced layout only where Grid is supported */
@supports (display: grid) {
  .gallery {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
  }
}
```

**Example: writing and loading a polyfill**

```javascript
// A simplified polyfill for Array.prototype.at (ES2022)
if (!Array.prototype.at) {
  Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, 'at', {
    value: function at(index) {
      const len = this.length;
      let i = Math.trunc(index) || 0;     // NaN or undefined -> 0, 2.7 -> 2
      if (i < 0) i += len;                // negative index counts from the end
      return i < 0 || i >= len ? undefined : this[i];
    },
    writable: true,
    configurable: true,
    enumerable: false,                    // keep it out of for...in loops, like built-ins
  });
}

// Load a polyfill only when needed, so modern browsers don't pay for it
if (!('structuredClone' in globalThis)) {
  await import('./polyfills/structured-clone.js');
}
```

**Supply-chain caution.** In 2024 the popular `polyfill.io` CDN domain changed owners and started serving malicious code to the sites that embedded it. Prefer self-hosted or bundled polyfills (for example core-js through Babel's `useBuiltIns: 'usage'`) over scripts loaded from third-party domains you don't control.

**Key Takeaways**

- Detect features, not browsers. UA sniffing is fragile and goes out of date.
- Use `in` checks, `typeof`, `CSS.supports()` and `@supports`, and wrap features that can fail at runtime in `try/catch`.
- Polyfills add missing APIs. Transpilers rewrite unsupported syntax. Neither replaces the other.
- Load polyfills conditionally and self-host them to reduce bundle size and supply-chain risk.
- Progressive enhancement starts from a version that works for everyone and adds features where they are available.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write feature checks for the Clipboard API, the Geolocation API and the `<dialog>` element, logging which are supported in your browser.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a polyfill for `Object.hasOwn(obj, prop)` that only installs itself when missing, does not show up during enumeration, and behaves correctly for objects created with `Object.create(null)`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is feature detection preferred over user-agent sniffing, and is there any case where UA sniffing is still justified?" *Hint:* think about features that technically exist but are broken in one specific engine version, and about analytics, compared with deciding which code path to run.

<a id="2-document-structure-and-presentation"></a>
## 2. Document Structure and Presentation

Every web page is built from two separate layers: HTML describes what the content *is* (its structure and meaning), and CSS describes how that content *looks* (its presentation and layout). This chapter covers the HTML document model, including semantics, forms, media and accessibility. It then covers the core mechanics of CSS, such as the cascade and the box model, and the layout systems used to build interfaces that adapt to any screen. These foundations make pages more accessible, easier to maintain and easier to script, so everything that follows on the DOM, JavaScript and front-end frameworks depends on them.

<a id="21-html-document-model"></a>
### 2.1 HTML Document Model

This subchapter covers how an HTML document is put together: its skeleton and metadata, the elements that carry meaning, collect input and embed media, and the practices that make content usable by everyone.

#### Document Structure and Metadata

When a browser receives an HTML file, it has to answer several questions before it can show anything. Which set of rendering rules should it follow? How should the bytes be decoded into characters? What language is the text in? How wide is the screen it should lay out for? What title should appear in the tab? An HTML document answers these questions in a fixed skeleton at its very top. If the skeleton is wrong, you get garbled characters, pages that appear zoomed out on phones, or layouts that follow rules from 1999.

**Elements, tags and attributes.** HTML is a *markup language*. You wrap content in **tags** to create **elements**, and you configure elements with **attributes** written as `name="value"` pairs inside the start tag.

```text
<a href="/about" class="nav-link">About us</a>
\________________________________/\______/\__/
            start tag              content end tag
   \___________/ \______________/
     attribute       attribute
```

Some elements, called **void elements**, cannot have content and so have no end tag: `<meta>`, `<link>`, `<img>`, `<input>`, `<br>`, `<hr>`, `<source>`. A trailing slash (`<br />`) is allowed but ignored in HTML.

Elements nest inside each other, and this nesting forms a **tree**. The browser parses the markup into that tree, called the **DOM** (Document Object Model, covered in depth in Chapter 6), and everything else (CSS styling, JavaScript, accessibility) works on that tree rather than on the raw text.

**The document skeleton.** Every HTML document has the same top-level shape:

```text
Document
 +-- <!DOCTYPE html>            -> rendering mode switch, not an element
 +-- html  (lang="en")          -> root element; declares the language
      +-- head                  -> metadata: not rendered on the page
      |    +-- meta charset
      |    +-- meta viewport
      |    +-- title
      |    +-- link (stylesheet, icon, ...)
      |    +-- script
      +-- body                  -> everything the user sees
           +-- header
           +-- main
           +-- footer
```

**The DOCTYPE.** `<!DOCTYPE html>` is not an HTML element. It is a switch that tells the browser to use **standards mode**. Without it, browsers fall back to **quirks mode**, which deliberately copies bugs from browsers of the late 1990s so that very old pages keep working.

| Mode | Triggered by | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| No-quirks (standards) | `<!DOCTYPE html>` | Follows the current CSS and HTML specifications |
| Limited-quirks | Some legacy transitional DOCTYPEs | Standards mode, except for a few table-cell image layout rules |
| Quirks | Missing or very old DOCTYPE | Emulates old bugs, for example a different box model in some contexts and fonts not inheriting into tables |

You can check the mode of any page from the console with `document.compatMode`. `"CSS1Compat"` means standards mode and `"BackCompat"` means quirks mode.

**Essential metadata.** The `<head>` holds information *about* the document:

| Element | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `<meta charset="utf-8">` | Character encoding | Must appear within the first 1024 bytes. A byte order mark or the HTTP `Content-Type` header overrides it. |
| `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` | Tells mobile browsers to lay out at the device's width | Without it, phones render a virtual page about 980px wide and shrink it |
| `<title>` | Tab text, bookmark name, search result headline | Required. Make each page's title unique. |
| `<meta name="description">` | Summary often shown in search results | Does not affect ranking directly |
| `<link rel="stylesheet" href="...">` | Loads CSS | Blocks rendering until it has loaded |
| `<link rel="icon" href="...">` | Favicon | SVG and PNG are both widely supported |
| `<link rel="canonical" href="...">` | Preferred URL when the same content has several URLs | Avoids duplicate-content problems in search engines |
| `<link rel="preload">` / `rel="preconnect"` | Resource hints | Start critical downloads or connections early |
| `<meta property="og:...">` | Open Graph data for link previews on social media and chat apps | Title, description, image, URL |
| `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` | Instructions for search crawlers | Use it on staging and private pages |

**Loading scripts.** A plain `<script>` stops the HTML parser: the browser must download and run the script before it can continue, because the script might change the document. The `defer` and `async` attributes avoid that pause.

```text
<script>        parse ======|           |====== parse continues
                            |-fetch-|run|

<script defer>  parse ====================================|run (in order)
                         |---- fetch ----|                   before DOMContentLoaded

<script async>  parse =============|run|==================
                         |- fetch -|      runs as soon as it arrives, any order
```

| Attribute | Blocks parsing? | Execution order | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | Yes | Document order | Rare today. Small inline scripts that must run immediately. |
| `defer` | No | Document order, after parsing | Application code that needs the DOM |
| `async` | No | Whenever each script finishes downloading | Independent scripts such as analytics |
| `type="module"` | No (deferred by default) | Document order, after parsing | Modern ES module code (Chapter 3) |

**A forgiving parser.** HTML parsers never reject a document. If you leave out `<html>`, `<head>` or `<body>`, the parser creates them. If you leave a `<p>` unclosed, it closes it for you. This forgiveness means invalid markup often *looks* fine but produces a different tree from the one you intended. Use the W3C Nu Html Checker (validator.w3.org/nu) to find these mistakes.

**Character references.** Characters that have a special meaning in markup must be escaped when you mean them as text: `&lt;` for `<`, `&gt;` for `>`, `&amp;` for `&`, `&quot;` for `"`. Others are conveniences, such as `&nbsp;` (non-breaking space) and `&copy;`.

**Example: a complete, production-ready skeleton**

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>                                   <!-- standards mode -->
<html lang="en">                                  <!-- language for screen readers, hyphenation, translation -->
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">                          <!-- first, so everything after it decodes correctly -->
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Pricing | Acme Cloud</title>             <!-- specific first, brand last -->
  <meta name="description" content="Simple monthly plans for teams of any size.">

  <link rel="canonical" href="https://acme.example/pricing">
  <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.example.net">  <!-- open the connection early -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/main.css">

  <!-- Link preview metadata -->
  <meta property="og:title" content="Acme Cloud Pricing">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.example/og/pricing.png">

  <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>        <!-- doesn't block parsing, runs after the DOM is built -->
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Visible content goes here -->
  <p>Prices start at &euro;9 per user &amp; month.</p>   <!-- character references -->
</body>
</html>
```

**Global attributes.** Some attributes are valid on every element:

| Attribute | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `id` | Unique identifier in the document (for links, labels, scripts) |
| `class` | Space-separated list of classes for CSS and JavaScript |
| `lang` / `dir` | Language and text direction (`ltr`, `rtl`, `auto`) for that subtree |
| `hidden` | Hides the element (equivalent to `display: none` unless CSS overrides it) |
| `tabindex` | Takes part in keyboard focus order (see Accessibility and ARIA Basics) |
| `title` | Advisory tooltip text. It is not a reliable way to label anything for accessibility. |
| `data-*` | Custom data for scripts (see HTML5 Feature Overview) |

**Key Takeaways**

- Always start with `<!DOCTYPE html>`. Without it, the browser renders in quirks mode.
- Declare `<meta charset="utf-8">` first, `lang` on `<html>`, and the viewport meta tag for mobile.
- `<head>` holds metadata that is not rendered. `<body>` holds visible content.
- Use `defer` (or `type="module"`) for application scripts and `async` for independent ones.
- The HTML parser silently repairs errors, so validate your markup instead of trusting how it looks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* From memory, write a valid skeleton for an Italian-language page called "Ricette" with a description and an SVG favicon. Run it through the Nu Html Checker until it reports no errors.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* A page displays "CafÃ©" instead of "Café". Explain which bytes were decoded with which encoding, list the three places where a document's encoding can be declared, and give their order of precedence.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `defer` and `async` on a script tag, and which would you use for an analytics snippet compared with your main application bundle?" *Hint:* think about whether execution order matters and whether the script needs the full DOM.

#### Semantic Elements

A page built only from `<div>` and `<span>` can look exactly like a well-structured one. Software that reads the page sees something very different, though. Screen readers, search engine crawlers, browser reader modes, translation tools and the next developer to open the file see only an undifferentiated pile of boxes. **Semantic elements** say what a piece of content *is*: navigation, the main content, a self-contained article, a date. Machines and people can then act on that meaning.

**Analogy:** two copies of the same book. One has a cover, a table of contents, chapter titles and footnotes. The other is a stack of unlabelled photocopies. The words are identical, but only the first can be navigated, indexed or summarised.

**Landmark (sectioning) elements.** These elements describe the major regions of a page. Assistive technologies expose them as **landmarks**, so a screen reader user can jump straight to the navigation or the main content.

| Element | Meaning | Implicit ARIA role |
|---|---|---|
| `<header>` | Introductory content for the page or for a section | `banner` (only when it is not inside `article`, `aside`, `main`, `nav` or `section`) |
| `<nav>` | A major block of navigation links | `navigation` |
| `<main>` | The dominant, unique content of the page. Use only one visible `<main>`. | `main` |
| `<article>` | Self-contained content that would make sense on its own (a post, a comment, a product card) | `article` |
| `<section>` | A thematic group of content, normally with its own heading | `region` (only when it has an accessible name) |
| `<aside>` | Content only loosely related to its surroundings (sidebars, call-outs) | `complementary` |
| `<footer>` | Closing information for the page or a section | `contentinfo` (only at page level) |
| `<search>` | A search or filtering form | `search` |

```text
+---------------------------------------------------+
| <header>  logo, site title                        |
|   <nav>   Home | Blog | About                     |
+-----------------------------------+---------------+
| <main>                            | <aside>       |
|   <h1>Latest posts</h1>           |  related      |
|   <article>                       |  links,       |
|     <h2>Post title</h2>           |  newsletter   |
|     <p>...</p>                    |               |
|     <footer>by Ada, <time></footer>               |
|   </article>                      |               |
|   <article>...</article>          |               |
+-----------------------------------+---------------+
| <footer>  copyright, contact links                |
+---------------------------------------------------+
```

**Choosing between `article`, `section` and `div`.**

```text
Could this content stand on its own (be shared, syndicated in a feed, reused)?
  yes --> <article>
  no  --> Is it a thematic group of content with its own heading?
            yes --> <section>
            no  --> Is it only a hook for styling or scripting?
                      yes --> <div>  (no semantic meaning, and that is fine)
```

**Headings.** `<h1>` to `<h6>` form the document outline that screen reader users browse, much like a table of contents. Choose the heading level for its place in the hierarchy, not for its default size (CSS controls size), and don't skip levels (for example `h2` straight to `h4`). The HTML specification once described an "outline algorithm" in which every section could restart at `<h1>`. No browser ever implemented it, and it was removed from the specification in 2022. Use explicit levels.

**Text-level semantics.** Inline elements carry meaning too:

| Element | Meaning | Not to be confused with |
|---|---|---|
| `<strong>` | Strong importance, seriousness or urgency | `<b>`: draws attention without extra importance (keywords, product names) |
| `<em>` | Stress emphasis that changes the meaning of a sentence | `<i>`: alternate voice (technical terms, foreign words, thoughts) |
| `<mark>` | Highlighted because of relevance (for example search matches) | Styling for decoration only |
| `<time datetime="2026-10-02">` | A date or time in machine-readable form | Plain text dates |
| `<abbr title="...">` | Abbreviation, with its expansion | |
| `<code>`, `<kbd>`, `<samp>`, `<var>` | Code, keyboard input, program output, variable | |
| `<blockquote>`, `<q>`, `<cite>` | Block quote, inline quote, title of a cited work | `<cite>` is for the *work*, not the person |
| `<figure>` + `<figcaption>` | Self-contained illustration, diagram or code listing with a caption | |
| `<address>` | Contact information for the nearest article or the page | Any postal address |
| `<ul>`, `<ol>`, `<dl>` | Unordered, ordered and description lists | Paragraphs separated by `<br>` |

**Example: from "div soup" to semantic markup**

```html
<!-- Before: correct visually, meaningless to software -->
<div class="header">
  <div class="menu">
    <div class="item"><a href="/">Home</a></div>
    <div class="item"><a href="/blog">Blog</a></div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="content">
  <div class="post">
    <div class="title">Understanding the Cascade</div>
    <div class="date">2 October 2026</div>
    <div class="text">The cascade decides which rule wins...</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

```html
<!-- After: the same layout, now with meaning -->
<header>
  <nav aria-label="Primary">                 <!-- the label tells apart several nav landmarks -->
    <ul>                                      <!-- screen readers announce "list, 2 items" -->
      <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
      <li><a href="/blog" aria-current="page">Blog</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</header>
<main>
  <article>
    <h1>Understanding the Cascade</h1>
    <p><time datetime="2026-10-02">2 October 2026</time></p>
    <p>The cascade decides which rule <em>wins</em>...</p>
  </article>
</main>
```

The benefits of semantic markup add up quickly:

- **Accessibility:** landmark and heading navigation, list item counts, correct announcements.
- **Search engines and previews:** crawlers can identify the main content and dates.
- **Built-in behaviour:** semantic elements such as `<button>` and `<a>` come with keyboard support for free.
- **Maintainability:** `<nav>` explains itself, while `<div class="x7">` does not.

**Key Takeaways**

- Semantic elements describe *meaning*. CSS controls appearance.
- Landmarks (`header`, `nav`, `main`, `aside`, `footer`, `search`) let assistive technology users jump around the page.
- Use `<article>` for self-contained content, `<section>` for a themed group with a heading, and `<div>` when there is no meaning to express.
- Pick heading levels by hierarchy, use one `h1` for the page topic, and don't skip levels.
- `<strong>`/`<em>` express importance and emphasis. `<b>`/`<i>` express a different kind of attention without changing importance.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite a recipe page made of `div`s (title, ingredient list, numbered steps, author, publication date) using semantic elements only, with no extra classes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Open a news website, enable the Accessibility pane in DevTools (or the full accessibility tree view), and list its landmarks and heading outline. Identify at least one semantic problem and propose a fix.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you use `<section>` rather than `<article>` or `<div>`?" *Hint:* consider whether the content makes sense on its own, whether it has a heading, and what a screen reader would announce in each case.

#### Forms and Input Controls

Forms are the Web's original way of sending data from a user to a server. Login pages, search boxes, checkouts and settings screens are all forms. A native HTML form works without any JavaScript: the browser collects the values, encodes them, sends an HTTP request and shows the response. Understanding this built-in behaviour lets you add JavaScript as an enhancement rather than rebuilding, badly, what the browser already does.

**How submission works.** When a form is submitted, the browser:

1. Collects every *successful* control. That means it has a `name`, is not disabled, and, for checkboxes and radio buttons, is checked.
2. Encodes the values as `name=value` pairs.
3. Sends them to the URL in `action` using the HTTP method in `method`.

| Attribute | Values | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | URL | Where to send the data (defaults to the current URL) |
| `method` | `get` (default), `post` | GET appends data to the URL query string. POST sends it in the request body. |
| `enctype` | `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (default), `multipart/form-data`, `text/plain` | How the body is encoded for POST. `multipart` is required for file uploads. |
| `novalidate` | boolean | Disables the browser's built-in validation |
| `autocomplete` | `on`, `off` | Default autofill behaviour for the form |

Use **GET** for safe, repeatable queries such as searches and filters, because the URL can be bookmarked and shared. Use **POST** for actions that change data or send sensitive values, which should not end up in URLs, server logs or browser history.

**Labels are not optional.** Every control needs a `<label>`. It gives the control an accessible name, and clicking the label focuses or toggles the control, which makes small checkboxes much easier to hit. Group related controls with `<fieldset>` and describe the group with `<legend>`.

**Input types.** The `type` attribute changes validation, the on-screen keyboard on mobile, and the native UI:

| Type | Purpose | Built-in behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `text`, `search` | Free text | `search` may show a clear button |
| `email`, `url` | Addresses | Format validation and a matching mobile keyboard |
| `password` | Secret text | Masked input. Password managers recognise it. |
| `tel` | Phone numbers | Numeric keypad. No format validation, because formats vary by country. |
| `number`, `range` | Numbers | `min`, `max`, `step`. `range` shows a slider. |
| `date`, `time`, `datetime-local`, `month`, `week` | Dates and times | Native picker. The value is always ISO format, such as `2026-10-02`. |
| `checkbox`, `radio` | Choices | Radios that share a `name` form a group with a single selection |
| `file` | File upload | `accept`, `multiple`. Requires `multipart/form-data`. |
| `color` | Colour picker | Value such as `#ff8800` |
| `hidden` | Data the user doesn't see | Not secret. It is visible in the page source and can be edited. |
| `submit`, `reset`, `button` | Buttons | Prefer the `<button>` element |

Other controls are `<select>` (with `<option>` and `<optgroup>`), `<textarea>` for multi-line text, `<output>` for calculated results, and `<datalist>` for autocomplete suggestions on a text input.

**The `<button>` trap.** A `<button>` inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`. A "Show password" button without `type="button"` will submit the form.

**Built-in validation.** Browsers check common constraints before submitting and show localised error messages:

| Attribute | Constraint |
|---|---|
| `required` | Must not be empty (or must be checked) |
| `minlength`, `maxlength` | Text length limits |
| `min`, `max`, `step` | Numeric and date ranges |
| `pattern` | Must match a regular expression (the whole value, implicitly anchored) |
| `type="email"` / `"url"` | Must be a well-formed address |

CSS can react to validity with `:valid`, `:invalid`, `:required`, `:checked` and `:disabled`. `:user-invalid` matches only after the user has interacted with the field, so empty required fields don't show errors as soon as the page loads.

**Example: a registration form**

```html
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Account</legend>

    <label for="username">Username</label>
    <input id="username" name="username" required minlength="3"
           pattern="[a-z0-9_]+" autocomplete="username"
           aria-describedby="username-hint">             <!-- links the hint below to the field -->
    <p id="username-hint">Lowercase letters, digits and underscores.</p>

    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="email">

    <label for="password">Password</label>
    <input id="password" name="password" type="password" required minlength="12"
           autocomplete="new-password">                  <!-- prompts the password manager to suggest one -->

    <label for="confirm">Confirm password</label>
    <input id="confirm" name="confirm" type="password" required>
  </fieldset>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Plan</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" checked> Free</label>  <!-- same name = one group -->
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro"> Pro</label>
  </fieldset>

  <label><input type="checkbox" name="newsletter"> Send me product news</label>

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
```

When the user submits with the Pro plan and the newsletter checked, the browser sends:

```http
POST /signup HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=ada_l&email=ada%40example.com&password=...&confirm=...&plan=pro&newsletter=on
```

Note that `@` is percent-encoded as `%40`, the checkbox sends `on` because it has no `value`, and an *unchecked* checkbox would send nothing at all.

**Example: custom validation with the Constraint Validation API**

```javascript
const password = document.querySelector('#password');
const confirm  = document.querySelector('#confirm');

function checkMatch() {
  // A non-empty message marks the field invalid; an empty string clears the error
  confirm.setCustomValidity(
    confirm.value === password.value ? '' : 'Passwords do not match.'
  );
}

password.addEventListener('input', checkMatch);
confirm.addEventListener('input', checkMatch);

// form.checkValidity() returns true/false; form.reportValidity() also shows the messages
```

```css
/* Show error styling only after the user has interacted with a field */
input:user-invalid {
  border-color: #c62828;
  outline: 2px solid #c62828;
}
```

**Client-side validation is not security.** It exists for a better user experience. Anyone can skip it with DevTools or by sending the request directly with `curl`. The server must always validate everything again (Chapters 12 and 17).

**Key Takeaways**

- Only controls with a `name` are submitted. An unchecked checkbox sends nothing.
- Use GET for repeatable queries and POST for changes or sensitive data. File uploads need `multipart/form-data`.
- Every control needs a `<label>`. Group related controls with `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`.
- Pick the most specific `type` to get validation, mobile keyboards and native pickers for free.
- `<button>` defaults to `type="submit"` inside forms. Set `type="button"` for other actions.
- Built-in and custom client-side validation improve the experience. The server must still validate.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a contact form with name, email, a topic `<select>`, a message `<textarea>` and a required consent checkbox. Set `action="https://httpbin.org/post"` and inspect the data that comes back.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend the registration form so that the error styling uses `:user-invalid`, the password field has a "Show" toggle button that does not submit the form, and the browser's own validation bubbles are replaced with messages written into an element linked through `aria-describedby`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What changes in the HTTP request when a form's `enctype` is `multipart/form-data`, and why is it required for file uploads?" *Hint:* compare how binary file bytes would fit into a percent-encoded string with how a multipart body uses boundaries and per-part headers.

#### Tables, Media and Embedded Content

Text alone rarely tells the whole story. Pages need grids of data, images, audio, video and sometimes whole documents from other sites. HTML has dedicated elements for each, and each comes with its own accessibility, performance and security concerns.

**Tables are for tabular data.** In the early Web, tables were used to lay out whole pages. That practice is long obsolete (use Flexbox and Grid, covered in 2.3). Today `<table>` should be used only for data with real rows and columns, where a screen reader can announce "row 3, Price column, 12 euros".

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| `<table>` | The table |
| `<caption>` | Title of the table (its accessible name) |
| `<thead>`, `<tbody>`, `<tfoot>` | Header, body and footer row groups |
| `<tr>` | A row |
| `<th scope="col">` / `<th scope="row">` | Header cell for a column or a row |
| `<td>` | Data cell |
| `colspan` / `rowspan` | Merges a cell across columns or rows |

**Example: an accessible data table**

```html
<table>
  <caption>Monthly plans</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Plan</th>
      <th scope="col">Users</th>
      <th scope="col">Price</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Starter</th>   <!-- row header: each cell in this row is "about" Starter -->
      <td>5</td>
      <td>€9</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Team</th>
      <td colspan="2">Contact sales</td>  <!-- spans the Users and Price columns -->
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

```text
              Monthly plans
+----------+-------+-------+
| Plan     | Users | Price |   <- thead, th scope="col"
+----------+-------+-------+
| Starter  |   5   |  €9   |   <- th scope="row" + td
| Team     | Contact sales |   <- colspan="2"
+----------+---------------+
```

**Images.** `<img>` needs two things in every case:

- **`alt` text** that describes the image's *purpose* in context. A purely decorative image gets an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip it. A missing `alt` makes many screen readers read the file name aloud.
- **`width` and `height`** attributes, so the browser can reserve space before the file arrives. This prevents the content from jumping around while the page loads, which is measured as **Cumulative Layout Shift**.

For performance, add `loading="lazy"` to images below the fold, and `fetchpriority="high"` to the main hero image.

**Responsive images.** A phone should not download a 2400px-wide photo meant for a 4K monitor. HTML provides two mechanisms:

| Need | Solution |
|---|---|
| Same image at different resolutions (**resolution switching**) | `srcset` with width descriptors and `sizes` on `<img>`. The browser chooses. |
| Different crops or formats (**art direction**, AVIF/WebP with a fallback) | `<picture>` with `<source>` children. The first match wins. |

```html
<!-- Resolution switching: the browser chooses the best file for the screen -->
<img src="hero-800.jpg"
     srcset="hero-400.jpg 400w, hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(min-width: 60em) 50vw, 100vw"
     alt="Team working around a whiteboard"
     width="1600" height="900"
     fetchpriority="high">
<!-- sizes: "the image will be half the viewport wide on large screens, full width otherwise" -->

<!-- Format fallback and art direction -->
<picture>
  <source type="image/avif" srcset="chart.avif">         <!-- smallest, used if supported -->
  <source type="image/webp" srcset="chart.webp">
  <source media="(max-width: 40em)" srcset="chart-cropped.png">
  <img src="chart.png" alt="Revenue grew 40% from Q1 to Q4" width="1200" height="600" loading="lazy">
</picture>
```

The `<img>` inside `<picture>` is required: it holds `alt`, the size and the final fallback.

**Audio and video.** `<audio>` and `<video>` play media natively, with no plugins.

```html
<video controls width="1280" height="720" poster="intro-poster.jpg" preload="metadata">
  <source src="intro.webm" type="video/webm">        <!-- the first supported format is used -->
  <source src="intro.mp4"  type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="intro.en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  <p>Your browser cannot play this video. <a href="intro.mp4">Download it</a>.</p>  <!-- fallback -->
</video>
```

| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `controls` | Shows the browser's play, volume and full-screen controls |
| `autoplay` | Browsers only allow it when the media is also `muted` (autoplay policies) |
| `muted`, `loop`, `playsinline` | `playsinline` stops iOS from forcing full screen |
| `preload` | `none`, `metadata` or `auto`: a hint about how much to download in advance |
| `poster` | Image shown before playback starts |

Captions (`<track>` with WebVTT files) are needed for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and they also help anyone watching with the sound off.

**Embedded content with `<iframe>`.** An `<iframe>` embeds a complete, separate document: maps, videos, payment widgets. The embedded page runs with the permissions of its own origin, so treat it as untrusted and restrict it.

```html
<iframe src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
        title="Product demo video"
        width="560" height="315"
        loading="lazy"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-presentation"
        allow="fullscreen; picture-in-picture"
        referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"></iframe>
<!-- title: the accessible name of the frame, which screen readers announce -->
<!-- sandbox: start with no permissions and add back only what is needed -->
<!-- allow: Permissions Policy that grants specific browser features -->
```

Never combine `allow-scripts` and `allow-same-origin` on a frame that loads content from *your own* origin: the framed script could then reach into its parent and remove the sandbox. A site can also refuse to be framed at all with the `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` header (Chapter 17).

The older `<object>` and `<embed>` elements were used for plugins such as Flash and Java applets, which no longer exist. Inline `<svg>` and `<canvas>` for graphics are covered in Chapter 7.

**Key Takeaways**

- Use tables only for tabular data, with a `<caption>`, `<th>` and `scope`.
- Every `<img>` needs a meaningful `alt` (or `alt=""` if it is decorative) plus `width` and `height` to prevent layout shift.
- Use `srcset`/`sizes` for resolution switching and `<picture>` for art direction or modern formats with fallbacks.
- `<video>` and `<audio>` accept several `<source>` formats. Add captions with `<track>`. Autoplay requires `muted`.
- Restrict iframes with `sandbox`, `allow` and a `title`, and lazy-load them when they are off-screen.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build an accessible table of a weekly timetable with days as columns and hours as row headers, including a lunch break that spans all days.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Serve a hero image in AVIF, WebP and JPEG at 480, 960 and 1920 pixels wide. Use the DevTools Network panel with device emulation to check which file each viewport downloads.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A page has a Cumulative Layout Shift problem caused by images and embeds. How do you fix it?" *Hint:* the browser needs to know an element's aspect ratio before the resource arrives. Think about `width`/`height` attributes, the CSS `aspect-ratio` property and reserved placeholders.

#### HTML5 Feature Overview

By the mid-2000s, web applications such as Gmail were being built with a language designed for documents. Video needed Flash, drawing needed plugins, and every site invented its own date picker. **HTML5** was the response: a large, backward-compatible update that turned HTML from a document format into an application platform.

**A short history.** After HTML 4.01 (1999), the W3C bet on XHTML 2.0, a strict XML-based language that was not compatible with existing pages. Browser vendors disagreed and formed the **WHATWG** in 2004 to evolve HTML incrementally. Their work became HTML5, which the W3C published as a Recommendation in October 2014. Since a 2019 agreement between the two bodies, the **HTML Living Standard** maintained by the WHATWG is the single authoritative specification. It has no version numbers, and it is updated continuously (see 1.3 Standards and Development Environment). "HTML5" now works as an umbrella term for the modern web platform rather than as a version.

**What HTML5 introduced:**

| Area | Additions | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| Semantics | `header`, `nav`, `main`, `article`, `section`, `aside`, `footer`, `figure`, `time`, `mark` | 2.1 Semantic Elements |
| Forms | New input types, `placeholder`, `required`, `pattern`, `autocomplete`, `datalist`, `output` | 2.1 Forms |
| Multimedia | `<audio>`, `<video>`, `<track>` | 2.1 Tables, Media |
| Graphics | `<canvas>`, inline `<svg>` and MathML | Chapter 7 |
| Interactivity | `<details>`/`<summary>`, `<dialog>`, `contenteditable`, drag and drop | This topic |
| Custom data | `data-*` attributes | This topic |
| APIs | Web Storage, History, Geolocation, Web Workers, WebSocket, File API | Chapters 5, 6, 10 |
| Offline | Application Cache (now removed), replaced by Service Workers | Chapter 15 |
| Parsing | One precise parsing algorithm, so every browser builds the same DOM even from broken markup | 2.1 Document Structure |

**Removed and obsolete features.** Presentational elements were dropped because styling belongs in CSS. Elements tied to old plugins or frames were dropped as well:

| Obsolete | Replace with |
|---|---|
| `<font>`, `<center>`, `<big>`, `<tt>`, `<strike>` | CSS (`font-*`, `text-align`, `text-decoration`) |
| `<frameset>`, `<frame>` | Normal layouts, or `<iframe>` where embedding is needed |
| `<applet>` | JavaScript or WebAssembly |
| `<acronym>` | `<abbr>` |
| `bgcolor`, `align`, `border` attributes | CSS |

**Content categories.** HTML5 replaced the simple "block vs inline" split with **content models**. Each element belongs to categories (such as *flow*, *phrasing*, *interactive* or *sectioning*) and specifies which categories it may contain. For example, `<p>` may only contain *phrasing* content, which is why `<p><div>...</div></p>` is invalid and the parser closes the `<p>` before the `<div>`. Interactive content cannot be nested inside other interactive content, so a `<button>` inside an `<a>` is invalid.

**Example: interactive elements that need no JavaScript**

```html
<!-- Disclosure widget: open and closed natively, keyboard-accessible -->
<details>
  <summary>What payment methods do you accept?</summary>
  <p>Cards, bank transfer and PayPal.</p>
</details>

<!-- An exclusive accordion: details elements that share a name close each other -->
<details name="faq"><summary>Shipping</summary><p>...</p></details>
<details name="faq"><summary>Returns</summary><p>...</p></details>

<!-- Popover: top-layer UI with light dismiss (click outside or Esc) and no JavaScript -->
<button popovertarget="user-menu">Account</button>
<div id="user-menu" popover>
  <a href="/profile">Profile</a>
  <a href="/logout">Log out</a>
</div>
```

```html
<!-- Modal dialog: focus moves into it, Esc closes it, the rest of the page is inert -->
<dialog id="confirm-delete">
  <form method="dialog">                     <!-- submitting closes the dialog -->
    <p>Delete this file permanently?</p>
    <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
    <button value="delete">Delete</button>   <!-- dialog.returnValue === "delete" -->
  </form>
</dialog>

<button id="delete-btn" data-file-id="4821" data-owner="ada">Delete file</button>

<script type="module">
  const dialog = document.querySelector('#confirm-delete');
  const btn = document.querySelector('#delete-btn');

  btn.addEventListener('click', () => dialog.showModal());   // showModal(), not show(), for a modal

  dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
    if (dialog.returnValue === 'delete') {
      // data-file-id becomes dataset.fileId (kebab-case is converted to camelCase)
      console.log('Deleting file', btn.dataset.fileId);
    }
  });
</script>
```

```css
/* The ::backdrop pseudo-element styles the layer behind a modal dialog */
dialog::backdrop {
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);
}
```

**Other useful additions:**

- `<template>`: inert markup that is parsed but not rendered, used as a blueprint for cloning (Chapter 6).
- `inert`: makes a subtree non-interactive and hides it from assistive technologies.
- `contenteditable`: lets the user edit an element's content in place.
- `hidden`: hides an element through markup.
- `spellcheck`, `translate`, `enterkeyhint`, `inputmode`: hints for spelling, translation and virtual keyboards.

**Key Takeaways**

- HTML5 turned HTML into an application platform with semantics, native media, graphics, richer forms and JavaScript APIs.
- The WHATWG HTML Living Standard is the single, continuously updated specification. "HTML5" is now an umbrella term.
- Presentational elements and attributes are obsolete. Use CSS instead.
- Content models define what each element may contain, which explains many parser surprises.
- `<details>`, `<dialog>` and `popover` provide accessible interactive UI with little or no JavaScript. `data-*` attributes store custom data for scripts.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build an FAQ section of five questions using `<details name="...">` so that only one answer is open at a time. Style the open state with the `[open]` attribute selector.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a "Rename file" modal with `<dialog>` that contains a form with a text input. Pre-fill the input from a `data-filename` attribute on the button that opened it, and log the new name only when the user confirms.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does the browser turn `<p><div>Hi</div></p>` into two separate paragraphs and a div, and how would you detect this kind of problem?" *Hint:* look up the content model of `<p>` and which end tags the parser can infer, then think about the DOM inspector and validators.

#### Accessibility and ARIA Basics

**Accessibility** (often shortened to *a11y*: "a", 11 letters, "y") means building pages that people can use regardless of disability: blind users with screen readers, people who cannot use a mouse, people with low vision, colour blindness, hearing loss or cognitive disabilities. The World Health Organization estimates that about 1.3 billion people, roughly 16% of the world's population, live with a significant disability. Accessibility is also a legal requirement in many places (the ADA in the US, the European Accessibility Act, in force since June 2025), and it improves the experience for everyone: captions in a noisy train, keyboard shortcuts for power users, readable contrast in bright sunlight.

**WCAG.** The **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines** (current version 2.2, published in 2023) define testable success criteria under four principles, known as **POUR**:

| Principle | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Perceivable** | Users can perceive the content | Text alternatives, captions, sufficient colour contrast |
| **Operable** | Users can operate the interface | Full keyboard access, enough time, no seizure-inducing flashes |
| **Understandable** | Content and behaviour are predictable | Clear labels, helpful error messages, consistent navigation |
| **Robust** | Works with current and future assistive technology | Valid markup, correct roles, names and states |

Each criterion has a conformance level: **A** (minimum), **AA** (the usual legal and contractual target) and **AAA** (enhanced).

**The accessibility tree.** Assistive technologies do not read your HTML directly. The browser builds a parallel **accessibility tree** from the DOM, and screen readers query it through operating system APIs. Each node exposes four key properties:

```text
DOM                                     Accessibility tree
<button aria-expanded="false">   -->    role:  button
  Menu                                  name:  "Menu"
</button>                               state: collapsed, focusable
                                        value: (none)

<div onclick="toggle()">Menu</div> --> role:  generic  (not focusable, not announced as clickable)
                                        name:  "Menu"
```

- **Role**: what the element is (button, link, checkbox, heading).
- **Name**: what it is called (from its content, a `<label>`, `alt`, `aria-label`...).
- **State/properties**: its current condition (checked, expanded, disabled, invalid).
- **Value**: for controls such as sliders and text fields.

**Native HTML first.** Most accessibility comes for free when you use the right element. A `<button>` is focusable, activates with both Enter and Space, has the `button` role and gets its name from its text. A `<div>` styled to look like a button has none of these.

```html
<!-- Inaccessible: no role, not focusable, mouse-only -->
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- The "fixed" div: all of this just to imitate a native element -->
<div class="btn" role="button" tabindex="0"
     onclick="save()"
     onkeydown="if (event.key === 'Enter' || event.key === ' ') { event.preventDefault(); save(); }">
  Save
</div>

<!-- The correct solution: one element, all behaviour built in -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>
```

**ARIA.** **WAI-ARIA** (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes that change how elements appear in the accessibility tree. ARIA changes *semantics only*: it adds no behaviour, no focusability and no keyboard handling. Its first rule is: **if a native HTML element or attribute already does what you need, use it instead of ARIA.** Surveys of large numbers of sites consistently find *more* accessibility errors on pages that use ARIA than on pages that don't, because incorrect ARIA overrides correct native semantics.

| Kind | Examples | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Roles | `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"`, `role="alert"`, `role="dialog"` | Declare what a custom widget is |
| Naming | `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby` | Provide or reference an accessible name |
| Description | `aria-describedby` | Link extra help or error text |
| States | `aria-expanded`, `aria-pressed`, `aria-checked`, `aria-selected`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-current` | Reflect dynamic state (your JavaScript must keep them up to date) |
| Visibility | `aria-hidden="true"` | Remove decorative content from the accessibility tree (never on focusable elements) |
| Live regions | `aria-live="polite"`, `role="status"`, `role="alert"` | Announce content that changes without moving focus |

**How the accessible name is chosen (simplified):**

```text
1. aria-labelledby   (references other elements' text)      highest priority
2. aria-label        (a string on the element itself)
3. Native labelling  (<label for>, alt, <caption>, <legend>, <figcaption>)
4. Element content   (for buttons, links, headings)
5. title attribute   (last resort, unreliable)               lowest priority
```

**Keyboard accessibility.** Many users navigate only with the keyboard: Tab and Shift+Tab move focus, Enter and Space activate, arrow keys move inside composite widgets, Esc closes.

| `tabindex` value | Effect |
|---|---|
| (absent) | Natural behaviour: interactive elements are focusable, others are not |
| `0` | Adds the element to the tab order in document order |
| `-1` | Focusable from JavaScript (`el.focus()`) but skipped by Tab. Useful for headings you jump to and dialog containers. |
| positive (`1`, `2`...) | Forces an order ahead of everything else. **Avoid**: it almost always creates a confusing order. |

Never remove the focus indicator without replacing it. Use `:focus-visible`, which shows focus styles for keyboard users without showing them on mouse clicks.

**Example: an accessible disclosure menu and a status message**

```html
<a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>   <!-- first focusable element on the page -->

<nav aria-label="Account">
  <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="account-menu">
    Account
  </button>
  <ul id="account-menu" hidden>
    <li><a href="/settings">Settings</a></li>
    <li><a href="/logout">Log out</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

<main id="main" tabindex="-1">                <!-- -1 so the skip link can move focus here -->
  <button type="button" id="save">Save draft</button>
  <p role="status" id="save-status"></p>      <!-- live region: changes are announced politely -->
</main>
```

```javascript
const toggle = document.querySelector('[aria-controls="account-menu"]');
const menu = document.querySelector('#account-menu');

toggle.addEventListener('click', () => {
  const open = toggle.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
  toggle.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(!open));  // announced as "expanded" / "collapsed"
  menu.hidden = open;
});

document.querySelector('#save').addEventListener('click', async () => {
  await saveDraft();
  // The live region already exists in the DOM, so changing its text triggers an announcement
  document.querySelector('#save-status').textContent = 'Draft saved.';
});
```

```css
.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  transform: translateY(-120%);          /* off-screen until focused */
}
.skip-link:focus {
  transform: none;
}

:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #1a73e8;            /* clear focus indicator for keyboard users */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
```

**Testing accessibility.** Automated tools (Lighthouse, axe DevTools, WAVE) reliably catch only some kinds of issue, such as missing `alt`, low contrast or missing labels. Whether a label is *meaningful* or a focus order makes *sense* needs a human. Manual checks:

1. Unplug the mouse and complete every task with the keyboard alone. Is focus always visible and in a logical order?
2. Use a screen reader: NVDA (Windows, free), VoiceOver (macOS and iOS, built in) or TalkBack (Android).
3. Zoom to 200% and 400%. Does the content reflow without horizontal scrolling?
4. Check the accessibility tree in DevTools for correct roles and names.

**Key Takeaways**

- Accessibility serves a large population, is often legally required, and improves usability for everyone.
- WCAG 2.2 organises requirements under Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust. AA is the usual target.
- Assistive technologies read the accessibility tree: role, name, state and value.
- Native HTML first. ARIA changes semantics only, never behaviour, and bad ARIA is worse than none.
- Everything must work with a keyboard, with a visible focus indicator. Avoid positive `tabindex`.
- Automated tools find only part of the problems. Test with a keyboard and a real screen reader.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run Lighthouse's accessibility audit on a page you built earlier in this chapter. Fix every reported issue, then navigate the whole page with the keyboard and fix anything Lighthouse missed.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build an accessible tabs component (three tabs and three panels) following the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices pattern: `role="tablist"`/`tab`/`tabpanel`, `aria-selected`, `aria-controls`, a roving `tabindex` and arrow-key navigation. Test it with a screen reader.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A teammate added `role="button"` to a clickable `<div>`. Is it accessible now?" *Hint:* list what a native `<button>` provides beyond its role (focus, which keys activate it, disabled state, form behaviour) and which of those ARIA supplies.

<a id="22-css-fundamentals"></a>
### 2.2 CSS Fundamentals

This subchapter explains how CSS finds elements, decides which rule wins, sizes and positions boxes, and brings them to life with motion.

#### Selectors and Combinators

Before CSS, presentation was mixed into the markup: `<font color="red">` on every heading of every page. Changing the brand colour meant editing thousands of tags. **CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)** separates presentation from structure. The HTML says *what* things are, and one stylesheet says how all of them look. To make that work, CSS needs a way to *point at* elements without touching the HTML. That is what **selectors** do.

**Anatomy of a rule.**

```text
selector       declaration block
   |       +------------------------+
   v       v                        v
 nav a  {  color: #1a73e8;  text-decoration: none;  }
           \____/ \_____/
          property  value
           \______________/
             declaration
```

**Attaching CSS to a document:**

| Method | Syntax | Use |
|---|---|---|
| External stylesheet | `<link rel="stylesheet" href="main.css">` | The default: cacheable and shared across pages |
| Embedded | `<style> ... </style>` in `<head>` | Critical above-the-fold CSS, single-page demos |
| Inline | `style="color: red"` attribute | Values computed by JavaScript. Hard to override and to maintain. |

**Basic selectors.**

| Selector | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `p` | Every `<p>` |
| Class | `.card` | Elements with `card` in their `class` list |
| ID | `#checkout` | The element with `id="checkout"` |
| Universal | `*` | Every element |
| Attribute | `[disabled]` | Elements that have the attribute |
| Attribute equals | `[type="email"]` | Exact value |
| Attribute prefix / suffix / contains | `[href^="https"]`, `[href$=".pdf"]`, `[class*="icon-"]` | Value starts with, ends with, contains |
| Attribute word | `[data-tags~="sale"]` | Space-separated list contains the word |
| Case-insensitive | `[href$=".PDF" i]` | Ignores ASCII case |
| Selector list | `h1, h2, h3` | Any of the listed selectors |

You can chain simple selectors with no spaces to require *all* of them on the same element: `button.primary[disabled]` means "a button with class `primary` that is disabled".

**Combinators** select elements by their *relationship* in the DOM tree:

| Combinator | Syntax | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Descendant | `article p` | Any `p` anywhere inside an `article` |
| Child | `ul > li` | `li` that are *direct* children of a `ul` |
| Next sibling | `h2 + p` | The `p` immediately after an `h2`, sharing the same parent |
| Subsequent sibling | `h2 ~ p` | Every `p` after an `h2`, sharing the same parent |

```text
<article>                     article p    article > p    h2 + p    h2 ~ p
  <h2>Title</h2>
  <p>Intro</p>                   yes           yes          yes       yes
  <p>Body</p>                    yes           yes          no        yes
  <blockquote>
    <p>Quote</p>                 yes           no           no        no
  </blockquote>
</article>
```

**Pseudo-classes** select elements by *state* or *position*, which plain markup can't express:

| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| User interaction | `:hover`, `:active`, `:focus`, `:focus-visible`, `:focus-within` |
| Form state | `:checked`, `:disabled`, `:required`, `:valid`, `:invalid`, `:user-invalid`, `:placeholder-shown` |
| Links | `:link`, `:visited`, `:target` (the element whose id matches the URL fragment) |
| Tree position | `:first-child`, `:last-child`, `:only-child`, `:nth-child(2n+1)`, `:nth-of-type(3)`, `:empty` |
| Logical | `:not(.x)`, `:is(h1, h2)`, `:where(ul, ol)`, `:has(img)` |

`:nth-child(an+b)` matches the children whose 1-based position equals `an+b` for some n = 0, 1, 2 and so on. For example, `2n+1` (or `odd`) gives 1, 3, 5..., `-n+3` gives the first three, and `3n` gives every third child.

`:has()` is the long-awaited "parent selector". It matches an element based on what it *contains* or what *follows* it: `.card:has(img)` styles cards that contain an image, and `label:has(+ input:invalid)` styles a label whose input is invalid.

**Pseudo-elements** (two colons) style a *part* of an element, or generate content that does not exist in the DOM:

| Pseudo-element | Targets |
|---|---|
| `::before`, `::after` | Generated boxes as the first or last child (require `content`) |
| `::first-line`, `::first-letter` | Typographic parts of a block of text |
| `::placeholder` | The placeholder text of an input |
| `::marker` | The bullet or number of a list item |
| `::selection` | Text highlighted by the user |
| `::backdrop` | The layer behind a modal `<dialog>` or a full-screen element |

**How browsers match.** Browsers evaluate selectors **right to left**. For `nav ul li a`, the browser first finds every `a`, then checks whether each one has an `li` ancestor, and so on. Modern engines are fast enough that selector performance rarely matters, but keeping selectors short and class-based still makes stylesheets easier to read and override.

**Example: selectors in practice**

```css
/* Links to external sites get an icon (generated content) */
a[href^="http"]:not([href*="example.com"])::after {
  content: " \2197";                       /* north-east arrow character */
}

/* Zebra-striped table rows */
tbody tr:nth-child(even) {
  background: #f5f7fa;
}

/* Spacing between consecutive paragraphs only (the "lobotomised owl" pattern, narrowed) */
.prose p + p {
  margin-top: 1em;
}

/* A form field container that contains an invalid input */
.field:has(input:user-invalid) {
  border-left: 4px solid #c62828;
}

/* Keyboard-only focus ring */
button:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #1a73e8;
}

/* Group selectors without repeating the rest */
:is(h1, h2, h3):hover > .anchor-link {
  opacity: 1;
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A rule is a selector plus a declaration block of `property: value` pairs.
- Basic selectors match by type, class, ID or attribute. Chaining them with no space requires all of them on the same element.
- Combinators (space, `>`, `+`, `~`) match by relationship in the DOM tree.
- Pseudo-classes match states and positions. Pseudo-elements style parts of an element or generate content.
- `:is()`, `:where()`, `:not()` and `:has()` make complex selections concise. `:has()` lets you select by descendants or by following siblings.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write selectors for: every PDF link, every `li` except the last one in a `ul`, the first paragraph after each `h2`, and every required input that is empty.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Without JavaScript, style a `<label>` in bold when its checkbox is checked, using both a sibling combinator layout (`input + label`) and a wrapping layout (`label:has(input:checked)`). Explain when each works.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why do browsers match selectors from right to left?" *Hint:* consider how many candidate elements remain after checking the rightmost part (the "key selector") compared with starting at the root and walking down every branch.

#### Cascade, Specificity and Inheritance

Any real page has many rules that target the same element: the browser's defaults, a CSS reset, a component library, your own styles, perhaps a user's custom stylesheet. They often disagree. Should this button be blue or grey? CSS needs a deterministic algorithm that always gives exactly one answer for every property of every element. That algorithm is the **cascade**, and it is the "C" in CSS.

**The cascade, step by step.** For each property of each element, the browser collects every declaration that applies, then sorts them by the following criteria. It stops at the first criterion that decides the winner:

```text
1. Origin and importance      (browser defaults vs user vs author, and !important)
        |  tie
2. Context                    (normal page vs shadow DOM encapsulation)
        |  tie
3. Element-attached styles    (the style="" attribute beats selector-based rules)
        |  tie
4. Cascade layers             (@layer order)
        |  tie
5. Specificity                (how precise the selector is)
        |  tie
6. Order of appearance        (the later declaration wins)
```

**1. Origins and importance.** Declarations come from three origins: the **user agent** (browser defaults, such as `h1` being bold and large), the **user** (accessibility settings or a custom stylesheet) and the **author** (you). `!important` *reverses* the normal order, so that users can always override authors when they really need to, for example to enforce a larger font size.

| Precedence (lowest to highest) |
|---|
| 1. User-agent normal |
| 2. User normal |
| 3. Author normal |
| 4. CSS animations (`@keyframes`) |
| 5. Author `!important` |
| 6. User `!important` |
| 7. User-agent `!important` |
| 8. CSS transitions |

Treat `!important` as a last resort, for example to override third-party inline styles or for utility classes that must always win. Each use makes the next override harder, which leads to an `!important` arms race.

**4. Cascade layers.** `@layer` lets you set the priority of whole groups of styles explicitly, regardless of their specificity. Layers declared later win over layers declared earlier, and styles that are not in any layer beat all layered styles.

```css
@layer reset, vendor, components, utilities;   /* declare the order once, up front */

@layer reset      { button { border: none; } }
@layer components { #app .btn { background: grey; } }   /* high specificity... */
@layer utilities  { .bg-blue { background: blue; } }    /* ...but this later layer wins */
```

**5. Specificity.** Specificity is a weight with three components, written **(A, B, C)** and compared from left to right like version numbers. A single ID therefore beats any number of classes.

| Component | Counted from |
|---|---|
| **A** | ID selectors (`#nav`) |
| **B** | Classes (`.btn`), attribute selectors (`[type]`), pseudo-classes (`:hover`) |
| **C** | Type selectors (`a`), pseudo-elements (`::before`) |
| Nothing | Universal `*`, combinators, `:where()` |
| Most specific argument | `:is()`, `:not()`, `:has()` |

| Selector | Specificity |
|---|---|
| `p` | (0, 0, 1) |
| `.card p` | (0, 1, 1) |
| `nav a:hover` | (0, 1, 2) |
| `input[type="email"]:focus` | (0, 2, 1) |
| `#main .card > p::first-line` | (1, 1, 2) |
| `:is(#a, .b) p` | (1, 0, 1), because `#a` is the most specific argument |
| `:where(#a, .b) p` | (0, 0, 1), because `:where()` contributes zero |

**6. Order of appearance.** When everything else ties, the declaration that appears last wins. "Last" follows the order in which stylesheets are loaded, and the order of rules within each stylesheet.

**Inheritance.** The cascade decides between declarations that *target* an element. But many elements have no declaration for a property at all. Then **inheritance** applies. Some properties pass their computed value from parent to child automatically, and others fall back to their initial value.

| Inherited by default | Not inherited |
|---|---|
| `color`, `font-*`, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`, `text-align`, `visibility`, `cursor`, `list-style`, custom properties | `margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`, `width`, `height`, `display`, `position`, `opacity`, `transform` |

The rule of thumb is that text-related properties are inherited and box-related ones are not. Setting `font-family` on `body` styles all the text on the page, but setting `border` on `body` does not give every element a border.

You can control inheritance explicitly with **global keywords**, which work on every property:

| Keyword | Result |
|---|---|
| `inherit` | Use the parent's computed value |
| `initial` | Use the property's initial value from the specification (for `display`, that is `inline`) |
| `unset` | `inherit` for inherited properties, `initial` for the others |
| `revert` | Roll back to the browser's default style for this element (for `div`, `display: block`) |
| `revert-layer` | Roll back to the value from the previous cascade layer |

`all: unset` resets every property at once, which is useful when you build a component from a native element such as `<button>`.

**Example: resolving a conflict by hand**

```html
<nav id="site-nav">
  <a class="link active" href="/">Home</a>
</nav>
```

```css
a               { color: black; }           /* (0,0,1)                                 */
.link           { color: grey; }            /* (0,1,0)                                 */
nav .active     { color: green; }           /* (0,1,1)                                 */
#site-nav a     { color: navy; }            /* (1,0,1)  <- highest specificity: wins   */
.link.active    { color: orange; }          /* (0,2,0)  two classes still lose to one ID */
```

The link is navy. To make `.active` win without adding an ID or `!important`, you could put `#site-nav a` into a lower `@layer`, or rewrite it as `:where(#site-nav) a` (specificity (0,0,1)).

**From declaration to pixels.** A property value goes through several stages. Understanding them explains what `getComputedStyle()` (Chapter 6) returns.

| Stage | Example for `width: 50%` |
|---|---|
| Declared | Every declaration that matched |
| Cascaded | The winner: `50%` |
| Specified | Cascaded value, or the inherited or initial value if there is none |
| Computed | Relative values resolved where possible: `50%` (a percentage width depends on layout) |
| Used | After layout: `400px` (half of an 800px container) |
| Actual | After device constraints, such as rounding to whole device pixels |

**Key Takeaways**

- The cascade resolves conflicts in this order: origin and importance, context, inline styles, layers, specificity, source order.
- `!important` reverses origin precedence. Use it sparingly.
- Specificity is (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements), compared left to right. `:where()` adds zero.
- `@layer` lets you set priority by architecture instead of selector weight. Unlayered styles beat layered ones.
- Text-related properties inherit and box-related ones don't. Use `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert` to control this.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Compute the specificity of `ul#menu li.item > a:hover`, `.btn.btn-primary:not(.disabled)` and `body :where(.card) h2::first-letter`. Order them from strongest to weakest.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* You import a third-party stylesheet that uses selectors like `#widget .title`. Using `@layer`, structure your CSS so that your simple class-based styles override it without IDs or `!important`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A colleague's style isn't applying even though it's the last rule in the file. Walk me through how you would debug it." *Hint:* use the DevTools Styles pane (struck-through declarations), think about specificity, inline styles, `!important`, cascade layers, invalid values and inheritance versus direct targeting.

#### The Box Model

To lay out a page, the browser has to turn every element into a rectangle with a precise position and size. The **box model** defines that rectangle. Every element generates a box made of four nested areas. Most "why is this 20 pixels wider than I said?" questions are about the box model.

```text
+--------------------------------------------------+
|                    margin                        |   transparent, outside the border,
|   +------------------------------------------+   |   separates the box from its neighbours
|   |                border                    |   |
|   |   +----------------------------------+   |   |
|   |   |            padding               |   |   |   takes the element's background
|   |   |   +--------------------------+   |   |   |
|   |   |   |         content          |   |   |   |   text, images, child boxes
|   |   |   |    width x height        |   |   |   |
|   |   |   +--------------------------+   |   |   |
|   |   +----------------------------------+   |   |
|   +------------------------------------------+   |
+--------------------------------------------------+
```

**`box-sizing`: what does `width` measure?**

| Value | `width` sets | Total rendered width for `width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 5px` |
|---|---|---|
| `content-box` (default) | The content area only | 300 + 2*20 + 2*5 = **350px** |
| `border-box` | Content + padding + border | **300px** (the content area shrinks to 250px) |

`border-box` matches how people think about sizes, so almost every modern project sets it globally:

```css
*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
```

**Display types.** The `display` property decides how a box takes part in layout. It has an *outer* type (how the box behaves among its siblings) and an *inner* type (how it lays out its children).

| `display` | Outer behaviour | Width and height | Vertical margin and padding |
|---|---|---|---|
| `block` | Starts on a new line and fills the available width | Respected | Push other boxes away |
| `inline` | Flows within a line of text | **Ignored** | Margins ignored vertically. Padding is painted but doesn't move other lines. |
| `inline-block` | Flows within a line, but is a box inside | Respected | Respected |
| `flex` / `grid` | Block-level box whose children use Flexbox or Grid | Respected | Respected |
| `inline-flex` / `inline-grid` | Inline-level versions | Respected | Respected |
| `none` | No box at all: removed from layout and the accessibility tree | | |
| `contents` | The element's own box disappears, and its children take its place | | |

**Margin collapsing.** In normal block flow, the vertical margins of adjacent blocks don't add up. They **collapse** into a single margin equal to the larger of the two.

```text
<h2 style="margin-bottom: 30px">     +--------------+
                                     |     h2       |
                                     +--------------+
                                           |  30px  (not 30 + 20 = 50px)
<p style="margin-top: 20px">         +--------------+
                                     |     p        |
                                     +--------------+
```

Collapsing happens in three situations:

1. Between adjacent siblings.
2. Between a parent and its first or last child when nothing separates them (no border, padding or inline content). The child's margin "escapes" through the parent.
3. Through an empty block, whose own top and bottom margins collapse.

It never happens with horizontal margins, inside flex or grid containers, with floated or absolutely positioned boxes, or across a **block formatting context** boundary. You can create one with `display: flow-root`.

**Overflow.** When content is larger than its box:

| `overflow` | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `visible` (default) | Content spills out and may overlap other content |
| `hidden` | Clipped. Still scrollable from JavaScript. Creates a block formatting context. |
| `clip` | Clipped, with no scrolling at all |
| `scroll` | Always shows scrollbars |
| `auto` | Shows scrollbars only when needed |

**Outline vs border.** `outline` is drawn outside the border and takes **no space**, so it never shifts the layout. That makes it ideal for focus indicators.

**Logical properties.** `margin-left` assumes left-to-right, horizontal text. **Logical properties** follow the writing direction instead: `inline` is the text direction and `block` is the direction in which lines stack. A layout written with them adapts automatically to Arabic, Hebrew or vertical Japanese.

| Physical | Logical (for horizontal left-to-right text) |
|---|---|
| `margin-left` / `margin-right` | `margin-inline-start` / `margin-inline-end` |
| `padding-top` + `padding-bottom` | `padding-block` |
| `width` / `height` | `inline-size` / `block-size` |
| `top` / `left` | `inset-block-start` / `inset-inline-start` |

**Example: box model in practice**

```css
.card {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  inline-size: 320px;                 /* = width in horizontal writing modes */
  padding: 16px 24px;                 /* vertical | horizontal */
  border: 1px solid #d0d7de;
  margin: 0 auto 24px;                /* top | horizontal (auto = centre a block) | bottom */
  overflow: auto;                     /* scroll if the content is too tall */
  max-block-size: 400px;
}

/* Contain children's margins and floats inside the card without clearfix hacks */
.card-body {
  display: flow-root;
}

/* An inline element ignores width and vertical margins; inline-block respects them */
.badge {
  display: inline-block;
  padding: 2px 8px;
  margin-block: 4px;
}
```

Use the DevTools **Computed** tab: it shows an interactive box model diagram with the exact content, padding, border and margin values of the selected element.

**Key Takeaways**

- Every box has content, padding, border and margin, from the inside out.
- `box-sizing: border-box` makes `width` include padding and border. Set it globally.
