- Block boxes stack and respect sizes. Inline boxes flow in text and ignore width, height and vertical margins.
- Vertical margins between blocks in normal flow collapse to the larger value. Flex, grid and `flow-root` prevent this.
- Prefer logical properties (`margin-inline`, `padding-block`) for layouts that work in any writing direction.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Calculate the rendered width of `div { width: 50%; padding: 2rem; border: 4px solid; }` inside a 1000px container, with `content-box` and with `border-box` (1rem = 16px).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* A `<section>` with a grey background contains an `<h2>` with `margin-top: 40px`, but the gap appears *above* the grey area instead of inside it. Explain why and give three different fixes.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `display: none`, `visibility: hidden` and `opacity: 0`?" *Hint:* compare whether each one keeps its space in the layout, whether it can still receive clicks and focus, whether it stays in the accessibility tree, and whether it can be animated.

#### Units, Colors and Typography

A size of "16px" or a colour of "red" seems simple, until users zoom in, switch to dark mode, rotate their phone or open the page on a 6K display. Choosing the right **units** makes layouts scale. Choosing **colours** with enough contrast keeps text readable. A solid **typography** setup is responsible for most of what makes a page look professional.

**Length units.**

| Unit | Relative to | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `px` | A CSS pixel (1/96 inch at a typical viewing distance, not one device pixel) | Borders, shadows, fine details |
| `em` | The element's own `font-size` (for `font-size` itself, the *parent's* font size) | Padding that scales with the component's text |
| `rem` | The *root* (`html`) font size, by default 16px | Font sizes and spacing scales |
| `%` | Depends on the property: the parent's font size for `font-size`, the containing block's *width* for width, padding and margin | Fluid widths |
| `ch` | Width of the "0" glyph | Readable line lengths (`max-width: 65ch`) |
| `lh` / `rlh` | The line height of the element / of the root | Vertical rhythm |
| `vw` / `vh` | 1% of the viewport width / height | Full-screen sections |
| `svh` / `lvh` / `dvh` | Small, large and *dynamic* viewport height (accounts for mobile browser toolbars) | Mobile full-height layouts (`min-height: 100dvh`) |
| `vmin` / `vmax` | The smaller / larger of `vw` and `vh` | Orientation-independent sizing |
| `cqi` / `cqb` | 1% of a query container's inline / block size | Components that size relative to their container (see 2.3) |

Watch out for two surprises:

- **`em` compounds.** With `li { font-size: 1.2em; }`, a list nested three levels deep has text at 1.2 x 1.2 x 1.2 = 1.728 times the base size. `rem` avoids this because it always refers to the root.
- **Vertical percentages refer to the width.** `padding-top: 50%` is half the containing block's *width*, not its height. Before the `aspect-ratio` property existed, this was the classic way to build fixed-ratio boxes.

**Accessibility note:** browsers let users set a larger default font size. Sizing text in `rem` respects that setting, while `font-size: 16px` on `html` overrides it.

**Math functions.**

```css
.sidebar  { width: calc(100% - 2 * var(--gap)); }    /* mix units freely */
.content  { width: min(100% - 2rem, 70ch); }          /* the smaller of the two */
.hero     { padding: max(2rem, 5vh); }                 /* the larger of the two */
h1        { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3.5rem); }  /* minimum, preferred, maximum */
```

**Colours.** CSS supports several colour notations. All modern browsers support the space-separated syntax with `/` for alpha.

| Notation | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Named | `rebeccapurple`, `transparent` | About 150 names |
| Hex | `#1a73e8`, `#1a73e880` (with alpha), `#fff` (short form) | Compact. Hard to adjust by hand. |
| `rgb()` | `rgb(26 115 232 / 50%)` | Red, green, blue 0 to 255 |
| `hsl()` | `hsl(217 82% 51%)` | Hue (degrees), saturation, lightness. Easy to make variations. |
| `oklch()` | `oklch(60% 0.18 255)` | Perceptual lightness, chroma, hue. Equal lightness values *look* equally light, which makes it the best choice for generating palettes. Also reaches wide-gamut (P3) colours. |
| `color-mix()` | `color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), white 20%)` | Tints, shades and blends computed by the browser |
| `currentColor` | `border: 1px solid currentColor` | The element's current `color` value |

**Contrast.** WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least **4.5:1** for normal text and **3:1** for large text (about 24px, or about 18.5px bold) and for meaningful non-text elements such as input borders and icons. DevTools shows the ratio in the colour picker. Never use colour as the *only* way to communicate something: add an icon or text to "red = error" for colour-blind users.

**Typography.**

| Property | Purpose | Advice |
|---|---|---|
| `font-family` | A list of fonts in order of preference | Always end with a generic family: `serif`, `sans-serif`, `monospace`, `system-ui` |
| `font-size` | Text size | `rem` for scales, `clamp()` for fluid headings |
| `font-weight` | Weight 100 to 900 | `400` is normal and `700` is bold. Load only the weights you use. |
| `line-height` | Space between lines | Use a **unitless** value such as `1.5`, so it scales with each child's font size |
| `letter-spacing`, `word-spacing` | Tracking | Slightly positive for uppercase labels |
| `text-align`, `text-transform`, `text-decoration` | Alignment, case, lines | `text-wrap: balance` for headings, `text-wrap: pretty` for paragraphs |
| `font-variant-numeric` | Number glyph styles | `tabular-nums` for aligned figures in tables |

**Web fonts** are loaded with `@font-face`. Use the WOFF2 format (best compression) and control what happens while the font downloads with `font-display`:

```css
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/Inter-Variable.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 100 900;          /* one variable font file covers the whole weight range */
  font-display: swap;            /* show fallback text immediately and swap when loaded */
}

:root {
  font-size: 100%;                                  /* respect the user's default (usually 16px) */
}

body {
  font-family: "Inter", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;                                 /* unitless: each child recalculates it */
  color: oklch(25% 0.02 255);                       /* near-black, softer than pure #000 */
  background: oklch(99% 0.005 255);
}

h1, h2, h3 {
  line-height: 1.2;                                 /* tighter for large text */
  text-wrap: balance;                               /* even line lengths in headings */
}

h1 { font-size: clamp(2rem, 1.2rem + 3vw, 3.5rem); }   /* fluid: scales between 32px and 56px */

.prose {
  max-width: 65ch;                                  /* about 65 characters per line is comfortable to read */
}

.price-table td {
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;               /* digits all the same width, so columns align */
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Use `rem` for font sizes and spacing, `em` for values that should scale with a component's text, `px` for hairlines, and `%`, `vw` and `fr` for fluid layouts.
- `em` compounds when nested. Percentages for padding and margin always refer to the containing block's *width*.
- `dvh` handles mobile browser toolbars better than `vh`.
- `calc()`, `min()`, `max()` and `clamp()` produce responsive values without media queries.
- Prefer `oklch()` and `color-mix()` for consistent palettes. Meet 4.5:1 contrast for body text.
- Use unitless `line-height`, a generic fallback font family, WOFF2 fonts and `font-display: swap`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a typographic scale for `h1` to `h4` and body text in `rem` with a ratio of 1.25. Check every text and background combination you use with the DevTools contrast checker.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `clamp()` expression for a heading that is 24px at a 360px viewport and 48px at a 1280px viewport, growing linearly in between. Show the arithmetic for the preferred value.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why might setting `html { font-size: 62.5%; }` or `html { font-size: 10px; }` be a problem, and what would you do instead?" *Hint:* consider which of the two respects a user who changed their browser's default font size, and what happens to `rem` values in each case.

#### Positioning and Stacking Contexts

By default, boxes are placed by **normal flow**: blocks stack from top to bottom, and inline content wraps from line to line. That covers most of a page, but not tooltips anchored to a button, a header that stays at the top while you scroll, a badge in the corner of an avatar, or modal overlays. The `position` property takes boxes out of normal flow, or shifts them within it. **Stacking contexts** then decide which box is painted in front when they overlap.

**The five `position` values.**

| Value | Stays in normal flow? | Offsets (`top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`) are relative to | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `static` (default) | Yes | Offsets are ignored | Everything |
| `relative` | Yes (its original space is kept) | Its own normal position | Small nudges. Anchor for absolute children. |
| `absolute` | **No** | The nearest *positioned* ancestor (any value other than `static`), or the initial containing block | Badges, tooltips, overlays inside a component |
| `fixed` | **No** | The viewport | Persistent headers, floating buttons, cookie banners |
| `sticky` | Yes, until a threshold is reached | Its nearest scrolling ancestor | Table headers and section titles that stick while scrolling |

```text
.avatar { position: relative; }          .badge { position: absolute; top: -4px; right: -4px; }

        +---------------+[3]   <- badge positioned against .avatar's padding box,
        |               |         because .avatar is the nearest positioned ancestor
        |    avatar     |
        |               |
        +---------------+
```

The **`inset`** shorthand sets all four offsets: `inset: 0` stretches an absolutely positioned element over its whole containing block.

**Pitfalls to know:**

- An absolutely positioned element with no positioned ancestor is placed against the initial containing block (roughly the first screen of the page), and it often ends up far from where you expected.
- Any ancestor with a `transform`, `filter`, `perspective`, `contain: paint` or `will-change: transform` becomes the containing block for its `fixed` descendants, so the "fixed" element scrolls with that ancestor. This often breaks modals that are rendered inside animated containers.
- `sticky` needs a threshold (for example `top: 0`). It sticks only within its parent, and it stops working if an ancestor between it and the scroller has `overflow: hidden` or `auto`.

**Floats.** `float: left | right` was used to build whole layouts for years. Its intended purpose, letting text wrap around an image, is still valid. For layout, use Flexbox and Grid (2.3).

**`z-index` and stacking contexts.** When boxes overlap, `z-index` controls which one appears in front. There are two important rules:

1. `z-index` only affects positioned elements (non-`static`) and flex or grid items.
2. `z-index` values are only compared **within the same stacking context**.

A **stacking context** is a group of elements that is painted as a single unit, like a sheet of paper. Inside it, children are ordered by their own `z-index`. But the whole sheet is placed in its parent context according to the *sheet's* `z-index`. A child can never rise above its context's siblings, however large its own value.

Common things that create a stacking context:

| Trigger | Example |
|---|---|
| The root element | `<html>` |
| A positioned element with a `z-index` other than `auto` | `position: relative; z-index: 1` |
| `position: fixed` or `sticky` | Always |
| `opacity` below 1 | `opacity: 0.99` |
| `transform`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, `perspective`, `clip-path`, `mask` | Any value other than `none` |
| A flex or grid item with a `z-index` other than `auto` | |
| `isolation: isolate` | Creates a context explicitly, with no side effects |
| `will-change` naming any of the properties above | `will-change: transform` |

**Example: the "z-index: 9999 doesn't work" bug**

```html
<header class="site-header">                       <!-- z-index: 10 -->
  <div class="dropdown">Menu items</div>           <!-- z-index: 9999 -->
</header>
<main class="content">                             <!-- z-index: 20 -->
  <div class="card">...</div>
</main>
```

```css
.site-header { position: relative; z-index: 10; }  /* creates stacking context A */
.dropdown    { position: absolute; z-index: 9999; }/* 9999 only counts *inside* A */
.content     { position: relative; z-index: 20; }  /* creates stacking context B */
```

```text
Root stacking context
 +-- A  .site-header  z=10
 |     +-- .dropdown  z=9999   <- compared only with other children of A
 +-- B  .content      z=20     <- B (20) is painted above A (10), and everything in A goes with it
```

The dropdown is painted *behind* the content, whatever its own value. The fix is to change the order at the level where the contexts are siblings: give `.site-header` a higher `z-index` than `.content`, or remove the `z-index` from `.content` if it doesn't need one.

**Painting order inside one stacking context** (from back to front):

```text
1. Background and borders of the element that forms the context
2. Positioned descendants with negative z-index
3. Non-positioned block boxes, in document order
4. Floats
5. Inline content (text, images)
6. Positioned descendants with z-index: auto or 0, in document order
7. Positioned descendants with positive z-index, lowest first
```

**The top layer.** Modal `<dialog>` elements, elements with the `popover` attribute and full-screen elements are rendered in the browser's **top layer**, above every stacking context in the document, with no `z-index` needed. This removes the main reason for `z-index: 99999` in modern code.

**Example: a sticky header and a positioned badge**

```css
.page-header {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;                         /* sticks once it reaches the top of the scroller */
  z-index: 10;                    /* above normal content scrolling underneath */
  background: white;              /* without a background, content shows through */
}

.avatar {
  position: relative;             /* establish the containing block for the badge */
  isolation: isolate;             /* own stacking context: internal z-indexes can't leak out */
}

.avatar .badge {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: -4px;        /* = top: -4px */
  inset-inline-end: -4px;         /* = right: -4px in left-to-right text */
  z-index: 1;                     /* compared only with other children of .avatar */
}

.overlay {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0;                       /* cover the whole viewport */
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `relative` keeps the element in flow. `absolute` and `fixed` remove it. `sticky` is in flow until it reaches its threshold.
- `absolute` positions against the nearest positioned ancestor, so set `position: relative` on the intended parent.
- `transform`, `filter` and similar properties on an ancestor change what `fixed` is relative to.
- `z-index` is only compared within the same stacking context. A child can never escape its parent context.
- Use `isolation: isolate` to contain z-index values inside a component. Use `<dialog>` and `popover` for UI that must appear above everything.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a product card with a "Sale" ribbon in its top-right corner using `position: absolute`, without the ribbon escaping the card.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a long table whose header row stays visible while you scroll, inside a container with `overflow: auto`. Then add `overflow: hidden` to an outer wrapper and explain what changes.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A modal with `position: fixed; z-index: 1000` appears behind a sidebar and scrolls with the page. What could cause both symptoms?" *Hint:* look for an ancestor with a `transform` or `filter`, and think about which stacking contexts the modal and the sidebar belong to. What would rendering the modal in the top layer change?

#### Transitions, Transforms and Animations

Motion explains change. A menu that slides in shows where it came from, a button that subtly presses down confirms a click, and a skeleton loader shows that something is happening. CSS provides three tools: **transforms** change an element's geometry visually, **transitions** animate between two states when a property changes, and **animations** run timelines defined with keyframes. All of them are declarative, and the browser can often run them off the main thread.

**Transforms.** `transform` moves, rotates, scales or skews an element *visually*, without affecting layout: surrounding elements don't move to make room for it.

| Function | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `translate(x, y)` | `translate(-50%, 0)` | Move. Percentages refer to the element's *own* size. |
| `scale(sx, sy)` | `scale(1.05)` | Resize |
| `rotate(angle)` | `rotate(45deg)` | Rotate around `transform-origin` (the centre by default) |
| `skew(ax, ay)` | `skewX(10deg)` | Slant |
| 3D | `perspective(600px) rotateY(30deg)`, `translateZ()` | Depth effects |

Transform functions are applied **from right to left**, so `translate(100px) rotate(45deg)` is not the same as `rotate(45deg) translate(100px)`. The individual properties `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` can be set and animated separately from each other.

**Transitions.** A transition says: "when this property's value changes, animate from the old value to the new one instead of jumping". The change can come from `:hover`, a class added by JavaScript, a media query, or anything else.

```text
transition: transform    0.2s       ease-out           0.05s
            \_______/    \__/       \______/           \___/
            property   duration  timing function       delay
```

| Timing function | Feel |
|---|---|
| `linear` | Constant speed, which looks mechanical (good for spinners and progress) |
| `ease` (default) | Speeds up quickly, then slows gently |
| `ease-in` | Starts slowly. Use it for elements leaving the screen. |
| `ease-out` | Ends slowly. Use it for elements entering, which feels responsive. |
| `ease-in-out` | Slow at both ends |
| `cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)` | A custom curve (y values outside 0 to 1 create overshoot) |
| `steps(n)` | Discrete jumps (sprite sheets, typewriter effects) |

Only *interpolable* values animate smoothly: lengths, colours, numbers and transforms. Discrete properties such as `display` used to change instantly, which made it impossible to fade an element in from `display: none`. Modern CSS solves this with `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` and `@starting-style`, which defines the "before" state for an element that has just appeared.

**Animations.** `@keyframes` defines a timeline with any number of steps. Animations can run automatically, loop and alternate direction, and they don't need a state change to start.

| Property | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `animation-name` | Which `@keyframes` to run | `pulse` |
| `animation-duration` | Length of one cycle | `1.5s` |
| `animation-timing-function` | Easing (applied between each pair of keyframes) | `ease-in-out` |
| `animation-delay` | Wait before starting (negative values start part-way through) | `200ms` |
| `animation-iteration-count` | Number of repetitions | `3`, `infinite` |
| `animation-direction` | Play order | `normal`, `reverse`, `alternate` |
| `animation-fill-mode` | Which styles apply before and after the run | `forwards` keeps the final frame |
| `animation-play-state` | Pause and resume | `paused` |

**Transitions vs animations.**

| | Transition | Animation |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | A property value changes | Starts when the animation is applied |
| States | Two (from, to) | Any number of keyframes |
| Looping | No | Yes |
| Best for | Hover and focus feedback, toggling UI states | Loaders, attention cues, multi-step choreography |

**Performance: animate `transform` and `opacity`.** Recall the rendering pipeline from Chapter 1: style, layout, paint, composite. What it costs to animate a property depends on the earliest stage it invalidates:

```text
Animating...        Style   Layout   Paint   Composite     Cost
width, top, margin   x        x        x        x          High: reflows the page on every frame
color, background    x                 x        x          Medium: repaints on every frame
transform, opacity   x                          x          Low: the GPU moves existing layers
```

To move something, animate `transform: translate()`, not `left` or `top`. To fade it, animate `opacity`. `will-change: transform` hints that the element should get its own layer ahead of time, but every layer uses memory, so add it only where you have measured a problem.

**Respect motion preferences.** Some users get dizzy or nauseous from motion (vestibular disorders) and enable "reduce motion" in their operating system. Honour that setting:

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;      /* effectively instant, but animation events still fire */
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}
```

**Example: a button, a fade-in panel and a loader**

```css
/* Transition: hover and press feedback */
.button {
  transition: transform 150ms ease-out, background-color 150ms ease-out;
}
.button:hover  { background-color: oklch(55% 0.18 255); }
.button:active { transform: scale(0.97); }        /* compositor-only: cheap */

/* Transition from display: none (discrete property) */
.panel {
  transition: opacity 200ms, translate 200ms, display 200ms allow-discrete;
}
.panel[hidden] {
  display: none;
  opacity: 0;
  translate: 0 8px;
}
@starting-style {
  .panel:not([hidden]) {                          /* the "from" state when the panel appears */
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 8px;
  }
}

/* Keyframe animation: infinite spinner */
@keyframes spin {
  to { rotate: 360deg; }                          /* "from" defaults to the current value */
}
.spinner {
  inline-size: 2rem;
  aspect-ratio: 1;
  border: 3px solid currentColor;
  border-block-start-color: transparent;          /* gap that makes the rotation visible */
  border-radius: 50%;
  animation: spin 0.8s linear infinite;
}

/* Keyframe animation: one-shot attention shake */
@keyframes shake {
  0%, 100% { translate: 0; }
  20%, 60% { translate: -6px; }
  40%, 80% { translate: 6px; }
}
.field.error {
  animation: shake 0.4s ease-in-out 1;
}
```

For animations controlled from JavaScript (pausing, reversing, chaining, reading progress), use the Web Animations API, covered in Chapter 6.

**Key Takeaways**

- Transforms change appearance without affecting layout. Functions apply from right to left.
- Transitions animate between two values when a property changes. Keyframe animations define multi-step timelines that can loop.
- Use `ease-out` for elements entering and `ease-in` for elements leaving. Keep UI transitions short (about 100 to 300ms).
- Animate `transform` and `opacity` for smooth 60fps motion. Avoid animating layout properties.
- `@starting-style` and `allow-discrete` allow enter and exit animations to and from `display: none`.
- Always provide a `prefers-reduced-motion` alternative.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a card that lifts on hover (moves 4px up and gains a stronger shadow) using a transition, and that does not move at all when reduced motion is enabled.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a three-dot "typing" indicator with a single `@keyframes` rule and staggered `animation-delay` values. Then record a performance profile in DevTools and confirm that no layout work happens during the animation.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is animating `transform: translateX()` smoother than animating `left`?" *Hint:* walk through the stages of the rendering pipeline that each property invalidates, and where the compositor thread runs.

<a id="23-layout-and-responsive-design"></a>
### 2.3 Layout and Responsive Design

This subchapter covers the modern layout systems and the techniques that make a single codebase adapt to every screen, from a small phone to a wide desktop monitor.

#### Flexbox Layout

For many years CSS had no real layout system. Developers built columns with tables, then with floats and clearfix hacks, and centring an element vertically was a running joke. **Flexbox** (the Flexible Box Layout module) was designed to distribute space among items along **one dimension**, a row or a column. It handles alignment, ordering and "fill the remaining space" with a few properties.

**Analogy:** books on a shelf. You choose whether they line up from the left or the right, whether gaps are spread evenly, whether some books may lean (shrink) or are allowed to spread out (grow), and whether a full shelf continues on the next one (wrap).

**Container and items.** `display: flex` turns an element into a **flex container**, and its direct children become **flex items**. Everything is described in terms of two axes:

```text
flex-direction: row (default)

       main start                                         main end
cross  +---------------------------------------------------------+
start  |  +--------+   +--------+   +--------+                   |
  |    |  | item 1 |   | item 2 |   | item 3 |    free space     |
  |    |  +--------+   +--------+   +--------+                   |
  v    +---------------------------------------------------------+
cross        ------------------ main axis ------------------>
end          justify-content works along the main axis
             align-items works along the cross axis
```

With `flex-direction: column`, the axes swap: the main axis runs vertically, so `justify-content` aligns vertically and `align-items` aligns horizontally.

**Container properties.**

| Property | Values | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `flex-direction` | `row`, `row-reverse`, `column`, `column-reverse` | Direction of the main axis |
| `flex-wrap` | `nowrap` (default), `wrap` | Whether items may move onto new lines |
| `flex-flow` | `row wrap` | Shorthand for direction and wrap |
| `justify-content` | `flex-start`, `center`, `flex-end`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly` | Distributes free space along the main axis |
| `align-items` | `stretch` (default), `flex-start`, `center`, `flex-end`, `baseline` | Aligns items along the cross axis within their line |
| `align-content` | Same values as `justify-content`, plus `stretch` | Distributes *lines* along the cross axis (only with wrapping) |
| `gap` | `1rem`, `1rem 2rem` | Space between items (row gap, column gap) |

**Item properties.**

| Property | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `flex-grow` | `0` | How much of the *positive* free space the item takes, relative to the others |
| `flex-shrink` | `1` | How much the item gives up when there isn't enough space |
| `flex-basis` | `auto` | The starting size before growing or shrinking (`auto` means use `width`, or the content size) |
| `flex` | `0 1 auto` | Shorthand for grow, shrink and basis |
| `align-self` | `auto` | Overrides `align-items` for this item |
| `order` | `0` | Changes the *visual* order (not the DOM or tab order) |

The `flex` shorthand has keywords that are worth memorising:

| Shorthand | Expands to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `flex: initial` | `0 1 auto` | Content-sized, can shrink but not grow |
| `flex: auto` | `1 1 auto` | Content-sized, then shares the free space |
| `flex: 1` | `1 1 0%` | Ignores content size and shares *all* the space equally |
| `flex: none` | `0 0 auto` | Rigid: exactly its content or width |

**How free space is shared.** Suppose a container is 600px wide and holds three items with a `flex-basis` of 100px each, so 300px of free space remains. With `flex-grow` values of 1, 1 and 2, the free space is split into 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 shares of 75px each. The items end up 175px, 175px and 250px wide. `flex-grow: 2` doesn't make an item twice as *wide*. It gives it twice as much of the *leftover* space.

**Two common pitfalls.**

- **Items refusing to shrink.** Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which means "never smaller than my content". A long URL or a wide `<pre>` block will overflow the container. The fix is `min-width: 0` (or `overflow: hidden`) on the item.
- **`order` breaks accessibility.** `order` changes only the visual position. Keyboard focus and screen readers still follow the DOM order, so users see one sequence and hear or tab through another. Reorder the HTML instead whenever the order carries meaning.

**Example: three common Flexbox patterns**

```css
/* 1. Perfect centring, horizontally and vertically */
.hero {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;          /* main axis */
  align-items: center;              /* cross axis */
  min-height: 60dvh;
}

/* 2. Navigation bar: logo on the left, links on the right */
.navbar {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 1rem;
}
.navbar .logo {
  margin-inline-end: auto;          /* an auto margin absorbs all free space and pushes the rest right */
}

/* 3. Wrapping card row: each card is at least 250px and the cards share the extra space */
.cards {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1.5rem;
}
.cards > .card {
  flex: 1 1 250px;                  /* grow, shrink, start at 250px */
}

/* A media object: fixed-size image next to text that fills the rest */
.media {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  align-items: flex-start;
}
.media img  { flex: none; }         /* never squash the image */
.media-body { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }  /* fill the rest and allow long words to wrap */
```

```html
<nav class="navbar">
  <a class="logo" href="/">Acme</a>
  <a href="/docs">Docs</a>
  <a href="/pricing">Pricing</a>
  <a href="/login">Log in</a>
</nav>
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Flexbox lays out items along one axis. `justify-content` works on the main axis and `align-items` on the cross axis.
- `flex: grow shrink basis`. Growing shares the *leftover* space. `flex: 1` shares all of the space equally.
- Use `gap` for spacing and `margin-*: auto` to push items apart.
- Add `min-width: 0` to flex items that must shrink below the width of their content.
- `order` changes only the visual order. Keep the DOM order meaningful for keyboard and screen reader users.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a footer with three groups of links that sit side by side on wide screens and wrap onto separate lines on narrow screens, using only Flexbox and `gap`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In a 900px container, three items have `flex: 1 1 200px`, `flex: 2 1 200px` and `flex: 0 0 300px`. Calculate each final width, then verify your answer with the DevTools flex inspector.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A flex item containing a long unbreakable string overflows its container even though `flex-shrink` is 1. Why?" *Hint:* look up the automatic minimum size of flex items and what `min-width: auto` resolves to.

#### CSS Grid Layout

Flexbox works on one line at a time: items on different rows don't line up with each other. Page layouts, dashboards and galleries need **two dimensions**, rows *and* columns that align across the whole area. **CSS Grid** provides exactly that: you define the tracks on the container, then place items into cells or areas.

**Analogy:** Flexbox is a bookshelf, where each shelf is filled independently. Grid is a spreadsheet, where every cell in a column has the same width and every cell in a row has the same height.

**Terminology.**

```text
        line 1     line 2          line 3     line 4
          |          |               |          |
line 1  --+----------+---------------+----------+--
          |  cell    |               |          |      <- row track 1
line 2  --+----------+---------------+----------+--
          |          |     area spanning 2x2    |      <- row track 2
line 3  --+----------+               +          +--
          |          |                          |      <- row track 3
line 4  --+----------+---------------+----------+--
           col track 1   col track 2   col track 3

Line:   the dividing lines, numbered from 1 (and from -1 counting from the end)
Track:  a row or a column between two lines
Cell:   the intersection of one row and one column
Area:   a rectangle of one or more cells
Gap:    the gutter between tracks
```

**Defining tracks.**

| Feature | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed and flexible sizes | `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 2fr` | `fr` is a fraction of the *remaining* space after fixed tracks |
| `repeat()` | `repeat(4, 1fr)` | Four equal columns |
| `minmax(min, max)` | `minmax(200px, 1fr)` | A track that is never smaller than 200px and grows to fill space |
| `auto-fill` | `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` | Creates as many columns as fit, keeping empty tracks |
| `auto-fit` | `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` | Same, but collapses empty tracks so the items stretch |
| Content keywords | `min-content`, `max-content`, `fit-content(300px)` | Size tracks from their content |
| `gap` | `gap: 1rem 2rem` | Row gap, column gap |

**Placing items.** Items fill cells automatically in order, unless you place them by line numbers or by named areas:

```css
.item {
  grid-column: 1 / 3;        /* from column line 1 to line 3 (spans 2 columns) */
  grid-row: 2 / span 2;      /* start at row line 2 and span 2 rows */
}
.full-width {
  grid-column: 1 / -1;       /* -1 = the last line: span the whole grid */
}
```

**Named areas** let you draw the layout as ASCII art directly in the CSS. Each string is a row, each word is a cell, and `.` is an empty cell. Every area must form a rectangle.

**The implicit grid.** If there are more items than the template defines cells for, Grid creates extra tracks automatically. Control their size with `grid-auto-rows` (for example `grid-auto-rows: minmax(100px, auto)`) and the fill direction with `grid-auto-flow` (`row`, `column`, or `dense` to backfill holes).

**Alignment.** Grid uses the same alignment vocabulary as Flexbox:

| Property | Aligns |
|---|---|
| `justify-items` / `align-items` | Each item inside its cell (inline and block axis) |
| `place-items` | Shorthand for both: `place-items: center` |
| `justify-content` / `align-content` | The whole grid inside the container, when the tracks are smaller than the container |
| `justify-self` / `align-self` | One item inside its cell |

**Subgrid.** A nested grid normally defines its own tracks, unrelated to its parent's. With `grid-template-rows: subgrid` (or `columns`), a grid item reuses its parent's tracks, so the titles, text and buttons inside a row of cards align with each other even when their content lengths differ.

**Example: a page layout with named areas**

```css
.page {
  display: grid;
  min-height: 100dvh;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;          /* header and footer fit their content; main fills the rest */
  grid-template-areas:
    "header  header"
    "sidebar main"
    "footer  footer";
  gap: 1rem;
}

.page > header { grid-area: header; }
.page > nav    { grid-area: sidebar; }
.page > main   { grid-area: main; }
.page > footer { grid-area: footer; }

/* On narrow screens, redraw the layout as a single column */
@media (width < 48rem) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header"
      "main"
      "sidebar"
      "footer";
  }
}
```

```text
Wide screens                          Narrow screens
+-------------------------------+     +-------------+
|            header             |     |   header    |
+---------+---------------------+     +-------------+
| sidebar |        main         |     |    main     |
|         |                     |     +-------------+
+---------+---------------------+     |   sidebar   |
|            footer             |     +-------------+
+-------------------------------+     |   footer    |
                                      +-------------+
```

**Example: a responsive gallery with no media queries, and aligned card contents**

```css
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 220px), 1fr));
  /* As many columns as fit, each at least 220px, and never wider than the container
     (min(100%, ...) prevents overflow on very small screens) */
  gap: 1rem;
}

.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 3;                     /* occupy 3 of the parent's implicit rows */
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;          /* image, text and button rows line up across all cards */
}
```

**Flexbox or Grid?**

| | Flexbox | Grid |
|---|---|---|
| Dimensions | One (a row *or* a column) | Two (rows *and* columns) |
| Approach | Content-out: item sizes drive the layout | Layout-in: the container defines the tracks |
| Alignment across rows | No, each line is independent | Yes |
| Overlapping items | Hard | Easy (place items in the same cells) |
| Typical uses | Navigation bars, button groups, centring, media objects | Page structure, galleries, dashboards, forms with aligned labels |

They work well together: a Grid page layout whose cells contain Flexbox components is the normal pattern.

**Key Takeaways**

- Grid lays out items in two dimensions with explicit row and column tracks.
- `fr` divides the remaining space. `minmax()`, `repeat()`, `auto-fit` and `auto-fill` create responsive tracks.
- Place items by line numbers (`1 / -1`, `span 2`) or by named `grid-template-areas`.
- `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks and `auto-fill` keeps them.
- `subgrid` aligns nested content to the parent's tracks.
- Use Grid for two-dimensional layout and Flexbox for one-dimensional alignment, and combine them freely.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Recreate a classic "holy grail" layout (header, footer, main content between two sidebars) with `grid-template-areas`, collapsing to a single column on small screens.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a photo gallery where some photos span two columns or two rows, and use `grid-auto-flow: dense` to fill the gaps. Then explain what effect `dense` has on keyboard navigation order.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` and `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))`?" *Hint:* try both with only two items in a very wide container and inspect the empty tracks in the DevTools grid overlay.

#### Media Queries and Breakpoints

A layout that looks right on a 1440px laptop is unusable on a 375px phone: the text is tiny, the columns are squeezed and the buttons are hard to tap. **Media queries** apply CSS only when conditions about the device or the user's preferences are true. This is the core mechanism of **responsive web design**, a term Ethan Marcotte coined in 2010 to describe fluid grids, flexible images and media queries working together.

**Prerequisite: the viewport meta tag.** Without `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` (see Document Structure and Metadata), a phone reports a viewport of about 980px and your small-screen queries never match.

**Syntax.**

```text
@media   screen    and   (min-width: 48rem)   and   (orientation: landscape)  { ... }
         \____/          \_______________/          \_______________________/
       media type          media feature                  media feature
     (all, screen, print)
```

| Operator | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `and` | `(min-width: 40rem) and (hover: hover)` | Both conditions must be true |
| `,` (or) | `(orientation: portrait), (max-width: 30rem)` | Either condition |
| `not` | `not print` | Negates the whole query |
| Range syntax | `(40rem <= width < 64rem)` | Modern, readable alternative to `min-width`/`max-width` |

**Useful media features.**

| Feature | Example | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `width` | `(width >= 48rem)` | The main responsive breakpoints |
| `orientation` | `(orientation: landscape)` | Layouts for rotated devices |
| `hover` / `pointer` | `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` | Enable hover effects only on mouse devices. Use bigger targets for `pointer: coarse` (touch). |
| `resolution` | `(resolution >= 2dppx)` | High-density screens |
| `prefers-color-scheme` | `(prefers-color-scheme: dark)` | Automatic dark mode |
| `prefers-reduced-motion` | `(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` | Turn off non-essential animation |
| `prefers-contrast` | `(prefers-contrast: more)` | Stronger borders and contrast |
| `forced-colors` | `(forced-colors: active)` | Windows high-contrast mode |
| `print` (type) | `@media print` | Hide navigation and show link URLs on paper |

**Choosing breakpoints.** Don't design for specific devices: there are thousands, and new sizes appear every year. Let the **content** decide. Resize the browser slowly, and add a breakpoint where the layout starts to look wrong (lines too long, cards too narrow). Many projects end up with a handful of breakpoints similar to these:

| Name | Approximate width | Typical layout |
|---|---|---|
| Small | < 40rem (640px) | Single column |
| Medium | 40 to 64rem (640 to 1024px) | Two columns, collapsible sidebar |
| Large | 64 to 80rem (1024 to 1280px) | Full multi-column layout |
| Extra large | > 80rem (1280px) | Wider gutters, constrained content width |

Using `em` or `rem` for breakpoints makes the layout respond to the user's zoom and default font size as well as to the screen width.

**Container queries.** Media queries respond to the *viewport*, but a reusable component cares about the space *it* is given. The same card might sit in a wide main column or in a narrow sidebar. **Container queries** let a component adapt to the size of its container:

```css
.card-slot {
  container-type: inline-size;          /* make this element a query container (width only) */
  container-name: card;                 /* optional name, to target a specific ancestor */
}

.card { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }

@container card (inline-size > 30rem) {
  .card {
    grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr;   /* image beside text when the slot is wide */
  }
}
```

| | Media query | Container query |
|---|---|---|
| Responds to | Viewport and device or user preferences | The size (or style) of an ancestor container |
| Best for | Page-level layout and user preferences | Reusable components |
| Declared with | `@media` | `container-type` on the ancestor, `@container` in the rule |

**Example: a responsive stylesheet with preferences and print styles**

```css
/* Base: small screens, no query needed (mobile-first, see the next topic) */
.layout { display: grid; gap: 1rem; padding-inline: 1rem; }

@media (width >= 40rem) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
}

@media (width >= 64rem) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 16rem 1fr 1fr; padding-inline: 2rem; }
}

/* Hover effects only where a real hover exists (not on touch screens) */
@media (hover: hover) {
  .card:hover { box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15); }
}

/* Automatic dark theme */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --bg: #0f1115; --text: #e6e6e6; }
}

/* Paper-friendly output */
@media print {
  nav, .ads, video { display: none; }
  a[href^="http"]::after { content: " (" attr(href) ")"; }  /* print the URL after each external link */
  body { font-size: 12pt; color: black; background: white; }
}
```

Queries can also be used in HTML (`<source media="...">` in `<picture>`, `<link rel="stylesheet" media="print">`) and in JavaScript with `window.matchMedia('(width >= 64rem)')`, which returns an object whose `matches` property you can check and whose `change` event you can listen to.

**Key Takeaways**

- Media queries apply CSS conditionally, based on viewport size, device capabilities and user preferences.
- The viewport meta tag is required for width-based queries to work on phones.
- Choose breakpoints where the content breaks, not at device sizes, and express them in `rem` or `em`.
- Use preference queries (`prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `hover`, `pointer`) as well as width.
- Container queries make components respond to their own available space rather than to the viewport.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a print stylesheet to an article page that hides the navigation and footer, removes background colours, and prints each external link's URL after the link text.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a product card that shows a stacked layout in a narrow container and a side-by-side layout in a wide one using container queries. Place the same card in a sidebar and in the main column to prove it adapts.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you use a container query instead of a media query?" *Hint:* think about a design-system component that is reused in many layouts and does not know where it will be placed.

#### Mobile-First Design

More than half of all web traffic now comes from phones. Phones also have the hardest constraints: small screens, touch input, variable networks and less CPU power. **Mobile-first design** means designing and writing CSS for the smallest, most constrained context first, then *progressively enhancing* the layout as more space and capability become available. It applies the progressive enhancement principle from Chapter 1 to layout.

**Analogy:** packing for a trip with only a carry-on bag forces you to decide what really matters. Moving up to a bigger suitcase later is easy. Squeezing a fully packed suitcase into a carry-on is not.

**Mobile-first vs desktop-first CSS.**

| | Mobile-first | Desktop-first |
|---|---|---|
| Base styles (no query) | Small screen | Large screen |
| Queries | `min-width` (`width >=`): *add* layout as space grows | `max-width` (`width <`): *undo* layout as space shrinks |
| Complexity on small devices | Lowest: simple single-column styles | Highest: full layout plus overrides |
| Design pressure | Prioritise content first | Tends to cram desktop content into small screens |
| Risk | Large screens looking sparse if neglected | Mobile becoming an afterthought |

```css
/* Desktop-first: write three columns, then undo them */
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
@media (width < 64rem) { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } }
@media (width < 40rem) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } }

/* Mobile-first: start simple (a single column is the default for grid), then add */
.grid { display: grid; }
@media (width >= 40rem) { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } }
@media (width >= 64rem) { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); } }
```

**Principles beyond the CSS.**

1. **Content prioritisation.** A small screen forces you to decide what really matters. The question is "what can we *add* on larger screens?", not "what do we *hide* on mobile?".
2. **Touch targets.** Fingers are far less precise than mouse pointers. WCAG 2.2 requires interactive targets of at least 24 x 24 CSS pixels (level AA), and platform guidelines recommend 44 to 48 pixels. Space targets apart so that taps don't land on the wrong one.
3. **No hover dependence.** Touch screens have no hover. Any information or menu that appears on hover needs a tap or focus equivalent.
4. **Performance budget.** Serve responsive images (`srcset`), lazy-load content below the fold, keep JavaScript bundles small, and test on mid-range devices over throttled networks. Search engines notice too: Google indexes the mobile version of each page (mobile-first indexing).
5. **Readable text without zooming.** Use a base font size of at least 16px. iOS Safari also zooms in on any input with a smaller font size when it receives focus.
6. **Device realities.** Mobile browser toolbars change the viewport height as the user scrolls (`100vh` doesn't fit; use `dvh`), and notched screens need safe-area padding.

**Example: a mobile-first article layout**

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">
<!-- viewport-fit=cover lets the page extend under the notch; env() then supplies safe margins -->
```

```css
/* 1. Base: phones. A single column, comfortable text, large tap targets */
body {
  font-size: 1rem;                                  /* 16px: no forced zoom on input focus */
  line-height: 1.6;
  padding-inline: max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-left));   /* respect notches and rounded corners */
}

.article-layout {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

.button {
  min-block-size: 44px;                              /* comfortable touch target */
  padding-inline: 1.25rem;
}

.hero { min-block-size: 70dvh; }                     /* dynamic viewport height: adjusts as toolbars appear */

/* 2. Tablets: more breathing room */
@media (width >= 40rem) {
  body { padding-inline: 2rem; }
  .article-layout { gap: 2rem; }
}

/* 3. Desktops: a sticky sidebar appears */
@media (width >= 64rem) {
  .article-layout {
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 16rem;     /* article plus sidebar */
    grid-template-areas: "article toc";              /* the toc comes first in the DOM but sits on the right */
    max-inline-size: 72rem;
    margin-inline: auto;
  }
  .article-layout > article { grid-area: article; }
  .toc {
    grid-area: toc;
    position: sticky;
    top: 2rem;
    align-self: start;                               /* otherwise the grid item stretches and can't stick */
  }
}

/* 4. Hover-only enhancements for precise pointers */
@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) {
  .button:hover { filter: brightness(1.1); }
}
```

```text
 Phone (< 40rem)       Tablet (40-64rem)          Desktop (>= 64rem)
+-------------+     +-------------------+     +----------------------------+
|   header    |     |      header       |     |          header            |
+-------------+     +-------------------+     +------------------+---------+
|    toc      |     |       toc         |     |                  |  toc    |
+-------------+     +-------------------+     |     article      | (sticky)|
|             |     |                   |     |                  |         |
|   article   |     |     article       |     |                  |         |
|             |     |                   |     +------------------+---------+
+-------------+     +-------------------+
```

Test with DevTools device emulation during development (Chapter 1), but always confirm on real devices: emulation does not reproduce real touch precision, CPU speed or browser toolbar behaviour.

**Key Takeaways**

- Write base styles for small screens and add complexity with `min-width` (`width >=`) queries.
- Mobile-first is a content strategy as well as a CSS technique: decide what matters most first.
- Make touch targets at least 24 x 24px (44 to 48px recommended) and never rely on hover alone.
- Use `dvh` for full-height sections, `env(safe-area-inset-*)` for notches, and a base font of at least 16px.
- Treat performance as part of the design: responsive images, lazy loading and small bundles.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Take a desktop-first stylesheet with three `max-width` queries and rewrite it mobile-first with `min-width` queries, producing the same result at every width.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Audit a page on a real phone or in Lighthouse's mobile mode. List every touch target smaller than 24 x 24px, every hover-only interaction and every horizontal scroll, and fix them.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your team's site was designed desktop-first and performs poorly on mobile. How would you plan a migration to mobile-first without a full rewrite?" *Hint:* think about which metrics to measure first, which templates get the most mobile traffic, and how to refactor queries component by component.

#### CSS Variables and Custom Properties

A design system has a brand colour, a spacing scale and border radii that are used hundreds of times. Hard-coding `#1a73e8` everywhere makes a rebrand a search-and-replace exercise, and dark mode would need a duplicate of every rule. **Custom properties** (usually called CSS variables) let you name a value once and reference it everywhere. Unlike preprocessor variables, they are **live**: they take part in the cascade, are inherited, and can change at runtime through media queries, classes or JavaScript.

**Syntax.**

```css
:root {
  --brand: #1a73e8;              /* define: the name starts with two dashes and is case-sensitive */
  --space-m: 1rem;
}

.button {
  background: var(--brand);                    /* use */
  padding: var(--space-m) calc(var(--space-m) * 2);
  color: var(--button-text, white);            /* a fallback, used if --button-text is not defined */
}
```

**Scoping and inheritance.** A custom property is an ordinary inherited property. Defining it on `:root` makes it global. Redefining it on an element changes it for that element's whole subtree. This is what makes theming and component variants easy:

```text
:root            --brand: blue
 +-- header                              uses var(--brand) -> blue
 +-- .danger-zone  --brand: red          (redefined here)
      +-- button                         uses var(--brand) -> red
```

**Custom properties vs preprocessor variables.**

| | Sass variable (`$brand`) | Custom property (`--brand`) |
|---|---|---|
| Resolved | At build time, then disappears | At runtime, in the browser |
| Cascade and inheritance | No | Yes, and it can be scoped to any element |
| Changes in media queries or with classes | No (you must duplicate the rules) | Yes (redefine the variable only) |
| Readable and writable from JavaScript | No | Yes (`style.setProperty('--x', ...)`) |
| Can hold any token sequence | n/a | Yes (it is validated only when used) |

**Invalid at computed-value time.** The browser cannot check that a variable's value fits a property until it substitutes the value. If the result is invalid, the declaration does **not** fall back to an earlier declaration in the cascade. The property becomes `unset` instead:

```css
:root { --size: red; }                 /* a nonsense value for a length, but defining it is legal */

p {
  font-size: 20px;
  font-size: var(--size);              /* invalid after substitution -> unset -> inherited size, NOT 20px */
}
```

**Registered properties with `@property`.** By default, custom properties are untyped strings, so the browser cannot interpolate them in animations. Registering a property gives it a type, an initial value and inheritance rules. A typed property can be transitioned, and invalid values fall back to the initial value:

```css
@property --angle {
  syntax: "<angle>";          /* the type: <length>, <color>, <number>, <percentage>, ... */
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}

.spinner-ring {
  background: conic-gradient(from var(--angle), #1a73e8, transparent);
  animation: rotate-gradient 2s linear infinite;
}

@keyframes rotate-gradient {
  to { --angle: 360deg; }     /* animating a gradient: only possible because --angle is typed */
}
```

**Example: light and dark theming with design tokens**

```css
:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;                        /* form controls and scrollbars follow the theme */

  /* Primitive tokens: raw values */
  --blue-500: oklch(58% 0.18 255);
  --gray-50:  oklch(98% 0.005 255);
  --gray-900: oklch(20% 0.02 255);

  /* Semantic tokens: what components use */
  --color-bg:     light-dark(var(--gray-50), var(--gray-900));   /* chooses based on color-scheme */
  --color-text:   light-dark(var(--gray-900), var(--gray-50));
  --color-accent: var(--blue-500);
  --radius: 8px;
  --space: 1rem;
}

/* Manual override from a theme switcher: <html data-theme="dark"> */
:root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
:root[data-theme="dark"]  { color-scheme: dark; }

body {
  background: var(--color-bg);
  color: var(--color-text);
}

/* Component API: the button exposes variables that callers can override */
.button {
  --button-bg: var(--color-accent);
  --button-pad: calc(var(--space) * 0.75);
  background: var(--button-bg);
  padding: var(--button-pad) calc(var(--button-pad) * 2);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
}
.button.danger  { --button-bg: oklch(55% 0.2 25); }   /* a variant changes only the variable */
.button.compact { --button-pad: calc(var(--space) * 0.4); }

/* Responsive tokens: one change applies everywhere */
@media (width >= 64rem) {
  :root { --space: 1.25rem; }
}
```

```javascript
// Reading and writing custom properties from JavaScript (see Chapter 6)
const root = document.documentElement;
root.style.setProperty('--color-accent', '#e8590c');                          // runtime rebrand
getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue('--radius').trim();                   // "8px"

// Pass pointer coordinates to CSS for a spotlight effect
card.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => {
  card.style.setProperty('--x', `${e.offsetX}px`);
  card.style.setProperty('--y', `${e.offsetY}px`);
});
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Custom properties (`--name`, `var(--name, fallback)`) are live values that cascade and inherit.
- Define global tokens on `:root` and override them on any subtree for themes and variants.
- Change variables in media queries and with classes instead of duplicating whole rules.
- A variable that produces an invalid value makes the property `unset`. It does not fall back to an earlier declaration.
- `@property` adds a type, which makes custom properties animatable and safer.
- Combine semantic tokens with `light-dark()` and `color-scheme` for theming with little code.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Refactor a stylesheet that repeats three colours and four spacing values into custom properties on `:root`, then add a dark theme by redefining only the colour variables.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a button component whose colour, size and radius are controlled entirely by variables such as `--btn-bg`, `--btn-size` and `--btn-radius`. Create three variants without repeating any property declarations.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can't you use a CSS custom property inside a media query condition, such as `@media (width >= var(--bp))`?" *Hint:* custom properties belong to elements and are resolved during the cascade, while media queries are evaluated against the whole document before any element is styled.

#### Preprocessors and Utility Frameworks

Plain CSS used to lack many features that large projects need: variables, nesting, reusable blocks, modules and loops. As stylesheets grew to thousands of lines, teams also ran into naming collisions and "append-only" CSS that nobody dared to delete. Two families of tools grew up around these problems. **Preprocessors** extend the language and compile it back to CSS. **Frameworks** provide ready-made styles, either as complete components or as small utility classes.

**Preprocessors.** A preprocessor is a language that compiles to CSS at build time:

```text
  styles.scss  --(sass compiler)-->  styles.css  --(PostCSS: autoprefixer, minify)-->  dist.css
   variables, nesting,                 plain CSS                                      shipped to
   mixins, modules                                                                    the browser
```

| Tool | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Sass** (SCSS syntax) | The most widely used. The reference implementation is Dart Sass (the `sass` npm package). LibSass and node-sass are deprecated. |
| **Less** | JavaScript-based. It was used by Bootstrap 3. |
| **Stylus** | Flexible, optional-punctuation syntax. Rarely chosen for new projects. |
| **PostCSS** | Not a language. It transforms CSS through plugins: **Autoprefixer** adds vendor prefixes based on Browserslist, `postcss-preset-env` compiles future CSS syntax, `cssnano` minifies. |

**Main Sass features:**

| Feature | Syntax | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Variables | `$gap: 1rem;` | Compile-time constants |
| Nesting | `.card { &:hover { } .title { } }` | Mirror the HTML structure. `&` refers to the parent selector. |
| Partials and modules | `@use 'tokens';` `tokens.$brand` | Split code into files with namespaces. (`@import` and global functions such as `map-get()` are deprecated in Dart Sass in favour of modules such as `sass:map`.) |
| Mixins | `@mixin focus-ring { }` / `@include focus-ring;` | Reusable blocks of declarations, with parameters |
| Functions | `@function rem($px) { @return math.div($px, 16) * 1rem; }` | Computed values |
| Control flow | `@each`, `@for`, `@if` | Generate repetitive classes |
| Extend | `@extend %placeholder;` | Share a selector's styles (can produce bloated, surprising output) |

**Example: SCSS and its compiled output**

```scss
// _tokens.scss
$breakpoints: (md: 40rem, lg: 64rem);
$brand: #1a73e8;

// card.scss
@use 'sass:color';
@use 'sass:map';
@use 'tokens' as t;

@mixin above($bp) {                                  // a reusable media-query mixin
  @media (width >= #{map.get(t.$breakpoints, $bp)}) { @content; }
}

.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid color.adjust(t.$brand, $lightness: 35%);

  &__title { font-weight: 700; }                     // & = .card  ->  .card__title (BEM naming)
  &:hover  { border-color: t.$brand; }

  @include above(md) { padding: 2rem; }
}

@each $name, $color in (info: #1a73e8, warn: #e8590c) {
  .badge-#{$name} { background: $color; }            // generates .badge-info and .badge-warn
}
```

```css
/* Compiled CSS */
.card { padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid #bcd6f8; }   /* brand blue, 35% lighter */
.card__title { font-weight: 700; }
.card:hover { border-color: #1a73e8; }
@media (width >= 40rem) { .card { padding: 2rem; } }
.badge-info { background: #1a73e8; }
.badge-warn { background: #e8590c; }
```

**Native CSS has caught up.** Many reasons to use a preprocessor are now built into browsers: custom properties (2.3), native **nesting** (supported in all major browsers since 2023), `color-mix()`, `@layer`, `calc()` and container queries. Preprocessors remain useful for loops, mixins and build-time logic, but small and medium projects can often use plain CSS with PostCSS.

```css
/* Native CSS nesting: no build step needed */
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  & .title { font-weight: 700; }
  &:hover  { border-color: var(--brand); }
  @media (width >= 40rem) { padding: 2rem; }
}
```

**Naming and scoping.** Global class names collide. Several approaches address this:

| Approach | Idea | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **BEM** (Block, Element, Modifier) | A naming convention with flat, low specificity | `.card`, `.card__title`, `.card--featured` |
| **CSS Modules** | The build tool renames classes to be unique per file | `.title` becomes `.Card_title__x7f2` |
| **CSS-in-JS** | Styles written in JavaScript next to components | styled-components, Emotion (Chapter 14) |
| **Cascade layers and `@scope`** | Native control of priority and reach | `@layer components { ... }` |

**Component frameworks: Bootstrap.** Bootstrap provides a responsive 12-column grid, ready-made components (navbars, modals, cards, forms) and JavaScript behaviour. Version 5 removed the jQuery dependency and is customised through Sass variables and CSS custom properties. It is fast for prototypes and internal tools, but sites built with it tend to look alike, and overriding its design takes effort.

```html
<!-- Bootstrap: semantic component classes plus grid classes -->
<div class="container">
  <div class="row">
    <div class="col-12 col-md-6">                <!-- full width on mobile, half from the md breakpoint -->
      <div class="card">
        <div class="card-body">
          <h5 class="card-title">Pro plan</h5>
          <a href="/buy" class="btn btn-primary">Buy</a>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

**Utility-first frameworks: Tailwind CSS.** Instead of semantic component classes, utility-first CSS provides a large set of small, single-purpose classes (`p-4` sets padding, `text-center` centres text) that you compose directly in the markup. Tailwind's build step scans your source files and generates *only* the classes you actually use, so the final CSS stays small regardless of the size of the framework. Since version 4 (2025), configuration is written in CSS itself:

```css
/* app.css (Tailwind v4) */
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --color-brand: oklch(58% 0.18 255);    /* generates bg-brand, text-brand, border-brand, ... */
  --font-display: "Inter", sans-serif;   /* generates font-display */
}
```

```html
<!-- Tailwind: styling by composing utilities; sm:, md:, hover:, dark: are variants -->
<article class="rounded-lg border border-gray-200 p-4 md:p-8 shadow-sm
                hover:shadow-md transition-shadow dark:bg-gray-900 dark:border-gray-700">
  <h2 class="font-display text-xl font-bold text-gray-900 dark:text-white">Pro plan</h2>
  <p class="mt-2 text-gray-600">Everything in Free, plus priority support.</p>
  <a href="/buy"
     class="mt-4 inline-block rounded-md bg-brand px-4 py-2 text-white
            hover:brightness-110 focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-2">
    Buy
  </a>
</article>
```

**Choosing an approach.**

| | Hand-written CSS | Sass + BEM | Bootstrap | Tailwind |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Learning curve | CSS only | Low extra | Learn the component API | Learn the utility vocabulary |
| Design freedom | Total | Total | Limited without customisation | High, within a design-token system |
| Speed to prototype | Slow | Medium | Very fast | Fast |
| CSS size growth | Grows with features | Grows with features | Large unless unused parts are removed | Stays small (only the classes used) |
| HTML readability | Clean | Clean | Moderate | Long class lists |
| Typical fit | Small sites, full control | Long-lived custom designs | Admin panels, prototypes | Component-based apps (React, Vue) |

The common criticisms of utility-first CSS are long class attributes and a mix of styling and structure. Its defenders reply that in component-based apps the component *is* the abstraction, so the styling lives in one place anyway, and that a constrained token system keeps designs consistent.

**Key Takeaways**

- Preprocessors such as Sass add variables, nesting, mixins, modules and loops, then compile to plain CSS. Use `@use`, not the deprecated `@import`.
- PostCSS transforms CSS with plugins. Autoprefixer handles vendor prefixes based on Browserslist.
- Native CSS now covers nesting, variables, layers and colour functions, which reduces the need for preprocessors.
- BEM, CSS Modules and cascade layers address naming collisions and specificity at scale.
- Bootstrap provides complete components quickly. Tailwind provides composable utilities and generates only the CSS you use.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite a 50-line plain CSS file using Sass partials, a variables module and nesting. Compile it with `npx sass` and compare the output with the original.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build the same pricing card three times: with BEM classes in plain CSS using native nesting, with Bootstrap, and with Tailwind. Compare the size of the HTML, the size of the CSS shipped, and how long it takes to change the accent colour across all of them.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your team is debating Tailwind versus CSS Modules for a new React application. What trade-offs would you discuss?" *Hint:* consider bundle size, consistency through design tokens, readability of the markup, onboarding, how styles get deleted when a component is removed, and how dynamic class names interact with the build-time class scanner.

<a id="3-javascript-language-core"></a>
## 3. JavaScript Language Core

JavaScript is the only programming language that every browser runs natively, and through Node.js it also runs on servers, build tools and command-line programs. This chapter covers the core of the language itself, independent of any browser API: its values and types, variables and scope, operators and control flow, functions and closures, error handling and the module systems used to organise code into files. Nearly every confusing behaviour you will meet later in DOM scripting, asynchronous code and frameworks can be traced back to one of these fundamentals, so they are worth learning precisely.

<a id="31-types-values-and-variables"></a>
### 3.1 Types, Values and Variables

This subchapter covers what kinds of values JavaScript has, how variables hold them, where those variables are visible, and the rules the language follows when it converts one type into another.

#### Primitive Types and Wrapper Objects

Before you can reason about any JavaScript program, you need to know what kind of thing a value is. The kind decides how the value is copied, how it is compared, and whether it can be changed. JavaScript splits every value into two families: **primitives**, which are simple and immutable, and **objects**, which are collections of properties that can be shared and modified.

**The seven primitive types.** A primitive is a value that is not an object and has no properties of its own.

| Type | Example values | `typeof` result | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `string` | `"hello"`, `'a'`, `` `x` `` | `"string"` | Immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units |
| `number` | `42`, `3.14`, `NaN`, `Infinity` | `"number"` | 64-bit floating point, the only "ordinary" numeric type |
| `bigint` | `10n`, `2n ** 64n` | `"bigint"` | Arbitrary-precision integers (ES2020) |
| `boolean` | `true`, `false` | `"boolean"` | |
| `undefined` | `undefined` | `"undefined"` | "No value has been assigned" |
| `null` | `null` | `"object"` | "Intentionally empty". The `typeof` result is a historical bug. |
| `symbol` | `Symbol("id")` | `"symbol"` | Unique identifiers, mainly used as property keys (ES2015) |

Everything else is an **object**: plain objects, arrays, functions, dates, regular expressions, maps, DOM nodes, errors. `typeof` returns `"object"` for all of them except functions, which return `"function"`.

**Values versus references.** A variable that holds a primitive holds the value itself. A variable that holds an object holds a *reference* to an object that lives elsewhere in memory. Copying a variable copies whatever it holds.

```text
let a = 7;            let p = { x: 1 };
let b = a;            let q = p;

  a: 7                  p: ref --+
  b: 7  (own copy)               +--> { x: 1 }   <- one object, two references
                        q: ref --+

b = 8  -> a is still 7          q.x = 2  -> p.x is also 2
```

Primitives are also **immutable**: no operation can change a primitive in place. `"abc".toUpperCase()` returns a *new* string. Reassigning a variable (`s = s + "!"`) makes it point to a different value; the original value is untouched. Chapter 4 covers object references, copying and cloning in depth.

**Wrapper objects and autoboxing.** If primitives have no properties, how does `"abc".length` work? When you access a property on a string, number, boolean, symbol or bigint, the engine temporarily wraps the primitive in the matching **wrapper object** (`String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `Symbol`, `BigInt`), reads the property from it (usually a method inherited from `String.prototype` and so on), then discards the wrapper. This is called **autoboxing**. Engines optimise the wrapper away, but the behaviour is as if it existed.

```text
"abc".toUpperCase()
   |
   +-> new String("abc")     (temporary wrapper, conceptually)
          |
          +-> String.prototype.toUpperCase  -> "ABC"
   wrapper discarded
```

Because the wrapper is thrown away, properties you *assign* to a primitive are lost. In strict mode (3.4) the assignment throws instead of failing silently. `null` and `undefined` have no wrappers, so accessing any property on them throws a `TypeError`.

**Calling wrappers with and without `new`.**

| Expression | Result | Use it? |
|---|---|---|
| `Number("42")` | `42` (primitive) | Yes: explicit conversion |
| `String(123)` | `"123"` (primitive) | Yes |
| `Boolean("")` | `false` (primitive) | Yes |
| `new Number(42)` | A `Number` object | No |
| `new Boolean(false)` | A `Boolean` object, which is **truthy** | No |
| `new Symbol()` / `new BigInt(1)` | `TypeError` | Not allowed |

**Example: primitives, wrappers and their traps**

```javascript
"use strict";

const word = "hello";
console.log(word.length);          // 5: autoboxed to a String wrapper, then discarded
console.log(word.toUpperCase());   // "HELLO": a new string; word is unchanged
console.log(word);                 // "hello"

try {
  word.custom = 1;                 // assigning a property to a primitive
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.name);             // "TypeError" in strict mode (silently ignored in sloppy mode)
}

const n1 = 42;
const n2 = new Number(42);         // an object wrapping 42: avoid
console.log(typeof n1, typeof n2); // "number" "object"
console.log(n1 === n2);            // false: primitive vs object
console.log(n1 == n2);             // true: == unwraps the object (see Type Coercion)

const flag = new Boolean(false);
if (flag) console.log("runs!");    // runs: every object is truthy, even this one

console.log(typeof null);          // "object": a bug kept for backward compatibility
console.log(typeof function () {});// "function"
console.log(typeof []);            // "object": use Array.isArray to detect arrays
```

**Detecting types reliably.** `typeof` is correct for every primitive except `null`. For the rest, use dedicated checks:

```javascript
const isNull   = (v) => v === null;
const isObject = (v) => v !== null && typeof v === "object";   // excludes null and functions
Array.isArray([1, 2]);                                        // true
Object.prototype.toString.call(new Date());                   // "[object Date]": works for built-ins
```

**Key Takeaways**

- JavaScript has seven primitive types (`string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `symbol`). Everything else is an object.
- Primitives are immutable and copied by value. Variables holding objects hold references, so copies share the same object.
- Accessing a property on a primitive autoboxes it in a temporary wrapper object. Properties assigned to primitives are lost.
- Use `Number()`, `String()` and `Boolean()` without `new` for conversion. Never create wrapper objects with `new`.
- `typeof null === "object"` is a historical bug. Test for `null` with `=== null`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Predict the `typeof` result for: `0n`, `NaN`, `null`, `[]`, `class {}`, `Symbol.iterator`, `undefined`, `new String("")`. Then check your answers in the browser console.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function `typeName(value)` that returns `"null"`, `"array"`, `"date"`, `"regexp"`, `"function"` or the `typeof` result for anything else. Explain why `Object.prototype.toString.call` is more reliable than `instanceof` for objects that come from an `<iframe>`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If strings are primitives and have no properties, how does `'abc'.length` work, and why does `s.foo = 1; s.foo` return `undefined`?" *Hint:* describe what happens to the object the engine creates for the property access.

#### Numbers, BigInt and Numeric Precision

Most languages offer several numeric types: 8-, 16-, 32- and 64-bit integers, single and double floats. JavaScript originally offered exactly one, `number`, a 64-bit floating-point value. That choice keeps the language simple, but it means integers lose precision above a certain size and decimal fractions such as `0.1` cannot be stored exactly. To write correct code for money, IDs, counters or scientific values, you need to know where those limits are.

**IEEE 754 double precision.** Every `number` is stored in 64 bits, split into three fields:

```text
 1 bit    11 bits          52 bits
+------+------------+-----------------------------+
| sign |  exponent  |         fraction            |
+------+------------+-----------------------------+
value = (-1)^sign  x  1.fraction (binary)  x  2^(exponent - 1023)
```

The 52-bit fraction (plus one implicit bit) gives about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits. Consequences:

| Limit | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` | `2^53 - 1` = 9 007 199 254 740 991 | Largest integer `n` such that `n` and `n + 1` are both exactly representable |
| `Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER` | `-(2^53 - 1)` | Smallest such integer |
| `Number.MAX_VALUE` | about `1.8e308` | Largest finite number. Beyond it you get `Infinity`. |
| `Number.MIN_VALUE` | `5e-324` | Smallest positive number |
| `Number.EPSILON` | `2^-52`, about `2.2e-16` | Gap between 1 and the next representable number |

Above `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, not every integer can be stored, so `2 ** 53 + 1 === 2 ** 53` is `true`. This matters for 64-bit database IDs and Twitter-style snowflake IDs: send them as strings in JSON.

**Why `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`.** In base 10, `1/3` has no finite representation (`0.333...`). In base 2, `1/10` has none either, so `0.1` is stored as the closest double, which is very slightly off. The tiny errors in `0.1` and `0.2` add up to a result that is not the closest double to `0.3`.

```javascript
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);                 // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);         // false

// Compare floats with a tolerance instead of ===
const nearlyEqual = (a, b, eps = Number.EPSILON) =>
  Math.abs(a - b) <= eps * Math.max(1, Math.abs(a), Math.abs(b));   // relative tolerance
console.log(nearlyEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)); // true

// Money: work in integer minor units (cents), format only for display
const priceCents = 1999;                // 19.99
const totalCents = priceCents * 3;      // 5997: exact integer arithmetic
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-GB", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" })
  .format(totalCents / 100));           // "€59.97"
```

**Special values.** Floating-point arithmetic never throws. Invalid or overflowing operations produce special values instead:

| Value | Produced by | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Infinity`, `-Infinity` | `1 / 0`, `-1 / 0`, overflow (`1e308 * 10`) | `Number.isFinite(x)` rejects them |
| `NaN` ("not a number") | `0 / 0`, `Math.sqrt(-1)`, `Number("abc")` | Still `typeof "number"`. `NaN !== NaN`. |
| `-0` | `-1 / Infinity`, `Math.round(-0.4)` | `-0 === 0` is `true`. `Object.is(-0, 0)` is `false`. |

`NaN` is the only value not equal to itself. Detect it with `Number.isNaN(x)`. The older global `isNaN(x)` converts its argument first, so `isNaN("hello")` is `true`, which is rarely what you want.

**Writing numeric literals.**

```javascript
255;          // decimal
0xff;         // hexadecimal  -> 255
0o377;        // octal        -> 255
0b1111_1111;  // binary with a numeric separator -> 255
1_000_000;    // separators (ES2021) are only for readability
2.5e-3;       // exponent notation -> 0.0025
```

**Parsing and converting.**

| Expression | Result | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `Number("42")` / `+"42"` | `42` | Whole string must be numeric (whitespace is trimmed) |
| `Number("12px")` | `NaN` | Strict |
| `Number("")` | `0` | A common surprise |
| `parseInt("12px", 10)` | `12` | Reads leading digits, stops at the first invalid character |
| `parseFloat("3.5kg")` | `3.5` | Same, for decimals |
| `parseInt("0.0000005")` | `0` | String is read as-is |
| `parseInt(0.0000005)` | `5` | The number is first converted to the string `"5e-7"` |

Always pass the radix to `parseInt`, and only pass it strings.
