**Rounding and formatting.** `Math.round`, `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil` and `Math.trunc` return numbers. `toFixed(digits)` returns a *string* and inherits binary representation errors: `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is `"1.00"` because `1.005` is actually stored as `1.00499999...`. `Math.round(-2.5)` is `-2`, because it rounds halves towards positive infinity. For user-facing output, prefer `Intl.NumberFormat`, which handles locales, currencies and grouping.

**Integer-only operations.** Bitwise operators (`|`, `&`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`) convert their operands to 32-bit signed integers. `x | 0` truncates, but silently breaks for values above `2^31 - 1`. Use `Math.trunc` instead.

**BigInt.** When you need integers larger than `2^53 - 1` with exact arithmetic (cryptography, 64-bit IDs, large factorials), use `bigint`. Write a literal with an `n` suffix or convert with `BigInt()`.

```javascript
const big = 2n ** 64n;                      // 18446744073709551616n: exact
console.log(typeof big);                    // "bigint"
console.log(9007199254740993n);             // exact, unlike 9007199254740993 (a number)

console.log(7n / 2n);                       // 3n: division truncates towards zero
console.log(-7n / 2n);                      // -3n

// 1n + 1;                                  // TypeError: cannot mix BigInt and other types
console.log(1n + BigInt(1));                // 2n: convert explicitly
console.log(Number(2n ** 60n));             // converts back, possibly losing precision

console.log(1n == 1, 1n === 1, 2n > 1);     // true false true: comparisons across types work
// JSON.stringify({ id: 1n });              // TypeError: BigInt is not serialisable by default
console.log(JSON.stringify({ id: String(1n) })); // '{"id":"1"}': serialise as a string
// BigInt(1.5);                             // RangeError: not an integer
```

| | `number` | `bigint` |
|---|---|---|
| Range | About ±1.8e308, exact integers up to 2^53 - 1 | Unlimited (memory-bound) integers |
| Fractions | Yes (binary floating point) | No |
| Speed | Hardware-fast | Slower, grows with size |
| `Math.*` functions | Yes | No |
| Mixing in arithmetic | | Must convert explicitly; mixing throws `TypeError` |
| JSON | Native | Throws unless you convert to a string |

**Key Takeaways**

- `number` is an IEEE 754 64-bit float. Integers are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1).
- Decimal fractions are approximate. Compare floats with a tolerance and store money as integer minor units.
- `NaN` is not equal to itself. Use `Number.isNaN` and `Number.isFinite`, not the global `isNaN` and `isFinite`.
- `Number()` is strict, `parseInt`/`parseFloat` read a numeric prefix. Always pass a radix to `parseInt`.
- `bigint` provides exact, arbitrary-size integers but cannot be mixed with `number` without explicit conversion.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `sumPrices(prices)` that adds an array of prices such as `[0.1, 0.2, 19.99]` and returns a correctly rounded string with two decimals. Do it once with floats and `toFixed`, and once with integer cents. Find an input for which the two versions disagree.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `factorial(n)` with `bigint` and compute `factorial(25n)`. Then compute the same value with `number` and explain from the 52-bit fraction why the last digits differ.
> 3. *(Interview)* "An API returns `{ "id": 1234567890123456789 }` and after `JSON.parse` your code fetches the wrong record. What happened, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* consider what happens to integers above 2^53 during parsing, and where the fix belongs (server output format or a custom parser).

#### Strings and Template Literals

Text is everywhere in web development: URLs, HTML, user input, JSON, log messages. JavaScript strings look simple, but two details cause many bugs. Strings are immutable, so every "modification" creates a new string. And strings are sequences of UTF-16 *code units*, not characters, so lengths and indices can be surprising for text outside the Basic Multilingual Plane. Template literals, added in ES2015, made building strings much easier and enabled a powerful feature called tagged templates.

**Three ways to write a string.**

| Syntax | Interpolation | Multi-line | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'single'` | No | No | Most code (style-guide preference) |
| `"double"` | No | No | Same as single quotes, no functional difference |
| `` `backtick` `` | `${expression}` | Yes | Building strings from values, multi-line text |

Escape sequences work in all three: `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab), `\\` (backslash), `\'`, `\"`, `\u00e9` (`é`), `\u{1D11E}` (any code point).

**Immutability.** You can read characters with `s[0]` or `s.at(-1)`, but you cannot write them. `s[0] = "X"` is silently ignored (or throws in strict mode). Every method returns a new string.

**Essential methods.**

| Method | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `at(i)` | `"hello".at(-1)` | `"o"` (negative indices count from the end) |
| `slice(start, end)` | `"hello".slice(1, 3)` | `"el"` (negative indices allowed) |
| `includes`, `startsWith`, `endsWith` | `"hello".startsWith("he")` | `true` |
| `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf` | `"hello".indexOf("l")` | `2` (`-1` if not found) |
| `split(sep)` | `"a,b,c".split(",")` | `["a", "b", "c"]` |
| `trim`, `trimStart`, `trimEnd` | `"  hi ".trim()` | `"hi"` |
| `padStart`, `padEnd` | `"7".padStart(3, "0")` | `"007"` |
| `replace`, `replaceAll` | `"a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+")` | `"a+b+c"` (`replace` with a string changes only the first match) |
| `toUpperCase`, `toLowerCase` | `"Straße".toUpperCase()` | `"STRASSE"` (length can change) |
| `repeat(n)` | `"ab".repeat(3)` | `"ababab"` |
| `localeCompare` | `"é".localeCompare("f", "fr")` | `-1` (language-aware ordering) |
| `normalize(form)` | `"e\u0301".normalize("NFC")` | `"é"` as one code point |

**UTF-16 and code units.** Each string element is a 16-bit code unit. Characters with code points above U+FFFF (many CJK ideographs, musical and mathematical symbols, and emoji) need two code units, called a **surrogate pair**. `length` and index access count code units, while `for...of`, spread and `Array.from` iterate by code point.

```javascript
const clef = "\u{1D11E}";               // MUSICAL SYMBOL G CLEF: one code point, two code units
console.log(clef.length);               // 2
console.log(clef[0]);                   // "\uD834": half of a surrogate pair, not a real character
console.log([...clef].length);          // 1: iteration is by code point
console.log(clef.codePointAt(0));       // 119070 (0x1D11E)

// Accents can be composed (1 code point) or decomposed (letter + combining mark)
const a = "caf\u00e9";                  // "café"
const b = "cafe\u0301";                 // also displays as "café"
console.log(a === b);                   // false
console.log(a.normalize() === b.normalize()); // true: normalise before comparing user input

// What a reader perceives as one character is a "grapheme cluster"
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter("en", { granularity: "grapheme" });
console.log([...seg.segment(b)].length); // 4
```

**Comparing strings.** `<` and `>` compare code unit by code unit, so all uppercase ASCII letters sort before lowercase ones (`"Z" < "a"` is `true`) and accented letters sort after `z`. For user-visible sorting use `localeCompare` or, for many comparisons, a reusable `Intl.Collator`.

**Template literals.** Backtick strings can embed any expression with `${...}`, and can span lines. The expression is converted to a string with the normal ToString rules (see Type Coercion and Equality Rules).

```javascript
const user = { name: "Ada", items: 3 };
const msg = `Hello ${user.name}, you have ${user.items} item${user.items === 1 ? "" : "s"}.`;
console.log(msg);                       // "Hello Ada, you have 3 items."

const html = `
  <ul>
    ${["a", "b"].map((x) => `<li>${x}</li>`).join("")}
  </ul>`;                               // newlines and indentation are kept literally
```

**Tagged templates.** If you put a function name directly before a template literal, the function is called with the literal's static string parts and the evaluated values separately. The tag can process the values (escape them, translate, build a query) before joining the parts.

```text
tag`Hi ${name}, you owe ${amount}!`

tag(
  ["Hi ", ", you owe ", "!"],   <- strings: always one more than the values
  name,                         <- values, already evaluated
  amount
)
```

```javascript
// A tag that HTML-escapes every interpolated value, preventing injection (Chapter 6)
const escapeHtml = (v) =>
  String(v).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) =>
    ({ "&": "&amp;", "<": "&lt;", ">": "&gt;", '"': "&quot;", "'": "&#39;" })[c]);

function safeHtml(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce(
    (out, str, i) => out + str + (i < values.length ? escapeHtml(values[i]) : ""),
    ""
  );
}

const comment = '<img src=x onerror="alert(1)">';
console.log(safeHtml`<p>${comment}</p>`);
// "<p>&lt;img src=x onerror=&quot;alert(1)&quot;&gt;</p>"

console.log(String.raw`C:\new\table`);  // "C:\new\table": built-in tag that skips escape processing
```

Tagged templates power libraries such as `lit-html`, `styled-components` and SQL query builders that turn values into bound parameters.

**Key Takeaways**

- Strings are immutable. Every method returns a new string.
- `length` and indices count UTF-16 code units. Characters above U+FFFF use two. Iterate with `for...of` or spread to get code points, and use `Intl.Segmenter` for user-perceived characters.
- Normalise (`normalize()`) before comparing text that may contain accents, and use `localeCompare` or `Intl.Collator` for sorting.
- Template literals support `${}` interpolation and multi-line text.
- A tagged template passes static parts and values separately to a function, which enables safe escaping and DSLs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `capitalize(s)` that upper-cases the first letter of each word in a sentence, using `split`, `map`, `at` or `slice`, and `join`. Make sure it handles multiple spaces.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `reverse(s)` that correctly reverses `"ab\u{1D11E}c"` and compare it with `s.split("").reverse().join("")`. Explain why the naive version produces broken output.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Implement a tagged template `sql` so that ``sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` `` returns `{ text: 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', params: [id] }`." *Hint:* the strings array has one more element than the values array; number the placeholders as you join them.

#### Booleans, null and undefined

Programs constantly need to represent "yes or no" and "there is nothing here". JavaScript has one type for the first (`boolean`) and, unusually, two separate values for the second: `undefined` and `null`. They behave differently in default parameters, JSON, arithmetic and equality, so knowing which one appears where, and which one to use yourself, prevents a whole class of bugs.

**Booleans.** The `boolean` type has exactly two values, `true` and `false`. Comparisons and the `!` operator produce booleans. Any value can be converted with `Boolean(value)` or the double negation `!!value`, following the truthy and falsy rules in Truthy and Falsy Values.

**`undefined`: "not set (yet)".** The language itself produces `undefined` whenever a value is missing:

| Situation | Example | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Declared variable without initial value | `let x;` | `undefined` |
| Missing function argument | `function f(a) {}` called as `f()` | `a` is `undefined` |
| Missing object property | `({}).name` | `undefined` |
| Array hole or out-of-range index | `[1, 2][5]` | `undefined` |
| Function without `return` | `(function () {})()` | `undefined` |
| `void` operator | `void 0` | `undefined` |

**`null`: "deliberately empty".** The language almost never produces `null` on its own. It appears when a program or an API deliberately states that there is no value: `document.querySelector(".missing")` returns `null`, a prototype chain ends in `null`, and `JSON` uses `null` for empty fields. A useful convention: **`undefined` means "absent", `null` means "present but empty"**.

**How the two differ.**

| Behaviour | `undefined` | `null` |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof` | `"undefined"` | `"object"` (historical bug) |
| `Number(x)` | `NaN` | `0` |
| `x + 1` | `NaN` | `1` |
| Triggers a default parameter | Yes | No |
| Triggers a destructuring default | Yes | No |
| `JSON.stringify({ a: x })` | `"{}"` (the key is dropped) | `'{"a":null}'` |
| `x == null` | `true` | `true` |
| `x === null` | `false` | `true` |
| `x ?? "fallback"` (3.2) | `"fallback"` | `"fallback"` |

**Example: the differences in practice**

```javascript
function greet(name = "guest") {           // default applies only when name is undefined
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}
console.log(greet());                      // "Hello, guest"
console.log(greet(undefined));             // "Hello, guest"
console.log(greet(null));                  // "Hello, null": null is a real value

console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: null })); // '{"b":null}'

// "Missing" vs "present but undefined"
const config = { debug: undefined };
console.log(config.debug === undefined);   // true
console.log(config.verbose === undefined); // true: cannot tell the two apart this way
console.log("debug" in config);            // true: the key exists
console.log(Object.hasOwn(config, "verbose")); // false: the key does not exist

// One check for both "empty" values
function isMissing(v) {
  return v == null;                        // true for null and undefined only (see Equality)
}
console.log(isMissing(0), isMissing(""), isMissing(null)); // false false true
```

**Why `typeof null` is `"object"`.** In the first JavaScript implementation, values carried a small type tag, and the tag for objects was `0`. `null` was represented as the null pointer, whose bits were all zero, so `typeof` read it as an object. Fixing it would break existing websites, so the bug became part of the specification.

**`undefined` is not a keyword.** `undefined` is a read-only property of the global object, so you cannot overwrite it globally in modern engines. You *can* still declare a local variable named `undefined`, which is why older code writes `void 0` to get a guaranteed `undefined`. Linters forbid shadowing it, and you will rarely need `void 0` today.

**Choosing between them in your own code.**

- Let the language produce `undefined`. Do not assign `undefined` explicitly unless you are deliberately "unsetting" something.
- Use `null` when an API or data structure needs to say "this field exists and is empty", for example in JSON payloads and database records.
- When consuming values, treat both as "no value" with `== null` or `??`, unless the distinction matters.

**Key Takeaways**

- `boolean` has two values. Convert other values with `Boolean(x)` or `!!x`.
- `undefined` is what the language gives you for missing values. `null` is an intentional "empty" set by code.
- Default parameters and destructuring defaults trigger only for `undefined`, never for `null`.
- `JSON.stringify` drops `undefined` properties but keeps `null` ones. `Number(null)` is `0` but `Number(undefined)` is `NaN`.
- `x == null` is the idiomatic check for "null or undefined". Use `in` or `Object.hasOwn` to check whether a key exists.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For each expression, predict the result: `null + 1`, `undefined + 1`, `null == 0`, `null == undefined`, `null === undefined`, `typeof undefined`, `typeof undeclaredVariable`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* A PATCH endpoint receives JSON. A field set to `null` must clear the database value, and a field that is absent must be left unchanged. Write `applyPatch(record, patch)` that implements this correctly, and explain why `if (patch.email)` is the wrong test.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`, and when would you use each one?" *Hint:* talk about who produces each value, defaults, JSON and the `== null` idiom.

#### Symbols

As programs grow and combine code from many libraries, property names start to collide. If two libraries both add a property called `id` or `meta` to the same object, one silently overwrites the other. ES2015 introduced **symbols** to solve this: a symbol is a primitive value that is guaranteed to be unique, so a property keyed by a symbol can never clash with any other key. Symbols also give the language a way to define **protocols**, hooks such as "how to iterate this object", without reserving ordinary property names.

**Creating symbols.** Call `Symbol()` with an optional description. The description is only a debugging label. Two symbols with the same description are still different.

```javascript
const id1 = Symbol("id");
const id2 = Symbol("id");
console.log(id1 === id2);          // false: every call creates a new unique value
console.log(id1.description);      // "id"
console.log(typeof id1);           // "symbol"
// new Symbol("id");               // TypeError: Symbol is not a constructor
```

**Symbols as property keys.** Use bracket notation, or a computed key in an object literal.

```javascript
const META = Symbol("meta");

const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  [META]: { fetchedAt: Date.now() },  // computed key: the symbol, not the string "META"
};

console.log(user[META].fetchedAt);    // works with the original symbol reference
console.log(Object.keys(user));       // ["name"]: symbol keys are skipped
console.log(JSON.stringify(user));    // '{"name":"Ada"}': skipped here too
for (const k in user) console.log(k); // "name" only

console.log(Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(user)); // [Symbol(meta)]
console.log(Reflect.ownKeys(user));              // ["name", Symbol(meta)]
```

| Operation | Includes string keys | Includes symbol keys |
|---|---|---|
| `for...in`, `Object.keys`, `Object.entries` | Yes | No |
| `JSON.stringify` | Yes | No |
| `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` | No | Yes |
| `Reflect.ownKeys` | Yes | Yes |
| `Object.assign`, object spread `{...obj}` | Yes | Yes |

Symbol keys are **hidden, not private**. Anyone with access to the object can list them with `Reflect.ownKeys`. For true privacy, use closures (3.3) or private class fields (Chapter 4).

**The global symbol registry.** Sometimes separate pieces of code (different modules, or a page and an iframe) need to agree on the *same* symbol. `Symbol.for(key)` looks the key up in a runtime-wide registry and creates the symbol only the first time.

```javascript
const a = Symbol.for("app.logger");
const b = Symbol.for("app.logger");   // returns the existing symbol
console.log(a === b);                 // true
console.log(Symbol.keyFor(a));        // "app.logger"
console.log(Symbol.keyFor(Symbol("x"))); // undefined: not a registered symbol
```

Use a namespaced key (`"mylib.feature"`), because the registry is shared by all code in the realm.

**Well-known symbols: language protocols.** The language defines built-in symbols, available as static properties of `Symbol`, that let your objects plug into core behaviour:

| Symbol | Lets an object define... | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `Symbol.iterator` | How to iterate it (see Generators and Iterators) | `for...of`, spread, destructuring, `Array.from` |
| `Symbol.asyncIterator` | Asynchronous iteration | `for await...of` (Chapter 5) |
| `Symbol.toPrimitive` | Conversion to a primitive (see Type Coercion and Equality Rules) | `+obj`, `` `${obj}` ``, `obj == 1` |
| `Symbol.toStringTag` | The label in `Object.prototype.toString` | `"[object MyType]"` |
| `Symbol.hasInstance` | Custom `instanceof` behaviour | `x instanceof C` |

**Example: making an object iterable and convertible**

```javascript
const temperature = {
  celsius: 21.5,
  [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {          // hint: "number", "string" or "default"
    return hint === "string" ? `${this.celsius} °C` : this.celsius;
  },
  get [Symbol.toStringTag]() { return "Temperature"; },
};

console.log(+temperature);              // 21.5 (hint "number")
console.log(`${temperature}`);          // "21.5 °C" (hint "string")
console.log(Object.prototype.toString.call(temperature)); // "[object Temperature]"

const week = {
  days: ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"],
  [Symbol.iterator]() {                 // the iteration protocol: return an object with next()
    let i = 0;
    return { next: () => ({ value: this.days[i], done: i++ >= this.days.length }) };
  },
};
console.log([...week]);                 // ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
```

**Converting symbols.** Symbols refuse implicit conversion to strings or numbers, to stop them from accidentally turning into ordinary property names. Use `String(sym)` or `sym.description` explicitly.

```javascript
const s = Symbol("token");
console.log(String(s));     // "Symbol(token)"
// s + "";                  // TypeError: Cannot convert a Symbol value to a string
// `${s}`;                  // TypeError as well
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `Symbol(description)` creates a unique primitive. The description is only a label.
- Symbol-keyed properties never collide with other keys and are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys` and `JSON.stringify`, but they are not private.
- `Symbol.for(key)` returns a shared symbol from a global registry, for coordination across modules or realms.
- Well-known symbols such as `Symbol.iterator` and `Symbol.toPrimitive` let your objects customise built-in language behaviour.
- Symbols throw on implicit string conversion. Convert them explicitly with `String()` or `.description`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create an object with two string keys and one symbol key. Log the results of `Object.keys`, `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`, `Reflect.ownKeys` and `JSON.stringify` and explain each one.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `Money` object with `amount` and `currency` whose `Symbol.toPrimitive` returns the amount for numeric hints and a formatted string such as `"12.50 EUR"` for string hints. Test it with `+m`, `` `${m}` `` and `m > 10`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why did JavaScript add symbols instead of just reserving a property name like `__iterator__`?" *Hint:* think about existing code on the web that might already use that name, and about what `Object.keys` or `JSON.stringify` would expose.

#### var, let and const

A variable is a name bound to a value. Until 2015, JavaScript had only `var` for declaring variables, and `var` has rules that surprise programmers coming from almost any other language: it ignores blocks, it can be redeclared, and it can be used before the line that declares it. ES2015 added `let` and `const`, which behave the way most people expect. Modern code uses `const` and `let`, but you will read `var` in older code and tutorials, so you need to understand all three.

**Comparison.**

| | `var` | `let` | `const` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | Function (or global) | Block `{ }` | Block `{ }` |
| Hoisted | Yes, initialised to `undefined` | Yes, but uninitialised (TDZ) | Yes, but uninitialised (TDZ) |
| Use before declaration | Gives `undefined` | `ReferenceError` | `ReferenceError` |
| Redeclare in same scope | Allowed | `SyntaxError` | `SyntaxError` |
| Reassign | Yes | Yes | No (`TypeError`) |
| Must be initialised | No | No | Yes |
| Top-level declaration in a classic script creates a `window` property | Yes | No | No |
| New binding per loop iteration | No | Yes | Yes (for `for...of` and `for...in`) |

Hoisting and the TDZ are covered in the next topic.

**Function scope versus block scope.** A `var` declared inside an `if` or `for` block belongs to the whole enclosing function. `let` and `const` belong only to the block in which they are declared.

```javascript
function demo() {
  if (true) {
    var a = 1;     // function-scoped: visible in the whole function
    let b = 2;     // block-scoped: visible only inside this if-block
    const c = 3;   // block-scoped
  }
  console.log(a);  // 1
  // console.log(b); // ReferenceError: b is not defined
}
demo();
```

**`const` means a constant binding, not a constant value.** You cannot reassign a `const` variable, but if it holds an object you can still change the object's contents. To make an object itself read-only, use `Object.freeze` (Chapter 4).

```javascript
const settings = { theme: "dark" };
settings.theme = "light";       // allowed: the object is mutated, the binding is unchanged
// settings = {};               // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

const frozen = Object.freeze({ theme: "dark" });
frozen.theme = "light";         // ignored (TypeError in strict mode): the object is frozen
```

**The classic loop bug.** Because `var` creates a single variable for the whole function, every callback created in the loop shares it. By the time the callbacks run, the loop has finished. `let` creates a fresh binding for each iteration, so each callback captures its own value.

```javascript
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("var", i), 0);   // logs 3, 3, 3: one shared i
}

for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("let", j), 0);   // logs 0, 1, 2: one j per iteration
}
```

```text
var:   one binding  i ----------------------------> 3 when callbacks run
        callback#1 --+
        callback#2 --+--> all read the same i
        callback#3 --+

let:   iteration 0: j=0 <-- callback#1
       iteration 1: j=1 <-- callback#2
       iteration 2: j=2 <-- callback#3
```

**Globals.** At the top level of a classic `<script>`, `var x` and function declarations become properties of the global object (`window.x`), where any other script can overwrite them. Top-level `let` and `const` are global variables too, but they are not added to `window`. In ES modules (3.4), top-level declarations of any kind are local to the module. Assigning to an undeclared name (`total = 5` without a declaration) creates a global property in sloppy mode and throws a `ReferenceError` in strict mode.

**Recommended practice.**

1. Use `const` by default. Most variables are never reassigned, and `const` makes that explicit.
2. Use `let` when the variable really needs to be reassigned (counters, accumulators, state that changes).
3. Do not use `var` in new code. Linters (`no-var`, `prefer-const`) enforce this automatically.

**Key Takeaways**

- `var` is function-scoped, redeclarable and initialised to `undefined` when hoisted. `let` and `const` are block-scoped and cannot be used before their declaration.
- `const` prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the object it refers to.
- `let` in a loop header creates a new binding per iteration, which fixes the classic closure-in-a-loop bug.
- Top-level `var` in a classic script pollutes `window`. Top-level `let` and `const` do not.
- Default to `const`, use `let` when you must reassign, and avoid `var`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite a 20-line snippet that uses only `var` so that it uses `const` wherever possible and `let` elsewhere. Run ESLint with `prefer-const` to confirm your choices.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Fix the `var` loop above in three different ways without changing `var` to `let`: with an IIFE, with `forEach`, and with the third argument of `setTimeout`. Explain why each one works.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If `const` means constant, why can I push items into a `const` array?" *Hint:* distinguish between the variable binding and the object the binding refers to.

#### Scope, Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone

When your code uses a name such as `total`, the engine needs to find out which variable that name refers to. **Scope** is the set of rules that answers this question. **Hoisting** describes when declarations come into existence, and the **temporal dead zone (TDZ)** describes the period in which a `let`, `const` or `class` exists but cannot yet be used. Together they explain error messages such as "Cannot access 'x' before initialization" and why some functions can be called before they appear in the file.

**Lexical scope.** JavaScript uses **lexical** (static) scoping: the scope of a variable is determined by *where it is written* in the source code, not by where or how a function is called. Scopes nest like boxes:

```text
+-- global / module scope -------------------------------------+
|  const appName = "Shop";                                      |
|                                                               |
|  +-- function checkout(cart) ------------------------------+  |
|  |  const tax = 0.2;                                        |  |
|  |                                                          |  |
|  |  +-- block: for (const item of cart) { ... } ---------+  |  |
|  |  |  const line = item.price * (1 + tax);               |  |  |
|  |  |  console.log(appName, line);  // sees tax, appName  |  |  |
|  |  +-----------------------------------------------------+  |  |
|  +----------------------------------------------------------+  |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+

Lookup goes from the inside out: block -> function -> module/global.
Inner scopes see outer variables. Outer scopes never see inner ones.
```

| Scope type | Created by | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| Global | The page or runtime | Built-ins, top-level declarations of classic scripts |
| Module | Each ES module file | Top-level declarations of that module |
| Function | Every function call | Parameters, `var`, `let`, `const`, inner functions |
| Block | `{ }` in `if`, `for`, `while`, `try`, bare blocks | `let`, `const`, `class` (and functions in strict mode) |

If no scope in the chain defines the name, the result is a `ReferenceError: x is not defined`. When an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer one, it **shadows** the outer variable within the inner scope.

**Hoisting: the creation phase.** Before running the code in a scope, the engine scans it and registers every declaration. That is why declarations behave as if they had been "hoisted" (moved) to the top of their scope. They are not literally moved; they are created before execution starts. What differs is how they are *initialised*:

| Declaration | Created at scope entry | Initial value | Access before the declaration line |
|---|---|---|---|
| `function f() {}` | Yes | The complete function | Works: the function can be called |
| `var x` | Yes | `undefined` | Gives `undefined` |
| `let x`, `const x` | Yes | Uninitialised | `ReferenceError` (TDZ) |
| `class C {}` | Yes | Uninitialised | `ReferenceError` (TDZ) |
| `import` | Yes (module linking) | Bound to the exporting module | Works (live binding) |

```javascript
console.log(sum(2, 3));    // 5: function declarations are hoisted complete
console.log(count);        // undefined: var is hoisted and initialised to undefined
// console.log(limit);     // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'limit' before initialization

function sum(a, b) { return a + b; }
var count = 10;
let limit = 5;
```

**The temporal dead zone.** For `let`, `const` and `class`, the TDZ is the period between entering the scope and executing the declaration. The name already exists (it shadows any outer variable with the same name), but any access throws. The zone is *temporal*: it depends on when code runs, not on where it is written.

```javascript
let x = "outer";
{
  // TDZ for the inner x starts here
  // console.log(x);       // ReferenceError: the inner x already shadows the outer one
  let x = "inner";         // TDZ ends
  console.log(x);          // "inner"
}

function later() {
  return value;            // fine to *write* this before the declaration...
}
const value = 42;
console.log(later());      // 42: ...because it is *called* after initialisation

// typeof is not safe inside the TDZ
// typeof y;               // ReferenceError
let y;
console.log(typeof notDeclaredAnywhere); // "undefined": undeclared names are fine for typeof

// Parameters have their own TDZ, evaluated left to right
function f(a = b, b = 1) {}
// f();                    // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
```

Why have a TDZ at all, when `var` simply gives `undefined`? Reading a variable before it is initialised is almost always a bug, and for `const` there would be no sensible value to return before initialisation. The TDZ turns that silent bug into an immediate error.

**Key Takeaways**

- Scope is lexical: it is decided by where code is written. Lookup goes outward from the innermost scope.
- There are global, module, function and block scopes. `let`, `const` and `class` are block-scoped.
- All declarations are hoisted (created when the scope is entered), but only function declarations are fully initialised and `var` starts as `undefined`.
- `let`, `const` and `class` are in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs. Accessing them earlier throws a `ReferenceError`, even with `typeof`.
- The TDZ is about time, not position: a function can refer to a later `const` as long as it is called after the `const` is initialised.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write down what this logs, then run it: `var a = 1; function f() { console.log(a); var a = 2; } f();`. Explain the result in terms of hoisting.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Draw the scope chain for a module that contains a function with a nested `for` loop and an inner arrow function. For each variable, mark which scopes can see it and identify one case of shadowing.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Are `let` and `const` hoisted?" *Hint:* the answer is yes, but explain what is different from `var` and give an example in which an inner `let` causes a `ReferenceError` even though an outer variable with the same name exists.

#### Type Coercion and Equality Rules

JavaScript was designed to keep running even when given "wrong" types. Ask it to subtract a string from a number, and instead of raising an error it converts the string to a number. This automatic conversion, called **implicit coercion**, explains both the convenience and the most famous puzzles of the language (`[] + {}`, `"5" - 2` versus `"5" + 2`). You do not need to memorise every rule, but you do need to know the three basic conversions, how `+` decides between adding and concatenating, and how `==` differs from `===`.

**Explicit and implicit coercion.** *Explicit* coercion is when you ask for the conversion: `Number(x)`, `String(x)`, `Boolean(x)`. *Implicit* coercion is when an operator does it for you: `x - 1`, `` `${x}` ``, `if (x)`. Both follow the same internal rules.

**Abstract operations.** The specification defines a few internal conversion operations that every operator uses:

| Operation | Converts to | Triggered by |
|---|---|---|
| ToPrimitive | A primitive | Any operator applied to an object |
| ToNumber | `number` | `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, unary `+`, `<`, `>`, `==` with numbers |
| ToString | `string` | `+` with a string, template literals, `String()`, property keys |
| ToBoolean | `boolean` | `if`, `while`, `!`, `&&`, `||`, ternary (see Truthy and Falsy Values) |

**ToNumber and ToString tables.**

| Value | ToNumber | ToString |
|---|---|---|
| `""` | `0` | `""` |
| `"  42  "` | `42` | `"  42  "` |
| `"42px"` | `NaN` | `"42px"` |
| `true` / `false` | `1` / `0` | `"true"` / `"false"` |
| `null` | `0` | `"null"` |
| `undefined` | `NaN` | `"undefined"` |
| `[]` | `0` (via `""`) | `""` |
| `[7]` | `7` (via `"7"`) | `"7"` |
| `[1, 2]` | `NaN` (via `"1,2"`) | `"1,2"` |
| `{}` | `NaN` (via `"[object Object]"`) | `"[object Object]"` |
| `-0` | `-0` | `"0"` |
| `Symbol()` | `TypeError` | `TypeError` (implicit) |

**ToPrimitive: how objects become primitives.** When an operator needs a primitive and receives an object, the engine:

```text
1. If obj[Symbol.toPrimitive] exists, call it with a hint ("number", "string" or "default").
2. Otherwise, with hint "string":         try obj.toString(), then obj.valueOf()
             with hint "number"/"default": try obj.valueOf(),  then obj.toString()
   The first one that returns a primitive wins. If neither does: TypeError.
```

For plain objects and arrays, `valueOf()` returns the object itself (not a primitive), so `toString()` is used. That is why arrays become comma-separated strings and plain objects become `"[object Object]"`. `Date` objects are the exception: with the `"default"` hint they prefer strings.

**The `+` operator.** `+` both adds numbers and concatenates strings, so it needs a rule to choose:

```text
a + b
  1. Convert both operands with ToPrimitive (hint "default").
  2. If either result is a string -> convert both to strings and concatenate.
  3. Otherwise                    -> convert both to numbers and add.
```

All other arithmetic operators (`-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `**`) always convert to numbers.

```javascript
console.log("5" + 2);       // "52": a string is present, so concatenation
console.log("5" - 2);       // 3: - always converts to numbers
console.log("5" * "2");     // 10
console.log(1 + true);      // 2: true -> 1
console.log(1 + null);      // 1: null -> 0
console.log(1 + undefined); // NaN
console.log([] + []);       // "": both arrays become ""
console.log([] + {});       // "[object Object]"
console.log([1, 2] + [3]);  // "1,23"
console.log(1 + 2 + "3");   // "33": evaluated left to right, (1 + 2) + "3"
console.log("1" + 2 + 3);   // "123"
```

**Relational comparison (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`).** After ToPrimitive, if *both* operands are strings, they are compared code unit by code unit. Otherwise both are converted to numbers.

```javascript
console.log("10" < "9");    // true: string comparison, "1" comes before "9"
console.log(10 < "9");      // false: numeric comparison, 10 < 9
console.log("a" < "b");     // true
console.log(null >= 0);     // true: null -> 0 for relational operators...
console.log(null == 0);     // false: ...but == has its own rule for null (see below)
```

**Strict equality (`===`).** Returns `true` only if both operands have the same type and the same value. There is no coercion. Two exceptions come from floating point: `NaN === NaN` is `false`, and `+0 === -0` is `true`. Objects are equal only if they are the *same* object (same reference).

**Loose equality (`==`).** If the types differ, `==` converts operands following this algorithm:

```text
x == y
  same type?                         -> compare like ===
  null == undefined (either order)   -> true    (and null/undefined equal nothing else)
  number == string                   -> ToNumber(string), compare again
  boolean == anything                -> ToNumber(boolean), compare again
  object == primitive                -> ToPrimitive(object), compare again
  bigint == number/string            -> compare mathematical values
  otherwise                          -> false
```

The boolean rule causes most surprises: booleans become numbers *before* anything else, so `x == true` does **not** mean "x is truthy".

| Expression | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `"" == 0` | `true` | `""` becomes `0` |
| `"0" == 0` | `true` | `"0"` becomes `0` |
| `"" == "0"` | `false` | Same type: different strings |
| `"0" == false` | `true` | `false` becomes `0`, then `"0"` becomes `0` |
| `"2" == true` | `false` | `true` becomes `1`, and `2 != 1`, although `"2"` is truthy |
| `[] == false` | `true` | `false` becomes `0`, `[]` becomes `""` then `0` |
| `[] == ![]` | `true` | `![]` is `false`, then as above |
| `null == 0` | `false` | `null` equals only `null` and `undefined` |
| `null == undefined` | `true` | Special rule |
| `NaN == NaN` | `false` | `NaN` equals nothing |
| `[1, 2] == "1,2"` | `true` | The array becomes `"1,2"` |
| `{} == {}` | `false` | Two different objects |

**Three equality algorithms.**

| Algorithm | Used by | `NaN` vs `NaN` | `+0` vs `-0` | Coerces types |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loose (`==`) | `==`, `!=` | `false` | `true` | Yes |
| Strict (`===`) | `===`, `!==`, `indexOf`, `switch` | `false` | `true` | No |
| SameValueZero | `includes`, `Map`, `Set` | `true` | `true` | No |
| SameValue | `Object.is` | `true` | `false` | No |

```javascript
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN));    // -1: indexOf uses ===
console.log([NaN].includes(NaN));   // true: includes uses SameValueZero
console.log(Object.is(-0, 0));      // false
```

**Recommended practice.** Use `===` and `!==` everywhere. Convert explicitly (`Number(input)`) when you need a different type. The one common exception is `x == null`, which concisely checks for both `null` and `undefined`, and which most style guides (including ESLint's `eqeqeq` with the `"null": "ignore"` option) allow.

**Key Takeaways**

- Operators coerce through a few internal operations: ToPrimitive, ToNumber, ToString and ToBoolean.
- `+` concatenates if either operand (after ToPrimitive) is a string. All other arithmetic operators convert to numbers.
- Relational operators compare strings lexically only when both operands are strings.
- `==` converts booleans to numbers first, treats `null` and `undefined` as equal only to each other, and converts objects to primitives. `===` never coerces.
- Use `===` by default, `== null` for "null or undefined", and `Object.is` or `includes` when `NaN` or `-0` matter.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Predict, then verify: `"3" * "4"`, `"3" + 4 + 5`, `3 + 4 + "5"`, `true + true`, `[] + 1`, `[2] * [3]`, `"b" + "a" + +"a" + "a"`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create an object `counter` whose `Symbol.toPrimitive` returns an incrementing number each time it is converted, so that `counter == 1 && counter == 2 && counter == 3` is `true`. Then explain why the same trick cannot make `counter === 1` true.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Walk me through how JavaScript evaluates `[] == ![]`." *Hint:* evaluate `![]` first using ToBoolean, then apply the `==` steps one at a time.

#### Truthy and Falsy Values

Conditions in JavaScript do not require booleans. You can write `if (user)`, `while (queue.length)` or `name || "Anonymous"` with any value, and the language decides whether that value counts as true or false. That decision is the ToBoolean conversion. Its rule is short, but a few entries in it (`0`, `""`, `NaN`) cause real bugs when they are valid data rather than "missing".

**The falsy list.** A value is **falsy** if ToBoolean converts it to `false`. There are exactly eight falsy values (nine with one legacy oddity). Every other value is **truthy**.

| Falsy value | Type |
|---|---|
| `false` | boolean |
| `0`, `-0` | number |
| `0n` | bigint |
| `""` (empty string) | string |
| `null` | null |
| `undefined` | undefined |
| `NaN` | number |
| `document.all` | Legacy browser object, deliberately falsy for old feature detection |

**Values that are truthy but look falsy.**

| Truthy value | Why it surprises people |
|---|---|
| `"0"`, `"false"`, `" "` | Non-empty strings are always truthy |
| `[]` | Every object is truthy, including empty arrays |
| `{}` | Also an object |
| `new Boolean(false)` | A wrapper object, so truthy (see Primitive Types and Wrapper Objects) |
| `-1`, `Infinity` | Only `0`, `-0` and `NaN` are falsy numbers |
| `function () {}` | Functions are objects |

**Where ToBoolean applies.** `if`, `else if`, `while`, `do...while`, `for` conditions, the ternary `? :`, `!`, `Boolean(x)`, and the left operand of `&&` and `||` (3.2). Note that `==` does *not* use ToBoolean. `if ("2")` runs, but `"2" == true` is `false` (see Type Coercion and Equality Rules).

**Example: idioms and the bugs they hide**

```javascript
// Concise existence checks: fine when falsy values can never be valid data
const el = document.querySelector("#menu");
if (el) el.classList.add("open");                 // el is an object or null

// Bug: 0 is valid data but falsy
function setVolume(level) {
  const volume = level || 50;                     // setVolume(0) gives 50!
  return volume;
}
console.log(setVolume(0));                        // 50: wrong

function setVolumeFixed(level) {
  const volume = level ?? 50;                     // only null/undefined fall back (3.2)
  return volume;
}
console.log(setVolumeFixed(0));                   // 0: correct

// Bug: an empty array is truthy
const results = [];
if (results) console.log("always runs");          // [] is truthy
if (results.length) console.log("never runs");    // 0 is falsy: correct check

// Empty object check
const filters = {};
console.log(Object.keys(filters).length === 0);   // true

// Filtering falsy entries from a list
console.log(["a", "", null, "b", undefined, 0].filter(Boolean)); // ["a", "b"]

// Converting to a real boolean, e.g. for an API that expects one
const hasDiscount = !!user?.coupon;               // true or false, never the coupon object
```

**Choosing the right check.**

| You want to know whether... | Write | Not |
|---|---|---|
| A value is present (not `null`/`undefined`) | `x != null` or `x ?? fallback` | `if (x)` when `0` or `""` is valid |
| A string is non-empty | `str.length > 0` or `str !== ""` | `if (str)` when `str` might be a non-string |
| An array has items | `arr.length > 0` | `if (arr)` |
| A number is a usable value | `Number.isFinite(n)` | `if (n)` |
| A value is exactly `true` | `x === true` | `x == true` |

**Key Takeaways**

- The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy.
- All objects are truthy, including `[]`, `{}` and `new Boolean(false)`. Non-empty strings like `"0"` and `"false"` are truthy too.
- Conditions, `!`, `&&`, `||` and the ternary use ToBoolean. `==` does not.
- Truthiness checks are fine for objects that may be `null`. For numbers and strings where `0` or `""` are valid, use `??` or explicit checks.
- Check arrays with `.length` and objects with `Object.keys(o).length`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a table with ten values of your choice and classify each as truthy or falsy. Verify with `Boolean(value)`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Find and fix the bug: `function paginate(items, page) { page = page || 1; ... }` should allow page `0` for a zero-based API, and `function label(n) { return n ? n + " items" : "none"; }` should print `"0 items"`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is `if ([])` true but `[] == false` also true?" *Hint:* one uses ToBoolean, the other uses the loose-equality algorithm, which converts both sides to numbers.

<a id="32-expressions-operators-and-control-flow"></a>
### 3.2 Expressions, Operators and Control Flow

This subchapter covers how JavaScript computes values with operators, how it decides which code to run with conditionals and loops, and the modern syntax for unpacking and spreading data.

#### Arithmetic, Logical and Comparison Operators

A program is built from **expressions** (pieces of code that produce a value, such as `price * qty` or `isAdmin && canEdit`) and **statements** (pieces of code that perform an action, such as `if`, `for` or a variable declaration). Operators are the building blocks of expressions. Most of them look familiar from other C-style languages, but several details are specific to JavaScript: `%` is a remainder rather than a modulo, `**` binds to the right, logical operators return operands rather than booleans, and some operator combinations are syntax errors without parentheses.

**Arithmetic operators.**

| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `+` | Addition or concatenation | `2 + 3` / `"2" + 3` | `5` / `"23"` |
| `-` | Subtraction | `7 - 10` | `-3` |
| `*` | Multiplication | `4 * 2.5` | `10` |
| `/` | Division (always floating point) | `7 / 2` | `3.5` |
| `%` | Remainder (sign follows the dividend) | `-7 % 3` | `-1` |
| `**` | Exponentiation (ES2016) | `2 ** 10` | `1024` |
| `++` / `--` | Increment and decrement | `i++`, `++i` | See below |
| unary `+` / `-` | Convert to number / negate | `+"42"` | `42` |

Division by zero does not throw: `1 / 0` is `Infinity` and `0 / 0` is `NaN` (see Numbers, BigInt and Numeric Precision).

```javascript
// % is a remainder: the result has the sign of the left operand
console.log(-7 % 3);                        // -1, not 2
const mod = (n, m) => ((n % m) + m) % m;    // true modulo, always in [0, m)
console.log(mod(-7, 3));                    // 2: useful for wrapping carousel indices

// ** is right-associative
console.log(2 ** 3 ** 2);                   // 512, i.e. 2 ** (3 ** 2)
// console.log(-2 ** 2);                    // SyntaxError: ambiguous, write (-2) ** 2

// Prefix vs postfix increment
let i = 5;
console.log(i++);                           // 5: returns the old value, then increments
console.log(++i);                           // 7: increments, then returns the new value
```

**Assignment operators.** Every arithmetic and bitwise operator has a compound form: `x += 2` means `x = x + 2`, and so on (`-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `**=`, `<<=`, `|=`, ...). The logical assignment operators `||=`, `&&=` and `??=` are covered in the next topic. Assignment is itself an expression whose value is the assigned value, which is why `a = b = 0` works (it is right-associative).

**Comparison operators.**

| Operator | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `===`, `!==` | Strict equality and inequality | No coercion (see Type Coercion and Equality Rules) |
| `==`, `!=` | Loose equality and inequality | Coerces types |
| `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` | Relational | Compares strings lexically only if both operands are strings |

Any comparison involving `NaN` returns `false`, including `NaN <= NaN`. Note that `a <= b` is not defined as `a < b || a == b`: it is defined as `!(b < a)` with special handling for `NaN`, which is why `null >= 0` is `true` while `null == 0` is `false`.

**Logical operators.** `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not). `!` always returns a boolean. `&&` and `||` return **one of their operands**, not necessarily a boolean, and they **short-circuit**. The next topic covers them in detail.

**Bitwise operators.** `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` (sign-propagating) and `>>>` (zero-fill) work on 32-bit signed integers. They are mainly used for flag sets, binary protocols, hashing and graphics.

```javascript
const READ = 0b001, WRITE = 0b010, EXEC = 0b100;  // permission flags
let perms = READ | WRITE;                          // combine: 0b011
console.log((perms & WRITE) !== 0);                // true: test a flag
perms &= ~WRITE;                                   // clear a flag: 0b001
console.log(perms.toString(2));                    // "1"
```

**Other operators.**

| Operator | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof x` | Type name as a string | `typeof 1` gives `"number"` |
| `x instanceof C` | Prototype chain check (Chapter 4) | `[] instanceof Array` |
| `key in obj` | Property existence, including inherited | `"length" in []` gives `true` |
| `delete obj.key` | Remove a property | Returns `true` on success |
| `void expr` | Evaluate, return `undefined` | `void 0` |
| `cond ? a : b` | Conditional (ternary) | `age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor"` |
| `a, b` | Comma: evaluate both, return `b` | Mostly in `for` headers |
| `new C()` | Create an instance (Chapter 4) | `new Date()` |

**Precedence and associativity.** When an expression contains several operators, **precedence** decides which binds tighter, and **associativity** decides the order for operators of equal precedence. An abridged table, from highest to lowest:

| Precedence | Operators | Associativity |
|---|---|---|
| Highest | `( )` grouping, `.`, `?.`, `[ ]`, `f()`, `new C()` | Left |
| | Postfix `x++`, `x--` | |
| | `!`, `~`, unary `+`/`-`, prefix `++`/`--`, `typeof`, `void`, `delete`, `await` | Right |
| | `**` | Right |
| | `*`, `/`, `%` | Left |
| | `+`, `-` | Left |
| | `<<`, `>>`, `>>>` | Left |
| | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `in`, `instanceof` | Left |
| | `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==` | Left |
| | `&`, then `^`, then `|` | Left |
| | `&&` | Left |
| | `||`, `??` | Left |
| | `? :` | Right |
| | `=`, `+=`, `&&=`, `??=`, ... , `=>`, `yield` | Right |
| Lowest | `,` | Left |

```javascript
console.log(1 + 2 * 3);          // 7: * binds tighter than +
console.log((1 + 2) * 3);        // 9
console.log(true || false && false); // true: && binds tighter, so true || (false && false)
console.log(typeof 1 + 1);       // "number1": typeof binds tighter than +
// a ?? b || c;                  // SyntaxError: ?? cannot be mixed with || or && without parentheses
```

When in doubt, add parentheses. They cost nothing and make intent explicit for the next reader.

**Key Takeaways**

- Expressions produce values; statements perform actions. Operators build expressions.
- `/` always produces a float, `%` is a remainder whose sign follows the dividend, and `**` is right-associative.
- `x++` returns the old value, `++x` the new one. Assignment is an expression that returns the assigned value.
- `&&` and `||` return one of their operands, not necessarily a boolean. Bitwise operators work on 32-bit integers.
- Precedence decides grouping. Use parentheses whenever it is not obvious, and they are mandatory when mixing `??` with `&&` or `||`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a function that converts a number of seconds into `"hh:mm:ss"` using only `/`, `%`, `Math.floor` and `padStart`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a permissions system with bit flags for `READ`, `WRITE`, `DELETE` and `ADMIN`, with functions `grant`, `revoke`, `has` and `list`. What is the maximum number of flags you can store this way, and why?
> 3. *(Interview)* "What do `typeof typeof 1` and `[] + null + 1` evaluate to?" *Hint:* evaluate from the inside out for the first one, and left to right with the `+` concatenation rule for the second.

#### Short-Circuit, Nullish Coalescing and Optional Chaining

Real data is full of gaps: optional configuration options, API responses with missing fields, DOM queries that find nothing. Code that handles these gaps used to be full of nested `if` statements and `obj && obj.a && obj.a.b` chains. JavaScript now has a compact set of operators for this job. To use them correctly, you need to understand short-circuit evaluation and the difference between "falsy" and "nullish".

**Short-circuit evaluation.** `&&` and `||` evaluate the left operand first and only evaluate the right one if it can still change the result. They return the value of whichever operand decided the result:

```text
a || b   ->  a is truthy?  return a (b is never evaluated)
             otherwise     return b

a && b   ->  a is falsy?   return a (b is never evaluated)
             otherwise     return b
```

```javascript
console.log("Ada" || "guest");   // "Ada"
console.log("" || "guest");      // "guest"
console.log(0 || null || "x");   // "x": returns the first truthy operand
console.log(1 && "yes");         // "yes": returns the last operand if all are truthy
console.log(null && "yes");      // null: returns the first falsy operand

// The right side is not evaluated at all
let calls = 0;
const count = () => ++calls;
false && count();
true || count();
console.log(calls);              // 0
```

Because evaluation stops early, `&&` is sometimes used as a compact "if": `isLoggedIn && showDashboard()`. It works, but a plain `if` statement is usually clearer for statements with side effects. In JSX (Chapter 14), `{items.length && <List />}` renders `0` when the list is empty, which is a well-known bug: use `items.length > 0 &&` instead.

**Nullish coalescing (`??`).** `||` falls back for *every* falsy value, so it wrongly replaces valid values such as `0`, `""` and `false`. The **nullish coalescing** operator `??` (ES2020) falls back only when the left side is `null` or `undefined` (the "nullish" values).

| Left value | `left || "default"` | `left ?? "default"` |
|---|---|---|
| `undefined` | `"default"` | `"default"` |
| `null` | `"default"` | `"default"` |
| `0` | `"default"` | `0` |
| `""` | `"default"` | `""` |
| `false` | `"default"` | `false` |
| `NaN` | `"default"` | `NaN` |
| `"value"` | `"value"` | `"value"` |

```javascript
function createSlider(options) {
  const min = options.min ?? 0;             // 0 if missing, but a passed 0 is kept as well
  const max = options.max ?? 100;
  const label = options.label ?? "Volume";  // "" is a valid (empty) label
  const animate = options.animate ?? true;  // false must not become true
  return { min, max, label, animate };
}
console.log(createSlider({ min: -10, animate: false, label: "" }));
// { min: -10, max: 100, label: "", animate: false }
```

`??` cannot be combined directly with `&&` or `||`: `a || b ?? c` is a `SyntaxError`. Write `(a || b) ?? c` to make the intended grouping explicit.

**Optional chaining (`?.`).** Accessing a property of `null` or `undefined` throws a `TypeError`. Optional chaining (ES2020) checks the value *before* the `?.`: if it is nullish, the whole expression stops and evaluates to `undefined` instead of throwing.

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `obj?.prop` | Property access |
| `obj?.[expr]` | Computed property access |
| `fn?.(args)` | Call only if `fn` is not nullish |
| `obj.method?.()` | Call the method only if it exists |

```javascript
const order = { customer: { address: null }, items: [] };

// Before ES2020
const cityOld = order && order.customer && order.customer.address && order.customer.address.city;

// With optional chaining
const city = order?.customer?.address?.city;   // undefined, no TypeError
console.log(city ?? "Unknown city");           // "Unknown city": ?. and ?? work well together

console.log(order.items?.[0]?.name);           // undefined
order.onShip?.();                              // not called, because onShip is undefined

// Short-circuit applies to the rest of the chain
const n = null;
console.log(n?.a.b.c);                         // undefined: .b.c is never evaluated
```

Optional chaining has limits. It cannot appear on the left of an assignment (`obj?.a = 1` is a `SyntaxError`). It only guards against `null` and `undefined`: if `obj.method` exists but is not a function, `obj.method?.()` still throws. And using `?.` everywhere hides real bugs: if `order` must always exist, write `order.customer` so that a missing order fails loudly where it happens.

**Logical assignment operators (ES2021).** These combine a logical operator with assignment, and they also short-circuit: if the condition is not met, **no assignment happens at all** (so setters are not triggered and frozen objects do not throw).

| Operator | Equivalent to | Assigns when the left side is... |
|---|---|---|
| `a ||= b` | `a || (a = b)` | Falsy |
| `a &&= b` | `a && (a = b)` | Truthy |
| `a ??= b` | `a ?? (a = b)` | `null` or `undefined` |

```javascript
const cache = {};
function getUser(id) {
  cache[id] ??= { id, loadedAt: Date.now() };  // create the entry only the first time
  return cache[id];
}

const opts = { retries: 0, timeout: undefined };
opts.retries ??= 3;    // stays 0: 0 is not nullish
opts.timeout ??= 5000; // becomes 5000

let token = "abc";
token &&= token.trim(); // transform only if present
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `&&` and `||` short-circuit and return the operand that decided the result, not necessarily a boolean.
- `||` replaces every falsy value. `??` replaces only `null` and `undefined`, so it is the correct choice for defaults when `0`, `""` or `false` are valid.
- `?.` stops a property access or call chain at a nullish value and returns `undefined`. It cannot be used as an assignment target.
- `||=`, `&&=` and `??=` assign only when needed, and skip the assignment entirely otherwise.
- `??` cannot be mixed with `&&` or `||` without parentheses. Do not use `?.` to hide values that should always exist.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite `const port = config && config.server && config.server.port ? config.server.port : 8080;` with `?.` and `??`. Test it with `port: 0`. Does the original handle that case correctly?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `memoize(fn)` helper for single-argument functions that uses a `Map` and `??=`-style logic. Explain why `cache[key] ||= fn(key)` would recompute results for keys whose result is `0` or `""`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `a || b` and `a ?? b`, and why does `a ?? b || c` throw a syntax error?" *Hint:* compare the sets of values that trigger the fallback, and consider why the language designers forced an explicit grouping.

#### Conditional Statements and switch

Programs need to choose between paths: show an error or a success message, apply a discount or not, route a request to the right handler. JavaScript offers `if...else`, the conditional operator `? :` and the `switch` statement for this. The choice between them is mostly about readability, but `switch` has two traps (fall-through and shared scope) that are worth learning in advance.

**`if`, `else if`, `else`.** The condition is converted with ToBoolean (see Truthy and Falsy Values). Always use braces, even for single statements: it prevents bugs when a second line is added later.

```javascript
function shippingCost(country, total) {
  if (total >= 100) {
    return 0;                      // free shipping over 100
  } else if (country === "IT") {
    return 5;
  } else if (["FR", "DE", "ES"].includes(country)) {
    return 9;
  } else {
    return 20;
  }
}
```

**Guard clauses.** Deeply nested `if` blocks are hard to follow. Handle the special and error cases first, return early, and leave the main logic unindented.

```javascript
// Nested
function publish(post, user) {
  if (post) {
    if (user.canPublish) {
      if (!post.published) {
        post.published = true;
        return "published";
      } else return "already published";
    } else return "forbidden";
  } else return "no post";
}

// Guard clauses: same logic, flat structure
function publishFlat(post, user) {
  if (!post) return "no post";
  if (!user.canPublish) return "forbidden";
  if (post.published) return "already published";

  post.published = true;           // the "happy path" reads top to bottom
  return "published";
}
```

**The conditional (ternary) operator.** `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` is an *expression*, so it can appear where `if` cannot: in a variable initialiser, a template literal, an argument or a return value.

```javascript
const label = count === 1 ? "item" : "items";
const cls = `btn ${isPrimary ? "btn-primary" : "btn-secondary"}`;
```

Nested ternaries quickly become unreadable. If you need more than one level, use `if` statements or a lookup table.

**`switch`.** `switch` compares one value against several cases using **strict equality** (`===`). Execution jumps to the first matching `case` and continues *until a `break`* (or `return`, or `throw`), even through the following cases. This **fall-through** is occasionally useful for grouping cases, and frequently a bug.

```javascript
function httpCategory(status) {
  switch (Math.floor(status / 100)) {
    case 2:
      return "success";
    case 3:
      return "redirect";
    case 4:
    case 5:                        // grouped cases: intentional fall-through
      return "error";
    default:                       // runs when nothing matches; can be anywhere, usually last
      return "unknown";
  }
}

function describe(day) {
  let kind;
  switch (day) {
    case "sat":
      kind = "weekend";            // BUG: missing break, falls through to the next case
    case "mon":
      kind = "weekday";
      break;
  }
  return kind;
}
console.log(describe("sat"));      // "weekday"
```

**Scope inside `switch`.** All `case` clauses share a single block scope, so declaring the same `let` or `const` in two cases is a `SyntaxError`, and a declaration in one case is in its TDZ in the others. Wrap each case body in braces to give it its own scope.

```javascript
switch (action.type) {
  case "add": {                    // braces create a block per case
    const item = action.payload;
    cart.push(item);
    break;
  }
  case "remove": {
    const item = action.payload;   // no clash with the declaration above
    cart = cart.filter((x) => x.id !== item.id);
    break;
  }
}
```

**`switch (true)`.** Since cases can be any expression, `switch (true)` matches the first case expression that evaluates to exactly `true`. It works but surprises many readers; an `if...else if` chain is usually clearer.

**Lookup tables.** When each branch only maps an input to a value or a function, an object or a `Map` is shorter than `switch` and can be extended or passed around as data.

```javascript
const handlers = {
  add: (cart, item) => [...cart, item],
  remove: (cart, item) => cart.filter((x) => x.id !== item.id),
  clear: () => [],
};

function reducer(cart, action) {
  const handler = Object.hasOwn(handlers, action.type) ? handlers[action.type] : null;
  return handler ? handler(cart, action.payload) : cart;   // unknown actions leave cart unchanged
}
```

`Object.hasOwn` matters here: without it, `action.type === "toString"` would find the inherited `Object.prototype.toString`.

**Choosing a construct.**

| Situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| One or two conditions, or conditions on different variables | `if` / `else if` |
| Choosing between two values in an expression | Ternary |
| Many discrete values of one variable, with statements in each branch | `switch` with `break` (or `return`) in every case |
| Pure mapping from a key to a value or function | Object or `Map` lookup table |
| Validation and error cases before the main logic | Guard clauses with early `return` |

**Key Takeaways**

- `if` uses truthiness. Always use braces, and prefer guard clauses with early returns over deep nesting.
- The ternary operator is an expression. Keep it to one level.
- `switch` uses `===` and falls through until `break`, `return` or `throw`. Every non-empty case needs one of them unless fall-through is intentional and commented.
- All `case` clauses share one scope. Wrap case bodies in `{ }` when they declare variables.
- For pure key-to-value or key-to-function mapping, a lookup object or `Map` is often cleaner than `switch`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `grade(score)` that returns `"A"` to `"F"` for scores from 0 to 100, first with `if...else if`, then with guard clauses that reject non-numbers and out-of-range values.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Convert a 6-case `switch` that maps keyboard keys (`"ArrowUp"`, `"w"`, ...) to movement vectors into a lookup table. Handle unknown keys and make sure that a key named `"constructor"` does not match anything.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What does this print, and why: `switch ('1') { case 1: console.log('number'); case '1': console.log('string'); default: console.log('default'); }`?" *Hint:* think about the comparison algorithm `switch` uses and what happens after a match without `break`.

#### Loops and Iteration Statements

Repeating work over a range of numbers, the items of a list or the keys of an object is one of the most common tasks in any program. JavaScript has five loop statements plus array iteration methods, and they are not interchangeable. In particular, `for...in` and `for...of` look almost identical but iterate over completely different things, and choosing the wrong one is a classic bug.

**The loop statements.**

| Loop | Iterates over | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `for (init; cond; step)` | A counter you control | Index ranges, stepping backwards or by 2, early exit |
| `while (cond)` | Until the condition becomes false | Unknown number of iterations, such as reading until a queue is empty |
| `do { } while (cond)` | Same, but the body runs at least once | Retry and prompt loops |
| `for (const v of iterable)` | **Values** of an iterable | Arrays, strings, `Map`, `Set`, `NodeList`, generators |
| `for (const k in object)` | **Enumerable string keys**, including inherited ones | Plain objects (with care) |
| `array.forEach(fn)` | Array elements via a callback | Side effects per element; cannot `break` |

```javascript
// Classic for: full control over the index
for (let i = 10; i > 0; i -= 2) console.log(i);  // 10 8 6 4 2

// while: unknown number of iterations
const queue = ["a", "b", "c"];
while (queue.length > 0) {
  const job = queue.shift();
  console.log("processing", job);
}

// do...while: body runs at least once
let attempt = 0;
do {
  attempt++;
} while (attempt < 3 && Math.random() < 0.5);
```

**`for...of` versus `for...in`.**

```javascript
const colours = ["red", "green"];
colours.extra = "oops";                       // a non-index property on the array

for (const c of colours) console.log(c);      // "red", "green": values of the iterable
for (const k in colours) console.log(k);      // "0", "1", "extra": string keys, extra included!

for (const ch of "hi") console.log(ch);       // "h", "i"

const prices = { apple: 1.2, pear: 0.9 };
// for (const p of prices) {}                 // TypeError: prices is not iterable
for (const [fruit, price] of Object.entries(prices)) {
  console.log(`${fruit}: ${price}`);          // iterate a plain object via entries
}

const scores = new Map([["ada", 10], ["linus", 7]]);
for (const [name, score] of scores) console.log(name, score);  // Maps yield [key, value]
```

```text
                for...in                         for...of
works on        any object                       iterables (Symbol.iterator, see 3.3)
yields          keys (always strings)            values
inherited       yes, enumerable inherited keys   n/a
on arrays       indices as "0", "1" + extras     elements, in order
on objects      own + inherited keys             TypeError (use Object.keys/values/entries)
```

Use `for...of` for arrays and other iterables. Use `Object.keys`, `Object.values` or `Object.entries` with `for...of` for plain objects; they return only own enumerable keys. Reserve `for...in` for the rare cases where you want inherited keys too.

**`break`, `continue` and labels.** `break` exits the innermost loop (or `switch`), and `continue` skips to the next iteration. To break out of an outer loop from an inner one, label the outer loop.

```javascript
const grid = [
  [1, 2, 3],
  [4, -1, 6],
  [7, 8, 9],
];

let found = null;
search: for (let r = 0; r < grid.length; r++) {     // label the outer loop
  for (let c = 0; c < grid[r].length; c++) {
    if (grid[r][c] < 0) {
      found = { r, c };
      break search;                                  // exits both loops
    }
  }
}
console.log(found);                                  // { r: 1, c: 1 }
```

If you find yourself using labels often, extracting the inner logic into a function and using `return` is usually more readable.

**Loops and array methods.** Arrays have iteration methods (`forEach`, `map`, `filter`, `find`, `some`, `every`, `reduce`, covered in Chapter 4) that express intent better than a loop when you are transforming or querying data. Loops remain the right tool when you need `break`, `await` inside the body in sequence, or complex control flow. Note that `return` inside a `forEach` callback only ends that callback, not the iteration, and `break` is a syntax error there.

**Common pitfalls.**

| Pitfall | Example | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Off-by-one | `i <= arr.length` | Use `<`, or `for...of` |
| Modifying an array while iterating it | `splice` inside `for` over the same array | Iterate backwards, or build a new array with `filter` |
| Infinite loop | Forgetting to update the condition variable | Update it in one obvious place |
| Callbacks capturing `var` | `var i` with `setTimeout` | Use `let` (see var, let and const) |
| Re-reading an expensive length | `i < getItems().length` | Compute once before the loop |
| `for...in` on arrays | Inherited or extra keys, string indices | Use `for...of` |

`for await...of`, which iterates over asynchronous data sources, is covered in Chapter 5.

**Key Takeaways**

- `for` gives full control of a counter; `while` and `do...while` loop until a condition changes; `do...while` always runs once.
- `for...of` iterates the **values** of iterables. `for...in` iterates **string keys** of any object, including inherited ones. Do not use `for...in` on arrays.
- Iterate plain objects with `Object.keys`, `Object.values` or `Object.entries` combined with `for...of`.
- `break` and `continue` affect the innermost loop. Labels let you target an outer loop.
- `forEach` cannot be stopped with `break`. Use a loop or `some`/`find` when you need early exit.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Print a multiplication table from 1 to 10 using nested `for` loops, then print only the rows for odd numbers using `continue`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Given `const inventory = { apples: 3, pears: 0, plums: 7 }`, log every fruit with a quantity above zero in three ways: `for...in` with `Object.hasOwn`, `Object.entries` with `for...of`, and `Object.entries` with `filter` and `forEach`. Explain why the first version needs `Object.hasOwn`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `for...in` and `for...of`?" *Hint:* compare what each one iterates (keys or values), which objects each works on, and how each treats inherited properties.

#### Destructuring Assignment

Code often needs to pull several values out of an object or array into separate variables: the `x` and `y` of a point, the `status` and `data` of a response, the first and second elements of a pair. Writing `const status = res.status; const data = res.data;` is repetitive. **Destructuring** (ES2015) lets you write a pattern that mirrors the shape of the data on the left of an assignment, and JavaScript fills in the variables.

```text
const { name, age } = { name: "Ada", age: 36, city: "London" };
        \_________/
        pattern mirrors the object shape -> name = "Ada", age = 36

const [first, second] = ["red", "green", "blue"];
       \___________/
       pattern mirrors the array positions -> first = "red", second = "green"
```

**Array destructuring.** Elements are matched by **position**. It works on any iterable, not just arrays.

```javascript
const rgb = [255, 128, 0];
const [r, g, b] = rgb;                     // r = 255, g = 128, b = 0

const [, second] = rgb;                    // skip elements with empty slots: second = 128
const [head, ...tail] = rgb;               // rest element: head = 255, tail = [128, 0]
const [x = 0, y = 0, z = 0, w = 1] = rgb;  // defaults for missing positions: w = 1

let a = 1, c = 2;
[a, c] = [c, a];                           // swap without a temporary variable

const [firstChar] = "hello";               // strings are iterable: "h"
const [[k, v]] = new Map([["id", 7]]);     // nested pattern on a Map: k = "id", v = 7
```

**Object destructuring.** Properties are matched by **name**, in any order.

```javascript
const response = {
  status: 200,
  data: { user: { id: 7, name: "Ada" }, tags: ["admin"] },
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
};

const { status } = response;                          // status = 200
const { status: code } = response;                    // rename: code = 200 (no "status" variable)
const { timeout = 3000 } = response;                  // default: timeout = 3000
const { retries: maxRetries = 2 } = response;         // rename and default together

const { data: { user: { name } } } = response;        // nested: name = "Ada" ("data" is not a variable)
const { data: { tags: [firstTag] } } = response;      // mixed object and array patterns: "admin"
const { headers: { "content-type": contentType } } = response; // non-identifier keys need renaming

const key = "status";
const { [key]: dynamic } = response;                  // computed key: dynamic = 200

const { headers, ...rest } = response;                // rest: rest = { status, data }
```

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `{ a }` | Variable `a` from property `a` |
| `{ a: b }` | Variable `b` from property `a` ("property: target") |
| `{ a = 1 }` | Default if `a` is `undefined` |
| `{ a: b = 1 }` | Rename and default |
| `{ a: { b } }` | Nested: variable `b` from `a.b` |
| `{ [expr]: v }` | Computed property name |
| `{ ...rest }` | Remaining own enumerable properties (must be last) |

**Rules and pitfalls.**

- Defaults apply only when the value is `undefined`, not `null` (see Booleans, null and undefined).
- Destructuring `null` or `undefined` throws: `const { a } = null` is a `TypeError`. Nested patterns throw if an intermediate level is missing, so give intermediate levels defaults: `const { data: { user } = {} } = res`.
- When assigning to **existing** variables with an object pattern, wrap the statement in parentheses. Otherwise the `{` is parsed as the start of a block: `({ a, b } = obj);`.
- A line that starts with `[` or `(` can be joined to the previous line if that line has no semicolon. `[a, c] = [c, a]` after a line without `;` is a common ASI bug.

**Destructuring function parameters.** This is the most common use of destructuring in modern code. It gives functions **named, optional arguments** with defaults, and makes the expected shape visible in the signature.

```javascript
function createUser({ name, role = "viewer", active = true } = {}) {   // "= {}" allows createUser()
  return { name, role, active };
}

console.log(createUser({ name: "Ada", role: "admin" }));  // { name: "Ada", role: "admin", active: true }
console.log(createUser());                                // { name: undefined, role: "viewer", active: true }

// Arrays of pairs from Object.entries or Map, destructured in the loop header
const stock = { apples: 3, pears: 0 };
for (const [fruit, qty] of Object.entries(stock)) {
  console.log(fruit, qty);
}

// Callbacks
const users = [{ id: 1, name: "Ada" }, { id: 2, name: "Linus" }];
console.log(users.map(({ name }) => name));               // ["Ada", "Linus"]

// Functions that "return multiple values"
function minMax(nums) {
  return [Math.min(...nums), Math.max(...nums)];
}
const [lo, hi] = minMax([4, 9, 1]);                       // lo = 1, hi = 9
```

Return an array when the values have an obvious order (like React's `useState` returning `[value, setValue]`) and an object when they are better identified by name.

**Key Takeaways**

- Array destructuring matches by position and works on any iterable. Object destructuring matches by property name.
- `{ a: b }` renames: the left side is the property, the right side is the variable. Defaults use `=` and apply only to `undefined`.
- Rest patterns (`...rest`) collect the remaining elements or properties and must come last.
- Destructuring `null` or `undefined` throws. Give parameters and nested levels a default of `{}` where data may be missing.
- Parameter destructuring gives functions named, optional arguments with defaults.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Given `const movie = { title: "Alien", year: 1979, ratings: [8.5, 9.1] }`, extract `title`, `year` renamed to `released`, and the first rating, all in one statement.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `formatAddress({ street, city, zip, country = "Italy" } = {})` that returns a formatted multi-line string. Make it safe to call with no argument, with `null` values for some fields, and with a nested `geo: { lat, lng }` object that may be missing.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `{ a, b } = obj;` throw a syntax error while `const { a, b } = obj;` works?" *Hint:* think about how the parser interprets a `{` at the start of a statement.

#### Spread and Rest Syntax

Combining arrays, copying objects, passing a list of values to a function, and accepting any number of arguments are everyday tasks. Before ES2015 they needed `concat`, `apply`, `Object.assign` and the `arguments` object. The `...` syntax replaces all of them. The same three dots do two opposite jobs depending on where they appear: **spread** expands a collection into individual elements, and **rest** collects individual elements into a collection.

```text
SPREAD: expands (on the right side, in calls and literals)
   [...[1, 2], 3]           ->  [1, 2, 3]
   f(...[1, 2])             ->  f(1, 2)
   { ...{ a: 1 }, b: 2 }    ->  { a: 1, b: 2 }

REST: collects (on the left side, in parameters and patterns)
```
