**The ES2023 "change by copy" methods.** `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with` are non-mutating twins of the classic mutating methods. They make immutable updates read naturally:

```javascript
const scores = [42, 7, 19];

const ranked = scores.toSorted((a, b) => b - a);   // [42, 19, 7]
const fixed  = scores.with(1, 8);                  // [42, 8, 19]
const noMid  = scores.toSpliced(1, 1);             // [42, 19]

console.log(scores);                               // [42, 7, 19]: never changed

// Before ES2023, the equivalent required copying first:
const rankedOld = [...scores].sort((a, b) => b - a);
```

**A bug from mutation.** A function that sorts its input changes the caller's data:

```javascript
function topThree(items) {
  return items.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score).slice(0, 3);  // sort mutates items!
}

const players = [{ n: "A", score: 1 }, { n: "B", score: 3 }, { n: "C", score: 2 }];
topThree(players);
console.log(players.map((p) => p.n));   // ["B", "C", "A"]: the caller's order was destroyed

function topThreeSafe(items) {
  return items.toSorted((a, b) => b.score - a.score).slice(0, 3);   // input untouched
}
```

**Choosing a family.** Mutation is fine, and slightly faster, for arrays that a single function creates and owns, such as a local result being built with `push`. Prefer non-mutating methods for data that is shared, passed in from outside, or held in framework state.

**Key Takeaways**

- Mutating methods: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`, `fill`, `copyWithin`, and index assignment.
- Non-mutating methods: `slice`, `concat`, `map`, `filter`, `flat`, `flatMap`, and the ES2023 `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with`.
- `slice` copies a range. `splice` removes and inserts in place and returns the removed elements.
- `sort` and `reverse` mutate and return the same array. Use `toSorted` and `toReversed` for copies.
- Never mutate arrays you do not own (function parameters, shared state).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Starting from `const q = [1, 2, 3]`, use mutating methods to implement a queue (add at the end, remove from the front) and a stack (add and remove at the end). Print the return value of each call.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement `insertAt(arr, index, item)`, `removeAt(arr, index)` and `move(arr, from, to)` without mutating `arr`, first using only `slice` and spread, then using `toSpliced`. Freeze the input in your tests to prove it is never modified.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What does `[3, 1, 2].sort().reverse()` return, and how many arrays are created along the way?" *Hint:* check what `sort` and `reverse` return, and compare it with what `toSorted().toReversed()` would do.

#### Iteration Methods: map, filter and reduce

Most work on arrays follows a handful of shapes: do something with each item, transform each item, keep the items that match, combine all items into one value, or ask whether any or all items satisfy a condition. You could write each of these as a `for` loop (3.2), but then every loop looks the same and the reader has to decode the body to find out which shape it is. Array iteration methods name the shape. They are higher-order functions (3.3): you pass a callback, and the method takes care of the looping.

**The callback signature.** Every iteration method calls your callback with three arguments: `(element, index, array)`. Most callbacks use only the first.

**The core methods.**

| Method | Callback returns | Method returns | Use it to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `forEach(fn)` | Ignored | `undefined` | Run a side effect for each element |
| `map(fn)` | New value | New array of the same length | Transform each element |
| `filter(fn)` | Truthy or falsy | New array with matching elements | Select elements |
| `reduce(fn, init)` | New accumulator | Final accumulator | Combine elements into one value |
| `some(fn)` | Truthy or falsy | `true` if any element matches (stops early) | "Is there at least one...?" |
| `every(fn)` | Truthy or falsy | `true` if all elements match (stops early) | "Are all...?" |

```javascript
const orders = [
  { id: 1, customer: "Ada",   total: 120, paid: true },
  { id: 2, customer: "Linus", total: 80,  paid: false },
  { id: 3, customer: "Ada",   total: 45,  paid: true },
];

const totals = orders.map((o) => o.total);                    // [120, 80, 45]
const unpaid = orders.filter((o) => !o.paid);                 // [{ id: 2, ... }]
const revenue = orders.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0);  // 245
const anyUnpaid = orders.some((o) => !o.paid);                // true
const allLarge = orders.every((o) => o.total > 50);           // false

orders.forEach((o, i) => console.log(`#${i + 1}: order ${o.id}`));
```

**Chaining into a pipeline.** Because `map` and `filter` return arrays, calls can be chained. Each step reads as one sentence of the algorithm.

```text
orders --filter(paid)--> [order 1, order 3] --map(total)--> [120, 45] --reduce(+)--> 165
```

```javascript
const paidRevenue = orders
  .filter((o) => o.paid)                 // keep paid orders
  .map((o) => o.total)                   // keep only their totals
  .reduce((sum, t) => sum + t, 0);       // add them up
console.log(paidRevenue);                // 165
```

**How `reduce` works.** `reduce` carries an **accumulator** through the array. The callback receives the current accumulator and the current element, and returns the next accumulator. The second argument of `reduce` is the starting accumulator.

```text
[120, 80, 45].reduce((sum, t) => sum + t, 0)

 step   sum (in)   t     returns
  1        0      120      120
  2      120       80      200
  3      200       45      245   <- result
```

Always pass the initial value. Without it, `reduce` uses the first element as the accumulator and starts at the second. That breaks when the accumulator should have a different type than the elements, and calling it on an empty array throws a `TypeError`.

```javascript
// [].reduce((a, b) => a + b);          // TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value
console.log([].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)); // 0

// Grouping: the accumulator is an object, not a number
const byCustomer = orders.reduce((groups, o) => {
  (groups[o.customer] ??= []).push(o);   // create the bucket on first use (3.2)
  return groups;                         // always return the accumulator!
}, {});
console.log(Object.keys(byCustomer));    // ["Ada", "Linus"]

// ES2024 has a built-in for this exact task
const grouped = Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.customer);
```

**Pitfalls.**

```javascript
// 1. map passes (element, index, array): functions with optional parameters misbehave
console.log(["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt));          // [1, NaN, NaN]: parseInt("2", 1), parseInt("3", 2)
console.log(["1", "2", "3"].map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))); // [1, 2, 3]

// 2. forEach cannot be stopped with break, and return only ends the current callback
[1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => { if (n === 2) return; console.log(n); }); // logs 1 and 3

// 3. Using map only for side effects creates a useless array: use forEach or for...of
// 4. Async callbacks: forEach does not wait for promises (Chapter 5)
```

**Choosing between methods and loops.** Iteration methods are clearer for transforming and querying data. A `for...of` loop is better when you need `break`, `continue`, `await` in sequence, or very hot loops where creating intermediate arrays matters.

**Key Takeaways**

- Iteration methods call `fn(element, index, array)` for each element and name the intent: `map` transforms, `filter` selects, `reduce` combines, `some` and `every` test.
- `map` and `filter` return new arrays and can be chained into readable pipelines.
- Always give `reduce` an initial value, and always return the accumulator from its callback.
- `Object.groupBy` and `Map.groupBy` (ES2024) replace hand-written grouping reducers.
- Watch for callbacks with extra optional parameters (`parseInt`) and for `forEach` not supporting `break` or `await`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Given an array of products with `name`, `price` and `inStock`, produce the names of in-stock products costing less than 50, sorted alphabetically, using one chained expression.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement your own `myMap`, `myFilter` and `myReduce` as plain functions that take an array and a callback. Match the built-in behaviour for the callback arguments, the missing initial value case (including the `TypeError` for empty arrays), and holes.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Can every array method be implemented with `reduce`? Show `map` and `filter` in terms of `reduce`, and explain when you would *not* use `reduce`." *Hint:* the accumulator can be an array. Think about readability and about operations that need to stop early.

#### Searching, Sorting and Flattening

Beyond transforming data, applications constantly ask questions of arrays: "is this tag already selected?", "which user has this ID?", "show the products ordered by price", "turn these nested lists into one list". JavaScript provides specialised methods for each of these. They are clearer and often faster than a general-purpose `filter` or `reduce`, and some of them have surprising default behaviour that you need to know.

**Searching.**

| Method | Returns | Comparison | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `includes(value)` | `true` / `false` | SameValueZero (`NaN` matches `NaN`) | Best for "is it present?" |
| `indexOf(value)` / `lastIndexOf(value)` | Index or `-1` | Strict equality `===` | Cannot find `NaN` |
| `find(fn)` / `findLast(fn)` | First / last matching element, or `undefined` | Your predicate | `findLast` is ES2023 |
| `findIndex(fn)` / `findLastIndex(fn)` | Index of the match, or `-1` | Your predicate | |

```javascript
const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Ada", role: "admin" },
  { id: 2, name: "Linus", role: "user" },
  { id: 3, name: "Grace", role: "admin" },
];

console.log(users.find((u) => u.id === 2)?.name);          // "Linus"
console.log(users.findLast((u) => u.role === "admin").name); // "Grace": searches from the end
console.log(users.findIndex((u) => u.name === "Bob"));       // -1: not found

console.log(["a", "b"].includes("b"));    // true
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN));          // -1: NaN !== NaN
console.log([NaN].includes(NaN));         // true

const target = { id: 1 };
console.log([{ id: 1 }].includes(target)); // false: objects are compared by reference
```

To search for an object by its contents, use `find` or `some` with a predicate. If you repeatedly look up items by key in a large array, build a `Map` once (see Map, Set, WeakMap and WeakSet) instead of scanning with `find` each time.

**Sorting: the default comparison is textual.** `sort()` without arguments converts elements to strings and compares them by UTF-16 code units. That is correct for simple ASCII strings and wrong for numbers.

```javascript
console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort());         // [1, 10, 100, 9]: compared as "1" < "10" < "100" < "9"
console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort((a, b) => a - b)); // [1, 9, 10, 100]
```

**The comparator contract.** A comparator `(a, b)` returns a negative number if `a` should come first, a positive number if `b` should come first, and `0` if their order does not matter. Since ES2019 sorting is **stable**: elements that compare equal keep their original relative order. Stability is what makes multi-key sorting work.

```javascript
const people = [
  { name: "Émile", age: 30 },
  { name: "ada", age: 25 },
  { name: "Zoe", age: 30 },
];

// Numbers: subtract
people.toSorted((a, b) => a.age - b.age);

// Strings: localeCompare handles case and accents correctly for a language
people.toSorted((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name, "en", { sensitivity: "base" }));
// ada, Émile, Zoe   (plain < comparison would give "Zoe", "ada", "Émile")

// Several keys: age descending, then name ascending
people.toSorted((a, b) => b.age - a.age || a.name.localeCompare(b.name));
// || falls through to the next key only when the first comparison returns 0

// Many comparisons on large arrays: reuse a collator, it is faster than localeCompare
const collator = new Intl.Collator("de", { numeric: true });
["file10", "file2", "file1"].sort(collator.compare);  // ["file1", "file2", "file10"]
```

Remember that `sort` mutates (see Mutating vs Non-Mutating Methods). Use `toSorted` when the array is shared.

**Flattening.** Nested arrays appear when each item produces several results: the tags of each post, the rows of each page. `flat(depth)` concatenates sub-arrays into the parent, one level deep by default. `flatMap(fn)` maps and then flattens one level, which also lets a callback return an empty array to drop an element.

```javascript
const nested = [1, [2, 3], [4, [5, [6]]]];
console.log(nested.flat());          // [1, 2, 3, 4, [5, [6]]]
console.log(nested.flat(Infinity));  // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]: flatten every level

const posts = [
  { title: "A", tags: ["js", "web"] },
  { title: "B", tags: ["css"] },
];
const allTags = posts.flatMap((p) => p.tags);        // ["js", "web", "css"]

// flatMap as map + filter in one pass: return [] to skip, [x] to keep
const parsed = ["1", "x", "3"].flatMap((s) => {
  const n = Number(s);
  return Number.isNaN(n) ? [] : [n];
});
console.log(parsed);                                 // [1, 3]
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Use `includes` for presence (it finds `NaN`), `find` and `findIndex` for predicates, and `findLast` to search from the end.
- `indexOf` and `includes` compare objects by reference. Use a predicate to match by content.
- Default `sort()` compares strings, so it misorders numbers. Always pass a comparator.
- Comparators return negative, zero or positive. Sorting is stable, so `||` chains several keys.
- Use `localeCompare` or `Intl.Collator` for human-readable text, and `flat` or `flatMap` to collapse nested arrays.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Sort `[5, 25, 100, 1]` ascending and descending with comparators, and sort `["banana", "Apple", "cherry"]` case-insensitively.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Given a list of employees with `department`, `salary` and `name`, produce a list sorted by department (A to Z), then salary (highest first), then name. Then write `binarySearch(sortedNumbers, target)` that returns the index or `-1`, and compare its speed with `indexOf` on an array of one million numbers.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `[1, 2, 10].sort()` return `[1, 10, 2]`, and why must a comparator return a number instead of a boolean such as `a > b`?" *Hint:* read what the default comparison converts elements to, and consider what the sort algorithm learns when the comparator returns `false`, which converts to `0`.

#### Array-Like Objects and Conversion

Some values look like arrays but are not. The DOM method `document.querySelectorAll` returns a `NodeList`, the old `arguments` object inside functions has indexed elements and a `length`, and strings can be indexed by position. You can read their elements by index, yet calling `map` on many of them fails. Knowing the difference between an *array*, an *array-like* and an *iterable*, and how to convert between them, is a daily need in browser code.

**Three different capabilities.**

| Concept | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Array** | A real `Array`, with all array methods | `[1, 2]`, `Array.from(x)` |
| **Array-like** | Any object with a numeric `length` and index keys `0..length-1` | `arguments`, `NodeList`, `HTMLCollection`, strings, `{ 0: "a", length: 1 }` |
| **Iterable** | Any object with a `[Symbol.iterator]` method, usable with `for...of` and spread (3.3) | Arrays, strings, `Map`, `Set`, `NodeList`, generators |

These overlap but are not the same. A `NodeList` is both array-like and iterable. `{ length: 2 }` is array-like but not iterable. A `Set` is iterable but not array-like (no index access).

```text
  iterable only          iterable AND array-like            array-like only
+---------------+   +-------------------------------+   +----------------------+
| Map, Set,     |   | Array, string, arguments,     |   | { 0: "a", length: 1 }|
| generators    |   | NodeList, HTMLCollection,     |   | (hand-made objects)  |
|               |   | typed arrays                  |   |                      |
+---------------+   +-------------------------------+   +----------------------+
 for...of, spread        everything works               indices + length only:
 work; no [i] access                                    no for...of, no spread
```

**Converting to a real array.**

| Technique | Works on | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Array.from(x)` | Iterables **and** array-likes | Most general. Optional second argument maps each element. |
| `[...x]` | Iterables only | Throws `TypeError` for non-iterable array-likes |
| `Array.prototype.slice.call(x)` | Array-likes | Legacy (pre-ES2015) idiom using method borrowing (4.4) |

```javascript
function legacySum() {
  // arguments is array-like: it has indices and length but no reduce
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
console.log(legacySum(1, 2, 3));                    // 6 (prefer rest parameters, 3.3)

const arrayLike = { 0: "a", 1: "b", length: 2 };
console.log(Array.from(arrayLike));                 // ["a", "b"]
// console.log([...arrayLike]);                     // TypeError: arrayLike is not iterable

console.log(Array.from({ length: 3 }));             // [undefined, undefined, undefined]
console.log(Array.from("abc", (c) => c.toUpperCase())); // ["A", "B", "C"]: map while converting
```

**DOM collections.** `querySelectorAll` returns a **static** `NodeList`, a snapshot that supports `forEach` but not `map` or `filter`. Properties such as `element.children` and `getElementsByClassName` return a **live** `HTMLCollection`, which updates automatically when the document changes (Chapter 6). Convert to an array before transforming, and especially before removing elements while iterating over a live collection.

```javascript
const links = document.querySelectorAll("a");                // static NodeList
const external = Array.from(links)
  .filter((a) => a.hostname !== location.hostname)
  .map((a) => a.href);

const items = document.getElementsByClassName("item");       // live HTMLCollection
for (const el of [...items]) el.classList.remove("item");    // iterate over a snapshot copy
// Iterating `items` directly would skip elements, because each removal shrinks the live collection
```

**Strings and Unicode.** Strings are array-like by UTF-16 code unit, but iterable by code point. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (many emoji and some CJK characters) take two code units, so the two conversions give different results (3.1).

```javascript
const s = "a\u{1F600}b";                           // "a", one emoji, "b"
console.log(s.length);                             // 4: the emoji is two UTF-16 code units
console.log(Array.prototype.slice.call(s).length); // 4: array-like view splits the pair
console.log([...s].length);                        // 3: iteration yields whole code points
console.log(Array.from(s).length);                 // 3: Array.from prefers the iterator
```

**Calling array methods directly.** Many array methods are intentionally generic: they work on any array-like `this`. You can borrow them without converting (see Method Borrowing and Mixins):

```javascript
const upper = Array.prototype.map.call("hey", (c) => c.toUpperCase()); // ["H", "E", "Y"]
```

**Key Takeaways**

- An array-like has `length` and index keys. An iterable has `[Symbol.iterator]`. A real array is both and has every array method.
- `Array.from` converts both array-likes and iterables, and can map at the same time. Spread works only on iterables.
- `querySelectorAll` returns a static `NodeList`. `children` and `getElementsBy*` return live collections, so iterate over a copy when modifying the DOM.
- Converting a string by iteration (`[...s]`, `Array.from`) keeps code points together. Index-based access splits surrogate pairs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On any web page, use `querySelectorAll("h2")` and `Array.from` to produce an array of heading texts, then print how many headings contain a given word.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `toArray(value)` that returns a real array for arrays (a copy), iterables, array-likes and single values (wrapped in an array), and returns `[]` for `null` and `undefined`. Test it with a `Set`, a string, `arguments`, `{ length: 2, 0: "x" }` and the number `5`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `document.getElementsByClassName('x')` sometimes skip elements when you remove the class inside a `for` loop over it, while `querySelectorAll` does not?" *Hint:* compare live and static collections, and trace the indices as the collection changes.

#### Map, Set, WeakMap and WeakSet

For years, JavaScript developers used plain objects as dictionaries and arrays as sets, because there was nothing else. Both have problems. Object keys are always strings, so you cannot key by an object or keep `1` and `"1"` apart. Inherited keys such as `"toString"` or `"__proto__"` can collide with your data. There is no built-in size, and order rules are quirky. Checking membership in an array means scanning it. ES2015 added dedicated collection types that solve these problems: `Map`, `Set`, and their "weak" variants for attaching data to objects without keeping those objects alive.

**`Map`: a true key-value dictionary.** Keys can be *any* value, including objects and functions. Entries are kept in insertion order, and the map knows its `size`.

```javascript
const visits = new Map();
const home = { path: "/" };

visits.set(home, 1);               // an object as key
visits.set("1", "string key");
visits.set(1, "number key");       // distinct from "1"

console.log(visits.get(home));     // 1
console.log(visits.get(1), visits.get("1"));  // "number key" "string key"
console.log(visits.has(home), visits.size);   // true 3
visits.delete("1");

for (const [key, value] of visits) console.log(key, value);   // insertion order

// Converting between Map and objects
const m = new Map(Object.entries({ a: 1, b: 2 }));
const o = Object.fromEntries(m);   // { a: 1, b: 2 }
```

| | Plain object | `Map` |
|---|---|---|
| Key types | Strings and symbols | Any value |
| Accidental keys | Inherited from the prototype (`toString`, `__proto__`) | None |
| Size | `Object.keys(o).length` | `m.size` |
| Iteration order | Integer-like keys first, then insertion order | Insertion order |
| Iteration | Through `Object.keys` / `entries` | Directly iterable |
| Frequent add/delete | Not optimised for it | Optimised for it |
| JSON | Native | Must convert (`Object.fromEntries` or `[...m]`) |
| Best for | Records with a fixed shape | Dictionaries with dynamic or non-string keys |

**`Set`: a collection of unique values.** Adding a value that is already present does nothing. Membership tests with `has` are fast regardless of size, unlike `array.includes`, which scans. Equality uses SameValueZero: `NaN` equals `NaN`, and objects are compared by reference.

```javascript
const tags = new Set(["js", "css"]);
tags.add("js");                          // no effect: already present
tags.add("html");
console.log(tags.size, tags.has("css")); // 3 true

const unique = [...new Set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])];   // [3, 1, 2]: the idiomatic de-duplication

// ES2025 set algebra
const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
const b = new Set([2, 3, 4]);
console.log(a.union(b));                 // Set {1, 2, 3, 4}
console.log(a.intersection(b));          // Set {2, 3}
console.log(a.difference(b));            // Set {1}
console.log(a.isSubsetOf(new Set([1, 2, 3, 4])));  // true
```

**Weak collections.** In a normal `Map`, a key object is kept alive as long as the map exists, even if nothing else references it. When you attach data to objects you do not control (DOM nodes, objects from a library), this causes memory leaks. `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` hold their keys **weakly**: an entry does not prevent the garbage collector from reclaiming its key. When the key object becomes unreachable elsewhere, the entry disappears (see Memory Model and Garbage Collection).

The price is that weak collections cannot be iterated and have no `size`: their contents depend on when garbage collection runs, so listing them would give unpredictable results. Their keys must be objects (or, since ES2023, non-registered symbols).

```javascript
// Cache derived data per object without leaking memory
const layoutCache = new WeakMap();

function measure(element) {
  if (!layoutCache.has(element)) {
    layoutCache.set(element, element.getBoundingClientRect());   // computed once per element
  }
  return layoutCache.get(element);
}
// When an element is removed from the DOM and dropped by your code, its cache entry can be collected

// Mark objects without modifying them
const processed = new WeakSet();
function processOnce(obj) {
  if (processed.has(obj)) return;
  processed.add(obj);
  // ... work ...
}
```

| | `Map` | `WeakMap` | `Set` | `WeakSet` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stores | Key-value pairs | Key-value pairs | Values | Values |
| Key / value types | Any | Objects (and non-registered symbols) as keys | Any | Objects (and non-registered symbols) |
| Keeps keys alive | Yes | No | Yes | No |
| Iterable, `size`, `clear` | Yes | No | Yes | No |
| Typical use | Dictionaries, lookups, counting | Per-object metadata, caches, private data | Unique values, fast membership | Tagging objects |

**Key Takeaways**

- Use `Map` for dictionaries whose keys are dynamic, non-string or numerous. Use plain objects for fixed-shape records.
- `Map` keeps insertion order, accepts any key, has `size`, and is directly iterable.
- `Set` stores unique values with fast `has`. `[...new Set(arr)]` removes duplicates, and ES2025 adds `union`, `intersection` and `difference`.
- `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` hold object keys weakly, so attached data is collected with its key. In exchange they are not iterable and have no `size`.
- Neither `Map` nor `Set` serialises to JSON automatically. Convert with `Object.fromEntries` or spread.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Count word frequencies in a paragraph with a `Map`, then print the five most frequent words. Repeat with a plain object and note what happens with the word `"constructor"`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement an LRU (least recently used) cache class with a capacity, `get(key)` and `set(key, value)`, using the fact that a `Map` iterates in insertion order. Moving a key to the "most recent" end can be done by deleting and re-inserting it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can't you iterate a `WeakMap` or read its size? When would you choose a `WeakMap` over a `Map`?" *Hint:* think about what the garbage collector is allowed to do with a key at any moment, and give an example involving DOM elements.

#### Typed Arrays and ArrayBuffer

Regular arrays can hold any mix of values, which makes them flexible but unsuitable for raw binary data. Images, audio samples, files read from disk, WebGL vertex buffers, WebAssembly memory and network protocols all deal in bytes and fixed-size numbers: "a 32-bit float, then two unsigned 16-bit integers". For this JavaScript provides **typed arrays**: fixed-length, densely packed arrays of a single numeric type, stored in a contiguous block of memory.

**Buffers and views.** The design separates storage from interpretation:

- An **`ArrayBuffer`** is a fixed-length block of raw bytes. You cannot read or write it directly.
- A **view** gives the bytes a meaning. A **typed array** (such as `Uint8Array` or `Float32Array`) treats the bytes as a sequence of numbers of one type. A **`DataView`** reads and writes individual values of any type at any byte offset, with explicit byte order.

Several views can share one buffer, so the same bytes can be read in different ways at the same time.

```text
const buf = new ArrayBuffer(8);              8 bytes of raw memory

byte offset:     0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
               +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
ArrayBuffer    | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 |
               +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
Uint8Array     | [0]| [1]| [2]| [3]| [4]| [5]| [6]| [7]|   8 elements, 1 byte each
Uint16Array    |  [0]    |  [1]    |  [2]    |  [3]    |   4 elements, 2 bytes each
Float32Array   |       [0]         |       [1]         |   2 elements, 4 bytes each
DataView       | any type at any offset: getUint16(1), setFloat32(4, x, true) ...
```

**The typed array family.**

| Type | Bytes per element | Range / meaning | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Int8Array` / `Uint8Array` | 1 | -128..127 / 0..255 | Raw bytes, files, network data |
| `Uint8ClampedArray` | 1 | 0..255, values clamped instead of wrapped | Canvas pixel data (Chapter 7) |
| `Int16Array` / `Uint16Array` | 2 | -32768..32767 / 0..65535 | Audio samples, indices |
| `Int32Array` / `Uint32Array` | 4 | 32-bit integers | Counters, hashes |
| `Float32Array` | 4 | Single-precision float | WebGL vertex data, audio (Web Audio API) |
| `Float64Array` | 8 | Same as `number` | Scientific data |
| `BigInt64Array` / `BigUint64Array` | 8 | 64-bit integers as `bigint` | 64-bit IDs, file offsets |

**Behaviour differences from regular arrays.** The length is fixed, so there is no `push`, `pop` or `splice`. Elements are initialised to `0`. Values that do not fit the type are converted: integers wrap around (modulo 2^n), clamped arrays saturate, and floats lose precision.

```javascript
const bytes = new Uint8Array([10, 255, 256, -1, 3.7]);
console.log(bytes);                        // Uint8Array [10, 255, 0, 255, 3]: wrapped and truncated

const pixels = new Uint8ClampedArray([300, -5]);
console.log(pixels);                       // Uint8ClampedArray [255, 0]: clamped to the range

const f = new Float32Array([0.1]);
console.log(f[0]);                         // 0.10000000149011612: single precision

const doubled = new Float64Array([1, 2, 3]).map((x) => x * 2); // most array methods exist
console.log(Array.isArray(doubled));       // false: it is a typed array, not an Array
```

**Sharing versus copying.** `subarray(start, end)` creates a new *view* on the same buffer, so writes through it affect the original. `slice(start, end)` copies the bytes into a new buffer.

```javascript
const data = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3, 4]);
const view = data.subarray(1, 3);          // shares memory
const copy = data.slice(1, 3);             // independent copy
view[0] = 99;
console.log(data[1], copy[0]);             // 99 2
```

**Reading a binary format with `DataView`.** Binary formats specify the **endianness** (byte order) of multi-byte numbers. Typed arrays always use the platform's native order, which is little-endian on almost all hardware. `DataView` lets you choose the order explicitly, which is essential for file formats and network protocols. The example reads the width and height of a PNG image, which the format stores as big-endian 32-bit integers at byte offsets 16 and 20.

```javascript
async function pngSize(url) {
  const buffer = await (await fetch(url)).arrayBuffer();   // the file as raw bytes (Chapter 5)
  const view = new DataView(buffer);

  const signature = new Uint8Array(buffer, 0, 8);          // a typed-array view on bytes 0..7
  if (signature[1] !== 0x50 || signature[2] !== 0x4e || signature[3] !== 0x47) {   // "PNG"
    throw new Error("Not a PNG file");
  }
  return {
    width: view.getUint32(16, false),     // false = big-endian, as the PNG spec requires
    height: view.getUint32(20, false),
  };
}
```

**Text and binary.** `TextEncoder` converts a string to UTF-8 bytes (a `Uint8Array`), and `TextDecoder` converts bytes back to a string. Many APIs accept or return buffers directly: `fetch` (`response.arrayBuffer()`), `FileReader` and `Blob.arrayBuffer()`, WebSockets, `crypto.subtle` and WebGL.

```javascript
const encoded = new TextEncoder().encode("héllo");    // Uint8Array(6): "é" takes 2 bytes in UTF-8
console.log(encoded.length);                          // 6
console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(encoded));       // "héllo"
```

**Key Takeaways**

- An `ArrayBuffer` is raw, fixed-size memory. Typed arrays and `DataView` are views that interpret its bytes.
- Typed arrays hold one numeric type, have a fixed length, start filled with zeros, and wrap, clamp or round values that do not fit.
- `subarray` shares memory with the original. `slice` copies.
- Use `DataView` for mixed-type binary formats and explicit endianness. Typed arrays use the platform's native byte order.
- `TextEncoder` and `TextDecoder` convert between strings and UTF-8 bytes.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a `Uint8Array` of length 4, write the values 0, 128, 255 and 256 into it, and explain each stored value. Then view the same buffer as a `Uint32Array` and print its single element.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `toHex(buffer)` that returns a hexadecimal string such as `"89504e47"` for an `ArrayBuffer`, and use it with `crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(text))` to compute the SHA-256 hash of a string.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is endianness, and why does `new Uint16Array(new Uint8Array([1, 0]).buffer)[0]` return `1` on most machines? How would you read a big-endian value portably?" *Hint:* write out which byte is most significant in each order, and look at the second parameter of `DataView.prototype.getUint16`.

<a id="43-object-oriented-programming"></a>
### 4.3 Object-Oriented Programming

This subchapter covers how the classic ideas of object-oriented programming map onto JavaScript, how `this` is determined, and the `class` syntax with its fields, static members, private members, inheritance and accessors.

#### Encapsulation, Inheritance and Polymorphism in JavaScript

As programs grow, the main difficulty is not writing code but keeping it understandable. Object-oriented programming (OOP) addresses this by bundling data with the operations that act on it, so that each piece of the program is a self-contained "thing" with a clear interface: a shopping cart that knows how to add items and compute its total, a modal dialog that knows how to open and close. Three ideas make this work: **encapsulation**, **inheritance** and **polymorphism**. JavaScript supports all three, but its mechanisms differ from class-based languages such as Java or C#, and knowing those differences prevents a lot of confusion.

**Encapsulation** means hiding an object's internal state behind a public interface, so other code cannot put it into an invalid state. Think of a vending machine: you press buttons and receive drinks, but you cannot reach into the coin box. In JavaScript you can encapsulate with closures (3.3) or with private class fields (see Static Members and Private Fields).

**Inheritance** means defining a new kind of object as a specialisation of an existing one, reusing its behaviour. In JavaScript inheritance is **prototypal**: objects delegate property lookups to another object, their prototype (4.4). The `class` and `extends` keywords are a convenient syntax over this mechanism.

**Polymorphism** means code can work with different kinds of objects through a common interface, and each object responds in its own way. JavaScript is dynamically typed, so polymorphism needs no declared interfaces: any object with the right method works. This is called **duck typing** (see Abstract Patterns and Duck Typing).

**How JavaScript compares with a class-based language.**

| Concept | Java | JavaScript |
|---|---|---|
| Blueprint | Classes are compile-time types | `class` creates a constructor function plus a prototype object at runtime |
| Inheritance | Class hierarchy, copied structure | Chain of live prototype objects that lookups delegate to |
| Encapsulation | `private`, `protected`, `public` | Closures, `#private` fields. No `protected`. |
| Interfaces | `interface`, checked by the compiler | No interfaces. Duck typing at runtime, or TypeScript (Chapter 9) |
| Polymorphism | Overriding plus static types | Overriding plus duck typing |
| Changing structure at runtime | Not possible | Objects and prototypes can be modified at any time |
| Objects without a class | Not possible | Normal: object literals |

**One example, two styles.** The same encapsulated, polymorphic "shape" model can be written with factory functions and closures, or with classes.

```javascript
// Style 1: factory functions + closures (encapsulation through scope)
function createCircle(radius) {
  return {
    name: "circle",
    area: () => Math.PI * radius ** 2,       // radius is captured, not exposed as a property
  };
}
function createSquare(side) {
  return { name: "square", area: () => side ** 2 };
}

// Style 2: classes (encapsulation through private fields, inheritance through extends)
class Shape {
  describe() {
    return `${this.constructor.name} with area ${this.area().toFixed(2)}`;  // calls the subclass's area
  }
}
class Circle extends Shape {
  #radius;                                     // private field
  constructor(radius) { super(); this.#radius = radius; }
  area() { return Math.PI * this.#radius ** 2; }
}
class Square extends Shape {
  #side;
  constructor(side) { super(); this.#side = side; }
  area() { return this.#side ** 2; }
}

// Polymorphism: this code works with any object that has area(), whatever its origin
const shapes = [new Circle(1), new Square(2), createCircle(2)];
const totalArea = shapes.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s.area(), 0);
console.log(totalArea.toFixed(2));             // "19.71"
console.log(shapes[0].describe());             // "Circle with area 3.14"
```

Both styles are idiomatic. Classes are better when you create many instances (methods are shared through the prototype rather than recreated per object) and when you want `instanceof` and inheritance. Factories are simpler for small objects and give real privacy without new syntax.

**Composition over inheritance.** Deep inheritance hierarchies are brittle: a change in a base class ripples through every subclass. A common guideline in JavaScript, as in other languages, is to prefer **composition**, building objects that *contain* or *combine* behaviours, and to keep inheritance shallow. Mixins (4.4) are one form of composition.

**Key Takeaways**

- Encapsulation hides state behind an interface, inheritance specialises existing behaviour, and polymorphism lets one piece of code work with many kinds of objects.
- JavaScript inheritance is prototypal: objects delegate to other live objects. `class` is syntax over that mechanism.
- Encapsulate with closures or `#private` fields. There is no `protected`.
- Polymorphism relies on duck typing: any object with the expected methods works.
- Prefer composition and shallow hierarchies over deep inheritance trees.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `createCounter()` factory that returns an object with `increment`, `decrement` and `value` methods, where the count cannot be modified directly from outside.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Model three payment methods (card, PayPal, bank transfer), each with a `pay(amount)` method that returns a different receipt string. Write a `checkout(cart, method)` function that works with any of them. Implement it once with classes and once with plain objects, and compare.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Is JavaScript an object-oriented language if it did not have classes until ES2015?" *Hint:* separate the idea of OOP (objects, encapsulation, polymorphism) from one implementation of it (classes), and describe what JavaScript used instead.

#### The this Binding Rules

Methods need a way to refer to the object they were called on: `cart.total()` must add up *this* cart's items, not some other cart's. JavaScript provides the keyword `this` for that. Unlike in Java, `this` in a regular function is **not** fixed when the function is written. It is decided *each time the function is called*, by *how* it is called. This flexibility lets one function be shared by many objects, but it is also why a method passed as a callback can suddenly lose its object. 3.3 introduced arrow functions and `call`, `apply` and `bind`. This topic gives the complete rules.

**The four rules for regular functions**, from highest to lowest priority:

| Rule | Call form | `this` is | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. `new` binding | `new F()` | The newly created object | `new Date()` |
| 2. Explicit binding | `f.call(obj)`, `f.apply(obj)`, `f.bind(obj)()` | `obj` | `greet.call(user)` |
| 3. Implicit binding | `obj.f()` | The object before the dot | `user.greet()` |
| 4. Default binding | `f()` | `undefined` in strict mode, `globalThis` in sloppy mode | `greet()` |

**Arrow functions** do not follow these rules at all: they have no `this` of their own and use the `this` of the surrounding scope at the place they were *defined* (lexical `this`). `call`, `apply`, `bind` and `new` cannot change it.

```text
How is the function called?
 |
 +-- Is it an arrow function? ----------------> this of the enclosing scope (lexical)
 +-- With new?  -------------------------------> the new object
 +-- With call / apply, or is it a bound fn? --> the object passed in
 +-- As obj.method() or obj[key]()? -----------> obj
 +-- Plainly, as fn()? ------------------------> undefined (strict) / globalThis (sloppy)
```

```javascript
"use strict";

function whoAmI() { return this?.name ?? String(this); }

const ada = { name: "Ada", whoAmI };
const linus = { name: "Linus" };

console.log(ada.whoAmI());              // "Ada": implicit (rule 3)
console.log(whoAmI.call(linus));        // "Linus": explicit (rule 2)
console.log(whoAmI());                  // "undefined": default in strict mode (rule 4)

const bound = whoAmI.bind(linus);
console.log(bound.call(ada));           // "Linus": a bound function ignores later call/apply
ada.bound = bound;
console.log(ada.bound());               // "Linus": explicit binding beats implicit binding

function Person(name) { this.name = name; }
const BoundPerson = Person.bind({ name: "ignored" });
console.log(new BoundPerson("Grace").name); // "Grace": new beats bind (rule 1)
```

**Losing `this`.** Implicit binding depends on the call site literally having the form `obj.method()`. As soon as the function is taken off the object and called on its own, it falls back to the default binding. This happens in three common situations:

```javascript
"use strict";

class Timer {
  seconds = 0;
  tick() { this.seconds++; }
}
const t = new Timer();

// 1. Passing a method as a callback
// setInterval(t.tick, 1000);          // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'seconds')

// 2. Storing the method in a variable or destructuring it
const { tick } = t;
// tick();                             // same TypeError: called as a plain function

// 3. Event handlers: the DOM calls the function with this = the element (Chapter 6)
// button.addEventListener("click", t.tick);   // this is the button, not t
```

**Three fixes.**

```javascript
// Fix 1: wrap the call in an arrow function, so the call site is t.tick() again
setInterval(() => t.tick(), 1000);

// Fix 2: bind once and pass the bound function
setInterval(t.tick.bind(t), 1000);

// Fix 3: define the method as an arrow-function class field (one copy per instance)
class SafeTimer {
  seconds = 0;
  tick = () => { this.seconds++; };    // this is captured from the instance when the field is created
}
const st = new SafeTimer();
setInterval(st.tick, 1000);            // works
```

Fix 3 is convenient for event handlers in UI components, but each instance gets its own function instead of sharing one through the prototype, and subclasses cannot call it with `super.tick()`.

**`this` in other places.**

| Location | `this` |
|---|---|
| Top level of an ES module | `undefined` |
| Top level of a classic script | `globalThis` (`window` in browsers) |
| Inside a class body (methods, constructor) | Class bodies are always strict, so the default binding is `undefined` |
| Class field initialiser | The instance being constructed |
| Static method called as `C.m()` | The class `C` itself |
| DOM event handler (regular function) | `event.currentTarget`, the element the listener is attached to |
| Callback with a `thisArg` (`arr.map(fn, obj)`) | `obj` |

**Key Takeaways**

- `this` in a regular function is decided at call time. In priority order: `new`, then explicit (`call`, `apply`, `bind`), then implicit (`obj.f()`), then the default (`undefined` in strict mode).
- Arrow functions take `this` from the scope where they are defined, and nothing can rebind it.
- Passing `obj.method` as a value loses `obj`. Fix it with an arrow wrapper, `bind`, or an arrow-function class field.
- Class bodies and modules are strict, so a lost `this` is `undefined` and fails loudly instead of silently using the global object.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Predict the output of `const o = { n: 1, f() { return this.n; }, g: () => this?.n }; console.log(o.f(), o.g(), (0, o.f)?.call({ n: 2 }));` in an ES module, then run it and explain each value.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `Counter` class whose `increment` method is attached to a button with `addEventListener`. Show the bug, then fix it in three different ways, and use the browser's memory tools or a simple instance count to compare how many function objects each fix creates for 1,000 counters.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the value of `this` inside `setTimeout(obj.method, 0)`, and why?" *Hint:* the timer calls the function it received without any object in front of it. Consider strict and sloppy mode, and what `setTimeout` does in browsers versus Node.js.

#### Classes and the class Syntax

Before ES2015, JavaScript had no `class` keyword. Developers built "classes" by hand from constructor functions and prototype objects (4.4), and every library had its own helpers for it. The `class` syntax standardised this pattern, made it far more readable, and added features that are hard to emulate, such as private fields. It is important to understand that a class is not a new kind of entity: it is still a function with a prototype object. The syntax simply sets them up correctly for you.

**Anatomy of a class.**

```javascript
class Temperature {
  unit = "C";                          // public instance field: created on each instance

  constructor(degrees) {               // runs when you call new Temperature(...)
    this.degrees = degrees;            // another own property of the instance
  }

  toFahrenheit() {                     // method: stored once on Temperature.prototype
    return this.degrees * 9 / 5 + 32;
  }

  toString() {                         // overrides Object.prototype.toString
    return `${this.degrees} °${this.unit}`;
  }
}

const t = new Temperature(21);
console.log(t.toFahrenheit());         // 69.8
console.log(`${t}`);                   // "21 °C": template literals call toString
console.log(Object.keys(t));           // ["unit", "degrees"]: fields and constructor props are own
console.log(Object.hasOwn(t, "toFahrenheit")); // false: methods live on the prototype
```

**What the class declaration creates.**

```text
 Temperature (a function)           Temperature.prototype            Object.prototype
+------------------------+         +-------------------------+      +----------------+
| the constructor code   |-------->| constructor: Temperature|----->| toString, ...  |
| prototype: ref --------+         | toFahrenheit()          |      +----------------+
+------------------------+         | toString()              |
                                   +-------------------------+
                                              ^
                                              | [[Prototype]]
                                    t  +--------------------+
                                       | unit: "C"          |   own data: one copy per instance
                                       | degrees: 21        |
                                       +--------------------+
```

```javascript
console.log(typeof Temperature);                                     // "function"
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(t) === Temperature.prototype);    // true
```

**Classes versus hand-written constructor functions.** The result is similar, but the class syntax adds safety:

| Behaviour | `class` | `function` constructor (4.4) |
|---|---|---|
| Calling without `new` | `TypeError: Class constructor ... cannot be invoked without 'new'` | Runs, with `this` undefined or global |
| Strict mode | Always, for the whole class body | Only if you opt in |
| Methods enumerable | No (do not show up in `for...in`) | Yes, if assigned to the prototype |
| Hoisting | Hoisted but in the temporal dead zone (like `let`, 3.1) | Fully hoisted |
| Fields, `#private`, `static` blocks | Supported | Not available |
| `super` | Supported | Not available |

**Fields versus methods.** A **field** (`unit = "C"`) is created as an own property of each instance, after `super()` returns (in a subclass) and before the rest of the constructor runs. Field initialisers can use `this` and earlier fields. A **method** is defined once on the prototype and shared by all instances. Do not put mutable shared data such as arrays on the prototype. Use fields, so that each instance gets its own copy.

```javascript
class Cart {
  items = [];                                // each cart gets its own array
  createdAt = Date.now();                    // initialiser runs per instance
  count = () => this.items.length;           // arrow-function field: a per-instance function

  add(item) { this.items.push(item); return this; }   // shared prototype method
}

const c1 = new Cart().add("pen");
const c2 = new Cart();
console.log(c1.items, c2.items);             // ["pen"] []: not shared
console.log(c1.add === c2.add, c1.count === c2.count); // true false
```

**Class expressions.** Like functions, classes can be expressions, which can be assigned, passed or returned. This is the basis of the mixin pattern in 4.4.

```javascript
const Point = class {
  constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
};

function makeEntity(kind) {
  return class { kind = kind; };             // a new class created at runtime
}
console.log(new (makeEntity("user"))().kind);    // "user"
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A class is a constructor function plus a prototype object. `typeof` a class is `"function"`.
- `constructor` initialises instances. Methods are stored once on `Class.prototype` and shared.
- Fields are own properties created per instance. Use them for per-instance state, including arrays and objects.
- Classes must be called with `new`, are always strict, have non-enumerable methods, and are in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs.
- Class expressions let you create and return classes dynamically.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `Rectangle` class with `width` and `height`, methods `area()` and `perimeter()`, and a `toString()` that returns `"Rectangle 3x4"`. Check which properties are own and which are inherited.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Rewrite the following constructor function as a class, keeping its behaviour identical: `function Stack() { this.items = []; } Stack.prototype.push = function (x) { this.items.push(x); return this; }; Stack.prototype.peek = function () { return this.items.at(-1); };`. Then list three behavioural differences between the two versions that you can observe at runtime.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Are JavaScript classes just syntactic sugar?" *Hint:* show which parts can be reproduced with functions and prototypes, and which cannot (private fields, the `new` check, `super` in object methods, correctly extending built-ins such as `Array`).

#### Static Members and Private Fields

Not every piece of behaviour belongs to an individual instance. A factory method that parses a string into a `Temperature`, a counter of how many users have been created, a table of constants: these belong to the class as a whole. Conversely, some instance data must not be reachable from outside at all, such as a password hash or an internal cache whose consistency the class must guarantee. **Static members** and **private members** cover these two needs.

**Static members** belong to the class (the constructor function) itself, not to its instances. Built-in examples are `Array.from`, `Object.keys`, `Number.isNaN` and `Date.now`. Inside a static method, `this` is the class.

```javascript
class User {
  static #count = 0;                       // private static field
  static ROLES = Object.freeze(["admin", "editor", "viewer"]);   // public static constant

  static fromJSON(json) {                  // static factory method
    const { name, role } = JSON.parse(json);
    return new this(name, role);           // this = the class (or a subclass, see extends)
  }

  static get count() { return User.#count; }

  constructor(name, role = "viewer") {
    if (!User.ROLES.includes(role)) throw new RangeError(`Unknown role: ${role}`);
    this.name = name;
    this.role = role;
    User.#count++;
  }
}

const u = User.fromJSON('{"name":"Ada","role":"admin"}');
console.log(User.count);                   // 1
console.log(u.ROLES);                      // undefined: static members are not on instances
```

**Static initialisation blocks** (ES2022) run once when the class is defined. They are useful for setup that needs several statements, such as reading configuration or building lookup tables.

```javascript
class Config {
  static values;
  static {
    const env = globalThis.process?.env ?? {};   // Node.js environment, or {} in browsers
    this.values = { debug: env.DEBUG === "1", region: env.REGION ?? "eu" };
  }
}
```

**Private members.** A name that starts with `#` is **private**: it can be accessed only by code written inside the class body. This is enforced by the language. Using it outside the class is a *syntax error*, so the code does not even run. Fields, methods, getters and setters, both static and instance, can all be private.

```javascript
class BankAccount {
  #balance = 0;                                 // private field: must be declared in the class body
  #history = [];

  deposit(amount) {
    this.#validate(amount);
    this.#balance += amount;
    this.#history.push({ type: "deposit", amount });
    return this;
  }

  withdraw(amount) {
    this.#validate(amount);
    if (amount > this.#balance) throw new Error("Insufficient funds");
    this.#balance -= amount;
    this.#history.push({ type: "withdraw", amount });
    return this;
  }

  get balance() { return this.#balance; }       // read-only public view

  #validate(amount) {                           // private method
    if (!(amount > 0)) throw new RangeError("Amount must be positive");
  }

  static isAccount(obj) { return #balance in obj; }   // brand check (ES2022)
}

const acc = new BankAccount().deposit(100).withdraw(30);
console.log(acc.balance);                  // 70
// acc.#balance = 1e6;                     // SyntaxError: Private field '#balance' must be declared in an enclosing class
// acc.balance = 1e6;                      // no setter: TypeError in strict code, silently ignored in sloppy mode
console.log(Object.keys(acc));             // []: private fields are invisible to reflection
console.log(BankAccount.isAccount(acc), BankAccount.isAccount({})); // true false
```

**Properties of `#private` names.**

- They are **not properties** in the usual sense: `Object.keys`, `Reflect.ownKeys`, `JSON.stringify`, spread and `structuredClone` do not see them.
- They are **per class, not per object**: any code inside the class can access `#balance` of *another* instance of the same class, which is useful for methods such as `equals(other)`.
- They are **not inherited for access**: a subclass's code cannot read its parent's `#fields`. Expose a getter or a protected-by-convention method instead.
- Accessing a private field on an object that does not have it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks safely.
- They do not work through a `Proxy` (4.4): inside a method called on a proxy, `this` is the proxy, which has no private fields.

**Ways to hide data in JavaScript.**

| Technique | Privacy | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `_name` convention | None, a social contract | Still common in older code |
| Closures (factory functions, 3.3) | Real | Methods are created per instance |
| `WeakMap` keyed by instance (4.2) | Real | The pre-ES2022 class pattern |
| Symbol keys (3.1) | Weak: visible through `Reflect.ownKeys` | Avoids name collisions, not access |
| `#private` members | Real, enforced by the syntax | Modern default for classes |

**Key Takeaways**

- `static` members live on the class itself: use them for factories, constants and class-wide state. Inside static methods, `this` is the class.
- `static { ... }` blocks run once at class definition time.
- `#name` creates a truly private field, method or accessor. Outside access is a syntax error, and reflection cannot see it.
- Private names are accessible to all code inside the class body, for any instance, but not to subclasses.
- Use `#field in obj` as a reliable brand check that an object was created by the class.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a static `compare(a, b)` method to a `Version` class (with `major`, `minor` and `patch`), and use it to sort an array of versions with `toSorted(Version.compare)`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a `Password` class that stores only a private hash (any simple function will do for practice), exposes `verify(plain)`, and serialises to `{"type":"password"}` through `toJSON` so the hash never leaks. Verify that neither `JSON.stringify`, `Object.keys` nor `console.log` reveal the hash.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between a property named with a Symbol and a `#private` field? Which one would a library use to avoid name collisions, and which to enforce invariants?" *Hint:* try to access each from outside the class with `Reflect.ownKeys`, and consider what happens when a subclass or a `Proxy` is involved.

#### Class Inheritance with extends and super

Often a new kind of object is "the same as an existing one, plus a little more": an `AdminUser` is a `User` with extra permissions, a `ValidationError` is an `Error` with a field name, a custom element is an `HTMLElement` with its own behaviour. Inheritance lets you reuse the parent's code and add to it or override parts. In JavaScript, `extends` builds the prototype links described in 4.4, and `super` lets the child call into the parent.

**`extends` and `super` basics.**

```javascript
class Animal {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
  speak() { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; }
  static create(name) { return new this(name); }     // this = whichever class it is called on
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name, breed) {
    super(name);                 // run Animal's constructor: required before using this
    this.breed = breed;
  }
  speak() {                      // override
    return `${super.speak()}: woof`;  // call the parent's version
  }
}

const rex = new Dog("Rex", "beagle");
console.log(rex.speak());                 // "Rex makes a sound: woof"
console.log(rex instanceof Dog, rex instanceof Animal);  // true true
console.log(Dog.create("Fido").speak());  // "Fido makes a sound: woof": static methods are inherited
```

**Two prototype chains.** `class Dog extends Animal` links *instances* to the parent's prototype and links the *classes* themselves, which is why static methods are inherited.

```text
 Instance chain                                  Static (constructor) chain

 rex ---> Dog.prototype ---> Animal.prototype     Dog ---> Animal ---> Function.prototype
          speak()            speak()                       create()
          constructor        constructor
                                  |
                                  v
                           Object.prototype ---> null
```

**Rules for derived constructors.**

- If a subclass defines a constructor, it **must** call `super(...)` before accessing `this`. Otherwise it throws a `ReferenceError`. The parent constructor is what creates and initialises the object.
- If a subclass does not define a constructor, a default one is created: `constructor(...args) { super(...args); }`.
- `super.method(...)` calls the parent's version of a method with the current `this`. It works in methods, getters, setters and static methods, and in object-literal shorthand methods.

```javascript
class Broken extends Animal {
  constructor(name) {
    // this.tag = "x";           // ReferenceError: Must call super constructor before accessing 'this'
    super(name);
    this.tag = "x";              // OK after super()
  }
}
```

**Initialisation order and a classic pitfall.** When you call `new Child()`: the child constructor starts, calls `super()`, the parent's fields are initialised and the parent constructor body runs, *then* the child's fields are initialised, and finally the rest of the child constructor runs. A parent constructor that calls an overridden method therefore sees a child whose fields do not exist yet.

```javascript
class Widget {
  constructor() { this.render(); }               // calls the overridden render()
  render() {}
}
class Label extends Widget {
  text = "Hello";                                // initialised only AFTER Widget's constructor returns
  render() { console.log(`Rendering: ${this.text}`); }
}
new Label();                                     // "Rendering: undefined"
```

Avoid calling overridable methods from constructors. Use an explicit `init()` or render step called after construction instead.

**Extending built-ins.** With `class`, built-in constructors such as `Error`, `Array`, `Map` and `HTMLElement` can be subclassed correctly, something that was not possible with ES5 functions. Custom errors (3.4) and custom elements (Web Components) depend on this.

```javascript
class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message) {
    super(message);                              // sets message and the stack trace
    this.name = "HttpError";
    this.status = status;
  }
}

class Stack extends Array {
  peek() { return this.at(-1); }
}
const s = Stack.from([1, 2, 3]);                 // static methods are inherited
console.log(s.peek(), s.map((x) => x * 2) instanceof Stack);   // 3 true: map returns a Stack
```

**Extending expressions.** The expression after `extends` can be any expression that evaluates to a constructor (or `null`). This lets you compute the parent class at runtime, which is how mixins work (4.4): `class Admin extends Serializable(User) {}`.

**Key Takeaways**

- `class B extends A` links `B.prototype` to `A.prototype` (instances inherit methods) and `B` to `A` (static methods are inherited).
- A derived constructor must call `super(...)` before using `this`. Omitting the constructor forwards all arguments to the parent.
- `super.method()` calls the parent's implementation with the current `this`.
- Parent constructors run before child fields are initialised, so do not call overridable methods from a constructor.
- `class` can correctly extend built-ins such as `Error`, `Array` and `HTMLElement`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create `Vehicle` with `wheels` and `describe()`, and subclasses `Car` and `Bike` that override `describe()` while reusing the parent's text through `super.describe()`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a `ValidationError extends Error` with a `field` property, and an `ApiError extends Error` with `status`. Write a function that catches errors from a fake API call and handles each type differently with `instanceof`. Check that `error.stack` and `error.name` are correct for each.
> 3. *(Interview)* "In what order are fields initialised and constructors executed in a three-level hierarchy `A <- B <- C`? Why might a method called from `A`'s constructor see `undefined` for a field declared in `C`?" *Hint:* add `console.log` statements in each field initialiser and constructor, and remember that `super()` must return before the subclass's fields exist.

#### Getters, Setters and Accessors

Sometimes a value looks like a plain property to the outside but needs logic behind it. A `fullName` should always reflect the current first and last name. A `celsius` setter should reject temperatures below absolute zero. A `width` property should trigger a redraw when it changes. You could expose methods such as `getFullName()` and `setWidth(w)`, but then every caller has to remember to use them, and switching a plain property to a method later breaks all callers. **Accessor properties** solve this: they are read and written with normal property syntax, but run a function each time.

**Getters and setters.** `get name()` runs when the property is read. `set name(value)` runs when it is assigned. You can define either or both, in object literals and in classes.

```javascript
const person = {
  first: "Ada",
  last: "Lovelace",
  get fullName() {                         // computed on every read
    return `${this.first} ${this.last}`;
  },
  set fullName(value) {                    // runs on assignment
    [this.first, this.last] = value.split(" ");
  },
};

console.log(person.fullName);              // "Ada Lovelace": no parentheses, it reads like data
person.fullName = "Grace Hopper";          // calls the setter
console.log(person.first);                 // "Grace"
```

**Validation and derived values in a class.** A private field stores the real value, and public accessors guard it.

```javascript
class Temperature {
  #celsius = 0;

  get celsius() { return this.#celsius; }
  set celsius(value) {
    if (typeof value !== "number" || value < -273.15) {
      throw new RangeError(`Invalid temperature: ${value}`);
    }
    this.#celsius = value;
  }

  get fahrenheit() { return this.#celsius * 9 / 5 + 32; }      // derived
  set fahrenheit(f) { this.celsius = (f - 32) * 5 / 9; }        // reuses the celsius setter's validation

  static get absoluteZero() { return -273.15; }                  // static getter
}

const t = new Temperature();
t.fahrenheit = 212;
console.log(t.celsius);                    // 100
// t.celsius = -300;                       // RangeError: Invalid temperature: -300
```

**Lazy computation and caching.** A getter can compute an expensive value only on first access and then replace itself with a plain data property, so later reads cost nothing.

```javascript
const report = {
  rows: Array.from({ length: 100_000 }, (_, i) => i),
  get total() {
    const value = this.rows.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);            // computed once
    Object.defineProperty(this, "total", { value, writable: false }); // replace accessor with data (4.4)
    return value;
  },
};
```

**Where accessors live.** In a class, getters and setters are defined on the **prototype**, not on each instance. This has consequences:

- `Object.keys(instance)`, spread and `JSON.stringify` do not include them (unless you add a `toJSON`).
- A setter on the parent class is bypassed if a subclass declares a *field* with the same name, because fields are defined directly on the instance.

**Pitfalls.**

```javascript
"use strict";

class Bad {
  set name(v) { this.name = v; }       // assigns to itself: calls the setter again, forever
}
// new Bad().name = "x";               // RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

class ReadOnly {
  get id() { return 42; }              // getter without a setter
}
// new ReadOnly().id = 1;              // TypeError in strict mode: has only a getter (ignored in sloppy mode)
```

Store the backing value under a different name (a `#private` field is ideal) to avoid infinite recursion. Keep getters fast and free of side effects: a reader expects `obj.x` to be cheap and repeatable. Use a method instead when the work is expensive, asynchronous or changes state.

| | Data property | Accessor property |
|---|---|---|
| Stores a value | Yes | No (computes it) |
| Defined with | `x: 1`, `this.x = 1`, a field | `get x() {}`, `set x(v) {}` |
| Reading runs code | No | Yes |
| Can validate writes | No | Yes |
| Read-only form | `writable: false` (4.4) or freeze | Getter without a setter |

**Key Takeaways**

- Getters and setters let a property run code on read and write while keeping the `obj.prop` syntax.
- Use them for derived values, validation, lazy initialisation, and keeping a stable public API when the internals change.
- Store the underlying value elsewhere (ideally a `#private` field) to avoid infinite recursion in setters.
- Class accessors live on the prototype, so they are invisible to `Object.keys`, spread and JSON.
- A getter without a setter makes a read-only property. Assigning to it throws in strict mode.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a `get area()` and a `get isSquare()` to a `Rectangle` class, and a `set size(n)` that sets both width and height.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `Slider` class with a `value` accessor that clamps the value to `[min, max]`, rounds it to a `step`, and calls an `onChange` callback only when the stored value actually changes. Make `min`, `max` and `step` read-only after construction.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `get total() { ... }` and `total() { ... }` on a class? When would you prefer each?" *Hint:* consider the call syntax, the expectations a reader has about cost and side effects, serialisation, and whether the value can take arguments.

#### Abstract Patterns and Duck Typing

Class-based languages let you declare an **abstract class** (a base class that cannot be instantiated and that forces subclasses to implement certain methods) and **interfaces** (a contract listing the methods a type must provide). The compiler then checks that every object passed to a function fulfils the contract. JavaScript has neither feature. Instead, it relies on conventions enforced at runtime and on **duck typing**: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck". Code checks whether an object can *do* what is needed, not what class it belongs to.

**Emulating an abstract class.** `new.target` refers to the constructor that was called with `new`. A base class can refuse to be instantiated directly, and declare "abstract" methods that throw until a subclass overrides them.

```javascript
class Exporter {
  constructor() {
    if (new.target === Exporter) {               // only subclasses may be instantiated
      throw new TypeError("Exporter is abstract");
    }
  }

  // Template method: fixed algorithm, with a step provided by subclasses
  export(rows) {
    const body = rows.map((r) => this.formatRow(r)).join("\n");
    return this.header() + body;
  }

  header() { return ""; }                         // optional hook with a default
  formatRow(row) {                                // "abstract" method
    throw new Error(`${this.constructor.name} must implement formatRow()`);
  }
}

class CsvExporter extends Exporter {
  header() { return "name,age\n"; }
  formatRow({ name, age }) { return `${name},${age}`; }
}

console.log(new CsvExporter().export([{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }]));  // "name,age\nAda,36"
// new Exporter();                                // TypeError: Exporter is abstract
```

This is the **template method pattern**: the base class defines the algorithm, and subclasses fill in the steps. The checks happen at runtime, so a missing implementation is reported only when the method is called.

**Duck typing.** Instead of `instanceof`, check for the capability you are about to use. This makes code work with objects from other libraries, other frames, plain object literals and test doubles.

```javascript
// Accept anything that has a write(text) method: a file stream, a DOM wrapper, a test mock
function logTo(sink, message) {
  if (typeof sink?.write !== "function") {
    throw new TypeError("sink must have a write(text) method");
  }
  sink.write(`[${new Date().toISOString()}] ${message}\n`);
}

const memorySink = { lines: [], write(text) { this.lines.push(text); } };
logTo(memorySink, "started");                 // works: no class or inheritance needed
console.log(memorySink.lines.length);         // 1
```

**Protocols: the language's own duck typing.** The language itself relies on duck typing through well-known method names and symbols. Implementing them lets your objects plug into built-in syntax.

| Protocol | Required member | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| Iterable | `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an iterator | `for...of`, spread, `Array.from`, destructuring (3.3) |
| Thenable | `then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` | `await`, `Promise.resolve` (Chapter 5) |
| JSON | `toJSON()` | `JSON.stringify` (4.1) |
| Primitive conversion | `[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint)`, `valueOf()`, `toString()` | Arithmetic, template literals, `==` (3.1) |
| Disposable | `[Symbol.dispose]()` | `using` declarations (explicit resource management, recent engines only) |

```javascript
class Range {
  constructor(from, to) { this.from = from; this.to = to; }

  *[Symbol.iterator]() {                        // a generator method implements the iterable protocol
    for (let i = this.from; i <= this.to; i++) yield i;
  }
}

const r = new Range(1, 5);
console.log([...r]);                            // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
for (const n of r) if (n % 2 === 0) console.log(n);  // 2, 4

const isIterable = (x) => x != null && typeof x[Symbol.iterator] === "function";
console.log(isIterable(r), isIterable({}));     // true false
```

**Duck typing versus nominal checks.**

| | Duck typing (`typeof x.m === "function"`) | Nominal (`x instanceof C`) |
|---|---|---|
| Accepts | Any object with the right shape | Only objects whose prototype chain contains `C.prototype` |
| Objects from other frames or library copies | Work | Fail (4.4) |
| Test doubles | Plain objects work | Must extend or fake the class |
| Risk | Accidental matches (an unrelated `write` method) | Over-restrictive |

For compile-time checking of shapes, TypeScript adds **structural** interfaces on top of JavaScript (Chapter 9). They formalise duck typing without changing runtime behaviour.

**Key Takeaways**

- JavaScript has no `abstract` or `interface` keywords. Emulate abstract classes with `new.target` checks and methods that throw until overridden.
- The template method pattern puts the algorithm in the base class and the variable steps in subclasses.
- Duck typing checks capabilities (`typeof obj.method === "function"`) rather than ancestry, which makes code more flexible and easier to test.
- Built-in features rely on protocols such as iterables, thenables and `toJSON`. Implement them to integrate your objects with the language.
- TypeScript interfaces add structural, compile-time checks of the same idea.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Make a `Playlist` class iterable over its songs with `[Symbol.iterator]`, so that `[...playlist]` and `for...of` work.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create an abstract `Storage` base class with abstract `get(key)` and `set(key, value)`, and two implementations: `MemoryStorage` (using a `Map`) and `LocalStorage` (wrapping `window.localStorage` with JSON). Write a `Settings` class that works with either, and test it with a plain object literal that has the same two methods.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is a thenable, and why does `await` accept objects that are not `Promise` instances?" *Hint:* relate it to duck typing and to interoperability between promise libraries written before native promises existed.

<a id="44-implementation-of-objects-and-constructors"></a>
### 4.4 Implementation of Objects and Constructors

This subchapter looks beneath the `class` syntax at the machinery JavaScript actually uses: constructor functions, the prototype chain, property descriptors, delegation, type checks, meta-programming with `Proxy` and `Reflect`, and how the engine stores objects and reclaims their memory.

#### Constructor Functions and the new Operator

Long before `class` existed, JavaScript code created many objects of the same kind with **constructor functions**: ordinary functions meant to be called with the `new` operator. Classes compile down to the same mechanism, most older libraries and many tutorials still use the pattern, and the built-ins (`Date`, `Error`, `Map`) behave like constructors. Understanding exactly what `new` does is the key to understanding prototypes.

**The pattern.** By convention, constructor names start with a capital letter. Per-instance data is assigned to `this` inside the function. Shared methods are put on the function's `prototype` object, so all instances share one copy.

```javascript
function Person(name, born) {
  this.name = name;              // own data for each instance
  this.born = born;
}

Person.prototype.age = function (year = new Date().getFullYear()) {   // shared method
  return year - this.born;
};

const ada = new Person("Ada", 1815);
const alan = new Person("Alan", 1912);
console.log(ada.age(1852), alan.name);     // 37 "Alan"
console.log(ada.age === alan.age);         // true: one function shared through the prototype
```

**What `new F(args)` does**, step by step:

1. Creates a new empty object.
2. Sets that object's internal `[[Prototype]]` link to `F.prototype`.
3. Calls `F` with `this` bound to the new object, passing `args`.
4. If `F` returns an object, that object becomes the result. Otherwise (no `return`, or a primitive), the new object from step 1 is the result.

```text
new Person("Ada", 1815)

 1. obj = {}
 2. obj.[[Prototype]] = Person.prototype        obj ----> Person.prototype ----> Object.prototype
 3. Person.call(obj, "Ada", 1815)                         age()
      obj.name = "Ada"; obj.born = 1815
 4. return obj   (unless Person returned an object)
```

The four steps can be written as an ordinary function, which is a common interview exercise:

```javascript
function myNew(F, ...args) {
  const obj = Object.create(F.prototype);        // steps 1 and 2
  const result = F.apply(obj, args);             // step 3
  return result !== null && (typeof result === "object" || typeof result === "function")
    ? result                                     // step 4: an explicitly returned object wins
    : obj;
}

const grace = myNew(Person, "Grace", 1906);
console.log(grace.age(1950), grace instanceof Person);  // 44 true
```

**Forgetting `new`.** A constructor called without `new` is just a function call, and `this` follows the default binding (4.3). In sloppy mode, `this` is the global object, so properties leak onto `window`. In strict mode, `this` is `undefined` and the first assignment throws. Defensive constructors check `new.target`, which is `undefined` when the function was not called with `new`:

```javascript
function Point(x, y) {
  if (!new.target) return new Point(x, y);   // repair the call (or throw a TypeError)
  this.x = x;
  this.y = y;
}
console.log(Point(1, 2) instanceof Point);   // true
```

Classes make this check automatic: calling a class without `new` always throws.

**What can be a constructor.** Regular `function` declarations and expressions and classes have a `prototype` and can be used with `new`. Arrow functions, shorthand methods, generators and async functions cannot: `new (() => {})` throws `TypeError: ... is not a constructor`.

**Built-in constructors with and without `new`.** Some built-ins behave differently when called without `new`: `Date()` returns a *string*, while `new Date()` returns a `Date` object. `String(x)`, `Number(x)` and `Boolean(x)` convert, while their `new` forms create wrapper objects (3.1). `Array(3)` and `new Array(3)` are equivalent, as are `Error("x")` and `new Error("x")`. `Symbol` and `BigInt` must *not* be called with `new`.

**Key Takeaways**

- A constructor function sets per-instance data on `this`. Methods placed on `F.prototype` are shared by all instances.
