- `new F()` creates an object linked to `F.prototype`, runs `F` with `this` set to it, and returns it unless `F` returns another object.
- Without `new`, `this` is the global object (sloppy) or `undefined` (strict). Guard with `new.target`, or use `class`.
- Arrow functions, methods, generators and async functions cannot be constructors.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `Book(title, pages)` constructor with a prototype method `readingTime(pagesPerHour)`. Create two books and confirm that they share the method but not the data.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend `myNew` so that it throws a `TypeError` when `F` is not constructible (hint: arrow functions have no `prototype` property). Test it with a function that explicitly returns an object, one that returns a primitive, and a class (and explain why calling a class with `F.apply` fails).
> 3. *(Interview)* "Walk me through what happens, step by step, when the engine evaluates `new Foo(1)`." *Hint:* cover object creation, the prototype link, `this`, and the special rule for the return value.

#### The Prototype Chain

When you call `[1, 2].map(...)`, the array has no own property called `map`, yet the call works. When you call `toString()` on an object literal you never gave a `toString`, it also works. Both work because of the **prototype chain**, the mechanism behind all inheritance in JavaScript. Instead of copying methods into every object, objects *delegate* lookups they cannot satisfy to another object. It is similar to asking a colleague: if you do not know the answer, you ask your team lead, who may ask the department head, and so on until someone knows or the chain ends.

**The `[[Prototype]]` link.** Every object has a hidden internal slot called `[[Prototype]]` that refers to another object or to `null`. Read it with `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`. Following these links from object to object forms the chain, which always ends at `null`.

```text
const arr = [1, 2];

 arr                   Array.prototype          Object.prototype          null
+-------------+       +-----------------+       +------------------+
| 0: 1        |  ---> | map, filter,    |  ---> | toString,        |  ---> null
| 1: 2        |       | push, at, ...   |       | hasOwnProperty,  |
| length: 2   |       | constructor     |       | valueOf, ...     |
+-------------+       +-----------------+       +------------------+

arr.map       -> not own -> found on Array.prototype
arr.toString  -> not own -> Array.prototype has its own toString, found there first
arr.valueOf   -> not own -> not on Array.prototype -> found on Object.prototype
arr.missing   -> not own -> not found anywhere -> reaches null -> undefined
```

**Reading walks the chain, writing does not.** A property *read* searches the object itself, then its prototype, and so on. The first match wins. A property *write* (`obj.x = 1`) normally creates or updates an **own** property on `obj` itself, even if the prototype has a property with the same name. The own property then **shadows** the inherited one.

```javascript
const defaults = { color: "blue", size: "M" };
const order = Object.create(defaults);     // order's prototype is defaults (see Object.create)
order.size = "L";                          // creates an own property: shadows defaults.size

console.log(order.color);                  // "blue": inherited
console.log(order.size);                   // "L": own property found first
console.log(defaults.size);                // "M": the prototype was not modified

delete order.size;                         // remove the own property...
console.log(order.size);                   // "M": ...and the inherited one is visible again
```

Two exceptions to "writes create own properties": if the inherited property is an **accessor** with a setter, the setter runs instead (4.3). If it is a **read-only** data property (`writable: false`), the write fails, and throws in strict mode.

**The chain is live.** Prototypes are ordinary objects referenced by link, not copied. Adding a method to a prototype makes it instantly available to every object that delegates to it, including objects created earlier.

```javascript
function Dog(name) { this.name = name; }
const rex = new Dog("Rex");

Dog.prototype.bark = function () { return `${this.name}: woof`; };  // added after rex was created
console.log(rex.bark());                   // "Rex: woof"
```

This is how polyfills (Chapter 1) add missing methods to built-ins. Modifying built-in prototypes in application code ("monkey patching"), however, risks clashing with future standard methods and with other libraries, and is strongly discouraged.

**Shared mutable state on prototypes.** Because every instance sees the same prototype object, a mutable value stored there is shared by all instances. That is right for methods and wrong for data:

```javascript
function Team() {}
Team.prototype.members = [];               // one array for ALL teams

const a = new Team(), b = new Team();
a.members.push("Ada");                     // reading a.members finds the prototype's array, then mutates it
console.log(b.members);                    // ["Ada"]: b sees it too
```

Put per-instance data in the constructor or in class fields.

**Objects without a prototype.** `Object.create(null)` creates an object whose chain ends immediately. It has no inherited `toString`, `hasOwnProperty` or `__proto__`, which makes it a safe dictionary for arbitrary string keys (although a `Map` is usually better, 4.2).

**Performance.** Lookups along short chains are very fast, because engines cache where they found each property (see Memory Model and Garbage Collection). Very deep chains and, above all, changing an existing object's prototype at runtime with `Object.setPrototypeOf` defeat these optimisations. Set the prototype when you create the object instead.

**Key Takeaways**

- Every object has a `[[Prototype]]` link to another object or `null`. Read it with `Object.getPrototypeOf`.
- Reading a property searches the object, then its prototypes in order, and returns `undefined` if the chain ends at `null`.
- Writing a property creates an own property that shadows the inherited one, unless the inherited property is a setter or read-only.
- Prototypes are shared and live: changes are visible to every object linked to them. Keep methods on prototypes and data on instances.
- Avoid `Object.setPrototypeOf` on existing objects, and do not modify built-in prototypes in application code.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a function `chainOf(obj)` that returns an array of the prototypes of `obj` up to `null`, using `Object.getPrototypeOf` in a loop. Try it with `[]`, `{}`, `new Date()`, `function () {}` and `Object.create(null)`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create `base = { greet() { return "hi " + this.name; } }` and two objects that delegate to it. Show shadowing by giving one of them its own `greet`, then use `delete` to restore the inherited behaviour. Then make `base.greet` read-only with `Object.defineProperty` and observe what happens when you try to shadow it in strict mode.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Explain how `'abc'.toUpperCase()` and `[].push(1)` find their methods, given that the values have no such own properties." *Hint:* combine autoboxing (3.1) with the prototype chain of `String.prototype` and `Array.prototype`.

#### prototype vs Dunder Proto

Two similar names cause more confusion than anything else in JavaScript's object model: the `prototype` property of functions, and `__proto__` (read "dunder proto", short for "double underscore proto"). They are related but mean completely different things. A function's `prototype` is the object that *will become* the `[[Prototype]]` of instances created with `new`. An object's `__proto__` is a getter and setter for *its own* `[[Prototype]]` link.

**Side by side.**

| | `F.prototype` | `obj.__proto__` |
|---|---|---|
| Exists on | Constructible functions and classes | Objects that inherit from `Object.prototype` |
| Kind | An ordinary data property | An accessor (getter/setter) defined on `Object.prototype` |
| Meaning | "Instances created by `new F` will link to this object" | "The object `obj` currently links to" |
| Standard status | Core language | Legacy, kept for compatibility (Annex B). Avoid it. |
| Modern replacement | | `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` / `Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, p)` |

**The triangle.** For any constructor `F` and instance `x = new F()`:

```text
            new F()
   F  ----------------------->  x
   |                            |
   | .prototype                 | [[Prototype]]   (read via Object.getPrototypeOf(x),
   v                            v                   or the legacy x.__proto__)
 F.prototype  <-----------------+
   |
   | .constructor  (points back to F)
   v
   F
```

```javascript
function F() {}
const x = new F();

console.log(F.prototype === Object.getPrototypeOf(x));   // true: the core relationship
console.log(x.__proto__ === F.prototype);                // true: legacy accessor, same link
console.log(F.prototype.constructor === F);              // true: the back-reference
console.log(x.constructor === F);                        // true: inherited from F.prototype

console.log(Object.hasOwn(x, "prototype"));              // false: ordinary objects have no .prototype
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(F) === Function.prototype); // true: F itself is a function object
console.log(F.prototype === Function.prototype);         // false: two very different objects
```

The last two lines show the most common confusion. `F.prototype` is where *instances* of `F` look for methods. `F`'s own `[[Prototype]]` is `Function.prototype`, which is where `F` *itself* finds `call`, `apply` and `bind`.

**Why `__proto__` is discouraged.** It works only on objects that inherit from `Object.prototype`, because it is an inherited accessor. On an object created with `Object.create(null)`, `obj.__proto__` is just an ordinary key. It is also a well-known attack vector: code that copies user-controlled keys into objects (for example, a naive deep merge of parsed JSON) can be tricked into writing to `__proto__` and modifying `Object.prototype` for the entire application. This attack is called **prototype pollution**.

```javascript
function naiveMerge(target, source) {
  for (const key in source) {
    if (typeof source[key] === "object" && source[key] !== null) {
      target[key] ??= {};
      naiveMerge(target[key], source[key]);   // recurses into target["__proto__"] = Object.prototype!
    } else {
      target[key] = source[key];
    }
  }
  return target;
}

const payload = JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}');  // JSON.parse creates an own "__proto__" key
naiveMerge({}, payload);
console.log({}.isAdmin);                      // true: every object in the program is now "admin"
delete Object.prototype.isAdmin;              // clean up

// Defences: skip "__proto__", "constructor" and "prototype" keys, use Object.hasOwn,
// build dictionaries with Object.create(null) or Map, or freeze Object.prototype
```

**`__proto__` in object literals is different.** Inside an object literal, `__proto__: value` (non-computed and not shorthand) is standard syntax that sets the new object's prototype. It is a concise and well-optimised way to create an object with a given prototype:

```javascript
const animal = { eats: true };
const rabbit = { __proto__: animal, jumps: true };   // sets [[Prototype]], creates no own key
console.log(rabbit.eats, Object.hasOwn(rabbit, "__proto__"));  // true false

const literalKey = { ["__proto__"]: animal };        // computed key: an ordinary own property
console.log(Object.hasOwn(literalKey, "__proto__")); // true
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `F.prototype` is a property of functions: the object that becomes the `[[Prototype]]` of `new F()` instances.
- `obj.__proto__` is a legacy accessor for `obj`'s own `[[Prototype]]`. Use `Object.getPrototypeOf` and `Object.setPrototypeOf` instead.
- `F.prototype.constructor === F`, and instances inherit that `constructor` back-reference.
- A function's own prototype is `Function.prototype`, which is different from its `prototype` property.
- Merging untrusted keys can write through `__proto__` and pollute `Object.prototype`. Filter dangerous keys or use null-prototype objects and `Map`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For `class A {}` and `const a = new A()`, evaluate and explain: `A.prototype === Object.getPrototypeOf(a)`, `Object.getPrototypeOf(A) === Function.prototype`, `a.prototype`, `a.constructor === A`, `A.prototype.constructor === A`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Fix `naiveMerge` so that it is safe against prototype pollution, and write a test that proves it using the malicious payload above plus a `constructor.prototype` variant (`{"constructor": {"prototype": {"polluted": true}}}`).
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `Foo.prototype` and `foo.__proto__`, and when are they the same object?" *Hint:* draw the triangle between a constructor, its `prototype` object and an instance.

#### Object.create and Prototypal Delegation

Constructors and classes are one way to set up prototype links, but they hide the link behind `new`. `Object.create(proto)` makes the link explicit: it creates a new, empty object whose `[[Prototype]]` is exactly the object you pass. This exposes the essence of JavaScript's object model: objects linking to other objects, with no class in between. Thinking in terms of **delegation** instead of "classes and instances" often makes the model easier to reason about.

**`Object.create(proto, descriptors?)`.** The first argument is the prototype (an object or `null`). The optional second argument defines own properties using property descriptors (see Property Descriptors and defineProperty).

```javascript
const vehicle = {
  describe() { return `${this.name} has ${this.wheels} wheels`; },
};

const bike = Object.create(vehicle);         // bike --[[Prototype]]--> vehicle
bike.name = "Bike";
bike.wheels = 2;
console.log(bike.describe());                // "Bike has 2 wheels": delegated to vehicle

const car = Object.create(vehicle, {
  name: { value: "Car", enumerable: true },
  wheels: { value: 4, enumerable: true },
});
console.log(car.describe());                 // "Car has 4 wheels"
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(car) === vehicle);  // true
```

**Delegation versus copying.** In a class-based language, an instance gets its own copy of the structure defined by its class. In JavaScript, an object holds only its own data and *delegates* everything else to its prototype at lookup time. Compare a tutorial copied onto each student's desk (copying) with one shared reference book that everyone consults (delegation): updating the shared book updates it for everyone at once.

**OLOO: "objects linked to other objects".** You can design whole programs with plain objects and `Object.create`, without constructors or classes. Behaviour lives in prototype objects, and an `init` method replaces the constructor.

```javascript
const Widget = {
  init(width, height) {
    this.width = width;
    this.height = height;
    return this;
  },
  render() { return `<div style="width:${this.width}px;height:${this.height}px"></div>`; },
};

const Button = Object.create(Widget);        // Button delegates to Widget
Button.setup = function (width, height, label) {
  this.init(width, height);                  // delegated call, this = the button object
  this.label = label;
  return this;
};
Button.render = function () {
  return Widget.render.call(this).replace("></div>", `>${this.label}</div>`);  // explicit "super" call
};

const ok = Object.create(Button).setup(80, 30, "OK");   // ok -> Button -> Widget -> Object.prototype
console.log(ok.render());     // '<div style="width:80px;height:30px">OK</div>'
```

**Pre-ES2015 inheritance between constructors.** Before `extends`, inheritance between constructor functions was wired by hand with `Object.create`. You will still see this in older libraries, and it is exactly what `extends` does for you:

```javascript
function Animal(name) { this.name = name; }
Animal.prototype.speak = function () { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; };

function Dog(name) {
  Animal.call(this, name);                            // like super(name): run the parent constructor
}
Dog.prototype = Object.create(Animal.prototype);      // link the prototypes
Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog;                      // restore the back-reference that was overwritten
Dog.prototype.speak = function () {
  return Animal.prototype.speak.call(this) + ": woof"; // like super.speak()
};

console.log(new Dog("Rex").speak());                  // "Rex makes a sound: woof"
```

**Three ways to build the same model.**

| | Constructor function | `class` | `Object.create` (OLOO) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Create instance | `new F()` | `new C()` | `Object.create(proto).init()` |
| Shared behaviour on | `F.prototype` | `C.prototype` (implicit) | The prototype object itself |
| Inheritance | `Object.create` plus manual wiring | `extends` | `Object.create(parentProto)` |
| Parent calls | `Parent.prototype.m.call(this)` | `super.m()` | `Parent.m.call(this)` |
| `instanceof` | Works | Works | Use `proto.isPrototypeOf(obj)` |
| Private state | Closures | `#private` | Closures or `WeakMap` |

**Key Takeaways**

- `Object.create(proto)` creates an object whose `[[Prototype]]` is `proto`. `Object.create(null)` creates one with no prototype.
- Delegation means objects share behaviour by linking to a prototype at lookup time, not by copying it.
- OLOO designs use plain objects, `Object.create` and `init` methods instead of constructors.
- Before `extends`, inheritance was set up with `Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype)`, restoring `constructor`, and calling `Parent.call(this, ...)`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use `Object.create` to make `admin` delegate to `user`, which delegates to `person`. Give each level one method, and call all three methods on `admin`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a minimal `Object.create` polyfill `create(proto)` using only a temporary constructor function and `new`, as was done before ES5. Explain why your version cannot support `null` as the prototype.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why do we write `Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog` after `Dog.prototype = Object.create(Animal.prototype)`? What breaks if we forget?" *Hint:* check what `new Dog().constructor` returns in both cases and where that property is found.

#### Property Descriptors and defineProperty

So far, a property has looked like a simple key-value pair. In reality, every property also carries hidden **attributes** that control whether it can be changed, whether it shows up in loops, and whether it can be deleted or reconfigured. These attributes explain why `Math.PI` cannot be reassigned, why array methods do not appear in `for...in`, and how `Object.freeze` works. You can read and set them with **property descriptors**.

**Two kinds of properties, two kinds of descriptors.**

| Attribute | Data property | Accessor property | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | Yes | | The stored value |
| `writable` | Yes | | Can the value be changed by assignment? |
| `get` | | Yes | Function called on read |
| `set` | | Yes | Function called on write |
| `enumerable` | Yes | Yes | Does it appear in `for...in`, `Object.keys`, spread and JSON? |
| `configurable` | Yes | Yes | Can it be deleted, and can its attributes be changed? |

**Reading descriptors.**

```javascript
const user = { name: "Ada" };
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(user, "name"));
// { value: "Ada", writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true }

console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Math, "PI"));
// { value: 3.141592653589793, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false }

console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Array.prototype, "map").enumerable);  // false
```

**Defining properties precisely.** `Object.defineProperty(obj, key, descriptor)` creates or modifies a single property. `Object.defineProperties(obj, { key: descriptor, ... })` does several at once. The crucial detail is the defaults: attributes you omit default to `false` when a property is *created* by `defineProperty`, whereas properties created by assignment or literals have every attribute set to `true`.

```javascript
"use strict";

const order = { items: [] };

Object.defineProperty(order, "id", {
  value: "ord_42",              // writable, enumerable and configurable all default to false
});

Object.defineProperty(order, "total", {
  get() { return this.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0); },
  enumerable: true,             // show it in Object.keys and JSON
});

order.items.push({ price: 10 }, { price: 5 });
console.log(order.total);                     // 15
console.log(Object.keys(order));              // ["items", "total"]: id is hidden (not enumerable)
console.log(JSON.stringify(order));           // '{"items":[...],"total":15}'

try { order.id = "hacked"; } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name); }  // "TypeError": not writable
try { delete order.id; } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name); }      // "TypeError": not configurable
```

**`configurable: false` is (almost) permanent.** Once a property is non-configurable, you cannot delete it, turn it into an accessor, or change its `enumerable` flag. The only change still allowed is lowering `writable` from `true` to `false` (and changing `value` while it is still writable). Attempts to do anything else throw a `TypeError`.

**How the integrity functions use descriptors.** The functions from 4.1 are shortcuts over descriptors:

| Function | Effect in descriptor terms |
|---|---|
| `Object.preventExtensions(o)` | Marks `o` non-extensible. Existing descriptors unchanged. |
| `Object.seal(o)` | Non-extensible, plus `configurable: false` on every own property |
| `Object.freeze(o)` | Sealed, plus `writable: false` on every data property (setters still run) |

**Copying with descriptors.** Spread and `Object.assign` read values, so getters are evaluated once and copied as plain values, and non-enumerable properties are skipped (4.1). To copy properties *as they are*, including accessors and attributes, copy the descriptors:

```javascript
const source = {
  first: "Ada",
  last: "Lovelace",
  get full() { return `${this.first} ${this.last}`; },
};

const flat = { ...source };
flat.first = "Grace";
console.log(flat.full);              // "Ada Lovelace": full was copied as a frozen-in-time string

const faithful = Object.defineProperties({}, Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors(source));
faithful.first = "Grace";
console.log(faithful.full);          // "Grace Lovelace": the getter was copied

// A shallow clone that also keeps the prototype
const clone = (o) => Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(o), Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors(o));
```

**Typical uses.** Hidden metadata (`enumerable: false`) that should not appear in JSON or loops; constants on objects (`writable: false`); lazily computed properties (see Getters, Setters and Accessors); and libraries that add properties to objects they do not own without disturbing enumeration, as polyfills do.

**Key Takeaways**

- Data properties have `value` and `writable`. Accessor properties have `get` and `set`. Both have `enumerable` and `configurable`.
- Properties created by assignment or literals have every attribute set to `true`. Attributes omitted in `defineProperty` default to `false`.
- Non-writable properties reject assignment, non-enumerable properties are hidden from enumeration and JSON, and non-configurable properties cannot be deleted or redefined.
- `seal` and `freeze` work by setting `configurable` and `writable` to `false` on every property.
- Use `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors` with `defineProperties` or `Object.create` to copy accessors faithfully.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Print the descriptors of `Math.PI`, of `"length"` on an array, and of a property you create with an object literal. Explain each attribute's value.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `defineConstants(obj, map)` that adds every entry of `map` to `obj` as a non-writable, non-configurable, enumerable property. Then write `hide(obj, key)` that makes an existing property non-enumerable without changing its value. Verify both with `Object.keys` and `JSON.stringify`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can't you `delete Math.PI` or reassign it, and how could you create a property with the same behaviour on your own object?" *Hint:* inspect its descriptor, and recall the default attribute values of `Object.defineProperty`.

#### Method Borrowing and Mixins

Inheritance gives an object *one* parent. Real designs often need behaviour from several unrelated sources: a `User` that is also serialisable, observable and validatable, or an array-like `NodeList` that would benefit from an array method. Two techniques share behaviour without forcing a class hierarchy. **Method borrowing** calls another object's method on your object for a single use. **Mixins** permanently add a set of methods to a class or object.

**Method borrowing.** Most built-in methods are intentionally *generic*: they only require `this` to look like the right kind of object. With `call` and `apply` (3.3), you can run them on any compatible object.

```javascript
// Array methods on array-likes (4.2)
function joinArgs() {
  return Array.prototype.join.call(arguments, "-");    // arguments has no join method
}
console.log(joinArgs("a", "b", "c"));                  // "a-b-c"

// Object.prototype methods on objects that might shadow or lack them
const dict = Object.create(null);
dict.key = 1;
console.log(Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(dict, "key"));  // true (modern: Object.hasOwn)

// Accurate type tags (see instanceof and Type Introspection)
console.log(Object.prototype.toString.call([]));       // "[object Array]"

// Functions that expect separate arguments, applied to an array
console.log(Math.max.apply(null, [3, 9, 2]));          // 9 (modern: Math.max(...arr))
```

**Object mixins with `Object.assign`.** A mixin is an object containing methods intended to be copied into other objects or prototypes. `Object.assign` copies them onto a class's prototype, so every instance gains them.

```javascript
const Serializable = {
  serialize() { return JSON.stringify(this); },
};

const Observable = {
  on(event, fn) {
    ((this._handlers ??= {})[event] ??= []).push(fn);    // lazily create storage per instance
    return this;
  },
  emit(event, data) {
    (this._handlers?.[event] ?? []).forEach((fn) => fn(data));
  },
};

class User {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
}
Object.assign(User.prototype, Serializable, Observable);   // copy methods onto the prototype

const u = new User("Ada");
u.on("rename", (n) => console.log(`renamed to ${n}`));
u.emit("rename", "Grace");                                 // "renamed to Grace"
console.log(u.serialize());                                // '{"name":"Ada","_handlers":{...}}'
```

Notice the problems with this approach. Methods with the same name silently overwrite each other (the last mixin wins). `Object.assign` evaluates getters instead of copying them (see Property Descriptors and defineProperty). Mixin state (`_handlers`) leaks into JSON, because mixins cannot use `#private` fields. And `super` does not work inside copied methods as it would in a class.

**Subclass factory mixins.** A more robust pattern uses the fact that `extends` accepts any expression (4.3). Each mixin is a function that takes a base class and returns a subclass of it. Applying several mixins builds a linear inheritance chain, so `super` works and there are no silent overwrites: a later mixin *overrides* and can call the earlier one.

```javascript
const Timestamped = (Base) => class extends Base {
  createdAt = new Date();
  touch() { this.updatedAt = new Date(); return this; }
};

const Validated = (Base) => class extends Base {
  validate() {
    if (!this.name) throw new Error("name is required");
    return super.validate?.() ?? true;     // chains to an earlier validate if present
  }
};

class Entity { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } }
class Product extends Validated(Timestamped(Entity)) {}

const p = new Product("Lamp").touch();
console.log(p.validate(), p.createdAt instanceof Date);   // true true
```

```text
Product -> Validated(...) -> Timestamped(...) -> Entity -> Object
  (each mixin application creates one anonymous class in the chain)
```

| | Method borrowing | `Object.assign` mixin | Subclass factory mixin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | One call | Every instance (copied onto the prototype) | Every instance (through the chain) |
| Name collisions | Not applicable | Silent overwrite | Explicit override, `super` available |
| Accessors | Not applicable | Flattened to values | Preserved |
| Private fields | Not applicable | Not possible | Supported inside each mixin |
| `instanceof` the mixin | No | No | Not directly (each application is a new class) |

**Key Takeaways**

- Method borrowing runs a generic method on another object with `call` or `apply`, for example array methods on array-likes.
- `Object.assign(C.prototype, mixin)` adds methods to every instance, but collisions overwrite silently and getters are flattened.
- Subclass factory mixins (`Base => class extends Base {}`) compose behaviour into a linear chain that supports `super`, accessors and private fields.
- Mixins are a form of composition: use them for orthogonal capabilities (serialisation, events, timestamps), not for "is a" relationships.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use `Array.prototype.filter.call` on a `NodeList` or on `{ 0: 3, 1: 8, 2: 5, length: 3 }` to keep only the values greater than 4.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write an `EventEmitter` subclass factory mixin with `on`, `off` and `emit` that stores handlers in a `#private` `Map`. Apply it to two unrelated classes and show that their handlers do not leak into `JSON.stringify`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "JavaScript only supports single inheritance. How would you give a class behaviour from two independent sources, and what are the trade-offs?" *Hint:* compare copying methods onto the prototype with chaining class factories, and mention composition by holding helper objects as fields.

#### instanceof and Type Introspection

Code often needs to know what kind of value it has received: an error handler that treats `HttpError` differently from `TypeError`, a function that accepts either a string or an array, a serialiser that handles dates specially. JavaScript offers several ways to ask "what is this?", and each has blind spots. `typeof` (3.1) only distinguishes broad categories. This topic covers the tools for objects and when each one can be trusted.

**How `instanceof` works.** `x instanceof C` does not check how `x` was created. It walks `x`'s prototype chain and returns `true` if it finds `C.prototype` anywhere on it.

```javascript
function myInstanceof(x, C) {
  if (x === null || (typeof x !== "object" && typeof x !== "function")) return false; // primitives
  let proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(x);
  while (proto !== null) {
    if (proto === C.prototype) return true;
    proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto);   // keep climbing the chain
  }
  return false;
}

class Animal {}
class Dog extends Animal {}
const d = new Dog();
console.log(d instanceof Dog, d instanceof Animal, d instanceof Object);  // true true true
console.log(myInstanceof(d, Animal));                                    // true
```

**Where `instanceof` misleads.**

```javascript
// 1. Primitives are never instances
console.log("text" instanceof String);           // false: a primitive, not a String object

// 2. The prototype chain can be changed after creation
const fake = Object.setPrototypeOf({}, Dog.prototype);
console.log(fake instanceof Dog);                // true, although no Dog constructor ever ran

// 3. Objects from another realm (iframe, worker message, vm context) have different built-ins
const iframe = document.createElement("iframe");
document.body.append(iframe);
const FrameArray = iframe.contentWindow.Array;
const foreign = new FrameArray(1, 2);
console.log(foreign instanceof Array);           // false: a different Array.prototype
console.log(Array.isArray(foreign));             // true: realm-independent check
```

The cross-realm problem matters in browsers (iframes, `postMessage`), in Node.js (`vm` contexts), and whenever two copies of the same library are loaded in a bundle: each copy has its own class, so `instanceof` fails between them.

**Customising `instanceof`.** A class can define `static [Symbol.hasInstance](x)` to decide what counts as an instance. This is rarely needed, but it allows duck-typed `instanceof` checks:

```javascript
class Iterable {
  static [Symbol.hasInstance](x) { return x != null && typeof x[Symbol.iterator] === "function"; }
}
console.log([1] instanceof Iterable, "abc" instanceof Iterable, {} instanceof Iterable);
// true true false
```

**Other introspection tools.**

| Tool | Answers | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof x` | Primitive type, or `"object"` / `"function"` | `typeof null === "object"` (3.1) |
| `x instanceof C` | Is `C.prototype` on `x`'s chain? | Fails across realms. `false` for primitives. |
| `proto.isPrototypeOf(x)` | Is `proto` on `x`'s chain? | Works for OLOO objects with no constructor |
| `Object.getPrototypeOf(x) === C.prototype` | Is `x` a *direct* instance of `C`? | Excludes subclasses |
| `x.constructor === C` / `x.constructor.name` | What constructor does `x` claim? | Easily overwritten. Missing on null-prototype objects. |
| `Array.isArray(x)` | Is `x` an array? | Realm-safe. The right way to detect arrays. |
| `Object.prototype.toString.call(x)` | Built-in tag such as `"[object Date]"` | Realm-safe for built-ins. Customisable with `Symbol.toStringTag`. |
| `#field in x` | Was `x` constructed by this class? | Unforgeable brand check (4.3) |
| Duck typing | Does `x` have the methods I need? | Most flexible (4.3) |

```javascript
const tag = (x) => Object.prototype.toString.call(x).slice(8, -1);   // "[object Date]" -> "Date"
console.log(tag(null), tag([]), tag(new Date()), tag(/x/), tag(new Map())); // Null Array Date RegExp Map

class Temperature {
  get [Symbol.toStringTag]() { return "Temperature"; }   // custom tag
}
console.log(tag(new Temperature()));                      // "Temperature"
console.log(String(new Temperature()));                   // "[object Temperature]"
```

**Choosing a check.** Use `typeof` for primitives and functions, `Array.isArray` for arrays, `instanceof` for your own classes and errors within one program, `#field in obj` when you must be certain an object came from your class, and duck typing when you only need a capability.

**Key Takeaways**

- `x instanceof C` checks whether `C.prototype` appears anywhere on `x`'s prototype chain. It does not check how `x` was created.
- `instanceof` returns `false` for primitives and fails for objects from other realms or from duplicate copies of a library.
- Use `Array.isArray` for arrays and `Object.prototype.toString.call` for built-in type tags. Both are realm-safe.
- `constructor` and `toStringTag` can be overwritten, so treat them as hints. Private brand checks (`#x in obj`) cannot be forged.
- Prefer duck typing when you only need to know what an object can do.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `describe(value)` that returns `"null"`, `"array"`, `"date"`, a class name for class instances, or the `typeof` result otherwise. Test it with ten different values.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create an iframe, construct a `Date` and an `Error` inside it, and compare the results of `instanceof`, `Object.prototype.toString.call` and duck typing (`typeof x.getTime === "function"`) for each. Explain every `false`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does `instanceof` work, and how can it give a wrong answer?" *Hint:* implement it with `Object.getPrototypeOf` in a loop, then think of `setPrototypeOf`, multiple realms, `Symbol.hasInstance` and primitives.

#### Proxy and Reflect APIs

Normally, the operations performed on an object (reading a property, assigning one, checking `in`, deleting, calling a function) have fixed built-in behaviour. A **`Proxy`** lets you intercept these fundamental operations and redefine them. It wraps a **target** object, and a **handler** object provides **traps**, functions that run instead of the default behaviour. Think of a receptionist in front of an office: every request goes through them, and they can forward it unchanged, modify it, log it, or refuse it. The companion **`Reflect`** object provides the default behaviour of every operation as a plain function, so traps can easily forward requests to the target. Together they enable validation layers, default values, logging, and the reactivity systems of frameworks such as Vue 3 and MobX.

**Basic structure.**

```javascript
const target = { name: "Ada" };

const handler = {
  get(target, key, receiver) {                         // intercepts property reads
    console.log(`read ${String(key)}`);
    return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);         // forward to the default behaviour
  },
};

const proxy = new Proxy(target, handler);
console.log(proxy.name);        // logs "read name", then "Ada"
proxy.age = 36;                 // no set trap: the default runs and writes to target
console.log(target.age);        // 36
```

**The main traps.** Every internal operation has a trap with the same name as its `Reflect` method.

| Trap / `Reflect` method | Intercepts |
|---|---|
| `get(target, key, receiver)` | `proxy.key`, `proxy[key]` |
| `set(target, key, value, receiver)` | `proxy.key = value` (must return `true` on success) |
| `has(target, key)` | `key in proxy` |
| `deleteProperty(target, key)` | `delete proxy.key` |
| `ownKeys(target)` | `Object.keys`, `Reflect.ownKeys`, `for...in` |
| `getOwnPropertyDescriptor` / `defineProperty` | Descriptor reads and `Object.defineProperty` |
| `getPrototypeOf` / `setPrototypeOf` | Prototype access, `instanceof` |
| `apply(target, thisArg, args)` | Calling a proxied function |
| `construct(target, args, newTarget)` | `new proxy(...)` |

**Why `Reflect` exists.** `Reflect` methods do exactly what the language would do by default, but with a function-call interface. They return booleans instead of throwing for operations that can fail (`Reflect.set`, `Reflect.defineProperty`), and they take a `receiver` argument so getters and setters run with the correct `this`. Forwarding with `Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)` rather than `target[key]` keeps inherited getters working correctly through the proxy.

**Example: validation.**

```javascript
"use strict";

function typed(schema) {
  return new Proxy({}, {
    set(target, key, value, receiver) {
      const expected = schema[key];
      if (!expected) throw new TypeError(`Unknown property "${key}"`);
      if (typeof value !== expected) {
        throw new TypeError(`"${key}" must be a ${expected}, got ${typeof value}`);
      }
      return Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver);   // returns true on success
    },
  });
}

const person = typed({ name: "string", age: "number" });
person.name = "Ada";
// person.age = "36";        // TypeError: "age" must be a number, got string
// person.email = "a@b.c";   // TypeError: Unknown property "email"
```

**Example: negative indices and defaults.**

```javascript
const pythonic = (arr) => new Proxy(arr, {
  get(target, key, receiver) {
    if (typeof key === "string" && /^-\d+$/.test(key)) {   // property keys arrive as strings
      key = String(target.length + Number(key));           // -1 -> length - 1
    }
    return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);
  },
});
console.log(pythonic(["a", "b", "c"])[-1]);                // "c"

const withDefaults = (obj, fallback) => new Proxy(obj, {
  get: (t, k, r) => (k in t ? Reflect.get(t, k, r) : fallback),
});
const labels = withDefaults({ save: "Save" }, "(missing label)");
console.log(labels.save, labels.cancel);                   // "Save" "(missing label)"
```

**Example: reactivity.** The core idea behind reactive frameworks fits in a few lines: intercept writes and notify subscribers.

```javascript
function reactive(obj, onChange) {
  return new Proxy(obj, {
    set(target, key, value, receiver) {
      const old = target[key];
      const ok = Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver);
      if (ok && old !== value) onChange(key, old, value);    // notify only on real changes
      return ok;
    },
  });
}

const state = reactive({ count: 0 }, (k, o, n) => console.log(`${k}: ${o} -> ${n}`));
state.count++;        // "count: 0 -> 1": the UI could re-render here
```

**Limits and costs.**

- **Invariants.** Traps cannot lie about the target in ways that break the language's guarantees. For example, a `get` trap must report the real value of a non-writable, non-configurable property, or the engine throws a `TypeError`.
- **Identity.** A proxy is a different object from its target: `proxy !== target`, and code that holds the target bypasses the traps.
- **Private fields and internal slots.** Built-ins such as `Map`, `Set` and `Date`, and classes with `#private` fields, store data in internal slots that a proxy does not have. Calling `proxy.method()` runs with `this` set to the proxy and throws a `TypeError`. The usual fix is a `get` trap that binds methods to the target.
- **Performance.** Every intercepted operation runs a function, so proxies are much slower than plain objects in hot code.
- **Revocation.** `Proxy.revocable(target, handler)` returns `{ proxy, revoke }`. After `revoke()`, every operation on the proxy throws, which is useful for handing out access temporarily.

**Key Takeaways**

- A `Proxy` wraps a target and lets handler traps intercept fundamental operations such as `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `apply` and `construct`.
- `Reflect` provides the default behaviour of each operation. Forward with `Reflect.method(...args)` and pass `receiver` so accessors keep the correct `this`.
- Typical uses include validation, default values, logging and debugging, access control and reactive state.
- A `set` trap must return `true`, and traps must respect invariants of non-configurable properties.
- Proxies do not have the target's internal slots or `#private` fields, are slower than plain objects, and are a different object from the target.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `logged(obj)` proxy that logs every property read and write with its key and value, and use it to discover which properties a library function reads from an options object you pass to it.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `readonlyDeep(obj)`, a proxy that throws on any `set`, `deleteProperty` or `defineProperty` at any depth by wrapping nested objects lazily in the `get` trap. Compare it with `deepFreeze` from 4.1: which one protects the original object, and which only protects access through the wrapper?
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `new Proxy(new Map(), {}).get('a')` throw, and how would you make a proxy around a `Map` work?" *Hint:* consider what `this` is when the `get` method runs, and where a `Map` actually stores its entries.

#### Memory Model and Garbage Collection

In JavaScript you never free memory yourself. You create objects, and the engine reclaims them when they are no longer needed. This is convenient, but it does not make memory problems impossible. Long-running single-page applications, servers and browser extensions regularly suffer from **memory leaks**: objects your program no longer needs but still references, so the collector cannot free them. It also helps to know how engines lay out objects in memory, because a few coding habits make objects significantly faster.

**Stack and heap.** Conceptually, a running program uses two memory regions. The **call stack** holds a frame for each active function call, with its local variables and arguments. Primitives can live there directly. The **heap** is a large pool where objects, arrays, functions and closures' captured variables live. Variables on the stack hold references into the heap. (Engines are free to optimise beyond this model, but it is the right mental picture.)

```text
 Call stack                      Heap
+---------------------+         +-------------------------------+
| render()            |         |                               |
|   items: ref -------+-------->| [ {..}, {..}, {..} ]          |
|   count: 3          |         |        |                      |
+---------------------+         |        +--> { id: 1, ... }    |
| main()              |         |                               |
|   config: ref ------+-------->| { theme: "dark" }             |
+---------------------+         |                               |
  frames are discarded          |  { old: "data" }  <- unreachable: garbage
  when functions return         +-------------------------------+
```

**Reachability.** The garbage collector does not ask "will this object be used again?" (which is impossible to know in general). It asks "can the program still *reach* this object?". It starts from a set of **roots**: global variables, the variables of every function on the call stack, and active handles held by the host such as pending timers, registered event listeners and the DOM tree. Every object reachable from a root by following references is kept alive. Everything else is garbage and can be reclaimed.

**Mark-and-sweep.** Modern collectors are based on **mark-and-sweep**: mark every object reachable from the roots, then sweep (free) everything unmarked. Because reachability is what counts, circular references are not a problem. Two objects that reference each other but are unreachable from the roots are collected together. (Early reference-counting collectors, such as the one in old Internet Explorer for DOM objects, leaked on cycles.)

**Generational collection.** Most objects die young: temporary arrays, intermediate strings, callback closures. Engines such as V8 exploit this by splitting the heap into a **young generation**, collected very frequently with a fast copying "scavenger", and an **old generation** for objects that survived several collections, collected less often with an incremental and concurrent mark-sweep-compact. Most collection work runs in small steps or on background threads to avoid long pauses that would drop animation frames.

**How engines store objects: hidden classes.** A dictionary for every object would be slow. Instead, engines give each object a **hidden class** (called a "map" in V8 and a "shape" in SpiderMonkey) that describes its layout: which properties it has, in what order, at which offsets. Objects created the same way share a hidden class, and property access code caches the offset (an **inline cache**), making `obj.x` nearly as fast as a field access in C. Some habits keep objects on this fast path:

```javascript
// Good: same properties, same order, set in one place (a constructor or literal)
class Point { constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } }
const pts = [new Point(1, 2), new Point(3, 4)];        // all share one hidden class

// Slower: different insertion orders produce different hidden classes
const a = {}; a.x = 1; a.y = 2;
const b = {}; b.y = 2; b.x = 1;                        // different shape from a

// Slower: delete can move an object to the slow "dictionary mode"
const c = { x: 1, y: 2 };
delete c.x;                                            // prefer c.x = undefined if the shape matters
```

These are micro-optimisations: they matter for hot code processing many objects, not for ordinary application logic.

**Common leaks and their fixes.**

| Leak | Why the memory stays reachable | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Forgotten timers | `setInterval` callbacks are roots, and so is everything their closures capture | `clearInterval` when the owner goes away |
| Forgotten event listeners | The listener (and its closure) is referenced by the target, often `window` or `document` | `removeEventListener`, or `{ signal }` with an `AbortController` |
| Detached DOM nodes | A removed element is still referenced from a JavaScript variable or cache | Drop references, or use a `WeakMap` keyed by the element |
| Unbounded caches | A `Map` or array that only grows | Size limits (LRU, 4.2), expiry, or `WeakMap` |
| Accidental globals | Assigning to an undeclared variable in sloppy mode creates a global | Strict mode (3.4) |
| Large captured scopes | A long-lived closure keeps alive the variables it captures (3.3) | Capture only what you need, and null out large data |

```javascript
class LiveSearch {
  #controller = new AbortController();
  #results = [];

  constructor(input) {
    const { signal } = this.#controller;
    input.addEventListener("input", (e) => this.#search(e.target.value), { signal });
    window.addEventListener("resize", () => this.#layout(), { signal });  // window is a long-lived root
    this.timer = setInterval(() => this.#refresh(), 30_000);
  }

  destroy() {
    this.#controller.abort();     // removes BOTH listeners at once
    clearInterval(this.timer);    // the interval no longer references this object
    this.#results = [];           // release large data early
  }

  #search(q) {} #layout() {} #refresh() {}
}
// Without destroy(), the window listener and the interval keep every LiveSearch alive forever,
// together with its input element and results, even after the component is removed from the page.
```

**Weak references.** `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` (4.2) hold their keys without keeping them alive. For rarer cases, ES2021 added `WeakRef` (a reference that does not prevent collection; `deref()` returns the object or `undefined`) and `FinalizationRegistry` (a callback that *may* run some time after an object is collected). Collection timing is unpredictable, so never use them for program logic that must run, only for optional cleanup and caches.

**Finding leaks.** In Chrome DevTools, the **Memory** panel can take **heap snapshots**. Take one, perform an action several times (open and close a dialog), take another, and compare: objects whose count keeps growing are leaking. The **retainers** view shows the chain of references from a root that keeps an object alive, which tells you which reference to break. The **Performance** panel's memory graph shows whether the heap returns to its baseline after garbage collection.

**Key Takeaways**

- Objects live on the heap and are referenced from the stack, globals and host structures. Memory is reclaimed automatically when an object becomes unreachable from the roots.
- Mark-and-sweep collectors handle circular references. Generational collection makes short-lived objects cheap.
- A leak is memory that is still reachable but no longer needed: forgotten timers and listeners, detached DOM nodes, unbounded caches and long-lived closures.
- Always provide a teardown path (`clearInterval`, `AbortController` for listeners) for long-lived resources.
- Engines optimise objects that share a hidden class: initialise the same properties in the same order and avoid `delete` in hot code.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a page with a button that creates 10,000 objects and stores them in a global array, and another button that clears the array. Watch the JavaScript heap size in DevTools' Performance monitor while clicking both, and force a garbage collection to see the memory return.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a small modal component that adds a `keydown` listener to `document` and a `setInterval` when opened. Open and close it 50 times without cleanup, take heap snapshots before and after, and find the leaked instances in the comparison view. Then fix the leak with an `AbortController` and `clearInterval`, and verify with a new snapshot.
> 3. *(Interview)* "JavaScript has a garbage collector, so how can a JavaScript application leak memory?" *Hint:* distinguish "unreachable" from "no longer needed", and give examples involving roots that the browser holds on your behalf.

<a id="5-asynchronous-programming-in-javascript"></a>
## 5. Asynchronous Programming in JavaScript

Web applications are full of operations that take an unknown amount of time, such as network requests, timers, user input and file reads. JavaScript still runs your code on a single thread. This chapter explains how the language handles waiting without freezing: the event loop and its queues, then the three generations of asynchronous code (callbacks, promises and `async`/`await`), and finally how the browser talks to servers with `XMLHttpRequest` and `fetch`. Almost every bug that involves "it works sometimes" or "the value is `undefined` here" in front-end code comes from a misunderstanding of the ideas in this chapter.

<a id="51-the-concurrency-model"></a>
### 5.1 The Concurrency Model

This subchapter explains how a single-threaded language can handle many things at once: the call stack, the event loop that feeds it, the queues that decide what runs next, the timing APIs built on top of them, and why blocking the thread is the cardinal sin of front-end code.

#### Single-Threaded Execution and the Call Stack

Many languages handle concurrent work with multiple threads, each running its own code at the same time with shared memory. That model is powerful but notoriously hard to get right: two threads writing the same variable at the same time produce race conditions, and protecting data with locks leads to deadlocks. JavaScript was designed in 1995 to script a web page, where the main shared resource is the DOM. Letting several threads mutate the DOM at once would have made every page a minefield. So JavaScript runs on **one thread**: at any moment exactly one piece of your JavaScript is executing, and it runs until it finishes.

This property is called **run-to-completion**. Once a function starts, nothing else in your JavaScript can interrupt it: no event handler, no timer callback, no network response. They all wait until the current code has finished. This makes reasoning simple (no locks, no data races on ordinary variables) but has a cost: if your code runs for a long time, everything else waits too.

**The call stack.** To keep track of where it is, the engine uses a **call stack**: a stack of **frames**, one per function call that has started but not yet returned. Each frame holds the function's local variables, its arguments and the position to return to.

- Calling a function **pushes** a new frame on top of the stack.
- Returning from a function **pops** its frame.
- The frame on top is the code currently running.
- When the stack is empty, the engine is idle and can pick up the next piece of work.

Think of a stack of plates in a cafeteria: you can only add or remove the top plate. A function that calls another function puts a new plate on top and cannot continue until that plate is removed.

```javascript
function square(n) {
  return n * n;
}

function sumOfSquares(a, b) {
  return square(a) + square(b);   // two nested calls
}

function main() {
  const result = sumOfSquares(3, 4);
  console.log(result);            // 25
}

main();
```

The stack evolves like this (each row is a snapshot, with the top of the stack on the left):

```text
time  call stack (top -> bottom)            event
----  ------------------------------------  ----------------------------------
 t1   main                                  main() is called
 t2   sumOfSquares | main                   main calls sumOfSquares(3, 4)
 t3   square | sumOfSquares | main          square(3) runs, returns 9, is popped
 t4   square | sumOfSquares | main          square(4) runs, returns 16, is popped
 t5   sumOfSquares | main                   sumOfSquares returns 25, is popped
 t6   console.log | main                    console.log prints 25, is popped
 t7   main                                  main returns, is popped
 t8   (empty)                               the engine is free for the next task
```

**Stack traces.** When an error is thrown, the engine records the frames on the stack at that moment. That is the **stack trace** you see in the console, read from the innermost call (top) to the outermost (bottom).

```javascript
function c() { throw new Error("boom"); }
function b() { c(); }
function a() { b(); }
a();
// Uncaught Error: boom
//     at c (app.js:1:22)    <- top of the stack: where the error happened
//     at b (app.js:2:16)
//     at a (app.js:3:16)
//     at app.js:4:1         <- bottom: the top-level script
```

**Stack overflow.** The stack has a limited size (typically a few thousand to tens of thousands of frames, depending on the engine and frame size). Unbounded recursion fills it and the engine throws a `RangeError`.

```javascript
function forever(n) {
  return forever(n + 1);  // no base case: every call adds a frame
}
forever(0);               // RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

**What "single-threaded" does and does not mean.** Only the execution of *your JavaScript* is single-threaded. The browser itself is heavily multi-threaded: network requests, image decoding, timers, disk access and parts of rendering happen on other threads. When those operations finish, they do not interrupt your code. They put a callback in a queue, and the event loop (next topic) runs it later on the main thread.

```text
+--------------------------- Browser process ---------------------------+
|                                                                        |
|   Main thread (one at a time)          Other browser threads           |
|   +-----------------------+            +--------------------------+    |
|   |  JavaScript engine    |  request   |  Network stack           |    |
|   |  +-----------------+  | ---------> |  Timers                  |    |
|   |  |   Call stack    |  |            |  File system, decoders   |    |
|   |  +-----------------+  | <--------- |  (run in parallel)       |    |
|   |  Style, layout, paint |  callback  +--------------------------+    |
|   +-----------------------+  queued                                    |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

You can run JavaScript on true parallel threads with **Web Workers** (6.4), but each worker has its own stack, its own event loop and no access to the DOM. Workers talk to the main thread by passing messages, not by sharing ordinary variables.

**Key Takeaways**

- JavaScript runs your code on a single thread. Code runs to completion: nothing interrupts a running function.
- The call stack holds one frame per active function call. Calling pushes a frame, returning pops it, and the top frame is the code that is running.
- Stack traces are snapshots of the call stack at the moment an error is created.
- Unbounded recursion exhausts the stack and throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.
- The browser is multi-threaded. Only your JavaScript runs on one thread, and results from other threads come back as queued callbacks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write three functions `first`, `second` and `third`, where each calls the next and `third` calls `console.trace()`. Run the code and match each line of the printed trace to a frame on the call stack.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a recursive `depth()` function that counts how many times it can call itself before a `RangeError` is thrown (catch the error and print the counter). Compare the result in two different browsers, then add three large local variables to the function and observe how the limit changes.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If JavaScript is single-threaded, how can a page download five images at the same time while the user scrolls?" *Hint:* separate "the thread that runs JavaScript" from "the threads the browser uses to do I/O", and explain how results come back.

#### The Event Loop

If JavaScript can only do one thing at a time and code runs to completion, something has to decide *what runs next* once the call stack is empty. A click happened, a timer expired and a network response arrived, all while your code was busy. They must be run one by one, in some order, without being lost. The component that coordinates this is the **event loop**.

An analogy: a restaurant with a single chef (the main thread). Waiters (browser threads) take orders, fetch ingredients and watch the oven in parallel, but only the chef cooks. When a waiter has something for the chef, they pin a ticket on a rail (the queue). The chef finishes the current dish completely (run-to-completion), then takes the next ticket. The chef never stops in the middle of a dish to look at the rail.

**The basic algorithm.** Simplified, the event loop in a browser repeats these steps forever:

```text
while (true) {
  1. Take the oldest task from a task queue (if any) and run it until the call stack is empty.
  2. Run ALL microtasks in the microtask queue, including any added while doing so.
  3. If it is time to render a frame (about every 16.7 ms at 60 Hz):
       a. run requestAnimationFrame callbacks
       b. recalculate styles, layout, paint
  4. If there is spare time before the next frame, run idle callbacks (requestIdleCallback).
  5. If there is nothing to do, sleep until something is queued.
}
```

Each turn of this loop is called a **tick** or an **iteration**. The details of tasks versus microtasks are covered in the next topic. Here the key idea is the overall flow:

```text
             +---------------------+
             |     Call stack      |  <-- runs one thing at a time
             +----------^----------+
                        | event loop moves work here when the stack is empty
   +--------------------+----------------------+
   |                    |                      |
+--+-------------+  +---+------------+  +------+---------+
| Microtask queue|  |  Task queue(s) |  | Render steps   |
| promise        |  |  click, timer, |  | rAF, style,    |
| reactions      |  |  network, msg  |  | layout, paint  |
+----------------+  +---^------------+  +----------------+
                        |
            +-----------+-------------+
            |   Browser / Web APIs    |  setTimeout, fetch, DOM events...
            |   (other threads)       |
            +-------------------------+
```

**Following one example.** Consider this code:

```javascript
console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("B");          // runs in a later task
}, 0);

console.log("C");
// Output: A, C, B
```

Step by step:

1. The whole script is itself a task. `console.log("A")` runs and prints `A`.
2. `setTimeout` is a Web API. The engine hands the callback and the delay to the browser's timer system and returns immediately. Nothing is printed.
3. `console.log("C")` prints `C`. The script ends and the call stack is empty.
4. Meanwhile the timer (0 ms) has expired, and the browser has put the callback in the task queue.
5. The event loop sees an empty stack, takes the callback task and runs it: `B` is printed.

`B` comes last even with a delay of `0`, because a callback can only run when the stack is empty. A delay is a *minimum waiting time*, not a guarantee.

**Rendering waits too.** The browser can only repaint the page between tasks (step 3). If you change the DOM several times in one task, the user only ever sees the final state. If one task runs for 2 seconds, the page cannot repaint for 2 seconds, which is what users experience as a frozen page.

```javascript
const box = document.querySelector("#box");
box.style.background = "red";
box.style.background = "blue";  // the user never sees red: no render step ran in between
```

**One loop per agent.** Every window (and each same-origin group of iframes) has its own event loop. Each Web Worker has its own as well. Node.js has a different event loop built on the libuv library, with more phases (timers, I/O callbacks, `setImmediate`, close callbacks), covered in 11.3. The concepts of tasks, microtasks and run-to-completion are the same.

**Key Takeaways**

- The event loop repeatedly takes one task, runs it to completion, drains the microtask queue, and gives the browser a chance to render.
- Asynchronous APIs hand work to the browser and return immediately. Their callbacks are queued and run later, only when the call stack is empty.
- A timer delay is a minimum, never an exact time.
- Rendering happens between tasks, so a long task freezes both input handling and painting.
- Each window and each worker has its own event loop. Node.js uses a different loop implementation built on the same principles.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Predict the output order of a script that logs `1`, schedules `setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0)`, schedules `setTimeout(() => console.log(3), 10)`, and logs `4`. Run it to check.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a button that, when clicked, sets a status element to "Working..." and then runs a loop that takes about 3 seconds before setting it to "Done". Explain why "Working..." never appears. Fix it so the text is visible before the heavy work starts, using only `setTimeout`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the event loop, and why does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` not run `fn` immediately?" *Hint:* describe the relationship between the call stack, the queue and the condition that must be true before a queued callback runs.

#### Task Queue and Microtask Queue

The previous topic described "the queue" as if there were only one. In reality there are two very different kinds of queue, and their priority rules explain output orders that otherwise look random. The distinction exists because some work must happen "as soon as possible, but after the current code", before the browser handles any other event or repaints. Promise reactions are the main example: when a promise settles, its handlers should run before anything else gets a chance to observe an inconsistent state.

**Tasks (macrotasks).** A **task** is a unit of work scheduled by the browser. Sources include:

- running a `<script>` element
- `setTimeout` and `setInterval` callbacks
- user input events (click, keydown, input...)
- network events (XHR `load`, WebSocket `message`)
- `postMessage` and `MessageChannel` messages

The browser may keep several task queues (for example one for user input and one for timers) and can choose which queue to serve next, typically prioritising user input. Inside a single queue, order is first in, first out. **Only one task runs per event loop iteration.**

**Microtasks.** A **microtask** is a smaller unit of work that runs right after the current task (or the current callback) finishes, *before* the next task and before rendering. Sources include:

- promise reactions (callbacks passed to `then`, `catch`, `finally`)
- the continuation of an `async` function after `await`
- `queueMicrotask(fn)`
- `MutationObserver` callbacks

**The microtask queue is drained completely.** After each task, the event loop runs microtasks until the queue is empty, *including microtasks added by other microtasks*. This is the key rule.

```text
One event loop iteration:

  +------------------+   +------------------------------+   +-----------+
  | run ONE task     |-->| run ALL microtasks           |-->| maybe     |--> next iteration
  | (e.g. a click    |   | (and those they schedule)    |   | render    |
  |  handler)        |   | until the queue is empty     |   |           |
  +------------------+   +------------------------------+   +-----------+
```

**The classic ordering puzzle.**

```javascript
console.log("1: script start");

setTimeout(() => console.log("2: timeout"), 0);       // task

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log("3: promise 1"))            // microtask
  .then(() => console.log("4: promise 2"));           // microtask, queued when promise 1 finishes

queueMicrotask(() => console.log("5: microtask"));    // microtask

console.log("6: script end");

// Output:
// 1: script start
// 6: script end
// 3: promise 1
// 5: microtask
// 4: promise 2
// 2: timeout
```

Why:

1. The script is the current task. It prints `1` and `6`, and schedules one task (the timeout) and two microtasks (`promise 1`, `microtask`).
2. The script task ends, so the microtask queue is drained: `promise 1` runs (and its completion queues `promise 2`), then `microtask` runs, then `promise 2` runs because the queue must be empty before moving on.
3. Only then does the event loop take the next task: `timeout`.

The state of the queues just after the script ends:

```text
Microtask queue: [ promise 1 ] [ microtask ]
Task queue:      [ timeout ]

After running promise 1:
Microtask queue: [ microtask ] [ promise 2 ]   <- promise 2 joins the end of the same drain
Task queue:      [ timeout ]
```

**Comparison.**

| | Task (macrotask) | Microtask |
|---|---|---|
| Typical sources | `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, events, network callbacks, `postMessage` | Promise reactions, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver` |
| How many per iteration | One | All of them, until the queue is empty |
| Runs before rendering? | Rendering may happen between two tasks | Always before the next render |
| Can starve the page? | No, other tasks and renders interleave | Yes, a microtask that keeps scheduling microtasks blocks forever |

**Microtask starvation.** Because the queue is drained completely, a microtask that always schedules another one never lets the event loop move on. The page freezes as badly as with an infinite loop, even though each microtask is short.

```javascript
function spin() {
  queueMicrotask(spin);   // each microtask schedules another: the queue never empties
}
// spin();                // freezes the tab: no task, no click, no render ever runs again

function polite() {
  setTimeout(polite, 0);  // each call is a new task: the browser can render and handle input between them
}
```

**`queueMicrotask` in practice.** Use it when you need to defer work until the current synchronous code has finished, but before anything else happens. A typical use is batching: many synchronous changes are collected, and one microtask processes them all.

```javascript
const pending = [];
let scheduled = false;

function logChange(change) {
  pending.push(change);
  if (!scheduled) {
    scheduled = true;
    queueMicrotask(() => {           // runs once, after all synchronous calls
      console.log("Batch:", pending.splice(0));
      scheduled = false;
    });
  }
}

logChange("a"); logChange("b"); logChange("c");
// Batch: ["a", "b", "c"]  (a single log, not three)
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Tasks come from timers, events, network callbacks and messages. The event loop runs one task per iteration.
- Microtasks come from promise reactions, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask` and `MutationObserver`.
- After every task the microtask queue is drained completely, including microtasks added during the drain.
- Promise callbacks therefore always run before a `setTimeout(..., 0)` callback scheduled at the same time.
- A chain of microtasks that never ends starves the event loop and freezes the page. Use a task (`setTimeout`) when you want to yield to the browser.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a script that mixes two `console.log` calls, one `setTimeout(..., 0)`, one `Promise.resolve().then(...)` and one `queueMicrotask(...)`. Write down your predicted output order before running it.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Predict the output of a `setTimeout` callback that itself calls `Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("inner micro"))` and `setTimeout(() => console.log("inner task"), 0)`, placed next to a second top-level `setTimeout` that logs `"second task"`. Explain the order in terms of iterations of the event loop.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between a microtask and a macrotask? Give an example where the difference changes the program's output." *Hint:* focus on how many of each run per event loop iteration, and when rendering can happen.

#### Timers and requestAnimationFrame

Programs often need to do something later (show a tooltip after 500 ms), repeatedly (poll a server every 30 seconds) or once per screen refresh (animate an element). JavaScript cannot simply "sleep", because sleeping would block the only thread. Instead, the browser provides scheduling APIs that queue a callback for the right moment.

**`setTimeout` and `clearTimeout`.** `setTimeout(callback, delay, ...args)` asks the browser to queue `callback` as a task after at least `delay` milliseconds. It returns a numeric ID that you can pass to `clearTimeout` to cancel it.

```javascript
const id = setTimeout((name) => {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}`);
}, 1000, "Ada");               // extra arguments are passed to the callback

// Changed our mind before the second elapsed:
clearTimeout(id);              // the callback will never run
```

A common pattern is a "delay" helper that returns a promise (see Promisification of Callback APIs, 5.2):

```javascript
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
await sleep(500);              // pauses only this async function, not the thread
```

**Why timers are not precise.** The delay is a minimum. The actual delay is longer when:

- the main thread is busy: the callback waits until the current task and the microtasks have finished
- timers are nested deeply: after five levels of nested `setTimeout` calls, browsers clamp the delay to at least 4 ms
- the tab is in the background: browsers throttle timers to at most about once per second, and some (for example Chrome) throttle chained timers in long-hidden pages to once per minute
- the device is in a power-saving mode

```javascript
const start = performance.now();
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log(`Asked for 0 ms, waited ${performance.now() - start} ms`);
}, 0);
for (let i = 0; i < 1e8; i++) {}   // busy loop: the timer callback must wait for it
// "Asked for 0 ms, waited 85.3 ms" (varies)
```

**`setInterval` and its pitfalls.** `setInterval(callback, delay)` queues the callback repeatedly, every `delay` ms, until `clearInterval(id)` is called. Two problems are common:

1. **Drift and pile-up.** The interval does not wait for the previous callback to finish. If a callback takes longer than the interval, runs pile up back to back. Browsers skip some runs rather than queueing infinitely, but timing becomes irregular.
2. **Overlapping async work.** If the callback starts an asynchronous request, a slow response can overlap with the next run.

A **recursive `setTimeout`** schedules the next run only after the current one has completed, which guarantees a gap between runs:

```javascript
// setInterval: runs every 5 s even if the previous request has not finished
const intervalId = setInterval(pollServer, 5000);

// Recursive setTimeout: waits 5 s AFTER each request completes
let timeoutId;
async function pollLoop() {
  await pollServer();                       // finish this run completely...
  timeoutId = setTimeout(pollLoop, 5000);   // ...then schedule the next one
}
pollLoop();

// Stop either version when it is no longer needed (for example, when a component is removed)
clearInterval(intervalId);
clearTimeout(timeoutId);
```

```text
setInterval(fn, 100) with fn taking 60 ms:
  |--fn--|    |--fn--|    |--fn--|
  0     60   100   160   200   260     -> starts are 100 ms apart, gaps are only 40 ms

recursive setTimeout(fn, 100):
  |--fn--|          |--fn--|          |--fn--|
  0     60         160   220         320     -> gaps are always 100 ms
```

**`requestAnimationFrame`.** Animating with `setTimeout(step, 16)` is a bad idea: the timer is not aligned with the display's refresh, so some frames get two updates and others none (visible as stutter), and it keeps running in background tabs. `requestAnimationFrame(callback)` (often shortened to rAF) asks the browser to run `callback` **just before the next repaint**. The browser calls it once per frame (60 times per second on a 60 Hz screen, 120 on a 120 Hz screen) and pauses it entirely in hidden tabs.

The callback receives a high-resolution timestamp. Base the animation on elapsed time, not on a frame counter, so that it runs at the same speed on every screen.

```javascript
const ball = document.querySelector("#ball");
const speed = 200;          // pixels per second
let start = null;
let frameId;

function step(timestamp) {  // timestamp: ms since page load, same clock as performance.now()
  if (start === null) start = timestamp;
  const elapsed = timestamp - start;
  const x = Math.min((elapsed / 1000) * speed, 400);   // time-based, frame-rate independent

  ball.style.transform = `translateX(${x}px)`;

  if (x < 400) {
    frameId = requestAnimationFrame(step);  // must re-request every frame
  }
}

frameId = requestAnimationFrame(step);
// cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);           // stops the animation
```

```text
Where each callback runs within one frame (about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz):

| task | microtasks | rAF callbacks | style | layout | paint | idle (requestIdleCallback) |
                     ^ read/write DOM here; changes appear in this frame's paint
```

**`requestIdleCallback`.** For low-priority work (sending analytics, pre-computing data), `requestIdleCallback(cb, { timeout })` runs `cb` when the browser has spare time in a frame. The callback receives a deadline object whose `timeRemaining()` tells you how long you may work. It is not available in all browsers (Safari does not support it), so feature-detect it.

**Choosing a scheduling API.**

| API | Runs | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `setTimeout(fn, ms)` | Once, as a task, after at least `ms` | Delays, deferring work to a later task, yielding to the browser |
| `setInterval(fn, ms)` | Repeatedly, every `ms` | Simple periodic work that is short and synchronous |
| Recursive `setTimeout` | Repeatedly, with a gap after each run | Polling and async periodic work |
| `requestAnimationFrame(fn)` | Once, before the next repaint | Visual updates and animations |
| `requestIdleCallback(fn)` | When the browser is idle | Low-priority background work |
| `queueMicrotask(fn)` | After the current code, before any task | Batching, consistent async ordering |

**Key Takeaways**

- `setTimeout` and `setInterval` queue tasks after a minimum delay. Busy threads, nesting, background tabs and power saving make the real delay longer.
- Always keep the returned ID and clear timers you no longer need. Forgotten intervals are a classic memory leak (4.4).
- Prefer a recursive `setTimeout` to `setInterval` when each run does asynchronous work or must not overlap.
- Use `requestAnimationFrame` for animations. It is synchronised with the display, paused in hidden tabs, and should use the timestamp to compute progress.
- Use `requestIdleCallback` for work that can wait, with a fallback where it is not supported.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a countdown from 10 to 0 that updates a `<span>` once per second using a recursive `setTimeout`, and provide a "Stop" button that cancels it.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Animate a square moving 300 px to the right over exactly 2 seconds, first with `setInterval(step, 16)` moving 2.4 px per step, then with `requestAnimationFrame` and elapsed time. Switch to another tab for 5 seconds during each animation and compare the results when you return.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why should you use `requestAnimationFrame` instead of `setTimeout` for animations?" *Hint:* talk about synchronisation with the refresh rate, behaviour in background tabs, and where the callback runs in the frame.

#### Blocking vs Non-Blocking Code

Everything in this subchapter leads to one practical rule: **never block the main thread**. Blocking code keeps the call stack busy for a long time, so the event loop cannot process clicks, run timers or repaint.
