Non-blocking code starts an operation, returns immediately, and handles the result later in a callback. Understanding the difference lets you design code that keeps the page responsive.

**An analogy.** In a blocking coffee shop, the cashier takes your order, makes your coffee and hands it to you before taking the next order. The line does not move while the machine runs. In a non-blocking coffee shop, the cashier takes your order, gives you a number and serves the next customer. When your coffee is ready, your number is called. The cashier (the main thread) is never idle waiting for the machine (I/O).

**Blocking code.** Code is blocking when it does not return until its work is done. In the browser, two kinds of blocking matter:

1. **Long computations**: loops over huge arrays, complex parsing, image processing written in JavaScript.
2. **Synchronous I/O**: APIs that wait for an external resource before returning. Most are deprecated or absent in browsers, but some remain: `alert`, `confirm` and `prompt`, synchronous `XMLHttpRequest` (deprecated on the main thread) and large synchronous `localStorage` operations.

```javascript
// Blocking: the page is frozen for the whole duration
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  const start = Date.now();
  while (Date.now() - start < 3000) {}     // busy-wait for 3 seconds
  status.textContent = "Done";             // clicks, scrolling and animations were frozen meanwhile
});

// Non-blocking: start the operation, handle the result later
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  status.textContent = "Loading...";       // this paint happens right after the handler returns
  fetch("/api/report")                     // network I/O happens on another thread
    .then((res) => res.json())
    .then((data) => {
      status.textContent = `Loaded ${data.items.length} items`;
    });
  // the handler returns immediately; the page stays responsive
});
```

```text
Blocking (3 s computation in a click handler):
main thread: [click handler ==============================] [render]
user clicks:        x     x       x            <- all wait; nothing repaints

Non-blocking (fetch):
main thread: [handler][render]  ...idle, handles input...  [then callback][render]
network:              [===========request in flight==========]
```

**Measuring "too long".** The browser treats any task that runs longer than **50 ms** as a **long task**. Humans perceive a delay above roughly 100 ms between an action and its visible response as lag, and the Core Web Vitals metric **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint) measures exactly this. Long tasks are marked in red in the DevTools Performance panel.

**Strategies for heavy computation.** Some work cannot be avoided, but it can be moved or split:

| Strategy | How | When |
|---|---|---|
| Chunking | Process a slice of the data, then yield to the event loop with `setTimeout` (or `scheduler.yield()` where supported) and continue | Large loops that must touch the DOM or main-thread state |
| Web Workers (6.4) | Run the computation on a separate thread and post the result back | CPU-heavy pure computation (parsing, compression, image filters) |
| Better algorithms | Reduce the complexity, cache results, avoid repeated DOM reads | Always the first thing to check |
| Server-side | Do the work on the server or at build time | Data that is the same for every user |

**Chunking example.** Split a big job into chunks and yield between them so that the browser can render and handle input:

```javascript
function yieldToMain() {
  // Use the Scheduler API where available, otherwise fall back to a new task
  if (globalThis.scheduler?.yield) return scheduler.yield();
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}

async function processAll(items, processItem) {
  let lastYield = performance.now();
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    processItem(items[i]);
    if (performance.now() - lastYield > 40) {   // stay under the 50 ms long-task budget
      await yieldToMain();                      // let the browser paint and handle input
      lastYield = performance.now();
    }
  }
}

processAll(hugeArray, (item) => { /* expensive work */ });
```

Note that yielding through a **microtask** (for example `await Promise.resolve()`) does *not* help: microtasks run before rendering and input handling, so the page stays frozen. You must yield through a task.

**Non-blocking does not mean parallel.** A non-blocking API lets the *waiting* happen elsewhere. Your callbacks still run one at a time on the main thread. Ten `fetch` calls can be in flight at once (concurrency), but their `then` callbacks never run at the same time (no parallelism).

| Term | Meaning | JavaScript example |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous | The caller waits for the result before continuing | `JSON.parse(text)` |
| Asynchronous | The caller continues, and the result is delivered later | `fetch(url)` |
| Blocking | The thread cannot do anything else while waiting | A 3-second `while` loop, `alert()` |
| Non-blocking | The thread is free while the operation is in progress | Any I/O API with a callback or promise |
| Concurrent | Several operations are in progress during the same period | Three requests in flight at once |
| Parallel | Several computations execute at the same instant | Code running in a Web Worker alongside the main thread |

**Key Takeaways**

- Blocking code keeps the call stack busy, so input, timers and rendering all stall. Non-blocking code starts work and handles the result in a later callback.
- Tasks longer than 50 ms are long tasks. Delays above about 100 ms feel laggy and hurt INP.
- Split heavy loops into chunks and yield with a *task* (`setTimeout`, `scheduler.yield()`), not a microtask.
- Move CPU-heavy pure computation to a Web Worker.
- Asynchronous I/O gives you concurrency, not parallelism. Callbacks still run one at a time.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a CSS animation (a spinning square) to a page, then add a button that runs a 3-second `while` loop. Observe what happens to the animation and to text selection while the loop runs.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function that computes the prime numbers below 5,000,000 and displays a progress bar while doing so. First write it as one loop (the bar will not update), then refactor it to process the range in chunks and yield between chunks so that the progress bar animates smoothly.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism, and which one does the browser's event loop give you?" *Hint:* consider ten simultaneous `fetch` calls versus ten simultaneous CPU-heavy loops, and where Web Workers fit.

<a id="52-callbacks-and-promises"></a>
### 5.2 Callbacks and Promises

This subchapter follows how asynchronous code evolved in JavaScript, from plain callbacks and their structural problems to promises, the standard object that represents a future result, and the tools for composing promises and converting older callback APIs.

#### Callback Pattern and Error-First Convention

An asynchronous operation returns before its result exists, so the result cannot be the function's return value. The oldest and simplest solution is to pass the operation a function to call when the result is ready: a **callback**. Functions are first-class values in JavaScript (3.3), so passing one as an argument is natural.

An analogy: leaving your phone number at a busy restaurant. You do not stand at the counter waiting. The restaurant calls you back when a table is free.

**Synchronous vs asynchronous callbacks.** Not every callback is asynchronous. `array.map(fn)` calls `fn` immediately, before `map` returns. An asynchronous callback is called *later*, after the function that received it has returned.

```javascript
// Synchronous callback: runs before forEach returns
[1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => console.log("sync", n));
console.log("after forEach");      // printed after all three "sync" lines

// Asynchronous callback: runs in a later task
setTimeout(() => console.log("async"), 0);
console.log("after setTimeout");   // printed BEFORE "async"
```

**Event-style callbacks.** DOM events use callbacks that can fire many times:

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {   // called on every click
  console.log("Clicked at", event.clientX, event.clientY);
});
```

**Completion-style callbacks.** For a one-shot operation the callback receives the outcome. Here is a small function that loads a script and reports success or failure:

```javascript
function loadScript(src, callback) {
  const script = document.createElement("script");
  script.src = src;
  script.onload = () => callback(null, script);                          // success
  script.onerror = () => callback(new Error(`Failed to load ${src}`));   // failure
  document.head.append(script);
}

loadScript("/js/chart.js", (err, script) => {
  if (err) {
    console.error(err.message);
    return;                              // stop here on failure
  }
  console.log("Loaded", script.src);
});
```

**The error-first convention.** Errors in asynchronous code cannot be caught with a `try/catch` around the call, because by the time the error happens the `try` block has long finished:

```javascript
try {
  setTimeout(() => {
    throw new Error("too late");    // thrown in a later task, with a different call stack
  }, 0);
} catch (e) {
  console.log("never reached");     // the try block finished before the callback ran
}
```

So errors must be *delivered* to the callback, not thrown. Node.js standardised the **error-first callback** (also called "Node-style" or "errback"), which many browser libraries also follow:

1. The callback is the **last** argument of the function.
2. The callback's **first** parameter is an error: `null` (or `undefined`) on success, an `Error` object on failure.
3. The remaining parameters hold the result and are only meaningful when the error is empty.
4. The callback is called **exactly once**.

```javascript
// Node.js: reading a file with an error-first callback
const fs = require("node:fs");

fs.readFile("config.json", "utf8", (err, text) => {
  if (err) {                         // ALWAYS check the error first
    console.error("Could not read config:", err.code);   // e.g. "ENOENT"
    return;
  }
  const config = JSON.parse(text);   // safe: text exists when err is null
  console.log(config.port);
});
```

**Writing your own error-first API.** Always call the callback asynchronously, even when the result is available immediately (for example from a cache). A function that is *sometimes* synchronous and *sometimes* asynchronous makes the order of operations unpredictable for callers. This problem is known as "releasing Zalgo".

```javascript
const cache = new Map();

function getUser(id, callback) {
  if (cache.has(id)) {
    // Wrong: callback(null, cache.get(id)) would run synchronously here
    queueMicrotask(() => callback(null, cache.get(id)));   // always asynchronous
    return;
  }
  fetchUserFromServer(id, (err, user) => {
    if (err) return callback(err);
    cache.set(id, user);
    callback(null, user);
  });
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A callback is a function passed to another function to be called later. Callbacks can be synchronous (`map`, `forEach`) or asynchronous (`setTimeout`, events, I/O).
- `try/catch` around an asynchronous call cannot catch errors that happen later in the callback.
- Error-first callbacks take `(err, result)`: check `err` first and return early on failure.
- A callback-based API should be consistently asynchronous and call its callback exactly once.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `delayedSum(a, b, callback)` that waits 500 ms and then calls `callback(null, a + b)`, or calls `callback(new TypeError(...))` immediately (but asynchronously) if either argument is not a number. Use it with a proper error-first handler.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `loadImage(url, callback)` function that follows the error-first convention, using an `Image` object's `onload` and `onerror`. Then write a test that proves the callback is never called synchronously, even when the image is already in the browser cache.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why do Node.js callbacks put the error as the first argument instead of throwing an exception?" *Hint:* think about which call stack is active when the asynchronous operation fails, and what would happen if the caller forgot to handle the error.

#### Callback Hell and Inversion of Control

Callbacks work well for one asynchronous step. Real tasks usually need several steps in sequence, each depending on the previous result: authenticate, then fetch the profile, then fetch the orders, then render. With callbacks, each step must be nested inside the previous step's callback. Two distinct problems follow: one about readability and one about trust.

**Problem 1: callback hell (the pyramid of doom).** The code drifts to the right with every step, and error handling is repeated at every level.

```javascript
login(credentials, (err, session) => {
  if (err) return showError(err);
  getProfile(session.userId, (err, profile) => {
    if (err) return showError(err);
    getOrders(profile.id, (err, orders) => {
      if (err) return showError(err);
      getShippingStatus(orders[0].id, (err, status) => {
        if (err) return showError(err);
        render(profile, orders, status);       // the actual logic, five levels deep
      });
    });
  });
});
```

```text
login(...
    getProfile(...
        getOrders(...
            getShippingStatus(...
                render(...)        <- the "pyramid of doom"
```

The shape itself is a symptom of deeper problems:

- **Error handling is duplicated** at every level, and forgetting one `if (err)` silently swallows an error.
- **Control flow is hard to express.** Loops, conditionals, retries and "run these three in parallel and wait for all" require hand-written counters and flags.
- **Variables leak between levels** through closures, so any level can accidentally modify state used by another.

Refactoring into named functions flattens the indentation, but the logic is still scattered across functions that each know who comes next:

```javascript
function start() { login(credentials, onLogin); }
function onLogin(err, session) {
  if (err) return showError(err);
  getProfile(session.userId, onProfile);    // each step hard-codes the next one
}
function onProfile(err, profile) { /* ... */ }
```

**Running callbacks in parallel by hand.** Waiting for several independent operations shows how much bookkeeping callbacks require:

```javascript
function loadAll(urls, callback) {
  const results = new Array(urls.length);
  let remaining = urls.length;
  let failed = false;

  urls.forEach((url, i) => {
    getJSON(url, (err, data) => {
      if (failed) return;                 // ignore results after the first error
      if (err) {
        failed = true;
        return callback(err);
      }
      results[i] = data;                  // keep the original order
      if (--remaining === 0) callback(null, results);
    });
  });
}
```

**Problem 2: inversion of control.** This is the more serious problem. When you pass a callback to a function, you hand control of your program's continuation to someone else's code. You *trust* that code to call your callback correctly. With third-party libraries, that trust can be misplaced. The callback might be:

| Failure | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Called too early (synchronously) | Code after the call runs in an unexpected order |
| Called too late or never | The program hangs silently, with no error |
| Called more than once | A payment is charged twice, a list is rendered twice |
| Called with the wrong arguments | Errors are silently ignored or misinterpreted |
| Errors thrown inside it are swallowed | Bugs disappear without a trace |

```javascript
// You give a third-party analytics library control over your checkout flow:
analytics.trackPurchase(order, () => {
  chargeCreditCard(order);   // what if the library retries and calls this twice?
});
```

To protect yourself, you end up wrapping every callback in defensive code: a flag that ignores second calls, a timer that fails if the callback never arrives, and so on. Every project reinvents these guards.

**What the solution needs.** A better primitive should:

1. Let the asynchronous function **return a value** that represents the future result, so that the caller keeps control.
2. Guarantee that the outcome is delivered **exactly once**, and **always asynchronously**.
3. Propagate errors automatically through a sequence of steps, like exceptions in synchronous code.
4. Compose easily: sequences, parallel groups, races.

This is exactly what promises provide (next topic).

**Key Takeaways**

- Sequencing dependent callbacks creates deeply nested code, with error handling repeated at each level.
- Parallel work and other control flow (loops, retries) with callbacks requires manual counters and flags.
- Inversion of control means trusting other code to call your continuation exactly once, at the right time, with the right arguments.
- Promises solve both problems: the caller keeps a value representing the result, and the promise guarantees single, asynchronous delivery.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Using `setTimeout`-based callbacks, write code that logs "Step 1", "Step 2" and "Step 3", one second apart, where each step starts only after the previous one finishes. Notice the nesting.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a wrapper `once(callback)` that returns a function which calls `callback` only on its first invocation and logs a warning on subsequent ones. Then write `withTimeout(callback, ms)` that calls `callback(new Error("timeout"))` if the wrapped function has not been invoked within `ms`. Use both to protect a deliberately misbehaving fake library function.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is inversion of control in the context of callbacks, and how do promises address it?" *Hint:* compare who holds the continuation in each model, and list the guarantees a promise makes that a plain callback cannot.

#### Promise States and Lifecycle

A **promise** is an object that represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. Instead of passing your continuation into the operation, the operation *returns* a promise and you attach your continuation to it. Control stays with you.

An analogy: an order receipt with a number. When you order at a food counter, you immediately get a receipt (the promise). The food (the value) does not exist yet. Later, your number is called (fulfilled) or you are told the kitchen ran out (rejected). You can hand the receipt to a friend, and they can also wait for the food. Whatever happens, the outcome is announced once and never changes.

**The three states.**

```text
                    resolve(value)
               +----------------------> FULFILLED (has a value)
               |
   PENDING ----+
               |
               +----------------------> REJECTED  (has a reason, usually an Error)
                    reject(error) or a thrown error

   FULFILLED and REJECTED are "settled" states: final and immutable.
```

| State | Meaning | Data |
|---|---|---|
| `pending` | The operation has not completed yet | None |
| `fulfilled` | The operation succeeded | A **value** |
| `rejected` | The operation failed | A **reason** (by convention an `Error`) |

A promise that is either fulfilled or rejected is called **settled**. Once settled, a promise never changes state again, and its value or reason never changes.

**Creating a promise.** The `Promise` constructor takes an **executor** function, which receives two functions: `resolve` and `reject`. The executor runs **synchronously**, immediately, inside the constructor. It typically starts an asynchronous operation and calls `resolve` or `reject` when it completes.

```javascript
const coinFlip = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  console.log("Executor runs now");             // synchronous
  setTimeout(() => {
    if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
      resolve("heads");                         // fulfil with a value
    } else {
      reject(new Error("tails"));               // reject with an Error
    }
  }, 1000);
});

console.log("After constructor");               // printed after "Executor runs now"

coinFlip.then(
  (value) => console.log("Won:", value),        // runs if fulfilled
  (error) => console.log("Lost:", error.message) // runs if rejected
);
```

**The guarantees.**

- **Settles at most once.** Calls to `resolve` or `reject` after the first one are ignored.
- **Handlers always run asynchronously**, as microtasks, even if the promise is already settled when the handler is attached.
- **Late handlers still work.** Attaching `then` to a promise that settled an hour ago calls the handler with the stored value.
- **A thrown error in the executor rejects the promise**, so you do not need a `try/catch` inside it for synchronous code.

```javascript
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  resolve(1);
  resolve(2);                  // ignored: already settled
  reject(new Error("x"));      // ignored
});
p.then((v) => console.log(v)); // 1

const q = new Promise(() => {
  throw new Error("oops");     // equivalent to calling reject(new Error("oops"))
});
q.catch((e) => console.log("Caught:", e.message));   // "Caught: oops"

Promise.resolve("ready").then((v) => console.log(v));
console.log("sync");           // printed first: handlers are always asynchronous
```

**"Resolved" is not the same as "fulfilled".** Calling `resolve` with another promise (or any **thenable**, an object with a `then` method) does not fulfil immediately. The outer promise *follows* the inner one and adopts its eventual state. The outer promise is then "resolved" (its fate is locked in) but still pending.

```javascript
const inner = new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve("inner value"), 1000));
const outer = new Promise((resolve) => resolve(inner));   // resolved, but still pending

outer.then((v) => console.log(v));   // after 1 s: "inner value" (not the inner promise object)
```

This adoption mechanism is what makes promise chaining work (next topic), and it is why `Promise.resolve(x)` and `await x` work with promises from other libraries that expose a compatible `then` method.

**Shortcuts.**

```javascript
Promise.resolve(42);                 // an already-fulfilled promise (or follows x if x is a thenable)
Promise.reject(new Error("no"));     // an already-rejected promise

// ES2024: create a promise and get its resolve/reject functions outside the executor
const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
button.addEventListener("click", () => resolve("clicked"), { once: true });
promise.then(console.log);
```

**Inspecting state.** There is no public property to read a promise's state synchronously, on purpose: code should react to settlement through handlers, not poll. In DevTools, logging a promise shows its internal `[[PromiseState]]` and `[[PromiseResult]]`.

**Unhandled rejections.** If a promise is rejected and no rejection handler is ever attached, the browser fires an `unhandledrejection` event on `window` and logs "Uncaught (in promise)". Node.js crashes the process by default. Always handle rejections (see Error Handling in Async Code, 5.3).

**Key Takeaways**

- A promise represents a future result. It is `pending`, then settles once to `fulfilled` (with a value) or `rejected` (with a reason), and never changes again.
- The executor runs synchronously. A throw inside it rejects the promise.
- Handlers always run asynchronously as microtasks, even on an already-settled promise, and handlers attached late still receive the result.
- Resolving with a promise or thenable makes the outer promise follow it. "Resolved" means locked in, not necessarily fulfilled.
- Always reject with `Error` objects so that stack traces are preserved, and always handle rejections.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a promise `wait(ms)` that fulfils with the string `"done after <ms> ms"`. Attach a handler to it twice, once immediately and once inside a `setTimeout` of 3 seconds, and confirm that both handlers receive the value.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `loadImage(url)` that returns a promise which fulfils with the `HTMLImageElement` on load and rejects with an `Error` on failure. Use `Promise.withResolvers()` for one version and the constructor for another, and test both with a valid and an invalid URL.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between a promise being resolved and being fulfilled?" *Hint:* consider what happens when you call `resolve` with another pending promise.

#### Chaining then, catch and finally

A single promise replaces a single callback. The real power of promises appears with sequences: the method `then` **returns a new promise**, so steps can be chained in a flat list instead of nested pyramids, and errors flow down the chain like exceptions flow up a call stack.

**How `then` works.** `p.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` registers handlers and immediately returns a new promise `p2`. When `p` settles, the relevant handler runs, and **what the handler does determines the state of `p2`**:

| The handler... | `p2` becomes |
|---|---|
| Returns a plain value `v` | Fulfilled with `v` |
| Returns nothing | Fulfilled with `undefined` |
| Returns a promise or thenable | Follows it: settles the same way, at the same time |
| Throws an error `e` | Rejected with `e` |
| Is missing for the outcome that occurred | Settles the same way as `p` (pass-through) |

**Flattening the pyramid.** The callback example from the previous topic, assuming each function now returns a promise:

```javascript
login(credentials)
  .then((session) => getProfile(session.userId))    // returning a promise: next step waits for it
  .then((profile) => getOrders(profile.id))
  .then((orders) => getShippingStatus(orders[0].id))
  .then((status) => render(status))
  .catch((err) => showError(err))                   // ONE handler for an error in ANY step
  .finally(() => hideSpinner());                    // runs in both cases
```

```text
login --> then --> then --> then --> then --> catch --> finally
  |         |        |        |        |        ^
  +---------+--------+--------+--------+--------+
      a rejection anywhere skips the remaining then handlers
      and jumps to the nearest catch
```

**Passing values along.** Each handler receives what the previous one returned.

```javascript
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then((x) => x * 10)          // 20
  .then((x) => {
    console.log(x);             // 20
    // no return statement: the next handler gets undefined
  })
  .then((x) => console.log(x)); // undefined
```

**Forgetting to return** is the most common chaining bug. Without `return`, the chain does not wait for the inner promise, and its result is lost:

```javascript
// Wrong: the inner promise is not returned
getUser(1)
  .then((user) => {
    getOrders(user.id);              // starts the request but does not return it
  })
  .then((orders) => console.log(orders));   // undefined, and logged BEFORE the orders arrive

// Right
getUser(1)
  .then((user) => getOrders(user.id))      // arrow with expression body returns implicitly
  .then((orders) => console.log(orders));
```

**`catch`.** `p.catch(onRejected)` is shorthand for `p.then(undefined, onRejected)`. A `catch` **recovers**: if its handler returns normally, the promise it returns is *fulfilled*, and the chain continues on the success path. To keep the chain rejected, rethrow.

```javascript
fetchPrice("AAPL")
  .catch((err) => {
    console.warn("Using cached price:", err.message);
    return cachedPrice;          // recovery: the chain continues with this value
  })
  .then((price) => display(price));   // runs with the live OR the cached price

fetchPrice("AAPL")
  .catch((err) => {
    logToServer(err);
    throw err;                   // rethrow: the next catch still sees the error
  })
  .then(display)                 // skipped on failure
  .catch(showError);
```

**`then(a, b)` versus `then(a).catch(b)`.** They are not equivalent. With the two-argument form, `b` does *not* catch errors thrown inside `a`:

```javascript
p.then(
  (v) => { throw new Error("bug in success handler"); },
  (e) => console.log("Not called for the error above")   // only handles rejections of p
);

p.then((v) => { throw new Error("bug in success handler"); })
 .catch((e) => console.log("Caught:", e.message));      // handles both p's rejection and the bug
```

**`finally`.** `p.finally(onFinally)` runs a cleanup function whether `p` fulfils or rejects. The handler receives **no arguments**, and normally does not change the outcome: the value or error passes through. The exception is when `onFinally` throws or returns a rejected promise; then the chain rejects with that new error.

```javascript
showSpinner();
fetchData()
  .then(render)
  .catch(showError)
  .finally(() => hideSpinner());    // always runs; the spinner never gets stuck

Promise.resolve(5)
  .finally(() => 99)                // return value of finally is ignored
  .then((v) => console.log(v));     // 5
```

**Branching versus chaining.** Calling `then` twice on the *same* promise creates two independent branches, not a chain:

```javascript
const p = Promise.resolve(1);

p.then((x) => x + 1).then((x) => console.log("chain:", x));   // chain: 2
p.then((x) => console.log("branch:", x));                      // branch: 1 (gets p's value, not 2)
```

```text
       +--> then(x + 1) --> then(log)     <- chain
  p ---+
       +--> then(log)                     <- separate branch
```

**Nesting when you need earlier values.** Sometimes a later step needs a value from an earlier step. Nesting one level is acceptable, or you can carry an object forward (and `async/await`, 5.3, makes this trivial):

```javascript
getUser(1)
  .then((user) =>
    getOrders(user.id).then((orders) => ({ user, orders }))   // bundle both values
  )
  .then(({ user, orders }) => render(user, orders));
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `then` always returns a new promise whose state depends on what the handler returns or throws.
- Return promises from handlers so that the chain waits for them. A missing `return` is the most common bug.
- A rejection skips `then` handlers until the nearest `catch`. A `catch` that returns normally recovers the chain, and rethrowing keeps it rejected.
- `then(a, b)` does not catch errors thrown in `a`. Prefer `then(a).catch(b)`.
- `finally` is for cleanup. It receives no arguments and passes the original outcome through unless it throws.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Starting from `Promise.resolve(3)`, build a chain that doubles the value, adds 4, then logs it. Then insert a step that throws an error when the value is greater than 5, and add a `catch` that logs the message and a `finally` that logs "done".
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Given `getUser(id)`, `getPosts(userId)` and `getComments(postId)` (implement them as fake functions that return promises after a random delay), build a single flat chain that logs the comments of the first post of user 1. Make `getPosts` randomly reject, and ensure that the chain shows a fallback message and still logs "finished" at the end.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is logged by `Promise.reject(new Error('x')).catch(e => 'recovered').then(v => console.log(v))`, and why?" *Hint:* consider what state the promise returned by `catch` is in when its handler returns normally.

#### Promise Combinators

Chaining handles *sequential* steps. Many real situations involve several *independent* operations at once: load a user's profile, settings and notifications in parallel, use whichever of two mirrors answers first, or give up if a request takes more than 5 seconds. The `Promise` class provides four static methods, called **combinators**, that take an iterable of promises and return a single promise.

**`Promise.all`: everything must succeed.** Fulfils with an array of all values, **in the same order as the input** (not the completion order). It rejects as soon as **any** input rejects, with that reason ("fail-fast").

```javascript
const [user, settings, notifications] = await Promise.all([
  fetchJSON("/api/user"),            // all three requests start immediately...
  fetchJSON("/api/settings"),
  fetchJSON("/api/notifications"),   // ...and run concurrently
]);
// total time is about the slowest request, not the sum of the three
```

Fail-fast does *not* cancel the other operations. They keep running; their results are simply ignored. Cancellation needs `AbortController` (5.3).

**`Promise.allSettled`: wait for everything, never reject.** Fulfils, once all inputs have settled, with an array of outcome objects: `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }`. Use it when partial success is acceptable.

```javascript
const results = await Promise.allSettled([
  sendEmail(a), sendEmail(b), sendEmail(c),
]);

const failed = results
  .map((r, i) => ({ ...r, index: i }))
  .filter((r) => r.status === "rejected");

console.log(`${results.length - failed.length} sent, ${failed.length} failed`);
failed.forEach((f) => console.error(`#${f.index}:`, f.reason.message));
```

**`Promise.race`: the first to settle wins.** Settles the same way as the first input to settle, fulfilled *or* rejected. The classic use is a timeout:

```javascript
function timeout(ms) {
  return new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`Timed out after ${ms} ms`)), ms)
  );
}

const data = await Promise.race([
  fetchJSON("/api/slow-report"),
  timeout(5000),                      // rejects if the request is not done in 5 s
]);
```

(For `fetch`, `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` is better because it actually stops the request, see 5.3.)

**`Promise.any`: the first to succeed wins.** Fulfils with the first *fulfilled* value and ignores rejections. It rejects only if **all** inputs reject, with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` property lists every reason.

```javascript
try {
  const image = await Promise.any([
    loadImage("https://cdn1.example.com/logo.png"),
    loadImage("https://cdn2.example.com/logo.png"),   // whichever mirror succeeds first
  ]);
  document.body.append(image);
} catch (err) {
  console.error(err instanceof AggregateError);       // true: every mirror failed
  console.error(err.errors);                          // [Error, Error]
}
```

**Comparison.**

| Combinator | Fulfils when | Rejects when | Result | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Promise.all` | All fulfil | The first rejection | Array of values (input order) | Independent requests that are all required |
| `Promise.allSettled` | All settle | Never | Array of `{status, value \| reason}` | Batch jobs where partial failure is fine |
| `Promise.race` | The first settles by fulfilling | The first settles by rejecting | The first value or reason | Timeouts, "first response wins" |
| `Promise.any` | The first fulfils | All reject | The first value, or an `AggregateError` | Redundant sources, fallbacks |

```text
Inputs:          A: ----ok(1)            B: --ok(2)          C: ------fail(x)
Promise.all         ------------------------------------ fail(x)   (at C's time)
Promise.allSettled  ------------------------------------ [{ok 1},{ok 2},{fail x}]
Promise.race        -- ok(2)                                        (B settled first)
Promise.any         -- ok(2)                                        (B fulfilled first)
```

**Edge cases.**

- Non-promise values in the input are treated as already-fulfilled promises: `Promise.all([1, fetchX()])` works.
- With an **empty** array, `all` and `allSettled` fulfil immediately with `[]`, `any` rejects immediately with an `AggregateError`, and `race` stays pending forever.
- The input is any iterable, so a `Set` or a generator also works.

**Key Takeaways**

- Combinators turn many promises into one. All of them start waiting at once, so the operations run concurrently.
- `all` needs every operation to succeed and fails fast. `allSettled` always reports every outcome.
- `race` follows the first to settle (success or failure). `any` follows the first success and fails only if everything fails.
- Combinators do not cancel the losing or remaining operations. Use `AbortController` for that.
- Results of `all` and `allSettled` are in input order, regardless of completion order.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `delay(ms, value)` that fulfils with `value` after `ms`. Use `Promise.all` with delays of 300, 100 and 200 ms and confirm that the results come back in input order and that the total time is about 300 ms.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement your own `promiseAll(iterable)` using only `new Promise` and `then`, handling input order, non-promise values, fail-fast rejection and the empty input case. Test it against the built-in `Promise.all`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose `Promise.allSettled` over `Promise.all`, and `Promise.any` over `Promise.race`?" *Hint:* think about whether a single failure should abort the whole operation, and whether a fast failure should win.

#### Promisification of Callback APIs

Promises arrived in the language in ES2015, but many APIs were designed earlier around callbacks and events: Node's original `fs` module, `setTimeout`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `FileReader`, `IndexedDB`, and countless libraries. To use them with promise chains and `async/await`, you wrap them in a function that returns a promise. This is called **promisification**.

**The general recipe.** Call the old API inside a promise executor, and connect its success and failure signals to `resolve` and `reject`.

```javascript
// Callback-based original: readConfig(path, (err, data) => {...})
function readConfigAsync(path) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    readConfig(path, (err, data) => {
      if (err) reject(err);      // error-first: error -> reject
      else resolve(data);        // success -> resolve
    });
  });
}

readConfigAsync("app.json").then(console.log).catch(console.error);
```

**Timers.** `setTimeout` has no error, only completion:

```javascript
const delay = (ms, value) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms, value));

delay(1000, "hi").then(console.log);   // "hi" after 1 s
```

**A generic `promisify` for error-first functions.** Because the error-first convention is uniform, one helper can convert any such function. The callback is appended as the last argument.

```javascript
function promisify(fn) {
  return function (...args) {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      fn.call(this, ...args, (err, result) => {   // keep `this` for methods (3.3, call/apply/bind)
        if (err) reject(err);
        else resolve(result);
      });
    });
  };
}

const loadScriptAsync = promisify(loadScript);   // from the error-first topic
await loadScriptAsync("/js/chart.js");
```

Node.js provides this helper as `util.promisify`, and most core modules now have promise versions built in:

```javascript
// Node.js
import { promisify } from "node:util";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";        // promise-based fs, no wrapping needed
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

const text = await readFile("config.json", "utf8");
await sleep(500);
```

**Promisifying event-based APIs.** Objects that fire events (`load`/`error`, `success`/`error`) are promisified the same way. Listen for the success event and the failure event, and remove both listeners after the first one fires so that nothing leaks.

```javascript
function readFileAsText(file) {             // wraps the browser's FileReader
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const reader = new FileReader();
    reader.onload = () => resolve(reader.result);
    reader.onerror = () => reject(reader.error);
    reader.readAsText(file);
  });
}

function once(target, eventName) {          // wait for the next occurrence of any DOM event
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    target.addEventListener(eventName, resolve, { once: true });   // auto-removed after firing
  });
}

const input = document.querySelector("input[type=file]");
await once(input, "change");
const text = await readFileAsText(input.files[0]);
```

**When not to promisify.** A promise settles once. It is a poor fit for things that happen **many times**: clicks, WebSocket messages, sensor readings. For repeated events, keep callbacks, or use async iterators or streams (5.3).

| Source | Promisify? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| One-shot callback (`readFile`, `setTimeout`) | Yes | Exactly one outcome |
| One-shot event (`load`, `DOMContentLoaded`) | Yes | Wait once for the first occurrence |
| Repeated events (`click`, `message`) | No (or only "the next one") | A promise cannot deliver several values |
| API that already returns promises | No | Do not wrap promises in `new Promise` (an anti-pattern) |

**The explicit-construction anti-pattern.** Wrapping an existing promise in `new Promise` adds code, and often loses errors:

```javascript
// Anti-pattern: redundant, and a throw inside then is never forwarded to reject
function getUserName(id) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    fetch(`/api/users/${id}`)
      .then((res) => res.json())
      .then((user) => resolve(user.name));   // missing .catch(reject): rejections are lost
  });
}

// Correct: just return the chain
function getUserName(id) {
  return fetch(`/api/users/${id}`)
    .then((res) => res.json())
    .then((user) => user.name);
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Promisification wraps a callback or event API in a function that returns a promise, mapping success to `resolve` and failure to `reject`.
- Error-first functions can be converted generically (`util.promisify` in Node.js). Many modern APIs already offer promise versions.
- For event-based APIs, handle both the success and the failure event, and remove listeners after settling.
- Promises fit one-shot results. Repeated events need callbacks, async iterators or streams.
- Never wrap a promise in `new Promise`. Return the existing chain instead.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Promisify `navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(success, error)` into `getPosition()` and log the latitude and longitude with `then`/`catch`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `promisifyAll(obj)` that, for every function-valued property `name` of `obj`, adds a property `nameAsync` that is the promisified version (bound to `obj`). Test it on an object with two error-first methods that use `this`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the 'explicit promise construction' anti-pattern, and what bug does it commonly introduce?" *Hint:* consider what happens when the inner chain rejects and nobody calls `reject`.

<a id="53-asyncawait-and-advanced-patterns"></a>
### 5.3 async/await and Advanced Patterns

This subchapter covers `async`/`await`, the syntax that lets promise-based code read like synchronous code, and the patterns built on it: error handling, controlling concurrency, consuming asynchronous sequences, cancelling work, and limiting how often operations run.

#### async Functions and await Semantics

Promise chains are much better than nested callbacks, but they are still not how we naturally write logic. Loops, conditionals and variables that span several steps become awkward when every step is a separate `then` callback. ES2017 introduced `async` functions and the `await` operator. They are built entirely on promises, but they let you write asynchronous code in the same shape as synchronous code.

**`async` functions always return a promise.** Marking a function `async` changes its return value:

- If the body returns a value `v`, the function returns a promise fulfilled with `v`.
- If the body throws, the function returns a promise rejected with the error.
- If the body returns a promise, the returned promise follows it.

```javascript
async function getAnswer() {
  return 42;                      // wrapped: the caller receives Promise<42>
}

async function fail() {
  throw new Error("nope");        // becomes a rejected promise, not a synchronous throw
}

console.log(getAnswer());          // Promise { 42 }
getAnswer().then(console.log);     // 42
fail().catch((e) => console.log(e.message));   // "nope"
```

All function forms can be `async`:

```javascript
async function declaration() {}
const expression = async function () {};
const arrow = async () => {};
const obj = { async method() {} };
class Service { async load() {} }
```

**`await` pauses the function, not the thread.** `await expr` waits for the promise `expr` to settle:

- If it fulfils, `await` evaluates to the value.
- If it rejects, `await` **throws** the reason at that line, so you can use ordinary `try/catch`.
- If `expr` is not a promise, it is wrapped with `Promise.resolve`, so `await 5` gives `5` (after a microtask).

```javascript
// With then chains
function showUserOrders(id) {
  return getUser(id)
    .then((user) => getOrders(user.id).then((orders) => ({ user, orders })))
    .then(({ user, orders }) => render(user, orders));
}

// With async/await: same behaviour, reads top to bottom
async function showUserOrders(id) {
  const user = await getUser(id);         // pause until the user arrives
  const orders = await getOrders(user.id); // `user` is still in scope: no bundling needed
  render(user, orders);
}
```

**What happens during an `await`.** When the engine reaches `await`, it suspends the async function: it saves its local variables and position (much like a generator, 3.3) and **returns to the caller**. The call stack unwinds and the event loop is free to run other work. When the awaited promise settles, the rest of the function is scheduled as a **microtask** and resumes exactly where it stopped.

```javascript
async function demo() {
  console.log("2: demo starts");     // runs synchronously, as part of the call
  await null;                        // suspend; the rest becomes a microtask
  console.log("4: demo resumes");
}

console.log("1: before");
demo();
console.log("3: after");             // the caller continues while demo is suspended

// 1: before
// 2: demo starts
// 3: after
// 4: demo resumes
```

```text
Call stack over time:

[main]-[demo]-(await: demo suspended, returns a pending promise)-[main continues]-(stack empty)
                                                                                     |
                                                     microtask: [demo resumes] <-----+
```

So an async function runs **synchronously up to its first `await`**. This explains why code before the first `await` happens immediately on call.

**Top-level `await`.** In ES modules (`<script type="module">`, `.mjs` files), `await` is allowed at the top level of the module. Modules that import this module wait until it has finished evaluating.

```javascript
// config.mjs
const response = await fetch("/config.json");
export const config = await response.json();   // importers receive a ready config
```

In classic scripts and inside non-async functions, `await` is a syntax error.

**`await` in callbacks.** `await` only works directly inside an `async` function. A common mistake is using it inside a callback passed to a non-async function, such as `forEach`:

```javascript
async function saveAll(items) {
  items.forEach(async (item) => {
    await save(item);              // awaits inside the arrow function only
  });
  console.log("All saved?");       // printed immediately: forEach does not wait for promises
}

async function saveAllCorrectly(items) {
  for (const item of items) {
    await save(item);              // sequential: one after another
  }
  console.log("All saved");        // printed after the last save
}
```

**Comparison.**

| | Callbacks | Promise chains | `async`/`await` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sequencing | Nesting | Flat chain of `then` | Ordinary statements |
| Error handling | `if (err)` at every level | `.catch()` | `try/catch` |
| Sharing variables between steps | Closures | Bundling or nesting | Ordinary local variables |
| Loops and conditionals | Manual recursion | Awkward | Ordinary `for`, `if`, `while` |
| Underlying mechanism | Functions | Promises | Promises plus suspension |

**Key Takeaways**

- An `async` function always returns a promise. Returned values fulfil it and thrown errors reject it.
- `await` suspends only the current async function, never the thread. The rest of the function resumes as a microtask.
- An async function runs synchronously until its first `await`.
- A rejected awaited promise throws at the `await` line, so `try/catch` works.
- `await` inside a callback does not make the outer function wait. `forEach` ignores promises; use `for...of` or `Promise.all`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite the following chain as an `async` function: `getUser(1).then(u => getPosts(u.id)).then(posts => console.log(posts.length))`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Predict the output order of a script that logs `"A"`, calls an async function that logs `"B"`, awaits `Promise.resolve()`, then logs `"C"`, and finally logs `"D"` after the call, with a `setTimeout(() => console.log("E"), 0)` placed before everything. Explain each step in terms of tasks and microtasks.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Does `await` block the JavaScript thread? What actually happens when execution reaches an `await`?" *Hint:* describe what happens to the async function's state, what the caller receives, and how execution resumes.

#### Error Handling in Async Code

Asynchronous errors are easy to lose. A rejection that nobody handles does not stop the program in the browser. It just logs a warning while the user stares at a spinner forever. This topic shows where errors go in each style, how to catch them reliably, and how to detect the ones you missed.

**`try/catch/finally` with `await`.** Inside an async function, a rejected `await` throws, so the synchronous error-handling tools apply (3.4):

```javascript
async function loadDashboard() {
  showSpinner();
  try {
    const user = await getUser();
    const stats = await getStats(user.id);
    render(user, stats);
  } catch (err) {
    // catches a rejection from getUser or getStats AND any error thrown by render
    showError(`Could not load the dashboard: ${err.message}`);
  } finally {
    hideSpinner();                 // runs on success and on failure
  }
}
```

**Errors propagate through `await` like exceptions through calls.** If you do not catch an error in an async function, its returned promise rejects, and the error reaches whoever awaits that function. You only need to handle errors at the level that can do something useful about them.

```javascript
async function getStats(id) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/stats/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);   // turn HTTP errors into rejections
  return res.json();
}
// No try/catch here: loadDashboard decides how to show the error.
```

**Handling an error for one step only.** A single `try` around many awaits is convenient but coarse. For a step with its own fallback, either use a small `try` block or attach `.catch` to that one promise:

```javascript
async function loadProfile(id) {
  const user = await getUser(id);                        // errors propagate to the caller
  const avatar = await getAvatar(id).catch(() => DEFAULT_AVATAR);   // local fallback
  return { user, avatar };
}
```

**`return` vs `return await` inside `try`.** Returning a promise from inside a `try` block *without* awaiting it means its rejection happens after the function has already left the `try`. The `catch` will not see it.

```javascript
async function withoutAwait() {
  try {
    return fetchData();            // the rejection escapes: catch is skipped
  } catch (err) {
    return "fallback";
  }
}

async function withAwait() {
  try {
    return await fetchData();      // the rejection is thrown here, inside try
  } catch (err) {
    return "fallback";             // works as intended
  }
}
```

Outside a `try` block, `return await` and `return` behave the same.

**Floating promises.** A promise that is created and then ignored is called **floating**. If it rejects, the error goes nowhere useful.

```javascript
async function onSubmit() {
  saveDraft();                     // floating: no await, no catch; failures are invisible
  await submitForm();
}

async function onSubmitFixed() {
  saveDraft().catch((err) => console.warn("Draft not saved:", err));   // deliberately fire-and-forget
  await submitForm();
}
```

Linters such as typescript-eslint's `no-floating-promises` rule detect these automatically.

**Errors that escape all promises.** A `throw` inside a plain callback scheduled by another API (a timer, an event listener) is not connected to any promise, so neither `.catch` nor an outer `try/catch` can catch it:

```javascript
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    throw new Error("lost");       // uncaught: this callback runs outside the executor
  }, 100);
}).catch(() => console.log("never called"));      // the promise stays pending forever

new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    try {
      resolve(riskyOperation());
    } catch (err) {
      reject(err);                 // forward the error explicitly
    }
  }, 100);
});
```

**Global safety nets.** Use these to log errors you failed to handle, not as your error-handling strategy.

```javascript
// Browser: promise rejections with no handler
window.addEventListener("unhandledrejection", (event) => {
  reportToServer(event.reason);    // the rejection reason
  event.preventDefault();          // optional: suppress the default console message
});

// Browser: synchronous errors that reach the top of the stack
window.addEventListener("error", (event) => {
  reportToServer(event.error);
});

// Node.js
process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => {
  console.error("Unhandled rejection:", reason);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
```

**Rejecting with `Error` objects.** Always reject (and throw) instances of `Error` or a subclass, never strings. Only `Error` objects carry a stack trace, and code that checks `err.message` or `err instanceof NetworkError` relies on it. The `cause` option (ES2022) lets you wrap a low-level error without losing it:

```javascript
try {
  await db.save(order);
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error(`Saving order ${order.id} failed`, { cause: err });   // keeps the original error
}
```

**Summary of where errors go.**

| Code | Where the error goes | How to handle it |
|---|---|---|
| `throw` in an async function | Rejects the function's promise | `try/catch` in the caller with `await`, or `.catch` |
| Rejected `await` | Thrown at the `await` line | `try/catch` around it |
| `throw` inside `then` | Rejects the promise returned by `then` | `.catch` later in the chain |
| Floating promise rejects | `unhandledrejection` event | `await` it or attach `.catch` |
| `throw` in a timer or event callback | Global `error` event | `try/catch` inside the callback |

**Key Takeaways**

- In async functions, use `try/catch/finally` around `await` exactly as with synchronous code.
- Let errors propagate to the level that can handle them. Convert non-exception failures (such as HTTP 500) into thrown errors.
- Use `return await` inside `try` blocks, otherwise the `catch` misses the rejection.
- Never leave promises floating: `await` them or attach a `.catch`.
- `unhandledrejection` and `error` events are safety nets for logging, not a substitute for local handling.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write an async function `safeParse(url)` that fetches a URL and parses it as JSON, returning `null` and logging a warning if the request fails, the status is not OK, or the body is not valid JSON.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a page with a global `unhandledrejection` handler that displays a toast message. Write three buttons that each produce a different kind of async error (a floating rejected promise, a rejection inside a `then` with no `catch`, and a `throw` inside a `setTimeout`) and observe which ones reach the handler. Explain why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Inside a `try` block in an async function, what is the difference between `return promise` and `return await promise`?" *Hint:* consider when the rejection happens relative to the function leaving the `try` block.

#### Sequential vs Parallel Execution

`async/await` makes asynchronous code look sequential, and that is both its strength and its trap. Writing `await` before each call makes each operation **wait for the previous one**, even when they are independent. A page that loads three unrelated resources one after another takes three times longer than necessary.

**The waterfall problem.**

```javascript
// Sequential: about 300 + 200 + 400 = 900 ms
async function loadPageSlow() {
  const user = await fetchJSON("/api/user");          // 300 ms
  const news = await fetchJSON("/api/news");          // 200 ms, but did not need to wait for user
  const weather = await fetchJSON("/api/weather");    // 400 ms
  return { user, news, weather };
}

// Concurrent: about max(300, 200, 400) = 400 ms
async function loadPageFast() {
  const [user, news, weather] = await Promise.all([
    fetchJSON("/api/user"),
    fetchJSON("/api/news"),
    fetchJSON("/api/weather"),
  ]);
  return { user, news, weather };
}
```

```text
Sequential:
user    [=====300=====]
news                   [===200===]
weather                           [=======400=======]        total ~900 ms

Concurrent:
user    [=====300=====]
news    [===200===]
weather [=======400=======]                                  total ~400 ms
```

**The rule.** Requests start when the function that creates the promise is *called*, not when the promise is awaited. To run operations concurrently, **start them all first, then await**.

```javascript
async function loadPage() {
  const userPromise = fetchJSON("/api/user");        // starts now
  const newsPromise = fetchJSON("/api/news");        // starts now, in parallel

  const user = await userPromise;
  const news = await newsPromise;
  return { user, news };
}
```

This works, but has a trap: if `newsPromise` rejects while the function is still awaiting `userPromise`, nothing is handling it yet, and the browser may report an unhandled rejection. `Promise.all` attaches handlers to all promises immediately, so prefer it.

**Real dependencies stay sequential.** When one step needs the result of another, it must wait. Mix both patterns:

```javascript
async function loadOrderPage(orderId) {
  const order = await getOrder(orderId);              // needed by everything below

  const [customer, items, shipping] = await Promise.all([
    getCustomer(order.customerId),                    // these three only depend on order
    getItems(order.itemIds),
    getShipping(order.shippingId),
  ]);

  return { order, customer, items, shipping };
}
```

```text
getOrder  [====]
customer        [======]
items           [===]
shipping        [========]
```

**Loops: sequential vs concurrent.**

```javascript
const ids = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

// Sequential: one at a time, in order. Use when order matters or the server needs gentle use.
const sequential = [];
for (const id of ids) {
  sequential.push(await getUser(id));
}

// Concurrent: all at once. Use for independent, few operations.
const concurrent = await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => getUser(id)));
// map returns an array of promises immediately; Promise.all waits for all of them
```

**Limited concurrency.** Firing 1,000 requests at once can overwhelm the server, hit rate limits, or saturate the browser (which limits HTTP/1.1 connections to about 6 per host and queues the rest). The middle ground is a **concurrency limit**: run at most `n` operations at the same time.

```javascript
async function mapWithLimit(items, limit, fn) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;                              // index of the next item to process

  async function worker() {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const i = next++;                      // claim an index (safe: single-threaded)
      results[i] = await fn(items[i], i);
    }
  }

  // Start `limit` workers that pull from the shared index until it runs out
  const workers = Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker);
  await Promise.all(workers);
  return results;                            // in input order
}

const thumbnails = await mapWithLimit(imageUrls, 4, (url) => createThumbnail(url));
```

```text
limit = 3, eight jobs of different lengths:
worker 1: [job0=====][job3==][job6=======]
worker 2: [job1==][job4========][job7==]
worker 3: [job2======][job5===]
```

**Choosing a strategy.**

| Strategy | Code | Time | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sequential | `for...of` with `await` | Sum of all durations | Steps depend on each other, order matters, or side effects must not overlap |
| Fully concurrent | `Promise.all(items.map(fn))` | Longest duration | Few independent operations |
| Limited concurrency | Worker pool (`mapWithLimit`) | Roughly total / limit | Many independent operations, rate limits |
| Concurrent with partial failure | `Promise.allSettled(...)` | Longest duration | Each result is optional |

**Key Takeaways**

- An operation starts when its function is called. `await` only waits for a result that is already on its way.
- Writing `await` before each independent call creates a waterfall. Start independent operations together and combine them with `Promise.all`.
- Keep steps sequential only when there is a real data dependency, and parallelise everything that depends on the same step.
- `ids.map(async ...)` with `Promise.all` is concurrent. `for...of` with `await` is sequential.
- For large batches, limit concurrency with a worker pool to respect servers and browser connection limits.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Using a `delay(ms, value)` helper, write two functions that each obtain three values from delays of 500, 700 and 300 ms: one sequential and one concurrent. Measure both with `performance.now()`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Given a list of 20 user IDs and a fake `getUser(id)` that takes 200 to 600 ms, fetch all users with a concurrency limit of 4. Log when each request starts and ends to verify that no more than 4 are ever in flight, and confirm that results are in input order.
> 3. *(Interview)* "This code takes 3 seconds; how would you make it faster? `const a = await f(); const b = await g(); const c = await h(a);`" *Hint:* identify which calls depend on which results, then decide which ones can overlap.

#### Async Iterators and for await of

A promise delivers one value. Some data arrives as a **sequence** of values over time: the pages of a paginated API, the chunks of a large download, the lines of a log file, messages from a server. You want to loop over them, but each item is only available asynchronously. Regular iterators (3.3) cannot do this, because their `next()` must return the item synchronously. **Async iterators** extend the iteration protocol to asynchronous sequences.

**The protocol.** Recall that a synchronous iterator has a `next()` method returning `{ value, done }`. An **async iterator** has a `next()` method that returns a **promise** of `{ value, done }`. An object is **async iterable** if it has a `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` method that returns an async iterator.

| | Sync iteration | Async iteration |
|---|---|---|
| Iterable method | `[Symbol.iterator]()` | `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` |
| `next()` returns | `{ value, done }` | `Promise<{ value, done }>` |
| Loop | `for (const x of it)` | `for await (const x of it)` |
| Generator syntax | `function*` with `yield` | `async function*` with `yield` and `await` |

**`for await...of`.** This loop awaits each `next()` result before running the body. It can only be used inside an async function or at the top level of a module.

```javascript
async function* countdown(from) {          // an async generator
  for (let i = from; i > 0; i--) {
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1000));
    yield i;                               // deliver one value, then pause until asked again
  }
}

for await (const n of countdown(3)) {      // waits about one second per iteration
  console.log(n);                          // 3, 2, 1
}
console.log("Liftoff");
```

**Async generators.** As in the example above, the simplest way to create an async iterator is an `async function*`. Inside it you can both `await` (to wait for data) and `yield` (to hand a value to the consumer). The generator is **lazy**: it only produces the next value when the consumer asks for it, so a slow consumer automatically slows down the producer (this is called **backpressure**).

**Real example: pagination.** Many APIs return results in pages, with a link to the next page. An async generator hides the paging logic and exposes a simple stream of items:

```javascript
async function* fetchAllIssues(repoUrl) {
  let url = `${repoUrl}/issues?per_page=100`;
  while (url) {
    const res = await fetch(url);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const issues = await res.json();
    yield* issues;                         // yield each item of this page, one by one

    url = parseNextLink(res.headers.get("Link"));   // null on the last page
  }
}

for await (const issue of fetchAllIssues("https://api.example.com/repos/acme/app")) {
  console.log(issue.title);
  if (issue.title.includes("critical")) break;     // stop early: no further pages are fetched
}
```

**Early exit and cleanup.** When the loop exits early (`break`, `return`, or a thrown error), `for await` calls the iterator's `return()` method. For an async generator, this runs any `finally` block inside it, which is the place to release resources such as connections or reader locks.

```javascript
async function* readLines(stream) {
  const reader = stream.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
  let buffer = "";
  try {
    while (true) {
      const { value, done } = await reader.read();
      if (done) break;
      buffer += value;
      const lines = buffer.split("\n");
      buffer = lines.pop();                // keep the incomplete last line for the next chunk
      yield* lines;
    }
    if (buffer) yield buffer;
  } finally {
    reader.releaseLock();                  // runs on normal end, on break, and on error
  }
}
```

**Built-in async iterables.**

- `ReadableStream` (the body of a `fetch` response, 5.4) is async iterable in current browsers and Node.js. Feature-detect it with `Symbol.asyncIterator in ReadableStream.prototype`.
- In Node.js: readable streams, `fs.promises.opendir` directory handles, `readline` interfaces, and `events.on(emitter, name)`.
- `Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable)` collects every value into an array.

```javascript
const res = await fetch("/large-log.txt");
for await (const chunk of res.body) {      // chunk is a Uint8Array
  console.log(`Received ${chunk.byteLength} bytes`);
}

const firstTen = await Array.fromAsync(countdown(10));   // [10, 9, ..., 1]
```

**`for await` over an array of promises.** `for await` also works on a *sync* iterable of promises, awaiting each in turn. All the promises were already started, so this is concurrent, but results are still processed in array order. If a later promise rejects while you are still awaiting an earlier one, the rejection is unhandled at first, so prefer `Promise.all` or `Promise.allSettled` for arrays of promises.

**Key Takeaways**

- Async iterators deliver a sequence of values over time. `next()` returns a promise of `{ value, done }`.
- `for await...of` consumes async iterables, awaiting each item in turn. It is only valid in async functions and modules.
- `async function*` generators combine `await` and `yield`. They are lazy, so they produce data only as fast as the consumer reads it.
- Breaking out of `for await` calls `return()` on the iterator, running the generator's `finally` block for cleanup.
- Streams (including `fetch` response bodies) are async iterable in modern environments.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write an async generator `ticker(n, ms)` that yields the numbers 1 to `n`, one every `ms` milliseconds, and consume it with `for await...of`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write an async generator `paginate(fetchPage)` where `fetchPage(page)` returns a promise of `{ items, hasMore }`. Then write a helper `take(asyncIterable, n)` (itself an async generator) that yields only the first `n` items, and verify with logging that no extra pages are requested once `n` items have been taken.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `for await (const x of arrayOfPromises)` and `await Promise.all(arrayOfPromises)`?" *Hint:* compare when processing of each result begins, what happens if a later promise rejects early, and the order of side effects.

#### Cancellation with AbortController

Promises have no built-in way to say "never mind". Yet cancellation is common in user interfaces: the user types a new search query before the previous results arrive, navigates away from a page mid-download, or closes a dialog that was loading data. Without cancellation, stale responses can overwrite fresh ones, and bandwidth and battery are wasted. The web platform's standard cancellation mechanism is `AbortController`.

**Two objects, two roles.**

- An `AbortController` is the **remote control**. Whoever owns it can call `controller.abort(reason)`.
- Its `controller.signal` is an `AbortSignal`, the **receiver**. You pass it to cancellable operations. It has an `aborted` flag, a `reason`, and fires an `abort` event.

This separation is deliberate: you can hand the signal to many operations without giving them the power to cancel each other.

```text
   AbortController -- abort() -->  AbortSignal  --event--> fetch #1     (rejects with AbortError)
     (caller keeps)                (passed down) --event--> fetch #2
                                                 --event--> addEventListener (listeners removed)
                                                 --event--> your own async function
```

**Cancelling a fetch.**

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();

fetch("/api/big-report", { signal: controller.signal })
  .then((res) => res.json())
  .then((data) => render(data))
  .catch((err) => {
    if (err.name === "AbortError") {
      console.log("Request cancelled");   // expected: not a real failure
    } else {
      showError(err);
    }
  });

cancelButton.onclick = () => controller.abort();   // stops the request, including the body download
```

When aborted, the `fetch` promise (or the pending `res.json()`) rejects with a `DOMException` named `"AbortError"`. Always distinguish it from real errors, so that cancelling does not show an error message to the user.

**Timeouts.** `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` returns a signal that aborts automatically after `ms` milliseconds, with a `DOMException` named `"TimeoutError"`. `AbortSignal.any([...signals])` creates a signal that aborts when any of the given signals aborts, which lets you combine user cancellation with a timeout:

```javascript
const userCancel = new AbortController();

try {
  const res = await fetch("/api/search?q=js", {
    signal: AbortSignal.any([userCancel.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(8000)]),
  });
  render(await res.json());
} catch (err) {
  if (err.name === "TimeoutError") showError("The server is taking too long.");
  else if (err.name !== "AbortError") showError(err.message);
}
```

**Cancelling stale requests (search-as-you-type).** Abort the previous request each time a new one starts. This also prevents the race condition in which a slow, old response arrives after a fast, new one and overwrites it.

```javascript
let currentController = null;

searchInput.addEventListener("input", async () => {
  currentController?.abort();                    // cancel the previous search, if any
  currentController = new AbortController();
  const { signal } = currentController;

  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(searchInput.value)}`, { signal });
    const results = await res.json();
    renderResults(results);                      // only the latest request gets here
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name !== "AbortError") showError(err);
  }
});
```

**Removing event listeners.** `addEventListener` accepts a `signal` option. When the signal aborts, the listener is removed. One `abort()` can tear down a whole group of listeners, which is ideal for component cleanup.

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const { signal } = controller;

window.addEventListener("resize", onResize, { signal });
window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { signal });
document.addEventListener("keydown", onKey, { signal });

function destroyComponent() {
  controller.abort();          // removes all three listeners at once
}
```

**Making your own functions cancellable.** Accept a `signal` option, check it before starting, and listen for its `abort` event to stop work and reject.

```javascript
function delay(ms, { signal } = {}) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    signal?.throwIfAborted();                       // reject immediately if already aborted

    const id = setTimeout(() => {
      signal?.removeEventListener("abort", onAbort);
      resolve();
    }, ms);

    function onAbort() {
      clearTimeout(id);                             // stop the underlying work
      reject(signal.reason);                        // an AbortError DOMException by default
    }
    signal?.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true });
  });
}

async function processBatch(items, { signal }) {
  for (const item of items) {
    signal.throwIfAborted();                        // check between steps of long work
    await processItem(item, { signal });            // pass the signal down to nested operations
  }
}
```

**What cancellation is not.** Aborting a request stops the browser from waiting for the response. It does not undo work the server has already done. If a `POST /orders` request is aborted, the order may still have been created. Design non-idempotent operations accordingly (10.4).

**Key Takeaways**

- `AbortController` creates the cancel action (`abort()`). Its `AbortSignal` is passed to operations that should be cancellable.
- An aborted `fetch` rejects with a `DOMException` named `"AbortError"`. Handle it separately from real errors.
- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives a built-in timeout ("TimeoutError"), and `AbortSignal.any` combines signals.
- Abort the previous request when starting a new one to avoid stale responses overwriting fresh ones.
- Pass `{ signal }` to `addEventListener` to remove many listeners with one call. Accept a `signal` in your own async functions and pass it down.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a "Cancel" button to a page that starts a `fetch` for a large file. Clicking it should abort the request and display "Cancelled" (not an error message).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `fetchWithTimeout(url, { timeout, signal })` that aborts after `timeout` ms or when the caller's `signal` aborts, whichever comes first, and throws a custom `TimeoutError` class for timeouts. Test the three outcomes: success, timeout and caller cancellation.
> 3. *(Interview)* "In a search-as-you-type feature, results sometimes show for an older query than the one typed. Why does this happen and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* consider responses arriving out of order, and two fixes: cancellation, and ignoring responses that are not the latest.

#### Throttling, Debouncing and Retry Logic

Some events fire far more often than you want to react to them: `input` fires on every keystroke, `scroll` and `resize` can fire dozens of times per second, and `mousemove` even more. Running an expensive handler (a network request, a layout calculation) on each one wastes resources and makes the page sluggish. Other operations fail occasionally for transient reasons (a dropped connection, a server under load) and succeed if simply tried again. This topic covers three patterns for controlling *when* and *how often* an asynchronous operation runs.

**Debouncing: wait until things calm down.** A **debounced** function delays execution until a certain time has passed *without* any new call. Every new call resets the timer. An analogy: an elevator door waits a few seconds after the last person enters before closing. Each new person resets the wait.

Use it when only the **final** state matters: search suggestions after the user stops typing, saving a draft, validating a field, recalculating a layout after resizing stops.

```javascript
function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timerId;
  return function (...args) {
    clearTimeout(timerId);                       // cancel the previously scheduled call
    timerId = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), wait);   // schedule a fresh one
  };
}

const search = debounce((query) => {
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`);   // one request per pause in typing
}, 300);

input.addEventListener("input", (e) => search(e.target.value));
```

**Throttling: at most once per interval.** A **throttled** function runs at most once every `interval` ms, no matter how often it is called. Calls in between are dropped (or one trailing call is kept). An analogy: a tap that drips once per second regardless of how hard you open it.

Use it when you need **regular updates during** a continuous activity: updating a scroll progress bar, infinite scroll checks, sending the cursor position in a collaborative app, rate-limiting a "Like" button.

```javascript
function throttle(fn, interval) {
  let lastRun = 0;
  let trailingId = null;
  let lastArgs, lastThis;

  return function (...args) {
    lastArgs = args;                             // always remember the most recent call
    lastThis = this;
    const remaining = interval - (Date.now() - lastRun);

    if (remaining <= 0) {                        // enough time has passed: run now
      clearTimeout(trailingId);
      trailingId = null;
      lastRun = Date.now();
      fn.apply(lastThis, lastArgs);
    } else if (!trailingId) {                    // schedule one trailing call for the end of the interval
      trailingId = setTimeout(() => {
        lastRun = Date.now();
        trailingId = null;
        fn.apply(lastThis, lastArgs);            // uses the latest arguments, not the ones from scheduling time
      }, remaining);
    }
  };
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", throttle(updateProgressBar, 100));
```

For purely visual updates, throttling to the frame rate with `requestAnimationFrame` is often the best choice:

```javascript
let ticking = false;
window.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
  if (!ticking) {
    ticking = true;
    requestAnimationFrame(() => {                // at most once per frame
      updateProgressBar();
      ticking = false;
    });
  }
});
```

```text
Raw events:     x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x . . . . . . . . x x x . . . . .
Throttle(100):  X       X       X       X     X(trailing)     X     X
Debounce(300):                                    X                       X
                                                  ^ 300 ms after the last event
```

| | Debounce | Throttle |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | Once, after calls stop for `wait` ms | At most once per `interval` ms, during the activity |
| Continuous activity | Never runs until it stops | Runs regularly |
| Use for | Search box, autosave, resize end, form validation | Scroll position, drag, mousemove, rate-limited buttons |
| Analogy | Elevator door | Dripping tap |

**Retry with exponential backoff.** Network operations sometimes fail transiently.
