Retrying immediately and repeatedly can make things worse (if the server is overloaded, thousands of clients hammering it prevents recovery). **Exponential backoff** waits longer after each failure (for example 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s, 4 s...). Adding **jitter** (randomness) prevents many clients from retrying in sync.

Rules for safe retries:

- Retry only **transient** failures: network errors, timeouts, HTTP 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504. Never retry 400, 401, 403 or 404: the result will be the same.
- Retry only **idempotent** operations (GET, PUT, DELETE) unless the server supports idempotency keys. Retrying a `POST /payments` could charge twice.
- Respect a `Retry-After` header when the server sends one.
- Cap the number of attempts and the maximum delay, and support cancellation.

```javascript
class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(response) {
    super(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    this.status = response.status;
  }
}

const RETRYABLE = new Set([408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]);

async function fetchWithRetry(url, options = {}, { retries = 4, baseDelay = 500, maxDelay = 8000 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, options);
      if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res);
      return res;
    } catch (err) {
      const retryable =
        err.name !== "AbortError" &&                       // never retry a deliberate cancel
        (err instanceof TypeError ||                       // fetch throws TypeError on network failure
          (err instanceof HttpError && RETRYABLE.has(err.status)));

      if (!retryable || attempt >= retries) throw err;     // give up

      const exp = Math.min(maxDelay, baseDelay * 2 ** attempt);   // 500, 1000, 2000, 4000...
      const wait = Math.random() * exp;                    // "full jitter": anywhere in [0, exp)
      console.warn(`Attempt ${attempt + 1} failed (${err.message}); retrying in ${Math.round(wait)} ms`);
      await delay(wait, { signal: options.signal });       // cancellable delay from the previous topic
    }
  }
}
```

```text
attempt 1  X
            <-0.5s->
attempt 2           X
                     <---1s--->
attempt 3                      X
                                <-------2s------->
attempt 4                                         OK
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Debounce when only the final value matters: run once after the calls stop.
- Throttle when you need steady updates during continuous activity: run at most once per interval. For visual updates, throttle with `requestAnimationFrame`.
- Retry only transient errors and idempotent operations, with a capped number of attempts.
- Use exponential backoff with jitter so that retries do not overload a struggling server, and respect `Retry-After`.
- Make delays and retries cancellable, and never retry an `AbortError`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Attach a `mousemove` handler that increments a counter, and display three counters side by side: raw calls, throttled calls (200 ms) and debounced calls (200 ms). Move the mouse continuously, then stop, and explain the differences.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend `debounce` so that the returned function has `cancel()` and `flush()` methods (`flush` runs a pending call immediately), and add a `leading` option that runs on the first call instead of the last. Write tests with fake timers or real short delays.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your mobile app retries failed requests every second. During an outage, the server stays down even after the bug is fixed. What is happening and how would you change the retry policy?" *Hint:* think about the combined load of all clients, synchronised retries, and which errors deserve a retry at all.

<a id="54-client-server-communication-from-the-browser"></a>
### 5.4 Client-Server Communication from the Browser

This subchapter applies the asynchronous techniques of the chapter to the most common asynchronous operation on the Web: an HTTP request made from JavaScript. It covers the original `XMLHttpRequest` API, the modern `fetch` API and its building blocks, common body formats, the cross-origin rules that govern which requests are allowed, and streaming large downloads and uploads.

#### XMLHttpRequest and the AJAX Model

In the early Web, every interaction with the server meant a full page load: click a link or submit a form, and the browser discarded the current page and rendered a new one from scratch. Even changing a single number on the page required a round trip of the entire document. Around 2000, browsers gained an object that let JavaScript send HTTP requests in the background and update only part of the page. In 2005 the term **AJAX** (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML) was coined for this technique, and applications such as Gmail and Google Maps showed that web pages could feel like desktop applications.

**The AJAX model.**

```text
Classic model:                              AJAX model:

Browser            Server                   Browser (page stays loaded)      Server
  | -- GET /page ---> |                       | -- XHR GET /api/items -------> |
  | <-- full HTML --- |                       | <-- small data (XML/JSON) ---- |
  | (page replaced)   |                       | JS updates one part of the DOM  |
  | -- POST form ---> |                       | -- XHR POST /api/items ------> |
  | <-- full HTML --- |                       | <-- {"ok": true} ------------- |
  | (page replaced)   |                       | JS updates one part of the DOM  |
```

The "X" (XML) is historical. Today the data is almost always JSON, but the name stuck. The same model underlies every single-page application, whether it uses XHR, `fetch`, or a library on top of them.

**Using `XMLHttpRequest`.** XHR is an event-based API. You create an object, configure it, attach handlers and send it:

```javascript
const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.open("GET", "/api/products?category=books");   // method, URL (async by default)
xhr.responseType = "json";                         // parse the body automatically
xhr.timeout = 10000;                               // ms; fires "timeout" if exceeded

xhr.onload = () => {                               // the response arrived (ANY status code)
  if (xhr.status >= 200 && xhr.status < 300) {
    renderProducts(xhr.response);                  // already parsed thanks to responseType
  } else {
    showError(`Server error: ${xhr.status}`);
  }
};
xhr.onerror = () => showError("Network error");    // DNS failure, offline, CORS blocked...
xhr.ontimeout = () => showError("Request timed out");

xhr.send();                                        // body goes here for POST/PUT
```

**The `readyState` lifecycle.** Older code uses `onreadystatechange` and checks `readyState`:

| `readyState` | Constant | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `UNSENT` | Object created, `open()` not called |
| 1 | `OPENED` | `open()` called |
| 2 | `HEADERS_RECEIVED` | Response headers and status are available |
| 3 | `LOADING` | Body is downloading (`responseText` holds partial data) |
| 4 | `DONE` | The operation is complete (success or failure) |

```javascript
xhr.onreadystatechange = () => {
  if (xhr.readyState === XMLHttpRequest.DONE && xhr.status === 200) {
    console.log(xhr.responseText);
  }
};
```

**Sending data and headers.**

```javascript
const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.open("POST", "/api/orders");
xhr.setRequestHeader("Content-Type", "application/json");   // after open(), before send()
xhr.onload = () => console.log(xhr.status, xhr.getResponseHeader("Location"));
xhr.send(JSON.stringify({ productId: 7, quantity: 2 }));
```

**Progress events and abort.** XHR's one remaining advantage over `fetch` is **upload progress**: `xhr.upload.onprogress` reports how many bytes have been sent. `xhr.abort()` cancels a request.

```javascript
xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => {
  if (e.lengthComputable) progressBar.value = e.loaded / e.total;
};
cancelButton.onclick = () => xhr.abort();          // fires the "abort" event
```

**Synchronous XHR.** Passing `false` as the third argument to `open` makes `send()` block until the response arrives. On the main thread this freezes the page and is deprecated. Browsers log warnings and restrict it. Never use it.

**Why XHR was superseded.** XHR works, but its event-based design predates promises: no chaining, manual promisification, scattered handlers, and a confusing API (`responseText` vs `response`, `readyState` numbers, header methods). `fetch` (next topic) replaces it for almost all new code. You still need to read XHR in legacy code, older libraries (jQuery's `$.ajax`, 8.2, and Axios in the browser use it internally), and when you need upload progress.

**Key Takeaways**

- AJAX means updating part of a page with data fetched in the background instead of reloading the whole page. Today the data is usually JSON.
- XHR is event-based: `open`, configure, attach `onload`/`onerror`/`ontimeout`, then `send`.
- `onload` fires for every HTTP status. Check `xhr.status` yourself. `onerror` only fires for network-level failures.
- `readyState` goes from 0 to 4. `responseType` controls how the body is parsed.
- Synchronous XHR is deprecated. XHR remains useful mainly for upload progress events and legacy code.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use XHR to load `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users` with `responseType = "json"` and render the user names in a list. Display a message for both a non-2xx status and a network error (test with a wrong domain).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `xhrRequest({ method, url, body, headers, timeout })` that returns a promise, rejects on network error, timeout and abort with distinct error messages, and resolves with `{ status, headers, data }`. Use it to send a JSON `POST` request.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What problem did AJAX solve, and why is it still called AJAX even though most applications no longer use XML?" *Hint:* contrast full-page reloads with partial updates, and consider what part of the name describes the technique versus the data format.

#### The Fetch API

`fetch` is the modern, promise-based replacement for XHR, available in all browsers, in Web Workers, and natively in Node.js (version 18 and later), Deno and Bun. It is built from reusable objects (`Request`, `Response`, `Headers`, next topic) that are also used by Service Workers (15.2), and it integrates naturally with `async/await`, `AbortController` and streams.

**The basic call.** `fetch(resource, options)` starts a request and returns a promise of a `Response`.

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/api/products");   // waits for the status line and headers
const products = await response.json();          // waits for the body and parses it
```

Notice the **two awaits**. The first promise fulfils as soon as the headers arrive, so you can inspect the status before downloading a possibly large body. Reading the body is a second asynchronous step.

```text
fetch() called ----> headers received ----------> body fully received
                     fetch promise fulfils        response.json() fulfils
                     (status, headers available)  (data available)
```

**The most important surprise: HTTP errors do not reject.** The `fetch` promise rejects only for **network-level failures**: the server is unreachable, DNS fails, the connection drops, CORS blocks the response, or the request is aborted. A 404 or 500 response is a *successful* HTTP exchange from fetch's point of view, so the promise **fulfils**. You must check `response.ok` (true for status 200 to 299) yourself.

```javascript
async function getJSON(url, options) {
  const response = await fetch(url, options);
  if (!response.ok) {                                         // 404, 500, etc.
    throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status} ${response.statusText} for ${url}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

try {
  const user = await getJSON("/api/users/42");
} catch (err) {
  // TypeError for network failures, our Error for HTTP failures,
  // DOMException "AbortError" for cancellation
  showError(err.message);
}
```

| Situation | `fetch` promise | `response.ok` |
|---|---|---|
| 200 OK | Fulfils | `true` |
| 201 Created, 204 No Content | Fulfils | `true` |
| 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error | **Fulfils** | `false` |
| Server unreachable, DNS failure, offline | Rejects (`TypeError`) | Not applicable |
| Blocked by CORS | Rejects (`TypeError`) | Not applicable |
| Aborted | Rejects (`DOMException` `AbortError`) | Not applicable |

**Options.** The second argument configures the request:

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/api/orders", {
  method: "POST",                                 // default "GET"
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Authorization": `Bearer ${token}`,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ productId: 7, quantity: 2 }),   // string, FormData, Blob, URLSearchParams...
  credentials: "same-origin",                     // when to send cookies (default)
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000),             // cancellation/timeout (5.3)
});
```

| Option | Common values | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `method` | `"GET"`, `"POST"`, `"PUT"`, `"PATCH"`, `"DELETE"` | HTTP method (10.1) |
| `headers` | Object, array of pairs, or `Headers` | Request headers |
| `body` | String, `FormData`, `URLSearchParams`, `Blob`, `ArrayBuffer`, `ReadableStream` | Request payload (not allowed with GET/HEAD) |
| `credentials` | `"same-origin"` (default), `"include"`, `"omit"` | Whether to send cookies and HTTP auth |
| `mode` | `"cors"` (default), `"same-origin"`, `"no-cors"` | Cross-origin behaviour (see CORS below) |
| `cache` | `"default"`, `"no-store"`, `"reload"`, `"no-cache"`, `"force-cache"` | Interaction with the HTTP cache |
| `redirect` | `"follow"` (default), `"error"`, `"manual"` | What to do with 3xx responses |
| `signal` | `AbortSignal` | Cancellation |
| `keepalive` | `true` | Let the request outlive the page (analytics on unload) |

**Building URLs safely.** Never concatenate user input into a URL without encoding it. Use `URL` and `URLSearchParams`:

```javascript
const url = new URL("/api/search", location.origin);
url.searchParams.set("q", userInput);            // encodes spaces, &, =, etc.
url.searchParams.set("page", 2);
const res = await fetch(url);                    // /api/search?q=rock+%26+roll&page=2
```

**A small reusable client.** Most applications wrap `fetch` once, centralising the base URL, headers, JSON handling and error checking:

```javascript
async function api(path, { method = "GET", body, headers = {}, signal } = {}) {
  const response = await fetch(`/api${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: {
      Accept: "application/json",
      ...(body !== undefined && { "Content-Type": "application/json" }),
      ...headers,
    },
    body: body !== undefined ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
    signal,
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text().catch(() => "");   // server error message, if any
    throw new Error(`${method} ${path} failed: ${response.status} ${detail}`);
  }
  return response.status === 204 ? null : response.json(); // 204 has no body to parse
}

const order = await api("/orders", { method: "POST", body: { productId: 7 } });
```

**`fetch` vs XHR.**

| | `XMLHttpRequest` | `fetch` |
|---|---|---|
| Style | Events and callbacks | Promises |
| HTTP error statuses | `onload` fires, check `status` | Promise fulfils, check `ok` |
| Cancellation | `xhr.abort()` | `AbortController` signal |
| Timeout | `xhr.timeout` | `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` |
| Download progress | `onprogress` event | Read `response.body` stream (see Streaming) |
| Upload progress | `xhr.upload.onprogress` | Not available |
| Streaming | No (partial `responseText` only) | Yes, `ReadableStream` bodies |
| Available in Service Workers and Node.js | No | Yes |

**Key Takeaways**

- `fetch(url, options)` returns a promise of a `Response`. Reading the body (`json()`, `text()`...) is a second asynchronous step.
- The promise rejects only on network failures, CORS blocks and aborts. HTTP error statuses fulfil, so always check `response.ok`.
- Configure method, headers, body, credentials, cache and cancellation through the options object.
- Build URLs with `URL` and `URLSearchParams` to encode user input correctly.
- Wrap `fetch` in a small helper that centralises headers, JSON handling and error checking.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Fetch `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1` and display its title. Then change the URL to `/posts/999999` and make your code show "Post not found" based on the status, not on a missing field.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build the `api()` helper above, extend it to support a query object (`api("/products", { query: { page: 2, sort: "price" } })`), and add a 10-second default timeout that callers can override or combine with their own `signal`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A colleague's code catches no errors when the server returns 500, even though it has a `.catch()`. Why?" *Hint:* consider what fetch considers a failure, and what the `ok` property is for.

#### Request, Response and Headers Objects

`fetch` is a thin function on top of three classes that model HTTP messages. Most of the time you use them implicitly, but knowing them lets you inspect responses properly, clone and modify requests, build responses yourself (in Service Workers, tests and mocks), and understand why a body can only be read once.

**`Headers`.** A `Headers` object is a case-insensitive, multi-valued map of HTTP header fields.

```javascript
const headers = new Headers({ "Content-Type": "application/json" });
headers.append("Accept-Language", "en");
headers.set("X-Request-Id", crypto.randomUUID());   // replace any existing value

console.log(headers.get("content-type"));            // "application/json" (names are case-insensitive)
console.log(headers.has("Authorization"));           // false
headers.delete("Accept-Language");

for (const [name, value] of headers) {               // iterable, names come back lower-cased
  console.log(name, value);
}
```

- `append` adds a value (several values are joined with `", "`), `set` replaces.
- `getSetCookie()` returns the separate `Set-Cookie` values where the environment exposes them (Node.js). Browsers never expose `Set-Cookie` to JavaScript.
- Some headers are **forbidden** in browser requests and silently ignored if you set them, because the browser must control them: for example `Host`, `Cookie`, `Origin`, `Referer`, `Content-Length` and `Connection`.

**Reading response headers.**

```javascript
const res = await fetch("/api/report");
console.log(res.headers.get("Content-Type"));       // "application/json; charset=utf-8"
console.log(res.headers.get("ETag"));               // null if missing or not exposed by CORS
```

**`Response`.** A `Response` represents the reply. Its main properties are:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status`, `statusText` | `404`, `"Not Found"` (`statusText` is often empty with HTTP/2) |
| `ok` | `true` if `status` is 200 to 299 |
| `headers` | A read-only `Headers` object |
| `url` | Final URL, after redirects |
| `redirected` | `true` if any redirect was followed |
| `type` | `"basic"` (same origin), `"cors"`, `"opaque"` (no-cors) |
| `body` | A `ReadableStream` of bytes, or `null` |
| `bodyUsed` | `true` once the body has been read |

**Body methods** read the whole body and return a promise:

| Method | Result | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `json()` | Parsed JavaScript value | JSON APIs |
| `text()` | String (decoded as UTF-8) | HTML, plain text, CSV |
| `blob()` | `Blob` | Images, files to download or display |
| `arrayBuffer()` | `ArrayBuffer` | Binary formats (4.2, Typed Arrays) |
| `bytes()` | `Uint8Array` | Binary data, newer shorthand for `arrayBuffer` |
| `formData()` | `FormData` | Multipart or URL-encoded bodies (mostly in Service Workers) |

**A body can only be read once.** The body is a stream: once consumed, the data is gone. A second read rejects with a `TypeError`. If you need it twice (for example to log the raw text and also parse it), clone the response first or read it as text and parse it yourself.

```javascript
const res = await fetch("/api/data");
const copy = res.clone();                   // must be cloned BEFORE reading
const data = await res.json();
const raw = await copy.text();              // works: the clone has its own body

// await res.text();                        // TypeError: body has already been consumed

// Alternative: read once as text, then parse
const text = await (await fetch("/api/data")).text();
let parsed;
try {
  parsed = JSON.parse(text);
} catch {
  console.error("Server did not return JSON:", text.slice(0, 200));
}
```

**Displaying a binary response.**

```javascript
const res = await fetch("/images/chart.png");
const blob = await res.blob();
const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);      // a temporary blob: URL pointing at the data
img.src = url;
img.onload = () => URL.revokeObjectURL(url);   // free the memory once displayed
```

**Constructing `Response` objects.** You can create responses yourself, which is essential in Service Workers and convenient for tests:

```javascript
const notFound = new Response("Not here", { status: 404, headers: { "Content-Type": "text/plain" } });
const jsonRes = Response.json({ ok: true }, { status: 201 });   // sets Content-Type: application/json
const failure = Response.error();                                // a network-error response

// Mocking fetch in a test
globalThis.fetch = async () => Response.json([{ id: 1, name: "Test product" }]);
```

**`Request`.** A `Request` represents an outgoing request. `fetch(url, options)` creates one internally, but you can create it yourself to reuse or derive it:

```javascript
const base = new Request("/api/items", {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
});

const withPost = new Request(base, {        // copy everything, override some fields
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: "Lamp" }),
  headers: { ...Object.fromEntries(base.headers), "Content-Type": "application/json" },
});

console.log(withPost.method, withPost.url); // "POST", "https://example.com/api/items"
const res = await fetch(withPost);
```

`Request` has the same body methods and the same read-once rule as `Response`, plus properties mirroring the fetch options (`method`, `headers`, `credentials`, `mode`, `signal`...).

```text
                        +-------------------------+
 fetch(input, init) --> | Request                 | -- network --> +--------------------------+
                        |  method, url, headers   |                | Response                 |
                        |  body (stream, once)    |                |  status, ok, headers     |
                        |  credentials, signal... |                |  body (stream, once)     |
                        +-------------------------+                |  json() text() blob()... |
                                                                   +--------------------------+
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `Headers` is a case-insensitive map. Some request headers are forbidden and controlled by the browser.
- `Response` exposes `status`, `ok`, `headers`, `url`, `type` and a body that can be read with `json()`, `text()`, `blob()`, `arrayBuffer()` and others.
- Bodies are streams and can only be consumed once. Use `clone()` before reading if you need the body twice.
- `Request` and `Response` can be constructed directly, which is useful for reusable request templates, Service Workers and test mocks.
- Use `URL.createObjectURL` to display binary responses, and revoke the URL afterwards.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Fetch any page from your own site and log every response header with a `for...of` loop over `response.headers`, along with `status`, `type`, `url` and `redirected`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `loggingFetch(input, init)` wrapper that logs the method, URL, status and duration of every request, and also logs the first 200 characters of the response body, while still returning a response whose body the caller can read normally.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does calling `response.json()` twice fail, and how can you work around it?" *Hint:* think about what `response.body` is, and what `clone()` does to it.

#### Working with JSON and FormData

The body of a request has to be encoded in a format that both sides agree on, announced by the `Content-Type` header. Picking the wrong format, or the wrong header, is a frequent source of "the server receives an empty body" bugs. In practice browsers send three formats: JSON for APIs, URL-encoded data for simple forms, and multipart form data for forms that include files.

| Format | `Content-Type` | Body type in JS | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| JSON | `application/json` | `JSON.stringify(obj)` | REST and JSON APIs (10.4) |
| URL-encoded | `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` | `URLSearchParams` | Simple forms without files, OAuth token endpoints |
| Multipart | `multipart/form-data; boundary=...` | `FormData` | Forms with files, mixed text and binary |
| Raw binary | `application/octet-stream`, `image/png`... | `Blob`, `File`, `ArrayBuffer` | Uploading a single file as-is |

**Sending JSON.** Serialise with `JSON.stringify` (4.1) and set the `Content-Type` yourself. Without the header, `fetch` sends a string body as `text/plain`, and many servers will not parse it.

```javascript
const res = await fetch("/api/users", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },   // required for JSON
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: "Ada", roles: ["admin"], joined: new Date() }),
});
// Dates become ISO strings, undefined and functions are dropped (4.1)
```

**Receiving JSON.** `response.json()` parses the body and rejects with a `SyntaxError` if the body is not valid JSON, for example when an error page in HTML is returned. Check the status (and optionally the content type) before parsing:

```javascript
const res = await fetch("/api/users/42");
const isJson = res.headers.get("Content-Type")?.includes("application/json");

if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
if (!isJson) throw new Error("Expected JSON but got " + res.headers.get("Content-Type"));

const user = await res.json();
```

**`URLSearchParams` for URL-encoded bodies.** Passing a `URLSearchParams` object as the body automatically sets `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded;charset=UTF-8`.

```javascript
const body = new URLSearchParams({ grant_type: "password", username: "ada", password: "s3cret" });
await fetch("/oauth/token", { method: "POST", body });
// body sent: grant_type=password&username=ada&password=s3cret
```

**`FormData`.** A `FormData` object is a list of name/value pairs, where values can be strings or files. You can build it by hand or capture an entire `<form>` element in one line. Passed as the body, it is encoded as `multipart/form-data`.

```html
<form id="profile-form">
  <input name="displayName" value="Ada">
  <input name="avatar" type="file" accept="image/*">
  <input name="interests" type="checkbox" value="math" checked>
  <input name="interests" type="checkbox" value="music" checked>
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
```

```javascript
const form = document.querySelector("#profile-form");

form.addEventListener("submit", async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();                       // stop the classic full-page form submission

  const data = new FormData(form);              // reads every named, enabled control
  data.append("clientTime", new Date().toISOString());   // add extra fields

  console.log(data.get("displayName"));          // "Ada"
  console.log(data.getAll("interests"));        // ["math", "music"]: repeated names are kept

  const res = await fetch("/api/profile", {
    method: "POST",
    body: data,                                 // DO NOT set Content-Type yourself
  });
  if (!res.ok) showError("Saving failed");
});
```

**Never set `Content-Type` for `FormData`.** The multipart format separates fields with a random **boundary** string, which must appear in the header (`multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX`). The browser generates it. If you set the header manually, the boundary is missing and the server cannot parse the body.

What a multipart body looks like on the wire:

```text
POST /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----Bnd7x

------Bnd7x
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="displayName"

Ada
------Bnd7x
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="avatar"; filename="me.png"
Content-Type: image/png

<binary bytes of the image>
------Bnd7x--
```

**Converting between formats.**

```javascript
const formData = new FormData(form);

// FormData -> plain object (repeated names keep only the last value) -> JSON
const obj = Object.fromEntries(formData);
await fetch("/api/profile", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(obj),                     // only useful if the form has no files
});

// FormData -> URLSearchParams (text fields only)
const params = new URLSearchParams(formData);
await fetch(`/api/search?${params}`);           // a GET with the form's values in the query string
```

**Key Takeaways**

- The `Content-Type` header must match the body format, or the server will not parse it.
- For JSON, call `JSON.stringify` and set `Content-Type: application/json` yourself. Check `ok` before calling `response.json()`.
- `URLSearchParams` produces URL-encoded bodies and query strings, and sets the header automatically.
- `FormData` captures forms (including files and repeated fields) and is sent as multipart. Never set its `Content-Type` manually, because the browser must add the boundary.
- Use `Object.fromEntries(formData)` to turn a file-less form into an object for JSON APIs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a contact form (name, email, message) and submit it with `fetch` and `FormData` to `https://httpbin.org/post`. Display the `form` field of the echoed response.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `toFormData(obj)` that converts a nested object such as `{ user: { name: "Ada", tags: ["a", "b"] }, avatar: fileObject }` into `FormData` using bracket notation (`user[name]`, `user[tags][]`). Send it to `httpbin.org/post`, then do the same with JSON, and compare what the server receives.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A file upload works in Postman but the server receives no file when sent from the browser with `fetch`. The code sets `Content-Type: multipart/form-data`. What is wrong?" *Hint:* look at what a multipart `Content-Type` header must contain, and who generates it.

#### Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

If any website could use JavaScript to read responses from any other site, a malicious page could read your webmail, your bank balance or your company's intranet, because the browser would attach your cookies to the requests. The **same-origin policy** prevents this: by default, a script may only *read* responses from its own **origin**. **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the standard way for a server to relax that rule and say "this other origin is allowed to read my responses".

**What an origin is.** An origin is the triple **scheme + host + port**. Two URLs have the same origin only if all three match.

| URL compared with `https://app.example.com` | Same origin? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `https://app.example.com/api/users` | Yes | Only the path differs |
| `http://app.example.com` | No | Different scheme |
| `https://api.example.com` | No | Different host (subdomains count) |
| `https://app.example.com:8443` | No | Different port |

**What the same-origin policy restricts.** It restricts *reading*, not sending. A page can embed cross-origin images, scripts and stylesheets, and submit forms to other sites. What it cannot do without permission is *read* a cross-origin response with `fetch` or XHR, or send certain kinds of requests. (Preventing unwanted cross-site *writes* is the job of CSRF protections, 10.3.)

**Simple requests.** A cross-origin request is "simple" if it could have been produced by an ordinary HTML form:

- method `GET`, `HEAD` or `POST`
- only CORS-safelisted headers (`Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Content-Language`, and `Content-Type` with a limited set of values)
- `Content-Type`, if present, is `text/plain`, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` or `multipart/form-data`

For a simple request, the browser sends it directly with an `Origin` header and checks the response:

```text
Browser (page on https://app.example.com)                 Server https://api.other.com
  | GET /products                                           |
  | Origin: https://app.example.com              ---------> |
  |                                                         |
  | <--------- 200 OK                                       |
  |            Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
  |                                                         |
  | Browser checks the header: matches -> JS can read the response
  | (if missing or different: response hidden, fetch rejects with TypeError)
```

**Preflighted requests.** Anything else, such as a `PUT` or `DELETE`, a JSON body (`Content-Type: application/json`), or an `Authorization` header, could have effects that a form could never produce. Before sending it, the browser asks for permission with a **preflight** request: an `OPTIONS` request that describes the real request.

```text
Browser                                                   Server
  | OPTIONS /orders                                         |
  | Origin: https://app.example.com                         |
  | Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT                      |
  | Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization
  |                                              ---------> |
  | <--------- 204 No Content                               |
  |            Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
  |            Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
  |            Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
  |            Access-Control-Max-Age: 600      (cache this answer for 10 min)
  |                                                         |
  | PUT /orders  (the actual request)            ---------> |
  | <--------- 200 OK + Access-Control-Allow-Origin         |
```

If the preflight response does not allow the method or headers, the actual request is never sent, and `fetch` rejects with a `TypeError`.

**Response headers set by the server.**

| Header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | Origin allowed to read: an exact origin, or `*` for any origin |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` | Methods allowed (preflight) |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` | Request headers allowed (preflight) |
| `Access-Control-Max-Age` | Seconds the browser may cache the preflight result |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` | `true` to allow requests that carry cookies or HTTP auth |
| `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` | Response headers JavaScript may read beyond the safelisted ones (for example `ETag`, `X-Total-Count`) |

**Credentials.** By default, cross-origin `fetch` does not send cookies. To send them:

```javascript
await fetch("https://api.other.com/me", { credentials: "include" });
```

The server must then reply with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and an **explicit** origin in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The wildcard `*` is not allowed with credentials. The cookies themselves must also allow cross-site sending (`SameSite=None; Secure`, 10.2).

**Configuring the server (Express example, 12.2).**

```javascript
const ALLOWED = new Set(["https://app.example.com", "http://localhost:5173"]);

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const origin = req.headers.origin;
  if (ALLOWED.has(origin)) {
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin);       // echo the allowed origin, never blindly
    res.set("Vary", "Origin");                            // caches must store per-origin responses
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", "true");
  }
  if (req.method === "OPTIONS") {                         // answer preflights
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Methods", "GET, POST, PUT, DELETE");
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "Content-Type, Authorization");
    res.set("Access-Control-Max-Age", "600");
    return res.sendStatus(204);
  }
  next();
});
```

**Common misconceptions.**

- **CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server.** `curl`, Postman and server-to-server calls ignore it. CORS protects *users' browsers*, not your API. Your API still needs authentication and authorisation.
- **CORS errors cannot be fixed from front-end code.** Only the server (or a proxy on your own origin, such as a development server proxy) can grant access.
- **`mode: "no-cors"` does not bypass CORS.** It produces an **opaque** response: status `0`, no headers, no readable body. It is only useful for fire-and-forget requests or caching in Service Workers.
- **CORS error details are hidden from JavaScript** on purpose. The `TypeError` says only "Failed to fetch". Check the browser console and the Network panel for the real reason.

**Key Takeaways**

- An origin is scheme + host + port. The same-origin policy stops scripts from reading cross-origin responses without permission.
- Simple requests are sent directly. Other requests (custom methods, JSON bodies, `Authorization`) are preceded by an `OPTIONS` preflight.
- The server grants access with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. The browser enforces them.
- Requests with credentials need `credentials: "include"`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and an explicit origin (no `*`).
- CORS protects users in browsers, not APIs. It is fixed on the server, and `no-cors` gives an unreadable opaque response.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Serve a page on `http://localhost:3000` and a tiny API on `http://localhost:4000`. Fetch the API from the page and observe the CORS error in the console and the Network panel. Fix it by adding `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the API.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Change the request to a `PUT` with a JSON body and an `Authorization` header. Observe the preflight in the Network panel, make the API answer it correctly, and use `Access-Control-Max-Age` to stop repeated preflights. Then add cookies with `credentials: "include"` and make that work too.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If CORS is not a server-side security mechanism, what does it actually protect, and why can't an attacker simply call your API with curl to get around it?" *Hint:* think about whose cookies and network position a malicious web page could use, compared with an attacker's own command line.

#### Streaming Responses and File Uploads

`response.json()` and `response.text()` wait for the **entire** body before giving you anything. That is fine for small API responses, but not for a 2 GB video file, a long-running server process that reports progress line by line, or a language model that generates text word by word. Streams let you process data **as it arrives**, chunk by chunk, with constant memory, and show progress to the user. Uploads raise the opposite problem: sending large files from the browser efficiently and with feedback.

**Response bodies are streams.** `response.body` is a `ReadableStream` of `Uint8Array` chunks. You read it with a reader, one chunk at a time:

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/videos/lecture.mp4");
const reader = response.body.getReader();
const total = Number(response.headers.get("Content-Length")) || 0;   // 0 if unknown (e.g. compressed)
let received = 0;
const chunks = [];

while (true) {
  const { done, value } = await reader.read();   // value is a Uint8Array chunk
  if (done) break;
  chunks.push(value);
  received += value.byteLength;
  if (total) progressBar.value = received / total;   // download progress
}

const blob = new Blob(chunks, { type: response.headers.get("Content-Type") });
video.src = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
```

```text
Server ---[chunk 1]---[chunk 2]---[chunk 3]--- ... ---[chunk n]---| done
             |           |           |                    |
          read()      read()      read()               read() -> { done: true }
          process     process     process              finish
```

Note that `Content-Length` may be missing, or describe the compressed size while the stream delivers decompressed bytes, so treat progress as approximate.

**Decoding text streams.** For text, pipe the byte stream through a `TextDecoderStream`, which correctly handles multi-byte characters split across chunks.

```javascript
const res = await fetch("/api/logs/stream");
const textStream = res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream());

for await (const text of textStream) {          // async iteration (5.3), where supported
  logView.textContent += text;                  // append as it arrives
}
```

**Streaming structured data (NDJSON).** Servers often stream newline-delimited JSON: one JSON object per line. Combine the line-splitting generator from 5.3 with `JSON.parse`:

```javascript
async function* ndjson(response) {
  for await (const line of readLines(response.body)) {   // readLines from "Async Iterators"
    if (line.trim()) yield JSON.parse(line);
  }
}

const res = await fetch("/api/search/stream?q=lamps");
for await (const result of ndjson(res)) {
  appendResult(result);                         // results appear one by one, as the server finds them
}
```

The same idea underlies **Server-Sent Events** (`EventSource`), a standard text format for server push over one HTTP response, and the token-by-token output of AI chat interfaces. WebSocket (10.5) is the alternative when communication must be two-way.

**Uploading files.** A file chosen by the user is a `File` object (a `Blob` with a name and a modification date). There are two common ways to upload it:

```javascript
const input = document.querySelector("input[type=file]");
const file = input.files[0];

// 1. Multipart: the file plus other fields, as an HTML form would send it
const data = new FormData();
data.append("title", "Holiday photo");
data.append("photo", file);                     // file name and type are included automatically
await fetch("/api/photos", { method: "POST", body: data });

// 2. Raw body: just the bytes, with metadata in headers or the URL
await fetch(`/api/photos/${encodeURIComponent(file.name)}`, {
  method: "PUT",
  headers: { "Content-Type": file.type || "application/octet-stream" },
  body: file,                                   // the browser streams it from disk
});
```

Before uploading, validate on the client for user experience (size, type), and **always validate again on the server**: client checks are trivially bypassed.

```javascript
const MAX = 10 * 1024 * 1024;                    // 10 MB

function validateUpload(file) {
  if (file.size > MAX) return "The file must be smaller than 10 MB.";
  if (!["image/png", "image/jpeg"].includes(file.type)) return "PNG or JPEG only.";
  return null;                                   // valid
}

const problem = validateUpload(file);
if (problem) showError(problem);                 // otherwise proceed with the upload
```

**Upload progress.** `fetch` has no upload progress events. When you need a progress bar for an upload, use XHR's `upload.onprogress`:

```javascript
function uploadWithProgress(url, formData, onProgress) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
    xhr.open("POST", url);
    xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => {
      if (e.lengthComputable) onProgress(e.loaded / e.total);   // fraction of bytes sent
    };
    xhr.onload = () => (xhr.status < 300 ? resolve(xhr.response) : reject(new Error(`HTTP ${xhr.status}`)));
    xhr.onerror = () => reject(new TypeError("Network error"));
    xhr.send(formData);
  });
}

await uploadWithProgress("/api/photos", data, (p) => (progressBar.value = p));
```

**Chunked (resumable) uploads.** For very large files, split the file into pieces with `Blob.slice` and upload them one by one. If the connection drops, only the current chunk must be resent. Production systems use protocols such as tus or cloud providers' multipart upload APIs, but the core idea is simple:

```javascript
async function uploadInChunks(file, uploadId, chunkSize = 5 * 1024 * 1024) {
  for (let start = 0; start < file.size; start += chunkSize) {
    const chunk = file.slice(start, start + chunkSize);       // a Blob view: no copy in memory
    await fetchWithRetry(`/api/uploads/${uploadId}`, {       // retry logic from 5.3
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        "Content-Range": `bytes ${start}-${start + chunk.size - 1}/${file.size}`,
      },
      body: chunk,
    });
    progressBar.value = (start + chunk.size) / file.size;   // progress per completed chunk
  }
}
```

**Streaming request bodies.** In Chromium-based browsers, a `ReadableStream` can also be used as a request body (with the option `duplex: "half"`, over HTTP/2 or later), for example to compress data while it is uploaded. Support is not universal, so feature-detect it and keep a fallback.

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| Small JSON response | `response.json()` |
| Large download with progress | `response.body.getReader()` and `Content-Length` |
| Text or line-by-line data as it arrives | `pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream())`, async iteration, NDJSON |
| One-way server push of events | Server-Sent Events (`EventSource`) |
| Upload a file with other fields | `FormData` with `fetch` |
| Upload with a progress bar | XHR `upload.onprogress` |
| Very large or unreliable uploads | `Blob.slice` chunks with retries |

**Key Takeaways**

- `response.body` is a `ReadableStream` of byte chunks. Read it incrementally for progress, low memory use and early display.
- Decode text streams with `TextDecoderStream`, and split them into lines or NDJSON records with an async generator.
- Upload files with `FormData` (multipart with other fields) or directly as the body (raw bytes). Validate on the client for convenience and on the server for security.
- `fetch` has no upload progress events. Use XHR `upload.onprogress` when a progress bar is required.
- Split very large uploads into `Blob.slice` chunks so that failures only resend one piece.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Download a large image with `fetch`, read the body with a reader, and show a percentage counter based on `Content-Length`. Display the image when the download completes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a small Node.js server that streams 20 NDJSON lines, one every 300 ms. On the client, render each object as soon as its line arrives, and add a "Stop" button that aborts the stream with an `AbortController` and releases the reader.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you implement an upload of a 4 GB video from the browser that survives a network interruption at 90%?" *Hint:* consider splitting the file, how the server tracks which parts it has received, how the client finds out where to resume, and what to do on transient failures.

<a id="6-browser-apis-dom-style-and-events"></a>
## 6. Browser APIs: DOM, Style and Events

Chapters 3 to 5 treated JavaScript as a language. This chapter is about what the browser gives that language to work with: the DOM, a live tree of objects that represents the page, the APIs that read and change its styles and geometry, and the event system that turns user actions into function calls. It ends with the browser features that every non-trivial front end relies on, including storage, routing, background threads and observers. Frameworks such as React (Chapter 14) are built on these APIs, so understanding them explains both how frameworks work and how to debug them when they do not.

<a id="61-the-dom-model-and-document-manipulation"></a>
### 6.1 The DOM Model and Document Manipulation

This subchapter explains how the browser represents an HTML document as a tree of objects, and how to find, read, create, change and observe the nodes of that tree efficiently and safely.

#### DOM Tree, Nodes and Node Types

An HTML file is just text. JavaScript cannot do anything useful with a long string of angle brackets: finding "the third paragraph" or "every button inside the form" would mean writing a parser. So the browser parses the text once and builds an in-memory **object model** of the document. Every tag, every piece of text and every comment becomes an object with properties and methods, and these objects are linked to each other in a tree. This is the **Document Object Model (DOM)**: a standard, language-neutral API (maintained by WHATWG as the *DOM Living Standard*) that represents a document as a tree of **nodes**.

An analogy: the HTML file is the architect's blueprint, and the DOM is the building constructed from it. Once the building exists, you renovate the building, not the blueprint. Changing the DOM changes what the user sees. The original HTML source is not modified, which is why "View Source" and the Elements panel of DevTools can show different things.

**From markup to tree.** Consider this document:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Shop</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1 class="title">Cart</h1>
    <!-- items go here -->
    <p>Total: <strong>42 EUR</strong></p>
  </body>
</html>
```

The parser produces this tree (`#text` nodes that contain only whitespace are shown as `"\n  "`):

```text
Document
├── DocumentType  (html)
└── Element <html lang="en">
    ├── Element <head>
    │   ├── Text "\n    "
    │   ├── Element <title>
    │   │   └── Text "Shop"
    │   └── Text "\n  "
    ├── Text "\n  "
    └── Element <body>
        ├── Text "\n    "
        ├── Element <h1 class="title">
        │   └── Text "Cart"
        ├── Text "\n    "
        ├── Comment " items go here "
        ├── Text "\n    "
        ├── Element <p>
        │   ├── Text "Total: "
        │   └── Element <strong>
        │       └── Text "42 EUR"
        └── Text "\n  "
```

Three things in this tree surprise most beginners:

1. **Text is a separate node.** The `<h1>` element does not contain the string "Cart" directly. It has a child `Text` node whose value is "Cart".
2. **Whitespace between tags becomes text nodes too.** The line breaks and indentation in the source are preserved as `Text` nodes. This matters when you navigate with `firstChild` or `childNodes` (see *Traversing the DOM Tree*).
3. **The parser repairs and completes markup.** Missing `<html>`, `<head>` or `<body>` tags are created automatically, a `<tbody>` is inserted into tables that lack one, and unclosed tags are closed. The DOM reflects the repaired document, not your source.

**Node types.** Every node has a `nodeType` number and a `nodeName` string:

| Node type | `nodeType` | Constant | `nodeName` | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Element | 1 | `Node.ELEMENT_NODE` | Upper-case tag name, such as `"P"` | `<p>`, `<div>` |
| Text | 3 | `Node.TEXT_NODE` | `"#text"` | The characters inside an element |
| Comment | 8 | `Node.COMMENT_NODE` | `"#comment"` | `<!-- ... -->` |
| Document | 9 | `Node.DOCUMENT_NODE` | `"#document"` | `document` |
| DocumentType | 10 | `Node.DOCUMENT_TYPE_NODE` | `"html"` | `<!DOCTYPE html>` |
| DocumentFragment | 11 | `Node.DOCUMENT_FRAGMENT_NODE` | `"#document-fragment"` | `template.content`, shadow roots |

Attributes (`Attr`, type 2) are also technically nodes, but they are not children of the element and are not part of the tree. Types 4, 5, 6, 7 and 12 exist for XML and are rarely seen in HTML pages.

**The interface hierarchy.** DOM objects are instances of a hierarchy of interfaces (classes, in JavaScript terms). Methods defined higher up are available to everything below:

```text
EventTarget                       addEventListener, dispatchEvent
└── Node                          parentNode, childNodes, appendChild, textContent
    ├── Document                  getElementById, createElement
    ├── DocumentFragment          (lightweight container, see later topic)
    ├── CharacterData             data, length
    │   ├── Text
    │   └── Comment
    └── Element                   id, classList, querySelector, getAttribute
        ├── HTMLElement           style, dataset, hidden, click()
        │   ├── HTMLInputElement  value, checked, validity
        │   ├── HTMLAnchorElement href, download
        │   └── ... (one per tag)
        └── SVGElement            (Chapter 7)
```

You can verify the chain in the console with the prototype chain (4.3):

```javascript
const input = document.createElement("input");

input instanceof HTMLInputElement;  // true
input instanceof HTMLElement;       // true
input instanceof Element;           // true
input instanceof Node;              // true
input instanceof EventTarget;       // true: every node can receive events

// Walk the prototype chain explicitly
let proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(input);
while (proto) {
  console.log(proto.constructor.name);  // HTMLInputElement, HTMLElement, Element, Node, EventTarget, Object
  proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto);
}
```

**Node versus Element.** Many APIs exist in two flavours: one that works with all nodes (including text and comments) and one that works with elements only. `childNodes` returns every child node, while `children` returns only element children. Most of the time you want the element version.

```javascript
const p = document.querySelector("p");

p.childNodes.length;   // 2: Text "Total: " and <strong>
p.children.length;     // 1: only <strong>

for (const node of p.childNodes) {
  console.log(node.nodeType, node.nodeName, JSON.stringify(node.textContent));
}
// 3 "#text"  "Total: "
// 1 "STRONG" "42 EUR"
```

**The DOM is live.** The objects you hold are the real page. Changing a property updates the screen on the next rendering opportunity (5.1), and changes made by other code (another script, a browser extension, the user editing a `contenteditable` region) are visible through the same objects.

**Key Takeaways**

- The DOM is a tree of objects built by the browser from the HTML source. Scripts read and change the DOM, never the source file.
- Elements, text, comments and the document itself are all nodes, distinguished by `nodeType` and `nodeName`.
- Text is stored in separate `Text` child nodes, and whitespace between tags also produces `Text` nodes.
- The parser repairs markup (implicit `<head>`, `<body>`, `<tbody>`), so the tree may differ from the source.
- DOM interfaces form an inheritance chain: `EventTarget`, `Node`, `Element`, `HTMLElement`, then one interface per tag.
- Prefer element-only APIs (`children`, `firstElementChild`) unless you specifically need text or comment nodes.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a table in HTML without a `<tbody>` and inspect it in the Elements panel. Then log `document.querySelector("table").children[0].tagName` and explain the result.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function `describe(node, depth = 0)` that prints the tree under a node with indentation, showing `nodeName` for elements and the trimmed text for non-empty text nodes, and skipping whitespace-only text nodes. Run it on `document.body`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between the HTML source of a page and its DOM?" *Hint:* consider parser error correction, scripts that modify the page after loading, and what "View Source" shows compared with DevTools.

#### The window and document Objects

Every script running in a page needs a starting point: something that represents "this browser tab" and something that represents "this page". The browser provides two root objects for that. `window` represents the browsing context (the tab or frame, its viewport, its history, its timers), and `document` represents the loaded page (the root of the DOM tree). The APIs hanging off `window` that are not about the document (location, history, screen, navigator) are traditionally called the **BOM**, the Browser Object Model.

```text
window  (global object, one per tab or iframe)
├── document         the DOM tree of the current page
├── location         current URL; assigning it navigates
├── history          session history (6.4)
├── navigator        browser and device info, clipboard, geolocation (6.4)
├── screen           physical screen size and colour depth
├── localStorage     per-origin storage (6.4)
├── innerWidth / innerHeight, scrollX / scrollY, devicePixelRatio
└── setTimeout, fetch, alert, requestAnimationFrame, ...
```

**`window` is the global object.** In a browser, `window` is the object that holds global variables and functions. This is why you can write `setTimeout(...)` instead of `window.setTimeout(...)`, and `document` instead of `window.document`. The standard name that works in every environment (browser, worker, Node.js) is `globalThis`.

```javascript
// In a classic (non-module) script:
var appName = "Shop";        // var at top level creates a property on window
let version = 2;             // let/const live in the global scope but NOT on window
function init() {}           // function declarations also become window properties

console.log(window.appName); // "Shop"
console.log(window.version); // undefined
console.log(window.init === init);       // true
console.log(globalThis === window);      // true in the main thread
```

In an ES module (3.4), top-level `var` and function declarations are scoped to the module and do not create `window` properties. This is one of the reasons modules avoid accidental global pollution.

**Named access on `window`.** For historical reasons, every element with an `id` is also exposed as a global variable of the same name:

```html
<button id="save">Save</button>
<script>
  console.log(save);           // <button id="save">: works, but do not rely on it
  console.log(window.save);    // same element
</script>
```

This is fragile: a global variable with the same name shadows it, and ids such as `name` or `location` collide with real `window` properties. Always select elements explicitly (next topic).

**Useful `window` members.**

| Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `innerWidth`, `innerHeight` | Viewport size in CSS pixels, including the scrollbar |
| `scrollX`, `scrollY`, `scrollTo()` | Page scroll position and programmatic scrolling (6.2) |
| `devicePixelRatio` | Device pixels per CSS pixel (2 or 3 on high-density screens) |
| `location.href`, `location.assign()`, `location.reload()` | Read or change the current URL |
| `matchMedia(query)` | Evaluate a CSS media query from JavaScript |
| `getComputedStyle(el)` | Final style values of an element (6.2) |
| `open()`, `close()`, `opener` | Open and control other windows (subject to popup blocking) |
| `alert()`, `confirm()`, `prompt()` | Blocking modal dialogs (avoid in production; use `<dialog>`) |

```javascript
// Respond to a media query from JavaScript
const dark = window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)");
console.log(dark.matches);                       // true or false right now
dark.addEventListener("change", (e) => {
  console.log("dark mode is now", e.matches);    // fires when the OS setting changes
});
```

**The `document` object.** `document` is the root `Document` node of the tree and the factory for new nodes. Its most used members:

| Member | Returns |
|---|---|
| `document.documentElement` | The `<html>` element |
| `document.head`, `document.body` | The `<head>` and `<body>` elements |
| `document.title` | The page title (read and write) |
| `document.URL`, `document.referrer` | Current URL and the page that linked here |
| `document.readyState` | `"loading"`, `"interactive"` (DOM parsed) or `"complete"` (all resources loaded) |
| `document.activeElement` | The element that currently has focus |
| `document.forms`, `document.images`, `document.links` | Live collections of those elements |
| `document.createElement()`, `createTextNode()` | Factories for new nodes |
| `document.cookie` | Cookies as a single string (Chapter 10) |

**When is the DOM ready?** A script can only find elements that the parser has already created. A classic script in the `<head>` runs before `<body>` exists:

```html
<head>
  <script>
    console.log(document.querySelector("h1"));  // null: <h1> has not been parsed yet
  </script>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello</h1>
</body>
```

There are three standard fixes. The first is the modern default:

```html
<!-- 1. defer (or type="module", which defers automatically): runs after parsing -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>

<!-- 2. Put the script at the end of <body> -->

<!-- 3. Wait for the DOMContentLoaded event (6.3) -->
<script>
  document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {
    console.log(document.querySelector("h1"));  // <h1>Hello</h1>
  });
</script>
```

**Frames have their own pair.** Each `<iframe>` has its own `window` and `document`, accessible via `iframe.contentWindow` and `iframe.contentDocument`, but only if the iframe is same-origin. Cross-origin frames can only communicate through `postMessage` (Chapter 17 covers the security model).

**Key Takeaways**

- `window` represents the tab or frame and is the global object. `document` represents the page and is the root of the DOM.
- Top-level `var` and function declarations in classic scripts become `window` properties. `let`, `const` and module code do not.
- Elements with an `id` are exposed as globals. Never rely on this: select elements explicitly.
- `document` provides shortcuts (`body`, `head`, `documentElement`, `activeElement`) and node factories (`createElement`).
- A script can only access elements that have already been parsed. Use `defer`, modules or `DOMContentLoaded`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* In the console of any page, log `document.readyState`, `document.title`, `window.innerWidth` and `window.devicePixelRatio`. Resize the window and zoom in, then log them again and explain what changed.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a script placed in the `<head>` (without `defer`) that logs the number of `<p>` elements at three moments: immediately, on `DOMContentLoaded` and on `load`. Add a large image to the page and explain the differences between the timestamps.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `window`, `document` and `globalThis`?" *Hint:* think about which one is the global object, which one is a node in the tree, and which name also works inside a Web Worker or Node.js.

#### Element Selection Methods

Before you can change an element, you need a reference to it. The DOM offers two generations of selection methods. The older ones (`getElementById`, `getElementsByTagName`, `getElementsByClassName`) each search by one specific criterion. The newer ones (`querySelector`, `querySelectorAll`) accept any CSS selector, so everything you learned about selectors in Chapter 2 becomes a query language for JavaScript.

**`getElementById`.** Returns the unique element with that `id`, or `null`. It exists only on `document` (ids are unique per document) and is the fastest lookup because browsers keep an index of ids.

```javascript
const form = document.getElementById("checkout");   // no "#" prefix
if (form === null) {
  throw new Error("checkout form missing");
}
```

**`querySelector` and `querySelectorAll`.** Accept any CSS selector. `querySelector` returns the first matching element in document order (or `null`). `querySelectorAll` returns a **static `NodeList`** of every match.

```javascript
const firstButton = document.querySelector("button");
const submit      = document.querySelector("form#checkout button[type='submit']");
const required    = document.querySelectorAll("input:required:not(:disabled)");
const odds        = document.querySelectorAll("tbody tr:nth-child(odd)");

required.forEach((input) => input.classList.add("highlight"));  // NodeList has forEach

// NodeList has no map/filter: convert to an array first
const names = Array.from(required, (input) => input.name);
const empty = [...required].filter((input) => input.value === "");
```

**Searching inside an element.** All these methods (except `getElementById`) also exist on elements, and then they only search that element's descendants. This is faster and avoids accidental matches elsewhere on the page.

```javascript
const card = document.querySelector(".product-card");
const price = card.querySelector(".price");   // only inside this card
```

One subtlety: the selector is still matched against the **whole document**. Only the results are restricted to descendants. Use `:scope` to anchor the selector to the element itself:

```html
<div id="outer">
  <div class="item">A
    <div class="item">B</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

```javascript
const outer = document.getElementById("outer");
outer.querySelectorAll("div .item").length;         // 2: "div" can match outer itself
outer.querySelectorAll(":scope > .item").length;    // 1: only direct children of outer
```

**Live versus static collections.** The older plural methods return **live** collections that update automatically when the document changes. `querySelectorAll` returns a snapshot.

```javascript
const liveItems   = document.getElementsByClassName("item");  // live HTMLCollection
const staticItems = document.querySelectorAll(".item");       // static NodeList

console.log(liveItems.length, staticItems.length);  // 3 3

const extra = document.createElement("li");
extra.className = "item";
document.querySelector("ul").append(extra);

console.log(liveItems.length, staticItems.length);  // 4 3: only the live one changed
```

Live collections cause a classic bug when you remove elements while iterating:

```javascript
const items = document.getElementsByClassName("item");  // live

// BUG: removing an element shifts the collection, so every other item is skipped
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
  items[i].remove();
}

// Fix: iterate over a static copy
for (const item of Array.from(items)) {
  item.remove();
}
```

**Testing elements: `matches` and `closest`.** Two methods test a selector against an element instead of searching for one:

- `element.matches(selector)` returns `true` if the element itself matches.
- `element.closest(selector)` walks up from the element (including itself) and returns the nearest ancestor that matches, or `null`. It is essential for event delegation (6.3).

```javascript
const button = document.querySelector("button.delete");

button.matches(".delete");               // true
button.matches("form button");           // true if inside a form
const row = button.closest("tr");        // the table row containing the button
const id = button.closest("[data-id]")?.dataset.id;  // nearest ancestor with data-id
```

**Escaping awkward ids and classes.** Ids may legally start with a digit or contain characters that are special in CSS (`.`, `:`). `querySelector("#1st")` throws a `SyntaxError`. Use `CSS.escape`:

```javascript
const userId = "42:admin";
document.querySelector(`#${CSS.escape(userId)}`);  // "#42\:admin" is a valid selector
document.getElementById(userId);                    // no escaping needed here
```

**Comparison.**

| Method | Argument | Returns | Live? | Available on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `getElementById(id)` | Id without `#` | `Element` or `null` | n/a | `document` only |
| `getElementsByClassName(names)` | Space-separated classes | `HTMLCollection` | Live | `document`, elements |
| `getElementsByTagName(tag)` | Tag name or `"*"` | `HTMLCollection` | Live | `document`, elements |
| `getElementsByName(name)` | `name` attribute | `NodeList` | Live | `document` only |
| `querySelector(sel)` | Any CSS selector | `Element` or `null` | n/a | `document`, elements, fragments |
| `querySelectorAll(sel)` | Any CSS selector | `NodeList` | Static | `document`, elements, fragments |
| `closest(sel)` | Any CSS selector | Ancestor `Element` or `null` | n/a | Elements |

**Performance in practice.** Selection is rarely the bottleneck in real applications. What matters is not selecting the same elements repeatedly inside loops or frequently fired handlers: select once, store the reference, and reuse it.

**Key Takeaways**

- `querySelector` and `querySelectorAll` accept any CSS selector and are the default choice. `getElementById` remains the fastest lookup by id.
- Calling a selection method on an element restricts results to its descendants. Use `:scope` to anchor the selector itself.
- `getElementsBy*` methods return live collections. `querySelectorAll` returns a static snapshot.
- Never remove elements while iterating a live collection. Copy it to an array first.
- `matches` tests an element, `closest` finds the nearest matching ancestor.
- Use `CSS.escape` when building selectors from data.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Given a list of products with classes `product` and `on-sale`, select all products on sale with one `querySelectorAll` call and log their names using `Array.from` with a mapping function.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function `$$(selector, root = document)` that returns a real array of matching elements, and a function `findRow(button)` that returns the `data-id` of the table row containing a button. Test both against a table with nested elements inside the cells.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between a live `HTMLCollection` and a static `NodeList`, and when can it cause a bug?" *Hint:* write a loop that modifies the document while iterating, and trace what happens to the indices.

#### Traversing the DOM Tree

Selection searches the whole tree for elements that match a pattern. Often you already have one element and need its neighbours: the parent row of a clicked cell, the next item in a list, the label just before an input. Traversal properties move through the tree one step at a time along its links, like moving through a family tree with "parent", "first child" and "next sibling".

**The two families of navigation properties.** Each direction exists twice: once for all nodes (including text and comments) and once for elements only.

```text
                     parentNode / parentElement
                                ^
                                |
 previousSibling        +---------------+        nextSibling
 previousElementSibling | current node  |  nextElementSibling
          <-------------+---------------+------------->
                         |             |
              firstChild |             | lastChild
       firstElementChild v             v lastElementChild
                   [ child ][ child ][ child ]
                       childNodes (all nodes, live NodeList)
                       children   (elements only, live HTMLCollection)
```

| All nodes | Elements only |
|---|---|
| `parentNode` | `parentElement` |
| `childNodes` | `children` |
| `firstChild`, `lastChild` | `firstElementChild`, `lastElementChild` |
| `previousSibling`, `nextSibling` | `previousElementSibling`, `nextElementSibling` |
| (none) | `childElementCount` |

**Why the element-only versions exist.** Because whitespace creates text nodes, the "all nodes" properties often return something you did not expect:

```html
<ul id="menu">
  <li>Home</li>
  <li>Shop</li>
</ul>
```

```javascript
const menu = document.getElementById("menu");

menu.firstChild;              // #text "\n  ": the line break before the first <li>
menu.firstElementChild;       // <li>Home</li>

const home = menu.firstElementChild;
home.nextSibling;             // #text "\n  "
home.nextElementSibling;      // <li>Shop</li>
home.parentNode === menu;     // true
```

`parentNode` and `parentElement` differ only at the top of the tree: for `<html>`, `parentNode` is `document` while `parentElement` is `null`, because `document` is not an element.

**Common traversal patterns.**

```javascript
// All siblings of an element, excluding itself
function siblings(el) {
  return [...el.parentElement.children].filter((child) => child !== el);
}

// Index of an element among its siblings (e.g. which tab was clicked)
function indexInParent(el) {
  return [...el.parentElement.children].indexOf(el);
}

// All ancestors up to <html>
function ancestors(el) {
  const result = [];
  for (let node = el.parentElement; node; node = node.parentElement) {
    result.push(node);
  }
  return result;
}

// Is an element inside another? (also true when a === b)
const insideDialog = dialog.contains(document.activeElement);
```

**Recursive walking.** To visit every node below a root (depth-first, in document order), recursion on `childNodes` is the simplest approach (3.3 covers recursion):

```javascript
// Count words in all text nodes under a root, skipping <script> and <style>
function countWords(node) {
  if (node.nodeType === Node.TEXT_NODE) {
    return node.data.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length;
  }
  if (node.nodeType === Node.ELEMENT_NODE && /^(SCRIPT|STYLE)$/.test(node.nodeName)) {
    return 0;
  }
  let total = 0;
  for (const child of node.childNodes) {
    total += countWords(child);
  }
  return total;
}

console.log(countWords(document.body));
```

**`TreeWalker`: a built-in iterator.** For large trees, or when you need to filter by node type, `document.createTreeWalker` gives you an iterator that does not recurse on the JavaScript stack:

```javascript
// Highlight every occurrence of a word in the text of <main>
const walker = document.createTreeWalker(
  document.querySelector("main"),
  NodeFilter.SHOW_TEXT,                            // visit text nodes only
  {
    acceptNode(node) {                             // optional extra filter
      return node.data.includes("JavaScript")
        ? NodeFilter.FILTER_ACCEPT
        : NodeFilter.FILTER_SKIP;
    },
  }
);

const matches = [];
while (walker.nextNode()) {
  matches.push(walker.currentNode);                // collect first: do not mutate while walking
}
console.log(`${matches.length} text nodes mention JavaScript`);
```

**Comparing positions.** `a.compareDocumentPosition(b)` returns a bit mask describing where `b` is relative to `a` (before, after, containing, contained). It is rarely needed, but useful for sorting nodes in document order:

```javascript
nodes.sort((a, b) =>
  a.compareDocumentPosition(b) & Node.DOCUMENT_POSITION_FOLLOWING ? -1 : 1
);
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Traversal properties move one step at a time: parent, children, first and last child, previous and next sibling.
- Each property has an "all nodes" form and an "elements only" form. Prefer the element form to avoid whitespace text nodes.
- `childNodes` and `children` are live collections.
- `contains` tests ancestry, and `closest` finds a matching ancestor.
- For full-tree visits, recurse on `childNodes` or use a `TreeWalker` with a `NodeFilter`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Given a `<ul>` with five `<li>` items, start from the third item and log the text of its previous and next element siblings, its parent's tag name and its index among its siblings.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function `textNodesContaining(root, word)` using a `TreeWalker`, then wrap each occurrence of the word in a `<mark>` element. Hint: `Text.splitText(offset)` splits a text node in two.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `element.firstChild` sometimes return a text node when the first thing inside the element is a tag?" *Hint:* consider what the parser does with the characters between the opening tag and the first child tag.

#### Creating, Inserting and Removing Nodes

Most interfaces change after the page loads: items are added to a cart, notifications appear, rows are deleted. All of this comes down to three operations on the tree: creating nodes, attaching them at a position, and detaching them. The modern DOM API for this is short and readable. Older methods still appear in a lot of code, so you need to recognise both.

**Creating nodes.** `document.createElement(tag)` creates an element that is not yet in the document. It is invisible until you attach it.

```javascript
const item = document.createElement("li");    // a detached <li>
item.className = "cart-item";
item.textContent = "Coffee beans";            // creates a child Text node
item.dataset.sku = "CB-500";                  // data-sku="CB-500"

const note = document.createTextNode(" (gift)");  // an explicit Text node
item.append(note);

console.log(item.isConnected);                // false: not in the document yet
document.querySelector("#cart").append(item);
console.log(item.isConnected);                // true
```

**Modern insertion methods.** These methods accept any number of nodes **and strings** (strings are inserted as text, never parsed as HTML):

```text
            el.before(...)
          <div id="el">        <- el
            el.prepend(...)
            ...existing children...
            el.append(...)
          </div>
            el.after(...)
```

| Method | Inserts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `parent.append(...nodes)` | As last children | Most common |
| `parent.prepend(...nodes)` | As first children | |
| `el.before(...nodes)` | As previous siblings | |
| `el.after(...nodes)` | As next siblings | |
| `el.replaceWith(...nodes)` | In place of `el` | `el` is detached |
| `el.remove()` | Nothing (detaches `el`) | |
| `parent.replaceChildren(...nodes)` | Replaces all children | With no arguments, empties the element |

```javascript
const list = document.querySelector("#todo");

list.append("Last item as text", document.createElement("hr"));  // mixed nodes and strings
list.prepend(makeItem("Urgent"));

const second = list.children[1];
second.before(makeItem("Inserted before the second"));
second.replaceWith(makeItem("Replacement"));

list.replaceChildren();               // remove every child in one call

function makeItem(text) {
  const li = document.createElement("li");
  li.textContent = text;
  return li;
}
```

**Legacy methods.** These are called on the parent and take a single node:

| Legacy | Modern equivalent |
|---|---|
| `parent.appendChild(node)` | `parent.append(node)` |
| `parent.insertBefore(node, ref)` | `ref.before(node)` (or `parent.append` if `ref` is `null`) |
| `parent.replaceChild(newNode, old)` | `old.replaceWith(newNode)` |
| `parent.removeChild(node)` | `node.remove()` |

One difference is useful: `appendChild` returns the appended node, while `append` returns `undefined`.

**`insertAdjacent*` methods.** These insert relative to an element using one of four position strings, which match the diagram above: `"beforebegin"`, `"afterbegin"`, `"beforeend"`, `"afterend"`.

```javascript
const card = document.querySelector(".card");
card.insertAdjacentText("afterbegin", "New: ");                 // text, never parsed
card.insertAdjacentElement("afterend", document.createElement("hr"));
card.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", "<small>Updated</small>"); // parses HTML: see the sanitization topic
```

`insertAdjacentHTML` parses a string and inserts the resulting nodes without destroying the existing children. That makes it safer for performance than `innerHTML +=`, which re-parses and rebuilds everything (next topics). It carries the same injection risk as `innerHTML`, though.

**Inserting an existing node moves it.** A node can only have one parent. Appending a node that is already in the document moves it. It is not copied:

```javascript
const a = document.querySelector("#list-a");
const b = document.querySelector("#list-b");

b.append(a.firstElementChild);   // moved from list A to list B; list A loses it
```

**Copying with `cloneNode`.** To duplicate a node, clone it. `cloneNode(true)` copies the whole subtree, while `cloneNode()` copies only the node itself. Clones keep attributes but **not** event listeners added with `addEventListener`, and they keep duplicate `id`s, which you must fix.

```javascript
const original = document.querySelector("#row-template-example");
const copy = original.cloneNode(true);   // deep clone
```
