```javascript
copy.id = "row-2";                        // ids must stay unique
original.after(copy);
```

**Removing nodes and memory.** `remove()` detaches a node from the tree. If your code still holds a reference to it (in a variable, an array, or a closure), it stays in memory, as a "detached DOM node" that you can find in DevTools heap snapshots. Release references to elements you remove, and remove event listeners on long-lived objects that point at them (4.4 covered memory leaks).

**Building many nodes.** Every insertion into the live document can invalidate layout. Insert in a single operation where possible. `append` with spread arguments, or a `DocumentFragment` (later topic), builds the nodes off-document first:

```javascript
const products = [{ name: "Tea" }, { name: "Coffee" }, { name: "Cocoa" }];
const items = products.map((p) => {
  const li = document.createElement("li");
  li.textContent = p.name;
  return li;
});
document.querySelector("#products").append(...items);  // one insertion
```

For very large arrays, spread can exceed the engine's argument limit (tens of thousands of arguments), so use a fragment instead.

**Key Takeaways**

- `createElement` makes detached nodes. They appear only once they are inserted into the document.
- `append`, `prepend`, `before`, `after`, `replaceWith`, `remove` and `replaceChildren` are the modern API. They accept several nodes and strings.
- Strings passed to these methods are inserted as text, never parsed as HTML.
- Inserting a node that is already in the tree moves it. Use `cloneNode(true)` to copy it (listeners are not copied).
- Removed nodes stay in memory while references to them exist.
- Build nodes first and insert them in one operation to minimise layout work.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a to-do list with an input and an "Add" button. Each added item must contain the text and a "Delete" button that removes only that item. Use `createElement`, `append` and `remove` only.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function `moveSelected(from, to)` that moves every checked item from one list to another, preserving order, and a "Duplicate" action that clones an item with a new unique id. Verify that cloned delete buttons do not work until you attach listeners, and explain why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What happens if you `append` an element that is already somewhere else in the document?" *Hint:* think about how many parents a node can have, and what that implies for drag-and-drop between lists.

#### Attributes, Properties and Dataset

An HTML attribute and a DOM property often have the same name: `<input value="5">` and `input.value`. It is tempting to assume they are the same thing, but they are not, and confusing them causes real bugs, particularly with form fields. The distinction is easiest to grasp as **initial configuration** versus **current state**. Attributes are what the HTML author wrote, stored as strings. Properties are the live state of the JavaScript object, with real types.

**Attribute API.** These methods work on the attribute strings:

```javascript
const link = document.querySelector("a");

link.getAttribute("href");            // "/docs" exactly as written in the HTML
link.setAttribute("target", "_blank");
link.hasAttribute("download");        // false
link.removeAttribute("title");
link.toggleAttribute("hidden");       // add if missing, remove if present

for (const attr of link.attributes) { // all attributes as Attr objects
  console.log(attr.name, attr.value);
}
```

**Properties.** Most standard attributes are **reflected** as properties of the element object, but the property may have a different name, type or value:

```javascript
const link = document.querySelector('a[href="/docs"]');

link.getAttribute("href");   // "/docs"                         (string as authored)
link.href;                   // "https://example.com/docs"      (resolved absolute URL)

const box = document.querySelector('input[type="checkbox"]');
box.getAttribute("checked"); // "" or null                      (string or absent)
box.checked;                 // true or false                   (boolean)

const td = document.querySelector("td[colspan]");
td.getAttribute("colspan");  // "2"                             (string)
td.colSpan;                  // 2                               (number)
```

| Attribute | Property | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| `class` | `className` (string), `classList` (6.2) | `class` is a reserved word in old JavaScript |
| `for` (on `<label>`) | `htmlFor` | Same reason |
| `href`, `src` | `href`, `src` | Property returns the resolved absolute URL |
| `checked`, `disabled`, `hidden` | Same names | Property is a boolean |
| `tabindex`, `colspan` | `tabIndex`, `colSpan` | Property is a number, camelCase |
| `style` | `style` | Property is a `CSSStyleDeclaration` object (6.2) |
| `value` (on `<input>`) | `defaultValue` | `value` property is the **current** value |
| `aria-label` | `ariaLabel` | ARIA reflection, supported in modern browsers |

**The `value` trap.** For form fields, the `value` attribute is only the **initial** value. Once the user types, the `value` property changes and the attribute does not:

```html
<input id="qty" value="1">
```

```javascript
const qty = document.getElementById("qty");
// The user types "3" into the field...
qty.value;                  // "3": current state
qty.getAttribute("value");  // "1": still the initial value
qty.defaultValue;           // "1": the property that reflects the attribute

// Form reset restores the attribute value
qty.form?.reset();          // qty.value is "1" again
```

The same split exists for checkboxes: the `checked` attribute is `defaultChecked`, and the `checked` property is the current state. Always use properties to read and set the current state of form controls.

**Boolean attributes.** For boolean attributes, **presence** means `true`, whatever the value. This is a frequent source of bugs:

```javascript
button.setAttribute("disabled", "false");  // STILL disabled: the attribute is present
button.disabled = false;                    // correct: removes the attribute
button.removeAttribute("disabled");         // also correct
button.toggleAttribute("disabled", isBusy); // add or remove based on a boolean
```

**Custom data with `data-*` and `dataset`.** HTML reserves attributes that start with `data-` for your own data. They are valid on any element, ignored by the browser, and accessible through the `dataset` property, which converts kebab-case names to camelCase:

```html
<article id="p1" data-product-id="1042" data-price="19.90" data-in-stock>
  Coffee grinder
</article>
```

```javascript
const product = document.getElementById("p1");

product.dataset.productId;          // "1042"   (data-product-id)
product.dataset.price;              // "19.90"  always a string
Number(product.dataset.price);      // 19.9     convert explicitly
"inStock" in product.dataset;       // true     (data-in-stock="" is present)

product.dataset.lastViewed = Date.now();  // creates data-last-viewed="1727..."
delete product.dataset.inStock;           // removes data-in-stock
```

`dataset` values are always strings, so store numbers and booleans carefully, and avoid storing large or structured data in the DOM. Keep that in JavaScript (a `Map` keyed by element or id works well). Data attributes are also selectable from CSS, which makes them good for state that styling depends on:

```css
[data-status="error"] { border-color: crimson; }
```

**Non-standard attributes.** Arbitrary attributes such as `<div tooltip="...">` are not reflected as properties: `div.tooltip` is `undefined`, and `getAttribute("tooltip")` works but the markup is invalid HTML. Use `data-tooltip` instead.

**Key Takeaways**

- Attributes are the authored strings in the HTML. Properties are the typed, live state of the DOM object.
- Many attributes are reflected as properties with different names (`className`, `htmlFor`) or types (boolean, number, absolute URL).
- For form controls, `value` and `checked` properties are the current state. The attributes are the defaults (`defaultValue`, `defaultChecked`).
- A boolean attribute is true whenever it is present, even with the value `"false"`. Set the property or remove the attribute instead.
- Use `data-*` attributes and `dataset` for custom data. Values are always strings.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create an `<input value="hello">`, type something else into it, then log `input.value`, `input.getAttribute("value")` and `input.defaultValue`. Call `form.reset()` and log them again.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Render a product grid from an array of objects, storing each product's id and price in `data-*` attributes. Add buttons that sort the grid by price by reading `dataset` and re-appending the elements in the new order.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why doesn't `setAttribute('disabled', 'false')` enable a button?" *Hint:* look up how HTML defines boolean attributes, and compare with the `disabled` property.

#### innerHTML, textContent and Sanitization

Creating every node with `createElement` is safe but verbose. Assigning a string of HTML is much shorter, and the browser's parser does the work. That convenience comes with the most common security vulnerability on the web: **cross-site scripting (XSS)**, where data controlled by an attacker is interpreted as markup or script. Choosing the right property for each job is mostly a question of whether you want your string to be **parsed as HTML** or **treated as text**.

**The four content properties.**

| Property | Reads | Writes | Parses HTML? | Layout-aware? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `innerHTML` | Serialised HTML of the children | Replaces children by parsing the string | Yes | No |
| `outerHTML` | Serialised HTML including the element itself | Replaces the element itself | Yes | No |
| `textContent` | Concatenated text of all descendant text nodes | Replaces children with one text node | No | No |
| `innerText` | Text as rendered (respects CSS, line breaks) | Replaces children with text and `<br>` | No | Yes (forces layout) |

```html
<div id="box">Hello <b>world</b><span style="display:none"> hidden</span></div>
```

```javascript
const box = document.getElementById("box");

box.innerHTML;    // 'Hello <b>world</b><span style="display:none"> hidden</span>'
box.textContent;  // "Hello world hidden"   includes hidden text, no layout needed
box.innerText;    // "Hello world"          only rendered text, triggers layout
```

**`textContent` for text.** When the string is meant to be text (a user name, a comment, a product title, anything that came from a server or user input), use `textContent`. The browser never interprets it:

```javascript
const comment = '<img src=x onerror="alert(document.cookie)">';

output.textContent = comment;  // safe: displays the characters literally
output.innerHTML = comment;    // XSS: the broken image triggers onerror, running the attacker's code
```

Note that `<script>` tags inserted with `innerHTML` are **not executed**. That is not a protection, because event handler attributes such as `onerror`, `onload` and `onfocus` are executed, as are `javascript:` URLs in links.

**`innerHTML` replaces everything.** Assigning `innerHTML` destroys all existing child nodes and creates new ones. This has consequences beyond security:

```javascript
const list = document.querySelector("#list");
const firstItem = list.firstElementChild;
firstItem.addEventListener("click", onClick);

list.innerHTML += "<li>New</li>";   // serialise, concatenate, re-parse ALL children

firstItem.isConnected;              // false: the old <li> was destroyed and recreated
// Its listener is gone, any typed input text is lost, focus is lost, and the
// whole list was rebuilt just to add one item.
```

Use `append` or `insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", ...)` to add content without rebuilding the rest.

**Building markup from data safely.** If you do build HTML strings (for templates, or code that predates the DOM methods), every interpolated value must be escaped. Escaping converts the five special characters into entities:

```javascript
function escapeHTML(value) {
  return String(value)
    .replaceAll("&", "&amp;")    // must be first
    .replaceAll("<", "&lt;")
    .replaceAll(">", "&gt;")
    .replaceAll('"', "&quot;")
    .replaceAll("'", "&#39;");
}

const user = { name: "<b>Eve</b>", bio: '"><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>' };

card.innerHTML = `
  <h2>${escapeHTML(user.name)}</h2>
  <p title="${escapeHTML(user.bio)}">Bio</p>
`;
```

Escaping is context-dependent. It protects element content and quoted attribute values. It does **not** make a value safe inside `href` (a `javascript:` URL contains no special characters), inside a `<script>` block, inside an event handler attribute, or inside CSS. For URLs, validate the scheme:

```javascript
function safeUrl(url) {
  const parsed = new URL(url, location.href);
  return ["http:", "https:", "mailto:"].includes(parsed.protocol) ? parsed.href : "#";
}
```

The tagged template literal from Chapter 3 that escapes every interpolated value is a tidy way to apply escaping consistently.

**Sanitization: when you must accept HTML.** Sometimes the content genuinely is HTML: a rich-text editor's output, a Markdown preview, an email body. Escaping would destroy the formatting. Instead, you **sanitize** it: parse it, keep an allowlist of harmless elements and attributes, and remove everything else (scripts, event handlers, `javascript:` URLs, `<iframe>`, and so on). Do not write your own sanitizer, because the HTML parser has many surprising behaviours that attackers exploit. Use a maintained library:

```javascript
import DOMPurify from "dompurify";

const dirty = '<p>Hi <a href="javascript:alert(1)">click</a><img src=x onerror=alert(2)></p>';
preview.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty);
// <p>Hi <a>click</a><img src="x"></p>   dangerous attributes removed
```

Browsers are also adding native support. The **HTML Sanitizer API** provides `element.setHTML(string)`, which parses and sanitizes in one step, and **Trusted Types** lets a site enforce, through Content Security Policy, that dangerous sinks such as `innerHTML` only accept values produced by approved sanitizing functions. Check current browser support before relying on either without a fallback. Chapter 17 covers XSS defences in depth.

**Choosing the right tool.**

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Display a plain string (from the user, a server or a URL) | `textContent` |
| Build a few elements with dynamic data | `createElement` and `textContent` |
| Insert a large static fragment written by you | `<template>` (next topic) or `innerHTML` with a constant string |
| Build HTML from data in a string template | Escape every value, validate URLs |
| Display user-provided HTML | Sanitize (DOMPurify or `setHTML`) |
| Read visible text for copying or display | `innerText` (sparingly, as it forces layout) |

**Key Takeaways**

- `innerHTML` parses its string as HTML. Assigning untrusted data to it is an XSS vulnerability, even though inserted `<script>` tags do not run.
- `textContent` treats strings as text and is the safe default for dynamic content.
- `innerText` reflects rendered text and forces a layout calculation. `textContent` includes hidden text and is cheap.
- `innerHTML +=` destroys and rebuilds all children, losing listeners, state and focus.
- Escape values in HTML templates, validate URL schemes separately, and sanitize with a library when HTML input is required.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a comment box that displays submitted comments. Implement it once with `innerHTML` and test the payload `<img src=x onerror="alert('xss')">`, then fix it with `textContent`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a tagged template function `html` that escapes every interpolated value except values wrapped in a `raw()` marker object, and use it to render a list of user profiles that includes a link built with a validated URL.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If `<script>` tags inserted with `innerHTML` do not execute, why is `innerHTML` still dangerous?" *Hint:* list other places in HTML where the browser runs JavaScript or follows URLs.

#### DocumentFragment and Template Elements

Two problems keep returning when you build UI with the DOM API. First, inserting many nodes one by one into the live document is wasteful, because each insertion modifies the visible tree. Second, building a complex structure (a card with an image, a title, a price and three buttons) with `createElement` calls is long, hard to read, and separates the markup from the HTML where designers expect to find it. `DocumentFragment` solves the first problem and `<template>` solves the second, and they work together.

**`DocumentFragment`: a temporary container.** A fragment is a lightweight node with no parent that is never part of the document. You build a subtree inside it, then insert the fragment. At that moment its **children** move into the document and the fragment itself becomes empty, so it leaves no wrapper element behind.

```text
Before insertion                After list.append(fragment)

fragment                        <ul id="list">
├── <li>Tea</li>                ├── (existing items)
├── <li>Coffee</li>             ├── <li>Tea</li>
└── <li>Cocoa</li>              ├── <li>Coffee</li>
                                └── <li>Cocoa</li>
                                fragment  (now empty)
```

```javascript
const names = ["Tea", "Coffee", "Cocoa"];
const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();   // or: new DocumentFragment()

for (const name of names) {
  const li = document.createElement("li");
  li.textContent = name;
  fragment.append(li);           // cheap: the fragment is not rendered
}

document.querySelector("#list").append(fragment);     // one insertion into the live DOM
console.log(fragment.childNodes.length);              // 0
```

Modern browsers are good at batching DOM changes made in the same task, so the performance gain over appending directly is often small. The real problems appear when you **read layout** between insertions (see *Reflow, Repaint and DOM Performance*). Fragments are still the clearest way to express "build everything, then insert once", and they work with any number of nodes (unlike `append(...array)`).

**`<template>`: inert markup.** A `<template>` element holds HTML that the parser processes but does **not render or activate**. Its content is not displayed, images inside it are not downloaded, scripts are not run, and it is not found by `document.querySelector`. It is a blueprint you clone whenever you need a new instance.

```html
<template id="product-card">
  <article class="card">
    <img class="card-img" alt="">
    <h3 class="card-title"></h3>
    <p class="card-price"></p>
    <button class="card-buy" type="button">Add to cart</button>
  </article>
</template>

<section id="catalog"></section>
```

The template's children live in `template.content`, which is a `DocumentFragment`. Clone it deeply, fill in the data with safe properties, and insert it:

```javascript
const template = document.getElementById("product-card");
const catalog = document.getElementById("catalog");

const products = [
  { id: 1, title: "Grinder", price: 49.9, image: "/img/grinder.jpg" },
  { id: 2, title: "Kettle",  price: 35,   image: "/img/kettle.jpg"  },
];

const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();

for (const product of products) {
  const card = template.content.cloneNode(true);       // deep copy of the fragment

  // Query inside the clone BEFORE inserting it: afterwards the fragment is empty
  card.querySelector(".card").dataset.id = product.id;
  card.querySelector(".card-img").src = product.image;
  card.querySelector(".card-img").alt = product.title;
  card.querySelector(".card-title").textContent = product.title;  // text, never parsed
  card.querySelector(".card-price").textContent =
    new Intl.NumberFormat("en", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }).format(product.price);

  fragment.append(card);
}

catalog.append(fragment);
```

This pattern combines the readability of HTML with the safety of `textContent`. It is the vanilla-JavaScript equivalent of a component, and it is how many lightweight libraries render lists.

**A common mistake: keeping a reference to the clone.** After `catalog.append(card)`, the variable `card` refers to an empty fragment. If you need the inserted element later (for example, to attach listeners), grab it before inserting:

```javascript
const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
const article = clone.firstElementChild;   // the <article> itself
catalog.append(clone);
article.querySelector(".card-buy").addEventListener("click", addToCart);  // works
```

Even better, use event delegation (6.3) on `#catalog`, so new cards need no listeners at all.

**`importNode` versus `cloneNode`.** `document.importNode(template.content, true)` also produces a deep copy, with the copied nodes owned by `document`. For templates in the same document, both work. The difference matters for custom elements and for templates that come from another document.

**Templates and Web Components.** `<template>` is one of the building blocks of Web Components, together with custom elements and Shadow DOM. A custom element typically clones a template into its shadow root, and shadow roots are themselves `DocumentFragment` subclasses (nodeType 11).

**Key Takeaways**

- A `DocumentFragment` is an off-document container. Appending it moves its children into the document and leaves it empty.
- Fragments express "build everything, then insert once" and avoid repeated live insertions.
- A `<template>` holds inert markup: it is parsed but not rendered, its images do not load and its scripts do not run.
- Clone `template.content` with `cloneNode(true)`, fill it with `textContent` and properties, then insert it.
- Query and grab references inside a cloned fragment before inserting it.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Render 1,000 numbered `<li>` items into a list, once by appending each item directly and once through a `DocumentFragment`. Measure both with `performance.now()` and explain why the difference is small or large.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a `<template>` for a table row with name, email and a "Remove" button. Load an array of users and render the table from the template, then add a search box that re-renders only the rows that match, using `replaceChildren`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why would you use a `<template>` element instead of a hidden `<div>` containing the same markup?" *Hint:* think about what the browser does with images, scripts, ids and `querySelector` results in each case.

#### Reflow, Repaint and DOM Performance

The DOM API makes it look as if changing an element is a cheap property assignment. Behind each change, the browser may have to recalculate styles, recompute the size and position of many elements, and redraw pixels. Section 1.1 introduced the rendering pipeline. This topic explains how your JavaScript interacts with it, and the single most common performance mistake in DOM code: forcing the browser to do that work many times in a single frame.

**The pipeline, revisited.** After a script changes the DOM or styles, the browser normally does the following work once, when the current task has finished and it is time to render:

```text
JavaScript ──> Style ──> Layout ──> Paint ──> Composite
 (changes)    (which      (size and   (draw      (assemble layers
              rules        position    pixels      on the GPU)
              apply)       of boxes)   into
                                       layers)
```

- **Style recalculation**: works out which CSS rules apply to each changed element.
- **Layout** (also called **reflow**): computes geometry (widths, heights, positions). A change to one element can affect its parent, siblings and children, so layout often touches large parts of the page.
- **Paint** (also called **repaint**): fills in the pixels of text, colours, borders and shadows.
- **Composite**: combines the painted layers, applying `transform` and `opacity` on the GPU.

**What each kind of change costs.**

| Change | Style | Layout | Paint | Composite |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `width`, `height`, `margin`, `padding`, `font-size`, `top`, `left`, adding or removing nodes, changing text | Yes | **Yes** | Yes | Yes |
| `color`, `background-color`, `box-shadow`, `visibility`, `outline` | Yes | No | **Yes** | Yes |
| `transform`, `opacity` (on an element with its own layer) | Yes | No | No | **Yes** |

This is why animations should use `transform` and `opacity` (6.2 and Chapter 2): they skip layout and paint entirely.

**Lazy rendering and forced synchronous layout.** Browsers are lazy on purpose. When you change a style, they mark the layout as dirty and wait, so that ten changes in one task cost one layout. The laziness breaks when your code **reads** a value that depends on layout. To return an accurate answer, the browser must run style and layout **immediately, synchronously, in the middle of your script**. This is a **forced synchronous layout** (or forced reflow).

Properties and methods that force layout when the layout is dirty include:

- `offsetWidth`, `offsetHeight`, `offsetTop`, `offsetLeft`
- `clientWidth`, `clientHeight`, `clientTop`, `clientLeft`
- `scrollWidth`, `scrollHeight`, `scrollTop`, `scrollLeft`
- `getBoundingClientRect()`, `getClientRects()`
- `getComputedStyle()` (when reading layout-dependent properties)
- `innerText`, `focus()`, `scrollIntoView()`, `window.scrollY`

**Layout thrashing.** One forced layout is fine. The problem is interleaving reads and writes in a loop, which forces a layout on every iteration:

```javascript
const boxes = document.querySelectorAll(".box");

// BAD: read, write, read, write... one forced layout per box
for (const box of boxes) {
  const width = box.parentElement.offsetWidth;   // READ: forces layout (layout is dirty)
  box.style.width = `${width / 2}px`;            // WRITE: makes the layout dirty again
}
```

With 500 boxes, this triggers 500 layouts in one task. The timeline in the DevTools Performance panel shows a wall of purple "Layout" bars, each flagged with a "Forced reflow" warning.

```text
Thrashing:   [R L W][R L W][R L W][R L W] ... x500   (L = full layout)
Batched:     [R R R R ... R][W W W W ... W] -> one layout at render time
```

**Fix 1: batch reads, then writes.**

```javascript
// GOOD: all reads first (at most one layout), then all writes (no layout until render)
const widths = [...boxes].map((box) => box.parentElement.offsetWidth);   // reads
boxes.forEach((box, i) => {
  box.style.width = `${widths[i] / 2}px`;                                // writes
});
```

**Fix 2: schedule writes for the next frame.** When reads and writes come from different parts of the code (separate components, separate handlers), you cannot easily reorder them. Defer writes with `requestAnimationFrame` (5.1), so all of them run together just before the next render:

```javascript
function onScroll() {
  const y = window.scrollY;                    // read now
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    header.classList.toggle("compact", y > 80);  // write in the next frame
  });
}
```

Libraries such as *fastdom* formalise this by queuing all reads and all writes and flushing them in two phases per frame.

**Other techniques.**

```javascript
// 1. Change classes, not many individual style properties
card.classList.add("expanded");            // one style invalidation; CSS does the rest

// 2. Hide, modify, show: changes to display:none subtrees do not cause layout
list.hidden = true;
rebuildHugeList(list);                     // no layout while hidden
list.hidden = false;                       // one layout

// 3. Cache layout values that do not change
const headerHeight = header.offsetHeight;  // read once, outside the hot path
```

```css
/* 4. Limit how far a layout change can spread */
.widget {
  contain: layout paint;          /* this box's internals cannot affect the outside */
}

/* 5. Skip rendering work for off-screen sections entirely */
.feed-item {
  content-visibility: auto;       /* layout and paint only when near the viewport */
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 300px;  /* placeholder size to keep the scrollbar stable */
}
```

**Measuring.** Do not optimise by guesswork. Record a trace in the DevTools Performance panel while interacting with the page. Long purple Layout blocks with a red corner and the warning "Forced reflow is a likely performance bottleneck" point to the exact line of JavaScript that caused the read. The Rendering drawer's "Paint flashing" option highlights repainted areas in green.

**Key Takeaways**

- After DOM and style changes, browsers run style, layout, paint and composite. Layout is usually the most expensive step.
- Browsers postpone layout until it is needed. Reading geometry (`offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`, `scrollTop`) while layout is dirty forces it to happen synchronously.
- Alternating reads and writes in a loop causes layout thrashing. Batch all reads before all writes, or defer writes with `requestAnimationFrame`.
- Animate `transform` and `opacity`, toggle classes instead of setting many styles, and use `contain` and `content-visibility` to limit work.
- Confirm problems with the Performance panel before optimising.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create 300 `.box` elements and run the "BAD" loop above. Record it in the Performance panel and find the forced reflow warnings. Then apply the batched version and compare the total scripting and rendering time.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a "masonry" layout that positions cards by reading each card's height and writing `transform: translate(...)` values. Implement it first with interleaved reads and writes, then with a read phase and a write phase, and measure the difference with 1,000 cards.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is layout thrashing and how do you avoid it?" *Hint:* explain why reading a geometry property is not free when there are pending style changes, and describe at least two ways to group reads and writes.

#### MutationObserver

Sometimes code needs to react when the DOM changes, but it does not control the code that makes the change. Examples include a third-party widget that injects content, a browser extension that must process newly loaded comments, an accessibility script that labels elements as a framework creates them, or a test that waits for an element to appear. Polling the DOM with `setInterval` is wasteful and slow to react. The original solution, *Mutation Events* (`DOMNodeInserted` and similar), fired synchronously on every single change and made pages extremely slow. They have been deprecated and removed from modern browsers. Their replacement is `MutationObserver`.

**How it works.** You create an observer with a callback, then tell it which node to watch and which kinds of change interest you. The browser records matching changes as `MutationRecord` objects and delivers them **in batches**, as a **microtask** (5.1), after the code that made the changes has finished. A loop that adds 1,000 nodes produces a single callback with 1,000 records, not 1,000 callbacks.

```javascript
const observer = new MutationObserver((records, obs) => {
  for (const record of records) {
    console.log(record.type, record.target);
  }
});

observer.observe(document.querySelector("#feed"), {
  childList: true,      // children added or removed
  subtree: true,        // ...anywhere below the target, not just direct children
  attributes: true,     // attribute changes
  attributeFilter: ["class", "data-state"],   // ...only these attributes
  attributeOldValue: true,                    // include the previous value
  characterData: false, // changes to Text node contents
});

// Later, when no longer needed:
observer.disconnect();
```

At least one of `childList`, `attributes` or `characterData` must be true, otherwise `observe` throws a `TypeError`.

**The `MutationRecord`.**

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | `"childList"`, `"attributes"` or `"characterData"` |
| `target` | The node that changed (the parent, for `childList`) |
| `addedNodes`, `removedNodes` | `NodeList`s of nodes added or removed (`childList`) |
| `previousSibling`, `nextSibling` | Where the added or removed nodes were |
| `attributeName` | Name of the changed attribute (`attributes`) |
| `oldValue` | Previous value, if `attributeOldValue` or `characterDataOldValue` was requested |

**Example: enhance elements as they appear.** Suppose a chat widget injects messages, and you want to convert every timestamp to the reader's local time:

```javascript
function localiseTimes(root) {
  // root may be the added element itself or contain matching elements
  const times = root.matches?.("time[datetime]")
    ? [root]
    : root.querySelectorAll?.("time[datetime]") ?? [];
  for (const time of times) {
    time.textContent = new Date(time.dateTime).toLocaleTimeString();
  }
}

const chat = document.querySelector("#chat");
localiseTimes(chat);                                   // handle existing content first

const observer = new MutationObserver((records) => {
  for (const record of records) {
    for (const node of record.addedNodes) {
      if (node.nodeType === Node.ELEMENT_NODE) {       // skip text and comment nodes
        localiseTimes(node);
      }
    }
  }
});
observer.observe(chat, { childList: true, subtree: true });
```

**Example: wait for an element.** A promise-based helper, useful in tests and scripts that run before a framework has rendered:

```javascript
function waitForElement(selector, { root = document, timeout = 5000 } = {}) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const existing = root.querySelector(selector);
    if (existing) return resolve(existing);

    const observer = new MutationObserver(() => {
      const el = root.querySelector(selector);
      if (el) {
        observer.disconnect();
        clearTimeout(timer);
        resolve(el);
      }
    });
    observer.observe(root, { childList: true, subtree: true });

    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      observer.disconnect();
      reject(new Error(`Timed out waiting for ${selector}`));
    }, timeout);
  });
}

const banner = await waitForElement(".cookie-banner");
```

**Pitfalls.**

- **Infinite loops.** If the callback modifies the nodes it observes in a way that matches the options, it triggers itself again. Either check whether the work is already done (for example, a `data-processed` flag), or disconnect, modify, and observe again.
- **Cost of `subtree: true` on `document`.** Observing the whole document with every option on a busy page creates many records. Observe the smallest subtree possible and filter attributes with `attributeFilter`.
- **Batched records lose intermediate states.** You see that a node was added and removed, but by the time the callback runs it may already be detached. Check `node.isConnected` if it matters.
- **`takeRecords()`.** Before disconnecting, call `observer.takeRecords()` to retrieve and process records that are queued but not yet delivered.

**The observer family.** `MutationObserver` is one of several observers with the same shape (constructor with callback, `observe`, `disconnect`). `IntersectionObserver` and `ResizeObserver` are covered in 6.4.

**Key Takeaways**

- `MutationObserver` reports DOM changes (children, attributes, text) to a callback without polling.
- Records are batched and delivered as a microtask after the changing code finishes, which keeps observation cheap.
- Configure `childList`, `attributes` and `characterData`, plus `subtree`, `attributeFilter` and old-value options, to receive only what you need.
- Process existing content first, then observe for future changes.
- Avoid callbacks that re-trigger themselves, keep the observed subtree small, and `disconnect` when done.
- It replaces the deprecated, synchronous Mutation Events.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Observe a `<ul>` for `childList` changes and log the number of added and removed items in each callback. Add three items in one function call and confirm you receive one callback with three records.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a script that adds `target="_blank" rel="noopener"` to every external link in a container, including links added later by other code. Make sure your own attribute changes do not cause an infinite loop.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why were Mutation Events replaced by `MutationObserver`?" *Hint:* compare when each one runs relative to the code that changes the DOM, and how many times each fires for a loop of 1,000 insertions.

<a id="62-css-management-and-manipulation"></a>
### 6.2 CSS Management and Manipulation

This subchapter covers how JavaScript reads and changes presentation: inline styles, classes, computed values, CSS custom properties, whole stylesheets, element geometry and scrolling, and animations controlled from script.

#### Inline Styles via the style Property

Chapter 2 established that presentation belongs in CSS. Some values, though, are only known at runtime: the position of an element being dragged, the width of a progress bar, a colour picked by the user. For these, JavaScript writes styles directly onto an element through its `style` property, which represents the element's **inline style** (the same thing as the `style="..."` attribute).

**Reading and writing individual properties.** `element.style` is a `CSSStyleDeclaration` object. CSS property names become camelCase properties, and every value is a **string with units**:

```javascript
const bar = document.querySelector(".progress-bar");

bar.style.width = "75%";                  // width: 75%
bar.style.backgroundColor = "seagreen";   // background-color -> backgroundColor
bar.style.borderTopLeftRadius = "4px";    // border-top-left-radius
bar.style.cssFloat = "left";              // "float" is a reserved word in old JS

bar.style.width = 75;                     // IGNORED: a number has no unit
bar.style.width = "75 px";                // IGNORED: invalid CSS, no error is thrown
bar.style.width = `${percent}%`;          // build values with template literals
```

Invalid values are silently discarded and the previous value stays in place. If a style "does not work", log `element.style.cssText` to see what was actually stored.

**The `setProperty` family.** These methods use the real CSS (kebab-case) names and support `!important` and custom properties:

```javascript
bar.style.setProperty("background-color", "seagreen");
bar.style.setProperty("width", "75%", "important");   // width: 75% !important
bar.style.setProperty("--fill", "0.75");              // custom properties need setProperty
bar.style.getPropertyValue("--fill");                 // "0.75"
bar.style.removeProperty("width");                    // remove one inline declaration
```

**Removing an inline style.** Assigning an empty string removes the declaration, so the value from the stylesheets applies again:

```javascript
bar.style.display = "none";   // hide
bar.style.display = "";       // restore whatever CSS says (block, flex, grid...)
```

This is better than setting `display = "block"`, which would hard-code a value that may be wrong for that element.

**Several properties at once with `cssText`.** `cssText` reads or replaces the whole inline style as a string. Assigning it **overwrites** all existing inline declarations:

```javascript
tooltip.style.cssText = "position: absolute; top: 10px; left: 20px;";  // replaces everything
tooltip.style.cssText += "z-index: 10;";                               // append instead

// Object.assign is a readable alternative that keeps other declarations
Object.assign(tooltip.style, { top: `${y}px`, left: `${x}px` });
```

**`style` reads only inline styles.** This is the most common misunderstanding. `element.style` knows nothing about stylesheets:

```html
<style> .card { padding: 16px; color: navy; } </style>
<div class="card" style="margin: 8px">...</div>
```

```javascript
const card = document.querySelector(".card");
card.style.margin;    // "8px": set inline
card.style.padding;   // "": set in a stylesheet, so not visible here
card.style.color;     // ""
// To read the value that actually applies, use getComputedStyle (later topic)
```

**Inline styles and the cascade.** Inline declarations have higher specificity than any selector, so they override stylesheet rules (except `!important` ones). This is useful for dynamic values but makes the CSS hard to override later, for example in a dark theme or a media query. Rule of thumb:

| Use inline styles for | Use classes for |
|---|---|
| Continuous, computed values: positions, sizes, percentages, transforms | Discrete states: open/closed, active, error, loading |
| Values that change every frame (dragging, following the pointer) | Anything a designer may want to restyle |
| One-off values specific to one element | Themes, responsive variants |

Even for continuous values, a good pattern is to set a **custom property** inline and let the stylesheet decide how to use it (see *Manipulating CSS Variables from JavaScript*).

**Content Security Policy.** A strict CSP (`style-src` without `'unsafe-inline'`) blocks `style="..."` attributes in markup and `setAttribute("style", ...)`. It does **not** block setting individual properties through the CSSOM, such as `el.style.width = "10px"` or `el.style.setProperty(...)`. Code that uses the object API keeps working under strict policies (Chapter 17).

**Key Takeaways**

- `element.style` reads and writes the inline style only, using camelCase names and string values with units.
- Invalid values are ignored silently. Assigning `""` removes a declaration and lets stylesheets apply again.
- Use `setProperty` for kebab-case names, `!important` and custom properties. `cssText` replaces the whole inline style.
- `element.style` does not show values from stylesheets. Use `getComputedStyle` for those.
- Prefer inline styles for continuous computed values and classes for discrete states.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a progress bar whose width is set from a range input (`<input type="range">`). Display the percentage inside the bar, and change its background colour to red below 20% using only `element.style`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Make an element follow the mouse pointer inside a container by setting `transform: translate(...)` on `pointermove`. Then rewrite it so that JavaScript only sets two custom properties and the stylesheet computes the transform.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `element.style.color` return an empty string even though the text is visibly red?" *Hint:* consider which declarations the `style` object represents and where the red colour is declared.

#### classList and Dynamic Class Manipulation

Most visual changes in an interface are switches between a few known states: a menu is open or closed, a field is valid or invalid, a tab is active or not. These states are best described in CSS, where all the related property changes (colour, border, icon, animation) live together, and JavaScript's only job is to say **which state the element is in**. The tool for that is the element's class list.

**`className`: the old string API.** `className` gives the `class` attribute as one string. Editing it requires string manipulation, which is error-prone:

```javascript
el.className;                          // "btn btn-primary"
el.className += " active";             // easy to forget the leading space
el.className = el.className.replace("active", "");  // also removes "inactive"!
```

**`classList`: the token API.** `classList` is a `DOMTokenList`, a set-like view of the classes with safe methods:

```javascript
const btn = document.querySelector(".btn");

btn.classList.add("active", "large");        // add one or more (duplicates ignored)
btn.classList.remove("large");               // remove (no error if absent)
btn.classList.contains("active");            // true
btn.classList.replace("btn-primary", "btn-danger");  // returns true if replaced
btn.classList.toggle("active");              // remove if present, add if absent; returns new state
btn.classList.toggle("disabled", !isValid);  // with a second argument: force add (true) or remove (false)

btn.classList.length;                         // number of classes
[...btn.classList];                           // ["btn", "btn-danger", "active"]
btn.classList.value;                          // same as className
```

The second argument of `toggle` is the most useful form. It ties a class directly to a boolean condition, so there is no need for `if/else` around `add` and `remove`:

```javascript
form.classList.toggle("has-errors", errors.length > 0);
nav.classList.toggle("sticky", window.scrollY > header.offsetHeight);
```

**Pattern: state in classes, styling in CSS.** A disclosure panel (accordion section):

```html
<section class="panel">
  <button class="panel-toggle" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="p1">Shipping</button>
  <div class="panel-body" id="p1">Free shipping over 50 EUR.</div>
</section>
```

```css
.panel-body             { display: none; }
.panel.is-open .panel-body { display: block; }
.panel-toggle::after    { content: "+"; }
.panel.is-open .panel-toggle::after { content: "-"; }
```

```javascript
document.querySelector(".panel-toggle").addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const panel = event.currentTarget.closest(".panel");
  const open = panel.classList.toggle("is-open");           // returns the new state
  event.currentTarget.setAttribute("aria-expanded", open);  // keep assistive tech informed
});
```

The JavaScript knows nothing about how "open" looks. A designer can change the appearance, add a transition or restyle it for mobile without touching the script.

**Classes, attributes or ARIA?** Classes are not the only way to express state. The table summarises the common options:

| Mechanism | Example | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Class | `.is-open`, `.has-error` | Purely visual states |
| `data-*` attribute | `[data-state="loading"]` | States with more than two values |
| ARIA attribute | `[aria-expanded="true"]`, `[aria-selected="true"]` | States that must be announced by screen readers |
| Native attribute or pseudo-class | `[hidden]`, `:disabled`, `:checked`, `:invalid`, `[open]` | States the browser already understands |

When an accessible attribute exists, styling it directly (`[aria-expanded="true"] + .panel-body`) avoids keeping a class and an attribute in sync.

**Exclusive states: one active item.** For tabs and similar widgets, remove the class from the previous item and add it to the new one:

```javascript
function activateTab(tabs, index) {
  tabs.forEach((tab, i) => {
    const selected = i === index;
    tab.classList.toggle("active", selected);
    tab.setAttribute("aria-selected", selected);
  });
}
```

**Restarting a CSS animation.** Removing and immediately re-adding a class does nothing, because the browser never sees the intermediate state (both changes happen in the same task). You need to force a style flush between them, or wait a frame:

```javascript
function shake(el) {
  el.classList.remove("shake");
  void el.offsetWidth;            // forces style and layout: the removal is applied
  el.classList.add("shake");      // the animation starts again
}
```

This is one of the few legitimate uses of a forced layout. The Web Animations API (last topic in this subchapter) offers a cleaner alternative.

**Key Takeaways**

- `classList` provides `add`, `remove`, `toggle`, `contains` and `replace`, and is safer than editing `className` as a string.
- `toggle(name, condition)` binds a class to a boolean in one call and returns the resulting state.
- Express discrete UI states as classes, `data-*` or ARIA attributes, and keep their styling in CSS.
- Prefer ARIA or native attributes when the state is meaningful to assistive technology.
- Removing and re-adding a class in the same task has no visible effect unless a style flush happens in between.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement a dark-mode toggle button that toggles a `dark` class on `<html>`, with all colour changes defined in CSS.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build an accessible tab component with three tabs and panels. Clicking a tab activates it and its panel using `classList.toggle` with a condition and updates `aria-selected`. The left and right arrow keys move between tabs.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is toggling a class usually better than setting several style properties from JavaScript?" *Hint:* consider separation of concerns, the cascade, media queries, transitions and the number of style invalidations.

#### getComputedStyle and Resolved Values

`element.style` only reflects inline declarations, but the final appearance of an element is the result of the whole cascade: user-agent styles, every matching rule, inheritance, media queries and inline styles. When JavaScript needs to know the value that **actually applies** (what font size an element ended up with, whether it is currently `display: none`, how wide its padding is) it asks the browser with `getComputedStyle`.

**Basic usage.**

```javascript
const card = document.querySelector(".card");
const styles = getComputedStyle(card);       // read-only, live CSSStyleDeclaration

styles.display;                               // "flex"
styles.fontSize;                              // "16px": always absolute, even if CSS says 1rem
styles.color;                                 // "rgb(0, 0, 128)": even if CSS says "navy"
styles.getPropertyValue("padding-left");      // "16px": kebab-case form
styles.getPropertyValue("--accent");          // custom properties work too

// Pseudo-elements: pass the pseudo-element as the second argument
getComputedStyle(card, "::before").content;   // '"New"'
```

The returned object is **live**: if the element's styles change later, reading a property again returns the new value. It is also read-only, and assigning to it throws an error.

**Which value do you get?** Section 2.2 described the stages a value passes through: declared, cascaded, specified, computed, used and actual. `getComputedStyle` returns what the CSSOM specification calls the **resolved value**. For most properties, this is the *computed* value. For properties whose value depends on layout (such as `width`, `height`, `top`, `margin` and `padding`), it is the *used* value, in pixels, after layout.

| CSS declaration | `getComputedStyle` returns | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `color: navy` | `"rgb(0, 0, 128)"` | Colours are normalised to `rgb()` / `rgba()` |
| `font-size: 1.25rem` | `"20px"` | Relative lengths resolved to pixels |
| `width: 50%` (in a 600px parent) | `"300px"` | Used value after layout |
| `width: auto` | `"412.5px"` | Used value (may be fractional) |
| `line-height: 1.5` | `"24px"` or `"normal"` | Depends on the property and browser |
| No declaration for `margin-top` on a `<div>` | `"0px"` | Initial value |
| `display: none` on an ancestor | `width` returns `"auto"` | Elements not rendered have no layout |

**Common uses.**

```javascript
// 1. Is the element actually visible? (a class or media query may hide it)
function isDisplayed(el) {
  return getComputedStyle(el).display !== "none" && el.getClientRects().length > 0;
}
// Modern browsers also offer el.checkVisibility(), which checks display, ancestors and more.

// 2. Read a duration defined in CSS to synchronise JavaScript with a transition
const ms = parseFloat(getComputedStyle(toast).transitionDuration) * 1000;  // "0.3s" -> 300

// 3. Read numeric values: parseFloat strips the unit
const paddingX =
  parseFloat(getComputedStyle(box).paddingLeft) +
  parseFloat(getComputedStyle(box).paddingRight);

// 4. Determine the effective background colour for contrast checks
const bg = getComputedStyle(document.body).backgroundColor;  // "rgb(255, 255, 255)"
```

**Shorthand properties.** Read **longhand** properties (`paddingLeft`, `borderTopWidth`, `marginBlockStart`). Whether a shorthand such as `border` or `background` returns a combined string differs between browsers and properties, and some return an empty string.

**Performance.** `getComputedStyle` is a read from the rendering engine. If styles are dirty, it forces a style recalculation, and if you read a layout-dependent property, a layout too. This makes it one of the triggers of forced synchronous layout described in 6.1. Read once and cache the values, or read before you write.

**Typed values: the CSS Typed OM.** Parsing strings like `"20px"` is clumsy. The CSS Typed Object Model offers `element.computedStyleMap()`, which returns typed objects:

```javascript
const map = card.computedStyleMap();
const size = map.get("font-size");   // CSSUnitValue { value: 20, unit: "px" }
size.value + 4;                      // 24: no parseFloat needed
```

Typed OM is supported in Chromium-based browsers and Safari but not everywhere, so feature-detect it (`"computedStyleMap" in Element.prototype`) and fall back to `getComputedStyle`.

**Key Takeaways**

- `getComputedStyle(el, pseudo?)` returns the resolved style after the whole cascade, as a live, read-only object.
- Values are normalised: lengths in pixels, colours in `rgb()`, layout-dependent properties as used values.
- Read longhand properties, and use `parseFloat` to extract numbers from strings with units.
- Pass `"::before"` or `"::after"` as the second argument to read pseudo-element styles.
- It can force style recalculation and layout, so avoid calling it repeatedly between writes.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Give an element `font-size: 1.5em` inside a parent with `font-size: 20px`. Log `el.style.fontSize` and `getComputedStyle(el).fontSize` and explain both results.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function `waitForTransition(el)` that reads `transition-duration` and `transition-delay` from the computed style (they may contain several comma-separated values) and returns a promise that resolves after the longest total. Compare with listening for the `transitionend` event.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between a computed value and a used value, and which one does `getComputedStyle` return for `width`?" *Hint:* think about what a percentage width depends on, and when that information becomes available.

#### Manipulating CSS Variables from JavaScript

CSS custom properties (section 2.3) are variables that live in the cascade: they inherit, can be overridden per element, and change with media queries. That makes them the best bridge between JavaScript and CSS. Instead of JavaScript writing final property values (`transform`, `background`, `box-shadow`), it writes a few **input values**, and the stylesheet decides how to use them. Think of JavaScript as turning dials on a control panel that the designer built.

**Writing and reading custom properties.** Custom properties are not exposed as camelCase properties of `style`. Use `setProperty`, `getPropertyValue` and `removeProperty` with the full name including the two dashes:

```javascript
const root = document.documentElement;   // <html>: variables set here are global

root.style.setProperty("--accent", "#e4572e");   // inline style on <html>
root.style.getPropertyValue("--accent");         // "#e4572e" (inline only)

// The value that actually applies (from any stylesheet or ancestor):
getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue("--accent").trim();   // "#e4572e"

root.style.removeProperty("--accent");           // back to the stylesheet value
```

Custom property values are stored as strings. Older browsers kept the leading whitespace from the declaration (`--gap: 8px` read back as `" 8px"`), so `.trim()` is a cheap safety measure.

**Scope follows the cascade.** A variable set on an element is visible to it and all its descendants. Set global values on `:root` (`document.documentElement`) and local values on a component:

```css
:root      { --accent: royalblue; }
.card      { border-top: 4px solid var(--accent); }
.button    { background: var(--accent); }
```

```javascript
// Change one card only; the rest of the page keeps the global value
document.querySelector(".card.promo").style.setProperty("--accent", "crimson");
```

**Pattern: JavaScript provides numbers, CSS provides units and formulas.**

```css
.spotlight {
  /* JavaScript sets --x and --y as unitless pointer coordinates (0-1) */
  background: radial-gradient(
    circle at calc(var(--x, 0.5) * 100%) calc(var(--y, 0.5) * 100%),
    rgb(255 255 255 / 0.25),
    transparent 40%
  );
}

.parallax-layer {
  /* --depth is set per layer in HTML; --scroll is set by JavaScript */
  transform: translateY(calc(var(--scroll, 0) * var(--depth) * -1px));
}
```

```javascript
const spotlight = document.querySelector(".spotlight");

spotlight.addEventListener("pointermove", (e) => {
  const rect = spotlight.getBoundingClientRect();
  spotlight.style.setProperty("--x", (e.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width);
  spotlight.style.setProperty("--y", (e.clientY - rect.top) / rect.height);
});

window.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--scroll", window.scrollY);
}, { passive: true });
```

The script contains no visual decisions. Changing the effect (a stronger gradient, a different parallax direction) only requires editing CSS.

**Pattern: user-selected themes.** Store the user's choices as variables and persist them (6.4 covers `localStorage`):

```javascript
const themeInput = document.querySelector("#accent-picker");   // <input type="color">

themeInput.addEventListener("input", () => {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--accent", themeInput.value);
  localStorage.setItem("accent", themeInput.value);
});

const saved = localStorage.getItem("accent");
if (saved) document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--accent", saved);
```

**Animating variables: `@property`.** By default, the browser does not know what type a custom property holds, so it cannot interpolate between two values and transitions on it jump instantly. Registering the property with a type makes it animatable. You can register it in CSS (`@property`) or from JavaScript:

```javascript
CSS.registerProperty({
  name: "--progress",
  syntax: "<percentage>",   // a typed value: now the browser can interpolate it
  inherits: false,
  initialValue: "0%",
});
```

```css
.ring {
  transition: --progress 600ms ease-out;   /* now actually animates */
  background: conic-gradient(seagreen var(--progress), #ddd 0);
}
```

```javascript
ring.style.setProperty("--progress", "72%");   // smoothly animates the conic gradient
```

**Performance.** Changing a variable invalidates the style of every element that **inherits** it and uses it. Setting `--scroll` on `<html>` on every scroll event forces style recalculation across the whole page if many elements reference it. Set frequently changing variables on the **smallest element** that needs them, and register non-inherited properties with `inherits: false` when descendants do not need them.

**Key Takeaways**

- Set custom properties with `style.setProperty("--name", value)`. Read the effective value with `getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue("--name")`.
- Variables inherit, so set global values on `document.documentElement` and local values on components.
- Let JavaScript provide raw numbers and let CSS apply units and formulas with `calc()`, keeping visual logic in stylesheets.
- Register a typed property with `CSS.registerProperty` or `@property` to make it animatable.
- Frequently changing variables should be set on the smallest possible element to limit style recalculation.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a page with `--accent` defined on `:root` and used by buttons, links and borders. Add an `<input type="color">` that changes it live, and restore the saved value on reload.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a circular progress indicator using a registered `--progress` property and `conic-gradient`. Animate it from 0% to a value read from a `data-value` attribute when it scrolls into view.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What are the advantages of setting a CSS custom property from JavaScript instead of setting `transform` directly?" *Hint:* consider who owns the visual logic, how media queries and themes can reuse the value, and how many elements one write can affect.

#### The CSSOM and Stylesheet Objects

Just as HTML is parsed into the DOM, CSS is parsed into the **CSSOM** (CSS Object Model): a tree of objects representing stylesheets and their rules. The previous topics touched individual elements. The CSSOM lets JavaScript work at the level of **rules**: list them, inspect them, add new ones, disable entire stylesheets. Most applications rarely need this, but it is how CSS-in-JS libraries, theme engines, DevTools and Web Components manage styles.

**The structure.**

```text
document.styleSheets              StyleSheetList (one entry per <link rel=stylesheet> and <style>)
└── CSSStyleSheet                 href, disabled, media, ownerNode
    └── cssRules                  CSSRuleList
        ├── CSSStyleRule          selectorText ".card", style (CSSStyleDeclaration)
        ├── CSSMediaRule          media "(min-width: 768px)", cssRules (nested rules)
        ├── CSSKeyframesRule      name "fade", cssRules (CSSKeyframeRule)
        ├── CSSImportRule         href, styleSheet
        └── CSSFontFaceRule, CSSLayerBlockRule, CSSContainerRule, ...
```

**Inspecting rules.**

```javascript
for (const sheet of document.styleSheets) {
  console.log(sheet.href ?? "(inline <style>)", sheet.ownerNode);
  try {
    for (const rule of sheet.cssRules) {
      if (rule instanceof CSSStyleRule) {
        console.log(rule.selectorText, rule.style.cssText);
      } else if (rule instanceof CSSMediaRule) {
        console.log("@media", rule.conditionText, rule.cssRules.length, "rules");
      }
    }
  } catch (err) {
    // Cross-origin stylesheets (e.g. from a CDN without CORS) cannot be read
    console.warn("Cannot read rules of", sheet.href, err.name);  // "SecurityError"
  }
}
```

Reading `cssRules` from a stylesheet loaded from another origin throws a `SecurityError` unless the `<link>` has `crossorigin` and the server sends the right CORS headers (5.4). This prevents a page from reading private stylesheets of other sites.

**Modifying rules.** Changing a rule affects **every element** that matches its selector, now and in the future, which an inline style cannot do:

```javascript
const sheet = document.querySelector("#theme").sheet;   // the CSSStyleSheet of a <style id="theme">

// Insert a new rule at the end; returns its index
const index = sheet.insertRule(".highlight { outline: 2px solid gold; }", sheet.cssRules.length);

// Modify an existing rule's declarations
const cardRule = [...sheet.cssRules].find((r) => r.selectorText === ".card");
cardRule.style.setProperty("border-radius", "12px");

// Delete a rule by index
sheet.deleteRule(index);

// Disable or enable a whole stylesheet
sheet.disabled = true;
```

`insertRule` throws a `SyntaxError` for invalid CSS. It inserts only one rule per call.

**Constructable stylesheets.** Creating a `<style>` element just to get a stylesheet is clumsy. Constructable stylesheets are created directly in JavaScript and attached with `adoptedStyleSheets`:

```javascript
const sheet = new CSSStyleSheet();
sheet.replaceSync(`
  .toast { position: fixed; bottom: 1rem; right: 1rem; padding: .75rem 1rem; }
  .toast.error { background: crimson; color: white; }
`);
// replace() is the asynchronous version and returns a promise

document.adoptedStyleSheets = [...document.adoptedStyleSheets, sheet];

// Updating the sheet later updates every document or shadow root that adopted it
sheet.replaceSync(".toast { bottom: 2rem; }");
```

Their main benefit appears with Web Components. One stylesheet object can be shared by hundreds of shadow roots without being parsed or stored again for each one:

```javascript
const buttonStyles = new CSSStyleSheet();
buttonStyles.replaceSync("button { font: inherit; padding: .5em 1em; }");

class FancyButton extends HTMLElement {
  constructor() {
    super();
    const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" });
    shadow.adoptedStyleSheets = [buttonStyles];   // shared, parsed once
    shadow.innerHTML = "<button><slot></slot></button>";
  }
}
customElements.define("fancy-button", FancyButton);
```

**When to use which.**

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| Change one element | `element.style` or `classList` |
| Change every element matching a selector, including future ones | Modify or insert a CSSOM rule, or (simpler) a custom property on `:root` |
| Load or swap a theme file | Add or remove a `<link rel="stylesheet">`, or toggle `sheet.disabled` |
| Styles generated at runtime by a library | Constructable stylesheets |
| Encapsulated component styles | `adoptedStyleSheets` on a shadow root |

**Key Takeaways**

- The CSSOM represents stylesheets as objects: `document.styleSheets` contains `CSSStyleSheet` objects whose `cssRules` hold typed rule objects.
- `insertRule`, `deleteRule` and rule `style` objects change styles for every matching element at once.
- Cross-origin stylesheets cannot be read without CORS and throw a `SecurityError`.
- Constructable stylesheets (`new CSSStyleSheet()`, `replaceSync`, `adoptedStyleSheets`) create and share styles without `<style>` elements, which is ideal for Web Components.
- For most dynamic styling, classes and custom properties are simpler than editing rules.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* List every rule in the page's stylesheets, printing its type and selector, and handle cross-origin sheets gracefully. Test with a Google Fonts stylesheet on the page.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a "high contrast" switch that creates a constructable stylesheet once and adds or removes it from `document.adoptedStyleSheets` without creating it again.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would a CSS-in-JS library inject styles generated at runtime, and why might it use `insertRule` instead of appending text to a `<style>` element?" *Hint:* think about parsing cost, how many rules are re-parsed on each change, and what DevTools can display.

#### Element Geometry, Box Metrics and Scrolling

Positioning a tooltip next to a button, detecting whether the user scrolled to the bottom of a list, or centring a modal all require knowing **where** elements are and **how big** they are. The DOM exposes several families of geometry properties, each measuring a different box from a different reference point. Mixing them up is the source of most "off by a few pixels" bugs, so this topic maps each property to the box it measures.

**The boxes of an element.** Recall the box model from Chapter 2. Assume an element with `width: 200px; padding: 10px; border: 5px; overflow: auto`, whose content is 600px tall, and a 15px vertical scrollbar:

```text
 offsetLeft/offsetTop: position of the border box relative to offsetParent
 |
 v
 +---------------------------------------------+  <- border box
 | border (clientLeft/clientTop = 5)            |     offsetWidth  = 5+10+200+10+5 = 230
 |  +-------------------------------------+---+ |     (includes scrollbar)
 |  | padding                             | s | |
 |  |  +-----------------------------+    | c | |  <- padding box minus scrollbar
 |  |  | content                     |    | r | |     clientWidth = 10+185+10 = 205
 |  |  |                             |    | o | |     (200 - 15 scrollbar = 185 content)
 |  |  |    scrollTop = how far the  |    | l | |
 |  |  |    content is scrolled      |    | l | |
 |  |  +-----------------------------+    |   | |
 |  +-------------------------------------+---+ |
 +---------------------------------------------+
   scrollHeight = full height of content + padding, including the hidden overflow
```

**The properties.**

| Property | Measures | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `offsetWidth`, `offsetHeight` | Border box (content + padding + border + scrollbar) | Integers (rounded) |
| `offsetTop`, `offsetLeft` | Position relative to `offsetParent` (nearest positioned ancestor, or `<body>`) | Integers |
| `clientWidth`, `clientHeight` | Padding box minus scrollbar: the visible inner area | Integers, `0` for inline elements |
| `clientTop`, `clientLeft` | Width of the top and left borders | Integers |
| `scrollWidth`, `scrollHeight` | Full content size including overflow that is scrolled out of view | Integers |
| `scrollTop`, `scrollLeft` | How far the content is scrolled | Writable, may be fractional |
| `getBoundingClientRect()` | Border box relative to the **viewport**, after CSS transforms | Fractional `DOMRect` |

**`getBoundingClientRect()`: the precise, modern choice.** It returns a `DOMRect` with `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `top`, `right`, `bottom` and `left`, in fractional CSS pixels, **relative to the viewport**. It accounts for transforms (a scaled element reports its visual size), which the `offset*` properties do not.

```javascript
const rect = button.getBoundingClientRect();
// DOMRect { x: 120.5, y: 310, width: 96, height: 40, top: 310, right: 216.5, bottom: 350, left: 120.5 }

// Viewport coordinates change as the page scrolls. For document coordinates, add the scroll offset:
const pageTop  = rect.top + window.scrollY;
const pageLeft = rect.left + window.scrollX;

// Is the element fully visible in the viewport right now?
const fullyVisible =
  rect.top >= 0 && rect.left >= 0 &&
  rect.bottom <= window.innerHeight && rect.right <= window.innerWidth;
```

For continuous visibility tracking, use `IntersectionObserver` (6.4) instead of calling this on every scroll event.

**Example: position a tooltip below a button.**

```javascript
function showTooltip(anchor, tooltip) {
  const a = anchor.getBoundingClientRect();     // READ phase
  const tipWidth = tooltip.offsetWidth;

  let left = a.left + a.width / 2 - tipWidth / 2;              // centred under the anchor
  left = Math.max(8, Math.min(left, window.innerWidth - tipWidth - 8));  // keep on screen

  tooltip.style.position = "fixed";              // WRITE phase: fixed = viewport coordinates
  tooltip.style.top = `${a.bottom + 8}px`;
  tooltip.style.left = `${left}px`;
}
```

Using `position: fixed` with `getBoundingClientRect` values keeps everything in the same coordinate system (the viewport). For simple anchoring, CSS anchor positioning increasingly removes the need for this code.

**Viewport and document dimensions.**

```javascript
window.innerWidth;                          // viewport width including the vertical scrollbar
document.documentElement.clientWidth;       // viewport width excluding the scrollbar (usable layout width)
document.documentElement.scrollHeight;      // total document height
window.scrollY;                             // vertical scroll of the page (alias: pageYOffset)
window.visualViewport?.height;              // visible area on mobile, shrinks with on-screen keyboard or pinch zoom
```

**Scrolling programmatically.**

```javascript
window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "smooth" });   // back to top
window.scrollBy({ top: window.innerHeight * 0.8 }); // one "page" down
list.scrollTop = list.scrollHeight;                  // jump a scroll container to the bottom (chat)

section.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", block: "start" });   // bring an element into view
field.scrollIntoView({ block: "center" });                        // centre it vertically

// Has the user scrolled to the bottom of a container? (with a 1px tolerance for rounding)
const atBottom = list.scrollHeight - list.scrollTop - list.clientHeight < 1;
```

Respect user preferences: CSS `scroll-behavior: smooth` combined with `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` lets users who dislike motion opt out of smooth scrolling. Fixed headers can cover elements scrolled into view. Fix this in CSS with `scroll-margin-top` on the targets, not by subtracting pixels in JavaScript.

**Remember: geometry reads force layout.** Every property in this topic is a layout read. Use the read-then-write discipline from 6.1, and avoid reading geometry inside `scroll` or `pointermove` handlers more often than once per frame.

**Key Takeaways**

- `offset*` measures the border box relative to the `offsetParent`, `client*` measures the visible inner area without borders and scrollbars, and `scroll*` measures the full scrollable content.
- `getBoundingClientRect()` returns fractional, viewport-relative coordinates that include transforms. Add `scrollX` and `scrollY` to get document coordinates.
- `document.documentElement.clientWidth` excludes the scrollbar, while `window.innerWidth` includes it.
- Scroll with `scrollTo`, `scrollBy`, `scrollTop` and `scrollIntoView`, and handle fixed headers with `scroll-margin-top`.
- All geometry reads can force a synchronous layout.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a scrollable `<div>` with a border, padding and long content. Log all `offset*`, `client*` and `scroll*` values and verify each one against the box-model diagram.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a "scroll to top" button that appears after the user scrolls down 1.5 viewport heights, and a reading-progress bar at the top of the page computed from `scrollY`, `scrollHeight` and `clientHeight`. Update the bar at most once per animation frame.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `offsetWidth`, `clientWidth`, `scrollWidth` and `getBoundingClientRect().width`?" *Hint:* draw the box model, mark which parts each one includes, and consider what happens with a `transform: scale(2)`.

#### The Web Animations API

There are three ways to animate in the browser. CSS transitions and keyframe animations (Chapter 2) are declarative and efficient but hard to control from code: you cannot easily pause one, reverse it from its current point, or know when it finishes. `requestAnimationFrame` (5.1) gives total control but makes you compute every frame yourself, on the main thread. The **Web Animations API (WAAPI)** combines the two. You describe keyframes in JavaScript, the browser runs the animation with the same engine as CSS animations (on the compositor for `transform` and `opacity`), and you get an `Animation` object with playback controls and promises.

**`element.animate()`.** It takes keyframes and timing options and returns an `Animation` that starts immediately:

```javascript
const box = document.querySelector(".box");

const animation = box.animate(
  [
    { transform: "translateX(0)",     opacity: 1 },   // keyframe at offset 0
    { transform: "translateX(200px)", opacity: 0.5, offset: 0.7 },  // optional explicit offset
    { transform: "translateX(300px)", opacity: 1 },   // keyframe at offset 1
  ],
  {
    duration: 800,           // milliseconds (CSS uses seconds; WAAPI uses ms)
    easing: "ease-in-out",   // any CSS easing, including cubic-bezier() and linear()
    delay: 100,
    iterations: 2,           // Infinity for endless
    direction: "alternate",  // normal, reverse, alternate, alternate-reverse
    fill: "forwards",        // keep the final keyframe's styles after finishing
  }
);
```

Keyframes can also be written as an object of arrays, which is convenient for simple two-state animations:

```javascript
box.animate({ opacity: [0, 1], transform: ["scale(0.9)", "scale(1)"] }, 200);  // number = duration
```

**Controlling playback.**

```javascript
animation.pause();
animation.play();
animation.reverse();             // plays backwards from the current point
animation.playbackRate = 2;      // double speed (negative values play backwards)
animation.currentTime = 400;     // seek to 400 ms (scrubbing)
animation.finish();              // jump to the end
animation.cancel();              // remove all effects, back to the original styles

animation.playState;             // "idle", "running", "paused" or "finished"
```

**Knowing when it ends.** `animation.finished` is a promise (5.2) that resolves when the animation completes, which makes sequencing straightforward with `async`/`await`:

```javascript
async function showToast(toast) {
  toast.hidden = false;
  await toast.animate(
    [{ transform: "translateY(100%)" }, { transform: "translateY(0)" }],
    { duration: 250, easing: "ease-out" }
  ).finished;

  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000));   // stay visible for 3 seconds

  await toast.animate({ opacity: [1, 0] }, 200).finished;
  toast.hidden = true;
}
```

The promise is rejected with an `AbortError` if the animation is cancelled, so wrap awaits in `try/catch` when cancellation is possible.

**`fill: "forwards"` and `commitStyles()`.** After an animation finishes, its effect disappears and the element snaps back to its CSS styles. `fill: "forwards"` keeps the final state, but the animation object stays alive and overrides the element's styles indefinitely, which also blocks later changes. A cleaner approach is to write the final state into the element and cancel the animation:

```javascript
const anim = panel.animate({ transform: ["none", "translateX(-100%)"] }, { duration: 300, fill: "forwards" });
await anim.finished;
anim.commitStyles();   // writes the current animated values into panel.style
anim.cancel();         // releases the animation
```

**Interrupting smoothly.** Because WAAPI knows the current progress, you can reverse an animation that is halfway through, for example a menu that the user closes while it is opening:

```javascript
let menuAnim = null;

function toggleMenu(open) {
  if (menuAnim && menuAnim.playState === "running") {
    menuAnim.reverse();                      // turn around from the current point
    return;
  }
  menuAnim = menu.animate(
    { clipPath: ["inset(0 0 100% 0)", "inset(0 0 0 0)"] },
    { duration: 300, easing: "ease-out", fill: "both", direction: open ? "normal" : "reverse" }
  );
}
```

**Controlling CSS animations from JavaScript.** CSS transitions and animations are also exposed as `Animation` objects (`CSSTransition`, `CSSAnimation`):

```javascript
for (const anim of document.getAnimations()) {   // every running animation on the page
  anim.playbackRate = 0.1;                         // slow everything down for debugging
}
spinner.getAnimations()[0]?.pause();              // pause a CSS @keyframes spinner
await Promise.all(card.getAnimations().map((a) => a.finished));  // wait for CSS transitions
```

**Respecting reduced motion.** Some users get motion sickness from animations. Check the preference before animating large movements:

```javascript
const reduceMotion = matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
el.animate(keyframes, { duration: reduceMotion ? 0 : 400 });
```

**Choosing an animation technique.**

| Technique | Best for | Control from JS | Runs on compositor |
|---|---|---|---|
| CSS transition | State changes (hover, open/closed) triggered by a class | Limited (events only) | Yes, for `transform` and `opacity` |
| CSS `@keyframes` | Decorative, looping or entrance animations | Limited | Yes, for `transform` and `opacity` |
| Web Animations API | Interactive, interruptible, sequenced or data-driven animations | Full (pause, seek, reverse, promises) | Yes, for `transform` and `opacity` |
| `requestAnimationFrame` | Physics, canvas drawing, values CSS cannot express | Full, but manual | No (main thread) |

Newer extensions let WAAPI animations be driven by scroll position instead of time (`ScrollTimeline` and `ViewTimeline`, the JavaScript side of CSS scroll-driven animations). Check browser support before using them.

**Key Takeaways**

- `element.animate(keyframes, options)` runs a keyframe animation and returns an `Animation` object. Durations are in milliseconds.
- The `Animation` object supports `play`, `pause`, `reverse`, `playbackRate`, `currentTime`, `finish` and `cancel`.
