- `animation.finished` is a promise, ideal for sequencing with `await`.
- Prefer `commitStyles()` plus `cancel()` over leaving `fill: "forwards"` animations alive.
- `getAnimations()` exposes CSS transitions and animations as the same objects, so they can be controlled from script.
- Animate `transform` and `opacity` for compositor performance, and honour `prefers-reduced-motion`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Animate a card that fades and slides in from below when a button is clicked, using `element.animate`. Log a message when the animation finishes, using the `finished` promise.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build an image carousel where clicking "Next" while a slide animation is running reverses or finishes the current animation cleanly instead of stacking animations. Add a range input that scrubs a long animation by setting `currentTime`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose the Web Animations API over a CSS transition, and when over `requestAnimationFrame`?" *Hint:* compare control over playback, who computes intermediate frames, and which thread does the work.

<a id="63-the-event-system"></a>
### 6.3 The Event System

This subchapter explains how the browser notifies your code about user actions and state changes: how to register handlers, what an event object contains, how events travel through the tree, how to cancel default behaviour, and how to design with delegation and custom events.

#### Event-Driven Programming Model

A command-line program usually runs from top to bottom: read input, compute, print, exit. A web page cannot work like that. It has no idea when, or whether, the user will click, type, scroll or resize the window, and it must also react to network responses and timers. So browser code is organised the other way around: you **register functions** that say "when *this* happens to *that* element, call me", and then your script ends. The browser waits for things to happen and calls your functions. This is **event-driven programming**, and it is an instance of *inversion of control* (5.2): the browser, not your code, decides when your code runs.

An analogy is a hotel front desk with a guest book of requests: "wake me at 7", "tell me when my taxi arrives". The guests (handlers) do not stand in the lobby waiting. The receptionist (the browser) watches for each condition and phones the right guest when it occurs.

**Vocabulary.**

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Event | A notification that something happened | A click, a key press, a form submission |
| Event type | The name of the kind of event | `"click"`, `"keydown"`, `"submit"` |
| Event target | The object on which the event occurred | The `<button>` that was clicked |
| Event listener (handler) | The function called when the event occurs | `function onSave(event) { ... }` |
| Event object | Information about the occurrence, passed to the listener | Mouse position, key pressed |
| Default action | What the browser does by itself in response | Following a link, submitting a form |

**How events fit into the event loop.** When the user clicks, the operating system notifies the browser, which works out which element is under the pointer and queues a **task** (5.1). When the call stack is empty, the event loop runs the task, and the browser calls every relevant listener **synchronously, one after another**. Each listener runs to completion, and nothing else happens (not even rendering) until all of them have returned.

```text
 user clicks ──> browser hit-tests ──> task queued ──> event loop picks task
                 (which element?)                       │
                                                         v
                         listener 1 ──> listener 2 ──> ... ──> microtasks ──> render
```

The practical consequence: a slow listener freezes the page. Keep handlers short and move heavy work elsewhere (5.1 and Web Workers in 6.4).

**Three ways to register a handler.** The web has accumulated three mechanisms:

```html
<!-- 1. HTML attribute (inline handler): code in a string, runs in global scope -->
<button onclick="save()">Save</button>
```

```javascript
// 2. DOM property: exactly one handler per event type per element
const button = document.querySelector("#save");
button.onclick = function (event) { save(); };
button.onclick = function (event) { log(); };   // REPLACES the previous handler
button.onclick = null;                            // removes it

// 3. addEventListener: any number of listeners, with options (next topic)
button.addEventListener("click", save);
button.addEventListener("click", log);            // both run, in registration order
```

| Mechanism | Multiple handlers | Options (capture, once, passive) | Separation of HTML and JS | Works under strict CSP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `onclick="..."` attribute | No | No | No | No (needs `'unsafe-inline'`) |
| `el.onclick = fn` | No (last one wins) | No | Yes | Yes |
| `el.addEventListener("click", fn)` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Inline attributes mix behaviour into markup, execute strings of code with surprising scope rules and are blocked by a strict Content Security Policy. `addEventListener` is the standard choice. DOM properties remain acceptable for quick scripts where a single handler is intended.

**Not only elements.** Any `EventTarget` can emit events: `window` (`resize`, `scroll`, `online`), `document` (`DOMContentLoaded`, `visibilitychange`), `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `AbortSignal`, `IndexedDB` requests, `Worker`s and even your own objects (see *Custom Events and Event Dispatching*). Everything in this subchapter applies to all of them.

**Key Takeaways**

- Browser code is event-driven: you register listeners, and the browser calls them when events occur.
- Events are delivered as tasks. All listeners for one event run synchronously, to completion, before rendering.
- Long-running listeners block input and rendering, so keep them short.
- Prefer `addEventListener`. `on*` properties allow one handler per type, and inline `on*` attributes should be avoided.
- Every `EventTarget` (window, document, elements, network objects, your own classes) uses the same event model.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Register two click handlers on one button with `onclick`, then two with `addEventListener`. Log which ones run and explain the difference.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a click handler that runs a loop for two seconds, and next to the button add a CSS `:hover` effect and a text input. Click the button and try to type and hover during the two seconds. Describe what you observe in terms of the event loop.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why are inline event handler attributes such as `onclick=\"...\"` considered bad practice?" *Hint:* consider maintainability, the number of handlers allowed, scope, and Content Security Policy.

#### Event Registration with addEventListener

`addEventListener` is the core method of the event system. It looks simple, but its options and the rules for removing listeners determine whether an application stays fast and leak-free.

**Signature.**

```javascript
target.addEventListener(type, listener, options);
target.removeEventListener(type, listener, options);
```

- `type`: the event name, without the `on` prefix (`"click"`, not `"onclick"`). Case-sensitive.
- `listener`: a function, or an object with a `handleEvent` method.
- `options`: an object (or, in old code, a boolean meaning `capture`).

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `capture` | `false` | Run during the capture phase instead of the bubble phase (see *Capturing, Targeting and Bubbling Phases*) |
| `once` | `false` | Remove the listener automatically after its first call |
| `passive` | `false`* | Promise not to call `preventDefault()`, allowing the browser to scroll without waiting |
| `signal` | none | An `AbortSignal`: when it aborts, the listener is removed |

\* Chromium-based browsers and Firefox default `passive` to `true` for `touchstart`, `touchmove`, `wheel` and `mousewheel` listeners registered on `window`, `document` or `<body>`.

```javascript
const button = document.querySelector("#buy");

button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log("clicked", event.target);
});

button.addEventListener("click", startTutorial, { once: true });   // only the first click

window.addEventListener("scroll", updateProgressBar, { passive: true });
```

**Duplicate registrations are ignored.** Adding the *same function* with the same `type` and `capture` value twice registers it only once. Two *different* functions with identical code are two listeners, which is why anonymous functions are a problem when you need to remove them.

**Removing listeners.** `removeEventListener` must receive **the same function reference** and the same `capture` value used when adding:

```javascript
// BUG: two different function objects; nothing is removed
el.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("hi"));
el.removeEventListener("click", () => console.log("hi"));

// Correct: keep a reference
function onClick() { console.log("hi"); }
el.addEventListener("click", onClick);
el.removeEventListener("click", onClick);

// BUG: capture flag differs; nothing is removed
el.addEventListener("click", onClick, { capture: true });
el.removeEventListener("click", onClick);                     // needs { capture: true }
```

**Removing many listeners at once with `AbortController`.** The `signal` option (5.3 introduced `AbortController`) removes a whole group of listeners with one call, and works with anonymous functions:

```javascript
function openModal(modal) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const { signal } = controller;

  document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
    if (e.key === "Escape") close();
  }, { signal });

  modal.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    if (e.target === modal) close();   // click on the backdrop
  }, { signal });

  window.addEventListener("resize", () => position(modal), { signal });

  function close() {
    modal.hidden = true;
    controller.abort();                // removes all three listeners at once
  }
}
```

This pattern is the cleanest way to avoid memory leaks from listeners on long-lived objects (`window`, `document`) that refer to short-lived components.

**`this` inside listeners.** For a regular function, `this` is the element the listener is attached to (`event.currentTarget`). Arrow functions do not have their own `this`, so they keep the surrounding one (3.3 and 4.3):

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  this.classList.toggle("active");        // this === button
});

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log(this);                       // NOT the button: outer this (undefined in modules)
});
```

Relying on `event.currentTarget` instead of `this` works with both kinds of function and is clearer.

**Methods as listeners.** Passing an object's method loses its `this` (4.3). Bind it, wrap it, or use a class field arrow function:

```javascript
class Counter {
  count = 0;
  constructor(button) {
    button.addEventListener("click", this.increment);   // this.increment keeps the instance
  }
  increment = () => {                                    // class field arrow function
    this.count++;
  };
}
```

The `handleEvent` interface is another option: pass the object itself, and the browser calls its `handleEvent` method with `this` set to the object:

```javascript
const tracker = {
  clicks: 0,
  handleEvent(event) {
    if (event.type === "click") this.clicks++;
  },
};
document.addEventListener("click", tracker);
document.removeEventListener("click", tracker);   // same object reference
```

**Passive listeners and scroll performance.** When a `touchmove` or `wheel` listener might call `preventDefault()`, the browser must wait for it to finish before scrolling, because the listener could cancel the scroll. A slow listener then makes scrolling stutter. Declaring `{ passive: true }` tells the browser it can scroll immediately. Calling `preventDefault()` inside a passive listener is ignored, with a console warning. To prevent scrolling on touch (for example in a drawing canvas), prefer the CSS property `touch-action: none` (see *Mouse, Keyboard, Pointer and Touch Events*).

**Key Takeaways**

- `addEventListener(type, listener, options)` supports `capture`, `once`, `passive` and `signal`.
- The same function added twice with the same type and capture flag is registered only once.
- `removeEventListener` needs the identical function reference and capture flag. Anonymous functions cannot be removed this way.
- Use an `AbortController` signal to remove groups of listeners with one `abort()` call.
- In regular function listeners `this` is `currentTarget`. Arrow functions inherit `this`, so prefer `event.currentTarget`.
- Mark scroll-related listeners as `passive` so they never delay scrolling.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a "Start" button that logs a message only the first time it is clicked, using `{ once: true }`, and a second button that removes a click listener from a third button.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `makeDraggable(el)` function that adds `pointermove` and `pointerup` listeners to `document` when dragging starts and removes them all with a single `AbortController` when it ends. Verify in DevTools (Elements panel, Event Listeners tab) that no listeners remain after dragging.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `el.removeEventListener('click', () => doSomething())` not work, and what are the alternatives?" *Hint:* think about function identity, and about two mechanisms that do not require keeping a reference.

#### The Event Object and Its Properties

When an event occurs, the listener needs details: which element was clicked, where the pointer was, which key was pressed, whether Shift was held down. The browser packages these into an **event object** and passes it as the only argument to every listener. All event objects share a common base interface, `Event`, and specialised event types add the relevant information.

**The base `Event` properties.**

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | The event name, such as `"click"` |
| `target` | The element where the event **originated** (the deepest element, such as a `<span>` inside a button) |
| `currentTarget` | The element whose listener is **running now** (where you attached the listener) |
| `eventPhase` | `1` capture, `2` at target, `3` bubble (`0` when not being dispatched) |
| `bubbles` | Whether the event bubbles up the tree |
| `cancelable` | Whether `preventDefault()` can cancel its default action |
| `defaultPrevented` | Whether some listener already called `preventDefault()` |
| `isTrusted` | `true` if generated by the browser from a real user action, `false` if created by script |
| `timeStamp` | Milliseconds since the page started loading (comparable with `performance.now()`) |
| `composedPath()` | Array of every object the event will pass through, from target to `window` |

**`target` versus `currentTarget`.** This distinction is essential for event delegation (later topic):

```html
<ul id="menu">
  <li><a href="/shop"><span class="icon">*</span> Shop</a></li>
</ul>
```

```javascript
document.getElementById("menu").addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log(event.target);          // <span class="icon"> if the icon was clicked
  console.log(event.currentTarget);   // <ul id="menu">: where the listener is attached
  console.log(event.target.closest("a"));  // <a href="/shop">: the link, whatever part was clicked
});
```

`currentTarget` is only meaningful while the listener is running. Afterwards it is `null`, which surprises people who log the event and inspect it later or read it after an `await`:

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", async (event) => {
  const el = event.currentTarget;        // copy it first
  await fetch("/api/like", { method: "POST" });
  console.log(event.currentTarget);      // null: dispatch is over
  el.classList.add("liked");             // works
});
```

**Specialised event interfaces.** Each family of events has its own interface that extends `Event` (some through `UIEvent`):

```text
Event
├── UIEvent
│   ├── MouseEvent         clientX/Y, pageX/Y, button, buttons, altKey, ctrlKey, shiftKey, metaKey
│   │   ├── PointerEvent   pointerId, pointerType, pressure, width, height, isPrimary
│   │   ├── WheelEvent     deltaX, deltaY, deltaMode
│   │   └── DragEvent      dataTransfer
│   ├── KeyboardEvent      key, code, repeat, isComposing, modifier keys
│   ├── FocusEvent         relatedTarget
│   ├── InputEvent         data, inputType ("insertText", "deleteContentBackward", ...)
│   └── TouchEvent         touches, targetTouches, changedTouches
├── SubmitEvent            submitter (the button that submitted the form)
├── CustomEvent            detail (your own data)
├── ProgressEvent          loaded, total, lengthComputable
├── StorageEvent           key, oldValue, newValue (6.4)
└── PopStateEvent          state (6.4)
```

```javascript
document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
  // e is a KeyboardEvent
  if ((e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey) && e.key === "s") {
    e.preventDefault();                    // stop the browser's "Save page" dialog
    saveDocument();
  }
});

canvas.addEventListener("pointerdown", (e) => {
  // e is a PointerEvent
  console.log(e.pointerType, e.clientX, e.clientY, e.pressure);  // "pen" 312 140 0.42
});

form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
  // e is a SubmitEvent
  console.log(e.submitter?.value);         // which submit button was used ("draft" or "publish")
});
```

**Exploring an event.** The fastest way to learn an event's properties is to log it and expand it in the console, or to run `monitorEvents(element, "click")` in Chrome DevTools, which logs every event of that type on the element.

**`isTrusted` and synthetic events.** Events created by script (see *Custom Events and Event Dispatching*) have `isTrusted === false`. Browsers reserve some privileged actions, such as opening pop-ups, entering fullscreen or writing to the clipboard, for trusted events that come from a real user gesture (called *user activation*).

**Key Takeaways**

- Every listener receives an event object that describes the occurrence. Specialised interfaces (`MouseEvent`, `KeyboardEvent`, `PointerEvent`, `SubmitEvent`...) add details.
- `target` is where the event started, and `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running.
- `currentTarget` is `null` once dispatch ends, so copy it before any `await`.
- `bubbles`, `cancelable`, `defaultPrevented` and `eventPhase` describe how the event is travelling and whether it can be cancelled.
- `isTrusted` distinguishes real user events from script-created ones, and some powerful APIs require a real user gesture.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add one click listener to `document` that logs `type`, `target.tagName`, `currentTarget`, `eventPhase`, `clientX` and `clientY`. Click several different elements and compare the output.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a keyboard shortcut handler that supports combinations such as "Ctrl+Shift+K" written as strings in a configuration object, and ignores events that occur while the user is typing in an input, a textarea or a `contenteditable` element.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `event.target` and `event.currentTarget`?" *Hint:* attach a listener to a list and click on a nested element inside one item.

#### Capturing, Targeting and Bubbling Phases

When you click a `<span>` inside a `<button>` inside a `<form>`, you have arguably clicked all of them. The DOM's answer is that the event **travels through the tree**, so listeners on the span, the button, the form, the body, the document and the window can all react. The order of that journey is defined precisely, in three phases. Understanding it explains how delegation works, why some listeners run before others, and what "stopping propagation" actually stops.

**The three phases.** The browser first computes the **propagation path**: the target and all its ancestors up to `window`. Then:

1. **Capture phase** (`eventPhase === 1`): the event travels **down** from `window` to the target's parent, calling listeners registered with `capture: true`.
2. **Target phase** (`eventPhase === 2`): the event is at the target itself. Listeners on the target run, capturing ones first, then non-capturing ones.
3. **Bubble phase** (`eventPhase === 3`): the event travels back **up** from the target's parent to `window`, calling listeners registered without `capture` (the default).

```text
                      window
              1 |                  ^ 3
                v                  |
                    document
              1 |                  ^ 3
                v                  |
                     <html>
              1 |                  ^ 3      Capture (1): top-down,
                v                  |        listeners with { capture: true }
                     <body>
              1 |                  ^ 3      Bubble (3): bottom-up,
                v                  |        default listeners
                     <form>
              1 |                  ^ 3
                v                  |
                    <button>
              1 |                  ^ 3
                v                  |
                 +---------------------+
                 |   <span> TARGET (2) |    Target (2): capture listeners,
                 +---------------------+    then bubble listeners on the target
```

**Seeing it in action.**

```html
<form id="f"><button id="b" type="button"><span id="s">Go</span></button></form>
```

```javascript
const ids = ["f", "b", "s"];
for (const id of ids) {
  const el = document.getElementById(id);
  el.addEventListener("click", (e) => console.log("capture", id, e.eventPhase), { capture: true });
  el.addEventListener("click", (e) => console.log("bubble ", id, e.eventPhase));
}

// Clicking the text "Go" logs:
// capture f 1
// capture b 1
// capture s 2     <- at the target
// bubble  s 2     <- at the target
// bubble  b 3
// bubble  f 3
```

**Why two directions?** Bubbling is what you want almost all the time: the most specific element reacts first, and more general containers can react afterwards (or handle many children at once with delegation). Capturing is useful when an ancestor must see the event **before** any descendant can handle or stop it. Typical uses are global logic such as closing open menus on any click, analytics, or debugging tools.

```javascript
// Close any open dropdown when the user clicks outside it.
// Capture phase: runs even if some inner component calls stopPropagation() during bubbling.
document.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  for (const dropdown of document.querySelectorAll(".dropdown.open")) {
    if (!dropdown.contains(e.target)) dropdown.classList.remove("open");
  }
}, { capture: true });
```

**Not every event bubbles.** Some events only make sense for the element itself, so they have `bubbles: false`. They still go through the capture phase and the target phase, so a capturing listener on an ancestor can still observe them.

| Does not bubble | Bubbling alternative |
|---|---|
| `focus`, `blur` | `focusin`, `focusout` |
| `mouseenter`, `mouseleave` | `mouseover`, `mouseout` |
| `pointerenter`, `pointerleave` | `pointerover`, `pointerout` |
| `load`, `error` on elements such as `<img>` | Listen in capture phase on an ancestor |
| `scroll` on an element (the document's `scroll` does reach `window`) | Capture on `document`, or listen on the element |
| `invalid` on form controls | Capture on the `<form>` |

```javascript
// Catch every broken image on the page with one listener
document.addEventListener("error", (e) => {
  if (e.target instanceof HTMLImageElement) {
    e.target.src = "/img/placeholder.svg";
  }
}, { capture: true });      // required: "error" does not bubble
```

**Shadow DOM and `composed`.** Events that cross a Web Component's shadow boundary are **retargeted**: listeners outside the component see the host element as `target`, hiding the internal structure. Custom events only cross the boundary if created with `composed: true`.

**Key Takeaways**

- Events travel in three phases: capture (window down to the target's parent), target, and bubble (back up to window).
- Listeners default to the bubble phase. Pass `{ capture: true }` to run during capture.
- At the target, capturing listeners run before non-capturing ones.
- Bubbling enables ancestors to handle events from many descendants. Capturing lets ancestors act before descendants.
- Some events do not bubble (`focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter`, element `load` and `error`). Use their bubbling variants or capture-phase listeners.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Reproduce the form/button/span example and predict the log order before clicking. Then remove the capture listeners and predict again.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a nested comment thread where clicking a comment highlights it, but clicking a reply nested inside must highlight only the reply. Solve it once with `stopPropagation` and once by checking `event.target.closest(".comment") === event.currentTarget`, then compare.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Describe the path of a click event on a deeply nested element. When would you use a capture-phase listener?" *Hint:* name the three phases and give an example where an ancestor must see the event before any child can stop it.

#### preventDefault and stopPropagation

Events do two independent things after your listeners run. The browser may perform a **default action** (a link navigates, a form submits, a checkbox toggles), and the event **propagates** to other elements. Two methods control these separately. They are often confused, and calling the wrong one, or both by habit, is a common source of bugs.

**Default actions.** Many events trigger built-in behaviour:

| Event | Default action |
|---|---|
| `click` on `<a href>` | Navigate to the URL |
| `submit` on `<form>` | Send the form and load the response page |
| `click` on a checkbox or radio | Toggle its checked state |
| `keydown` (Space, arrows, Page Down) | Scroll the page |
| `keydown` in a text field | Insert the character |
| `wheel`, `touchmove` | Scroll or zoom |
| `contextmenu` | Open the browser context menu |
| `dragstart` on an image or link | Start a native drag |

**`preventDefault()` cancels the default action** but does not stop the event travelling. Other listeners still run.

```javascript
// Single-page application: handle navigation in JavaScript (6.4)
document.querySelector("nav").addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const link = event.target.closest("a[href^='/']");
  if (!link) return;
  event.preventDefault();                 // do not load a new page
  router.navigate(link.pathname);
});

// Submit a form with fetch instead of a page load (5.4)
form.addEventListener("submit", async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const response = await fetch(form.action, { method: "POST", body: new FormData(form) });
  showResult(await response.json());
});

// Restrict a field to digits
digitsInput.addEventListener("beforeinput", (event) => {
  if (event.data && /\D/.test(event.data)) event.preventDefault();   // block non-digit insertions
});
```

`preventDefault()` only works if `event.cancelable` is `true`, and it is ignored in passive listeners. Other listeners can detect that it was called through `event.defaultPrevented`, which is a cooperative way for components to say "I handled this".

**`return false`.** In an `on*` property or attribute handler, returning `false` is equivalent to `preventDefault()`. In `addEventListener` listeners, the return value is **ignored**. (In jQuery, Chapter 8, `return false` means both `preventDefault()` and `stopPropagation()`, which adds to the confusion.)

**`stopPropagation()` stops the journey** through the tree. Listeners on later elements in the path do not run. Listeners on the **current** element still run, and the default action still happens.

**`stopImmediatePropagation()`** also prevents the remaining listeners on the current element from running.

```javascript
const card = document.querySelector(".card");
const like = card.querySelector(".like");

card.addEventListener("click", () => openDetails(card));   // clicking a card opens it

like.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  event.stopPropagation();                // the like button must not also open the card
  toggleLike(card);
});
```

**Summary of effects.**

| Call | Default action | Other listeners on the same element | Listeners on later elements in the path |
|---|---|---|---|
| (nothing) | Happens | Run | Run |
| `preventDefault()` | **Cancelled** | Run | Run |
| `stopPropagation()` | Happens | Run | **Skipped** |
| `stopImmediatePropagation()` | Happens | **Skipped** | **Skipped** |

**Why to be careful with `stopPropagation`.** Stopping propagation makes the event invisible to everything above, including code you do not know about: analytics, "click outside to close" logic, accessibility tools, other components using delegation. A dropdown that closes on outside clicks breaks as soon as any child stops propagation. Before using it, consider the alternatives:

```javascript
// Alternative 1: the ancestor checks where the click came from
card.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  if (event.target.closest(".like, a, button")) return;   // let interactive children handle it
  openDetails(card);
});

// Alternative 2: the child marks the event as handled, the ancestor respects it
like.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();          // or set a flag on a WeakSet of handled events
  toggleLike(card);
});
card.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  if (event.defaultPrevented) return;
  openDetails(card);
});
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `preventDefault()` cancels the browser's default action (navigation, submission, scrolling, toggling) but does not stop propagation.
- `stopPropagation()` stops the event from reaching further elements in the path, but listeners on the current element still run and the default action still happens.
- `stopImmediatePropagation()` also skips the remaining listeners on the current element.
- `return false` only cancels the default action in `on*` handlers. It does nothing in `addEventListener` listeners.
- Use `stopPropagation` sparingly. Checking `event.target` or `event.defaultPrevented` keeps events visible to other code.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a link and a form. Prevent the link from navigating and log its `href` instead, and prevent the form from submitting and log its data with `new FormData(form)`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a card component with a "Delete" button inside it. Clicking the card selects it, and clicking "Delete" removes it without selecting it. Implement it without `stopPropagation`, and add a document-level "click outside deselects" handler that keeps working.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `preventDefault`, `stopPropagation` and `return false`?" *Hint:* separate "what the browser does" from "who else hears about the event", and remember that the answer for `return false` depends on how the handler was registered.

#### Event Delegation

Imagine a list of 5,000 table rows, each with "Edit" and "Delete" buttons, where rows are added and removed as the user works. Attaching two listeners to every button means 10,000 function registrations, extra memory, and code that must remember to attach listeners whenever a row is created and remove them when it is deleted. **Event delegation** solves this with one listener on a common ancestor, relying on bubbling: since clicks on any button bubble up to the table, the table can handle them all and work out which button was clicked.

An analogy is a company switchboard: instead of every employee having an outside line, all calls arrive at one number and the operator routes each one according to the extension requested.

**The basic pattern.**

1. Attach one listener to a stable container that exists for the lifetime of the items.
2. In the listener, find the relevant element with `event.target.closest(selector)`.
3. Ignore events that do not come from a matching element, or whose match is outside the container.

```html
<table id="users">
  <tbody>
    <tr data-id="17">
      <td>Ada Lovelace</td>
      <td>
        <button type="button" data-action="edit"><svg>...</svg> Edit</button>
        <button type="button" data-action="delete">Delete</button>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <!-- ...thousands more rows, added and removed dynamically... -->
  </tbody>
</table>
```

```javascript
const table = document.getElementById("users");

const actions = {
  edit(row)   { openEditor(row.dataset.id); },
  delete(row) { if (confirm("Delete user?")) row.remove(); },
};

table.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest("button[data-action]");  // the <svg> inside also works
  if (!button || !table.contains(button)) return;               // click was elsewhere

  const row = button.closest("tr");
  actions[button.dataset.action]?.(row);                        // dispatch by data-action
});
```

New rows work immediately, without any extra code, because the listener is on the table, not on the rows.

**Why `closest` and not `target`.** `event.target` is the innermost element clicked, such as an `<svg>` icon or a `<span>` inside a button. Checking `event.target.matches("button")` fails in those cases. `closest` walks up from the target to the nearest matching ancestor, so it handles any internal structure.

**Why the `contains` check.** `closest` can walk **beyond** the container. If the whole table were inside a `<button>` (an unusual case), or if the selector were generic (`"div"`), the match could be an ancestor of the container. Checking `container.contains(match)` makes the delegation robust.

**Benefits.**

| Aspect | One listener per item | Delegation |
|---|---|---|
| Listeners registered | One per item (thousands) | One |
| Items added later | Must attach listeners each time | Handled automatically |
| Items removed | Must remove listeners to avoid leaks | Nothing to do |
| Initial render cost | Higher | Lower |
| Code location | Spread across render code | Centralised |

**Limitations and solutions.**

- **Non-bubbling events.** `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter` and `mouseleave` do not bubble. Delegate with `focusin`, `focusout`, `mouseover` and `mouseout`, or use a capture-phase listener.
- **`stopPropagation` in children** prevents the event from reaching the delegate. This is one more reason to avoid it.
- **Very frequent events** such as `mousemove` and `pointermove` can be delegated, but the listener runs for every movement over the whole container. Keep the matching logic cheap.
- **Over-delegation.** Putting every handler for the whole application on `document` makes the code hard to follow and runs every listener for every click. Delegate to the nearest stable container of the component.

**Delegation with `mouseover` and `mouseout`.** Hover effects with delegation need care, because `mouseover` fires again each time the pointer moves between children of the same item. Compare `relatedTarget` (the element the pointer came from or goes to) to detect real entry and exit:

```javascript
list.addEventListener("mouseover", (e) => {
  const item = e.target.closest("li");
  if (!item || item.contains(e.relatedTarget)) return;  // moving inside the same item
  showPreview(item);
});
```

Delegation is also how frameworks handle events. React (Chapter 14), for example, attaches its listeners to the root container and dispatches internally to the right component's handler.

**Key Takeaways**

- Event delegation uses one listener on a container to handle events from many descendants, relying on bubbling.
- Use `event.target.closest(selector)` to find the relevant element, and `container.contains(match)` to confirm it belongs to the container.
- Delegation automatically handles elements added later and needs no cleanup when they are removed.
- Use `data-action`-style attributes to route events to handlers.
- Non-bubbling events need their bubbling counterparts (`focusin`, `mouseover`) or capture-phase listeners.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a to-do list where each item has "Done" and "Remove" buttons, handled by a single listener on the `<ul>`. Add new items dynamically and confirm the buttons work without new listeners.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a form-validation module that uses one `focusout` listener on the `<form>` to validate whichever field lost focus, and one `input` listener to clear the error message on the field being edited. Fields can be added dynamically.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is event delegation, and what are its limitations?" *Hint:* explain which event-system feature makes it possible, then think about events that do not follow that feature and about code that stops it.

#### Mouse, Keyboard, Pointer and Touch Events

Input devices differ widely: a mouse has buttons and hovers, a keyboard produces keys and characters, a touchscreen has several fingers and no hover, and a pen has pressure and tilt. The web platform added an event family for each device over the years: mouse events in the 1990s, touch events with the iPhone, and **pointer events** as a unified model. Knowing which to use, and which coordinates and key properties to read, avoids the most common input bugs.

**Mouse events.**

| Event | Fires when | Bubbles |
|---|---|---|
| `mousedown`, `mouseup` | A button is pressed or released | Yes |
| `click` | Primary button pressed and released on the same element (also triggered by keyboard activation of buttons and links) | Yes |
| `dblclick` | Two clicks in quick succession | Yes |
| `auxclick` | Non-primary button click (middle button) | Yes |
| `contextmenu` | Right click or context-menu key | Yes |
| `mousemove` | Pointer moves over the element | Yes |
| `mouseover`, `mouseout` | Pointer enters or leaves the element **or any child** | Yes |
| `mouseenter`, `mouseleave` | Pointer enters or leaves the element itself | No |
| `wheel` | Wheel or trackpad scroll gesture | Yes |

For one click, the order is `mousedown`, `mouseup`, `click` (and for a double click, two of those sequences followed by `dblclick`). `event.button` identifies which button changed (`0` primary, `1` middle, `2` secondary). `event.buttons` is a bit mask of all buttons **currently held** (`1` primary, `2` secondary, `4` middle), which is useful during `mousemove`.

**Coordinate systems.** Mouse and pointer events provide several sets of coordinates:

| Properties | Relative to | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `clientX`, `clientY` | Viewport | Comparing with `getBoundingClientRect()`, `position: fixed` |
| `pageX`, `pageY` | Whole document (client + scroll) | Absolute positioning in the document |
| `offsetX`, `offsetY` | Padding box of the **target** element | Quick local position (unreliable when the target is a child) |
| `screenX`, `screenY` | Physical screen | Rarely needed |

```javascript
// Position relative to a canvas, robust even if the click lands on a child element
canvas.addEventListener("pointerdown", (e) => {
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
  const y = e.clientY - rect.top;
  drawDot(x, y);
});
```

**Keyboard events.** Use `keydown` and `keyup` (the old `keypress` event is deprecated). Keyboard events go to the **focused element** (or `<body>` if nothing is focused).

| Property | Meaning | Example (US layout, Shift+A) | Example (French AZERTY, "A" key) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `key` | The **character or meaning** produced, depends on layout and modifiers | `"A"` | `"a"` |
| `code` | The **physical key** position, independent of layout | `"KeyA"` | `"KeyQ"` |
| `repeat` | `true` when auto-repeating because the key is held | | |
| `ctrlKey`, `shiftKey`, `altKey`, `metaKey` | Modifier state | | |
| `isComposing` | `true` during IME composition (Chinese, Japanese, Korean input) | | |

Use `key` for shortcuts tied to meaning ("Ctrl+S", "Escape", "Enter", "ArrowLeft"). Use `code` for position-based controls such as WASD movement in a game, which should work on any layout.

```javascript
document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
  if (e.isComposing) return;                     // the user is composing text with an IME
  if (e.target.closest("input, textarea, [contenteditable]")) return;  // do not hijack typing

  switch (e.key) {
    case "ArrowRight": nextSlide(); break;
    case "ArrowLeft":  previousSlide(); break;
    case "Escape":     closeOverlay(); break;
    case "?":          showHelp(); break;
  }
});
```

To react to **text changes** in a field, use the `input` event (next topic), not keyboard events. Text can also arrive by paste, drag and drop, autocomplete, voice dictation or an on-screen keyboard, none of which produce reliable key events.

**Pointer events: one model for all devices.** Pointer events mirror mouse events (`pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`, `pointerover`, `pointerout`, `pointerenter`, `pointerleave`) and add `pointercancel`. They work for mouse, pen and touch with the same code, and add device information:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pointerId` | Unique id for this pointer (each finger gets its own) |
| `pointerType` | `"mouse"`, `"pen"` or `"touch"` |
| `isPrimary` | The first finger in a multi-touch gesture, or the mouse |
| `pressure` | 0 to 1 (0.5 for mouse buttons pressed, real values for pens) |
| `width`, `height` | Contact geometry (touch) |
| `tiltX`, `tiltY`, `twist` | Pen orientation |

**Pointer capture.** During a drag, the pointer often moves outside the element faster than the element follows, and events stop arriving. `setPointerCapture` routes all events of that pointer to the element until it is released:

```javascript
const handle = document.querySelector(".slider-handle");
const track = handle.parentElement;

handle.addEventListener("pointerdown", (e) => {
  handle.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);         // receive moves even outside the handle
});

handle.addEventListener("pointermove", (e) => {
  if (!handle.hasPointerCapture(e.pointerId)) return;   // only while dragging
  const rect = track.getBoundingClientRect();
  const ratio = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, (e.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width));
  handle.style.setProperty("--value", ratio);           // CSS positions the handle
});

handle.addEventListener("pointerup", (e) => {
  handle.releasePointerCapture(e.pointerId);     // also released automatically on pointerup
});
```

```css
.slider-handle {
  touch-action: none;   /* tell the browser not to scroll or zoom when dragging this on touch */
}
```

Without `touch-action: none`, a touch drag starts scrolling the page, and the browser fires `pointercancel` and stops sending pointer events to your code.

**Touch events.** `touchstart`, `touchmove`, `touchend` and `touchcancel` predate pointer events and expose lists of touch points (`touches`, `targetTouches`, `changedTouches`). They remain useful for some multi-touch gestures and for code that must support very old browsers. For new code, pointer events are simpler and cover all devices. Browsers also fire compatibility mouse events (`mousedown`, `click`) after touches, so a `click` listener works for taps without touch-specific code.

**Which family to use.**

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Activating a button or link | `click` (works for mouse, touch, keyboard and assistive technology) |
| Drag, draw, swipe, custom sliders | Pointer events, `setPointerCapture`, `touch-action` |
| Hover effects | CSS `:hover`, or `pointerenter`/`pointerleave` |
| Shortcuts and key controls | `keydown` with `key` (or `code` for physical layouts) |
| Text input in fields | `input` and `beforeinput`, not key events |
| Wheel zoom or custom scroll | `wheel` (non-passive only if you must prevent scrolling) |

**Key Takeaways**

- `click` is device-independent (mouse, touch, keyboard), so use it for activation.
- `mouseover`/`mouseout` bubble and fire for children, while `mouseenter`/`mouseleave` do not bubble and fire only for the element.
- `clientX`/`clientY` are viewport coordinates and pair with `getBoundingClientRect()`. `pageX`/`pageY` add the scroll offset.
- Keyboard `key` is the produced character or meaning, and `code` is the physical key. Ignore events during IME composition.
- Pointer events unify mouse, pen and touch. Use `setPointerCapture` for drags and `touch-action` to stop the browser taking over gestures.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a box that logs `clientX`, `pageX`, `offsetX`, `button` and `buttons` on `mousedown` and `mousemove`. Scroll the page and click again, and explain the differences between the coordinate values.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a drawing pad on a `<canvas>` using pointer events that supports mouse, pen (with line width based on `pressure`) and multiple simultaneous fingers, each identified by `pointerId`. Prevent the page from scrolling while drawing.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `event.key` and `event.code`, and which should a game use for WASD movement?" *Hint:* think about users with AZERTY or Dvorak keyboards.

#### Form, Focus and Document Lifecycle Events

Beyond raw input devices, the browser emits higher-level events about **meaning**: a field's value changed, a form was submitted, an element received focus, the DOM is ready, the page is being hidden. These are the events most application logic should be built on, because they already account for the many ways users interact with a page.

**Form events.**

| Event | Target | Fires when | Bubbles |
|---|---|---|---|
| `input` | `<input>`, `<textarea>`, `<select>`, `contenteditable` | The value changes, on every keystroke, paste, drop or autocomplete | Yes |
| `beforeinput` | Same | Just before the value changes. Cancelable, exposes `inputType` and `data` | Yes |
| `change` | Same | The change is **committed**: on blur for text fields, immediately for checkboxes, radios, selects and file inputs | Yes |
| `submit` | `<form>` | The form is submitted (Enter in a field or a submit button) | Yes |
| `reset` | `<form>` | The form is reset | Yes |
| `invalid` | Form controls | A control fails constraint validation during submission or `checkValidity()` | No |

```javascript
const search = document.querySelector("#search");
const email = document.querySelector("#email");

search.addEventListener("input", debounce(() => {      // live search (5.3 covers debounce)
  runSearch(search.value);
}, 300));

email.addEventListener("change", () => {                // validate once the user is done
  email.setCustomValidity(isCompanyEmail(email.value) ? "" : "Use your company email");
  email.reportValidity();
});

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));  // { email: "...", plan: "pro" }
  console.log("submitted by", event.submitter?.name);   // which button
  save(data);
});
```

Listen for `submit` on the **form**, not `click` on the submit button. Pressing Enter in a text field also submits the form, and a click handler would miss it. To submit from JavaScript and still run validation and the `submit` event, call `form.requestSubmit()`. `form.submit()` skips both.

**Focus events.**

| Event | Bubbles | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `focus` | No | Element received focus |
| `blur` | No | Element lost focus |
| `focusin` | Yes | Like `focus`, but bubbles: use for delegation |
| `focusout` | Yes | Like `blur`, but bubbles |

`FocusEvent.relatedTarget` is the element losing focus (for `focus`/`focusin`) or receiving focus (for `blur`/`focusout`). It is how a composite widget, such as a menu or a combobox, knows whether focus moved **outside** the widget or just between its own parts:

```javascript
menu.addEventListener("focusout", (e) => {
  if (!menu.contains(e.relatedTarget)) {   // focus left the menu entirely
    closeMenu();
  }
});
```

Use `el.focus()` to move focus programmatically (for example to the first field of a dialog), and `document.activeElement` to find the currently focused element. The CSS pseudo-class `:focus-visible` shows focus rings for keyboard users without showing them on mouse clicks.

**Document lifecycle events.** A page goes through a series of states, from parsing to unloading. Each transition fires an event:

```text
  navigation starts
        │
        v
  readyState = "loading"        parsing HTML, running classic scripts
        │
        v
  readyState = "interactive"    DOM fully parsed, deferred and module scripts run
        │──> DOMContentLoaded   (on document) DOM ready; images and stylesheets may still load
        v
  readyState = "complete"       all subresources (images, iframes, styles) loaded
        │──> load               (on window)
        v
  ... user interacts ...
        │──> visibilitychange   tab hidden or shown (document.visibilityState)
        │──> pagehide           leaving the page (event.persisted = true if kept in bfcache)
        v
  page restored from back/forward cache
        └──> pageshow           (event.persisted = true)
```

| Event | Target | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `DOMContentLoaded` | `document` | Initialising scripts that need the DOM (unnecessary with `defer` or modules) |
| `load` | `window` | Work that needs images or all resources, such as measuring image sizes |
| `readystatechange` | `document` | Reacting to every `readyState` transition |
| `visibilitychange` | `document` | Pausing video, timers and polling when the tab is hidden; saving state |
| `pagehide`, `pageshow` | `window` | Leaving the page, and returning from the back/forward cache |
| `beforeunload` | `window` | Warning about unsaved changes |

**Saving state reliably.** The `unload` event is deprecated and unreliable (especially on mobile, where pages are often discarded without warning), and its presence prevents the browser from keeping the page in the **back/forward cache (bfcache)**, which makes back navigation instant. The recommended pattern is to save on `visibilitychange` when the page becomes hidden. That is the last event guaranteed to fire on mobile:

```javascript
document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === "hidden") {
    // sendBeacon queues a small POST that survives the page being closed
    navigator.sendBeacon("/analytics", JSON.stringify(collectMetrics()));
    saveDraftToStorage();
  }
});

window.addEventListener("pageshow", (event) => {
  if (event.persisted) refreshStaleData();   // restored from bfcache: JS state is intact but old
});
```

**Warning about unsaved changes.** Browsers show a generic confirmation dialog (custom messages are ignored) when a `beforeunload` listener cancels the event, and only if the user has interacted with the page. Add the listener only while there are unsaved changes:

```javascript
function onBeforeUnload(event) {
  event.preventDefault();      // standard way to request the confirmation dialog
  event.returnValue = "";      // legacy requirement for some browsers
}

editor.addEventListener("input", () => window.addEventListener("beforeunload", onBeforeUnload));
saveButton.addEventListener("click", () => window.removeEventListener("beforeunload", onBeforeUnload));
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `input` fires on every value change from any source. `change` fires when a change is committed. `beforeinput` can cancel a change before it happens.
- Handle `submit` on the form, call `preventDefault()` for JavaScript submission, and use `requestSubmit()` to submit programmatically with validation.
- `focus` and `blur` do not bubble. `focusin` and `focusout` do, and `relatedTarget` tells you where focus came from or went.
- `DOMContentLoaded` means the DOM is parsed, and `load` means every resource is loaded.
- Save state on `visibilitychange` (hidden), avoid `unload`, handle bfcache restores with `pageshow`, and add `beforeunload` only while there are unsaved changes.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Attach `input` and `change` listeners to a text field, a checkbox and a `<select>`, logging each event. Describe exactly when each one fires for each control.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a note editor that saves a draft to `localStorage` whenever the tab is hidden, restores it on load, and warns about unsaved changes on navigation only when the current text differs from the last saved version.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `DOMContentLoaded` and `load`, and why is `unload` discouraged?" *Hint:* consider which resources each event waits for, and how the back/forward cache and mobile tab discarding behave.

#### Custom Events and Event Dispatching

The browser is not the only source of events. Your own components can announce what happens inside them, such as "item added to cart", "filter changed" or "upload finished", using the same mechanism as built-in events. Other parts of the application listen without the component knowing who they are. This decouples the code: the cart widget does not import the header badge or the analytics module, it just announces the change, and anyone interested listens. It is the *publish/subscribe* (observer) pattern, implemented by the platform.

**Creating and dispatching a `CustomEvent`.** `CustomEvent` adds a `detail` property for your own data:

```javascript
// Inside the cart component
function addToCart(product) {
  cart.items.push(product);

  const event = new CustomEvent("cart:add", {
    detail: { product, count: cart.items.length },  // any data
    bubbles: true,       // default false: set true so ancestors and delegates can listen
    cancelable: true,    // allow listeners to veto with preventDefault()
    composed: false,     // true to cross shadow DOM boundaries
  });

  const allowed = cartElement.dispatchEvent(event);   // false if a listener called preventDefault()
  if (!allowed) {
    cart.items.pop();    // a listener vetoed the action
  }
}

// Anywhere else, e.g. the header badge
document.addEventListener("cart:add", (event) => {
  badge.textContent = event.detail.count;
});

// A rule that can veto the action
document.addEventListener("cart:add", (event) => {
  if (event.detail.count > 10) {
    event.preventDefault();
    alert("Maximum 10 items");
  }
});
```

**Dispatch is synchronous.** Unlike events from the browser, which are queued as tasks, `dispatchEvent` calls all listeners **immediately** and returns only when they have all finished. This is why the return value can report whether one of them called `preventDefault()`:

```javascript
console.log("before");
el.addEventListener("ping", () => console.log("listener"));
el.dispatchEvent(new Event("ping"));
console.log("after");
// before, listener, after: no event loop involved
```

An exception thrown in a listener does not stop the other listeners or reach the code that called `dispatchEvent`. It is reported as an uncaught error instead.

**Naming conventions.** Event names are case-sensitive strings. Use lowercase names with a namespace prefix to avoid collisions with built-in and third-party events, for example `cart:add`, `cart:remove` or `filters-change`. Do not reuse built-in names such as `change` for custom meaning, since other code expects their standard behaviour.

**Simulating built-in events.** You can construct built-in event types (`new MouseEvent("click", {...})`, `new KeyboardEvent("keydown", {...})`), but dispatching them generally does **not** perform default actions. A synthetic `keydown` does not type a character or scroll the page, and a synthetic `submit` event does not submit the form. The notable exception is `click`: dispatching a `MouseEvent("click")` runs the element's activation behaviour (a link navigates, a checkbox toggles). Synthetic events are marked `isTrusted: false`, so privileged actions that require user activation still fail. To trigger the real behaviour, call the corresponding method:

| Goal | Use |
|---|---|
| Activate a button or link like a user click | `el.click()` (dispatches a `click` and runs its activation behaviour) |
| Focus an element | `el.focus()` |
| Submit a form with validation and the `submit` event | `form.requestSubmit()` |
| Notify listeners that a value was changed by script | `el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", { bubbles: true }))` |

The last row is common in test code and integrations. Setting `input.value` from script does **not** fire `input` or `change`, so frameworks listening to those events will not notice unless you dispatch one.

**Events on your own objects: extending `EventTarget`.** Any class can become an event source by extending `EventTarget`, without needing a DOM element:

```javascript
class Store extends EventTarget {
  #state;
  constructor(initial) {
    super();
    this.#state = initial;
  }
  get state() {
    return this.#state;
  }
  set(patch) {
    const previous = this.#state;
    this.#state = { ...previous, ...patch };
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("change", {
      detail: { previous, current: this.#state },
    }));
  }
}

const store = new Store({ theme: "light", user: null });

store.addEventListener("change", ({ detail }) => {
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = detail.current.theme;
});

store.set({ theme: "dark" });   // listeners run synchronously
```

This tiny store already supports multiple subscribers, `once`, and removal with an `AbortSignal`, because it inherits the whole `addEventListener` machinery. It is the core idea behind many state-management libraries (14.4).

**Key Takeaways**

- `new CustomEvent(type, { detail, bubbles, cancelable, composed })` creates an event carrying your own data in `detail`.
- `dispatchEvent` runs listeners synchronously and returns `false` if a cancelable event was cancelled with `preventDefault()`.
- Custom events are not bubbling by default. Set `bubbles: true` so ancestors and delegates can hear them, and `composed: true` to cross shadow roots.
- Synthetic built-in events have `isTrusted: false` and mostly do not trigger default actions (`click` is the exception). Use `click()`, `focus()` and `requestSubmit()` to trigger real behaviour.
- Any class can extend `EventTarget` to become a lightweight, standard event emitter.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a "Like" button component that dispatches a bubbling `like:toggle` event with `{ id, liked }` in `detail`, and a listener on `document` that updates a total counter.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a `Timer` class extending `EventTarget` that emits `tick` (every second, with the remaining time), `pause` and `done` events. Build a UI that subscribes to it, and use an `AbortController` to unsubscribe the UI when it is closed.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does dispatching a custom event differ from a browser-generated event in terms of timing and trust?" *Hint:* consider when listeners run relative to the `dispatchEvent` call, what `isTrusted` reports, and whether default actions run.

<a id="64-other-browser-capabilities"></a>
### 6.4 Other Browser Capabilities

This subchapter surveys the browser APIs that turn a document into an application: storing data on the client, managing URLs without reloading, accessing device features, running code in the background and observing visibility and size changes efficiently.

#### Web Storage: localStorage and sessionStorage

HTTP is stateless (Chapter 10), and a page's JavaScript variables disappear when the page is reloaded or closed. Many small pieces of state should survive that: the user's theme, a half-written comment, the last-selected tab, a dismissed banner. Before 2009 the only client-side option was **cookies**, which are tiny (about 4 KB), awkward to use from JavaScript, and **sent to the server with every request**, wasting bandwidth on data the server never needs. The **Web Storage** API provides two simple key-value stores that stay in the browser.

**The API.** `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` share the same interface (`Storage`):

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
localStorage.getItem("theme");           // "dark"
localStorage.getItem("missing");         // null (not undefined)
localStorage.removeItem("theme");
localStorage.clear();                    // remove everything for this origin
localStorage.length;                     // number of keys
localStorage.key(0);                     // name of the first key (order not guaranteed)
```

**Strings only.** Keys and values are always strings. Other values are converted with `String()`, which silently corrupts objects:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("count", 5);
typeof localStorage.getItem("count");    // "string": "5"

localStorage.setItem("user", { name: "Ada" });
localStorage.getItem("user");            // "[object Object]": data lost

// Serialise structured data with JSON (4.1)
localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify({ name: "Ada", visits: 3 }));
const user = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user") ?? "null");   // { name: "Ada", visits: 3 }
```

Dates come back as strings, and `Map`, `Set`, `undefined` and functions are not preserved by JSON.

**`localStorage` versus `sessionStorage`.**

| Aspect | `localStorage` | `sessionStorage` |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Until deleted by script, the user or browser storage policies | Until the tab is closed (survives reloads) |
| Scope | Shared by all tabs and windows of the same **origin** | One per tab and origin. A duplicated tab gets a copy |
| Typical use | Preferences, cached data, drafts | Multi-step form progress, per-tab state |

**Origin scoping.** Storage is isolated by **origin** (scheme + host + port). `https://shop.example.com` and `https://blog.example.com` have separate stores, and so do `http://` and `https://` versions of the same site. This is what keeps other sites from reading your data.

**The `storage` event: syncing tabs.** When one tab changes `localStorage`, other tabs of the same origin receive a `storage` event on `window`. The tab that made the change does not receive it.

```javascript
// Log out in every open tab when the user logs out in one
window.addEventListener("storage", (event) => {
  // event.key, event.oldValue, event.newValue, event.url, event.storageArea
  if (event.key === "session" && event.newValue === null) {
    location.assign("/login");
  }
});
```

For richer cross-tab messaging, `BroadcastChannel` sends arbitrary messages between same-origin tabs.

**Limits and failure modes.** Production code must handle storage failures, because storage can be unavailable or full:

- **Quota**: about 5 MB per origin in most browsers (measured in UTF-16 characters, so roughly 2.5 million characters). Exceeding it throws a `QuotaExceededError`.
- **Disabled or restricted**: some privacy settings, embedded iframes with blocked third-party storage, and older private-browsing modes throw on access.
- **Eviction**: browsers may clear storage under disk pressure, and Safari's tracking prevention can delete script-writable storage for sites the user has not visited for a period of days.

```javascript
const storage = {
  get(key, fallback = null) {
    try {
      const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return raw === null ? fallback : JSON.parse(raw);
    } catch {
      return fallback;              // storage blocked or corrupted JSON
    }
  },
  set(key, value) {
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value));
      return true;
    } catch (err) {
      console.warn("Could not save", key, err.name);   // QuotaExceededError, SecurityError
      return false;
    }
  },
};
```

**Synchronous and therefore blocking.** Every `getItem` and `setItem` call blocks the main thread while the browser reads or writes, and the first access may load the whole store from disk. Small values are fine, but storing megabytes of JSON and parsing it on every change causes jank. Use IndexedDB (next topic) for large or structured data.

**Security: never store secrets.** Any JavaScript running on the origin can read Web Storage, including injected scripts in an XSS attack (6.1, Chapter 17). Storing authentication tokens in `localStorage` exposes them to theft. `HttpOnly` cookies, which JavaScript cannot read at all, are safer for session identifiers (Chapter 10).

**Client-side storage options compared.**

| Feature | Cookies | `localStorage` | `sessionStorage` | IndexedDB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Capacity | About 4 KB per cookie | About 5 MB | About 5 MB | Large (a share of free disk space) |
| Sent to the server | With every request | No | No | No |
| API | String parsing (`document.cookie`) | Synchronous key-value | Synchronous key-value | Asynchronous, transactional |
| Data types | Strings | Strings | Strings | Structured clone (objects, Blobs, Dates, Maps) |
| Readable by JS | Unless `HttpOnly` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Available in Workers | No | No | No | Yes |

**Key Takeaways**

- `localStorage` persists per origin across sessions. `sessionStorage` lasts for one tab's session.
- Both store only strings. Serialise with `JSON.stringify` and parse with `JSON.parse`, handling `null` for missing keys.
- The `storage` event notifies other tabs of the same origin about changes.
- The API is synchronous and limited to about 5 MB. Wrap access in `try/catch` and use IndexedDB for large data.
- Web Storage is readable by any script on the origin. Never store secrets or session tokens in it.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Save the content of a `<textarea>` to `localStorage` on every `input` event and restore it when the page loads. Then switch to `sessionStorage` and compare the behaviour when closing and reopening the tab.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a theme switcher that stores the choice in `localStorage` and updates every open tab instantly via the `storage` event. Make it work when storage is disabled, falling back to the operating system's `prefers-color-scheme`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Where would you store a JWT access token in a browser application, and why not `localStorage`?" *Hint:* consider which code can read each storage mechanism, and what an XSS vulnerability would allow an attacker to do.

#### IndexedDB Basics

Some applications need much more than a few preferences: an email client that works offline, a note-taking app with thousands of notes, a photo editor that keeps images between sessions, a cache of API responses. These need a lot of space, queries by fields other than the key, binary data, and an API that does not block the main thread. **IndexedDB** is the browser's built-in transactional database for this. It is a **NoSQL object store**: you store JavaScript objects (not rows and columns), retrieve them by key, and query them through indexes.

**Concepts.**

```text
Origin (https://notes.example.com)
└── Database "notes-app"  (version 2)
    ├── Object store "notes"         keyPath: "id", autoIncrement
    │   ├── records: { id: 1, title: "Ideas", tags: ["work"], updated: Date, ... }
    │   ├── index "by-updated"        on field "updated"
    │   └── index "by-tag"            on field "tags" (multiEntry: one entry per tag)
    └── Object store "attachments"   key: provided explicitly
        └── records: Blob, File, ArrayBuffer...
```

| Concept | Meaning | Relational analogy |
|---|---|---|
| Database | Named container per origin, with an integer **version** | Database |
| Object store | Collection of records with unique keys | Table |
| Key / `keyPath` | How each record is identified (a property path, or an explicit key, optionally auto-incremented) | Primary key |
| Index | Lookup structure on a field of the records | Secondary index |
| Transaction | Group of operations that succeed or fail together, `readonly` or `readwrite` | Transaction |
| Cursor | Iterator over a range of records | Cursor |

Values are copied with the **structured clone algorithm**, which supports objects, arrays, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `Blob`, `File`, `ArrayBuffer` and typed arrays, but not functions or DOM nodes.

**Opening a database and defining its schema.** The schema can only change inside the `upgradeneeded` event, which fires when the database is created or when you open it with a higher version number:

```javascript
function openDatabase() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const request = indexedDB.open("notes-app", 2);   // name, version

    request.onupgradeneeded = (event) => {
      const db = request.result;
      // event.oldVersion tells you which migrations to run (0 = brand-new database)
      if (event.oldVersion < 1) {
        const notes = db.createObjectStore("notes", { keyPath: "id", autoIncrement: true });
        notes.createIndex("by-updated", "updated");
      }
      if (event.oldVersion < 2) {
        const notes = request.transaction.objectStore("notes");
        notes.createIndex("by-tag", "tags", { multiEntry: true });   // added in version 2
      }
    };

    request.onsuccess = () => resolve(request.result);
    request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
    request.onblocked = () => console.warn("Close other tabs to upgrade the database");
  });
}
```

**Reading and writing.** Every operation happens inside a transaction and returns an `IDBRequest` with `success` and `error` events. The original API predates promises (Chapter 5), so a small helper makes it pleasant to use:

```javascript
// Convert an IDBRequest into a promise
const promisify = (request) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    request.onsuccess = () => resolve(request.result);
    request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
  });

const db = await openDatabase();

// Write: a readwrite transaction on one store
async function saveNote(note) {
  const tx = db.transaction("notes", "readwrite");
  const id = await promisify(tx.objectStore("notes").put({ ...note, updated: new Date() }));
  // put = insert or replace; add = insert only (fails if the key exists)
  return id;
}

// Read by primary key
async function getNote(id) {
  const tx = db.transaction("notes", "readonly");
  return promisify(tx.objectStore("notes").get(id));    // undefined if not found
}

// Query an index: all notes tagged "work"
async function notesWithTag(tag) {
  const index = db.transaction("notes").objectStore("notes").index("by-tag");
  return promisify(index.getAll(tag));
}

// Range query with a cursor: the 10 most recently updated notes
async function recentNotes(limit = 10) {
  const index = db.transaction("notes").objectStore("notes").index("by-updated");
  const results = [];
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const request = index.openCursor(null, "prev");      // newest first
    request.onsuccess = () => {
      const cursor = request.result;
      if (!cursor || results.length === limit) return resolve(results);
      results.push(cursor.value);
      cursor.continue();                                 // fires onsuccess again
    };
    request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
  });
}
```

`IDBKeyRange` expresses ranges: `IDBKeyRange.bound(a, b)`, `lowerBound(a)`, `upperBound(b)` and `only(x)`. These can be passed to `getAll` or `openCursor`.

**The transaction auto-commit trap.** A transaction commits automatically as soon as it has no pending requests and control returns to the event loop. If you `await` something unrelated (such as a `fetch`) in the middle of a transaction, it has already committed by the time you continue, and further requests throw `TransactionInactiveError`:

```javascript
const tx = db.transaction("notes", "readwrite");
const store = tx.objectStore("notes");
const note = await promisify(store.get(1));          // OK: an IndexedDB request
const extra = await fetch("/api/enrich").then((r) => r.json());   // tx commits here!
store.put({ ...note, ...extra });                    // TransactionInactiveError

// Fix: do the network work first, then open a transaction for the database work only
```

**Libraries.** Because the raw API is verbose, most projects use a thin wrapper. `idb` (by Jake Archibald) adds promises with almost no abstraction, while Dexie offers a higher-level query API.

**Storage quotas and persistence.** IndexedDB can store a large share of free disk space, but the browser may evict it under storage pressure ("best-effort" storage). An application can check usage and ask for persistent storage:

```javascript
const { usage, quota } = await navigator.storage.estimate();
console.log(`${(usage / 1e6).toFixed(1)} MB of ${(quota / 1e6).toFixed(0)} MB used`);

const persisted = await navigator.storage.persist();   // true if the browser grants it
```

IndexedDB is also available in Web Workers and service workers, which makes it the standard storage for offline-capable Progressive Web Apps (Chapter 15).

**Key Takeaways**

- IndexedDB is an asynchronous, transactional object database per origin, suitable for large and structured data, including binary data.
- Databases contain object stores (collections keyed by a `keyPath` or explicit key) and indexes on record fields.
- Schema changes happen only in `upgradeneeded`, triggered by opening with a higher version. Use `oldVersion` to run migrations.
- Every operation runs in a transaction and returns a request. Wrap requests in promises or use a library such as `idb`.
- Transactions auto-commit when idle. Never `await` unrelated asynchronous work inside one.
- Use `navigator.storage.estimate()` and `persist()` to monitor quota and request durable storage.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a database with a `contacts` store (`keyPath: "email"`). Add three contacts, read one by key, and inspect the result in the DevTools Application panel.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build an offline-capable notes list that stores notes in IndexedDB with an index on `updated`, shows them newest first, supports tag search through a `multiEntry` index, and migrates from version 1 to version 2 by adding the tag index without losing data.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose IndexedDB over `localStorage`?" *Hint:* compare data size, data types, blocking behaviour, querying needs and availability in workers.

#### History API and Client-Side Routing

In a traditional website, every link click loads a whole new HTML page from the server. A **single-page application (SPA)** loads one page and replaces its content with JavaScript, which is faster and allows smooth transitions. But if the URL never changes, the app breaks basic web expectations: the Back button leaves the app entirely, refreshing loses your place, and you cannot bookmark or share a link to a specific view. The **History API** lets JavaScript change the URL and add entries to the session history **without loading a new page**, so an SPA can behave like a set of real pages. Code that maps URLs to views is called a **client-side router**.

**The session history.** Each tab keeps a stack of visited entries, with a pointer to the current one. `history.back()`, `history.forward()` and `history.go(n)` move the pointer, exactly like the browser buttons.

**`pushState` and `replaceState`.**

```javascript
history.pushState(state, "", url);      // ADD a new entry after the current one and make it current
history.replaceState(state, "", url);   // REPLACE the current entry
history.state;                          // the state object of the current entry
```

- `state`: any structured-cloneable data associated with the entry (for example, a scroll position or the id of an open item). It is returned to you later.
- The second parameter is unused (historically a title). Pass `""`.
- `url`: the new URL, which must be **same-origin**. It can be relative (`"/products/42"`, `"?page=2"`, `"#reviews"`).

Neither method loads anything or fires an event. The address bar changes and that is all, so your code must render the new view itself.

```text
Session history after: load /, pushState /products, pushState /products/42, back()

  [ / ] [ /products ] [ /products/42 ]
               ^ current          (forward entry still available)

pushState("/cart") from here discards the forward entries:

  [ / ] [ /products ] [ /cart ]
                          ^ current
```

**`popstate`: responding to Back and Forward.** When the user navigates between entries created by `pushState` (with the Back or Forward buttons or `history.back()`), the page is not reloaded. Instead, `window` receives a `popstate` event with the entry's `state`. `pushState` and `replaceState` do **not** fire `popstate`.

**A minimal router.**

```javascript
const routes = [
  { pattern: new URLPattern({ pathname: "/" }),              view: renderHome },
  { pattern: new URLPattern({ pathname: "/products/:id" }),  view: renderProduct },
  { pattern: new URLPattern({ pathname: "/cart" }),          view: renderCart },
];
// URLPattern is a recent built-in; a regular expression per route works everywhere.

function render(url) {
  for (const { pattern, view } of routes) {
    const match = pattern.exec(url);
    if (match) {
      view(match.pathname.groups);        // e.g. { id: "42" }
      return;
    }
  }
  renderNotFound();
}

function navigate(url) {
  history.pushState({}, "", url);         // 1. update the URL and history
  render(location.href);                  // 2. render the new view ourselves
}

// Intercept clicks on internal links with event delegation (6.3)
document.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const link = event.target.closest("a[href]");
  if (
    !link ||
    link.origin !== location.origin ||    // external link: let the browser handle it
    link.target === "_blank" ||
    link.hasAttribute("download") ||
    event.button !== 0 ||                 // middle click opens a new tab
    event.metaKey || event.ctrlKey || event.shiftKey || event.altKey
  ) return;

  event.preventDefault();
  navigate(link.href);
});

window.addEventListener("popstate", () => render(location.href));   // Back / Forward
render(location.href);                                              // initial page load
```

**Hash-based routing.** Older SPAs used URLs such as `/#/products/42`. Changing `location.hash` never reloads the page, and the `hashchange` event fires on every change. It needs no server configuration, but the URLs are less clean and the fragment is not sent to the server, which matters for server rendering and analytics.

**The server must cooperate.** With path-based routing, a user can reload or open `https://shop.example.com/products/42` directly. The browser then requests that path from the server, which must return the SPA's `index.html` (a *fallback* route) instead of a 404. Express (Chapter 12), static hosts and CDNs all provide a setting for this.

**Responsibilities a router takes on.** Because no real navigation happens, the browser no longer does several things for you:

| Concern | What the router must do |
|---|---|
| Page title | Update `document.title` for each view |
| Scroll position | Scroll to top on new navigation, and restore the position on Back (`history.scrollRestoration = "manual"` lets you take full control) |
| Focus and accessibility | Move focus to the new main heading or content, and announce the change for screen-reader users |
| Loading and errors | Show progress, and handle data that fails to load |
| Pending work | Cancel fetches for the previous view (`AbortController`, 5.3) |

**The Navigation API.** A newer API, `window.navigation`, centralises all of this. A single `navigate` event fires for link clicks, form submissions, Back/Forward and programmatic navigations, and `event.intercept({ handler })` converts it into a same-document navigation:

```javascript
navigation.addEventListener("navigate", (event) => {
  if (!event.canIntercept || event.hashChange || event.downloadRequest) return;
```
