```javascript
  const url = new URL(event.destination.url);
  if (url.origin !== location.origin) return;

  event.intercept({
    async handler() {
      await render(url.href);   // the browser handles the URL, focus and scroll restoration
    },
  });
});
```

It removes the need for click interception and `popstate` handling. Chromium shipped it first and other engines have been adding it, so check support and keep a History API fallback where needed.

**Key Takeaways**

- `history.pushState` and `replaceState` change the URL and session history without loading a page or firing events. Your code must render the new view.
- `popstate` fires when the user moves between history entries with Back and Forward. It does not fire for `pushState`.
- A client-side router intercepts internal link clicks, calls `pushState`, renders the matching view and re-renders on `popstate`.
- The server must return the application's HTML for every client-side route so that reloads and deep links work.
- A router must handle titles, scroll, focus and cancellation that the browser normally manages. The Navigation API simplifies this where supported.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a page with three buttons that call `pushState` with different URLs and states, and a `popstate` listener that displays `history.state`. Use the Back and Forward buttons and observe the URL and the displayed state.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a small SPA with home, product list, product detail (`/products/:id`) and 404 views, using the router pattern above. Update `document.title`, move focus to each view's `<h1>`, and restore scroll positions when going back. Serve it with a fallback route so that reloading a deep link works.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does a client-side router work, and what breaks if the server is not configured for it?" *Hint:* trace a link click, a Back button press and a page reload on a deep URL separately.

#### Geolocation, Notifications and Clipboard

Some browser APIs reach beyond the page: the device's location, the operating system's notification centre, the system clipboard. Because these can expose private data or be used to annoy users, they share a common security model. They are only available in **secure contexts** (HTTPS or `localhost`), many require the user's **permission**, and some only work in response to a **user gesture** such as a click. Learning that model once makes every device API easier to use.

**The permission model.**

```text
  page calls the API ──> secure context? ──no──> API missing or rejects
                               │ yes
                               v
                  permission state for this origin?
             ┌────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────┐
          "granted"     "prompt"       "denied"
             │              │              │
          proceed     browser asks     fails immediately
                      the user         (the user must change site settings)
```

The **Permissions API** lets you check the current state without triggering a prompt, so you can explain why you need a permission before asking:

```javascript
const status = await navigator.permissions.query({ name: "geolocation" });
console.log(status.state);                            // "granted", "prompt" or "denied"
status.addEventListener("change", () => console.log("now", status.state));
```

**Geolocation.** `navigator.geolocation` gives the device's position from GPS, Wi-Fi, cell towers or IP address. The API uses callbacks:

```javascript
navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(
  (position) => {
    const { latitude, longitude, accuracy } = position.coords;   // accuracy in metres
    showOnMap(latitude, longitude, accuracy);
  },
  (error) => {
    // error.code: 1 PERMISSION_DENIED, 2 POSITION_UNAVAILABLE, 3 TIMEOUT
    showMessage(error.code === error.PERMISSION_DENIED
      ? "Location access was denied. Enter your city instead."
      : "Could not determine your location.");
  },
  {
    enableHighAccuracy: false,  // true uses GPS: slower and uses more battery
    timeout: 10_000,            // give up after 10 seconds
    maximumAge: 60_000,         // accept a cached position up to 1 minute old
  }
);

// Continuous tracking (navigation, fitness apps)
const watchId = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(updateMarker, handleError);
navigator.geolocation.clearWatch(watchId);   // stop tracking
```

Promisifying it (5.2) makes it fit into `async` code:

```javascript
const getPosition = (options) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(resolve, reject, options));

const { coords } = await getPosition({ timeout: 10_000 });
```

**Notifications.** The Notifications API displays system notifications outside the page. Permission must be requested with `Notification.requestPermission()`, and browsers ignore or silently block requests that are not triggered by a user gesture:

```javascript
enableAlertsButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  if (!("Notification" in window)) return;

  const permission = await Notification.requestPermission();   // "granted", "denied", "default"
  if (permission !== "granted") return;

  const notification = new Notification("Order shipped", {
    body: "Your order #1042 is on its way.",
    icon: "/img/logo-192.png",
    tag: "order-1042",          // a newer notification with the same tag replaces this one
  });
  notification.addEventListener("click", () => {
    window.focus();
    location.assign("/orders/1042");
  });
});
```

Notifications created this way only work while the page is open. To notify users when the site is closed, a **service worker** receives messages from the server through the Push API and shows the notification (`registration.showNotification`). This is covered with Progressive Web Apps in Chapter 15.

**Clipboard.** The asynchronous Clipboard API (`navigator.clipboard`) replaces the old `document.execCommand("copy")`:

```javascript
copyButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  try {
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(codeBlock.textContent);   // needs a secure context and focus
    copyButton.textContent = "Copied";
  } catch (err) {
    copyButton.textContent = "Copy failed";                      // permission or focus problem
  }
});

// Reading is more sensitive: browsers ask for permission or show a "Paste" confirmation
const text = await navigator.clipboard.readText();

// Rich content: images and HTML with ClipboardItem
const blob = await (await fetch("/chart.png")).blob();
await navigator.clipboard.write([new ClipboardItem({ "image/png": blob })]);
```

You can also customise what users copy and paste with the `copy`, `cut` and `paste` events, which expose `event.clipboardData`:

```javascript
// Paste images from the clipboard into an editor
editor.addEventListener("paste", (event) => {
  const file = [...event.clipboardData.files].find((f) => f.type.startsWith("image/"));
  if (file) {
    event.preventDefault();
    insertImage(URL.createObjectURL(file));
  }
});
```

**Requirements at a glance.**

| API | Secure context | Permission prompt | User gesture required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Geolocation | Yes | Yes | No (but asking on load is bad practice) |
| Notifications | Yes | Yes | Yes, for `requestPermission` in most browsers |
| `clipboard.writeText` | Yes | No (Chromium may use a permission) | Usually, and the document must be focused |
| `clipboard.readText` | Yes | Yes, or a per-use paste confirmation | Yes in most browsers |

**Good practice.** Ask for a permission **in context**, at the moment its value is obvious (a "Find stores near me" button, not a prompt on page load). Users who deny a prompt are rarely asked again, because the browser remembers the decision. Always provide a fallback path (manual city entry, an in-page message, a selectable text field).

**Key Takeaways**

- Device APIs require secure contexts. Many need explicit permission, and some need a user gesture.
- Use `navigator.permissions.query` to check state without prompting, and request permissions in context, with a fallback if denied.
- Geolocation uses callbacks with success, error (codes 1 to 3) and options (`enableHighAccuracy`, `timeout`, `maximumAge`). Promisify it for `async` code.
- `Notification.requestPermission()` must be called from a user gesture. Notifications for closed pages require a service worker and Push.
- `navigator.clipboard.writeText` and `readText` are promise-based. Reading is more restricted than writing. `copy` and `paste` events customise clipboard behaviour.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a "Copy" button to every `<pre>` block on a page using event delegation and `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, showing "Copied" for two seconds afterwards.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a "Find the nearest store" feature: check the geolocation permission state, explain the request in a message before prompting, compute the distance to a list of stores with the haversine formula, and fall back to a city search box when permission is denied or the request times out.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why do browsers require HTTPS and a user gesture for APIs like notifications and clipboard access?" *Hint:* consider what a malicious page or a network attacker could do with each capability if the restrictions did not exist.

#### Web Workers and Background Threads

Chapter 5 established that JavaScript runs your code on a single main thread, shared with rendering and input handling. A computation that takes 500 ms (parsing a large file, filtering 100,000 records, applying an image filter) freezes the page for 500 ms, whatever async syntax wraps it. Promises and `async` functions help with **waiting**, not with **computing**. To compute without freezing the page, the work must run on another thread. **Web Workers** provide exactly that: real OS threads that run JavaScript in parallel with the main thread.

**The isolation model.** A worker runs in its own global scope (`self`, of type `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope`), with its own event loop and its own memory. It has **no access to the DOM**, `window` or `document`, which would require locking and make the DOM unsafe. Workers and the page communicate only by **passing messages**, like two people in separate offices who talk by sending letters, never by sharing a desk.

```text
 Main thread                                     Worker thread
 ┌──────────────────────────┐   postMessage()   ┌──────────────────────────┐
 │ DOM, events, rendering   │ ────────────────> │ onmessage: compute       │
 │ worker.onmessage(...)    │ <──────────────── │ postMessage(result)      │
 └──────────────────────────┘   postMessage()   └──────────────────────────┘
   window, document                               self, no DOM
                                                  fetch, IndexedDB, timers, WebSocket available
```

**A first worker.**

```javascript
// primes.worker.js: runs in the worker thread
self.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  const { limit } = event.data;
  const primes = [];
  for (let n = 2; n <= limit; n++) {               // deliberately slow CPU work
    let isPrime = true;
    for (let d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
      if (n % d === 0) { isPrime = false; break; }
    }
    if (isPrime) primes.push(n);
  }
  self.postMessage({ count: primes.length, last: primes.at(-1) });
});
```

```javascript
// main.js: runs in the page
const worker = new Worker(new URL("./primes.worker.js", import.meta.url), { type: "module" });

worker.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  output.textContent = `${event.data.count} primes, the largest is ${event.data.last}`;
});
worker.addEventListener("error", (event) => {
  console.error("Worker failed:", event.message);
});

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  output.textContent = "Computing...";               // the page stays responsive meanwhile
  worker.postMessage({ limit: 5_000_000 });
});

// When no longer needed:
// worker.terminate();      from the page, or self.close() from inside the worker
```

`{ type: "module" }` lets the worker use `import` statements (3.4). Classic workers use `importScripts("lib.js")` instead.

**What can be sent: structured clone and transfer.** Messages are **copied** with the structured clone algorithm (the same one IndexedDB uses): plain objects, arrays, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `Blob`, `ArrayBuffer`, typed arrays and more. Functions, DOM nodes and class instances' prototypes are not preserved. Copying a 200 MB buffer is slow, so large binary data can be **transferred** instead: ownership moves to the other thread in constant time, and the sender's copy becomes unusable.

```javascript
const pixels = new Uint8ClampedArray(4 * 4000 * 3000);    // 48 MB image buffer
worker.postMessage({ pixels }, [pixels.buffer]);           // second argument: transfer list
console.log(pixels.byteLength);                            // 0: the buffer now belongs to the worker
```

**A request/response wrapper.** Raw messages have no built-in notion of "the answer to *this* request". A small wrapper adds ids and promises so that callers can simply `await`:

```javascript
// main.js
function createWorkerClient(url) {
  const worker = new Worker(url, { type: "module" });
  const pending = new Map();
  let nextId = 0;

  worker.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
    const { id, result, error } = data;
    const { resolve, reject } = pending.get(id);
    pending.delete(id);
    error ? reject(new Error(error)) : resolve(result);
  };

  return {
    call(method, ...args) {
      return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        const id = nextId++;
        pending.set(id, { resolve, reject });
        worker.postMessage({ id, method, args });
      });
    },
  };
}

// worker.js
const api = {
  sum: (numbers) => numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0),
  sortBy: (rows, key) => rows.toSorted((a, b) => (a[key] > b[key] ? 1 : -1)),
};
self.onmessage = ({ data: { id, method, args } }) => {
  try {
    self.postMessage({ id, result: api[method](...args) });
  } catch (err) {
    self.postMessage({ id, error: err.message });
  }
};

// usage
const client = createWorkerClient("./worker.js");
const total = await client.call("sum", bigArray);
```

Libraries such as *Comlink* generalise this pattern, letting you call worker functions as if they were local async functions.

**Kinds of workers.**

| Kind | Created with | Shared by | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dedicated worker | `new Worker(url)` | The page that created it | Offload CPU work |
| Shared worker | `new SharedWorker(url)` | All same-origin tabs that connect to it | Share one connection or cache across tabs |
| Service worker | `navigator.serviceWorker.register(url)` | All pages in its scope, even when closed | Network proxy, offline caching, push (Chapter 15) |
| Worklets | `CSS.paintWorklet.addModule()`, `audioContext.audioWorklet` | The rendering or audio pipeline | Tiny hooks into rendering and audio processing |

**Costs and limits.**

- Starting a worker takes time and memory (a new JavaScript environment). Create workers once and reuse them, or keep a pool sized to `navigator.hardwareConcurrency`.
- Message copying costs grow with data size. Send only what is needed, and transfer large buffers.
- True shared memory (`SharedArrayBuffer` with `Atomics`) exists, but is only available on **cross-origin isolated** pages (served with the `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` headers) as a defence against Spectre-style attacks.
- Workers cannot touch the DOM. For graphics, `OffscreenCanvas` lets a worker draw into a canvas (Chapter 7).

**Key Takeaways**

- Web Workers run JavaScript on separate threads, so CPU-heavy work does not freeze the page. `async` code alone does not achieve this.
- Workers have no DOM access and communicate with the page only through `postMessage` and `message` events.
- Messages are copied with structured clone. Transfer `ArrayBuffer`s to move large data without copying.
- Wrap message passing in a request/response protocol with ids and promises (or use Comlink).
- Dedicated, shared and service workers serve different purposes. Reuse workers because they are expensive to start.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the prime-counting loop on the main thread with a CSS spinner on the page and observe the freeze. Move it into a worker and confirm the spinner keeps turning.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a CSV viewer that reads a large file with `<input type="file">`, sends the file to a worker that parses it and computes column statistics, and reports progress messages every 10,000 rows. Make the "Cancel" button terminate the worker.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If JavaScript is single-threaded, how do Web Workers achieve parallelism, and why can't they access the DOM?" *Hint:* consider separate event loops and memory, message passing versus shared state, and what concurrent DOM mutation would require.

#### Intersection and Resize Observers

Two questions come up constantly in UI code: "Is this element visible on screen?" (to lazy-load images, load the next page of an infinite list, start a video or record an ad impression) and "Has this element changed size?" (to redraw a chart, switch a component's layout or truncate text). The traditional answers were `scroll` and `resize` listeners that call `getBoundingClientRect()` and read `offsetWidth`. These run constantly, force layout on the main thread (6.1) and miss many cases: a `resize` event fires when the **window** changes, not when an element changes size because a sidebar collapsed. The observer APIs make the browser do this tracking efficiently and report only actual changes, with the same shape as `MutationObserver` (6.1).

**`IntersectionObserver`.** It reports when a target element starts or stops intersecting a **root** (the viewport by default, or a scrollable ancestor), crossing given **thresholds**:

```javascript
const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
  (entries, obs) => {
    for (const entry of entries) {
      // entry.isIntersecting, entry.intersectionRatio (0..1), entry.target,
      // entry.boundingClientRect, entry.intersectionRect, entry.rootBounds, entry.time
      if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        console.log(entry.target.id, "is visible at", entry.intersectionRatio);
      }
    }
  },
  {
    root: null,                    // null = the viewport; or a scrollable container element
    rootMargin: "0px 0px 200px 0px",  // grow the root box: trigger 200px BEFORE entering the viewport
    threshold: [0, 0.5, 1],        // call back when visibility crosses 0%, 50% and 100%
  }
);

document.querySelectorAll("section").forEach((s) => observer.observe(s));
```

The callback also runs once for each target as soon as observation starts, reporting its initial state.

**Lazy-loading images.** Native `loading="lazy"` on `<img>` and `<iframe>` covers the simple case without any JavaScript. The observer is useful for custom behaviour, such as background images or loading components:

```javascript
const lazy = new IntersectionObserver((entries, obs) => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    if (!entry.isIntersecting) continue;
    const img = entry.target;
    img.src = img.dataset.src;          // start the real download
    obs.unobserve(img);                 // done with this one
  }
}, { rootMargin: "300px" });            // start a little before it scrolls into view

document.querySelectorAll("img[data-src]").forEach((img) => lazy.observe(img));
```

**Infinite scroll with a sentinel.** Put an empty element after the list and observe it. When it becomes visible, load the next page:

```javascript
const sentinel = document.querySelector("#load-more-sentinel");
let page = 1;
let loading = false;

const loader = new IntersectionObserver(async ([entry]) => {
  if (!entry.isIntersecting || loading) return;
  loading = true;
  const items = await fetch(`/api/items?page=${++page}`).then((r) => r.json());
  renderItems(items);                   // appending pushes the sentinel down again
  if (items.length === 0) loader.disconnect();   // no more data
  loading = false;
});
loader.observe(sentinel);
```

Other uses include highlighting the current section in a table of contents, pausing videos and animations that scroll out of view, and reporting ad or product impressions (for example "50% visible", with a threshold of `0.5`).

**`ResizeObserver`.** It reports when an **element's** size changes, for any reason: window resize, content change, a sibling collapsing, a font loading, or a CSS class change.

```javascript
const chartContainer = document.querySelector(".chart");

const resizeObserver = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    // contentBoxSize and borderBoxSize are arrays (one item per fragment, e.g. in multi-column layouts)
    const { inlineSize: width, blockSize: height } = entry.contentBoxSize[0];
    redrawChart(entry.target, width, height);
  }
});

resizeObserver.observe(chartContainer);                   // content box by default
// resizeObserver.observe(el, { box: "border-box" });     // or observe the border box
```

`entry.contentRect` is an older `DOMRect`-based property that is still widely used. `inlineSize` and `blockSize` are the writing-mode-aware width and height.

**Avoiding resize loops.** If the callback changes the observed element's size, it triggers another observation. The browser processes these in passes during the same frame, and if it cannot settle it reports the console error "ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications" and defers the rest to the next frame. Avoid resizing the observed element itself in its callback. Change children, or defer the change with `requestAnimationFrame`.

**Container queries first.** Since container queries (`@container`, Chapter 2) let CSS adapt a component to its container's size, a `ResizeObserver` is no longer needed for purely visual changes. Use it when JavaScript must act on the size, for example to redraw a canvas, pick an image resolution, or virtualise a list.

**The observer family.**

| Observer | Reports | Typical uses |
|---|---|---|
| `MutationObserver` (6.1) | DOM tree, attribute and text changes | Reacting to third-party DOM changes |
| `IntersectionObserver` | Visibility relative to the viewport or a container | Lazy loading, infinite scroll, impressions, scroll spy |
| `ResizeObserver` | Element size changes | Responsive canvases and charts, component-level layout logic |
| `PerformanceObserver` | Performance entries (long tasks, paints, layout shifts) | Real-user performance monitoring (Chapter 17) |

All share the same lifecycle: create with a callback, `observe(target, options)`, `unobserve(target)`, `disconnect()`. Callbacks are batched and run asynchronously, so they never block the change that triggered them.

**Key Takeaways**

- `IntersectionObserver` reports when elements enter or leave the viewport or a container, without scroll listeners or forced layout.
- Configure it with `root`, `rootMargin` (to trigger early) and `threshold` (the visibility ratios that trigger callbacks). Call `unobserve` when a target no longer needs tracking.
- `ResizeObserver` reports element size changes from any cause, which `window` `resize` events cannot.
- Do not resize an observed element inside its own `ResizeObserver` callback, and prefer CSS container queries for purely visual adaptation.
- Mutation, Intersection, Resize and Performance observers share one pattern: callback, `observe`, `unobserve`, `disconnect`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a long page with ten sections and a fixed table of contents. Use an `IntersectionObserver` to highlight the link of the section currently in view.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a component that draws a sine wave on a `<canvas>` sized to its container, using a `ResizeObserver` and `devicePixelRatio` for sharp rendering. Place it in a layout with a collapsible sidebar and confirm that it redraws when the sidebar toggles, even though the window size does not change.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you implement infinite scrolling, and why is `IntersectionObserver` preferable to a scroll listener?" *Hint:* compare how often each approach runs code, whether it forces layout, and how a sentinel element simplifies the logic.

<a id="7-graphics-and-rendering-apis"></a>
## 7. Graphics and Rendering APIs

HTML and CSS (Chapter 2) lay out boxes of text, but charts, maps, diagrams, games, photo editors and 3D product viewers need direct control over shapes and pixels. The web platform offers three complementary technologies for this: **SVG**, a vector format whose shapes live in the DOM; the **Canvas 2D API**, a bitmap you paint with JavaScript; and **WebGL**, which runs your own programs on the GPU for hardware-accelerated 2D and 3D rendering. Understanding how each one models an image, and what that model costs, is what lets you choose the right tool and keep the result sharp, accessible and fast.

<a id="71-svg-api-for-vector-rendering"></a>
### 7.1 SVG API for Vector Rendering

This subchapter covers Scalable Vector Graphics: how vector images differ from bitmaps, how an SVG document is structured, and how to draw, style, transform, reuse, script, animate and add interaction to its shapes.

#### Vector vs Raster Graphics

A screen is a grid of pixels, so every image eventually becomes a grid of coloured dots. There are, however, two very different ways of *describing* an image before that happens.

- A **raster** (or **bitmap**) image stores the dots themselves: a fixed grid of pixels, each with a colour. A 200×200 PNG is 40,000 colour values.
- A **vector** image stores *instructions*: "a circle centred at (100, 100) with radius 80, filled red". The dots are computed only when the image is displayed, at whatever size is needed.

An analogy: a raster image is a mosaic. Up close you see the tiles, and to make it twice as big you can only make the tiles bigger. A vector image is a set of instructions handed to a painter ("draw a circle this big, here"). Ask for a bigger picture and the painter simply paints it bigger, with the same crisp edges.

**What happens when you scale.**

```text
Raster circle, 8x8 pixels         Same raster scaled 2x            Vector circle scaled 2x
                                   (each pixel becomes 2x2)         (re-rasterised at new size)
  . . # # # # . .                  . . . . # # # # # # # # . . . .     smooth edge computed
  . # # # # # # .                  . . . . # # # # # # # # . . . .     from the equation
  # # # # # # # #                  . . # # # # # # # # # # # # . .     (x-cx)^2 + (y-cy)^2 = r^2
  # # # # # # # #                  . . # # # # # # # # # # # # . .     at the new resolution,
  ...                              ... jagged "staircase" edges        so no staircase appears
```

Both kinds are rasterised in the end, because the display is raster. The difference is **when**: a vector image postpones rasterisation until the final size and pixel density are known. This matters more than ever on high-density displays, where one CSS pixel may be 2 or 3 device pixels (`window.devicePixelRatio`). A vector icon is sharp at every density, while a bitmap icon needs a separate file per density (`srcset`, Chapter 2).

**Comparison.**

| Aspect | Raster (PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, GIF) | Vector (SVG, also fonts and PDF) |
|---|---|---|
| Stores | A grid of pixel colours | Geometric shapes, paths and text |
| Scaling up | Blurs or pixelates | Stays sharp at any size |
| File size grows with | Number of pixels | Number and complexity of shapes |
| Best for | Photographs, complex textures, camera output | Icons, logos, charts, diagrams, maps, UI illustrations |
| Editing individual parts | Hard (pixels have no identity) | Easy (each shape is an object) |
| Rendering cost | Fixed: copy pixels | Grows with shape count and effects |
| Text inside | Burned in, not selectable | Real text, selectable and searchable |

**Where the web technologies sit.** SVG is a vector format. Canvas 2D has a vector-like *drawing* API (`arc`, `lineTo`), but its *result* is a bitmap: once drawn, the circle is just pixels. WebGL also produces a bitmap, rasterised by the GPU. This distinction drives most of the trade-offs in this chapter.

**A vector image is just text.** Here is a complete SVG icon. It is small, compresses well with gzip or Brotli, and can be edited in any text editor:

```xml
<!-- check.svg: 3 shapes, under 300 bytes, sharp at 16px or 1600px -->
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24">
  <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="11" fill="#2e7d32"/>
  <path d="M6 12 l4 4 l8 -8" fill="none" stroke="white" stroke-width="2.5"
        stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/>
</svg>
```

A photograph, by contrast, has no simple geometric description: converting it to vectors ("tracing") produces either a huge file or a cartoon-like approximation. Choose by content, not by habit.

**Key Takeaways**

- Raster images store pixels at a fixed resolution. Vector images store shapes and are rasterised on demand at any size.
- Vectors stay sharp on any display density and are usually smaller for flat, geometric artwork. Rasters are the right choice for photographs and rich textures.
- Vector rendering cost grows with the number of shapes, raster cost with the number of pixels.
- SVG is vector and lives in the DOM. Canvas and WebGL produce bitmaps, even though you draw on them with geometric commands.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Save the `check.svg` example and a 24×24 PNG screenshot of it. Display both with `<img>` at `width="384"` and describe the difference. Compare the file sizes before and after gzip.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* For each of the following, choose raster or vector and justify the choice: a company logo, a product photo, a line chart with 50 points, a scatter plot with 500,000 points, a satellite map tile, a QR code.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why might an SVG be the wrong choice for a chart even though it is resolution-independent?" *Hint:* think about what each data point costs in the DOM and how rendering time grows with element count.

#### SVG Document Structure and Coordinate System

Before drawing anything, you need to know what an SVG document is, how it gets into a page, and where "(10, 20)" actually is on screen.

**SVG is XML.** SVG (*Scalable Vector Graphics*) is an XML vocabulary standardised by the W3C (SVG 1.1, with SVG 2 adding many refinements). Each shape is an element, each property an attribute. A standalone `.svg` file must declare the SVG namespace so that XML parsers know what `<circle>` means:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>          <!-- optional XML prolog -->
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"          <!-- required in standalone files -->
     width="300" height="200"                    <!-- size of the viewport -->
     viewBox="0 0 300 200">                      <!-- user coordinate system (see Transformations) -->
  <title>Two shapes</title>                      <!-- accessible name, also a tooltip -->
  <desc>A blue rectangle partly covered by an orange circle.</desc>

  <defs>                                         <!-- definitions: not drawn by themselves -->
    <linearGradient id="sky"> ... </linearGradient>
  </defs>

  <rect x="20" y="20" width="160" height="100" fill="steelblue"/>  <!-- painted first -->
  <circle cx="170" cy="110" r="60" fill="orange"/>                  <!-- painted on top -->
</svg>
```

**Painting order is document order.** SVG uses the *painter's algorithm*: later elements are painted over earlier ones. CSS `z-index` does not apply to shapes inside an SVG, so to bring a shape to the front you move it later in the document (for example `svg.append(shape)`).

**Ways to put SVG on a page.**

| Method | Example | Scriptable from page | Styleable by page CSS | Cached separately |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inline SVG | `<svg>...</svg>` inside HTML | Yes (part of the DOM) | Yes | No (part of the HTML) |
| Image | `<img src="logo.svg" alt="...">` | No (scripts inside never run) | No | Yes |
| CSS background | `background-image: url(icon.svg)` | No | No | Yes |
| Embedded document | `<object data="map.svg" type="image/svg+xml">` or `<iframe>` | Through `contentDocument`, same-origin only | No | Yes |

Inline SVG is what the rest of this subchapter assumes. Inside HTML, the parser knows `<svg>` and switches to the SVG namespace automatically, so `xmlns` can be omitted.

**The coordinate system.** SVG uses a 2D Cartesian system, but with one twist that surprises everyone who remembers school maths: **y grows downward**.

```text
 (0,0) ───────────────────────────► x  (300,0)
   │
   │      ● (60, 40)
   │
   │                   ● (200, 120)
   │
   ▼
   y  (0,200)                           (300,200)
```

- The origin `(0, 0)` is the top-left corner of the viewport.
- Coordinates are in **user units**. Without a `viewBox`, one user unit equals one CSS pixel. With a `viewBox`, user units are scaled to fit the viewport, which is what makes SVG "scalable".
- Coordinates can be fractional and negative. Content outside the viewport is clipped (unless `overflow: visible`).
- Angles in `rotate()` are in degrees and, because y points down, positive angles rotate **clockwise**.

**Accessibility.** A meaningful inline SVG should expose a name to assistive technologies, while a decorative one should be hidden:

```html
<!-- meaningful graphic -->
<svg role="img" aria-labelledby="chart-title" viewBox="0 0 400 200">
  <title id="chart-title">Monthly sales, January to June</title>
  <!-- ... -->
</svg>

<!-- decorative icon next to visible text -->
<button><svg aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">...</svg> Save</button>
```

SVG files exported from design tools often contain editor metadata, unused definitions and excessive decimal places. An optimiser such as **SVGO** routinely shrinks them by 30 to 70 percent.

**Key Takeaways**

- SVG is an XML vocabulary. Standalone files need `xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"`; inline SVG in HTML does not.
- Only inline SVG (and same-origin `<object>`) can be styled and scripted from the page. `<img>` and CSS backgrounds treat SVG as a sealed image.
- The origin is top-left and y points down. Positive rotations are clockwise.
- Elements are painted in document order. There is no `z-index` for shapes.
- Give meaningful SVG `role="img"` and a `<title>`, and hide decorative SVG with `aria-hidden="true"`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a standalone SVG of 400×300 user units containing a sun (circle) in the top-right corner and a ground strip (rectangle) along the bottom. Open it directly in the browser, then include it with `<img>` and inline.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Put an SVG containing a `<script>` that changes a shape's colour on load into a page three ways: inline, `<img>` and `<object>`. Record where the script runs and explain why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you bring an SVG shape to the front when the user hovers it?" *Hint:* consider the painting model of SVG and what DOM operation changes it.

#### Basic Shapes and the Path Element

SVG gives you a handful of convenient shape elements for common cases and one universal element, `<path>`, that can draw anything. In fact every basic shape is just a shorthand for a particular path.

**Basic shapes.**

| Element | Key attributes | Draws |
|---|---|---|
| `<rect>` | `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, optional `rx`, `ry` (corner radii) | Rectangle, optionally rounded |
| `<circle>` | `cx`, `cy`, `r` | Circle |
| `<ellipse>` | `cx`, `cy`, `rx`, `ry` | Axis-aligned ellipse |
| `<line>` | `x1`, `y1`, `x2`, `y2` | Straight segment (needs a `stroke` to be visible) |
| `<polyline>` | `points="x1,y1 x2,y2 ..."` | Open chain of segments |
| `<polygon>` | `points="..."` | Closed chain (last point joins the first) |

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 320 120" width="320" height="120">
  <rect x="10" y="10" width="80" height="60" rx="8" fill="#90caf9"/>
  <circle cx="140" cy="40" r="30" fill="#ef9a9a"/>
  <ellipse cx="220" cy="40" rx="40" ry="20" fill="#a5d6a7"/>
  <line x1="10" y1="100" x2="300" y2="100" stroke="black"/>     <!-- no fill: lines have no area -->
  <polyline points="10,90 60,80 110,95 160,70" fill="none" stroke="purple"/>
  <polygon points="270,10 300,70 240,70" fill="#ffcc80"/>       <!-- a triangle -->
</svg>
```

**The path element.** `<path d="...">` describes an outline with a compact command language. Think of it as instructions to a pen: "lift the pen and move to (10, 10), draw a line to (50, 10), draw a curve to ...". Each command is a letter followed by numbers. An **uppercase** letter uses **absolute** coordinates, a **lowercase** letter uses coordinates **relative** to the current pen position.

| Command | Parameters | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `M` / `m` | `x y` | Move to (start a new sub-path without drawing) |
| `L` / `l` | `x y` | Line to |
| `H` / `h` | `x` | Horizontal line to |
| `V` / `v` | `y` | Vertical line to |
| `Z` / `z` | none | Close path (straight line back to the sub-path start) |
| `C` / `c` | `x1 y1 x2 y2 x y` | Cubic Bézier curve with two control points |
| `S` / `s` | `x2 y2 x y` | Smooth cubic: first control point mirrored from the previous curve |
| `Q` / `q` | `x1 y1 x y` | Quadratic Bézier curve with one control point |
| `T` / `t` | `x y` | Smooth quadratic: control point mirrored |
| `A` / `a` | `rx ry rotation large-arc sweep x y` | Elliptical arc to `(x, y)` |

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 120" width="300" height="120">
  <!-- A house: absolute moves and lines, then close -->
  <path d="M 20 110 V 60 L 60 20 L 100 60 V 110 Z" fill="#ffe0b2" stroke="#6d4c41"/>

  <!-- The same outline with relative commands: each step is an offset from the previous point -->
  <path d="m 120 110 v -50 l 40 -40 l 40 40 v 50 z" fill="none" stroke="#6d4c41"/>

  <!-- An S-shaped cubic curve -->
  <path d="M 220 100 C 220 20, 290 100, 290 20" fill="none" stroke="crimson" stroke-width="3"/>
</svg>
```

**Bézier curves.** A curve is defined by its end points and **control points** that "pull" the curve towards them without the curve passing through them:

```text
      P1 (control)                 P2 (control)
        o . . . . .         . . . .o
       .           .  ___ .
      .         ____---    .
     .     __---             .
    ●--''                     ●
  P0 (start)                P3 (end)

  "M P0 C P1, P2, P3": the curve leaves P0 heading towards P1
  and arrives at P3 coming from the direction of P2.
```

`S` and `T` mirror the previous control point, which guarantees a smooth join (no visible corner) between consecutive curves.

**Arcs.** The `A` command is the trickiest. Given a start point, an end point and radii, there are generally **four** possible elliptical arcs. Two flags pick one: `large-arc` (1 = the arc longer than 180°) and `sweep` (1 = drawn in the positive-angle, clockwise direction). Arcs are what you need for pie and donut charts:

```javascript
// Build the "d" attribute of a pie slice centred at (cx, cy)
function pieSlice(cx, cy, r, startAngle, endAngle) {      // angles in radians, 0 = 3 o'clock
  const x1 = cx + r * Math.cos(startAngle);
  const y1 = cy + r * Math.sin(startAngle);                // y down => angles go clockwise
  const x2 = cx + r * Math.cos(endAngle);
  const y2 = cy + r * Math.sin(endAngle);
  const largeArc = endAngle - startAngle > Math.PI ? 1 : 0;
  return `M ${cx} ${cy} L ${x1} ${y1} A ${r} ${r} 0 ${largeArc} 1 ${x2} ${y2} Z`;
  //                      move to centre, line to arc start, arc to end (sweep=1), back to centre
}

// A 30% slice starting at 12 o'clock
const start = -Math.PI / 2;
document.querySelector("#slice").setAttribute("d", pieSlice(100, 100, 80, start, start + 0.3 * 2 * Math.PI));
```

**Fill rules and holes.** A path can contain several sub-paths (several `M` commands). Whether an inner sub-path becomes a hole depends on `fill-rule`. With `evenodd`, a point is inside if a ray from it crosses the outline an odd number of times, so a circle inside a circle produces a ring regardless of direction. With the default `nonzero`, the inner sub-path must be drawn in the opposite direction to become a hole.

```html
<!-- Donut: outer square and inner square, evenodd makes the inner one a hole -->
<path fill-rule="evenodd" fill="teal"
      d="M 10 10 H 110 V 110 H 10 Z   M 40 40 H 80 V 80 H 40 Z"/>
```

Paths also expose geometry helpers used for animation and layout: `path.getTotalLength()` returns the outline length, and `path.getPointAtLength(d)` returns the point at distance `d` along it.

**Key Takeaways**

- Use `<rect>`, `<circle>`, `<ellipse>`, `<line>`, `<polyline>` and `<polygon>` for simple shapes. `<path>` can draw any outline.
- Path commands are letters followed by numbers. Uppercase is absolute, lowercase is relative to the current point.
- Bézier curves are shaped by control points the curve does not pass through. `S` and `T` create smooth joins.
- The arc command needs two flags (`large-arc`, `sweep`) to choose one of four possible arcs.
- `fill-rule="evenodd"` is the simplest way to cut holes in a shape.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Draw a five-pointed star twice: once with `<polygon>` and once with `<path>` using only `M`, `L` and `Z`. Then switch the path to relative commands.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Using the `pieSlice` function, write `renderPie(svg, values)` that draws one slice per value with a different colour, so that the slices together make a full circle. Handle the case of a single value equal to 100% (a full circle cannot be one arc).
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does the SVG arc command need both a large-arc flag and a sweep flag?" *Hint:* draw two ellipses of the given radii through the same two points and count the arcs.

#### Text, Groups and Reusable Symbols

Real graphics need labels, need to treat several shapes as one unit, and often repeat the same artwork many times. SVG provides text elements, grouping, and a definition-and-reuse mechanism for all three needs.

**Text.** `<text>` draws real, selectable, searchable text. Its `x` and `y` set the **baseline** position of the first character, not the top-left corner:

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 120" width="300" height="120" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">
  <line x1="150" y1="0" x2="150" y2="120" stroke="#ddd"/>          <!-- guide at x=150 -->

  <text x="150" y="30" text-anchor="start">start</text>              <!-- begins at x -->
  <text x="150" y="60" text-anchor="middle">middle</text>            <!-- centred on x -->
  <text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="end">end</text>                  <!-- ends at x -->

  <text x="10" y="112" font-size="14">
    Total: <tspan font-weight="bold" fill="crimson">42</tspan>      <!-- styled run of text -->
    <tspan dy="-6" font-size="9">*</tspan>                           <!-- shifted up 6 units -->
  </text>
</svg>
```

- `text-anchor` (`start`, `middle`, `end`) controls horizontal alignment, and `dominant-baseline` (for example `middle` or `hanging`) controls vertical alignment.
- `<tspan>` styles or repositions part of a text (`x`, `y` for absolute, `dx`, `dy` for relative offsets).
- SVG text **does not wrap automatically**. Break lines yourself with several `<tspan x="..." dy="1.2em">`, or embed HTML with `<foreignObject>` when you need real paragraph layout.
- `<textPath href="#curve">` lays text along any path, for example a curved label on a map.

**Groups.** `<g>` groups elements. Attributes and transforms set on the group are inherited by its children, and the group can be styled, moved, hidden or listened to as one unit:

```html
<g transform="translate(200, 40)" fill="gold" stroke="black" class="marker">
  <circle r="12"/>                         <!-- inherits fill and stroke -->
  <text y="30" text-anchor="middle" stroke="none" fill="black">Rome</text>
</g>
```

**Define once, use many times.** `<defs>` holds content that is not rendered directly. `<use>` renders a copy of any element by reference, and `<symbol>` is a container designed for reuse that can have its own `viewBox`:

| Element | Rendered by itself | Own `viewBox` | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<g>` | Yes | No | Group visible shapes |
| `<defs>` | No | No | Hold gradients, filters, markers, templates |
| `<symbol>` | No (only through `<use>`) | Yes | Icons and reusable artwork |
| `<use>` | Yes (a copy of its target) | No | Instantiate a symbol or element at `x`, `y` with `width`, `height` |

**Icon sprites.** The most common real-world use is an icon system: all icons as symbols in one sprite, each one drawn with `<use>`. Using `currentColor` lets each instance take its colour from CSS `color`:

```html
<!-- Sprite, usually at the top of <body> or in an external icons.svg -->
<svg style="display:none">
  <symbol id="icon-heart" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
    <path fill="currentColor"
          d="M12 21 C 5 15, 2 12, 2 8 A 5 5 0 0 1 12 6 A 5 5 0 0 1 22 8 C 22 12, 19 15, 12 21 Z"/>
  </symbol>
  <symbol id="icon-star" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
    <polygon fill="currentColor" points="12,2 15,9 22,9 16.5,14 18.5,21 12,17 5.5,21 7.5,14 2,9 9,9"/>
  </symbol>
</svg>

<!-- Instances: same artwork, any size, colour from CSS -->
<button class="like">
  <svg width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#icon-heart"/></svg> Like
</button>
<svg width="48" height="48" style="color: goldenrod"><use href="#icon-star"/></svg>

<!-- External sprite file (must be same-origin) -->
<svg width="24" height="24"><use href="/icons.svg#icon-star"/></svg>
```

```css
.like { color: #999; }
.like:hover { color: crimson; }          /* the heart turns red: fill="currentColor" follows */
```

**Styling inside `<use>`.** The copy created by `<use>` lives in a closed shadow tree, so selectors from the page such as `.like path` cannot reach it. Style instances through **inherited** properties (`fill`, `stroke`, `color`) set on the `<use>` element, through `currentColor`, or through CSS custom properties (`fill: var(--icon-accent)` inside the symbol).

Older code writes `xlink:href` instead of `href`. Plain `href` is the SVG 2 form and works in all current browsers.

**Key Takeaways**

- `<text>` positions by baseline. Align with `text-anchor` and `dominant-baseline`, style runs with `<tspan>`, and break lines manually because SVG text does not wrap.
- `<g>` groups elements so they share attributes, transforms and event handling.
- `<defs>` stores non-rendered definitions. `<symbol>` (with its own `viewBox`) plus `<use>` is the standard pattern for reusable icons.
- Content cloned by `<use>` cannot be selected from outside. Use inherited properties, `currentColor` and CSS custom properties to vary instances.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a sprite with three icons (home, search, user) as `<symbol>`s and display them at 16, 32 and 64 pixels in three different colours using only CSS.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function `wrapText(textEl, string, maxWidth)` that splits a string into words and appends `<tspan>` lines so that no line is wider than `maxWidth`, using `getComputedTextLength()` on a temporary `<tspan>` to measure.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your icon component uses `<use href="#icon">` and a designer wants the icon to have two colours that change on hover. How would you do it?" *Hint:* think about what crosses the shadow boundary of `<use>`: inheritance, `currentColor` and custom properties.

#### Fills, Strokes, Gradients and Filters

Shapes are only geometry until they are painted. SVG paints every shape in two layers, the **fill** (its interior) and the **stroke** (its outline), and either can be a flat colour, a gradient or a pattern. Filters then add image-processing effects such as blur and shadows.

**Attributes or CSS.** Most painting properties can be set as *presentation attributes* (`fill="red"`) or as CSS (`fill: red`). Presentation attributes have the lowest priority: any CSS rule overrides them, even `* { fill: black }`. This is convenient, because exported SVG can carry defaults in attributes while your stylesheet overrides them.

```css
.chart .bar { fill: steelblue; }          /* wins over fill="..." attributes */
.chart .bar:hover { fill: orange; }
```

**Fill and stroke properties.**

| Property | Values and notes |
|---|---|
| `fill`, `stroke` | Colour, `none`, `currentColor` or `url(#paintServerId)` |
| `fill-opacity`, `stroke-opacity`, `opacity` | 0 to 1. `opacity` applies to the whole element after painting |
| `fill-rule` | `nonzero` (default) or `evenodd` |
| `stroke-width` | Width in user units. The stroke is **centred** on the outline, half inside and half outside |
| `stroke-linecap` | `butt` (default), `round`, `square`: the shape of open line ends |
| `stroke-linejoin` | `miter` (default), `round`, `bevel`: the shape of corners |
| `stroke-dasharray`, `stroke-dashoffset` | Dash pattern (for example `"8 4"`) and where the pattern starts |
| `vector-effect` | `non-scaling-stroke` keeps the stroke width constant when the shape is scaled |
| `paint-order` | `stroke` paints the stroke under the fill (useful for outlined text) |

```text
stroke-linecap:   butt  ═══════|      round ═══════)      square ═══════]
                  (ends at the point)  (half-circle)        (extends by half the width)

stroke-linejoin:  miter: sharp pointed corner   round: rounded corner   bevel: corner cut off flat
```

**Gradients.** A gradient is a *paint server* defined in `<defs>` and referenced with `url(#id)`. Colour **stops** are placed along the gradient at offsets from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%):

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 120" width="300" height="120">
  <defs>
    <!-- left-to-right by default (x1=0 y1=0 x2=1 y2=0), relative to each shape's bounding box -->
    <linearGradient id="sunset" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">   <!-- top to bottom -->
      <stop offset="0" stop-color="#ff9800"/>
      <stop offset="0.6" stop-color="#e91e63"/>
      <stop offset="1" stop-color="#3f51b5"/>
    </linearGradient>

    <!-- centre highlight that fades to transparent; fx, fy move the focal point -->
    <radialGradient id="glow" cx="0.5" cy="0.5" r="0.5" fx="0.35" fy="0.35">
      <stop offset="0" stop-color="white" stop-opacity="0.9"/>
      <stop offset="1" stop-color="white" stop-opacity="0"/>
    </radialGradient>
  </defs>

  <rect width="300" height="120" fill="url(#sunset)"/>
  <circle cx="230" cy="50" r="40" fill="#ffeb3b"/>
  <circle cx="230" cy="50" r="40" fill="url(#glow)"/>              <!-- layered on top -->
</svg>
```

By default, gradient coordinates use `gradientUnits="objectBoundingBox"`: 0 to 1 spans the bounding box of *the shape being painted*, so one gradient fits any shape. Set `gradientUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` to give the gradient absolute coordinates shared by all shapes (for example one continuous gradient across all bars of a chart). `spreadMethod` (`pad`, `reflect`, `repeat`) decides what happens beyond the end stops. `<pattern>` works the same way but tiles arbitrary SVG content, for example hatching in a chart.

**Clipping, masking and markers.** `<clipPath>` cuts a shape to the outline of another (hard edges), `<mask>` uses the luminance of another graphic as variable transparency (soft edges), and `<marker>` attaches artwork such as arrowheads to the ends or vertices of lines and paths, which is essential for diagrams:

```html
<defs>
  <marker id="arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5"
          markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">
    <path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 Z" fill="context-stroke"/>   <!-- same colour as the line where supported -->
  </marker>
</defs>
<line x1="20" y1="20" x2="180" y2="20" stroke="black" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
```

**Filters.** A `<filter>` is a small image-processing graph. Each *filter primitive* (`fe...`) takes an input image (`in`), produces an output (`result`) and can be chained to other primitives. `SourceGraphic` and `SourceAlpha` are the element itself and its alpha channel:

```html
<defs>
  <!-- Hand-built drop shadow: blur the alpha, offset it, then draw the original on top -->
  <filter id="shadow" x="-20%" y="-20%" width="140%" height="140%">   <!-- room for the blur -->
    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="3" result="blur"/>
    <feOffset in="blur" dx="2" dy="3" result="offsetBlur"/>
    <feMerge>
      <feMergeNode in="offsetBlur"/>      <!-- bottom layer: the shadow -->
      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>   <!-- top layer: the original -->
    </feMerge>
  </filter>

  <!-- Same result with the shortcut primitive -->
  <filter id="shadow2"><feDropShadow dx="2" dy="3" stdDeviation="3" flood-opacity="0.4"/></filter>
</defs>

<rect x="20" y="20" width="120" height="60" rx="10" fill="white" filter="url(#shadow)"/>
```

Other useful primitives include `feColorMatrix` (desaturate, recolour), `feTurbulence` (procedural noise, paper and cloud textures) and `feDisplacementMap` (distortion). The CSS `filter` property can apply an SVG filter to *HTML* elements too (`filter: url(#shadow)`), and simple CSS filter functions (`blur()`, `drop-shadow()`) are shorthands for common filter graphs. Filters are computed per pixel and can be expensive on large or animated areas.

**Key Takeaways**

- Every shape has a fill and a stroke. Strokes are centred on the outline and are shaped by `linecap`, `linejoin` and `dasharray`.
- Presentation attributes lose to any CSS rule, so stylesheets can override exported SVG.
- Gradients and patterns are paint servers in `<defs>`, used with `url(#id)`. Their default coordinates are relative to each shape's bounding box.
- `<clipPath>` gives hard-edged cut-outs, `<mask>` soft transparency, `<marker>` arrowheads and line decorations.
- Filters chain primitives through `in` and `result`. They are powerful but cost per-pixel work.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Draw a button-shaped rounded rectangle with a vertical linear gradient, a 1-unit darker stroke and a drop shadow. Then override its fill colour from a stylesheet on hover.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Draw five bars of different heights. Apply one gradient with the default `objectBoundingBox` units and then with `userSpaceOnUse`, and explain the visual difference. Add an arrowhead marker to an x-axis line.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does a 1-unit stroke on a shape positioned at integer coordinates sometimes look blurry, and how can you fix it?" *Hint:* the stroke is centred on the geometry; where do its edges fall relative to the pixel grid?

#### Transformations and viewBox Scaling

Two mechanisms change *where* and *how big* things appear without editing their coordinates: the `transform` attribute moves, rotates and scales individual elements, and the `viewBox` scales the entire drawing to fit its viewport. Together they are what puts the "Scalable" in SVG.

**The transform attribute.** A transform maps the element's coordinate system to its parent's:

| Function | Effect |
|---|---|
| `translate(tx, ty)` | Shift by `tx`, `ty` |
| `scale(s)` or `scale(sx, sy)` | Scale around the origin. A negative factor mirrors |
| `rotate(angle)` / `rotate(angle, cx, cy)` | Rotate clockwise by degrees around the origin, or around `(cx, cy)` |
| `skewX(angle)`, `skewY(angle)` | Shear along one axis |
| `matrix(a, b, c, d, e, f)` | Arbitrary affine transform: `x' = a·x + c·y + e`, `y' = b·x + d·y + f` |

Every combination of these is one 3×3 matrix, which is why `matrix()` can express them all:

```text
| x' |   | a  c  e |   | x |
| y' | = | b  d  f | · | y |       translate(tx,ty) = matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, tx, ty)
| 1  |   | 0  0  1 |   | 1 |       scale(s)        = matrix(s, 0, 0, s, 0, 0)
```

**Order matters.** A list of transforms is applied to the shape's points **from right to left**. An equivalent way to read it, which many people find easier, is left to right, with each function changing the coordinate system that the next one works in:

```html
<!-- Moves the coordinate system to (100, 50), then rotates it: the square spins in place at (100, 50) -->
<rect width="40" height="40" x="-20" y="-20" transform="translate(100, 50) rotate(45)"/>

<!-- Rotates first, then translates along the ROTATED axes: the square ends up somewhere else -->
<rect width="40" height="40" x="-20" y="-20" transform="rotate(45) translate(100, 50)"/>
```

Drawing a shape centred on `(0, 0)` and then translating it, as above, is a habit worth adopting: rotations and scales then happen around the shape's centre.

**CSS transforms on SVG.** CSS `transform` also works on SVG elements, but with a different default origin. For SVG elements, `transform-origin` defaults to `0 0` of the SVG's user space (`transform-box: view-box`), not to the element's centre as for HTML. To rotate a shape around its own centre with CSS:

```css
.gear {
  transform-box: fill-box;        /* percentages and origin refer to the shape's own bounding box */
  transform-origin: center;
  transition: transform 0.4s;
}
.gear:hover { transform: rotate(90deg); }
```

**viewBox: a camera over the drawing.** `viewBox="minX minY width height"` defines which rectangle of user space is visible. The browser maps that rectangle onto the viewport (the element's `width` × `height` on the page). An analogy: the drawing is a large sheet of paper, the `viewBox` is the window of a camera aimed at part of it, and the viewport is the photo print size.

```text
       User space (infinite)                       Viewport on the page (600 x 300 CSS px)
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐             ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │    viewBox="0 0 100 50"      │   scaled    │                                        │
   │   ┌───────────────┐          │   x6 to fit │   every user unit is now 6 CSS px      │
   │   │   ●  ▲        │          │  ─────────► │     ●      ▲                           │
   │   │               │          │             │                                        │
   │   └───────────────┘          │             └────────────────────────────────────────┘
   └──────────────────────────────┘
```

When the aspect ratio of the `viewBox` differs from that of the viewport, `preserveAspectRatio` decides what happens:

| Value | Behaviour | CSS analogy |
|---|---|---|
| `xMidYMid meet` (default) | Scale uniformly so the whole `viewBox` fits, centred | `object-fit: contain` |
| `xMidYMid slice` | Scale uniformly to cover the viewport, cropping overflow | `object-fit: cover` |
| `none` | Stretch non-uniformly to fill exactly | `object-fit: fill` |
| `xMinYMin ...`, `xMaxYMax ...` | Align to the left/top or right/bottom instead of centring | `object-position` |

**Responsive SVG.** Give the SVG a `viewBox`, author everything in those units, and let CSS size the element:

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 60" class="chart" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart">
  <rect x="10" y="20" width="15" height="40"/>   <!-- coordinates in a fixed 100x60 space -->
  <rect x="35" y="5"  width="15" height="55"/>
</svg>
<style>
  .chart { width: 100%; height: auto; }          /* height follows the 100:60 ratio */
</style>
```

**Zooming and panning.** Because the `viewBox` is just four numbers, changing it zooms and pans the whole drawing, and every shape is re-rasterised sharply:

```javascript
const svg = document.querySelector("#map");
let vb = { x: 0, y: 0, w: 1000, h: 600 };

function setViewBox() {
  svg.setAttribute("viewBox", `${vb.x} ${vb.y} ${vb.w} ${vb.h}`);
}

function zoom(factor, cx, cy) {             // zoom around the user-space point (cx, cy)
  vb.x = cx - (cx - vb.x) / factor;         // keep (cx, cy) fixed on screen
  vb.y = cy - (cy - vb.y) / factor;
  vb.w /= factor;                           // factor > 1 zooms in (smaller visible area)
  vb.h /= factor;
  setViewBox();
}
```

A nested `<svg>` element creates a new viewport with its own `viewBox`, which is a convenient way to place a self-contained sub-drawing (for example a chart inside a dashboard) with its own coordinate system.

**Key Takeaways**

- `transform` composes `translate`, `scale`, `rotate`, `skew` and `matrix` into one affine matrix. The order changes the result.
- Draw shapes around `(0, 0)` and position them with `translate` so that rotations and scales happen around their centre.
- CSS transforms on SVG use the user-space origin by default. Set `transform-box: fill-box; transform-origin: center` to transform around the shape itself.
- `viewBox` maps a rectangle of user space onto the viewport, and `preserveAspectRatio` works like `object-fit`.
- A `viewBox` with CSS width and `height: auto` makes SVG responsive. Animating the `viewBox` implements zoom and pan.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Draw a clock face in a `viewBox="-100 -100 200 200"` (origin at the centre). Draw twelve hour marks with a single `<line>` definition reused through `<use>` and `rotate(30 * i)`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement mouse-wheel zoom around the cursor and drag-to-pan for an SVG map by updating its `viewBox`. Use the `zoom` function above and convert the cursor position to user units (see the next two topics).
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `width`/`height` and `viewBox` on an `<svg>` element?" *Hint:* one says how big the window is on the page, the other says which part of the drawing appears in that window.

#### Scripting SVG through the DOM

Inline SVG elements are DOM nodes like any other (Chapter 6): they inherit from `Element` through `SVGElement`, so `querySelector`, `classList`, `addEventListener` and `remove` all work. This is what makes SVG a natural choice for data-driven graphics. There are, however, a few SVG-specific rules.

**Creating elements requires the namespace.** `document.createElement("circle")` creates an *HTML* element called `circle`, which is unknown and never renders. SVG elements must be created in the SVG namespace:

```javascript
const SVG_NS = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";

const wrong = document.createElement("circle");             // HTMLUnknownElement: invisible
const right = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, "circle");   // SVGCircleElement: renders

right.setAttribute("cx", 50);           // ordinary attributes need no namespace
right.setAttribute("cy", 50);
right.setAttribute("r", 20);
right.classList.add("dot");
document.querySelector("svg").append(right);
```

Markup strings are an alternative. When `innerHTML` or `insertAdjacentHTML` is used on an element that is already inside an `<svg>`, the HTML parser creates SVG elements correctly:

```javascript
svg.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", `<circle cx="80" cy="50" r="10" fill="tomato"/>`);
```

The usual caution from Chapter 6 applies twice over: never insert untrusted strings, because SVG can carry `<script>` elements, `on*` attributes and `javascript:` links.

**Reading and writing geometry.** Attributes are the simplest interface. SVG also exposes typed "animated" properties (`circle.r.baseVal.value`), but they are verbose and rarely used. The most useful SVG-specific methods measure geometry:

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `el.getBBox()` | Bounding box in the element's own user units (ignores its transform and stroke) |
| `el.getBoundingClientRect()` | Bounding box in viewport CSS pixels (like HTML elements) |
| `path.getTotalLength()` / `getPointAtLength(d)` | Outline length and a point along it |
| `textEl.getComputedTextLength()` | Rendered width of a text run |
| `el.getCTM()` / `el.getScreenCTM()` | Matrix from the element's coordinates to its viewport / to the screen |
| `shape.isPointInFill(point)` / `isPointInStroke(point)` | Hit tests in user units |

```javascript
// Fit a background rectangle behind a label, whatever its length
const label = svg.querySelector("#label");
const box = label.getBBox();
const bg = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, "rect");
Object.entries({ x: box.x - 4, y: box.y - 2, width: box.width + 8, height: box.height + 4, rx: 3 })
  .forEach(([k, v]) => bg.setAttribute(k, v));
bg.setAttribute("fill", "#fff8e1");
label.before(bg);                                    // insert before so it is painted underneath
```

**A data-driven bar chart.** A small helper that creates elements from an attribute object keeps chart code readable:

```javascript
function svgEl(tag, attrs = {}, parent) {
  const el = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, tag);
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(attrs)) el.setAttribute(key, value);
  if (parent) parent.append(el);
  return el;
}

function barChart(container, data, { width = 400, height = 200, pad = 24 } = {}) {
  const svg = svgEl("svg", { viewBox: `0 0 ${width} ${height}`, role: "img" });
  const max = Math.max(...data.map((d) => d.value));
  const barW = (width - pad * 2) / data.length;

  const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();   // build off-DOM, insert once
  data.forEach((d, i) => {
    const h = (d.value / max) * (height - pad * 2);
    const g = svgEl("g", { transform: `translate(${pad + i * barW}, ${height - pad})` }, frag);
    svgEl("rect", { x: 2, y: -h, width: barW - 4, height: h, class: "bar", "data-index": i }, g);
    svgEl("text", { x: barW / 2, y: 16, "text-anchor": "middle", "font-size": 11 }, g)
      .textContent = d.label;                        // textContent is safe with user data
  });
  svg.append(frag);
  container.replaceChildren(svg);
  return svg;
}

barChart(document.querySelector("#chart"), [
  { label: "Jan", value: 30 }, { label: "Feb", value: 45 }, { label: "Mar", value: 22 },
]);
```

Libraries such as **D3.js** formalise this idea with *data joins*, which match data items to existing elements and decide which elements to add, update or remove when the data changes.

**Loading an external SVG into the DOM.** An SVG in `<img>` cannot be scripted. To manipulate an external file, fetch it and insert its root:

```javascript
const text = await fetch("/img/floorplan.svg").then((r) => r.text());
const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString(text, "image/svg+xml");
const root = doc.documentElement;                   // the <svg> element
// If the file is not fully trusted, sanitise it (for example with DOMPurify) before inserting
document.querySelector("#plan").append(document.importNode(root, true));
```

**Performance limits.** Each shape is a DOM node with style, layout and event bookkeeping. A few hundred to a few thousand elements are comfortable. Tens of thousands, especially when animated, become slow, and that is the point to consider Canvas (7.2) or WebGL (7.3).

**Key Takeaways**

- Inline SVG elements are regular DOM nodes, so all DOM APIs from Chapter 6 apply.
- Create SVG elements with `document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", tag)`. `createElement` produces invisible HTML elements.
- Use `setAttribute` for geometry, and `getBBox`, `getTotalLength` and `getScreenCTM` to measure.
- Build charts from data with a small element-creation helper and a `DocumentFragment`, and set text with `textContent`.
- Sanitise untrusted SVG before inserting it, and move to Canvas or WebGL when element counts reach the tens of thousands.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create 20 circles at random positions with `createElementNS`. Then try the same with `createElement` and inspect both in DevTools to see the difference.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend `barChart` with a y-axis (line plus five tick labels) and an `update(newData)` function that reuses existing `<rect>` elements, adds missing ones and removes extra ones instead of rebuilding the chart.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `document.createElement('circle')` not draw anything inside an `<svg>`?" *Hint:* consider how the DOM decides which interface an element implements, and what the HTML parser does differently when it sees `<circle>` inside `<svg>`.

#### SVG Events and Interactivity

Because SVG shapes are DOM elements, they receive the same events as HTML elements (6.3): `click`, `pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `keydown` and so on, with capturing, bubbling and delegation. The interesting differences are in **what counts as a hit** and **which coordinates** you get.

**Hit testing follows the geometry.** An HTML element is hit anywhere inside its rectangular box. An SVG shape is hit only where it is actually painted: a click in the empty corner of a circle's bounding box does not hit the circle. The `pointer-events` property controls this precisely:

| `pointer-events` | Shape receives events when the pointer is over |
|---|---|
| `visiblePainted` (default) | Its fill or stroke, if painted (not `none`) and visible |
| `visible` | Its fill or stroke area, painted or not, if visible |
| `painted` | Painted areas, even if `visibility: hidden` |
| `fill` / `stroke` | Only the fill area / only the stroke area |
| `all` | Fill or stroke area, regardless of painting and visibility |
| `none` | Never: events pass through to what is underneath |

A frequent surprise: a shape with `fill="none"` is clickable only on its thin stroke. Use `fill="transparent"` or `pointer-events: all` to make the interior clickable, and add a wide invisible stroke to make thin lines easier to hit:

```html
<!-- Visible 1px line, plus an invisible 12px "hit area" on top -->
<g class="edge">
  <line x1="0" y1="0" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="#555"/>
  <line x1="0" y1="0" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="transparent" stroke-width="12"/>
</g>
```

`pointer-events: none` is equally useful the other way round: labels drawn over shapes should not steal clicks from the shapes beneath them.

**From screen pixels to SVG units.** `event.clientX` and `clientY` are in viewport CSS pixels, but shapes are positioned in user units, which differ whenever a `viewBox` or a transform is involved. `getScreenCTM()` returns the matrix from user units to screen pixels, so its inverse converts the other way:

```javascript
// Convert a pointer event to the user coordinates of `svg` (or of any element inside it)
function toUserSpace(event, el) {
  const point = new DOMPoint(event.clientX, event.clientY);
  return point.matrixTransform(el.getScreenCTM().inverse());
}
```

**Drag and drop with pointer events.** Pointer events (6.3) cover mouse, touch and pen with one code path. Pointer capture keeps delivering `pointermove` to the dragged element even when the pointer moves faster than the shape:

```javascript
const svg = document.querySelector("#board");
let drag = null;                                       // { el, dx, dy } while dragging

svg.addEventListener("pointerdown", (e) => {
  const el = e.target.closest(".draggable");          // event delegation on the root
  if (!el) return;
  const p = toUserSpace(e, svg);
  drag = { el, dx: p.x - +el.getAttribute("cx"), dy: p.y - +el.getAttribute("cy") };
  el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);                  // keep receiving events for this pointer
  el.classList.add("dragging");
});

svg.addEventListener("pointermove", (e) => {
  if (!drag) return;
  const p = toUserSpace(e, svg);
  drag.el.setAttribute("cx", p.x - drag.dx);          // keep the grab offset
  drag.el.setAttribute("cy", p.y - drag.dy);
});

svg.addEventListener("pointerup", () => {
  drag?.el.classList.remove("dragging");
  drag = null;
});
```

```css
.draggable { cursor: grab; touch-action: none; }      /* stop touch scrolling from stealing the drag */
.draggable.dragging { cursor: grabbing; }
.draggable:hover { stroke: black; stroke-width: 2; }  /* :hover works on shapes too */
```

**Tooltips.** A `<title>` child gives a shape a native tooltip and an accessible name with no code. For richer tooltips, position an HTML element using the shape's `getBoundingClientRect()` or the pointer's `clientX`/`clientY`.

**Keyboard and accessibility.** Shapes are not focusable by default. An interactive shape needs `tabindex="0"`, an appropriate `role` (for example `button`), an accessible name (`<title>` or `aria-label`) and keyboard handlers. Alternatively, wrap shapes in an SVG `<a href="...">`, which is focusable and keyboard-activatable like an HTML link.

```html
<circle cx="50" cy="50" r="20" class="draggable" tabindex="0" role="button"
        aria-label="Node A, press arrow keys to move"><title>Node A</title></circle>
```

**Key Takeaways**

- SVG shapes receive standard DOM events, so delegation, pointer events and pointer capture work as in HTML.
- Hit testing follows painted geometry. `fill="none"` makes interiors unclickable; `pointer-events` and transparent hit areas fix it.
- Convert `clientX`/`clientY` to user units with `new DOMPoint(x, y).matrixTransform(el.getScreenCTM().inverse())`.
- Use `<title>` for simple tooltips, and `tabindex`, `role`, accessible names and key handlers (or SVG `<a>`) for keyboard access.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Draw a 3×3 grid of squares with `fill="none"` and a stroke. Make a click on any square toggle its fill, first observing the problem with unfilled shapes and then fixing it with `pointer-events`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a node graph editor: draggable circles connected by lines whose end points follow the circles while dragging. Make it work inside an SVG with `viewBox="0 0 100 100"` displayed at 600×600 pixels, and support moving the focused node with arrow keys.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A user reports that dragging works on desktop but scrolls the page on a phone. What is happening and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* look at how the browser decides whether a touch gesture is a scroll before your handlers run.

#### SVG Animation with SMIL and CSS

Motion helps users follow changes: a bar growing to its new value, a line drawing itself, a loading spinner. SVG can be animated in three ways: declaratively inside the SVG with **SMIL** elements, with **CSS** transitions and keyframes, or imperatively with **JavaScript** (`requestAnimationFrame`, 5.1, or the Web Animations API, 6.2).

**SMIL animation elements.** SMIL (*Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language*) animations are child elements that animate their parent:

| Element | Animates |
|---|---|
| `<animate>` | Any attribute, numeric or colour (`r`, `x`, `fill`, `d`, `points`, `viewBox`, ...) |
| `<animateTransform>` | The `transform` attribute (`type="rotate"`, `scale`, `translate`, ...) |
| `<animateMotion>` | Position along a path, optionally rotating to follow it |
| `<set>` | Sets a value at a moment without interpolation |

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 120 60" width="240" height="120">
  <!-- Spinner: rotate around (30, 30) forever -->
  <circle cx="30" cy="30" r="20" fill="none" stroke="#1976d2" stroke-width="5"
          stroke-dasharray="90 40" stroke-linecap="round">
    <animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="rotate"
                      from="0 30 30" to="360 30 30" dur="1s" repeatCount="indefinite"/>
  </circle>

  <!-- Pulse on click: the animation starts when the circle is clicked -->
  <circle cx="90" cy="30" r="10" fill="tomato">
    <animate attributeName="r" values="10;20;10" dur="0.6s" begin="click"
             calcMode="spline" keySplines="0.4 0 0.2 1; 0.4 0 0.2 1"/>   <!-- easing per segment -->
  </circle>
</svg>
```

Key SMIL attributes are `attributeName`, `from`/`to` or `values` (a semicolon-separated list), `dur`, `repeatCount`, `begin` (a time, an event such as `click`, or another animation's end such as `intro.end`), `fill="freeze"` (keep the final value instead of reverting) and `keyTimes`/`keySplines` for timing control. SMIL can animate attributes that CSS cannot reach in every browser, such as `points`, `viewBox` and path data. Like CSS embedded in the file, it also keeps running inside an SVG loaded with `<img>`, where scripts never run (although an `<img>` receives no events, so `begin="click"` will not fire there). Chrome once announced its deprecation, then reversed the decision, and it is supported in all modern browsers.

**Moving along a path.**

```html
<path id="route" d="M10 80 C 60 0, 140 160, 190 80" fill="none" stroke="#ccc"/>
<polygon points="-6,-4 6,0 -6,4" fill="black">          <!-- a small arrow centred on (0,0) -->
  <animateMotion dur="3s" repeatCount="indefinite" rotate="auto">
    <mpath href="#route"/>                               <!-- follow the path, turning with it -->
  </animateMotion>
</polygon>
```

**CSS animation.** CSS transitions and keyframes (Chapter 2) work on SVG presentation properties: `fill`, `stroke`, `opacity`, `stroke-dasharray`, `stroke-dashoffset` and `transform`. SVG 2 also turned several geometry attributes into CSS properties (`cx`, `cy`, `r`, `rx`, `ry`, `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, and `d` for paths), although support for animating them, especially `d`, is not uniform, so check compatibility. CSS is usually the best choice for hover states and state transitions in inline SVG, because it lives with the rest of your styles and respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.

**The line-drawing effect.** A classic technique makes a path appear to draw itself: make the dash as long as the whole path, then slide the dash pattern from "all gap" to "all dash":

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 100" width="400" height="200">
  <path class="draw" d="M10 90 L60 30 L100 60 L190 10" fill="none" stroke="teal" stroke-width="3"/>
</svg>
```

```css
.draw {
  stroke-dasharray: var(--len);       /* one dash as long as the path, then an equal gap */
  stroke-dashoffset: var(--len);      /* shift the pattern so the gap covers the path */
  animation: draw 2s ease-out forwards;
}
@keyframes draw { to { stroke-dashoffset: 0; } }   /* slide the dash into view */

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .draw { animation: none; stroke-dashoffset: 0; }
}
```

```javascript
// Measure the path once and give CSS the exact length
const path = document.querySelector(".draw");
path.style.setProperty("--len", path.getTotalLength());
```

`pathLength="1"` on the path is an alternative: it tells the browser to treat the path as 1 unit long for dash calculations, so `stroke-dasharray: 1; stroke-dashoffset: 1` works without JavaScript.

**Morphing.** Interpolating between two `d` values (with SMIL `<animate attributeName="d">`, CSS `d`, or a library) works only if both paths have the same number and type of commands. Otherwise browsers jump instead of interpolating, and libraries such as Flubber or GSAP's MorphSVG are used to normalise the paths.

**Choosing an approach.**

| Approach | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| SMIL | Works inside `<img>`-embedded SVG, event-based sequencing, path motion, any attribute | Separate syntax, harder to control from JavaScript, no reduced-motion media query inside |
| CSS | Familiar, declarative, hover and state classes, media queries, often GPU-composited `transform`/`opacity` | Only CSS properties; geometry property support varies |
| JavaScript (rAF, Web Animations API, GSAP) | Full control, data-driven, physics, interruption and sequencing | More code; runs on the main thread unless only `transform`/`opacity` are animated via WAAPI |

**Key Takeaways**

- SVG can be animated with SMIL elements, CSS, or JavaScript.
- SMIL (`<animate>`, `<animateTransform>`, `<animateMotion>`, `<set>`) animates any attribute, sequences with `begin`, and works in SVG used as an image.
- CSS animates fill, stroke, opacity, transform and dash properties well, and should be the default for interactive inline SVG.
- The line-drawing effect animates `stroke-dashoffset` from the path length to zero.
- Morphing requires paths with matching command structure. Always provide a `prefers-reduced-motion` alternative.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a loading spinner twice: once with `<animateTransform>` and once with a CSS `@keyframes` rotation using `transform-box: fill-box`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Animate a line chart so that the line draws itself over 1.5 seconds and then each data point fades in one after another. Use `pathLength` for the line and CSS `animation-delay` computed from the point's index. Disable the effect under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
