Two more practical details: type errors do **not** stop `tsc` from emitting JavaScript unless you set `noEmitOnError`, and you can run TypeScript in the browser-based TypeScript Playground (typescriptlang.org/play) to see errors and output side by side.

**Key Takeaways**

- Dynamic typing checks types at runtime, as each operation executes; static typing checks them before the program runs.
- Static vs dynamic (when types are checked) is independent of strong vs weak (how much implicit conversion happens).
- TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript whose types are checked by the compiler and then erased, so they have no runtime cost and no runtime effect.
- Its type system is structural (shape matters, not names), gradual (`any` and plain JavaScript can be mixed in) and deliberately not fully sound.
- Data that enters at runtime (network, storage, user input) is not verified by TypeScript and needs runtime validation.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* In the TypeScript Playground, paste the JavaScript `shippingLabel` function, add the `Order` interface and a parameter annotation, and read the error. Then call the function with an object that lacks `customer.name` and read the new error.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Place JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java and C on a two-axis grid (static/dynamic, strong/weak). For each language, write a one-line code example that justifies where you placed it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Our TypeScript project compiled with zero errors, yet production crashed with `Cannot read properties of undefined`. How is that possible?" *Hint:* think about erased types, `any`, type assertions and data that crosses a runtime boundary.

#### Primitive and Special Types

TypeScript's types mirror JavaScript's runtime types (Chapter 3.1) and add a few types that exist only in the type system to describe "anything", "nothing" and "impossible".

**Primitive types.** Each JavaScript primitive has a matching lowercase type:

| Type | Values | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `string` | Text | `'hi'`, `` `Total: ${n}` `` |
| `number` | IEEE 754 doubles, including `NaN` and `Infinity` | `42`, `3.14`, `-0` |
| `bigint` | Integers of arbitrary size | `9007199254740993n` |
| `boolean` | `true`, `false` | `true` |
| `symbol` | Unique identifiers (`unique symbol` for a specific `const` one) | `Symbol('id')` |
| `undefined` | The value `undefined` | `undefined` |
| `null` | The value `null` | `null` |

Always use the lowercase names. `String`, `Number` and `Boolean` with a capital letter are the types of the rarely used wrapper *objects* (`new String('x')`) and should never appear in annotations.

```typescript
const productName: string = 'Keyboard';
const price: number = 49.9;
const orderId: bigint = 9_007_199_254_740_993n; // larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
const inStock: boolean = true;
const cacheKey: symbol = Symbol('cache');
let discount: number | undefined;               // declared now, maybe assigned later
let coupon: string | null = null;               // explicitly "no value"
```

**`null`, `undefined` and `strictNullChecks`.** Without `strictNullChecks`, `null` and `undefined` can be assigned to every type, which reproduces the "billion-dollar mistake" of Java and C. With it (part of `strict`, which is on by default in TypeScript 7), absence must be part of the type and handled explicitly:

```typescript
let title: string = 'Report';
title = null;                           // error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'string'.

const heading = document.querySelector('h1'); // HTMLHeadingElement | null
heading.textContent = 'Hi';             // error TS18047: 'heading' is possibly 'null'.
if (heading) heading.textContent = 'Hi'; // OK after the check
```

**Special types.**

| Type | Meaning | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `any` | Switches type checking off for this value | Migration from JavaScript, last-resort escape hatch |
| `unknown` | "Some value, I don't know what yet"; must be checked before use | `JSON.parse` results, `catch` variables, untrusted input |
| `never` | No value can ever have this type | Functions that always throw, impossible branches |
| `void` | "The return value should not be used" | Return type of functions without a meaningful result |
| `object` | Any non-primitive (objects, arrays, functions) | Parameters that must be objects |
| `{}` | Any value except `null` and `undefined`, *including primitives* | Rarely what you mean |

These types form a hierarchy. Think of each type as a set of values: `unknown` contains every value (the **top type**), `never` contains none (the **bottom type**), and everything else lies between them.

```text
                       unknown          top: every value is assignable TO it
                          |
  string  number  bigint  boolean  symbol  object  null  undefined
     |       |               |             /  |  \
  'GET'     42             true       {...} [...] (...) => ...    more specific types
     \       \               \           \   |   /
                         never          bottom: assignable to every type, has no values

  any  stands outside this picture: it is assignable to and from (almost) everything,
       and switches checking off wherever it flows
```

**`any` vs `unknown`.** Both accept any value; the difference is what you may do with it afterwards.

```typescript
function parseAny(text: string): any {
  return JSON.parse(text);
}
function parseSafe(text: string): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(text);
}

const a = parseAny('{"count": 1}');
a.items.map((x: number) => x * 2);    // compiles, crashes at runtime: there is no "items"
const n: number = a;                  // compiles: any is silently assignable to everything

const u = parseSafe('{"count": 1}');
u.count;                              // error TS18046: 'u' is of type 'unknown'.
if (typeof u === 'object' && u !== null && 'count' in u && typeof u.count === 'number') {
  console.log(u.count + 1);           // OK: each check narrows the type a little further
}
```

| | `any` | `unknown` |
|---|---|---|
| Accepts any value | Yes | Yes |
| Can be assigned to other types | Yes, silently | Only to `unknown` and `any` |
| Property access and calls | Allowed without checks | Error until the type is narrowed |
| Spreads to other values | Yes (`a.b.c` is also `any`) | No |
| Use it when | You must opt out of checking | You have a value you have not validated yet |

**`void` and `never`.**

```typescript
function logEvent(name: string): void {
  console.log(`[event] ${name}`);  // returns undefined; callers should ignore the result
}

function fail(message: string): never {
  throw new Error(message);        // never returns normally
}

function parsePort(value: string): number {
  const port = Number(value);
  if (Number.isInteger(port) && port > 0 && port < 65536) return port;
  return fail(`Invalid port: ${value}`); // OK: never is assignable to number
}

// A callback typed as returning void may still return a value; it is just ignored.
const ids: number[] = [];
[1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => ids.push(n)); // push returns a number, forEach expects void: allowed
```

**`object` vs `{}`.**

```typescript
let o: object = { a: 1 };
o = [1, 2];          // OK: arrays are objects
o = 'text';          // error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'object'.

let e: {} = 'text';  // OK: {} means "not null or undefined", so primitives are accepted
e = null;            // error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type '{}'.
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Use the lowercase primitive types `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `symbol`, `null` and `undefined`, never the capitalised wrapper types.
- With `strictNullChecks`, absence must be written into the type (`string | null`) and handled before use.
- `unknown` is the safe "any value" type: everything is assignable to it, but you must narrow it before using it. `any` turns checking off and spreads.
- `never` is the empty type (impossible values, functions that never return); `void` means "ignore the return value".
- `object` means non-primitive; `{}` means any value except `null` and `undefined`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Declare annotated variables for a product price, a 20-digit order number, an availability flag, a unique metadata key and a middle name that may be missing. Try assigning a wrong value to each and read the errors.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `function toNumber(value: unknown): number` that accepts numbers, numeric strings and booleans and throws a `TypeError` otherwise, without using `any`. Then change the parameter to `any` and list the mistakes the compiler no longer catches.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Explain the difference between `any`, `unknown` and `never`, and give a situation where each is the right choice." *Hint:* think of them as "checking off", "top type" and "bottom type", and ask in which direction assignment is allowed for each.

#### Type Annotations and Inference

TypeScript needs to know the type of every expression, but you do not have to write it everywhere. You **annotate** where the compiler has nothing to work from or where you want to state a contract, and let it **infer** the rest.

**Analogy:** think of labels in a shared kitchen. The jars on the shelf that everyone uses (function signatures, exported values) must be labelled. The spoonful you just took out of a labelled jar (a local variable) obviously contains the same thing, and labelling it again only adds noise.

**Annotation syntax.** A colon after the name, followed by the type:

```typescript
let count: number = 0;                          // variable
const tags: string[] = [];                      // needed: an empty array gives nothing to infer from

function greet(name: string, greeting = 'Hello'): string { // parameter, default value, return type
  return `${greeting}, ${name}`;                // greeting is inferred as string from its default
}

function log(message: string, level?: 'info' | 'warn'): void { // optional parameter
  console.log(level ?? 'info', message);        // level: 'info' | 'warn' | undefined
}

const user: { id: number; email: string; nickname?: string } = { // object type, optional property
  id: 1,
  email: 'ada@example.com',
};
```

**Where inference comes from.**

1. **Initialisers:** `let total = 0` makes `total` a `number`.
2. **Return statements:** the return type of a function is inferred from what it returns.
3. **Contextual typing:** the expected type flows *into* an expression, typically a callback.
4. **Best common type:** an array literal gets the union of its element types.

```typescript
let total = 0;                         // number
const prices = [9.99, 25, 4.5];        // number[]
const mixed = [1, 'two', null];        // (string | number | null)[]

function average(values: number[]) {   // return type inferred as number
  return values.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v, 0) / values.length;
}

// Contextual typing: no annotations on the callbacks, yet everything is typed
window.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  console.log(event.key);              // event: KeyboardEvent, inferred from 'keydown'
});
const labels = prices.map((p) => p.toFixed(2)); // p: number, labels: string[]
```

**Widening.** The inferred type depends on whether the value can change:

| Declaration | Inferred type | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `let method = 'GET'` | `string` | A `let` can be reassigned to any string |
| `const method = 'GET'` | `'GET'` | A `const` can never change, so the literal type is kept |
| `const req = { method: 'GET' }` | `{ method: string }` | Object properties are mutable, so they widen |
| `const req = { method: 'GET' } as const` | `{ readonly method: 'GET' }` | `as const` keeps literals and makes everything `readonly` |

**When to annotate.**

| Situation | Annotate? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Function parameters | Yes, unless contextually typed | Nothing to infer from; otherwise implicit `any` (an error under `noImplicitAny`) |
| Return types of exported functions | Recommended | Documents the contract and catches accidental changes to it |
| Local variables with an initialiser | No | Inference is exact |
| Empty arrays, variables assigned later | Yes | The initial value carries no information |
| Object literals that must match a known type | Yes, or use `satisfies` | Enables checks for missing and extra properties |

**Assertions and `satisfies`.** Sometimes you know more than the compiler. A **type assertion** (`value as Type`) tells it to trust you. It does nothing at runtime, and TypeScript only allows it when the two types overlap. The **non-null assertion** (`value!`) removes `null` and `undefined` from a type. The **`satisfies` operator** checks a value against a type *without* replacing the inferred type with the annotated one.

```typescript
const input = document.querySelector('#email') as HTMLInputElement; // "trust me, it exists and is an input"
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;                    // "trust me, it is not null"
const n = 'hello' as number;
// error TS2352: Conversion of type 'string' to type 'number' may be a mistake...

type Route = { path: string; auth: boolean };

// With an annotation, the variable's type becomes exactly Record<string, Route>:
const routesA: Record<string, Route> = {
  home: { path: '/', auth: false },
  admin: { path: '/admin', auth: true },
};
routesA.adminn;          // no error: any string key is allowed, the typo goes unnoticed

// With satisfies, the value is checked, but the precise inferred type is kept:
const routesB = {
  home: { path: '/', auth: false },
  admin: { path: '/admin', auth: true },
} satisfies Record<string, Route>;
routesB.adminn;          // error TS2551: Property 'adminn' does not exist on type ... Did you mean 'admin'?
routesB.admin.path;      // string
```

| Form | Checks the value? | Resulting type | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `const x: T = value` | Yes | `T` (widened to the annotation) | None, but specific information is lost |
| `const x = value satisfies T` | Yes | The inferred type of `value` | None |
| `const x = value as T` | Only that the types overlap | `T` | You can be wrong, and nothing checks it at runtime |
| `value!` | No | The type without `null`/`undefined` | A runtime `TypeError` if you are wrong |

**Key Takeaways**

- Annotate parameters, public return types and variables without a useful initialiser; let inference handle the rest.
- Contextual typing gives callbacks their parameter types from the place where they are passed.
- `let` widens literals to their base type, `const` keeps them, and `as const` keeps them deeply and makes them `readonly`.
- `as` and `!` are unchecked promises to the compiler; `satisfies` checks a value against a type and keeps the precise inferred type.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Before hovering in your editor, predict the inferred type of: `let a = 1`, `const b = 1`, `const c = [1, 'x']`, `const d = { kind: 'circle', r: 2 }`, `const e = { kind: 'circle' } as const`. Then hover over each to check.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `theme` object with `colors` and `spacing` entries. Check it once with an annotation `Record<string, string | number>` and once with `satisfies`, and compare what you can do with `theme.colors` in each case.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Should you add type annotations everywhere in a TypeScript code base?" *Hint:* talk about where inference is exact, where it has nothing to work from, and what explicit return types give you at module boundaries.

#### Arrays, Tuples and Enums

JavaScript has one array type for every purpose; TypeScript distinguishes lists of same-typed elements (arrays), fixed-length records accessed by position (tuples), and adds enums for named sets of constants.

**Arrays.** Two equivalent spellings, plus read-only variants:

```typescript
const scores: number[] = [90, 85, 77];
const names: Array<string> = ['Ada', 'Grace'];         // generic syntax, same type as string[]
const currencies: readonly string[] = ['EUR', 'USD'];  // also written ReadonlyArray<string>

scores.push(100);       // OK
currencies.push('GBP'); // error TS2339: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly string[]'.

function sum(values: readonly number[]): number { // accepts both mutable and readonly arrays
  return values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

Indexing an array gives the element type even when the index is out of range: `scores[10]` is typed `number` although its value is `undefined`. The option `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (9.3) changes the type to `number | undefined`.

**Tuples.** A tuple is an array with a fixed length where each position has its own type. It is useful for small groups of values where the position carries the meaning:

```typescript
type Point = [number, number];
type HttpHeader = [name: string, value: string];   // labelled elements, documentation only
type Range = [start: number, end?: number];        // optional last element
type Row = [id: number, ...cells: string[]];       // rest element: one number, then any number of strings

const origin: Point = [0, 0];
const header: HttpHeader = ['Content-Type', 'application/json'];
const row: Row = [7, 'Ada', 'Lovelace', 'London'];

const [hName, hValue] = header;                    // destructuring keeps the per-position types

const entries = Object.entries({ a: 1, b: 2 });   // [string, number][]

// Returning several values, as React's useState does
function useToggle(initial: boolean): [boolean, () => void] {
  let value = initial;
  return [value, () => { value = !value; }];
}
const [isOpen, toggle] = useToggle(false);

const bad: Point = [1, 2, 3];
// error TS2322: Type '[number, number, number]' is not assignable to type 'Point'.
//               Source has 3 element(s) but target allows only 2.
```

Tuples are still arrays at runtime, so `origin.push(5)` compiles. Use `readonly [number, number]` when the length must really stay fixed. `as const` on an array literal produces a readonly tuple of literal types:

```typescript
const rgb = [255, 128, 0] as const; // readonly [255, 128, 0]
```

**Enums.** An enum gives names to a set of related constants. Unlike almost every other TypeScript feature, it is not just a type: it emits a JavaScript object.

```typescript
enum Direction {
  Up,      // 0
  Down,    // 1
  Left,    // 2
  Right,   // 3
}

enum Role {
  Admin = 'ADMIN',
  Editor = 'EDITOR',
  Viewer = 'VIEWER',
}

function move(d: Direction): void {}
move(Direction.Left);   // OK
const raw: number = 42;
move(raw);              // OK, unfortunately: any number is accepted for a numeric enum

function setRole(r: Role): void {}
setRole(Role.Admin);    // OK
setRole('ADMIN');       // error TS2345: Argument of type '"ADMIN"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Role'.
```

The emitted JavaScript for `Direction` shows the runtime object, including a *reverse mapping* from numbers to names:

```javascript
var Direction;
(function (Direction) {
    Direction[Direction["Up"] = 0] = "Up";        // Direction.Up === 0 and Direction[0] === "Up"
    Direction[Direction["Down"] = 1] = "Down";
    Direction[Direction["Left"] = 2] = "Left";
    Direction[Direction["Right"] = 3] = "Right";
})(Direction || (Direction = {}));
```

Because enums generate code, they are not supported by tools that only *strip* types, such as Node.js's built-in TypeScript support (9.3), and the `erasableSyntaxOnly` option forbids them. Many teams therefore use a union of string literals or a constant object instead:

```typescript
// Alternative 1: a union of literal types (no runtime value)
type Status = 'draft' | 'published' | 'archived';

// Alternative 2: an "as const" object (runtime values plus a derived type)
const Theme = {
  Light: 'light',
  Dark: 'dark',
} as const;
type Theme = (typeof Theme)[keyof typeof Theme]; // 'light' | 'dark'

function applyTheme(t: Theme): void {
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = t;
}
applyTheme(Theme.Dark);  // OK
applyTheme('light');     // OK: plain literals are accepted too
Object.values(Theme);    // ['light', 'dark']: easy to iterate, e.g. for a <select>
```

| Option | Runtime object | Accepts plain literals | Iterable | Works with type stripping |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Numeric `enum` | Yes, with reverse mapping | Any `number` | Awkward (names and numbers mixed) | No |
| String `enum` | Yes | No | Yes | No |
| `const enum` | No (values inlined) | No | No | No, and problematic with `isolatedModules` |
| Union of string literals | No | Yes | No | Yes |
| `as const` object + derived type | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

**Key Takeaways**

- `T[]` and `Array<T>` are the same type; use `readonly T[]` for arrays that must not be mutated, especially for parameters.
- Tuples are fixed-length arrays with a type per position; they can have labels, optional and rest elements, and should be `readonly` if the length matters.
- Enums are one of the few TypeScript features that emit runtime code; numeric enums accept any number, and string enums reject plain string literals.
- Unions of string literals and `as const` objects are the common, erasable alternatives to enums.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Declare a list of product prices, a read-only list of supported language codes and an RGB color as a tuple. Try to `push` onto the read-only list and to assign a 4-element array to the RGB tuple.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Convert `enum LogLevel { Debug, Info, Warn, Error }` to an `as const` object and a derived `LogLevel` type. Write `shouldLog(level: LogLevel, threshold: LogLevel): boolean` that keeps the original ordering (*hint:* an ordered `readonly` array of levels and `indexOf`).
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why do some teams forbid `enum` in their TypeScript code?" *Hint:* consider emitted code, type-stripping tools, the assignability of numeric enums and how string enums treat plain strings.

#### Union and Intersection Types

Real data is rarely "exactly one type". An ID may be a number or a string, a function may return a result or `null`, and an entity may combine several independent traits. **Union types** (`A | B`) and **intersection types** (`A & B`) let you express these combinations.

**Types as sets of values.** The clearest way to reason about unions and intersections is to treat every type as the set of values it allows:

```text
  string                       -> { "", "a", "hello", ... }
  'GET' | 'POST'               -> { 'GET', 'POST' }
  string | number              -> all strings  plus  all numbers         union: values in A OR B
  { id: number } & { name: string }
                               -> objects having BOTH id and name        intersection: values in A AND B
  string & number              -> { }  which is  never                   no value is both
```

**Union types.** A value of type `A | B` is *either* an `A` or a `B`, and you do not know which. You can therefore only use what is valid for *every* member of the union, until you check which one you have (narrowing, see the last topic of 9.1):

```typescript
function formatId(id: string | number): string {
  id.toUpperCase();          // error TS2339: Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string | number'.
  if (typeof id === 'string') {
    return id.toUpperCase(); // id: string inside this branch
  }
  return id.toFixed(0);      // id: number here, because the string case has returned
}

formatId(42);       // OK
formatId('a-17');   // OK
formatId(true);     // error TS2345: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | number'.
```

The same rule applies to unions of object types: only properties common to all members are accessible.

```typescript
type Cat = { name: string; meow(): void };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

function greet(pet: Cat | Dog): void {
  console.log(pet.name); // OK: every member has name
  pet.bark();            // error TS2339: Property 'bark' does not exist on type 'Cat | Dog'.
}
```

Unions with `null` and `undefined` are the most common of all, and the optional chaining and nullish coalescing operators (Chapter 3.2) are designed for them:

```typescript
function cityOf(user: { address?: { city: string } } | null): string {
  return user?.address?.city ?? 'unknown';  // safe on every path
}
```

**Intersection types.** A value of type `A & B` is *both* an `A` and a `B`, so it has every property of both. Intersections are used to compose types from smaller pieces:

```typescript
type WithId = { id: string };
type Timestamped = { createdAt: Date; updatedAt: Date };
type Article = WithId & Timestamped & { title: string; body: string };

const post: Article = {
  id: 'p1',
  title: 'Hello',
  body: '...',
  createdAt: new Date(),
  updatedAt: new Date(),
};

// Object.assign is typed with an intersection of its arguments
const settings = Object.assign({ theme: 'dark' }, { fontSize: 14 });
settings.fontSize; // number: settings is { theme: string } & { fontSize: number }
```

When the parts contradict each other, the intersection silently becomes impossible instead of reporting an error:

```typescript
type A = { id: string };
type B = { id: number };
type C = A & B;         // id: string & number, which is never

const c: C = { id: 1 }; // error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'never'.
```

**Why unions seem to have "fewer" properties.** The set view explains a common confusion. A union is a *bigger* set of values, so you know *less* about any given value and fewer properties are guaranteed. An intersection is a *smaller* set of values, so you know *more* about each value and more properties are guaranteed.

| | Union `A \| B` | Intersection `A & B` |
|---|---|---|
| Values allowed | Values of A, plus values of B | Values that are both A and B |
| Size of the set of values | Larger (or equal) | Smaller (or equal) |
| Properties you can use | Only those common to A and B | All properties of A and of B |
| Typical use | Alternatives: `string \| null`, `'asc' \| 'desc'`, result-or-error | Composition: mixins, adding fields to an existing type |
| Contradictory parts | Simply both alternatives | Collapse to `never` |

**Key Takeaways**

- Think of types as sets of values: a union is the set union, an intersection is the set intersection.
- With a union you can only use what all members share until you narrow the value to one member.
- An intersection has all the properties of its parts; conflicting parts collapse to `never` without a clear error.
- `T | null` and `T | undefined` are the standard way to model optional values under `strictNullChecks`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `padLeft(value: string, padding: string | number): string`, which adds `padding` spaces when it is a number and prepends it as text when it is a string.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Define `HasEmail = { email: string }` and `HasPhone = { phone: string }`. Write `notify(contact: HasEmail | HasPhone, message: string)` that uses whichever channel is available, and `notifyBoth(contact: HasEmail & HasPhone, message: string)`. Note which property accesses the compiler rejects in each function and explain why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does a union of two object types let you access fewer properties than either type alone, while an intersection lets you access more?" *Hint:* compare the set of values allowed with the set of properties that every one of those values is guaranteed to have.

#### Type Aliases vs Interfaces

Writing `{ id: number; email: string }` everywhere would be repetitive and fragile. TypeScript offers two ways to give a type a name: **type aliases** and **interfaces**. They overlap heavily for object types, which is why choosing between them is a frequent question.

**Type aliases.** `type Name = ...` gives a name to *any* type expression: primitives, unions, tuples, functions, objects, and the computed types of 9.2.

```typescript
type UserId = string;
type Status = 'active' | 'suspended';
type Coordinates = [lat: number, lng: number];
type Comparator<T> = (a: T, b: T) => number;
type User = {
  readonly id: UserId;        // cannot be reassigned after creation
  email: string;
  status: Status;
  nickname?: string;          // optional: may be missing
};
```

**Interfaces.** `interface Name { ... }` declares an object type: properties, methods, call or construct signatures, and index signatures.

```typescript
interface Product {
  readonly sku: string;
  name: string;
  price: number;
  tags?: string[];
  discount(percent: number): number;  // method signature
}

interface PriceTable {
  [currency: string]: number;         // index signature: any string key maps to a number
}

const prices: PriceTable = { EUR: 10, USD: 11 };
```

**Extending.** Interfaces extend other interfaces; aliases combine with intersections. The two behave differently on conflicts:

```typescript
interface Animal {
  name: string;
}
interface Dog extends Animal {   // Dog has name and breed
  breed: string;
}

type AnimalT = { name: string };
type DogT = AnimalT & { breed: string };  // same shape, built with an intersection

interface BadDog extends Animal { // error TS2430: Interface 'BadDog' incorrectly extends interface 'Animal'.
  name: number;                   //   Types of property 'name' are incompatible.
}
type BadDogT = AnimalT & { name: number }; // no error here: name silently becomes never
```

**Declaration merging.** Two interface declarations with the same name in the same scope are merged into one. This is how you *augment* existing types, such as adding a property that a script tag places on `window` (9.2 covers `declare global` in modules):

```typescript
export {};  // declare global is only allowed in a module (a file with an import or export)

declare global {
  interface Window {
    analytics: { track(event: string, data?: object): void };  // merged into the built-in Window
  }
}

window.analytics.track('signup', { plan: 'pro' });  // OK

type Settings = { theme: string };
type Settings = { fontSize: number }; // error TS2300: Duplicate identifier 'Settings'.
```

**Excess property checks.** Structural typing normally allows extra properties (see the first topic). But when an object *literal* is assigned directly to a typed location, TypeScript treats extra properties as probable typos:

```typescript
interface Options {
  timeout?: number;
  retries?: number;
}

const a: Options = { timeout: 1000, retrys: 3 };
// error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'retrys' does not exist in type 'Options'.

const raw = { timeout: 1000, retrys: 3 };
const b: Options = raw;  // no error: not a fresh literal, so only the shape is compared
```

**Comparison.**

| Feature | `interface` | `type` |
|---|---|---|
| Object shapes | Yes | Yes |
| Unions, tuples, primitives, function types, mapped and conditional types | No | Yes |
| Extension | `extends`; conflicting properties are an error | `&`; conflicting properties become `never` |
| Declaration merging and augmentation | Yes | No (duplicate identifier) |
| Used with `implements` in classes | Yes | Yes, if it is an object type |
| Name shown in hovers and errors | Always the interface name | Sometimes expanded into its structure |
| Checking performance in large projects | Slightly better (`extends` relations are cached) | Large intersections are recomputed |

**Which one to use?** Both are correct for object types, and consistency matters more than the choice. A common convention:

- Use `interface` for object shapes, especially public APIs and library types that consumers may need to augment.
- Use `type` for everything else: unions, tuples, function types, and types computed from other types.
- Enforce the convention with the `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-definitions` lint rule.

**Analogy:** an interface is a contract form that can be amended by later addenda (declaration merging). A type alias is a nickname: a label you can stick on any type at all, but once written it cannot be changed.

**Key Takeaways**

- A type alias names any type; an interface declares an object type.
- `interface ... extends` reports conflicting properties, whereas an intersection silently turns them into `never`.
- Only interfaces support declaration merging, which is how built-in and library types are augmented.
- Fresh object literals get excess property checks, which catch typos in option names.
- Pick one convention (for example, interfaces for object shapes and aliases for everything else) and enforce it with a linter.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Model a `BlogPost` with a read-only `id`, a `title`, an optional `subtitle` and a `tags` array, once as an interface and once as a type alias. Try reassigning `id` and omitting `title`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create an interface `Animal { name: string }` and a `Dog` that extends it while redeclaring `name: number`. Repeat with type aliases and `&`. Explain the different outcomes and which one you would prefer to find in a code review.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose an interface over a type alias, and when is a type alias the only option?" *Hint:* think about augmenting third-party types, unions and computed types.

#### Literal Types and Type Narrowing

Many values in a program come from a small, fixed set: an HTTP method, a button size, a log level. **Literal types** describe such sets exactly, and **narrowing** is how TypeScript follows your `if` statements to work out which specific type a value has at each point in the code.

**Literal types.** Any string, number or boolean literal can be used as a type that contains only that value. Combined in a union, literal types describe a finite set of options, and the editor autocompletes them:

```typescript
type HttpMethod = 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';
type DiceRoll = 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6;

function request(url: string, method: HttpMethod): void {}

request('/api/users', 'GET');   // OK
request('/api/users', 'get');   // error TS2345: Argument of type '"get"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'HttpMethod'.
```

**Losing literal types through widening.** As seen in the inference topic, `let` and object properties widen literals to their base type, which causes a classic error:

```typescript
const req = { url: '/api/users', method: 'GET' };  // method: string
request(req.url, req.method);
// error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'HttpMethod'.

// Three fixes:
const req1: { url: string; method: HttpMethod } = { url: '/api/users', method: 'GET' }; // annotate
const req2 = { url: '/api/users', method: 'GET' } as const;                             // keep all literals
const req3 = { url: '/api/users', method: 'GET' as const };                             // keep one literal
request(req2.url, req2.method); // OK
```

**Template literal types** build string types from other types, using the same syntax as template strings:

```typescript
type CssLength = `${number}px` | `${number}rem` | `${number}%`;
type Side = 'top' | 'right' | 'bottom' | 'left';
type MarginProperty = `margin-${Side}`; // 'margin-top' | 'margin-right' | 'margin-bottom' | 'margin-left'

const width: CssLength = '12px';        // OK
const height: CssLength = '12';         // error TS2322: Type '"12"' is not assignable to type 'CssLength'.
```

**Narrowing.** When a value has a union type, TypeScript performs **control flow analysis**: it follows every branch, `return`, `throw` and assignment, and computes a more specific type for the variable at each point.

```text
function describe(x: string | number | null)
            |
   if (x === null) -------------------> x: null          -> return 'nothing'
            |
            v   x: string | number
   if (typeof x === 'string') --------> x: string        -> return x.trim()
            |
            v   x: number
   return x.toFixed(2)
```

```typescript
function describe(x: string | number | null): string {
  if (x === null) return 'nothing';
  if (typeof x === 'string') return x.trim();
  return x.toFixed(2);  // only number is left
}
```

**Narrowing techniques.**

| Technique | Example | What remains in the true branch |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof` | `typeof x === 'string'` | One of `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `symbol`, `undefined`, `object`, `function` |
| Truthiness | `if (x)` | The type without `null`, `undefined` and falsy literals |
| Equality | `x === null`, `x === 'GET'` | The matching member(s) |
| `in` | `'bark' in pet` | Members that have that property |
| `instanceof` | `err instanceof TypeError` | Instances of that class |
| `Array.isArray` | `Array.isArray(v)` | Array members |
| Assignment | `x = 'a'` | The type of the assigned value, within the declared type |
| Type predicates, discriminants | `isUser(v)`, `switch (s.kind)` | See 9.2 |

```typescript
function area(shape: number | [number, number] | { w: number; h: number } | null): number {
  if (!shape) return 0;                          // removes null (and the number 0)
  if (typeof shape === 'number') return shape ** 2; // a square side
  if (Array.isArray(shape)) return shape[0] * shape[1];
  return shape.w * shape.h;                      // only the object is left
}

function handleError(err: unknown): string {
  if (err instanceof Error) return err.message;  // err: Error
  if (typeof err === 'string') return err;       // err: string
  return 'Unknown error';
}
```

**Pitfalls.**

```typescript
// 1. typeof null is "object" (Chapter 3.1), so this does not exclude null
function keys(value: object | null): string[] {
  if (typeof value === 'object') {
    return Object.keys(value);
    // error TS2769: No overload matches this call... ('value' is possibly 'null')
  }
  return [];
}

// 2. Truthiness also removes valid falsy values
function label(count: number | undefined): string {
  if (count) return `${count} items`;  // 0 falls through to the "no data" branch
  return 'no data';
}

// 3. Narrowing of a mutable property is not kept inside a callback,
//    because the property might change before the callback runs
function schedule(config: { delay?: number }): void {
  if (config.delay !== undefined) {
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log(config.delay.toFixed(0));
      // error TS18048: 'config.delay' is possibly 'undefined'.
    }, 0);
    const delay = config.delay;        // fix: copy the narrowed value into a const
    setTimeout(() => console.log(delay.toFixed(0)), 0);
  }
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Literal types describe exact values; unions of literals model fixed sets of options with autocompletion.
- Literals widen in `let` variables and object properties; use an annotation or `as const` to keep them.
- Template literal types build string patterns such as `` `${number}px` ``.
- Control flow analysis narrows union types through `typeof`, truthiness, equality, `in`, `instanceof`, `Array.isArray` and assignments.
- Watch out for `typeof null === 'object'`, truthiness removing `0` and `''`, and narrowing that is lost inside callbacks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Define `type Size = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'` and `buttonClass(size: Size): string`. Call it with a value from `let s = 'md'` and fix the resulting error in two different ways.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `formatValue(v: string | number | boolean | Date | null | string[]): string` and use at least five different narrowing techniques. Then add `bigint` to the union and confirm the compiler tells you where handling is missing (*hint:* declare an explicit return type).
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does TypeScript know that `x` is a `string` inside `if (typeof x === 'string') { ... }`, and why can that knowledge disappear inside a callback?" *Hint:* control flow analysis, and the fact that a callback may run later, after other code has changed the value.

<a id="92-advanced-typing"></a>
### 9.2 Advanced Typing

This subchapter covers the tools for writing reusable and precise types: generics and their constraints, function and constructor types, type guards and discriminated unions, the built-in utility types, type-level programming with mapped and conditional types, and declaration files that describe code TypeScript did not compile itself.

#### Generics and Type Parameters

Suppose you write a function that returns the first element of an array. It works for arrays of anything, but how do you type it? With `any`, the function accepts everything but forgets what it was given. Writing one version per element type does not scale. **Generics** solve this: a function (or type, or class) takes a **type parameter**, a placeholder that is filled with a concrete type each time it is used.

**Analogy:** a function's ordinary parameters are placeholders for *values*; type parameters are placeholders for *types*. A generic `Box<T>` is like a shipping container with a blank label: the container works the same for every cargo, and the label is filled in when it is loaded, so whoever unloads it knows what is inside.

```typescript
function firstAny(items: any[]): any {
  return items[0];
}
const a = firstAny(['x', 'y']);   // any: the information "string" is lost

function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
const s = first(['x', 'y']);      // string | undefined (T inferred as string)
const d = first([new Date()]);    // Date | undefined
const n = first<number>([1, 2]);  // explicit type argument, rarely needed
```

The key property is that the type parameter *connects* the input and the output: whatever element type goes in comes back out.

**How type arguments are inferred.** At each call, TypeScript infers type parameters from the arguments, including from what a callback returns:

```typescript
function map<T, U>(items: readonly T[], fn: (item: T, index: number) => U): U[] {
  const result: U[] = [];
  items.forEach((item, i) => result.push(fn(item, i)));
  return result;
}

const lengths = map(['a', 'bb', 'ccc'], (s) => s.length); // number[]
```

```text
map(['a', 'bb', 'ccc'],  (s) => s.length)
         |                 |        |
     T = string      s: string    U = number      (U comes from the callback's return type)
result type: U[]  =  number[]
```

**Generic types, interfaces and classes.** Types can be parameterised too, and many built-in types already are: `Array<T>`, `Promise<T>`, `Map<K, V>`, `Set<T>`, `Record<K, V>`.

```typescript
interface ApiResponse<T> {
  data: T;
  status: number;
  receivedAt: Date;
}

type Pair<A, B> = [first: A, second: B];

class Stack<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];

  push(item: T): void {
    this.items.push(item);
  }
  pop(): T | undefined {
    return this.items.pop();
  }
  get size(): number {
    return this.items.length;
  }
}

const history = new Stack<string>();   // explicit: there is no constructor argument to infer from
history.push('/home');
history.push(42);                      // error TS2345: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'.

const userResponse: ApiResponse<{ id: number; name: string }> = {
  data: { id: 1, name: 'Ada' },
  status: 200,
  receivedAt: new Date(),
};
const entry: Pair<string, number> = ['retries', 3];
const cache = new Map<string, Promise<Response>>(); // nested generics
```

**Generics and asynchronous code.** An `async` function always returns `Promise<T>`, and generic helpers are a common way to type HTTP calls. Be aware of what such a helper does and does not guarantee:

```typescript
async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return (await res.json()) as T;  // T is a promise you make, not something TypeScript verifies
}

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}
const me = await getJson<User>('/api/me'); // me: User, but only as trustworthy as the server
```

**The rule of thumb for type parameters.** A type parameter should relate at least two things, usually appearing in two places (two parameters, or a parameter and the return type). A type parameter that appears only once is a disguised `any` or a disguised type assertion:

```typescript
// Bad: T appears only in the return type; callers can pick any T and nothing checks it
function parse<T>(json: string): T {
  return JSON.parse(json);
}
const port = parse<number>('"not a number"'); // compiles; port is actually a string

// Better: return unknown and validate (type guards, later in 9.2)
function parseSafe(json: string): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(json);
}
```

One syntax detail: in `.tsx` files, `<T>` before an arrow function is read as a JSX tag. Write `<T,>(value: T) => value` or use a constraint (next topic).

**Key Takeaways**

- Generics add type parameters to functions, interfaces, type aliases and classes, so one definition works for many types while keeping track of which one is in use.
- Type arguments are usually inferred from the call's arguments; specify them explicitly only when there is nothing to infer from.
- A good type parameter links inputs to outputs; one that appears only once is a disguised `any`.
- Generic HTTP helpers such as `getJson<T>` are only assertions: the response is not checked at runtime.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `last<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined` and `wrap<T>(value: T): T[]`. Hover over the results of a few calls to see what `T` was inferred as.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement `groupBy<T>(items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string): Record<string, T[]>` and use it to group a list of orders by customer. Then write a generic `Queue<T>` class with `enqueue`, `dequeue`, `peek` and `size`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is wrong with the signature `function parse<T>(json: string): T`?" *Hint:* count how many times `T` appears and ask who checks that the parsed value really is a `T`.

#### Constraints and Default Type Arguments

Inside a generic function, an unconstrained `T` could be *anything*, so TypeScript lets you do almost nothing with it: you cannot read `.length` or call a method. A **constraint** (`T extends Something`) limits which types callers may supply, and in exchange lets the function use the members of `Something`. A **default type argument** (`T = Something`) says which type to use when none is given or inferred.

**Constraints with `extends`.** `T extends X` means "T must be assignable to X". Inside the function, `T` can be used as an `X`; outside, the caller still gets back their specific type:

```typescript
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length >= b.length ? a : b;   // OK: every T has a length
}

longest('abc', 'de');        // string
longest([1, 2], [1, 2, 3]);  // number[]: the specific type is preserved, not { length: number }
longest(10, 20);             // error TS2345: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type '{ length: number; }'.
```

**`keyof` constraints.** `keyof T` is the union of the property names of `T`, and `T[K]` is the type of property `K` in `T` (both are covered in detail later in 9.2). Together with a constraint they produce a type-safe property getter:

```typescript
function getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}

const user = { id: 1, name: 'Ada', admin: false };
getProperty(user, 'name');   // string
getProperty(user, 'admin');  // boolean
getProperty(user, 'email');  // error TS2345: Argument of type '"email"' is not assignable to parameter of type '"admin" | "id" | "name"'.
```

**A constraint is a lower bound, not the type itself.** The caller chooses `T`, and it may be a subtype with more properties than the constraint. You therefore cannot return "some value that matches the constraint" where a `T` is expected:

```typescript
function withMinLength<T extends { length: number }>(value: T, min: number): T {
  if (value.length >= min) return value;
  return { length: min };
  // error TS2322: Type '{ length: number; }' is not assignable to type 'T'.
  //   '{ length: number; }' is assignable to the constraint of type 'T', but 'T' could be
  //   instantiated with a different subtype of constraint '{ length: number; }'.
}
```

If the caller passed a `string`, the function would return a plain object and break the promise that the result is a string.

**Constraints that relate type parameters.** One type parameter can be constrained by another, and object constraints are common for merge-style helpers:

```typescript
function merge<T extends object, U extends object>(a: T, b: U): T & U {
  return { ...a, ...b };
}
const merged = merge({ host: 'localhost' }, { port: 8080 }); // { host: string } & { port: number }

function copyFields<T extends U, U extends object>(target: T, source: U): T {
  return Object.assign(target, source);   // source may only contain fields that target also has
}
```

**Default type arguments.** A type parameter can have a default, used when the type is written without arguments or when nothing can be inferred:

```typescript
interface ApiError {
  code: string;
  message: string;
}

type Result<T, E = ApiError> =
  | { ok: true; value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

const r1: Result<number> = { ok: true, value: 42 };                        // E defaults to ApiError
const r2: Result<number, string> = { ok: false, error: 'timeout' };        // E given explicitly

function createStore<S = Record<string, unknown>>(initial?: S) {
  let state = initial ?? ({} as S);
  return {
    get: (): S => state,
    set: (next: S): void => { state = next; },
  };
}
createStore();              // S = Record<string, unknown>: nothing to infer, the default applies
createStore({ count: 0 });  // S = { count: number }: inference wins over the default
```

Rules for defaults: parameters with defaults must come after those without, a default must satisfy the parameter's constraint (`<T extends object = {}>`), and inferred types take precedence over defaults.

**`const` type parameters.** Generic inference normally widens literals. Adding the `const` modifier to a type parameter infers the narrowest type, as if the caller had written `as const`:

```typescript
function defineRoutes<const T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T): T {
  return paths;
}
const routes = defineRoutes(['/', '/about', '/blog']);
// readonly ['/', '/about', '/blog'] instead of string[]
type RoutePath = (typeof routes)[number]; // '/' | '/about' | '/blog'
```

**Blocking inference with `NoInfer`.** Sometimes a parameter should be *checked* against `T` but not *contribute* to inferring it:

```typescript
function createMachine<S extends string>(states: S[], initial: NoInfer<S>): S {
  return initial;
}
createMachine(['idle', 'loading', 'done'], 'idle');  // OK
createMachine(['idle', 'loading', 'done'], 'idel');
// error TS2345: Argument of type '"idel"' is not assignable to parameter of type '"done" | "idle" | "loading"'.
// Without NoInfer, S would be inferred as 'idle' | 'loading' | 'done' | 'idel' and the typo accepted.
```

| Pattern | Meaning | Example use |
|---|---|---|
| `<T extends string>` | Only string types (keeps literals) | Event names, route paths |
| `<T extends object>` | Only non-primitive types | Merging, cloning |
| `<K extends keyof T>` | One of `T`'s property names | Getters, setters, `pluck`, `sortBy` |
| `<F extends (...args: any[]) => unknown>` | Any function | Wrappers such as `debounce`, `memoize` |
| `<T = Default>` | Fallback when nothing is given or inferred | Library types such as `ApiResponse<T = unknown>` |
| `<const T>` | Infer literal and tuple types | Configuration objects, route tables |
| `NoInfer<T>` | Check against `T` without inferring from here | Default values, initial states |

**Key Takeaways**

- `T extends X` restricts what callers may pass and lets the implementation use `X`'s members, while callers keep their specific type.
- `K extends keyof T` with `T[K]` produces type-safe access to properties by name.
- A constraint is a lower bound: you cannot return an arbitrary value of the constraint type where `T` is expected.
- Default type arguments apply when a type is written without arguments or nothing can be inferred; inference wins over defaults.
- `const` type parameters keep literal types, and `NoInfer` stops a parameter from influencing inference.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][]` and use it to extract the `email` of every user in an array. Try to pluck a key that does not exist.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Using the `Result<T, E = ApiError>` type above, write `parseJson(text: string): Result<unknown, SyntaxError>` and `safeDivide(a: number, b: number): Result<number>` (relying on the default for `E`). Write a caller that handles both cases without type assertions.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does TypeScript reject returning `{ length: min }` from a function declared as `<T extends { length: number }>(value: T, min: number) => T`?" *Hint:* who chooses `T`, and what could `T` be besides `{ length: number }`?

#### Function and Constructor Types

Functions are values in JavaScript (Chapter 3.3): they are passed as callbacks, stored in objects and returned from other functions. TypeScript therefore needs a way to write the type of a function, and also the type of a *class* used as a value.

**Function type expressions.** The most common form looks like an arrow function with types instead of a body:

```typescript
type BinaryOp = (a: number, b: number) => number;
type Predicate<T> = (value: T) => boolean;

const add: BinaryOp = (a, b) => a + b;    // a and b are contextually typed as number
const isEven: Predicate<number> = (n) => n % 2 === 0;

function applyAll(values: number[], op: BinaryOp, initial: number): number {
  return values.reduce(op, initial);
}
```

Parameter names in a function type are documentation only. A function with *fewer* parameters is assignable to a type with more, because JavaScript ignores extra arguments: that is why `[1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => ...)` is valid although `forEach` passes three arguments.

**Call signatures and method signatures.** When a function also has properties, describe it with an object type containing a **call signature**. Methods inside object types can be written in method or property syntax:

```typescript
interface Formatter {
  (value: number): string;   // call signature: the object can be called
  locale: string;            // and it also has properties
}

const euro = ((value: number) => `${value.toFixed(2)} EUR`) as Formatter;
euro.locale = 'it-IT';
euro(9.5); // "9.50 EUR"

interface Repository {
  findById(id: string): Promise<User | null>;    // method syntax
  save: (user: User) => Promise<void>;           // property syntax
}
interface User {
  id: string;
}
```

**Optional, default, rest and `this` parameters.**

```typescript
function buildUrl(path: string, query?: Record<string, string>): string {  // optional
  return query ? `${path}?${new URLSearchParams(query)}` : path;
}

function sumAll(...values: number[]): number {          // rest parameter: always an array type
  return values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

function onClick(this: HTMLButtonElement, event: MouseEvent): void {
  this.disabled = true;     // `this` is typed by a fake first parameter, erased in the output
}
document.querySelector('button')?.addEventListener('click', onClick);
```

**Overloads.** When the *return type* depends on *which arguments* are passed, declare several **overload signatures** followed by one implementation. Callers only see the overloads; the implementation signature must be compatible with all of them:

```typescript
function parseDate(iso: string): Date;
function parseDate(timestamp: number): Date;
function parseDate(year: number, month: number, day: number): Date;
function parseDate(a: string | number, month?: number, day?: number): Date { // implementation: not callable directly
  if (typeof a === 'string') return new Date(a);
  if (month !== undefined && day !== undefined) return new Date(a, month - 1, day);
  return new Date(a);
}

parseDate('2026-10-03');  // OK
parseDate(2026, 10, 3);   // OK
parseDate(2026, 10);
// error TS2575: No overload expects 2 arguments, but overloads do exist that expect either 1 or 3 arguments.
```

Prefer a union parameter when the return type is the same in all cases; overloads are for "different inputs, different outputs", such as `document.createElement('img')` returning an `HTMLImageElement`.

**Parameter variance.** A function that handles only dogs cannot stand in for a function that must handle any animal, because someone might call it with a cat. With `strictFunctionTypes` (part of `strict`), TypeScript enforces this for function-typed properties:

```typescript
interface Animal {
  name: string;
}
interface Dog extends Animal {
  bark(): void;
}

type AnimalHandler = (animal: Animal) => void;
const handleDog = (dog: Dog): void => dog.bark();

const handler: AnimalHandler = handleDog;
// error TS2322: Type '(dog: Dog) => void' is not assignable to type 'AnimalHandler'.
//   Types of parameters 'dog' and 'animal' are incompatible.
```

Parameters declared with *method syntax* (`handle(animal: Animal): void`) are checked more loosely (bivariantly) for compatibility with existing JavaScript patterns, which is one reason some style guides prefer property syntax for callbacks.

**Constructor types.** A class name is two things at once: a *type* describing its instances, and a *value*, the constructor function. To accept a class as an argument, use a **construct signature** (`new (...) => T`):

```typescript
class Logger {
  log(msg: string): void {
    console.log(msg);
  }
}

function create<T>(ctor: new () => T): T {
  return new ctor();
}
const logger = create(Logger);       // Logger

let instance: Logger = new Logger(); // "Logger" as a type: the instance side
let klass: typeof Logger = Logger;   // "typeof Logger": the constructor (static) side
type FromCtor = InstanceType<typeof Logger>; // Logger again
```

| Written as | Means | Example value |
|---|---|---|
| `Logger` | The type of instances | `new Logger()` |
| `typeof Logger` | The type of the class itself (constructor plus static members) | `Logger` |
| `new () => Logger` | Anything constructible without arguments that produces a `Logger` | `Logger`, or a subclass |
| `abstract new () => Logger` | The same, but abstract classes are also accepted | An abstract base class |

Construct signatures enable **mixins**, functions that take a class and return an extended class:

```typescript
type Constructor<T = {}> = new (...args: any[]) => T;

function Timestamped<TBase extends Constructor>(Base: TBase) {
  return class extends Base {
    createdAt = new Date();
  };
}

class Person {
  name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

const TimestampedPerson = Timestamped(Person);
const p = new TimestampedPerson('Ada');
console.log(p.name, p.createdAt.toISOString()); // both members are typed
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Function types are written `(param: Type) => Return`; use a call signature in an object type when the function also has properties.
- Functions with fewer parameters are assignable to function types with more parameters.
- Use overloads only when the return type depends on the arguments; otherwise use a union parameter.
- Under `strictFunctionTypes`, function-typed properties check parameters contravariantly; method syntax is checked more loosely.
- A class name used as a type means its instances; `typeof ClassName` and `new (...) => T` describe the constructor.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Define `type Predicate<T> = (value: T) => boolean` and write `filterBy<T>(items: readonly T[], ...predicates: Predicate<T>[]): T[]`, which keeps items that pass every predicate.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write overloads for `createElement(tag: 'a'): HTMLAnchorElement`, `createElement(tag: 'img'): HTMLImageElement` and `createElement(tag: string): HTMLElement`. Then replace them with a single generic signature using `K extends keyof HTMLElementTagNameMap` and compare the two versions.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between using `Logger` and `typeof Logger` as a type annotation?" *Hint:* a class declaration creates both an instance type and a constructor value with its own static members.

#### Type Guards and Discriminated Unions

The narrowing techniques of 9.1 work with JavaScript operators that the compiler understands, such as `typeof` and `instanceof`. Real programs also need *custom* checks ("is this object a valid `User`?") and need to model data that can be in one of several well-defined states. **Type guards** teach the compiler about custom checks, and **discriminated unions** model alternatives so that narrowing becomes automatic.

**User-defined type guards.** A function whose return type is a **type predicate**, `value is Type`, tells the compiler that when the function returns `true`, the argument has that type:

```typescript
interface User {
  id: number;
  email: string;
}

function isUser(value: unknown): value is User {
  return (
    typeof value === 'object' && value !== null &&
    'id' in value && typeof value.id === 'number' &&
    'email' in value && typeof value.email === 'string'
  );
}

const data: unknown = await (await fetch('/api/me')).json();
if (isUser(data)) {
  console.log(data.email);  // data: User
} else {
  console.error('Unexpected response', data);
}
```

The compiler trusts the predicate completely: if the function body checks the wrong things, the "guarantee" is wrong. Keep guards small and test them, or generate them from a schema library (9.3).

**Assertion functions.** Instead of returning a boolean, an assertion function throws when the check fails, and narrows the type for all code after the call:

```typescript
function assertDefined<T>(value: T, name: string): asserts value is NonNullable<T> {
  if (value === null || value === undefined) {
    throw new Error(`${name} is missing`);
  }
}

const root = document.getElementById('app');   // HTMLElement | null
assertDefined(root, '#app');
root.append('Loaded');                         // root: HTMLElement from here on
```

**Inferred type predicates.** Since TypeScript 5.5, simple arrow functions like `x => x !== null` are recognised as type guards automatically, which fixes a long-standing annoyance with `filter`:

```typescript
const maybeNumbers = [1, null, 3, undefined, 5];
const numbers = maybeNumbers.filter((x) => x != null); // number[] (previously (number | null | undefined)[])
```

**Discriminated unions.** A discriminated (or *tagged*) union is a union of object types that share one property, the **discriminant**, whose type is a different literal in each member. Checking that property narrows the whole object:

```text
                         RemoteData<T>
    status:  'idle'   |   'loading'   |   'success'     |   'error'          <- discriminant
               |              |               |                 |
              { }            { }        { data: T }     { error: Error }     <- member-specific fields

    switch (state.status) selects exactly one member, so only its fields are accessible
```

```typescript
type RemoteData<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error };

function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled case: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

function render(state: RemoteData<User[]>): string {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
      return 'Press "Load" to fetch users';
    case 'loading':
      return 'Loading...';
    case 'success':
      return `${state.data.length} users`;       // data exists only in this member
    case 'error':
      return `Failed: ${state.error.message}`;   // error exists only in this member
    default:
      return assertNever(state);                 // state: never if every case is handled
  }
}
```

**Exhaustiveness checking.** The `default` branch receives whatever has not been handled. If every member is handled, that is `never`, and the call compiles. If someone later adds `{ status: 'cancelled' }` to the union, the compiler points to every `switch` that forgot it:

```text
error TS2345: Argument of type '{ status: "cancelled"; }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'.
```

**Making illegal states unrepresentable.** Compare a discriminated union with the common "bag of flags" design:

```typescript
// Flags: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations, most of them meaningless
interface LoadStateFlags {
  isLoading: boolean;
  data?: User[];
  error?: Error;
}
const nonsense: LoadStateFlags = { isLoading: true, data: [], error: new Error('?') }; // compiles

// Discriminated union: exactly the 4 valid states, and nothing else compiles
const invalid: RemoteData<User[]> = { status: 'loading', data: [] };
// error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'data' does not exist in type '{ status: "loading"; }'.
```

The same pattern models Redux-style actions, WebSocket messages, form steps and parse results. Requirements: the discriminant must be a property with literal types (strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, `undefined`) present in every member, and you narrow with `===`, `!==` or `switch`.

| Guard kind | Syntax | Narrows | Checked by the compiler? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Built-in operators | `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, `===` | Automatically | Yes |
| Type predicate | `(v: unknown): v is T` | In the `true` branch (and `false` branch) | No: you write the check |
| Inferred predicate | `(x) => x !== null` | Automatically | Yes |
| Assertion function | `asserts v is T` | After the call | No: you write the check |
| Discriminant check | `switch (v.kind)` | Automatically | Yes |

**Key Takeaways**

- A type predicate (`value is T`) turns a boolean function into a type guard; the compiler trusts it, so it must be correct.
- Assertion functions (`asserts value is T`) throw on failure and narrow the type for the code that follows.
- Discriminated unions use a shared literal property to tell members apart; checking it narrows the whole object.
- A `never`-typed default branch gives exhaustiveness checking: adding a new member breaks the build wherever it is not handled.
- Prefer discriminated unions over combinations of boolean flags to make invalid states impossible to construct.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `isString(value: unknown): value is string` and use it with `filter` on an `unknown[]` to obtain a `string[]`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Model `Shape` as a discriminated union of `circle`, `rectangle` and `triangle` with a `kind` field. Write `area(shape: Shape): number` with an exhaustive `switch`. Add `square` to the union and fix every error the compiler reports.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you type the state of a checkout form so that it can never show a success message and an error message at the same time?" *Hint:* list the valid states, give each a literal tag and only the fields that make sense in it.

#### Utility Types

Applications describe the same entity in several variations: the full `User` stored in the database, the subset a client sends to create one, the partial update a `PATCH` request carries, and the public version without the password hash. Writing each variation by hand duplicates fields that then drift apart. **Utility types** are built-in generic types that *derive* new types from existing ones, so there is a single source of truth.

**Analogy:** a database table and its views. The `User` interface is the table; `Pick`, `Omit` and `Partial` are views over it. Add a column to the table and every view that should include it updates automatically.

**Deriving types from a model.**

```typescript
interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  name: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer';
  createdAt: Date;
}

type NewUser = Omit<User, 'id' | 'createdAt'>;             // what a client sends to create a user
type UserPatch = Partial<Pick<User, 'email' | 'name'>>;   // the fields a PATCH request may change
type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>;              // safe to send to the browser
type FrozenUser = Readonly<User>;                          // no property can be reassigned

type Permissions = Record<User['role'], string[]>;         // one entry per role, none forgotten
const permissions: Permissions = {
  admin: ['*'],
  editor: ['posts:write'],
};
// error TS2741: Property 'viewer' is missing in type '{ admin: string[]; editor: string[]; }'
//               but required in type 'Permissions'.

function updateUser(user: User, patch: UserPatch): User {
  return { ...user, ...patch };
}
updateUser({} as User, { role: 'admin' });
// error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'role' does not exist in type 'Partial<Pick<User, "email" | "name">>'.
```

**Working with unions.**

```typescript
type Role = User['role'];                              // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'
type StaffRole = Exclude<Role, 'viewer'>;              // 'admin' | 'editor'
type DomEvent = 'click' | 'keydown' | 'keyup' | 'focus';
type KeyEvent = Extract<DomEvent, `key${string}`>;     // 'keydown' | 'keyup'
type MaybeName = string | null | undefined;
type Name = NonNullable<MaybeName>;                    // string
```

**Deriving types from functions and classes.** The type query `typeof` turns a value (such as a function) into its type, and utility types pick it apart. This keeps types in sync with code that already exists:

```typescript
async function fetchUser(id: string, opts?: { signal?: AbortSignal }) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, opts);
  return (await res.json()) as PublicUser;
}

type FetchUserArgs = Parameters<typeof fetchUser>;              // [id: string, opts?: { signal?: AbortSignal }]
type FetchUserResult = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>>;   // PublicUser

class HttpClient {
  constructor(readonly baseUrl: string, readonly timeoutMs = 5000) {}
}
type ClientArgs = ConstructorParameters<typeof HttpClient>;     // [baseUrl: string, timeoutMs?: number]
type Client = InstanceType<typeof HttpClient>;                  // HttpClient
```

**Reference table.**

| Utility type | Result | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Partial<T>` | All properties optional | Update payloads, options objects |
| `Required<T>` | All properties required | Options after defaults are applied |
| `Readonly<T>` | All properties `readonly` | Immutable state |
| `Pick<T, K>` | Only the keys `K` | Summary or projection types |
| `Omit<T, K>` | All keys except `K` | Removing secrets or server-generated fields |
| `Record<K, V>` | An object with keys `K` and values `V` | Lookup tables, exhaustive maps |
| `Exclude<U, X>` | Members of union `U` not assignable to `X` | Removing options |
| `Extract<U, X>` | Members of union `U` assignable to `X` | Selecting options |
| `NonNullable<T>` | `T` without `null` and `undefined` | After validation |
| `ReturnType<F>` | Return type of function type `F` | Types of factory results |
| `Parameters<F>` | Parameter types of `F` as a tuple | Wrappers that forward arguments |
| `ConstructorParameters<C>` | Constructor parameter types as a tuple | Factories |
| `InstanceType<C>` | Instance type of a constructor type | Dependency injection containers |
| `Awaited<T>` | The value a promise resolves to (recursively) | Results of `async` functions |
| `NoInfer<T>` | `T`, excluded from inference | See constraints and defaults |
| `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize` | Transformed string literal types | Event and method names |

**Caveats.**

```typescript
// 1. Readonly and Partial are shallow: nested objects are unaffected
type Settings = { theme: { color: string } };
const s: Readonly<Settings> = { theme: { color: 'red' } };
s.theme = { color: 'blue' };   // error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'theme' because it is a read-only property.
s.theme.color = 'blue';        // allowed: theme's own properties are still mutable

// 2. Omit does not check that the keys exist; Pick does
type NoSecret = Omit<User, 'passwrodHash'>;  // typo, no error, and passwordHash is still included
type OnlyName = Pick<User, 'nmae'>;
// error TS2344: Type '"nmae"' does not satisfy the constraint 'keyof User'.
```

When a derived type grows complicated, give its intermediate steps names: `type UserPatch = Partial<Pick<User, EditableField>>` with `type EditableField = 'email' | 'name'` reads better than one long expression.

**Key Takeaways**

- Utility types derive variations of a type from a single source of truth instead of duplicating fields.
- `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, `Omit` and `Record` transform object types; `Exclude`, `Extract` and `NonNullable` filter unions.
- `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, `Awaited`, `InstanceType` and `ConstructorParameters` extract types from existing functions and classes via `typeof`.
- `Readonly` and `Partial` are shallow, and `Omit` does not report misspelled keys.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Given `interface Product { id: number; name: string; price: number; description: string; stock: number }`, derive `ProductDraft` (no `id`), `ProductSummary` (`id`, `name`, `price`) and `ProductUpdate` (`id` required, everything else optional).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `toPublic(user: User): PublicUser` that removes `passwordHash` with object rest destructuring. Then write a `Record<Role, (user: PublicUser) => boolean>` of access checks and confirm the compiler complains when a role is missing.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does `Omit<User, 'pasword'>` compile without an error while `Pick<User, 'pasword'>` does not, and how would you write a stricter `Omit`?" *Hint:* compare the constraints on the key parameter of each type (`keyof any` vs `keyof T`).

#### Mapped and Conditional Types

Utility types are not magic: they are ordinary generic types written in TypeScript's own type language, using **mapped types** (loops over keys) and **conditional types** (if-then-else on types). Learning these tools lets you read library type definitions and write your own transformations.

**The building blocks.** Three type operators turn values and object types into other types:

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof value` | The type of a value (in a type position) | `typeof config` |
| `keyof T` | Union of the property names of `T` | `keyof User` is `'id' \| 'email' \| ...` |
| `T[K]` | Type of property `K` in `T` (indexed access) | `User['role']` |
| `T[number]` | Element type of an array or tuple type | `(typeof roles)[number]` |

```typescript
const config = { apiUrl: 'https://api.example.com', retries: 3, debug: false };

type Config = typeof config;        // { apiUrl: string; retries: number; debug: boolean }
type ConfigKey = keyof Config;      // 'apiUrl' | 'retries' | 'debug'
type Retries = Config['retries'];   // number
type ConfigValue = Config[ConfigKey]; // string | number | boolean

const roles = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = (typeof roles)[number]; // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer': the array is the single source of truth
```

**Mapped types.** A mapped type builds an object type by iterating over a union of keys, much like `Array.prototype.map` builds an array by iterating over elements:

```typescript
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };            // for each key K of T: optional, same type
type MyReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };     // "-" removes a modifier
type Concrete<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };            // removes "?": the same as Required<T>
type Flags<T> = { [K in keyof T]: boolean };              // same keys, different value type

type ConfigFlags = Flags<Config>; // { apiUrl: boolean; retries: boolean; debug: boolean }
```

**Key remapping** with `as` changes the key names, usually with a template literal type. Mapping a key to `never` removes it:

```typescript
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};
type ConfigGetters = Getters<Config>;
// { getApiUrl: () => string; getRetries: () => number; getDebug: () => boolean }

type PickByValue<T, V> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends V ? K : never]: T[K];    // keep a key only if its value type matches
};
type NumericConfig = PickByValue<Config, number>;         // { retries: number }
```

```text
Getters<Config>, evaluated key by key:

  K           new key  `get${Capitalize<K>}`     new value  () => Config[K]
  'apiUrl'    'getApiUrl'                        () => string
  'retries'   'getRetries'                       () => number
  'debug'     'getDebug'                         () => boolean
```

**Conditional types.** `T extends U ? X : Y` is a ternary operator on types: if `T` is assignable to `U`, the result is `X`, otherwise `Y`.

```typescript
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type A = IsString<'hello'>;  // true
type B = IsString<42>;       // false
```

**`infer`** declares a type variable inside the `extends` clause and captures part of the matched type, like a capture group in a regular expression:

```typescript
type ElementType<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type E1 = ElementType<string[]>;                 // string

type MyReturnType<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type R1 = MyReturnType<() => Promise<number>>;   // Promise<number>

type UnwrapPromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? UnwrapPromise<V> : T; // recursive
type V1 = UnwrapPromise<Promise<Promise<string>>>; // string
```

**Distribution over unions.** When the checked type is a bare type parameter and receives a union, the conditional type is applied to each member separately and the results are joined. This is how `Exclude` works. Wrapping both sides in a tuple turns distribution off:

```typescript
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
type Ex = MyExclude<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'a'>;      // 'b' | 'c'   ('a' -> never, 'b' -> 'b', 'c' -> 'c')

type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
type D1 = ToArray<string | number>;             // string[] | number[]   (distributed)

type ToArrayAll<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never;
type D2 = ToArrayAll<string | number>;          // (string | number)[]   (not distributed)
```

**Recursive types** apply a transformation at every level, fixing the shallowness of the built-in `Readonly`:

```typescript
type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => unknown
  ? T                                                // leave functions alone
  : T extends object
    ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> } // recurse into objects and arrays
    : T;                                             // primitives stay as they are

type AppState = { user: { name: string; tags: string[] } };
const state: DeepReadonly<AppState> = { user: { name: 'Ada', tags: ['admin'] } };
state.user.name = 'Grace';  // error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'name' because it is a read-only property.
state.user.tags.push('x');  // error TS2339: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly string[]'.
```

**A practical example: a typed event emitter.** A mapped type over an event map links each event name to its payload type, so subscribers and publishers cannot disagree:

```typescript
type AppEvents = {
  login: { userId: string };
  logout: undefined;
  error: Error;
};

class Emitter<Events extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  private listeners: { [K in keyof Events]?: Array<(payload: Events[K]) => void> } = {};

  on<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, listener: (payload: Events[K]) => void): void {
    const list = this.listeners[event] ?? [];
    list.push(listener);
    this.listeners[event] = list;
  }

  emit<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, payload: Events[K]): void {
```
