```typescript
    this.listeners[event]?.forEach((listener) => listener(payload));
  }
}

const bus = new Emitter<AppEvents>();
bus.on('login', (p) => console.log(p.userId));   // p: { userId: string }
bus.emit('login', { userId: 'u1' });             // OK
bus.emit('login', { id: 'u1' });
// error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'id' does not exist in type '{ userId: string; }'.
bus.emit('signup', undefined);
// error TS2345: Argument of type '"signup"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'keyof AppEvents'.
```

`AppEvents` is declared with `type`, not `interface`, on purpose: interfaces do not satisfy the `Record<string, unknown>` constraint, because they may be augmented later with keys of any type.

Type-level programming is powerful but costly to read and to compile. Prefer the built-in utility types, give complex types descriptive names, and test them with a few example aliases or `expectTypeOf` assertions (from Vitest) the way you would test functions.

**Key Takeaways**

- `typeof`, `keyof` and indexed access (`T[K]`, `T[number]`) derive types from values and from other types.
- Mapped types iterate over keys (`[K in keyof T]`), can add or remove `readonly` and `?`, and can rename or drop keys with `as`.
- Conditional types (`T extends U ? X : Y`) choose between types; `infer` captures part of a matched type.
- Conditional types distribute over unions when checking a bare type parameter; `[T] extends [U]` prevents it.
- Recursive mapped types such as `DeepReadonly` apply a transformation at every level of nesting.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write your own `MyPick<T, K extends keyof T>` and `MyRecord<K extends PropertyKey, V>` with mapped types, and check them against the built-in versions on a `User` type.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `Setters<T>`, which turns `{ name: string; age: number }` into `{ setName(value: string): void; setAge(value: number): void }`, and `FunctionKeys<T>`, the union of keys whose values are functions.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Explain what makes a conditional type distributive, and give an example where distribution produces a surprising result." *Hint:* compare `T extends unknown ? T[] : never` with `[T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never` for `T = string | number`, and consider what happens with `T = never`.

#### Declaration Files and Ambient Types

Most of the JavaScript ecosystem was not written in TypeScript, and even TypeScript libraries are published as compiled JavaScript. To type-check code that uses them, the compiler needs a description of their types without their implementation. That description is a **declaration file** (`.d.ts`), and the types it introduces are called **ambient**, because they describe things that exist somewhere else at runtime.

**Analogy:** a declaration file is like the specification sheet of an electronic component. An engineer designing a circuit needs the pin layout and voltage ratings, not the chip's internal design. Likewise, the compiler needs the names and types of a library's exports, not their code.

**What a `.d.ts` file contains.** Only types and `declare` statements, never executable code:

```typescript
// math-utils.d.ts: describes math-utils.js, which contains the actual implementation
export declare function clamp(value: number, min: number, max: number): number;
export declare const PRECISION: number;
export interface Range {
  min: number;
  max: number;
}
export declare class Vector2 {
  constructor(x: number, y: number);
  readonly x: number;
  readonly y: number;
  add(other: Vector2): Vector2;
}
```

You rarely write such files for your own code: with `"declaration": true` the compiler generates them next to the emitted JavaScript.

```text
src/math-utils.ts  --tsc-->  dist/math-utils.js     (implementation, runs)
                             dist/math-utils.d.ts   (types only, read by the compiler of consumers)
                             dist/math-utils.d.ts.map (optional: "go to definition" jumps to the .ts source)
```

**The `declare` keyword.** `declare` says "this exists at runtime; trust me, here is its type". It never emits code:

```typescript
declare const __APP_VERSION__: string;               // injected by the bundler at build time
declare function gtag(command: 'event', name: string, params?: object): void; // from a <script> tag

console.log(`Version ${__APP_VERSION__}`);
gtag('event', 'page_view');
```

**Where the types of a package come from.** When you write `import x from 'some-lib'`, TypeScript looks for types in this order:

```text
import { format } from 'some-lib'
        |
        v
1. Types bundled with the package     package.json "exports" -> "types" condition,
                                      or the "types"/"typings" field, or index.d.ts
        |  not found
        v
2. DefinitelyTyped                    node_modules/@types/some-lib/index.d.ts
                                      (community-maintained, installed with npm i -D @types/some-lib)
        |  not found
        v
3. Your own declaration               declare module 'some-lib' { ... } in a .d.ts in your project
        |  not found
        v
error TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module 'some-lib'.
```

**Ambient module declarations.** For an untyped package, or for non-JavaScript imports handled by a bundler, declare the module yourself in a `.d.ts` file that is part of the project (for example `src/types/modules.d.ts`):

```typescript
// src/types/modules.d.ts
declare module 'tiny-slugify' {
  export interface SlugifyOptions {
    separator?: string;
    lowercase?: boolean;
  }
  export default function slugify(text: string, options?: SlugifyOptions): string;
}

declare module '*.svg' {            // wildcard: every import ending in .svg
  const url: string;
  export default url;
}

declare module '*.module.css' {     // CSS Modules: class names mapped to generated names
  const classes: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;
  export default classes;
}
```

The quick escape hatch `declare module 'tiny-slugify';` (with no body) makes every import from the module `any`. It silences the error, but you lose all checking.

**Global augmentation and module augmentation.** Thanks to declaration merging (9.1), you can add members to existing types. In a file that is a module, global types are augmented inside `declare global`, and a package's types inside `declare module 'package'`:

```typescript
// src/types/globals.d.ts
export {};  // makes this file a module, so the blocks below are augmentations

declare global {
  interface Window {
    __APP_CONFIG__: { apiUrl: string; featureFlags: Record<string, boolean> };
  }
}

declare module 'express-serve-static-core' {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; role: 'admin' | 'member' };  // added by an authentication middleware (Chapter 12)
  }
}
```

**The standard library declarations.** The built-in JavaScript and browser APIs are themselves described by declaration files shipped with TypeScript (`lib.es2024.d.ts`, `lib.dom.d.ts` and so on). The `lib` compiler option selects which ones are loaded (9.3), and `types` selects which `@types` packages are included automatically. A triple-slash directive can pull in a specific one from a single file:

```typescript
/// <reference types="vite/client" />
// makes Vite's ambient types (import.meta.env, asset imports) available in this project
```

**Script files and module files in declarations.** A `.d.ts` file *without* top-level `import` or `export` is a global script: everything it declares is visible everywhere. With an `import` or `export`, it becomes a module, and you must use `declare global` to add globals. Mixing these up is the most common reason an augmentation "does nothing".

| Need | Write |
|---|---|
| Types for your own TypeScript library | Nothing: set `"declaration": true` |
| A JavaScript package without types | `npm i -D @types/name`, otherwise `declare module 'name' { ... }` |
| Assets imported through a bundler (`.svg`, `.css`) | Wildcard `declare module '*.svg'`, or the bundler's client types |
| Globals created by `<script>` tags or the bundler | `declare const`, or `declare global { interface Window { ... } }` |
| Extra fields on a library's types | Module augmentation: `declare module 'lib' { interface X { ... } }` |
| Skip type-checking `.d.ts` files of dependencies | `"skipLibCheck": true` (faster builds, common in applications) |

**Key Takeaways**

- Declaration files (`.d.ts`) contain only types and describe JavaScript that exists elsewhere; the compiler generates them for your code with `"declaration": true`.
- `declare` introduces ambient values, functions, modules and globals without emitting code.
- Package types come from the package itself, then from `@types/*` on DefinitelyTyped, and otherwise from your own `declare module`.
- Declaration merging inside `declare global` and `declare module 'x'` augments existing global and library types.
- A `.d.ts` file with a top-level `import` or `export` is a module, and global declarations in it must go inside `declare global`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* In a Vite or plain TypeScript project, import an `.svg` file and read the error. Fix it with a wildcard module declaration and check that the imported value is typed as `string`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a small JavaScript module `currency.js` exporting `format(amount, currency)` and a `RATES` object. Write `currency.d.ts` next to it, import the module from a `.ts` file with `allowJs` disabled, and verify that wrong argument types are reported.
> 3. *(Interview)* "You added a property to `Window` in a `.d.ts` file, but the compiler still says it does not exist. What are the likely causes?" *Hint:* is the file included by `tsconfig.json`, and is it a script or a module?

<a id="93-typescript-in-practice"></a>
### 9.3 TypeScript in Practice

This subchapter moves from the type system to real projects: object-oriented code with classes, interfaces and decorators, the module system, configuring the compiler and choosing a strictness level, the build pipeline from `.ts` to running JavaScript, and typing the browser, Node.js and third-party libraries.

#### Classes, Access Modifiers and Abstract Classes

JavaScript classes (Chapter 4.3) are syntax for constructor functions and prototypes. TypeScript keeps their runtime behaviour and adds what class-based languages such as Java and C# offer: declared and typed fields, access modifiers, `readonly` members, abstract classes and checked overrides.

**Declared fields and initialisation.** In TypeScript every field is declared with its type in the class body. With `strictPropertyInitialization` (part of `strict`), each field must be initialised where it is declared or in the constructor:

```typescript
class Article {
  title: string;                  // assigned in the constructor: OK
  views = 0;                      // initialiser: type number is inferred
  tags: string[] = [];
  summary?: string;               // optional: may stay undefined
  body: string;
  // error TS2564: Property 'body' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor.
  publishedAt!: Date;             // "!" definite assignment: you promise it is set before use (e.g. by a framework)

  constructor(title: string) {
    this.title = title;
  }
}
```

**Access modifiers.** TypeScript has three modifiers, and JavaScript itself now has private fields with `#`:

```typescript
class BankAccount {
  static readonly bankName = 'TS Bank';   // shared by the class, read-only
  readonly id: string;                    // can be set only in the declaration or the constructor
  public owner: string;                   // public is the default; writing it is optional
  protected balance = 0;                  // this class and its subclasses
  private history: number[] = [];         // this class only (checked at compile time)
  #pin: string;                           // this class only (enforced at runtime by JavaScript)

  constructor(id: string, owner: string, pin: string) {
    this.id = id;
    this.owner = owner;
    this.#pin = pin;
  }

  deposit(amount: number): void {
    this.balance += amount;
    this.history.push(amount);
  }

  checkPin(pin: string): boolean {
    return pin === this.#pin;
  }
}

const account = new BankAccount('acc-1', 'Ada', '1234');
account.owner = 'Grace';  // OK
account.id = 'acc-2';     // error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'id' because it is a read-only property.
account.balance;          // error TS2445: Property 'balance' is protected and only accessible within class 'BankAccount' and its subclasses.
account.history;          // error TS2341: Property 'history' is private and only accessible within class 'BankAccount'.
account.#pin;             // error TS18013: Property '#pin' is not accessible outside class 'BankAccount' because it has a private identifier.
account['history'];       // allowed: bracket access is an intentional escape hatch for TypeScript's private
```

| | `private` (TypeScript) | `#field` (JavaScript) |
|---|---|---|
| Enforced | At compile time only | At runtime, by the engine |
| Visible in the emitted JavaScript | Yes, as a normal property | No, truly hidden |
| Accessible via `obj['name']`, `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify` | Yes | No |
| Accessible from other instances of the same class | Yes | Yes |
| Typical use | Encapsulation within a TypeScript code base | Library code, security-relevant state |

**Parameter properties.** A shorthand that declares and assigns a field directly from a constructor parameter. It is widely used (for example in Angular and NestJS), but it generates code, so it is not *erasable syntax* (see the compilation topic) and is rejected by Node.js type stripping:

```typescript
class UserService {
  constructor(
    private readonly baseUrl: string,      // declares this.baseUrl and assigns it
    protected timeoutMs = 5000,
  ) {}

  url(path: string): string {
    return `${this.baseUrl}${path}`;
  }
}
```

**Inheritance and `override`.** Subclasses can redefine methods. The `override` keyword states the intention explicitly, and the option `noImplicitOverride` makes it mandatory, so renaming a base method breaks the subclasses that relied on it instead of silently creating a new method:

```typescript
class Shape {
  describe(): string {
    return 'a shape';
  }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
  constructor(public radius: number) {
    super();
  }
  override describe(): string {           // checked: Shape really has describe()
    return `a circle of radius ${this.radius}`;
  }
  override describ(): string {
    // error TS4117: This member cannot have an 'override' modifier because it is not declared in the base class 'Shape'.
    //   Did you mean 'describe'?
    return '';
  }
}
```

**Abstract classes.** An abstract class is a partial implementation: it cannot be instantiated, and it declares `abstract` members that subclasses must implement. It fits the *template method* pattern, where the base class fixes an algorithm and subclasses fill in the steps:

```typescript
abstract class Exporter<Row> {
  constructor(protected readonly rows: Row[]) {}

  protected abstract header(): string;           // no body: subclasses must implement it
  protected abstract formatRow(row: Row): string;

  export(): string {                             // template method: the algorithm is fixed here
    return [this.header(), ...this.rows.map((r) => this.formatRow(r))].join('\n');
  }
}

type Product = { name: string; price: number };

class CsvExporter extends Exporter<Product> {
  protected header(): string {
    return 'name,price';
  }
  protected formatRow(p: Product): string {
    return `${p.name},${p.price}`;
  }
}

const csv = new CsvExporter([{ name: 'Pen', price: 1.5 }]).export(); // "name,price\nPen,1.5"
const base = new Exporter<Product>([]);
// error TS2511: Cannot create an instance of an abstract class.

class JsonExporter extends Exporter<Product> {
  // error TS2515: Non-abstract class 'JsonExporter' does not implement inherited abstract member formatRow from class 'Exporter<Product>'.
  protected header(): string {
    return '[';
  }
}
```

**Classes are structural too.** Two classes with the same public shape are interchangeable as types, even if they are unrelated. A `private` or `protected` member changes this: only instances of the class that declared it (or its subclasses) are compatible.

```typescript
class Celsius {
  constructor(public value: number) {}
}
class Meters {
  constructor(public value: number) {}
}
const distance: Meters = new Celsius(20);   // allowed: same shape { value: number }
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Fields are declared with types, and `strictPropertyInitialization` requires them to be initialised; `!` is an unchecked promise that they will be.
- `public`, `protected` and `private` are compile-time checks only; `#private` fields are enforced by the JavaScript engine at runtime.
- `readonly` fields can be assigned only in their declaration or the constructor; parameter properties declare and assign fields in one step but are not erasable syntax.
- `override` together with `noImplicitOverride` keeps subclasses in sync with their base classes.
- Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and force subclasses to implement abstract members; they fit the template method pattern.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `Counter` class with a `private` count, `increment()` and `reset()` methods and a `readonly` `name`. Try to change `count` and `name` from outside the class, then convert `count` to a `#count` field and compare the emitted JavaScript.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement an abstract `Notifier` class with an abstract `send(to: string, message: string): Promise<void>` and a concrete `notifyAll(recipients: string[], message: string)` that sends to everyone and collects failures. Add `EmailNotifier` and `SmsNotifier` subclasses.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between TypeScript's `private` and JavaScript's `#private`, and when would you choose each?" *Hint:* think about compile time vs runtime, what `JSON.stringify` and `Object.keys` see, and code that is consumed from plain JavaScript.

#### Implementing Interfaces and Decorators

Interfaces describe *what* an object can do; classes describe *how*. The `implements` clause connects the two, which is the basis of loosely coupled, testable designs. Decorators, the second topic here, attach reusable behaviour such as logging, caching or framework registration to classes and their members.

**`implements`.** A class that `implements` an interface is checked to provide every member of that interface with a compatible type. A class can implement several interfaces:

```typescript
interface Logger {
  info(message: string): void;
  error(message: string, cause?: unknown): void;
}

interface Disposable {
  dispose(): void;
}

class ConsoleLogger implements Logger, Disposable {
  info(message: string): void {
    console.log(`[info] ${message}`);
  }
  error(message: string, cause?: unknown): void {
    console.error(`[error] ${message}`, cause);
  }
  dispose(): void {}
}

class BrokenLogger implements Logger {
  // error TS2420: Class 'BrokenLogger' incorrectly implements interface 'Logger'.
  //   Property 'error' is missing in type 'BrokenLogger' but required in type 'Logger'.
  info(message: string): void {}
}
```

`implements` is only a check. It does not change the class's type, and it does not give the method parameters their types:

```typescript
class LazyLogger implements Logger {
  info(message) {}           // error TS7006: Parameter 'message' implicitly has an 'any' type.
  error(message: string): void {}
}
```

**Programming to interfaces.** Code that depends on an interface instead of a concrete class can be given any implementation: a real one in production, a fake one in tests. This is the *dependency inversion* principle, and it is the core idea behind dependency injection frameworks:

```typescript
interface Clock {
  now(): Date;
}

class SignupService {
  constructor(
    private readonly logger: Logger,     // depends on abstractions, not on ConsoleLogger
    private readonly clock: Clock,
  ) {}

  register(email: string): { email: string; registeredAt: Date } {
    const registeredAt = this.clock.now();
    this.logger.info(`New signup: ${email}`);
    return { email, registeredAt };
  }
}

// Production wiring
const service = new SignupService(new ConsoleLogger(), { now: () => new Date() });

// Test wiring: plain objects satisfy the interfaces structurally
const lines: string[] = [];
const testService = new SignupService(
  { info: (m) => lines.push(m), error: () => {} },
  { now: () => new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z') },
);
testService.register('ada@example.com');   // lines: ['New signup: ada@example.com']
```

| | Interface | Abstract class |
|---|---|---|
| Exists at runtime | No | Yes (it is a class) |
| Can contain implementation | No | Yes |
| Can contain state (fields with values) | No | Yes |
| A class can use | Any number (`implements A, B`) | Only one (`extends`) |
| Satisfied by plain objects | Yes, structurally | Only if they match its public shape (and it has no private members) |
| Use when | Defining a contract between parts of the system | Sharing code between closely related classes |

**Decorators.** A decorator is a function, applied with `@name` before a class or class member, that receives the decorated element and can observe, replace or extend it. The idea comes from the *decorator* design pattern: wrapping behaviour around existing code without modifying it.

**Analogy:** a decorator is like a frame put around a painting. The painting (the method) stays the same, but the frame adds something around it, such as a label, lighting or an alarm (logging, timing, retries).

There are two incompatible decorator systems in TypeScript:

| | Standard decorators | Legacy ("experimental") decorators |
|---|---|---|
| Specification | TC39 decorators proposal (stage 3) | Early TypeScript design from 2015 |
| Enabled by | Default since TypeScript 5.0 | `"experimentalDecorators": true` |
| Decorator signature | `(value, context) => replacement` | `(target, propertyKey, descriptor)` |
| Parameter decorators | No | Yes |
| Type metadata (`emitDecoratorMetadata`) | No | Yes |
| Used by | New code, recent library versions | Angular, NestJS, TypeORM, and other established frameworks |

**A standard method decorator.** The decorator receives the original method and a `context` object, and returns a replacement method:

```typescript
function logged<This, Args extends unknown[], Return>(
  target: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return,
  context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return>,
) {
  const name = String(context.name);
  return function (this: This, ...args: Args): Return {
    console.log(`-> ${name}(${args.map((a) => JSON.stringify(a)).join(', ')})`);
    const result = target.call(this, ...args);     // call the original method
    console.log(`<- ${name}`);
    return result;
  };
}

class Calculator {
  @logged
  add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b;
  }
}

new Calculator().add(2, 3);
// -> add(2, 3)
// <- add
```

**Decorator factories.** To configure a decorator, write a function that *returns* a decorator. Here, a retry policy for asynchronous methods:

```typescript
function retry(times: number) {
  return function <This, Args extends unknown[], Return>(
    target: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Promise<Return>,
    context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Promise<Return>>,
  ) {
    return async function (this: This, ...args: Args): Promise<Return> {
      let lastError: unknown;
      for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= times; attempt++) {
        try {
          return await target.call(this, ...args);
        } catch (err) {
          lastError = err;
          console.warn(`${String(context.name)} failed (attempt ${attempt}/${times})`);
        }
      }
      throw lastError;
    };
  };
}

class PriceApi {
  @retry(3)                              // the factory is called once, with 3
  async latest(symbol: string): Promise<number> {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/prices/${symbol}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    return (await res.json()) as number;
  }
}
```

**Initialisers and auto-binding.** `context.addInitializer` runs code when each instance is constructed. This decorator binds a method to its instance, so it keeps the correct `this` when passed as an event listener (Chapter 6.3):

```typescript
function bound(_target: unknown, context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext) {
  const name = context.name;
  context.addInitializer(function (this: any) {
    this[name] = this[name].bind(this);
  });
}

class Toolbar {
  clicks = 0;
  @bound
  handleClick(): void {
    this.clicks++;              // `this` is the Toolbar, even when called as a detached function
  }
}

const toolbar = new Toolbar();
document.querySelector('#save')?.addEventListener('click', toolbar.handleClick);
```

**Legacy decorators in frameworks.** In Angular or NestJS code you will meet the legacy form, often with constructor parameter decorators and runtime type metadata used for dependency injection:

```typescript
// Requires "experimentalDecorators": true and "emitDecoratorMetadata": true (NestJS example)
import { Controller, Get, Param } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('users')                       // class decorator: registers a route prefix
export class UsersController {
  constructor(private readonly users: UsersService) {}   // injected using emitted metadata

  @Get(':id')                              // method decorator: maps GET /users/:id
  findOne(@Param('id') id: string) {       // parameter decorator: legacy decorators only
    return this.users.findById(id);
  }
}
```

Decorators generate code, so they need a compiler (TypeScript, Babel, SWC or esbuild) to transform them; type-stripping tools cannot run them.

**Key Takeaways**

- `implements` checks that a class satisfies one or more interfaces, but does not change the class's type or infer parameter types.
- Depending on interfaces instead of concrete classes enables dependency injection and simple test fakes.
- Use interfaces for contracts and abstract classes for shared implementation; a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.
- Decorators are functions applied with `@` that wrap or annotate classes and members; factories (`@retry(3)`) configure them.
- Standard decorators (TypeScript 5.0+) and legacy decorators (`experimentalDecorators`) are incompatible; frameworks such as Angular and NestJS still use the legacy form.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Define an interface `Cache<V>` with `get`, `set` and `delete`, and implement it twice: `MemoryCache` with a `Map`, and `StorageCache` with `localStorage` and JSON serialisation.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a standard `@memoize` method decorator that caches results by the JSON of the arguments, and a `@timed(label)` decorator factory that logs how long each call takes. Apply both to the same method and observe the order in which they run.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How do interfaces make code easier to test? Show it with a class that depends on the current time and on an HTTP client." *Hint:* constructor injection of a `Clock` and an `HttpClient` interface, with fakes in the test.

#### Modules and Namespaces

TypeScript uses the standard ES module system of Chapter 3.4: `import` and `export`, one module per file. It adds type-only imports and exports, has to work out how module specifiers map to files (module resolution), and still supports namespaces, its older way of organising code.

**Scripts vs modules.** A file with a top-level `import` or `export` is a module, with its own scope. A file without either is a *script*, and its top-level declarations are global. Two script files that both declare `const config` therefore produce `error TS2451: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'config'`. Add `export {}` to turn a file into a module, or set `"moduleDetection": "force"` (as `tsc --init` does) to treat every file as a module.

**Importing and exporting types.** Types can be exported and imported like values. Because types disappear in the emitted JavaScript, TypeScript lets you mark imports that are *only* types:

```typescript
// api.ts
export interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
}
export type UserId = User['id'];
export async function fetchUser(id: UserId): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  return (await res.json()) as User;
}

// profile.ts
import { fetchUser, type User } from './api.js';   // inline "type": this name is erased
import type { UserId } from './api.js';            // the whole import is erased

export type { User };                              // re-export a type only
export async function showProfile(id: UserId): Promise<User> {
  return fetchUser(id);
}
```

**Why type-only imports matter.** Fast transpilers (esbuild, SWC, Babel, Node.js type stripping) process one file at a time and cannot know whether an imported name is a type, which must be removed, or a value, which must be kept. Marking type imports removes the guesswork. Two options enforce it:

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `isolatedModules` | Reports code that a single-file transpiler cannot compile correctly (for example re-exporting a type without `export type`) |
| `verbatimModuleSyntax` | Imports and exports are emitted exactly as written, minus anything marked `type`; importing a type without `type` is an error |

```typescript
// With "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
import { User } from './api.js';
// error TS1484: 'User' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import when 'verbatimModuleSyntax' is enabled.
```

**Module resolution.** Given `import { x } from './utils.js'` or `from 'lodash-es'`, the compiler must find the file that provides the types. The `module` and `moduleResolution` options tell it which runtime or tool will resolve the import later, so that it follows the same rules:

| Setting | Models | Relative imports | Typical project |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"module": "nodenext"` | Node.js's real rules for ESM and CommonJS | Need the runtime extension: `'./utils.js'` for `utils.ts` | Node.js applications and libraries |
| `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` with `"module": "esnext"` or `"preserve"` | Vite, webpack, esbuild and similar tools | Extensions optional: `'./utils'` | Front-end applications built with a bundler |

```typescript
// tsconfig: "module": "nodenext", and package.json has "type": "module"
import { slugify } from './utils';
// error TS2835: Relative import paths need explicit file extensions in ECMAScript imports when
//   '--moduleResolution' is 'node16' or 'nodenext'. Did you mean './utils.js'?
import { slugify as ok } from './utils.js';  // correct: refers to the emitted utils.js, type-checked against utils.ts
```

If you prefer writing `./utils.ts`, enable `allowImportingTsExtensions` (with `noEmit`, for bundlers and runtimes that run `.ts` directly) or `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` (when `tsc` emits JavaScript, it rewrites `.ts` to `.js`).

**Path aliases.** Long relative paths such as `'../../../lib/date'` can be replaced by aliases. The `paths` option only teaches the *type checker* about them; the bundler or runtime must be configured to resolve them too. The standard alternative that works everywhere is Node.js **subpath imports** in `package.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "shop",
  "type": "module",
  "imports": {
    "#lib/*": "./src/lib/*"
  }
}
```

```typescript
import { formatDate } from '#lib/date.js';   // understood by Node.js, bundlers and TypeScript alike
```

**CommonJS interoperability.** Many npm packages are still CommonJS (`module.exports = ...`). TypeScript lets you import them with ES syntax (`import express from 'express'`); this default-import interoperability (formerly the `esModuleInterop` option) is always enabled in TypeScript 7. The older form `import fs = require('fs')` still exists for CommonJS output but generates code and is not erasable.

**Namespaces.** Before ES modules existed, TypeScript provided *internal modules*, now called **namespaces**: named objects that group related code and hide what is not exported.

```typescript
namespace Validation {
  const lettersRegexp = /^[A-Za-z]+$/;          // not exported: private to the namespace
  export function isLetters(s: string): boolean {
    return lettersRegexp.test(s);
  }
  export const MAX_LENGTH = 64;
}

Validation.isLetters('Hello');   // true
Validation.lettersRegexp;        // error TS2339: Property 'lettersRegexp' does not exist on type 'typeof Validation'.
```

A namespace compiles to an object built by an immediately invoked function (Chapter 3.3), the same *module pattern* that was common in pre-ES2015 JavaScript:

```javascript
var Validation;
(function (Validation) {
    const lettersRegexp = /^[A-Za-z]+$/;
    function isLetters(s) {
        return lettersRegexp.test(s);
    }
    Validation.isLetters = isLetters;
    Validation.MAX_LENGTH = 64;
})(Validation || (Validation = {}));
```

Namespaces are legacy in application code: ES modules do the same job, work with every tool, and support tree shaking (Chapter 3.4). They remain useful in *declaration files*, where they describe libraries that expose a global object (for example `declare namespace google.maps { ... }`), and for grouping types such as `NodeJS.ProcessEnv`.

| | ES modules | Namespaces |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | JavaScript (ES2015) | TypeScript only |
| Unit | One file | A named block, possibly spread across files |
| Runtime output | `import`/`export` kept | An object built by an IIFE |
| Tree shaking, bundlers, Node.js | Fully supported | Poorly supported; not erasable syntax |
| Use today | All new code | Declaration files for global libraries |

**Key Takeaways**

- A file with a top-level `import` or `export` is a module; without one, its declarations are global.
- `import type` and inline `type` modifiers mark imports that are erased; `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `isolatedModules` make code safe for single-file transpilers.
- Choose `module: "nodenext"` for code run by Node.js (relative imports need `.js` extensions) and `moduleResolution: "bundler"` for code processed by a bundler.
- `paths` only affects type checking; subpath imports (`#lib/*` in `package.json`) work with every tool.
- Namespaces are a legacy, non-erasable way to organise code; use ES modules, and keep namespaces for declaration files.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Split a small program into `models.ts` (only interfaces), `service.ts` (functions) and `main.ts`. Use `import type` for the models and enable `verbatimModuleSyntax` to check that you did it correctly.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create the same two-file project twice: once with `"module": "nodenext"` and run with `node`, once with `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` and built with Vite. Note which import specifiers each one accepts, and why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why do fast transpilers such as esbuild need `isolatedModules`, and what kind of code breaks without it?" *Hint:* a transpiler that sees one file at a time cannot tell whether `export { User } from './api'` re-exports a type or a value.

#### tsconfig and Compiler Options

A TypeScript project is defined by a `tsconfig.json` file: which files belong to it, which environment the code runs in, how strictly it is checked and what, if anything, the compiler emits. Running `tsc` without arguments looks for `tsconfig.json` in the current directory and uses it. Editors read the same file, so the editor and the build agree.

**Structure of the file.** `tsconfig.json` allows comments and trailing commas:

```jsonc
{
  "extends": "@tsconfig/node24/tsconfig.json",  // inherit a shared base configuration
  "compilerOptions": {
    // ...options, grouped below
  },
  "include": ["src"],                           // files to compile (globs); defaults to everything
  "exclude": ["**/*.test.ts"],                  // removed from "include" (not from imports)
  "files": [],                                  // an explicit list, for small projects
  "references": [{ "path": "../shared" }]       // project references (monorepos)
}
```

**The main option groups.**

| Group | Option | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Type checking | `strict` and its family | How strictly code is checked (next topic) |
| Language and environment | `target` | Which JavaScript syntax version to emit (`es2022`, `esnext`...) |
| | `lib` | Which built-in API declarations exist (`es2024`, `dom`, `dom.iterable`, `webworker`) |
| | `types` | Which `@types/*` packages are loaded globally (`["node"]`) |
| | `jsx` | How to handle JSX (`react-jsx`, `preserve`) |
| Modules | `module`, `moduleResolution` | Module format and resolution rules (previous topic) |
| | `resolveJsonModule` | Allows `import data from './data.json'` with inferred types |
| | `paths` | Import aliases for the type checker |
| Emit | `outDir`, `rootDir` | Where emitted files go, and the source root they mirror |
| | `declaration`, `declarationMap` | Emit `.d.ts` files (and maps back to the source) |
| | `sourceMap` | Emit `.js.map` files for debugging |
| | `noEmit` | Only type-check (another tool produces the JavaScript) |
| | `noEmitOnError` | Do not write output if there are type errors |
| Interop | `isolatedModules`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `erasableSyntaxOnly` | Compatibility with single-file transpilers and type stripping |
| | `allowJs`, `checkJs` | Include and optionally check JavaScript files |
| Performance | `skipLibCheck` | Do not re-check dependencies' `.d.ts` files |
| | `incremental`, `composite` | Cache results between builds; enable project references |

**`target` vs `lib`.** These two are often confused:

```text
target: "es2017"   -> the OUTPUT syntax:   a?.b  is rewritten to  a === null || a === void 0 ? void 0 : a.b
lib: ["es2024"]    -> the APIs you may CALL: Object.groupBy, Array.prototype.findLast ... are allowed

Neither adds polyfills: if lib promises Object.groupBy but the browser lacks it,
the code type-checks and still fails at runtime. Polyfills are a separate concern (Chapter 1.3).
```

**Example: a browser application built with Vite.** The bundler produces the JavaScript, so `tsc` only checks types:

```jsonc
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "lib": ["es2023", "dom", "dom.iterable"],
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "types": ["vite/client"],          // import.meta.env, asset imports

    "noEmit": true,                    // Vite emits; tsc --noEmit runs in CI and the editor
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,

    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
```

**Example: a Node.js library published to npm.** Here `tsc` emits JavaScript and declaration files:

```jsonc
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2023",
    "lib": ["es2023"],                 // no "dom": this code runs in Node.js
    "module": "nodenext",              // also sets moduleResolution: nodenext
    "types": ["node"],

    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "sourceMap": true,

    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"],
  "exclude": ["src/**/*.test.ts"]
}
```

**Defaults and recent changes.** TypeScript 7 (2026), the native rewrite of the compiler, changed several defaults: `strict` is on, `target` and `module` default to `esnext`, and `types` defaults to an empty list, so `@types/node` must be listed explicitly. Legacy options that were deprecated in TypeScript 6.0 have been removed, including `target: "es5"`, `moduleResolution: "node10"` and `"classic"`, `baseUrl`, `outFile`, the `amd`, `umd` and `system` module formats and `esModuleInterop: false`. Old tutorials often still use them, so expect to update configurations copied from older projects.

**Shared bases and project references.** The `@tsconfig/bases` project publishes recommended configurations per runtime (`@tsconfig/node24`, `@tsconfig/strictest` and others) to `extends` from. Large repositories split into several projects with `"composite": true` and `references`, and build them in dependency order with `tsc --build` (`tsc -b`), which only rebuilds what changed.

```text
packages/
  shared/tsconfig.json     "composite": true
  api/tsconfig.json        "references": [{ "path": "../shared" }]
  web/tsconfig.json        "references": [{ "path": "../shared" }]
tsconfig.json              "files": [], "references": [ shared, api, web ]   -> tsc -b builds all three
```

**Useful diagnostic commands.**

| Command | Shows |
|---|---|
| `tsc --init` | Creates a commented `tsconfig.json` with recommended settings |
| `tsc --showConfig` | The final configuration after `extends` and defaults |
| `tsc --explainFiles` | Every file in the program and why it was included |
| `tsc --traceResolution` | How each import was resolved to a file |
| `tsc --noEmit --watch` | Continuous type checking without output |
| `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` | Time and memory per compilation phase |

**Key Takeaways**

- `tsconfig.json` defines a project: its files (`include`, `exclude`), its environment (`target`, `lib`, `types`, `module`) and its checking and emit options.
- `target` controls the emitted syntax and `lib` the APIs the code may use; neither provides polyfills.
- Front-end projects usually type-check with `noEmit` and let a bundler emit; libraries emit JavaScript, `.d.ts` files and source maps with `tsc`.
- TypeScript 7 enables `strict` by default, defaults `target` and `module` to `esnext`, and removes legacy options such as `es5` output, `baseUrl` and `outFile`.
- `extends` shares configuration, and project references with `tsc -b` structure large repositories into incremental builds.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run `tsc --init` in an empty folder, read every option it enabled, and use `tsc --showConfig` to see the effective configuration. Add `"lib": ["es2020"]` and try calling `Object.groupBy`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a small Node.js package with the library configuration above, build it, and inspect `dist/`: the `.js`, `.d.ts`, `.d.ts.map` and `.js.map` files. Import it from a second project and use "Go to Definition" on one of its functions.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A project compiles without errors, but crashes in an older browser with `Object.groupBy is not a function`. Which configuration options are involved, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* separate what `target` and `lib` promise from what the browser actually provides.

#### Strict Mode and Type Safety Levels

TypeScript is gradual: the same compiler can accept almost any JavaScript, or reject everything that is not provably safe. Where a project sits on that spectrum is decided by configuration. The `strict` flag is the most important switch, but it is only one level on a longer ladder.

**Why strictness is configurable.** When TypeScript appeared, its users had large JavaScript code bases to migrate. Enforcing `null` checks or forbidding implicit `any` from the first day would have produced thousands of errors. Each strict check was therefore introduced as a separate opt-in flag, and `strict` was added as a single switch for the whole family. In TypeScript 7, `strict` is on by default.

**The `strict` family.** `"strict": true` enables all of these at once (and future strict checks automatically):

| Flag | What it catches | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `noImplicitAny` | Parameters and variables whose type would silently be `any` | `function f(x) {}` |
| `strictNullChecks` | Use of possibly `null`/`undefined` values | `document.querySelector('a').href` |
| `strictFunctionTypes` | Unsafe callback parameter types (see 9.2) | Passing a `Dog` handler where an `Animal` handler is required |
| `strictBindCallApply` | Wrong arguments to `bind`, `call` and `apply` | `fn.call(undefined, 'x')` when `fn` expects a number |
| `strictPropertyInitialization` | Class fields that are never initialised | `name: string;` with no assignment |
| `noImplicitThis` | `this` of implicit type `any` | `this` inside a standalone `function` |
| `useUnknownInCatchVariables` | Treats `catch (err)` as `unknown` instead of `any` | `err.message` without a check |
| `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` | Iterator results from built-ins typed precisely | `iterator.next().value` may be `undefined` |
| `alwaysStrict` | Emits `"use strict"` (always on in TypeScript 7) | Strict mode JavaScript semantics |

The `catch` variable case is one of the most common in everyday code:

```typescript
async function loadConfig(): Promise<string> {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/config.json');
    return await res.text();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err.message);   // error TS18046: 'err' is of type 'unknown'.
    if (err instanceof Error) console.error(err.message);  // OK
    return '{}';
  }
}
```

**Beyond `strict`.** Some checks are not included in `strict` because they require more code changes, but they catch real bugs:

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` | Index access on arrays and records includes `undefined` |
| `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` | `prop?: string` means "missing or a string", and assigning `undefined` explicitly is an error |
| `noImplicitOverride` | Requires `override` on overriding methods |
| `noImplicitReturns` | Every code path of a function must return a value |
| `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` | Forbids non-empty `case` blocks without `break` or `return` |
| `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` | Requires `obj['key']` instead of `obj.key` for index-signature properties |
| `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters` | Reports unused declarations (often left to a linter instead) |

```typescript
// With "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true
const scores: Record<string, number> = { ada: 90 };
const s = scores['grace'];    // number | undefined
s.toFixed(1);                 // error TS18048: 's' is possibly 'undefined'.

const items = ['a', 'b'];
const third = items[2];       // string | undefined
for (const item of items) {
  item.toUpperCase();         // OK: iteration never yields a missing element
}
```

```typescript
// With "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true
interface Options {
  label?: string;
}
const a: Options = {};                    // OK: the property is missing
const b: Options = { label: undefined };
// error TS2375: Type '{ label: undefined; }' is not assignable to type 'Options' with 'exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true'.
//   Consider adding 'undefined' to the types of the target's properties.
```

**A ladder of type safety levels.**

```text
Level 0  Plain JavaScript + // @ts-check or "checkJs"   JSDoc comments give types; no build step changes
Level 1  TypeScript, "strict": false, "allowJs"           Migration in progress; implicit any accepted
Level 2  "strict": true                                   The baseline for new projects (default in TypeScript 7)
Level 3  strict + noUncheckedIndexedAccess,               Index access, optional properties and overrides
         exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noImplicitOverride    are also checked
Level 4  Level 3 + typescript-eslint "strict-type-checked" Lint rules forbid explicit any, unsafe any flows,
                                                           floating promises, unnecessary conditions
Level 5  Level 4 + runtime validation at every boundary    Network, storage and user input are verified
```

Level 0 deserves a closer look, because it brings type checking to projects that cannot add a build step:

```javascript
// @ts-check
/**
 * @param {number} price
 * @param {number} [quantity=1]
 * @returns {string}
 */
function formatTotal(price, quantity = 1) {
  return (price * quantity).toFixed(2);
}

formatTotal('9.99'); // error: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.
```

**Escape hatches, ranked by risk.** Strict code still needs occasional overrides. Prefer the safer ones and make every use visible in code review:

| Escape hatch | Effect | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `// @ts-expect-error reason` | Suppresses an error on the next line, and *reports an error if there is none* | Low: becomes visible once the problem is fixed |
| `value satisfies T` | Checks without changing the type | None |
| `value as T` | Unchecked assertion | Medium: wrong if the data does not match |
| `value!` | Removes `null` and `undefined` | Medium: a `TypeError` if wrong |
| `// @ts-ignore` | Suppresses any error on the next line, forever | High: hides future errors too |
| `any` | Disables checking and spreads to everything it touches | Highest |

**Migrating a code base to `strict`.** Turning on every flag at once can produce thousands of errors. A proven approach:

1. Enable `strict` and add one flag at a time if the full set is too much, starting with `noImplicitAny`, then `strictNullChecks`.
2. Fix errors file by file or directory by directory; in large projects, temporarily suppress the remaining errors with `// @ts-expect-error` comments so that new code is checked strictly from day one.
3. Ratchet: track the number of suppressions in CI and allow it only to go down.
4. Add lint rules (`@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any`, `no-floating-promises`) once the compiler errors are gone.

**The runtime boundary.** No compiler flag checks data that arrives at runtime. The strictest projects validate input with a schema library and *derive* the static type from the schema, so the two cannot drift apart:

```typescript
import { z } from 'zod';

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  age: z.number().int().nonnegative().optional(),
});
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;  // { id: string; email: string; age?: number | undefined }

async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  return UserSchema.parse(await res.json());   // throws a detailed error if the data is wrong
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `strict` enables a family of checks (`noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictFunctionTypes` and others) and is the default in TypeScript 7.
- `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` and `noImplicitOverride` are valuable checks outside `strict`.
- Type safety is a ladder: from `// @ts-check` with JSDoc, through `strict`, to type-aware lint rules and runtime validation.
- Prefer `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`, and `satisfies` over `as`; treat `any` as the last resort.
- Static types end at runtime boundaries; validate external data with a schema and derive the type from it.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Take a 30-line JavaScript file, add `// @ts-check` and JSDoc annotations, and fix the errors the editor reports. Then rename it to `.ts` and replace the JSDoc with TypeScript annotations.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In an existing project, enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. Count the new errors, fix five of them in different ways (a guard, a default value, `Array.prototype.at` with a check, restructuring the loop), and decide whether to keep the flag.
> 3. *(Interview)* "You join a team whose large code base has `strict: false` and around 400 uses of `any`. How do you improve type safety without stopping feature work?" *Hint:* incremental flags, suppressions with a ratchet in CI, lint rules for new code, and focusing first on the boundaries where data enters the system.

#### Compilation, Transpilation and Source Maps

Browsers and Node.js run JavaScript, so TypeScript always goes through a build step, even if it is hidden inside a tool. Understanding that step explains why type errors and runtime errors are separate, why fast tools skip type checking, and how a debugger can show TypeScript lines while running JavaScript.

**Two jobs, often done by different tools.**

- **Type checking** needs the whole program: every file, every `.d.ts`, every import. It is the slow part.
- **Transpiling** (source-to-source compilation) removes types and optionally rewrites newer syntax for older runtimes. It can be done one file at a time, and very quickly.

```text
                          +------------------------------------------+
  src/*.ts  ------------> |  tsc --noEmit  (type checking only)      | ---> errors in the editor, CI
     |                    +------------------------------------------+
     |
     |                    +------------------------------------------+
     +------------------> |  Transpiler: esbuild, SWC, Babel, tsc,   | ---> *.js (+ *.js.map)
                          |  or a runtime that strips types (Node.js,|      runs in the browser or Node.js
                          |  Deno, Bun)                              |
                          +------------------------------------------+
     Transpilers do not check types: code with type errors still runs.
```

| Tool | Type checks | Speed | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tsc` | Yes | Fast since TypeScript 7 (native, parallel); slower in 5.x/6.x | Libraries, CI checks, `.d.ts` generation |
| esbuild, SWC, Oxc | No | Very fast | Inside Vite, webpack, Next.js and test runners |
| Babel (`@babel/preset-typescript`) | No | Moderate | Existing Babel pipelines |
| Node.js type stripping | No | Instant (types replaced by spaces) | Scripts, servers, tooling |
| Deno, Bun | No by default (`deno check` checks) | Instant | Runtimes with built-in TypeScript support |

The usual setup is therefore: a fast transpiler in development and in the bundle, plus `tsc --noEmit` in the editor and in CI as the gatekeeper.

**Downlevelling.** The `target` option decides which syntax the output may use. Newer syntax is rewritten for older targets:

```typescript
// input
const city = user?.address?.city ?? 'unknown';
```

```javascript
// output with "target": "es2019" (no optional chaining or ?? yet)
var _a;
var _b;
const city = (_b = (_a = user === null || user === void 0 ? void 0 : user.address) === null || _a === void 0 ? void 0 : _a.city) !== null && _b !== void 0 ? _b : 'unknown';

// output with "target": "es2022": unchanged apart from removed types
```

Some features need helper functions in the output (for example class private fields for old targets). `importHelpers` imports them from the `tslib` package instead of copying them into every file. Downlevelling rewrites *syntax* only; missing *APIs* such as `Array.prototype.findLast` require polyfills (see `target` vs `lib` in the previous topics).

**Erasable syntax and type stripping.** Most TypeScript syntax is *erasable*: deleting it leaves valid JavaScript with the same behaviour. A few older features generate code instead, and tools that only strip types cannot handle them:

| Erasable (types only) | Not erasable (generates code) |
|---|---|
| Type annotations, `interface`, `type` | `enum` (except `declare enum`) |
| Generics, `as`, `satisfies`, `!` | `namespace` with values |
| `import type`, `export type` | Parameter properties: `constructor(private x: number)` |
| `declare` statements | `import x = require('...')`, `export =` |
| Access modifiers on normal fields | Decorators (need a transform) |

Node.js 22.18 and later (and Node.js 24) run `.ts` files directly by replacing type annotations with whitespace, so line and column positions do not change and no source maps are needed:

```bash
node server.ts                  # runs, as long as the file only uses erasable syntax
node --experimental-transform-types legacy.ts   # also transforms enums, namespaces, parameter properties
```

```text
SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode
```

Setting `"erasableSyntaxOnly": true` makes `tsc` report non-erasable syntax as errors, so code stays runnable by type-stripping tools:

```typescript
// With "erasableSyntaxOnly": true
enum Color { Red, Green }
// error TS1294: This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.
```

**Source maps.** After transpiling, bundling and minifying, the JavaScript that runs looks nothing like the TypeScript you wrote. A **source map** is a JSON file that maps each position in the generated code back to a file, line and column in the original source. Browser developer tools and Node.js read it to show stack traces and breakpoints in TypeScript.

```text
dist/app.js                               dist/app.js.map                         src/app.ts
-----------------------------             ------------------------------------    --------------------------
"use strict";                             {                                       const greet = (n: string) =>
const greet = (n) => `Hi ${n}`;    <----    "version": 3,                     ---->   `Hi ${n}`;
...                                         "file": "app.js",
//# sourceMappingURL=app.js.map            "sources": ["../src/app.ts"],
     ^ link from the code to its map        "sourcesContent": ["...original..."],   (only with inlineSources)
                                            "mappings": "AAAA,MAAM,KAAK,GAAG..."     <- Base64 VLQ segments:
                                          }                                           generated column ->
                                                                                     source file, line, column
```

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `sourceMap` | Writes `app.js.map` next to `app.js` and adds the `sourceMappingURL` comment |
| `inlineSourceMap` | Embeds the map as a base64 `data:` URL inside `app.js` (convenient, but larger files) |
| `inlineSources` | Puts the original TypeScript into the map, so the debugger needs no access to `src/` |
| `declarationMap` | Maps `.d.ts` files back to the source, so "Go to Definition" opens the `.ts` file of a library |

Node.js does not apply source maps to stack traces unless asked:

```bash
node --enable-source-maps dist/server.js
# Error: Invalid order
#     at createOrder (/app/src/orders.ts:42:11)     <- original TypeScript position instead of dist/orders.js
```

In production, a common practice is to generate source maps but not serve them publicly ("hidden" source maps), and upload them to an error-tracking service that uses them to de-minify stack traces.

**Watch mode and incremental builds.** `tsc --watch` keeps the compiler running and re-checks only what changed. `incremental` stores information about the previous build in a `.tsbuildinfo` file, so the next `tsc` run starts faster, and `tsc -b` uses it across project references. TypeScript 7 is a native port of the compiler (written in Go) that checks files in parallel. It is typically around ten times faster than the JavaScript-based 5.x compiler, which makes running full type checks on every save practical even in large repositories.

**Key Takeaways**

- Type checking (whole program, slower) and transpiling (per file, fast) are separate jobs; fast transpilers do not check types, so run `tsc --noEmit` in CI.
- `target` controls downlevelling of syntax; missing runtime APIs need polyfills, not a lower `target`.
- Erasable syntax can be removed without changing behaviour; enums, namespaces, parameter properties and decorators generate code and break type stripping. `erasableSyntaxOnly` enforces the difference.
- Node.js 22.18+ runs erasable `.ts` files directly; Deno and Bun also run TypeScript without a separate build step.
- Source maps link generated JavaScript back to TypeScript for debuggers and stack traces; use `--enable-source-maps` in Node.js and keep production maps private.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Compile a file that uses optional chaining, `??` and a class with a `#private` field with `--target es2017` and with `--target es2022`. Compare the two outputs and explain each difference.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a small Node.js project with `sourceMap: true`, throw an error inside a nested function, and run it with and without `--enable-source-maps`. Then open the `.js.map` file and identify `sources`, `names` and `mappings`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Our Vite application builds successfully even though it contains type errors. Why, and how should the pipeline be set up?" *Hint:* which tool inside Vite transforms TypeScript, what it does with types, and where `tsc --noEmit` belongs.

#### Typing DOM, Node and Third-Party Libraries

Most TypeScript code spends its time calling APIs it did not define: the browser's DOM, Node.js modules and npm packages. All of them are typed through declaration files, and each has its own patterns and pitfalls.

**The DOM.** The browser APIs are declared in `lib.dom.d.ts`, enabled by including `"dom"` (and `"dom.iterable"` for `for...of` over `NodeList`) in `lib`. Their types follow the interface hierarchy of Chapter 6.1:

```text
EventTarget
  └─ Node
       └─ Element
            └─ HTMLElement
                 ├─ HTMLInputElement      (value, checked, files ...)
                 ├─ HTMLAnchorElement     (href, download ...)
                 ├─ HTMLCanvasElement     (getContext ...)
                 └─ ... one interface per tag, mapped in HTMLElementTagNameMap
```

**Selecting elements.** The return type depends on how you select:

```typescript
const link = document.querySelector('a');              // HTMLAnchorElement | null (tag name: precise)
const field = document.querySelector('#email');        // Element | null (a CSS selector string: generic)
const byId = document.getElementById('email');         // HTMLElement | null

// Option 1: generic type argument (an unchecked claim, like "as")
const email = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#email');

// Option 2: an instanceof check (verified at runtime)
const el = document.getElementById('email');
if (el instanceof HTMLInputElement) {
  console.log(el.value);                               // el: HTMLInputElement
}

// Option 3: a small helper that fails fast with a clear message
function $<T extends Element>(selector: string, type: new () => T): T {
  const node = document.querySelector(selector);
  if (!(node instanceof type)) throw new Error(`${selector} is not a ${type.name}`);
  return node;
}
const amount = $('#amount', HTMLInputElement);         // HTMLInputElement, verified
const items = document.querySelectorAll('li.item');    // NodeListOf<Element>
```

**Events.** `addEventListener` uses event maps to type the event object from the event name. The `target` of an event, however, is only typed as `EventTarget | null`, because the event may come from any descendant (event delegation, Chapter 6.3):

```typescript
const form = document.querySelector('form')!;

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {            // event: SubmitEvent
  event.preventDefault();
  const data = new FormData(form);
  console.log(data.get('email'));                        // FormDataEntryValue | null
});

document.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {           // e: KeyboardEvent
  if (e.key === 'Escape') closeDialog();
});

const list = document.querySelector('ul')!;
list.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  e.currentTarget;                                       // EventTarget | null: the ul the listener is on
  e.target.closest('li');
  // error TS18047: 'e.target' is possibly 'null'.
  // error TS2339: Property 'closest' does not exist on type 'EventTarget'. (a target may be a non-Element node)
  if (e.target instanceof Element) {
    const item = e.target.closest('li');                 // HTMLLIElement | null
    item?.classList.toggle('done');
  }
});

function closeDialog(): void {}
```

**Custom events.** Declare the detail type with `CustomEvent<T>`, and add your event to the global event map so that listeners are typed automatically:

```typescript
export {};  // a module, so "declare global" is allowed

interface CartUpdatedDetail {
  itemCount: number;
  total: number;
}

declare global {
  interface DocumentEventMap {
    'cart:updated': CustomEvent<CartUpdatedDetail>;
  }
}

document.dispatchEvent(
  new CustomEvent<CartUpdatedDetail>('cart:updated', { detail: { itemCount: 3, total: 59.9 } }),
);

document.addEventListener('cart:updated', (e) => {
  console.log(e.detail.total.toFixed(2));               // e: CustomEvent<CartUpdatedDetail>
});
```

**`fetch` and JSON.** `response.json()` is typed as returning `Promise<any>`, which silently disables checking for everything that follows. Treat it as `unknown` and validate it (the type guards of 9.2, or a schema as in the strict mode topic):

```typescript
const res = await fetch('/api/cart');
const body: unknown = await res.json();   // explicitly unknown: must be checked before use
```

**Node.js.** Node's APIs are typed by the `@types/node` package. Install the version that matches your Node.js major version and list it in `types`:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @types/node@24
```

```typescript
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { createServer, type IncomingMessage, type ServerResponse } from 'node:http';
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';

const text = await readFile('config.json', 'utf8');        // string (Buffer without an encoding)

createServer((req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end(`You requested ${req.url ?? '/'}`);
}).listen(3000);

// Typed events: map each event name to its listener arguments
const jobs = new EventEmitter<{ done: [jobId: string, ms: number]; failed: [jobId: string, error: Error] }>();
jobs.on('done', (id, ms) => console.log(`${id} took ${ms} ms`)); // id: string, ms: number
jobs.emit('done', 'job-1', 120);
jobs.emit('done', 'job-1');
// error TS2554: Expected 3 arguments, but got 2.   (the "ms" argument is missing)
```

Environment variables are typed as `string | undefined`. You can document the expected ones by augmenting `NodeJS.ProcessEnv`, but remember this is a claim; validate them once at startup:

```typescript
export {};  // a module, so "declare global" is allowed

declare global {
  namespace NodeJS {
    interface ProcessEnv {
      DATABASE_URL?: string;
      PORT?: string;
    }
  }
}

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
if (!process.env.DATABASE_URL) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL is not set');
```

**Mixing environments.** Including both `dom` and `@types/node` in one project leads to conflicts, the classic one being timers: `setTimeout` returns a `number` in the browser and a `NodeJS.Timeout` in Node.js. Write `ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>` to stay portable, and split code for different environments (browser, server, tests) into separate `tsconfig` projects, each with its own `lib` and `types`.

```typescript
let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;   // number or NodeJS.Timeout, depending on the environment
function debounceSave(save: () => void): void {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  timer = setTimeout(save, 300);
}
```

**Third-party libraries.** For any npm package there are three situations:

| Situation | How to recognise it | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Types bundled with the package | `package.json` has `types` or a `types` export condition; npm shows a "TS" badge | Nothing: `import` just works |
| Types on DefinitelyTyped | npm shows a "DT" badge; `@types/<name>` exists | `npm install -D @types/<name>`, matching the library's major and minor version |
| No types anywhere | `error TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module '<name>'` | Write `declare module '<name>' { ... }` for the parts you use (9.2) |

Packages with a scope map to DefinitelyTyped names with a double underscore: the types for `@babel/core` are published as `@types/babel__core`.

**Example: jQuery and its plugins.** jQuery (Chapter 8) is a library typed on DefinitelyTyped. Installing `@types/jquery` types `$`, the wrapped sets and the event objects. A jQuery plugin adds methods to `$.fn` at runtime, and you describe it by *augmenting* the global `JQuery` interface:

```typescript
// npm install jquery && npm install -D @types/jquery
import $ from 'jquery';

declare global {
  interface JQuery<TElement = HTMLElement> {
    highlight(options?: { color?: string; durationMs?: number }): this;  // returns this for chaining
  }
}

$.fn.highlight = function (this: JQuery, options = {}) {
  const { color = 'yellow', durationMs = 800 } = options;
  return this.css('background-color', color).delay(durationMs).queue(function (next) {
    $(this).css('background-color', '');
    next();
  });
};

$('.price').highlight({ color: '#ffe08a' }).addClass('updated');  // typed and chainable
$('.price').highlight({ colour: 'red' });
// error TS2561: Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'colour' does not exist in type
//   '{ color?: string | undefined; durationMs?: number | undefined; }'. Did you mean to write 'color'?
```

**Choosing libraries with good types.** The quality of a package's types now matters as much as its API. Prefer packages that ship their own types, check that their generics produce useful inference (for example, query builders that infer result types from the query), and treat a package that needs `any` everywhere as a maintenance cost.

**Key Takeaways**

- DOM types come from `lib.dom.d.ts`; `querySelector` is precise for tag names, and `instanceof` checks or explicit type arguments are needed for other selectors.
- Event types come from event maps, but `event.target` is only `EventTarget | null`; narrow it with `instanceof` before use. Custom events are typed with `CustomEvent<T>` and by augmenting the event map.
- `response.json()` returns `any`; treat the result as `unknown` and validate it.
- Node.js is typed by `@types/node` (matching the runtime version, listed in `types`); use `node:` imports, typed `EventEmitter`s and validated environment variables.
- Library types are bundled, on DefinitelyTyped (`@types/*`), or written by you; plugins and globals are typed by augmenting existing interfaces.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a small to-do page in TypeScript: select the form, input and list without non-null assertions, add items on submit, and toggle them with a delegated click listener on the list.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a Node.js script that reads a JSON file of orders with `node:fs/promises`, validates it with a type guard, and emits typed `processed` and `invalid` events from a typed `EventEmitter`. Run it with Node.js type stripping, making sure it only uses erasable syntax.
> 3. *(Interview)* "You install an npm package and the compiler reports `TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module`. Walk through your options, from best to worst." *Hint:* check for a newer version with bundled types, then `@types`, then a hand-written `declare module` for the parts you use, and only as a last resort an empty `declare module`.

<a id="10-the-http-protocol-and-web-communication"></a>
## 10. The HTTP Protocol and Web Communication

Every page load, API call, login and live notification on the Web travels over HTTP or a protocol that starts its life as an HTTP request. Chapter 1.1 introduced the request-response cycle and Chapter 5.4 showed how browser code sends requests with `fetch`; this chapter looks at the protocol itself and at what applications build on top of it. It covers the HTTP message model, methods, status codes, caching and protocol versions (10.1), how state is added to a stateless protocol with cookies and sessions (10.2), how users and clients prove who they are and what they may do (10.3), how to design resource-oriented APIs (10.4), and how to push data in real time with Server-Sent Events, WebSocket and WebRTC (10.5). Server-side implementation details follow in Chapters 11 and 12, and attacks such as XSS and CSRF are treated in depth in Chapter 17.

<a id="101-the-http-protocol"></a>
### 10.1 The HTTP Protocol

This subchapter dissects HTTP from the message format upwards: the request-response cycle, methods and their guarantees, status codes, headers, content negotiation, caching, connection management, the evolution from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/3, the TLS layer that makes HTTPS, and the intermediaries that sit between clients and servers.

#### Request-Response Cycle and Statelessness

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) was designed in 1989-1991 to fetch hypertext documents, and its core model has survived every revision since: a **client** opens a connection, sends a **request** naming a resource, and a **server** sends back exactly one **response**. The client always speaks first; a server cannot send an HTTP response nobody asked for.

A useful analogy is a shop counter with no memory. Each customer walks up, asks for one item, receives it (or an explanation of why not), and leaves. If the same customer comes back, the clerk does not recognise them unless they show something, such as a loyalty card. That card is what cookies and tokens are to HTTP (10.2, 10.3).

```text
  Client (browser, curl, mobile app)                     Server
  ----------------------------------                     ------
          |   1. DNS lookup: example.com -> 203.0.113.10    |
          |   2. TCP (or QUIC) connection, TLS handshake    |
          |------------------------------------------------>|
          |   3. Request:  GET /products/42 HTTP/1.1        |
          |------------------------------------------------>|
          |                                   4. Process:   |
          |                                   route, read   |
          |                                   DB, render    |
          |   5. Response: HTTP/1.1 200 OK + body           |
          |<------------------------------------------------|
          |   6. Connection kept open for the next request  |
          |      (or closed)                                |
```

**What "stateless" means.** Each request must carry everything the server needs to process it. The protocol itself keeps no record of earlier requests: request 2 on the same connection is not "the follow-up to request 1" as far as HTTP is concerned. This is a deliberate design choice:

| Benefit of statelessness | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Horizontal scaling | Any server behind a load balancer can answer any request |
| Simple failure recovery | A crashed server loses no conversation state; the client simply retries elsewhere |
| Cacheability | A response depends only on the request, so intermediaries can reuse it |
| Simpler servers | No per-client memory has to be allocated, tracked or expired at the protocol level |

The cost is that anything resembling a "conversation" (a shopping cart, a login) must be rebuilt on top: either the client resends identifying data on every request (a cookie or a token), or the server stores state in a shared database keyed by an identifier the client sends.

**Stateless protocol, stateful applications.** Statelessness is a property of the protocol, not a ban on state. Servers keep plenty of state (databases, sessions); the rule is only that the *meaning* of a request must not depend on hidden protocol-level history.

```bash
# Two independent requests: the second one knows nothing about the first
curl -i https://api.example.com/cart          # 401 Unauthorized: who are you?
curl -i https://api.example.com/cart \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi..."  # 200 OK: the request now identifies the caller itself
```

**Key Takeaways**

- HTTP is a client-initiated request-response protocol: one request, one response.
- Stateless means each request is self-contained; the protocol does not remember previous requests.
- Statelessness enables load balancing, caching and simple recovery; state is layered on with cookies, sessions and tokens.
- Servers can still be stateful internally; what must not exist is implicit state in the protocol conversation.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use `curl -v https://example.com` and label each phase of the output: DNS/TCP connection, TLS, request, response headers, body.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Explain why a load balancer can send consecutive requests from the same browser to different servers without breaking a plain HTTP application, and what breaks if the application keeps login state in a server's memory.
> 3. *(Interview)* "HTTP is stateless, yet I stay logged in to my bank for twenty minutes. How?" *Hint:* distinguish protocol state from application state, and follow the identifier that is sent with every request.

#### Request and Response Message Format

An HTTP/1.1 message is plain text that a human can read and type. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode the same information in binary frames (see later in this subchapter), but the logical structure is identical, so learning the text format teaches you all versions.

**Request structure.** A request line, header fields, an empty line, and an optional body:

```http
POST /api/orders?notify=true HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
User-Agent: curl/8.9.1
Accept: application/json
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 46

{"productId": 42, "quantity": 2, "gift": true}
```

```text
POST                     /api/orders?notify=true      HTTP/1.1
 ^ method                 ^ request target             ^ protocol version
                            (path + query string)

Host: shop.example.com    <- header field: name, colon, value (names are case-insensitive)
...                       <- more headers
                          <- empty line (CRLF CRLF) ends the header section
{"productId": 42, ...}    <- body: exactly Content-Length bytes (or chunked, see below)
```

**Response structure.** A status line, headers, an empty line and an optional body:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:15:02 GMT
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 58
Location: /api/orders/9817

{"id": 9817, "status": "pending", "total": {"EUR": 59.8}}
```

| Part | Request | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Start line | `METHOD target VERSION` | `VERSION status-code reason-phrase` |
| Headers | Describe the request, client and body | Describe the response, server and body |
| Empty line | Mandatory separator | Mandatory separator |
| Body | Optional (usually present for POST, PUT, PATCH) | Optional (absent for 204, 304 and HEAD responses) |

**Line endings and the `Host` header.** Lines end with CRLF (`\r\n`). In HTTP/1.1 the `Host` header is mandatory: one IP address often hosts many sites (virtual hosting), and `Host` tells the server which one you want. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 its role is taken by the `:authority` pseudo-header.

**Knowing where the body ends.** Because a connection carries several messages in sequence, the receiver must know exactly where one body stops. There are two mechanisms:

- `Content-Length: 46`: the body is exactly 46 bytes.
- `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`: the body is sent in pieces, each prefixed with its size in hexadecimal, ending with a zero-sized chunk. This lets a server stream a response whose total size it does not know in advance.

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

7
Hello, 
6
world!
0

```

**Typing a request by hand.** Since HTTP/1.1 is text, you can speak it over a raw TCP connection:

```bash
# Open a TCP connection and type the request yourself (port 80, no TLS)
printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc example.com 80

# The same with TLS (port 443), using openssl as the "pipe"
printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' \
```
