| Meaningless | No information leakage | No user ID, timestamp or counter inside |
| Unique and server-issued | Prevent fixation and collisions | Server generates; never accept client-chosen IDs |

```javascript
import { randomBytes } from 'node:crypto';

const sessionId = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'); // 256 bits from a CSPRNG
// NOT: Math.random(), Date.now(), incrementing counters, or hashes of the username
```

**A minimal session implementation.** Frameworks provide this (`express-session`, Chapter 12), but writing it once makes the mechanism clear:

```javascript
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { randomBytes } from 'node:crypto';

const sessions = new Map();                        // sid -> { data, expiresAt } (demo: in memory)
const TTL_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000;                     // 30 minutes idle timeout

function getSession(req, res) {
  const sid = /(?:^|;\s*)sid=([^;]+)/.exec(req.headers.cookie ?? '')?.[1];
  const existing = sid && sessions.get(sid);
  if (existing && existing.expiresAt > Date.now()) {
    existing.expiresAt = Date.now() + TTL_MS;      // sliding expiration: extend on activity
    return existing.data;
  }
  const newSid = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');
  const session = { data: {}, expiresAt: Date.now() + TTL_MS };
  sessions.set(newSid, session);
  res.setHeader('Set-Cookie', `sid=${newSid}; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`); // add Secure on HTTPS
  return session.data;
}

createServer((req, res) => {
  const session = getSession(req, res);
  session.views = (session.views ?? 0) + 1;        // state survives across requests
  res.end(`You have viewed this page ${session.views} times\n`);
}).listen(3000);
```

**Signed session cookies.** Libraries often sign the session ID cookie with a secret (for example `sid=s%3AQ2x9....signature`). The signature does not make the random ID more secure, but it lets the server reject forged or malformed IDs cheaply before touching the store.

**Key Takeaways**

- A session is server-side state associated with a client through a session ID, normally stored in a cookie.
- Session IDs act as temporary passwords: generate them with a CSPRNG, with at least 128 bits of entropy, and put no meaning in them.
- Create a new ID at login and destroy the session at logout.
- Session data lives on the server, so it can be large, sensitive and changed or revoked at any time.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the minimal session server, open it in two different browsers, and explain why each browser has its own counter.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend the example with `/login?user=ada` and `/logout` routes that store and delete the user name, regenerating the session ID on login.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is `sessionId = sha256(username + Date.now())` a bad session ID?" *Hint:* estimate how many guesses an attacker who knows the username and the approximate login time would need.

#### Session Stores and Expiration

Where session data lives determines how an application scales, how fast each request is, and what happens when a server restarts. Expiration policies decide how long a stolen or forgotten session stays usable.

**The problem with in-memory sessions.** The `Map` in the previous example works on a single process only:

```text
              +--> Node process A: sessions { Zp4L: user 7 }
Load balancer |
              +--> Node process B: sessions { }        <- request with sid=Zp4L: "not logged in"
  Also: a restart or deployment wipes every session; memory grows without bound.
```

Two fixes exist: **sticky sessions** (the load balancer always routes a client to the same server, which is fragile when that server dies) or, preferably, a **shared session store**.

| Store | Strengths | Weaknesses | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-process memory | Fastest, zero setup | Lost on restart, not shared, leaks memory | Development only |
| **Redis / Valkey** | Very fast, built-in key expiry (TTL), shared | Extra service to run | The most common production choice |
| Relational DB (PostgreSQL, MySQL) | Already available, durable, queryable | Slower; expired rows must be cleaned up | Moderate traffic, audit needs |
| MongoDB | Flexible documents, TTL indexes | Extra load on the main database | MongoDB-based stacks |
| Signed/encrypted cookie (client-side) | No store at all | 4 KB limit, hard to revoke, data sent on every request | Small, non-sensitive session data |

```javascript
// Express + express-session + Redis store (details in Chapter 12)
import express from 'express';
import session from 'express-session';
import { RedisStore } from 'connect-redis';
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const redisClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
await redisClient.connect();

const app = express();
app.set('trust proxy', 1);                         // behind a TLS-terminating proxy (10.1)
app.use(session({
  store: new RedisStore({ client: redisClient, prefix: 'sess:' }),
  secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,              // signs the session ID cookie
  name: '__Host-sid',
  resave: false,                                   // don't write unchanged sessions back
  saveUninitialized: false,                        // don't create sessions for anonymous visitors
  rolling: true,                                   // refresh expiry on every response (sliding)
  cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge: 30 * 60 * 1000 },
}));
```

**Expiration policies.** A session should end even if the user never clicks "log out", to limit the window in which a stolen ID is useful.

| Policy | Rule | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Idle timeout** (sliding) | Expires after N minutes without activity | Abandoned sessions on shared computers |
| **Absolute timeout** | Expires N hours after creation, regardless of activity | Caps the lifetime of a stolen ID |
| **Explicit logout** | Server deletes the session | User intent |
| **Forced invalidation** | Server deletes all of a user's sessions | Password change, suspected compromise, account deletion |

Typical values: 15-30 minutes idle for banking and admin tools, hours or days for low-risk consumer apps, combined with an absolute limit. Expiry must be enforced **on the server**; the cookie's `Max-Age` is only a hint to the browser and can be ignored by an attacker who copied the ID.

```text
Redis keys with TTL implement both timeouts naturally:

SET sess:Zp4L '{"userId":7,"createdAt":1791018000}' EX 1800   <- idle timeout 30 min
(on each request) EXPIRE sess:Zp4L 1800                         <- slide the window
(on each request) if now - createdAt > 8h -> DEL sess:Zp4L      <- absolute timeout check

"Log out everywhere": keep a set user:7:sessions -> {Zp4L, Ab9q, ...} and delete them all.
```

**Key Takeaways**

- In-memory sessions break with multiple processes or restarts; production uses a shared store.
- Redis/Valkey is the usual store thanks to speed and built-in TTLs; databases work for lower traffic.
- Combine an idle (sliding) timeout with an absolute timeout, and enforce both on the server.
- Invalidate all of a user's sessions on password change or compromise.
- Avoid creating sessions for anonymous visitors unless needed (`saveUninitialized: false`).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Explain what users experience if an app keeps sessions in memory and is deployed three times a day.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add an absolute timeout to the minimal session server from the previous topic, storing `createdAt` and rejecting sessions older than eight hours even if they are active.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you implement 'log out of all other devices' in a session-based application?" *Hint:* you need an index from user to session IDs, and you must keep the current session.

#### Session Hijacking and Fixation Risks

Because a session ID is equivalent to the user's credentials for its lifetime, attackers try to **obtain** a valid ID (hijacking) or **plant** one they already know (fixation). Defending sessions is mostly about denying both.

**Session hijacking: stealing the ID.**

| Attack vector | How the ID is stolen | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Network sniffing | Cookie sent over plain HTTP | HTTPS everywhere, `Secure` flag, HSTS |
| XSS | Injected script reads `document.cookie` | `HttpOnly`, output encoding, CSP (Chapter 17) |
| URL leakage | ID in URL ends up in logs, `Referer`, shared links | Never put session IDs in URLs |
| Malware / infostealers | Cookies copied from the browser's profile | Short lifetimes, re-authentication for sensitive actions, device binding |
| Prediction / brute force | Guessable IDs | CSPRNG IDs with at least 128 bits |
| Logs and error pages | Server logs headers or dumps request objects | Redact `Cookie` and `Authorization` in logs |

**Session fixation: planting the ID.** The attacker does not steal the victim's ID; they make the victim use an ID the attacker already knows:

```text
1. Attacker visits bank.example and receives sid=EVIL123 (anonymous session).
2. Attacker gets the victim's browser to use sid=EVIL123:
     - a link like https://bank.example/?sid=EVIL123 on apps accepting IDs from URLs, or
     - a cookie set via a compromised or user-controlled subdomain (Domain=bank.example).
3. Victim logs in. The application marks session EVIL123 as "user = victim".
4. Attacker, still holding sid=EVIL123, is now logged in as the victim.
```

**The fix: regenerate the session ID on every privilege change.** At login (and at any elevation, such as entering admin mode), issue a fresh ID and discard the old one. An ID known before login then becomes useless.

```javascript
// Express + express-session: regenerate at login
app.post('/login', async (req, res, next) => {
  const user = await verifyCredentials(req.body.email, req.body.password);
  if (!user) return res.status(401).render('login', { error: 'Invalid credentials' });

  req.session.regenerate((err) => {          // new ID, old session destroyed
    if (err) return next(err);
    req.session.userId = user.id;
    req.session.createdAt = Date.now();
    req.session.save((err) => (err ? next(err) : res.redirect(303, '/account')));
  });
});

app.post('/logout', (req, res, next) => {
  req.session.destroy((err) => {             // remove server-side state
    if (err) return next(err);
    res.clearCookie('__Host-sid', { path: '/', secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' });
    res.redirect(303, '/');
  });
});
```

Other fixation defences: never accept session IDs from URL parameters, only accept IDs the server issued (reject unknown IDs instead of adopting them), and use the `__Host-` prefix so subdomains cannot inject the cookie.

**Additional hardening.**

- **Re-authentication** for sensitive actions (changing email or password, payments): ask for the password or an MFA step again even within a valid session.
- **Binding hints**: record the user agent and approximate location at login and flag significant changes. Binding strictly to IP address breaks mobile users whose IPs change, so it is rarely enforced.
- **Session listing**: show users their active sessions (device, location, last activity) and let them revoke them.
- **Device-bound credentials**: newer browser features such as Device Bound Session Credentials tie a session to a key stored in the device's secure hardware, so a copied cookie stops working elsewhere.

**Key Takeaways**

- Hijacking steals a valid session ID; fixation tricks the victim into using an ID the attacker knows.
- HTTPS + `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, strong random IDs and no IDs in URLs defend against hijacking.
- Regenerating the session ID at login and privilege changes defeats fixation.
- Logout must destroy the server-side session, not only clear the cookie.
- Require re-authentication for sensitive operations and let users view and revoke sessions.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For each defence (`Secure`, `HttpOnly`, regeneration at login, short idle timeout), name the attack it primarily mitigates.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Reproduce session fixation against the minimal session server from earlier: log in in one browser using a session ID copied from another, without regeneration. Then add regeneration and show the attack fails.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If we only clear the cookie on logout but leave the session in Redis, what is the risk?" *Hint:* consider an attacker who copied the cookie value earlier.

#### Cookies vs Tokens vs Web Storage

Modern applications can keep credentials in cookies, in tokens sent through the `Authorization` header, or in browser storage. The choice affects security (XSS and CSRF exposure), architecture (single domain vs many APIs) and which clients you can support. The debate is often framed as "cookies vs JWT", but that mixes two separate questions: **where** the credential is stored and transported, and **what** it contains.

```text
                   WHAT is in it?
                   opaque random ID (server lookup)    self-contained token (JWT, signed claims)
WHERE is it?      +---------------------------------+-------------------------------------------+
Cookie            | classic session cookie          | JWT stored in an HttpOnly cookie          |
(sent auto.)      |                                 |                                           |
                  +---------------------------------+-------------------------------------------+
JS-managed        | opaque access token in memory,  | JWT in memory or localStorage,            |
(Authorization    | introspected by the API         | sent as Authorization: Bearer             |
 header)          |                                 |                                           |
                  +---------------------------------+-------------------------------------------+
```

**Browser storage options.**

| Storage | Capacity | Sent automatically | Readable by JS | Lifetime | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cookie | ~4 KB each | Yes, to matching domain/path | Unless `HttpOnly` | Session or `Max-Age` | Domain + path |
| `localStorage` | ~5-10 MB per origin | No | Yes | Until cleared | Origin, all tabs |
| `sessionStorage` | ~5 MB per origin | No | Yes | Until the tab closes | Origin, single tab |
| In-memory variable | Unlimited | No | Yes (only by that page's code) | Until page reload | One page instance |
| IndexedDB | Large (quota-based) | No | Yes | Until cleared | Origin |

**The security trade-off.**

| | `HttpOnly` cookie | Token in `localStorage` + `Authorization` header |
|---|---|---|
| **XSS** | Script cannot read the credential (but can still act within the page) | Script can read and **exfiltrate** the token for use anywhere |
| **CSRF** | Browser attaches it automatically, so CSRF is possible; mitigate with `SameSite` and CSRF tokens | Not sent automatically, so CSRF does not apply |
| **Cross-domain APIs** | Hard: cookies are tied to a domain, need CORS with credentials | Easy: send the header to any API |
| **Mobile / server clients** | Awkward (need a cookie jar) | Natural |
| **Revocation** | Easy with server sessions | Hard for self-contained tokens (10.3) |

Since XSS can do serious damage in either case, the deciding factor is usually: an `HttpOnly` cookie stops a stolen credential from being *taken away*, while CSRF is now well-mitigated by `SameSite` and tokens. For browser-based apps on your own domain, current guidance (including OWASP's) therefore favours **`HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookies**, and recommends never putting long-lived tokens in `localStorage`.

**Common patterns.**

| Application type | Recommended approach |
|---|---|
| Server-rendered site or SPA served from the same site as its API | Session cookie (`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`) |
| SPA calling third-party or multiple APIs | **Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)**: a small server on the SPA's domain holds tokens and gives the browser only a session cookie |
| SPA that must hold tokens itself | Short-lived access token in memory; refresh token in an `HttpOnly` cookie scoped to the refresh endpoint |
| Native mobile app | Tokens in the OS secure storage (Keychain, Android Keystore), sent in `Authorization` |
| Server-to-server | API keys or OAuth client-credentials tokens in headers (10.3) |

```javascript
// Same-origin SPA using a session cookie: no token handling in JavaScript at all
const res = await fetch('/api/orders', { credentials: 'same-origin' }); // default: cookie sent
// Cross-site API with cookies: needs credentials: 'include' + CORS with an explicit origin (5.4)

// Token-based alternative: the code must attach the token itself
let accessToken = null;                         // kept in memory, not localStorage
const res2 = await fetch('https://api.example.com/orders', {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` },
});
```

**What belongs in Web Storage.** Non-sensitive client state: UI preferences, drafts, cached API data for offline use, feature flags. Never passwords, long-lived tokens or personal data that should not survive on a shared computer.

**Key Takeaways**

- Separate *where* a credential lives (cookie or JS-managed) from *what* it is (opaque ID or self-contained token).
- `HttpOnly` cookies resist token theft through XSS but need CSRF protection; JS-managed tokens avoid CSRF but are exposed to XSS.
- For same-site web apps, prefer `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookies; use a BFF when an SPA needs third-party tokens.
- `localStorage` persists indefinitely and is readable by any script on the origin; keep credentials out of it.
- Native and server clients naturally use tokens in the `Authorization` header.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Fill in a table for cookie, `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`: survives closing the tab? survives closing the browser? shared between tabs? sent automatically to the server?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Sketch the request flow for a React SPA on `app.example.com` that uses a BFF on the same domain to call a third-party API with OAuth tokens. Mark where each credential is stored.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A colleague proposes storing JWTs in `localStorage` because 'cookies are vulnerable to CSRF'. How do you respond?" *Hint:* compare what an XSS attacker can do with each, and how `SameSite` changed the CSRF picture.

<a id="103-authentication-and-authorization"></a>
### 10.3 Authentication and Authorization

This subchapter covers how web applications establish who a user or client is and what they may do: the HTTP authentication framework, password-based and session-based login, password storage, JSON Web Tokens, token lifecycles, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, API keys, role-based access control and multi-factor authentication.

#### Authentication vs Authorization

Two questions sit in front of every protected resource, and they are easy to confuse because both are often handled by the same "auth" code:

- **Authentication (AuthN)**: *Who are you?* Verifying an identity claim, for example by checking a password, a token signature or a fingerprint.
- **Authorization (AuthZ)**: *What are you allowed to do?* Deciding whether an authenticated (or anonymous) identity may perform a specific action on a specific resource.

At an airport, showing your passport at security is authentication (it proves you are Ada Lovelace); your boarding pass for gate B12 is authorization (it allows Ada onto *this* flight, not every flight).

```text
 Request: DELETE /api/projects/17  Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
     |
     v
 +------------------------+   fails -> 401 Unauthorized + WWW-Authenticate
 | 1. Authentication      |            ("we don't know who you are")
 |    verify token -> user 7
 +------------------------+
     |
     v
 +------------------------+   fails -> 403 Forbidden
 | 2. Authorization       |            ("we know you, and the answer is no")
 |    may user 7 delete   |            or 404 to hide the resource's existence
 |    project 17?         |
 +------------------------+
     |
     v
  Handler executes
```

| | Authentication | Authorization |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Who is the caller? | May the caller do this? |
| Input | Credentials (password, token, key, certificate, biometric) | Identity + action + resource + context |
| Output | An identity (user ID, client ID) and its attributes | Allow or deny |
| Failure status | `401 Unauthorized` | `403 Forbidden` (or `404`) |
| Typical mechanisms | Passwords, sessions, JWT, OAuth/OIDC, passkeys, MFA | Roles (RBAC), ownership checks, attributes (ABAC), scopes |
| Happens | Once per login, then verified per request | On every request, for every action |

**Authorization must be checked on the server, per resource.** The most common authorization bug is not a broken login but a missing ownership check: the API verifies that the caller is logged in, then returns `/api/invoices/1002` without checking that invoice 1002 belongs to them. This is **Broken Object Level Authorization** (also called IDOR), at the top of the OWASP API Security Top 10.

```javascript
// Express-style handler: authentication alone is NOT enough
app.get('/api/invoices/:id', requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const invoice = await db.invoices.findById(req.params.id);
  if (!invoice) return res.sendStatus(404);
  if (invoice.ownerId !== req.user.id && !req.user.roles.includes('accountant')) {
    return res.sendStatus(404);              // authorization: hide other users' invoices
  }
  res.json(invoice);
});
```

Hiding a button in the UI is not authorization: anyone can send the HTTP request directly with `curl`.

**Key Takeaways**

- Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides permissions for an action on a resource.
- Failed authentication means `401`; failed authorization means `403` (or `404` to hide existence).
- Authorization is evaluated on every request, on the server, including ownership checks per object.
- Client-side checks improve the user experience but provide no security.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Classify each as authentication or authorization: checking a TOTP code, checking that a user is an admin, verifying a JWT signature, checking that a document belongs to the caller, validating an API key.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Find an endpoint in a project of yours that loads a record by ID and check whether it verifies ownership. Write a test that requests another user's record and expects 403 or 404.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does the HTTP spec call the 401 status 'Unauthorized' if it is about authentication?" *Hint:* historical naming, and look at which header must accompany a 401.

#### HTTP Basic Authentication

HTTP defines a generic **authentication framework**: a server challenges with `401` and a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming a scheme; the client retries with an `Authorization` header in that scheme. **Basic** is the simplest scheme (RFC 7617): the client sends a username and password with every request.

```text
Browser                                                 Server
  | GET /admin                                            |
  |------------------------------------------------------>|
  | 401 Unauthorized                                      |
  | WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Admin area", charset="UTF-8"
  |<------------------------------------------------------|
  |   (browser shows its built-in login dialog)           |
  | GET /admin                                            |
  | Authorization: Basic YWRhOmMwbXB1dDNy                 |
  |------------------------------------------------------>|
  | 200 OK                                                |
  |<------------------------------------------------------|
  The browser then resends the header automatically for this realm.
```

**Encoding is not encryption.** The credential is just `username:password` encoded in Base64, which anyone can decode:

```bash
echo -n 'ada:c0mput3r' | base64        # YWRhOmMwbXB1dDNy
echo 'YWRhOmMwbXB1dDNy' | base64 -d    # ada:c0mput3r   <- trivially reversible
curl -u ada:c0mput3r https://example.com/admin   # curl builds the header for you
```

Basic authentication is therefore only acceptable **over HTTPS**.

**A server-side implementation.**

```javascript
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

const USER = 'ada';
const PASS = process.env.ADMIN_PASSWORD;            // never hardcode real credentials

function safeEqual(a, b) {                          // constant-time comparison
  const bufA = Buffer.from(a), bufB = Buffer.from(b);
  return bufA.length === bufB.length && timingSafeEqual(bufA, bufB);
}

createServer((req, res) => {
  const [scheme, encoded] = (req.headers.authorization ?? '').split(' ');
  if (scheme === 'Basic' && encoded) {
    const decoded = Buffer.from(encoded, 'base64').toString('utf8');
    const sep = decoded.indexOf(':');               // password may contain ':'; username may not
    const user = decoded.slice(0, sep), pass = decoded.slice(sep + 1);
    if (sep > 0 && safeEqual(user, USER) && safeEqual(pass, PASS)) {
      return res.end('Welcome to the admin area\n');
    }
  }
  res.writeHead(401, { 'WWW-Authenticate': 'Basic realm="Admin area", charset="UTF-8"' });
  res.end('Authentication required\n');
}).listen(3000);
```

`timingSafeEqual` prevents attackers from guessing the secret character by character by measuring how long the comparison takes. In a real system the password would be checked against a stored hash (see Password Hashing below).

**Strengths and weaknesses.**

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Universally supported by browsers, `curl`, HTTP libraries | Password sent with **every** request (more exposure) |
| Stateless, no sessions or cookies | No logout: browsers cache credentials until closed |
| Trivial to implement, good for scripts and internal tools | Browser dialog cannot be styled; no "forgot password", MFA or lockout UI |
| | Credentials can leak through logs or misconfigured proxies |

**Where it is still used.** Protecting staging sites and internal dashboards (often configured in nginx rather than in the app), machine-to-machine calls where the "password" is an API key (several APIs accept the key as the Basic username), and the OAuth token endpoint, where clients authenticate with their client ID and secret using Basic.

**Key Takeaways**

- The HTTP authentication framework uses `401` + `WWW-Authenticate` for the challenge and `Authorization` for the credentials.
- Basic sends `base64(username:password)` on every request: encoded, not encrypted; HTTPS is mandatory.
- Compare secrets in constant time and check against stored password hashes.
- Basic suits scripts, internal tools and staging protection, not consumer login.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Decode the header `Authorization: Basic Z3Vlc3Q6aHVudGVyMg==` by hand or with `base64 -d` and explain why seeing it in a log is a security incident.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Protect a static directory with Basic authentication in nginx (`auth_basic` and an `htpasswd` file) and access it with `curl -u`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is it hard to implement a logout button for Basic authentication?" *Hint:* who stores the credentials, and when does the browser stop sending them?

#### Digest Access Authentication

Digest authentication (RFC 7616, originally RFC 2617) was designed in the 1990s to fix Basic's biggest flaw at a time when HTTPS was rare: the password never travels over the wire. Instead the client proves it knows the password by sending a **hash** computed from the password and a one-time value supplied by the server.

**The challenge-response idea.** The server sends a random **nonce**; the client returns `hash(username, password, nonce, request details)`. An eavesdropper sees only the hash, which is useless for a different nonce, so recorded responses cannot be replayed later.

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Digest realm="api@example.com",
                  qop="auth",
                  algorithm=SHA-256,
                  nonce="7ypf/xlj9XXwfDPEoM4URrv/xwf94BcCAzFZH4GiTo0v",
                  opaque="FQhe/qaU925kfnzjCev0ciny7QMkPqMAFRtzCUYo5tdS"
```

```http
GET /dir/index.html HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Digest username="Mufasa", realm="api@example.com",
               uri="/dir/index.html", algorithm=SHA-256,
               nonce="7ypf/xlj9XXwfDPEoM4URrv/xwf94BcCAzFZH4GiTo0v",
               nc=00000001, cnonce="f2/wE4q74E6zIJEtWaHKaf5wv/H5QzzpXusqGemxURZJ",
               qop=auth,
               response="753927fa0e85d155564e2e272a28d1802ca10daf4496794697cf8db5856cb6c1",
               opaque="FQhe/qaU925kfnzjCev0ciny7QMkPqMAFRtzCUYo5tdS"
```

**How the response is computed.**

```text
HA1      = H(username ":" realm ":" password)
HA2      = H(method ":" uri)
response = H(HA1 ":" nonce ":" nc ":" cnonce ":" qop ":" HA2)

H        = MD5 (legacy) or SHA-256 (RFC 7616)
nc       = nonce count: increments for each request with the same nonce (replay detection)
cnonce   = client nonce: random value chosen by the client
```

```javascript
// Computing a Digest response (client side) in Node.js
import { createHash, randomBytes } from 'node:crypto';

const H = (s) => createHash('sha256').update(s).digest('hex');

function digestResponse({ username, password, realm, nonce, method, uri, nc = '00000001' }) {
  const cnonce = randomBytes(16).toString('hex');
  const ha1 = H(`${username}:${realm}:${password}`);
  const ha2 = H(`${method}:${uri}`);
  const response = H(`${ha1}:${nonce}:${nc}:${cnonce}:auth:${ha2}`);
  return { cnonce, nc, response };      // sent in the Authorization header with the other fields
}
```

**Why Digest faded.**

| Problem | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Server must store `HA1` or the plain password | `HA1` is password-equivalent for that realm and cannot be a slow, salted hash like bcrypt or Argon2 |
| Weak algorithm in practice | Most deployments used MD5, which is fast to brute-force |
| No server authentication | A man-in-the-middle can downgrade the client to Basic |
| Limited protection | Only the credentials are protected; the request and response bodies travel in clear text |
| Same UX problems as Basic | Browser dialog, no logout, no MFA |

Once HTTPS became universal, it protected *everything* (not just credentials) and let servers store passwords with modern hashing. Digest survives mainly in embedded devices, IP cameras, SIP telephony and some legacy enterprise systems; `curl --digest` and most HTTP libraries still support it.

**Key Takeaways**

- Digest is a challenge-response scheme: the client sends a hash of the password combined with a server nonce, never the password itself.
- Nonces, nonce counts and client nonces defend against replay.
- The server must store password-equivalent data (`HA1`), which conflicts with modern password hashing.
- HTTPS plus form or token authentication has replaced Digest on the Web; it lingers in devices and legacy systems.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Explain in your own words why capturing one Digest `Authorization` header does not let an attacker reuse it a minute later, while capturing a Basic header does.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Use `curl --digest -u user:passwd -v https://httpbin.org/digest-auth/auth/user/passwd` and identify the nonce, cnonce and response values in the exchange.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Digest never sends the password, so why is it considered less secure than Basic over HTTPS?" *Hint:* compare what each scheme forces the server to store and what TLS protects.

#### Form-Based and Session-Based Login

Almost every website logs users in with its own HTML form, not with the browser's Basic/Digest dialog. The form collects credentials, the server verifies them, and a **session** (10.2) remembers the result. This gives full control over the user experience: branding, "remember me", password reset, MFA, rate limiting and error messages.

**The complete flow.**

```text
1. GET /login                          -> HTML form (with a CSRF token)
2. POST /login  email=...&password=... -> server:
     a. rate-limit by account and IP
     b. look up user by email
     c. verify password against stored hash (constant time)
     d. regenerate session ID, store userId in session
     e. 303 See Other, Location: /dashboard   + Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=...
3. GET /dashboard  Cookie: __Host-sid=... -> session lookup -> user 7 -> page
4. POST /logout                        -> destroy session, clear cookie, redirect
```

**The login form.**

```html
<form method="post" action="/login">
  <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="r4nd0m-t0k3n">          <!-- CSRF protection, Chapter 17 -->
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="username" required></label>
  <label>Password
    <input type="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password" required>
  </label>
  <button>Sign in</button>
</form>
```

The `autocomplete` values let password managers fill and save credentials correctly; on a sign-up form use `autocomplete="new-password"`.

**Server side (Express-style).**

```javascript
import argon2 from 'argon2';

app.post('/login', loginRateLimiter, async (req, res, next) => {
  const { email, password } = req.body;
  const user = await db.users.findByEmail(email.toLowerCase());

  // Verify even when the user does not exist, so response time does not reveal valid emails
  const hash = user?.passwordHash ?? DUMMY_HASH;
  const ok = await argon2.verify(hash, password);

  if (!user || !ok) {
    return res.status(401).render('login', { error: 'Invalid email or password' }); // generic message
  }
  req.session.regenerate((err) => {                // prevent session fixation (10.2)
    if (err) return next(err);
    req.session.userId = user.id;
    res.redirect(303, '/dashboard');               // Post/Redirect/Get (10.1)
  });
});

function requireLogin(req, res, next) {           // reusable authentication middleware
  if (req.session.userId) return next();
  res.redirect(303, `/login?next=${encodeURIComponent(req.originalUrl)}`);
}
app.get('/dashboard', requireLogin, (req, res) => res.render('dashboard'));
```

**Security checklist for login forms.**

| Concern | Practice |
|---|---|
| Credentials in transit | HTTPS only; never send the form over HTTP |
| User enumeration | Same message and similar timing for "unknown email" and "wrong password" (also for reset and sign-up flows) |
| Brute force and credential stuffing | Rate limit per account and per IP, progressive delays, CAPTCHA after failures, check passwords against breach lists |
| Session fixation | Regenerate the session ID after login |
| CSRF on login and logout | CSRF tokens and `SameSite` cookies; logout must be `POST`, not a GET link |
| Open redirects | Only accept relative, same-site `next` URLs after login |
| "Remember me" | A separate long-lived, random, revocable token stored hashed on the server, not a longer session |
| Password managers | Correct `autocomplete`, allow paste, no maximum length below 64 characters |

**Key Takeaways**

- Form-based login posts credentials to the server, which verifies them and creates a session cookie.
- Regenerate the session on login, redirect with `303`, and destroy the session on logout (via `POST`).
- Return identical errors for unknown users and wrong passwords to prevent enumeration.
- Rate limiting, breach-password checks and CSRF protection are part of a correct login implementation.
- Use proper `autocomplete` attributes so password managers work.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write the HTML for a sign-up form with email, password and password confirmation, using the correct `autocomplete` values.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement login, logout and a protected `/dashboard` with `express-session`, including the `?next=` redirect, and validate that `next` cannot point to another site.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you design 'remember me' so that a stolen remember-me cookie can be detected and revoked?" *Hint:* look up the selector/validator pattern and token rotation on each use.

#### Password Hashing and Salting

Databases leak: through SQL injection, stolen backups, misconfigured cloud buckets or insiders. Since people reuse passwords, a leaked password table exposes users on *other* sites too. A server should therefore never store passwords in a form that can be turned back into the original password, and should make guessing as slow as possible.

**Why not encryption or plain hashing.**

| Storage | Problem |
|---|---|
| Plain text | Leak = every password exposed immediately |
| Encryption (AES) | Reversible: whoever gets the key (often stored next to the data) gets every password |
| Fast hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) | GPUs compute billions of guesses per second; identical passwords give identical hashes; precomputed tables (rainbow tables) work |
| Fast hash + salt | Defeats precomputed tables, but brute force is still very fast |
| **Slow, salted password hash** (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2) | Each guess is deliberately expensive; each password has a unique salt |

**Salt.** A random value (at least 16 bytes), generated per password and stored next to the hash. It ensures that two users with the password `summer2026` get different hashes and that an attacker must attack each hash separately. The salt is not secret.

**Work factor.** Password hashing functions are intentionally slow and tunable: you choose parameters so that one hash takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds on your server. For a legitimate login that is unnoticeable; for an attacker trying billions of guesses it is crippling. Memory-hard functions (Argon2id, scrypt) also require lots of RAM per guess, which neutralises GPUs and custom hardware.

**Pepper (optional).** A secret key stored outside the database (in a secrets manager or HSM), mixed in with an HMAC, so that a database dump alone is not enough to start cracking.

| Algorithm | Recommendation (OWASP, current) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Argon2id** | Preferred: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 degree of parallelism (or stronger) | Winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015) |
| scrypt | N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1 | Built into Node.js `crypto` |
| bcrypt | Cost 10 or more | Widely available; truncates input at 72 bytes |
| PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 | 600,000 iterations or more | Needed for FIPS-140 compliance; not memory-hard |

**Argon2id in Node.js** (the `argon2` npm package stores algorithm, parameters, salt and hash in one self-describing string):

```javascript
import argon2 from 'argon2';

const hash = await argon2.hash('correct horse battery staple'); // argon2id with a random salt by default
console.log(hash);
// $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$Zl0yQ0p...$Wq4mG8...
//  ^algo     ^ver ^memory KiB, iterations, parallelism  ^salt  ^hash

const ok = await argon2.verify(hash, 'correct horse battery staple'); // true
```

**scrypt with only the standard library.**

```javascript
import { scrypt, randomBytes, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';
import { promisify } from 'node:util';

const scryptAsync = promisify(scrypt);
const PARAMS = { N: 2 ** 17, r: 8, p: 1, maxmem: 256 * 1024 * 1024 }; // ~128 MiB per hash

export async function hashPassword(password) {
  const salt = randomBytes(16);                                  // unique per password
  const key = await scryptAsync(password.normalize('NFKC'), salt, 64, PARAMS);
  return `scrypt$${salt.toString('base64')}$${key.toString('base64')}`;
}

export async function verifyPassword(password, stored) {
  const [, saltB64, keyB64] = stored.split('$');
  const expected = Buffer.from(keyB64, 'base64');
  const actual = await scryptAsync(password.normalize('NFKC'), Buffer.from(saltB64, 'base64'),
                                   expected.length, PARAMS);
  return timingSafeEqual(actual, expected);                      // constant-time comparison
}
```

**Upgrading old hashes.** Because the stored string records the algorithm and parameters, you can raise the work factor over time: on each successful login, if the stored hash uses outdated parameters, rehash the (now known) password with the new ones (`argon2.needsRehash(hash)` does this check). Legacy MD5/SHA-1 tables can be migrated immediately by wrapping them (`argon2(md5(password))`) and then rehashing properly at the next login.

**Password policy (NIST SP 800-63B).** Require at least 8 characters (15 or more when the password is the only factor), allow at least 64 characters and all Unicode characters including spaces, check new passwords against lists of breached passwords (for example the Have I Been Pwned range API), and **do not** force periodic changes or arbitrary composition rules ("one uppercase, one symbol").

**Key Takeaways**

- Never store passwords in plain text, encrypted, or with fast hashes like SHA-256.
- Use a slow, salted, preferably memory-hard function: Argon2id first, then scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2.
- Salts are unique per password and not secret; peppers are secret and stored outside the database.
- Store algorithm and parameters with the hash so you can rehash with stronger settings at login.
- Follow modern policy: length over complexity, breached-password checks, no forced rotation.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Hash the same password twice with `argon2.hash` and explain why the outputs differ yet both verify.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Measure how long one hash takes with bcrypt cost 10, 12 and 14 and with Argon2id at the default settings on your machine. Pick parameters that take about 100-250 ms and justify the choice.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your company discovers its user table stores unsalted SHA-1 password hashes. What do you do, today and over the next months?" *Hint:* wrap existing hashes immediately, rehash at login, consider forcing resets, and think about disclosure.

#### JSON Web Tokens: Structure and Claims

A session cookie is an opaque ticket: the server must look it up to know who it belongs to. A **JSON Web Token** (JWT, RFC 7519, pronounced "jot") is a self-contained ticket: it carries the user's identity and attributes inside it, protected by a digital signature so nobody can alter them. Any server that has the verification key can trust it without a database lookup, which is attractive for distributed systems and APIs.

**Structure.** A JWT is three Base64url-encoded parts separated by dots:

```text
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsIm5hbWUiOiJBZGEiLCJyb2xlIjoiYWRtaW4iLCJpYXQiOjE3OTEwMTgwMDAsImV4cCI6MTc5MTAxODkwMH0.Lf3...signature...
|_________ header _________________| |_______________________________ payload ________________________________________________| |__ signature __|
```

```jsonc
// Header: how the token is signed
{ "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" }

// Payload: the claims (statements about the subject)
{
  "sub": "42",
  "name": "Ada",
  "role": "admin",
  "iat": 1791018000,
  "exp": 1791018900
}

// Signature: HMACSHA256(base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload), secret)
```

**Signed, not encrypted.** Base64url is an encoding; anyone holding the token can read the payload:

```javascript
const [, payload] = token.split('.');
console.log(JSON.parse(Buffer.from(payload, 'base64url').toString())); // { sub: '42', name: 'Ada', ... }
```

The signature guarantees **integrity and authenticity** (the payload was issued by someone with the key and has not been changed), not confidentiality. Never put passwords, personal data or secrets in a JWT payload. (Encrypted tokens exist, JWE, but are much less common.)

**Registered claims.** RFC 7519 defines short standard claim names:

| Claim | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `iss` | Issuer | Who created and signed the token (`https://auth.example.com`) |
| `sub` | Subject | Whom the token is about (user ID), unique within the issuer |
| `aud` | Audience | Who the token is intended for (`https://api.example.com`); recipients must reject tokens not meant for them |
| `exp` | Expiration time | Seconds since the Unix epoch after which the token must be rejected |
| `nbf` | Not before | Token is not valid before this time |
| `iat` | Issued at | When the token was created |
| `jti` | JWT ID | Unique identifier, useful for revocation lists and replay detection |

Applications add **private claims** (`role`, `tenant`, `scope`). Keep tokens small: they are sent on every request, and HTTP headers have size limits (often 8-16 KB at proxies).

**JWT vs opaque session ID.**

| | Opaque session ID | JWT |
|---|---|---|
| Content | Random string | Signed claims |
| Validation | Lookup in session store | Signature check + claim checks, no lookup |
| Revocation | Delete from store: immediate | Hard: valid until `exp` unless you add a deny list |
| Size | ~32-64 bytes | Hundreds of bytes to several KB |
| Data freshness | Always current (read from store) | Frozen at issue time (a revoked role remains in the token) |
| Best fit | Browser sessions for one application | Short-lived API access tokens across services, federated identity (ID tokens) |

**Key Takeaways**

- A JWT is `header.payload.signature`, each part Base64url-encoded.
- The payload is readable by anyone; the signature only prevents tampering. Keep secrets out.
- Registered claims (`iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `jti`) standardise identity and validity.
- JWTs avoid server lookups but are hard to revoke and freeze data at issue time, so keep them short-lived.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Paste a sample JWT into a decoder (or decode it with `Buffer.from(part, 'base64url')`) and identify the algorithm, subject and expiry time as a human-readable date.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Change one character of a JWT's payload (for example the role) and re-encode it. Explain why a correctly implemented server rejects it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose server-side sessions over JWTs for a web application?" *Hint:* consider revocation, number of services, data freshness and the size of each request.

#### JWT Signing, Verification and Algorithms

The security of a JWT rests entirely on its signature and on how strictly the receiver verifies it. Most real-world JWT vulnerabilities come not from the cryptography but from verifiers that accept the wrong algorithm, skip claim checks or trust the header.

**Two families of algorithms.**

| Family | Examples | Key | Who can sign | Who can verify |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HMAC** (symmetric) | `HS256`, `HS384`, `HS512` | One shared secret | Anyone with the secret | Anyone with the secret |
| **Asymmetric** | `RS256` (RSA), `PS256` (RSA-PSS), `ES256` (ECDSA P-256), `EdDSA` (Ed25519) | Private/public key pair | Only the private key holder | Anyone with the public key |

```text
HS256: auth server and every API share the SAME secret
       -> any API that can verify can also forge tokens

RS256/ES256/EdDSA: auth server signs with its PRIVATE key
       -> APIs verify with the PUBLIC key, published as a JWKS
          (JSON Web Key Set) at e.g. https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
       -> compromising an API does not let anyone mint tokens
```

Use HMAC when the same service issues and verifies tokens; use asymmetric keys when tokens cross service or organisation boundaries. Each key has an ID (`kid` in the header) so the issuer can rotate keys while old tokens remain verifiable.

**Signing and verifying with `jose`** (a dependency-free library that works in Node.js, browsers, Deno and edge runtimes):

```javascript
import { SignJWT, jwtVerify } from 'jose';

const secret = new TextEncoder().encode(process.env.JWT_SECRET); // at least 256 random bits for HS256

// Issue a token
const token = await new SignJWT({ role: 'admin' })     // private claims
  .setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'HS256' })
  .setSubject('42')
  .setIssuer('https://auth.example.com')
  .setAudience('https://api.example.com')
  .setIssuedAt()
  .setExpirationTime('15m')                            // short-lived
  .sign(secret);

// Verify a token: signature AND claims
try {
  const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, secret, {
    algorithms: ['HS256'],                             // allowlist: never trust the header's alg
    issuer: 'https://auth.example.com',
    audience: 'https://api.example.com',
    clockTolerance: 30,                                // seconds of allowed clock skew
  });
  console.log(payload.sub, payload.role);              // '42' 'admin'
} catch (err) {
  // JWTExpired, JWSSignatureVerificationFailed, JWTClaimValidationFailed, ...
  console.error('Rejected:', err.code);
}
```

```javascript
// Asymmetric verification against a remote JWKS (keys fetched and cached by kid)
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose';

const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL('https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json'));
const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, {
  algorithms: ['ES256', 'RS256'],
  issuer: 'https://auth.example.com',
  audience: 'https://api.example.com',
});
```

**Classic attacks and their defences.**

| Attack | How it works | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| `alg: none` | Attacker sets the header to `{"alg":"none"}` and removes the signature; naive libraries accept it | Allowlist algorithms; modern libraries reject `none` by default |
| Algorithm confusion | Server expects RS256; attacker sends an HS256 token signed with the server's **public** key as the HMAC secret | Allowlist algorithms per key; never let the token choose |
| Weak HMAC secret | Short or guessable secrets can be brute-forced offline from any token | At least 256 random bits from a CSPRNG, stored in a secrets manager |
| Missing claim checks | Expired tokens or tokens for another service are accepted | Always validate `exp`, `iss`, `aud` (and `nbf`) |
| Header injection (`jku`, `x5u`, `kid`) | Attacker points the verifier to their own key or injects paths into `kid` | Never fetch keys from URLs in the token; treat `kid` as a lookup key only |
| `decode` instead of `verify` | Code reads claims without verifying the signature | Use the library's verify function; decode only for debugging |

**Key Takeaways**

- HMAC algorithms share one secret between signer and verifiers; asymmetric algorithms let anyone verify with a public key while only the issuer can sign.
- Publish public keys as a JWKS and rotate keys with `kid`.
- Always verify the signature with an algorithm allowlist, then check `exp`, `iss` and `aud`.
- Use long random secrets for HMAC and never trust key locations or algorithms from the token header.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Generate a 256-bit secret with `node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'))"`, then sign and verify a token with `jose`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Generate an Ed25519 key pair with `generateKeyPair('EdDSA')` from `jose`, export the public key as a JWK, serve it as a JWKS from a small server, and verify tokens in a second process using `createRemoteJWKSet`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Explain the RS256-to-HS256 algorithm confusion attack and why it worked." *Hint:* what does the attacker know about an RS256 verification key, and what does an HMAC verifier do with the key it is given?

#### Access Tokens, Refresh Tokens and Revocation

Self-contained tokens create a dilemma. Long-lived tokens are convenient but dangerous: a stolen token works until it expires and cannot easily be revoked. Very short-lived tokens are safer but would force users to log in constantly. The standard solution splits the job between two tokens.

| | Access token | Refresh token |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Authorise API calls | Obtain new access tokens |
| Sent to | Every API request (`Authorization: Bearer`) | Only the authorization server's token endpoint |
| Lifetime | Short: 5-15 minutes typical | Long: days to months, often with absolute and idle limits |
| Format | Often JWT (verified locally) or opaque | Opaque random string, stored (hashed) on the server |
| Revocation | Usually waits for expiry | Immediate: delete it from the database |

```text
Client                                   Auth server                       API
  | login (password, OAuth code...)        |                                |
  |--------------------------------------->|                                |
  |  access token (15 min) + refresh token |                                |
  |<---------------------------------------|                                |
  |  GET /orders  Authorization: Bearer AT ------------------------------->| verify JWT locally
  |<------------------------------------------------------------------------| 200
  |              ... 15 minutes later ...                                   |
  |  GET /orders  Authorization: Bearer AT ------------------------------->| exp passed
  |<------------------------------------------------------------------------| 401 (invalid_token)
  |  POST /token  grant_type=refresh_token  refresh_token=RT1              |
  |--------------------------------------->| RT1 valid? rotate:            |
  |  new AT + new RT2  (RT1 invalidated)   |   mark RT1 used, issue RT2     |
  |<---------------------------------------|                                |
  |  retry GET /orders with new AT ---------------------------------------->| 200
```

The refresh token is checked against a database on every use, so revocation (logout, password change, admin action) takes effect within one access-token lifetime at most.

**Refresh token rotation and reuse detection.** Each refresh returns a *new* refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old refresh token is ever presented again, either the legitimate client or a thief is replaying a stolen copy; the server cannot tell which, so it revokes the whole token family and forces a new login.

```javascript
// Token endpoint sketch with rotation and reuse detection
import { randomBytes, createHash } from 'node:crypto';
const sha256 = (s) => createHash('sha256').update(s).digest('hex');

app.post('/token', async (req, res) => {
  const presented = req.cookies.refresh_token;                 // HttpOnly cookie (browser) or body (native)
  const record = await db.refreshTokens.findByHash(sha256(presented ?? ''));

  if (!record || record.expiresAt < Date.now()) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'invalid_grant' });
  if (record.usedAt) {                                          // reuse: likely theft
    await db.refreshTokens.revokeFamily(record.familyId);
    return res.status(401).json({ error: 'invalid_grant' });
  }

  await db.refreshTokens.markUsed(record.id);
  const newRefresh = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');
  await db.refreshTokens.insert({ hash: sha256(newRefresh), userId: record.userId,
                                  familyId: record.familyId, expiresAt: Date.now() + 30 * 864e5 });
  const accessToken = await issueAccessToken(record.userId);   // short-lived JWT

  res.cookie('refresh_token', newRefresh, {
    httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict', path: '/token', maxAge: 30 * 864e5,
  });
  res.json({ access_token: accessToken, token_type: 'Bearer', expires_in: 900 });
});
```

Refresh tokens are stored **hashed** (like passwords, but a fast hash is fine because they are long and random) so a database leak does not expose usable tokens.

**Revoking access tokens before they expire.** If waiting up to 15 minutes is unacceptable:

| Technique | How | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Short lifetimes | 5 minutes or less | More refresh traffic |
| Deny list | Store revoked `jti` values (or "tokens issued before time T for user U") in Redis until they expire | One cache lookup per request: partially gives up statelessness |
| Token versioning | User record has a `tokenVersion`; increment on logout-all; tokens carry the version | One lookup (often cached) |
| Introspection | Opaque access tokens checked with the auth server (RFC 7662) | A network call per request (cache briefly) |

**Client-side handling.** A client should refresh proactively shortly before expiry, or reactively on a `401`, and must avoid firing several refreshes at once when many requests fail simultaneously (otherwise rotation reuse detection will log the user out):

```javascript
let refreshing = null;                                     // shared in-flight refresh promise

async function apiFetch(url, options = {}, retried = false) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { ...options, headers: { ...options.headers,
                                 Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` } });
  if (res.status !== 401 || retried) return res;
  refreshing ??= refreshAccessToken().finally(() => { refreshing = null; }); // one refresh at a time
  await refreshing;
  return apiFetch(url, options, true);                     // retry once with the new token
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Short-lived access tokens limit damage from theft; long-lived refresh tokens avoid constant logins.
- Refresh tokens are opaque, stored hashed, sent only to the token endpoint, and revocable instantly.
- Rotate refresh tokens on every use and revoke the whole family when reuse is detected.
- Immediate access-token revocation needs extra state: deny lists, token versions or introspection.
- Clients should refresh once, share the in-flight refresh, and retry the original request.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Explain why the refresh token cookie in the example uses `Path=/token` and `SameSite=Strict`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the token endpoint with an in-memory store, then write a test that uses a refresh token twice and verifies that the second use revokes the newer token as well.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A user changes their password because they think their account is compromised. With JWT access tokens and refresh tokens, how do you make sure the attacker loses access?" *Hint:* consider both token types and how long each would otherwise remain valid.

#### Bearer Tokens and the Authorization Header

A **bearer token** (RFC 6750) is a token whose mere possession grants access, just like cash or a concert ticket: whoever *bears* it can use it, with no further proof of identity. Most API access tokens, including JWTs issued by OAuth servers, are bearer tokens sent in the `Authorization` header.

**The header format.**

```http
GET /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIwMjYtMDkifQ.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIs...
```

`Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>` is the general HTTP authentication syntax; `Bearer` is the scheme, as `Basic` and `Digest` were in earlier topics. Tokens can technically also be sent as a form field or a query parameter, but query parameters end up in logs, browser history and `Referer` headers, so the header is the only recommended method.

**Errors use `WWW-Authenticate`.**

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api", error="invalid_token", error_description="The access token expired"
```

| Situation | Status | `error` value |
|---|---|---|
| No token | `401` | (none, just `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api"`) |
| Malformed request | `400` | `invalid_request` |
| Expired, revoked or invalid token | `401` | `invalid_token` |
| Valid token, missing permission (scope) | `403` | `insufficient_scope` (with `scope="orders:write"`) |

**Validating bearer tokens in middleware.**

```javascript
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose';

const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL('https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json'));

export function requireToken(requiredScope) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    const match = /^Bearer (\S+)$/i.exec(req.get('Authorization') ?? '');
    if (!match) {
      res.set('WWW-Authenticate', 'Bearer realm="api"');
      return res.sendStatus(401);
    }
    try {
      const { payload } = await jwtVerify(match[1], JWKS, {
        issuer: 'https://auth.example.com', audience: 'https://api.example.com',
        algorithms: ['ES256'],
      });
      const scopes = String(payload.scope ?? '').split(' ');   // OAuth scopes are space-separated
      if (requiredScope && !scopes.includes(requiredScope)) {
        res.set('WWW-Authenticate', `Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="${requiredScope}"`);
        return res.sendStatus(403);
      }
      req.auth = payload;                                      // available to route handlers
      next();
    } catch {
      res.set('WWW-Authenticate', 'Bearer error="invalid_token"');
      res.sendStatus(401);
    }
  };
}

// app.get('/v1/orders', requireToken('orders:read'), listOrders);
```

**The bearer weakness and sender-constrained tokens.** Because possession is enough, a token leaked through logs, a malicious browser extension or a compromised proxy can be replayed from anywhere until it expires. Mitigations:

- short lifetimes and narrow scopes and audiences;
- HTTPS only, never in URLs, redacted from logs;
- **sender-constrained tokens**, which bind the token to a key the client holds: **DPoP** (RFC 9449) makes the client sign a small proof JWT for each request with its private key, and **mTLS-bound tokens** (RFC 8705) tie the token to the client's TLS certificate. A thief who copies the token alone cannot use it.

```http
GET /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
Authorization: DPoP eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIs...          <- access token bound to the client's key
DPoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJkcG9wK2p3dCIsImFsZyI6IkVTMjU2...     <- per-request proof signed with that key
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Bearer tokens grant access to whoever presents them; treat them like cash.
- Send them in `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, never in URLs.
- Respond with `401` + `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"` for bad tokens and `403` + `insufficient_scope` for missing permissions.
- Limit damage with short lifetimes, narrow scopes and audiences; DPoP or mTLS binding makes stolen tokens useless.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Call a public API that uses bearer tokens (for example the GitHub REST API with a personal access token) using `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ..."` and observe the response with a valid, an invalid and no token.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Wire the `requireToken` middleware into an Express app with two routes needing different scopes, and test all four error cases from the table.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What does DPoP protect against that HTTPS alone does not?" *Hint:* HTTPS protects the token in transit; think about where else a token can leak and what an attacker would additionally need.

#### OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

Imagine a printing service that needs your photos from a cloud drive. Giving it your cloud password would let it read your email, change your password and keep access forever. **OAuth 2.0** (RFC 6749) solves this **delegated authorization** problem: you authorise the printing app to access *only your photos*, *for a limited time*, without ever showing it your password. The analogy is a hotel key card: reception (the authorization server) issues a card that opens only your room, expires at checkout and can be deactivated, without handing out the master key.

**Roles.**

| Role | Example |
|---|---|
| **Resource owner** | You, the user who owns the photos |
| **Client** | The printing app requesting access |
| **Authorization server** | The cloud provider's login and consent service; issues tokens |
| **Resource server** | The cloud provider's photo API; accepts access tokens |

**Authorization Code flow with PKCE.** The recommended flow for web apps, SPAs and mobile apps alike:

```text
User        Client (print app)              Authorization server            Photo API
 |  "Connect drive"  |                               |                           |
 |------------------>| 1. create code_verifier (random), code_challenge = SHA256(verifier)
 |                   | 2. redirect browser to:                                   |
 |<------------------|    /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=print-app      |
 |                   |      &redirect_uri=https://print.app/callback             |
 |                   |      &scope=photos.read&state=xyz                         |
 |                   |      &code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256       |
 |-------------------------------------------------->| 3. user logs in at the    |
 |                   |                               |    provider, sees consent:|
 |                   |                               |    "Print app wants to    |
 |                   |                               |     read your photos"     |
 |<--------------------------------------------------| 4. redirect back:         |
 |  /callback?code=SplxlOB&state=xyz                 |                           |
 |------------------>| 5. check state == xyz         |                           |
 |                   | 6. POST /token  code=SplxlOB, code_verifier=..., client auth
 |                   |------------------------------>| verify SHA256(verifier)   |
 |                   |                               |   == stored challenge     |
 |                   |<------------------------------|                           |
 |                   |  access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, scope           |
 |                   | 7. GET /photos  Authorization: Bearer access_token ------>|
 |                   |<---------------------------------------------------------|
```

- The **authorization code** travels through the browser (front channel) but is short-lived and useless alone.
- Tokens are obtained on the **back channel** (`POST /token`), out of the browser's URL bar.
- **`state`** ties the callback to the request the client started, defeating CSRF on the callback.
- **PKCE** (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) ensures that whoever redeems the code is the client that started the flow, even if the code was intercepted. It is required for public clients (SPAs, mobile) and recommended for all.

```javascript
// Creating the PKCE pair (works in browsers and Node.js via Web Crypto)
const verifier = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32))
  .reduce((s, b) => s + b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0'), '');        // 64 hex chars
const digest = await crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(verifier));
const challenge = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new Uint8Array(digest)))
  .replace(/\+/g, '-').replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/=+$/, '');       // base64url, no padding
```

**Grant types.**

| Grant | Use | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Authorization Code + PKCE | Users signing in through web, SPA and mobile apps | Recommended |
| Client Credentials | Machine-to-machine; no user involved | Recommended |
| Device Authorization | TVs, CLIs: user approves on another device | Recommended for input-constrained devices |
| Refresh Token | Renew access tokens | Recommended (with rotation for public clients) |
| Implicit | Tokens returned directly in the URL fragment | **Deprecated** (leaks tokens) |
| Resource Owner Password | Client collects the user's password | **Deprecated** (defeats the purpose) |

OAuth 2.1, a consolidation currently being finalised by the IETF, formally removes Implicit and Password and makes PKCE mandatory.

**OAuth is not authentication.** An access token says "the bearer may read photos"; it is meant for the API, not for the client, and does not reliably tell the client *who the user is*. Using it to "log in with X" led to many vulnerabilities. **OpenID Connect (OIDC)** is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that fixes this:

- The client requests the `openid` scope (plus `profile`, `email`).
- The token response also contains an **ID token**: a JWT *for the client* stating who the user is and how they authenticated.
- A standard `/userinfo` endpoint, a discovery document (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`) and a JWKS make integration uniform across providers.

```jsonc
// Decoded ID token payload
{
  "iss": "https://accounts.example.com",
  "sub": "248289761001",                 // stable user identifier at this provider: use it, not email
  "aud": "print-app",                    // must equal your client_id
  "exp": 1791019800,
  "iat": 1791016200,
  "nonce": "n-0S6_WzA2Mj",               // must match the nonce you sent (replay protection)
  "email": "ada@example.com",
  "email_verified": true,
  "auth_time": 1791016190,
  "amr": ["pwd", "otp"]                  // authentication methods used (here: password + OTP)
}
```

| | OAuth 2.0 | OpenID Connect |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Delegated authorization: access an API on the user's behalf | Authentication: learn who the user is (single sign-on, "Sign in with...") |
| Main artifact | Access token (for the resource server) | ID token (for the client) + access token |
| Token format | Not specified (opaque or JWT) | ID token is always a JWT |

In practice, use a certified library (`openid-client` for Node.js, Auth.js, or your provider's SDK) or a hosted identity provider (Auth0/Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google, Keycloak, Cognito) rather than implementing the flows by hand.

**Key Takeaways**

- OAuth 2.0 delegates limited, revocable API access to a client without sharing the user's password.
- Use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE for apps with users and Client Credentials for machines; Implicit and Password grants are deprecated.
- `state` protects the redirect from CSRF; PKCE protects the authorization code from interception.
- OAuth alone is not authentication; OpenID Connect adds the ID token, `userinfo` and discovery for login.
- Identify users by `iss` + `sub`, validate `aud` and `nonce`, and rely on well-tested libraries.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Fetch `https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` and find the authorization endpoint, token endpoint, JWKS URI and supported scopes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Register an OAuth app with GitHub and implement "Sign in with GitHub" in Express using the Authorization Code flow with `state`, exchanging the code on the server and displaying the user's login name.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why was the Implicit flow deprecated, and what replaced it for single-page applications?" *Hint:* where did the token appear, and what does PKCE allow a public client to do safely?

#### API Keys and Role-Based Access Control

Not every caller is a person with a password. Scripts, partner integrations and backend services need credentials too, and once a caller is identified, the application must decide what each one may do. This topic covers the simplest machine credential, the API key, and the most common permission model, role-based access control.

**API keys.** An API key is a long random secret that identifies a *project or client* (rather than a user) and is sent with every request:

```http
GET /v1/forecast?city=Turin HTTP/1.1
Host: api.weather.example
Authorization: Bearer wx_live_4eC39HqLyjWDarjtT1zdp7dc        <- or a custom header such as X-API-Key
```

| Use API keys for | Avoid API keys for |
|---|---|
| Server-to-server calls, scripts, CI jobs | Identifying end users |
| Metering, quotas and billing per customer | Secrets embedded in front-end or mobile code (they can be extracted) |
| Simple partner integrations | Fine-grained delegated access (use OAuth) |

**Managing keys safely.**

```javascript
import { randomBytes, createHash } from 'node:crypto';

// Issue: show the full key to the user ONCE; store only its hash and a prefix
function createApiKey(env = 'live') {
  const secret = randomBytes(24).toString('base64url');
  const key = `wx_${env}_${secret}`;                    // recognisable prefix helps secret scanners
  return {
    key,                                                // display once, never store
    record: {
      prefix: key.slice(0, 12),                         // shown in the dashboard to identify the key
      hash: createHash('sha256').update(key).digest('hex'),
      scopes: ['forecast:read'],
      createdAt: new Date(),
      lastUsedAt: null,
    },
  };
}

// Verify: hash the presented key and look it up
async function authenticateKey(presented) {
  const hash = createHash('sha256').update(presented).digest('hex');
  return db.apiKeys.findActiveByHash(hash);             // null if unknown or revoked
}
```

Good practice: scope keys to the minimum permissions, allow several keys per account so they can be rotated without downtime, record last use, support immediate revocation, and use recognisable prefixes so tools like GitHub secret scanning can detect leaked keys.

**Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).** Assigning permissions to each user individually becomes unmanageable as an application grows. RBAC adds an indirection: permissions are granted to **roles**, and users are assigned roles.

```text
 Users            Roles                 Permissions
 -----            -----                 -----------
 ada    ------->  admin     ---------->  users:manage, posts:delete, posts:publish, posts:write, posts:read
 linus  ------->  editor    ---------->  posts:publish, posts:write, posts:read
 grace  --+---->  author    ---------->  posts:write, posts:read
          +---->  billing   ---------->  invoices:read
 guest  ------->  viewer    ---------->  posts:read
```

```javascript
const ROLE_PERMISSIONS = {
  admin:  ['users:manage', 'posts:delete', 'posts:publish', 'posts:write', 'posts:read'],
  editor: ['posts:publish', 'posts:write', 'posts:read'],
  author: ['posts:write', 'posts:read'],
  viewer: ['posts:read'],
};

function can(user, permission) {
  return user.roles.some((role) => ROLE_PERMISSIONS[role]?.includes(permission));
}

function requirePermission(permission) {               // Express middleware
  return (req, res, next) => (can(req.user, permission) ? next() : res.sendStatus(403));
}

app.delete('/api/posts/:id', requireAuth, requirePermission('posts:delete'), deletePost);
```

Check **permissions**, not role names, in code (`can(user, 'posts:delete')` instead of `user.role === 'admin'`), so roles can be reorganised without touching every handler.

**When roles are not enough.** RBAC answers "may editors publish posts?" but not "may Grace edit *this* post?". Real applications combine models:

| Model | Decision based on | Example |
|---|---|---|
| RBAC | User's roles | Editors may publish |
| Ownership / ACL | Relationship to the specific resource | Authors may edit *their own* drafts |
| ABAC (attribute-based) | Attributes of user, resource, action and context | Accountants may read invoices of their region during business hours |
| ReBAC (relationship-based) | Graph of relationships | Members of a shared folder may view documents inside it (Google Zanzibar-style systems such as OpenFGA, SpiceDB) |

```javascript
// RBAC + ownership combined
function canEditPost(user, post) {
  if (can(user, 'posts:publish')) return true;                       // editors and admins: any post
  return can(user, 'posts:write') && post.authorId === user.id && post.status === 'draft';
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- API keys identify client applications, not users; store only their hashes, scope them and support rotation and revocation.
- Never ship secret API keys in browser or mobile code.
- RBAC maps users to roles and roles to permissions; check permissions in code, not role names.
- Combine RBAC with ownership checks (or ABAC/ReBAC) for per-resource decisions.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Design roles and permissions for a school platform with students, teachers and administrators, covering courses, grades and user accounts.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement API key creation, hashed storage, verification middleware and revocation for an Express API, and show that revoking a key immediately returns `401`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A front-end developer puts the company's payment provider secret key in the React app's environment variables. What is the problem, and what is the right architecture?" *Hint:* everything bundled into front-end code is public; distinguish publishable keys from secret keys.

#### Multi-Factor Authentication Concepts

Passwords are phished, reused across sites and leaked in breaches. **Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** requires proof from two or more *different categories* of evidence, so that compromising one factor is not enough.

| Factor category | Something you... | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge | know | Password, PIN, security questions (weak) |
| Possession | have | Phone with an authenticator app, hardware security key, device-bound passkey |
| Inherence | are | Fingerprint, face recognition (usually used to unlock a possession factor locally) |

Two passwords are still one factor (both are knowledge). A fingerprint that unlocks a passkey on your phone combines possession (the phone's key) and inherence (the fingerprint).

**Common second factors, from weakest to strongest.**

| Method | How it works | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| SMS / voice codes | Code sent to the phone number | SIM swapping, SS7 interception, phishable; NIST classes it as "restricted" |
| Email codes / magic links | Code or link sent to the inbox | Only as strong as the email account |
| **TOTP** apps | Time-based codes from a shared secret (Google Authenticator, 1Password, Aegis) | Phishable: a fake site can relay the code in real time |
| Push notifications | Approve a prompt in an app | "MFA fatigue": users approve spammed prompts; mitigated by number matching |
| **WebAuthn / passkeys** | Public-key challenge-response bound to the site's origin | Phishing-resistant; requires compatible devices (all modern platforms) |

**How TOTP works** (RFC 6238). At enrolment the server generates a random secret and shows it as a QR code; the app and server then derive the same 6-digit code from the secret and the current 30-second time step:

```text
T    = floor(unix_time / 30)                  <- changes every 30 seconds
HMAC = HMAC-SHA1(secret, T as 8-byte integer)
code = dynamic_truncate(HMAC) mod 10^6        <- 6 digits, e.g. 492039

QR code content:
otpauth://totp/Example:ada@example.com?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=Example&digits=6&period=30
```

```javascript
// TOTP verification in Node.js with only the standard library (HOTP RFC 4226 + time steps)
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

function hotp(secret, counter, digits = 6) {
  const buf = Buffer.alloc(8);
  buf.writeBigUInt64BE(BigInt(counter));
  const hmac = createHmac('sha1', secret).update(buf).digest();
  const offset = hmac[hmac.length - 1] & 0x0f;                        // dynamic truncation
  const bin = (hmac.readUInt32BE(offset) & 0x7fffffff) % 10 ** digits;
  return String(bin).padStart(digits, '0');
}

function verifyTotp(secret, code, window = 1) {                       // secret: Buffer (base32-decoded)
  const step = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000 / 30);
  for (let i = -window; i <= window; i++) {                           // tolerate small clock drift
    const expected = Buffer.from(hotp(secret, step + i));
    const given = Buffer.from(String(code));
    if (given.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(given, expected)) return true;
  }
  return false;   // also: remember the last accepted step to prevent reuse of the same code
}
```

**Why passkeys are phishing-resistant.** With WebAuthn, the authenticator (phone, laptop, security key) creates a key pair *per site*. At login the server sends a challenge; the authenticator signs it only if the browser confirms that the page's origin matches the site the key was created for. A pixel-perfect fake on `examp1e.com` gets nothing usable, because there is no code for the user to type into it.

```javascript
// Browser side of a passkey login (server-generated options; libraries like SimpleWebAuthn help)
const options = await (await fetch('/webauthn/login/options', { method: 'POST' })).json();
const credential = await navigator.credentials.get({
  publicKey: {
    challenge: base64urlToBuffer(options.challenge),   // random, single-use, from the server
```
