Before package managers, reusing someone else's library meant downloading a ZIP file, copying it into your project and repeating the process by hand for every update and every dependency of that library. A **package manager** automates this: you declare *what* you need, and it finds, downloads, verifies and installs the right versions, along with everything they depend on.

**Three things called "npm".**

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| The npm **registry** | A public database of packages at `https://registry.npmjs.org`, run by npm Inc. (owned by GitHub/Microsoft) |
| The npm **CLI** | The `npm` command installed with Node.js |
| npmjs.com | The website for searching packages and managing accounts and organisations |

The registry is the largest software package registry in the world, with millions of packages. A **package** is a directory (published as a tarball) containing a `package.json` file; a **module** is anything Node can load with `require` or `import`. Most packages are modules, but some only provide command-line tools.

**What happens during `npm install express`.**

```text
 1. Resolve    ask the registry for express's metadata (GET registry.npmjs.org/express)
               choose the newest version matching the requested range
 2. Recurse    read its dependencies and resolve each one, building a dependency tree
 3. Dedupe     hoist compatible versions to the top of node_modules to avoid duplicates
 4. Fetch      download tarballs (or take them from the local cache, ~/.npm/_cacache)
 5. Verify     check each tarball against its integrity hash (sha512)
 6. Extract    unpack into node_modules/
 7. Scripts    run lifecycle scripts such as postinstall (unless disabled)
 8. Record     write package.json (if adding) and package-lock.json
```

**How Node finds packages.** When code calls `require('express')` or `import 'express'`, Node looks for a `node_modules/express` directory in the current folder, then in the parent folder, and so on up to the root of the file system. This simple algorithm is why `node_modules` is local to each project.

```text
project/
├── package.json
├── package-lock.json
├── node_modules/
│   ├── express/            <- direct dependency
│   ├── body-parser/        <- dependency of express, hoisted to the top level
│   └── debug/
│       └── node_modules/
│           └── ms/         <- nested because another package needs a different ms version
└── src/
    └── app.js              <- require('express') walks up and finds ../node_modules/express
```

**The small-module culture.** The npm ecosystem favours many small packages. This makes reuse easy, but trees grow quickly: a typical web application can have over a thousand transitive dependencies. The 2016 **left-pad** incident, when an 11-line package was unpublished and broke builds worldwide, led npm to restrict unpublishing; later incidents (see "Auditing and Supply Chain Risks" below) showed the security cost of large trees.

**Evaluating a package before adding it.** Check the weekly downloads, the date of the last release, open issues, the number of maintainers, its own dependency count, its licence and whether it ships TypeScript types. Tools like `npm view <pkg>` and `npm explain <pkg>` help from the command line.

```bash
npm search markdown parser        # search the registry
npm view express versions --json  # all published versions
npm view express dependencies     # what installing it pulls in
npm ls                            # the installed tree of the current project
npm explain ms                    # why is this package installed? which packages depend on it?
```

**Key Takeaways**

- npm is three things: a public registry, a command-line client and a website.
- Installing resolves version ranges, builds a dependency tree, downloads and verifies tarballs, and writes `node_modules` and a lock file.
- Node resolves bare package names by walking up the directory tree looking for `node_modules`.
- Small-module culture makes dependency trees large; evaluate packages before adding them.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create an empty project, install `express`, and count how many packages end up in `node_modules` (`npm ls --all` or `ls node_modules | wc -l`).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Use `npm explain` on a transitive dependency of a real project and draw the chain of packages that leads to it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What criteria do you use before adding a new dependency to a production project?" *Hint:* think about maintenance, security history, size of its own tree, licence, alternatives in the standard library, and the cost of removing it later.

#### package.json Anatomy

Every Node.js project and every npm package has a `package.json` at its root. It is the project's identity card and manifest: it says what the project is called, how to run it, what it depends on and, for packages, what files to expose to users.

**Creating one.**

```bash
npm init          # interactive questions
npm init -y       # accept the defaults
npm pkg set type=module scripts.start="node src/index.js"   # edit fields from the CLI
```

**An annotated example for an application.**

```jsonc
{
  "name": "order-service",          // lowercase, URL-safe; must be unique on the registry if published
  "version": "1.4.2",               // semantic version (next topics)
  "private": true,                  // refuse to publish by accident; typical for applications
  "type": "module",                 // .js files are ES modules
  "description": "REST API for orders",
  "license": "MIT",
  "engines": { "node": ">=22.12" }, // supported Node versions
  "scripts": {                      // commands run with `npm run <name>`
    "start": "node src/index.js",
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file=.env src/index.js",
    "test": "node --test"
  },
  "dependencies": {                 // needed at run time
    "express": "^5.1.0"
  },
  "devDependencies": {              // needed only for development and builds
    "typescript": "~5.9.2"
  }
}
```

(`package.json` itself must be strict JSON; the comments above are for explanation only.)

**Additional fields for a library.**

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `main` | Legacy entry point for `require('pkg')` |
| `exports` | Modern, explicit map of entry points; hides everything not listed |
| `types` | Entry point for TypeScript declarations |
| `bin` | Command-line executables to install (`{ "mytool": "./bin/cli.js" }`) |
| `files` | Allow-list of files to include in the published tarball |
| `repository`, `homepage`, `bugs` | Links shown on npmjs.com |
| `keywords`, `author`, `contributors` | Metadata for search and credit |
| `peerDependencies` | Packages the host project must provide (next topic) |
| `sideEffects` | Tells bundlers which files are safe to tree-shake |

**The `exports` field.** It defines the package's public interface and can serve different files depending on conditions such as `import` vs `require` or `node` vs `browser`:

```json
{
  "name": "tiny-date",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "import": "./dist/index.js",
      "require": "./dist/index.cjs"
    },
    "./format": "./dist/format.js",
    "./package.json": "./package.json"
  }
}
```

With this map, `import 'tiny-date'` and `import 'tiny-date/format'` work, while `import 'tiny-date/dist/internal.js'` fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`. That protection lets authors refactor internals without breaking users. Conditions are matched in object order, so `types` comes first and `default` (if present) last.

**Subpath imports.** The related `imports` field defines private aliases (they must start with `#`) usable only inside the package, which replaces fragile `../../../` paths:

```json
{ "imports": { "#db": "./src/db/index.js", "#utils/*": "./src/utils/*.js" } }
```

```javascript
import { pool } from '#db';
import { slugify } from '#utils/strings';
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `package.json` describes the project: name, version, module type, scripts, dependencies and supported engines.
- `"private": true` prevents accidental publishing of applications.
- `exports` defines a package's public entry points and conditional variants (`import`, `require`, `types`, `browser`); unlisted paths are inaccessible.
- `imports` provides internal `#` aliases; `bin` installs commands; `files` controls what is published.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run `npm init -y`, then use `npm pkg set` to add a `start` script, set `type` to `module` and add an `engines` field. Inspect the resulting file.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a local package with an `exports` map exposing `.` and `./math`, link it into another project with `npm install ../my-lib`, and verify that importing an unexported internal file fails.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What problems does the `exports` field solve compared with `main`?" *Hint:* think about encapsulation of internal files, dual CommonJS/ESM packages, TypeScript types and environment-specific builds.

#### Dependencies, devDependencies and peerDependencies

Not every package a project uses is needed in the same situations. A web framework must be present in production; a test runner is needed only on developers' machines and in CI; a React component library needs React but must not bring its own copy. npm expresses these situations with separate dependency fields.

**The dependency fields.**

| Field | Meaning | Installed when | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dependencies` | Required at run time | Always, including when your package is installed by others | `express`, `pg`, `zod` |
| `devDependencies` | Needed only to develop, test or build | In your project only; skipped with `npm install --omit=dev` and never installed for consumers of your package | `typescript`, `vitest`, `eslint` |
| `peerDependencies` | Must be provided by the host project; your package plugs into it | npm 7+ installs missing peers automatically and errors on conflicts | A React library requires `react` |
| `optionalDependencies` | Nice to have; installation failures are ignored | When possible | Platform-specific native binaries |
| `bundleDependencies` | Shipped inside your tarball | With your package | Rare: offline or patched copies |

```bash
npm install express              # -> dependencies
npm install -D typescript        # -> devDependencies (--save-dev)
npm install -O fsevents          # -> optionalDependencies
npm uninstall lodash             # remove from package.json and node_modules
npm install --omit=dev           # production install: skip devDependencies
```

**Why peer dependencies exist.** Imagine a plugin for a framework. If the plugin listed the framework under `dependencies`, the application could end up with *two* copies of it: its own and the plugin's nested copy. For libraries with internal state or identity checks (React hooks, `instanceof` checks), two copies cause subtle bugs such as "Invalid hook call".

```text
Wrong: plugin lists react in dependencies         Right: plugin lists react in peerDependencies

app/node_modules/                                 app/node_modules/
├── react@19        <- app's copy                 ├── react@19        <- single shared copy
└── ui-kit/                                       └── ui-kit/         <- uses the app's react
    └── node_modules/
        └── react@18    <- second copy: two React instances, hooks break
```

```json
{
  "name": "ui-kit",
  "peerDependencies": {
    "react": "^18.0.0 || ^19.0.0"
  },
  "peerDependenciesMeta": {
    "react-dom": { "optional": true }
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "react": "^19.1.0"
  }
}
```

The library also lists React under `devDependencies` so its own tests can run. Keep peer ranges *wide*: the narrower the range, the more likely it is to conflict with the host. When peers conflict, npm reports `ERESOLVE`; `--legacy-peer-deps` skips peer installation and should be a temporary workaround, not a fix.

**Applications vs libraries.** For an application deployed from source, the split between `dependencies` and `devDependencies` mainly affects the size of production installs and Docker images. For a published library it is critical: everything in `dependencies` is installed on every user's machine.

**Overrides.** Sometimes a transitive dependency has a bug or vulnerability and the intermediate package has not updated yet. `overrides` forces a version throughout the tree:

```json
{
  "overrides": {
    "semver": "^7.6.3",
    "some-lib": { "debug": "4.4.0" }
  }
}
```

(yarn calls this field `resolutions`; pnpm supports `pnpm.overrides`.)

**Key Takeaways**

- `dependencies` are needed at run time; `devDependencies` only for development and builds and are never installed for consumers.
- `peerDependencies` declare that the host must supply a package, preventing duplicate copies of frameworks.
- Keep peer ranges wide and duplicate peers in `devDependencies` for local testing.
- `overrides` pins a transitive dependency version when the direct dependency cannot be updated.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Classify each of these for a TypeScript Express API: `express`, `typescript`, `@types/express`, `pino`, `vitest`, `dotenv`, `tsx`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a Docker image with `npm ci` and with `npm ci --omit=dev`, and compare the sizes of `node_modules`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why should a React component library declare React as a peer dependency rather than a regular dependency?" *Hint:* think about how many copies of React end up in the application bundle and what React's hooks rely on.

#### Semantic Versioning and Version Ranges

When a package releases a new version, consumers need to know whether upgrading is safe. **Semantic Versioning** (SemVer) encodes this promise in the version number itself, and npm's version *ranges* let a project accept safe updates automatically while refusing risky ones.

**The SemVer contract.** A version is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, optionally followed by a pre-release tag and build metadata:

```text
   2 . 7 . 4 - beta.1 + build.5
   |   |   |    |         |
   |   |   |    |         +-- build metadata (ignored for precedence)
   |   |   |    +------------ pre-release: 2.7.4-beta.1 < 2.7.4
   |   |   +----------------- PATCH: backwards-compatible bug fixes
   |   +--------------------- MINOR: backwards-compatible new features
   +------------------------- MAJOR: breaking changes
```

Versions `0.x.y` are special: the API is considered unstable, and by convention a MINOR change (`0.3` to `0.4`) can be breaking.

**Range syntax used in `package.json`.**

| Range | Meaning | Accepts | Rejects |
|---|---|---|---|
| `4.18.2` | Exactly this version | `4.18.2` | everything else |
| `^4.18.2` | Compatible: same major (default for `npm install`) | `4.18.2`, `4.19.0`, `4.99.9` | `5.0.0`, `4.18.1` |
| `^0.3.1` | For 0.x, caret locks the minor | `0.3.1`, `0.3.9` | `0.4.0` |
| `~4.18.2` | Patch updates only | `4.18.2`, `4.18.9` | `4.19.0` |
| `>=4.0.0 <5.0.0` | Explicit comparator range | as written | |
| `4.x` or `4` | Any 4.x.y | `4.0.0`, `4.20.1` | `5.0.0` |
| `1.2.3 - 1.4.0` | Inclusive hyphen range | `1.2.3` to `1.4.0` | |
| `^1.0.0 \|\| ^2.0.0` | Either range | `1.5.0`, `2.1.0` | `3.0.0` |
| `*` or `""` | Any version | everything | nothing (avoid) |
| `latest`, `next` | A distribution tag, resolved at install time | | |

Pre-release versions are only matched by ranges that explicitly mention a pre-release on the same `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, so `^2.0.0` does not silently install `2.1.0-beta.1`.

**Trying ranges in code.** The `semver` package (used by npm itself) evaluates ranges:

```javascript
import semver from 'semver';

semver.satisfies('4.19.1', '^4.18.2');   // true
semver.satisfies('5.0.0', '^4.18.2');    // false
semver.satisfies('0.4.0', '^0.3.1');     // false: caret on 0.x locks the minor
semver.maxSatisfying(['1.2.0', '1.3.5', '2.0.0'], '~1.3.0'); // '1.3.5'
semver.inc('1.4.2', 'minor');            // '1.5.0'
```

**Bumping your own version.**

```bash
npm version patch        # 1.4.2 -> 1.4.3, commits and tags v1.4.3 in git
npm version minor        # 1.4.3 -> 1.5.0
npm version major        # 1.5.0 -> 2.0.0
npm version prerelease --preid=rc   # 2.0.0 -> 2.0.1-rc.0
```

**SemVer is a promise, not a guarantee.** Maintainers decide what counts as "breaking", and mistakes happen: a patch release can break your code. Ranges give flexibility, but reproducible builds come from lock files (next topic). Tools such as Renovate or Dependabot propose updates as pull requests so CI can verify them.

**Key Takeaways**

- SemVer: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for compatible features, PATCH for compatible fixes; `0.x` is unstable.
- `^` allows minor and patch updates (only patch updates for `0.x`), `~` allows patch updates, an exact version allows nothing.
- Pre-releases are excluded from ranges unless explicitly requested.
- Ranges express what is compatible; lock files decide what is actually installed.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For each range `^2.3.1`, `~2.3.1`, `2.x` and `^0.2.5`, list which of these versions it accepts: `2.3.0`, `2.3.9`, `2.4.0`, `3.0.0`, `0.2.9`, `0.3.0`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* You maintain a library at 1.6.3. Decide the next version for each change: a bug fix; a new optional parameter; renaming an exported function; dropping support for Node 18. Justify each.
> 3. *(Interview)* "If `^` already restricts updates to compatible versions, why do we still need a lock file?" *Hint:* consider two developers installing a month apart, a maintainer mistake in a minor release, and transitive dependencies you do not control.

#### Lock Files and Reproducible Installs

`package.json` lists *ranges*, so the same file can produce different `node_modules` trees on different days as new versions are published. A build that passed yesterday can fail today without any change to your code. **Lock files** record the exact result of a resolution so every install reproduces it.

**What `package-lock.json` contains.** For every package in the tree: the exact version, where it was downloaded from and an integrity hash.

```json
{
  "name": "order-service",
  "lockfileVersion": 3,
  "packages": {
    "": {
      "name": "order-service",
      "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" }
    },
    "node_modules/express": {
      "version": "5.1.0",
      "resolved": "https://registry.npmjs.org/express/-/express-5.1.0.tgz",
      "integrity": "sha512-<base64-encoded SHA-512 of the tarball>",
      "dependencies": { "accepts": "^2.0.0", "body-parser": "^2.2.0" }
    }
  }
}
```

The `integrity` field is a Subresource Integrity hash: if the downloaded tarball does not match, installation fails. This protects against corrupted downloads and tampered mirrors.

**`npm install` vs `npm ci`.**

| | `npm install` | `npm ci` |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Development: add, update, resolve | CI and production: reproduce exactly |
| Reads | `package.json` and the lock file | The lock file (must agree with `package.json`) |
| Modifies the lock file | Yes, when ranges or the tree change | Never; fails if out of sync |
| Existing `node_modules` | Updated incrementally | Deleted and recreated |
| Speed | Variable | Predictable, cache-friendly |

```bash
# On a developer machine
npm install zod             # adds zod, updates package.json and package-lock.json
git add package.json package-lock.json
git commit -m "Add zod"

# In CI and Dockerfiles
npm ci                      # installs exactly what the lock file says, or fails
npm ci --omit=dev           # production image
```

**Rules for teams.**

- **Commit the lock file** for applications. Every developer, CI run and deployment then uses identical versions.
- Update dependencies deliberately (`npm update`, `npm outdated`, `npm install pkg@latest`) and review lock file diffs in pull requests. A large unexpected diff deserves a question.
- Resolve merge conflicts in the lock file by resolving `package.json` first and then running `npm install`, which regenerates the lock file; do not edit it by hand.
- Libraries should commit their lock file too (for reproducible CI), but note that it is **not published**: consumers resolve the library's ranges themselves. (`npm-shrinkwrap.json` is a publishable variant, appropriate only for CLI tools.)

**Updating.**

```bash
npm outdated                # current, wanted (max in range) and latest versions
npm update                  # update within ranges, refresh the lock file
npm install express@latest  # move to a new major deliberately
```

Each package manager has its own format: `package-lock.json` (npm), `yarn.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `bun.lock`. Use one manager per project and commit only its lock file.

**Key Takeaways**

- A lock file records the exact version, source and integrity hash of every package in the tree.
- `npm install` may update the lock file; `npm ci` installs exactly what it says and fails if it is out of sync.
- Commit the lock file, use `npm ci` in CI and production, and review lock file changes.
- Library lock files are not published; consumers resolve the library's ranges themselves.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Install a package, delete `node_modules`, run `npm ci`, and confirm with `npm ls` that the same versions are installed.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Change a dependency range in `package.json` without running `npm install`, then run `npm ci` and explain the error. Fix it properly.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A build works locally but fails in CI with an error inside a dependency. How do you investigate?" *Hint:* compare the installed versions in both environments, check whether CI uses `npm ci` and the committed lock file, and look at Node and npm versions.

#### npm Scripts and Task Automation

Projects need repeatable commands: start the server, run tests, build, lint, format. Instead of documenting long command lines in a README, put them in the `scripts` field of `package.json` so everyone (and CI) runs them the same way with `npm run <name>`.

**Basics.**

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file=.env src/index.js",
    "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.build.json",
    "start": "node dist/index.js",
    "test": "node --test",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "format": "prettier --write .",
    "check": "npm run lint && npm run build && npm test"
  }
}
```

```bash
npm run dev          # run any script by name
npm start            # shortcuts exist for start, test, stop, restart
npm test
npm run             # list available scripts
npm test -- --test-reporter=spec   # arguments after -- are passed to the script's command
```

**Why local tools "just work".** When npm runs a script, it adds `node_modules/.bin` to the `PATH`. Packages that declare a `bin` field install executables there, so `"lint": "eslint ."` uses the project's own ESLint version, not a global one. Scripts also receive environment variables such as `npm_package_name` and `npm_package_version`.

**Pre and post scripts.** A script named `preX` runs before `X`, and `postX` after it:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "prebuild": "rm -rf dist",
    "build": "tsc",
    "postbuild": "node scripts/copy-assets.js"
  }
}
```

**Lifecycle scripts.** Some names are run automatically by npm itself:

| Script | When it runs |
|---|---|
| `prepare` | After `npm install` in the project, and before `npm publish` and `npm pack` (often used to build or install git hooks) |
| `prepublishOnly` | Only before `npm publish` |
| `preinstall`, `install`, `postinstall` | When the package is installed, including as someone else's dependency |

Install scripts of *dependencies* run arbitrary code on your machine during `npm install`. They are needed for native add-ons, but they are also the most common vector for malicious packages (see "Auditing and Supply Chain Risks" later in this subchapter).

**Cross-platform scripts.** Scripts run in `sh` on Unix and `cmd.exe` on Windows by default, so shell-specific syntax breaks portability:

| Problem | Portable alternative |
|---|---|
| `rm -rf dist` | `node -e "fs.rmSync('dist',{recursive:true,force:true})"` or the `rimraf` package |
| `NODE_ENV=production node app.js` | `node --env-file=.env.production app.js` or the `cross-env` package |
| `cmd1 & cmd2` (parallel) | `npm-run-all2` / `concurrently` packages, or `npm run a --workspaces` |

For complex logic, write a small Node script (`scripts/build.mjs`) and call it from `package.json`: it is portable and testable.

**`node --run`.** Node 22 added `node --run <script>`, which executes a script from `package.json` directly. It starts faster than `npm run` because it skips npm's own start-up, but intentionally does not run `pre`/`post` scripts.

**Key Takeaways**

- `scripts` turns project commands into named, shared, documented tasks run with `npm run`.
- `node_modules/.bin` is on the `PATH` during scripts, so the project's pinned tool versions are used.
- `preX`/`postX` wrap scripts; lifecycle scripts such as `prepare` and `postinstall` run automatically.
- Write portable scripts; move complex logic into Node files.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add `dev`, `start`, `test` and `lint` scripts to a project and run each. Then run `npm run` to list them.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a `check` script that runs lint, type-checking and tests, failing fast if any step fails, and make it work on both Windows and Linux.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is it better to run `npm run lint` than to install ESLint globally and run `eslint .`?" *Hint:* think about version consistency across developers and CI, and how `node_modules/.bin` is used.

#### Global Packages and npx

Some packages are tools you run from the terminal rather than libraries you import: project generators, CLIs for cloud platforms, one-off utilities. npm offers two ways to use them: install them globally, or run them on demand with `npx`.

**Global installs.**

```bash
npm install -g npm-check-updates   # installs into a global prefix, adds `ncu` to the PATH
ncu                                # now available in every directory
npm ls -g --depth=0                # list global packages
npm root -g                        # where global packages live
npm uninstall -g npm-check-updates
```

Global packages have drawbacks: one version is shared by every project, the version is not recorded in any project file, and on some systems global installs need administrator rights (avoid `sudo npm install -g`; use a version manager, which gives you a user-owned prefix). The modern recommendation is: **install project tools locally** as devDependencies, and reserve global installs for a few personal utilities.

**`npx`: run without installing permanently.** `npx <command>` first looks for the command in the local project's `node_modules/.bin`; if it is not there, it downloads the package into a cache, runs it and leaves your project untouched.

```bash
npx eslint .                         # uses the project's local eslint
npx create-vite@latest my-app        # run a project generator once, always the latest version
npx -y cowsay "hello"                # -y: skip the confirmation prompt
npx --package=typescript tsc --init  # the package name differs from the command name
npm exec -- prettier --check .       # npm exec is the same mechanism, npx is its shorthand
```

`npm create <name>` is a further shortcut: `npm create vite@latest` runs the `create-vite` package.

**Security note.** `npx some-package` downloads and executes code from the registry. A typo (`npx create-reac-app`) can run a malicious look-alike package. Check the name, prefer well-known scoped packages, and pin a version (`npx tool@1.2.3`) in scripts and documentation.

| Approach | Version control | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Local devDependency + `npm run` / `npx` | Pinned in `package.json` and lock file | Tools the project depends on (linters, compilers, test runners) |
| `npx pkg@version` | Specified in the command | One-off generators and occasional utilities |
| `npm install -g` | Not recorded anywhere | Personal tools you use across all projects |

**Key Takeaways**

- Global installs make a command available everywhere but are unversioned per project; prefer local devDependencies.
- `npx` runs a local binary if present, otherwise downloads and runs the package temporarily.
- `npm create x` runs the `create-x` package, the standard way to scaffold projects.
- Running packages with `npx` executes remote code: check names and pin versions.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use `npx` to run `npm-check-updates` in a project without installing it, and interpret its output.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Install a tool globally and the same tool at a different version locally. Show which version runs with the bare command, with `npx` and inside an npm script.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Should a project's README tell contributors to install the TypeScript compiler globally?" *Hint:* consider reproducibility, multiple projects on one machine and CI.

#### Publishing and Scoped Packages

Publishing turns your code into a package anyone (or only your organisation) can install. Doing it well means controlling what goes into the tarball, versioning correctly, and protecting the account and pipeline that publish it.

**Scopes.** A scope is a namespace that starts with `@`: `@angular/core`, `@types/node`, `@acme/logger`. Scopes belong to a user or organisation on npm, which prevents name squatting and makes ownership obvious. Scoped packages are private by default (requires a paid plan) unless published with `--access public`.

```json
{
  "name": "@acme/logger",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": { ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" } },
  "files": ["dist", "README.md"],
  "publishConfig": { "access": "public" },
  "repository": { "type": "git", "url": "git+https://github.com/acme/logger.git" }
}
```

**Before publishing: inspect the tarball.** Accidentally published `.env` files and private keys are a real and recurring problem. Use the `files` allow-list rather than an `.npmignore` deny-list, and check the result:

```bash
npm pack --dry-run     # lists every file that would be included, and the tarball size
npm pack               # creates acme-logger-1.0.0.tgz for local testing
npm install ../logger/acme-logger-1.0.0.tgz   # test it in another project like a real user
```

**Publishing.**

```bash
npm login                      # authenticate (use 2FA)
npm version minor              # bump version, commit and tag
npm publish                    # upload; runs prepublishOnly/prepare first
npm publish --tag next         # publish a pre-release without moving the `latest` tag
npm dist-tag add @acme/logger@2.0.0 latest   # promote it later
npm deprecate @acme/logger@"<1.2.0" "Security fix in 1.2.0, please upgrade"
```

A published version is immutable: you cannot overwrite `1.0.0`, only publish `1.0.1`. Unpublishing is allowed only within 72 hours and only under conditions (for example, no other package depends on it), to avoid another left-pad.

**Publishing from CI securely.** Long-lived publish tokens stored in CI secrets are attractive to attackers. Current best practice:

- **Trusted publishing** (OIDC): npm trusts a specific GitHub Actions or GitLab workflow to publish without any stored token.
- **Provenance**: `npm publish --provenance` attaches a signed statement linking the tarball to the source commit and build workflow, shown on npmjs.com.
- Enforce 2FA on maintainer accounts and organisations.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/publish.yml (excerpt)
permissions:
  id-token: write        # allow the workflow to request an OIDC token for trusted publishing
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    with: { node-version: 24, registry-url: 'https://registry.npmjs.org' }
  - run: npm ci
  - run: npm test
  - run: npm publish --provenance --access public
```

**Private registries.** Companies host internal packages on GitHub Packages, GitLab, Artifactory, Verdaccio or npm organisations. An `.npmrc` file maps scopes to registries:

```text
# .npmrc
@acme:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com
//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}
```

Always use a scope for internal packages. An unscoped internal name (`acme-utils`) can be hijacked by someone publishing the same name publicly, the **dependency confusion** attack.

**Key Takeaways**

- Scopes (`@org/name`) namespace packages by owner and are private by default; use `--access public` for open source.
- Use `files` and `npm pack --dry-run` to control and verify exactly what is published.
- Versions are immutable; use dist-tags (`latest`, `next`) for release channels and `npm deprecate` to steer users.
- Publish from CI with trusted publishing and provenance; use scoped names for internal packages to prevent dependency confusion.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run `npm pack --dry-run` on a project without a `files` field and identify files that should not be published.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Set up a local Verdaccio registry, publish a scoped package to it, and install it from another project using an `.npmrc` scope mapping.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is a dependency confusion attack and how do you protect an organisation against it?" *Hint:* consider how a package manager chooses between a public and a private registry for the same unscoped name.

#### Monorepos and Workspaces

As a product grows, it often consists of several related packages: a web front end, an API, a shared validation library, a design system. Keeping them in separate repositories makes cross-cutting changes painful (change the library, publish, bump the version in each consumer). A **monorepo** keeps them in one repository, and **workspaces** let the package manager treat them as one project.

**Layout.**

```text
acme/
├── package.json          <- root: "workspaces": ["packages/*", "apps/*"]
├── package-lock.json     <- one lock file for everything
├── node_modules/         <- shared, hoisted dependencies
│   └── @acme/
│       └── validation -> ../../packages/validation   (symlink)
├── packages/
│   └── validation/
│       └── package.json  <- "name": "@acme/validation"
└── apps/
    ├── api/
    │   └── package.json  <- depends on "@acme/validation": "*"
    └── web/
        └── package.json  <- depends on "@acme/validation": "*"
```

```json
{
  "name": "acme",
  "private": true,
  "workspaces": ["packages/*", "apps/*"],
  "scripts": {
    "build": "npm run build --workspaces --if-present",
    "test": "npm test --workspaces --if-present"
  }
}
```

**How it works.** `npm install` at the root installs every workspace's dependencies into a single `node_modules` and **symlinks** each workspace package there. When `apps/api` imports `@acme/validation`, Node resolves it to the local source folder: changes are visible immediately, with no publishing.

```bash
npm install                                   # install everything
npm install zod -w @acme/validation           # add a dependency to one workspace
npm run test -w apps/api                      # run a script in one workspace
npm run build --workspaces                    # run in all workspaces
npm ls @acme/validation                       # check the link
```

**Benefits and costs.**

| Benefits | Costs |
|---|---|
| Atomic changes across packages in one commit and pull request | Larger repository, slower clones and CI unless optimised |
| Single version of shared tooling and dependencies | Requires discipline in boundaries and ownership |
| Easy local development without publishing | Running every test on every change becomes slow |
| One place for CI, linting and formatting rules | Package managers' hoisting can hide undeclared dependencies |

**Build orchestration.** Workspaces handle installation and linking, but not *task ordering* or caching. Tools such as **Turborepo** and **Nx** add a task graph (build `validation` before `api`), cache results by input hash, and run only tasks affected by a change. **Changesets** manages versioning and changelogs when workspace packages are published.

```jsonc
// turbo.json: build depends on dependencies' builds; outputs are cached
{
  "tasks": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["dist/**"] },
    "test": { "dependsOn": ["build"] }
  }
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A monorepo keeps related packages in one repository; workspaces make the package manager install and link them together.
- Workspace packages are symlinked into the root `node_modules`, so local changes are visible without publishing.
- Use `-w <name>` and `--workspaces` to target one or all packages.
- Add Turborepo or Nx for task ordering and caching, and Changesets for coordinated versioning.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a monorepo with workspaces `packages/greet` and `apps/cli`, where the CLI imports a function from `greet`. Verify that editing `greet` immediately affects the CLI.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `build` step to both workspaces (for example with `tsc`) and configure a root script that builds them in dependency order.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What are the trade-offs between a monorepo and separate repositories for a front end, a back end and a shared library?" *Hint:* consider atomic changes, CI time, access control, release independence and tooling requirements.

#### Auditing and Supply Chain Risks

When you install a package, you run code written by strangers, plus code written by everyone *they* depend on. A typical application trusts hundreds of maintainers. Attackers know this: compromising one popular package reaches thousands of companies at once. This is called a **software supply chain attack**.

**How attacks happen.**

| Attack | Description | Real examples |
|---|---|---|
| Compromised maintainer account | Phished or reused credentials let an attacker publish a malicious version | `ua-parser-js` (2021); `chalk`, `debug` and other widely used packages via a phished maintainer (September 2025) |
| Malicious new maintainer | An attacker gains trust, takes over maintenance and adds a payload | `event-stream` targeting a Bitcoin wallet (2018) |
| Self-propagating worm | Malware steals npm tokens from installs and republishes itself in the victim's packages | "Shai-Hulud" (2025) |
| Typosquatting | Packages with names close to popular ones (`crossenv` vs `cross-env`) | Hundreds removed every year |
| Dependency confusion | Public package with the same name as a company's internal package | Demonstrated against major tech companies (2021) |
| Protestware / sabotage | A maintainer deliberately breaks their own package | `colors` and `faker` (2022), `node-ipc` (2022) |

Most payloads run in **install scripts** (`postinstall`) or on first import, and try to steal environment variables, cloud credentials, SSH keys, npm tokens or cryptocurrency.

**`npm audit`: known vulnerabilities.** npm compares your lock file against the GitHub Advisory Database:

```bash
npm audit                     # report known vulnerabilities by severity, with dependency paths
npm audit --omit=dev          # only what ships to production
npm audit fix                 # apply compatible (in-range) upgrades
npm audit fix --force         # allow major upgrades: may break things, review carefully
npm audit signatures          # verify registry signatures and provenance attestations
```

Read reports critically. A "critical" ReDoS issue in a dev-only build tool that never sees untrusted input is far less urgent than a moderate issue in your HTTP request parser. `npm audit` also only knows about *reported* vulnerabilities; it cannot detect a malicious version published an hour ago.

**Defensive practices.**

- **Fewer dependencies.** Prefer the standard library: Node now has `fetch`, `util.parseArgs`, `fs.glob`, the test runner, `crypto.randomUUID()` and `structuredClone`, which replace many small packages.
- **Lock and reproduce.** Commit lock files; use `npm ci` so CI installs exactly what was reviewed.
- **Delay new versions.** Many attacks are detected within hours or days. Tools such as Renovate can wait a few days (a "minimum release age") before proposing updates; pnpm has a similar setting.
- **Restrict install scripts.** `npm ci --ignore-scripts` (or `ignore-scripts=true` in `.npmrc`) blocks them; pnpm 10 and Bun run dependency scripts only for an allow-list of trusted packages.
- **Protect secrets.** Do not keep long-lived tokens in environment variables of developer machines and CI jobs that install packages; use OIDC and short-lived credentials.
- **Monitor.** Dependabot or Renovate for updates, GitHub security alerts, and specialised scanners (Socket, Snyk) that look at *behaviour* of new versions (network access, install scripts, obfuscated code).
- **Software Bill of Materials (SBOM).** `npm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx` lists every component, so you can answer "are we affected?" quickly when a new incident is announced.

```text
# .npmrc for a security-conscious project
ignore-scripts=true          # no lifecycle scripts; `npm run x` still runs x, but not prex/postx
audit-level=high             # npm audit exits with an error only for high and critical findings
save-exact=true              # record exact versions instead of ^ ranges for new dependencies
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Every dependency is code you trust; supply-chain attacks target popular packages and maintainer accounts to reach many victims.
- Common vectors are compromised accounts, typosquatting, dependency confusion and malicious install scripts.
- `npm audit` finds *known* vulnerabilities in the locked tree; triage by real exposure, not only severity labels.
- Reduce dependencies, lock versions, delay fresh releases, restrict install scripts, protect tokens and keep an SBOM.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run `npm audit` on an existing project, pick one finding, and trace the dependency path to the vulnerable package. Decide whether it affects production.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure a project with `ignore-scripts=true`, install a package that needs a build step (for example a native add-on), and work out how to allow just that package's script safely.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A popular package you depend on was just reported to contain malware in its latest version. What do you do in the next hour?" *Hint:* determine whether you installed the affected version (lock files, SBOM, CI logs), what the payload could access, which credentials must be rotated, and how to pin a safe version.

#### Alternative Managers: yarn and pnpm

npm is the default, but not the only client for the npm registry. **yarn** and **pnpm** were created to fix npm's historical weaknesses (speed, determinism, disk usage) and pushed npm to improve. All three install the same packages from the same registry; they differ in *how* they lay out `node_modules` and in their extra features.

**yarn.** Released by Facebook in 2016, when npm was slow and had no lock file. It introduced `yarn.lock`, parallel downloads and an offline cache, ideas npm 5 adopted in 2017. Yarn 2+ ("Berry") is a rewrite with:

- **Plug'n'Play (PnP)**: no `node_modules` at all; a `.pnp.cjs` file maps package names to zip archives in a cache. Installs are near-instant and undeclared dependencies fail loudly, but some tools need adapters.
- `nodeLinker: node-modules` to fall back to a traditional layout.
- Strong workspace support, constraints and plugins.

**pnpm.** "Performant npm" uses a **content-addressable store**: every version of every file is stored once on disk (for example in `~/.local/share/pnpm/store`), and projects get **hard links** to it. Its `node_modules` is **strict**: only declared dependencies are visible at the top level, and everything else lives in `node_modules/.pnpm` and is wired together with symlinks.

```text
npm (hoisted, flat)                         pnpm (strict, symlinked)

node_modules/                               node_modules/
├── express/                                ├── express -> .pnpm/express@5.1.0/node_modules/express
├── body-parser/   <- importable even       └── .pnpm/
├── debug/            though app never          ├── express@5.1.0/node_modules/
└── ...               declared it               │   ├── express/          (hard links to store)
                      ("phantom dependency")    │   └── body-parser -> ../../body-parser@2.2.0/...
                                                └── body-parser@2.2.0/node_modules/body-parser/
```

The **phantom dependency** problem is worth understanding: with npm's flat layout, your code can `require('debug')` without declaring it, because Express happened to install it. It works until Express drops `debug`, then breaks mysteriously. pnpm prevents this by design.

**Comparison.**

| Aspect | npm | yarn (Berry) | pnpm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ships with Node | Yes | No (via Corepack or install) | No (via Corepack or install) |
| Lock file | `package-lock.json` | `yarn.lock` | `pnpm-lock.yaml` |
| Layout | Flat, hoisted `node_modules` | Plug'n'Play or `node_modules` | Strict symlinked `node_modules` |
| Disk usage across projects | One copy per project | Shared cache (zips) | One copy per machine (hard links) |
| Phantom dependencies | Possible | Prevented with PnP | Prevented |
| Workspaces | Yes | Yes, rich features | Yes, very popular for monorepos (`pnpm-workspace.yaml`) |
| Dependency install scripts | Run by default | Run by default | Allow-list required (pnpm 10+) |

**Commands side by side.**

| Task | npm | yarn | pnpm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Install all | `npm install` | `yarn` | `pnpm install` |
| CI install | `npm ci` | `yarn install --immutable` | `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` |
| Add | `npm install zod` | `yarn add zod` | `pnpm add zod` |
| Add dev | `npm install -D vitest` | `yarn add -D vitest` | `pnpm add -D vitest` |
| Run script | `npm run build` | `yarn build` | `pnpm build` |
| Run binary once | `npx tool` | `yarn dlx tool` | `pnpm dlx tool` |

**Pinning the manager.** The `packageManager` field records which manager and version a project uses, and Corepack (or the manager itself) enforces it:

```json
{ "packageManager": "pnpm@10.15.0" }
```

**Choosing.** npm is the zero-setup default and perfectly adequate for most projects. pnpm is a strong choice for monorepos and large projects because of speed, disk savings and strictness. Yarn PnP suits teams that want the strictest guarantees and are willing to configure tools for it. Bun's installer (`bun install`) is another fast, npm-compatible option. Whatever you pick, use one manager per repository and commit only its lock file.

**Key Takeaways**

- yarn and pnpm use the same registry as npm but differ in install layout, speed and features.
- pnpm's content-addressable store saves disk space and its strict layout prevents phantom dependencies.
- Yarn Berry's Plug'n'Play removes `node_modules` entirely in favour of a resolution map.
- Pin the manager with `packageManager`, use one per project and commit only its lock file.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Install the same project with npm and with pnpm in two copies of the directory, and compare install time and the structure of `node_modules`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a project that imports a transitive dependency it does not declare. Show that it works with npm and fails with pnpm, then fix it correctly.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is a phantom dependency and why can it break a working application after an unrelated update?" *Hint:* think about hoisting in a flat `node_modules` and what happens when a direct dependency changes its own dependencies.

<a id="113-asynchronous-and-non-blocking-io"></a>
### 11.3 Asynchronous and Non-Blocking I/O

This subchapter explains the core of Node's performance model: why blocking I/O is a problem on a single thread, how libuv's event loop schedules work in phases, what the thread pool does, how `process.nextTick` and `setImmediate` fit in, the three styles of asynchronous APIs, the difference between concurrency and parallelism, and how to detect code that blocks the loop. It builds on the browser event loop of Chapter 5.1.

#### Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O

I/O (reading files, querying databases, calling other services) is slow compared with the CPU. A modern CPU executes billions of instructions per second; a network round trip to a database in the same data centre takes around half a millisecond, enough time for a million instructions. What a program does *while waiting* determines how many clients it can serve.

| Operation | Typical latency | In "CPU time" terms |
|---|---|---|
| L1 cache reference | ~1 ns | 1 second |
| Main memory reference | ~100 ns | ~2 minutes |
| Read 4 KB from an SSD | ~20-100 µs | ~6-28 hours |
| Round trip within a data centre | ~500 µs | ~6 days |
| Round trip across continents | ~150 ms | ~5 years |

**Blocking I/O.** A blocking call does not return until the operation is complete. The thread that made the call can do nothing else in the meantime. With one thread per request, that is acceptable: other requests have their own threads. In Node.js, where *all* JavaScript runs on one thread, a blocking call freezes the entire server.

**Non-blocking I/O.** A non-blocking call starts the operation and returns immediately. The result is delivered later, through a callback, a promise or an event, when the event loop picks up the completion.

```javascript
const fs = require('node:fs');

// Blocking: the thread waits inside readFileSync; nothing else can run
console.log('1. before');
const data = fs.readFileSync('big.log', 'utf8');
console.log('2. read', data.length, 'chars');
console.log('3. after');
// Output: 1, 2, 3 — and during the read, every other client of this process waits too

// Non-blocking: readFile returns immediately; the callback runs later
console.log('A. before');
fs.readFile('big.log', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
  if (err) throw err;
  console.log('C. read', data.length, 'chars');
});
console.log('B. after');
// Output: A, B, C — the thread was free between B and C
```

**The effect on a server.**

```text
Blocking handler, 3 requests, each needs 100 ms of I/O and 1 ms of CPU

 time ->  0        100       200       300 ms
 req 1    [CPU][-------I/O------]
 req 2                           [CPU][-------I/O------]
 req 3                                                  [CPU][-------I/O------]
 last response after ~303 ms; the thread is idle 99% of the time

Non-blocking handler, same 3 requests

 req 1    [CPU][-------I/O------][cb]
 req 2     [CPU][-------I/O------][cb]
 req 3      [CPU][-------I/O------][cb]
 last response after ~104 ms; I/O waits overlap
```

**When synchronous APIs are fine.** Node offers `*Sync` variants of many functions on purpose. They are simpler and appropriate where nothing else needs to run concurrently: start-up code (reading configuration before the server starts listening), command-line tools and build scripts. Inside request handlers they are almost always a mistake.

**Key Takeaways**

- I/O is orders of magnitude slower than computation, so what a thread does while waiting matters.
- Blocking calls stop the only JavaScript thread, freezing all other work in the process.
- Non-blocking calls start the operation and return; results arrive later via callbacks, promises or events.
- Synchronous APIs are fine at start-up and in scripts, but not in code that serves concurrent requests.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a script that reads a large file once with `readFileSync` and once with `readFile`, logging messages before and after each call, and explain the output order.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create an HTTP server where `/slow` uses `readFileSync` on a large file and `/fast` returns "ok". Use `autocannon` or a loop of `curl` requests to show how `/slow` affects `/fast`, then fix it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Is it ever acceptable to use `fs.readFileSync` in a Node.js server?" *Hint:* distinguish start-up time from request time, and consider what else the process is doing at that moment.

#### The Node Event Loop Phases

The browser event loop (Chapter 5.1) picks one task, runs it, drains microtasks and possibly renders. Node.js has no rendering, but it has many kinds of events: timers, socket data, completed file reads, `setImmediate` callbacks, closing handles. libuv organises them into **phases** that run in a fixed order. Each iteration of the loop is called a **tick**.

**The phases.**

```text
             ┌───────────────────────────┐
   ┌───────> │          timers           │  setTimeout / setInterval callbacks whose time has come
   │         └─────────────┬─────────────┘
   │         ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
   │         │     pending callbacks     │  some I/O callbacks deferred from the previous tick
   │         └─────────────┬─────────────┘    (e.g. certain TCP errors)
   │         ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
   │         │       idle, prepare       │  internal use only
   │         └─────────────┬─────────────┘
   │         ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
   │         │           poll            │  retrieve new I/O events and run their callbacks;
   │         │                           │  wait here for I/O if nothing else is scheduled
   │         └─────────────┬─────────────┘
   │         ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
   │         │           check           │  setImmediate callbacks
   │         └─────────────┬─────────────┘
   │         ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
   └──────── │      close callbacks      │  'close' events, e.g. socket.on('close')
             └───────────────────────────┘

  Between every individual callback in every phase:
    1. drain the process.nextTick queue
    2. drain the promise microtask queue
    (repeat until both are empty)
```

**What each phase does.**

| Phase | Runs | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| timers | Expired `setTimeout`/`setInterval` callbacks | A timer's delay is a *minimum*, not a guarantee |
| pending callbacks | System-level callbacks deferred from the previous iteration | Rarely relevant in application code |
| poll | Callbacks for completed I/O (incoming data, finished file reads) | If no timers or immediates are pending, the loop *blocks* here waiting for I/O, using no CPU |
| check | `setImmediate` callbacks | Runs right after poll, which is why `setImmediate` exists |
| close callbacks | `'close'` handlers of destroyed handles | |

**The poll phase is the heart of the loop.** When nothing else is scheduled, Node sits in the poll phase inside `epoll_wait` (Linux) or its equivalent, with the thread sleeping until the kernel reports activity on a socket or the thread pool completes a task. This is why an idle Node server uses almost no CPU. The poll phase also calculates how long it may block: until the nearest timer is due.

**Microtasks between callbacks.** Since Node 11, the `nextTick` queue and the promise microtask queue are drained after *each* callback, not only between phases, which matches browser behaviour.

**Predicting the order.**

```javascript
// order.cjs — run with: node order.cjs
const fs = require('node:fs');

console.log('1 sync');

setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log('immediate'));
process.nextTick(() => console.log('2 nextTick'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3 promise'));

fs.readFile(__filename, () => {
  console.log('readFile callback (poll phase)');
  setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout inside I/O'), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log('immediate inside I/O'));   // always first: check comes right after poll
});

console.log('1b sync');
```

```text
1 sync
1b sync
2 nextTick
3 promise
timeout                         <- these two may swap (see below)
immediate
readFile callback (poll phase)
immediate inside I/O            <- always before the timeout scheduled in the same callback
timeout inside I/O
```

1. Synchronous code runs first, to completion.
2. Before the loop starts, the `nextTick` queue, then the promise queue, are drained.
3. The first loop iteration enters the timers phase. Whether the 0 ms timer (internally 1 ms) has already expired depends on how long start-up took, so `timeout` and `immediate` can appear in either order at the top level.
4. Inside an I/O callback (poll phase), the next phase is always check, so `setImmediate` deterministically runs before a new timer.

**A note on ES modules.** In an ES module, top-level code is itself evaluated as part of a promise job, so the promise microtask queue is drained *before* the `nextTick` queue gets its turn: in `order.mjs`, `3 promise` prints before `2 nextTick`. Code should never depend on this fine-grained ordering; it is shown only to explain surprising logs.

**Key Takeaways**

- Node's loop runs phases in order: timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, close callbacks.
- The poll phase handles completed I/O and is where the loop sleeps when there is nothing to do.
- `setImmediate` runs in the check phase, right after poll; timers run in the timers phase.
- After every callback, the `nextTick` queue and then the promise microtask queue are drained completely.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the `order.cjs` example several times and observe whether `timeout` and `immediate` change order. Then explain why the pair inside the `readFile` callback never changes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Predict the output of a program in which a `setImmediate` callback schedules a `process.nextTick`, a promise and another `setImmediate`. Run it to check your prediction and explain it phase by phase.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Walk me through what happens in the event loop when an HTTP request arrives at a Node.js server and the handler queries a database." *Hint:* follow the request from the kernel's socket notification in the poll phase, through the handler, the database driver's socket write, back to the poll phase and the response.

#### The Thread Pool and Offloaded Work

Node is often called single-threaded, but a running Node process has several threads. Only **one runs your JavaScript**. Others belong to V8 (garbage collection, compilation) and to **libuv's thread pool**, which performs operations that cannot be done without blocking at the operating-system level.

**Why some operations need threads.** Network sockets are well supported by OS readiness mechanisms (`epoll`, `kqueue`, IOCP): the kernel can tell libuv "this socket has data". Regular files are different. On most platforms, `epoll` does not work for regular files, and a `read()` on a file always blocks until the data comes from the disk. DNS lookups through `getaddrinfo` are also blocking C library calls. libuv's solution is to run these calls on a pool of worker threads, so the main thread does not block.

**What uses the thread pool.**

| Uses the thread pool | Does not (handled by the OS asynchronously) |
|---|---|
| Asynchronous `fs` operations (except `fs.watch`) | TCP and UDP sockets (`net`, `http`, `dgram`) |
| `dns.lookup()` (used by default when connecting to a hostname) | `dns.resolve*()` (uses c-ares over the network) |
| Async `crypto`: `pbkdf2`, `scrypt`, `randomBytes`, `randomFill`, key generation | Pipes, TTYs, child process I/O |
| Async `zlib` compression and decompression | Timers |
| Native add-ons that use `uv_queue_work` | Signals |

**The default size is 4.** With more than four simultaneous thread-pool tasks, the rest queue up. The effect is easy to observe:

```javascript
// pool.cjs — six expensive hashes at once
const crypto = require('node:crypto');
const start = Date.now();

for (let i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
  crypto.pbkdf2('secret', 'salt', 500_000, 64, 'sha512', () => {
    console.log(`hash ${i} done after ${Date.now() - start} ms`);
  });
}
```

```text
$ node pool.cjs                        $ UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=6 node pool.cjs
hash 1 done after 410 ms               hash 1 done after 430 ms
hash 3 done after 412 ms               hash 2 done after 433 ms
hash 2 done after 414 ms               hash 4 done after 435 ms
hash 4 done after 418 ms               hash 3 done after 436 ms
hash 5 done after 822 ms   <- waited   hash 5 done after 438 ms
hash 6 done after 825 ms   <- waited   hash 6 done after 440 ms
(timings vary with the machine and the number of cores)
```

```text
                      main thread (JavaScript, event loop)
                                 |
              pbkdf2 x6          |          completion events
          +----------------------+------------------------+
          v                                               ^
   +--------------+                                       |
   |  work queue  |  tasks 5, 6 wait here                 |
   +------+-------+                                       |
          v                                               |
   [ T1 ] [ T2 ] [ T3 ] [ T4 ]   libuv thread pool --------+
```

**Tuning.** Set `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (up to 1024) as an environment variable *before* the process starts; setting it later from JavaScript is unreliable because the pool may already exist. Increasing it helps when many file or crypto operations run concurrently, but more threads than CPU cores does not make CPU-bound work faster, and each thread costs memory.

**A hidden bottleneck: DNS.** `http.get('http://api.example.com')` resolves the hostname with `dns.lookup()`, which uses the pool. A slow DNS server can occupy all four threads, and then even unrelated `fs.readFile` calls wait. Remedies include caching DNS results, using IP addresses for internal services, or increasing the pool size.

**The thread pool is not for your JavaScript.** You cannot submit a JavaScript function to libuv's pool. To run *your own* CPU-heavy JavaScript in parallel, use worker threads (11.5).

**Key Takeaways**

- Only one thread runs JavaScript; libuv keeps a pool of threads (4 by default) for blocking system work.
- File system operations, `dns.lookup`, async crypto and zlib use the pool; network sockets do not.
- When more tasks than threads are submitted, they queue; `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (set before start-up) changes the size.
- Your own JavaScript cannot run on the pool; CPU-heavy JavaScript belongs in worker threads.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the `pbkdf2` example with pool sizes 1, 2, 4 and 8, record the completion times and explain the pattern.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Start eight `crypto.pbkdf2` calls and, at the same time, a single `fs.readFile` of a small file. Measure when the file read completes, and explain why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Our Node service has high latency on file uploads only when many users log in at the same time. What could be happening?" *Hint:* think about which resource password hashing and file writes might share.

#### process.nextTick vs setImmediate

Node offers several ways to say "run this later". The two Node-specific ones have confusing names: `process.nextTick` runs *before* the next tick of the event loop, and `setImmediate` runs *after* the current poll phase, not immediately. Their names are historical accidents that cannot be changed without breaking the ecosystem.

**Comparison.**

| API | Queue | When it runs | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `process.nextTick(fn)` | nextTick queue (Node-specific) | After the current operation, before promise microtasks and before the loop continues | Let callers attach listeners before an event is emitted; consistently async callbacks in libraries |
| `queueMicrotask(fn)` / `Promise.then` | Promise microtask queue | After the nextTick queue is empty, before the loop continues | Standard, portable way to defer a little |
| `setImmediate(fn)` | check phase | In the check phase of the current or next loop iteration | Yield to I/O, split long work into chunks |
| `setTimeout(fn, 0)` | timers phase | In a later timers phase, after at least 1 ms | Delays; portable "run later" in browsers |

```javascript
setImmediate(() => console.log('4 setImmediate'));
setTimeout(() => console.log('3/4 setTimeout'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('2 promise'));
process.nextTick(() => console.log('1 nextTick'));
// CommonJS output: 1 nextTick, 2 promise, then timeout and immediate (order varies at top level)
```

**Why `process.nextTick` exists.** A classic case: an object emits an event from its constructor before the caller has had a chance to attach a listener.

```javascript
const EventEmitter = require('node:events');

class Connection extends EventEmitter {
  constructor() {
    super();
    // Wrong: this.emit('ready') here would fire before anyone could listen.
    // Right: defer the emit until the current synchronous code has finished.
    process.nextTick(() => this.emit('ready'));
  }
}

const conn = new Connection();
conn.on('ready', () => console.log('connected'));   // attached in time, so this runs
```

The same idea applies to callbacks: an API should be **always synchronous or always asynchronous**, never "sometimes". Calling the callback synchronously when a value is cached and asynchronously otherwise (sometimes called "releasing Zalgo") produces order-dependent bugs.

```javascript
const cache = new Map();

function getUser(id, cb) {
  if (cache.has(id)) {
    // Calling cb(null, cache.get(id)) directly would be synchronous on the cached path only
    process.nextTick(cb, null, cache.get(id));   // keep the API consistently asynchronous
    return;
  }
  db.findUser(id, (err, user) => {
    if (!err) cache.set(id, user);
    cb(err, user);
  });
}
```

**The danger: starving the loop.** The nextTick queue is drained completely before the loop moves on, including ticks added by ticks. Recursive `nextTick` therefore blocks all I/O forever:

```javascript
function spin() {
  process.nextTick(spin);       // never yields: timers, sockets and immediates never run
}
spin();
setTimeout(() => console.log('never printed'), 10);
```

`setImmediate` does not have this problem: immediates scheduled during the check phase run in the *next* iteration, so I/O gets a turn in between. This makes it the right tool for splitting long computations:

```javascript
// Process a large array in chunks, letting I/O run between chunks
function processAll(items, handle, done) {
  let i = 0;
  function chunk() {
    const end = Math.min(i + 1000, items.length);
    for (; i < end; i++) handle(items[i]);
    if (i < items.length) setImmediate(chunk);   // yield to the event loop, then continue
    else done();
  }
  chunk();
}
```

**Recommendation.** Prefer `queueMicrotask` or promises for "after this code, before anything else", `setImmediate` for "after pending I/O", and reserve `process.nextTick` for library code that needs its specific guarantees. The Node documentation itself recommends `setImmediate` in most cases because it is easier to reason about.

**Key Takeaways**

- `process.nextTick` runs before promise microtasks and before the loop continues; `setImmediate` runs in the check phase after poll.
- `nextTick` lets callers attach listeners before an event fires and keeps APIs consistently asynchronous.
- Recursive `nextTick` (or microtasks) starves the event loop; recursive `setImmediate` does not.
- Use `setImmediate` to break up long work so I/O callbacks can run in between.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a script that schedules one callback with each of `process.nextTick`, `queueMicrotask`, `setImmediate` and `setTimeout(fn, 0)` inside an `fs.readFile` callback, and explain the output order.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a function that sums the numbers from 1 to 100 million in chunks using `setImmediate`, while a `setInterval` prints a heartbeat every 100 ms. Show that the heartbeat keeps printing, then switch to `process.nextTick` and observe the difference.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `process.nextTick` and `setImmediate`, and which would you use to break a CPU-heavy loop into chunks?" *Hint:* focus on when each queue is drained relative to the poll phase, and what that means for pending I/O.

#### Callback, Promise and async/await APIs in Node

Node's core APIs were designed in 2009, before promises existed in JavaScript, so they use **error-first callbacks**. Promises arrived in ES2015 and `async`/`await` in ES2017; Node has since added promise-based versions of most core modules. You will meet all three styles in real code and need to convert between them.

**Error-first callbacks.** The convention: the last argument is a callback whose first parameter is an error (or `null`), followed by results.

```javascript
const fs = require('node:fs');

fs.readFile('config.json', 'utf8', (err, text) => {
  if (err) {                          // always check the error first
    console.error('cannot read config:', err.code);   // e.g. 'ENOENT'
    return;                           // and return, or the code below runs with text undefined
  }
  const config = JSON.parse(text);    // note: a throw here is NOT caught by anything above
  console.log(config.port);
});
```

Nested callbacks for sequential steps quickly become hard to read ("callback hell", Chapter 5.2), and errors must be checked at every level.

**Promise-based core APIs.** Many core modules have promise variants:

| Callback module | Promise variant |
|---|---|
| `node:fs` | `node:fs/promises` |
| `node:timers` | `node:timers/promises` (`setTimeout`, `setInterval` as async iterator) |
| `node:dns` | `node:dns/promises` |
| `node:stream` (`pipeline`, `finished`) | `node:stream/promises` |
| `node:readline` | `node:readline/promises` |
| `node:events` | `events.once()` and `events.on()` return a promise / async iterator |

```javascript
// ES module with top-level await
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';

try {
  const config = JSON.parse(await readFile('config.json', 'utf8'));
  await sleep(500);                                          // promise-based delay
  config.updatedAt = new Date().toISOString();
  await writeFile('config.json', JSON.stringify(config, null, 2));
} catch (err) {
  console.error('update failed:', err.message);             // catches I/O and JSON errors alike
}
```

**Converting callbacks to promises.** `util.promisify` wraps any function that follows the error-first convention:

```javascript
const { promisify } = require('node:util');
const { execFile } = require('node:child_process');

const execFileAsync = promisify(execFile);

async function gitBranch() {
  const { stdout } = await execFileAsync('git', ['branch', '--show-current']);
  return stdout.trim();
}
```

For functions that do not follow the convention, wrap them manually with `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)`. The reverse, `util.callbackify`, turns an async function into a callback-style one for legacy interfaces.

**Running operations concurrently.** `await` in a loop runs operations one after another. When they are independent, start them together:

```javascript
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const files = ['a.json', 'b.json', 'c.json'];

// Sequential: total time = sum of all reads
for (const f of files) await readFile(f, 'utf8');

// Concurrent: total time = slowest read
const contents = await Promise.all(files.map(f => readFile(f, 'utf8')));

// Concurrent, tolerating individual failures
const results = await Promise.allSettled(files.map(f => readFile(f, 'utf8')));
for (const r of results) {
  if (r.status === 'rejected') console.warn('failed:', r.reason.code);
}
```

**Cancellation.** Many Node APIs accept an `AbortSignal`, the same mechanism `fetch` uses:

```javascript
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(2000);                 // abort after 2 seconds
try {
  const data = await readFile('huge.bin', { signal });
} catch (err) {
  if (err.name === 'AbortError') console.log('read cancelled');
  else throw err;
}
```

**Unhandled rejections crash the process.** Since Node 15, a promise that rejects with no handler terminates the process (`--unhandled-rejections=throw` is the default). This is deliberate: silently ignored errors leave applications in unknown states. Always `await` or `.catch()` promises, including "fire and forget" ones.

```javascript
// Fire and forget, but handle the error
sendAnalyticsEvent(evt).catch(err => logger.warn({ err }, 'analytics failed'));
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Node's classic APIs use error-first callbacks: `(err, result) => {}`; always check and return on `err`.
- Promise variants (`fs/promises`, `timers/promises`, `stream/promises`, ...) work naturally with `async`/`await` and `try`/`catch`.
- `util.promisify` converts error-first functions; `Promise.all`/`allSettled` run independent operations concurrently.
- Many APIs accept an `AbortSignal` for cancellation; unhandled promise rejections terminate the process.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite a callback-based script that reads two files, concatenates them and writes the result, using `fs/promises` and `async`/`await`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a function `mapLimit(items, limit, fn)` that runs an async function over an array with at most `limit` operations in flight at once, and use it to read 100 files with a limit of 10.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What happens in Node.js if a promise rejects and nobody handles it, and why did Node change the behaviour?" *Hint:* compare the old warning-only behaviour with the current default, and think about what state a server is in after an error nobody noticed.

#### Concurrency vs Parallelism in Node

"Node can handle 10,000 requests at once" and "Node is single-threaded" are both true, because they describe different things. **Concurrency** is about *dealing with* many tasks at once by interleaving them; **parallelism** is about *doing* many tasks at the same instant on multiple CPU cores.

An analogy: a single chef who starts the pasta water, chops vegetables while it heats, and stirs the sauce in between is working *concurrently*. Two chefs each cooking a dish at the same time are working *in parallel*.

```text
Concurrency (one JS thread, interleaved)

 thread  [A1][B1][C1]......[A2]..[C2][B2]
          |   |   |          ^     ^   ^
          |   |   +-- I/O ---|-----+   |       I/O waits overlap,
          |   +------ I/O ---|---------+       CPU work never does
          +---------- I/O ---+

Parallelism (several threads or processes, simultaneous)

 core 1  [A1][A2][A3][A4]
 core 2  [B1][B2][B3][B4]
 core 3  [C1][C2][C3][C4]
```

**What Node gives you.**

| Kind of work | Single Node process | How to get more |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting on network and disk | Highly concurrent: thousands of in-flight operations | Usually not needed |
| Built-in blocking system work (fs, crypto, zlib) | Parallel on the libuv thread pool | Increase `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` |
| Your own CPU-heavy JavaScript | Sequential on one core; blocks everything else | Worker threads (11.5), child processes |
| Serving more requests than one core can compute | Limited to one core | Cluster module, multiple containers behind a load balancer (11.5) |

**I/O concurrency in practice.** Firing many requests concurrently costs almost nothing on the JavaScript side:

```javascript
// 50 HTTP calls in flight at once, on a single thread
const ids = Array.from({ length: 50 }, (_, i) => i + 1);
console.time('all');
const users = await Promise.all(
  ids.map(id => fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${(id % 10) + 1}`).then(r => r.json()))
);
console.timeEnd('all');   // roughly the time of the slowest request, not 50 times one request
```

**CPU work does not interleave.** Promises do not make computation parallel. Wrapping a loop in `async` does not move it off the main thread:

```javascript
async function heavy() {             // async does NOT mean "runs in the background"
  let x = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 2e9; i++) x += i;  // still runs on the main thread, blocking it
  return x;
}

setTimeout(() => console.log('timer'), 10);
await Promise.all([heavy(), heavy()]);   // runs one after the other; the timer waits for both
```

**Limit concurrency when it hurts others.** Unlimited concurrency can overwhelm a downstream service, exhaust database connection pools or hit API rate limits. Use a fixed concurrency limit (a pool or a library such as `p-limit`) and connection pools in database drivers.

**Shared state is still simple.** Because JavaScript code itself never runs in parallel within a thread, there are no data races on ordinary variables: a function runs to completion before another callback starts. But there *are* logical races across `await` points:

```javascript
// Race across an await: two concurrent requests can both read 100 and both write 90
async function withdraw(accountId, amount) {
  const balance = await db.getBalance(accountId);      // other requests can run while we wait
  if (balance < amount) throw new Error('insufficient funds');
  await db.setBalance(accountId, balance - amount);    // may overwrite a concurrent update
}
// Fix: let the database do it atomically, e.g.
// UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Concurrency is interleaving many tasks; parallelism is running them at the same instant on several cores.
- One Node process is highly concurrent for I/O, and uses the thread pool in parallel for some built-in work.
- Your JavaScript runs on one core: `async` does not make computation parallel; use workers or more processes.
- No low-level data races, but logical races across `await` points still require atomic operations or locks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Time 20 sequential `fetch` calls against 20 concurrent calls with `Promise.all`, and explain the difference.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Simulate the `withdraw` race with an in-memory "database" whose methods `await` a random delay, show that two concurrent withdrawals can overdraw the account, and fix it with a per-account promise-based lock.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Is Node.js concurrent, parallel, both or neither?" *Hint:* answer separately for JavaScript execution, for I/O, for the libuv thread pool and for a cluster of processes.

#### Diagnosing Event Loop Blocking

When the event loop is blocked, every request in the process slows down at once, including health checks, which can cause orchestrators to restart healthy-but-busy instances. The symptoms (latency spikes, timeouts, a CPU at 100% on one core) are easy to see; finding the responsible code needs measurement.

**Common causes.**

| Cause | Example | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous I/O in handlers | `fs.readFileSync`, `execSync`, `crypto.pbkdf2Sync` | Use asynchronous variants |
| Large JSON | `JSON.parse` / `JSON.stringify` on tens of megabytes | Paginate, stream (NDJSON), or parse in a worker |
| Catastrophic regex backtracking (ReDoS) | `/^(a+)+$/` against `'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!'` | Safer patterns, input length limits, linear-time regex engines |
| Heavy computation | Image resizing, PDF generation, sorting huge arrays | Worker threads, native libraries, a separate service |
| Unbounded loops over user input | Processing an uploaded 1-million-row CSV in one go | Streams and chunking |
| Excessive garbage collection | Allocating huge temporary arrays per request | Reduce allocations, stream data |

**Measuring loop delay.** The idea: schedule a timer and measure how late it fires. Node provides precise tools in `perf_hooks`:

```javascript
import { monitorEventLoopDelay, performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';

const histogram = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 });  // sample every 20 ms
histogram.enable();

let lastElu = performance.eventLoopUtilization();

setInterval(() => {
  const elu = performance.eventLoopUtilization(lastElu);      // delta since last sample
  lastElu = performance.eventLoopUtilization();
  console.log({
```
