> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is `req.params.id === 42` always false in Express, and what can go wrong with `Number(req.params.id)`?" *Hint:* consider the types the router produces and what `Number` returns for `''`, `'1e3'`, `'0x10'` and `' 7 '`.

#### Route Handlers and express.Router

A route can have **several handlers**. Each one receives `(req, res, next)` and either responds or calls `next()` to pass control to the following handler. This lets small, reusable functions (authentication, validation, loading a resource) be combined per route:

```javascript
app.get('/admin/reports', authenticate, requireRole('admin'), listReports);
app.post('/books', [authenticate, validateBook], createBook);   // arrays are flattened, so lists can be reused
```

**Skipping the rest of a route.** `next('route')` skips the remaining handlers of the current route and continues with the next matching route. It is useful for conditional behaviour such as feature flags:

```javascript
app.get('/checkout', (req, res, next) => {
  if (!req.user?.betaFeatures) return next('route');   // skip renderNewCheckout
  next();
}, renderNewCheckout);

app.get('/checkout', renderClassicCheckout);           // reached by users without the flag
```

**Grouping methods on one path.** `app.route()` avoids repeating a path:

```javascript
app.route('/books')
  .get(listBooks)
  .post(createBook);

app.route('/books/:id')
  .get(getBook)
  .patch(updateBook)
  .delete(deleteBook)
  .all((req, res) => res.set('Allow', 'GET, PATCH, DELETE').sendStatus(405));  // other methods: 405, not 404
```

Without the final `.all()`, a `PUT /books/42` would fall through to the 404 handler, because Express does not generate `405 Method Not Allowed` on its own.

**express.Router: mini-applications.** As an API grows, defining every route on `app` in one file becomes unmanageable. `express.Router()` creates an isolated group of routes and middleware, a "mini-app" without its own server or settings, that can be **mounted** at a path:

```javascript
// src/books/books.router.js
import { Router } from 'express';

export const booksRouter = Router();
booksRouter.get('/', listBooks);                 // GET  /api/v1/books
booksRouter.post('/', createBook);               // POST /api/v1/books
booksRouter.get('/:id', getBook);                // GET  /api/v1/books/42

// Nested router: reviews belong to a book
const reviewsRouter = Router({ mergeParams: true });   // makes :bookId from the parent visible
reviewsRouter.get('/', (req, res) => res.json(reviews.forBook(Number(req.params.bookId))));
booksRouter.use('/:bookId/reviews', reviewsRouter);
```

```javascript
// src/app.js
app.use('/api/v1/books', booksRouter);
app.use('/api/v1/users', usersRouter);
```

When a router is mounted, Express strips the mount path from the URL the router sees and records it in `req.baseUrl`. For `GET /api/v1/books/42/reviews?sort=new`:

```text
 app
  +-- /api/v1/books  --> booksRouter       req.baseUrl = '/api/v1/books'             req.path = '/42/reviews'
        +-- /:bookId/reviews --> reviewsRouter
                                           req.baseUrl = '/api/v1/books/42/reviews'  req.path = '/'
                                           req.params  = { bookId: '42' }   (only with mergeParams: true)
                                           req.originalUrl = '/api/v1/books/42/reviews?sort=new'  (never changes)
```

Because a router does not know where it is mounted, the same router can be reused at different paths, and API versioning becomes a matter of mounting: `app.use('/api/v1', v1Router)` and `app.use('/api/v2', v2Router)`.

**Router options.**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `mergeParams` | `false` | Keep `req.params` from parent routers |
| `caseSensitive` | `false` | Treat `/Books` and `/books` as different |
| `strict` | `false` | Treat `/books` and `/books/` as different |

`next('router')` leaves the current router entirely and continues with whatever comes after it in the parent, for example to bypass a versioned router for certain clients.

**Key Takeaways**

- A route can chain several handlers; each responds or calls `next()`. Arrays of handlers can be reused.
- `next('route')` skips to the next matching route; `next('router')` exits the current router.
- `app.route(path)` groups handlers for one path; add `.all()` to return `405` for unsupported methods.
- `express.Router()` creates mountable mini-apps; mounting strips the prefix into `req.baseUrl`, and `mergeParams` exposes parent parameters.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Split an app with `/books` and `/authors` routes into two routers in separate files, mounted under `/api/v1`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add nested routes `/api/v1/authors/:authorId/books` that reuse a books router. Log `req.baseUrl`, `req.path` and `req.params` at each level, with and without `mergeParams`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you version a public REST API in Express so that v1 and v2 share most of their code?" *Hint:* consider mounting routers, a shared service layer, and a v2 router that delegates unchanged paths to v1 with `next('router')` or reuses its handlers.

#### Project Structure and Configuration

Express prescribes no structure, so small projects often end up as one `app.js` with hundreds of routes, database queries inside handlers and settings read from `process.env` everywhere. That code is hard to test (every test needs HTTP and a database), hard to change (the same rule is copied into many handlers) and hard to deploy (missing configuration is only discovered when a request fails). A clear structure separates **what the HTTP layer does** from **what the business rules are** from **how data is stored**.

**Layered architecture.**

```text
 HTTP request
     |
     v
 +-----------------+   paths, middleware, mapping URL -> handler
 | router          |
 +--------+--------+
          v
 +-----------------+   reads req (params, query, body), calls a service,
 | controller      |   turns the result into a response (often inline in small apps)
 +--------+--------+
          v
 +-----------------+   business rules: "an ISBN must be unique", "only owners may delete"
 | service         |   no req/res: usable from HTTP, CLI scripts, queues and tests
 +--------+--------+
          v
 +-----------------+   data access: SQL, MongoDB, external APIs; one interface,
 | repository      |   several implementations (real, in-memory for tests)
 +-----------------+
```

The key rule: **dependencies point downwards**. Services never import Express; repositories never know about HTTP status codes. This is what makes each layer replaceable and testable.

**Organising files.** Two common layouts:

| Layout | Example | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| By layer | `routes/`, `controllers/`, `services/`, `models/` | Familiar, fine for small apps | One feature is spread over many folders |
| By feature (vertical slices) | `books/`, `users/`, `orders/`, each with its router, service, repository, schemas | Features stay together; easy to find, move or delete | Shared code needs a clear home (`lib/`, `middleware/`) |

A feature-based layout for a medium-sized API:

```text
src/
  app.js                   createApp(deps): middleware, routers, 404, error handler (no listen)
  server.js                loads config, creates real dependencies, listens, shuts down
  config.js                validated, frozen configuration object
  lib/
    http-error.js          HttpError class (12.2)
    logger.js
  middleware/
    authenticate.js
    validate.js
    error-handler.js
  books/
    books.router.js        routes + handlers
    books.service.js       business rules
    books.repository.js    data access
    books.schemas.js       validation schemas (12.3)
  users/
    ...
test/
  books.test.js
```

**Dependency injection with an app factory.** Instead of each module importing a global database connection, `createApp()` receives its dependencies. Production passes real ones; tests pass in-memory ones:

```javascript
// src/app.js
import express from 'express';
import { createBooksRouter } from './books/books.router.js';
import { createBookService } from './books/books.service.js';

export function createApp({ bookRepository, authenticate, logger }) {
  const app = express();
  app.use(express.json());
  app.use('/api/v1/books', createBooksRouter({ books: createBookService(bookRepository), authenticate, logger }));
  return app;
}
```

```javascript
// src/server.js
import { config } from './config.js';
import { createApp } from './app.js';
import { createPgBookRepository } from './books/books.repository.js';
import { authenticateJwt } from './middleware/authenticate-jwt.js';
import { createPool } from './lib/db.js';

const pool = createPool(config.DATABASE_URL);
const app = createApp({
  bookRepository: createPgBookRepository(pool),   // tests pass an in-memory repository instead
  authenticate: authenticateJwt,                  // ...and a fake authentication middleware
  logger: console,
});
app.listen(config.PORT);
```

**Configuration.** Following the *twelve-factor app* principle, configuration that differs between environments (ports, database URLs, secrets, allowed origins) comes from **environment variables**, not from code. Node can load a `.env` file itself (`node --env-file=.env`, 11.5), so packages such as `dotenv` are optional. Environment variables are untyped strings, so validate them once at start-up and fail fast:

```javascript
// src/config.js
import { z } from 'zod';

const schema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']).default('development'),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),    // "3000" -> 3000
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
  SESSION_SECRET: z.string().min(32, 'use at least 32 random characters'),
  CORS_ORIGINS: z.string().default('')
    .transform((s) => s.split(',').map((o) => o.trim()).filter(Boolean)),   // "a,b" -> ['a', 'b']
  LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(['fatal', 'error', 'warn', 'info', 'debug', 'trace']).default('info'),
});

const parsed = schema.safeParse(process.env);
if (!parsed.success) {
  console.error('Invalid configuration:');
  for (const issue of parsed.error.issues) console.error(`  ${issue.path.join('.')}: ${issue.message}`);
  process.exit(1);                         // crash at start-up, not on the first request that needs the value
}

export const config = Object.freeze(parsed.data);
```

```json
{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file=.env src/server.js",
    "start": "node src/server.js",
    "test": "node --env-file=.env.test --test"
  }
}
```

In production, the platform (Docker, Kubernetes, a PaaS) sets the variables, so `start` does not load a file. Commit a `.env.example` with placeholder values and never commit real secrets (Chapter 17).

**What `NODE_ENV=production` changes.** Express caches compiled templates and hides stack traces in its default error page; many libraries also enable optimisations. Set it in every production deployment, but do not use it as the only switch for application features: prefer explicit configuration variables.

**Key Takeaways**

- Separate routing/HTTP, business rules (services) and data access (repositories); dependencies point only downwards.
- Organising by feature keeps related code together as the application grows.
- An app factory that receives its dependencies makes the application easy to test and to wire differently per environment.
- Read configuration from environment variables, validate and type it once at start-up, freeze it, and fail fast when it is invalid.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `config.js` that requires `PORT` and `DATABASE_URL`, start the app without them and check that it exits with a clear message.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Refactor a single-file Express app (routes with inline data access) into router, service and repository layers for one feature. Then write a test that uses the service with an in-memory repository, without HTTP.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Where should business rules live in an Express application, and why not in route handlers?" *Hint:* think about reuse from other entry points (queues, CLI scripts), testability without HTTP, and what happens when the same rule is needed by two routes.

<a id="122-the-middleware-pipeline"></a>
### 12.2 The Middleware Pipeline

This subchapter explains the idea at the heart of Express: a request passes through a chain of middleware functions, each of which can inspect it, modify it, answer it or hand it on. It covers execution order, the levels at which middleware can be attached, the built-in and most common third-party middleware, how to write your own, and how errors (synchronous and asynchronous) travel through the pipeline.

#### Middleware Concept and Execution Order

Many concerns apply to *many* routes at once: logging, security headers, CORS, parsing bodies, checking authentication, compressing responses. Putting that code into every route handler would duplicate it everywhere. **Middleware** solves this by turning request handling into a pipeline of small functions, each responsible for one concern.

An analogy is airport departure. Every passenger passes check-in, security and passport control before reaching the gate. Each checkpoint can let you continue, turn you away, or call for help if something is wrong; and some checkpoints only apply to some passengers (passport control only for international flights). Middleware works the same way.

**The signature.** A middleware function receives the request, the response and a function `next`:

```javascript
function middleware(req, res, next) {
  // 1. inspect or modify req / res
  // 2. then exactly one of:
  //    - send a response (the pipeline stops here)
  //    - call next()      (continue with the next middleware or route)
  //    - call next(err)   (skip to error-handling middleware)
}
```

Route handlers are middleware too; they are simply the last in line and normally respond instead of calling `next()`.

```text
 request
    |
    v
 +--------+  next()  +--------------+  next()  +--------------+  next()  +---------------+
 | logger | -------> | express.json | -------> | authenticate | -------> | route handler | --> res.json(...)
 +--------+          +--------------+          +------+-------+          +---------------+
                                                      |
                                       res.status(401)|  or next(err)
                                                      v
                                        response sent / error-handling middleware
```

**Execution order follows registration order.** Express keeps one ordered list of middleware and routes. For each request it walks the list from the top and runs every entry whose method and path match, until something responds:

```javascript
import express from 'express';
const app = express();

app.use((req, res, next) => { console.log('1 app-level: every request'); next(); });
app.use('/api', (req, res, next) => { console.log('2 only paths under /api'); next(); });

app.get('/api/hello', (req, res) => {
  console.log('3 route handler');
  res.send('hi');
  console.log('4 still runs: sending does not stop the function');
});

app.use((req, res) => {                     // reached only if nothing above responded
  console.log('5 not found');
  res.status(404).send('not found');
});

app.listen(3000);
// GET /api/hello -> 1, 2, 3, 4
// GET /other     -> 1, 5
// GET /api/nope  -> 1, 2, 5
```

**Running code after the response.** Express middleware is a *linear* chain: `next()` starts the next function but does not return a promise that waits for it. Code after `await next()` therefore runs too early:

```javascript
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  const start = performance.now();
  await next();                                       // next() returns undefined: nothing is awaited
  console.log(performance.now() - start);             // about 0 ms, measured before the handler finished
});

// Correct: listen for the response's 'finish' event (or 'close' for aborted requests)
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const start = performance.now();
  res.on('finish', () => {
    console.log(`${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} ${res.statusCode} ${(performance.now() - start).toFixed(1)}ms`);
  });
  next();
});
```

Koa (12.3) uses a different design, the "onion" model, in which `await next()` really waits for everything downstream.

**Two classic bugs.**

| Bug | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Middleware neither responds nor calls `next()` | The request hangs until the client or server times out | Every code path must end in a response, `next()` or `next(err)` |
| Middleware responds *and* calls `next()` | `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` when a later handler also responds | `return` after responding |

**Key Takeaways**

- Middleware is a function `(req, res, next)` that handles one concern and then responds, calls `next()` or calls `next(err)`.
- Express runs matching middleware and routes in registration order; nothing after a response runs unless it was already called.
- `next()` does not wait for downstream code; use `res.on('finish')` for work after the response.
- A request hangs when no code path responds or calls `next`; it fails when two paths respond.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write three middleware functions that log their names and register them so that a request to `/api/x` logs them in the order B, A, C. Explain the order using registration order and path matching.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a response-time logger that records method, URL, status and duration, and also logs requests whose client disconnected before the response finished (compare the `finish` and `close` events).
> 3. *(Interview)* "In Express, why does `await next()` not let you measure how long the rest of the pipeline took?" *Hint:* look at what `next()` returns, and compare with Koa's composition of middleware as nested promises.

#### Application, Router and Route-Level Middleware

Middleware can be attached at different levels, which decides **which requests** it runs for. Choosing the right level keeps concerns local: security headers apply to everything, authentication to a group of routes, a specific validation to one route.

| Level | Registered with | Runs for |
|---|---|---|
| Application | `app.use(fn)` | Every request |
| Application, with path | `app.use('/admin', fn)` | Requests whose path is `/admin` or starts with `/admin/` |
| Router | `router.use(fn)` | Every request that *enters* that router |
| Route | `app.get('/x', fn, handler)` | Only that method and path |
| Error-handling | `app.use((err, req, res, next) => ...)` | Only after `next(err)` or a thrown error (see below) |

**Path prefixes.** `app.use('/admin', fn)` matches `/admin`, `/admin/` and `/admin/users`, but not `/administrator`: matching works on whole path segments. Inside `fn`, the prefix is stripped: `req.baseUrl` is `'/admin'` and `req.path` is the rest. Route methods (`app.get(...)`) instead match the *whole* path.

**A realistic arrangement.**

```javascript
import express, { Router } from 'express';

const app = express();
app.use(helmet());                                        // application level: every response gets security headers
app.use(express.json());

const publicRouter = Router();
publicRouter.get('/health', (req, res) => res.json({ status: 'ok' }));
publicRouter.post('/auth/login', login);

const adminRouter = Router();
adminRouter.use(authenticate, requireRole('admin'));      // router level: everything under /api/admin
adminRouter.get('/users', listUsers);
adminRouter.delete('/users/:id', auditLog('user.delete'), deleteUser);   // route level: only this route

app.use('/api', publicRouter);
app.use('/api/admin', adminRouter);
```

Which middleware runs for each request:

| Request | helmet | json | authenticate + requireRole | auditLog |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/health` | yes | yes | no | no |
| `GET /api/admin/users` | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `DELETE /api/admin/users/7` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `GET /api/admin/nothing-here` | yes | yes | yes (then 404) | no |

**The router-level trap.** Router-level middleware runs for every request that *enters* the router, even if none of its routes match. Mounting a protected router at a shared prefix therefore protects more than intended:

```javascript
const privateRouter = Router();
privateRouter.use(authenticate);              // runs for EVERY request entering this router
privateRouter.get('/orders', listOrders);

app.use('/api', privateRouter);               // registered first, at /api...
app.use('/api', publicRouter);                // ...so GET /api/health now requires a login: it enters privateRouter first
```

Fixes: mount routers with different authentication needs at distinct prefixes (`/api/public`, `/api/private`), register public routers first, or attach authentication at route level.

**Key Takeaways**

- Application-level middleware applies to all requests (optionally under a path prefix), router-level to requests entering the router, route-level to one route.
- `app.use(path, ...)` matches path prefixes by segment and strips the prefix into `req.baseUrl`; route methods match the full path.
- Router-level middleware runs even when no route in the router matches; mind where routers are mounted.
- Attach each concern at the narrowest level that covers all the routes that need it.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build the arrangement above with stub functions that log their names, and verify the table by sending each request.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Reproduce the router-level trap, then fix it in two different ways. Write down which fix you would prefer in a large codebase and why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Where would you put authentication middleware in an Express app with both public and private endpoints?" *Hint:* compare app-level with an allowlist, router-level with separate prefixes, and route-level; consider what happens when a developer adds a new route and forgets something.

#### Built-In Middleware

Express 3 shipped with about twenty bundled middleware functions from Connect. Express 4 removed almost all of them so they could evolve independently, and later re-added the most essential ones. Express 5 includes five:

| Middleware | Based on | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `express.json()` | `body-parser` | Parse `application/json` bodies into `req.body` |
| `express.urlencoded()` | `body-parser` | Parse HTML form posts (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) |
| `express.text()` | `body-parser` | Read `text/plain` bodies as a string |
| `express.raw()` | `body-parser` | Read bodies as a `Buffer` (for signatures and binary data) |
| `express.static(root)` | `serve-static` | Serve files from a directory |

**Why body parsing is opt-in.** The request body is a stream (11.4). Reading it costs memory and time, the right format and size limit differ by route, and some routes (file uploads, proxies) must not have their body consumed at all. Express therefore leaves the decision to you.

**Body parsers.**

```javascript
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));                         // the default limit, stated explicitly
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false, limit: '20kb' }));   // HTML forms
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | `'100kb'` | Maximum body size; larger bodies are rejected with `413` |
| `type` | the parser's MIME type | Which `Content-Type` values to parse (string, array or function) |
| `strict` (json) | `true` | Accept only objects and arrays at the top level |
| `extended` (urlencoded) | `false` in Express 5 | `true` uses `qs` and allows nested objects like `a[b]=1` |
| `inflate` | `true` | Accept gzip/deflate/brotli-encoded bodies |
| `verify` | none | `verify(req, res, buf)` callback to inspect the raw bytes |

Each parser runs only when the request's `Content-Type` matches; otherwise it calls `next()` without touching the body. In Express 5, `req.body` is then `undefined` (in Express 4 it was `{}`), so code like `const { title } = req.body` throws a `TypeError` when a client forgets the `Content-Type` header. Validation (12.3) handles this.

Body-parser failures are passed to `next(err)` with a `status` and a `type`, which an error handler can map to clear responses:

| `err.type` | `err.status` | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| `'entity.parse.failed'` | 400 | Malformed JSON |
| `'entity.too.large'` | 413 | Body above `limit` |
| `'encoding.unsupported'` | 415 | Unknown `Content-Encoding` |
| `'charset.unsupported'` | 415 | Unsupported charset |
| `'request.aborted'` | 400 | Client disconnected during upload |

**Per-route limits and the ordering trap.** Once a body has been parsed, later parsers skip it. A global parser with a small limit therefore rejects large bodies *before* a route-specific parser with a larger limit is reached. Register the special route first, or apply the global parser only to the routers that need it:

```javascript
app.post('/api/imports', express.json({ limit: '5mb' }), importBooks);   // registered before the global parser
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));                              // all other routes
```

**Raw bodies for webhook signatures.** Payment providers and similar services sign the *exact bytes* they send. Parsing and re-serialising JSON can change those bytes (key order, whitespace), so the signature must be checked on the raw body:

```javascript
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

app.post('/webhooks/payments',
  express.raw({ type: 'application/json', limit: '1mb' }),    // req.body is a Buffer with the exact bytes
  (req, res) => {
    const expected = createHmac('sha256', process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET).update(req.body).digest('hex');
    const received = req.get('X-Signature') ?? '';
    const valid = received.length === expected.length &&      // timingSafeEqual requires equal lengths
      timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(received), Buffer.from(expected));
    if (!valid) return res.sendStatus(401);
    const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString('utf8'));       // parse only after verifying
    paymentEvents.enqueue(event);
    res.sendStatus(204);
  });

app.use(express.json());                                       // registered after: the webhook keeps its raw body
```

**Static files.** `express.static(root, options)` serves files from a directory, with correct MIME types, `ETag`/`Last-Modified` validation, `Range` requests and protection against path traversal (`/../../etc/passwd` is rejected).

```javascript
import path from 'node:path';

const publicDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, '..', 'public');

app.use('/static', express.static(publicDir, {
  maxAge: '1d',              // Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
  index: false,              // do not serve index.html for directory requests
  dotfiles: 'ignore',        // the Express 5 default: .env, .git are invisible
  setHeaders(res, filePath) {
    if (filePath.endsWith('.pdf')) res.set('Content-Disposition', 'inline');
  },
}));
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `maxAge` | `0` | `Cache-Control` max-age (milliseconds or a string such as `'1y'`) |
| `immutable` | `false` | Adds `immutable` to `Cache-Control`; use with fingerprinted file names |
| `index` | `'index.html'` | File served for directory paths; `false` to disable |
| `dotfiles` | `'ignore'` | `'allow'`, `'deny'` (403) or `'ignore'` (404) for names starting with `.` |
| `fallthrough` | `true` | On a missing file call `next()`; `false` sends a `404` error instead |
| `etag`, `lastModified` | `true` | Validation headers for conditional requests |
| `setHeaders` | none | Function to add headers per file |

Several static directories can be stacked; Express tries them in registration order. Never point `express.static` at the project root, which would expose source code and configuration.

**Key Takeaways**

- Express 5 includes `json`, `urlencoded`, `text`, `raw` and `static`; everything else is a separate package.
- Body parsers run only for matching `Content-Type`s, enforce a size limit (default 100 KB) and leave `req.body` `undefined` otherwise.
- The first parser to read a body wins: order route-specific parsers before global ones.
- Use `express.raw()` when the exact bytes matter (webhook signatures); use `express.static()` with explicit caching and dotfile options.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Send the same JSON body with and without `Content-Type: application/json` and log `req.body` in each case. Then send malformed JSON and a 200 KB body and note the status codes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a webhook endpoint that verifies an HMAC signature over the raw body, plus a script that signs and sends test events. Show that pretty-printing the JSON before sending breaks verification.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A route that accepts large JSON imports keeps returning 413 even though it uses `express.json({ limit: '10mb' })`. Why?" *Hint:* think about which parser reads the body first and what later parsers do with an already parsed request.

#### Third-Party Middleware

Most functionality around Express lives in separate npm packages that follow the same `(req, res, next)` contract. The table lists the ones found in most production applications:

| Package | Purpose | Chapter reference |
|---|---|---|
| `helmet` | Sets security headers (CSP, HSTS, `X-Content-Type-Options`, ...) | 17.1 |
| `cors` | Answers CORS preflights and sets `Access-Control-*` headers | 5.4, 17.1 |
| `compression` | gzip/brotli compression of responses | 10.1 |
| `pino-http`, `morgan` | Request logging (structured JSON / text lines) | 11.6 |
| `cookie-parser` | Parses the `Cookie` header into `req.cookies`, verifies signed cookies | 12.3 |
| `express-session` | Server-side sessions | 10.2, 12.3 |
| `express-rate-limit` | Limits requests per client and time window | 10.4 |
| `multer` | `multipart/form-data` file uploads | 12.3 |
| `passport` | Authentication strategies (local, OAuth, JWT, ...) | 12.3 |
| `http-proxy-middleware` | Forwards requests to other services | 12.3 |
| `csrf-csrf`, `csrf-sync` | CSRF tokens (the older `csurf` is deprecated) | 17.1 |

**A typical production stack, in order.** Order follows a simple logic: observe everything first, reject cheaply early, do expensive work late.

```javascript
import express from 'express';
import helmet from 'helmet';
import cors from 'cors';
import compression from 'compression';
import pinoHttp from 'pino-http';
import { rateLimit } from 'express-rate-limit';
import cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';

export function createApp({ config, logger }) {
  const app = express();
  app.set('trust proxy', 1);                              // needed for correct req.ip in logs and rate limits

  app.use(pinoHttp({ logger }));                          // 1. log every request, including rejected ones
  app.use(helmet());                                      // 2. security headers on every response, even errors
  app.use(cors({                                          // 3. answer preflights before auth and body parsing
    origin: config.CORS_ORIGINS,                          //    explicit allowlist (an array of origins)
    credentials: true,                                    //    allow cookies; incompatible with origin '*'
    maxAge: 600,                                          //    browsers may cache the preflight for 10 minutes
  }));
  app.use(compression());                                 // 4. omit if the reverse proxy already compresses
  app.use('/api', rateLimit({                             // 5. reject floods before doing real work
    windowMs: 60_000,
    limit: 120,                                           //    120 requests per minute per IP
    standardHeaders: 'draft-7',                           //    RateLimit header as in the IETF draft
    legacyHeaders: false,                                 //    no X-RateLimit-* headers
  }));
  app.use(cookieParser(config.COOKIE_SECRET));            // 6. cookies, then bodies
  app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));

  // 7. routers, 8. 404 handler, 9. error handler
  return app;
}
```

**helmet** sets about a dozen headers with safe defaults, among them `Content-Security-Policy`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy`, and removes `X-Powered-By`. The default CSP is strict; pages that load scripts or images from other origins need adjustments, which are merged with the defaults:

```javascript
app.use(helmet({
  contentSecurityPolicy: {
    directives: {
      'script-src': ["'self'", 'https://cdn.example.com'],
      'img-src': ["'self'", 'data:', 'https://images.example.com'],
    },
  },
}));
```

**cors** accepts a function for dynamic decisions, for example allowing any subdomain of your own site:

```javascript
app.use(cors({
  origin(origin, callback) {
    // origin is undefined for same-origin requests and non-browser clients (curl, servers)
    const allowed = !origin || /^https:\/\/([a-z0-9-]+\.)?example\.com$/.test(origin);
    callback(null, allowed);                  // true -> echo the origin; false -> no CORS headers
  },
  credentials: true,
}));
```

**Rate limiting with several instances.** By default `express-rate-limit` counts in the memory of one process. With several instances behind a load balancer each keeps its own count, so the effective limit is multiplied. Use a shared store (for example `rate-limit-redis`, Chapter 13) and stricter limits on sensitive routes such as login.

**Choosing a package.** Middleware runs on every request and often handles untrusted input, so evaluate it like any dependency (11.2): maintenance activity and open security advisories, Express 5 compatibility, number of transitive dependencies, and whether the problem is small enough to solve in twenty lines yourself.

**Key Takeaways**

- Most Express features come from third-party middleware with the same `(req, res, next)` contract.
- Order the stack deliberately: logging, security headers, CORS, compression, rate limiting, cookies, bodies, routes, 404, errors.
- Configure `helmet` and `cors` explicitly for your origins; never combine `credentials: true` with a wildcard origin.
- Rate-limit counters must live in a shared store when the app runs on several instances.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add `helmet` to an app and compare the response headers before and after with `curl -I`. Look up what three of the new headers do.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure `cors` for a front end at `http://localhost:5173` that sends cookies. From the browser console, verify that a `PUT` with a JSON body triggers a preflight that succeeds, and that the same request from another origin fails.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does the position of the rate limiter and the logger in the middleware stack matter?" *Hint:* consider which requests each one sees if placed before or after authentication, body parsing and static files, and what you lose in logs if the limiter rejects first.

#### Writing Custom Middleware

Application-specific cross-cutting concerns, such as loading the current user, checking roles, attaching request IDs or switching to maintenance mode, are best written as your own middleware. A few patterns cover nearly every case.

**1. A plain function.** For behaviour that needs no configuration:

```javascript
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

const VALID_ID = /^[\w-]{8,64}$/;

export function requestId(req, res, next) {
  const incoming = req.get('X-Request-Id');
  req.id = incoming && VALID_ID.test(incoming) ? incoming : randomUUID();   // never log arbitrary client input
  res.set('X-Request-Id', req.id);                // lets clients and proxies correlate logs
  next();
}
```

**2. A factory for configurable middleware.** A function that takes options and *returns* the middleware. Options are checked once at start-up, not on every request:

```javascript
export function requireRole(...roles) {
  if (roles.length === 0) throw new Error('requireRole() needs at least one role');   // fails at boot
  return (req, res, next) => {
    if (!req.user) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'authentication required' });
    if (!roles.includes(req.user.role)) return res.status(403).json({ error: 'insufficient permissions' });
    next();
  };
}

router.delete('/:id', requireRole('admin', 'editor'), deleteBook);
```

```javascript
export function maintenanceMode({ isEnabled, allowPaths = ['/health'] }) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    if (!isEnabled() || allowPaths.some((p) => req.path.startsWith(p))) return next();
    res.set('Retry-After', '300').status(503).json({ error: 'down for maintenance, try again later' });
  };
}

app.use(maintenanceMode({ isEnabled: () => featureFlags.get('maintenance') }));
```

**3. Asynchronous middleware.** Express 5 forwards a rejected promise to the error handler automatically (see "Handling Async Errors"), so `async` middleware can simply `await`:

```javascript
export function loadCurrentUser(users) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    const userId = req.session?.userId;
    if (userId) req.user = (await users.findById(userId)) ?? undefined;   // a DB failure goes to the error handler
    next();
  };
}
```

**4. Composition.** Middleware lists are just arrays, so related steps can be bundled under one name:

```javascript
export const adminOnly = [authenticate, requireRole('admin')];

router.get('/stats', adminOnly, getStats);
router.delete('/users/:id', adminOnly, auditLog('user.delete'), deleteUser);
```

**Where to store per-request data.**

| Location | Typical content | Visible to |
|---|---|---|
| `req.user`, `req.id`, `req.valid` | Data about the request and caller | All later middleware and handlers |
| `res.locals` | Data for rendering the response (flash messages, CSRF token, current user for templates) | Later middleware, handlers and templates (merged into `res.render` locals) |
| `app.locals` | Application-wide constants | Everything, all requests: never per-request data |

In TypeScript, properties added to `req` must be declared through **declaration merging**, so every file sees the same type:

```typescript
// src/types/express.d.ts
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      id: string;
      user?: { id: string; role: 'admin' | 'editor' | 'member' };
    }
  }
}
export {};
```

**Checklist for good middleware.**

- Every code path ends with a response, `next()` or `next(err)`, and `return`s after responding.
- It does one thing and is named after it (`requireRole`, not `checks`).
- Configuration is passed to a factory and validated at start-up.
- It does not trust client input it attaches to `req` or logs (validate IDs, limit lengths).
- Expensive work runs only when needed (check the path or method first).
- It is exported separately so it can be unit tested (see "Testing Express Applications").

**Key Takeaways**

- Write middleware as plain functions for fixed behaviour and as factories for configurable behaviour.
- `async` middleware is safe in Express 5 because rejections reach the error handler.
- Arrays of middleware compose naturally into reusable bundles such as `adminOnly`.
- Put request data on `req`, view data on `res.locals`, and only constants on `app.locals`; declare added properties in TypeScript with declaration merging.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a middleware that rejects requests without an `X-Api-Key` header matching a value from configuration, returning `401` with a JSON error.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a factory `cacheControl({ maxAge, private: isPrivate })` that sets `Cache-Control` only for successful `GET` responses. (Hint: headers must be set before the response is sent; compare setting them up front with checking `res.statusCode` later.)
> 3. *(Interview)* "Design a middleware that enforces per-user feature flags for a set of routes. What would its API look like, and how would you test it?" *Hint:* think about a factory taking the flag name, where the flag data comes from (cached), what status to return when the flag is off, and how to inject a fake flag store in tests.

#### Error-Handling Middleware

Errors happen in every layer: malformed JSON, failed validation, a missing record, a database timeout, a bug. Without a plan, each handler formats errors differently, some leak stack traces, and some forget to respond at all. Express provides one central place for all of this: **error-handling middleware**.

**The four-argument signature.** Express recognises an error handler by its **arity**: a function declared with exactly four parameters.

```javascript
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {      // four parameters: this is an error handler
  res.status(500).json({ error: 'internal server error' });
});
```

Express checks `fn.length`, so all four parameters must be declared even if `next` is unused. A default value or rest parameter reduces `length` (`(err, req, res, next = noop) => {}` has length 3) and silently turns the handler into normal middleware.

**How errors travel.** When a middleware calls `next(err)` or throws (synchronously, or by rejecting a promise in Express 5), Express skips all remaining *normal* middleware and routes and jumps to the next *error-handling* middleware:

```text
 normal chain:   logger --> json --> auth --> route handler
                                       |            |
                         next(err) ----+            +---- throw / rejected promise
                                       v            v
 error chain:              (all normal middleware below is skipped)
                           errorReporter(err, ...) --next(err)--> errorResponder(err, ...) --> response
```

`next('route')` and `next('router')` are the only string values with special meaning; any other argument passed to `next` is treated as an error.

**An error class carrying HTTP information.** Throwing plain `Error`s loses the intended status. A small class lets any layer say *what* went wrong; the error handler decides *how* to present it:

```javascript
// src/lib/http-error.js
export class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message, { code, details, headers, cause } = {}) {
    super(message, { cause });
    this.name = 'HttpError';
    this.status = status;
    this.code = code;              // stable machine-readable code, e.g. 'BOOK_NOT_FOUND'
    this.details = details;        // e.g. a list of validation issues
    this.headers = headers;        // e.g. { 'Retry-After': '30' }
    this.expose = status < 500;    // client errors may be shown; server errors may not
  }
}
```

(The `http-errors` package, used internally by Express, provides the same idea: `createError(404, 'book not found')`.)

**A complete error handler.** It normalises different error kinds, logs according to severity, hides internals in production and answers with a consistent format. Here the format is Problem Details (RFC 9457, 10.4):

```javascript
// src/middleware/error-handler.js
import { HttpError } from '../lib/http-error.js';

export function notFound(req, res, next) {             // normal middleware, registered after all routes
  next(new HttpError(404, `no route for ${req.method} ${req.path}`, { code: 'ROUTE_NOT_FOUND' }));
}

function normalize(err) {
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return err;
  if (err.type === 'entity.parse.failed') return new HttpError(400, 'malformed JSON body', { code: 'INVALID_JSON' });
  if (err.type === 'entity.too.large') return new HttpError(413, 'request body too large', { code: 'BODY_TOO_LARGE' });
  const status = Number.isInteger(err.status) && err.status >= 400 && err.status < 600 ? err.status : 500;
  const message = status < 500 && err.expose ? err.message : 'internal server error';   // http-errors convention
  return new HttpError(status, message, { cause: err });
}

export function errorHandler({ isProduction }) {
  return (err, req, res, next) => {
    if (res.headersSent) return next(err);       // response already started: let Express abort the connection

    const httpErr = normalize(err);
    const log = req.log ?? console;              // pino-http attaches req.log
    if (httpErr.status >= 500) log.error({ err, requestId: req.id }, 'request failed');
    else log.warn({ status: httpErr.status, code: httpErr.code, requestId: req.id }, httpErr.message);

    if (httpErr.headers) res.set(httpErr.headers);
    res.status(httpErr.status).type('application/problem+json').json({
      type: 'about:blank',
      title: httpErr.message,
      status: httpErr.status,
      code: httpErr.code,
      errors: httpErr.details,                   // validation issues, if any
      instance: req.originalUrl,
      requestId: req.id,                         // users can quote it to support
      ...(!isProduction && { stack: err.stack }),// never send stack traces in production
    });
  };
}
```

```javascript
// src/app.js (end of the pipeline)
app.use('/api/v1/books', booksRouter);
app.use(notFound);                                         // after all routes
app.use(errorHandler({ isProduction: config.NODE_ENV === 'production' }));   // last
```

Handlers can now simply throw:

```javascript
router.get('/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const book = await books.findById(Number(req.params.id));
  if (!book) throw new HttpError(404, 'book not found', { code: 'BOOK_NOT_FOUND' });
  res.json(book);
});
```

**Express's default error handler.** If no custom handler responds, Express's built-in one does. It uses `err.status` (or `err.statusCode`) if it is a valid 4xx/5xx code, otherwise `500`; sets `err.headers`; sends an HTML page with the stack trace in development and only the status message in production; and, if headers were already sent, destroys the connection. A custom handler should keep that last behaviour by delegating with `next(err)` when `res.headersSent` is `true`.

**404 is not an error handler.** "No route matched" is detected by an ordinary middleware registered after all routes (`notFound` above). It runs only when nothing responded, and passes a 404 error into the error chain so all errors share one format.

**Chaining error handlers.** Several error handlers can be stacked, for example one that reports to an error-tracking service and calls `next(err)`, followed by the one that responds. Error handlers can also be attached to a router to give part of an API a different format (an HTML error page for `/admin`, JSON for `/api`).

**Key Takeaways**

- Error-handling middleware has exactly four declared parameters and is registered after all routes.
- `next(err)` or a thrown error skips normal middleware and jumps to the next error handler.
- Use an error class carrying status, code and details; normalise library errors (body parser, validation) in one place.
- Log server errors with stack traces, return a consistent format, hide internals in production, and delegate to Express when headers were already sent.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add `notFound` and `errorHandler` to an app, then trigger a 404, malformed JSON, a thrown `HttpError(409)` and a `TypeError`, and compare the four responses.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a second error handler in front of the responder that counts errors by status code and code in memory, exposed at `GET /internal/error-stats`. Verify that the counting handler never sends a response itself.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does Express use the number of declared parameters to identify error handlers, and what problems can this cause?" *Hint:* consider `Function.prototype.length`, default parameters, wrappers that use `(...args)`, and how minifiers or decorators might change the signature.

#### Handling Async Errors

Most handlers are asynchronous: they await databases, files and other services. The question is what happens when an awaited operation fails.

**The problem in Express 4.** Express 4 called handlers synchronously and caught only synchronous exceptions. An `async` function never throws synchronously: it *returns a rejected promise*, which Express 4 ignored:

```javascript
// Express 4
app.get('/books/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const book = await db.findBook(req.params.id);   // the database is down: the promise rejects
  res.json(book);
});
// Result: no response is ever sent (the client hangs until timeout), and Node reports an
// unhandled rejection, which crashes the process by default since Node 15.
```

The usual Express 4 workarounds were a try/catch in every handler, or a wrapper:

```javascript
// Express 4: forward rejections to next() explicitly
const asyncHandler = (fn) => (req, res, next) => Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next);

app.get('/books/:id', asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  res.json(await db.findBook(req.params.id));
}));
```

The `express-async-errors` package did the same by patching Express globally.

**Express 5: promises are first-class.** Express 5 checks whether a middleware, route handler or `router.param` callback returns a promise and, if it rejects, calls `next(err)` with the rejection reason (or a generic error if the reason is falsy). Handlers can simply throw:

```javascript
// Express 5: no wrapper needed
app.get('/books/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const book = await db.findBook(req.params.id);   // a rejection here reaches the error handler
  if (!book) throw new HttpError(404, 'book not found');
  res.json(book);
});
```

**What Express 5 still cannot catch.** Express only sees the promise returned by the function it called. Errors that occur *outside* that promise chain escape it:

```javascript
import fs from 'node:fs';

// 1. Callback APIs: the callback runs later, on a new call stack, outside any promise Express sees
app.get('/legacy', (req, res) => {
  fs.readFile('missing.txt', (err, data) => {
    if (err) throw err;                    // uncaughtException: the process crashes instead of a 500
    res.send(data);
  });
});
// Fix: forward explicitly, or use the promise API
app.get('/legacy', (req, res, next) => {
  fs.readFile('missing.txt', (err, data) => (err ? next(err) : res.send(data)));
});
app.get('/modern', async (req, res) => res.send(await fs.promises.readFile('missing.txt')));

// 2. Fire-and-forget promises: started but never awaited
app.post('/orders', async (req, res) => {
  const order = await orders.create(req.body);
  sendConfirmationEmail(order);            // a rejection here is unhandled
  res.status(201).json(order);
});
// Fix: handle the failure where the work is started
//   sendConfirmationEmail(order).catch((err) => req.log.error({ err }, 'confirmation email failed'));
// or better, put the job in a queue that retries.

// 3. Timers and event emitters
app.get('/later', (req, res) => {
  setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('boom'); }, 10);   // escapes everything
});
```

**Streams.** Errors in streams are emitted as `'error'` events, not thrown. Use `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises`, which turns stream errors into a rejected promise that Express 5 forwards:

```javascript
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';

app.get('/reports/:name', async (req, res) => {
  const file = resolveReportPath(req.params.name);   // validates the name, prevents path traversal
  res.type('pdf');
  await pipeline(createReadStream(file), res);       // ENOENT, read errors, client aborts -> rejection
});
```

If the file is missing, the error occurs before any bytes are sent, and the error handler can still answer (map `err.code === 'ENOENT'` to 404 in `normalize`). If it fails half-way, `res.headersSent` is `true` and the error handler must delegate so the connection is closed, signalling to the client that the response is incomplete.

**Requests that never finish.** A handler awaiting a promise that never settles (a hung connection to another service) produces neither a response nor an error. Defend with time limits at each level:

```javascript
// Outgoing calls: always set a timeout
const stock = await fetch(`${INVENTORY_URL}/stock/${id}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000) });

// Per-request deadline middleware
export function deadline(ms) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      if (!res.headersSent) next(new HttpError(503, 'request timed out', { code: 'TIMEOUT' }));
    }, ms);
    res.on('close', () => clearTimeout(timer));      // response finished or client disconnected
    next();
  };
}
app.use('/api', deadline(10_000));
```

Node's server also has `server.requestTimeout` (default 300 seconds) and `server.headersTimeout` as a last resort.

**Process-level safety nets.** Errors that escape everything end in `process.on('uncaughtException')` and `process.on('unhandledRejection')`. Use them only to log and exit (11.5); the process supervisor then restarts it. Do not try to keep serving: the application may be in an inconsistent state.

**Key Takeaways**

- Express 4 ignored rejected promises; handlers needed try/catch or an `asyncHandler` wrapper.
- Express 5 forwards rejected promises from middleware, handlers and `param` callbacks to the error handler, so `async` handlers can simply throw.
- Callbacks, timers, event emitters and un-awaited promises are outside Express's reach: forward with `next(err)`, use promise APIs, `pipeline`, or `.catch()` where work starts.
- Put timeouts on outgoing calls and requests, and keep process-level handlers as log-and-exit safety nets.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write an `async` route that awaits a rejected promise and observe the behaviour in Express 5. Then install Express 4 in a separate folder and compare.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Find the error-handling problems in a route that reads a file with `fs.readFile` callbacks, fires an un-awaited analytics call and pipes a stream with `.pipe()`. Rewrite it so that every failure reaches the error handler or is logged.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A colleague says Express 5 means we no longer need to think about async errors. Do you agree?" *Hint:* list which error sources go through the promise returned by the handler and which do not, and what happens to a request whose awaited promise never settles.

<a id="123-building-services-with-express"></a>
### 12.3 Building Services with Express

This subchapter combines the building blocks of 12.1 and 12.2 into complete services: a REST resource with validation, cookie- and session-based state, authentication with Passport and JWT, file uploads, server-rendered pages, hosting single-page applications and fronting other services, automated testing, and finally a comparison with the main alternative frameworks.

#### Implementing REST Endpoints

Chapter 10.4 described what a good REST API looks like: resources identified by URIs, HTTP methods mapped to operations, meaningful status codes, pagination and consistent errors. This topic implements one complete resource, a collection of books, using the project structure from 12.1 and the error handling from 12.2.

**The contract first.** Before writing code, define the endpoints and their responses:

| Method and path | Purpose | Success | Typical errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/books?page=&limit=&author=` | List, paginated and filtered | `200` with `{ data, page, limit, total }` | `422` invalid query |
| `GET /api/v1/books/:id` | Read one | `200` | `404` |
| `POST /api/v1/books` | Create | `201` + `Location` header | `401`, `409` duplicate ISBN, `422` |
| `PATCH /api/v1/books/:id` | Partial update | `200` with the updated book | `401`, `404`, `422` |
| `DELETE /api/v1/books/:id` | Delete | `204` without body | `401`, `404` |

**Repository: data access behind an interface.** An in-memory implementation is enough to build and test the API; a SQL or MongoDB version (Chapter 13) exposes the same methods.

```javascript
// src/books/books.repository.js
export function createInMemoryBookRepository() {
  const rows = new Map();
  let nextId = 1;

  return {
    async list({ offset, limit, author }) {
      let items = [...rows.values()];
      if (author) items = items.filter((b) => b.author.toLowerCase().includes(author.toLowerCase()));
      return { items: items.slice(offset, offset + limit), total: items.length };
    },
    async findById(id) { return rows.get(id) ?? null; },
    async findByIsbn(isbn) { return [...rows.values()].find((b) => b.isbn === isbn) ?? null; },
    async insert(data) {
      const book = { id: nextId++, tags: [], ...data, createdAt: new Date().toISOString() };
      rows.set(book.id, book);
      return book;
    },
    async update(id, changes) {
      const current = rows.get(id);
      if (!current) return null;
      const book = { ...current, ...changes, updatedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
      rows.set(id, book);
      return book;
    },
    async remove(id) { return rows.delete(id); },
  };
}
```

**Service: business rules, no HTTP objects.** The service decides what is allowed. It throws `HttpError` (12.2) for simplicity; a stricter design throws domain errors (`NotFoundError`, `ConflictError`) and lets the error handler map them to status codes.

```javascript
// src/books/books.service.js
import { HttpError } from '../lib/http-error.js';

export function createBookService(repo) {
  async function get(id) {
    const book = await repo.findById(id);
    if (!book) throw new HttpError(404, `book ${id} not found`, { code: 'BOOK_NOT_FOUND' });
    return book;
  }

  return {
    get,
    list: (query) => repo.list(query),
    async create(data) {
      if (await repo.findByIsbn(data.isbn)) {
        throw new HttpError(409, 'a book with this ISBN already exists', { code: 'DUPLICATE_ISBN' });
      }
      return repo.insert(data);
    },
    async update(id, changes) {
      await get(id);                                   // 404 if missing
      return repo.update(id, changes);
    },
    async remove(id) {
      if (!(await repo.remove(id))) throw new HttpError(404, `book ${id} not found`, { code: 'BOOK_NOT_FOUND' });
    },
  };
}
```

**Schemas: the shape of valid input.** They are explained in the next topic; here they define what each endpoint accepts.

```javascript
// src/books/books.schemas.js
import { z } from 'zod';

export const bookIdParams = z.object({ id: z.coerce.number().int().positive() });

export const bookListQuery = z.object({
  page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
  author: z.string().trim().max(100).optional(),
});

export const bookCreateBody = z.object({
  title: z.string().trim().min(1).max(200),
  author: z.string().trim().min(1).max(100),
  isbn: z.string().regex(/^(97[89])?\d{9}[\dX]$/, 'invalid ISBN-10 or ISBN-13'),
  year: z.number().int().min(1450).max(new Date().getFullYear() + 1),
  tags: z.array(z.string().trim().toLowerCase().min(1).max(30)).max(10).optional(),
}).strict();                                           // unknown fields are an error, not silently stored

export const bookPatchBody = bookCreateBody.partial()
  .refine((value) => Object.keys(value).length > 0, 'send at least one field to update');
```

**Router: HTTP in, HTTP out.** Each handler reads validated input, calls the service and chooses status code and headers. Because Express 5 forwards rejected promises, there is no try/catch.

```javascript
// src/books/books.router.js
import { Router } from 'express';
import { validate } from '../middleware/validate.js';
import { bookIdParams, bookListQuery, bookCreateBody, bookPatchBody } from './books.schemas.js';

export function createBooksRouter({ books, authenticate }) {
  const router = Router();

  router.get('/', validate({ query: bookListQuery }), async (req, res) => {
    const { page, limit, author } = req.valid.query;
    const { items, total } = await books.list({ offset: (page - 1) * limit, limit, author });
    res.json({ data: items, page, limit, total });
  });

  router.get('/:id', validate({ params: bookIdParams }), async (req, res) => {
    res.json(await books.get(req.valid.params.id));
  });

  router.post('/', authenticate, validate({ body: bookCreateBody }), async (req, res) => {
    const book = await books.create(req.valid.body);
    res.status(201)
      .location(`${req.baseUrl}/${book.id}`)           // where the new resource lives
      .json(book);
  });

  router.patch('/:id', authenticate, validate({ params: bookIdParams, body: bookPatchBody }), async (req, res) => {
    res.json(await books.update(req.valid.params.id, req.valid.body));
  });

  router.delete('/:id', authenticate, validate({ params: bookIdParams }), async (req, res) => {
    await books.remove(req.valid.params.id);
    res.sendStatus(204);                               // success, no body
  });

  return router;
}
```

**Trying it out.**

```bash
TOKEN=...   # obtained from the login endpoint ("Authentication with Passport and JWT")

curl -si -X POST localhost:3000/api/v1/books \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","isbn":"9780441172719","year":1965}'
# HTTP/1.1 201 Created
# Location: /api/v1/books/1
# {"id":1,"tags":[],"title":"Dune",...}

curl -s 'localhost:3000/api/v1/books?author=herbert&limit=10'
# {"data":[{"id":1,...}],"page":1,"limit":10,"total":1}

curl -s -X PATCH localhost:3000/api/v1/books/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"price": 9}'
# 422 application/problem+json: unrecognized key "price"
```

**Details that make an API pleasant.**

- **Consistent envelopes:** lists always return `{ data, ... }` with pagination metadata; single resources return the object itself; errors always use the problem format from 12.2.
- **Correct status codes:** `201` + `Location` for creation, `204` for deletion, `409` for conflicts with existing state, `422` for well-formed but invalid input.
- **Idempotency:** `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` must be safe to retry (10.1). For `POST`, support an `Idempotency-Key` header if clients may retry payments or orders.
- **Caching:** Express adds weak `ETag`s to `res.json` responses automatically, so `GET` requests with `If-None-Match` receive `304 Not Modified` without extra code.

**Key Takeaways**

- Define the contract (paths, methods, status codes, payloads) before implementing.
- Split each resource into repository (data), service (rules) and router (HTTP); handlers stay short.
- Use precise status codes and headers: `201` with `Location`, `204`, `404`, `409`, `422`.
- In Express 5, async handlers can throw `HttpError`s and rely on the central error handler.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add `PUT /api/v1/books/:id` that replaces a whole book (all fields required), and explain how its semantics differ from `PATCH`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add sorting (`?sort=year` or `?sort=-year`, with an allowlist of sortable fields) and cursor-based pagination (`?after=<id>`). Return a `Link` header with the next page URL using `res.links()`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Two clients load the same book and both send a `PATCH`. How do you prevent the second one from silently overwriting the first?" *Hint:* think about a version number or `ETag` returned with the resource, an `If-Match` request header, and the `412 Precondition Failed` status.

#### Request Validation and Sanitization

Everything in a request (path, query, headers, cookies, body) is chosen by the client, and some clients are attackers. The type annotations in your code and the form on your front end do not constrain what arrives: anyone can send any bytes with `curl`. **Validation** at the boundary turns untrusted input into data with a known shape before any business logic sees it.

Three related but distinct activities are often confused:

| Activity | Question | Example | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Validation | Is this input acceptable? | `year` is an integer between 1450 and next year | At the boundary; reject with `400`/`422` |
| Normalisation (sanitisation) | Can I put it into a canonical form? | Trim whitespace, lower-case emails, Unicode NFC | At the boundary, as part of parsing |
| Output encoding | Is this safe in the context where I *output* it? | HTML-escape a title in a template, parameterise SQL | Where data leaves (templates, queries) |

A common mistake is to "sanitise" input by HTML-escaping it on arrival. The stored data is then wrong for every other use (JSON APIs, emails, search) and still unsafe in other contexts (URLs, JavaScript). Validate and normalise on input; **encode on output** (17.1).

**Schema validation with Zod.** A schema declares the expected shape once and produces both validation and a typed, normalised result. Unknown keys are stripped by default (or rejected with `.strict()`), strings can be trimmed, and query strings can be coerced to numbers:

```javascript
import { z } from 'zod';

const registerBody = z.object({
  email: z.string().trim().toLowerCase().email().max(254),
  password: z.string().min(12).max(128),
  displayName: z.string().trim().normalize('NFC').min(1).max(50),
  birthYear: z.number().int().min(1900).max(new Date().getFullYear()).optional(),
});

const result = registerBody.safeParse({ email: '  Ada@Example.COM ', password: 'short', displayName: 'Ada', role: 'admin' });
// result.success === false
// result.error.issues: [{ path: ['password'], message: 'Too small: expected string to have >=12 characters', ... }]
// On success, result.data would contain email 'ada@example.com' and no 'role' key (stripped).
```

**A reusable validation middleware.** It validates any combination of `params`, `query` and `body`, collects all problems into one `422` response, and stores the parsed values in `req.valid`. (`req.query` cannot be replaced, because it is a read-only getter in Express 5.)

```javascript
// src/middleware/validate.js
import { HttpError } from '../lib/http-error.js';

export function validate(schemas) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    const valid = {};
    const issues = [];
    for (const part of ['params', 'query', 'body']) {
      if (!schemas[part]) continue;
      const result = schemas[part].safeParse(req[part] ?? {});    // missing body -> {} -> "required" errors
      if (result.success) valid[part] = result.data;
      else issues.push(...result.error.issues.map((i) => ({ in: part, path: i.path.join('.'), message: i.message })));
    }
    if (issues.length > 0) {
      return next(new HttpError(422, 'request validation failed', { code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', details: issues }));
    }
    req.valid = { ...req.valid, ...valid };
    next();
  };
}
```

Response for an invalid request:

```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "request validation failed",
  "status": 422,
  "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "errors": [
    { "in": "body", "path": "year", "message": "Too big: expected number to be <=2027" },
    { "in": "body", "path": "isbn", "message": "invalid ISBN-10 or ISBN-13" }
  ],
  "instance": "/api/v1/books"
}
```

**Common rules.**

| Input | Rules |
|---|---|
| Strings | Maximum length always; trim; pattern or enum where possible |
| Numbers from query/params | Coerce, require integer, set min/max (pagination limits!) |
| IDs | Exact format (positive integer, UUID, ObjectId) |
| Emails, URLs | Format check plus length; restrict URL schemes to `https:` |
| Arrays | Maximum item count and per-item rules |
| Objects | Strip or reject unknown keys; limit nesting |
| Dates | ISO 8601 format and a sensible range |
| Free text | Length limit; for rich text, an HTML allowlist sanitiser (below) |

**Mass assignment.** Passing `req.body` directly to the database lets clients write fields they should never control:

```javascript
// Vulnerable: the body {"displayName": "Ada", "role": "admin"} makes the caller an administrator
app.patch('/api/me', authenticate, async (req, res) => {
  res.json(await users.update(req.user.id, req.body));
});

// Safe: only fields in the schema survive
const updateMeBody = z.object({ displayName: z.string().trim().min(1).max(50), bio: z.string().max(500) })
  .partial().strict();
app.patch('/api/me', authenticate, validate({ body: updateMeBody }), async (req, res) => {
  res.json(await users.update(req.user.id, req.valid.body));
});
```

**Prototype pollution.** `JSON.parse` turns a key named `"__proto__"` into an ordinary property. A naive recursive merge then writes into `Object.prototype`, changing *every* object in the process:

```javascript
function naiveMerge(target, source) {
  for (const key of Object.keys(source)) {
    if (typeof source[key] === 'object' && source[key] !== null) {
      target[key] ??= {};
      naiveMerge(target[key], source[key]);    // key '__proto__': target.__proto__ is Object.prototype
    } else {
      target[key] = source[key];
    }
  }
}

naiveMerge({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}'));
console.log({}.isAdmin);                       // true: every object now looks like an admin
```

Defences: validate with schemas that strip unknown keys before merging; skip `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` in merge utilities; use `Object.create(null)` or `Map` for dictionaries built from input; and keep libraries such as `lodash` up to date. Node's `--disable-proto=delete` flag removes the `__proto__` accessor entirely.

**Rich text.** When users may submit limited HTML (comments, biographies), escaping would destroy the formatting and storing it raw enables XSS. Use an allowlist sanitiser:

```javascript
import sanitizeHtml from 'sanitize-html';

const cleanBio = sanitizeHtml(req.valid.body.bio, {
  allowedTags: ['b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'a', 'p', 'ul', 'ol', 'li'],
  allowedAttributes: { a: ['href'] },
  allowedSchemes: ['https', 'mailto'],        // blocks javascript: URLs
});
```

**express-validator.** A popular alternative expresses rules as a chain of middleware per field:

```javascript
import { body, validationResult, matchedData } from 'express-validator';

router.post('/register',
  body('email').trim().isEmail().normalizeEmail(),
  body('password').isLength({ min: 12, max: 128 }),
  (req, res) => {
    const result = validationResult(req);
    if (!result.isEmpty()) return res.status(422).json({ errors: result.array() });
    const { email, password } = matchedData(req);   // only fields that were validated
    // ...
  });
```

| Approach | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Zod (or Valibot, ArkType) | One schema for validation and TypeScript types; reusable on the front end | Not Express-specific: you write the small middleware |
| express-validator | Express-native, many built-in validators and sanitisers | Rules spread over middleware chains; no types derived |
| JSON Schema with Ajv | Language-neutral, can be shared with OpenAPI documentation (10.4) | Verbose; types need a generator |

**Validation in depth.** Boundary validation checks *shape*. Business rules that need state (ISBN unique, stock available) belong in the service, and database constraints (unique indexes, foreign keys, `NOT NULL`) are the last line of defence against race conditions between check and insert.

**Key Takeaways**

- Treat every part of the request as untrusted; validate at the boundary with schemas and reject with clear `422` responses.
- Normalise input (trim, case, Unicode) during validation; encode output for its context instead of escaping input.
- Allowlist fields to prevent mass assignment, and strip dangerous keys to prevent prototype pollution.
- Keep shape validation at the edge, business rules in services and integrity constraints in the database.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a Zod schema for a "create event" request (title, ISO start date, optional end date after start, up to 20 attendee emails) and test it with valid and invalid objects.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend `validate` to accept a `headers` schema (for example a required `Idempotency-Key` in UUID format), and add tests showing that unknown body fields are rejected when the schema is strict.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Should you HTML-escape user input before storing it in the database?" *Hint:* consider how many output contexts the same data appears in (HTML, JSON, CSV, email, URLs), and what goes wrong when data is escaped twice or for the wrong context.

#### Cookie and Session Middleware

HTTP is stateless (10.2): each request arrives without memory of the previous ones. Cookies give the browser a way to send a value back on every request, and sessions use a cookie containing only an ID to find server-side state. Chapter 10 explained the mechanisms and their security attributes; this topic shows how Express applications use them.

**Reading and writing cookies.** Express can *set* cookies on its own (`res.cookie`), but reading them requires `cookie-parser`, which parses the `Cookie` header into `req.cookies` and verifies **signed cookies** into `req.signedCookies`:

```javascript
import cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';

app.use(cookieParser(config.COOKIE_SECRET));     // secret enables signed cookies

app.post('/preferences/theme', express.urlencoded({ extended: false }), (req, res) => {
  const theme = req.body.theme === 'dark' ? 'dark' : 'light';   // allowlist the value
  res.cookie('theme', theme, {
    maxAge: 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,           // milliseconds in Express (Max-Age in seconds on the wire)
    sameSite: 'lax',
    secure: true,
    httpOnly: false,                             // deliberately readable by front-end JavaScript
  });
  res.redirect(303, '/settings');
});

app.get('/settings', (req, res) => {
  res.render('settings', { theme: req.cookies.theme ?? 'light' });
});
```

| `res.cookie` option | Cookie attribute | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `maxAge` / `expires` | `Max-Age` / `Expires` | Without either, a session cookie (deleted when the browser closes) |
| `httpOnly` | `HttpOnly` | Hidden from JavaScript; use for all credentials |
| `secure` | `Secure` | Only sent over HTTPS |
| `sameSite` | `SameSite` | `'strict'`, `'lax'` or `'none'` (the last requires `secure`) |
| `domain`, `path` | `Domain`, `Path` | Scope of the cookie |
| `signed` | (value prefixed with `s:` and an HMAC) | Integrity, not secrecy |
| `partitioned` | `Partitioned` | CHIPS: third-party cookies isolated per top-level site |

**Signed cookies** append an HMAC computed with the secret. If a client changes the value, `req.signedCookies.name` is `false` instead of the tampered value. The content is still readable by anyone, so never put secrets in it.

**Deleting cookies.** `res.clearCookie(name, options)` sends an expired cookie. It only removes the original if `path` and `domain` match those used to set it; a mismatch leaves the old cookie in place, which is a common cause of "logout does not work" bugs.

**Sessions with express-session.** `express-session` creates a session ID, stores it in a signed cookie, and loads the session data from a **store** into `req.session` on every request. Changes are saved automatically at the end of the request. 10.2 showed a production configuration with a Redis store; the key options are:

```javascript
import session from 'express-session';

app.use(session({
  store: sessionStore,                     // Redis, PostgreSQL, ... (the default MemoryStore leaks and is per-process)
  secret: config.SESSION_SECRET,           // signs the ID cookie; an array allows key rotation
  name: '__Host-sid',                      // not the default 'connect.sid', which reveals the stack
  resave: false,                           // do not rewrite unchanged sessions
  saveUninitialized: false,                // no session (and no cookie) until something is stored
  cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: 30 * 60 * 1000 },
}));
```

**Login and logout.** The session API is callback-based; small promise helpers keep handlers readable:

```javascript
// src/lib/session.js
const call = (req, method) => new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
  req.session[method]((err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve())));
export const regenerateSession = (req) => call(req, 'regenerate');
export const saveSession = (req) => call(req, 'save');
export const destroySession = (req) => call(req, 'destroy');
```

```javascript
// src/auth/auth.router.js
router.post('/login', loginLimiter, validate({ body: loginBody }), async (req, res) => {
  const { email, password } = req.valid.body;
  const user = await users.verifyCredentials(email, password);    // password hashing: 10.3
  if (!user) throw new HttpError(401, 'invalid email or password'); // same message for both cases

  await regenerateSession(req);                // new session ID: defeats session fixation (10.2)
  req.session.userId = user.id;                // store only what you need, not the whole user object
  await saveSession(req);                      // persisted before the client gets the cookie
  res.json({ id: user.id, displayName: user.displayName });
});

router.post('/logout', async (req, res) => {
  await destroySession(req);                   // removes the data from the store
  res.clearCookie('__Host-sid', { path: '/', httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' });
  res.sendStatus(204);
});
```

```javascript
// src/middleware/require-session.js
export function requireSession(users) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    if (!req.session.userId) throw new HttpError(401, 'login required');
    const user = await users.findById(req.session.userId);
    if (!user) {                               // user deleted since login
      await destroySession(req);
      throw new HttpError(401, 'login required');
    }
    req.user = user;
    next();
  };
}
```

| `req.session` API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `req.session.<key> = value` | Store data (must be JSON-serialisable for most stores) |
| `req.sessionID` | The session ID |
| `req.session.regenerate(cb)` | New ID, empty data: call on login and privilege changes |
| `req.session.destroy(cb)` | Delete the session from the store |
| `req.session.save(cb)` | Save immediately (before redirects, for example) |
| `req.session.cookie.maxAge` | Adjust the lifetime of this session (for "remember me") |

**Client-side sessions.** `cookie-session` stores the (signed) data in the cookie itself, with no server store. It suits small, non-sensitive state, but the 4 KB limit applies, data travels with every request, and sessions cannot be revoked server-side.

**CSRF.** Cookies are sent automatically, so a malicious site can make the browser send authenticated requests to your app (cross-site request forgery, 17.1). `SameSite=Lax` blocks cookies on cross-site `POST`s in modern browsers, and is the first defence. For defence in depth, check the `Origin` header on state-changing requests, or use tokens (`csrf-csrf`, `csrf-sync`):

```javascript
export function sameOriginOnly(allowedOrigins) {
  const allowed = new Set(allowedOrigins);
  return (req, res, next) => {
    if (['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS'].includes(req.method)) return next();   // safe methods change nothing
    const referer = req.get('Referer');
    const origin = req.get('Origin') ?? (referer && URL.canParse(referer) ? new URL(referer).origin : undefined);
    if (!origin || !allowed.has(origin)) {
      return next(new HttpError(403, 'cross-site request blocked', { code: 'CSRF_ORIGIN' }));
    }
    next();
  };
}
app.use(sameOriginOnly(['https://app.example.com']));
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `res.cookie` sets cookies; `cookie-parser` reads them and verifies signatures (integrity, not confidentiality).
- `clearCookie` must use the same `path` and `domain` as the original cookie.
