- `express-session` needs a real store, a strong secret, secure cookie flags and `saveUninitialized: false`; regenerate the session on login and destroy it on logout.
- Protect cookie-authenticated, state-changing routes against CSRF with `SameSite` plus an origin check or tokens.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement a page-view counter stored in a signed cookie. Edit the cookie in DevTools and observe that `req.signedCookies` reports `false`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement login, logout and a protected `/api/me` route with `express-session` and a Redis store. Verify with DevTools that the session ID changes at login and that the old ID no longer works after logout.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Users report that after logging out they are still logged in when they reload the page. What would you check?" *Hint:* compare the attributes used to set and clear the cookie, whether the session is destroyed in the store, and whether a cached page or a second cookie (different path or domain) is involved.

#### Authentication with Passport and JWT

Authentication in a web service has two parts: **verifying credentials once** (a password, an OAuth login with Google, a passkey) and **recognising the caller on every later request** (a session cookie or a token). Chapter 10.3 explained the concepts: password hashing, sessions versus JWTs, access and refresh tokens, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. This topic implements them in Express with two widely used tools: **Passport**, which standardises the first part, and **JSON Web Tokens**, a common format for the second.

**Passport's model.** Passport is authentication middleware with more than 500 **strategies**, one per authentication method. Each strategy knows how to extract credentials from a request and calls your **verify callback** to find the user. The rest of the application never sees the method used.

| Concept | Role |
|---|---|
| Strategy (`passport-local`, `passport-google-oauth20`, `passport-jwt`, ...) | Extracts and checks credentials for one method |
| Verify callback | Your code: given credentials, return a user, `false` (failed) or an error |
| `passport.authenticate(name, options)` | Middleware that runs a strategy |
| `serializeUser` / `deserializeUser` | What to store in the session (an ID), and how to load the user from it |
| `req.user`, `req.isAuthenticated()` | Set for authenticated requests |
| `req.login(user, cb)` / `req.logout(cb)` | Establish or end a login session |

**Local strategy with sessions.** Suits server-rendered applications and SPAs served from the same site:

```text
 POST /login {email, password}
     |
     v
 passport.authenticate('local') --> verify callback: find user, verify hash --> user
     |
     v
 req.login(user): regenerates the session, serializeUser(user) -> session.passport.user = user.id
     |
 later requests: cookie --> session store --> deserializeUser(id) --> req.user
```

```javascript
import passport from 'passport';
import { Strategy as LocalStrategy } from 'passport-local';
import argon2 from 'argon2';

passport.use(new LocalStrategy({ usernameField: 'email' }, async (email, password, done) => {
  try {
    const user = await users.findByEmail(email.trim().toLowerCase());
    const valid = user !== null && await argon2.verify(user.passwordHash, password);
    if (!valid) return done(null, false, { message: 'Invalid email or password' });   // failure, not error
    return done(null, user);
  } catch (err) {
    return done(err);                                       // infrastructure error -> error handler
  }
}));

passport.serializeUser((user, done) => done(null, user.id));          // keep the session small
passport.deserializeUser(async (id, done) => {
  try { done(null, (await users.findById(id)) ?? false); }            // false: user no longer exists
  catch (err) { done(err); }
});

app.use(session({ /* as in the previous topic */ }));
app.use(passport.initialize());
app.use(passport.session());                                // restores req.user from the session

app.post('/login',
  loginLimiter,                                             // slow down password guessing
  passport.authenticate('local', { failureRedirect: '/login?error=1' }),
  (req, res) => res.redirect(303, '/dashboard'));           // Passport regenerates the session on login

app.post('/logout', (req, res, next) => {
  req.logout((err) => (err ? next(err) : res.redirect(303, '/')));   // callback required since Passport 0.6
});

const requireLogin = (req, res, next) => (req.isAuthenticated() ? next() : res.redirect('/login'));
app.get('/dashboard', requireLogin, (req, res) => res.render('dashboard', { user: req.user }));
```

**Social login (OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect).** The same structure works with an external identity provider; only the strategy and routes change:

```javascript
import { Strategy as GoogleStrategy } from 'passport-google-oauth20';

passport.use(new GoogleStrategy({
  clientID: config.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID,
  clientSecret: config.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET,
  callbackURL: 'https://app.example.com/auth/google/callback',
}, async (accessToken, refreshToken, profile, done) => {
  try { done(null, await users.findOrCreateByGoogleId(profile.id, profile.emails?.[0]?.value)); }
  catch (err) { done(err); }
}));

app.get('/auth/google', passport.authenticate('google', { scope: ['openid', 'email', 'profile'] }));
app.get('/auth/google/callback',
  passport.authenticate('google', { failureRedirect: '/login' }),
  (req, res) => res.redirect(303, '/dashboard'));
```

**JWT access tokens.** For APIs used by mobile apps, other services or SPAs on another domain, the server issues a short-lived signed token at login, and clients send it in the `Authorization: Bearer` header (10.3). No session store is needed: any instance with the key can verify it. The `jose` library implements JWT with modern, promise-based APIs:

```javascript
// src/auth/tokens.js
import { SignJWT, jwtVerify } from 'jose';

const key = new TextEncoder().encode(config.JWT_SECRET);   // HS256: at least 32 random bytes
const ISSUER = 'https://api.example.com';
const AUDIENCE = 'bookshelf-clients';

export function issueAccessToken(user) {
  return new SignJWT({ role: user.role })                  // custom claims: keep them few and non-sensitive
    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'HS256' })
    .setSubject(String(user.id))
    .setIssuer(ISSUER)
    .setAudience(AUDIENCE)
    .setIssuedAt()
    .setExpirationTime('15m')                               // short-lived: limits the damage of a leak
    .sign(key);
}

export async function verifyAccessToken(token) {
  const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, key, {
    issuer: ISSUER,
    audience: AUDIENCE,
    algorithms: ['HS256'],                                  // never let the token choose the algorithm
  });
  return { id: payload.sub, role: payload.role };
}
```

```javascript
// src/middleware/authenticate-jwt.js
export async function authenticateJwt(req, res, next) {
  const [scheme, token] = (req.get('Authorization') ?? '').split(' ');
  if (scheme !== 'Bearer' || !token) {
    throw new HttpError(401, 'missing bearer token', { headers: { 'WWW-Authenticate': 'Bearer' } });
  }
  try {
    req.user = await verifyAccessToken(token);
  } catch {                                                 // expired, bad signature, wrong audience...
    throw new HttpError(401, 'invalid or expired token',
      { headers: { 'WWW-Authenticate': 'Bearer error="invalid_token"' } });
  }
  next();
}
```

```javascript
// Login for API clients: verify the password, return tokens
router.post('/token', loginLimiter, validate({ body: loginBody }), async (req, res) => {
  const user = await users.verifyCredentials(req.valid.body.email, req.valid.body.password);
  if (!user) throw new HttpError(401, 'invalid email or password');
  const refreshToken = await refreshTokens.issue(user.id);  // random, stored hashed, revocable (10.3)
  res.cookie('refresh_token', refreshToken, {
    httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict',
    path: '/api/auth/token',                                // only sent to the token endpoints
    maxAge: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  });
  res.json({ accessToken: await issueAccessToken(user), tokenType: 'Bearer', expiresIn: 900 });
});

router.post('/token/refresh', async (req, res) => {
  const record = await refreshTokens.consume(req.cookies.refresh_token);   // single use; detects reuse
  if (!record) throw new HttpError(401, 'invalid refresh token');
  const user = await users.findById(record.userId);
  const rotated = await refreshTokens.issue(user.id);       // rotation: a new refresh token every time
  res.cookie('refresh_token', rotated, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict', path: '/api/auth/token', maxAge: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 });
  res.json({ accessToken: await issueAccessToken(user), tokenType: 'Bearer', expiresIn: 900 });
});
```

The same verification is available as a Passport strategy, which is convenient when an application already uses Passport for other methods:

```javascript
import { Strategy as JwtStrategy, ExtractJwt } from 'passport-jwt';

passport.use(new JwtStrategy({
  jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),
  secretOrKey: config.JWT_SECRET,
  algorithms: ['HS256'],
  issuer: 'https://api.example.com',
  audience: 'bookshelf-clients',
}, (payload, done) => done(null, { id: payload.sub, role: payload.role })));

router.get('/me', passport.authenticate('jwt', { session: false }), (req, res) => res.json(req.user));
```

**Authorization comes after authentication.** Knowing *who* the caller is does not say *what* they may do. Role checks fit in middleware (`requireRole`, 12.2); ownership checks need the resource and belong in the handler or service:

```javascript
router.delete('/:id', authenticateJwt, validate({ params: bookIdParams }), async (req, res) => {
  const book = await books.get(req.valid.params.id);
  const isOwner = book.ownerId === req.user.id;
  if (!isOwner && req.user.role !== 'admin') throw new HttpError(403, 'you can only delete your own books');
  await books.remove(book.id);
  res.sendStatus(204);
});
```

**Choosing between the two.**

| | Session cookie (+ Passport) | JWT bearer token |
|---|---|---|
| Typical clients | Browser apps on the same site | Mobile apps, third-party clients, service-to-service, SPAs on other domains |
| State on the server | Session store | None for access tokens (refresh tokens are stored) |
| Revocation | Delete the session | Wait for expiry, or keep a deny-list |
| CSRF exposure | Yes (cookies sent automatically): use `SameSite` and checks | No, if the token is sent in a header |
| XSS exposure | Low with `HttpOnly` cookies | High if the token is stored where scripts can read it |

**Security checklist.** Rate-limit login and token endpoints; return the same message for unknown users and wrong passwords; pin the JWT algorithm and check issuer, audience and expiry; keep access tokens short-lived; never put personal or secret data in JWT payloads; serve everything over HTTPS; regenerate sessions at login.

**Key Takeaways**

- Passport separates authentication methods (strategies) from your user lookup (verify callbacks) and integrates with sessions through serialise/deserialise.
- JWT access tokens let any instance authenticate requests without a session store; verify them with a pinned algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry.
- Pair short-lived access tokens with rotated, revocable refresh tokens in `HttpOnly` cookies scoped to the token endpoint.
- Authentication identifies the caller; authorization (roles, ownership) must still be checked for every protected action.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement `POST /api/auth/token` and a protected `GET /api/me` with `jose`. Decode a token in the terminal and verify that tampering with its payload causes a `401`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add refresh-token rotation with reuse detection: if an already-used refresh token is presented, revoke all refresh tokens for that user. Write a test that simulates a stolen token being used after the legitimate client has refreshed.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you log out a user everywhere immediately in a system that uses JWT access tokens?" *Hint:* consider short expiry, revoking refresh tokens, a per-user token version or `iat` cut-off checked on each request, and the cost of each option.

#### File Uploads with Multer

Uploading files from an HTML form or `fetch` uses `multipart/form-data` (11.6): the body is split into parts by a boundary string, each part with its own headers, and files can be very large. Parsing this by hand means streaming, handling limits and cleaning up partial files. **Multer** is Express middleware built on the `busboy` streaming parser that does this for you: text fields go to `req.body`, files to `req.file` or `req.files`.

**Client side.**

```html
<form action="/api/v1/books/42/cover" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="cover" accept="image/jpeg,image/png,image/webp">
  <button>Upload</button>
</form>
```

```javascript
const form = new FormData();
form.append('cover', fileInput.files[0]);
await fetch('/api/v1/books/42/cover', { method: 'POST', body: form });   // do NOT set Content-Type: the browser adds the boundary
```

**Configuring Multer.** A Multer instance combines a storage engine, limits and a file filter:

```javascript
// src/books/cover-upload.js
import multer from 'multer';
import path from 'node:path';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { HttpError } from '../lib/http-error.js';

export const COVER_TYPES = new Map([['image/jpeg', '.jpg'], ['image/png', '.png'], ['image/webp', '.webp']]);
export const coversDir = path.join(config.DATA_DIR, 'covers');      // outside the source tree and public/

export const uploadCover = multer({
  storage: multer.diskStorage({
    destination: coversDir,                                          // a string: Multer creates the directory
    filename: (req, file, cb) => cb(null, randomUUID() + COVER_TYPES.get(file.mimetype)),  // never trust originalname
  }),
  limits: {
    fileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024,                                       // 5 MB per file
    files: 1,                                                        // at most one file
    fields: 10,                                                      // and a few text fields
    fieldSize: 10 * 1024,
  },
  fileFilter: (req, file, cb) => {
    if (COVER_TYPES.has(file.mimetype)) return cb(null, true);
    cb(new HttpError(415, 'only JPEG, PNG or WebP images are accepted', { code: 'UNSUPPORTED_FILE_TYPE' }));
  },
});
```

**Using it in a route.** The `mimetype` checked by `fileFilter` comes from the client and can lie. After the upload, check the file's **magic bytes** (its real format) and delete it if it does not match:

```javascript
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import { fileTypeFromFile } from 'file-type';

router.post('/:id/cover',
  authenticateJwt,
  validate({ params: bookIdParams }),
  uploadCover.single('cover'),                             // field name must match the form
  async (req, res) => {
    if (!req.file) throw new HttpError(400, 'a "cover" image file is required');
    const detected = await fileTypeFromFile(req.file.path);           // reads the first bytes of the file
    if (!detected || !COVER_TYPES.has(detected.mime)) {
      await fs.rm(req.file.path, { force: true });                    // clean up rejected files
      throw new HttpError(415, 'file content is not a supported image', { code: 'UNSUPPORTED_FILE_TYPE' });
    }
    await books.setCover(req.valid.params.id, req.file.filename);
    res.status(201).json({ coverUrl: `/media/covers/${req.file.filename}`, size: req.file.size });
  });
```

| Method | Accepts | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `upload.single('cover')` | One file in field `cover` | `req.file` |
| `upload.array('photos', 5)` | Up to 5 files in field `photos` | `req.files` (array) |
| `upload.fields([{ name: 'cover', maxCount: 1 }, { name: 'gallery', maxCount: 8 }])` | Several named fields | `req.files.cover`, `req.files.gallery` |
| `upload.none()` | Text fields only | `req.body`; any file causes an error |
| `upload.any()` | Any files | `req.files`: avoid, it accepts everything |

`req.file` contains `fieldname`, `originalname`, `mimetype`, `size` and, depending on the storage, `destination`, `filename` and `path` (disk) or `buffer` (memory).

**Errors.** Limit violations produce a `multer.MulterError` with a `code`. Map them in the error handler's `normalize` function (12.2):

```javascript
import multer from 'multer';

if (err instanceof multer.MulterError) {
  const status = err.code === 'LIMIT_FILE_SIZE' ? 413 : 400;   // LIMIT_FILE_COUNT, LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE, ...
  return new HttpError(status, err.message, { code: err.code });
}
```

**Storage options.**

| Storage | How | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| `diskStorage` | Streams to a local file | One server, or a shared volume |
| `memoryStorage` | Keeps the whole file in `req.file.buffer` | Small files processed immediately (resize, then upload elsewhere); dangerous without strict limits |
| Custom engine (for example `multer-s3`) | Streams to object storage | Multiple instances, containers with ephemeral disks |
| Direct-to-storage with presigned URLs | The app only issues a signed upload URL; the browser uploads to S3/GCS directly | Large files; keeps traffic off the app servers |

```text
 Presigned upload flow
 browser --POST /api/uploads {type, size}--> Express: validate, authorise, create a presigned PUT URL
 browser <--------- { uploadUrl, key } -----
 browser --PUT file--------------------------> object storage (checks signature, size, type)
 browser --POST /api/books/42/cover {key}--> Express: verify the object exists, record it
```

**Serving uploaded files safely.** An uploaded file is attacker-controlled content. An "image" that is really HTML with a script, served from your domain with the wrong type, becomes stored XSS.

```javascript
app.use('/media/covers', express.static(coversDir, {
  index: false,
  dotfiles: 'deny',
  setHeaders(res) {
    res.set('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff');               // browsers must trust Content-Type
    res.set('Content-Security-Policy', "default-src 'none'");   // nothing in the file may execute
  },
}));
```

Further measures: serve user content from a separate domain (`usercontent.example.com`) so it cannot read your cookies; re-encode images (for example with `sharp`), which also strips metadata such as GPS location; scan files with an antivirus service where required; enforce per-user quotas; and never use `originalname` to build paths.

**Key Takeaways**

- Multer parses `multipart/form-data` as a stream, putting text fields in `req.body` and files in `req.file`/`req.files`.
- Always set limits (size, count, fields), generate file names on the server, and verify the real content type from the file's bytes.
- Map `MulterError` codes to `413`/`400` in the central error handler, and delete rejected files.
- Serve uploads with `nosniff` and a restrictive CSP, ideally from a separate domain; consider presigned URLs for large files and multiple instances.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build an avatar upload endpoint that accepts one PNG or JPEG up to 1 MB and returns its URL. Try a 2 MB file, a text file renamed to `.png`, and a request with two files.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Use `memoryStorage` with `sharp` to resize uploads to 400x600, convert them to WebP, and store only the processed version. Measure memory use while uploading ten files concurrently, then explain why the limits matter.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What can go wrong when users upload files to your web application, and how do you defend against each risk?" *Hint:* consider size and count (denial of service), file names (path traversal), content type spoofing (stored XSS), malware, privacy metadata, and storage on ephemeral containers.

#### Template Engines and Server-Side Views

Not every web application is a JSON API plus a single-page front end. Admin panels, content sites, e-mail templates and progressively enhanced forms are often simpler and faster to build with **server-side rendering (SSR)**: the server produces finished HTML for every page, and the browser just displays it. Pages load fast, work without JavaScript and are easy for search engines to index.

A **template engine** turns a template (HTML with placeholders and simple logic) plus data into an HTML string. It is like a mail merge: one letter template, many personalised letters.

```text
 template  views/books/list.ejs        data  { books: [...], user: {...} }
        \                                  /
         +-------> template engine <------+
                        |
                        v
                 HTML string --> res.send() --> browser
```

**Express's view system.** Express does not include a template engine, but it defines how one plugs in: you configure a directory and an engine, and `res.render()` finds the file, merges the data and sends the result.

```javascript
import path from 'node:path';

app.set('views', path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'views'));   // where templates live
app.set('view engine', 'ejs');                                // default extension and engine (npm i ejs)

app.locals.siteName = 'Bookshelf';                            // available in every template

app.get('/books', async (req, res) => {
  const { items } = await books.list({ offset: 0, limit: 50 });
  res.render('books/list', { title: 'All books', books: items });   // renders views/books/list.ejs
});
```

The data available in a template is the merge of `app.locals`, `res.locals` and the object passed to `res.render`, with later sources taking precedence. In production (`NODE_ENV=production`) the `view cache` setting is on, so templates are compiled only once.

**EJS: JavaScript inside HTML.** EJS uses plain JavaScript in tags, so there is little new syntax to learn:

```ejs
<%# views/books/list.ejs %>
<%- include('../partials/header', { title }) %>

<h1><%= title %></h1>

<% if (books.length === 0) { %>
  <p>No books yet. <a href="/books/new">Add the first one</a>.</p>
<% } else { %>
  <ul>
    <% for (const book of books) { %>
      <li>
        <a href="/books/<%= book.id %>"><%= book.title %></a>
        by <%= book.author %> (<%= book.year %>)
      </li>
    <% } %>
  </ul>
<% } %>

<%- include('../partials/footer') %>
```

| EJS tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<%= value %>` | Output, **HTML-escaped** (`<` becomes `&lt;`): use for all data |
| `<%- value %>` | Output **raw**, unescaped: only for trusted HTML such as `include()` results |
| `<% code %>` | Run JavaScript (loops, conditions), no output |
| `<%# comment %>` | Comment, not included in the output |

Escaped output is what prevents a book titled `<script>alert(1)</script>` from executing in every visitor's browser. Using `<%-` with user data is one of the most common sources of XSS in server-rendered Express apps.

**Shared data with `res.locals`.** Values that every page needs (the logged-in user, flash messages, a CSRF token) are set once in middleware instead of in every `res.render` call:

```javascript
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.locals.currentUser = req.user ?? null;          // for the navigation bar
  res.locals.flash = req.session.flash ?? null;       // one-time message from the previous request
  delete req.session.flash;                           // ...shown only once
  res.locals.csrfToken = req.session.csrfToken;       // for hidden form fields
  next();
});
```

**Forms: Post/Redirect/Get.** After a successful `POST`, respond with a redirect (`303 See Other`) instead of rendering a page. Otherwise reloading the result page resubmits the form. On validation errors, re-render the form with the submitted values and messages, with status `422`:

```javascript
router.get('/books/new', (req, res) => res.render('books/new', { values: {}, errors: {} }));

router.post('/books', express.urlencoded({ extended: false }), async (req, res) => {
  const input = { ...req.body, year: Number(req.body.year) };          // form fields are always strings
  const result = bookCreateBody.safeParse(input);
  if (!result.success) {
    const errors = Object.fromEntries(result.error.issues.map((i) => [i.path.join('.'), i.message]));
    return res.status(422).render('books/new', { values: req.body, errors });   // keep what the user typed
  }
  const book = await books.create(result.data);
  req.session.flash = { type: 'success', message: `"${book.title}" was added.` };
  res.redirect(303, `/books/${book.id}`);                              // Post/Redirect/Get
});
```

```ejs
<%# views/books/new.ejs (excerpt) %>
<form method="post" action="/books" novalidate>
  <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="<%= csrfToken %>">
  <label>Title
    <input name="title" value="<%= values.title ?? '' %>" required maxlength="200">
  </label>
  <% if (errors.title) { %><p class="error"><%= errors.title %></p><% } %>
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
```

**Other engines.**

| Engine | Syntax style | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| EJS | HTML with `<% %>` JavaScript tags | Minimal learning curve; layouts via `include` |
| Pug | Indentation-based, no closing tags | Concise; mixins and inheritance; the syntax must be learned |
| Handlebars (`express-handlebars`) | `{{ }}` "logic-less" templates with helpers | Layouts and partials built in; logic moves to helpers |
| Nunjucks | Jinja2-like `{% %}` blocks | Template inheritance with `extends`/`block`; familiar to Python developers |
| JSX on the server (React `renderToString`, Hono JSX) | Components | Typed components; the bridge to full SSR frameworks |

```pug
//- views/books/list.pug: the same list in Pug
extends ../layout
block content
  h1= title
  ul
    each book in books
      li
        a(href=`/books/${book.id}`)= book.title
        |  by #{book.author}
```

**Where server-rendered views fit today.** Classic templates suit content-heavy sites and internal tools, often enhanced with small amounts of JavaScript (or libraries such as htmx that swap HTML fragments returned by the server). Highly interactive interfaces usually use a front-end framework (Chapter 14), sometimes with framework-level SSR, while Express serves the API and the built assets (next topic).

**Key Takeaways**

- Template engines merge templates with data into HTML; Express connects them through `views`, `view engine` and `res.render`.
- Template data comes from `app.locals`, `res.locals` and the render call; use `res.locals` for per-request shared values.
- Always use escaped output for data (`<%= %>` in EJS); raw output of user data causes XSS.
- Follow Post/Redirect/Get after successful form submissions, and re-render with `422` and the user's input on errors.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build list, detail and "new book" pages with EJS, sharing a header and footer partial and showing the logged-in user's name in the header.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add flash messages and full validation feedback to the form, including CSRF protection. Then render a book with the title `<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>` using `<%=` and `<%-` and explain the difference.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose server-rendered templates over a React single-page application for a new project?" *Hint:* consider interactivity requirements, SEO and first-load performance, team skills, the amount of client-side state, and hybrid approaches such as htmx or framework SSR.

#### Serving SPAs and API Gateways

Express often runs at the edge of a system in one of two roles: **hosting a single-page application** (the built output of React, Vue or Angular together with its API) and acting as an **API gateway**, a single entry point that forwards requests to internal services.

**Hosting an SPA.** A build tool (Vite, webpack) produces static files: an `index.html` and fingerprinted assets such as `assets/index-3f9a1c.js`. Express must do three things: serve the API, serve the assets with good caching, and return `index.html` for every client-side route so that reloading `/books/42` works (the *history fallback*, 6.4).

```text
 GET /api/v1/books        --> API router                         (JSON)
 GET /api/unknown         --> JSON 404                           (never index.html)
 GET /assets/index-3f9a.js --> express.static, cached for a year (file name changes when content changes)
 GET /favicon.ico         --> express.static, short cache
 GET /books/42            --> index.html, no-cache               (the SPA router renders the page)
 GET /missing.png         --> 404                                (not HTML: no fallback)
```

```javascript
import path from 'node:path';

const distDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, '..', 'client', 'dist');

app.use('/api', apiRouter);                                        // 1. API first
app.use('/api', (req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: 'not found' }));   // 2. unknown API paths stay JSON

app.use('/assets', express.static(path.join(distDir, 'assets'), {
  immutable: true,
  maxAge: '1y',                                                    // 3. fingerprinted: cache "forever"
  fallthrough: false,                                              //    a missing asset is a 404, not index.html
}));
app.use(express.static(distDir, { index: false, maxAge: '1h' }));  // favicon.ico, robots.txt, ...

app.get('/{*path}', (req, res, next) => {                          // 4. history fallback (GET and HEAD)
  if (!req.accepts('html')) return next();                         //    only for browsers navigating to a page
  res.sendFile('index.html', {
    root: distDir,
    headers: { 'Cache-Control': 'no-cache' },                      //    always revalidate: it points to the current assets
  });
});
```

`index.html` must not be cached for long, because it references the current asset file names; the assets themselves can be cached for a year because a new build produces new names.

**Development versus production.** During development the front end runs on the Vite dev server (with hot reloading) and *proxies* API calls to Express, so both appear to come from one origin. In production Express serves the built files itself, and front end and API share one origin: no CORS configuration is needed and cookies can use `SameSite=Strict`.

```javascript
// client/vite.config.js (development only)
export default {
  server: {
    proxy: { '/api': 'http://localhost:3000' },   // the browser talks to Vite; Vite forwards /api to Express
  },
};
```

**API gateway and backend for frontend (BFF).** When a system is split into several services (users, orders, inventory), clients should not need to know every service's address, authenticate against each, or make many round trips. A gateway in front of them centralises cross-cutting concerns:

```text
                         +---------------------------------------+
 browser / mobile -----> | Express gateway                       |
                         |  TLS, CORS, rate limits, auth (once), |
                         |  request IDs, logging, aggregation    |
                         +----+--------------+--------------+----+
                              |              |              |
                              v              v              v
                        users-service  orders-service  inventory-service   (internal network only)
```

| Responsibility | How in Express |
|---|---|
| Routing to services | `http-proxy-middleware` per path prefix |
| Authentication | Verify the token once, pass a trusted identity header downstream |
| Rate limiting, CORS, security headers | The middleware from 12.2, in one place |
| Aggregation (BFF) | A route that calls several services and combines the results |
| Observability | Request IDs forwarded to every service |

**Proxying.**

```javascript
import { createProxyMiddleware, fixRequestBody } from 'http-proxy-middleware';

app.use('/api/orders',
  authenticateJwt,                                   // verify the token at the edge
  createProxyMiddleware({
    target: 'http://orders-service:4000/orders',     // the mount path is stripped: /api/orders/42 -> /orders/42
    changeOrigin: true,                              // Host header becomes orders-service:4000
    proxyTimeout: 5_000,                             // fail instead of waiting forever
    on: {
      proxyReq: (proxyReq, req) => {
        proxyReq.setHeader('X-User-Id', req.user.id);    // trusted identity (overwrites any client-sent value)
        proxyReq.setHeader('X-Request-Id', req.id);
        fixRequestBody(proxyReq, req);                   // re-send the body if a body parser already consumed it
      },
    },
  }));
```

Body parsers and proxies conflict: if `express.json()` has already read the request stream, the proxy has nothing left to forward and the upstream service waits for a body that never comes. Either mount proxies *before* body parsers or re-serialise the body with `fixRequestBody`. Internal services must accept identity headers only from the gateway (network policies, mutual TLS), or anyone could send `X-User-Id: 1`.

**Aggregation in a BFF.** A dashboard that needs data from two services can get it in one request from the client's point of view, with independent failures handled gracefully:

```javascript
const getJson = async (url, signal) => {
  const r = await fetch(url, { signal });
  if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`${url} answered ${r.status}`);
  return r.json();
};

app.get('/api/dashboard', authenticateJwt, async (req, res) => {
  const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(2_000);                       // shared deadline for both calls
  const userId = encodeURIComponent(req.user.id);
  const [profile, orders] = await Promise.allSettled([             // in parallel, and one failure does not hide the other
    getJson(`${config.USERS_URL}/users/${userId}`, signal),
    getJson(`${config.ORDERS_URL}/orders?user=${userId}&limit=5`, signal),
  ]);
  res.json({
    profile: profile.status === 'fulfilled' ? profile.value : null,
    recentOrders: orders.status === 'fulfilled' ? orders.value : [],
    degraded: profile.status === 'rejected' || orders.status === 'rejected',
  });
});
```

For pure routing at very high throughput, dedicated proxies (nginx, Envoy, cloud API gateways) are more efficient. An Express gateway is worthwhile when the edge needs application logic: aggregation, custom authentication, response shaping for a specific client.

**Key Takeaways**

- To host an SPA: API routes first, a JSON 404 for unknown API paths, long-cached fingerprinted assets, and an `index.html` fallback (with `no-cache`) only for HTML navigation requests.
- Use the dev server's proxy in development and same-origin hosting in production to avoid CORS.
- An Express gateway centralises authentication, rate limiting and logging, and forwards requests with `http-proxy-middleware`; beware of body parsers consuming the stream.
- A BFF aggregates several services for one client, in parallel, with timeouts and graceful degradation.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a Vite + React (or plain HTML/JS) front end with client-side routes, serve its `dist` folder with Express, and verify that reloading a deep link works while `/api/nope` and `/missing.png` return 404.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create two small services (users and orders) and an Express gateway that authenticates with JWT, proxies `/api/users` and `/api/orders`, and exposes an aggregated `/api/dashboard`. Stop one service and check how the gateway responds.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What are the risks of an API gateway forwarding user identity to internal services in a header?" *Hint:* consider who else can reach the internal services, whether clients can inject the same header, and mechanisms such as network isolation, mutual TLS or signed internal tokens.

#### Testing Express Applications

Without automated tests, every change to a middleware order, a validation rule or an error mapping must be checked by hand, and regressions reach users. Express applications are well suited to testing because the app is just a function that handles requests: a test can call it without a real network, a browser or a deployed server.

**What to test at which level.**

| Level | Tests | Example | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | One function in isolation | `requireRole` returns 403 for members; service rejects duplicate ISBN | Milliseconds |
| Integration (HTTP) | The app through HTTP, with fake or test dependencies | `POST /api/v1/books` returns 201 and `Location`; invalid body returns 422 | Tens of milliseconds |
| Integration (data) | Repositories against a real test database | SQL queries, unique constraints | Slower; needs a database (Chapter 13) |
| End-to-end | Browser + deployed stack | Login and add a book through the UI (17.2) | Seconds |

Most tests should be fast unit and HTTP integration tests; a few end-to-end tests cover critical journeys.

**HTTP tests with supertest.** `supertest` takes an Express app, starts it on an ephemeral port for the duration of a request, and offers a fluent API for requests and assertions. Combined with the app factory from 12.1 and Node's built-in test runner (11.2), each test gets a fresh app with in-memory dependencies:

```javascript
// test/books.test.js
import { describe, it, beforeEach } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import request from 'supertest';
import { createApp } from '../src/app.js';
import { createInMemoryBookRepository } from '../src/books/books.repository.js';

const fakeAuth = (req, res, next) => { req.user = { id: '1', role: 'admin' }; next(); };   // replace real auth

describe('Books API', () => {
  let app;
  beforeEach(() => {
    app = createApp({ bookRepository: createInMemoryBookRepository(), authenticate: fakeAuth });  // isolated state per test
  });

  const dune = { title: 'Dune', author: 'Frank Herbert', isbn: '9780441172719', year: 1965 };

  it('creates a book and returns its location', async () => {
    const res = await request(app)
      .post('/api/v1/books')
      .send(dune)                                       // serialised as JSON, Content-Type set
      .expect('Content-Type', /json/)
      .expect(201);
    assert.equal(res.body.title, 'Dune');
    assert.equal(res.headers.location, `/api/v1/books/${res.body.id}`);
  });

  it('rejects duplicates with 409', async () => {
    await request(app).post('/api/v1/books').send(dune).expect(201);
    const res = await request(app).post('/api/v1/books').send(dune).expect(409);
    assert.equal(res.body.code, 'DUPLICATE_ISBN');
  });

  it('returns 422 with details for invalid input', async () => {
    const res = await request(app).post('/api/v1/books').send({ ...dune, year: 'old' }).expect(422);
    assert.ok(res.body.errors.some((e) => e.path === 'year'));
  });

  it('returns a problem document for unknown books', async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get('/api/v1/books/999').expect(404);
    assert.match(res.headers['content-type'], /application\/problem\+json/);
  });
});
```

```bash
node --test                                  # runs test/**/*.test.js
node --test --experimental-test-coverage     # with a coverage report
```

**Testing authentication flows.** For token-based APIs, obtain a token (or sign one with the test key) and send it with `.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`)`. For session-based apps, `request.agent(app)` keeps cookies between requests like a browser:

```javascript
it('keeps the user logged in between requests', async () => {
  const agent = request.agent(app);            // stores Set-Cookie and sends Cookie on later requests
  await agent.post('/api/auth/login').send({ email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct horse battery staple' }).expect(200);
  await agent.get('/api/me').expect(200);
  await agent.post('/api/auth/logout').expect(204);
  await agent.get('/api/me').expect(401);
});
```

supertest talks plain HTTP, so cookies marked `Secure` are not sent back. Make the `secure` flag (and a `__Host-` cookie name, which requires it) depend on configuration, and disable it in the test environment.

**Unit-testing middleware.** Middleware is a function; call it with minimal fake objects:

```javascript
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { requireRole } from '../src/middleware/require-role.js';

function fakeRes() {
  return {
    statusCode: 200, body: undefined,
    status(code) { this.statusCode = code; return this; },
    json(body) { this.body = body; return this; },
  };
}

test('requireRole lets admins through', (t) => {
  const next = t.mock.fn();                                   // records calls
  requireRole('admin')({ user: { role: 'admin' } }, fakeRes(), next);
  assert.equal(next.mock.callCount(), 1);
});

test('requireRole rejects members with 403', (t) => {
  const res = fakeRes();
  const next = t.mock.fn();
  requireRole('admin')({ user: { role: 'member' } }, res, next);
  assert.equal(res.statusCode, 403);
  assert.equal(next.mock.callCount(), 0);
});
```

**Dependencies outside the app.**

| Dependency | Strategy |
|---|---|
| Database | In-memory repository for HTTP tests; a real database for repository tests (Docker or Testcontainers), reset per test with transactions or truncation |
| Outgoing HTTP calls | Inject a client and fake it, or intercept `fetch` with undici's `MockAgent` or MSW |
| Time | Inject a clock, or use `t.mock.timers` in `node:test` |
| Configuration | A dedicated `.env.test` and an explicit `config` object passed to `createApp` |

**Key Takeaways**

- An app factory with injected dependencies makes Express apps testable without a network, a real database or global state.
- supertest drives the app through HTTP and asserts status codes, headers and bodies; `request.agent` keeps cookies for session flows.
- Middleware and services are plain functions: unit-test them with simple fakes and mocks.
- Most tests should be fast unit and HTTP integration tests; test error paths (`404`, `409`, `422`, `401`) as carefully as success paths.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write supertest tests for every endpoint of the books API, including one success and one error case each.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Test the login/logout flow with `request.agent`, and test that the rate limiter returns `429` after the configured number of failed logins (inject a small limit through configuration).
> 3. *(Interview)* "How do you keep integration tests for an Express API fast and reliable?" *Hint:* think about app factories, fresh state per test, which dependencies to fake and which to run for real, parallel test execution, and avoiding fixed ports and sleeps.

#### Alternatives: Koa, Fastify and NestJS

Express's design dates from 2010, before promises, `async`/`await` and TypeScript were common. Newer frameworks keep its core idea (functions handling requests) but make different trade-offs: Koa redesigns the middleware model around `async`/`await`, Fastify focuses on performance and schemas, NestJS adds an opinionated architecture, and Hono targets every JavaScript runtime. Knowing them helps you choose, and most concepts from this chapter transfer directly.

**Koa: the onion model.** Koa was created by the original Express team. It has no built-in router or body parser, and replaces `req`/`res` with a single **context** object `ctx`. Its main difference is the middleware model: `await next()` really waits for everything downstream, so each middleware wraps the ones after it like layers of an onion.

```text
          request
             |
 +-----------v----------------------------------------+
 | timing:  before await next()                       |
 |   +-------v----------------------------------+     |
 |   | errors:  try { await next() }            |     |
 |   |   +-------v--------------------------+   |     |
 |   |   | router: ctx.body = book          |   |     |
 |   |   +-------+--------------------------+   |     |
 |   | } catch (err) { ctx.status = ... }       |     |
 |   +-------+----------------------------------+     |
 | timing:  after await next(): set header            |
 +-----------+----------------------------------------+
             v
          response (sent by Koa after the whole chain has resolved)
```

```javascript
import Koa from 'koa';
import Router from '@koa/router';

const app = new Koa();

app.use(async (ctx, next) => {                    // wraps everything downstream
  const start = performance.now();
  await next();                                   // in Koa this really waits
  ctx.set('X-Response-Time', `${Math.round(performance.now() - start)}ms`);
});

app.use(async (ctx, next) => {                    // error handling is a plain try/catch
  try {
    await next();
  } catch (err) {
    ctx.status = err.status ?? 500;
    ctx.body = { error: err.expose ? err.message : 'internal server error' };
  }
});

const router = new Router();
router.get('/books/:id', async (ctx) => {
  const book = await books.findById(Number(ctx.params.id));
  if (!book) ctx.throw(404, 'book not found');    // throws an HttpError with expose = true
  ctx.body = book;                                // assigning an object means "respond with JSON"
});

app.use(router.routes()).use(router.allowedMethods());   // allowedMethods adds 405 and OPTIONS handling
app.listen(3000);
```

**Fastify: speed through schemas.** Fastify asks you to describe inputs and outputs with JSON Schema. It uses the schemas to validate and coerce requests (with Ajv) and to compile a fast JSON serialiser for responses, which also drops fields not in the schema (preventing accidental data leaks). It has built-in logging (pino), an encapsulated **plugin** system, and lifecycle **hooks** (`onRequest`, `preHandler`, `onSend`, `onResponse`, `onError`) instead of one generic middleware chain.

```javascript
import Fastify from 'fastify';

const app = Fastify({ logger: true });                     // structured logging built in

const Book = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: { id: { type: 'integer' }, title: { type: 'string' }, author: { type: 'string' } },
  required: ['id', 'title', 'author'],
};

app.get('/books/:id', {
  schema: {
    params: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'integer', minimum: 1 } }, required: ['id'] },
    response: { 200: Book },                               // serialiser compiled from the schema
  },
}, async (request, reply) => {
  const book = await books.findById(request.params.id);    // already validated and coerced to a number
  if (!book) return reply.code(404).send({ error: 'book not found' });
  return book;                                             // the returned value is the response body
});

app.register(async (admin) => {                            // encapsulated plugin: the hook applies only inside
  admin.addHook('onRequest', authenticateAdmin);
  admin.get('/stats', async () => ({ books: await books.count() }));
}, { prefix: '/admin' });

await app.listen({ port: 3000, host: '0.0.0.0' });
```

In "hello world" benchmarks Fastify handles several times more requests per second than Express. In real applications, where database calls dominate, the difference is smaller but still noticeable under high load. Existing Express middleware can be used through `@fastify/express` or `@fastify/middie` during a migration.

**NestJS: architecture included.** NestJS is a TypeScript framework inspired by Angular. It runs on top of Express (version 5 by default since NestJS 11) or Fastify and adds a structure: **modules** group features, **controllers** handle routes, **providers** (services) are created and injected by a **dependency injection** container, and cross-cutting concerns have dedicated building blocks: **guards** (authorization), **pipes** (validation and transformation), **interceptors** (wrapping handlers, like Koa middleware) and **exception filters** (error mapping).

```typescript
// books/books.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, ParseIntPipe, NotFoundException, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { BooksService } from './books.service';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';

@Controller('books')
export class BooksController {
  constructor(private readonly books: BooksService) {}        // injected by the DI container

  @Get(':id')
  async findOne(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {      // the pipe validates and converts the parameter
    const book = await this.books.findById(id);
    if (!book) throw new NotFoundException('book not found'); // turned into a 404 by the exception filter
    return book;                                               // serialised to JSON
  }

  @Get(':id/notes')
  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)                                     // authorization as a declarative guard
  notes(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {
    return this.books.notesFor(id);
  }
}
```

```typescript
// books/books.module.ts and main.ts (imports of BooksService and AppModule omitted)
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { BooksController } from './books.controller';

@Module({ controllers: [BooksController], providers: [BooksService] })
export class BooksModule {}

const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);    // Express adapter by default; FastifyAdapter is available
await app.listen(3000);
```

The same layered architecture that 12.1 built by convention is enforced by the framework, which helps large teams stay consistent, at the cost of more concepts, decorators and boilerplate.

**Hono: web standards on every runtime.** Hono is a small framework built on the standard `Request`/`Response` objects of the Fetch API. The same code runs on Node.js, Deno, Bun, Cloudflare Workers and other edge platforms (11.1):

```javascript
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { serve } from '@hono/node-server';

const app = new Hono();
app.get('/books/:id', async (c) => {
  const book = await books.findById(Number(c.req.param('id')));
  return book ? c.json(book) : c.json({ error: 'book not found' }, 404);
});

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 });   // on Bun or Workers you would export app instead
```

**Comparison.**

| | Express | Koa | Fastify | NestJS | Hono |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Style | Minimal, linear middleware | Minimal, onion middleware | Plugins, hooks, schemas | Opinionated, modules, DI, decorators | Minimal, Web-standard `Request`/`Response` |
| Async errors | Native since v5 | Native (try/catch around `next`) | Native | Native (exception filters) | Native |
| Validation | Bring your own | Bring your own | JSON Schema built in | Pipes (`class-validator`, Zod) | Validator middleware (Zod and others) |
| Performance | Baseline | Somewhat faster | Among the fastest on Node | Depends on adapter | Very fast, especially on Bun and edge runtimes |
| TypeScript | Via `@types/express` | Via types package | Built-in types, type providers | TypeScript-first | TypeScript-first |
| Ecosystem | Largest | Moderate | Large, official plugins | Large, integrated modules | Growing quickly |
| Typical fit | Most apps, learning, legacy | Small services wanting clean async | High-throughput APIs | Large teams and enterprise codebases | Edge and multi-runtime apps |

**How to choose.**

- An existing Express codebase, a team that knows it, or a need for a specific middleware: stay with Express 5.
- A new API where throughput or strict schemas matter: Fastify.
- A large application with many developers who benefit from enforced structure: NestJS.
- Deployment to edge or serverless runtimes, or code shared between runtimes: Hono.
- Whatever you pick, the concepts of this chapter (pipelines of handlers, validation at the boundary, central error handling, layered services, app factories for testing) carry over.

**Key Takeaways**

- Koa replaces Express's linear chain with the onion model, where `await next()` waits for downstream middleware; it ships without router or body parser.
- Fastify uses JSON Schemas for validation and fast serialisation, and organises code into encapsulated plugins with lifecycle hooks.
- NestJS adds modules, dependency injection, guards, pipes, interceptors and filters on top of Express or Fastify.
- Hono builds on Web-standard `Request`/`Response` and runs unchanged across Node.js, Deno, Bun and edge platforms.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement `GET /books/:id` and `POST /books` in Express, Koa and Fastify, and compare how each handles parameters, body parsing, validation and errors.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Benchmark the three implementations with `autocannon` for a JSON response, first with an in-memory result and then with a simulated 20 ms database delay. Explain why the relative differences shrink.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your team must build a new API platform with 30 developers. Express, Fastify or NestJS?" *Hint:* weigh performance needs against consistency across teams, onboarding cost, testability, the existing middleware you depend on, and the fact that NestJS can run on Fastify.

<a id="13-storage-and-data-persistence"></a>
## 13. Storage and Data Persistence

A web server's memory is temporary: it disappears when the process restarts, it is not shared between instances, and it is far too small for a growing user base. Every real application therefore keeps its data in a dedicated store. This chapter first builds the vocabulary needed to choose and use one: relational and NoSQL models, consistency guarantees, connection management and data modelling (13.1). It then studies the two stores most often paired with Node.js. MongoDB is a general-purpose document database (13.2). Redis is an in-memory data structure server used for caching, sessions, rate limiting and messaging (13.3). It builds on the Node.js runtime (Chapter 11) and on the Express services from Chapter 12, whose in-memory repositories, session stores and rate limiters this chapter finally backs with real storage.

<a id="131-persistence-concepts-for-web-applications"></a>
### 13.1 Persistence Concepts for Web Applications

This subchapter covers the ideas that apply to every database, whatever the product: the relational and NoSQL families, the guarantees they give (ACID, BASE, CAP), the main data models, how applications talk to a database through drivers and connection pools, and how to design data around the way a web application actually reads and writes it.

#### Relational vs NoSQL Data Stores

**Why a database at all?** Imagine storing users in a JSON file. It works for one user and one process. Then two requests write at the same time and one overwrites the other. The file grows to 2 GB and every lookup reads all of it. The server crashes halfway through a write and leaves the file corrupted. A **database management system (DBMS)** solves these problems once: concurrent access, fast lookups (indexes), crash safety, a query language, access control, backups and replication.

**The relational model.** Proposed by Edgar F. Codd in 1970, the relational model stores data in **tables** (relations) made of **rows** (tuples) and **columns** (attributes). Every column has a type, and the set of tables and columns (the **schema**) is declared in advance. Rows are linked through **keys**: a **primary key** identifies a row, and a **foreign key** points to the primary key of another table. Data is queried with **SQL**, a declarative language: you describe *what* you want, and the database's **query planner** decides *how* to fetch it. Popular relational databases (RDBMS) include PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, Microsoft SQL Server and Oracle.

Relational design favours **normalisation**: each fact is stored exactly once, and related data is split into separate tables that are recombined with **joins** at query time. Think of a well-organised library card catalogue: authors in one drawer, books in another, each card pointing to the other by number. Nothing is duplicated, so nothing can become inconsistent.

```sql
-- Schema: declared up front, enforced by the database
CREATE TABLE authors (
  id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE books (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title      TEXT NOT NULL,
  isbn       CHAR(13) UNIQUE NOT NULL,              -- the database rejects duplicates
  author_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES authors(id) -- foreign key: must point to an existing author
);

-- Recombine the normalised data with a join
SELECT b.title, a.name AS author
FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
WHERE a.name = 'Frank Herbert';
```

**NoSQL.** In the late 2000s, companies such as Google (Bigtable, 2006) and Amazon (Dynamo, 2007) needed to spread data across thousands of commodity machines with predictable latency. Joins and multi-row transactions across machines are expensive, so they built stores that gave them up in exchange for horizontal scale and flexible schemas. "NoSQL" (usually read as "not only SQL") is an umbrella term for these non-relational stores. It is not one model but several (see "Document, Key-Value, Column and Graph Models"):

- **Document stores** (MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore) keep self-contained JSON-like documents.
- **Key-value stores** (Redis, Valkey, DynamoDB, etcd) map a key to a value.
- **Wide-column stores** (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase) organise data in rows with flexible column families, partitioned across nodes.
- **Graph databases** (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune) store nodes and relationships as first-class data.

The same book in a document store keeps related data *together* instead of normalising it:

```javascript
// MongoDB document: the author is embedded; one read returns everything a page needs
{
  _id: ObjectId('66fe1c2a9b1e8a3f4c2d7e10'),
  title: 'Dune',
  isbn: '9780441172719',
  author: { id: 17, name: 'Frank Herbert' },   // duplicated from the authors collection on purpose
  tags: ['sci-fi', 'classic'],                 // arrays are native: no extra join table
  ratings: { count: 1287, average: 4.6 }
}
```

**Comparison.**

| Aspect | Relational (SQL) | NoSQL (typical) |
|---|---|---|
| Data shape | Tables of rows with fixed columns | Documents, key-value pairs, wide rows, graphs |
| Schema | Declared and enforced up front (schema-on-write) | Flexible; often enforced by the application (schema-on-read) or optional validators |
| Relationships | Foreign keys and joins | Embedding, duplication, application-side joins, `$lookup` |
| Query language | Standard SQL | Product-specific APIs (MongoDB query language, Redis commands, CQL, Cypher) |
| Transactions | Multi-row, multi-table ACID by default | Single-record atomicity always; multi-record transactions in some products |
| Scaling | Vertical first; read replicas; sharding is possible but harder | Designed for horizontal partitioning (sharding) |
| Strengths | Integrity, ad hoc queries, reporting, complex relationships | Flexible shapes, very high throughput on known access patterns, easy scale-out |
| Weaknesses | Schema migrations on huge tables, scaling writes across machines | Ad hoc queries and cross-entity integrity are harder; denormalised data can drift |

**The lines are blurring.** PostgreSQL stores and indexes JSON (`JSONB`), and MongoDB offers multi-document ACID transactions and schema validation. Distributed SQL databases (CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, Google Spanner) shard relational data horizontally. The choice is rarely "SQL or NoSQL forever"; it is about which model fits each workload.

**Polyglot persistence.** Many web systems use several stores, each for what it does best:

```text
                       +----------------------------+
  browser --> API ---> | PostgreSQL / MongoDB       |  system of record: users, orders, products
                |      +----------------------------+
                +----> | Redis                      |  cache, sessions, rate limits, queues
                |      +----------------------------+
                +----> | Elasticsearch / OpenSearch |  full-text search over products
                |      +----------------------------+
                +----> | S3-compatible object store |  images, uploads, backups
                       +----------------------------+
```

The **system of record** is the authoritative copy. Every other store holds derived data that can be rebuilt from it. Keep that distinction clear: losing a cache is an inconvenience, losing the system of record is a disaster.

**Choosing.** Ask questions, not slogans:

1. How are entities related, and how often do you query across those relationships in unpredictable ways? Many ad hoc relationships favour relational.
2. Do the records of one kind have very different shapes, or does the shape change often? That favours documents.
3. Which operations must be atomic across several records (money transfers, stock reservations)?
4. What are the read/write volumes and latency targets, and will one machine be enough for years? It usually is.
5. What does the team already know how to operate, back up and monitor?

**Key Takeaways**

- A DBMS provides concurrency control, indexing, crash safety, querying and replication that files cannot.
- Relational databases store normalised tables with a declared schema, linked by keys and recombined with SQL joins.
- NoSQL is a family of models (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) that trade joins and sometimes cross-record transactions for flexibility and horizontal scale.
- Modern products blur the boundary (`JSONB` in PostgreSQL, transactions in MongoDB); choose by workload, not by trend.
- Polyglot persistence pairs a system of record with specialised stores for caching, search and files.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Model a blog with users, posts and comments twice: once as relational tables with primary and foreign keys, once as MongoDB documents. Write the query that returns a post with its author name and comments in each model.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* For an e-commerce site, list five kinds of data (catalogue, carts, orders, sessions, product search) and choose a store for each. Justify each choice in one sentence and identify the system of record.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL, and when would you not?" *Hint:* talk about data shape variability, relationships queried ad hoc, transactional requirements, the team's operational experience, and the fact that PostgreSQL also stores JSON.

#### ACID vs BASE and the CAP Theorem

A database's **guarantees** decide which bugs your application can and cannot have. If two customers buy the last item at the same moment, will both orders succeed? If the server loses power right after confirming a payment, is the payment still there after the restart? These questions are answered by the consistency models below.

**ACID.** A **transaction** is a group of operations treated as a single unit. Relational databases (and MongoDB for multi-document transactions) guarantee four properties:

| Property | Meaning | Bank transfer example |
|---|---|---|
| **Atomicity** | All operations happen, or none do | Debit and credit both apply, or neither does |
| **Consistency** | The transaction moves the database from one valid state to another; constraints (unique, foreign keys, checks) always hold | A `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint is never violated |
| **Isolation** | Concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states | Another reader never sees money that has left one account but not arrived in the other |
| **Durability** | Once committed, data survives crashes | After "transfer complete", a power failure does not undo it |

Durability is usually implemented with a **write-ahead log (WAL)**: the change is appended to a log file and flushed to disk before the commit is acknowledged. After a crash, the database replays the log.

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
-- if anything fails before this point, ROLLBACK undoes both updates
COMMIT;
```

**Isolation levels.** Perfect isolation (each transaction behaves as if it ran alone) is expensive, so SQL defines weaker levels. Each level permits fewer **anomalies**:

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom read | Typical default in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read uncommitted | possible | possible | possible | rarely used |
| Read committed | prevented | possible | possible | PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle |
| Repeatable read | prevented | prevented | possible (prevented in PostgreSQL) | MySQL InnoDB |
| Serializable | prevented | prevented | prevented | opt-in |

- *Dirty read*: you see data another transaction has not committed (and may roll back).
- *Non-repeatable read*: reading the same row twice in one transaction returns different values.
- *Phantom read*: re-running a range query returns new rows that another transaction inserted.

A classic bug at read committed is the **lost update**: two requests read `stock = 1`, both compute `stock - 1 = 0` in application code, and both write `0`; two items are sold, one is in stock. The fix is to let the database do the arithmetic atomically (`UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`), to lock the row (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), or to use optimistic concurrency with a version number.

**Distributed systems and CAP.** Once data is replicated across several machines (for availability or scale), a new problem appears: the network between them can fail. The **CAP theorem** (Eric Brewer, 2000; proved by Gilbert and Lynch, 2002) says that a distributed data store cannot guarantee all three of the following at the same time:

- **Consistency (C)**: every read sees the most recent write (linearizability; not the same "C" as in ACID).
- **Availability (A)**: every request to a non-failing node receives a response.
- **Partition tolerance (P)**: the system keeps working even if messages between nodes are lost.

Partitions *will* happen in any real network, so P is not optional. The real choice is what to do **during** a partition:

```text
            Node A  ----X----  Node B          the link between A and B is broken
          (has write v2)     (still has v1)

  A client asks Node B for the value. Node B can:

  CP: refuse to answer (error or timeout)  --> stays consistent, gives up availability
  AP: answer v1 (stale)                    --> stays available, gives up consistency
```

| Choice | Behaviour during a partition | Examples (default configurations) |
|---|---|---|
| CP | Minority side rejects writes (and possibly reads) until the partition heals | MongoDB with majority write concern, etcd, ZooKeeper, HBase |
| AP | Every side keeps accepting reads and writes; conflicts reconciled later | Cassandra, DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads), CouchDB |

**PACELC** (Daniel Abadi) extends CAP with the more common case: if there is a **P**artition, choose **A** or **C**; **E**lse (normal operation), choose between **L**atency and **C**onsistency. Even without failures, waiting for several replicas to confirm a write costs latency. Many databases let you choose per operation (MongoDB write and read concerns, Cassandra consistency levels).

**BASE.** Systems that favour availability describe their guarantees as **BASE**:

- **Basically Available**: the system answers, even if some data is stale or some parts are degraded.
- **Soft state**: the state may change over time without new input, as replicas converge.
- **Eventual consistency**: if writes stop, all replicas eventually return the same value.

An analogy: ACID is a bank counter where the clerk will not let you leave until the ledger is updated and signed. BASE is a social network's "like" counter: different users may briefly see 41 or 42 likes, and nobody is harmed because it converges within a second.

**ACID vs BASE.**

| Aspect | ACID | BASE |
|---|---|---|
| Priority | Correctness of every operation | Availability and scale |
| Consistency | Strong, immediate | Eventual |
| Typical uses | Payments, inventory, bookings, account balances | Feeds, counters, analytics, product views, caches |
| Cost | Coordination, locking, latency | Application must tolerate and sometimes reconcile stale or conflicting data |

**Practical guidance for web applications.**

- Identify the few operations that must be strongly consistent (money, stock, unique usernames) and protect them with transactions, atomic updates or unique constraints.
- Accept eventual consistency where users will not notice (counters, recommendation lists, search indexes updated a second later).
- Watch out for **read-your-own-writes**: a user saves a profile and the next page, read from a lagging replica, shows the old value. Route such reads to the primary or use causal consistency (see "Replica Sets and Sharding").

**Key Takeaways**

- ACID transactions guarantee atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability; isolation comes in levels that permit different anomalies.
- Lost updates happen when application code reads, modifies and writes; prefer atomic updates, locks or optimistic versioning.
- CAP: during a network partition a replicated store must choose between consistency and availability; PACELC adds the latency/consistency trade-off during normal operation.
- BASE systems are basically available with eventual consistency; they suit data where brief staleness is harmless.
- Most applications mix models: strong consistency for critical operations, eventual consistency elsewhere.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For each feature, state whether it needs strong or eventual consistency and why: checking out a cart, the "views" counter on a video, changing a password, the list of "people you may know".
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write two concurrent scripts that each read a stock value, decrement it in JavaScript and write it back, 1,000 times, against any database. Show the lost updates, then fix it with an atomic update and verify the final count.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Is MongoDB CP or AP?" *Hint:* the answer depends on configuration; discuss primary elections, write concern `majority` versus `w: 1`, and reads from secondaries.

#### Document, Key-Value, Column and Graph Models

A **data model** is the shape in which a database lets you store and query information. The model decides which questions are cheap to ask. A useful analogy is storage furniture: a filing cabinet (documents), a wall of numbered lockers (key-value), a giant spreadsheet split across rooms (wide-column), and a corkboard with pins and strings (graph). You can store anything in any of them, but each makes certain retrievals effortless and others painful.

**Key-value model.** The simplest model: a key maps to an opaque value. The store can find a value by its exact key extremely quickly, but it cannot search *inside* values or ask "which keys have a value greater than 10?" unless it adds extra structures. Redis extends the idea with typed values (lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets) that support server-side operations.

```text
 key                         value
 ------------------------    ----------------------------------------
 session:9f2c...             {"userId":42,"role":"admin"}            (string, JSON-encoded)
 ratelimit:203.0.113.7       17                                      (counter)
 cart:42                     { "sku-1": 2, "sku-9": 1 }              (Redis hash)
```

*Strengths:* very low latency, trivial to partition by key. *Weaknesses:* only lookups by key; relationships and secondary queries are your job. *Use for:* caches, sessions, feature flags, counters, rate limits.

**Document model.** Each record is a **document**: a nested structure of fields, arrays and sub-documents (JSON or a binary form of it, such as BSON). Documents of the same kind are grouped in **collections**. Unlike key-value stores, the database understands the document's structure: it can query and index any field, including nested ones and array elements.

```javascript
// One document holds an order with its line items: the unit that is read and written together
{
  _id: 'ord_1029',
  customer: { id: 42, name: 'Ada Lovelace' },
  status: 'paid',
  items: [
    { sku: 'BK-DUNE', qty: 1, price: 9.99 },
    { sku: 'BK-EMMA', qty: 2, price: 7.50 }
  ],
  total: 24.99
}
```

*Strengths:* maps naturally to objects in code, no impedance mismatch, flexible shapes, one read for an aggregate. *Weaknesses:* many-to-many relationships and cross-document consistency need care. *Use for:* content, catalogues, user profiles, orders, most general application data.

**Wide-column (column-family) model.** Data is stored in tables with a **partition key** that decides which node holds the row and **clustering columns** that sort rows within a partition. Rows in the same table can have different columns. It is optimised for massive write volumes and queries that read one partition in order. Cassandra and ScyllaDB are the main examples. Note that "wide-column" is different from "columnar" analytic databases (ClickHouse, BigQuery), which store each column contiguously to speed up aggregations.

```sql
-- Cassandra Query Language (CQL): readings partitioned by sensor, sorted by time
CREATE TABLE readings (
  sensor_id  text,
  day        date,
  ts         timestamp,
  value      double,
  PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts)       -- (partition key), clustering column
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC);

-- Efficient: reads one partition, already sorted
SELECT ts, value FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 's-17' AND day = '2026-10-03' LIMIT 100;
-- Not allowed without a full scan: WHERE value > 30 (not part of the key)
```

*Strengths:* linear write scalability, high availability, time-ordered data. *Weaknesses:* you must design a table per query; no joins; limited ad hoc queries. *Use for:* IoT telemetry, event logs, messaging histories at very large scale.

**Graph model.** Data is stored as **nodes** (entities) and **edges** (relationships), both with properties. Traversing a relationship is a pointer hop rather than a join, so queries that follow many hops ("friends of friends who like the same band") stay fast however large the data grows.

```text
 (:User {name:'Ada'}) -[:FOLLOWS]-> (:User {name:'Alan'}) -[:LIKES]-> (:Band {name:'Kraftwerk'})
          |                                                                 ^
          +--------------------------[:LIKES]-------------------------------+
```

```text
// Cypher (Neo4j): recommend bands liked by people Ada follows, but not yet by Ada
MATCH (me:User {name: 'Ada'})-[:FOLLOWS]->(:User)-[:LIKES]->(b:Band)
WHERE NOT (me)-[:LIKES]->(b)
RETURN b.name, count(*) AS score
ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5;
```

*Strengths:* deep relationship queries, path finding, recommendations, fraud rings. *Weaknesses:* less suited to bulk aggregate scans; harder to shard. *Use for:* social graphs, knowledge graphs, access-control graphs, network topologies.

**Other specialised models** often found next to the main database:

| Model | Examples | Typical web use |
|---|---|---|
| Time series | TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus | Metrics, monitoring, sensor data |
| Search engine (inverted index) | Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Meilisearch | Full-text search, faceted navigation |
| Vector | pgvector, MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, Qdrant | Semantic search, retrieval for AI features |
| Object storage | Amazon S3 and compatibles | Files, images, backups |

**Summary comparison.**

| Model | Unit of data | Lookup by | Relationships | Scale-out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Key-value | Value behind a key | Key only | None (application) | Easiest |
| Document | Nested document | Any indexed field | Embedding, references | Good (sharding) |
| Wide-column | Row in a partition | Partition key + clustering columns | None; one table per query | Excellent |
| Graph | Node and edge | Pattern traversal | First-class | Harder |
| Relational | Row in a table | Any indexed column, joins | Foreign keys, joins | Harder for writes |

**Key Takeaways**

- Key-value stores give the fastest lookups by key and little else; Redis adds typed values with server-side operations.
- Document stores keep nested, flexible records and can query and index fields inside them.
- Wide-column stores partition rows by key for enormous write throughput but require one table design per query.
- Graph databases make multi-hop relationship traversal cheap.
- Pick a model by the questions your application asks most often.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Represent a user with two addresses and three roles in each of the four models. Which representation makes "find all admins" easiest, and which makes "load user 42" easiest?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Design a Cassandra-style table for "the last 50 messages in a chat room" and explain your partition and clustering keys. What happens if one room becomes extremely popular?
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why are graph databases faster than SQL joins for friend-of-friend queries?" *Hint:* compare index lookups per join step with index-free adjacency, and consider how cost grows with depth.

#### Connection Pooling and Drivers

**What a driver does.** Your application does not speak a database's wire protocol by itself. A **driver** (client library) does that work: it opens TCP connections, performs TLS and authentication, encodes queries and parameters into the protocol (PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol, MongoDB's OP_MSG with BSON, Redis's RESP), decodes results into language values, and handles timeouts, retries and server discovery in clusters. Examples for Node.js: `pg` (PostgreSQL), `mysql2`, the official `mongodb` driver, and `redis` or `ioredis`. Higher-level libraries sit on top: **query builders** (Knex, Kysely), **ORMs** for relational databases (Prisma, Drizzle, Sequelize, TypeORM) and **ODMs** for documents (Mongoose, 13.2).

```text
 your code  -->  ODM / ORM (optional)  -->  driver  -->  wire protocol over TCP/TLS  -->  database
 repo.find()     Mongoose, Prisma           mongodb, pg   BSON / PostgreSQL messages
```

**Why connections are expensive.** Opening a database connection involves a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, authentication (often a deliberately slow SCRAM hash exchange), and on PostgreSQL the creation of a whole server process with its own memory. That can take from a few milliseconds on a local network to over 100 ms across regions. A web request that opens and closes its own connection pays that cost every time, and the database pays even more.

**Connection pooling.** A **pool** keeps a set of open connections and lends them out. A request borrows a connection, runs its queries, and returns it; the next request reuses it immediately. An analogy is a taxi rank: instead of building a car for every passenger and scrapping it at the destination, a fixed fleet of taxis waits at the rank, and passengers queue when all are busy.

```text
              +----------------- pool (max 10) -----------------+
 request A -->| [conn 1: busy A] [conn 2: busy B] [conn 3: idle] |---> database
 request B -->| [conn 4: idle]   ...                             |
 request C -->| waiting queue: (empty) --> gets conn 3           |
              +--------------------------------------------------+
```

Node.js is single-threaded, but database work is I/O: while one query waits for the network, the event loop runs other requests. A pool with several connections lets those queries run concurrently on the database.

**A pool in practice (PostgreSQL with `pg`).**

```javascript
// src/db/pg.js: one pool per process, created once at start-up
import pg from 'pg';

export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
```
