```javascript
  await client.connect();                          // optional (operations auto-connect), but fails fast at start-up
  await db.command({ ping: 1 });                   // verify credentials and connectivity
  await ensureIndexes();
}

async function ensureIndexes() {                   // idempotent: does nothing if the index already exists
  await db.collection('books').createIndexes([
    { key: { isbn: 1 }, unique: true },
    { key: { 'author.name': 1, createdAt: -1 } },
  ]);
}
```

```javascript
// src/server.js: start-up and graceful shutdown (11.5, 12.1)
import { client, connectMongo } from './db/mongo.js';
import { createApp } from './app.js';

await connectMongo();
const server = createApp().listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  server.close(async () => {
    await client.close();                          // close pooled connections cleanly
    process.exit(0);
  });
});
```

**ObjectIds from URLs.** Route parameters are strings; `_id` values are ObjectIds. Convert and validate them, otherwise `{ _id: '66fe...' }` matches nothing (a string is not an ObjectId):

```javascript
import { ObjectId } from 'mongodb';

export function parseObjectId(value) {
  if (!/^[0-9a-f]{24}$/i.test(value)) {          // ObjectId.isValid() also accepts any 12-character string
    throw new HttpError(400, 'invalid id', { code: 'INVALID_ID' });
  }
  return new ObjectId(value);
}
```

**A MongoDB repository for the bookshelf API.** In 12.3 the service depended on a repository with `list`, `findById`, `findByIsbn`, `insert`, `update` and `remove`. A MongoDB implementation exposes the same interface, so the service and routes need no changes (apart from validating IDs as ObjectId strings instead of integers):

```javascript
// src/books/books.mongo-repository.js
import { ObjectId } from 'mongodb';

const toBook = ({ _id, ...rest }) => ({ id: _id.toHexString(), ...rest });   // hide Mongo's _id from API clients

export function createMongoBookRepository(db) {
  const books = db.collection('books');

  return {
    async list({ offset, limit, author }) {
      const filter = author
        ? { 'author.name': { $regex: `^${escapeRegex(author)}`, $options: 'i' } }   // escape user input in regexes
        : {};
      const [items, total] = await Promise.all([
        books.find(filter).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).skip(offset).limit(limit).toArray(),
        books.countDocuments(filter),
      ]);
      return { items: items.map(toBook), total };
    },

    async findById(id) {
      const doc = await books.findOne({ _id: new ObjectId(id) });
      return doc && toBook(doc);
    },

    async findByIsbn(isbn) {
      const doc = await books.findOne({ isbn });
      return doc && toBook(doc);
    },

    async insert(data) {
      const doc = { tags: [], ...data, createdAt: new Date() };
      const { insertedId } = await books.insertOne(doc);    // the driver also sets doc._id
      return toBook({ ...doc, _id: insertedId });
    },

    async update(id, changes) {
      const doc = await books.findOneAndUpdate(
        { _id: new ObjectId(id) },
        { $set: { ...changes, updatedAt: new Date() } },
        { returnDocument: 'after' },
      );
      return doc && toBook(doc);
    },

    async remove(id) {
      const { deletedCount } = await books.deleteOne({ _id: new ObjectId(id) });
      return deletedCount === 1;
    },
  };
}

const escapeRegex = (s) => s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
```

**Handling driver errors.** Server errors are `MongoServerError` instances with a numeric `code`. The most common one in web applications is **11000, duplicate key**, raised by unique indexes. Map it to `409 Conflict` in the error handler (12.2). This also closes the race in the service's "check ISBN, then insert" logic: two concurrent requests can both pass the check, but the unique index rejects the second insert.

```javascript
import { MongoServerError } from 'mongodb';

// in the central error handler (12.2)
if (err instanceof MongoServerError && err.code === 11000) {
  return res.status(409).json({ error: 'duplicate value', fields: Object.keys(err.keyValue ?? {}) });
}
```

Network errors (`MongoNetworkError`) and server selection timeouts (`MongoServerSelectionError`) indicate infrastructure problems: return `503` and make your health check report the database as down.

**TypeScript.** Collections accept a document type, which types filters, updates and results:

```typescript
import type { ObjectId } from 'mongodb';

interface BookDoc {
  _id: ObjectId;
  title: string;
  isbn: string;
  author: { name: string };
  tags: string[];
  createdAt: Date;
}

const books = db.collection<BookDoc>('books');
await books.updateOne({ isbn: '9780441172719' }, { $set: { title: 'Dune' } });   // checked against BookDoc
// await books.updateOne({}, { $set: { titel: 'x' } });                          // compile-time error: unknown field
```

Note that these types are only compile-time hints: the database does not know about them, so validate input at the boundary and consider `$jsonSchema` on the server.

**Testing.** Integration tests should run against a real MongoDB: a Docker container in CI, Testcontainers, or the `mongodb-memory-server` package, which downloads and starts a real `mongod` binary for the test run. Use a separate database per test file and drop it afterwards.

**Key Takeaways**

- Use the official `mongodb` driver with one `MongoClient` per process; connect and create indexes at start-up and close the client on shutdown.
- Convert route parameters to `ObjectId` after validating them; strings do not match ObjectIds.
- A repository with the same interface as the in-memory one lets services and routes stay unchanged.
- Map duplicate key errors (code 11000) to `409` and network errors to `503`; rely on unique indexes for uniqueness under concurrency.
- Typed collections catch mistakes at compile time but do not validate data at runtime.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Connect to MongoDB from a Node.js script, insert three books and print them sorted by title, closing the client at the end.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Replace the in-memory repository of the 12.3 bookshelf API with `createMongoBookRepository`. Update the ID validation schema, map error 11000 to `409`, and run the existing Supertest suite against `mongodb-memory-server`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can the 'check if exists, then insert' pattern create duplicates, and how do you prevent it?" *Hint:* think about two concurrent requests between the check and the insert, and what a unique index guarantees.

#### Object Modeling with Mongoose

**What Mongoose adds.** The driver is deliberately thin: it stores whatever you give it. Mongoose is an **ODM** (Object Document Mapper) that adds an application-level schema on top of the driver: declared field types with casting, defaults, validation, middleware (hooks), relationships with `populate`, virtual properties, and model classes with methods. It trades some performance and transparency for structure and convenience, similar to an ORM in the relational world.

| Concern | Native driver | Mongoose |
|---|---|---|
| Schema | Optional (`$jsonSchema` on the server) | Declared in code, applied to every document |
| Type casting | None: `'10'` stays a string | `'10'` cast to `10` for a `Number` path |
| Validation | Your own code or server validator | Built-in and custom validators |
| Hooks | None | `pre`/`post` middleware |
| Relationships | Manual or `$lookup` | `ref` + `populate()` |
| Result objects | Plain objects | Document instances with methods and change tracking (or plain objects with `lean()`) |
| Overhead | Minimal | Higher (document hydration, change tracking) |

**Connecting.**

```javascript
import mongoose from 'mongoose';

await mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGO_URL, { maxPoolSize: 20, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5_000 });
mongoose.connection.on('disconnected', () => console.warn('MongoDB disconnected'));

// on shutdown
await mongoose.disconnect();
```

Mongoose **buffers** model operations until the connection is open, which can hide connection problems as hanging requests; set `mongoose.set('bufferCommands', false)` or connect before starting the HTTP server.

**Schema and model.**

```javascript
// src/books/book.model.js
import mongoose from 'mongoose';
const { Schema, model } = mongoose;

const bookSchema = new Schema(
  {
    title:  { type: String, required: true, trim: true },
    isbn:   { type: String, required: true, unique: true },     // creates a unique INDEX (not a validator)
    price:  { type: Number, required: true, min: 0 },
    author: { type: Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Author', required: true },  // reference for populate()
    tags:   { type: [String], default: [] },
    status: { type: String, enum: ['draft', 'published'], default: 'draft' },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,                                              // adds createdAt and updatedAt automatically
    toJSON: {                                                      // shape of res.json(book)
      virtuals: true,
      transform(_doc, ret) { delete ret._id; delete ret.__v; return ret; },
    },
  },
);

bookSchema.index({ author: 1, createdAt: -1 });                    // compound index declared on the schema

// Virtual: computed, not stored
bookSchema.virtual('priceWithVat').get(function () { return Math.round(this.price * 122) / 100; });

// Instance method: available on each document
bookSchema.methods.publish = function () { this.status = 'published'; return this.save(); };

// Static: available on the model
bookSchema.statics.findByIsbn = function (isbn) { return this.findOne({ isbn }); };

export const Book = model('Book', bookSchema);                     // collection name: 'books' (lowercased, pluralised)
```

**Using models.**

```javascript
// Create: validation and casting run before the insert
const book = await Book.create({ title: ' Dune ', isbn: '9780441172719', price: '9.99', author: authorId });
book.title;   // 'Dune' (trimmed)
book.price;   // 9.99 (cast from string)

// Read
const one = await Book.findById(id);                             // casts the string id to ObjectId for you
const list = await Book.find({ tags: 'sci-fi' }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20).select('title price');

// Update a document instance: change tracking saves only modified paths
one.price = 8.99;
await one.save();                                                // runs validators and save middleware

// Update directly in the database (faster, but see the validation caveats in the next topic)
await Book.updateOne({ _id: id }, { $inc: { price: 1 } });

await Book.deleteOne({ _id: id });
```

**Queries are thenables.** `Book.find(...)` returns a `Query` object that you can keep chaining; it executes when awaited. Call `.exec()` to get a real promise with better stack traces. Since Mongoose 7, callback APIs are gone: everything is promise-based.

**`lean()` for read-heavy endpoints.** By default each result is **hydrated** into a full Mongoose document with getters, setters and change tracking, which costs CPU and memory. For read-only API responses, `lean()` returns plain objects and is several times faster:

```javascript
const books = await Book.find({ status: 'published' }).select('title price').lean();   // plain objects
```

Lean results do not have virtuals, methods or defaults applied (plugins exist to add virtuals back).

**`populate`: following references.** `populate` replaces an ObjectId with the referenced document, by running a second query:

```javascript
const book = await Book.findById(id).populate('author', 'name country').lean();
// { title: 'Dune', author: { _id: ..., name: 'Frank Herbert', country: 'US' }, ... }
```

`populate` is convenient, but it is an application-side join: populating a list of 100 books issues one extra query with `$in` for all authors (not 100), but nested populates and large lists multiply queries. For hot paths, consider embedding (extended reference pattern) or `$lookup`.

**Strictness.** By default schemas are **strict**: fields not in the schema are silently dropped on save. That protects against mass assignment (a client sending `{ role: 'admin' }`), but validating request bodies at the boundary (12.3) is still the primary defence.

**Key Takeaways**

- Mongoose is an ODM that adds schemas, casting, validation, middleware, virtuals, methods and `populate` on top of the driver.
- Define a `Schema` with types and options, then compile it into a `Model` used for all queries.
- `timestamps`, `toJSON` transforms, indexes, virtuals, instance methods and statics are declared on the schema.
- Use `lean()` for read-only queries to avoid document hydration overhead.
- `populate` performs extra queries; use it with care on hot paths and large lists.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Define `Author` and `Book` models with a reference from book to author, create two authors and four books, and list books with populated author names.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Measure the time to load 10,000 books with and without `lean()` and compare heap usage with `process.memoryUsage()`. Explain the difference.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose the native driver over Mongoose?" *Hint:* weigh performance, transparency of the generated queries, team familiarity, the need for flexible document shapes, and where validation already happens (zod, `$jsonSchema`).

#### Mongoose Schemas, Validation and Middleware

**Validation in Mongoose.** Before a document is saved, Mongoose **casts** each value to its schema type and then runs **validators**. If anything fails, the save is rejected with a `ValidationError` and nothing reaches the database.

**Built-in validators.**

| Type | Validators |
|---|---|
| All | `required` |
| `Number` | `min`, `max`, `enum` |
| `String` | `minLength`, `maxLength`, `match` (regex), `enum` |
| `Date` | `min`, `max` |
| `Array` | custom validators on the array or on its items |

Each validator accepts a custom message, either as an array `[value, message]` or an object:

```javascript
const userSchema = new Schema({
  email: {
    type: String,
    required: [true, 'email is required'],
    lowercase: true,                                               // setter: normalise before validation
    trim: true,
    match: [/^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$/, 'invalid email address'],
    unique: true,                                                  // index, NOT a validator (see below)
  },
  username: { type: String, required: true, minLength: 3, maxLength: 30 },
  age: { type: Number, min: [13, 'must be at least 13'], max: 130 },
  role: { type: String, enum: { values: ['user', 'editor', 'admin'], message: '{VALUE} is not a valid role' }, default: 'user' },
  passwordHash: { type: String, required: true, select: false },   // excluded from query results unless asked for
});
```

**Custom and async validators.**

```javascript
const eventSchema = new Schema({
  startsAt: { type: Date, required: true },
  endsAt: {
    type: Date,
    required: true,
    validate: {
      validator(value) { return value > this.startsAt; },          // 'this' is the document during save()
      message: 'endsAt must be after startsAt',
    },
  },
  venueId: {
    type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
    validate: {
      async validator(id) { return !!(await Venue.exists({ _id: id })); }, // async validators return a promise
      message: 'venue does not exist',
    },
  },
});
```

**Handling validation errors.** A `ValidationError` has an `errors` object keyed by path; map it to `422` in the error handler, the same status used for schema validation in 12.3. Values that cannot be cast (for example `'abc'` for a `Number`, or an invalid ObjectId in `findById`) produce a `CastError`.

```javascript
import mongoose from 'mongoose';

// central error handler (12.2)
if (err instanceof mongoose.Error.ValidationError) {
  const details = Object.values(err.errors).map((e) => ({ path: e.path, message: e.message }));
  return res.status(422).json({ error: 'validation failed', details });
}
if (err instanceof mongoose.Error.CastError) {
  return res.status(400).json({ error: `invalid value for ${err.path}` });
}
if (err.code === 11000) {
  return res.status(409).json({ error: 'duplicate value', fields: Object.keys(err.keyValue) });
}
```

**Three caveats that cause real bugs.**

1. **`unique` is not a validator.** It only creates a unique index. Validation passes, and the duplicate is rejected later by the database with error 11000. If the collection already contains duplicates, the index build fails and uniqueness is not enforced at all.
2. **Update queries skip validators by default.** `save()` and `create()` validate; `updateOne`, `updateMany` and `findOneAndUpdate` do not, unless you pass `runValidators: true`. Even then, update validators only check the paths in the update, and in custom validators `this` is the *query*, not the document.
3. **Update queries skip document middleware.** `pre('save')` hooks do not run for `updateOne` or `findOneAndUpdate`.

```javascript
await User.updateOne({ _id: id }, { $set: { age: -5 } });                          // accepted!
await User.updateOne({ _id: id }, { $set: { age: -5 } }, { runValidators: true });  // ValidationError
// Or enable globally: mongoose.set('runValidators', true)
```

**Middleware (hooks).** Middleware are functions that run before (`pre`) or after (`post`) certain operations, like Express middleware for database operations. There are four kinds, and `this` refers to something different in each:

| Kind | Operations | `this` is |
|---|---|---|
| Document middleware | `validate`, `save`, `updateOne`/`deleteOne` called on a document | The document |
| Query middleware | `find`, `findOne`, `findOneAndUpdate`, `updateOne`, `updateMany`, `deleteOne`, `deleteMany`, `countDocuments` ... | The query |
| Aggregate middleware | `aggregate` | The aggregation object |
| Model middleware | `insertMany`, `bulkWrite` | The model |

**Example: hashing passwords on save.**

```javascript
import bcrypt from 'bcrypt';

userSchema.pre('save', async function () {
  if (!this.isModified('passwordHash')) return;                // only when the password changed
  this.passwordHash = await bcrypt.hash(this.passwordHash, 12); // async hooks: no need to call next()
});

userSchema.methods.checkPassword = function (plain) {
  return bcrypt.compare(plain, this.passwordHash);
};

// Usage: set the plain value, the hook replaces it with a hash before writing
const user = new User({ email, username, passwordHash: plainPassword });
await user.save();

// Login: passwordHash has select: false, so request it explicitly
const found = await User.findOne({ email }).select('+passwordHash');
```

Because of caveat 3, a password changed with `User.updateOne({ $set: { passwordHash: 'new' } })` would be stored **in plain text**. Either always change passwords through `save()`, or add a `pre('findOneAndUpdate')`/`pre('updateOne')` hook that hashes the value in `this.getUpdate()`.

**Example: query middleware for soft delete.**

```javascript
// Hide soft-deleted documents from every find query automatically
userSchema.pre(/^find/, function () {                          // regex: find, findOne, findOneAndUpdate, ...
  if (this.getOptions().withDeleted) return;                     // escape hatch for admin tools
  this.where({ deletedAt: null });
});

userSchema.methods.softDelete = function () {
  this.deletedAt = new Date();
  return this.save();
};
```

**Post hooks and error-handling middleware.** A `post` hook receives the result. A post hook with **three parameters** `(error, res, next)` is error-handling middleware and can translate errors:

```javascript
userSchema.post('save', function (doc) {
  logger.info({ userId: doc._id }, 'user saved');
});

userSchema.post('save', function (error, _doc, next) {
  if (error.code === 11000) next(new HttpError(409, 'email already registered'));
  else next(error);
});
```

**Plugins: reusable schema behaviour.** A plugin is a function that adds fields, hooks or methods to any schema:

```javascript
// src/db/plugins/audit.js
export function auditPlugin(schema) {
  schema.add({ createdBy: Schema.Types.ObjectId, updatedBy: Schema.Types.ObjectId });
  schema.pre('save', function () {
    const actor = this.$locals.actorId;                          // set by the service before save
    if (this.isNew) this.createdBy = actor;
    this.updatedBy = actor;
  });
}

bookSchema.plugin(auditPlugin);        // or mongoose.plugin(auditPlugin) for all schemas
```

**Where to validate?** In a layered Express application, validation happens in several places with different purposes. Request schemas (zod, 12.3) reject malformed HTTP input early with clear messages. Mongoose validators protect the data's invariants whichever code path writes it. Unique indexes and `$jsonSchema` validators are the last line of defence, enforced by the database itself under concurrency.

**Key Takeaways**

- Mongoose casts values, then runs built-in (`required`, `min`, `enum`, `match`, ...) and custom (sync or async) validators before saving.
- Map `ValidationError` to `422`, `CastError` to `400` and duplicate key errors (11000) to `409`.
- `unique` is an index, not a validator; update queries skip validators unless `runValidators` is set, and skip `save` middleware entirely.
- Document, query, aggregate and model middleware run before or after operations; `this` differs for each kind.
- Plugins package reusable fields and hooks; validation belongs at the request boundary, in the model and in the database.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add validators to a `Product` schema: required name of 2–100 characters, non-negative price, category from a fixed list. Show the `errors` object returned for an invalid product.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a user model with password hashing in `pre('save')`, then demonstrate the plain-text bug with `findOneAndUpdate` and fix it with a query hook.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A Mongoose schema declares `email: { unique: true }`, yet the database contains duplicate emails. How is that possible?" *Hint:* consider when the index is built, what happens if duplicates already existed, `autoIndex` settings in production, and the fact that `unique` is not a validator.

<a id="133-redis"></a>
### 13.3 Redis

Redis is an in-memory data structure server: it keeps strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets and more in RAM and manipulates them with atomic commands in well under a millisecond. Earlier chapters already relied on it for sessions (10.2, 12.3), distributed rate limiting (10.6, 12.3) and WebSocket fan-out (10.5). This subchapter explains how it works and how to use it well: data types and expiration, atomicity and transactions, pub/sub, caching, sessions, rate limiting and queues, persistence, high availability and the Node.js clients.

#### In-Memory Data Store Concepts

**Why keep data in memory?** Reading from RAM takes about 100 nanoseconds; a random read from an SSD takes about 100 microseconds, and a database query including network, parsing, planning and disk is typically 1–10 milliseconds. An in-memory store removes disk access from the request path, so a whole command round trip (mostly network time) completes in a fraction of a millisecond. That makes it ideal for data that is read or updated on almost every request: sessions, counters, caches, rate limits.

An analogy: the database is a warehouse, safe and enormous but a drive away. Redis is the shelf behind the counter: small and quick to reach, holding the items asked for most often.

**What Redis is.** Redis (REmote DIctionary Server), created by Salvatore Sanfilippo in 2009, is a server that maps **keys** to **typed values** and exposes commands that operate on those values on the server side:

```text
 client                      Redis server (one process, data in RAM)
 ---------------------       ------------------------------------------------
 INCR page:views    ---->    key "page:views" -> integer 41 -> becomes 42
                    <----    (integer) 42
 LPUSH jobs "email:17" -->   key "jobs" -> list ["email:16"] -> ["email:17","email:16"]
 ZADD lb 870 "ada"  ---->    key "lb" -> sorted set {ada:870, bob:640, ...}
```

Because operations like "increment", "append to list" or "add to sorted set" run *inside* Redis, many clients can share the same structures without race conditions (see "Atomic Operations and Transactions").

**The single-threaded execution model.** Redis executes commands one at a time on a single main thread, using an event loop much like Node.js (11.3). There are no locks, and every individual command is atomic: no other command can observe a half-applied change. Since Redis 6, network reading and writing can use extra I/O threads, but command execution remains sequential. The consequence: **one slow command blocks everyone**. Commands that touch every element of a large structure (`KEYS *`, `SMEMBERS` on a set of millions, `HGETALL` on a huge hash, `FLUSHALL` without `ASYNC`) can freeze the server for seconds. Use `SCAN`-family commands to iterate incrementally.

**Memory is the limit.** All data must fit in RAM. Configure a ceiling and an **eviction policy**, which decides what happens when the ceiling is reached:

| Policy | Behaviour when `maxmemory` is reached | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `noeviction` (default) | Writes fail with an OOM error | Data that must not disappear (queues, sessions) |
| `allkeys-lru` | Evict the least recently used key | General-purpose cache |
| `allkeys-lfu` | Evict the least frequently used key | Cache with stable popular items |
| `volatile-lru` / `volatile-lfu` | Same, but only among keys with a TTL | Mixed cache + persistent data in one instance |
| `volatile-ttl` | Evict keys closest to expiring | Caches with meaningful TTLs |
| `allkeys-random` / `volatile-random` | Evict randomly | Rarely the best choice |

```text
# redis.conf
maxmemory 2gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
```

Mixing a cache (evictable) with sessions or queues (not evictable) in one instance is risky: under memory pressure the cache policy may evict the data you needed to keep. Use separate instances or logical separation by policy.

**Durability.** "In memory" does not mean "lost on restart": Redis can write snapshots and an append-only log to disk (see "Persistence with RDB and AOF"). But Redis is usually **not the system of record** (13.1): it holds data that can be recomputed or that is acceptable to lose in a disaster.

**The ecosystem and licensing.** In 2024 Redis changed its licence from BSD to source-available licences; the Linux Foundation then forked the last BSD version as **Valkey**, which major cloud providers adopted. Redis 8 (2025) added the open-source AGPLv3 as a licensing option and bundled former modules (JSON, search, time series, probabilistic structures). Valkey and Redis remain protocol-compatible for everything in this chapter, and the same clients work with both. Managed offerings include Amazon ElastiCache and MemoryDB, Google Memorystore, Azure Managed Redis, Redis Cloud and Upstash.

**Trying it out.**

```bash
docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8          # or: valkey/valkey:8
docker exec -it redis redis-cli                          # interactive client

127.0.0.1:6379> SET greeting "hello"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET greeting
"hello"
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO memory                              # used_memory_human, maxmemory, fragmentation
127.0.0.1:6379> exit

docker exec -it redis redis-cli --latency                # measure round-trip latency continuously
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Redis keeps typed data structures in RAM and serves commands in well under a millisecond.
- Commands execute one at a time on a single thread: each command is atomic, but slow commands block everyone; iterate with `SCAN`.
- All data must fit in memory; set `maxmemory` and an eviction policy that matches the data's purpose.
- Redis can persist to disk but is usually not the system of record.
- Valkey is a protocol-compatible open-source fork; clients and commands in this chapter work with both.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Start Redis with Docker, set and read a few keys with `redis-cli`, and inspect `INFO memory` and `INFO stats`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Set `maxmemory 10mb` with `allkeys-lru`, write keys in a loop until memory is full, and observe evictions in `INFO stats` (`evicted_keys`). Repeat with `noeviction` and observe the error.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Redis is single-threaded. How can it handle hundreds of thousands of operations per second?" *Hint:* consider in-memory data, non-blocking I/O multiplexing, no locking overhead, simple O(1) operations and pipelining.

#### Keys, Expiration and TTL

**Keys.** A Redis key is a binary-safe string (up to 512 MB, but keep keys short). There are no tables or collections, so structure comes from **naming conventions**. The common convention uses colons to build a hierarchy:

```text
 <app>:<object-type>:<id>[:<field>]

 shop:user:42                 hash with the user's profile
 shop:user:42:cart            hash sku -> quantity
 shop:product:9:views         counter
 sess:Yp3x...                 session (prefix set by connect-redis)
 ratelimit:login:203.0.113.7  rate-limit counter
 cache:v3:book:66fe1c...      cached JSON, with a version for mass invalidation
```

A consistent prefix per feature makes keys discoverable (`SCAN MATCH shop:user:*`), allows per-feature memory analysis, and enables ACL rules that restrict a client to some prefixes.

**Generic key commands.**

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `EXISTS key [key ...]` | Number of the given keys that exist |
| `DEL key [key ...]` | Delete synchronously |
| `UNLINK key [key ...]` | Delete, freeing memory in a background thread (prefer for large values) |
| `TYPE key` | `string`, `list`, `hash`, `set`, `zset`, `stream` |
| `RENAME key newkey` | Rename (overwrites `newkey`) |
| `SCAN cursor MATCH pattern COUNT n` | Iterate keys incrementally without blocking |
| `KEYS pattern` | List matching keys: **blocks the server**, never use in production |
| `OBJECT ENCODING key`, `MEMORY USAGE key` | Inspect internal representation and size |

```bash
# Iterate safely: SCAN returns a new cursor and a batch; stop when the cursor is 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0 MATCH shop:user:* COUNT 100
1) "1792"                       # next cursor
2) 1) "shop:user:42"
   2) "shop:user:7"
127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 1792 MATCH shop:user:* COUNT 100
...
```

**Expiration (time to live).** Any key can be given a **TTL**, after which Redis deletes it automatically. This is one of Redis's most valuable features: caches refresh themselves, sessions end, rate-limit windows reset, and one-time tokens disappear, all without cleanup jobs.

```bash
SET otp:42 "731904" EX 300        # set value and expire in 300 seconds, atomically
TTL otp:42                        # (integer) 297: seconds remaining
PTTL otp:42                       # milliseconds remaining
EXPIRE cart:42 86400              # set/replace the TTL of an existing key (1 day)
EXPIREAT promo:summer 1790000000  # expire at a Unix timestamp
PERSIST cart:42                   # remove the TTL: the key lives forever
TTL no-such-key                   # (integer) -2: key does not exist
SET counter 0
TTL counter                       # (integer) -1: key exists, no TTL
```

**SET options worth memorising.**

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `EX seconds` / `PX milliseconds` | Set a TTL together with the value |
| `EXAT` / `PXAT timestamp` | Expire at an absolute Unix time |
| `NX` | Only set if the key does **not** exist (locks, "first writer wins") |
| `XX` | Only set if the key **already** exists |
| `KEEPTTL` | Keep the existing TTL instead of clearing it |
| `GET` | Return the old value |

`EXPIRE` also accepts conditions (Redis 7+): `NX` (only if no TTL), `XX` (only if a TTL exists), `GT` / `LT` (only if the new TTL is greater/less).

**TTL rules that cause bugs.**

- **Overwriting a key with `SET` removes its TTL** (unless `KEEPTTL`). A cached value refreshed without `EX` becomes permanent.
- Commands that *modify* a value (`INCR`, `LPUSH`, `HSET`, `SADD`) keep the existing TTL.
- `RENAME` transfers the TTL to the new name.
- The TTL applies to the **whole key**. A hash cannot normally expire individual fields; Redis 7.4 added per-field TTLs for hashes (`HEXPIRE`), but separate keys remain the portable approach.

**How expiration works.** Redis combines two mechanisms:

```text
 passive (lazy):  when a client accesses a key, Redis checks its expiry and deletes it if past due
 active:          about 10 times per second, Redis samples random keys with a TTL and deletes the expired ones;
                  if many sampled keys were expired, it repeats immediately
```

So expired keys are never *returned*, but they may occupy memory briefly. Replicas do not expire keys on their own: they wait for the primary to send a `DEL`, which keeps replicas consistent.

**Avoiding synchronized expiry.** If 10,000 cache keys are written at the same moment with the same TTL, they also expire at the same moment and the database receives 10,000 queries at once. Add **jitter**:

```javascript
const ttl = 3600 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 300);   // 60-65 minutes
await redis.set(key, value, { EX: ttl });
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Keys are strings; use a consistent `app:type:id:field` naming convention and keep keys short.
- Iterate with `SCAN`, never `KEYS`, and delete large values with `UNLINK`.
- `SET ... EX/PX` sets a value and TTL atomically; `NX`/`XX` make writes conditional; `TTL` returns `-1` (no expiry) or `-2` (missing).
- `SET` without `KEEPTTL` clears an existing TTL; modifying commands keep it.
- Expired keys are removed lazily and by active sampling; add jitter to TTLs to avoid mass expiry.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a one-time password key valid for 5 minutes, check its TTL, overwrite it with a plain `SET` and check the TTL again. Explain the result.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a Node.js script that deletes all keys matching `cache:v2:*` using `SCAN` and `UNLINK` in batches, and measure how long it takes for 1 million keys.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is `KEYS *` dangerous in production when `SCAN` is not?" *Hint:* relate the single-threaded execution model to an O(N) command, and explain the guarantees `SCAN` gives (and does not give) about duplicates and concurrent changes.

#### Data Types: Strings, Lists, Hashes and Sets

**Why typed values?** A plain key-value store would make you `GET` a JSON array, modify it in your application and `SET` it back: two round trips and a race condition. Redis values have **types** with their own commands, so the change happens atomically on the server. Choosing the right type is the most important Redis design decision.

**Strings.** The basic type: a byte sequence up to 512 MB. It holds text, serialised JSON, binary data, or a number that Redis can increment.

```bash
SET user:42:name "Ada"
GET user:42:name                       # "Ada"
MSET a 1 b 2                           # several keys in one command
MGET a b missing                       # 1) "1" 2) "2" 3) (nil)
INCR page:home:views                   # (integer) 1: atomic, creates the key at 0 if missing
INCRBY page:home:views 10              # (integer) 11
INCRBYFLOAT balance:42 2.5
APPEND log:today "line\n"
SETRANGE / GETRANGE                    # byte ranges
```

Strings also power two compact structures: **bitmaps** (`SETBIT`, `BITCOUNT`: one bit per user ID, for example daily active users in 12 MB for 100 million users) and **HyperLogLog** (`PFADD`, `PFCOUNT`: approximate count of distinct items with about 0.81% error in at most 12 KB).

**Lists.** Ordered sequences of strings, implemented so that pushing and popping at both ends is O(1). Use them for queues, stacks, recent-items feeds and capped logs.

```bash
LPUSH notifications:42 "n3" "n2"       # push to the head (left)
RPUSH notifications:42 "n4"            # push to the tail (right)
LRANGE notifications:42 0 -1           # whole list: n2 n3 n4  (indexes; -1 = last)
LLEN notifications:42
LPOP notifications:42                  # remove and return the head
LTRIM notifications:42 0 99            # keep only the first 100 elements (capped list)

# Blocking pop: wait up to 5 s for an element (a worker waiting for jobs)
BLPOP jobs 5
# Atomically move an element to another list (reliable queue, see "Rate Limiting and Job Queues")
LMOVE jobs jobs:processing LEFT RIGHT
```

Accessing the middle of a long list (`LINDEX`, `LINSERT`) is O(N); lists are not arrays.

**Hashes.** A map of field-value pairs stored under one key, like a small object. Ideal for records whose fields are read or updated individually, and very memory-efficient when small.

```bash
HSET user:42 name "Ada" email "ada@example.com" logins 0
HGET user:42 email                     # "ada@example.com"
HMGET user:42 name email
HINCRBY user:42 logins 1               # atomic per-field counter
HGETALL user:42                        # all fields (fine for small hashes)
HDEL user:42 email
HEXISTS user:42 email                  # 0
HLEN user:42

HINCRBY cart:42 sku-9 2                # shopping cart: field = SKU, value = quantity
```

**Hash or JSON string?** Store an object as a hash when fields are updated independently (counters, partial updates) or read partially. Store it as a JSON string when it is always read and written whole and has nested structure. (Redis 8 also includes a native JSON type with path-level commands.)

**Sets.** Unordered collections of unique strings with O(1) add, remove and membership test, plus server-side set algebra.

```bash
SADD post:7:likes "u42" "u17"          # (integer) 2: number of NEW members
SADD post:7:likes "u42"                # (integer) 0: already present
SISMEMBER post:7:likes "u42"           # 1
SCARD post:7:likes                     # 2: cardinality
SREM post:7:likes "u17"
SMEMBERS post:7:likes                  # all members (use SSCAN for big sets)

SADD user:42:follows u1 u2 u3
SADD user:17:follows u2 u3 u9
SINTER user:42:follows user:17:follows # u2 u3: follows in common
SDIFF user:17:follows user:42:follows  # u9: suggestion for user 42
SRANDMEMBER giveaway:entrants 3        # pick 3 random winners (SPOP also removes them)
```

**Choosing a type.**

| Need | Type | Example key |
|---|---|---|
| Single value, counter, cached JSON | String | `cache:book:9`, `views:post:7` |
| Queue, recent N items, timeline | List | `queue:emails`, `feed:42` |
| Object with independently updated fields | Hash | `user:42`, `cart:42` |
| Unique membership, tags, "who liked" | Set | `post:7:likes`, `online:users` |
| Ranking, ordering by score or time | Sorted set (next topic) | `leaderboard:2026-10` |
| Append-only event log with consumer groups | Stream | `events:orders` |
| Distinct counts at huge scale | HyperLogLog | `uniques:2026-10-03` |

**Complexity matters.** Redis documentation lists the time complexity of every command. Commands that are O(1) or O(log N) are safe at any size. O(N) commands on large values (`SMEMBERS`, `HGETALL`, `LRANGE 0 -1`) should be replaced by their `SCAN` variants (`SSCAN`, `HSCAN`, `ZSCAN`) or bounded ranges.

**Key Takeaways**

- Typed values let Redis modify data atomically on the server instead of read-modify-write in the application.
- Strings hold text, JSON or numbers (`INCR`); bitmaps and HyperLogLog are compact counting structures built on strings.
- Lists are fast at both ends: queues, feeds and capped logs with `LTRIM`; blocking pops wait for data.
- Hashes store objects with independently updated fields; sets store unique members with fast membership and set algebra.
- Check command complexity and avoid O(N) commands on large values.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Model a shopping cart with a hash: add items, change a quantity with `HINCRBY`, remove an item and list the cart.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement "recently viewed products" (last 10, no duplicates, most recent first) with a list, using `LREM`, `LPUSH` and `LTRIM` in one `MULTI`. Then discuss why a sorted set might be better.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you count unique daily visitors for a site with 50 million users using little memory?" *Hint:* compare a set, a bitmap keyed by user ID, and HyperLogLog in terms of memory, accuracy and the ability to list visitors.

#### Sorted Sets and Ranking Use Cases

**The idea.** A **sorted set** (`zset`) is a set of unique members where each member has a numeric **score**, and members are kept ordered by score. You can add or update a member in O(log N), get its rank in O(log N), and read any range by rank or score. Doing that in a relational database for millions of rows on every request ("what is my position on the leaderboard?") is expensive; in Redis it is a single fast command.

Internally, large sorted sets combine a **skip list** (for ordered traversal and ranges) with a **hash table** (for O(1) score lookup by member); small ones use a compact list.

```text
 leaderboard (ordered by score, ascending internally)
 rank (ZRANK)    0       1        2        3
 member         bob     carol    ada      dan
 score          640     720      870      910
 rank (ZREVRANK) 3       2        1        0     <- "position" in a high-score table
```

**Core commands.**

```bash
ZADD lb 870 ada 640 bob 720 carol 910 dan   # add members with scores
ZINCRBY lb 50 bob                            # bob: 690 (atomic, creates member if missing)
ZSCORE lb ada                                # "870"
ZREVRANK lb ada                              # (integer) 1: second place (0-based)
ZCARD lb                                     # 4

# Top 3 (highest first), with scores
ZRANGE lb 0 2 REV WITHSCORES                 # dan 910, ada 870, carol 720

# By score range: players between 700 and 900
ZRANGE lb 700 900 BYSCORE WITHSCORES
ZCOUNT lb 700 900                            # how many

# Remove
ZREM lb bob
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE lb -inf 100                 # drop low scores
ZREMRANGEBYRANK lb 0 -1001                   # keep only the top 1000

# Conditional updates (ZADD flags)
ZADD lb GT 900 ada                           # only update if the new score is GREATER (keep personal best)
ZADD lb NX 0 newbie                          # only add new members, never update existing ones
```

When scores are equal, members are ordered lexicographically. Scores are 64-bit floating-point numbers, so integers up to 2^53 are exact.

**Use case 1: leaderboards.**

```javascript
// node-redis
export async function recordScore(gameId, userId, score) {
  // GT flag: only raise the score (keep personal best); raw command because option syntax differs across client versions
  await redis.sendCommand(['ZADD', `lb:${gameId}`, 'GT', String(score), userId]);
}

export async function topTen(gameId) {
  return redis.zRangeWithScores(`lb:${gameId}`, 0, 9, { REV: true });        // [{ value, score }, ...]
}

export async function myPosition(gameId, userId) {
  const rank = await redis.zRevRank(`lb:${gameId}`, userId);
  return rank === null ? null : rank + 1;                                     // 1-based for display
}

// "Players around me": 2 above and 2 below
export async function neighbours(gameId, userId) {
  const rank = await redis.zRevRank(`lb:${gameId}`, userId);
  if (rank === null) return [];
  return redis.zRangeWithScores(`lb:${gameId}`, Math.max(0, rank - 2), rank + 2, { REV: true });
}
```

Periodic leaderboards use one key per period (`lb:weekly:2026-W40`) with a TTL, and `ZUNIONSTORE` can combine them (for example, a monthly board from weekly ones, summing scores).

**Use case 2: time-ordered data (score = timestamp).**

```bash
# Recent activity per user, scored by Unix milliseconds
ZADD activity:42 1790000000123 "login"
ZADD activity:42 1790000050000 "order:991"
ZRANGE activity:42 +inf 1789990000000 BYSCORE REV LIMIT 0 20   # latest 20 since a time
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE activity:42 -inf 1787400000000                # drop entries older than 30 days
```

**Use case 3: delayed jobs and scheduling.** Store job IDs scored by the time they should run; a worker periodically takes the jobs whose score is in the past. `ZPOPMIN` removes the earliest atomically.

```javascript
await redis.zAdd('delayed', { score: Date.now() + 15 * 60_000, value: 'reminder:991' });  // run in 15 min

// worker loop (simplified; a Lua script makes "read due jobs and remove them" atomic across workers)
const due = await redis.zRangeByScore('delayed', 0, Date.now(), { LIMIT: { offset: 0, count: 100 } });
```

**Use case 4: trending and top-N with decay.** Increment a score per view (`ZINCRBY trending:2026-10-03 1 post:7`) in hourly keys, then `ZUNIONSTORE` the last 24 hours with `WEIGHTS` that give older hours less weight.

**Use case 5: autocomplete.** When all members have the same score, sorted sets order them lexicographically, and `ZRANGE ... BYLEX` returns members with a given prefix:

```bash
ZADD autocomplete 0 "redis" 0 "react" 0 "relational" 0 "rest"
ZRANGE autocomplete "[re" "[re\xff" BYLEX LIMIT 0 10      # react, redis, relational, rest
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A sorted set keeps unique members ordered by a floating-point score; updates, ranks and range reads are O(log N).
- `ZADD` (with `GT`, `LT`, `NX`, `XX` flags), `ZINCRBY`, `ZRANGE` (with `REV`, `BYSCORE`, `BYLEX`, `LIMIT`) and `ZREVRANK` cover most needs.
- Leaderboards, "around me" views, time-ordered feeds, delayed jobs, trending lists and prefix autocomplete are natural fits.
- Use one key per period with a TTL, and combine periods with `ZUNIONSTORE`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a leaderboard for five players, update two scores, and print the top three and one player's position.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a sliding "last 24 hours" trending list for blog posts using hourly sorted sets and `ZUNIONSTORE` with weights, and expose it as `GET /api/trending`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you show a user's global rank among 100 million players in real time?" *Hint:* compare `COUNT(*) WHERE score > ?` in SQL with `ZREVRANK`, and discuss memory per member and sharding by score range when one instance is not enough.

#### Atomic Operations and Transactions

**The concurrency problem.** A web application usually runs several processes (11.6, cluster and containers), each handling many requests concurrently. If two of them read a value, modify it in JavaScript and write it back, one update can be lost:

```text
 process A: GET stock -> 1                     process B: GET stock -> 1
 process A: SET stock 0  (sold one)            process B: SET stock 0  (sold one)
 result: 2 items sold, stock says 0, real stock -1
```

Redis provides four tools to avoid this, from simplest to most powerful.

**1. Single commands are atomic.** Because commands run one at a time, a command that reads and modifies in one step is safe:

```bash
DECRBY stock:sku-9 1            # atomic decrement: returns the new value
SET lock:report "worker-3" NX PX 30000   # atomic "set if absent": only one worker gets the lock
HINCRBY cart:42 sku-9 1
SADD seen:emails "a@b.c"        # returns 1 if new, 0 if already present: atomic de-duplication
```

Prefer designs that need only one command.

**2. `MULTI` / `EXEC` transactions.** Commands sent between `MULTI` and `EXEC` are queued and then executed **sequentially without any other client's command in between**:

```bash
MULTI
INCR user:42:orders
LPUSH user:42:recent "order:991"
LTRIM user:42:recent 0 9
EXEC
# 1) (integer) 8
# 2) (integer) 11
# 3) OK
```

Redis transactions differ from SQL transactions in two important ways:

- **No rollback.** If a command fails at runtime (for example `INCR` on a non-numeric value), the others still execute. Only errors detected while queueing (syntax errors) abort the whole transaction.
- **No reads inside.** Commands are queued, so you cannot use a value read inside the transaction to decide what to write later in the same transaction.

**3. `WATCH`: optimistic locking.** For read-modify-write logic, `WATCH` keys before reading. If any watched key changes before `EXEC`, the transaction is discarded (`EXEC` returns null) and you retry:

```javascript
// node-redis: transfer loyalty points without going negative
async function transferPoints(from, to, amount) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const conn = redis.duplicate();                          // WATCH state is per connection: use a dedicated one
    await conn.connect();
    try {
      await conn.watch(`points:${from}`);
      const balance = Number(await conn.get(`points:${from}`) ?? 0);
      if (balance < amount) throw new Error('insufficient points');
      const result = await conn.multi()
        .decrBy(`points:${from}`, amount)
        .incrBy(`points:${to}`, amount)
        .exec();                                             // aborted if points:{from} changed since WATCH
      if (result !== null) return;                           // committed
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.name !== 'WatchError') throw err;              // node-redis throws WatchError on abort
    } finally {
      await conn.close();                                    // node-redis v5 (v4: quit())
    }
  }
  throw new Error('too much contention, try again');
}
```

`WATCH` is per connection, which is why this example uses a dedicated connection; in production, node-redis's `executeIsolated` (v4) or a client pool (v5) avoid creating a connection per call. This complexity is one reason Lua scripts are often preferred.

**4. Lua scripts and functions.** A Lua script runs **atomically** on the server: no other command executes while it runs. It can read, branch and write, which makes it the most flexible tool for atomic logic:

```lua
-- transfer-points.lua
-- KEYS[1] = points:from, KEYS[2] = points:to, ARGV[1] = amount
local balance = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
local amount = tonumber(ARGV[1])
if balance < amount then
  return redis.error_reply('INSUFFICIENT_POINTS')
end
redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], amount)
redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[2], amount)
return balance - amount
```

```javascript
// node-redis: run the script with its keys and arguments (all arguments travel as strings)
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const transferLua = await readFile(new URL('./transfer-points.lua', import.meta.url), 'utf8');

const remaining = await redis.eval(transferLua, {
  keys: ['points:42', 'points:17'],
  arguments: ['100'],
});

// Optimisation: load once, then call by SHA1 digest to avoid resending the source
const sha = await redis.scriptLoad(transferLua);
await redis.evalSha(sha, { keys: ['points:42', 'points:17'], arguments: ['100'] });
```

If the server restarts, its script cache is emptied and `EVALSHA` fails with `NOSCRIPT`; reload the script and retry. node-redis's `scripts` option and ioredis's `defineCommand` (see "Redis Clients in Node.js") handle this automatically.

Rules for scripts: pass every key the script touches in `KEYS` (required for Redis Cluster routing), keep scripts short (they block the server while running), and make them deterministic. Redis 7 also offers **functions** (`FUNCTION LOAD`, `FCALL`), which are named, persisted libraries of scripts.

**Pipelining is not a transaction.** **Pipelining** sends many commands without waiting for each reply, saving network round trips. It improves throughput dramatically but does not make the commands atomic: other clients' commands can interleave.

```text
 without pipelining:  cmd1 -> reply1 -> cmd2 -> reply2 -> cmd3 -> reply3   (3 round trips)
 with pipelining:     cmd1, cmd2, cmd3 -> reply1, reply2, reply3            (1 round trip)
```

node-redis pipelines automatically: commands issued in the same event-loop tick are sent together, so `await Promise.all([redis.get(a), redis.get(b)])` uses one round trip.

**Distributed locks.** `SET lock:name <random-token> NX PX 30000` acquires a lock that expires automatically if the holder crashes. Release it only if you still own it, which requires a script (a plain `DEL` could delete a lock another process acquired after yours expired):

```lua
-- release: delete only if the token matches
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
end
return 0
```

A Redis lock is fine for efficiency (avoid doing the same work twice). For correctness-critical mutual exclusion, remember that a paused process can outlive its lock's TTL; protect the resource itself with a fencing token or database constraint.

**Key Takeaways**

- Each Redis command is atomic; design operations to need a single command where possible (`INCR`, `SET NX`, `HINCRBY`, `SADD`).
- `MULTI`/`EXEC` executes queued commands without interleaving, but has no rollback and cannot read inside the transaction.
- `WATCH` adds optimistic locking: the transaction aborts if a watched key changed, and the client retries.
- Lua scripts (and Redis 7 functions) run atomically with full read-branch-write logic; pass all keys in `KEYS`.
- Pipelining reduces round trips but is not atomic; distributed locks need tokens, TTLs and safe release.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use `MULTI`/`EXEC` to increment a counter and append to a capped list in one transaction. Then make one command fail at runtime and observe that the other still applies.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a "reserve stock" Lua script that decrements `stock:<sku>` only if enough units remain and records the reservation in a hash, and test it with 100 concurrent requests for 10 units.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between a Redis transaction and a SQL transaction?" *Hint:* compare atomicity, isolation, rollback behaviour and the ability to read inside the transaction; mention `WATCH` and Lua.

#### Publish and Subscribe Messaging

**The idea.** **Publish/subscribe (pub/sub)** decouples senders from receivers: publishers send messages to a named **channel** without knowing who is listening, and every client currently subscribed to that channel receives a copy. It is like a radio broadcast: the station transmits, anyone tuned in hears it, and anyone who was not tuned in misses it.

```text
                         channel "chat:room:7"
 publisher (instance A) ---PUBLISH---> [ Redis ] ---> subscriber: instance A
                                           |-------> subscriber: instance B
                                           +-------> subscriber: instance C
```

**Commands.**

```bash
# terminal 1
SUBSCRIBE chat:room:7 notifications           # the connection enters subscriber mode
PSUBSCRIBE chat:room:*                        # pattern subscription

# terminal 2
PUBLISH chat:room:7 '{"user":"ada","text":"hi"}'
# (integer) 2   <- number of clients that received it (0 if nobody is listening)
```

**Delivery semantics.** Redis pub/sub is **fire-and-forget (at-most-once)**:

- Messages are not stored. A subscriber that is disconnected, restarting or slow simply misses them.
- There are no acknowledgements or retries.
- A subscriber that cannot keep up has its output buffer grow until Redis disconnects it.

That is acceptable for ephemeral real-time signals (chat messages already persisted in a database, "user is typing", cache invalidation broadcasts, live dashboard updates) and unacceptable for work that must not be lost (orders, emails to send). For those, use lists or streams (see "Rate Limiting and Job Queues").

**Subscriber connections are special.** A connection in subscribe mode can only issue subscription commands (with the classic RESP2 protocol), so applications use a **dedicated connection** for subscribing:

```javascript
// node-redis: fan out WebSocket messages across several server instances (10.5)
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const pub = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
const sub = pub.duplicate();                         // second connection, same options
await Promise.all([pub.connect(), sub.connect()]);

// Every instance subscribes; each delivers to ITS OWN connected sockets
await sub.subscribe('chat:room:7', (message, channel) => {
  const event = JSON.parse(message);
  for (const ws of localSocketsInRoom('7')) ws.send(JSON.stringify(event));
});

// Pattern subscriptions receive the concrete channel name too
await sub.pSubscribe('chat:room:*', (message, channel) => {
  const roomId = channel.split(':').at(-1);
  broadcastLocally(roomId, message);
});

// Any instance can publish when one of its clients sends a message
export async function sendToRoom(roomId, event) {
  await saveMessage(roomId, event);                  // persist first: pub/sub is not storage
  await pub.publish(`chat:room:${roomId}`, JSON.stringify(event));
}
```

This is exactly what the Socket.IO Redis adapter (10.5) does internally.

**Cache invalidation across instances.** Applications that keep a small in-process cache (an LRU map in each Node.js instance) can broadcast "key X changed" on a channel so every instance drops its local copy. Missed messages are tolerable if local entries also have a short TTL.

**Keyspace notifications.** Redis can publish events about its own keys (set, expired, evicted, ...) on special channels, enabled with `notify-keyspace-events`:

```bash
CONFIG SET notify-keyspace-events Ex          # E: keyevent channels, x: expired events
SUBSCRIBE __keyevent@0__:expired              # receive the names of keys as they expire
```

They are useful for debugging and some automation, but they inherit pub/sub's at-most-once semantics, and expiry events fire when Redis actually deletes the key, not at the exact TTL instant.

**Sharded pub/sub.** In Redis Cluster, classic `PUBLISH` is broadcast to every node, which limits scalability. Redis 7 added **sharded pub/sub** (`SPUBLISH`, `SSUBSCRIBE`), where a channel lives on the node owning its hash slot.

**Pub/sub vs streams vs lists.**

| Feature | Pub/sub | List (queue) | Stream |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delivery | To all current subscribers | To one consumer | To each consumer group; one consumer per group |
| Persistence | None | Until popped | Until trimmed |
| Missed while offline | Lost | Kept | Kept; consumers resume from their last ID |
| Acknowledgement | No | Manual pattern (`LMOVE`) | Built in (`XACK`, pending list) |
| Typical use | Real-time fan-out, notifications | Simple work queues | Event logs, reliable queues, multiple consumer groups |

**Key Takeaways**

- Pub/sub delivers each message to every client currently subscribed to the channel; patterns subscribe to many channels at once.
- Delivery is at-most-once with no storage or acknowledgements: offline or slow subscribers miss messages.
- Subscribers need a dedicated connection; publishers can use the normal client.
- Use pub/sub for ephemeral fan-out (WebSocket scaling, cache invalidation), and lists or streams for work that must not be lost.
- Keyspace notifications publish key events; sharded pub/sub scales channels in Redis Cluster.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open two `redis-cli` sessions, subscribe in one and publish in the other. Then publish while the subscriber is disconnected and observe that the message is lost.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run two instances of a WebSocket chat server on different ports and use Redis pub/sub so that messages sent to one instance reach clients of the other.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Would you use Redis pub/sub to send order confirmation emails?" *Hint:* consider what happens when the email worker restarts, scaling to several workers (does each get a copy?), and how streams with consumer groups or a job queue solve both problems.

#### Caching Strategies and Invalidation

**Why cache.** A **cache** stores the result of an expensive operation (a database query, an external API call, a rendered fragment) so that later requests can reuse it. When the same data is read far more often than it changes, a cache reduces latency (Redis answers in under a millisecond), lowers load on the database, and absorbs traffic spikes. Phil Karlton's famous quip applies: "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things." Adding a cache is easy; keeping it correct is the hard part.

**Where caches live.** Redis is one layer among several (Chapter 10 covered HTTP caching):

```text
 browser cache --> CDN / reverse proxy --> application (in-process LRU) --> Redis --> database
 (Cache-Control)   (shared HTTP cache)     (per instance, fastest)          (shared)  (system of record)
```

**Caching patterns.**

| Pattern | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cache-aside** (lazy loading) | App checks cache; on miss, reads DB and fills cache | Simple; caches only what is used; cache failure is non-fatal | First request is slow; stale until TTL or invalidation |
| **Read-through** | Cache library loads from DB itself on miss | Clean application code | Needs a loader abstraction |
| **Write-through** | Every write goes to the cache and the DB synchronously | Cache always fresh for written keys | Write latency; caches data never read |
| **Write-behind** (write-back) | Writes go to cache; flushed to DB asynchronously | Very fast writes | Data loss risk; complex |
| **Refresh-ahead** | Popular keys refreshed before they expire | No miss latency for hot keys | Wasted work on keys no longer needed |

**Cache-aside in practice.** Cache-aside is the default choice for web applications:

```text
 GET /books/9
   1. GET cache:book:9 from Redis
   2. hit?  -> return it
   3. miss  -> query MongoDB, SET cache:book:9 <json> EX 600, return it

 PATCH /books/9
   1. update MongoDB (system of record)
   2. DEL cache:book:9   (next read repopulates it)
```

```javascript
// src/lib/cache.js: a small cache-aside helper
export function createCache(redis, { prefix = 'cache:v1:', defaultTtl = 600 } = {}) {
  return {
    async getOrLoad(key, loader, ttl = defaultTtl) {
      const fullKey = prefix + key;
      try {
        const cached = await redis.get(fullKey);
        if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);           // hit
      } catch (err) {
        logger.warn({ err }, 'cache read failed');                // Redis down: degrade to the database
      }
      const value = await loader();                               // miss: load from the system of record
      if (value !== undefined) {
        const jitter = Math.floor(Math.random() * ttl * 0.1);     // avoid synchronized expiry
        redis.set(fullKey, JSON.stringify(value), { EX: ttl + jitter })
          .catch((err) => logger.warn({ err }, 'cache write failed'));  // do not fail the request
      }
      return value;
    },
    invalidate: (key) => redis.unlink(prefix + key),
  };
}

// Usage in the books service (12.3)
const cache = createCache(redis);

export const bookService = {
  get: (id) => cache.getOrLoad(`book:${id}`, () => repo.findById(id)),
  async update(id, changes) {
    const book = await repo.update(id, changes);
    await cache.invalidate(`book:${id}`);                          // after the DB write succeeded
    return book;
  },
};
```

**Invalidation strategies.**

1. **TTL only.** Accept data up to N seconds stale. Simple and robust; pick N per data type (exchange rates: 60 s; product descriptions: 1 h).
2. **Delete on write.** After updating the database, delete the cache key. Delete rather than overwrite: overwriting races with concurrent writers, and deleting lets the next read load the true value.
3. **Versioned keys.** Include a version in the key prefix (`cache:v3:`). Bumping the version (on deploys that change the cached shape, or to flush a whole category) makes old keys unreachable; they expire on their own.
4. **Tag-based invalidation.** Keep a set of keys per tag (`SADD tag:author:17 cache:v1:book:9 ...`) and delete all of them when the author changes.
5. **Event-driven.** A change stream (13.2) or message triggers invalidation, which also catches writes made by other services or scripts.

**The race in cache-aside.** Even "update DB, then delete cache" has a rare race: a reader misses, reads the old value from the DB, the writer updates the DB and deletes the key, then the reader writes the *old* value into the cache. A TTL bounds how long that stale value survives; for stricter needs, delay a second delete (delete again a few hundred milliseconds later) or use versioned values.

**Cache stampede (dogpile).** When a popular key expires, hundreds of concurrent requests miss at once and all hit the database with the same expensive query. Mitigations:

| Technique | Idea |
|---|---|
| Request coalescing (single-flight) | In each process, concurrent misses for the same key share one loader promise |
| Lock on miss | `SET lock:key token NX PX 5000`; only the winner recomputes, others wait briefly or serve stale data |
| Stale-while-revalidate | Store the value with a "soft" expiry; after it passes, serve the stale value and refresh in the background |
| Probabilistic early refresh | Each request refreshes early with a probability that grows as expiry approaches |
| TTL jitter | Spread expiries of keys written together |

```javascript
// Single-flight: concurrent misses in this process share one database query
const inFlight = new Map();
async function loadOnce(key, loader) {
  if (inFlight.has(key)) return inFlight.get(key);
  const promise = loader().finally(() => inFlight.delete(key));
  inFlight.set(key, promise);
  return promise;
}
```

**Negative caching.** If many requests ask for something that does not exist (`/books/does-not-exist`, or an attacker probing IDs), every request misses and hits the database. Cache the "not found" result too, with a short TTL, using a sentinel value.

**What not to cache.** Data that must be exactly current (balances during a payment), data unique to one request, values that are cheaper to compute than to fetch, and personal data without thinking about who can read the cache and when it is deleted.

**Measure.** Track hit ratio (`INFO stats`: `keyspace_hits`, `keyspace_misses`, or your own metrics per key prefix), latency with and without the cache, and memory. A cache with a 20% hit ratio adds a network round trip to 80% of requests for little benefit.

**Key Takeaways**

- Caches cut latency and database load for data read far more often than it changes; invalidation is the hard part.
- Cache-aside is the default pattern: read the cache, load from the database on a miss, and invalidate after writes.
- Prefer deleting keys on write over overwriting; use TTLs as a safety net, versioned keys for mass invalidation, and events for writes from other systems.
- Protect hot keys against stampedes with single-flight, locks, stale-while-revalidate and TTL jitter; cache negative results.
- A Redis failure should degrade performance, not availability: fall back to the database.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add cache-aside caching to `GET /api/v1/books/:id` and measure latency with and without the cache using `autocannon`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Simulate a stampede: give a slow query (500 ms) a 5-second TTL and send 200 concurrent requests right after expiry. Count database queries, then add single-flight and a Redis lock and count again.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Users report seeing an old product price for a few minutes after it was changed. How would you investigate and fix it?" *Hint:* consider every cache layer (browser, CDN, Redis, in-process), the invalidation path after the write, the delete-vs-read race, and TTLs.

#### Redis as a Session Store

**Why Redis for sessions.** Server-side sessions (10.2) keep user state on the server and send the browser only a random session ID in a cookie. Where should that state live?

| Store | Problem |
|---|---|
| Process memory (`MemoryStore`) | Lost on restart, not shared between instances, leaks memory; for development only |
| Relational/document database | Works, but adds a database read (and often a write) to every request; needs a cleanup job for expired sessions |
| Redis | Shared by all instances, sub-millisecond reads, built-in TTL deletes expired sessions automatically |

Sessions are read on almost every request, are small, and have a natural expiry: a perfect fit for Redis.

**How it fits together.**

```text
 browser                              Express instance (any of N)                 Redis
 Cookie: sid=s%3AYp3x...signature --> express-session verifies the signature
                                      GET sess:Yp3x...                    -------> {"cookie":{...},"userId":42,"role":"user"}
                                      req.session = parsed object
                                      ... route handler runs ...
                                      if modified: SET sess:Yp3x... <json> EX <maxAge>
                                      else (rolling/touch): EXPIRE sess:Yp3x... <maxAge>
```

**Configuration.** 10.2 and 12.3 showed the basic set-up; here it is with the decisions explained:

```javascript
import session from 'express-session';
import { RedisStore } from 'connect-redis';
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const redisClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
redisClient.on('error', (err) => logger.error({ err }, 'redis error'));
await redisClient.connect();

app.set('trust proxy', 1);                       // Secure cookies behind a TLS-terminating proxy (12.1)
app.use(session({
  store: new RedisStore({
    client: redisClient,
    prefix: 'sess:',                             // key namespace: sess:<session id>
    ttl: 60 * 60 * 8,                            // seconds; used when the cookie has no maxAge
  }),
  name: 'sid',
  secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRETS.split(','), // array: first signs, all verify (key rotation)
  resave: false,                                 // do not rewrite unchanged sessions
  saveUninitialized: false,                      // no session (and no cookie) until something is stored
  rolling: true,                                 // reset the expiry on every response: idle timeout
  cookie: {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: true,
    sameSite: 'lax',
    maxAge: 1000 * 60 * 30,                      // 30 min idle timeout; Redis TTL follows this value
  },
}));
```

The Redis key's TTL is derived from the cookie's `maxAge`, so the server-side session and the cookie expire together. With `resave: false`, unchanged sessions are not rewritten; the store's `touch` method only refreshes the TTL (`EXPIRE`), which is cheaper.

**Idle and absolute timeouts.** `rolling` gives an idle timeout. Security guidelines (10.2) also recommend an **absolute** timeout regardless of activity. Store the login time in the session and enforce it in middleware:

```javascript
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const MAX_SESSION_AGE = 12 * 60 * 60 * 1000;                     // 12 hours
  if (req.session.userId && Date.now() - req.session.loginAt > MAX_SESSION_AGE) {
    return req.session.destroy(() => res.status(401).json({ error: 'session expired' }));
  }
  next();
});
```

**Login, regeneration and logout.**

```javascript
app.post('/login', async (req, res, next) => {
  const user = await authenticate(req.body.email, req.body.password);
  if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'invalid credentials' });

  req.session.regenerate(async (err) => {                         // new ID: prevents session fixation (10.2)
    if (err) return next(err);
    req.session.userId = user.id;
    req.session.loginAt = Date.now();
    await redisClient.sAdd(`user:${user.id}:sessions`, req.session.id);   // index sessions per user
    req.session.save((err2) => (err2 ? next(err2) : res.json({ ok: true })));
  });
});

app.post('/logout', (req, res, next) => {
  const { userId } = req.session;
  const sid = req.session.id;
  req.session.destroy(async (err) => {                            // DEL sess:<id> in Redis
    if (err) return next(err);
    if (userId) await redisClient.sRem(`user:${userId}:sessions`, sid);
    res.clearCookie('sid').status(204).end();
  });
});
```

**"Log out everywhere".** After a password change or a suspected compromise, all of a user's sessions must end. The set `user:<id>:sessions` maintained above makes that possible without scanning all keys:

```javascript
export async function destroyAllSessions(userId) {
  const key = `user:${userId}:sessions`;
  const sids = await redisClient.sMembers(key);
  if (sids.length) await redisClient.unlink([...sids.map((sid) => `sess:${sid}`), key]);
}
```

Entries in the set can outlive their sessions (sessions expire by TTL without anyone removing them from the set). Clean the set at login (`SMISMEMBER`/`EXISTS` checks), or give it a TTL as long as the absolute session timeout.

**Operational concerns.**

- **Eviction.** Sessions must not be evicted to make room for cache entries. Use `noeviction` or a `volatile-*` policy on an instance dedicated to sessions, or a separate instance from the cache.
- **Persistence.** Without persistence, a Redis restart logs everyone out. Enable AOF (see "Persistence with RDB and AOF") if that is unacceptable.
- **Availability.** If Redis is down, no request can load its session. Use a replicated, managed deployment, and decide whether authenticated routes fail closed (they should).
- **Size.** Keep sessions small: user ID, role, CSRF token, a few flags. Do not store whole user profiles or carts that can be loaded from the database; large sessions cost bandwidth on every request.
- **Security.** Session data is sensitive. Require authentication on Redis (ACL users), use TLS across networks, and never expose Redis to the internet.

**Sessions or tokens?** Redis sessions give instant revocation and small cookies, at the cost of a shared store. Stateless JWTs (10.3) avoid the store but make revocation hard, which is why deny lists for revoked tokens also end up in Redis.

**Key Takeaways**

- Redis is the standard session store: shared across instances, sub-millisecond, and its TTLs expire sessions automatically.
- `connect-redis` stores sessions as `sess:<id>` with a TTL derived from the cookie's `maxAge`; `rolling` gives an idle timeout.
- Regenerate the session ID at login, destroy it at logout, and enforce an absolute timeout in middleware.
- Index sessions per user in a set to support "log out everywhere".
- Protect session data from eviction and restarts with the right eviction policy, persistence and replication.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Configure `express-session` with a Redis store, log in, and inspect the session key and its TTL with `redis-cli`. Make a request and watch the TTL reset.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement `POST /api/me/sessions/revoke-all` that ends every session of the current user except the current one, and an endpoint that lists active sessions with their login time and user agent.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your application stores sessions and cache entries in the same Redis instance with `allkeys-lru`. What can go wrong?" *Hint:* consider memory pressure from a cache-heavy traffic spike and which keys the eviction policy may choose.

#### Rate Limiting and Job Queues

Two very common Redis workloads have the same shape: many application instances coordinate through shared, atomic state. A **rate limiter** counts requests per client across instances; a **job queue** hands work from the web tier to background workers.

**Rate limiting.** 10.6 introduced the algorithms and 12.3 used `express-rate-limit`. With several instances behind a load balancer, counters must be shared, or each instance enforces its own limit and the effective limit is multiplied (12.3). Redis implements every algorithm with atomic commands.

**Fixed window.** Count requests per key per time window. Simple and memory-cheap; allows bursts of up to twice the limit at window boundaries.

```javascript
// 100 requests per minute per client
export async function fixedWindow(redis, clientId, limit = 100, windowSec = 60) {
  const window = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000 / windowSec);
  const key = `rl:fw:${clientId}:${window}`;
  const [count] = await redis.multi()
    .incr(key)                                   // atomic increment (creates the key at 1)
    .expire(key, windowSec, 'NX')                // set the TTL only the first time (Redis 7+)
    .exec();
  return { allowed: count <= limit, remaining: Math.max(0, limit - count) };
}
```

The `MULTI` ensures the TTL is always set together with the first increment. Without it, a crash between `INCR` and `EXPIRE` would leave a counter that never expires and blocks the client forever.

**Sliding window log.** Store each request's timestamp in a sorted set and count those in the last N seconds. Exact, but memory grows with the limit:

```lua
-- KEYS[1] = rl:sw:<client>, ARGV[1] = now (ms), ARGV[2] = window (ms), ARGV[3] = limit, ARGV[4] = unique request id
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1] - ARGV[2])   -- drop timestamps outside the window
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1])
if count >= tonumber(ARGV[3]) then
  return 0                                                       -- rejected
end
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], ARGV[4])
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
return 1                                                         -- allowed
```

**Token bucket** (smooth rate with bursts) is also usually implemented as a short Lua script storing `tokens` and `lastRefill` in a hash. In practice, use a library rather than writing your own:

```javascript
import { rateLimit } from 'express-rate-limit';
import { RedisStore } from 'rate-limit-redis';

app.use('/api/auth/login', rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 10,                                     // 10 attempts per 15 minutes per IP
  standardHeaders: 'draft-8',                    // RateLimit headers for clients
  store: new RedisStore({
    prefix: 'rl:login:',
    sendCommand: (...args) => redisClient.sendCommand(args),   // adapter for node-redis
  }),
}));
```

**Choosing a key.** Limit by API key or user ID when the client is authenticated, and by IP otherwise (with `trust proxy` configured correctly, 12.1). For login endpoints, limit both per IP and per account to slow down credential stuffing and targeted guessing.

**Job queues: why.** Some work should not happen during the HTTP request: sending emails, resizing images, generating PDFs, calling slow third-party APIs. Doing it inline makes responses slow and loses the work if the process crashes. A **job queue** lets the web tier record "this needs doing" in milliseconds and return, while separate **worker** processes do the work, with retries.

```text
 HTTP request --> API: validate, save order, ENQUEUE "send-confirmation" --> 202/201 response
                                                  |
                                             [ Redis queue ]
                                                  |
                         worker 1 <---------------+---------------> worker 2
                         sends email, ACK                           resizes image, ACK
                         on failure: retry with backoff, then move to "failed"
```

**A minimal list-based queue.** `LPUSH` enqueues, a blocking pop dequeues. To avoid losing a job if a worker crashes mid-task, move it atomically to a processing list and remove it only when done (the **reliable queue** pattern):

```javascript
// producer
await redis.lPush('queue:emails', JSON.stringify({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), to, template: 'order-confirmation', orderId }));

// worker (dedicated connection: blocking commands hold the connection while waiting)
const worker = redis.duplicate();
await worker.connect();
for (;;) {
  const raw = await worker.blMove('queue:emails', 'queue:emails:processing', 'RIGHT', 'LEFT', 5); // wait up to 5 s
  if (!raw) continue;
  try {
    await sendEmail(JSON.parse(raw));
```
