This is deliberate: if your effect breaks when it runs twice (two WebSocket connections, a doubled analytics event), it also breaks in production when a user navigates away and back. The fix is a correct cleanup, not disabling Strict Mode.

**You might not need an effect.** Effects are an escape hatch, and overusing them is the most common React mistake:

| Situation | Instead of an effect |
|---|---|
| Compute a value from props or state | Compute it during render (`const total = items.reduce(...)`) |
| Expensive computation from props | `useMemo` (see "useMemo and useCallback") |
| Reset all state when a prop changes | Give the component a `key` (14.1) |
| React to a user action (submit, click) | Put the code in the event handler |
| Notify a parent about a change | Call the parent's callback in the same event handler |
| Subscribe to an external store | `useSyncExternalStore` (14.4) |

```jsx
// Wrong: an extra render and a moment of stale UI
const [fullName, setFullName] = useState('');
useEffect(() => setFullName(`${first} ${last}`), [first, last]);

// Right
const fullName = `${first} ${last}`;
```

**useLayoutEffect.** `useEffect` runs *after* the browser paints. When an effect must measure the DOM and adjust it before the user sees anything (positioning a tooltip from its measured height), use `useLayoutEffect`, which runs after DOM mutations but before paint. It blocks painting, so use it only when you see flicker.

**Reading the latest value without re-running: useEffectEvent.** Sometimes an effect needs a value but should not re-synchronise when it changes, for example logging a visit with the current theme without reconnecting when the theme changes. React 19.2 provides `useEffectEvent` for this: it wraps a function that always sees the latest props and state and is not a dependency.

```jsx
const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => showToast(`Connected to ${roomId}`, theme));
useEffect(() => {
  const c = createConnection(roomId);
  c.on('connected', onConnected);            // reads the latest theme without being a dependency
  c.connect();
  return () => c.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);                                // theme changes do not reconnect
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Use effects to synchronise a component with an external system; use event handlers for things caused by a specific user action.
- An effect has a setup, an optional cleanup and a dependency array; React runs cleanup before each re-run and on unmount.
- List every reactive value the effect reads as a dependency; fix the code instead of silencing the lint rule.
- Use cleanup (an `AbortController` or an `ignore` flag) to avoid fetch race conditions; Strict Mode double-runs effects in development to expose missing cleanups.
- Many effects are unnecessary: derive values during render, handle actions in handlers, reset with keys.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `useEffect` that sets `document.title` to "(N) Bookshelf" where N is the number of unread books, and verify it updates when N changes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a clock component that shows the current time and updates every second. Make it work correctly under Strict Mode, stop the interval on unmount, and add a prop that switches between 12- and 24-hour format without restarting the interval.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A colleague's component fetches data in `useEffect` and sometimes shows results for an old search term. What is wrong and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* responses arriving out of order, what the cleanup function is for, and why a caching library avoids the issue.

#### Component Lifecycle in Hook Terms

**The three phases.** Every component instance goes through the same life: it **mounts** (its first render is committed to the DOM), it **updates** (it re-renders zero or more times because of new props, state or context), and it **unmounts** (it is removed from the tree and its state is discarded). Class components (see "Class Components and Legacy Lifecycle Methods") exposed a method for each moment. Function components express the same moments through hooks, but the recommended way of *thinking* is different.

**One update, step by step.**

```text
                         +----------------------------------------------+
 trigger                 |  mount / setState / parent render / context  |
                         +----------------------------------------------+
                                             |
 RENDER                  call the component function: hooks return current state,
                         JSX is produced, children are rendered
                                             |
 COMMIT                  React updates the DOM
                                             |
                         ref callbacks / ref.current assigned
                                             |
                         useLayoutEffect: cleanups of the previous run, then setups
                                             |
 PAINT                   browser draws the frame
                                             |
                         useEffect: cleanups of the previous run, then setups
```

Within the tree, effects run **children first**: a child's effects run before its parent's, because a parent can only be "fully mounted" once its children are.

**Mapping lifecycle moments to hooks.**

| Lifecycle moment | Class component | Function component |
|---|---|---|
| Initialise state | `constructor` | `useState(initial)` / `useState(() => initial)` |
| Render | `render()` | The function body |
| After first mount | `componentDidMount` | `useEffect(fn, [])` |
| After updates of specific values | `componentDidUpdate(prevProps)` with comparisons | `useEffect(fn, [a, b])` |
| Before unmount | `componentWillUnmount` | Cleanup returned from `useEffect` |
| Skip re-render if props equal | `shouldComponentUpdate` / `PureComponent` | `memo(Component)` |
| Measure DOM before paint | `componentDidMount`/`componentDidUpdate` (synchronous) | `useLayoutEffect` |
| Catch render errors | `componentDidCatch`, `getDerivedStateFromError` | No hook: still needs a class error boundary (14.3) |

**Think in synchronisation, not in moments.** The table is useful when reading old code, but writing effects as "on mount, do X" leads to bugs. Consider an effect written with only a mount and unmount in mind:

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const sub = stockFeed.subscribe(symbol, setPrice);   // "on mount: subscribe"
  return () => sub.unsubscribe();                      // "on unmount: unsubscribe"
}, []);                                                // bug: symbol changes are ignored
```

If the `symbol` prop changes, the component keeps showing prices for the old symbol. The correct question is not "when does this run?" but "**what does this effect keep in sync, and with which values?**" Answer: it keeps a subscription in sync with `symbol`. That makes `[symbol]` the dependency list, and React calls cleanup and setup whenever `symbol` changes. Each effect describes *how to start* and *how to stop* synchronising; React decides when.

**Observing the lifecycle.** A small component that logs each step makes the order visible:

```jsx
function Lifecycle({ label }) {
  console.log(`render ${label}`);

  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    console.log(`layout effect ${label}`);
    return () => console.log(`layout cleanup ${label}`);
  }, [label]);

  useEffect(() => {
    console.log(`effect ${label}`);
    return () => console.log(`effect cleanup ${label}`);
  }, [label]);

  return <p>{label}</p>;
}
// mount "A":         render A, layout effect A, effect A
// update to "B":     render B, layout cleanup A, layout effect B, effect cleanup A, effect B
// unmount:           layout cleanup B, effect cleanup B
// (in Strict Mode dev you will additionally see the extra mount-unmount-mount cycle)
```

**Keeping a component alive while hidden.** Unmounting discards state. If you want to hide a tab but keep its state (scroll position, form inputs), you can render it and hide it with CSS, or, since React 19.2, wrap it in `<Activity mode="hidden">`. React then keeps the state but unmounts its effects while it is hidden, and re-creates them when it becomes visible.

**Key Takeaways**

- A component mounts, updates any number of times, and unmounts; unmounting discards its state.
- Order of one update: render, DOM commit, refs, layout effects, paint, effects; children's effects run before their parents'.
- Class lifecycle methods map to `useState`, `useEffect` with dependencies and cleanup, `useLayoutEffect` and `memo`; error boundaries still need classes.
- Design effects around what they synchronise and with which values, not around "on mount" and "on unmount".

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use the `Lifecycle` component above inside a parent that can toggle it and change its label. Record the log order with and without Strict Mode and explain each line.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Translate a class component that uses `componentDidMount`, `componentDidUpdate(prevProps)` (to refetch when `userId` changes) and `componentWillUnmount` into a function component. Show that the hook version needs fewer branches.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the equivalent of `componentDidMount` in hooks, and why is that the wrong question?" *Hint:* `useEffect(fn, [])` is the literal answer; then explain why dependencies describe synchronisation and what bug appears when props change.

#### useRef and DOM Access

**Why refs.** Sometimes a component must remember a value that is *not* used for rendering: a timer ID, the previous value of a prop, a WebSocket instance. Storing it in state would cause pointless re-renders. Other times a component must reach a real DOM node: to focus an input, measure an element, scroll into view, or hand a node to a non-React library such as a chart or a map. `useRef` covers both needs. React's documentation calls refs an **escape hatch**: a way to step outside the declarative model when you must.

**A mutable box.** `useRef(initial)` returns an object `{ current: initial }` that persists for the life of the component. You can read and write `ref.current` freely, and changing it does **not** trigger a render.

| | `useState` | `useRef` |
|---|---|---|
| Survives re-renders | Yes | Yes |
| Changing it triggers a render | Yes | No |
| Value in the current render | Snapshot (immutable) | Live (mutable `current`) |
| Use for | Anything shown on screen | Timer IDs, DOM nodes, instances of external objects |

```jsx
function Stopwatch() {
  const [elapsed, setElapsed] = useState(0);
  const intervalRef = useRef(null);            // the ID is never rendered: a ref is enough

  function start() {
    if (intervalRef.current) return;           // already running
    const startedAt = Date.now() - elapsed;
    intervalRef.current = setInterval(() => setElapsed(Date.now() - startedAt), 100);
  }
  function stop() {
    clearInterval(intervalRef.current);
    intervalRef.current = null;
  }

  useEffect(() => stop, []);                   // clear the interval if unmounted while running

  return (
    <>
      <p>{(elapsed / 1000).toFixed(1)} s</p>
      <button onClick={start}>Start</button>
      <button onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
    </>
  );
}
```

**Refs to DOM nodes.** Pass a ref object to the `ref` attribute of a DOM element. After the commit, React sets `ref.current` to the DOM node; on unmount it sets it back to `null`.

```jsx
function SearchBar() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  return (
    <>
      <input ref={inputRef} type="search" aria-label="Search books" />
      <button onClick={() => inputRef.current.focus()}>Focus search</button>  {/* imperative DOM call */}
    </>
  );
}
```

**Do not read or write refs during render.** During the render the DOM node may not exist yet, and a ref changed during render makes the component impure. Use refs in event handlers and effects. The one exception is lazy initialisation: `if (ref.current === null) ref.current = new ExpensiveThing();`.

**Integrating a non-React library.** A ref plus an effect is the standard bridge:

```tsx
function BookMap({ lat, lng }: { lat: number; lng: number }) {
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const mapRef = useRef<MapWidget | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const map = new MapWidget(containerRef.current!);      // library takes over this div
    mapRef.current = map;
    return () => { map.destroy(); mapRef.current = null; };
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    mapRef.current?.setCenter(lat, lng);                   // sync props into the imperative API
  }, [lat, lng]);

  return <div ref={containerRef} style={{ height: 300 }} />;  // React renders nothing inside it
}
```

**Passing refs to your own components.** Since React 19, `ref` is an ordinary prop for function components, so a design-system input can expose its inner DOM node:

```tsx
function TextInput({ label, ref, ...rest }: React.ComponentProps<'input'> & { label: string }) {
  return (
    <label>
      {label}
      <input ref={ref} {...rest} />          {/* the parent's ref reaches the DOM input */}
    </label>
  );
}
```

Before React 19 the same component had to be wrapped in `forwardRef((props, ref) => ...)`, which you will see in most existing libraries.

**Ref callbacks.** Instead of an object you can pass a function. React calls it with the node after mount; since React 19, the function may return a cleanup that runs on detach. This is useful for refs to a dynamic number of elements or for observers:

```jsx
<div
  ref={(node) => {
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => setWidth(entry.contentRect.width));
    observer.observe(node);
    return () => observer.disconnect();     // React 19: cleanup on unmount or when the callback changes
  }}
/>
```

**Exposing a limited API with useImperativeHandle.** If you want a parent to call `ref.current.focus()` but not to access the whole DOM node, define the methods it may use:

```jsx
function VideoPlayer({ src, ref }) {
  const videoRef = useRef(null);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    play: () => videoRef.current.play(),
    pause: () => videoRef.current.pause(),
  }), []);
  return <video ref={videoRef} src={src} />;
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `useRef` returns a persistent mutable `{ current }` box; changing it does not re-render.
- Use refs for values not shown on screen (timer IDs, instances) and to access DOM nodes via the `ref` attribute.
- Read and write refs in handlers and effects, not during render.
- A ref plus an effect is the standard way to integrate non-React libraries.
- In React 19, `ref` is a normal prop for function components (no `forwardRef`), and ref callbacks can return a cleanup; `useImperativeHandle` exposes a restricted API.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a login form that focuses the email input when it mounts and moves focus to the password field when the user presses Enter in the email field.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `usePrevious(value)` hook with `useRef` and `useEffect` and use it to show "up" or "down" next to a changing price. Explain why the ref is updated in an effect and not during render.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you use a ref instead of state?" *Hint:* ask whether the value affects what is rendered; mention timer IDs, DOM access, third-party instances, and the bug of displaying `ref.current` on screen.

#### useMemo and useCallback

**Why memoisation.** Every render re-runs the whole component body. Usually that is cheap. Two situations make it a problem: an expensive calculation that runs on every render even though its inputs did not change, and **referential identity**. Objects and functions created during render are new on every render, even if their contents are the same:

```javascript
({ a: 1 }) === ({ a: 1 })              // false: two different objects
(() => {}) === (() => {})              // false: two different functions
```

This matters when a new object or function is passed to a child wrapped in `memo`, or used as an effect dependency. The child sees "changed" props and re-renders, and the effect re-runs, although nothing really changed. **Memoisation** means caching a result and returning the cached value while the inputs stay the same.

**useMemo caches a value.**

```jsx
function BookStats({ books, year }) {
  const stats = useMemo(() => {
    // Imagine this scans tens of thousands of books
    const ofYear = books.filter((b) => b.year === year);
    return { count: ofYear.length, avgPages: average(ofYear.map((b) => b.pages)) };
  }, [books, year]);   // recomputed only when books or year change (compared with Object.is)

  return <p>{stats.count} books, {stats.avgPages} pages on average</p>;
}
```

**useCallback caches a function.** `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`: it returns the same function instance until a dependency changes.

```jsx
const BookRow = memo(function BookRow({ book, onToggle }) {   // memo: skip render if props are equal
  return (
    <li>
      <label>
        <input type="checkbox" checked={book.read} onChange={() => onToggle(book.id)} />
        {book.title}
      </label>
    </li>
  );
});

function ReadingList({ books, setBooks }) {
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('');

  // Without useCallback: a new function each render -> every memo'd BookRow re-renders on each keystroke
  const handleToggle = useCallback((id) => {
    setBooks((prev) => prev.map((b) => (b.id === id ? { ...b, read: !b.read } : b)));
  }, [setBooks]);       // setters from useState are stable, so this almost never changes

  return (
    <>
      <input value={filter} onChange={(e) => setFilter(e.target.value)} />
      <ul>
        {books.filter((b) => b.title.includes(filter)).map((b) => (
          <BookRow key={b.id} book={b} onToggle={handleToggle} />
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}
```

**memo, useMemo and useCallback work together.**

| Tool | Caches | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `memo(Component)` | The rendered output of a component | Skip re-rendering when all props are `Object.is`-equal to the previous ones |
| `useMemo(fn, deps)` | The return value of `fn` | Avoid expensive recalculation; keep object/array props stable |
| `useCallback(fn, deps)` | The function itself | Keep callback props and effect dependencies stable |

`useCallback` on its own does nothing useful: a stable function only helps if something compares it (a `memo` child, an effect dependency, another hook's dependency).

**When not to memoise.** Memoisation has a cost: extra code, dependency arrays to maintain, memory, and a comparison on every render. Wrapping everything "just in case" makes code harder to read for little gain. Reasonable rules:

- Measure first with the React DevTools Profiler (14.5). A calculation under about 1 ms is rarely worth caching.
- Memoise when you pass objects or functions to `memo` children, or when they are dependencies of effects or other hooks.
- Prefer structural fixes first: move state down so fewer components re-render, or pass JSX as `children` (14.5).
- `useMemo` is a performance hint, not a guarantee. React may discard the cache, so code must still be correct without it.

**The React Compiler.** Released as stable in October 2025, the React Compiler analyses components at build time and inserts memoisation automatically, at a finer granularity than you would write by hand. In projects that enable it, most manual `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `memo` calls become unnecessary. You still need to understand them to read existing code and to reason about referential identity.

**Key Takeaways**

- Objects and functions created during render are new each time; this defeats `memo` and re-triggers effects.
- `useMemo` caches a computed value and `useCallback` caches a function until their dependencies change.
- They are useful together with `memo` children, effect dependencies, and genuinely expensive computations.
- Do not memoise by default: measure, prefer structural fixes, and remember the cache is only a hint.
- The React Compiler can add memoisation automatically.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Generate 20,000 fake books and render a component that filters and sorts them by a text query and a sort key. Use `console.time` to measure the computation, then add `useMemo` and type into an unrelated input on the same page to see the difference.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In the `ReadingList` example, use React DevTools "Highlight updates" to show that every row re-renders on each keystroke without `memo` and `useCallback`. Then find a solution that needs neither, by restructuring which component owns the `filter` state.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `useMemo` and `useCallback`, and why might adding `useCallback` everywhere make an application slower?" *Hint:* one is defined in terms of the other; consider the cost of comparisons, closures and maintenance, and when nothing compares the function anyway.

#### useReducer for Complex State

**Why a reducer.** As a component grows, state updates scatter across many event handlers. Each handler knows how to change several pieces of state, and related changes can be forgotten. Consider a checkout form with `status`, `error`, `items` and `coupon`: the "submit", "success", "failure", "add item" and "apply coupon" handlers all touch overlapping state. A **reducer** moves all the update logic into one pure function. Handlers just describe *what happened* by dispatching an **action**, and the reducer decides *how the state changes*.

An analogy: instead of each employee editing the shared ledger directly, they file a slip saying "sold 2 items". One accountant (the reducer) applies every slip by the same rules.

**The pieces.**

```text
event handler --dispatch({ type: 'added', book })--> reducer(state, action) --> new state --> re-render
```

```tsx
type Book = { id: number; title: string; read: boolean };

type State = {
  books: Book[];
  status: 'idle' | 'saving' | 'error';
  error: string | null;
};

type Action =
  | { type: 'added'; book: Book }
  | { type: 'toggled'; id: number }
  | { type: 'removed'; id: number }
  | { type: 'save_started' }
  | { type: 'save_failed'; message: string }
  | { type: 'save_succeeded' };

// Pure function: no fetch, no mutation, same input -> same output
function shelfReducer(state: State, action: Action): State {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'added':
      return { ...state, books: [...state.books, action.book] };
    case 'toggled':
      return {
        ...state,
        books: state.books.map((b) => (b.id === action.id ? { ...b, read: !b.read } : b)),
      };
    case 'removed':
      return { ...state, books: state.books.filter((b) => b.id !== action.id) };
    case 'save_started':
      return { ...state, status: 'saving', error: null };
    case 'save_failed':
      return { ...state, status: 'error', error: action.message };
    case 'save_succeeded':
      return { ...state, status: 'idle' };
    default: {
      const unreachable: never = action;      // TypeScript errors here if an action type is unhandled
      return state;
    }
  }
}
```

```tsx
import { useReducer } from 'react';

function Shelf({ initialBooks }: { initialBooks: Book[] }) {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(shelfReducer, {
    books: initialBooks, status: 'idle', error: null,
  });

  async function handleSave() {
    dispatch({ type: 'save_started' });
    try {
      await saveShelf(state.books);                 // side effects stay in the handler
      dispatch({ type: 'save_succeeded' });
    } catch (e) {
      dispatch({ type: 'save_failed', message: (e as Error).message });
    }
  }

  return (
    <>
      <ul>
        {state.books.map((b) => (
          <li key={b.id}>
            <input type="checkbox" checked={b.read}
                   onChange={() => dispatch({ type: 'toggled', id: b.id })} />
            {b.title}
            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'removed', id: b.id })}>Remove</button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <button onClick={handleSave} disabled={state.status === 'saving'}>Save</button>
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
    </>
  );
}
```

**Benefits.** The reducer is a plain function, so you can unit test it without React (`expect(shelfReducer(s, { type: 'removed', id: 1 }).books).toHaveLength(0)`). Every possible change is visible in one place. Actions are a readable log of what happened, and you can `console.log` them while debugging. `dispatch` is stable across renders, so it can be passed to children or put in context without memoisation.

**Rules for reducers.** They must be pure, like render. Never mutate `state`; return a new object (or use Immer's `useImmerReducer`). Name actions after *what happened* (`'save_failed'`), not after the setter you want to call (`'set_error'`). Keep side effects such as `fetch` in handlers or effects.

**Choosing.**

| Criterion | `useState` | `useReducer` |
|---|---|---|
| Shape of state | Independent primitive values | Several related values that change together |
| Update logic | Simple, local to one handler | Shared by many handlers or with many cases |
| Readability | Less code for small cases | More upfront code, clearer at scale |
| Testing | Through the component | Reducer testable in isolation |
| Debugging | Inspect state | Log every action and resulting state |

You can mix both in one component. The reducer pattern is also the foundation of Redux (14.4), which applies it to state shared by the whole application.

**Key Takeaways**

- `useReducer(reducer, initialState)` returns `[state, dispatch]`; handlers dispatch actions and a pure reducer computes the next state.
- Reducers centralise update logic, are testable in isolation and make state transitions explicit.
- Reducers must be pure and immutable; side effects stay in handlers or effects.
- Prefer `useReducer` when several values change together or many handlers share update logic; `useState` remains best for simple, independent values.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite a counter with "increment", "decrement", "reset" and "set to N" buttons using `useReducer`, and write three unit tests for the reducer.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Model a multi-step "add book" wizard (details, cover upload, confirmation) with a reducer whose state includes the current step, the form data per step and a submission status. Make invalid transitions (jumping to confirmation without a title) impossible inside the reducer.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose `useReducer` over `useState`?" *Hint:* talk about related state, the number of update sites, testability, and the stability of `dispatch` when passing it deep into the tree.

#### useContext and Prop Drilling

**The problem: prop drilling.** Some data is needed by many components at different depths: the logged-in user, the theme, the language, feature flags. Passing it down as props means every intermediate component must accept and forward it, even when it does not use it:

```text
<App user theme>
  <Layout user theme>               does not use them, only forwards
    <Sidebar user theme>            does not use them, only forwards
      <Avatar user theme />         the only real consumer
```

This is called **prop drilling**. It couples intermediate components to data they do not care about and makes refactoring painful. First try composition (14.1); when data really is needed in many distant places, use **context**.

**Context.** Context lets a component provide a value to its whole subtree. Any descendant can read it directly, however deep, like a radio broadcast that every receiver in range can tune into without wires running through each room.

```tsx
// theme-context.tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo, useState } from 'react';

type Theme = 'light' | 'dark';
type ThemeContextValue = { theme: Theme; toggleTheme: () => void };

// 1. Create the context, with a default used when there is no provider above
const ThemeContext = createContext<ThemeContextValue | null>(null);

// 2. Provide it: a component that owns the state and wraps the tree
export function ThemeProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState<Theme>('light');
  const value = useMemo(
    () => ({ theme, toggleTheme: () => setTheme((t) => (t === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light')) }),
    [theme],                                         // a new object only when theme changes
  );
  return <ThemeContext value={value}>{children}</ThemeContext>;  // React 19; older: <ThemeContext.Provider value={value}>
}

// 3. Consume it through a custom hook that also checks for a missing provider
export function useTheme() {
  const ctx = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useTheme must be used inside <ThemeProvider>');
  return ctx;
}
```

```tsx
// main.tsx
<ThemeProvider>
  <App />
</ThemeProvider>

// Anywhere below, no props needed
function ThemeToggle() {
  const { theme, toggleTheme } = useTheme();
  return <button onClick={toggleTheme}>Switch to {theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light'} mode</button>;
}
```

**How lookup works.** `useContext(SomeContext)` returns the value of the *nearest* provider above the calling component. Providers can be nested and overridden for part of the tree (for example a dark sidebar inside a light page). Without any provider, the default from `createContext` is returned. React 19 also lets you read context with `use(SomeContext)`, which, unlike `useContext`, may be called inside conditions.

**Re-render behaviour.** When a provider's `value` changes (compared with `Object.is`), **every** component that reads that context re-renders, even if it only uses a part of the value that did not change. This leads to two practical rules:

1. **Keep the value stable.** Passing `value={{ theme, toggleTheme }}` creates a new object on every render of the provider and re-renders all consumers. Memoise it as above.
2. **Split contexts by how often they change.** Put the rarely changing user identity and the frequently changing shopping cart in separate contexts, and separate state from the functions that update it when that helps.

```text
AuthContext      { user, login, logout }     changes on login/logout
ThemeContext     { theme, toggleTheme }      changes rarely
CartContext      { items }                   changes often -> only cart widgets re-render
CartActionsCtx   { add, remove }             stable (dispatch-based) -> buttons never re-render
```

**When to use context.**

| Good fit | Poor fit |
|---|---|
| Theme, locale, authenticated user, feature flags | Data that changes many times per second (pointer position, form keystrokes) |
| Dependencies such as an API client or analytics service | Server data that needs caching and refetching (use a query library, 14.4) |
| Shared state of a compound component (`Tabs` and its `Tab`s) | Avoiding two levels of props (composition is simpler) |

Context is a **transport** mechanism, not a state management library. Combined with `useReducer` it is enough for many applications; larger ones may adopt Redux or a lighter store (14.4).

**Key Takeaways**

- Prop drilling passes data through components that do not use it; try composition first, then context.
- `createContext` creates a context, a provider (`<Ctx value>` in React 19, `<Ctx.Provider>` before) supplies a value, and `useContext`/`use` reads the nearest one.
- Wrap each context in a provider component and a custom hook that throws when the provider is missing.
- All consumers re-render when the value changes: memoise the value and split contexts by update frequency.
- Context transports values; it does not cache server data or replace a state library in large apps.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a `LocaleContext` with `'en'` and `'it'`, a provider with a switch button, and a `useT(key)` hook that reads translations from an object. Use it in two components at different depths.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build an `AuthProvider` exposing `user`, `login(email, password)` and `logout()` against the Chapter 12 login endpoint. Add a counter in each consumer that logs renders, then split state and actions into two contexts and show that a "Log out" button no longer re-renders when the user object changes.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Is React Context a replacement for Redux?" *Hint:* distinguish dependency injection from state management; discuss re-render granularity, selectors, middleware, DevTools and the size of the application.

#### Custom Hooks and the Rules of Hooks

**Why custom hooks.** Several components often need the same *stateful logic*: tracking whether the browser is online, debouncing a search term, reading and writing `localStorage`, subscribing to a WebSocket. Before hooks, sharing such logic required higher-order components or render props (14.3), which nested wrappers around components. A **custom hook** is simply a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks. It shares *logic*, and each component that calls it gets its *own* independent state.

```tsx
// useOnlineStatus.ts
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(() => navigator.onLine);
  useEffect(() => {
    const update = () => setOnline(navigator.onLine);
    window.addEventListener('online', update);
    window.addEventListener('offline', update);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('online', update);
      window.removeEventListener('offline', update);
    };
  }, []);
  return online;
}

// Two components, two independent subscriptions, one implementation
function SaveButton() {
  const online = useOnlineStatus();
  return <button disabled={!online}>{online ? 'Save' : 'Offline'}</button>;
}
function StatusBar() {
  return <footer>{useOnlineStatus() ? 'Connected' : 'Working offline'}</footer>;
}
```

More examples that appear in almost every project:

```tsx
// Debounce: return a value that only updates after `delay` ms without changes
export function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, delay = 300): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);            // a new keystroke cancels the pending update
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}

// Persisted state with the same API as useState
export function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string, initial: T) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(() => {
    try {
      const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return raw === null ? initial : (JSON.parse(raw) as T);
    } catch {
      return initial;                         // private mode, quota or corrupted JSON
    }
  });
  useEffect(() => {
    try { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value)); } catch { /* ignore */ }
  }, [key, value]);
  return [value, setValue] as const;          // tuple type, like useState
}

// Usage: search the API only when the user pauses typing
function Search() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useLocalStorage('lastQuery', '');
  const debouncedQuery = useDebouncedValue(query, 400);
  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <BookResults query={debouncedQuery} />
    </>
  );
}
```

**The Rules of Hooks.**

1. **Only call hooks at the top level** of a component or custom hook: never inside conditions, loops, nested functions, after an early `return`, or in `try`/`catch`.
2. **Only call hooks from React functions**: function components and custom hooks, not ordinary functions or class components.

**Why the rules exist.** Hooks have no names. React stores each component's hook data in a list and identifies each hook by its **call order**:

```text
render 1                         render 2 (if a hook is skipped by a condition)
slot 0: useState('Ada')          slot 0: useState('Ada')        OK
slot 1: useState(0)       <---   slot 1: useEffect(...)          React hands the effect the counter's slot: corrupted
slot 2: useEffect(...)           slot 2: ???
```

If a hook is called conditionally, the order changes between renders and each hook receives another hook's data. The rules guarantee that the order is identical on every render. Put the condition *inside* the hook instead:

```jsx
// Wrong
if (user) {
  useEffect(() => track(user.id), [user]);
}

// Right
useEffect(() => {
  if (user) track(user.id);
}, [user]);
```

React 19's `use()` is the documented exception: it may be called conditionally, because it reads a promise or context rather than storing per-component data.

**Enforce them with a linter.** `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` (included in the Vite template) reports rule violations (`rules-of-hooks`) and missing dependencies (`exhaustive-deps`). Treat its warnings as errors.

**Designing good custom hooks.** Name them after their purpose (`useOnlineStatus`), not their implementation (`useEventListenerEffect`). Return what the caller needs: a single value, a tuple like `useState`, or an object for many fields. Avoid lifecycle-style hooks such as `useMount(fn)`, which hide dependencies from the linter. And remember that a function that calls no hooks should not start with `use`; it is just a function.

**Key Takeaways**

- A custom hook is a `use`-prefixed function that calls other hooks; it shares logic, not state.
- Common examples: online status, debounce, local storage, media queries, data subscriptions.
- Call hooks only at the top level of components and custom hooks; React identifies hooks by call order.
- Put conditions inside hooks, never around them; `use()` is the only hook that may be called conditionally.
- Use `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` to enforce the rules and dependency lists.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `useWindowWidth()` that returns the current `window.innerWidth` and updates on resize, and use it to switch between a grid and a list layout.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write `useFetch<T>(url)` returning `{ data, error, status }` that aborts the previous request when the URL changes. Use it in two components and show that each has its own state. Then list three features a production data-fetching library adds on top of it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can't hooks be called inside an `if` statement?" *Hint:* explain how React associates hook state with call order on each render, and what the linter does about it.

#### Class Components and Legacy Lifecycle Methods

**Why study classes.** From 2015 until hooks arrived in React 16.8 (February 2019), class components were the only way to have state and lifecycle methods. Large existing codebases and many tutorials still use them, and **error boundaries** (14.3) can still only be written as classes. You need to read them fluently, even if you write new code with functions.

**Anatomy of a class component.**

```jsx
import { Component } from 'react';

class BookTimer extends Component {
  // State is a single object
  state = { seconds: 0, running: false };

  // Class field arrow functions keep `this` bound to the instance
  toggle = () => {
    this.setState((prev) => ({ running: !prev.running }));  // setState MERGES into this.state
  };

  componentDidMount() {
    this.intervalId = setInterval(() => {
      if (this.state.running) this.setState((s) => ({ seconds: s.seconds + 1 }));
    }, 1000);
  }

  componentDidUpdate(prevProps) {
    if (prevProps.bookId !== this.props.bookId) {           // manual comparison of what changed
      this.setState({ seconds: 0, running: false });
    }
  }

  componentWillUnmount() {
    clearInterval(this.intervalId);
  }

  render() {
    const { title } = this.props;                           // props are on this.props
    return (
      <div>
        <p>Reading "{title}" for {this.state.seconds} s</p>
        <button onClick={this.toggle}>{this.state.running ? 'Pause' : 'Start'}</button>
      </div>
    );
  }
}
```

Differences from function components:

| Aspect | Class component | Function component |
|---|---|---|
| Props and state | `this.props`, `this.state` (one object) | Function parameter; one `useState` per value |
| Updating state | `this.setState(partial)` shallow-merges | Setter replaces the value |
| Event handlers | Must bind `this` (constructor `bind` or class field arrows) | Closures, no `this` |
| Side effects | Split across `componentDidMount`, `componentDidUpdate`, `componentWillUnmount` | One `useEffect` per concern, setup and cleanup together |
| Logic reuse | HOCs and render props | Custom hooks |
| Reading values in async callbacks | `this.props` is mutable: may read *newer* props than the render that started the work | Closures capture the render's snapshot |

**The `this` binding problem.** Methods passed as callbacks lose their `this` (Chapter 4). Older code binds them in the constructor:

```jsx
constructor(props) {
  super(props);                            // required before using `this`
  this.state = { open: false };
  this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this);
}
handleClick() { this.setState({ open: true }); }
```

**The full lifecycle.**

```text
MOUNTING          constructor -> static getDerivedStateFromProps -> render -> componentDidMount
UPDATING          static getDerivedStateFromProps -> shouldComponentUpdate -> render
                  -> getSnapshotBeforeUpdate -> componentDidUpdate(prevProps, prevState, snapshot)
UNMOUNTING        componentWillUnmount
ERRORS            static getDerivedStateFromError -> componentDidCatch
```

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `shouldComponentUpdate(nextProps, nextState)` | Return `false` to skip rendering; `PureComponent` implements it with shallow comparison |
| `static getDerivedStateFromProps(props, state)` | Rarely needed: update state from props before every render |
| `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate(prevProps, prevState)` | Read DOM information (such as scroll position) just before it changes; the result goes to `componentDidUpdate` |
| `static getDerivedStateFromError(error)` | Return state to render a fallback after a descendant throws |
| `componentDidCatch(error, info)` | Log the error (side effects allowed) |

**Deprecated methods.** `componentWillMount`, `componentWillReceiveProps` and `componentWillUpdate` ran during the render phase, where async rendering may run them several times or discard their work. They were renamed with an `UNSAFE_` prefix in React 16.3, and Strict Mode warns about them. Replace them with `componentDidMount`, derived values or `componentDidUpdate`.

**Why hooks replaced classes.** Related logic was scattered across lifecycle methods (a subscription set up in one method and torn down in another), while unrelated logic lived together in the same method. Reusing stateful logic created wrapper hell. `this` was confusing. And classes were harder for tools to optimise. Hooks group code by concern rather than by lifecycle moment. Classes are still supported and not deprecated, but all new React features (concurrent rendering APIs, `use`, actions) target function components.

**Migrating a class to a function.**

```jsx
function BookTimer({ bookId, title }) {
  const [seconds, setSeconds] = useState(0);
  const [running, setRunning] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {                               // literal translation; simpler: render <BookTimer key={bookId} />
    setSeconds(0);
    setRunning(false);
  }, [bookId]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!running) return;                         // only tick while running
    const id = setInterval(() => setSeconds((s) => s + 1), 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, [running]);

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Reading "{title}" for {seconds} s</p>
      <button onClick={() => setRunning((r) => !r)}>{running ? 'Pause' : 'Start'}</button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Class components keep state in `this.state`, update it with merging `setState`, and need `this` binding for handlers.
- Lifecycle methods split by moment: mount (`componentDidMount`), update (`componentDidUpdate`, `shouldComponentUpdate`), unmount (`componentWillUnmount`), errors (`getDerivedStateFromError`, `componentDidCatch`).
- `UNSAFE_` methods are deprecated because they run in the render phase.
- Hooks replaced classes because they group logic by concern and make it reusable; classes remain necessary for error boundaries.
- Migrating means converting state fields to `useState`, lifecycle pairs to effects with cleanup, and `prevProps` comparisons to dependency arrays.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a class component `Toggle` with a button that shows "ON"/"OFF", once with constructor binding and once with a class field arrow function.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Convert a class component that subscribes to window resize in `componentDidMount`, unsubscribes in `componentWillUnmount`, and refetches data in `componentDidUpdate` when `props.userId` changes, into a function component with two effects and a custom hook.
> 3. *(Interview)* "In a class component, a handler shows a message using `this.props.user` three seconds after a click. What can go wrong that cannot happen in a function component?" *Hint:* `this` is mutable and always points to the latest props; closures capture the props of the render in which the handler was created.

<a id="143-patterns-and-application-structure"></a>
### 14.3 Patterns and Application Structure

With components and hooks in hand, the next question is how to organise them. This subchapter covers forms, the direction in which data flows between components, the older reuse patterns (higher-order components and render props) that hooks largely replaced, portals and error boundaries, the main approaches to styling, and the component libraries and design systems on which most production interfaces are built.

#### Controlled and Uncontrolled Forms

**Two places a value can live.** A text field has a value. In plain HTML the DOM keeps it, and you read it when you need it. In React you can leave it there or move it into state. That choice defines the two kinds of form inputs:

- A **controlled** input gets its value from React state (`value`) and reports every change (`onChange`). React state is the single source of truth, and the DOM displays it.
- An **uncontrolled** input keeps its value in the DOM. You may give it a starting value (`defaultValue`) and read it later, through a ref or from the submitted form data.

An analogy: a controlled input is a puppet that only moves when React pulls the strings; an uncontrolled input is an independent actor you check on at the end of the scene.

**Controlled inputs.**

```tsx
function NewBookForm({ onCreate }: { onCreate: (b: { title: string; author: string; year: number }) => void }) {
  const [title, setTitle] = useState('');
  const [author, setAuthor] = useState('');
  const [year, setYear] = useState('');                     // keep the raw string; convert on submit

  const titleError = title.trim().length === 0 ? 'Title is required' : null;  // validated on every keystroke

  function handleSubmit(e: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
    e.preventDefault();                                     // stop the browser's full-page submit
    if (titleError) return;
    onCreate({ title: title.trim(), author, year: Number(year) });
    setTitle(''); setAuthor(''); setYear('');               // resetting is just setting state
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit} noValidate>
      <label>
        Title
        <input value={title} onChange={(e) => setTitle(e.target.value)} aria-invalid={!!titleError} />
      </label>
      {titleError && <small role="alert">{titleError}</small>}

      <label>
        Author
        <input value={author} onChange={(e) => setAuthor(e.target.value)} />
      </label>

      <label>
        Year
        <input inputMode="numeric" value={year}
               onChange={(e) => setYear(e.target.value.replace(/\D/g, ''))} />  {/* reject non-digits as typed */}
      </label>

      <button type="submit" disabled={!!titleError}>Add book</button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

Because the value passes through your code on each keystroke, you can validate instantly, transform input (upper-case, strip characters), enable or disable buttons, and keep several fields in sync. A `value` without an `onChange` makes the field read-only, and React warns about it.

Other elements follow the same pattern with small differences:

| Element | Controlled prop | Read the change from |
|---|---|---|
| `<input type="text">`, `<textarea>` | `value` | `e.target.value` |
| `<input type="checkbox">` | `checked` | `e.target.checked` |
| `<input type="radio">` | `checked={choice === 'x'}` | `e.target.value` |
| `<select>` | `value` on the `<select>` (not `selected` on options) | `e.target.value` |
| `<select multiple>` | `value={['a', 'b']}` | `Array.from(e.target.selectedOptions, (o) => o.value)` |
| `<input type="file">` | Always uncontrolled (value is read-only) | `e.target.files` |

**Uncontrolled inputs.** For a simple form that you only read on submit, the DOM can keep the values. `FormData` collects them by `name`:

```jsx
function SearchForm({ onSearch }) {
  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(e.currentTarget);          // reads every named field from the DOM
    onSearch({ q: data.get('q'), genre: data.get('genre') });
  }
  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="q" defaultValue="" />                 {/* defaultValue, not value */}
      <select name="genre" defaultValue="all">
        <option value="all">All</option>
        <option value="sf">Science fiction</option>
      </select>
      <button>Search</button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

**Form actions in React 19.** React 19 lets you pass a function to a form's `action` prop. React calls it with the `FormData` on submit, tracks its pending state, and resets uncontrolled fields after success. `useActionState` stores the result of the last submission, and `useFormStatus` lets a child button know that its form is submitting:

```tsx
import { useActionState } from 'react';
import { useFormStatus } from 'react-dom';

type Result = { error?: string; ok?: boolean };

async function createBook(_prev: Result, formData: FormData): Promise<Result> {
  const res = await fetch('/api/v1/books', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(Object.fromEntries(formData)),
  });
  if (!res.ok) return { error: (await res.json()).title ?? 'Could not save' };   // problem+json title
  return { ok: true };
}

function SubmitButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();                    // reads the status of the enclosing <form>
  return <button disabled={pending}>{pending ? 'Saving...' : 'Save'}</button>;
}

export function QuickAddBook() {
  const [state, formAction] = useActionState(createBook, {});
  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="title" required />
      <input name="author" required />
      <SubmitButton />
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
      {state.ok && <p>Saved.</p>}
    </form>
  );
}
```

**Form libraries.** Large forms (dozens of fields, nested arrays, async validation) are tedious with one `useState` per field. **React Hook Form** registers mostly uncontrolled inputs and re-renders only what changes. It integrates with schema validators such as **Zod**, so the same schema can validate on the client and on the server (see "Request Validation and Sanitization" in 12.3):

```tsx
import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
import { zodResolver } from '@hookform/resolvers/zod';
import { z } from 'zod';

const bookSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().trim().min(1, 'Title is required'),
  author: z.string().trim().min(1),
  year: z.coerce.number().int().min(1450).max(new Date().getFullYear()),  // coerce: input values are strings
});
type BookInput = z.infer<typeof bookSchema>;

function BookForm({ onSubmit }: { onSubmit: (b: BookInput) => Promise<void> }) {
  const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } =
    useForm<BookInput>({ resolver: zodResolver(bookSchema) });

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
      <input {...register('title')} />                 {/* register wires name, ref, onChange, onBlur */}
      {errors.title && <small>{errors.title.message}</small>}
      <input {...register('author')} />
      <input {...register('year')} inputMode="numeric" />
      {errors.year && <small>{errors.year.message}</small>}
      <button disabled={isSubmitting}>Save</button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

**Choosing.**

| | Controlled | Uncontrolled |
|---|---|---|
| Source of truth | React state | The DOM |
| Initial value | `value` | `defaultValue` / `defaultChecked` |
| Instant validation and formatting | Easy | Harder (read via ref or on blur) |
| Re-renders per keystroke | One per change | None |
| Reset | Set state | `form.reset()` or remount with a new `key` |
| Typical use | Interactive forms, dependent fields, search-as-you-type | Simple submit-only forms, file inputs, form actions, form libraries |

Never switch an input between controlled and uncontrolled during its life (for example from `value={undefined}` to `value="x"`); React warns because it cannot tell who owns the value. Initialise controlled state with `''`, not `undefined`.

Whatever the approach, client validation is a convenience for the user. The server must validate again, because any request can be sent without your form.

**Key Takeaways**

- Controlled inputs store their value in React state (`value` + `onChange`); uncontrolled inputs keep it in the DOM (`defaultValue`, refs, `FormData`).
- Controlled inputs enable instant validation and formatting; uncontrolled inputs avoid re-renders and suit submit-only forms.
- React 19 form actions (`action={fn}`, `useActionState`, `useFormStatus`) handle submission and pending state with less code.
- Libraries such as React Hook Form with Zod scale to large forms and can share validation schemas with the server.
- Never switch an input between controlled and uncontrolled; always validate again on the server.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a controlled sign-up form with email, password and "confirm password" fields that shows a mismatch error as the user types and disables the submit button until the form is valid.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build the "add book" form for the Chapter 12 API three ways: controlled with `useState`, uncontrolled with a React 19 form action, and with React Hook Form and Zod. Show the API's `422` validation errors next to the right field in each version and compare the amount of code.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled component, and when would you choose each?" *Hint:* talk about the source of truth, re-renders per keystroke, validation timing, file inputs, and what form libraries do internally.

#### Lifting State Up and Unidirectional Data Flow

**The problem.** Two sibling components need the same data. A `GenreFilter` lets the user choose a genre, and a `BookList` must show only books of that genre. If the filter keeps the selected genre in its own state, the list cannot see it, because siblings cannot read each other's state and props flow only downward.

**The solution: lift state up.** Move the state to the closest common ancestor. The ancestor passes the *value* down to whoever displays it and a *callback* down to whoever changes it:

```text
                 BookshelfPage
              state: genre = 'sf'
             /                     \
   value + onChange               value
       |                             |
   GenreFilter                   BookList
 (displays, reports)          (displays only)
```

```jsx
function BookshelfPage({ books }) {
  const [genre, setGenre] = useState('all');                       // lifted: one source of truth
  const visible = genre === 'all' ? books : books.filter((b) => b.genre === genre);

  return (
    <>
      <GenreFilter value={genre} onChange={setGenre} />
      <BookList books={visible} />
      <p>{visible.length} books shown</p>                          {/* a third consumer is free */}
    </>
  );
}

function GenreFilter({ value, onChange }) {                        // now fully controlled by its parent
  return (
    <select value={value} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}>
      <option value="all">All genres</option>
      <option value="sf">Science fiction</option>
      <option value="fantasy">Fantasy</option>
    </select>
  );
}
```

`GenreFilter` has become a **controlled component** in the broader sense: its important value is driven by props, not by its own state. That makes it more reusable, because the parent decides where the value lives.

**Unidirectional data flow.** React applications follow one rule: **data flows down, events flow up**.

```text
            state (owned by one component)
                 |  props (data down)
                 v
            child components render it
                 |  callback calls (events up)
                 v
            owner updates its state  ---> re-render with new props
```

Every piece of state has exactly one owner, and only the owner changes it. When the screen shows a wrong value, you trace it upward through props to the single component that owns the state and inspect the handlers that change it. Compare this with **two-way data binding** (Angular's `[(ngModel)]`, Vue's `v-model`), where a field and a model update each other automatically. Two-way binding is convenient for forms. But when many bindings form a web, a change can trigger chains of updates whose origin is hard to find. React accepts some extra wiring (`value` + `onChange`) in exchange for traceability. (Both Angular and Vue also use one-way flow between components; their two-way binding is syntax sugar over a value plus an event.)

**Where should state live?** A practical procedure:

1. List every component that *reads* the state.
2. Find their closest common ancestor.
3. Put the state there, or in a component above it if that makes more sense.
4. If no reasonable component exists, create a wrapper component just to own it.

Then keep state as **low** as possible. Lifting state too high makes large parts of the tree re-render on every change. Colocating it with its only consumer is better for performance and readability (14.5). When state is needed by distant parts of the app, move to context or a store (14.4).

**The opposite move: pushing state down.** If after a refactor only one child reads a piece of state, move it back into that child. State placement is not a one-time decision; it follows the needs of the UI.

**Key Takeaways**

- Siblings cannot share state directly; lift it to their closest common ancestor and pass value and callback down.
- Data flows down through props and events flow up through callbacks; every piece of state has one owner.
- One-way flow makes changes traceable; two-way binding trades this for convenience in forms.
- Put state at the lowest common ancestor of its readers, and move it down again when fewer components need it.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build two inputs, Celsius and Fahrenheit, that always show the same temperature. Decide which single value to store, where to store it, and derive the other.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a bookshelf page with a search box, a genre filter, a sort selector, a list and a "N results" counter as separate components. Draw the component tree, mark where each piece of state lives, and justify each choice.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is unidirectional data flow, and how is it different from two-way binding?" *Hint:* describe ownership, how a bug is traced, and how frameworks with two-way binding implement it under the hood.

#### Higher-Order Components and Render Props

**Why these patterns existed.** Before hooks (2019), class components had no way to share *stateful* logic: you could not call a function that "adds a subscription to this component". The community developed two patterns based on composition. Hooks have replaced them for most purposes, but you will meet both in existing code and in some libraries.

**Higher-order components (HOCs).** A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a new component that wraps it with extra props or behaviour. It applies the idea of higher-order functions (Chapter 3) to components. The naming convention is `withSomething`:

```jsx
// A HOC that injects the current window width as a prop
function withWindowWidth(WrappedComponent) {
  function WithWindowWidth(props) {
    const [width, setWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth);
    useEffect(() => {
      const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
      window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
      return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
    }, []);
    return <WrappedComponent {...props} windowWidth={width} />;  // pass through + inject
  }
  WithWindowWidth.displayName =                                  // readable name in React DevTools
    `withWindowWidth(${WrappedComponent.displayName || WrappedComponent.name})`;
  return WithWindowWidth;
}

function Gallery({ windowWidth, books }) {
  const columns = windowWidth > 900 ? 4 : 2;
  return <Grid columns={columns} items={books} />;
}
export default withWindowWidth(Gallery);
```

Typical HOCs guard routes (`withAuth`), inject data (`connect` from older react-redux), add logging or error handling. Two HOCs remain common in modern React: `memo` (returns a component that skips renders) and `lazy` (14.5), although they are not usually described that way.

**Render props.** A **render prop** is a prop whose value is a function that returns JSX. The component owns the logic and calls the function with its data, and the caller decides what to render:

```jsx
function WindowWidth({ children }) {               // `children` used as the render function
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth);
  useEffect(() => {
    const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
    window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
  }, []);
  return children(width);                          // the caller's function decides the output
}

<WindowWidth>
  {(width) => <Grid columns={width > 900 ? 4 : 2} items={books} />}
</WindowWidth>
```

Render props are still useful when a component must let callers customise the rendering of *parts* of its output. Example: a virtualised list's `renderItem`, a combobox's option renderer, or a data table's cell renderer.

**The same logic as a hook.**

```jsx
function useWindowWidth() {
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth);
  useEffect(() => {
    const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
    window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
  }, []);
  return width;
}

function Gallery({ books }) {
  const width = useWindowWidth();                  // no wrapper, no extra tree level, explicit source
  return <Grid columns={width > 900 ? 4 : 2} items={books} />;
}
```

**Problems that hooks solved.** Stacking several HOCs or render props creates **wrapper hell**: deeply nested trees in DevTools and pyramids of callbacks in JSX.

```jsx
export default withRouter(withTheme(withAuth(withWindowWidth(Gallery))));
// Which HOC supplied `user`? Two HOCs both injecting `data` silently overwrite each other.
```

| | HOC | Render prop | Custom hook |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shape | `withX(Component)` returns a component | `<X>{(data) => ...}</X>` | `const data = useX()` |
| Extra components in the tree | One per HOC | One per render prop | None |
| Where data comes from | Implicit (injected props) | Explicit (function argument) | Explicit (return value) |
| Prop name collisions | Possible | No | No |
| Static typing | Awkward generics | Good | Good |
| Still a good choice for | Wrapping whole components (`memo`, auth guards in some routers) | Customising rendered parts (`renderItem`) | Sharing stateful logic (default) |

**Key Takeaways**

- A higher-order component is a function `withX(Component)` that returns a wrapped component with extra props or behaviour.
- A render prop is a function prop that a component calls to let the caller decide what to render.
- Both were invented to share stateful logic among class components; custom hooks now do this without extra tree levels or name collisions.
- HOCs still appear as `memo`, `lazy` and some library APIs; render props remain useful for customising parts of a component's output.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a `withLoading(Component)` HOC that renders "Loading..." when a `loading` prop is true and the wrapped component otherwise. Set a proper `displayName`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the same mouse-position tracker three ways (HOC, render prop and custom hook) and use each in a component that draws a dot at the pointer. Compare the component tree in React DevTools and the TypeScript types required.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why did hooks largely replace HOCs and render props?" *Hint:* mention wrapper hell, implicit prop injection and collisions, typing difficulties, and the cases where render props are still the right tool.

#### Portals and Error Boundaries

This topic covers two features that deal with situations the normal component tree handles badly: content that must escape its parent's box in the DOM, and errors that would otherwise unmount the whole application.

**The problem portals solve.** A modal dialog, tooltip or dropdown is often logically part of a deep component (a "Delete" button inside a book card), but visually it must float above everything. If it is rendered inside the card, CSS gets in the way. An ancestor with `overflow: hidden` clips it, and an ancestor with `transform` or its own stacking context traps its `z-index`.

**Portals.** `createPortal(children, domNode)` renders children into a *different DOM node*, usually one directly under `<body>`, while keeping them in the *same place in the React tree*:

```tsx
import { createPortal } from 'react-dom';

function Modal({ title, onClose, children }: { title: string; onClose: () => void; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const onKey = (e: KeyboardEvent) => e.key === 'Escape' && onClose();   // keyboard users can close it
    document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);
    return () => document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
  }, [onClose]);

  return createPortal(
    <div className="backdrop" onClick={onClose}>
      <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="modal-title" className="modal"
           onClick={(e) => e.stopPropagation()}>        {/* clicks inside do not close it */}
        <h2 id="modal-title">{title}</h2>
        {children}
      </div>
    </div>,
    document.body,                                      // DOM destination: outside every clipping ancestor
  );
}

function BookCard({ book, onDelete }) {
  const [confirming, setConfirming] = useState(false);
  return (
    <article className="book-card">                     {/* may have overflow: hidden, no problem */}
      <h3>{book.title}</h3>
      <button onClick={() => setConfirming(true)}>Delete</button>
      {confirming && (
        <Modal title="Delete book?" onClose={() => setConfirming(false)}>
          <button onClick={() => onDelete(book.id)}>Delete</button>
        </Modal>
      )}
    </article>
  );
}
```

```text
React tree (logical)                   DOM tree (physical)
<BookCard>                             <body>
  <article>                              <div id="root"> ... <article class="book-card"> ... </article>
    <Modal>   ---- portal ---->          <div class="backdrop"> <div role="dialog"> ... </div></div>
```

Because the portal stays in the React tree, it still receives context from its ancestors, and **React events bubble through the React tree**, not the DOM tree. A click inside the modal reaches `onClick` handlers on `BookCard`'s ancestors even though the DOM nodes are elsewhere. Keep this in mind when a parent handles clicks.

Portals do not make a dialog accessible by themselves. Move focus into it when it opens, trap Tab inside it, restore focus on close, and label it. The native `<dialog>` element with `showModal()` renders in the browser's **top layer** (above all `z-index`), adds a backdrop, makes the rest of the page inert and handles Escape. It is a good alternative to a hand-made portal modal. Component libraries (see "Component Libraries and Design Systems") provide tested implementations.

**The problem error boundaries solve.** If a component throws during rendering (for example `book.author.name` when `author` is `null`), React cannot know what the UI should look like. Since React 16, an uncaught render error **unmounts the entire application**, leaving a blank page. This is safer than showing a corrupted UI, but it means one broken widget takes the whole app down.

**Error boundaries.** An error boundary is a component that catches errors thrown while rendering its descendants, shows a fallback UI instead, and lets the rest of the application keep working. Like a circuit breaker in a house, it cuts power to one room instead of the whole building. Error boundaries must be **class components**, because there is no hook equivalent of the two methods they use:

```tsx
import { Component, type ErrorInfo, type ReactNode } from 'react';

type Props = { fallback: ReactNode; children: ReactNode };
type State = { hasError: boolean };

export class ErrorBoundary extends Component<Props, State> {
  state: State = { hasError: false };

  static getDerivedStateFromError(): State {
    return { hasError: true };                     // render phase: switch to the fallback
  }

  componentDidCatch(error: Error, info: ErrorInfo) {
    reportError(error, info.componentStack);       // commit phase: log to Sentry or similar
  }

  render() {
    return this.state.hasError ? this.props.fallback : this.props.children;
  }
}
```

```jsx
<Layout>
  <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Recommendations are unavailable.</p>}>
    <Recommendations />                {/* if it crashes, only this box shows the fallback */}
  </ErrorBoundary>
  <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Could not show the book list.</p>}>
    <BookList />
  </ErrorBoundary>
</Layout>
```

In practice most teams use the small **react-error-boundary** library, which provides an `<ErrorBoundary>` with `FallbackComponent`, a `resetErrorBoundary` function for "Try again" buttons, `resetKeys` and a `useErrorBoundary` hook to trigger the boundary from async code.

**What error boundaries do not catch.**

| Not caught | Why | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Errors in event handlers | They do not happen during rendering | `try`/`catch` in the handler and set error state |
| Async code (`setTimeout`, promise callbacks) | Runs outside React's render | Catch and store in state; or rethrow into render (`useErrorBoundary`) |
| Server-side rendering errors | Handled by the server framework | Framework error pages (`error.tsx` in Next.js) |
| Errors in the boundary itself | It cannot catch its own failure | A boundary higher up |

**Where to place boundaries.** One at the root to show a friendly "Something went wrong" page instead of a blank screen. One per route, so other pages still work. And one around independent widgets (sidebar, comments, third-party embeds). React 19 also accepts `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError` options on `createRoot` for central error reporting.

**Key Takeaways**

- `createPortal` renders children into another DOM node (often `document.body`) while keeping them in the same React tree, which avoids `overflow` and `z-index` clipping.
- Portal content still receives context, and its events bubble through React ancestors; accessibility (focus, labelling) is still your job, and `<dialog>` is a strong native alternative.
- An uncaught render error unmounts the whole app; error boundaries contain the failure and show a fallback.
- Error boundaries are class components using `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`; react-error-boundary provides a ready-made version.
- They do not catch errors in event handlers, async code, SSR or themselves; place them at the root, per route and around independent widgets.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a `Tooltip` that renders through a portal into `document.body` and positions itself under its trigger using `getBoundingClientRect`. Put the trigger in a container with `overflow: hidden` to prove the tooltip is not clipped.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Wrap three dashboard widgets in separate error boundaries, make one throw on a button click by setting state that causes a render error, and add a "Try again" button that resets only that boundary. Then make an event handler throw and explain why the boundary does not catch it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why are error boundaries still class components, and what errors do they miss?" *Hint:* name the two lifecycle methods involved, the render/commit split, and handle the uncaught cases (handlers, async, SSR) explicitly.

#### Styling with CSS Modules and CSS-in-JS

**Why styling is a problem in component apps.** CSS was designed for documents: every selector is **global**. In an application with hundreds of components written by many people, a rule like `.title { font-size: 2rem }` written for one card silently affects every other `.title`. Nobody dares delete old CSS because they cannot know what depends on it. Component-based styling solutions all try to give CSS the same properties as components: **local scope**, **colocation** with the component, and **dead-code elimination** when a component is deleted.

**Plain CSS and inline styles.** You can import a global stylesheet (`import './App.css'`) and use naming conventions such as BEM (`.book-card__title--highlighted`) to avoid collisions. The `style` prop is fine for truly dynamic values (a progress bar's width), but it cannot express hover states, media queries or pseudo-elements, and it bypasses the browser's style caching.

```jsx
<div className="progress"><div className="progress-fill" style={{ width: `${percent}%` }} /></div>
```

**CSS Modules.** A file named `*.module.css` is processed by the build tool (Vite, webpack and Next.js support it out of the box). Every class name is renamed to a unique one, and importing the file gives you an object that maps your names to the generated ones:

```css
/* BookCard.module.css */
.card { border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; padding: 1rem; }
.title { font-size: 1.25rem; margin: 0; }
.card:hover .title { text-decoration: underline; }          /* normal CSS: hover, nesting, media queries */
.highlighted { border-color: var(--accent); }
```

```tsx
import styles from './BookCard.module.css';
import clsx from 'clsx';                                     // tiny helper to join class names conditionally

export function BookCard({ book, highlighted }) {
  return (
    <article className={clsx(styles.card, highlighted && styles.highlighted)}>
      <h3 className={styles.title}>{book.title}</h3>         {/* rendered as class="_title_x7k2a_5" */}
    </article>
  );
}
```

CSS Modules have no runtime cost (the output is ordinary CSS files), work with server rendering, and keep you writing standard CSS. Combined with CSS custom properties (`var(--accent)`) for theming, they are a solid default.

**CSS-in-JS.** Libraries such as **styled-components** and **Emotion** let you write CSS inside JavaScript, usually with tagged template literals, and create components that carry their styles. Styles can depend on props:

```jsx
import styled from 'styled-components';

const Card = styled.article`
  border: 1px solid ${({ theme }) => theme.colors.border};
  border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 1rem;
  border-color: ${({ $highlighted, theme }) => ($highlighted ? theme.colors.accent : theme.colors.border)};
`;   /* $-prefixed "transient" props are not forwarded to the DOM */

<Card $highlighted={isFavourite}>...</Card>
```

These **runtime** CSS-in-JS libraries generate and inject `<style>` rules in the browser while rendering. That makes them very flexible, but it has costs: extra JavaScript, style computation on every render, and complications with server rendering, streaming and React Server Components (14.5). Since about 2023 the ecosystem has moved toward **zero-runtime** CSS-in-JS (vanilla-extract, Linaria, Panda CSS, StyleX), which keeps the authoring style but extracts static CSS at build time.

**Utility-first CSS.** **Tailwind CSS** takes a different approach: instead of writing CSS, you compose small single-purpose classes directly in the markup. The build step generates only the classes you use.

```jsx
<article className={`rounded-lg border p-4 ${highlighted ? 'border-indigo-500' : 'border-gray-200'}`}>
  <h3 className="m-0 text-xl hover:underline">{book.title}</h3>
</article>
```

Tailwind removes naming and global-scope problems and keeps the CSS bundle small. It enforces a consistent design scale (spacing, colours) but makes markup verbose; component extraction keeps it manageable.

**Comparison.**

| Approach | Scope | Runtime cost | Dynamic styles | SSR / Server Components | Typical tools |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global CSS + BEM | Global (by convention) | None | Classes, CSS variables | Yes | Plain CSS, Sass |
| Inline `style` | Element | Small | Fully dynamic values | Yes | Built in |
| CSS Modules | Local (generated names) | None | Class toggling, CSS variables | Yes | Vite, webpack, Next.js |
| Runtime CSS-in-JS | Local | Yes (style generation in browser) | Props-based, very flexible | Extra setup; not in Server Components | styled-components, Emotion |
| Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS | Local | None | Variants, CSS variables | Yes | vanilla-extract, Panda, StyleX |
| Utility-first | Utility classes | None | Class toggling | Yes | Tailwind CSS |

**Practical advice.** For new projects, CSS Modules or Tailwind are the common defaults, with CSS custom properties for theming and dark mode. Pass dynamic numeric values through CSS variables (`style={{ '--progress': '40%' }}`) so the rules stay in CSS. Whatever you choose, be consistent across the codebase.

**Key Takeaways**

- Global CSS scales badly in component apps; modern approaches aim for local scope, colocation and safe deletion.
- CSS Modules rename classes per file at build time, cost nothing at runtime and keep standard CSS.
- Runtime CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion) is flexible but adds runtime cost and complicates SSR and Server Components; zero-runtime variants avoid this.
- Tailwind composes utility classes in markup and ships only the classes used.
- Use the `style` prop or CSS variables for truly dynamic values; choose one approach and use it consistently.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Style a `BookCard` with a CSS Module, add a `highlighted` variant with `clsx`, and inspect the generated class names in DevTools.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement light and dark themes with CSS custom properties defined on `:root` and `[data-theme="dark"]`, toggled by the `ThemeProvider` from 14.2. Then reimplement the same card with Tailwind and compare the markup and CSS bundle size after `npm run build`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What are the trade-offs of runtime CSS-in-JS, and why has the ecosystem moved away from it?" *Hint:* consider style injection during render, bundle size, server rendering and streaming, React Server Components, and what zero-runtime libraries extract at build time.

#### Component Libraries and Design Systems
