**Why not build every component yourself.** A production-quality select box, date picker or modal is much harder than it looks. It must support keyboard navigation, focus management and screen readers (WAI-ARIA patterns), right-to-left languages, touch, positioning near viewport edges, and theming. Rebuilding these per project wastes time and usually produces inaccessible widgets. Teams therefore either adopt a **component library** or build an internal **design system**, often on top of one.

**Design system vs component library.**

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Design tokens** | Named design decisions: colours, spacing scale, typography, radii, shadows, motion (`--color-accent`, `space-4`) |
| **Component library** | Reusable, tested coded components (`Button`, `Dialog`, `Table`) |
| **Design system** | Tokens + components + guidelines (when to use what, tone of voice, accessibility rules) + design files + documentation, maintained as a product |

Examples of public design systems: Google's Material Design, IBM's Carbon, Shopify's Polaris, GitHub's Primer and Microsoft's Fluent. A design system is like a city's building code plus a catalogue of prefabricated parts: individual teams build different houses, but doors, stairs and signs work the same everywhere.

**Kinds of React component libraries.**

| Kind | Examples | You get | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fully styled | MUI (Material UI), Ant Design, Chakra UI, Mantine, Fluent UI | Complete components with a visual style and theming API | Fast to start; harder to match a custom brand; larger bundles |
| Headless (unstyled) | Radix UI Primitives, React Aria, Headless UI, Base UI, Ark UI | Behaviour and accessibility only; you supply the styles | Full visual control; more styling work |
| Copy-in ("open code") | shadcn/ui (Radix or Base UI + Tailwind) | Component source code copied into your repo | You own and modify the code; you also maintain it |

**Using a headless primitive.** A headless library provides correct behaviour (focus trap, Escape key, ARIA attributes, portal), and you add classes:

```tsx
import * as Dialog from '@radix-ui/react-dialog';
import styles from './ConfirmDialog.module.css';

export function ConfirmDialog({ trigger, title, onConfirm }) {
  return (
    <Dialog.Root>
      <Dialog.Trigger asChild>{trigger}</Dialog.Trigger>      {/* asChild: reuse the caller's button */}
      <Dialog.Portal>
        <Dialog.Overlay className={styles.overlay} />
        <Dialog.Content className={styles.content}>            {/* focus trapped, Escape closes */}
          <Dialog.Title>{title}</Dialog.Title>
          <Dialog.Close asChild><button>Cancel</button></Dialog.Close>
          <Dialog.Close asChild><button onClick={onConfirm}>Confirm</button></Dialog.Close>
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog.Root>
  );
}
```

Note the **compound component** API (`Dialog.Root`, `Dialog.Trigger`, `Dialog.Content`), introduced in 14.1: the parts share state through context, and you arrange them freely.

**Building your own design system components.** Good shared components:

- Wrap native elements and **forward** their props and `ref` (14.2), so consumers can add `aria-*`, `type` and event handlers.
- Expose a small set of **variants** (`variant="primary" | "secondary" | "danger"`, `size="sm" | "md"`) instead of arbitrary style props, so that the design stays consistent.
- Read colours and spacing from **tokens** (CSS variables), so theming and dark mode need no code changes.
- Are **accessible by default**: an `IconButton` requires an `aria-label` prop in its TypeScript type.

```tsx
type ButtonProps = React.ComponentProps<'button'> & {
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger';
  size?: 'sm' | 'md';
};

export function Button({ variant = 'primary', size = 'md', className, ...rest }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button className={clsx(styles.button, styles[variant], styles[size], className)} {...rest} />;
}
```

**Documenting with Storybook.** **Storybook** is a workshop where each component is rendered in isolation in all its states ("stories"). Designers review it, developers find existing components instead of rewriting them, and stories double as visual regression and accessibility tests.

```tsx
// Button.stories.tsx
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite';
import { Button } from './Button';

const meta = { component: Button, args: { children: 'Save' } } satisfies Meta<typeof Button>;
export default meta;

export const Primary: StoryObj<typeof meta> = {};
export const Danger: StoryObj<typeof meta> = { args: { variant: 'danger', children: 'Delete' } };
export const Disabled: StoryObj<typeof meta> = { args: { disabled: true } };
```

**Choosing a library.** Ask: Do we have a custom brand that must be matched exactly (favour headless or copy-in)? Do we need complex data components such as data grids and date pickers soon (fully styled libraries such as MUI or Ant Design ship them)? Does it work with our styling approach and with server rendering? What is its accessibility record, bundle size, maintenance activity and licence (some advanced components are commercial)?

**Key Takeaways**

- Accessible, robust widgets are hard to build; component libraries and design systems prevent each team from rebuilding them.
- A design system combines tokens, components, guidelines and documentation; a component library is its code part.
- Fully styled libraries are fastest to adopt, headless libraries give full visual control, and copy-in approaches (shadcn/ui) give you ownership of the source.
- Shared components should forward native props and refs, expose limited variants, use tokens and be accessible by default.
- Storybook documents components in isolation and supports visual and accessibility testing.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Install a fully styled library (MUI or Mantine) and build a book list page with its `Card`, `Button` and `TextField` components. Change the primary colour through its theme.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a `Select` on top of a headless library (Radix or React Aria), style it with CSS Modules and design tokens, and test it with only the keyboard and with a screen reader. Write three Storybook stories for it.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your company has three React apps with inconsistent UIs. How would you introduce a design system?" *Hint:* start from tokens and the most-used components, choose build vs buy (headless foundation), plan versioning and distribution as a package, documentation, adoption and ownership.

<a id="144-routing-data-and-state-management"></a>
### 14.4 Routing, Data and State Management

A real application has many screens, loads data from servers and shares state across distant components. This subchapter covers client-side routing with React Router, nested routes and guards, the patterns and pitfalls of loading data, a typed client for the Chapter 12 REST API, global state with Context and Redux, Redux Toolkit and its lighter alternatives, libraries specialised in caching server state, and live updates over WebSocket.

#### Client-Side Routing with React Router

**Why client-side routing.** In a traditional multi-page site every link triggers a full HTTP request, and the browser discards the current page, JavaScript state included, and loads a new one. A **single-page application** (SPA) loads one HTML page and then swaps views in JavaScript. Navigation becomes instant and state survives, but the application must take over the browser's routing duties: show the right view for the current URL, change the URL when the user navigates, support the Back and Forward buttons, deep links and bookmarks.

The browser provides the building blocks through the **History API** (Chapter 6): `history.pushState()` changes the URL without a request, and the `popstate` event fires on Back/Forward. A **router** library wraps them and maps URLs to components:

```text
user clicks <Link to="/books/42">
   -> router calls history.pushState(null, '', '/books/42')     (no HTTP request)
   -> router matches '/books/:id' and renders <BookDetails />
user presses Back
   -> browser fires popstate -> router re-matches '/books' -> renders <BookList />
user reloads /books/42
   -> real HTTP request: the server must return index.html for any app route (history fallback)
```

The last line is important: the server must answer every application URL with `index.html` and let the router take over (see "Serving SPAs and API Gateways" in 12.3).

| History mode | URL | Server configuration | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Browser history | `/books/42` | Needs a fallback to `index.html` | Clean URLs; the standard choice |
| Hash history | `/#/books/42` | None (the hash is never sent to the server) | For static hosting without rewrites |
| Memory history | Not in the address bar | None | Tests, embedded widgets, React Native |

**React Router.** React Router is the most widely used router for React. Version 7 (late 2024) merged the former Remix framework into it and ships as a single `react-router` package (`react-router-dom` remains as a re-export for older imports). It can be used in three **modes** of increasing scope:

| Mode | Setup | Adds |
|---|---|---|
| Declarative | `<BrowserRouter>`, `<Routes>`, `<Route>` | URL matching, links, navigation hooks |
| Data | `createBrowserRouter` + `<RouterProvider>` | Route `loader`s and `action`s, pending states, error elements |
| Framework | Vite plugin, `routes.ts`, file conventions | Type-safe route modules, code splitting, server rendering |

**Declarative mode.**

```tsx
// main.tsx
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from 'react-router';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<HomePage />} />
      <Route path="/books" element={<BookListPage />} />
      <Route path="/books/:id" element={<BookDetailsPage />} />   {/* :id is a dynamic segment */}
      <Route path="/about" element={<AboutPage />} />
      <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} />               {/* catch-all for unknown URLs */}
    </Routes>
  </BrowserRouter>,
);
```

React Router ranks routes by specificity, so the order of `<Route>` elements does not matter: `/books/new` wins over `/books/:id` for that URL.

**Navigating.** Use `<Link>` instead of `<a>`. A plain anchor causes a full page reload, losing all state. `<Link>` renders a real `<a href>`, so middle-click and "open in new tab" keep working, but it intercepts normal clicks and calls `pushState`. `<NavLink>` additionally knows whether it matches the current URL, which is useful for highlighting the active menu entry:

```tsx
import { Link, NavLink, useNavigate } from 'react-router';

function NavBar() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <NavLink to="/" end>Home</NavLink>                                   {/* end: exact match only */}
      <NavLink to="/books" className={({ isActive }) => (isActive ? 'active' : undefined)}>
        Books
      </NavLink>
    </nav>
  );
}

function BookRow({ book }) {
  const navigate = useNavigate();                       // programmatic navigation
  async function handleDelete() {
    await api.deleteBook(book.id);
    navigate('/books', { replace: true });              // replace: do not leave a history entry
  }
  return (
    <li>
      <Link to={`/books/${book.id}`}>{book.title}</Link>
      <button onClick={handleDelete}>Delete</button>
    </li>
  );
}
```

**Data mode.** In data mode, routes are defined as objects and each route can declare a **loader** that fetches its data *before* the route renders. Navigation then shows a pending state instead of rendering a component that immediately starts loading:

```tsx
import { createBrowserRouter, RouterProvider, useLoaderData } from 'react-router';

const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    path: '/books/:id',
    loader: async ({ params, request }) => {
      const res = await fetch(`/api/v1/books/${params.id}`, { signal: request.signal });  // aborted if the user navigates away
      if (res.status === 404) throw new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });           // shown by errorElement
      return res.json();
    },
    Component: BookDetailsPage,
    errorElement: <RouteError />,
  },
]);

function BookDetailsPage() {
  const book = useLoaderData();                // already loaded when the component renders
  return <h1>{book.title}</h1>;
}

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(<RouterProvider router={router} />);
```

**Alternatives.** TanStack Router offers fully type-safe routes and search parameters. Next.js (14.5) and React Router's framework mode use **file-based routing**, where the file system defines the routes.

**Key Takeaways**

- Client-side routing maps URLs to components and uses the History API (`pushState`, `popstate`) to change views without page reloads.
- The server must return `index.html` for every application route (history fallback) so deep links and reloads work.
- React Router v7 ships as `react-router` and has declarative, data and framework modes.
- Use `<Link>`/`<NavLink>` instead of `<a>` for internal links and `useNavigate` for programmatic navigation.
- Data mode loaders fetch data before a route renders and integrate with abort signals and error elements.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add React Router to the bookshelf app with routes for `/`, `/books`, `/books/:id` and a 404 page, plus a navigation bar whose active link is highlighted.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Convert the app to data mode: load the book list and book details with loaders, show a global "Loading..." bar using `useNavigation().state`, and render a custom error element when the API returns `404`. Build it and serve it from Express with a history fallback, then reload a deep link.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A user reloads `https://app.example.com/books/42` and gets a 404 from the server. Why, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* explain what the server receives on reload in a SPA with browser history, and the fallback rule for non-API, non-asset paths.

#### Nested Routes, Params and Navigation Guards

**Nested routes and layouts.** Most applications share layout between pages: a header and sidebar around every page, a tab bar around every page in a section. **Nested routes** model this directly. A parent route renders the shared layout and an `<Outlet />` where the matching child route appears, like a picture frame whose picture changes with the URL:

```tsx
<Routes>
  <Route element={<AppLayout />}>                        {/* layout route: no path, just wraps children */}
    <Route index element={<HomePage />} />               {/* index route: renders at the parent's exact path */}
    <Route path="books" element={<BooksLayout />}>
      <Route index element={<BookListPage />} />         {/* /books */}
      <Route path="new" element={<NewBookPage />} />     {/* /books/new */}
      <Route path=":id" element={<BookDetailsPage />} /> {/* /books/42 */}
      <Route path=":id/edit" element={<EditBookPage />} />
    </Route>
  </Route>
  <Route path="login" element={<LoginPage />} />         {/* outside the layout */}
  <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} />
</Routes>
```

```tsx
import { Outlet } from 'react-router';

function AppLayout() {
  return (
    <>
      <NavBar />
      <main><Outlet /></main>                            {/* child route renders here */}
      <Footer />
    </>
  );
}
```

```text
URL /books/42/edit
<AppLayout>                  NavBar + Footer stay mounted while navigating between books
  <BooksLayout>              section header ("Books") stays mounted
    <EditBookPage />         only this part changes
```

Because layouts stay mounted, their state (an open sidebar, a scroll position) survives navigation between their children.

**URL parameters.** Dynamic segments are read with `useParams`. They are always **strings** (or `undefined`), so validate and convert them:

```tsx
import { useParams } from 'react-router';

function BookDetailsPage() {
  const { id } = useParams();                            // '/books/42' -> { id: '42' }
  const bookId = Number(id);
  if (!Number.isInteger(bookId)) return <NotFoundPage />;
  return <BookDetails id={bookId} />;
}
```

**Search parameters as state.** Filters, sorting and pagination belong in the **query string** (`/books?author=herbert&page=2`), not only in component state. The URL can then be bookmarked, shared and restored by Back. `useSearchParams` works like `useState` for the query string:

```tsx
import { useSearchParams } from 'react-router';

function BookListPage() {
  const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();
  const page = Number(params.get('page') ?? '1');
  const author = params.get('author') ?? '';

  function goTo(p: number) {
    setParams((prev) => { prev.set('page', String(p)); return prev; });   // keeps other params
  }

  return (
    <>
      <input
        value={author}
        onChange={(e) => setParams({ author: e.target.value, page: '1' }, { replace: true })}  // no history entry per keystroke
      />
      <BookTable author={author} page={page} />
      <button disabled={page === 1} onClick={() => goTo(page - 1)}>Previous</button>
      <button onClick={() => goTo(page + 1)}>Next</button>
    </>
  );
}
```

**Relative links.** Inside nested routes, `to` values without a leading slash are relative to the current route: in `BookDetailsPage`, `<Link to="edit">` goes to `/books/42/edit` and `<Link to="..">` to the parent route.

**Navigation guards.** Some routes require a logged-in user or a specific role. A **guard** checks the condition before rendering and redirects otherwise. In declarative mode, a layout route can do this for all its children:

```tsx
import { Navigate, Outlet, useLocation } from 'react-router';

function RequireAuth({ role }: { role?: 'admin' }) {
  const { user, status } = useAuth();                    // from the AuthProvider (14.2)
  const location = useLocation();

  if (status === 'checking') return <Spinner />;         // do not redirect while the session is being restored
  if (!user) {
    // Remember where the user wanted to go, so login can send them back
    return <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location }} />;
  }
  if (role && user.role !== role) return <Forbidden />;
  return <Outlet />;
}

<Route element={<RequireAuth />}>
  <Route path="books/new" element={<NewBookPage />} />
</Route>
<Route element={<RequireAuth role="admin" />}>
  <Route path="admin/*" element={<AdminPage />} />
</Route>
```

```tsx
// LoginPage: after a successful login, return to the original destination
const location = useLocation();
const navigate = useNavigate();
const from = location.state?.from?.pathname ?? '/';
await login(email, password);
navigate(from, { replace: true });
```

In data mode, the same check can run in a parent route's `loader` (`if (!user) throw redirect('/login')`), so protected data is never even requested.

**Blocking navigation.** To warn about unsaved changes, `useBlocker` intercepts in-app navigation, and a `beforeunload` listener covers closing the tab:

```tsx
const blocker = useBlocker(({ currentLocation, nextLocation }) =>
  isDirty && currentLocation.pathname !== nextLocation.pathname);

{blocker.state === 'blocked' && (
  <ConfirmDialog title="Discard changes?" onConfirm={blocker.proceed} onCancel={blocker.reset} />
)}
```

**Guards are UX, not security.** Anyone can open DevTools and render any component, or call the API directly. A client-side guard only avoids showing pages that will not work. Every protected API endpoint must check authentication and authorisation on the server (see "API Keys and Role-Based Access Control" in 10.3).

**Key Takeaways**

- Nested routes render shared layouts with an `<Outlet />`; layouts stay mounted while child routes change.
- `useParams` reads dynamic segments as strings; validate and convert them.
- Keep filters, sorting and pagination in the query string with `useSearchParams` so they are shareable and survive reloads.
- Guards (a layout route with `<Navigate>`, or a loader with `redirect`) send unauthenticated users to login and remember where they were going; `useBlocker` protects unsaved changes.
- Client-side guards improve UX only; the server must enforce access control.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a `/books` section with a layout that shows a sub-navigation ("All", "Add new") and an `<Outlet />`, plus index, `new` and `:id` child routes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Store the book list's `author`, `sort` and `page` in the URL. Verify that Back restores the previous filter, that a copied link reproduces the same view, and that typing in the author field does not create one history entry per keystroke.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How do you implement protected routes in a React SPA, and why is that not enough to protect data?" *Hint:* describe a guard component or loader redirect, preserving the target location, handling the 'session still loading' state, and server-side enforcement of every API call.

#### Data Fetching and Loading States

**The core difficulty.** Fetching is asynchronous, so a component that displays remote data must handle several states, not just "here is the data". Forgetting any of them produces the classic bugs: a blank screen while loading, an infinite spinner after an error, an empty-looking list that is actually still loading.

**Model the states explicitly.** A request is in exactly one of a few states. Represent them with a **discriminated union**, not independent booleans, so impossible combinations cannot be represented:

```tsx
type AsyncState<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error };

// Booleans allow nonsense: { isLoading: true, isError: true, data: [...] }
```

```text
      fetch()            response ok
idle ---------> loading -------------> success
                   |                      |
                   | network/HTTP error   | refetch
                   v                      v
                 error  ---- retry ---> loading
```

```tsx
function useBooks(author: string) {
  const [state, setState] = useState<AsyncState<Book[]>>({ status: 'idle' });

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState({ status: 'loading' });
    api.listBooks({ author }, controller.signal)
      .then((page) => setState({ status: 'success', data: page.data }))
      .catch((error) => {
        if (!controller.signal.aborted) setState({ status: 'error', error });
      });
    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [author]);

  return state;
}

function BookListPage({ author }: { author: string }) {
  const state = useBooks(author);

  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
    case 'loading':
      return <BookListSkeleton />;
    case 'error':
      return <ErrorMessage error={state.error} />;
    case 'success':
      return state.data.length === 0
        ? <EmptyState message="No books by this author yet." />    // empty is not the same as loading
        : <BookList books={state.data} />;
  }
}
```

**Loading UI that feels fast.**

| Technique | Use when |
|---|---|
| **Skeleton screen** (grey shapes matching the final layout) | Content areas with a known shape; avoids layout shift |
| **Spinner** | Small areas or unknown shape; avoid full-page spinners |
| **Delayed indicator** (show only after ~200 ms) | Fast responses would otherwise cause a distracting flash |
| **Keep previous data** while refetching, dimmed | Pagination and filtering; avoids the content disappearing |
| **Optimistic update** | Mutations likely to succeed (likes, toggles); see "Consuming REST APIs from React" |

**Waterfalls.** When components fetch their own data in effects, a child cannot start fetching until its parent has loaded and rendered it. Requests that could run in parallel run one after the other:

```text
Fetch-on-render (each component fetches in its own effect)
  0ms   |--- GET /user ---|
  300ms                   |--- GET /user/7/shelves ---|
  600ms                                               |--- GET /shelves/3/books ---|
  900ms  page complete

Fetch in parallel (start all independent requests together)
  0ms   |--- GET /user ---|
  0ms   |--- GET /shelves (for current session) ---|
  0ms   |--- GET /books?shelf=3 ---|
  300ms  page complete
```

Ways to avoid waterfalls: start independent requests together (`Promise.all`); fetch at the **route level** with loaders (fetch-then-render) so data for the whole page starts loading on navigation; prefetch on hover or when a link becomes visible; and move data fetching to the server (14.5).

**Three strategies.**

| Strategy | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fetch-on-render | `useEffect` in each component | Simple, colocated | Waterfalls, no caching, race handling by hand |
| Fetch-then-render | Router loaders fetch before rendering the route | No waterfalls inside a route, data ready at render | Navigation waits for the slowest request |
| Render-as-you-fetch | Start fetching early, pass the promise, suspend where data is needed (`use` + Suspense) | Parallel, progressive display with Suspense boundaries | Needs a framework or library that caches promises |

**Suspense for data with `use`.** React 19's `use(promise)` reads a promise's value during render. If the promise is still pending, the component **suspends**, and the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary shows its fallback. If the promise rejects, the nearest error boundary catches it. The promise must be created *outside* render (by a loader, a cache or a parent) and kept stable; creating it inside the component would start a new request on every render.

```tsx
import { Suspense, use } from 'react';

function BookDetails({ bookPromise }: { bookPromise: Promise<Book> }) {
  const book = use(bookPromise);              // suspends until resolved
  return <h1>{book.title}</h1>;
}

function BookPage({ id }: { id: number }) {
  const [bookPromise] = useState(() => api.getBook(id));   // created once, outside the child's render
  return (
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Could not load the book.</p>}>
      <Suspense fallback={<BookSkeleton />}>
        <BookDetails bookPromise={bookPromise} />
      </Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  );
}
```

Suspense is covered in depth in 14.5. In practice, caching data libraries (see "Server State Caching Libraries") and frameworks manage the promises for you.

**Key Takeaways**

- Every remote-data view has loading, error, empty and success states; model them as a discriminated union, not independent booleans.
- Prefer skeletons, delayed indicators and keeping previous data to blank screens and flashing spinners.
- Fetching in each component's effect creates request waterfalls; start independent requests together or fetch at the route level.
- Strategies: fetch-on-render, fetch-then-render (loaders) and render-as-you-fetch (`use` + Suspense).
- `use(promise)` suspends until the promise resolves; the promise must be created outside render and cached.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a book details page with explicit loading, error (with a "Retry" button), not-found and success states. Throttle the network in DevTools to check each one.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a page that needs the current user, their shelves and the books on the first shelf. Implement it with nested effects, record the waterfall in the Network panel, then restructure it to remove the waterfall and compare the timings.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is a request waterfall in a React app, and how do you avoid it?" *Hint:* explain why fetching in effects serialises requests through the component tree, and mention parallel requests, route loaders, prefetching and server-side data fetching.

#### Consuming REST APIs from React

**Why a dedicated API layer.** Scattering `fetch` calls across components duplicates the base URL, headers, JSON parsing and error handling, and every component ends up handling HTTP details differently. A small **API client** module centralises them. Components then call `api.listBooks()` and receive typed data or a meaningful error, just as the Express services in Chapter 12 hide the database behind a repository.

**Types matching the API contract.** The bookshelf API from 12.3 returns books, paginated lists and `application/problem+json` errors:

```typescript
// src/api/types.ts
export type Book = {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  author: string;
  isbn: string;
  year: number;
  tags: string[];
};
export type NewBook = Omit<Book, 'id' | 'tags'> & { tags?: string[] };
export type Page<T> = { data: T[]; page: number; limit: number; total: number };

export type Problem = {          // RFC 9457 problem details, as produced by the 12.2 error handler
  type?: string;
  title: string;                 // human-readable message, e.g. 'request validation failed'
  status: number;
  detail?: string;
  code?: string;                 // machine-readable, e.g. 'VALIDATION_FAILED'
  errors?: { in: 'params' | 'query' | 'body'; path: string; message: string }[];
  requestId?: string;
};
```

**The client.**

```typescript
// src/api/client.ts
import type { Book, NewBook, Page, Problem } from './types';

const BASE = import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL ?? '/api/v1';

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(public status: number, public problem: Problem) {
    super(problem.detail ?? problem.title);
  }
}

let accessToken: string | null = null;                 // kept in memory, not localStorage
export const setAccessToken = (t: string | null) => { accessToken = t; };

async function request<T>(path: string, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<T> {
  const headers = new Headers(init.headers);
  headers.set('Accept', 'application/json');
  if (init.body) headers.set('Content-Type', 'application/json');
  if (accessToken) headers.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${accessToken}`);

  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, { ...init, headers, credentials: 'include' }); // send cookies too

  if (res.status === 204) return undefined as T;      // DELETE: no body
  const body = await res.json().catch(() => null);    // error pages may not be JSON

  if (!res.ok) {
    if (res.status === 401) window.dispatchEvent(new Event('auth:expired'));  // let the AuthProvider react
    throw new ApiError(res.status, body ?? { title: res.statusText, status: res.status });
  }
  return body as T;
}

export const api = {
  listBooks: (q: { page?: number; limit?: number; author?: string }, signal?: AbortSignal) => {
    const params = new URLSearchParams();
    Object.entries(q).forEach(([k, v]) => v !== undefined && v !== '' && params.set(k, String(v)));
    return request<Page<Book>>(`/books?${params}`, { signal });
  },
  getBook: (id: number, signal?: AbortSignal) => request<Book>(`/books/${id}`, { signal }),
  createBook: (b: NewBook) => request<Book>('/books', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(b) }),
  updateBook: (id: number, patch: Partial<NewBook>) =>
    request<Book>(`/books/${id}`, { method: 'PATCH', body: JSON.stringify(patch) }),
  deleteBook: (id: number) => request<void>(`/books/${id}`, { method: 'DELETE' }),
};
```

The type assertion `body as T` trusts the server. For APIs you do not control, validate responses at runtime with the same kind of Zod schemas used on the server, or generate the client from an OpenAPI specification (for example with openapi-typescript).

**Showing server validation errors.** The API answers `422` with a list of field errors. Map them to the form:

```tsx
async function handleSubmit(values: NewBook) {
  try {
    const book = await api.createBook(values);
    navigate(`/books/${book.id}`);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof ApiError && e.status === 422) {
      for (const err of e.problem.errors ?? []) setError(err.path as keyof NewBook, { message: err.message });
    } else if (e instanceof ApiError && e.status === 409) {
      setError('isbn', { message: 'A book with this ISBN already exists' });
    } else {
      setFormError('Could not save the book. Please try again.');
    }
  }
}
```

**Pagination.** The API returns `{ data, page, limit, total }`, so the UI can compute the number of pages:

```tsx
const totalPages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(result.total / result.limit));
<Pager page={result.page} totalPages={totalPages} onChange={goTo} />
```

For endless scrolling, request the next page when a sentinel element at the end of the list becomes visible (`IntersectionObserver`), and append the results.

**Optimistic updates.** For actions that almost always succeed, update the UI immediately and roll back on failure. React 19's `useOptimistic` shows a temporary value while an async action is in progress:

```tsx
import { useOptimistic, startTransition } from 'react';

function FavouriteButton({ book, onSaved }: { book: Book & { favourite: boolean }; onSaved: (b: Book) => void }) {
  const [optimisticFav, setOptimisticFav] = useOptimistic(book.favourite);

  function toggle() {
    startTransition(async () => {
      setOptimisticFav(!book.favourite);                       // shown immediately
      const saved = await api.updateBook(book.id, { tags: toggleTag(book.tags, 'favourite') });
      onSaved(saved);                                          // real value replaces the optimistic one
    });                                                        // if it throws, the optimistic value is discarded
  }

  return <button aria-pressed={optimisticFav} onClick={toggle}>{optimisticFav ? 'Favourite' : 'Add to favourites'}</button>;
}
```

**Cross-origin requests and authentication.**

| Setup | What to configure |
|---|---|
| Development | Vite proxy (`/api` to `localhost:3000`): same origin for the browser, no CORS |
| Production, same origin | Serve the SPA from the API server or put both behind one reverse proxy |
| Production, different origins | CORS on the API (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for the app's origin; `Allow-Credentials` if cookies are used) |

Where to keep credentials matters. A token in `localStorage` is readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS vulnerability leaks it. Safer options are a session or refresh token in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie, combined with a short-lived access token kept in memory (see "Access Tokens, Refresh Tokens and Revocation" in 10.3). Cookie-based authentication requires CSRF protection on state-changing requests.

**Key Takeaways**

- Centralise HTTP details (base URL, headers, JSON, errors, auth) in a typed API client; components call meaningful functions.
- Turn non-2xx responses into typed errors and map `422` validation problems back to form fields.
- Use the `total` and `limit` from paginated responses to drive pagers or infinite scroll.
- Optimistic updates (`useOptimistic`) make mutations feel instant and roll back on failure.
- Avoid CORS in development with a proxy; prefer `HttpOnly` cookies plus in-memory access tokens over `localStorage` for credentials.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write the API client above for the Chapter 12 bookshelf API and use it to show a paginated list with "Previous"/"Next" buttons and "Page X of Y".
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build create, edit and delete flows. Show `422` errors next to their fields, `409` on the ISBN field, and make deletion optimistic with a rollback and an error toast if the server refuses. Test the rollback by stopping the server.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Where should a React SPA store an authentication token?" *Hint:* compare `localStorage`, memory and `HttpOnly` cookies in terms of XSS, CSRF, page reloads and multiple tabs; mention refresh tokens.

#### Global State with Context and Redux

**Kinds of state.** Before choosing a "state management" tool, classify the state. Different kinds have different best homes:

| Kind | Examples | Best home |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI state | Is this dropdown open, input text | `useState` in the component |
| Shared UI state | Theme, sidebar collapsed, toasts | Context, or a small store |
| Server state (remote data cache) | Books, user profile, search results | A server-state library (see "Server State Caching Libraries") |
| URL state | Current page, filters, selected tab | The router (`useParams`, `useSearchParams`) |
| Form state | Field values, errors, dirty flags | The form or a form library |
| Complex client state | Editor documents, offline queues, wizards, undo history | `useReducer`, Redux or another store |

Many applications that "need Redux" turn out to need a server-state library plus a little context. True global *client* state is usually small.

**Context plus useReducer.** For moderate needs, combining the two hooks from 14.2 gives a lightweight store: a reducer defines the transitions, and context distributes `state` and `dispatch`:

```tsx
const CartStateContext = createContext<CartState | null>(null);
const CartDispatchContext = createContext<React.Dispatch<CartAction> | null>(null);

export function CartProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(cartReducer, { items: [] });
  return (
    <CartDispatchContext value={dispatch}>            {/* dispatch is stable: these consumers never re-render */}
      <CartStateContext value={state}>{children}</CartStateContext>
    </CartDispatchContext>
  );
}
```

The limitation is granularity. Every consumer of `CartStateContext` re-renders when *anything* in the cart state changes, even if it only shows the item count. Context has no built-in **selectors** that subscribe to a slice of the state. For large, frequently changing global state, a store library is more efficient.

**Redux.** Redux (2015, Dan Abramov and Andrew Clark) applies the reducer idea to the whole application, inspired by the Flux architecture and the Elm language. Its three principles:

1. **Single source of truth**: all global state lives in one object tree inside one **store**.
2. **State is read-only**: the only way to change it is to **dispatch an action**, a plain object describing what happened.
3. **Changes are made with pure functions**: **reducers** compute the next state from the previous state and the action.

```text
          +-------------------------------- store --------------------------------+
          |                                                                       |
 UI ---dispatch(action)---> middleware (logging, async) ---> rootReducer(state, action)
  ^       |                                                          |            |
  |       |                                                    new state          |
  |       +----------------------------------------------------------|------------+
  |                                                                  |
  +------ components re-render if their selected slice changed <----+
```

**Classic Redux, for reading older code.**

```javascript
// Action types and action creators
const BOOK_ADDED = 'books/added';
const bookAdded = (book) => ({ type: BOOK_ADDED, payload: book });

// Reducer: pure, immutable
function booksReducer(state = { items: [] }, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case BOOK_ADDED:
      return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.payload] };
    default:
      return state;
  }
}

// Store
import { createStore, combineReducers } from 'redux';   // createStore is deprecated in favour of RTK
const store = createStore(combineReducers({ books: booksReducer }));
store.dispatch(bookAdded({ id: 1, title: 'Dune' }));
store.getState();   // { books: { items: [{ id: 1, title: 'Dune' }] } }
```

**Connecting React with react-redux.** A `<Provider>` makes the store available, `useSelector` subscribes to a **slice** of state, and `useDispatch` returns `dispatch`. A component re-renders only when the value its selector returns changes (compared by reference), which solves the granularity problem of context:

```jsx
import { Provider, useSelector, useDispatch } from 'react-redux';

<Provider store={store}><App /></Provider>

function CartBadge() {
  const count = useSelector((state) => state.cart.items.length);  // re-renders only when the count changes
  return <span className="badge">{count}</span>;
}

function AddToCartButton({ book }) {
  const dispatch = useDispatch();
  return <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'cart/itemAdded', payload: book })}>Add</button>;
}
```

**What Redux gives you.** Predictable updates in one place; the **Redux DevTools** browser extension, which shows every action with the state before and after, and lets you "time-travel" by replaying actions; **middleware** for cross-cutting concerns (logging, analytics, async logic); and easy testing of reducers and selectors. Its traditional cost was **boilerplate**: action type constants, action creators, switch statements and hand-written immutable updates for every feature. Redux Toolkit (next topic) removes most of it.

**Key Takeaways**

- Classify state first: local UI, shared UI, server, URL, form and complex client state have different best homes.
- Context plus `useReducer` is a lightweight store, but every consumer re-renders on any change because context has no selectors.
- Redux keeps global state in one store, changed only by dispatched actions processed by pure reducers.
- `useSelector` subscribes to a slice and re-renders only when it changes; `useDispatch` sends actions.
- Redux offers DevTools time travel, middleware and testability; classic Redux is verbose, which Redux Toolkit addresses.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement a shopping cart with Context plus `useReducer` (add, remove, change quantity) and display a badge in the header and a list in a drawer.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a render counter to every cart consumer and observe how many re-render when a quantity changes. Re-implement the cart with classic Redux and `useSelector`, and compare the counters.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How do you decide whether an application needs Redux?" *Hint:* classify the state, estimate how much is truly global client state, consider re-render granularity, debugging needs, team size and existing code, and mention server-state libraries.

#### Redux Toolkit and Alternatives

**Redux Toolkit (RTK).** Redux Toolkit is the official, recommended way to write Redux. It keeps the same architecture but removes the boilerplate: it configures the store with good defaults, generates action creators and types from reducers, and uses **Immer** so reducers can be written with "mutating" syntax that produces immutable updates.

```bash
npm install @reduxjs/toolkit react-redux
```

```typescript
// src/features/cart/cartSlice.ts
import { createSlice, type PayloadAction } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

type CartItem = { bookId: number; title: string; quantity: number };
type CartState = { items: CartItem[] };

const initialState: CartState = { items: [] };

const cartSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'cart',                                    // prefix of generated action types: 'cart/itemAdded'
  initialState,
  reducers: {
    itemAdded(state, action: PayloadAction<{ bookId: number; title: string }>) {
      const existing = state.items.find((i) => i.bookId === action.payload.bookId);
      if (existing) existing.quantity += 1;        // looks like mutation: Immer turns it into a new object
      else state.items.push({ ...action.payload, quantity: 1 });
    },
    itemRemoved(state, action: PayloadAction<number>) {
      state.items = state.items.filter((i) => i.bookId !== action.payload);
    },
    cleared() {
      return initialState;                         // returning a value replaces the state
    },
  },
});

export const { itemAdded, itemRemoved, cleared } = cartSlice.actions;  // generated action creators
export default cartSlice.reducer;

// Selectors live next to the slice
export const selectCartCount = (s: RootState) => s.cart.items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.quantity, 0);
```

```typescript
// src/store.ts
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import { useDispatch, useSelector } from 'react-redux';
import cartReducer from './features/cart/cartSlice';

export const store = configureStore({
  reducer: { cart: cartReducer },                  // combines slice reducers; DevTools and thunk enabled
});                                                // dev checks: accidental mutation, non-serialisable values

export type RootState = ReturnType<typeof store.getState>;
export type AppDispatch = typeof store.dispatch;
export const useAppSelector = useSelector.withTypes<RootState>();   // typed hooks for the whole app
export const useAppDispatch = useDispatch.withTypes<AppDispatch>();
```

```tsx
function CartBadge() {
  const count = useAppSelector(selectCartCount);
  return <span className="badge">{count}</span>;
}
function AddButton({ book }: { book: Book }) {
  const dispatch = useAppDispatch();
  return <button onClick={() => dispatch(itemAdded({ bookId: book.id, title: book.title }))}>Add to cart</button>;
}
```

**Async logic with thunks.** A **thunk** is a function dispatched instead of an action. Its job is to perform async work and dispatch real actions. `createAsyncThunk` generates `pending`, `fulfilled` and `rejected` actions:

```typescript
import { createAsyncThunk } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

export const checkout = createAsyncThunk('cart/checkout', async (_: void, { getState }) => {
  const { cart } = getState() as RootState;
  return api.createOrder(cart.items);              // resolved value becomes action.payload
});

// in createSlice({ ..., extraReducers: (builder) => builder
//   .addCase(checkout.pending,   (s) => { s.status = 'submitting'; })
//   .addCase(checkout.fulfilled, (s) => { s.items = []; s.status = 'idle'; })
//   .addCase(checkout.rejected,  (s, a) => { s.status = 'error'; s.error = a.error.message ?? null; }) })
```

For server data, RTK includes **RTK Query** (`createApi`), a caching data layer comparable to the libraries in the next topic.

**Memoised selectors.** A selector that derives a new array (`state.books.filter(...)`) returns a new reference every time, which re-renders the component on every store update. `createSelector` (from Reselect, re-exported by RTK) memoises derived data:

```typescript
import { createSelector } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
const selectItems = (s: RootState) => s.cart.items;
export const selectExpensiveItems = createSelector([selectItems], (items) => items.filter((i) => i.quantity > 2));
```

**Alternatives.** Redux is no longer the default answer. Lighter libraries cover most needs with less ceremony:

```typescript
// Zustand: a store is a hook; components subscribe with selectors
import { create } from 'zustand';

type CartStore = {
  items: CartItem[];
  add: (b: { bookId: number; title: string }) => void;
  remove: (id: number) => void;
};

export const useCart = create<CartStore>()((set) => ({
  items: [],
  add: (b) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, { ...b, quantity: 1 }] })),
  remove: (id) => set((s) => ({ items: s.items.filter((i) => i.bookId !== id) })),
}));

// No provider needed
const count = useCart((s) => s.items.length);      // re-renders only when the length changes
const add = useCart((s) => s.add);
```

```typescript
// Jotai: state split into small independent atoms, composed like useState
import { atom, useAtom, useAtomValue } from 'jotai';
const itemsAtom = atom<CartItem[]>([]);
const countAtom = atom((get) => get(itemsAtom).length);  // derived atom
const count = useAtomValue(countAtom);
```

| Library | Model | Strengths | Consider when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Redux Toolkit | Single store, actions, reducers (Immer) | DevTools, middleware, conventions for large teams, RTK Query | Large apps, many developers, complex flows, existing Redux code |
| Zustand | Small hook-based stores with selectors | Minimal API, no provider, tiny | Most apps that need some global client state |
| Jotai | Atoms (bottom-up), derived atoms | Fine-grained updates, Suspense support | Many independent pieces of state, derived values |
| MobX | Observable objects, automatic tracking | Mutable style, very fine-grained reactivity | Teams comfortable with OOP and observables |
| XState | State machines and statecharts | Explicit states and transitions, visualisation | Complex workflows (checkout, wizards, media players) |
| Context + `useReducer` | Built in | No dependency | Small to medium apps, rarely changing global state |

**Key Takeaways**

- Redux Toolkit is the standard way to write Redux: `configureStore`, `createSlice` with Immer, generated action creators and typed hooks.
- `createAsyncThunk` handles async flows with pending/fulfilled/rejected actions; RTK Query handles server data.
- Use memoised selectors (`createSelector`) for derived data to avoid unnecessary re-renders.
- Zustand, Jotai, MobX and XState are lighter or differently shaped alternatives; choose by the shape and size of your client state.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Rewrite the cart from the previous topic with Redux Toolkit (`createSlice`, `configureStore`, typed hooks) and inspect actions in Redux DevTools.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the same cart with Zustand. Add persistence to `localStorage` with Zustand's `persist` middleware and a checkout thunk in the RTK version, and compare the code size and the developer experience of both.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does Redux Toolkit let you write `state.items.push(x)` in a reducer if Redux requires immutability?" *Hint:* explain Immer's draft proxy, structural sharing of the result, and what happens if you both mutate the draft and return a value.

#### Server State Caching Libraries

**Server state is different.** Data fetched from an API is not really *your* state. It is a **cached copy** of state that lives on the server. Other users can change it, it becomes stale, several components may request the same data at the same time, and it needs refetching, deduplication, pagination and invalidation after mutations. Managing it with `useState` + `useEffect` (or putting it into Redux by hand) means rebuilding a cache badly. **Server-state libraries** implement this cache for you.

Main features:

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Caching by key | Results are stored under a key such as `['books', { author, page }]`; other components reuse them |
| Deduplication | Ten components asking for the same key at the same time produce one request |
| Stale-while-revalidate | Show cached data immediately, refetch in the background, update when the new data arrives |
| Automatic refetch | On window focus, network reconnect, interval, or when the key changes |
| Invalidation | After a mutation, mark related keys stale so they refetch |
| Retries, pagination, infinite queries, prefetching, optimistic updates | Built in |

```text
Stale-while-revalidate timeline for key ['books']
t=0     component mounts -> cache empty -> status 'pending' -> request #1
t=300   response -> cache = v1 -> status 'success', render v1
t=60s   user leaves the tab, comes back -> data is stale -> render v1 immediately AND request #2
t=60.3s response -> cache = v2 -> re-render with v2 (no spinner shown)
```

**TanStack Query.** TanStack Query (formerly React Query) is the most widely used library of this kind.

```tsx
// main.tsx
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';

const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: { queries: { staleTime: 30_000 } },   // data is "fresh" for 30 s: no refetch within that time
});

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}><App /></QueryClientProvider>,
);
```

```tsx
// Queries: read data
import { useQuery, keepPreviousData } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function BookListPage({ author, page }: { author: string; page: number }) {
  const { data, isPending, isError, error, isFetching, refetch } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['books', { author, page }],                       // key changes -> new query
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => api.listBooks({ author, page, limit: 20 }, signal),  // aborted when no longer needed
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,                            // keep the old page visible while the next loads
  });

  if (isPending) return <BookListSkeleton />;
  if (isError) return <ErrorMessage error={error} onRetry={refetch} />;
  return (
    <div style={{ opacity: isFetching ? 0.6 : 1 }}>               {/* background refetch indicator */}
      <BookList books={data.data} />
    </div>
  );
}
```

```tsx
// Mutations: change data, then invalidate what may have changed
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useCreateBook() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: api.createBook,
    onSuccess: (book) => {
      queryClient.setQueryData(['book', book.id], book);          // seed the details cache
      queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['books'] });     // every list query refetches
    },
  });
}

function NewBookPage() {
  const createBook = useCreateBook();
  return (
    <BookForm
      onSubmit={(values) => createBook.mutateAsync(values)}
      submitting={createBook.isPending}
    />
  );
}
```

`invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['books'] })` matches every key that *starts with* `['books']`, so all filtered and paginated lists are refreshed. Designing keys hierarchically (`['books']`, `['books', filters]`, `['book', id]`) makes invalidation simple.

**Two time settings to understand.**

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `staleTime` | `0` | How long data counts as fresh. Fresh data is served from cache with no refetch |
| `gcTime` | 5 minutes | How long *unused* data stays in memory after the last component using it unmounts |

With the default `staleTime: 0`, every new mount and every window focus triggers a background refetch. Raise it for data that changes rarely.

**Optimistic updates with a cache.**

```typescript
useMutation({
  mutationFn: (id: number) => api.deleteBook(id),
  onMutate: async (id) => {
    await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['books'] });           // avoid overwriting by in-flight fetches
    const previous = queryClient.getQueriesData<Page<Book>>({ queryKey: ['books'] });
    queryClient.setQueriesData<Page<Book>>({ queryKey: ['books'] }, (old) =>
      old && { ...old, data: old.data.filter((b) => b.id !== id), total: old.total - 1 });
    return { previous };                                                // context for rollback
  },
  onError: (_err, _id, ctx) => ctx?.previous.forEach(([key, data]) => queryClient.setQueryData(key, data)),
  onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['books'] }),  // resync with the server
});
```

**Other libraries.**

| Library | Notes |
|---|---|
| TanStack Query | Framework-agnostic, rich features, excellent DevTools |
| SWR (Vercel) | Smaller API built around the stale-while-revalidate idea: `useSWR(key, fetcher)` |
| RTK Query | Part of Redux Toolkit; endpoints defined once, generates hooks; cache tags for invalidation |
| Apollo Client, urql, Relay | GraphQL clients with normalised caches |
| Router loaders / Server Components | Fetch per route or on the server; often combined with one of the above |

With a server-state library, the remaining *client* state is usually small enough for `useState`, context or a tiny store.

**Key Takeaways**

- Server state is a cache of remote data: it can go stale, is shared, and needs deduplication, refetching and invalidation.
- Server-state libraries cache results by key and implement stale-while-revalidate, retries, pagination and optimistic updates.
- In TanStack Query, `useQuery` reads by `queryKey`, `useMutation` writes, and `invalidateQueries` refreshes related keys after a mutation.
- `staleTime` controls when data refetches; `gcTime` controls how long unused data stays in memory.
- Moving server data to such a library usually removes most of the need for a global client-state store.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Replace the hand-written `useBooks` hook with `useQuery`. Open the TanStack Query DevTools, switch tabs and come back, and observe the background refetch. Then set `staleTime` to one minute and repeat.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement create, update and delete with `useMutation`, hierarchical keys and invalidation. Make delete optimistic with rollback, and prefetch a book's details when the user hovers over its link (`queryClient.prefetchQuery`).
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why not keep API data in Redux or in a global context?" *Hint:* list what a cache needs (staleness, deduplication, garbage collection, refetch triggers, invalidation, race handling) and how much code that is to write by hand.

#### Real-Time Updates with WebSocket

**When polling is not enough.** Chapter 10.5 introduced WebSocket, a persistent two-way connection over which the server can push messages, as well as server-sent events (SSE). In a React application, live features (a chat, presence indicators, "a new review was posted", stock levels) receive these messages and must merge them into the UI. The challenge is mostly about **lifecycle**: the connection is an external system, so it must be opened, kept and closed in step with the components that need it.

**A connection in an effect.** The simplest version opens a socket while a component is mounted:

```tsx
function LiveReviews({ bookId }: { bookId: number }) {
  const [reviews, setReviews] = useState<Review[]>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const ws = new WebSocket(`${location.protocol === 'https:' ? 'wss' : 'ws'}://${location.host}/ws`);
    ws.addEventListener('open', () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'subscribe', bookId })));
    ws.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
      const msg = JSON.parse(event.data);
      if (msg.type === 'review.created' && msg.review.bookId === bookId) {
        setReviews((prev) => [msg.review, ...prev]);        // updater: never reads a stale list
      }
    });
    return () => ws.close();                                // book changed or unmounted
  }, [bookId]);

  return <ReviewList reviews={reviews} />;
}
```

This works, but each component that needs live data opens its own connection, and nothing reconnects after a network drop.

**One shared connection.** Usually an application keeps **one** socket and lets many components subscribe to the messages they care about. A small module outside React owns the connection and handles reconnection with **exponential backoff**:

```typescript
// src/realtime/socket.ts
type Listener = (msg: ServerMessage) => void;
type Status = 'connecting' | 'open' | 'closed';

const listeners = new Set<Listener>();
const statusListeners = new Set<() => void>();
let ws: WebSocket | null = null;
let status: Status = 'closed';
let attempt = 0;

function setStatus(s: Status) { status = s; statusListeners.forEach((l) => l()); }

export function connect() {
  setStatus('connecting');
  ws = new WebSocket(`${location.origin.replace(/^http/, 'ws')}/ws`);
  ws.onopen = () => { attempt = 0; setStatus('open'); };
  ws.onmessage = (e) => { const msg = JSON.parse(e.data); listeners.forEach((l) => l(msg)); };
  ws.onclose = () => {
    setStatus('closed');
    const delay = Math.min(30_000, 1000 * 2 ** attempt++) * (0.5 + Math.random());  // backoff with jitter
    setTimeout(connect, delay);
  };
}

export function subscribe(listener: Listener) {
  listeners.add(listener);
  return () => listeners.delete(listener);                 // unsubscribe function
}

export function send(msg: ClientMessage) {
  if (ws?.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) ws.send(JSON.stringify(msg));
}

// For useSyncExternalStore
export const subscribeStatus = (cb: () => void) => { statusListeners.add(cb); return () => statusListeners.delete(cb); };
export const getStatus = () => status;
```

**Reading an external store: useSyncExternalStore.** The connection status lives outside React. `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot)` is the hook designed to read such values safely. It re-renders when the store changes and avoids inconsistent values ("tearing") during concurrent rendering:

```tsx
import { useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';
import { subscribeStatus, getStatus } from './socket';

export function useConnectionStatus() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribeStatus, getStatus);
}

function ConnectionBanner() {
  const status = useConnectionStatus();
  if (status === 'open') return null;
  return <div role="status" className="banner">Reconnecting... live updates are paused.</div>;
}
```

**Subscribing to messages with a hook.**

```tsx
export function useServerEvent<T extends ServerMessage['type']>(
  type: T,
  handler: (msg: Extract<ServerMessage, { type: T }>) => void,
) {
  const onEvent = useEffectEvent(handler);                  // always the latest handler, not a dependency
  useEffect(() => subscribe((msg) => {
    if (msg.type === type) onEvent(msg as Extract<ServerMessage, { type: T }>);
  }), [type]);
}
```

**Merging pushed data into the server-state cache.** When a server-state library holds the data, a pushed message can either update the cache directly or invalidate it so it refetches:

```tsx
function RealtimeSync() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();

  useServerEvent('book.updated', ({ book }) => {
    queryClient.setQueryData(['book', book.id], book);               // patch the details cache directly
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['books'] });          // lists may be affected: refetch
  });
  useServerEvent('book.deleted', ({ id }) => {
    queryClient.removeQueries({ queryKey: ['book', id] });
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['books'] });
  });
  return null;                                                       // a "behaviour-only" component
}
```

Sending small "something changed" events and letting the client refetch is simpler and safer than pushing full data. The REST API remains the authority (and enforces permissions), and messages missed during a disconnection are covered by refetching on reconnect.

**Practical concerns.**

| Concern | Approach |
|---|---|
| Strict Mode double effects | Ensure cleanup closes or unsubscribes; with a shared module, components only add and remove listeners |
| Missed messages while disconnected | On reconnect, invalidate queries (or request events since the last sequence number) |
| Authentication | Cookies are sent with the handshake; or send a token in the first message; never put long-lived tokens in the URL |
| High-frequency streams (prices, cursors) | Throttle updates, batch them per animation frame, update only the affected rows |
| Libraries | Socket.IO client (rooms, acknowledgements, automatic reconnection; needs a Socket.IO server), or SSE with `EventSource` for server-to-client only |

**Key Takeaways**

- A WebSocket connection is an external system: open it in an effect or a module, and always close or unsubscribe in cleanup.
- Prefer one shared connection with subscriptions and reconnection with exponential backoff and jitter.
- `useSyncExternalStore` reads values from stores outside React (such as connection status) safely under concurrent rendering.
- Merge pushed events into the server-state cache with `setQueryData` or invalidation; the REST API remains the source of truth.
- Handle missed messages, authentication and high-frequency updates explicitly.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Connect to the WebSocket server from Chapter 10.5 and render a live message list with an input to send messages. Verify under Strict Mode that only one connection stays open.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a WebSocket endpoint to the Chapter 12 API that broadcasts `book.created`, `book.updated` and `book.deleted` events. In the React app, keep one shared connection with backoff, show a "Reconnecting" banner, and update the TanStack Query cache. Open two browser windows and check that edits in one appear in the other.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you integrate a WebSocket feed into a React app that uses TanStack Query?" *Hint:* where the connection lives, how components subscribe, `setQueryData` vs `invalidateQueries`, and what happens to updates missed during a disconnection.

<a id="145-testing-and-optimization"></a>
### 14.5 Testing and Optimization

The last subchapter is about shipping React applications that load quickly, stay responsive and keep working as they change. It covers splitting the bundle and loading code on demand, Suspense and concurrent rendering, finding and fixing slow renders, testing components the way users use them, rendering React on the server with Next.js, and how React compares with Angular and Vue.

#### Code Splitting and Lazy Loading

**Why split.** By default, a bundler follows every `import` from `main.tsx` and produces one JavaScript file containing the whole application. As the app grows, every visitor downloads, parses and executes code for pages they never open: the admin dashboard, the charting library, the rich-text editor. On a mid-range phone over a mobile network, a few megabytes of JavaScript can delay interactivity by seconds. **Code splitting** breaks the bundle into chunks that load on demand, like a restaurant kitchen that prepares dishes when they are ordered instead of cooking the whole menu at opening time.

**The mechanism: dynamic `import()`.** A static `import` is resolved at build time and lands in the same chunk. A dynamic `import('./module')` (Chapter 3) returns a promise. Bundlers treat it as a **split point** and emit the module and its exclusive dependencies as a separate file, fetched only when the call runs:

```javascript
// The CSV library is downloaded only when the user clicks "Export"
async function handleExport(books) {
  const { unparse } = await import('papaparse');      // separate chunk, loaded on demand
  downloadFile('books.csv', unparse(books));
}
```

**Lazy components.** `React.lazy` turns a dynamic import of a component module into a component that suspends while its code loads. A `<Suspense>` boundary above it shows a fallback in the meantime:

```tsx
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const AdminPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/AdminPage'));          // module must have a default export
const StatsChart = lazy(() =>                                        // named export: map it to default
  import('./components/StatsChart').then((m) => ({ default: m.StatsChart })),
);

function Dashboard({ showStats }: { showStats: boolean }) {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<ChartSkeleton />}>
      {showStats && <StatsChart />}                                  {/* chunk requested on first render */}
    </Suspense>
  );
}
```

Declare lazy components at **module level**, never inside a component. Calling `lazy` during render creates a new component type each time, which remounts it and loses its state (14.1).

**Route-based splitting.** Routes are the natural split points, because users visit one page at a time. Splitting per route gives the biggest win for the least effort:

```tsx
const BookListPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/BookListPage'));
const BookDetailsPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/BookDetailsPage'));
const AdminPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/AdminPage'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>                {/* one boundary for all routes */}
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/books" element={<BookListPage />} />
        <Route path="/books/:id" element={<BookDetailsPage />} />
        <Route path="/admin/*" element={<AdminPage />} />
      </Routes>
    </Suspense>
  );
}
```

In React Router's data mode, a route's `lazy` property loads its component *and* loader in parallel with the data, avoiding a code-then-data waterfall. Framework mode and Next.js split every route automatically.

```text
Before                                After
index-9f2c.js   1.4 MB                index-a1b3.js            180 KB   (shell, router, home)
                                      BookListPage-7c1e.js      40 KB
                                      BookDetailsPage-3d9a.js   35 KB
                                      AdminPage-e2f0.js        620 KB   (only for admins)
                                      vendor-charts-5b7d.js    480 KB   (only when stats are shown)
```

**Preloading.** Lazy loading adds a delay at the moment the user navigates. Hide it by starting the download a little earlier, when intent is likely:

```tsx
const loadAdmin = () => import('./pages/AdminPage');   // the browser caches the module after the first call
const AdminPage = lazy(loadAdmin);

<Link to="/admin" onMouseEnter={loadAdmin} onFocus={loadAdmin}>Admin</Link>
```

**What to split, and how to check.** Good candidates are routes, heavy rarely used widgets (editors, charts, maps, PDF viewers) and content below the fold or behind interaction (modals, tabs). Bad candidates are small components shown on first render: each extra request has a cost, and splitting them only adds latency. Measure with a bundle analyser (`rollup-plugin-visualizer` for Vite, `@next/bundle-analyzer` for Next.js) and the browser's Network and Coverage panels. Also check that you import only what you use (`import debounce from 'lodash-es/debounce'` rather than the whole library), so that **tree shaking** can remove the rest.

**Failures after a deploy.** Chunk file names contain content hashes. If you deploy a new version while a user still has the old app open, their next lazy import requests a chunk that no longer exists and the import rejects. Mitigations: keep the previous build's assets available for a while, catch the error with an error boundary that offers to reload the page, and treat chunk-load errors as a signal to refresh.

**Key Takeaways**

- Code splitting turns dynamic `import()` calls into separate chunks that load on demand, reducing the JavaScript needed for the first page.
- `React.lazy` plus `<Suspense>` lazy-loads components; declare lazy components at module level.
- Split by route first, then by heavy, rarely used widgets; do not split small components needed on first render.
- Preload chunks on hover or focus to hide the delay; analyse bundles to find what to split.
- Plan for chunk-load failures after deployments (keep old assets, error boundary with reload).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Lazy-load every page of the bookshelf app with `React.lazy`, build the app, and compare the list of files and their sizes in `dist/assets` before and after.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a heavy charting library to a statistics page, run a bundle analyser, and make sure it ends up only in that page's chunk. Add hover preloading to the navigation link and measure the navigation delay with the Network panel throttled to "Fast 4G".
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you reduce the initial JavaScript of a large React SPA?" *Hint:* measure first (bundle analyser, Coverage), route-based splitting, lazy heavy dependencies, tree-shakable imports, removing duplicated libraries, and server rendering or Server Components for content that needs no client code.

#### Suspense and Concurrent Rendering

**Suspense: declaring loading states.** Before Suspense, every component that waited for something (code or data) had to track its own `isLoading` flag and render its own spinner. A page could show five spinners popping in at random moments. `<Suspense>` lets a component **suspend**, that is, signal "I cannot render yet", and lets an *ancestor* decide what to show meanwhile. It works like `try`/`catch` for waiting: the boundary catches the "not ready" signal, shows its `fallback`, and renders the children when they are ready.

```tsx
<Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
  <BookHeader id={id} />                         {/* both must be ready before the page appears */}
  <Suspense fallback={<ReviewsSkeleton />}>      {/* nested: reviews may arrive later on their own */}
    <Reviews bookId={id} />
  </Suspense>
</Suspense>
```

```text
time ->     0ms              200ms                    900ms
outer:      <PageSkeleton>   header ready -> page shown
inner:                       <ReviewsSkeleton>        reviews ready -> shown
```

You design the loading sequence by where you put boundaries. Everything inside one boundary appears together; nested boundaries reveal content progressively.

**What can suspend.** Lazy components (`React.lazy`), promises read with `use` (14.4), and data from Suspense-enabled libraries and frameworks (TanStack Query's `useSuspenseQuery`, Relay, Next.js Server Components). Data fetched in a plain `useEffect` does **not** suspend: the component has already rendered by the time the effect runs.

**Concurrent rendering.** Before React 18, rendering was **synchronous**: once React started rendering an update, it ran to completion, blocking the main thread. Typing into a search box that filtered a 10,000-row list could freeze each keystroke for 200 ms. With **concurrent rendering** (enabled by `createRoot`), React can prepare a new UI in the background, **interrupt** that work when something more urgent happens (a keystroke), and **discard** results that are already outdated. Pure rendering (14.1) is what makes this safe.

The tool for this is marking some updates as non-urgent **transitions**:

| Update type | Examples | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Urgent | Typing, clicking, pressing | Must reflect immediately; never interrupted |
| Transition | Filtering results, switching tabs, navigating | May be interrupted, shows the old UI until the new one is ready |

**useTransition.**

```tsx
import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';

function BookExplorer({ books }: { books: Book[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');           // urgent: the input must stay responsive
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('');         // transition: the expensive list follows later
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function handleChange(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {
    setQuery(e.target.value);                        // render the typed character right away
    startTransition(() => setFilter(e.target.value));  // low priority; interrupted by the next keystroke
  }

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={handleChange} aria-label="Filter books" />
      <div style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.5 : 1 }}>   {/* old results stay visible, dimmed */}
        <SlowBookList books={books} filter={filter} />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}
```

Transitions also change how Suspense behaves. If an update made in a transition causes an *already visible* boundary to suspend (for example navigating to a page whose code is not loaded), React keeps showing the current UI instead of replacing it with a fallback. Routers wrap navigations in transitions for this reason: you stay on the old page with a progress indicator, rather than flashing a skeleton.

**useDeferredValue.** When you do not control the state update (the value comes from props or a library), `useDeferredValue` gives you a copy of the value that "lags behind" during heavy renders:

```tsx
function Results({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);    // first renders with the old value, then the new one
  const isStale = query !== deferredQuery;
  return (
    <div style={{ opacity: isStale ? 0.5 : 1 }}>
      <SlowBookList filter={deferredQuery} />       {/* memo(SlowBookList) lets React skip the urgent render */}
    </div>
  );
}
```

**Actions.** React 19 extends transitions to async functions. An async function passed to `startTransition` (or to a form's `action`, 14.3) is an **action**: React tracks it as pending until it settles and integrates it with `useOptimistic` and `useActionState`.

**Concurrency is not parallelism.** Rendering still happens on the single main thread (Chapter 5). React splits the work into small units and yields to the browser between them (roughly every 5 ms), so input events can be handled. Code inside a single component that takes 300 ms still blocks; transitions help when the cost is spread across many components.

**Other concurrent features.** Streaming server rendering sends HTML progressively as Suspense boundaries resolve (see "Server-Side Rendering with Next.js"). **Selective hydration** makes the parts of a server-rendered page interactive in the order the user interacts with them. `<Activity>` (React 19.2) pre-renders hidden UI at low priority.

**Key Takeaways**

- `<Suspense fallback>` shows a fallback while descendants suspend (lazy code, `use(promise)`, Suspense-enabled data libraries); boundary placement designs the loading sequence.
- Concurrent rendering (enabled by `createRoot`) lets React interrupt and discard non-urgent rendering work.
- `useTransition` marks state updates as non-urgent and exposes `isPending`; `useDeferredValue` defers a value you receive.
- Transitions keep the current UI visible instead of showing fallbacks again; async transitions are actions in React 19.
- Concurrency is cooperative scheduling on one thread, not parallelism; a single slow component still blocks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a page with two nested Suspense boundaries around lazy components with artificial delays (`new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1500))` before the import) and observe how fallbacks appear and disappear.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a filter over 20,000 books where each row does some artificial work. Measure input lag with the Performance panel, then fix it once with `useTransition` and once with `useDeferredValue`, and explain which you would choose and why.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What problem does concurrent rendering solve, and how does `useTransition` use it?" *Hint:* blocking synchronous renders, urgent vs non-urgent updates, interruption and discarding of work, and why rendering must be pure.

#### Render Performance and Profiling

**Measure before optimising.** React is fast by default for most screens, and most "optimisations" applied blindly (wrapping everything in `memo`) add complexity without measurable benefit. Performance work follows a loop: **measure** a real slow interaction, **find** the cause, **fix** it with the simplest change, **measure again**.

**What users feel.** The Core Web Vitals give targets that relate to rendering:

| Metric | Measures | Good |
|---|---|---|
| **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint) | When the main content appears | <= 2.5 s |
| **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint) | Delay from a click or key press until the next frame | <= 200 ms |
| **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift) | Unexpected movement of content | <= 0.1 |

Slow React renders hurt INP most directly; large bundles and client-side data waterfalls hurt LCP.

**Tools.**

- **React DevTools Profiler**: record an interaction and see which components rendered, how long each took (flame graph and ranked views) and, with "Record why each component rendered" enabled, *why* (props changed, state changed, parent rendered, context changed, hooks changed).
- **Highlight updates when components render** (React DevTools setting): flashes a border around components as they render.
- **Browser Performance panel**: shows long tasks on the main thread, including React's work, layout and paint. Use CPU throttling (4x or 6x slowdown) to mimic a mid-range phone.
- **`<Profiler>` component**: measures render times in code, for example to send them to monitoring.

```tsx
import { Profiler } from 'react';

<Profiler id="BookList" onRender={(id, phase, actualDuration) => {
  if (actualDuration > 16) console.warn(`${id} ${phase} took ${actualDuration.toFixed(1)} ms`);  // over one frame
}}>
  <BookList books={books} />
</Profiler>
```
