Always profile a **production build** (`npm run build && npm run preview`, or React's profiling build). Development mode includes extra checks and Strict Mode double rendering, so it is several times slower.

**Common causes and fixes.** Most render performance problems come from rendering *too many* components or rendering *too often*, not from one slow component.

1. **State placed too high.** Typing in a search box at the top of `App` re-renders the whole page. Move the state down into the component that uses it (**colocation**), or split the component so the fast-changing part is isolated:

```tsx
// Before: every keystroke re-renders ExpensiveTree
function Page() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  return (<><input value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} /><ExpensiveTree /></>);
}

// After: the state lives in a small component; ExpensiveTree is untouched
function SearchInput() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  return <input value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} />;
}
function Page() {
  return (<><SearchInput /><ExpensiveTree /></>);
}
```

2. **Lift content up as `children`.** When a stateful wrapper must surround expensive content, pass the content as `children`. The elements are created by the parent, so they are the same objects when the wrapper re-renders, and React skips them:

```tsx
function ScrollTracker({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [y, setY] = useState(0);                      // changes often
  useEffect(() => {
    const onScroll = () => setY(window.scrollY);
    window.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { passive: true });
    return () => window.removeEventListener('scroll', onScroll);
  }, []);
  return <div><ProgressBar value={y} />{children}</div>;  // children are not re-rendered on scroll
}

<ScrollTracker><ExpensiveArticle /></ScrollTracker>
```

3. **Unstable props to memoised children.** New objects, arrays and functions created on every render defeat `memo`. Stabilise them with `useMemo`/`useCallback` (14.2) or move constants outside the component.

4. **Context values that change too often.** Every consumer re-renders. Memoise the provider value, split the context, or use a store with selectors (14.4).

5. **Long lists.** Rendering 10,000 rows creates 10,000 DOM nodes. **Virtualisation** (windowing) renders only the rows visible in the viewport plus a small buffer and reuses them while scrolling:

```tsx
import { useVirtualizer } from '@tanstack/react-virtual';

function VirtualBookList({ books }: { books: Book[] }) {
  const parentRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const virtualizer = useVirtualizer({
    count: books.length,
    getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current,
    estimateSize: () => 48,                          // estimated row height in px
    overscan: 5,                                     // extra rows above and below the viewport
  });

  return (
    <div ref={parentRef} style={{ height: 600, overflow: 'auto' }}>
      <div style={{ height: virtualizer.getTotalSize(), position: 'relative' }}>   {/* full scroll height */}
        {virtualizer.getVirtualItems().map((row) => (
          <div key={row.key}
               style={{ position: 'absolute', top: 0, transform: `translateY(${row.start}px)`, height: row.size, width: '100%' }}>
            {books[row.index].title}
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}
```

6. **Expensive work during render.** Cache it with `useMemo`, move it to the server, precompute it, or move it to a Web Worker.

7. **Urgent updates that cause heavy renders.** Use transitions or deferred values (see "Suspense and Concurrent Rendering").

| Symptom in the Profiler | Likely cause | First fix to try |
|---|---|---|
| Whole page renders on each keystroke | State too high | Move state down, split components |
| Memoised child renders, "props changed" with identical-looking values | New object/function each render | Stabilise with `useMemo`/`useCallback`, or React Compiler |
| Many components render on "context changed" | Broad, frequently changing context | Split context, memoise value, use a store with selectors |
| One commit takes long with thousands of rows | Too many DOM nodes | Virtualisation, pagination |
| Single component with high self time | Heavy computation in render | `useMemo`, precompute, Web Worker |

**The React Compiler.** The React Compiler (stable since October 2025) is a build-time plugin that automatically memoises components and values. It removes most of causes 3 and part of 4 without manual `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback`. It relies on your code following the Rules of React (pure render, no mutation of props and state), and its ESLint plugin reports code it cannot optimise. It does not fix state placement, long lists or heavy computations; those are still design decisions.

**Key Takeaways**

- Measure first, in a production build, with the React DevTools Profiler and the browser Performance panel; INP is the metric most affected by slow renders.
- Most problems come from rendering too many components too often: colocate state, pass stable content as `children`, keep props and context values stable.
- Virtualise long lists; memoise or move expensive computations; use transitions for heavy non-urgent updates.
- `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` are targeted tools; the React Compiler applies them automatically when code follows the Rules of React.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Record a Profiler session while typing in the bookshelf search box. Identify every component that renders per keystroke and the reason React DevTools gives for each.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a list of 10,000 books with a filter and a "select" checkbox per row. Profile it with 4x CPU throttling, then apply, one at a time, state colocation, `memo` with stable callbacks, and virtualisation. Record INP-like timings after each step in a table.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A page in your React app feels slow when typing. How do you investigate and fix it?" *Hint:* reproduce in a production build with throttling, profile, read "why did this render", then fix in order of simplicity: state placement, children as props, stable references, virtualisation, transitions.

#### Testing with Jest and React Testing Library

**What to test, and how.** Component tests should give you confidence that the UI works for users and should survive refactoring. A test that checks internal state names or the component's private methods breaks whenever you restructure the code, even though users notice nothing. The guiding principle of **React Testing Library** (RTL) is: *the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you.* Tests find elements the way users do (by role, label and text), interact the way users do (click, type), and assert on what users see.

```text
                 /\        E2E (Playwright, Cypress): a few critical journeys in a real browser
                /  \       against a real (or staging) back end
               /----\
              /      \     Integration/component tests (Vitest/Jest + RTL + MSW):
             /        \    most tests; render a page or feature with mocked network
            /----------\
           /            \  Unit tests: reducers, selectors, hooks, utility functions
          /--------------\
           static analysis: TypeScript, ESLint (react-hooks)
```

**The toolchain.**

| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| **Jest** or **Vitest** | Test runner: finds tests, runs them, provides `describe`/`it`/`expect` and mocking. Vitest reuses the Vite configuration and has a Jest-compatible API, so it is the natural choice in Vite projects; Jest is common in older and non-Vite projects |
| **jsdom** (or happy-dom) | A simulated DOM in Node.js, so components can render without a browser |
| **@testing-library/react** | `render`, `screen` and queries |
| **@testing-library/user-event** | Realistic user interactions (typing fires keydown, input, keyup) |
| **@testing-library/jest-dom** | Matchers such as `toBeInTheDocument`, `toBeDisabled`, `toHaveValue` |
| **MSW** (Mock Service Worker) | Intercepts network requests and returns mock responses, so components keep their real `fetch` code |

```bash
npm install -D vitest jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/user-event @testing-library/jest-dom msw
```

```typescript
// vite.config.ts (excerpt)
export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  test: {
    environment: 'jsdom',
    globals: true,                               // describe/it/expect without imports, like Jest
    setupFiles: ['./src/test/setup.ts'],
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/test/setup.ts
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { afterAll, afterEach, beforeAll } from 'vitest';
import { cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';
import { server } from './server';

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));  // fail on unmocked requests
afterEach(() => { server.resetHandlers(); cleanup(); });
afterAll(() => server.close());
```

**Queries and their priority.** RTL queries come in three families: `getBy*` throws if nothing (or more than one element) matches, `queryBy*` returns `null` (to assert absence), and `findBy*` returns a promise that waits for the element (for async UI). Prefer queries that reflect accessibility, because they also verify that the UI is accessible:

| Priority | Query | Finds |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })` | Elements by ARIA role and accessible name |
| 2 | `getByLabelText('Title')` | Form fields by their label |
| 3 | `getByPlaceholderText`, `getByText`, `getByDisplayValue` | Visible text |
| 4 | `getByAltText`, `getByTitle` | Images, titled elements |
| Last resort | `getByTestId('book-row')` | `data-testid` attributes, invisible to users |

**A first component test.**

```tsx
// Rating.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { vi } from 'vitest';
import { Rating } from './Rating';

it('reports the chosen rating', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  const onChange = vi.fn();                                        // mock function (jest.fn() in Jest)
  render(<Rating value={2} onChange={onChange} />);

  expect(screen.getByRole('radio', { name: '2' })).toBeChecked();  // aria-checked is reflected
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('radio', { name: '4' }));

  expect(onChange).toHaveBeenCalledWith(4);
});
```

**Testing with network: MSW.** Mocking `fetch` or the API module ties tests to implementation details. MSW intercepts requests at the network level, so the component, the API client and the error handling all run for real:

```typescript
// src/test/server.ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

export const books = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Dune', author: 'Frank Herbert', isbn: '9780441172719', year: 1965, tags: [] },
  { id: 2, title: 'Emma', author: 'Jane Austen', isbn: '9780141439587', year: 1815, tags: [] },
];

export const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/api/v1/books', ({ request }) => {
    const author = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('author')?.toLowerCase() ?? '';
    const data = books.filter((b) => b.author.toLowerCase().includes(author));
    return HttpResponse.json({ data, page: 1, limit: 20, total: data.length });
  }),
);
```

```tsx
// BookListPage.test.tsx
import { screen, waitForElementToBeRemoved } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { server } from '../test/server';
import { renderWithProviders } from '../test/utils';
import { BookListPage } from './BookListPage';

it('shows books and filters them by author', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  renderWithProviders(<BookListPage />);

  expect(await screen.findByText('Dune')).toBeInTheDocument();     // findBy waits for the fetch
  expect(screen.getByText('Emma')).toBeInTheDocument();

  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText(/author/i), 'austen');

  expect(await screen.findByText('Emma')).toBeInTheDocument();
  await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText('Dune'));  // Dune disappears after refetch
});

it('shows an error message when the API fails', async () => {
  server.use(                                                      // override for this test only
    http.get('/api/v1/books', () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ title: 'internal server error', status: 500 }, { status: 500 })),
  );
  renderWithProviders(<BookListPage />);
  expect(await screen.findByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent(/could not load/i);
});
```

Components that use routers, query clients or stores need those providers. A small helper keeps tests short and gives each test a fresh cache:

```tsx
// src/test/utils.tsx
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { MemoryRouter } from 'react-router';
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';

export function renderWithProviders(ui: React.ReactElement, { route = '/' } = {}) {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient({ defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false } } }); // fail fast in tests
  return render(
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <MemoryRouter initialEntries={[route]}>{ui}</MemoryRouter>
    </QueryClientProvider>,
  );
}
```

**Testing hooks and logic.** Pure functions (reducers, selectors, formatters) are tested directly, without React. Custom hooks can be tested through a component that uses them or with `renderHook`:

```tsx
import { renderHook, act } from '@testing-library/react';

it('debounces the value', () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  const { result, rerender } = renderHook(({ v }) => useDebouncedValue(v, 300), { initialProps: { v: 'a' } });
  rerender({ v: 'ab' });
  expect(result.current).toBe('a');                    // not yet updated
  act(() => { vi.advanceTimersByTime(300); });         // act flushes the resulting state update
  expect(result.current).toBe('ab');
  vi.useRealTimers();
});
```

**Good practices.**

- Use `user-event` over `fireEvent`; it simulates complete interactions (focus, key events, pointer events).
- Await `findBy*` for async UI instead of arbitrary `setTimeout` waits; RTL wraps updates in `act()` for you.
- Avoid large **snapshot tests**: they break on every markup change and are approved without reading. Small, targeted assertions document intent better.
- Do not test implementation details: no assertions on state variables, hook call counts or CSS class names users cannot perceive.
- Add automated accessibility checks (`vitest-axe`/`jest-axe`) to component tests and Storybook.
- Cover a few critical journeys (login, create a book, checkout) with **end-to-end** tests in **Playwright**, which drives real browsers against a running app.

**Key Takeaways**

- Test behaviour, not implementation: find elements by role and label, interact with `user-event`, assert on what users see.
- Vitest (Vite projects) or Jest runs tests in jsdom; RTL renders and queries; jest-dom adds DOM matchers.
- Use `getBy` for present elements, `queryBy` for absence, `findBy` for async UI; prefer role and label queries.
- Mock the network with MSW so the real API client and error handling are tested; wrap components in providers with a helper.
- Unit-test pure logic directly, use `renderHook` for hooks, keep snapshots small, and add a few Playwright E2E tests for critical flows.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Test the `NewBookForm` from 14.3: the submit button is disabled while the title is empty, typing a title enables it, and submitting calls `onCreate` with the trimmed values.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write MSW-backed tests for the book list page covering loading, empty, error and success states, pagination and the author filter. Then refactor the page to use TanStack Query and verify that the tests pass unchanged.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What does 'avoid testing implementation details' mean in React Testing Library?" *Hint:* give an example of a brittle test (state values, class names, snapshot) and its user-centric replacement, and explain why the replacement survives refactoring.

#### Server-Side Rendering with Next.js

**The limits of client-side rendering.** A Vite SPA sends an almost empty HTML page. The browser must download, parse and run the JavaScript, which then fetches data and finally renders content:

```text
CSR (client-side rendering)
  HTML (empty) -> JS bundle download -> JS executes -> fetch data -> render -> content visible
                                                                             (and interactive)

SSR (server-side rendering)
  server: fetch data -> render HTML -> send
  browser: HTML visible (content!) -> JS download -> hydrate -> interactive
```

CSR has three weaknesses: a slow first contentful paint on slow devices and networks, content that crawlers and link-preview bots may not see, and data requests that start only after the JavaScript runs. **Server-side rendering** (SSR) runs the same React components on the server, sends complete HTML, and then **hydrates** it in the browser.

**Hydration.** The server's HTML is "dry": it looks right but has no event handlers. **Hydration** means React runs in the browser, renders the same component tree, matches it against the existing DOM, and attaches event listeners and state without recreating the nodes. For this to work, the first client render must produce exactly the same output as the server. Anything that differs between them causes a **hydration mismatch**: `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `window.innerWidth`, `localStorage` or locale-dependent formatting. Read browser-only values in an effect (which runs only on the client) after hydration.

**Rendering strategies.**

| Strategy | When HTML is produced | Fresh data | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| CSR | In the browser | Yes, fetched by the client | Dashboards behind login, highly interactive tools |
| SSR (dynamic) | On the server, per request | Yes | Personalised or frequently changing pages |
| SSG (static generation) | At build time | Only as of the build | Documentation, marketing, blogs |
| ISR (incremental static regeneration) | At build time, regenerated in the background after N seconds or on demand | Eventually | Catalogues, product pages, news |
| Streaming SSR | On the server, sent progressively as Suspense boundaries resolve | Yes | Pages with fast and slow parts |

**Next.js.** Next.js (by Vercel) is the most widely used React framework. It provides file-based routing, all the rendering strategies above, React Server Components, server-side mutations, image and font optimisation, and an integrated build (Turbopack). Its modern router is the **App Router** (the `app/` directory, introduced in Next.js 13). The older **Pages Router** (`pages/` with `getServerSideProps` and `getStaticProps`) is still supported and common in existing projects.

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest bookshelf-next     # TypeScript, ESLint, App Router, optional Tailwind
```

```text
app/
+-- layout.tsx                 root layout: <html>, <body>, shared navigation
+-- page.tsx                   /
+-- books/
|   +-- page.tsx               /books
|   +-- loading.tsx            Suspense fallback for this segment (streaming)
|   +-- error.tsx              error boundary for this segment
|   +-- [id]/
|       +-- page.tsx           /books/42  (dynamic segment)
|       +-- not-found.tsx
+-- api/
    +-- health/route.ts        route handler: GET /api/health
```

**Server Components and Client Components.** In the App Router, components are **React Server Components** (RSC) by default. They run *only on the server* (at request time or at build time), can be `async`, can read databases and secrets directly, and send their rendered result to the browser **without their JavaScript**. Components that need state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs must be **Client Components**, marked with the `'use client'` directive at the top of the file. Client Components are rendered to HTML on the server too, then hydrated in the browser.

```tsx
// app/books/[id]/page.tsx  (Server Component: no 'use client')
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
import { FavouriteButton } from './FavouriteButton';

type Props = { params: Promise<{ id: string }> };        // params are async in recent Next.js versions

export async function generateMetadata({ params }: Props) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const book = await getBook(Number(id));
  return { title: book ? `${book.title} | Bookshelf` : 'Not found' };   // <title> and meta tags, rendered on the server
}

export default async function BookPage({ params }: Props) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const book = await getBook(Number(id));                 // runs on the server: direct DB or API call, secrets stay there
  if (!book) notFound();                                  // renders not-found.tsx with a 404 status

  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{book.title}</h1>
      <p>{book.author}, {book.year}</p>
      <FavouriteButton bookId={book.id} />                {/* interactive island: a Client Component */}
    </article>
  );
}

async function getBook(id: number) {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/api/v1/books/${id}`, {
    next: { revalidate: 60 },                             // ISR-style: cache the response for 60 s
  });
  if (res.status === 404) return null;
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`API error ${res.status}`); // caught by error.tsx
  return res.json() as Promise<Book>;
}
```

```tsx
// app/books/[id]/FavouriteButton.tsx
'use client';                                            // this file and its imports ship to the browser

import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';
import { toggleFavourite } from './actions';

export function FavouriteButton({ bookId }: { bookId: number }) {
  const [fav, setFav] = useState(false);
  const [pending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  return (
    <button disabled={pending}
            onClick={() => startTransition(async () => setFav(await toggleFavourite(bookId)))}>
      {fav ? 'Remove favourite' : 'Add favourite'}
    </button>
  );
}
```

**Server Functions (Server Actions).** A function in a file marked `'use server'` runs on the server but can be called from the client like an async function, or used as a form `action`. Next.js turns each call into a POST request behind the scenes:

```typescript
// app/books/[id]/actions.ts
'use server';

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';

export async function toggleFavourite(bookId: number): Promise<boolean> {
  const session = (await cookies()).get('sid')?.value;
  if (!session) throw new Error('Not authenticated');     // a public endpoint: always check auth and validate input
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/api/v1/me/favourites/${bookId}`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { Cookie: `sid=${session}` },
  });
  revalidatePath(`/books/${bookId}`);                     // refresh cached server-rendered output
  return (await res.json()).favourite;
}
```

**Streaming.** `loading.tsx` wraps a route segment in a Suspense boundary. The server sends the layout and the fallback immediately, then streams the page's HTML when its data is ready. You can also place `<Suspense>` boundaries inside a page so a slow recommendations section does not delay the main content.

**The Server/Client boundary.**

| | Server Component | Client Component (`'use client'`) |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | On the server only | Server (for HTML) and browser (hydration, interactivity) |
| JavaScript sent to the browser | None | The component and its imports |
| `async`/`await` data access, secrets, DB | Yes | No (call APIs or Server Functions) |
| `useState`, `useEffect`, event handlers, browser APIs | No | Yes |
| Can render the other kind | Yes, Client Components as children | Server Components only when passed in as `children`/props |

Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component cross the network, so they must be serialisable: plain data, dates, promises and JSX, but no ordinary functions (Server Functions are the exception). Keep `'use client'` as far down the tree as possible ("interactive islands"), so most of the page ships no JavaScript.

**Alternatives and trade-offs.** React Router's framework mode (the successor to Remix) offers SSR with loaders and actions, and TanStack Start offers SSR with type-safe routing. Astro renders mostly static pages with React islands. SSR needs a Node.js (or edge) runtime, adds server costs and operational complexity, and makes some mistakes (hydration mismatches, leaking secrets into Client Components) possible. For internal tools behind login, a Vite SPA is often the simpler and better choice. Caching APIs in Next.js have changed between major versions, so check the documentation of the version you use.

**Key Takeaways**

- CSR sends empty HTML and renders in the browser; SSR renders HTML on the server for faster first paint and better crawlability, then hydrates it.
- Hydration attaches React to server HTML and requires identical first renders; browser-only values belong in effects.
- Choose per page among CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR and streaming according to freshness, personalisation and cost.
- In the Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default (async, server-only, no client JavaScript); `'use client'` marks interactive Client Components; `'use server'` defines Server Functions.
- Server Functions are public endpoints: authenticate and validate in them; keep client boundaries small.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a Next.js App Router project with `/books` and `/books/[id]` pages that fetch from the Chapter 12 API in Server Components. View the page source to confirm that the book titles are in the HTML.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `loading.tsx`, an `error.tsx`, a `not-found.tsx` and `generateMetadata` to the details page, a Client Component that adds the book to favourites through a Server Function, and a slow "similar books" section streamed behind its own Suspense boundary. Compare the JavaScript sent to the browser with the Vite SPA version.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is hydration, and what causes a hydration mismatch?" *Hint:* explain server HTML vs client render, the requirement that the first client render matches, and examples such as dates, random values, `window` access and browser extensions modifying the DOM.

#### Comparison with Angular and Vue

**Three answers to the same problem.** React, Angular and Vue all build component-based UIs that update when state changes, and all can produce excellent applications. They differ in *how much* they include, *how* you write templates and *how* they detect changes. Understanding the differences helps you choose for a project and move between codebases.

**The same component in each.** A counter with a doubled value and a button:

```tsx
// React: a function; JSX; state via hooks; the function re-runs on each change
import { useState } from 'react';

export function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const doubled = count * 2;                               // recomputed on every render
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count} x 2 = {doubled}</button>;
}
```

```typescript
// Angular: a decorated class; HTML template with its own syntax; signals for reactivity
import { Component, computed, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-counter',
  template: `<button (click)="increment()">{{ count() }} x 2 = {{ doubled() }}</button>`,
})
export class Counter {
  count = signal(0);
  doubled = computed(() => this.count() * 2);              // recomputed only when count changes
  increment() { this.count.update((c) => c + 1); }
}
```

```vue
<!-- Vue: a single-file component; HTML-based template; reactive refs (Composition API) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref, computed } from 'vue';
const count = ref(0);
const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2);           // tracked dependency: updates when count changes
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">{{ count }} x 2 = {{ doubled }}</button>
</template>
```

**How each detects changes.**

- **React** re-runs the component function when state changes and diffs the virtual DOM (14.1). Reactivity is explicit (setters) and coarse-grained (per component); memoisation or the React Compiler narrows it.
- **Vue** wraps state in JavaScript **proxies** (`ref`, `reactive`). Reading a value during render records a dependency, and writing it re-renders exactly the components that read it. Templates are compiled with optimisation hints (static parts are skipped), and Vapor mode removes the virtual DOM for fine-grained DOM updates.
- **Angular** historically used **Zone.js** to patch async APIs and run change detection across the component tree after any event. Modern Angular uses **signals**, fine-grained reactive values that notify exactly the views that depend on them, and new applications are **zoneless** by default.

**Overview.**

| Aspect | React | Angular | Vue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kind | UI library; ecosystem chooses the rest | Complete framework ("batteries included") | Progressive framework: core plus official router and store |
| Maintained by | Meta and community | Google | Independent core team (Evan You), community funded |
| First release | 2013 | 2016 (rewrite of AngularJS from 2010) | 2014 |
| Language | JavaScript or TypeScript | TypeScript (required) | JavaScript or TypeScript |
| Templates | JSX: JavaScript expressions and `map` | HTML templates with `@if`, `@for`, bindings `[prop]`, `(event)` | HTML templates with `v-if`, `v-for`, `:prop`, `@event`; JSX optional |
| Reactivity | State setters, re-render and virtual DOM diff | Signals (formerly Zone.js change detection) | Proxy-based reactive refs, dependency tracking |
| Data binding | One-way; controlled inputs | One-way plus two-way `[(ngModel)]` | One-way plus two-way `v-model` |
| Routing | React Router, TanStack Router (third party) | `@angular/router` (built in) | Vue Router (official) |
| State management | Context, Redux Toolkit, Zustand, TanStack Query... | Services with dependency injection, signals, NgRx | Pinia (official) |
| Forms | Controlled inputs, React Hook Form | Template-driven and reactive forms (built in) | `v-model`, VeeValidate, FormKit |
| HTTP | `fetch` + libraries | `HttpClient` (built in, RxJS based) | `fetch` + libraries |
| CLI and tooling | Vite, framework CLIs | Angular CLI (generation, build, test) | `create-vue` (Vite), Vue DevTools |
| SSR framework | Next.js, React Router, TanStack Start | Angular SSR (built in) | Nuxt |
| Mobile | React Native (native UI) | Ionic, NativeScript | Ionic, Capacitor, NativeScript |
| Learning curve | Small core; many ecosystem choices to learn | Steeper: TypeScript, DI, RxJS, many concepts, but one way to do things | Gentle; templates familiar to HTML/CSS developers |
| Typical fit | Large ecosystem, flexible architectures, cross-platform with React Native | Large enterprise teams wanting consistency and conventions | Teams wanting an approachable, cohesive framework; progressive adoption in existing pages |

**Other options.** **Svelte** compiles components to direct DOM updates and uses "runes" for reactivity. **SolidJS** uses JSX like React, but with signals and no virtual DOM: components run once, and only the affected DOM nodes update. Both show that the virtual DOM is one design among several. Their ideas (signals, compilation) have influenced React's Compiler, Angular's signals and Vue's Vapor mode.

**Choosing.** Technical differences matter less than they appear: all three are fast enough for nearly every application. Choose based on the team's experience, the hiring market where you are, the existing codebase, how much structure the team wants from the framework (Angular) versus how much freedom it wants (React), the ecosystem libraries you need, and mobile or SSR requirements.

**Key Takeaways**

- React is a UI library with a large ecosystem; Angular is a complete, opinionated TypeScript framework; Vue is a progressive framework with official router and store.
- React uses JSX and re-renders components with virtual DOM diffing; Angular and Vue use HTML-based templates and fine-grained reactivity (signals, proxies).
- Angular and Vue provide two-way binding syntax for forms; React uses controlled inputs and one-way flow.
- Svelte and SolidJS show alternatives without a virtual DOM, and their ideas are spreading to the others.
- Choose based on team skills, existing code, desired structure, ecosystem needs and platform targets, not on micro-benchmarks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement the same "book list with a search filter" component in React, Vue (`<script setup>`) and Angular (standalone component with signals). Compare how each handles the input binding and the derived filtered list.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a one-page technical recommendation choosing a framework for a new bookshelf admin application for a team of six developers who know TypeScript but not React. Cover routing, forms, state, testing and SSR needs, and justify the choice against the other two.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does change detection differ between React, Vue and Angular?" *Hint:* re-running components plus virtual DOM diffing, proxy-based dependency tracking, and Zone.js versus signals; discuss granularity and what developers must do to avoid unnecessary work in each.

<a id="15-hybrid-mobile-and-progressive-web-applications"></a>
## 15. Hybrid Mobile and Progressive Web Applications

Most people now reach the Web from a phone, and many expect "an app" rather than "a website". This chapter covers the ways web technologies (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) reach mobile users, from the plain responsive site to the app sold in a store. It starts with the strategic choices and the constraints of mobile devices (15.1). Then it covers Progressive Web Apps, which add offline support, installation and push notifications to ordinary websites (15.2). The rest is about frameworks: jQuery Mobile, historically important and now deprecated (15.3); Apache Cordova and its successor Capacitor, which wrap a web app in a native shell (15.4); and Ionic, which gives that app a native-looking UI (15.5). The running example is a mobile client for the bookshelf API from Chapter 12.

<a id="151-mobile-web-strategies"></a>
### 15.1 Mobile Web Strategies

Before writing any code, a team has to decide how its product will reach phones. This subchapter compares native, hybrid and web approaches, explains the WebView component that hybrid apps are built on, and covers the realities of mobile development: small and varied screens, touch input, limited CPU and battery, and device features that are only partly available to web code.

#### Native vs Hybrid vs Web Applications

**Why the choice matters.** Suppose the bookshelf service needs a mobile presence. There are several ways to build it, and they differ in cost, reach, performance and access to device features. The decision is hard to reverse: it determines the languages the team writes, how updates reach users, and whether app store review stands between a bug fix and the users.

**The main families.**

- A **native app** is written in the platform's own language and UI toolkit: Swift or Objective-C with SwiftUI or UIKit on iOS, Kotlin or Java with Jetpack Compose or Android Views on Android. It is compiled for the device, distributed through the App Store or Google Play, and has full access to every platform API on release day.
- A **mobile web app** is an ordinary website designed for small screens. It runs in the browser, is reached by URL, and updates the moment you deploy. It can only use the APIs the browser exposes.
- A **Progressive Web App (PWA)** is a web app that also meets a set of requirements (HTTPS, a manifest, usually a service worker), so it can be installed on the home screen, work offline and receive push notifications (15.2).
- A **hybrid app** is a web app packaged inside a thin native shell. The shell shows the HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a **WebView** (an embedded browser component) and provides a **bridge** so JavaScript can call native code. It ships through the app stores like a native app. Apache Cordova (15.4), Capacitor and Ionic (15.5) belong here.
- A **cross-platform native app** is written once in a shared language but renders real native UI widgets or draws its own UI with a native graphics engine: React Native (JavaScript, native views), Flutter (Dart, own rendering engine), .NET MAUI (C#), Kotlin Multiplatform with Compose Multiplatform. These do not use a WebView for their UI, so they are related to this chapter but not part of it.

An analogy: a native app is a house built for one specific plot of land; a web app is a tent you can pitch anywhere but that offers fewer comforts; a hybrid app is a tent put up inside a prefabricated shell that gives it a front door, mailbox and electricity connection.

```text
                 Native              Hybrid                       Web / PWA
              +-----------+     +------------------+         +----------------+
  Your code   | Swift /   |     | HTML, CSS, JS    |         | HTML, CSS, JS  |
              | Kotlin UI |     +------------------+         +----------------+
              |           |     | WebView + bridge |         |    Browser     |
              |           |     +------------------+         |  (Chrome,      |
              |           |     | Native shell     |         |   Safari...)   |
              +-----------+     +------------------+         +----------------+
  Platform    |        iOS / Android operating system and hardware           |
              +---------------------------------------------------------------+
  Delivery      App store          App store                     URL (+ install)
```

**Comparing the approaches.**

| Criterion | Native | Hybrid (Cordova, Capacitor) | Web / PWA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Languages | Swift, Kotlin (two codebases) | HTML, CSS, JS/TS (one codebase) + native plugins when needed | HTML, CSS, JS/TS (one codebase) |
| UI | Platform widgets, best fidelity | Web UI styled to look native | Web UI |
| Performance | Best, especially for animation, graphics, heavy computation | Good for business apps; WebView limits heavy graphics | Good; depends on the browser and device |
| Device APIs | Everything, immediately | Everything a plugin exposes (plugins can be written) | Only what browsers support; strongest on Android Chromium |
| Offline | Yes | Yes (assets are bundled in the app) | Yes, with a service worker |
| Distribution | App stores (review, fees) | App stores (review, fees) | URL, search engines; optional store listing |
| Updates | Store release; users must update | Store release (web assets can sometimes be live-updated within store rules) | Instant on next load |
| Discoverability | Store search | Store search | Links, search engines, sharing |
| Team skills | iOS + Android specialists | Web developers + some native knowledge | Web developers |
| Typical cost | Highest | Medium | Lowest |

**How to decide.** No approach is best in general. Useful questions:

1. *Which device features does the product need?* If it needs background Bluetooth, deep OS integration (widgets, watch apps, CarPlay) or advanced camera processing, native or cross-platform native is likely. If it needs a camera, geolocation and notifications, all three can work.
2. *How demanding is the UI?* Games, video editors and complex gesture-driven interfaces benefit from native rendering. Forms, lists and content screens (most business apps) work well in a WebView.
3. *Must it be in the app stores?* Some audiences only look there, and some organizations distribute only through managed app stores. A PWA can also be listed in Google Play (Trusted Web Activity) and the Microsoft Store, but not in Apple's App Store without a native wrapper.
4. *What skills and budget does the team have?* A web team can ship a PWA or hybrid app without hiring iOS and Android specialists.
5. *How often does it change?* Frequent releases favor the web, where deployment is instant.

Many products combine approaches: a responsive website and PWA for reach, plus a hybrid or native app for users who want the store version, often sharing the same front-end code.

**Key Takeaways**

- Native apps use platform languages and toolkits: best performance and API access, highest cost, two codebases.
- Web apps and PWAs run in the browser from a URL: lowest cost, instant updates, limited to browser APIs.
- Hybrid apps package web code in a native shell with a WebView and a JavaScript-to-native bridge, and ship through app stores.
- Cross-platform native frameworks (React Native, Flutter) share code but render native or custom-drawn UI, not a WebView.
- Choose based on required device features, UI demands, store presence, team skills and release frequency.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For each of these products, choose native, hybrid or PWA and justify the choice in two sentences: a restaurant's ordering app, a 3D racing game, an internal expense-report tool for a company with managed devices, a news site.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a one-page decision record for the bookshelf mobile client. List the features (browse books, scan an ISBN barcode with the camera, offline reading list, reminders), evaluate each against the three approaches, and recommend one with its main risks.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you not build a hybrid app?" *Hint:* think about rendering-heavy UIs, features that depend on OS integration or background execution, and situations where the plugin you need does not exist or is unmaintained.

#### WebView-Based Architectures

**Why understand the WebView.** Every hybrid framework in this chapter is built on one component: the WebView. Its capabilities and limits are the capabilities and limits of your app. Knowing how it works explains why a hybrid app behaves differently on iOS and Android, why some CSS features are missing on old devices, and how JavaScript can trigger native code at all.

**What a WebView is.** A WebView is a browser engine without the browser around it: no address bar, no tabs, no bookmarks, just a rectangle that renders web content and runs JavaScript. A native app places it on screen like any other view. Many apps use WebViews for parts of their UI (help pages, checkout flows, in-app browsers), and hybrid apps use one for the whole UI.

| Platform | Component | Engine | How it is updated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android | `android.webkit.WebView` (Android System WebView) | Chromium (Blink + V8) | Through Google Play, independently of OS updates (Android 5+) |
| iOS / iPadOS | `WKWebView` | WebKit (JavaScriptCore) | Only with iOS updates |
| Windows (desktop) | WebView2 | Chromium (Edge) | Evergreen runtime |

On iOS, the WebView engine is tied to the OS version, so an app's available web features depend on which iOS versions its users run. The older `UIWebView` was deprecated and Apple has rejected new apps that use it since 2020. On Android the WebView is Chromium and auto-updates, so feature support usually tracks recent Chrome versions.

**The bridge.** A web page normally cannot touch the camera API of the operating system or read the native contacts database. A hybrid shell adds a **bridge**: a channel for messages between the JavaScript in the WebView and native code in the shell.

```text
 +-------------------------- Native app process ---------------------------+
 |                                                                          |
 |  +------------------- WebView ------------------+                        |
 |  |  index.html, app.js, styles.css              |                        |
 |  |                                              |                        |
 |  |  Camera.getPhoto({ quality: 80 })            |                        |
 |  |        |                         ^           |                        |
 |  +--------|-------------------------|-----------+                        |
 |           | 1. JSON message         | 4. result delivered as             |
 |           |    {plugin, method,     |    a JS callback / resolved        |
 |           |     args, callbackId}   |    Promise                         |
 |           v                         |                                    |
 |  +---------------- Bridge -----------------+                             |
 |  |  routes calls to registered plugins     |                             |
 |  +-----------------------------------------+                             |
 |           | 2. dispatch                 ^ 3. result {callbackId, data}   |
 |           v                             |                                |
 |  +-------------- Native plugin (Swift / Kotlin) -------------+           |
 |  |  opens the camera UI, waits for the photo, saves it       |           |
 |  +-----------------------------------------------------------+           |
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The bridge is asynchronous: JavaScript sends a message and gets the answer later through a callback or Promise, because the native work (opening a camera, asking for permission) may take seconds. Arguments and results are serialized (usually as JSON), so you cannot pass functions or DOM nodes across it.

**The platform primitives.** Frameworks hide these, but it helps to see them once. On Android, the shell can expose a Java or Kotlin object to JavaScript, and can run JavaScript in the page:

```kotlin
// Android (Kotlin): a minimal hand-written bridge
class NativeBridge(private val activity: Activity, private val webView: WebView) {

    @JavascriptInterface                    // only annotated methods are visible to JS
    fun vibrate(ms: Long) {
        val vibrator = activity.getSystemService(Vibrator::class.java)
        vibrator.vibrate(VibrationEffect.createOneShot(ms, VibrationEffect.DEFAULT_AMPLITUDE))
        // Native -> JS: run code in the page (must happen on the UI thread)
        activity.runOnUiThread {
            webView.evaluateJavascript("window.onNativeEvent('vibrated', $ms)", null)
        }
    }
}

// Setup in the Activity
webView.settings.javaScriptEnabled = true
webView.addJavascriptInterface(NativeBridge(this, webView), "AndroidBridge")
webView.loadUrl("https://appassets.androidplatform.net/assets/www/index.html")
```

```javascript
// In the page: AndroidBridge is now a global object
window.onNativeEvent = (name, data) => console.log('native says', name, data);
if (window.AndroidBridge) {
  AndroidBridge.vibrate(200); // calls the Kotlin method
}
```

On iOS, `WKWebView` uses message handlers instead: the page posts a message, and native code receives it.

```swift
// iOS (Swift): receive messages from JavaScript
class BridgeHandler: NSObject, WKScriptMessageHandler {
    weak var webView: WKWebView?

    func userContentController(_ controller: WKUserContentController,
                               didReceive message: WKScriptMessage) {
        guard message.name == "bridge",
              let body = message.body as? [String: Any] else { return }
        // ... do the native work, then reply by evaluating JavaScript
        webView?.evaluateJavaScript("window.onNativeEvent('done', null)")
    }
}

// Setup
let config = WKWebViewConfiguration()
let handler = BridgeHandler()
config.userContentController.add(handler, name: "bridge")
let webView = WKWebView(frame: .zero, configuration: config)
handler.webView = webView
```

```javascript
// In the page on iOS
window.webkit.messageHandlers.bridge.postMessage({ action: 'vibrate', ms: 200 });
```

Writing this by hand for every feature on two platforms is tedious, which is why frameworks such as Cordova and Capacitor exist: they provide one JavaScript API, a plugin registry on each platform, callback bookkeeping and a library of ready-made plugins.

**Where the web assets come from.** A hybrid app usually bundles its HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside the app package and serves them from a local origin, for example `https://localhost` on Android with Capacitor or `capacitor://localhost` on iOS. Serving them from a real-looking origin (rather than `file://`) matters: `file://` pages have an opaque origin, so cookies, `fetch` with CORS, service workers and many APIs behave badly or not at all. Some apps instead load a remote URL into the WebView; this allows instant updates but makes the app useless offline and is closely examined in app store review (Apple's guidelines reject apps that are just a repackaged website).

**Security considerations.** The bridge gives JavaScript native powers, so any script that runs in the WebView can use them. Rules that follow:

- Never load untrusted or third-party pages in the WebView that has the bridge. Open external links in the system browser or an in-app browser tab instead.
- Restrict navigation to your own origin (Cordova's `allow-navigation`, Capacitor's `server.allowNavigation`).
- Use a strict Content Security Policy (Chapter 17) so injected scripts cannot run.
- Treat data coming from JavaScript as untrusted input in native code (validate paths, sizes, URLs).

**Key Takeaways**

- A WebView is an embeddable browser engine; hybrid apps render their entire UI in one.
- Android's WebView is Chromium and updates through Google Play; iOS's `WKWebView` is WebKit and updates only with iOS.
- A bridge passes asynchronous, serialized messages between JavaScript and native code; frameworks add a plugin system on top.
- Serve bundled assets from a local `https`-like origin instead of `file://` so web APIs behave normally.
- The bridge grants native power to any script in the WebView: restrict navigation, avoid untrusted content and use a CSP.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Explain in your own words why a hybrid app might show a CSS feature correctly on a three-year-old Android phone but not on an iPhone that has not been updated for three years.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Design the message format for a small bridge that supports `getBatteryLevel()` and `share(text)`. Show the JSON sent from JavaScript, the JSON sent back, and how the JavaScript side matches each reply to the right pending Promise.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is it dangerous to open arbitrary links inside the WebView of a hybrid app?" *Hint:* consider what a third-party page could call through the bridge, and what the native side can do on the user's behalf.

#### Responsive and Adaptive Mobile UI

**Why mobile layout needs care.** Phones range from about 320 to 430 CSS pixels wide, tablets reach over 1000, foldables change size while the app is running, and the same device can be held in portrait or landscape. Notches, rounded corners and gesture bars cover parts of the screen. A layout designed for a 1440-pixel desktop simply shrunk down would be unreadable. Chapter 2 (2.3) introduced media queries and breakpoints; this topic covers what changes when the target is a phone.

**Responsive vs adaptive.** Two broad approaches exist:

| Approach | Idea | How | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Responsive | One layout that flows and rearranges continuously | Fluid grids, flexbox, grid, relative units, media and container queries | One codebase, works on unknown sizes | Same HTML and assets downloaded everywhere unless optimized |
| Adaptive | Several distinct layouts, one chosen per device class | Server picks a template (via Client Hints or user agent), or client picks components at breakpoints | Tailored experiences, smaller payloads per device | More layouts to maintain; device detection can be wrong |

In practice most sites are responsive at their core and adaptive in places: for example a bottom tab bar on phones and a side navigation on desktops, chosen at a breakpoint.

**The viewport meta tag.** Without it, mobile browsers assume the page was designed for a desktop and render it in a virtual viewport of about 980 pixels, then zoom out. Every mobile page needs:

```html
<!-- width=device-width: the layout viewport matches the device width in CSS pixels
     initial-scale=1: no initial zoom
     viewport-fit=cover: draw under notches and rounded corners (then use safe-area insets) -->
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">
```

Do not add `user-scalable=no` or `maximum-scale=1`: blocking zoom is an accessibility failure for users with low vision.

**Mobile-first CSS.** Write the base styles for the smallest screen, then add complexity for larger screens with `min-width` queries. Small screens get the simplest CSS, and you are forced to decide what really matters.

```css
/* Base: phone. Single column, bottom navigation */
.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-areas: "main" "nav";
  grid-template-rows: 1fr auto;
  min-height: 100dvh;                 /* dynamic viewport height: follows the browser's
                                         collapsing address bar, unlike 100vh */
}
.nav {
  grid-area: nav;
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-around;
  padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom); /* keep buttons above the iOS home indicator */
}

/* Tablet and up: navigation moves to the side */
@media (min-width: 48rem) {
  .layout {
    grid-template-areas: "nav main";
    grid-template-columns: 16rem 1fr;
    grid-template-rows: 1fr;
  }
  .nav { flex-direction: column; justify-content: flex-start; }
}
```

**Viewport units on mobile.** The classic `100vh` equals the height with the browser's address bar *hidden*, so content set to `100vh` overflows when the bar is visible. CSS now offers three variants: `svh` (small: bars visible), `lvh` (large: bars hidden) and `dvh` (dynamic: changes as bars move). Use `dvh` for full-screen app layouts, `svh` when content must never be hidden.

**Safe areas.** With `viewport-fit=cover`, the page extends under the notch and home indicator. The `env()` function returns the insets you must keep clear:

```css
.header {
  padding-top: max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-top));   /* at least 1rem, more under a notch */
  padding-left: env(safe-area-inset-left);            /* landscape: notch on the side */
  padding-right: env(safe-area-inset-right);
}
```

**Media features beyond width.** Screen width does not tell you how the user interacts. Interaction media features describe the input device:

```css
/* Primary input is a finger (imprecise, no hover): enlarge targets, avoid hover-only UI */
@media (pointer: coarse) {
  .toolbar button { min-width: 48px; min-height: 48px; }
}

/* Hover effects only where hovering is possible */
@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) {
  .card:hover { box-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15); }
}

/* Respect system preferences */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; }
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --bg: #121212; --text: #e8e8e8; }
}
```

**Container queries.** A component such as a book card may appear in a narrow sidebar and in a wide grid on the same screen. Media queries ask about the viewport; container queries ask about the component's container, so the component adapts wherever it is placed:

```css
.book-list { container-type: inline-size; }          /* make the list a query container */

.book-card { display: grid; gap: 0.5rem; }
@container (min-width: 30rem) {                      /* the container is at least 30rem wide */
  .book-card { grid-template-columns: 6rem 1fr; }    /* cover image beside the text */
}
```

**Responsive images.** A phone on a cellular connection should not download a 2400-pixel hero image. `srcset` and `sizes` let the browser choose:

```html
<img src="cover-400.jpg"
     srcset="cover-400.jpg 400w, cover-800.jpg 800w, cover-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(min-width: 48rem) 33vw, 100vw"
     alt="Cover of Dune" width="400" height="600" loading="lazy">
<!-- width/height reserve space before loading, preventing layout shift (CLS) -->
```

**Device detection.** Avoid parsing the `User-Agent` string to decide layout: it is long, frequently spoofed and being reduced by browsers. Prefer CSS media features and JavaScript feature detection. If the server must know (adaptive serving), Chromium browsers send **User-Agent Client Hints** such as `Sec-CH-UA-Mobile: ?1`.

**Key Takeaways**

- Every mobile page needs `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`; never disable zoom.
- Responsive design uses one fluid layout; adaptive design picks between distinct layouts; most sites mix both.
- Write mobile-first CSS and add `min-width` breakpoints for larger screens.
- Use `dvh`/`svh` instead of `100vh`, and `env(safe-area-inset-*)` with `viewport-fit=cover`.
- Use `pointer`, `hover`, `prefers-*` media features and container queries rather than width alone; serve sized images with `srcset`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build a bookshelf page with a header, a list of book cards and a bottom navigation bar on phones that becomes a left sidebar at 48rem. Test it in the browser's device emulation at 360 px and 1024 px.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Make the book card a container-query component that shows only the title under 20rem, title and author between 20rem and 30rem, and cover, title, author and description above 30rem. Place it both in a narrow sidebar and a wide main area.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `100vh` and `100dvh`, and why does it matter on phones?" *Hint:* think about what happens to the browser's address bar while scrolling and which height each unit measures.

#### Touch Interaction and Mobile Performance

**Why touch is different.** A mouse pointer is a precise, single point with a hover state. A finger is a wide, imprecise contact area of roughly 8 to 10 mm, it hides what it touches, it cannot hover, and several fingers can act at once. Phones also have slower CPUs, less memory and less reliable networks than the laptops developers test on. A page that feels fine on a desktop can feel sluggish and fiddly on a mid-range phone.

**Touch targets.** Small buttons cause mis-taps. Guidelines:

| Source | Recommended minimum target size |
|---|---|
| Apple Human Interface Guidelines | 44 x 44 points |
| Material Design (Android) | 48 x 48 dp, with about 8 dp between targets |
| WCAG 2.2, criterion 2.5.8 (level AA) | 24 x 24 CSS pixels (or enough spacing) |

A small icon can keep its visual size while its tappable area grows, using padding.

```css
.icon-button {
  /* 24px icon, 48px touch target */
  inline-size: 48px;
  block-size: 48px;
  display: inline-grid;
  place-items: center;
  touch-action: manipulation;          /* disables double-tap-to-zoom on this element,
                                          so taps fire immediately */
  -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; /* remove the grey flash on iOS/Android;
                                               provide your own :active style instead */
}
.icon-button:active { background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.08); }
```

**The 300 ms delay (history).** Early mobile browsers waited about 300 ms after a tap to see whether a second tap (double-tap zoom) would follow before firing `click`. Libraries such as FastClick worked around it. Modern browsers skip the delay on pages with `width=device-width` in the viewport meta tag, and `touch-action: manipulation` removes it for specific elements. You may still see the workaround in legacy code (including jQuery Mobile's `vclick`, 15.3).

**Use pointer events.** Chapter 6 (6.3) covered mouse, touch and pointer events. For new code, **pointer events** are the best choice: one API for mouse, pen and touch, with `pointerType` telling you which.

```javascript
// A swipe-to-delete gesture on a list item, using pointer events
const item = document.querySelector('.book-item');
let startX = 0;
let dx = 0;

item.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => {
  startX = e.clientX;
  item.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);   // keep receiving events even if the finger leaves the element
});

item.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => {
  if (!item.hasPointerCapture(e.pointerId)) return;
  dx = Math.min(0, e.clientX - startX);  // only allow dragging to the left
  item.style.transform = `translateX(${dx}px)`; // transform: cheap, compositor-only
});

item.addEventListener('pointerup', () => {
  if (dx < -120) item.remove();          // swiped far enough: delete
  else item.style.transform = '';        // snap back
  dx = 0;
});
```

```css
/* Tell the browser that horizontal panning on this element is handled by JavaScript,
   while vertical scrolling of the page still works natively */
.book-item { touch-action: pan-y; }
```

**Passive listeners.** When a page listens for `touchstart`, `touchmove` or `wheel`, the browser must wait for the handler to finish before scrolling, because the handler might call `preventDefault()`. Declaring a listener **passive** promises it will not, so scrolling stays smooth:

```javascript
window.addEventListener('touchmove', updateParallax, { passive: true });
```

Chrome and Safari already treat `touchstart`/`touchmove` listeners on `window`, `document` and `body` as passive by default.

**Measuring mobile performance.** Google's **Core Web Vitals** measure what users feel, and are measured on real users in the field:

| Metric | Measures | Good | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|
| LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) | Loading: when the main content appears | <= 2.5 s | > 4.0 s |
| INP (Interaction to Next Paint) | Responsiveness: delay from a tap to the next frame | <= 200 ms | > 500 ms |
| CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) | Visual stability: unexpected content movement | <= 0.1 | > 0.25 |

INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. Mobile devices fail INP far more often than desktops, because every millisecond of JavaScript costs more on a slower CPU.

**Techniques that matter most on phones.**

- **Ship less JavaScript.** Parsing and executing JavaScript is the biggest cost on mid-range phones. Use code splitting (`import()`), remove unused dependencies, and render HTML on the server where possible (14.5).
- **Keep the main thread free.** Break long tasks (over 50 ms) into smaller pieces; move heavy computation into a Web Worker (6.4). To give the browser a chance to handle input during long loops, yield regularly:

```javascript
// Process 5,000 books without blocking taps for the whole duration
async function indexBooks(books) {
  for (let i = 0; i < books.length; i++) {
    addToSearchIndex(books[i]);
    if (i % 200 === 0) {
      // Yield to the browser so pending input and rendering can run.
      // scheduler.yield() where available, otherwise a macrotask via setTimeout
      await (globalThis.scheduler?.yield?.() ?? new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0)));
    }
  }
}
```

- **Animate only `transform` and `opacity`.** These can be handled by the GPU compositor without recalculating layout. Animating `top`, `left`, `width` or `height` forces layout on every frame.
- **Avoid layout thrashing.** Reading layout (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`) after writing styles forces synchronous layout; batch reads, then writes.
- **Skip off-screen work.** `content-visibility: auto` lets the browser skip rendering off-screen sections; `loading="lazy"` defers images; virtualize long lists (render only visible rows).
- **Optimize images and fonts.** Use modern formats (AVIF, WebP), correct sizes (`srcset`) and `font-display: swap`.
- **Design for slow and flaky networks.** Test with network throttling, cache aggressively (15.2) and show skeleton screens instead of blank pages.

**Test on real devices.** Desktop emulation in DevTools simulates screen size and throttles CPU and network, but real mid-range Android phones expose problems emulation hides. Chrome's remote debugging (`chrome://inspect`) and Safari's Web Inspector let you profile a page running on a connected phone.

**Key Takeaways**

- Touch targets should be about 44 to 48 px; enlarge the hit area with padding rather than enlarging icons.
- Modern browsers have no 300 ms tap delay with a proper viewport; `touch-action: manipulation` removes it per element.
- Use pointer events for gestures, `touch-action` to declare what the browser should handle, and passive listeners for scroll-related events.
- Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) measure real user experience; mobile CPUs make INP the hardest to pass.
- Ship less JavaScript, break up long tasks, animate only `transform`/`opacity`, and test on real mid-range devices.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Audit a page you built earlier with DevTools device emulation: find every interactive element smaller than 44 x 44 px and fix it without changing the visual icon size.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement pull-to-refresh on a scrollable book list using pointer events and `touch-action`. It should only start when the list is scrolled to the top, follow the finger with a `transform`, and trigger a reload after 80 px.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A page feels laggy when users tap buttons on Android phones but fine on desktop. How do you investigate?" *Hint:* think about INP, CPU throttling in the Performance panel, long tasks, and what runs on the main thread when the tap happens.

#### Device Capabilities and Constraints

**Why this matters.** Mobile apps are attractive because phones have cameras, GPS, motion sensors, vibration motors and always-on connectivity. Before choosing web, PWA or hybrid, you need to know which of these a browser actually exposes, on which platforms, and under what conditions. You also need to design for what phones lack: plenty of battery, memory, storage and a reliable network.

**Web APIs for device features.** Support varies widely. Android Chromium is the most capable browser; Safari on iOS supports fewer device APIs; some APIs exist only in Chromium. The table summarizes the situation in 2026; always check current data (for example on caniuse.com or MDN) before relying on an API.

| Capability | Web API | Android Chrome | iOS Safari | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Location | `navigator.geolocation` (6.4) | Yes | Yes | Permission prompt; HTTPS only |
| Camera / microphone | `getUserMedia`, `<input type="file" capture>` | Yes | Yes | `capture` opens the camera directly on mobile |
| Motion and orientation | `DeviceMotionEvent`, `DeviceOrientationEvent` | Yes | Yes, after `requestPermission()` | iOS requires an explicit permission call from a user gesture |
| Vibration | `navigator.vibrate()` | Yes | No | |
| Native share sheet | `navigator.share()` | Yes | Yes | Must be called from a user gesture |
| Keep screen on | Screen Wake Lock API | Yes | Yes (16.4+) | |
| Push notifications | Push API + Notifications (15.2) | Yes | Home-screen web apps only (16.4+) | |
| App badge | Badging API (`navigator.setAppBadge`) | Installed apps | Home-screen web apps (16.4+) | |
| Bluetooth, USB, NFC, Serial | Web Bluetooth, WebUSB, Web NFC, Web Serial | Mostly yes | No | Chromium-only |
| Contacts | Contact Picker API | Yes | No | |
| Network type | `navigator.connection` | Yes | No | Chromium-only |
| Background sync | Background Sync API (15.2) | Yes | No | Chromium-only |

When an API is missing, a hybrid app fills the gap with a native plugin (15.4).

**Feature detection and progressive enhancement.** Never assume an API exists because the device is a phone. Check for it, use it when available, and provide a fallback when it is not:

```javascript
// Share a book: native share sheet when available, clipboard fallback otherwise
async function shareBook(book) {
  const data = { title: book.title, text: `Read "${book.title}"`, url: `/books/${book.id}` };

  if (navigator.canShare?.(data)) {            // optional chaining: undefined if unsupported
    try {
      await navigator.share(data);             // opens the OS share sheet
      return;
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;   // the user closed the sheet: not an error
      throw err;
    }
  }
  await navigator.clipboard.writeText(new URL(data.url, location.origin).href);
  showToast('Link copied');
}
```

```javascript
// Motion sensors: iOS needs an explicit permission request from a user gesture
async function enableShakeToUndo() {
  if (typeof DeviceMotionEvent?.requestPermission === 'function') {
    const state = await DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission(); // iOS 13+
    if (state !== 'granted') return;
  }
  window.addEventListener('devicemotion', (e) => {
    const a = e.accelerationIncludingGravity;
    if (a && Math.hypot(a.x, a.y, a.z) > 25) undoLastAction();
  });
}
document.querySelector('#enable-shake').addEventListener('click', enableShakeToUndo);
```

**Permissions.** Powerful features require user permission and a **secure context** (HTTPS or `localhost`). Good permission manners:

- Ask in context, right when the user tries the feature ("Scan barcode" button), not on page load. Prompts on load are often denied and some browsers suppress them.
- Explain the benefit before the prompt (a "pre-permission" screen in your own UI).
- Handle denial gracefully; a denied prompt usually cannot be re-shown by the page.
- Check status first with the Permissions API where supported: `await navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'geolocation' })` returns `granted`, `denied` or `prompt`.

**Constraints of mobile devices.**

| Constraint | Consequence | Design response |
|---|---|---|
| Battery | GPS, radio, wake locks and constant JavaScript drain it | Request location only when needed, batch network requests, stop timers when hidden |
| CPU and memory | Mid-range phones are several times slower than laptops; the OS kills background tabs and apps | Ship less JavaScript; save state so the app can be restored after being killed |
| Network | High latency, packet loss, offline periods, metered data | Cache assets and data, retry with backoff, offline-first design (15.2) |
| Storage | Quotas and eviction; Safari may clear script storage of non-installed sites after 7 days without a visit | Use `navigator.storage.persist()`; keep the server as source of truth |
| Background execution | Pages are frozen or discarded when hidden; JavaScript does not run in the background | Use the Page Lifecycle (`visibilitychange`), service worker events, or native plugins |
| Screen and input | Small screen, virtual keyboard covers half of it | Correct `inputmode`, `autocomplete` and `enterkeyhint` attributes; keep focused fields visible |

The `visibilitychange` event is the reliable signal that the user switched away. Mobile browsers may never fire `unload` or `beforeunload`, so save state when the page becomes hidden:

```javascript
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'hidden') {
    saveDraftToIndexedDB();                 // the page may be killed without further warning
    navigator.sendBeacon('/api/v1/analytics', JSON.stringify(pendingEvents)); // survives page close
    stopPolling();
  } else {
    startPolling();
  }
});
```

The virtual keyboard is a device constraint that HTML can help with:

```html
<!-- Numeric keypad, autofill hint, and a "search" action key on the keyboard -->
<input type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]*" autocomplete="off"
       enterkeyhint="search" placeholder="ISBN">
<input type="email" autocomplete="email" enterkeyhint="next">
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Browser support for device APIs varies: Android Chromium supports the most, iOS Safari fewer, and some APIs are Chromium-only.
- Always use feature detection with fallbacks; hybrid apps cover gaps with native plugins.
- Powerful APIs require HTTPS and permission; ask in context, after explaining why, and handle denial.
- Design for limited battery, CPU, memory, storage and network, and for pages being frozen or killed in the background.
- Save state on `visibilitychange` (not `unload`), and use `inputmode`, `autocomplete` and `enterkeyhint` for the virtual keyboard.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a small "capabilities" page that detects and lists which of these APIs the current browser supports: geolocation, vibration, Web Share, Wake Lock, Badging, Web Bluetooth, Background Sync. Open it on an Android phone and an iPhone and compare.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a "Find bookshops near me" button to the bookshelf client. It should check the permission state first, show an explanation before the first prompt, request location with a timeout, and display a manual city search if permission is denied or unavailable.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why should you not rely on `beforeunload` to save user data on mobile?" *Hint:* think about how mobile operating systems suspend and kill background tabs and apps, and which event fires reliably before that happens.

<a id="152-progressive-web-apps"></a>
### 15.2 Progressive Web Apps

A Progressive Web App is a website that the user can install, that works offline or on a bad connection, and that can re-engage users with notifications, while still being reached by URL and updated by deploying. This subchapter explains the defining characteristics, the Web App Manifest, service workers and their lifecycle, caching strategies, offline-first design, push notifications, installability and auditing.

#### PWA Characteristics and Criteria

**Why PWAs exist.** For years the choice was a website (easy to reach, instant updates, but no offline mode, no home screen icon, no notifications) or a native app (all of those, but a store download, a separate codebase, and slow updates). In 2015 Alex Russell and Frances Berriman coined the term **Progressive Web App** for sites that use new browser capabilities to get closer to native apps without giving up the web's strengths. "Progressive" refers to **progressive enhancement**: the app works as a normal website in any browser, and gains app-like features where the browser supports them.

**Characteristics.** A good PWA is commonly described as:

| Characteristic | Meaning | Enabled by |
|---|---|---|
| Progressive | Works for every user, regardless of browser; enhances where possible | Feature detection |
| Responsive | Fits any screen: phone, tablet, desktop | Responsive design (15.1) |
| Connectivity-independent | Works offline or on poor networks | Service worker + Cache API, IndexedDB |
| App-like | Feels like an app: own window, app shell navigation | Manifest `display`, app shell model |
| Fresh | Always up to date | Service worker update process |
| Safe | Served over HTTPS so content cannot be tampered with | TLS |
| Discoverable | Identifiable as an app by search engines and browsers | Manifest, metadata |
| Re-engageable | Can bring users back | Push notifications, badges |
| Installable | Can be added to the home screen, dock or start menu | Manifest + browser install criteria |
| Linkable | Shared and opened by URL, no installation needed | URLs, deep links |

**The three technical building blocks.**

```text
             +----------------------------------------------+
             |                Your web app                  |
             |       (responsive HTML, CSS, JavaScript)     |
             +----------------------------------------------+
   HTTPS ----|  required for service workers and most APIs  |
             +-----------------------+----------------------+
             |   Web App Manifest    |    Service Worker    |
             |   (JSON metadata:     |   (JS proxy between  |
             |    name, icons,       |    page and network: |
             |    display, colors)   |    caching, offline, |
             |   -> installability,  |    push, sync)       |
             |      app look & feel  |                      |
             +-----------------------+----------------------+
```

1. **HTTPS.** Service workers can intercept every request, so browsers only allow them on secure origins (plus `localhost` for development).
2. **Web App Manifest.** A JSON file that tells the browser the app's name, icons, colors, start URL and how it should be displayed when launched (next topic).
3. **Service worker.** A script that runs separately from the page and acts as a programmable network proxy. It enables offline support, caching, push notifications and background sync.

**Platform support.** PWAs work best on Chromium browsers (Chrome, Edge, Samsung Internet) on Android and desktop, where installation, push, background sync and many device APIs are available. Safari supports service workers, the manifest and installation through "Add to Home Screen" on iOS and "Add to Dock" on macOS. Since iOS 16.4, web apps added to the home screen can receive push notifications and set badges. Firefox supports service workers and push everywhere, and installation on Android; its desktop support for installing web apps is limited. A PWA must therefore treat installation and the advanced APIs as optional enhancements.

**PWA in the store.** A PWA can also be packaged for app stores: Google Play through a **Trusted Web Activity** (a Chrome tab without browser UI, created with tools such as Bubblewrap or PWABuilder) and the Microsoft Store directly. For Apple's App Store a native wrapper with real native value is needed.

**Key Takeaways**

- A PWA is a website that uses modern browser features to be installable, offline-capable and re-engageable, while remaining linkable and instantly updatable.
- "Progressive" means it works as a normal site everywhere and adds features where supported.
- The three building blocks are HTTPS, a Web App Manifest and a service worker.
- Chromium offers the most PWA features; Safari supports the core features with fewer extras; always treat advanced features as enhancements.
- PWAs can be listed in Google Play (Trusted Web Activity) and the Microsoft Store.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open three websites you use often, check in DevTools (Application panel) whether they have a manifest and a service worker, and list which PWA characteristics each one meets.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* For the bookshelf client, write a table mapping each PWA characteristic to a concrete feature (for example "connectivity-independent: the reading list is available offline") and the browser API that provides it, noting which ones will not work on iOS.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What makes a website a Progressive Web App?" *Hint:* name the technical requirements (secure origin, manifest, service worker), then explain the experience goals and why "progressive" is in the name.

#### The Web App Manifest

**Why a manifest.** When a user installs a website, the operating system needs information that HTML does not provide: which name to show under the icon, which icons in which sizes, which page to open, whether to show browser controls, which color the splash screen should have. The **Web App Manifest** is a JSON file that answers these questions in one place.

**Linking the manifest.** Every page of the app references it from `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest">
<!-- theme-color colors the browser UI / status bar; can vary by color scheme -->
<meta name="theme-color" content="#2e5d4b" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#16302a" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
<!-- iOS still uses this icon for the home screen in some versions -->
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/icons/apple-touch-icon-180.png">
```

Serve the file with the `application/manifest+json` media type (`.webmanifest` is the conventional extension; `.json` also works).
