**A complete manifest.**

```json
{
  "id": "/",
  "name": "Bookshelf - Your Reading List",
  "short_name": "Bookshelf",
  "description": "Track the books you own, read and want to read.",
  "start_url": "/?source=pwa",
  "scope": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "display_override": ["window-controls-overlay", "standalone"],
  "orientation": "any",
  "background_color": "#ffffff",
  "theme_color": "#2e5d4b",
  "lang": "en",
  "dir": "ltr",
  "categories": ["books", "productivity"],
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/icons/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icons/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icons/icon-maskable-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }
  ],
  "screenshots": [
    { "src": "/screens/list-narrow.png", "sizes": "1080x1920", "type": "image/png", "form_factor": "narrow", "label": "Your reading list" },
    { "src": "/screens/list-wide.png", "sizes": "1920x1080", "type": "image/png", "form_factor": "wide", "label": "Library overview" }
  ],
  "shortcuts": [
    { "name": "Add a book", "url": "/books/new", "icons": [{ "src": "/icons/add-96.png", "sizes": "96x96" }] },
    { "name": "Reading list", "url": "/reading-list" }
  ],
  "share_target": {
    "action": "/share",
    "method": "GET",
    "params": { "title": "title", "text": "text", "url": "url" }
  }
}
```

**Members explained.**

| Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `id` | Stable identity of the app. If omitted, `start_url` is used, so changing `start_url` would create a "different" app. Set it once and never change it. |
| `name` / `short_name` | Full name (install dialog, splash screen) and short name (under the home screen icon, about 12 characters). |
| `start_url` | Page opened when the app is launched. A query parameter lets analytics distinguish launches from the home screen. |
| `scope` | URLs considered part of the app. Navigating outside the scope opens the browser UI or a separate browser. |
| `display` | `fullscreen` (no system UI, for games), `standalone` (own window, no browser UI, like an app), `minimal-ui` (own window with minimal navigation controls), `browser` (normal tab). |
| `display_override` | Ordered list of preferred display modes, tried before `display`; for example `window-controls-overlay` on desktop draws the app into the title bar area. |
| `icons` | Icons in several sizes. At least 192x192 and 512x512 for Chromium installability. `purpose: "maskable"` marks an icon with safe padding that the OS may crop into a circle, squircle or other shape. |
| `background_color` | Splash screen background shown while the app loads. |
| `theme_color` | Color of the title bar or status bar. |
| `screenshots` | Shown in the richer install dialog on Android and desktop Chromium. |
| `shortcuts` | Quick actions in the long-press menu of the icon (Android) or the taskbar or dock menu (desktop). |
| `share_target` | Lets the installed app appear in the OS share sheet and receive shared content (Chromium). |
| `protocol_handlers`, `file_handlers` | Register the app for custom URL schemes or file types (desktop Chromium). |

**Maskable icons.** Android launchers display icons in different shapes. A regular icon gets shrunk inside a white circle; a maskable icon fills the shape. Design maskable icons with the important content within the central 80 percent circle (the "safe zone"); tools such as maskable.app preview the result.

**Display modes in CSS and JavaScript.** The app can detect how it was launched, for example to hide an "Install" button or show its own back button in standalone mode, where there is no browser back button:

```css
/* Only when launched as an installed app */
@media (display-mode: standalone), (display-mode: window-controls-overlay) {
  .install-banner { display: none; }
  .app-back-button { display: inline-flex; }
}
```

```javascript
const isInstalled =
  window.matchMedia('(display-mode: standalone)').matches ||
  window.navigator.standalone === true;      // legacy iOS Safari property
```

**Inspecting the manifest.** In Chrome DevTools, the **Application > Manifest** pane shows the parsed manifest, icon previews, warnings and installability problems.

**Key Takeaways**

- The manifest is a JSON file linked with `<link rel="manifest">` that describes the installed app's identity and appearance.
- Essential members: `name`, `short_name`, `start_url`, `display`, `icons` (192 and 512, plus a maskable icon), `theme_color`, `background_color`.
- Set `id` explicitly and keep it stable; `scope` defines which URLs belong to the app.
- `display: standalone` gives an app-like window; detect it with the `display-mode` media feature.
- Optional members such as `shortcuts`, `screenshots` and `share_target` integrate the app further with the OS.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a manifest for the bookshelf client with name, short name, start URL, standalone display, colors and two icons. Link it, and check the Application > Manifest pane in DevTools for warnings.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a maskable icon, two shortcuts and a `share_target` that accepts a shared URL. Implement the `/share` route so that sharing a book page from another app pre-fills the "Add a book" form.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What happens if you change `start_url` in a deployed PWA's manifest that has no `id`?" *Hint:* think about how the browser identifies an installed app and whether it would consider the result an update or a new app.

#### Service Worker Lifecycle

**Why service workers.** Normally, when the network is down, the browser shows its own error page and your code never gets a say. Earlier attempts to give pages offline power (the Application Cache, now removed) used a declarative file listing what to cache, and it behaved in surprising ways. The **service worker** takes the opposite approach: it gives you a JavaScript program that sits between your pages and the network and decides, request by request, what to answer.

Think of the service worker as a personal assistant at the front desk of your app. Every request from the page passes the desk. The assistant can forward it to the network, answer from a filing cabinet (the cache), or combine both. The assistant also works when the office (your page) is closed, for example to receive a push message.

**What a service worker is.**

- A JavaScript file running in its own **worker thread**, separate from any page. It has no DOM access; it communicates with pages through `postMessage`.
- **Event-driven:** the browser starts it when an event arrives (`fetch`, `push`, `sync`, `message`) and terminates it when idle. Do not keep state in global variables; store it in IndexedDB or the Cache API.
- **Scoped:** it controls pages under its scope, by default the directory containing the script. A worker at `/sw.js` controls the whole origin; one at `/app/sw.js` controls only `/app/`. That is why the file is usually placed at the site root.
- **Secure origins only:** HTTPS or `localhost`.
- **Fully asynchronous:** synchronous APIs such as `localStorage` and synchronous XHR are not available.

**Registration.** The page registers the worker. Do it after the page has loaded so the worker's setup does not compete with the first render:

```javascript
// main.js (page)
if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
  window.addEventListener('load', async () => {
    try {
      const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js', { scope: '/' });
      console.log('Service worker registered with scope', reg.scope);
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('Service worker registration failed', err);
    }
  });
}
```

**The lifecycle.** A service worker goes through a strict sequence of states. The design guarantees that only one version of your worker controls the pages at a time, so old pages never talk to a new worker that expects a different cache layout.

```text
  register('/sw.js')
          |
          v
   +-------------+   install event: precache the app shell
   | installing  |   event.waitUntil(promise) delays completion
   +-------------+   (rejection -> worker is discarded: "redundant")
          |
          v
   +-------------+   another version still controls open pages?
   |  installed  |-- yes --> waits here ("waiting") until all those tabs are closed
   |  (waiting)  |           (or the new worker calls self.skipWaiting())
   +-------------+
          | no old version (or skipWaiting)
          v
   +-------------+   activate event: delete old caches, migrate data
   | activating  |   event.waitUntil(promise)
   +-------------+
          |
          v
   +-------------+   handles fetch, push, sync, message events;
   |  activated  |   terminated when idle and restarted on the next event
   +-------------+
          |
          v
   +-------------+
   |  redundant  |   replaced by a newer version, or installation failed
   +-------------+
```

**A first-visit subtlety.** On the very first visit, the page loaded *before* the worker existed, so it is not controlled. The worker becomes active, but it only controls pages loaded afterwards, unless it calls `clients.claim()` during activation.

**A complete minimal worker.**

```javascript
// sw.js
const VERSION = 'v3';
const SHELL_CACHE = `shell-${VERSION}`;
const SHELL_ASSETS = ['/', '/index.html', '/app.js', '/styles.css', '/offline.html', '/icons/icon-192.png'];

// 1. INSTALL: download and store the app shell
self.addEventListener('install', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(                                  // installation succeeds only if this resolves
    caches.open(SHELL_CACHE).then((cache) => cache.addAll(SHELL_ASSETS))
  );
});

// 2. ACTIVATE: remove caches from previous versions
self.addEventListener('activate', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil((async () => {
    const names = await caches.keys();
    await Promise.all(
      names
        .filter((name) => name.startsWith('shell-') && name !== SHELL_CACHE)
        .map((name) => caches.delete(name))
    );
    await self.clients.claim();                     // take control of already-open pages now
  })());
});

// 3. FETCH: answer navigations from the network, falling back to an offline page
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  if (event.request.mode === 'navigate') {
    event.respondWith(
      fetch(event.request).catch(() => caches.match('/offline.html'))
    );
    return;
  }
  // Other requests: cache first, then network (strategies are covered in the next topic)
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then((cached) => cached ?? fetch(event.request))
  );
});
```

**How updates work.** The browser checks for a new version of `sw.js` on navigations to pages in scope (and on functional events), at most about once every 24 hours unless you call `registration.update()`. By default it bypasses the HTTP cache for the worker script itself (`updateViaCache: 'imports'`). If the file differs by even one byte, the new version installs and then **waits** until no tab uses the old version. This surprises developers: a user who keeps one tab open forever never gets the update.

Two common patterns for updating promptly:

1. **Skip waiting immediately** (`self.skipWaiting()` in `install`). Simple, but a page loaded by the old worker may then request assets that the new worker has already deleted. Safe only when assets are versioned in their filenames and old ones remain available.
2. **Ask the user** ("A new version is available. Reload?"), then tell the waiting worker to skip waiting:

```javascript
// sw.js: skip waiting only when the page asks
self.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
  if (event.data?.type === 'SKIP_WAITING') self.skipWaiting();
});
```

```javascript
// main.js: detect a waiting worker and offer a reload
const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js');

function offerUpdate(worker) {
  showBanner('A new version of Bookshelf is available.', 'Reload', () => {
    worker.postMessage({ type: 'SKIP_WAITING' });
  });
}

if (reg.waiting) offerUpdate(reg.waiting);           // a new version was already waiting
reg.addEventListener('updatefound', () => {
  const newWorker = reg.installing;
  newWorker.addEventListener('statechange', () => {
    // installed + an existing controller = an update (not the first install)
    if (newWorker.state === 'installed' && navigator.serviceWorker.controller) {
      offerUpdate(newWorker);
    }
  });
});

// When the new worker takes control, reload once so the page uses the new assets
let reloading = false;
navigator.serviceWorker.addEventListener('controllerchange', () => {
  if (!reloading) { reloading = true; window.location.reload(); }
});
```

**Debugging.** Chrome DevTools' **Application > Service workers** pane shows the active and waiting workers and has buttons to *Update*, *Unregister* and *Skip waiting*, plus an "Update on reload" checkbox that makes development bearable. `chrome://serviceworker-internals` lists every registration. A hard reload (Shift+Reload) bypasses the service worker for that load.

**Key Takeaways**

- A service worker is an event-driven script in its own thread that acts as a network proxy for pages in its scope; it has no DOM and no persistent globals.
- Lifecycle: `install` (precache) -> waiting (while an old version controls pages) -> `activate` (clean up) -> idle/handling events -> redundant.
- `event.waitUntil()` extends install and activate until a Promise settles; `clients.claim()` controls already-open pages.
- The browser installs a new worker when the script changes by one byte, but it waits until the old version's tabs close, unless `skipWaiting()` is called.
- Offer updates to the user with a "reload" prompt and a `SKIP_WAITING` message, and reload once on `controllerchange`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Register a service worker that logs every lifecycle event and every `fetch` URL. Change one character in the worker, reload, and observe the waiting state in DevTools. Then close all tabs and reopen.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the "new version available" banner for the bookshelf client using the `SKIP_WAITING` message pattern. Verify that the page reloads exactly once after the user accepts.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does a new service worker wait before activating, and when is `skipWaiting()` dangerous?" *Hint:* think about a page loaded with version 1's HTML that then requests files from a cache that version 2 has replaced.

#### Caching Strategies and the Cache API

**Why strategies.** Being able to intercept requests is only useful if you decide well what to answer. A cached stylesheet that never changes can always come from the cache. A list of books should be fresh, but showing yesterday's list is better than an error. A payment request must always go to the network. Different resources need different **caching strategies**.

**The Cache API.** The Cache API stores pairs of `Request` and `Response` objects. It is available in service workers and in pages (`window.caches`), and is separate from the browser's HTTP cache: nothing enters or leaves it unless your code puts it there or deletes it.

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `caches.open(name)` | Open (or create) a named cache, returns a `Cache` |
| `caches.match(request)` | Search all caches for a matching response |
| `caches.keys()` / `caches.delete(name)` | List and delete named caches |
| `cache.add(url)` / `cache.addAll(urls)` | Fetch URLs and store the responses (fails if any response is not OK) |
| `cache.put(request, response)` | Store a response you already have |
| `cache.match(request, options)` | Find a response; `{ ignoreSearch: true }` ignores the query string |
| `cache.delete(request)` / `cache.keys()` | Remove an entry, list requests |

A `Response` body can be read only once. When you want to both return a response to the page and store it, **clone** it: `cache.put(request, response.clone())`.

**The five classic strategies.**

```text
 Cache first                     Network first                   Stale-while-revalidate
 page -> SW -> cache?            page -> SW -> network            page -> SW -> cache (answer now)
          hit: return                     ok: store + return               \-> network (in background)
          miss: network,                  fail: cache                           -> update cache
                store + return                                                    (used next time)

 Network only                    Cache only
 page -> SW -> network           page -> SW -> cache
 (never cached)                  (only precached assets)
```

| Strategy | Speed | Freshness | Offline | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cache first | Fastest | Stale until the cache changes | Yes | Versioned static assets (`app.3f9a1c.js`), fonts, icons |
| Network first | Network speed; slow on bad networks unless a timeout is used | Fresh | Fallback to cache | HTML pages, API data that must be current |
| Stale-while-revalidate | Fast | One request behind | Yes | Avatars, non-critical API data, article lists |
| Network only | Network speed | Fresh | No | Payments, analytics, non-GET requests |
| Cache only | Fastest | Only what was precached | Yes | The precached app shell |

**Implementing them.**

```javascript
// sw.js: one function per strategy
const RUNTIME = 'runtime-v1';

async function cacheFirst(request) {
  const cached = await caches.match(request);
  if (cached) return cached;
  const response = await fetch(request);
  if (response.ok) {
    const cache = await caches.open(RUNTIME);
    cache.put(request, response.clone());          // clone: the body can only be consumed once
  }
  return response;
}

async function networkFirst(request, timeoutMs = 3000) {
  const cache = await caches.open(RUNTIME);
  try {
    // Race the network against a timeout so a slow connection falls back to the cache
    const response = await Promise.race([
      fetch(request),
      new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timeout')), timeoutMs)),
    ]);
    if (response.ok) cache.put(request, response.clone());
    return response;
  } catch {
    const cached = await cache.match(request);
    if (cached) return cached;
    return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: 'offline' }), {
      status: 503,
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    });
  }
}

async function staleWhileRevalidate(event) {
  const cache = await caches.open(RUNTIME);
  const cached = await cache.match(event.request);
  const network = fetch(event.request).then((response) => {
    if (response.ok) cache.put(event.request, response.clone());
    return response;
  });
  event.waitUntil(network.catch(() => {}));        // keep the worker alive until the update finishes
  return cached ?? network;                        // answer from cache if possible
}

// Routing: choose a strategy per request
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  const { request } = event;
  const url = new URL(request.url);

  if (request.method !== 'GET') return;            // let the browser handle POST, PUT, DELETE
  if (url.origin !== self.location.origin) return; // ignore third-party requests here

  if (url.pathname.startsWith('/api/v1/books')) {
    event.respondWith(networkFirst(request));
  } else if (url.pathname.startsWith('/covers/')) {
    event.respondWith(staleWhileRevalidate(event));
  } else if (/\.(js|css|woff2|png|svg)$/.test(url.pathname)) {
    event.respondWith(cacheFirst(request));
  }
  // Anything else: no respondWith -> the browser fetches normally
});
```

**Precaching vs runtime caching.** **Precaching** stores a known list of files during `install` (the app shell), so they are available offline before the user visits them. **Runtime caching** stores responses as they are requested. Both need limits: runtime caches grow without bound unless you delete old entries.

**Storage limits.** Origins get a share of disk space determined by the browser (often a large percentage of free disk, much less in some contexts). Check usage and ask for persistence so the browser does not evict data under storage pressure:

```javascript
const { usage, quota } = await navigator.storage.estimate();
console.log(`Using ${(usage / 1e6).toFixed(1)} MB of ${(quota / 1e6).toFixed(0)} MB`);

if (navigator.storage.persist) {
  const persisted = await navigator.storage.persist(); // may be granted automatically for installed apps
  console.log('Persistent storage:', persisted);
}
```

**Opaque responses.** A `no-cors` request to another origin (for example an image from a CDN without CORS headers) returns an **opaque** response: status 0, unreadable body. You can cache it, but you cannot check whether it succeeded, and browsers count it as several megabytes against the quota. Prefer CORS-enabled resources.

**Workbox.** Writing strategies, expiration and precache manifests by hand is error-prone. **Workbox**, a set of libraries maintained by Google's Chrome team, provides them ready-made, and build plugins generate the precache list with content hashes. With Vite, `vite-plugin-pwa` integrates Workbox and generates the manifest and worker.

```javascript
// sw.js with Workbox (bundled by a build tool)
import { precacheAndRoute, cleanupOutdatedCaches } from 'workbox-precaching';
import { registerRoute } from 'workbox-routing';
import { NetworkFirst, StaleWhileRevalidate, CacheFirst } from 'workbox-strategies';
import { ExpirationPlugin } from 'workbox-expiration';

precacheAndRoute(self.__WB_MANIFEST);  // list of hashed build files, injected at build time
cleanupOutdatedCaches();

registerRoute(
  ({ url }) => url.pathname.startsWith('/api/v1/'),
  new NetworkFirst({ cacheName: 'api', networkTimeoutSeconds: 3 })
);

registerRoute(
  ({ request }) => request.destination === 'image',
  new CacheFirst({
    cacheName: 'images',
    plugins: [new ExpirationPlugin({ maxEntries: 200, maxAgeSeconds: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 })],
  })
);

registerRoute(
  ({ request }) => request.destination === 'style' || request.destination === 'script',
  new StaleWhileRevalidate({ cacheName: 'assets' })
);
```

**Key Takeaways**

- The Cache API stores `Request`/`Response` pairs under named caches, fully controlled by your code and separate from the HTTP cache.
- Choose a strategy per resource: cache first for versioned static assets, network first for fresh data, stale-while-revalidate for data that may be slightly old, network only for non-GET and sensitive requests.
- Clone responses before caching them; use `event.waitUntil` for background work.
- Precache the app shell during `install`, limit runtime caches, and request persistent storage.
- Workbox and `vite-plugin-pwa` provide tested strategies, expiration and precache manifests.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a cache-first route for images to a service worker and verify in the Network panel that the second load of a page shows "(ServiceWorker)" as the source.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a maximum-entries limit for the runtime cache: after each `put`, delete the oldest entries so that at most 50 remain. Then compare your code with Workbox's `ExpirationPlugin`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Which caching strategy would you use for an HTML page, a hashed JavaScript bundle, and a user's profile picture, and why?" *Hint:* consider for each how often it changes, what a stale version costs, and what should happen offline.

#### Offline-First Design and Background Sync

**Why offline-first.** Caching assets makes the app *open* offline, but the user also wants to *work* offline: read their reading list on a plane, mark a book as finished in the subway, and have the change reach the server later. "Offline" is also not just a binary state: a connection with 5 seconds of latency ("Lie-Fi") is worse than none, because the app waits instead of falling back.

**Offline-first** is a design approach: the app reads and writes local data first, shows it immediately, and synchronizes with the server in the background. The network becomes an enhancement rather than a requirement.

```text
   Network-first app                         Offline-first app
   ------------------                        ------------------
   UI --request--> server                    UI <--read/write--> local store (IndexedDB)
   UI <--data----- server                                          |
   (spinner while waiting;                                         | sync when possible
    error if offline)                                              v
                                                                server
```

An analogy: a network-first app is like calling a shop every time you want to know what is on your shopping list; an offline-first app keeps the list in your pocket and syncs it with your partner's copy when you are both home.

**Building blocks.**

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| Store structured data locally | IndexedDB (6.4), via a small wrapper such as `idb` |
| Remember writes made offline | An "outbox" queue in IndexedDB |
| Send the queue when back online | Background Sync API (Chromium), or `online` event and app start as fallback |
| Detect connectivity | `navigator.onLine` and the `online`/`offline` events (only a hint: "online" means a network interface is up, not that the server is reachable) |
| Resolve conflicts | Timestamps, version numbers, server-side merge rules |

**Optimistic UI with an outbox.** When the user marks a book as read, the app updates IndexedDB and the UI immediately, then stores the request in an outbox to send later.

```javascript
// db.js: thin wrapper using the 'idb' library (promise-based IndexedDB)
import { openDB } from 'idb';

export const dbPromise = openDB('bookshelf', 1, {
  upgrade(db) {
    db.createObjectStore('books', { keyPath: 'id' });
    db.createObjectStore('outbox', { keyPath: 'id', autoIncrement: true });
  },
});

// Called by the UI
export async function markAsRead(bookId) {
  const db = await dbPromise;
  const tx = db.transaction(['books', 'outbox'], 'readwrite');   // one atomic transaction
  const book = await tx.objectStore('books').get(bookId);
  book.status = 'read';
  book.updatedAt = Date.now();
  await tx.objectStore('books').put(book);                       // local state updated first
  await tx.objectStore('outbox').add({
    method: 'PATCH',
    url: `/api/v1/books/${bookId}`,
    body: { status: 'read', updatedAt: book.updatedAt },
  });
  await tx.done;

  await requestSync();                                           // ask to flush the outbox
}

async function requestSync() {
  const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
  if ('sync' in reg) {
    await reg.sync.register('flush-outbox');                     // Background Sync (Chromium)
  } else {
    flushOutbox();                                               // fallback: try now (and on 'online')
  }
}
window.addEventListener('online', () => flushOutbox());
```

**Background Sync.** The Background Sync API lets the service worker run a task when the browser believes connectivity is available, even if the user has closed the page. If the task's Promise rejects, the browser retries later with backoff (a limited number of times).

```javascript
// sw.js
import { openDB } from 'idb';

self.addEventListener('sync', (event) => {
  if (event.tag === 'flush-outbox') {
    event.waitUntil(flushOutbox());    // rejection -> the browser retries later
  }
});

async function flushOutbox() {
  const db = await openDB('bookshelf', 1);
  const entries = await db.getAll('outbox');
  for (const entry of entries) {
    const response = await fetch(entry.url, {
      method: entry.method,
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(entry.body),
    });                                // a network error throws -> sync retried later
    if (response.ok || response.status === 409) {
      await db.delete('outbox', entry.id);  // done (or a conflict the server resolved)
    } else if (response.status >= 500) {
      throw new Error(`Server error ${response.status}`);  // retry later
    }
  }
}
```

Related APIs, all Chromium-only:

- **Periodic Background Sync** (`reg.periodicSync.register('refresh', { minInterval })`): refresh content periodically for installed apps; the browser decides the actual frequency based on engagement.
- **Background Fetch**: download large files (podcasts, videos) with a browser-managed progress UI, surviving page closure.

On Safari and Firefox, flush the outbox on app start, on the `online` event and on `visibilitychange` to visible.

**Conflicts.** If the user changes a book on the phone while offline and on the laptop while online, the two changes conflict. Common resolutions:

| Strategy | How | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Last write wins | Compare `updatedAt` timestamps; the newest change wins | Simple; silently loses the other change; device clocks may differ |
| Version numbers | Client sends the version it edited; server rejects with `409 Conflict` if it changed | Detects conflicts; the app must handle them (merge or ask the user) |
| Field-level merge | Merge non-overlapping field changes | More logic, fewer conflicts |
| CRDTs | Data types that merge automatically (Yjs, Automerge) | Ideal for collaborative editing; more complex |

**Offline UX.** Tell users what is happening without alarming them: a subtle "Offline: changes will sync later" indicator, a badge on items still in the outbox, and disabled actions that truly need the network (such as payments). Never lose user input.

**Key Takeaways**

- Offline-first apps read and write a local store first and sync with the server in the background; they also handle slow connections well.
- Use IndexedDB for data, an outbox queue for pending writes, and optimistic UI updates.
- Background Sync runs a service worker task when connectivity returns, with retries; it is Chromium-only, so add fallbacks (`online`, app start, visibility).
- `navigator.onLine` is only a hint; the real test is whether a request succeeds.
- Plan for conflicts: last write wins, version checks with `409`, field merges or CRDTs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add an offline indicator to the bookshelf client that appears on the `offline` event and disappears on `online`. Test it with DevTools' "Offline" network option.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the outbox pattern for adding and deleting books. Make changes offline, close the tab, go back online, and verify in the server logs that Background Sync sent the requests. Add the fallback for browsers without `SyncManager`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you handle two devices editing the same record while one was offline?" *Hint:* compare last-write-wins with optimistic concurrency (version numbers, `409 Conflict`), and think about what the user should see.

#### Push Notifications

**Why push.** Chapter 6 (6.4) showed the Notifications API, which works only while the page is open. Re-engagement needs messages that arrive when the app is closed: "The book you reserved is available", "Your reading streak ends tonight". **Web Push** delivers a message from your server to a user's browser, which wakes the service worker even if no tab is open.

**Two APIs, three parties.**

- The **Push API** lets a service worker subscribe to a push service and receive `push` events.
- The **Notifications API** displays the message (`registration.showNotification`).
- The **push service** is run by the browser vendor (Google's FCM for Chrome, Mozilla's autopush for Firefox, Apple's service for Safari). Your server never connects to the device directly; it sends messages to the push service, which delivers them.

```text
 1. subscribe (with VAPID public key)
 Browser/SW --------------------------------> Push service (FCM, Mozilla, Apple)
            <-------------------------------- returns PushSubscription
                                              { endpoint: "https://fcm.googleapis.com/...",
                                                keys: { p256dh, auth } }
 2. send subscription
 Page ----------------- POST /api/v1/push/subscriptions ------------------> Your server (stores it)

 3. later: send a message (encrypted payload, signed with VAPID private key)
 Your server ------------- POST {endpoint} ----------------> Push service

 4. deliver (device online; queued if offline, up to the TTL)
 Push service ------------------------------> Browser wakes SW -> 'push' event
                                                                -> showNotification()
 5. user taps the notification -> 'notificationclick' -> open / focus the app
```

**VAPID keys.** Voluntary Application Server Identification identifies your server to the push service. You generate one key pair; the public key goes to the browser when subscribing, the private key stays on the server to sign messages. Payloads are encrypted end to end with the subscription's keys, so the push service cannot read them.

```bash
npx web-push generate-vapid-keys
# Public Key:  BEl62iUYgUivxIkv69yViEuiBIa-Ib9-SkvMeAtA3LFgDzkrxZJjSgSnfckjBJuBkr3qBUYIHBQFLXYp5Nksh8U
# Private Key: (keep this secret, store it in an environment variable)
```

**Step 1: subscribe in the page.** Ask for permission only after a user action, and explain the benefit first. Browsers penalize or block sites that prompt on page load.

```javascript
// main.js
const VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY = 'BEl62iUY...';

function urlBase64ToUint8Array(base64) {
  // The key is URL-safe base64; PushManager wants raw bytes
  const padding = '='.repeat((4 - (base64.length % 4)) % 4);
  const b64 = (base64 + padding).replace(/-/g, '+').replace(/_/g, '/');
  return Uint8Array.from(atob(b64), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0));
}

document.querySelector('#notify-me').addEventListener('click', async () => {
  if (!('PushManager' in window)) {
    return showToast('Notifications are not supported here. On iPhone, add Bookshelf to your Home Screen first.');
  }
  const permission = await Notification.requestPermission();   // must follow a user gesture
  if (permission !== 'granted') return;

  const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
  const subscription = await reg.pushManager.subscribe({
    userVisibleOnly: true,                    // promise: every push shows a notification
    applicationServerKey: urlBase64ToUint8Array(VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY),
  });

  await fetch('/api/v1/push/subscriptions', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(subscription),       // PushSubscription has a toJSON() method
  });
});
```

**Step 2: send from the server.** The `web-push` package for Node.js handles encryption and VAPID signing. In the Express API from Chapter 12:

```javascript
// server/push.js
import webpush from 'web-push';

webpush.setVapidDetails(
  'mailto:admin@bookshelf.example',          // contact for the push service operator
  process.env.VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY,
  process.env.VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY
);

export async function notifyUser(userId, payload) {
  const subscriptions = await db.pushSubscriptions.find({ userId });
  await Promise.all(subscriptions.map(async (sub) => {
    try {
      await webpush.sendNotification(sub, JSON.stringify(payload), {
        TTL: 60 * 60,                         // seconds the push service keeps it if the device is offline
        urgency: 'normal',                    // very-low | low | normal | high (affects battery use)
        topic: 'reservation',                 // a newer message with the same topic replaces an undelivered one
      });
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.statusCode === 404 || err.statusCode === 410) {
        await db.pushSubscriptions.deleteOne({ endpoint: sub.endpoint }); // expired or unsubscribed
      } else {
        throw err;
      }
    }
  }));
}

// Example: notifyUser(42, { title: 'Book available', body: '"Dune" is ready for pickup', url: '/reservations' });
```

**Step 3: receive in the service worker.**

```javascript
// sw.js
self.addEventListener('push', (event) => {
  const data = event.data?.json() ?? { title: 'Bookshelf', body: 'You have an update.' };
  event.waitUntil(
    self.registration.showNotification(data.title, {
      body: data.body,
      icon: '/icons/icon-192.png',
      badge: '/icons/badge-72.png',     // small monochrome icon for the Android status bar
      tag: 'reservation',               // replaces an earlier notification with the same tag
      data: { url: data.url ?? '/' },   // arbitrary data available on click
      actions: [{ action: 'open', title: 'View' }],
    })
  );
});

self.addEventListener('notificationclick', (event) => {
  event.notification.close();
  const target = new URL(event.notification.data.url, self.location.origin).href;
  event.waitUntil((async () => {
    // Focus an existing window if the app is already open, otherwise open one
    const windows = await self.clients.matchAll({ type: 'window', includeUncontrolled: true });
    const existing = windows.find((w) => w.url === target);
    if (existing) return existing.focus();
    return self.clients.openWindow(target);
  })());
});
```

**Rules and platform notes.**

- `userVisibleOnly: true` is required by Chrome and Safari: every push must show a notification. Silent background pushes are not allowed on the web.
- On iOS and iPadOS (16.4+), push works only for web apps added to the Home Screen, and permission must be requested from a user gesture inside the installed app. Safari 18.4 added **Declarative Web Push**, a JSON message format the system can display without running a service worker.
- Subscriptions expire or get revoked; delete them when the push service returns `404` or `410`.
- Respect users: send fewer, relevant notifications, let users choose topics, and make unsubscribing easy (`subscription.unsubscribe()`).

**Key Takeaways**

- Web Push combines the Push API (receive messages in the service worker) and the Notifications API (display them), delivered through the browser vendor's push service.
- The server identifies itself with VAPID keys; payloads are encrypted end to end with the subscription's keys.
- Flow: request permission after a user gesture -> `pushManager.subscribe` -> store the subscription on the server -> send with a library such as `web-push` -> `push` event -> `showNotification`.
- Every push must show a notification; handle `notificationclick` to open or focus the app.
- iOS supports Web Push only for Home Screen web apps (16.4+); remove subscriptions that return `404`/`410`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Generate VAPID keys, subscribe a page to push, and send a test message to it using the `web-push` command-line tool.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add push to the bookshelf API: a `POST /api/v1/push/subscriptions` route, a subscription collection, and a notification when a reserved book becomes available. Clicking the notification must open the reservation page or focus it if already open.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can't a website send silent push messages to sync data in the background?" *Hint:* consider battery, privacy and abuse, and what `userVisibleOnly` promises; then mention which API is designed for background data sync instead.

#### Installability and the App Shell Model

**Why installation matters.** An icon on the home screen or in the dock is a constant reminder, launches without browser chrome, and gets its own entry in the app switcher. Installed PWAs also get privileges in some browsers: persistent storage, badges, push on iOS. But users rarely discover installation on their own, so it pays to understand when the browser offers it and how to prompt for it.

**Install criteria (Chromium).** Chrome and Edge offer installation (an icon in the address bar on desktop, an install banner or menu item on Android) when:

- The site is served over HTTPS (or `localhost`).
- It has a manifest linked from the page with `name` or `short_name`, `icons` including 192 px and 512 px, `start_url`, and `display` set to `fullscreen`, `standalone`, `minimal-ui` or `window-controls-overlay`.
- `prefer_related_applications` is not `true` (that member tells the browser to promote a native app instead).
- The user has interacted with the page (some engagement heuristics apply).

A service worker with a `fetch` handler was historically required; Chrome dropped that requirement in 2023, but you still need one for offline support and push.

**Install flows by platform.**

| Platform | How users install |
|---|---|
| Android (Chrome, Edge, Samsung Internet) | Install banner or "Install app" in the menu; creates a WebAPK, a real Android package generated by the browser |
| Desktop Chrome / Edge | Install icon in the address bar or menu; the app gets its own window, start menu or dock entry |
| iOS / iPadOS Safari (and other iOS browsers, 16.4+) | Share button -> "Add to Home Screen"; no programmatic prompt |
| macOS Safari (Sonoma and later) | File -> "Add to Dock" |
| Firefox | Android: "Install"; desktop: limited support |

**A custom install button.** Chromium fires `beforeinstallprompt` when the app is installable. You can prevent the default mini-infobar, save the event, and show your own install button at a good moment (for example after the user added their third book):

```javascript
// main.js
let deferredPrompt = null;
const installButton = document.querySelector('#install');

window.addEventListener('beforeinstallprompt', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();                 // do not show the browser's default prompt now
  deferredPrompt = event;                 // keep it to call prompt() later
  installButton.hidden = false;
});

installButton.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  if (!deferredPrompt) return;
  deferredPrompt.prompt();                // must be called from a user gesture, once per event
  const { outcome } = await deferredPrompt.userChoice;   // 'accepted' or 'dismissed'
  console.log('Install outcome:', outcome);
  deferredPrompt = null;
  installButton.hidden = true;
});

window.addEventListener('appinstalled', () => {
  installButton.hidden = true;
  analytics.track('pwa_installed');
});

// iOS has no beforeinstallprompt: show instructions instead
const isIOS = /iPad|iPhone|iPod/.test(navigator.userAgent) ||
              (navigator.platform === 'MacIntel' && navigator.maxTouchPoints > 1); // iPadOS reports as Mac
const isStandalone = window.matchMedia('(display-mode: standalone)').matches || navigator.standalone;
if (isIOS && !isStandalone) showHint('Tap Share, then "Add to Home Screen" to install Bookshelf.');
```

**The app shell model.** Native apps feel fast because their UI frame (toolbar, navigation, empty layouts) is installed on the device; only data comes from the network. The **app shell** model copies this: separate the minimal HTML, CSS and JavaScript needed to draw the UI frame (the **shell**) from the **content** (data). The shell is precached by the service worker, so on repeat visits it appears instantly, even offline, and content is filled in as it arrives.

```text
 +--------------------------------------+
 | [=]  Bookshelf               [search]|  <- shell: header, navigation, layout
 +--------------------------------------+     precached at install, loaded from cache
 |  +-------+  ##################       |
 |  |       |  ########                |  <- content: book data from /api/v1/books
 |  +-------+                          |     (network first, cached copy offline);
 |  +-------+  ##################       |     skeleton placeholders while loading
 |  |       |  ########                |
 |  +-------+                          |
 +--------------------------------------+
 |  Library    Reading list    Profile  |  <- shell: tab bar
 +--------------------------------------+
```

Steps to apply it:

1. Identify the shell: index HTML, core CSS, the application JavaScript bundle, logo and icons.
2. Precache those files during `install` (with hashed filenames, so updates are safe).
3. In the `fetch` handler, answer navigation requests with the cached shell (`/index.html`) for single-page apps, then let client-side routing render the right view.
4. Fetch content with network first or stale-while-revalidate, and show skeleton screens while it loads.

```javascript
// sw.js: serve the cached shell for every in-app navigation (SPA)
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  if (event.request.mode === 'navigate') {
    event.respondWith(
      caches.match('/index.html').then((shell) => shell ?? fetch(event.request))
    );
  }
});
```

**App shell and server rendering.** The app shell model fits client-rendered single-page apps (Chapter 14). With server-side rendering, a common alternative is to cache full HTML responses with network first (or stream a cached header and footer around network content), so the first visit benefits from server rendering and repeat visits still work offline.

**Key Takeaways**

- Chromium offers installation for HTTPS sites with a valid manifest (name, 192/512 icons, `start_url`, app-like `display`); a service worker is no longer strictly required but is needed for offline and push.
- `beforeinstallprompt` (Chromium only) lets you defer the prompt and show your own install button; `appinstalled` confirms installation.
- iOS installation is manual through "Add to Home Screen"; show instructions instead of a button.
- The app shell model precaches the UI frame and loads content separately, giving instant repeat loads and offline startup.
- For SPAs, answer navigation requests with the cached shell; show skeletons while content loads.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Make the bookshelf client installable in Chrome. Use DevTools' Application > Manifest pane to fix any installability errors, install it, and open it as a standalone window.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a custom install button that appears only after the user has added at least three books, and an iOS-specific hint for Safari users. Track install outcomes in the console.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the app shell model and when is it not a good fit?" *Hint:* think about what is cached, what is fetched, the first-visit experience, and how it interacts with server-side rendering and SEO.

#### Auditing with Lighthouse

**Why audit.** A PWA can look fine on the developer's fast laptop and still load slowly on a mid-range phone, fail accessibility checks or have a broken manifest. **Lighthouse** is an open-source tool from Google that loads a page under controlled conditions (by default a simulated mid-range mobile device on a slow 4G network), runs a series of audits and produces a report with scores and concrete recommendations.

**What Lighthouse checks.**

| Category | Examples of audits |
|---|---|
| Performance | First Contentful Paint, Largest Contentful Paint, Total Blocking Time, Cumulative Layout Shift, Speed Index; insights such as render-blocking resources, unused JavaScript, image sizes |
| Accessibility | Color contrast, alt text, form labels, ARIA usage, tap target size |
| Best Practices | HTTPS, no console errors, no deprecated APIs, correct image aspect ratios |
| SEO | Title and meta description, crawlable links, valid `robots.txt`, viewport meta tag |

**The PWA category was removed.** Lighthouse used to have a "PWA" category with a badge for installability and offline support. It was removed in Lighthouse 12 (2024), because the criteria had diverged across browsers and the checks were not good predictors of PWA quality. Installability is now checked in Chrome DevTools: **Application > Manifest** lists installability errors, and **Application > Service workers** shows the worker's state. Offline behavior is tested by enabling "Offline" in the Network panel or the Service workers pane and reloading. Older tutorials still refer to the PWA category; do not expect it in current tools.

**Lab metrics and the performance score.** Lighthouse measures **lab data**, a single simulated run, unlike the **field data** (Core Web Vitals from real users) described in 15.1. Because no user interacts during a lab run, INP cannot be measured; **Total Blocking Time (TBT)**, the time the main thread was blocked by long tasks during loading, is used as a proxy. The performance score (0 to 100) is a weighted average:

| Metric | Weight |
|---|---|
| Total Blocking Time | 30% |
| Largest Contentful Paint | 25% |
| Cumulative Layout Shift | 25% |
| First Contentful Paint | 10% |
| Speed Index | 10% |

Scores vary between runs (network, CPU load, browser extensions). Run audits several times, in an incognito window or from the command line, and compare medians rather than single numbers.

**Ways to run Lighthouse.**

1. **Chrome DevTools > Lighthouse panel:** choose categories and mobile or desktop, then "Analyze page load". Also available as "Timespan" (audit an interaction) and "Snapshot" (audit the current state) modes.
2. **PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev): runs Lighthouse on Google's servers and also shows field data from the Chrome UX Report when the site has enough traffic.
3. **Command line:**

```bash
# Run against a local production build (not the dev server: dev builds are unminified)
npx lighthouse http://localhost:4173 --view                       # opens the HTML report
npx lighthouse http://localhost:4173 --only-categories=performance,accessibility \
  --output=json --output-path=./reports/home.json                 # machine-readable result
npx lighthouse http://localhost:4173 --preset=desktop             # desktop configuration
```

4. **Node API**, for scripted audits:

```javascript
// audit.mjs: audit a page and fail if performance drops below 90
import lighthouse from 'lighthouse';
import * as chromeLauncher from 'chrome-launcher';

const chrome = await chromeLauncher.launch({ chromeFlags: ['--headless=new'] });
const result = await lighthouse('http://localhost:4173', {
  port: chrome.port,                       // Lighthouse drives Chrome through the DevTools protocol
  onlyCategories: ['performance', 'accessibility'],
  output: 'json',
});
await chrome.kill();

const { performance, accessibility } = result.lhr.categories;
console.log(`Performance ${performance.score * 100}, accessibility ${accessibility.score * 100}`);
if (performance.score < 0.9) process.exit(1);
```

**Lighthouse CI.** To catch regressions before they reach users, run Lighthouse on every pull request with **Lighthouse CI** (`@lhci/cli`). It runs several times, asserts against thresholds and can upload reports. The configuration lives in `lighthouserc.json`:

```json
{
  "ci": {
    "collect": {
      "startServerCommand": "npm run preview",
      "url": ["http://localhost:4173/", "http://localhost:4173/books/1"],
      "numberOfRuns": 3
    },
    "assert": {
      "assertions": {
        "categories:performance": ["error", { "minScore": 0.9 }],
        "categories:accessibility": ["error", { "minScore": 0.95 }],
        "largest-contentful-paint": ["warn", { "maxNumericValue": 2500 }],
        "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 0.1 }]
      }
    },
    "upload": { "target": "temporary-public-storage" }
  }
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/lighthouse.yml (excerpt)
- run: npm ci && npm run build
- run: npx @lhci/cli autorun          # collect, assert, upload according to lighthouserc.json
```

**Reading the report.** Treat the score as a summary, not a goal. The useful part is the list of opportunities and diagnostics: each names specific files and estimated savings. Fix the largest items first (usually JavaScript size, image sizes and render-blocking resources), then re-run. Pass/fail audits for accessibility are a starting point; automated tools find only a part of accessibility problems, so manual testing with a screen reader and keyboard is still needed.

**Key Takeaways**

- Lighthouse audits performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO under simulated mobile conditions and suggests concrete fixes.
- The PWA category was removed in Lighthouse 12; check installability in DevTools' Application panel and test offline mode manually.
- Lighthouse produces lab data (TBT replaces INP); real-user field data comes from the Chrome UX Report and your own monitoring.
- Run it from DevTools, PageSpeed Insights, the CLI or the Node API; audit production builds and compare several runs.
- Lighthouse CI asserts score and metric thresholds on every pull request to prevent regressions.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run Lighthouse in DevTools on the production build of the bookshelf client in mobile mode. Write down the three largest opportunities and fix one of them; re-run and compare.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Set up Lighthouse CI in a GitHub Actions workflow with assertions for performance, accessibility and CLS. Introduce a deliberate regression (a 2 MB unoptimized image) and confirm the workflow fails.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your Lighthouse performance score is 98, but users complain the site feels slow on their phones. How can both be true?" *Hint:* compare lab and field data, simulated devices with real ones, page load with interactions after load, and the pages Lighthouse tested with the pages users visit.

<a id="153-jquery-mobile"></a>
### 15.3 jQuery Mobile

jQuery Mobile was the most popular framework for mobile websites in the early 2010s. It is deprecated today, but it still runs in many older applications and Cordova projects, and its ideas (declarative widgets in HTML, page transitions, touch-friendly components, themes) shaped the frameworks that followed. This subchapter teaches enough of it to read and maintain existing code, and explains how to migrate away.

#### Framework Overview and Page Model

**Why jQuery Mobile existed.** Around 2010, smartphones were spreading quickly, but mobile browsers differed greatly (iOS Safari, the Android stock browser, BlackBerry, Windows Phone, Symbian), CSS flexbox and grid were not usable, and touch events behaved differently everywhere. Building a site that felt like an app (toolbars, sliding page transitions, big touch-friendly lists) meant writing a lot of fragile code. **jQuery Mobile**, released by the jQuery project in 2010 (1.0 in November 2011), offered a solution for web developers who already knew jQuery (Chapter 8): write semantic HTML with a few `data-` attributes, and the framework turns it into a touch-optimized, themed, app-like interface that works across many devices.

**Core ideas.**

- **Progressive enhancement:** the markup is plain HTML that works without JavaScript; jQuery Mobile enhances it into widgets.
- **Declarative configuration:** behavior is set with `data-*` attributes (`data-role="page"`, `data-theme="b"`), not with JavaScript calls.
- **Single-page navigation with AJAX:** links load new pages with AJAX and animate them in, while keeping the browser's back button working through the URL hash and History API.
- **Built on jQuery:** it depends on jQuery (1.4.5, the last stable release, supports jQuery 1.8 to 1.11 and 2.1) and extends it with widgets built on the jQuery UI widget factory.

**Setup.**

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Bookshelf</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://code.jquery.com/mobile/1.4.5/jquery.mobile-1.4.5.min.css">
  <script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-1.11.3.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    // mobileinit fires before jQuery Mobile initializes: the place to change defaults.
    // It must be bound AFTER jQuery and BEFORE jquery.mobile.js is loaded.
    $(document).on('mobileinit', function () {
      $.mobile.defaultPageTransition = 'slide';
    });
  </script>
  <script src="https://code.jquery.com/mobile/1.4.5/jquery.mobile-1.4.5.min.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
  <!-- pages go here -->
</body>
</html>
```

**The page model.** jQuery Mobile structures the UI as **pages**. A page is an element with `data-role="page"`, usually containing a header toolbar, a content area and a footer toolbar. Only one page is visible at a time.

```html
<div data-role="page" id="library">
  <div data-role="header">
    <h1>Library</h1>
  </div>

  <div role="main" class="ui-content">        <!-- 1.4 style; older code uses data-role="content" -->
    <p>Welcome to your bookshelf.</p>
    <a href="#reading" class="ui-btn ui-corner-all">Reading list</a>
  </div>

  <div data-role="footer" data-position="fixed">  <!-- stays at the bottom while scrolling -->
    <h4>3 books</h4>
  </div>
</div>
```

```text
 +----------------------------+
 |        Library             |  data-role="header"  (toolbar, title centered)
 +----------------------------+
 |                            |
 |  Welcome to your bookshelf |  role="main" class="ui-content"
 |  [     Reading list     ]  |
 |                            |
 +----------------------------+
 |         3 books            |  data-role="footer" data-position="fixed"
 +----------------------------+
```

**Single-page and multi-page documents.** One HTML file can contain several pages (a **multi-page template**); links to `#id` show the page with that ID. Alternatively, each page lives in its own file, and jQuery Mobile loads it with AJAX, inserts its first `data-role="page"` element into the DOM and transitions to it. In that case only the content of the first page in the loaded file is used, and scripts in its `<head>` are **not** executed, a common source of bugs.

```html
<!-- One file, two pages -->
<div data-role="page" id="library">
  <div data-role="header"><h1>Library</h1></div>
  <div role="main" class="ui-content">
    <a href="#reading">Go to reading list</a>
  </div>
</div>

<div data-role="page" id="reading">
  <div data-role="header">
    <a href="#library" data-rel="back" class="ui-btn ui-icon-back ui-btn-icon-left">Back</a>
    <h1>Reading list</h1>
  </div>
  <div role="main" class="ui-content"><p>Dune, Neuromancer</p></div>
</div>
```

**Page events instead of `$(document).ready`.** Because pages are loaded and shown dynamically, `$(document).ready` runs only once for the first document. Code that sets up a page must listen to page events:

| Event | Fires on | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `mobileinit` | `document`, before initialization | Configure global defaults |
| `pagecreate` | The page, once, after enhancement | Bind handlers, initialize plugins for that page |
| `pagecontainerbeforeshow` | The page container, before each transition in | Refresh data shown on the page |
| `pagecontainershow` | The page container, after the transition | Start animations, set focus |
| `pagecontainerbeforehide` / `pagecontainerhide` | Before and after leaving a page | Stop timers, save state |

```javascript
// Run once when the #reading page is first enhanced
$(document).on('pagecreate', '#reading', function () {
  $(this).find('.refresh').on('click', loadReadingList);
});

// Run every time a page becomes visible (1.4 API: events on the page container)
$(document).on('pagecontainerbeforeshow', function (event, ui) {
  if (ui.toPage.attr('id') === 'reading') loadReadingList();
});
```

Older code uses `pageinit`, `pagebeforeshow` and `pageshow` bound to individual pages; these were deprecated in 1.4 in favor of the `pagecontainer` events.

**Key Takeaways**

- jQuery Mobile (2010) turned semantic HTML with `data-*` attributes into touch-friendly, themed mobile interfaces on top of jQuery.
- A page is an element with `data-role="page"` containing a header, a content area (`role="main" class="ui-content"`) and a footer.
- Pages can share one HTML file (multi-page template) or be loaded with AJAX from separate files; scripts in AJAX-loaded `<head>` elements do not run.
- Configure defaults in a `mobileinit` handler bound before loading the library.
- Use `pagecreate` and `pagecontainer*` events instead of `$(document).ready`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a multi-page jQuery Mobile document with a "Library" page and a "Book details" page, each with a header and footer, and links between them.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Move the details page into its own file loaded through AJAX, put a script in its `<head>`, and observe that it does not run. Fix the problem by moving the setup code into a `pagecreate` handler in the main file.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why doesn't `$(document).ready` work for page setup in jQuery Mobile?" *Hint:* think about how many times the document is loaded versus how many times pages are inserted and shown.

#### Data Attributes and Widget Markup

**Why data attributes.** jQuery Mobile's main promise was that web designers could build mobile UIs without writing JavaScript. HTML5's custom `data-*` attributes were the vehicle: they are valid HTML, ignored by browsers, and readable by scripts. During initialization, jQuery Mobile scans each page, finds elements with known roles and options, and **enhances** them: it adds classes, wraps elements in extra markup and attaches widget behavior.

**How enhancement works.**

```text
  Your markup                                 After enhancement (simplified)
  -----------                                 ------------------------------
  <ul data-role="listview"                    <ul class="ui-listview ui-listview-inset
      data-inset="true">                              ui-corner-all ui-shadow">
    <li><a href="#b1">Dune</a></li>             <li><a href="#b1" class="ui-btn ui-btn-icon-right
  </ul>                                                 ui-icon-carat-r">Dune</a></li>
                                              </ul>
```

The framework reads the role (which widget), then the options (`data-inset`, `data-theme`, `data-icon` and so on), and calls the corresponding widget plugin, for example `$('ul').listview({ inset: true })`.

**Common roles and attributes.**

| Attribute | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `data-role` | `page`, `header`, `footer`, `listview`, `navbar`, `panel`, `popup`, `collapsible`, `controlgroup`, `flipswitch`, `table` | Which widget to create |
| `data-theme` | `a`, `b` | Color swatch (15.3, Themes) |
| `data-position` | `fixed` | Fixed toolbars |
| `data-inset` | `true` | Rounded, inset list or collapsible |
| `data-filter` | `true` | Adds a search box that filters list items |
| `data-icon` / `data-iconpos` | `star`, `left` | Icons on widgets that still use attributes |
| `data-mini` | `true` | Compact form element |
| `data-rel` | `back`, `popup`, `external` | Link behavior |
| `data-transition` | `slide`, `pop`, `fade` | Page transition |
| `data-ajax` | `false` | Disable AJAX loading for a link or form |
| `data-enhance` / `data-role="none"` | `false`, `none` | Prevent enhancement of a container or element |

**Buttons in 1.4.** Version 1.4 moved some widgets from data attributes to plain CSS classes for performance: a button is now just an anchor or `<button>` with classes. You will see both styles in existing code:

```html
<!-- jQuery Mobile 1.4: CSS classes -->
<a href="#add" class="ui-btn ui-corner-all ui-shadow ui-icon-plus ui-btn-icon-left">Add book</a>
<a href="#add" class="ui-btn ui-btn-inline ui-mini">Small inline button</a>

<!-- Older (1.3 and earlier) style, deprecated in 1.4 -->
<a href="#add" data-role="button" data-icon="plus" data-iconpos="left">Add book</a>

<!-- Grouped buttons -->
<div data-role="controlgroup" data-type="horizontal">
  <a href="#" class="ui-btn ui-corner-all">All</a>
  <a href="#" class="ui-btn ui-corner-all ui-btn-active">Unread</a>
  <a href="#" class="ui-btn ui-corner-all">Read</a>
</div>
```

**Other widgets.**

```html
<!-- Navbar: up to 5 buttons spread evenly; often inside a header or footer -->
<div data-role="footer" data-position="fixed">
  <div data-role="navbar">
    <ul>
      <li><a href="#library" class="ui-btn-active ui-state-persist" data-icon="home">Library</a></li>
      <li><a href="#reading" data-icon="star">Reading</a></li>
      <li><a href="#profile" data-icon="user">Profile</a></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- Collapsible: an accordion section -->
<div data-role="collapsible" data-collapsed="true">
  <h3>Book details</h3>
  <p>Published 1965. 412 pages.</p>
</div>

<!-- Panel: a slide-out drawer, a child of the page -->
<div data-role="panel" id="menu" data-display="overlay">
  <ul data-role="listview"><li><a href="#settings">Settings</a></li></ul>
</div>
<a href="#menu" class="ui-btn ui-icon-bars ui-btn-icon-notext ui-corner-all">Menu</a>
```

**Enhancing dynamic content.** Markup inserted after initialization is not enhanced automatically. Either trigger creation for a container or refresh an existing widget:

```javascript
// New markup containing widgets: enhance everything inside the container
$('#results').html(html).enhanceWithin();     // 1.4; older code used .trigger('create')

// Existing widget whose items changed: refresh it
$('#bookList').append('<li><a href="#b9">Hyperion</a></li>').listview('refresh');

// Programmatic widget calls follow the jQuery UI widget pattern
$('#menu').panel('open');
$('#darkMode').flipswitch('option', 'disabled', true);
```

**Key Takeaways**

- jQuery Mobile reads `data-role` and other `data-*` attributes and enhances matching elements into widgets by adding classes, markup and behavior.
- Common roles include `page`, `header`, `footer`, `listview`, `navbar`, `panel`, `popup`, `collapsible` and `controlgroup`.
- In 1.4 buttons use CSS classes (`ui-btn`, `ui-icon-*`, `ui-btn-icon-left`); `data-role="button"` is deprecated.
- Dynamically inserted markup must be enhanced with `.enhanceWithin()`; changed widgets need their `refresh` method.
- Widgets also have a jQuery UI-style JavaScript API (`.panel('open')`, `.listview('refresh')`).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a fixed footer navbar with three tabs and a slide-out panel menu to the bookshelf jQuery Mobile app.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Load the book list from `GET /api/v1/books` with `$.getJSON`, build `<li>` elements, append them to a `data-role="listview"` and refresh it. Add a collapsible with details inside each item, and make sure it is enhanced.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What does 'enhancement' mean in jQuery Mobile, and what are its performance costs?" *Hint:* think about how much DOM is added and changed for each widget on a slow 2012 phone, and why 1.4 moved buttons to plain CSS classes.

#### Navigation, Transitions and Dialogs

**Why a navigation system.** In a traditional site, each link loads a new document and the screen goes white between pages, which feels nothing like a native app. jQuery Mobile's navigation system intercepts links and form submissions, fetches the target with AJAX, inserts the page into the DOM and animates the change, while updating the URL so the back button, bookmarks and reloads still work.

**How navigation works.**

```text
 user taps <a href="details.html">
        |
        v
 jQuery Mobile intercepts the click (same-origin link, AJAX enabled)
        |
        v
 $.ajax('details.html') -> extract first [data-role="page"] -> enhance -> insert into DOM
        |
        v
 transition: current page slides out, new page slides in
        |
        v
 URL updated with history.pushState (or #hash on old browsers)
 -> the Back button triggers the reverse transition
```

**Links and their options.**

| Markup | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `<a href="#reading">` | Show the internal page with ID `reading` |
| `<a href="details.html">` | Load via AJAX and transition |
| `<a href="details.html" data-transition="flip">` | Use a specific transition |
| `<a href="#" data-rel="back">` | Go back in history (like the Back button) |
| `<a href="other.html" data-ajax="false">` or `rel="external"` | Normal full page load (needed for other multi-page documents, other origins, or file downloads) |
| `<a href="#library" data-direction="reverse">` | Play the transition backwards |

**Transitions.** Available values for `data-transition` include `fade` (the default in 1.4), `slide`, `slideup`, `slidedown`, `slidefade`, `pop`, `flip`, `turn`, `flow` and `none`. They use CSS 3D transforms where supported; on devices without them, jQuery Mobile falls back to `fade` (configurable with `$.mobile.maxTransitionWidth` and `$.mobile.transitionFallbacks`).

**Programmatic navigation.** In 1.4 you change pages through the **pagecontainer** widget:

```javascript
// Go to an internal page with a slide transition
$(':mobile-pagecontainer').pagecontainer('change', '#reading', {
  transition: 'slide',
  reverse: false,
});

// Load an external page, passing data through the query string
$(':mobile-pagecontainer').pagecontainer('change', 'details.html?id=7', {
  transition: 'pop',
});

// Older equivalent, deprecated in 1.4:
// $.mobile.changePage('#reading', { transition: 'slide' });
```

Passing data between pages is a recurring problem. Options are the query string (read it in `pagecontainerbeforeshow` from `ui.toPage.data('url')`), a shared JavaScript variable or module, or `sessionStorage`.

**Dialogs and popups.** jQuery Mobile has two ways to show content above the current page:

1. A **dialog** is a full page styled as a modal window, reached by navigation. In 1.4 you mark the page with `data-dialog="true"` (older code: link with `data-rel="dialog"`). It gets a close button and takes part in history (Back closes it).
2. A **popup** is a small overlay inside the current page (`data-role="popup"`), opened by a link with `data-rel="popup"` or with `.popup('open')`. Use it for menus, tooltips, confirmations and images.

```html
<!-- Dialog: a separate page -->
<div data-role="page" id="confirmDelete" data-dialog="true" data-close-btn="right">
  <div data-role="header"><h1>Delete book?</h1></div>
  <div role="main" class="ui-content">
    <p>This cannot be undone.</p>
    <a href="#" id="doDelete" class="ui-btn ui-corner-all ui-btn-b">Delete</a>
    <a href="#" data-rel="back" class="ui-btn ui-corner-all">Cancel</a>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- Popup: inside the current page -->
<a href="#sortMenu" data-rel="popup" data-transition="pop" class="ui-btn ui-btn-inline">Sort</a>
<div data-role="popup" id="sortMenu" data-theme="a">
  <ul data-role="listview" data-inset="true" style="min-width: 200px">
    <li data-role="list-divider">Sort by</li>
    <li><a href="#" data-sort="title">Title</a></li>
    <li><a href="#" data-sort="author">Author</a></li>
  </ul>
</div>
```

```javascript
$(document).on('click', '#sortMenu a[data-sort]', function () {
  sortBooks($(this).data('sort'));
  $('#sortMenu').popup('close');
});
```

**Pitfalls.** Because AJAX-loaded pages stay in the DOM (cached) or are removed (by default, only the first page is kept), IDs can be duplicated if the same file is loaded twice; scope selectors to the active page (`$.mobile.activePage` or `$(':mobile-pagecontainer').pagecontainer('getActivePage')`). Pages that keep server state should set `data-dom-cache="false"` (the default) to get fresh markup.

**Key Takeaways**

- jQuery Mobile intercepts links, loads pages with AJAX, animates transitions and keeps history and URLs working.
- `data-transition`, `data-rel="back"`, `data-direction="reverse"` and `data-ajax="false"` control link behavior.
- Navigate in code with `pagecontainer('change', target, options)`; `$.mobile.changePage` is deprecated.
- Dialogs are pages shown modally (`data-dialog="true"`); popups are overlays within the current page (`data-role="popup"`).
- Scope selectors to the active page, because several pages can be in the DOM at once.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a "Delete book?" dialog and a "Sort by" popup to the bookshelf app, with transitions, and verify that the Back button closes the dialog.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement a list-to-details flow: tapping a book in the list navigates to a single `details` page with `pagecontainer('change')`, passing the book ID; the details page loads the book from the API in `pagecontainerbeforeshow`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does jQuery Mobile keep the back button working while loading pages with AJAX?" *Hint:* think about the History API, hash fragments as a fallback, and what happens when the user reloads on a deep URL.

#### Mobile Form Controls and List Views

**Why special controls.** Native form controls in 2011 mobile browsers were small, inconsistent and hard to tap. jQuery Mobile replaced their appearance with large, finger-friendly, themed versions while keeping the real `<input>` and `<select>` elements underneath. Forms therefore still submit normally and degrade to native controls without JavaScript. Lists were the other workhorse of mobile UI (contacts, settings, messages), and jQuery Mobile's list view became its most recognizable widget.

**Form controls.** Most controls are enhanced automatically from standard HTML:

```html
<form id="bookForm" action="/books" method="post" data-ajax="false">
  <!-- Text input with a clear button -->
  <label for="title">Title</label>
  <input type="text" name="title" id="title" data-clear-btn="true" required>

  <!-- Search input gets a search icon and clear button -->
  <label for="q">Search</label>
  <input type="search" name="q" id="q">

  <!-- Slider from a range input -->
  <label for="rating">Rating</label>
  <input type="range" name="rating" id="rating" min="0" max="5" step="1" value="3" data-highlight="true">

  <!-- Flip switch (1.4): an on/off toggle from a checkbox -->
  <label for="finished">Finished</label>
  <input type="checkbox" data-role="flipswitch" name="finished" id="finished"
         data-on-text="Yes" data-off-text="No">

  <!-- Radio buttons grouped as a segmented control -->
  <fieldset data-role="controlgroup" data-type="horizontal">
    <legend>Format</legend>
    <input type="radio" name="format" id="f-paper" value="paper" checked>
    <label for="f-paper">Paper</label>
    <input type="radio" name="format" id="f-ebook" value="ebook">
    <label for="f-ebook">E-book</label>
  </fieldset>

  <!-- Select: native picker by default; data-native-menu="false" uses a custom themed menu -->
  <label for="genre">Genre</label>
  <select name="genre" id="genre" data-native-menu="false">
    <option value="sf">Science fiction</option>
    <option value="fantasy">Fantasy</option>
    <option value="history">History</option>
  </select>

  <input type="submit" value="Save" data-theme="b">
</form>
```

**Labels and layout.** Every control needs a `<label>`; jQuery Mobile styles it and uses it as the tappable surface for checkboxes and radios. To place labels beside fields on wider screens, wrap each pair in `<div class="ui-field-contain">` (called `data-role="fieldcontain"` before 1.4). Add `data-mini="true"` for compact controls.

**Changing values in code.** Enhanced controls show a custom UI, so after changing the underlying value in JavaScript, call the widget's `refresh` method:

```javascript
$('#rating').val(5).slider('refresh');
$('#finished').prop('checked', true).flipswitch('refresh');
$('#genre').val('fantasy').selectmenu('refresh');
$('input[name=format][value=ebook]').prop('checked', true);
$('input[name=format]').checkboxradio('refresh');
```

**AJAX form submission.** By default, jQuery Mobile submits forms with AJAX and displays the response as a new page. For APIs that return JSON, disable that with `data-ajax="false"` and handle submission yourself:

```javascript
$(document).on('submit', '#bookForm', function (event) {
  event.preventDefault();
  $.mobile.loading('show', { text: 'Saving...', textVisible: true }); // built-in spinner
  $.ajax({
    url: '/api/v1/books',
    method: 'POST',
    contentType: 'application/json',
    data: JSON.stringify(Object.fromEntries(new FormData(this))),
  })
    .done(() => $(':mobile-pagecontainer').pagecontainer('change', '#library'))
    .fail((xhr) => alert(`Could not save: ${xhr.status}`))
    .always(() => $.mobile.loading('hide'));
});
```

**List views.** A `<ul>` or `<ol>` with `data-role="listview"` becomes a touch-friendly list. Its features are added through markup:

```html
<ul data-role="listview" data-filter="true" data-filter-placeholder="Search books..."
    data-inset="true" data-autodividers="true" id="bookList">
  <!-- data-autodividers: dividers generated from the first letter of each item -->

  <li>
    <a href="#book-1">
      <img src="covers/dune-80.jpg" alt="">               <!-- thumbnail on the left -->
      <h2>Dune</h2>
      <p>Frank Herbert</p>
      <span class="ui-li-count">412</span>                 <!-- count bubble on the right -->
    </a>
  </li>

  <li>
    <!-- Split button: the main link opens details, the second link is a separate action -->
    <a href="#book-2"><h2>Neuromancer</h2><p>William Gibson</p></a>
    <a href="#confirmDelete" data-rel="popup" data-icon="delete">Delete</a>
  </li>

  <li data-role="list-divider">Wishlist</li>              <!-- manual divider -->
  <li><a href="#book-3">Hyperion</a></li>
  <li data-filtertext="Le Guin earthsea fantasy">A Wizard of Earthsea</li> <!-- extra search terms -->
</ul>
```

```text
 +--------------------------------------+
 | [ Search books...                  ] |   data-filter="true"
 +--------------------------------------+
 | D                                    |   auto divider
 | [img] Dune                     (412) |   thumbnail, heading, count bubble
 |       Frank Herbert              >   |
 | N                                    |
 | Neuromancer                    | (x) |   split button
 | William Gibson                 |     |
 +--------------------------------------+
```

The search filter is the separate `filterable` widget in 1.4; `data-filter="true"` on a list view still creates it for compatibility.

**Responsive tables and grids.** For tabular data, `data-role="table"` with `data-mode="reflow"` stacks cells vertically on narrow screens, and `data-mode="columntoggle"` lets the user hide columns. Simple column layouts use the grid classes `ui-grid-a` (2 columns) to `ui-grid-d` (5 columns) with `ui-block-a`, `ui-block-b` and so on.

**Key Takeaways**

- jQuery Mobile restyles native form controls into large, themed widgets while keeping real form elements underneath.
- Special controls include sliders (`type="range"`), flip switches (`data-role="flipswitch"`), segmented control groups and custom select menus (`data-native-menu="false"`).
- After changing a control's value in code, call its widget `refresh` method.
- Use `data-ajax="false"` and custom handlers for JSON APIs; `$.mobile.loading` shows a spinner.
- List views support thumbnails, count bubbles, split buttons, dividers and built-in filtering; tables can reflow or toggle columns.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build an "Add book" form with a text input, genre select, rating slider and "finished" flip switch, laid out with `ui-field-contain`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Make the book list filterable, with thumbnails, auto-dividers and a split "Delete" button that opens a confirmation popup and removes the item through `DELETE /api/v1/books/:id`, refreshing the list afterwards.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does jQuery Mobile require calling `refresh` after changing a value programmatically?" *Hint:* consider the relationship between the hidden native element and the visible enhanced markup, and which events fire when code (rather than the user) changes a value.

#### Themes and ThemeRoller

**Why a theme system.** Mobile apps need a consistent look: toolbars, buttons, lists and forms that share colors, borders and shadows. In 2011, before CSS custom properties, changing the look of a widget library meant editing many CSS rules. jQuery Mobile separated **structure** CSS (layout and sizing) from **theme** CSS (colors, gradients, fonts) and organized colors into **swatches** that can be applied to any widget with one attribute.

**Swatches.** A swatch is a named color scheme identified by a letter. Version 1.4 ships with two:

| Swatch | Look | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
