| `a` | Light: light grey bars, white content, dark text | Default for pages and content |
| `b` | Dark: dark bars and backgrounds, light text | Toolbars, emphasis, dark sections |

Versions up to 1.3 shipped five swatches, `a` to `e`, with glossy gradients. Custom themes can define up to 26 swatches (`a` to `z`).

**Applying swatches.**

```html
<div data-role="page" data-theme="a">                   <!-- page and its content -->
  <div data-role="header" data-theme="b">               <!-- dark toolbar -->
    <h1>Bookshelf</h1>
  </div>
  <div role="main" class="ui-content">
    <a href="#" class="ui-btn ui-btn-b ui-corner-all">Primary action</a>   <!-- 1.4 class form -->
    <ul data-role="listview" data-theme="a" data-divider-theme="b" data-count-theme="b">
      <li data-role="list-divider">Reading</li>
      <li><a href="#">Dune <span class="ui-li-count">2</span></a></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
```

Swatches are inherited: a widget without `data-theme` takes the swatch of its container. In CSS, swatches appear as classes such as `.ui-page-theme-a`, `.ui-bar-b`, `.ui-body-a` and `.ui-btn-b`.

**ThemeRoller.** **ThemeRoller for jQuery Mobile** (themeroller.jquerymobile.com) is a web-based visual editor: you pick colors for bars, bodies and buttons of each swatch, drag colors from the palette (including Adobe Kuler palettes at the time), preview the result live, and download a CSS file. The download contains the theme CSS; you then load the **structure-only** CSS from jQuery Mobile and your theme after it:

```html
<!-- Custom theme: structure CSS + your generated theme, instead of the default combined file -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="themes/bookshelf.min.css">              <!-- from ThemeRoller -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="themes/jquery.mobile.icons.min.css">    <!-- icons (1.4) -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://code.jquery.com/mobile/1.4.5/jquery.mobile.structure-1.4.5.min.css">
```

**Overriding styles.** For small changes, override theme classes in your own stylesheet loaded after the framework's. Because the framework applies its classes during enhancement, target those classes rather than your original markup:

```css
/* Brand color for swatch b buttons and toolbars */
.ui-page-theme-a .ui-btn.ui-btn-b,
.ui-bar-b {
  background-color: #2e5d4b;
  border-color: #234a3c;
  color: #fff;
  text-shadow: none;
}

/* Allow long titles in headers instead of cutting them with "..." */
.ui-header .ui-title {
  white-space: normal;
  margin: 0 3em;
}
```

**Icons.** Version 1.4 uses SVG icons with PNG fallback, applied through classes such as `ui-icon-star`, `ui-icon-delete`, `ui-icon-carat-r` and position classes `ui-btn-icon-left`, `ui-btn-icon-notext`. Custom icons are defined with CSS by setting a background image on a new `ui-icon-*` class.

**Key Takeaways**

- jQuery Mobile separates structure CSS from theme CSS; colors are grouped into lettered swatches.
- Version 1.4 ships swatches `a` (light) and `b` (dark); earlier versions had `a` to `e`; custom themes can have up to 26.
- Apply swatches with `data-theme` or classes like `ui-btn-b`; widgets inherit their container's swatch.
- ThemeRoller generates a custom theme CSS file, used together with the structure-only CSS.
- Override styles by targeting the framework's enhanced classes in a stylesheet loaded afterwards.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Apply swatch `b` to the header and footer of the bookshelf app and swatch `a` to the content; add one dark primary button.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a custom theme with ThemeRoller (or by hand) with a third swatch `c` in the bookshelf brand color, load it with the structure-only CSS, and use it for list dividers and the primary button.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you implement theming for a component library today, compared with jQuery Mobile's swatch approach?" *Hint:* think about CSS custom properties, `prefers-color-scheme`, and switching themes at runtime without loading new stylesheets.

#### Touch Events and Responsive Behavior

**Why custom events.** In jQuery Mobile's era, touch support was inconsistent: some devices fired touch events, some only mouse events, Windows Phone used Microsoft's pointer events, and `click` was delayed by about 300 ms. jQuery Mobile normalized this with its own set of events, so the same code worked everywhere.

**Touch and gesture events.**

| Event | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `tap` | A quick touch and release (no 300 ms delay) |
| `taphold` | A touch held for about 750 ms (`$.event.special.tap.tapholdThreshold`) |
| `swipe` | A horizontal drag of at least about 30 px within one second, with limited vertical movement |
| `swipeleft` / `swiperight` | A swipe in that direction |
| `scrollstart` / `scrollstop` | Scrolling begins or ends |
| `orientationchange` | The device rotates; `event.orientation` is `portrait` or `landscape` |
| `throttledresize` | A throttled version of `resize` |
| `vclick`, `vmousedown`, `vmouseup`, `vmousemove`, `vmouseover`, `vmouseout`, `vmousecancel` | Virtual mouse events: unified mouse and touch events |

```javascript
// Swipe left on a book to reveal actions; long-press to open a context menu
$(document).on('swipeleft', '#bookList li', function () {
  $(this).addClass('show-actions');
});
$(document).on('swiperight', '#bookList li', function () {
  $(this).removeClass('show-actions');
});
$(document).on('taphold', '#bookList li', function (event) {
  event.preventDefault();
  $('#bookMenu').data('bookId', $(this).data('id')).popup('open', { positionTo: this });
});

// Swipe between pages, a common jQuery Mobile pattern
$(document).on('swipeleft', '.ui-page', function () {
  const next = $(this).jqmData('next');            // jqmData reads data-* with the jQM namespace
  if (next) $(':mobile-pagecontainer').pagecontainer('change', next, { transition: 'slide' });
});

// Tune thresholds globally (before use)
$.event.special.swipe.horizontalDistanceThreshold = 60;   // require a longer swipe
```

**Responsive behavior.** jQuery Mobile was designed mostly for phones, but 1.3 added tools for larger screens:

- **Responsive grids** (`ui-grid-a` and so on) with CSS you can make collapse into one column under a breakpoint.
- **Reflow and column-toggle tables** (previous topic).
- **Panels** with `data-display="reveal"`, `push` or `overlay`, plus CSS to keep a panel permanently open on wide screens.
- **Fixed toolbars** that stay put while content scrolls.
- **Orientation classes**: the `<html>` element receives `portrait` or `landscape` classes.

```css
/* Show the panel permanently on wide screens, as a sidebar */
@media (min-width: 55em) {
  #menu.ui-panel-closed { visibility: visible; transform: none; width: 17em; }
  .ui-panel-page-content-open, .ui-page .ui-content { margin-left: 17em; }
}
```

**Lessons for today.** Most of what these events solved is now built into the platform:

| jQuery Mobile | Modern platform equivalent |
|---|---|
| `tap`, `vclick` (no delay) | `click` with `width=device-width` viewport, `touch-action: manipulation` |
| `vmouse*` events | Pointer events (`pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`) |
| `swipe`, `taphold` | Pointer events with small gesture code, or libraries such as Hammer.js successors, `@use-gesture` |
| `orientationchange` | `screen.orientation.addEventListener('change', ...)` or `(orientation: landscape)` media query |
| `throttledresize` | `ResizeObserver` |
| `scrollstart`/`scrollstop` | `scroll` with passive listeners and `scrollend` |
| Responsive grids | CSS grid, flexbox and container queries |

**Key Takeaways**

- jQuery Mobile normalized touch input with events such as `tap`, `taphold`, `swipe`, `swipeleft`, `swiperight` and virtual mouse events (`vclick`, `vmousedown`).
- Thresholds for gestures can be tuned through `$.event.special` settings.
- Responsive features include grids, reflow tables, panels, fixed toolbars and orientation classes.
- Modern browsers make these events unnecessary: use pointer events, `touch-action`, `ResizeObserver`, `screen.orientation` and CSS layout.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add swipe-left and swipe-right handlers to move between the Library and Reading list pages with a slide transition.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Rewrite the `taphold` context menu and the swipe-to-reveal actions without jQuery Mobile, using pointer events and a timer, and compare the amount of code and the behavior on a touch device.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why did libraries like jQuery Mobile and FastClick introduce a `tap` event, and why is it no longer needed?" *Hint:* recall double-tap-to-zoom, the 300 ms delay, and what browsers changed for pages with a mobile viewport.

#### Legacy Status and Modern Alternatives

**Why this topic.** Choosing a framework includes asking whether it will be maintained. jQuery Mobile is a cautionary example: hugely popular for a few years, then overtaken by platform improvements and newer frameworks. Developers still meet it in old intranets, kiosk apps and Cordova projects, and they need to know the risks and the migration options.

**Timeline.**

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 2010 | Project announced; alpha releases |
| 2011 | 1.0 released (November) |
| 2013 | 1.3: responsive tables, panels |
| 2014 | 1.4.x: performance work, CSS-class buttons, flat design, SVG icons; 1.4.5 is the last stable release |
| 2017 | 1.5.0-alpha.1, the last release of any kind |
| 2021 | Officially deprecated by the jQuery team (October); repository archived |

**Why it declined.**

- **Performance:** heavy DOM enhancement and the AJAX page system were slow on the low-end devices it targeted.
- **"Looks like jQuery Mobile":** apps had a recognizable generic style rather than a native look.
- **Platform progress:** flexbox, grid, media queries, pointer events, the History API and the disappearance of the 300 ms delay removed most reasons to use it.
- **Architecture shift:** component frameworks (React, Angular, Vue) and mobile-specific UI kits (Ionic) offered better ways to structure large apps.
- **Dependency age:** it requires jQuery 1.x or 2.x; the supported versions of jQuery (3.x and 4.x) are not officially compatible, and old jQuery versions have known security vulnerabilities.

**Risks of keeping it.** No security patches, incompatibility with current jQuery, breaking changes in browsers that no one will fix, and fewer developers who know it. For an internal tool that works and is rarely changed, keeping it temporarily may be acceptable; for anything public or actively developed, plan a migration.

**Modern alternatives.**

| Need | Alternative |
|---|---|
| Mobile-friendly responsive website | Plain modern CSS (grid, flexbox, container queries), or a CSS framework such as Bootstrap or Tailwind CSS |
| App-like mobile UI with native look | Ionic Framework (15.5) with Angular, React, Vue or plain JavaScript |
| Lightweight mobile UI components | Framework7, Onsen UI, Konsta UI |
| Installable, offline-capable web app | PWA techniques (15.2) |
| Store app from web code | Capacitor (15.4) with any front-end framework |
| Page transitions | View Transitions API (`document.startViewTransition`), framework routers |

**Migrating.** A big-bang rewrite is risky. An incremental approach:

1. **Inventory** the pages, widgets, page events and `data-*` options in use.
2. **Separate logic from markup:** move business logic and API calls out of page event handlers into plain modules that do not depend on jQuery Mobile.
3. **Pick the target** (for example Ionic with Vue, or plain HTML with modern CSS and a router) and build a mapping: `listview` to `ion-list`, `navbar` to `ion-tab-bar`, `popup` to `ion-popover` or `<dialog>`.
4. **Migrate page by page**, if the app can be split by URL, with `data-ajax="false"` links between old and new pages.
5. **Remove** jQuery Mobile, then decide whether jQuery itself is still needed (Chapter 8, 8.3).

The native `<dialog>` element and the View Transitions API replace two of jQuery Mobile's signature features with a few lines:

```javascript
// Page-like transition between two views with the View Transitions API
function showView(id) {
  const update = () => {
    document.querySelectorAll('.view').forEach((v) => (v.hidden = v.id !== id));
  };
  if (!document.startViewTransition) return update();   // fallback: no animation
  document.startViewTransition(update);                 // browser animates old -> new snapshot
}
```

```html
<!-- Native modal dialog instead of a jQuery Mobile dialog page -->
<dialog id="confirmDelete">
  <form method="dialog">
    <p>Delete this book?</p>
    <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
    <button value="delete">Delete</button>
  </form>
</dialog>
<script>
  const dlg = document.querySelector('#confirmDelete');
  dlg.addEventListener('close', () => { if (dlg.returnValue === 'delete') deleteBook(); });
  // dlg.showModal() opens it with focus trapping and Escape-to-close built in
</script>
```

**Key Takeaways**

- jQuery Mobile's last stable release is 1.4.5 (2014); the project was officially deprecated in 2021.
- It declined because of performance problems, a generic look, platform improvements that made it unnecessary, and the rise of component frameworks.
- Keeping it means no security fixes and dependence on old jQuery versions; plan migrations for active or public apps.
- Alternatives include modern CSS, Ionic, Framework7, PWA techniques and Capacitor; `<dialog>` and View Transitions replace dialogs and page transitions.
- Migrate incrementally: inventory, separate logic, map widgets, migrate page by page, then remove the library.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* List five jQuery Mobile features used in this subchapter and name the modern platform feature or library that replaces each.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Migrate the jQuery Mobile bookshelf list page to plain HTML with modern CSS, a native `<dialog>` for deletion and the View Transitions API between list and details. Keep the same API calls.
> 3. *(Interview)* "You inherit a working jQuery Mobile app used by 200 employees. Would you rewrite it?" *Hint:* weigh security exposure (internal or public), change frequency, the cost and risk of a rewrite, and incremental options; there is no single right answer, but you must justify yours.

<a id="154-apache-cordova"></a>
### 15.4 Apache Cordova

Apache Cordova packages a web application as a native iOS or Android app and gives its JavaScript access to device features through plugins. It defined the hybrid app model that later tools followed. This subchapter covers its architecture, command-line workflow, configuration, plugin system, common device APIs, permissions, building and debugging, store deployment, and Capacitor, its modern successor.

#### Cordova Architecture and the WebView Bridge

**Why Cordova.** In 2008, building an iPhone app required Objective-C, and an Android app required Java; web developers could not use their skills for store apps. At an iPhoneDevCamp hackathon, developers from the Canadian company Nitobi created **PhoneGap**: a native app containing a full-screen WebView plus a JavaScript library that exposed phone features. Adobe acquired Nitobi in 2011 and donated the core code to the Apache Software Foundation, where it became **Apache Cordova** (PhoneGap became Adobe's distribution of Cordova, with a cloud build service). Adobe ended PhoneGap and PhoneGap Build in 2020; Cordova continues as an Apache project.

**The architecture.** A Cordova app has three layers:

```text
 +------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |                     Native app (APK/AAB or IPA)                  |
 |                                                                  |
 |  +---------------------------+     +--------------------------+  |
 |  |     WebView               |     |   Native plugins         |  |
 |  |  www/index.html           |     |   Camera (Java/Kotlin,   |  |
 |  |  www/js/app.js            |     |     Objective-C/Swift)   |  |
 |  |  cordova.js  <------------+-----+-> Geolocation            |  |
 |  |  plugin JS interfaces     |     |   File, Device, ...      |  |
 |  |  navigator.camera.        |     |                          |  |
 |  |     getPicture(...)       |     |                          |  |
 |  +---------------------------+     +--------------------------+  |
 |        ^          bridge (cordova.exec)          ^               |
 |        +------------------------------------------+               |
 |                                                                  |
 |  Native shell: Activity (Android) / ViewController (iOS),        |
 |  loads config.xml, starts the WebView, registers plugins         |
 +------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

1. **Web application** (`www/`): your HTML, CSS and JavaScript, any framework or none.
2. **WebView**: Android System WebView or iOS `WKWebView` (15.1), rendering the app. `cordova.js`, injected per platform, implements the bridge on the JavaScript side.
3. **Plugins**: each plugin has a JavaScript interface and native implementations for each platform. All device access goes through plugins, including core features like the camera.

**The bridge: `cordova.exec`.** Every plugin call ends in one function:

```javascript
cordova.exec(successCallback, errorCallback, 'ServiceName', 'action', [arg1, arg2]);
```

Cordova assigns a callback ID, serializes the call, and passes it to the native side (on Android through a `@JavascriptInterface` object, on iOS through a `WKScriptMessageHandler`). The native plugin performs the action, possibly on a background thread, and sends back a `PluginResult` with the callback ID. Cordova finds the stored callbacks and calls the right one. Plugins can also keep a callback alive to send several results (for example a stream of location updates).

**`deviceready`: the most important event.** The bridge and plugins load asynchronously after the page. Calling a plugin before they are ready fails. Cordova fires **`deviceready`** on `document` when everything is available; it is the entry point of every Cordova app.

```javascript
// www/js/index.js
document.addEventListener('deviceready', onDeviceReady, false);

function onDeviceReady() {
  // Safe to use plugins from here on
  console.log(`Running cordova-${cordova.platformId}@${cordova.version}`);
  console.log(`Device: ${device.manufacturer} ${device.model}, OS ${device.version}`); // cordova-plugin-device

  // App lifecycle events, available after deviceready
  document.addEventListener('pause', () => saveState(), false);     // app goes to background
  document.addEventListener('resume', () => refreshData(), false);  // app returns to foreground
  document.addEventListener('backbutton', onBackButton, false);     // Android hardware/gesture back
}

function onBackButton(event) {
  event.preventDefault();                     // registering a handler overrides the default (exit)
  if (history.length > 1) history.back();
  else navigator.app.exitApp();               // Android only
}
```

If `deviceready` has already fired when a listener is added, Cordova calls the listener immediately, so late registration is safe.

**What the WebView loads.** Assets are copied into the app package. Modern platform versions serve them from a local HTTPS-like origin instead of `file://`: `https://localhost` on Android (since cordova-android 10, through `WebViewAssetLoader`) and, when configured with the `scheme` and `hostname` preferences, a custom scheme such as `app://localhost` on iOS. This makes `fetch`, cookies and CORS behave like a normal website (15.1).

**Key Takeaways**

- Cordova (originally PhoneGap, 2008) wraps a web app in a native shell with a WebView and exposes device features through plugins.
- The layers are the web app (`www/`), the WebView with `cordova.js`, and plugins with JavaScript and native parts.
- Every plugin call goes through `cordova.exec(success, error, service, action, args)`, an asynchronous bridge with callback IDs.
- Wait for `deviceready` before using any plugin; handle `pause`, `resume` and `backbutton` for lifecycle and navigation.
- Modern Cordova serves assets from a local `https`-like origin rather than `file://`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Draw the path of a `navigator.camera.getPicture()` call from JavaScript to the native camera and back, labeling `cordova.js`, the bridge, the plugin and the callback.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a small `whenReady()` function that returns a Promise resolved on `deviceready` in Cordova and immediately in a normal browser, so the same app code can run in both.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why must a Cordova app wait for `deviceready`, and what happens if it uses a plugin earlier?" *Hint:* think about the order in which the WebView loads the page, `cordova.js`, plugin modules and the native plugin registry.

#### CLI, Project Structure and Platforms

**Why a CLI.** A Cordova app is really several projects in one: the shared web code, an Android Gradle project and an iOS Xcode project, plus plugins that must be installed into each. Keeping these consistent by hand would be painful. The **Cordova CLI** manages it: it creates projects, adds platforms, installs plugins and copies the web code into each native project before building.

**Prerequisites.** Node.js and npm, plus each platform's native toolchain:

| Platform | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Android | JDK (version required by cordova-android), Android Studio or the Android SDK command-line tools, Gradle, environment variables `ANDROID_HOME` and `JAVA_HOME` |
| iOS | A Mac with Xcode, Xcode command-line tools, CocoaPods (for some plugins), an Apple Developer account for device builds and distribution |

`cordova requirements` checks the toolchain for each added platform.

**Typical workflow.**

```bash
npm install -g cordova                          # install the CLI

cordova create bookshelf com.example.bookshelf Bookshelf
#              folder    reverse-domain app ID  display name
cd bookshelf

cordova platform add android                    # adds platforms/android (Gradle project)
cordova platform add ios                        # macOS only: adds platforms/ios (Xcode project)
cordova platform ls                             # installed and available platforms

cordova plugin add cordova-plugin-camera        # installs the plugin into every platform
cordova plugin ls

cordova requirements                            # check JDK, SDK, Gradle, Xcode
cordova prepare                                 # copy www/ and config into platforms/
cordova build android                           # prepare + compile (debug build by default)
cordova emulate android                         # build and launch in an emulator
cordova run android --device                    # build and install on a connected device
cordova run ios --target="iPhone-16"            # a specific simulator
```

The same commands work through `npx cordova` with a project-local CLI, which keeps CLI versions consistent across a team.

**Project structure.**

```text
bookshelf/
+-- config.xml           # app metadata and configuration (next topic)
+-- package.json         # npm dependencies, including platforms and plugins;
|                        # the "cordova" section records which ones are installed
+-- www/                 # YOUR web app: the only source code you edit for the UI
|   +-- index.html
|   +-- css/
|   +-- js/index.js
+-- res/                 # icons and splash screens (convention, referenced from config.xml)
+-- platforms/           # GENERATED native projects: android/, ios/
+-- plugins/             # GENERATED: downloaded plugin sources
+-- hooks/               # optional scripts run at CLI steps (legacy; prefer package.json hooks)
+-- node_modules/
```

**Generated vs source.** `platforms/` and `plugins/` are build artifacts, regenerated from `package.json` and `config.xml` with `cordova prepare` (which restores missing platforms and plugins). Do not commit them, and do not edit files inside them: `cordova prepare` overwrites `platforms/*/www` and many native files. Native changes belong in plugins, `config.xml` (`<edit-config>`, `<config-file>`, `<resource-file>`) or hooks.

```json
{
  "name": "com.example.bookshelf",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "devDependencies": {
    "cordova-android": "^14.0.0",
    "cordova-ios": "^7.1.0",
    "cordova-plugin-camera": "^8.0.0"
  },
  "cordova": {
    "platforms": ["android", "ios"],
    "plugins": {
      "cordova-plugin-camera": {}
    }
  }
}
```

(Version numbers above are illustrative; check each package's current release and its supported platform versions.)

**Using a modern front-end build.** Cordova only knows `www/`. To use a framework with a bundler (Vite with React or Vue), build into `www/` and run Cordova afterwards:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build:web": "vite build --outDir www --emptyOutDir",
    "android": "npm run build:web && cordova run android",
    "ios": "npm run build:web && cordova run ios"
  }
}
```

Use relative asset paths (`base: './'` in Vite) and include `cordova.js` with a `<script src="cordova.js">` tag in `index.html`: the file does not exist in `www/` but is added to each platform during `prepare`.

**Platforms and their versions.** Each platform is an npm package (`cordova-android`, `cordova-ios`, plus `cordova-electron` and `cordova-browser`) with its own release cycle. A platform version determines the minimum and target OS versions, the WebView behavior and plugin compatibility. App stores require recent target SDK levels (Google Play requires targeting an Android API level within about a year of the latest release), so platform upgrades are regular maintenance work: `cordova platform rm android && cordova platform add android@latest`.

**Key Takeaways**

- The Cordova CLI creates projects, adds platforms, installs plugins, prepares and builds; native toolchains (Android SDK, Xcode) are still required.
- `www/` holds your web app; `config.xml` and `package.json` describe the app, its platforms and plugins.
- `platforms/` and `plugins/` are generated and should not be edited or committed; `cordova prepare` restores them.
- With a bundler, build into `www/` before running Cordova, use relative paths and reference `cordova.js`.
- Platform packages determine OS targets and must be upgraded regularly to meet store requirements.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a Cordova project for the bookshelf client, add the Android platform, run `cordova requirements`, and launch the default app in an emulator.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Replace the default `www/` with a Vite build of the React bookshelf front end from Chapter 14. Add npm scripts that build and run on Android, and confirm that a fresh clone without `platforms/` and `plugins/` builds after `cordova prepare`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A teammate fixed a bug by editing a Java file under `platforms/android`. Why is that a problem and what should they do instead?" *Hint:* think about what `cordova prepare` and fresh clones do, and the proper places for native changes (plugins, `config.xml`, hooks).

#### Application Configuration

**Why `config.xml`.** One file describes the app independently of platforms: identity, version, start page, which URLs the app may load, platform-specific preferences, icons and splash screens. During `cordova prepare`, Cordova translates it into each platform's native configuration (`AndroidManifest.xml`, `res/xml/config.xml`, `Info.plist`, Xcode settings). Its format comes from the W3C Widgets specification, hence the root element `<widget>`.

**A complete example.**

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<widget id="com.example.bookshelf"
        version="1.2.0"
        android-versionCode="10200"
        ios-CFBundleVersion="1.2.0.1"
        xmlns="http://www.w3.org/ns/widgets"
        xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
  <!-- id: app identifier (Android package name / iOS bundle ID); never change after publishing
       version: user-visible version; versionCode/CFBundleVersion: build numbers the stores compare -->

  <name>Bookshelf</name>
  <description>Track the books you own and read.</description>
  <author email="dev@bookshelf.example" href="https://bookshelf.example">Bookshelf Team</author>

  <content src="index.html" />                                  <!-- start page inside www/ -->

  <!-- Network access control -->
  <access origin="https://api.bookshelf.example" />            <!-- network requests (XHR, fetch, images) -->
  <allow-navigation href="https://bookshelf.example/help/*" /> <!-- URLs the WebView itself may navigate to -->
  <allow-intent href="https://*/*" />                          <!-- URLs the OS may open in other apps -->
  <allow-intent href="mailto:*" />
  <allow-intent href="tel:*" />

  <!-- Global preferences -->
  <preference name="Orientation" value="portrait" />
  <preference name="BackgroundColor" value="0xff2e5d4b" />
  <preference name="DisallowOverscroll" value="true" />        <!-- no rubber-band bounce on iOS -->

  <platform name="android">
    <preference name="android-minSdkVersion" value="24" />
    <preference name="android-targetSdkVersion" value="35" />
    <preference name="AndroidWindowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon" value="res/android/splash-icon.png" />
    <preference name="AndroidWindowSplashScreenBackground" value="#2e5d4b" />
    <icon density="mdpi" src="res/android/icon-48.png" />
    <icon density="xxxhdpi" src="res/android/icon-192.png" />
    <!-- Adaptive icon: separate foreground and background layers -->
    <icon foreground="res/android/fg.png" background="res/android/bg.png" density="xxxhdpi" />

    <!-- Add an entry to AndroidManifest.xml -->
    <config-file target="AndroidManifest.xml" parent="/manifest">
      <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />
    </config-file>
  </platform>

  <platform name="ios">
    <preference name="deployment-target" value="14.0" />
    <preference name="scheme" value="app" />                  <!-- serve assets from app://localhost -->
    <preference name="hostname" value="localhost" />
    <icon src="res/ios/icon-1024.png" width="1024" height="1024" />

    <!-- Merge a usage description into Info.plist (required for camera access) -->
    <edit-config target="NSCameraUsageDescription" file="*-Info.plist" mode="merge">
      <string>Bookshelf uses the camera to scan book barcodes.</string>
    </edit-config>
  </platform>
</widget>
```

**Network access: three different lists.** This trips up many developers:

| Element | Controls | Example consequence if missing |
|---|---|---|
| `<access origin>` | Which servers the app may make network requests to | `fetch('https://api.bookshelf.example/...')` blocked (on Android; iOS relies more on CSP and ATS) |
| `<allow-navigation>` | Which URLs the WebView itself may load as the top-level page or iframes | Navigating to the help site does nothing |
| `<allow-intent>` | Which URLs the app may ask the OS to open (browser, mail, phone, maps) | `tel:` links do nothing |

Keep each list as narrow as possible: `<access origin="*">` and `<allow-navigation href="*">` let any injected script load arbitrary content into a WebView with plugin access.

**Content Security Policy.** The CSP in `index.html` complements `config.xml` and is the main defense against injected scripts:

```html
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
      content="default-src 'self';
               connect-src 'self' https://api.bookshelf.example;
               img-src 'self' data: https://covers.bookshelf.example;
               style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
               script-src 'self'">
```

**Preferences.** Preferences configure the shell. Common ones include `Orientation`, `Fullscreen`, `BackgroundColor`, `DisallowOverscroll`, `StatusBarOverlaysWebView` (status bar plugin), `AndroidPersistentFileLocation` and `iosPersistentFileLocation` (file plugin), and the Android splash screen preferences. The exact list depends on the platform and plugin versions; check their documentation.

**Icons and splash screens.** Each platform needs many icon sizes and densities. Declare them with `<icon>` and `<splash>` (iOS uses storyboard launch screens) elements, or generate them from one source image with tools such as `cordova-res`. Since cordova-android 11, Android uses the system SplashScreen API configured through preferences.

**Key Takeaways**

- `config.xml` describes the app (ID, version, name, start page, preferences, icons) and is translated into native configuration during `prepare`.
- The `id` is the store identity and must never change after publishing; increase `version` and the build numbers for every release.
- `<access>`, `<allow-navigation>` and `<allow-intent>` control network requests, WebView navigation and external apps respectively; keep them narrow.
- Platform-specific settings go inside `<platform>`; `<config-file>` and `<edit-config>` modify `AndroidManifest.xml` and `Info.plist` without editing generated files.
- A strict Content Security Policy in `index.html` complements the allow lists.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Configure the bookshelf app's `config.xml` with name, description, version, portrait orientation and an `<access>` entry for the API origin only. Verify that a `fetch` to another origin is blocked on Android.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `tel:` support link, an allowed help-site navigation, a camera usage description for iOS and a matching CSP. Explain for each entry which attack or failure it prevents.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between `<access>`, `<allow-navigation>` and `<allow-intent>`?" *Hint:* separate the three cases: data requested by scripts, pages loaded inside the WebView, and URLs handed to the operating system.

#### The Plugin System and Native APIs

**Why plugins.** The WebView only offers standard web APIs. Everything else, from the barcode scanner to in-app purchases, is provided by **plugins**. A plugin is a package with a JavaScript interface and native code for each platform, registered in the native shell so `cordova.exec` can find it. The core team maintains plugins for common features, and thousands of community plugins exist on npm (search for the `ecosystem:cordova` keyword).

**Core and popular plugins.**

| Plugin | Provides |
|---|---|
| `cordova-plugin-camera` | `navigator.camera.getPicture()`: take photos or choose from the library |
| `cordova-plugin-geolocation` | `navigator.geolocation` backed by native location services (mainly for permission handling) |
| `cordova-plugin-file` | Read and write files in app directories (`cordova.file.dataDirectory`, etc.) |
| `cordova-plugin-device` | `device.platform`, `device.model`, `device.version`, `device.uuid` |
| `cordova-plugin-network-information` | `navigator.connection.type` (`wifi`, `4g`, `none`...) |
| `cordova-plugin-inappbrowser` | `cordova.InAppBrowser.open(url, target)`: show external pages safely, outside the main WebView |
| `cordova-plugin-statusbar` | Status bar color and overlay |
| `cordova-plugin-dialogs`, `cordova-plugin-vibration`, `cordova-plugin-media`, `cordova-plugin-media-capture` | Native dialogs, vibration, audio playback and recording, audio/video capture |

Some former core plugins were deprecated because the web platform now covers them: `cordova-plugin-device-motion` and `cordova-plugin-device-orientation` (use `DeviceMotionEvent`), `cordova-plugin-battery-status`, `cordova-plugin-whitelist` (built into platforms since cordova-android 10), and `cordova-plugin-splashscreen` on Android (built into cordova-android 11).

**Anatomy of a plugin.** A minimal custom plugin that returns a greeting from native code:

```text
cordova-plugin-greeter/
+-- package.json
+-- plugin.xml                    # manifest: JS modules, native sources, config changes
+-- www/greeter.js                # JavaScript interface exposed to the app
+-- src/android/Greeter.java      # Android implementation
+-- src/ios/CDVGreeter.swift      # iOS implementation
```

```xml
<!-- plugin.xml -->
<plugin xmlns="http://apache.org/cordova/ns/plugins/1.0"
        xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        id="cordova-plugin-greeter" version="1.0.0">
  <name>Greeter</name>

  <!-- Load www/greeter.js and expose its exports as window.Greeter -->
  <js-module src="www/greeter.js" name="Greeter">
    <clobbers target="Greeter" />
  </js-module>

  <platform name="android">
    <!-- Register the service name "Greeter" -> Java class -->
    <config-file target="res/xml/config.xml" parent="/*">
      <feature name="Greeter">
        <param name="android-package" value="com.example.greeter.Greeter" />
      </feature>
    </config-file>
    <source-file src="src/android/Greeter.java" target-dir="src/com/example/greeter" />
  </platform>

  <platform name="ios">
    <config-file target="config.xml" parent="/*">
      <feature name="Greeter">
        <param name="ios-package" value="CDVGreeter" />
      </feature>
    </config-file>
    <source-file src="src/ios/CDVGreeter.swift" />
  </platform>
</plugin>
```

```javascript
// www/greeter.js: the JavaScript interface
const exec = require('cordova/exec');

exports.greet = function (name, success, error) {
  exec(success, error, 'Greeter', 'greet', [name]);   // service, action, arguments
};

// Optional Promise wrapper for modern code
exports.greetAsync = (name) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) => exports.greet(name, resolve, reject));
```

```java
// src/android/Greeter.java
package com.example.greeter;

import org.apache.cordova.CallbackContext;
import org.apache.cordova.CordovaPlugin;
import org.json.JSONArray;
import org.json.JSONException;

public class Greeter extends CordovaPlugin {
    @Override
    public boolean execute(String action, JSONArray args, CallbackContext callbackContext)
            throws JSONException {
        if ("greet".equals(action)) {
            String name = args.getString(0);
            if (name.isEmpty()) {
                callbackContext.error("Name must not be empty");
                return true;
            }
            // Long work must not block the WebView thread: use cordova.getThreadPool()
            cordova.getThreadPool().execute(() ->
                callbackContext.success("Hello, " + name + " from Android"));
            return true;               // action recognized
        }
        return false;                  // unknown action -> "invalid action" error in JS
    }
}
```

```swift
// src/ios/CDVGreeter.swift
@objc(CDVGreeter) class CDVGreeter: CDVPlugin {
    @objc(greet:)
    func greet(_ command: CDVInvokedUrlCommand) {
        let name = command.arguments.first as? String ?? ""
        let result: CDVPluginResult
        if name.isEmpty {
            result = CDVPluginResult(status: CDVCommandStatus_ERROR, messageAs: "Name must not be empty")
        } else {
            result = CDVPluginResult(status: CDVCommandStatus_OK, messageAs: "Hello, \(name) from iOS")
        }
        commandDelegate.send(result, callbackId: command.callbackId)  // route back to the JS callback
    }
}
```

```javascript
// In the app, after deviceready
const message = await Greeter.greetAsync('Ada');
console.log(message);   // "Hello, Ada from Android"
```

Swift plugin code also needs the Cordova headers through a bridging header; older projects used the `cordova-plugin-add-swift-support` plugin to set this up, and plugins written in Objective-C avoid the question entirely.

Install a local plugin with `cordova plugin add ../cordova-plugin-greeter`. For development of the plugin itself, `plugman` and `--link` help avoid reinstalling after each change.

**Choosing third-party plugins.** Check the last release date, open issues, support for the current `cordova-android` and `cordova-ios` versions, and whether it targets the API levels stores require. An unmaintained plugin can block a platform upgrade and thus a store release. Wrapping plugin calls in your own small service module makes replacing a plugin easier.

**Key Takeaways**

- Plugins provide all native functionality; each has a JavaScript interface, native code per platform and a `plugin.xml` manifest.
- `plugin.xml` declares JS modules (`<js-module>`, `<clobbers>`), native sources, service registrations (`<feature>`) and manifest changes.
- On Android, a plugin extends `CordovaPlugin` and implements `execute`; on iOS, it subclasses `CDVPlugin` and sends a `CDVPluginResult` with the callback ID.
- Several former core plugins are deprecated because web APIs or the platforms now cover them.
- Evaluate plugin maintenance carefully and wrap plugin calls behind your own interfaces.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Install `cordova-plugin-device` and `cordova-plugin-network-information`, and show the device model, OS version and connection type on the bookshelf app's About page.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write the Greeter plugin for Android, install it locally, and add a Promise wrapper. Add an action `getFreeDiskSpace` that returns the number of free bytes using `StatFs`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How does a Cordova plugin return results asynchronously, and how would it send multiple results over time?" *Hint:* look at callback IDs, `CallbackContext`/`commandDelegate`, and the `keepCallback` flag of `PluginResult`.

#### Camera, Storage, Geolocation and Sensors

**Why these four.** They are the device features most hybrid apps need: photos (profile pictures, document scans, book covers), local storage (offline data, settings, files), location (nearby places, check-ins) and motion (shake gestures, orientation). Each has both a web API and a Cordova plugin, and knowing which one to use on which platform is part of the job.

**Camera.**

```javascript
// cordova-plugin-camera: photograph a book cover
function takeCoverPhoto() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    navigator.camera.getPicture(resolve, reject, {
      quality: 70,                                         // JPEG quality 0-100
      destinationType: Camera.DestinationType.FILE_URI,    // a file path; DATA_URL returns base64 (memory heavy)
      sourceType: Camera.PictureSourceType.CAMERA,         // or PHOTOLIBRARY
      encodingType: Camera.EncodingType.JPEG,
      targetWidth: 800,                                    // scale down: full-size photos are huge
      targetHeight: 1200,
      correctOrientation: true,                            // rotate according to EXIF
      saveToPhotoAlbum: false,
    });
  });
}

async function onAddCover(bookId) {
  try {
    const fileUri = await takeCoverPhoto();
    // The page's origin is https://localhost or app://localhost, so a file:// URI usually
    // cannot be shown directly: read the file (a File is a Blob) and use an object URL
    const file = await fileUriToFile(fileUri);
    document.querySelector('#cover').src = URL.createObjectURL(file);
    await uploadCover(bookId, file);                       // e.g. FormData + fetch
  } catch (err) {
    if (err !== 'No Image Selected') showToast(`Camera error: ${err}`);  // user cancel is not an error
  }
}

// cordova-plugin-file: native path -> File object
function fileUriToFile(uri) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    window.resolveLocalFileSystemURL(uri, (entry) => entry.file(resolve, reject), reject);
  });
}
```

Avoid `DATA_URL` for large images: a base64 string of a 12-megapixel photo can crash the app. Use `FILE_URI`, scale the image with `targetWidth`/`targetHeight`, and read the file only when needed.

In many cases a plain `<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="environment">` is enough even inside Cordova and needs no plugin.

**Storage options.**

| Option | Kind | Size | Persistence | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `localStorage` | Synchronous key-value strings | ~5 MB | Can be cleared by the OS under storage pressure (especially iOS) | Small settings only |
| IndexedDB | Asynchronous structured data | Large (quota) | Same WebView storage caveats | Offline data in the WebView |
| `cordova-plugin-file` | Files in app directories | Device storage | Persistent app storage | Photos, downloads, exports |
| SQLite plugins (`cordova-sqlite-storage`) | SQL database in native storage | Large | Persistent | Large structured data, complex queries |
| Secure storage plugins (Keychain, Android Keystore) | Encrypted key-value | Small | Persistent | Tokens, credentials |

WebView storage lives in the app's private data and is generally kept, but iOS may purge WebView data in low-storage situations, so important data belongs in native storage (files, SQLite) or on the server. Never store tokens in `localStorage`; use secure storage.

```javascript
// cordova-plugin-file: save the reading list as a JSON file in the app's private data directory
function writeJson(fileName, data) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    window.resolveLocalFileSystemURL(cordova.file.dataDirectory, (dir) => {
      dir.getFile(fileName, { create: true }, (fileEntry) => {
        fileEntry.createWriter((writer) => {
          writer.onwriteend = resolve;
          writer.onerror = reject;
          writer.write(new Blob([JSON.stringify(data)], { type: 'application/json' }));
        }, reject);
      }, reject);
    }, reject);
  });
}

function readJson(fileName) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    window.resolveLocalFileSystemURL(cordova.file.dataDirectory + fileName, (fileEntry) => {
      fileEntry.file((file) => {
        const reader = new FileReader();
        reader.onloadend = () => resolve(JSON.parse(reader.result));
        reader.readAsText(file);
      }, reject);
    }, reject);
  });
}
```

The callback-heavy API shows the plugin's age; wrap it in Promises once and use `async`/`await` elsewhere.

**Geolocation.** `cordova-plugin-geolocation` implements the same W3C API you already know (6.4). On iOS it mostly adds the required usage description; on Android it handles the runtime permission.

```javascript
// Track position while the user is on the "nearby bookshops" screen
let watchId = null;

function startTracking() {
  watchId = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(
    ({ coords }) => updateMap(coords.latitude, coords.longitude, coords.accuracy),
    (err) => showToast(`Location error (${err.code}): ${err.message}`), // 1 denied, 2 unavailable, 3 timeout
    { enableHighAccuracy: false, maximumAge: 60_000, timeout: 15_000 }  // low accuracy saves battery
  );
}

function stopTracking() {
  if (watchId !== null) navigator.geolocation.clearWatch(watchId);
  watchId = null;
}

document.addEventListener('pause', stopTracking);   // stop GPS when the app goes to background
document.addEventListener('resume', startTracking);
```

Background location (tracking while the app is not visible) is not possible from the WebView alone; it needs specialized native plugins and extra store review.

**Sensors.** Device motion and orientation use the standard `DeviceMotionEvent` and `DeviceOrientationEvent` (15.1) inside the WebView, with the same iOS permission call. Specialized sensors (barcode scanning, NFC, Bluetooth LE, biometrics) need dedicated community plugins, for example a barcode scanner plugin based on Google ML Kit or Apple's Vision framework.

**Key Takeaways**

- Use `cordova-plugin-camera` with `FILE_URI` and scaled dimensions; avoid base64 `DATA_URL` for large photos; `<input capture>` may be enough.
- Choose storage by need: `localStorage` for small settings, IndexedDB for WebView data, files or SQLite for large or important data, secure storage for secrets.
- `cordova-plugin-file` reads and writes files in app directories such as `cordova.file.dataDirectory`; wrap its callbacks in Promises.
- Geolocation uses the W3C API; stop watching on `pause` to save battery.
- Motion sensors use web events; specialized hardware needs dedicated plugins.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a "Take cover photo" button to the bookshelf book details screen that uses the camera plugin and displays the photo.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Store the offline reading list both in IndexedDB and as a JSON backup file in `cordova.file.dataDirectory`. On startup, restore from the file if IndexedDB is empty.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Where would you store an authentication token in a hybrid app, and why not in `localStorage`?" *Hint:* consider XSS, OS-level encryption, what Keychain and Keystore provide, and how WebView storage can be purged.

#### Permissions and Platform Differences

**Why permissions are tricky in hybrid apps.** Native platforms protect sensitive features with permissions, and their rules differ: what must be declared in which file, when the user is asked, what happens after a denial, and how the store reviews your justification. A hybrid app must satisfy two systems at once (the OS and, for web APIs, the WebView) on two platforms.

**Android permissions.**

- **Declared** in `AndroidManifest.xml` (`<uses-permission>`). Plugins add their own entries through `plugin.xml`; you add others through `<config-file>` in `config.xml`.
- **Normal** permissions (internet, vibration) are granted at install.
- **Dangerous** permissions (camera, location, microphone, contacts) must also be **requested at runtime** since Android 6 (API 23). Plugins usually request them automatically when you call them.
- Newer Android versions split permissions further: precise vs approximate location, separate background location, photo picker instead of broad storage access, `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` for notifications (Android 13).

Plugins request permissions through Cordova's API, and `cordova-plugin-android-permissions` exposes it to JavaScript when you need explicit control:

```javascript
// Explicitly check and request the camera permission on Android before showing a scanner UI
function ensureCameraPermission() {
  const perms = cordova.plugins.permissions;
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    perms.checkPermission(perms.CAMERA, (status) => {
      if (status.hasPermission) return resolve(true);
      perms.requestPermission(perms.CAMERA, (s) => resolve(s.hasPermission), () => resolve(false));
    });
  });
}
```

**iOS permissions.**

- Every protected resource needs a **usage description string** in `Info.plist` (for example `NSCameraUsageDescription`, `NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription`, `NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription`, `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`). Without it, the app crashes when it accesses the resource, and App Store review rejects it.
- The system shows the prompt the first time the feature is used, with your description. After a denial, the app cannot ask again; the user must change it in Settings.

```xml
<!-- config.xml: iOS usage descriptions -->
<platform name="ios">
  <edit-config target="NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription" file="*-Info.plist" mode="merge">
    <string>Bookshelf shows bookshops near you.</string>
  </edit-config>
  <edit-config target="NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription" file="*-Info.plist" mode="merge">
    <string>Bookshelf lets you choose a photo as a book cover.</string>
  </edit-config>
</platform>
```

Many plugins accept these strings as install-time variables: `cordova plugin add cordova-plugin-geolocation --variable GEOLOCATION_USAGE_DESCRIPTION="..."`.

**Platform differences beyond permissions.**

| Area | Android | iOS |
|---|---|---|
| WebView engine | Chromium, auto-updated | WebKit, tied to iOS version |
| Back navigation | System back button/gesture fires `backbutton`; app must handle it | No system back button; the app must provide back UI |
| Status bar and notch | Status bar color via plugin; edge-to-edge since Android 15 targets | Safe areas; `viewport-fit=cover` and `env(safe-area-inset-*)` |
| Keyboard | Usually resizes the WebView | Overlays content; may scroll the page; plugins help control it |
| File system paths | `cordova.file.externalDataDirectory` etc. | Different directory set; sandboxed paths |
| Push notifications | Firebase Cloud Messaging | Apple Push Notification service (APNs) |
| Store review | Faster, mostly automated | Stricter human review; rejects apps that are "just a website" |
| UI conventions | Material Design | Human Interface Guidelines |

Detect the platform at runtime when behavior must differ:

```javascript
const platform = cordova.platformId;            // 'android' | 'ios' | 'browser' | 'electron'
document.documentElement.classList.add(`platform-${platform}`);   // style per platform in CSS

if (platform === 'ios') {
  document.querySelector('#backButton').hidden = false;   // iOS: show an in-app back button
}
```

**Good practice.** Request permissions just in time with an explanation; degrade gracefully when denied (for example manual entry instead of barcode scanning); test on both platforms and on old and new OS versions; and document why each permission is needed, because store reviewers ask.

**Key Takeaways**

- Android requires permissions in `AndroidManifest.xml` and runtime requests for dangerous permissions; newer versions split permissions further.
- iOS requires a usage description in `Info.plist` for every protected resource; missing ones cause crashes and rejection.
- Add manifest entries and descriptions through `plugin.xml`, `config.xml` (`<config-file>`, `<edit-config>`) or plugin variables, never by editing generated files.
- Platforms differ in WebView engine, back navigation, keyboard, safe areas, push services and store review.
- Use `cordova.platformId` for platform-specific behavior and request permissions in context with graceful fallbacks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add the iOS usage descriptions needed for the camera, photo library and location features of the bookshelf app, and the corresponding Android permissions if any plugin does not add them.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the Android back button for the bookshelf app: close open dialogs first, then navigate back in the router, and exit only from the home screen after a "press back again to exit" toast.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A hybrid app works on Android but crashes on iOS the moment the user taps 'Scan'. What is your first suspicion?" *Hint:* think about what iOS requires before an app may access the camera, and where that is configured in a Cordova project.

#### Building, Emulating and Debugging

**Why a special workflow.** A hybrid app runs inside a native process on an emulator or device, so the usual "save and refresh the browser" loop does not apply directly. You need to build, deploy, inspect the WebView, and read native logs when a plugin fails.

**Build types and targets.**

```bash
cordova build android                  # debug APK: platforms/android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/
cordova build android --release        # release build (needs signing, next topic)
cordova build ios --emulator           # build for the iOS Simulator
cordova build ios --device             # build for a physical iPhone (needs signing)

cordova emulate android                # start the default AVD (Android Virtual Device) and install
cordova run android --list             # list available devices and emulators
cordova run android --target=Pixel_8_API_35
cordova run android --device           # USB-connected phone with USB debugging enabled
```

Emulators are fast for UI work; real devices are essential for performance, camera, sensors, push notifications and battery behavior.

**A faster development loop.** Most UI work does not need native features. Develop in a desktop browser with a dev server (Vite's hot reload), and make the app tolerate missing plugins:

```javascript
// services/camera.js: one interface, different implementations
export async function pickCoverImage() {
  if (window.cordova && navigator.camera) {
    return takeCoverPhoto();                    // native plugin (previous topic)
  }
  // Browser fallback for development and web builds
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const input = Object.assign(document.createElement('input'), { type: 'file', accept: 'image/*' });
    input.onchange = () => resolve(URL.createObjectURL(input.files[0]));
    input.click();
  });
}
```

The `browser` platform (`cordova platform add browser`, `cordova run browser`) runs the app in a desktop browser with browser implementations of some plugins, which helps for quick checks.

**Debugging the WebView.**

| Platform | Tool | How |
|---|---|---|
| Android | Chrome DevTools | Open `chrome://inspect/#devices` in desktop Chrome with the device connected or the emulator running; click "inspect" under the app's WebView. Works for debug builds (WebView debugging is enabled automatically). |
| iOS | Safari Web Inspector | Enable Web Inspector on the device (Settings > Safari > Advanced), then in desktop Safari open the Develop menu > device > app page. Debug builds are inspectable; release builds need `isInspectable` (iOS 16.4+). |

You get the full DevTools experience: console, DOM, network requests, breakpoints, performance profiles.

**Native logs and debugging.** When a plugin crashes or fails silently, the error is in native logs:

```bash
adb devices                                 # list connected Android devices
adb logcat | grep -iE "chromium|cordova|bookshelf|AndroidRuntime"   # WebView console + crashes
adb logcat *:E                              # errors only
```

For deeper problems, open the native project (`platforms/android` in Android Studio, `platforms/ios/Bookshelf.xcworkspace` in Xcode) and use the native debugger with breakpoints in plugin code. On iOS, the Xcode console shows native logs and WebView console output.

**Common problems.**

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Plugin object is `undefined` | Called before `deviceready`, plugin not installed for this platform, or `cordova.js` not loaded |
| White screen on start | JavaScript error during startup (check the WebView console), wrong `<content src>`, absolute asset paths with a bundler |
| Network requests fail on device but work in browser | Missing `<access>` entry, CSP `connect-src`, HTTP instead of HTTPS (blocked by default by Android and iOS App Transport Security), CORS with the local origin |
| Build fails after an update | Plugin incompatible with the platform version, wrong JDK or Gradle version |
| Works on Android, broken on iOS | Missing usage description, WebKit feature differences, custom-scheme file URLs |

**CORS with a local origin.** The app's origin is `https://localhost` (Android) or `app://localhost` (iOS), so your API must allow those origins in its CORS configuration, as in Chapter 12:

```javascript
// Express API: allow the hybrid app's origins
app.use(cors({
  origin: ['https://bookshelf.example', 'https://localhost', 'app://localhost', 'capacitor://localhost'],
  credentials: true,
}));
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `cordova build`, `emulate` and `run` build and deploy to emulators and devices; test on real devices for hardware features and performance.
- Develop most UI in a desktop browser with fallbacks for missing plugins, and deploy to devices for native features.
- Debug the WebView with `chrome://inspect` (Android) and Safari Web Inspector (iOS).
- Native errors appear in `adb logcat` and the Xcode console; native debuggers work on the generated projects.
- Allow the app's local origins (`https://localhost`, `app://localhost`) in your API's CORS settings.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the bookshelf app on an Android emulator, open it in `chrome://inspect`, set a breakpoint in the book list loading code and inspect a network request.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a `services/` layer for camera, storage and device info with Cordova and browser implementations, so the whole app runs with `vite dev` in a browser and with `cordova run` on a device without code changes.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A hybrid app shows a white screen on a device but works in the desktop browser. How do you debug it?" *Hint:* list where you would look (remote WebView console, native logs), and the usual suspects (asset paths, CSP, `deviceready`, startup errors).

#### Packaging and Store Deployment

**Why this step needs care.** Publishing is where many hybrid projects stall: signing keys, store accounts, review guidelines and metadata. Mistakes can be costly; losing the Android signing key used to mean you could never update your app again (Play App Signing now protects against that).

**Android: signing and Android App Bundles.** Google Play requires apps to be uploaded as **Android App Bundles** (`.aab`) for new apps since August 2021; Play then generates optimized APKs for each device. Every upload must be signed with your **upload key**; with **Play App Signing**, Google holds the final app signing key and can reset a lost upload key.

```bash
# 1. Create an upload keystore once (keep it and its passwords safe, outside the repo)
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore bookshelf-upload.keystore -alias upload \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000

# 2. Build a signed release bundle
cordova build android --release -- \
  --keystore=../keys/bookshelf-upload.keystore --alias=upload \
  --storePassword="$KEYSTORE_PASSWORD" --password="$KEY_PASSWORD" \
  --packageType=bundle
# Output: platforms/android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab
```

The same options can live in a `build.json` file (`cordova build android --release --buildConfig=build.json`). Keep that file and the keystore out of version control and inject secrets in CI.

**iOS: certificates, provisioning and archives.** iOS distribution requires an **Apple Developer Program** membership. You need a distribution certificate, an App ID matching `config.xml`'s `id`, and a provisioning profile. Xcode's automatic signing manages most of this.

```json
{
  "ios": {
    "release": {
      "developmentTeam": "ABCDE12345",
      "codeSignIdentity": "Apple Distribution",
      "packageType": "app-store",
      "automaticProvisioning": true
    }
  }
}
```

```bash
cordova build ios --release --device --buildConfig=build.json
# Or: open platforms/ios/Bookshelf.xcworkspace in Xcode -> Product > Archive -> Distribute App
```

Upload the archive to **App Store Connect** (from Xcode's Organizer or Apple's Transporter app), test with **TestFlight**, then submit for review.

**Store listings.** Both stores need metadata: name, description, screenshots for several device sizes, an icon, a privacy policy URL, age rating, and data-collection disclosures (Google Play's Data safety section, Apple's privacy "nutrition labels"). Use semantic versioning for `version` and increase the build numbers (`android-versionCode`, `ios-CFBundleVersion`) for every upload; stores reject duplicates.

**Review pitfalls for hybrid apps.**

- **Minimum functionality (Apple guideline 4.2):** an app that just shows a website in a WebView is rejected. Provide offline content, native integrations and an app-like experience.
- **Code updates:** you may update web assets over the air (for example with Capacitor live update services) only if the update does not change the app's primary purpose; Apple's guideline 3.3.2 (formerly 2.5.2) restricts downloading executable code.
- **Payments:** digital goods sold in the app must use in-app purchase on both stores, with regional exceptions.
- **Permissions:** every permission must be justified and used.
- **Target API level:** Google Play requires a recent `targetSdkVersion` for new apps and updates.

**Automating releases.** Repeated manual builds are error-prone. **fastlane** automates screenshots, signing, building and uploading to both stores; CI services (GitHub Actions with macOS runners, Bitrise, Codemagic) run it on every tag.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/android-release.yml (excerpt)
- run: npm ci && npm run build:web
- run: echo "$UPLOAD_KEYSTORE_B64" | base64 -d > upload.keystore
- run: >
    npx cordova build android --release -- --keystore=upload.keystore --alias=upload
    --storePassword="$KEYSTORE_PASSWORD" --password="$KEY_PASSWORD" --packageType=bundle
- uses: r0adkll/upload-google-play@v1          # or fastlane supply
  with:
    serviceAccountJsonPlainText: ${{ secrets.PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT }}
    packageName: com.example.bookshelf
    releaseFiles: platforms/android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab
    track: internal
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Google Play requires signed Android App Bundles; use Play App Signing and keep the upload keystore safe and out of the repository.
- iOS needs an Apple Developer membership, certificates and provisioning profiles; archive with Xcode or `cordova build ios --release`, then distribute through App Store Connect and TestFlight.
- Increase build numbers for every upload and prepare store metadata, privacy disclosures and screenshots.
- Hybrid apps must offer real app value (not a wrapped website), follow code-update and payment rules, and justify permissions.
- Automate builds and uploads with fastlane and CI, storing signing secrets in the CI's secret store.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Generate an upload keystore and build a signed release `.aab` of the bookshelf app. Inspect it with `bundletool` or Android Studio's APK Analyzer.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `build.json` and a CI workflow that builds signed Android bundles on every Git tag, reading the keystore and passwords from secrets. Upload to an internal testing track.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What can get a hybrid app rejected from the App Store that would not affect a native app?" *Hint:* think about minimum functionality, downloading code after review, and how much the app does beyond the website.

#### Capacitor as a Successor

**Why Capacitor.** By the late 2010s, Cordova showed its age: callback-based APIs, generated native projects that could not be edited safely, slow plugin maintenance and complicated configuration hooks. The Ionic team, the largest Cordova user, built **Capacitor** (1.0 in 2019) as a "spiritual successor": the same idea (web app + WebView + native plugins) with a modern developer experience. Capacitor is now the default runtime for Ionic apps (15.5) but works with any web framework.

**Key differences from Cordova.**

| Aspect | Cordova | Capacitor |
|---|---|---|
| Native projects | Generated in `platforms/`, overwritten by `prepare`, not committed | `android/` and `ios/` are **source artifacts**: committed, edited freely in Android Studio and Xcode |
| Configuration | `config.xml` | `capacitor.config.ts` (or `.json`) for Capacitor; native settings edited directly in native files |
| JavaScript API | Global objects, callbacks, `deviceready` | ES module imports, Promises, available immediately (no `deviceready`) |
| Plugins | `plugin.xml`, `cordova.exec` | npm packages with native code; Cordova plugins mostly still work |
| Web build | Expects `www/` | Any `webDir` (`dist`, `build`) from any bundler |
| Web support | Separate `browser` platform | Plugins ship web implementations, so the same code runs as a PWA |
| iOS dependencies | CocoaPods | Swift Package Manager (supported since Capacitor 6) or CocoaPods |
| Asset origin | `https://localhost` (Android), configurable (iOS) | `https://localhost` (Android), `capacitor://localhost` (iOS) |

**Workflow.**

```bash
npm install @capacitor/core
npm install -D @capacitor/cli
npx cap init Bookshelf com.example.bookshelf --web-dir=dist   # creates capacitor.config.ts

npm install @capacitor/android @capacitor/ios
npx cap add android                # creates android/ (commit it)
npx cap add ios                    # creates ios/ (commit it)

npm run build                      # build the web app into dist/
npx cap sync                       # copy dist/ into native projects + update native plugins
npx cap run android                # build and run on a device or emulator
npx cap open ios                   # open the Xcode project for native work, signing, archiving
```

Run `npx cap sync` after every web build or plugin install; `npx cap copy` copies only web assets (faster when plugins have not changed).

```typescript
// capacitor.config.ts
import type { CapacitorConfig } from '@capacitor/cli';

const config: CapacitorConfig = {
  appId: 'com.example.bookshelf',
  appName: 'Bookshelf',
  webDir: 'dist',
  server: {
    androidScheme: 'https',               // default in recent versions
    // url: 'http://192.168.1.20:5173',   // live reload during development (do not ship)
    // cleartext: true,
  },
  plugins: {
    SplashScreen: { launchShowDuration: 1000, backgroundColor: '#2e5d4b' },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Plugins with Promises.** Official plugins live under the `@capacitor/` scope: camera, geolocation, filesystem, preferences, push-notifications, local-notifications, share, haptics, network, app, status-bar, splash-screen, keyboard, device, and more. Community plugins are collected by the **Capacitor Community** organization and by Capawesome.

```typescript
// Camera, preferences and geolocation in Capacitor: modern, typed, Promise-based
import { Camera, CameraResultType, CameraSource } from '@capacitor/camera';
import { Preferences } from '@capacitor/preferences';
import { Geolocation } from '@capacitor/geolocation';
import { Capacitor } from '@capacitor/core';

export async function takeCoverPhoto(): Promise<string | undefined> {
  const photo = await Camera.getPhoto({
    quality: 70,
    width: 800,
    resultType: CameraResultType.Uri,     // a file URI; webPath is directly usable in <img>
    source: CameraSource.Prompt,          // ask: camera or photo library
  });
  return photo.webPath;                    // works on Android, iOS and the web implementation
}

export async function saveLastSearch(query: string) {
  await Preferences.set({ key: 'lastSearch', value: query });   // native key-value storage
}

export async function currentPosition() {
  const perm = await Geolocation.checkPermissions();
  if (perm.location !== 'granted') {
    const req = await Geolocation.requestPermissions();
    if (req.location !== 'granted') throw new Error('Location permission denied');
  }
  const { coords } = await Geolocation.getCurrentPosition({ enableHighAccuracy: false });
  return coords;
}

console.log(Capacitor.getPlatform());       // 'ios' | 'android' | 'web'
console.log(Capacitor.isNativePlatform());  // false in the browser
```

**Writing a Capacitor plugin.** The structure mirrors Cordova but with less ceremony. The JavaScript side registers a plugin by name with TypeScript types:

```typescript
// src/plugins/greeter.ts
import { registerPlugin } from '@capacitor/core';

export interface GreeterPlugin {
  greet(options: { name: string }): Promise<{ message: string }>;
}

export const Greeter = registerPlugin<GreeterPlugin>('Greeter', {
  web: () => ({ greet: async ({ name }) => ({ message: `Hello, ${name} from the web` }) }),
});
```

```java
// android/app/src/main/java/com/example/bookshelf/GreeterPlugin.java
@CapacitorPlugin(name = "Greeter")
public class GreeterPlugin extends Plugin {
    @PluginMethod
    public void greet(PluginCall call) {
        String name = call.getString("name", "");
        if (name.isEmpty()) { call.reject("Name must not be empty"); return; }
        JSObject ret = new JSObject();
        ret.put("message", "Hello, " + name + " from Android");
        call.resolve(ret);                         // resolves the JavaScript Promise
    }
}
// Register in MainActivity.onCreate: registerPlugin(GreeterPlugin.class) before super.onCreate
```

```swift
// ios/App/App/GreeterPlugin.swift
import Capacitor

@objc(GreeterPlugin)
public class GreeterPlugin: CAPPlugin, CAPBridgedPlugin {
    public let identifier = "GreeterPlugin"
    public let jsName = "Greeter"
    public let pluginMethods: [CAPPluginMethod] = [
        CAPPluginMethod(name: "greet", returnType: CAPPluginReturnPromise)
    ]

    @objc func greet(_ call: CAPPluginCall) {
        let name = call.getString("name") ?? ""
        guard !name.isEmpty else { call.reject("Name must not be empty"); return }
        call.resolve(["message": "Hello, \(name) from iOS"])
    }
}
```

**Migrating from Cordova.** Capacitor supports most Cordova plugins directly (`npm install cordova-plugin-x && npx cap sync`), which makes incremental migration possible:

1. Add Capacitor to the existing project (`npx cap init` with `webDir` set to `www`), add platforms.
2. Move icons, splash screens, permissions and preferences from `config.xml` into the native projects and `capacitor.config.ts`.
3. Keep Cordova plugins that work; replace those with official Capacitor equivalents over time.
4. Remove `deviceready` waits where code only uses Capacitor plugins (Cordova plugins in Capacitor still fire `deviceready`).
5. Delete `config.xml`, `platforms/`, `plugins/` and the Cordova CLI when nothing depends on them.

**Key Takeaways**

- Capacitor, created by the Ionic team in 2019, follows Cordova's hybrid model with modern tooling and is the default for Ionic apps.
- Native projects (`android/`, `ios/`) are committed source code you edit in Android Studio and Xcode; configuration lives in `capacitor.config.ts`.
- Plugins are npm packages with typed, Promise-based APIs and web implementations; no `deviceready` is needed.
- Core commands: `npx cap add`, `npx cap sync` (after each build or plugin change), `npx cap run`, `npx cap open`.
- Most Cordova plugins work in Capacitor, enabling incremental migration.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add Capacitor to the Vite bookshelf front end, add the Android platform, and run it on an emulator. Use `@capacitor/preferences` to remember the last search.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Migrate the Cordova bookshelf app to Capacitor: keep one Cordova plugin, replace camera and geolocation with `@capacitor/camera` and `@capacitor/geolocation`, move permissions into the native projects, and remove `config.xml`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does Capacitor commit native projects to source control while Cordova regenerates them?" *Hint:* weigh the cost of editing native code through configuration and hooks against the cost of merging native project changes during upgrades.

<a id="155-ionic-framework"></a>
### 15.5 Ionic Framework

Capacitor and Cordova put a web app on a phone, but they say nothing about how it looks: a plain web UI inside a store app feels out of place next to native apps. Ionic is a UI toolkit of mobile components that look and behave like native iOS and Android controls, built as Web Components and usable with Angular, React, Vue or plain JavaScript. This subchapter covers its architecture, components, framework integrations, navigation, native plugins, theming and the build-and-release workflow.

#### Ionic Architecture and Web Components

**Why Ionic.** Building a polished mobile UI from scratch means implementing toolbars that follow each platform's conventions, swipeable list items, pull-to-refresh, modals that slide up as sheets, page transitions that match iOS or Android, safe-area handling, and accessibility for all of them. **Ionic Framework** provides these as ready-made components. Combined with Capacitor (15.4), one codebase can ship to the App Store, Google Play and the web as a PWA.

**History in brief.**

| Version | Year | Architecture |
|---|---|---|
| Ionic 1 | 2013-2015 | AngularJS directives, Cordova |
| Ionic 2 and 3 | 2016-2017 | Angular (2+) components |
| Ionic 4 | 2019 | Rebuilt as **Web Components** with Stencil; framework-agnostic; React and Vue support followed |
| Ionic 5 to 8 | 2020-2024 | Refinements: new design updates, Capacitor as default runtime, standalone Angular components, improved theming (dark and high-contrast palettes) |

The company behind Ionic was acquired by OutSystems in 2022; the framework remains open source under the MIT license.

**Web Components as the foundation.** Web Components are browser standards for creating custom HTML elements: **Custom Elements** (define a new tag such as `<ion-button>` with its own behavior), **Shadow DOM** (encapsulated markup and styles), and **HTML templates and slots** (where child content goes). Because they are native to the browser, they work in any framework or none. Ionic writes its components once in **Stencil**, a compiler that outputs standard Web Components, and generates thin framework wrappers.

```text
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |                 Your app (Angular / React / Vue / plain JS)       |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
 | @ionic/angular | @ionic/react | @ionic/vue |  (no wrapper needed) |  framework bindings:
 | (directives,   | (React       | (Vue       |                      |  forms, routing,
 |  NavController)|  components, |  components|                      |  lifecycle hooks
 |                |  router)     |  router)   |                      |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |      @ionic/core: ~100 Web Components (<ion-button>, <ion-list>,  |
 |      <ion-modal>...), built with Stencil, Shadow DOM, CSS vars    |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |         Browser / WebView (Capacitor, Cordova) / PWA              |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |      Capacitor plugins (camera, push, filesystem...)  optional    |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Using Ionic without a framework.** Because the components are standard custom elements, one script tag is enough to try them:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">
  <script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@ionic/core/dist/ionic/ionic.esm.js"></script>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@ionic/core/css/ionic.bundle.css">
</head>
<body>
  <ion-app>
    <ion-header>
      <ion-toolbar color="primary">
        <ion-title>Bookshelf</ion-title>
      </ion-toolbar>
    </ion-header>
    <ion-content class="ion-padding">
      <ion-list id="books"></ion-list>
      <ion-button expand="block" id="add">Add book</ion-button>
    </ion-content>
  </ion-app>

  <script type="module">
    const list = document.querySelector('#books');
    const books = await (await fetch('/api/v1/books')).json();
    list.innerHTML = books.data
      .map((b) => `<ion-item><ion-label><h2>${b.title}</h2><p>${b.author}</p></ion-label></ion-item>`)
      .join('');   // real code must escape titles to avoid XSS (Chapter 17)

    document.querySelector('#add').addEventListener('click', async () => {
      const alert = document.createElement('ion-alert');      // overlays are elements too
      alert.header = 'Add book';
      alert.inputs = [{ name: 'title', placeholder: 'Title' }];
      alert.buttons = ['Cancel', { text: 'Add', handler: (data) => console.log(data.title) }];
      document.body.appendChild(alert);
      await alert.present();
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

**Properties, attributes and events.** Ionic components are configured through attributes (strings) or JavaScript properties (any type, such as the `inputs` array above), and emit custom events prefixed with `ion`, such as `ionChange`, `ionInput`, `ionFocus` and `ionRefresh`. Framework wrappers map these to the framework's idioms (`(ionChange)` in Angular, `onIonChange` in React, `@ionChange` in Vue).

**Shadow DOM implications.** Most Ionic components render their internals in a shadow root. Your global CSS cannot reach inside, which protects the components from accidental breakage, but it means you customize them through **CSS custom properties** and **shadow parts** instead of descendant selectors (15.5, Theming).

**Key Takeaways**
