- Ionic Framework is a library of mobile UI components that mimic native iOS and Android controls, usually deployed with Capacitor.
- Since Ionic 4, components are standard Web Components built with Stencil (`@ionic/core`), with thin wrappers for Angular, React and Vue.
- Components work with no framework at all through a script tag; they use attributes, properties and `ion`-prefixed events.
- Shadow DOM encapsulates component internals; customization uses CSS custom properties and shadow parts.
- Ionic is open source (MIT); Capacitor provides native access.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a plain HTML page using Ionic from a CDN with a toolbar, a list of three books and a button that opens an `ion-toast`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a tiny custom element `<book-badge status="read">` with Shadow DOM and a CSS custom property for its color. Compare how you style it from outside with how you style `ion-badge`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why did Ionic move from Angular components to Web Components in version 4?" *Hint:* think about framework lock-in, the size of the potential user base, maintenance of one component set versus several, and browser standards.

#### UI Components and Platform-Adaptive Styling

**Why platform-adaptive styling.** iOS and Android users have different expectations: on iOS, titles are centered, back buttons show a chevron with text, and modals slide up as cards; on Android (Material Design), titles are left-aligned, buttons have ripple effects, and toolbars have different heights and shadows. An app that looks like iOS on Android (or the reverse) feels foreign. Ionic solves this with **modes**: every component has an `ios` and an `md` (Material Design) style, and Ionic picks the right one for the platform automatically.

**Modes.**

| Platform | Default mode |
|---|---|
| iPhone, iPad | `ios` |
| Android | `md` |
| Desktop and other browsers | `md` |

```text
 ios mode                                  md mode
 +--------------------------------+        +--------------------------------+
 | < Library     Dune         Edit|        | <-  Dune                    :  |
 +--------------------------------+        +================================+  (shadow)
 | Frank Herbert                  |        | Frank Herbert                  |
 | -----------------------------  |        |                                |
 | Status                Read  >  |        | Status                   Read  |
 +--------------------------------+        +--------------------------------+
  centered title, text back button,         left-aligned title, arrow icon,
  thin separators, chevrons                 shadow, ripple on tap
```

You can force a mode for the whole app (useful for a consistent brand look or for testing) or for single components:

```html
<ion-button mode="ios">Always iOS style</ion-button>
```

```typescript
// React: global configuration before rendering
import { setupIonicReact } from '@ionic/react';
setupIonicReact({ mode: 'md' });          // the whole app uses Material Design styles

// Detect the platform in code
import { isPlatform } from '@ionic/react'; // also available in @ionic/core, Angular's Platform service
if (isPlatform('ios')) { /* ... */ }
if (isPlatform('capacitor')) { /* running in a native Capacitor app */ }
if (isPlatform('mobileweb')) { /* mobile browser, not native */ }
```

During development, append `?ionic:mode=ios` to the URL to preview the other mode in a desktop browser.

**Component overview.** Ionic has around 100 components. The most used:

| Group | Components |
|---|---|
| App structure | `ion-app`, `ion-header`, `ion-toolbar`, `ion-title`, `ion-buttons`, `ion-back-button`, `ion-content`, `ion-footer`, `ion-split-pane`, `ion-menu` |
| Navigation | `ion-router-outlet`, `ion-tabs`, `ion-tab-bar`, `ion-tab-button`, `ion-nav`, `ion-breadcrumbs` |
| Lists | `ion-list`, `ion-item`, `ion-label`, `ion-note`, `ion-item-sliding`, `ion-item-options`, `ion-reorder-group`, `ion-avatar`, `ion-thumbnail` |
| Forms | `ion-input`, `ion-textarea`, `ion-select`, `ion-checkbox`, `ion-toggle`, `ion-radio-group`, `ion-range`, `ion-datetime`, `ion-searchbar`, `ion-segment` |
| Buttons and indicators | `ion-button`, `ion-fab`, `ion-icon`, `ion-badge`, `ion-chip`, `ion-spinner`, `ion-progress-bar`, `ion-skeleton-text` |
| Overlays | `ion-modal` (including sheet modals), `ion-popover`, `ion-alert`, `ion-action-sheet`, `ion-toast`, `ion-loading` |
| Scrolling | `ion-refresher` (pull to refresh), `ion-infinite-scroll` |
| Layout | `ion-grid`, `ion-row`, `ion-col`, `ion-card` |

**A typical screen.**

```html
<ion-header>
  <ion-toolbar>
    <ion-buttons slot="start">
      <ion-menu-button></ion-menu-button>              <!-- opens the side menu -->
    </ion-buttons>
    <ion-title>Library</ion-title>
  </ion-toolbar>
  <ion-toolbar>
    <ion-searchbar debounce="300" placeholder="Search books"></ion-searchbar>
  </ion-toolbar>
</ion-header>

<ion-content>
  <!-- Pull to refresh: emits ionRefresh; call event.detail.complete() when done -->
  <ion-refresher slot="fixed">
    <ion-refresher-content></ion-refresher-content>
  </ion-refresher>

  <ion-list>
    <ion-item-sliding>                                 <!-- swipe left to reveal options -->
      <ion-item button detail="true">                  <!-- button: tappable; detail: chevron (ios) -->
        <ion-thumbnail slot="start"><img src="/covers/dune.jpg" alt=""></ion-thumbnail>
        <ion-label>
          <h2>Dune</h2>
          <p>Frank Herbert</p>
        </ion-label>
        <ion-badge slot="end" color="success">Read</ion-badge>
      </ion-item>
      <ion-item-options side="end">
        <ion-item-option color="danger" expandable>Delete</ion-item-option>
      </ion-item-options>
    </ion-item-sliding>
  </ion-list>

  <ion-infinite-scroll threshold="100px">             <!-- emits ionInfinite near the bottom -->
    <ion-infinite-scroll-content loading-text="Loading more books..."></ion-infinite-scroll-content>
  </ion-infinite-scroll>

  <ion-fab slot="fixed" vertical="bottom" horizontal="end">
    <ion-fab-button aria-label="Add book"><ion-icon name="add"></ion-icon></ion-fab-button>
  </ion-fab>
</ion-content>
```

**Slots.** Many components position children through **slots**: `slot="start"` and `slot="end"` place content at the leading and trailing edge (and flip automatically for right-to-left languages), `slot="fixed"` keeps elements outside the scrolling area of `ion-content`.

**Icons.** Ionic uses **Ionicons**, an open-source icon set with iOS and Material variants (`name="add"`, `name="trash-outline"`, `name="book-sharp"`). In bundled apps, icons are imported individually so unused ones are not shipped (next topic).

**Overlays in code.** Overlays can be declared inline (for example `<ion-modal trigger="open-filters">`) or created with controllers or hooks:

```typescript
// React: action sheet and toast with hooks
import { useIonActionSheet, useIonToast } from '@ionic/react';

function BookActions({ book, onDelete }: { book: Book; onDelete: (id: number) => void }) {
  const [presentSheet] = useIonActionSheet();
  const [presentToast] = useIonToast();

  const openActions = () =>
    presentSheet({
      header: book.title,
      buttons: [
        { text: 'Delete', role: 'destructive', handler: () => {
            onDelete(book.id);
            presentToast({ message: 'Book deleted', duration: 2000, position: 'bottom' });
        } },
        { text: 'Cancel', role: 'cancel' },
      ],
    });

  return <IonButton fill="clear" onClick={openActions}>More</IonButton>;
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Ionic components have two modes, `ios` and `md`, chosen automatically by platform; force them globally or per component with `mode`.
- Use `isPlatform()` (or Angular's `Platform`) to detect `ios`, `android`, `capacitor`, `mobileweb` and more.
- Core building blocks: `ion-header`/`ion-toolbar`/`ion-content` for screens, `ion-list`/`ion-item` for lists, overlays such as `ion-modal`, `ion-alert`, `ion-toast` and `ion-action-sheet`.
- Slots (`start`, `end`, `fixed`) position content and adapt to right-to-left layouts.
- Built-in mobile patterns include sliding items, pull to refresh, infinite scroll and floating action buttons.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build the bookshelf "Library" screen with a toolbar, searchbar, list of books with thumbnails and badges, and a floating "Add" button. Preview it in both modes using `?ionic:mode=ios`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add pull to refresh that reloads `GET /api/v1/books`, infinite scroll that loads the next page with `?page=` and `limit=`, and sliding items with a "Delete" option that asks for confirmation with `ion-alert`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Should an app use platform-specific styling or one consistent brand style on both platforms?" *Hint:* consider user expectations, brand identity, design and QA effort, and which components (navigation, dialogs) matter most for platform conventions.

#### Ionic with Angular, React and Vue

**Why framework integrations.** Web Components alone do not fit perfectly into frameworks: React historically passed only string attributes to custom elements, frameworks need two-way binding with form controls, routers must cooperate with Ionic's animated page stack, and pages need lifecycle hooks that fire when they are shown or hidden from the stack. The `@ionic/angular`, `@ionic/react` and `@ionic/vue` packages provide this glue.

**Creating a project.** The Ionic CLI scaffolds apps with Capacitor already configured:

```bash
npm install -g @ionic/cli
ionic start bookshelf tabs --type=react --capacitor     # starters: blank, tabs, sidemenu, list
ionic start bookshelf tabs --type=vue
ionic start bookshelf tabs --type=angular-standalone    # Angular with standalone components
cd bookshelf
ionic serve                                             # dev server with live reload in the browser
```

**The same page in three frameworks.** A book list with a search filter shows the differences.

*React* (`@ionic/react`): Ionic components are React components prefixed with `Ion`, and events use `onIon...` props. Every routed page must be wrapped in `IonPage` so the router can animate it.

```tsx
// src/pages/Library.tsx
import { IonPage, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent, IonSearchbar,
         IonList, IonItem, IonLabel, useIonViewWillEnter } from '@ionic/react';
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Library() {
  const [books, setBooks] = useState<Book[]>([]);
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');

  // Ionic lifecycle: runs every time the page is about to be shown (also when navigating back)
  useIonViewWillEnter(() => {
    fetch('/api/v1/books').then((r) => r.json()).then((res) => setBooks(res.data));
  });

  const visible = books.filter((b) => b.title.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()));

  return (
    <IonPage>
      <IonHeader>
        <IonToolbar><IonTitle>Library</IonTitle></IonToolbar>
      </IonHeader>
      <IonContent>
        <IonSearchbar value={query} debounce={250}
                      onIonInput={(e) => setQuery(e.detail.value ?? '')} />
        <IonList>
          {visible.map((b) => (
            <IonItem key={b.id} routerLink={`/books/${b.id}`} detail>
              <IonLabel><h2>{b.title}</h2><p>{b.author}</p></IonLabel>
            </IonItem>
          ))}
        </IonList>
      </IonContent>
    </IonPage>
  );
}
```

*Vue* (`@ionic/vue`): components are imported from `@ionic/vue` and used in templates; `v-model` works on Ionic inputs.

```vue
<!-- src/views/LibraryPage.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { IonPage, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent, IonSearchbar,
         IonList, IonItem, IonLabel, onIonViewWillEnter } from '@ionic/vue';
import { ref, computed } from 'vue';

const books = ref<Book[]>([]);
const query = ref('');

onIonViewWillEnter(async () => {
  books.value = (await (await fetch('/api/v1/books')).json()).data;
});

const visible = computed(() =>
  books.value.filter((b) => b.title.toLowerCase().includes(query.value.toLowerCase()))
);
</script>

<template>
  <ion-page>
    <ion-header>
      <ion-toolbar><ion-title>Library</ion-title></ion-toolbar>
    </ion-header>
    <ion-content>
      <ion-searchbar v-model="query" :debounce="250" />
      <ion-list>
        <ion-item v-for="b in visible" :key="b.id" :router-link="`/books/${b.id}`" detail>
          <ion-label><h2>{{ b.title }}</h2><p>{{ b.author }}</p></ion-label>
        </ion-item>
      </ion-list>
    </ion-content>
  </ion-page>
</template>
```

*Angular* (`@ionic/angular/standalone`): components are standalone Angular components; `ngModel` and reactive forms work through value accessors; Ionic's lifecycle methods are class methods.

```typescript
// src/app/library/library.page.ts
import { Component, computed, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { HttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
import { FormsModule } from '@angular/forms';
import { RouterLink } from '@angular/router';
import { IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent, IonSearchbar,
         IonList, IonItem, IonLabel } from '@ionic/angular/standalone';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-library',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [FormsModule, RouterLink, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent,
            IonSearchbar, IonList, IonItem, IonLabel],
  template: `
    <ion-header><ion-toolbar><ion-title>Library</ion-title></ion-toolbar></ion-header>
    <ion-content>
      <ion-searchbar [ngModel]="query()" (ngModelChange)="query.set($event)" [debounce]="250" />
      <ion-list>
        @for (b of visible(); track b.id) {
          <ion-item [routerLink]="['/books', b.id]" detail>
            <ion-label><h2>{{ b.title }}</h2><p>{{ b.author }}</p></ion-label>
          </ion-item>
        }
      </ion-list>
    </ion-content>
  `,
})
export class LibraryPage {
  private http = inject(HttpClient);
  books = signal<Book[]>([]);
  query = signal('');
  visible = computed(() =>
    this.books().filter((b) => b.title.toLowerCase().includes(this.query().toLowerCase())));

  ionViewWillEnter() {                         // Ionic lifecycle hook, called on every show
    this.http.get<{ data: Book[] }>('/api/v1/books').subscribe((res) => this.books.set(res.data));
  }
}
```

**Bootstrapping.** Each integration needs a setup step and the Ionic CSS:

| Framework | Setup |
|---|---|
| React | `setupIonicReact()` before rendering; import `@ionic/react/css/core.css` and optional utility CSS |
| Vue | `createApp(App).use(IonicVue).use(router)`; import `@ionic/vue/css/core.css` |
| Angular (standalone) | `provideIonicAngular({})` in `bootstrapApplication` providers; global styles include `@ionic/angular/css/core.css` |

**Icons in bundled apps.** To keep bundles small, icons are imported explicitly. In React and Vue pass the imported icon data: `<IonIcon icon={add} />` with `import { add } from 'ionicons/icons'`. In Angular standalone, register them once with `addIcons({ add, trashOutline })` from `ionicons`, then use `<ion-icon name="add">`.

**Page lifecycle hooks.** Ionic keeps previous pages in the DOM (hidden) in the navigation stack, so a framework's mount and unmount hooks do not run when the user navigates back. Ionic adds four hooks that do:

| Hook (Angular / React / Vue) | Fires |
|---|---|
| `ionViewWillEnter` / `useIonViewWillEnter` / `onIonViewWillEnter` | Before the page animates in (every time) |
| `ionViewDidEnter` / `useIonViewDidEnter` / `onIonViewDidEnter` | After the transition finishes |
| `ionViewWillLeave` / `useIonViewWillLeave` / `onIonViewWillLeave` | Before the page animates out |
| `ionViewDidLeave` / `useIonViewDidLeave` / `onIonViewDidLeave` | After it is hidden |

Use them to refresh data when returning to a page and to pause expensive work on hidden pages.

**Key Takeaways**

- `@ionic/angular`, `@ionic/react` and `@ionic/vue` wrap the Web Components with framework-native bindings, form integration, routing and lifecycle hooks.
- `ionic start <name> <template> --type=<framework> --capacitor` scaffolds a project; `ionic serve` runs it in the browser.
- React uses `Ion*` components with `onIon*` events and requires `IonPage` for routed pages; Vue supports `v-model`; Angular supports `ngModel` and reactive forms with standalone imports.
- Import icons explicitly to keep bundles small.
- Pages stay in the DOM when navigating; use Ionic's `ionViewWillEnter`-style hooks instead of mount hooks for "on every show" logic.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Scaffold an Ionic app with the tabs template in the framework you know best, and replace the first tab with the bookshelf Library page.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build the "Add book" form (title, author, genre select, rating range, "read" toggle) with validation using your framework's form tooling (React Hook Form, Vue `v-model` with a validation library, or Angular reactive forms) and Ionic inputs that show error text.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does Ionic provide its own page lifecycle hooks instead of relying on React's `useEffect` or Angular's `ngOnInit`?" *Hint:* think about what happens to the previous page's component when a new page is pushed onto the stack and when the user navigates back.

#### Navigation and Routing in Ionic

**Why mobile navigation is different.** Web routing replaces one view with another. Mobile apps instead maintain **stacks**: tapping a book pushes a details page on top of the list, which slides in from the right; going back pops it, revealing the list exactly as it was, scroll position included. Tab-based apps keep a separate stack per tab, so switching tabs and back returns to where you were in that tab. Ionic's router outlet combines URL-based routing (so deep links, the browser back button and PWAs work) with this stack behavior and native-style transitions.

```text
 Tab "Library" stack                Tab "Reading" stack
 +-------------------+              +-------------------+
 | /library/books/7  |  <- top      | /reading          |
 +-------------------+              +-------------------+
 | /library          |
 +-------------------+
 Switching to "Reading" and back keeps /library/books/7 on screen;
 the back button pops to /library with its scroll position preserved.
```

**`ion-router-outlet`.** Each framework's router renders pages into `ion-router-outlet` (instead of the plain framework outlet). It keeps previous pages in the DOM, applies push and pop animations, and supports the iOS swipe-back gesture.

**React with `@ionic/react-router`.** Ionic React's router integration has historically been built on React Router v5; check which React Router version your Ionic release supports.

```tsx
// src/App.tsx
import { IonApp, IonRouterOutlet, IonTabs, IonTabBar, IonTabButton, IonIcon, IonLabel,
         setupIonicReact } from '@ionic/react';
import { IonReactRouter } from '@ionic/react-router';
import { Route, Redirect } from 'react-router-dom';
import { library, bookmark, person } from 'ionicons/icons';

setupIonicReact();

export default function App() {
  return (
    <IonApp>
      <IonReactRouter>
        <IonTabs>
          <IonRouterOutlet>
            <Route exact path="/library" component={Library} />
            <Route exact path="/library/books/:id" component={BookDetails} />  {/* nested in Library tab */}
            <Route exact path="/reading" component={ReadingList} />
            <Route exact path="/profile" component={Profile} />
            <Route exact path="/"><Redirect to="/library" /></Route>
          </IonRouterOutlet>

          <IonTabBar slot="bottom">
            <IonTabButton tab="library" href="/library">
              <IonIcon icon={library} /><IonLabel>Library</IonLabel>
            </IonTabButton>
            <IonTabButton tab="reading" href="/reading">
              <IonIcon icon={bookmark} /><IonLabel>Reading</IonLabel>
            </IonTabButton>
            <IonTabButton tab="profile" href="/profile">
              <IonIcon icon={person} /><IonLabel>Profile</IonLabel>
            </IonTabButton>
          </IonTabBar>
        </IonTabs>
      </IonReactRouter>
    </IonApp>
  );
}
```

```tsx
// src/pages/BookDetails.tsx: back button and programmatic navigation
import { IonPage, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonButtons, IonBackButton, IonTitle, IonContent,
         IonButton, useIonRouter } from '@ionic/react';
import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom';

export default function BookDetails() {
  const { id } = useParams<{ id: string }>();
  const router = useIonRouter();

  async function remove() {
    await fetch(`/api/v1/books/${id}`, { method: 'DELETE' });
    router.goBack();                              // pop with the back animation
    // router.push('/library', 'root', 'replace') would reset the stack instead
  }

  return (
    <IonPage>
      <IonHeader>
        <IonToolbar>
          <IonButtons slot="start">
            {/* defaultHref: where to go if the page was opened directly (deep link, no history) */}
            <IonBackButton defaultHref="/library" />
          </IonButtons>
          <IonTitle>Book {id}</IonTitle>
        </IonToolbar>
      </IonHeader>
      <IonContent className="ion-padding">
        <IonButton color="danger" onClick={remove}>Delete</IonButton>
      </IonContent>
    </IonPage>
  );
}
```

**Vue with `@ionic/vue-router`.** It wraps Vue Router 4; routes are defined as usual, but created with Ionic's `createRouter`:

```typescript
// src/router/index.ts
import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from '@ionic/vue-router';
import TabsPage from '@/views/TabsPage.vue';

const routes = [
  { path: '/', redirect: '/tabs/library' },
  {
    path: '/tabs/',
    component: TabsPage,                              // contains ion-tabs, ion-router-outlet, ion-tab-bar
    children: [
      { path: 'library', component: () => import('@/views/LibraryPage.vue') },
      { path: 'library/books/:id', component: () => import('@/views/BookDetailsPage.vue') },
      { path: 'reading', component: () => import('@/views/ReadingPage.vue') },
    ],
  },
];

export default createRouter({ history: createWebHistory(import.meta.env.BASE_URL), routes });
```

In Vue components, `useIonRouter()` provides `push`, `back`, `canGoBack` and `navigate` with explicit animation direction.

**Angular.** Angular's router is used directly with `<ion-router-outlet>` in the root template (`IonRouterOutlet` in standalone imports). Ionic adds `NavController` for navigation with an explicit direction, and a `routerDirection` attribute for links:

```typescript
import { NavController } from '@ionic/angular/standalone';

export class BookDetailsPage {
  private nav = inject(NavController);
  saved() { this.nav.navigateBack('/tabs/library'); }        // back animation
  openAuthor(id: number) { this.nav.navigateForward(['/authors', id]); }
  logout() { this.nav.navigateRoot('/login'); }               // clear the stack
}
```

```html
<ion-item [routerLink]="['/books', book.id]" routerDirection="forward">...</ion-item>
```

**Navigation rules to remember.**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| Wrap every routed page in `IonPage` (React/Vue) | The outlet needs it to animate and manage the page |
| Navigate between tabs with the tab bar, not `push` across tabs | Each tab owns its stack; pushing a page of another tab corrupts the history |
| Use `ion-back-button` with `defaultHref` | Deep-linked pages have no history to go back to |
| Use `root` navigation for login/logout | Prevents navigating "back" into protected pages |
| Use modals, not routes, for short tasks | Modals (like "Filter" or "Add book") do not belong in the stack |
| Use `ion-nav` for navigation inside a modal | It provides its own push/pop stack without changing the URL |

Without a framework, Ionic provides `ion-router` with `ion-route` elements and `ion-nav` for the same stack navigation in plain JavaScript or Stencil apps.

**Key Takeaways**

- Mobile navigation uses stacks: push slides a page in, back pops it; tab apps keep one stack per tab.
- `ion-router-outlet` combines URL routing with stack behavior, transitions, preserved state and swipe-back.
- React uses `IonReactRouter`, Vue uses `@ionic/vue-router`, Angular uses its own router plus `NavController`; `useIonRouter` controls direction in React and Vue.
- `ion-back-button` with `defaultHref` handles deep links; root navigation resets the stack for login and logout.
- Keep each tab's pages within its own route prefix, and use modals (with `ion-nav` if needed) for short tasks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Set up a three-tab bookshelf app (Library, Reading, Profile) with a book details page inside the Library tab. Verify that switching tabs preserves the details page.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a login page outside the tabs with a route guard (React: a wrapper component; Vue: `beforeEach`; Angular: a `canActivate` function) and use root navigation on login and logout so the back button never returns to protected pages.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does Ionic keep previous pages in the DOM instead of unmounting them like a typical web router?" *Hint:* consider back-navigation speed, preserved scroll position and form state, swipe-back gestures, and the memory cost of deep stacks.

#### Ionic Native and Capacitor Plugins

**Why this topic.** Ionic gives the app a native look; plugins give it native abilities. The way Ionic apps access plugins has changed over time, and existing projects use different approaches. Knowing the history explains the imports you will see in older code.

**From Ionic Native to Awesome Cordova Plugins.** When Ionic apps ran on Cordova, the Ionic team maintained **Ionic Native**: TypeScript wrappers that turned callback-based Cordova plugins into Promises and Observables and made them injectable in Angular. In 2021 the project was renamed **Awesome Cordova Plugins** and handed to the community, because Ionic's focus had moved to Capacitor.

```typescript
// Older Ionic + Angular code (Ionic Native / Awesome Cordova Plugins wrapper + Cordova plugin)
import { BarcodeScanner } from '@awesome-cordova-plugins/barcode-scanner/ngx'; // was @ionic-native/...

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class ScanService {
  constructor(private scanner: BarcodeScanner) {}   // wrapper injected through Angular DI
  async scanIsbn() {
    const result = await this.scanner.scan();       // Promise instead of callbacks
    return result.cancelled ? null : result.text;
  }
}
```

**Today: Capacitor plugins.** New Ionic projects use Capacitor plugins directly. They are already Promise-based and typed, need no wrapper, and work the same in every framework.

| Source | Examples |
|---|---|
| Official `@capacitor/*` | `app`, `camera`, `filesystem`, `geolocation`, `haptics`, `keyboard`, `local-notifications`, `network`, `preferences`, `push-notifications`, `share`, `splash-screen`, `status-bar`, `device`, `browser`, `clipboard`, `toast`, `screen-orientation` |
| Capacitor Community (`@capacitor-community/*`) | SQLite, Bluetooth LE, AdMob, keep-awake, barcode scanning and others |
| Capawesome (`@capawesome/*`, `@capawesome-team/*`) | ML Kit barcode scanning, file picker, badges, NFC, app updates and others |
| Cordova plugins | Mostly compatible with Capacitor (`npm install cordova-plugin-x && npx cap sync`) |

**Wrapping plugins in services.** Keep plugin calls out of components. A service module hides platform checks, permissions and fallbacks, and makes components testable:

```typescript
// src/services/device-features.ts
import { Capacitor } from '@capacitor/core';
import { Haptics, ImpactStyle } from '@capacitor/haptics';
import { Share } from '@capacitor/share';
import { Network } from '@capacitor/network';
import { App } from '@capacitor/app';

export async function confirmTap() {
  if (Capacitor.isNativePlatform()) {
    await Haptics.impact({ style: ImpactStyle.Light });   // small vibration feedback on native
  }
}

export async function shareBook(book: Book) {
  const { value: canShare } = await Share.canShare();
  if (!canShare) return navigator.clipboard.writeText(`https://bookshelf.example/books/${book.id}`);
  await Share.share({
    title: book.title,
    text: `I'm reading "${book.title}" by ${book.author}`,
    url: `https://bookshelf.example/books/${book.id}`,
  });
}

export function onConnectivityChange(callback: (online: boolean) => void) {
  return Network.addListener('networkStatusChange', (s) => callback(s.connected)); // returns a handle
}

// Android back button: let Ionic's router handle back, exit only from the root
export function setupBackButton(canGoBack: () => boolean, goBack: () => void) {
  App.addListener('backButton', () => (canGoBack() ? goBack() : App.exitApp()));
}
```

```tsx
// In a React component: listeners must be removed on unmount
useEffect(() => {
  const handle = onConnectivityChange(setOnline);
  return () => { handle.then((h) => h.remove()); };   // addListener returns a Promise of a handle
}, []);
```

Ionic's router already handles the Android back button for navigation (with priorities so overlays close first); custom back logic should use Ionic's `ionBackButton` event or `useIonRouter().canGoBack()` to cooperate with it.

**Push notifications in a native Ionic app.** Native apps receive push through Firebase Cloud Messaging (Android) and APNs (iOS), not Web Push (15.2). `@capacitor/push-notifications` registers the device and returns a token that your server uses with FCM or APNs:

```typescript
import { Capacitor } from '@capacitor/core';
import { PushNotifications } from '@capacitor/push-notifications';

// router: the app's navigation object, e.g. from useIonRouter() or NavController
export async function registerPush(userId: number, router: { push(url: string): void }) {
  let perm = await PushNotifications.checkPermissions();
  if (perm.receive === 'prompt') perm = await PushNotifications.requestPermissions();
  if (perm.receive !== 'granted') return;

  await PushNotifications.addListener('registration', async ({ value: token }) => {
    await fetch('/api/v1/push/devices', {               // server stores the FCM/APNs token
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ userId, token, platform: Capacitor.getPlatform() }),
    });
  });
  await PushNotifications.addListener('pushNotificationActionPerformed', ({ notification }) => {
    const url = notification.data?.url;
    if (url) router.push(url);                          // deep link into the app
  });
  await PushNotifications.register();                    // triggers 'registration'
}
```

Android requires a Firebase project and its `google-services.json`; iOS requires enabling the Push Notifications capability in Xcode and an APNs key.

**Key Takeaways**

- Ionic Native wrapped Cordova plugins in Promises for Ionic apps; it was renamed Awesome Cordova Plugins in 2021 and is community maintained.
- New Ionic apps use Capacitor plugins (`@capacitor/*`, Capacitor Community, Capawesome) directly; most Cordova plugins still work.
- Wrap plugin calls in service modules that handle platform checks, permissions and fallbacks, and remove listeners on unmount.
- Ionic's router handles the Android back button; integrate custom logic through `ionBackButton` or `canGoBack()`.
- Native push uses FCM and APNs tokens through `@capacitor/push-notifications`, not Web Push.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add haptic feedback when the user marks a book as read and a native share button on the details page, with a clipboard fallback on the web.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add barcode scanning of ISBNs using a Capacitor barcode plugin. Wrap it in a service with a permission check and a manual-entry fallback, then look up the book details from your API and pre-fill the "Add book" form.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How do push notifications differ between an Ionic app running as a PWA and the same app running natively with Capacitor?" *Hint:* compare the delivery services, the subscription object versus device token, platform requirements (especially iOS), and the server-side libraries involved.

#### Theming and Custom Styling

**Why Ionic's theming works the way it does.** Ionic components use Shadow DOM (15.5, Architecture), so an ordinary rule like `ion-button .button-inner { ... }` cannot reach their internals. Instead, Ionic exposes **CSS custom properties** (variables) at two levels: global theme variables that affect every component, and component-specific variables. Where variables are not enough, **shadow parts** (`::part()`) expose selected internal elements for styling.

**The color system.** Ionic defines nine named colors: `primary`, `secondary`, `tertiary`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`, `light`, `medium` and `dark`. Most components accept a `color` attribute:

```html
<ion-button color="primary">Save</ion-button>
<ion-badge color="success">Read</ion-badge>
<ion-toolbar color="dark">...</ion-toolbar>
```

Each color is defined by six variables, because components need more than one shade (text on top of it, pressed states, transparent backgrounds):

```css
/* src/theme/variables.css: brand primary color */
:root {
  --ion-color-primary: #2e5d4b;            /* base */
  --ion-color-primary-rgb: 46, 93, 75;     /* same color as r, g, b for rgba() transparency */
  --ion-color-primary-contrast: #ffffff;   /* text/icons on top of the base */
  --ion-color-primary-contrast-rgb: 255, 255, 255;
  --ion-color-primary-shade: #29523f;      /* darker: pressed/active state (~12% darker) */
  --ion-color-primary-tint: #436d5d;       /* lighter: hover state (~10% lighter) */
}
```

The Ionic documentation includes a color generator that computes the shade, tint and RGB values from one base color.

**Custom colors.** To add a new named color (for example `favorite`), define its variables and a class that maps them to the `--ion-color-base` family that components read:

```css
:root {
  --ion-color-favorite: #c2185b;
  --ion-color-favorite-rgb: 194, 24, 91;
  --ion-color-favorite-contrast: #ffffff;
  --ion-color-favorite-contrast-rgb: 255, 255, 255;
  --ion-color-favorite-shade: #ab1550;
  --ion-color-favorite-tint: #c82f6b;
}
.ion-color-favorite {                       /* Ionic adds this class when color="favorite" */
  --ion-color-base: var(--ion-color-favorite);
  --ion-color-base-rgb: var(--ion-color-favorite-rgb);
  --ion-color-contrast: var(--ion-color-favorite-contrast);
  --ion-color-contrast-rgb: var(--ion-color-favorite-contrast-rgb);
  --ion-color-shade: var(--ion-color-favorite-shade);
  --ion-color-tint: var(--ion-color-favorite-tint);
}
```

```html
<ion-chip color="favorite">Favorite</ion-chip>
```

**Application-wide variables.** Beyond colors, global variables set the base look:

| Variable | Affects |
|---|---|
| `--ion-background-color`, `--ion-background-color-rgb` | Page and content backgrounds |
| `--ion-text-color`, `--ion-text-color-rgb` | Default text |
| `--ion-font-family` | Font of all components |
| `--ion-toolbar-background`, `--ion-toolbar-color` | Toolbars |
| `--ion-item-background`, `--ion-border-color` | List items and separators |
| `--ion-color-step-50` ... `--ion-color-step-950` (or the newer text/background step variables) | Neutral grey steps derived from background and text colors |

Variables can be scoped to a mode or platform with the classes Ionic sets on `<html>`:

```css
:root { --ion-font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif; }
.ios  { --ion-toolbar-background: #f7f7f7; }   /* only in ios mode */
.md   { --ion-toolbar-background: var(--ion-color-primary); --ion-toolbar-color: #fff; }
```

**Component variables and shadow parts.** Each component documents its own variables (in the "CSS Custom Properties" section of its API page) and its shadow parts:

```css
/* Rounded, taller buttons via component variables */
ion-button {
  --border-radius: 999px;
  --padding-start: 1.5rem;
  --padding-end: 1.5rem;
  --box-shadow: none;
}

/* A list item with a custom background and no inner border */
ion-item.book-item {
  --background: var(--ion-color-light);
  --inner-border-width: 0;
  --min-height: 72px;
}

/* Shadow parts: style an internal element directly when no variable exists */
ion-searchbar::part(icon) { color: var(--ion-color-primary); }
ion-segment-button::part(indicator-background) { height: 3px; }
```

**Dark mode and high contrast.** Ionic 8 ships palette stylesheets. Import one variant:

```typescript
// main.tsx (React) or main.ts (Vue/Angular global styles)
import '@ionic/react/css/palettes/dark.system.css';   // follows the OS setting (prefers-color-scheme)
// import '@ionic/react/css/palettes/dark.always.css'; // always dark
// import '@ionic/react/css/palettes/dark.class.css';  // dark when <html> has .ion-palette-dark
// High-contrast palettes are available in the same folder (high-contrast.*.css, high-contrast-dark.*.css)
```

The class variant enables a user-controlled toggle:

```typescript
// Toggle dark mode from a settings screen and remember the choice
import { Preferences } from '@capacitor/preferences';

export async function setDarkMode(enabled: boolean) {
  document.documentElement.classList.toggle('ion-palette-dark', enabled);
  await Preferences.set({ key: 'darkMode', value: String(enabled) });
}
```

**Utility classes and global CSS.** Ionic ships optional CSS utilities (imported in the starter templates): `ion-padding`, `ion-margin`, `ion-text-center`, `ion-hide-md-up` (responsive display), `ion-justify-content-between` and others. App-specific global styles go in a global stylesheet; component-scoped styles use your framework's mechanism (CSS modules, Vue scoped styles, Angular component styles), remembering that only variables and parts reach inside Ionic's shadow roots.

**Key Takeaways**

- Ionic components are styled through CSS custom properties and shadow parts, because Shadow DOM blocks ordinary descendant selectors.
- Nine named colors, each defined by base, RGB, contrast, shade and tint variables; custom colors need the variables plus an `.ion-color-<name>` class.
- Global variables (`--ion-background-color`, `--ion-text-color`, `--ion-font-family`, toolbar and item variables) set the overall look, optionally per mode with `.ios`/`.md`.
- Component variables (`--background`, `--border-radius`) and `::part()` customize individual components.
- Ionic 8 palettes provide system, always-on and class-based dark mode plus high-contrast themes.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Apply the bookshelf brand color as `primary` using the color generator values, and set a custom font for the whole app.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a custom `favorite` color used by chips and badges, a dark mode toggle in the Profile tab using the class-based palette with the choice persisted through `@capacitor/preferences`, and verify contrast in both modes.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can't you style the inner button of `ion-button` with a normal CSS selector, and what are the alternatives?" *Hint:* explain Shadow DOM encapsulation, then compare CSS custom properties (designed by the component author) and shadow parts (exposed elements).

#### Live Reload, Building and Distribution

**Why a dedicated workflow.** An Ionic app ends up in three places: the browser (development and PWA), Android and iOS. The development loop should stay as fast as web development, even when testing native features on a phone, and releasing should be repeatable for all targets.

**Development in the browser.** Most work happens with the web dev server:

```bash
ionic serve                     # Vite dev server with hot module replacement, opens the browser
ionic serve --external          # listen on all interfaces so a phone on the same Wi-Fi can open it
```

Use the browser's device emulation for layout and `?ionic:mode=ios` for the other platform's styles. Capacitor plugins run their web implementations (or throw "not implemented" for native-only ones, which your services should handle).

**Live reload on a device.** When you need native plugins, run the app on a device or emulator but load the web code from your dev server, so changes appear instantly without rebuilding the native app:

```bash
ionic cap run android -l --external   # -l: live reload; --external: use the machine's LAN IP
ionic cap run ios -l --external
```

Under the hood, this temporarily sets `server.url` in the Capacitor configuration to the dev server's address (`http://192.168.x.x:8100`). The phone and computer must be on the same network, and the dev server must not be blocked by a firewall. Never ship a build with `server.url` set: the app would try to load your laptop's address.

```text
 Development with live reload                   Production build
 +--------------------+                          +--------------------+
 | Phone (native app) |  http://192.168.1.20     | Phone (native app) |
 |  WebView ----------+----------> dev server    |  WebView ----------+--> bundled assets
 |  native plugins    |            (Vite, HMR)   |  native plugins    |    (https://localhost,
 +--------------------+                          +--------------------+     capacitor://localhost)
```

**Building for each target.**

```bash
# Web / PWA
ionic build                       # production build into dist/ (or www/ for Angular)
# deploy dist/ to any static host or CDN; add a manifest and service worker (vite-plugin-pwa,
# or @angular/pwa for Angular) to make it a PWA

# Native
ionic build && npx cap sync       # equivalently: ionic cap sync (builds and syncs)
npx cap open android              # Android Studio: Build > Generate Signed App Bundle
npx cap open ios                  # Xcode: Product > Archive > Distribute App
npx cap run android --target=<device-id>
```

Signing, store listings and review rules are the same as in 15.4 (Packaging and Store Deployment): Android App Bundles signed with an upload key for Google Play, archives signed with a distribution certificate for App Store Connect and TestFlight.

**Icons and splash screens.** Generate all sizes from one source image with `@capacitor/assets`:

```bash
# Place assets/icon-only.png (1024x1024), assets/icon-foreground.png, assets/icon-background.png,
# assets/splash.png and assets/splash-dark.png, then:
npx @capacitor/assets generate --iconBackgroundColor '#2e5d4b' --splashBackgroundColor '#2e5d4b'
# Writes Android adaptive icons, iOS app icons, splash screens and PWA icons
```

**Environment configuration.** Use build-time environment variables for API URLs, and make sure native builds point to the production API:

```typescript
// src/config.ts (Vite)
export const API_BASE = import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE ?? 'https://api.bookshelf.example';
// .env.development: VITE_API_BASE=http://192.168.1.20:3000   (reachable from the phone)
// .env.production:  VITE_API_BASE=https://api.bookshelf.example
```

**Live updates.** Native store releases take time (review can take a day or more). **Live update** services deliver new web assets (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) to installed apps without a store release, which is valuable for urgent fixes. Store rules allow this only for changes that do not alter the app's primary purpose, and native code changes (new plugins, permissions) still require a store release. Ionic's commercial **Appflow** service offered live updates and cloud builds; Ionic announced in 2025 that it is winding down its commercial products, including Appflow, so new projects typically use alternatives such as Capawesome Cloud, self-hosted update plugins, or CI pipelines with fastlane for builds.

**A release pipeline.**

```text
 git tag v1.4.0
      |
      v
 CI (GitHub Actions: Linux runner for web + Android, macOS runner for iOS)
      |-- npm ci, lint, unit tests, ionic build
      |-- web:     deploy dist/ to static hosting (PWA)
      |-- android: npx cap sync android -> Gradle bundleRelease (signed) -> Play internal track
      |-- ios:     npx cap sync ios -> fastlane (match for signing, gym to build, pilot to TestFlight)
      v
 Manual promotion: internal testing -> beta -> production in each store
```

Versioning: keep the web app version, Android `versionName`/`versionCode` (in `android/app/build.gradle`) and iOS `MARKETING_VERSION`/`CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION` (in Xcode) in sync, ideally with a script run by CI.

**Key Takeaways**

- Develop in the browser with `ionic serve`; use `ionic cap run <platform> -l --external` for live reload on devices with native plugins.
- Live reload works by pointing `server.url` at the dev server; never ship a build with it set.
- `ionic build` produces the web bundle for PWA hosting; `ionic cap sync` and the native IDEs produce signed store builds.
- Generate icons and splash screens with `@capacitor/assets`, and use environment variables for API URLs per build.
- Live updates can ship web-only fixes within store rules; automate builds and store uploads with CI and fastlane.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the bookshelf Ionic app on an Android device with live reload, change a label in the Library page, and observe the update without rebuilding.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure separate development and production API URLs, generate icons and splash screens from one source image, and produce a signed Android App Bundle and a PWA build from the same commit.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What can and cannot be delivered through a live update to an installed hybrid app?" *Hint:* separate web assets from native code and configuration (plugins, permissions, `Info.plist`, manifest), then consider what app store guidelines allow.

<a id="16-cross-platform-web-based-native-applications"></a>
## 16. Cross-Platform Web-Based Native Applications

Chapter 15 brought web technologies to phones. This chapter brings them to the desktop: applications installed on Windows, macOS and Linux, with their own windows, menus, tray icons and file access, written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It focuses on Electron, the framework behind VS Code, Slack and Discord. It covers Electron's multi-process architecture (16.1), its integration with the operating system (16.2), and how such apps are packaged, signed, secured and shipped (16.3), ending with alternatives such as Tauri and desktop PWAs. The running example is *Bookshelf Desktop*, a desktop client for the bookshelf API from Chapter 12.

<a id="161-electron-architecture"></a>
### 16.1 Electron Architecture

An Electron app is a set of cooperating processes, not a single web page. This subchapter explains why desktop apps are built with web technologies at all and how Electron combines Chromium and Node.js. It then covers the main and renderer processes, windows, the preload scripts that connect them safely, the messages they exchange and the events that drive the application from launch to quit.

#### Motivation for Web-Based Desktop Applications

**Why not just write a native app?** A company that wants a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux faces the same problem as on mobile (15.1), only worse. Each platform has its own languages and UI toolkits: C# with WinUI or WPF on Windows, Swift with SwiftUI or AppKit on macOS, C or C++ with GTK or Qt on Linux. Three codebases need three teams and three release cycles, and features arrive at different times on each platform. Meanwhile, the same company usually has a web app already, built by web developers, with a UI that users know.

**The idea.** Take a browser engine, remove the browser around it (address bar, tabs, bookmarks), put a JavaScript runtime with operating system access next to it, and package the two as an ordinary installable program. The web team then builds the desktop app with the skills, libraries and often the code it already has. The app ships as a normal executable, with a Start menu entry, Dock icon, file associations and auto-updates.

An analogy: a native app is a custom-built car for each country's roads. An Electron app is one car body (your web UI) placed on a standard chassis (Chromium plus Node.js) that is certified for every country. The chassis is heavy, but you design the body only once.

**A short history.**

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 2008 | Chromium Embedded Framework (CEF) lets C++ apps embed Chromium; used by Spotify and Steam |
| 2011 | node-webkit (later NW.js) combines WebKit/Chromium and Node.js in one process |
| 2013 | GitHub creates *Atom Shell* for its Atom editor |
| 2015 | Atom Shell is renamed Electron; Visual Studio Code is built on it |
| 2019 | Electron joins the OpenJS Foundation |
| 2022 | Tauri 1.0 offers a lightweight alternative based on the operating system's own WebView |
| Now | A new Electron major version roughly every 8 weeks, each tracking a recent Chromium release |

**Who uses it.** VS Code, Slack, Discord, Figma's desktop app, Obsidian, Notion, Signal Desktop, 1Password, Postman and GitHub Desktop are all Electron apps. Some well-known apps have also moved away from it: Microsoft Teams switched to Edge WebView2 in 2023 to reduce memory use. That shows the main trade-off.

**Benefits and costs.**

| Aspect | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Codebase | One codebase for three operating systems, often shared with the web app | Platform differences still appear (menus, tray, paths, signing) |
| Skills | Web developers can build it; huge npm ecosystem | Native expertise is still needed for packaging, signing and edge cases |
| Rendering | Same Chromium version on every machine: no browser compatibility testing | Look and feel is not native unless you work at it |
| OS access | Full Node.js plus Electron APIs: files, processes, network, menus, tray | A bug such as XSS can become remote code execution (16.3) |
| Size | Self-contained; no runtime for users to install | Every app ships its own Chromium: installers of roughly 80 to 150 MB |
| Memory | Multi-process isolation: one crashed window does not take down the app | Idle memory use is typically 100 MB or more, higher than a native app |
| Updates | Auto-update frameworks and fast iteration (16.2) | You must ship Chromium security fixes by updating Electron regularly |

**When it fits.** Electron is a good choice for tools centered on documents, communication or productivity, where the UI is mostly text, lists and forms, the team is web-oriented, and the same product exists on the web. It is a poor choice for tiny utilities where a 100 MB download is absurd, for apps that must feel exactly native, for low-memory devices and for heavy real-time graphics, unless the heavy work runs in native modules.

```text
               Native desktop               Electron                  Desktop PWA (16.3)
            +------------------+     +----------------------+     +----------------------+
 Your code  | C# / Swift / C++ |     | HTML, CSS, JS        |     | HTML, CSS, JS        |
            | per platform     |     | + Node.js main code  |     | + service worker     |
            +------------------+     +----------------------+     +----------------------+
 Runtime    | OS UI toolkit    |     | Bundled Chromium     |     | The user's installed |
            |                  |     | + Node.js + Electron |     | browser (Chrome/Edge)|
            +------------------+     +----------------------+     +----------------------+
 OS access  | Everything       |     | Everything (Node.js) |     | Browser APIs only    |
 Delivery   | Installer/store  |     | Installer/store      |     | URL + "Install"      |
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Web-based desktop apps let one web team ship to Windows, macOS and Linux from one codebase, often reusing web app code.
- Electron bundles Chromium and Node.js into an installable program with full operating system access.
- The main costs are download size, memory use, a non-native feel and a larger security responsibility.
- It suits productivity, communication and document tools; it suits tiny utilities and graphics-heavy apps poorly.
- Alternatives trade some of Electron's power for size and memory savings (16.3).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Install two Electron apps you use (for example VS Code and Slack). Find their installed size on disk and their memory use in the task manager with one window open, and compare them with a native app of similar purpose.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a half-page decision record for Bookshelf Desktop: the product must work offline with a local reading list, open `.epub` files, show reminders and run on all three desktop operating systems. Compare native, Electron and a desktop PWA, and recommend one.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why do so many desktop apps ship a whole browser, and what does that cost the user?" *Hint:* separate developer economics (one codebase, web skills, consistent rendering) from user costs (disk, memory, battery, update frequency, security surface).

#### Chromium and Node.js Integration

**Why two engines.** A browser can render UIs well, but it deliberately cannot touch the file system, start processes or open raw sockets. Node.js (Chapter 11) can do all of that but has no UI. Electron joins the two so that one application can do both, while still keeping them apart where safety requires it.

**What Electron is made of.**

```text
+--------------------------------- Electron binary ----------------------------------+
|                                                                                     |
|  +-------------------------- Chromium ---------------------------+                  |
|  |  Blink (HTML/CSS layout, DOM)   V8 (JavaScript engine)        |                  |
|  |  Network stack, GPU compositing, multi-process sandbox        |                  |
|  +----------------------------------------------------------------+                 |
|  +-------------------------- Node.js ----------------------------+                  |
|  |  libuv (event loop, file system, sockets, child processes)    |                  |
|  |  Core modules: fs, path, crypto, child_process, net, ...      |                  |
|  +----------------------------------------------------------------+                 |
|  +-------------------- Electron native layer ---------------------+                 |
|  |  app, BrowserWindow, Menu, Tray, dialog, Notification, ipcMain |                 |
|  |  (C++/Objective-C bindings to Win32, Cocoa, GTK)               |                 |
|  +----------------------------------------------------------------+                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Three parts work together:

- **Chromium** provides rendering, networking, the GPU process and Chromium's multi-process sandbox.
- **Node.js** provides the npm ecosystem and system access. Electron builds Node.js against Chromium's copy of V8, so there is only **one** V8 engine in each process, not two.
- **Electron's own native layer** wraps operating system features (windows, menus, tray icons, dialogs, notifications) and exposes them as JavaScript modules.

**Merging two event loops.** Chromium has its own message loop (for input, rendering and timers), and Node.js has libuv's event loop (for I/O). A process can only block on one loop at a time. Electron solves this by running libuv's polling in a helper thread: when libuv reports that I/O is ready, the helper posts a task to Chromium's message loop, which then runs the Node.js callbacks. For your code this means that `setTimeout`, Promises, `fs` callbacks and UI events all appear on the same single JavaScript thread, as in Node.js and in browsers (5.1).

**Versions are pinned.** Each Electron release bundles specific versions of Chromium, V8 and Node.js. Your app runs on exactly those versions on every user's machine, regardless of which browser they have installed. That ends browser compatibility testing, but it also means you are responsible for Chromium security patches: an app that is never updated keeps old, known vulnerabilities. Electron supports the latest three major versions with security fixes.

```javascript
// Print the versions bundled with the running Electron
console.log(process.versions.electron); // e.g. '44.x.y'
console.log(process.versions.chrome);   // Chromium version
console.log(process.versions.node);     // Node.js version
console.log(process.versions.v8);       // the single shared V8
```

**Which APIs exist where.** Not every module is available everywhere. Some APIs only make sense in the privileged main process (next topic), some only in a page, some in both.

| Module | Main process | Preload / renderer | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `app`, `BrowserWindow`, `Menu`, `Tray`, `dialog` | Yes | No | Application and window control |
| `ipcMain`, `globalShortcut`, `protocol`, `session`, `autoUpdater`, `utilityProcess` | Yes | No | Messaging, OS hooks, networking, updates |
| `Notification` (Electron module) | Yes | No (renderers use the Web Notification API) | Desktop notifications |
| `ipcRenderer`, `contextBridge`, `webFrame`, `webUtils` | No | Yes | Messaging and safe exposure to the page |
| `clipboard`, `nativeImage`, `crashReporter` | Yes | Partly (prefer main or web APIs) | Shared utilities |
| Node.js core (`fs`, `child_process`, ...) | Yes | Only if Node integration is enabled (avoid) | System access |

**A minimal project.** An Electron app is an npm package whose `main` field points at the main process script.

```json
{
  "name": "bookshelf-desktop",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "src/main.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "electron ."
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "electron": "^44.0.0"
  }
}
```

```javascript
// src/main.js: the smallest useful Electron app
const { app, BrowserWindow } = require('electron');
const path = require('node:path');

app.whenReady().then(() => {                  // wait until Electron has initialized
  const win = new BrowserWindow({ width: 1000, height: 700 });
  win.loadFile(path.join(__dirname, 'index.html')); // a normal HTML page
});
```

The `electron` npm package downloads a prebuilt binary for your operating system (the version number above is an example; install the current stable release with `npm install --save-dev electron`). Running `npm start` launches that binary, which reads `package.json`, runs `src/main.js` with Node.js, and shows a window rendered by Chromium. The examples in this chapter use CommonJS (`require`) because sandboxed preload scripts require it; the main process also supports ES modules.

**Key Takeaways**

- Electron = Chromium (rendering, networking, sandbox) + Node.js (system access, npm) + a native layer for OS features.
- Node.js and Chromium share one V8 per process; Electron merges libuv's loop into Chromium's message loop.
- Each Electron version pins Chromium and Node.js versions, giving consistent rendering but making you responsible for security updates.
- Modules are split by process: window, menu and OS modules live in the main process; `ipcRenderer` and `contextBridge` in preload scripts.
- An Electron app is an npm package whose `main` script is run by the Electron binary.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create the minimal project above, add an `index.html` that says "Bookshelf", and run it. Then print `process.versions` in the main process and compare the Chromium version with the Chrome you have installed.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In the main process, call `fs.promises.readdir(app.getPath('home'))` and log the result, then try to do the same from a `<script>` in `index.html`. Explain why the second attempt fails with the default settings.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why does Electron ship its own Chromium instead of using the browser installed on the user's machine?" *Hint:* consider version consistency, which APIs the app can rely on, Node.js integration with V8, and the costs this creates for size and patching.

#### Main Process vs Renderer Process

**Why more than one process.** Chrome runs each tab in a separate process so that a crashing or malicious page cannot take down or spy on the others. Electron inherits this model. An application with several windows, a background task and native integration needs one place that owns the application as a whole, and separate, less privileged places for each page.

**The main process.** Every Electron app has exactly **one** main process. It runs the script named in `package.json` in a full Node.js environment. It:

- creates and manages windows (`BrowserWindow`);
- owns application-level features: menus, tray, dialogs, notifications, global shortcuts, protocol handlers, auto-updates;
- reacts to application lifecycle events (`ready`, `window-all-closed`, `before-quit`);
- has full operating system access through Node.js.

It has no DOM and no visible UI of its own. Think of it as the building manager: it does not live in any apartment, but it holds all the keys and decides who gets which room.

**Renderer processes.** Each window (more precisely, each `webContents`: the web page inside a window) gets its own **renderer process**, which is a Chromium renderer. It runs HTML, CSS and JavaScript exactly as a browser tab does: DOM, `fetch`, Web Workers, IndexedDB. By default it has **no** Node.js access and is **sandboxed** (since Electron 20), so a compromised page has no more power than a web page in Chrome. Renderers are the tenants: each lives in its own apartment and must ask the manager for anything beyond its walls.

**Other processes.** Chromium also starts a GPU process and a network service process. Electron adds **utility processes** (`utilityProcess.fork()`), Node.js child processes for CPU-heavy or crash-prone work, which you can create yourself (16.3).

```text
                          +-----------------------------------------+
                          |            Main process (1)             |
                          |  Node.js + Electron APIs, no DOM        |
                          |  app, BrowserWindow, Menu, Tray, ipcMain|
                          +-----------------------------------------+
                             |  creates / controls     ^  IPC messages
             +---------------+---------------+---------+------------+
             v                               v                      |
 +-----------------------+     +-----------------------+     +------------------+
 | Renderer: Library win |     | Renderer: Settings win|     | Utility process  |
 | Chromium page (DOM)   |     | Chromium page (DOM)   |     | Node.js worker   |
 | sandboxed, no Node.js |     | sandboxed, no Node.js |     | (e.g. indexing)  |
 | + preload script      |     | + preload script      |     +------------------+
 +-----------------------+     +-----------------------+
             Chromium also runs: GPU process, network service process
```

**Dividing the work.** The guiding rule: the renderer does **presentation**, the main process does **privileged work**, and they talk through narrow, validated messages (see Inter-Process Communication below).

| Task | Where it belongs | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Rendering the book list, handling clicks | Renderer | It is UI |
| Calling the bookshelf REST API with `fetch` | Renderer (or main) | A normal web capability; move it to main if it uses secrets |
| Reading and writing local files | Main | Needs `fs`; the renderer has no file access |
| Showing an Open File dialog | Main | `dialog` exists only in main |
| Storing an API token securely | Main (`safeStorage`) | Keeps the secret out of web content |
| Parsing a 200 MB export | Utility process or Web Worker | Keeps the main process and UI responsive |

**A blocked main process freezes everything.** The main process handles events for all windows: menu clicks, window moves and resizes, and every IPC message. A synchronous file read of a large file or a long loop in the main process makes every window feel frozen, even though each renderer is a separate process. Keep the main process light and asynchronous.

```javascript
// main.js: BAD, blocks the main process (and thus every window) for seconds
const data = require('node:fs').readFileSync(hugeFile); // synchronous I/O
const index = buildSearchIndex(data);                    // long CPU work

// main.js: GOOD, asynchronous I/O and CPU work moved to a utility process
const { utilityProcess } = require('electron');
const fs = require('node:fs/promises');

const text = await fs.readFile(hugeFile, 'utf8');        // does not block the loop
const worker = utilityProcess.fork(path.join(__dirname, 'indexer.js'));
worker.postMessage({ text });                             // heavy work elsewhere
worker.on('message', (index) => { /* use the index */ });
```

**Crashes are contained.** If a renderer crashes or runs out of memory, only that window's content is lost. The main process receives a `render-process-gone` event and can reload the page or show an error (16.3). If the main process crashes, the whole app ends.

**Key Takeaways**

- One main process runs Node.js and Electron APIs, owns windows and OS integration, and has no DOM.
- Each window's page runs in its own sandboxed renderer process with web APIs only.
- Renderers handle presentation; privileged work goes to the main process through IPC.
- Blocking the main process freezes all windows; use async APIs and utility processes for heavy work.
- Process separation contains crashes and limits what a compromised page can do.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open two windows in a test app, then open the operating system's process list (or call `app.getAppMetrics()`) and identify the main, renderer, GPU and utility processes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In the main process, add a menu item that runs a three-second busy loop. While it runs, try to move, resize and type into both windows. Then move the loop into a `utilityProcess` and repeat. Describe the difference.
> 3. *(Interview)* "In Electron, which code should run in the main process and which in the renderer?" *Hint:* reason from privilege and responsiveness: what needs Node.js or OS APIs, what must never be exposed to web content, and what would block every window.

#### BrowserWindow and Window Lifecycle

**Why windows need managing.** On the web, the browser owns the window: the page lives inside a tab and cannot decide its own size or what happens when it closes. In a desktop app, *you* own the window. You decide its size and position, whether it remembers them, what happens when it closes, and how it behaves on each operating system. The `BrowserWindow` class in the main process handles all of this.

**Creating a window.** A `BrowserWindow` is a native window (Win32, Cocoa or GTK) that contains a `webContents`, the object that represents the web page and its renderer process.

```javascript
// main.js
const { app, BrowserWindow } = require('electron');
const path = require('node:path');

function createMainWindow() {
  const win = new BrowserWindow({
    width: 1100,
    height: 720,
    minWidth: 640,                      // prevent layouts from breaking
    minHeight: 480,
    title: 'Bookshelf',
    backgroundColor: '#1e1e1e',         // painted before the page loads: no white flash
    show: false,                        // create hidden, show when ready (see below)
    webPreferences: {
      preload: path.join(__dirname, 'preload.js'), // bridge script (see Preload Scripts below)
      contextIsolation: true,           // default since Electron 12; keep it
      sandbox: true,                    // default since Electron 20; keep it
      nodeIntegration: false,           // default; never enable it for app content
    },
  });

  win.once('ready-to-show', () => win.show()); // first paint is ready: show without flicker
  win.loadFile(path.join(__dirname, 'renderer', 'index.html'));
  return win;
}

app.whenReady().then(createMainWindow);
```

`loadFile` loads a local file, `loadURL` loads any URL (for example a development server at `http://localhost:5173`). Both return Promises that resolve when the page has finished loading.

**The window lifecycle.** A window goes through a sequence of events. The important distinction is between `close` (the user asked to close; you may still cancel) and `closed` (the window is gone; drop your references).

```text
  new BrowserWindow()            loadFile / loadURL
         |                              |
         v                              v
   [created, hidden] --> did-finish-load --> ready-to-show --> show()
                                                                  |
                    focus / blur / resize / move / maximize / minimize ... (while open)
                                                                  |
         user clicks X or win.close() --> 'close'  --(event.preventDefault()?)--> stays open
                                                  |
                                                  v
                                             'closed'  -> set references to null
```

```javascript
// Ask before closing a window with unsaved changes
let hasUnsavedChanges = false; // updated through IPC from the renderer

win.on('close', async (event) => {
  if (!hasUnsavedChanges) return;           // let it close
  event.preventDefault();                    // cancel this close attempt
  const { response } = await dialog.showMessageBox(win, {
    type: 'question',
    buttons: ['Cancel', 'Discard changes'],
    defaultId: 0,
    cancelId: 0,
    message: 'You have unsaved notes. Close anyway?',
  });
  if (response === 1) {
    hasUnsavedChanges = false;
    win.close();                             // try again; this time the handler lets it close
  }
});

win.on('closed', () => {
  mainWindow = null;                         // avoid using a destroyed window object
});
```

**Common window options.**

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `width`, `height`, `x`, `y`, `minWidth`, `maxHeight` | Size and position |
| `show: false` + `ready-to-show` | Avoids showing an empty or half-painted window |
| `backgroundColor` | Color painted before the page renders |
| `parent`, `modal: true` | Child window attached to a parent; modal blocks the parent |
| `frame: false` | Removes the native title bar and borders (you draw your own) |
| `titleBarStyle: 'hidden'` (+ `titleBarOverlay` on Windows/Linux) | Hides the title bar but keeps native window controls |
| `resizable`, `alwaysOnTop`, `fullscreenable`, `skipTaskbar` | Window behavior |
| `icon` | Window icon on Windows and Linux (macOS uses the app bundle icon) |
| `webPreferences` | Settings for the page: preload, isolation, sandbox, zoom, spellcheck |

**Custom title bars.** With `frame: false` or `titleBarStyle: 'hidden'`, you draw the title bar in HTML. The CSS property `-webkit-app-region: drag` marks areas that move the window. Interactive elements inside them need `no-drag`, otherwise they cannot be clicked.

```css
.titlebar { -webkit-app-region: drag; height: 32px; }   /* drag the window by this bar */
.titlebar button { -webkit-app-region: no-drag; }        /* buttons stay clickable */
```

**Remembering size and position.** Users expect a window to reopen where they left it. Save the bounds when the window closes, restore them on startup, and check that the saved position is still on a connected display.

```javascript
const { screen } = require('electron');
const fs = require('node:fs');
const statePath = path.join(app.getPath('userData'), 'window-state.json');

function loadBounds() {
  try {
    const saved = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(statePath, 'utf8'));
    const visible = screen.getAllDisplays().some(({ workArea: a }) =>
      saved.x >= a.x && saved.y >= a.y &&
      saved.x < a.x + a.width && saved.y < a.y + a.height);
    return visible ? saved : { width: saved.width, height: saved.height }; // monitor gone: let the OS place it
  } catch {
    return { width: 1100, height: 720 };     // first run or corrupted file
  }
}

// When creating: new BrowserWindow({ ...loadBounds(), ... })
// When closing:
win.on('close', () => fs.writeFileSync(statePath, JSON.stringify(win.getNormalBounds())));
```

(`getNormalBounds()` returns the size before maximizing, which is what you want to restore. Synchronous file writes are acceptable here because the file is tiny and the app is closing.)

**Multiple windows and views.** An app may open several windows: a library window, a settings window, a reader window per book. Keep references in a `Map` keyed by purpose or document, and focus an existing window instead of opening a duplicate. To show several web pages inside one window (for example an app UI plus an embedded web page), use `BaseWindow` with `WebContentsView` (Electron 30+), which replaced the deprecated `BrowserView`.

**Key Takeaways**

- `BrowserWindow` is a native window that hosts a `webContents` (a page in its own renderer process).
- Create windows with `show: false` and show them on `ready-to-show` to avoid flicker; set `backgroundColor`.
- `close` can be cancelled with `event.preventDefault()`; after `closed`, drop all references.
- Frameless and hidden title bars use `-webkit-app-region: drag` for draggable areas.
- Persist window bounds in `userData` and check they still fit on a connected display.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a main window and a modal "About Bookshelf" window that is a child of it. Verify that the main window cannot be used while the About window is open.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement window state persistence that also restores the maximized state, and test it by disconnecting a second monitor between runs (or by editing the saved coordinates to an off-screen position).
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is the difference between the `close` and `closed` events of a `BrowserWindow`, and where would you put an unsaved-changes check?" *Hint:* one is cancellable and happens before destruction; think about what is still safe to call on the window object in each.
#### Preload Scripts and Context Isolation

**The problem.** The renderer is deliberately powerless: no `fs`, no `dialog`, no `ipcRenderer`. But the Bookshelf UI must be able to say "export my reading list to a file". Early Electron apps solved this by enabling `nodeIntegration`, which gave every page full Node.js. Then any injected script, whether from an XSS bug, a compromised CDN dependency or a malicious book description, could run `require('child_process').exec(...)` on the user's machine. A safe design needs a narrow, controlled doorway between the page and the privileged world.

**Preload scripts.** A preload script is a JavaScript file that Electron runs in the renderer process **before** the page's own scripts. It has access to the DOM globals and to a small set of Electron renderer modules (`contextBridge`, `ipcRenderer`, `webFrame`, `webUtils`). In a sandboxed renderer (the default), it can `require` only those Electron modules plus a few Node.js polyfills (`events`, `timers`, `url`), not `fs` or `child_process`.

**Context isolation.** By default, the preload script and the page run in two separate JavaScript **worlds**: same DOM, but different global objects, different built-in prototypes and different variables. The page cannot see the preload's variables or modify the built-ins the preload uses (for example by overriding `Array.prototype.push` to intercept data). Chrome extensions use the same mechanism for content scripts.

The analogy is a bank teller's window. The customer (the page) and the vault (the main process) never share a room. The teller (the preload) sits behind bulletproof glass (context isolation) and offers only specific services through the slot (`contextBridge`): "deposit", "withdraw", "check balance", never "give me the vault keys".

```text
+------------------------------- Renderer process (sandboxed) ------------------------------+
|                                                                                            |
|   Isolated world (preload.js)                     Main world (your page: app.js, React)    |
|   +------------------------------+                +------------------------------------+   |
|   | require('electron')          |   contextBridge|  window.bookshelf.exportList(books)|   |
|   |   ipcRenderer, contextBridge |  ------------> |  window.bookshelf.onSyncStatus(cb) |   |
|   | own globals and prototypes   |  copies only   |  no require, no ipcRenderer        |   |
|   +------------------------------+  the exposed   +------------------------------------+   |
|               |                     functions                                              |
+---------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                | IPC
                v
        Main process: ipcMain.handle('books:export', ...)
```

**contextBridge.** `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld(name, api)` makes `api` available as `window[name]` in the page. Values crossing the bridge are copied (with the structured clone algorithm, similar to `postMessage`), and functions are wrapped in proxies, so the page receives callable functions but no references to the preload's internal objects.

```javascript
// preload.js: expose a minimal, purpose-specific API
const { contextBridge, ipcRenderer } = require('electron');

contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('bookshelf', {
  // Two-way calls: each returns a Promise resolved by the main process
  exportReadingList: (books) => ipcRenderer.invoke('books:export', books),
  openBookFile: () => ipcRenderer.invoke('books:open-file'),
  getAppVersion: () => ipcRenderer.invoke('app:version'),

  // One-way notification to main
  setUnsavedChanges: (flag) => ipcRenderer.send('editor:unsaved', Boolean(flag)),

  // Subscribe to events from main; return an unsubscribe function
  onSyncStatus: (callback) => {
    const listener = (_event, status) => callback(status); // do NOT pass the event object on
    ipcRenderer.on('sync:status', listener);
    return () => ipcRenderer.removeListener('sync:status', listener);
  },
});
```

```javascript
// renderer/app.js: ordinary front-end code (could be React from Chapter 14)
const result = await window.bookshelf.exportReadingList(books);
if (result.saved) showToast(`Saved to ${result.path}`);

const stop = window.bookshelf.onSyncStatus((s) => (statusBar.textContent = s));
// later, e.g. on component unmount: stop();
```

For TypeScript projects, declare the shape once so the renderer gets type checking (9.3):

```typescript
// renderer/global.d.ts
export {};
declare global {
  interface Window {
    bookshelf: {
      exportReadingList(books: Book[]): Promise<{ saved: boolean; path?: string }>;
      openBookFile(): Promise<{ name: string; content: string } | null>;
      getAppVersion(): Promise<string>;
      setUnsavedChanges(flag: boolean): void;
      onSyncStatus(cb: (status: string) => void): () => void;
    };
  }
}
```

**What not to expose.** The bridge is only as safe as the API you put on it.

```javascript
// DANGEROUS: each of these gives the page (and any injected script) far too much power
contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('api', {
  ipcRenderer,                                    // page can send ANY message on ANY channel
  send: (channel, data) => ipcRenderer.send(channel, data), // same problem, generic channel
  readFile: (p) => ipcRenderer.invoke('fs:read', p),        // arbitrary path: reads ~/.ssh/id_rsa
  on: (channel, cb) => ipcRenderer.on(channel, cb),         // leaks the IpcRendererEvent (event.sender)
});
```

Rules of thumb:

- Expose **one function per action**, with a fixed channel name inside the preload.
- Never expose `ipcRenderer` itself, a generic `send(channel)`, or functions that take arbitrary paths, commands or URLs.
- Do not forward the IPC `event` object to page callbacks.
- Validate arguments again in the main process (next topic); the preload is a convenience layer, not a security boundary on its own.
