**Settings that must stay on.** `contextIsolation: true`, `sandbox: true` and `nodeIntegration: false` are the defaults in current Electron. Code that turns any of them off, often copied from old tutorials, re-opens the path from XSS to full system compromise (16.3).

**Key Takeaways**

- A preload script runs in the renderer before the page, with access to `contextBridge` and `ipcRenderer` but no full Node.js when sandboxed.
- Context isolation runs the preload and the page in separate JavaScript worlds that share only the DOM.
- `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld` gives the page a copied, proxied API under a global name.
- Expose narrow, action-specific functions; never expose `ipcRenderer` or generic channels, paths or commands.
- Keep `contextIsolation`, `sandbox` and disabled `nodeIntegration` at their secure defaults.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a preload script that exposes `window.bookshelf.getAppVersion()` and display the version in the page footer.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In a test app, try to override `Array.prototype.map` from the page and check whether the preload's code is affected. Then set `contextIsolation: false` and repeat. Explain the result.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('ipc', ipcRenderer)` a security problem even with context isolation enabled?" *Hint:* isolation protects the preload's objects, but what can a script in the page do with an unrestricted channel to the privileged process?

#### Inter-Process Communication

**Why messages.** The renderer and main processes are separate operating system processes with separate memory. They cannot call each other's functions or share objects. The only way to cooperate is to send **messages**, as a browser talks to a server with HTTP, but over a local channel. Electron's **IPC** (inter-process communication) modules, `ipcMain` and `ipcRenderer`, provide named channels for these messages.

**Three patterns.**

| Pattern | Renderer side | Main side | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Renderer to main, one-way | `ipcRenderer.send(channel, ...args)` | `ipcMain.on(channel, (event, ...args) => ...)` | Notifications that need no answer ("document is dirty") |
| Renderer to main, request/response | `await ipcRenderer.invoke(channel, ...args)` | `ipcMain.handle(channel, async (event, ...args) => result)` | Most calls: open a dialog, read a file, get a setting |
| Main to renderer | `ipcRenderer.on(channel, (event, ...args) => ...)` | `win.webContents.send(channel, ...args)` | Pushing updates: sync status, menu commands, download progress |

Avoid `ipcRenderer.sendSync`: it blocks the renderer until main replies, and if main is busy the window freezes.

**A full round trip.** The export feature from the previous topic, end to end:

```text
 Renderer (page)              Preload                     Main process
 ---------------              -------                     ------------
 bookshelf.exportReadingList(books)
        |----------------------> ipcRenderer.invoke('books:export', books)
                                         |------------------------> ipcMain.handle('books:export')
                                                                    validate sender + args
                                                                    dialog.showSaveDialog(...)
                                                                    fs.writeFile(...)
                                         <------------------------- return { saved, path }
        <---------------------- Promise resolves
 showToast(...)
```

```javascript
// main.js: handlers registered once, at startup
const { app, ipcMain, dialog, BrowserWindow } = require('electron');
const fs = require('node:fs/promises');

// Accept messages only from our own UI (see the security notes below)
function isTrustedSender(frame) {
  if (!frame) return false;                          // frame was destroyed or navigated away
  const url = new URL(frame.url);
  return url.protocol === 'file:' || url.origin === 'app://bookshelf'; // our local content only
}

ipcMain.handle('app:version', () => app.getVersion());

ipcMain.handle('books:export', async (event, books) => {
  if (!isTrustedSender(event.senderFrame)) throw new Error('Untrusted sender');
  if (!Array.isArray(books) || books.length > 10_000) throw new Error('Invalid book list');

  const win = BrowserWindow.fromWebContents(event.sender); // the window that asked
  const { canceled, filePath } = await dialog.showSaveDialog(win, {
    defaultPath: 'reading-list.json',
    filters: [{ name: 'JSON', extensions: ['json'] }],
  });
  if (canceled || !filePath) return { saved: false };

  // Main chooses what to write: only known fields, not whatever the page sent
  const clean = books.map(({ id, title, author, read }) =>
    ({ id: Number(id), title: String(title), author: String(author), read: Boolean(read) }));
  await fs.writeFile(filePath, JSON.stringify(clean, null, 2), 'utf8');
  return { saved: true, path: filePath };
});

const dirtyWindows = new Set();                      // ids of windows with unsaved changes

ipcMain.on('editor:unsaved', (event, flag) => {
  const win = BrowserWindow.fromWebContents(event.sender);
  win.setDocumentEdited(flag);                       // macOS: dot in the close button
  dirtyWindows[flag ? 'add' : 'delete'](win.id);
});
```

```javascript
// main.js: pushing a message from main to one window
function reportSyncStatus(win, status) {
  if (!win.isDestroyed()) win.webContents.send('sync:status', status);
}
```

**Errors.** If an `ipcMain.handle` handler throws, the renderer's `invoke` Promise rejects. Only the error *message* crosses the boundary (stack traces and custom properties are lost), so return structured results like `{ ok: false, reason: 'not-found' }` when the UI needs details.

**What can be sent.** Arguments are serialized with the structured clone algorithm: plain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `ArrayBuffer`, typed arrays and `Error` objects work. Functions, DOM nodes, class instances' prototypes, Promises and Electron objects do not. For large binary data, send an `ArrayBuffer` or `Uint8Array` rather than an array of numbers.

**MessagePorts.** For high-volume or direct communication, Electron supports `MessageChannelMain` and transferring `MessagePort`s, the same API as Web Workers' `postMessage`. A common use is a direct channel between a renderer and a utility process, so that the main process does not have to relay every message.

**Security rules for IPC.**

- **Treat every message as untrusted input.** The renderer shows content from the network; assume it may be compromised. Validate types, sizes and values in main, exactly as an API server validates HTTP requests (12.3).
- **Validate the sender.** Check `event.senderFrame.url` so that messages from an embedded third-party frame or a page the window navigated to are rejected.
- **Expose capabilities, not primitives.** `books:export` with a save dialog chosen by the user is safe; `fs:write(path, data)` is not.
- **Name channels by feature** (`books:export`, `sync:status`) to keep the API surface visible and auditable.

**Key Takeaways**

- Processes communicate only by messages on named channels through `ipcMain` and `ipcRenderer`.
- Use `invoke`/`handle` for request/response, `send`/`on` for one-way, and `webContents.send` for main-to-renderer pushes.
- Arguments are copied with structured clone: no functions, DOM nodes or class instances.
- Errors thrown in a handler reject the renderer's Promise, but only the message survives.
- Validate the sender and every argument in main, and expose specific capabilities rather than generic primitives.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement `bookshelf.getAppVersion()` with `invoke`/`handle` and a "Check for sync" button that triggers a fake sync in main, which pushes three `sync:status` messages back to the window one second apart.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement `books:open-file`: main shows an Open dialog for `.json` files, reads the chosen file, validates it as a list of books (reject anything over 5 MB or with missing fields) and returns it. Write two malicious calls from the DevTools console and show that main rejects them.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you design the IPC API of an Electron app so that an XSS bug in the renderer does not compromise the user's machine?" *Hint:* think about the preload surface, channel granularity, sender validation, argument validation, and who chooses file paths and URLs.

#### Application Lifecycle Events

**Why lifecycle matters.** A web page lives and dies with its tab. A desktop application has a richer life: it starts, possibly before any window exists; it may keep running with no windows (common on macOS); the OS may ask it to open a file or URL; a second copy may be launched; the computer may sleep, resume or shut down. Handling these moments correctly is what makes an app feel native. The `app` module emits an event for each of them.

**The core sequence.**

```text
 launch
   |
   v
 'will-finish-launching'  (very early; set up crash reporting, open-url listeners on macOS)
   |
   v
 'ready' / app.whenReady() -----> create windows, menus, tray; register IPC handlers
   |
   |   while running: 'activate' (macOS Dock click), 'second-instance', 'open-file',
   |                  'open-url', 'browser-window-created', 'render-process-gone', ...
   v
 last window closed --> 'window-all-closed'  --> app.quit()   (Windows/Linux convention)
                                              \-> keep running (macOS convention)
   |
 quit requested (menu, Cmd+Q, app.quit(), OS shutdown)
   |
   v
 'before-quit'  --> 'close' on each window --> 'will-quit' --> 'quit'  --> process exits
 (cancellable)                                 (cancellable)
```

**The platform conventions.** On Windows and Linux, closing the last window quits the app. On macOS, apps usually stay running in the Dock with their menu bar, and clicking the Dock icon opens a new window. The standard boilerplate encodes both:

```javascript
// main.js
app.whenReady().then(() => {
  registerIpcHandlers();
  createMainWindow();

  // macOS: clicking the Dock icon with no windows open should open one
  app.on('activate', () => {
    if (BrowserWindow.getAllWindows().length === 0) createMainWindow();
  });
});

app.on('window-all-closed', () => {
  if (process.platform !== 'darwin') app.quit(); // macOS keeps the app alive
});
```

**Saving work before quitting.** `before-quit` fires once when quitting starts, before windows close. Use it to flush state. Because Electron does not wait for Promises in event handlers, asynchronous cleanup needs the "prevent, finish, quit again" pattern:

```javascript
let cleanupDone = false;

app.on('before-quit', async (event) => {
  if (cleanupDone) return;          // second pass: let the quit proceed
  event.preventDefault();           // pause the quit
  try {
    await syncPendingChanges();      // e.g. push offline edits to the bookshelf API
    await database.close();
  } finally {
    cleanupDone = true;
    app.quit();                      // quit again; handler now returns immediately
  }
});
```

Keep this work short: during operating system shutdown, the OS may kill the process if it takes too long.

**Single-instance apps.** Double-clicking the app icon again, or opening a file associated with the app, normally starts a **second process**. Most apps want one instance that receives the new request instead.

```javascript
const gotLock = app.requestSingleInstanceLock();

if (!gotLock) {
  app.quit();                        // another instance is running: it will handle this launch
} else {
  app.on('second-instance', (event, argv, workingDirectory) => {
    // argv contains the second launch's command line (files, deep links on Windows/Linux)
    if (mainWindow) {
      if (mainWindow.isMinimized()) mainWindow.restore();
      mainWindow.focus();
    }
    handleCommandLine(argv);          // e.g. open a file or a bookshelf:// link (16.2)
  });
  app.whenReady().then(createMainWindow);
}
```

**Other useful events.**

| Event (module) | When | Typical response |
|---|---|---|
| `open-file` (`app`, macOS) | User opens an associated file or drops it on the Dock icon | Open the file; may fire before `ready`, so queue it |
| `open-url` (`app`, macOS) | A registered custom URL scheme is opened (16.2) | Route the deep link |
| `browser-window-created`, `web-contents-created` (`app`) | Any window or page is created | Apply security handlers to every page (16.3) |
| `render-process-gone` (`webContents`/`app`) | A renderer crashed, was killed or ran out of memory | Log it, offer to reload (16.3) |
| `suspend`, `resume`, `lock-screen`, `unlock-screen` (`powerMonitor`) | System sleep or lock | Pause sync, reconnect WebSockets on resume |
| `shutdown` (`powerMonitor`, Linux and macOS) | OS is shutting down | Save state quickly |
| `updated` (`nativeTheme`) | User switched light/dark mode | Update UI if not using CSS `prefers-color-scheme` |

**Paths for app data.** Lifecycle code often reads and writes state. Use `app.getPath()` instead of hard-coding locations, because each operating system has its own conventions:

| Name | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| `userData` | `%APPDATA%\Bookshelf` | `~/Library/Application Support/Bookshelf` | `~/.config/Bookshelf` |
| `logs` | `%APPDATA%\Bookshelf\logs` | `~/Library/Logs/Bookshelf` | `~/.config/Bookshelf/logs` |
| `documents`, `downloads`, `temp`, `home` | Standard user folders | Standard user folders | Standard user folders |

**Key Takeaways**

- Create windows, menus and handlers after `app.whenReady()`; many APIs are not usable before it.
- Quit on `window-all-closed` except on macOS, and re-create a window on `activate`.
- For async cleanup in `before-quit`, prevent the quit, finish the work, then call `app.quit()` again.
- Use `requestSingleInstanceLock` and `second-instance` to route new launches, files and links to the running instance.
- Use `powerMonitor` for sleep/resume and `app.getPath()` for platform-correct data locations.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add the standard `activate` and `window-all-closed` handlers to Bookshelf Desktop and test the difference on macOS and on Windows or Linux (or simulate it by logging `process.platform`).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Make Bookshelf a single-instance app. When it is launched a second time with a file path argument (`electron . ./list.json`), the existing window should come to the front and open that file.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your Electron app loses user data when the computer goes to sleep with unsynchronized changes and the network is down on wake. Which lifecycle events would you use to fix it?" *Hint:* consider `powerMonitor` events, persisting locally before sync, and retrying on resume or when the network returns.

<a id="162-native-integration"></a>
### 16.2 Native Integration

An app that is only a web page in a window feels like a website. What makes it feel like a desktop application is integration with the operating system. This subchapter covers that integration: native menus, tray and Dock icons, file dialogs, notifications, keyboard shortcuts and the clipboard, custom URL schemes, and automatic updates. Each of these lives in the main process and is reached from the UI through the IPC patterns of 16.1.

#### Application and Context Menus

**Why native menus.** Desktop users expect a menu bar with File, Edit and View, keyboard shortcuts listed next to commands, and a right-click menu that matches the operating system's style. They also expect Cut, Copy, Paste and Undo to work in every text field. On macOS this is not optional: without an application menu, even Cmd+C and Cmd+V stop working in text fields. HTML can imitate menus, but only native menus appear in the macOS menu bar, follow accessibility settings and use the system's keyboard handling.

**Where menus appear.**

```text
 macOS                                          Windows / Linux
 +--------------------------------------------+ +--------------------------------------+
 |  Bookshelf  File  Edit  View  Window  Help | | [icon] Bookshelf             _ [] X  |  <- title bar
 +--------------------------------------------+ +--------------------------------------+
   ^ one global menu bar, at the top of the     | File  Edit  View  Help               |  <- menu bar
     screen; first menu is the app menu         +--------------------------------------+
     (About, Settings..., Quit)                 |  window content                      |
                                                  ^ menu bar inside each window
```

**Templates and roles.** Menus are built from a template: an array of plain objects. Each item has a `label` and either a `click` handler, a `role` or a `submenu`. A **role** is a built-in behavior that Electron implements natively and labels and localizes correctly for each platform: `undo`, `redo`, `cut`, `copy`, `paste`, `selectAll`, `reload`, `toggleDevTools`, `togglefullscreen`, `minimize`, `quit`, and whole standard menus such as `appMenu`, `editMenu`, `viewMenu` and `windowMenu`. Use roles whenever one exists.

**Accelerators** are keyboard shortcuts written as strings: `CmdOrCtrl+O` means Cmd+O on macOS and Ctrl+O elsewhere. Others: `Shift`, `Alt` (Option on macOS), `F5`, `Plus`, `Delete`.

```javascript
// main/menu.js
const { app, Menu, shell } = require('electron');

function buildAppMenu(getFocusedWindow) {
  const isMac = process.platform === 'darwin';

  // Helper: forward a command to the focused window's UI
  const sendToUI = (command) => () =>
    getFocusedWindow()?.webContents.send('menu:command', command);

  const template = [
    ...(isMac ? [{ role: 'appMenu' }] : []),        // macOS: About, Services, Hide, Quit...
    {
      label: 'File',
      submenu: [
        { label: 'New Note', accelerator: 'CmdOrCtrl+N', click: sendToUI('new-note') },
        { label: 'Open Book File...', accelerator: 'CmdOrCtrl+O', click: () => openBookFile() },
        { label: 'Export Reading List...', accelerator: 'CmdOrCtrl+E', click: sendToUI('export') },
        { type: 'separator' },
        isMac ? { role: 'close' } : { role: 'quit' },
      ],
    },
    { role: 'editMenu' },                             // Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Select All
    {
      label: 'View',
      submenu: [
        { role: 'reload' },
        ...(app.isPackaged ? [] : [{ role: 'toggleDevTools' }]), // DevTools only in development
        { type: 'separator' },
        { role: 'resetZoom' }, { role: 'zoomIn' }, { role: 'zoomOut' },
        { type: 'separator' },
        { role: 'togglefullscreen' },
      ],
    },
    { role: 'windowMenu' },
    {
      role: 'help',
      submenu: [
        { label: 'Documentation', click: () => shell.openExternal('https://bookshelf.example.com/docs') },
      ],
    },
  ];

  Menu.setApplicationMenu(Menu.buildFromTemplate(template));
}

module.exports = { buildAppMenu };
```

In the renderer, the preload exposes `onMenuCommand(cb)` (same pattern as `onSyncStatus` in 16.1), and the UI reacts to `'new-note'` or `'export'`.

**Dynamic items.** Items can be `enabled: false`, `type: 'checkbox'` with `checked`, or `type: 'radio'`. Give an item an `id` to find and change it later: `Menu.getApplicationMenu().getMenuItemById('export').enabled = books.length > 0`. For bigger changes, rebuild the menu from the template with new state.

**Context menus.** A right-click menu is a `Menu` shown with `menu.popup()`. Chromium reports right-clicks through the `context-menu` event of `webContents`, with details about what was clicked: selected text, whether the target is editable, link URL, image URL, misspelled word and spelling suggestions.

```javascript
// main.js: a context menu for every window
const { Menu } = require('electron');

function attachContextMenu(win) {
  win.webContents.on('context-menu', (_event, params) => {
    const template = [];

    // Spellchecker suggestions for a misspelled word in an editable field
    for (const suggestion of params.dictionarySuggestions.slice(0, 3)) {
      template.push({ label: suggestion, click: () => win.webContents.replaceMisspelling(suggestion) });
    }
    if (params.misspelledWord) template.push({ type: 'separator' });

    if (params.isEditable) template.push({ role: 'cut' }, { role: 'copy' }, { role: 'paste' });
    else if (params.selectionText) template.push({ role: 'copy' });

    if (params.selectionText) {
      template.push({ type: 'separator' }, {
        label: `Search books for "${params.selectionText.slice(0, 20)}"`,
        click: () => win.webContents.send('menu:command', 'search', params.selectionText),
      });
    }

    if (template.length) Menu.buildFromTemplate(template).popup({ window: win });
  });
}
```

For a context menu that depends on application data (for example "Mark as read" on a specific book card), let the renderer handle `contextmenu` in the DOM, call `event.preventDefault()`, and send the book id through IPC. Main then builds and pops up the menu.

**Key Takeaways**

- Build menus from templates with `Menu.buildFromTemplate` and install them with `Menu.setApplicationMenu`.
- Prefer roles (`editMenu`, `copy`, `quit`...): they are native, localized and correct per platform.
- macOS has one global menu bar with an app menu first; without an Edit menu, clipboard shortcuts break.
- Accelerators like `CmdOrCtrl+O` map to the right modifier on each platform.
- Context menus come from the `context-menu` event (or renderer IPC) and are shown with `menu.popup()`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build the File, Edit, View and Help menus above for Bookshelf Desktop and verify that Copy and Paste work in a text field on your platform.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a "Mark as read" context menu to book cards: the renderer sends the book id on right-click, main shows a menu with "Mark as read" or "Mark as unread" depending on the book's current state, and the choice is sent back to the UI.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why might copy and paste stop working in an Electron app on macOS, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* consider what implements those keyboard shortcuts on macOS and what happens when a custom application menu omits certain roles.

#### System Tray and Dock Integration

**Why stay visible without a window.** Some apps should keep working when their window is closed: a chat app that receives messages, a sync client, a music player, a clipboard manager. Users still need a way to see their status and reach them. The operating system provides a small, permanent place for this: the **system tray** (notification area) on Windows, the **menu bar extras** on macOS and the **status area** on many Linux desktops. The macOS **Dock** and the Windows **taskbar** also accept badges, progress bars and custom menus.

**Creating a tray icon.**

```javascript
// main/tray.js
const { app, Tray, Menu, nativeImage } = require('electron');
const path = require('node:path');

let tray = null;   // keep a module-level reference: if garbage-collected, the icon disappears

function createTray(showMainWindow) {
  // macOS: a file named "...Template.png" is treated as a template image,
  // drawn in black or white automatically to match the menu bar
  const iconFile = process.platform === 'darwin' ? 'trayTemplate.png' : 'tray.png';
  const icon = nativeImage.createFromPath(path.join(__dirname, '..', 'assets', iconFile));

  tray = new Tray(icon);
  tray.setToolTip('Bookshelf');
  tray.setContextMenu(Menu.buildFromTemplate([
    { label: 'Open Bookshelf', click: showMainWindow },
    { label: 'Sync now', click: () => syncNow() },
    { type: 'separator' },
    { label: 'Pause sync', type: 'checkbox', checked: false, click: (item) => setSyncPaused(item.checked) },
    { type: 'separator' },
    { label: 'Quit', click: () => app.quit() },
  ]));

  // Windows convention: left click opens the window (macOS shows the menu on click)
  tray.on('click', () => { if (process.platform === 'win32') showMainWindow(); });
  return tray;
}

module.exports = { createTray };
```

Provide icons at 16x16 and 32x32 (`tray.png` and `tray@2x.png`; Electron picks the right one for high-DPI screens). On Linux, tray support depends on the desktop environment (GNOME needs an AppIndicator extension), so the tray must never be the *only* way to reach a feature.

**"Close to tray".** If the app should keep running when its window is closed, hide the window instead of destroying it, but let a real quit through:

```javascript
let isQuitting = false;
app.on('before-quit', () => { isQuitting = true; });

mainWindow.on('close', (event) => {
  if (!isQuitting) {
    event.preventDefault();  // closing the window only hides it
    mainWindow.hide();
  }
});
```

Tell users this is happening (a one-time notification "Bookshelf is still running in the tray") and offer a setting to turn it off. An app that silently keeps running after its window closes surprises users.

**Dock and taskbar features.**

| Feature | API | Platform |
|---|---|---|
| Badge with a count | `app.setBadgeCount(3)` | macOS, some Linux desktops (Unity launcher) |
| Badge with text | `app.dock.setBadge('3')` | macOS |
| Overlay icon on the taskbar button | `win.setOverlayIcon(image, '3 unread')` | Windows |
| Progress bar in the Dock/taskbar | `win.setProgressBar(0.4)`; `-1` removes it; `2` shows indeterminate | All (Linux: Unity launcher only) |
| Attract attention | `app.dock.bounce('informational')` / `win.flashFrame(true)` | macOS / Windows and Linux |
| Dock menu | `app.dock.setMenu(menu)` | macOS |
| Jump list tasks | `app.setUserTasks([...])`, `app.setJumpList([...])` | Windows |
| Recent documents | `app.addRecentDocument(filePath)` | macOS and Windows |
| Hide from Dock (tray-only app) | `app.dock.hide()` | macOS |

```javascript
// Show export progress on the taskbar/Dock icon and the unread count as a badge
function reportExportProgress(win, done, total) {
  win.setProgressBar(done < total ? done / total : -1); // value between 0 and 1; -1 = remove
}

function setUnreadCount(win, count) {
  if (process.platform === 'darwin') {
    app.dock.setBadge(count ? String(count) : '');
  } else if (process.platform === 'win32') {
    win.setOverlayIcon(count ? badgeImage(count) : null, count ? `${count} new books` : '');
  } else {
    app.setBadgeCount(count);  // may be ignored by the desktop environment
  }
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `Tray` puts a permanent icon with a menu in the notification area; keep a reference so it is not garbage-collected.
- Use template images on macOS and provide 1x/2x icons; Linux tray support varies by desktop.
- "Close to tray" means hiding the window in `close` while letting a real quit through via `before-quit`.
- Badges, progress bars, jump lists and Dock menus are platform-specific; check `process.platform`.
- Never make the tray the only route to a feature, and make background behavior visible and configurable.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a tray icon to Bookshelf Desktop with "Open", "Sync now" and "Quit" items, and make "Open" restore a hidden window.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement close-to-tray with a setting stored in `userData`. Show the unread-book count as a Dock badge on macOS and as an overlay icon on Windows, and a taskbar progress bar while an export runs.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A user reports that your app's tray icon disappears after a few minutes. What is the most likely cause?" *Hint:* think about JavaScript object lifetimes and what keeps a native resource alive.

#### Native Dialogs and File System Access

**Why native dialogs.** A browser can let the user pick a file with `<input type="file">`, but it cannot let the page save to a chosen path, open a folder, or remember a file for later. A desktop app is expected to have Open and Save As dialogs that look like the operating system's, remember recent folders and respect sandboxing rules. In Electron, the `dialog` module shows these native dialogs, and Node.js `fs` (11.5) does the actual reading and writing, both in the main process.

**Dialog types.**

| Method | Returns | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `dialog.showOpenDialog(win, options)` | `{ canceled, filePaths }` | Choose one or more files or folders |
| `dialog.showSaveDialog(win, options)` | `{ canceled, filePath }` | Choose where to save |
| `dialog.showMessageBox(win, options)` | `{ response, checkboxChecked }` | Questions, confirmations, warnings |
| `dialog.showErrorBox(title, content)` | nothing | Fatal errors; works even before `ready` |

Passing the window as the first argument makes the dialog **modal** to that window (a sheet attached to the window on macOS). The `...Sync` variants exist but block the main process; prefer the Promise-based ones.

**Opening and saving files, safely.**

```javascript
// main/files.js
const { ipcMain, dialog, BrowserWindow, app } = require('electron');
const fs = require('node:fs/promises');
const path = require('node:path');

const MAX_SIZE = 5 * 1024 * 1024;   // refuse files larger than 5 MB

ipcMain.handle('books:open-file', async (event) => {
  const win = BrowserWindow.fromWebContents(event.sender);
  const { canceled, filePaths } = await dialog.showOpenDialog(win, {
    title: 'Import Reading List',
    defaultPath: app.getPath('documents'),
    properties: ['openFile'],            // also: 'openDirectory', 'multiSelections', 'showHiddenFiles'
    filters: [
      { name: 'Reading lists', extensions: ['json', 'csv'] },
      { name: 'All files', extensions: ['*'] },
    ],
  });
  if (canceled || filePaths.length === 0) return null;

  const filePath = filePaths[0];        // chosen by the USER, not by the page
  const { size } = await fs.stat(filePath);
  if (size > MAX_SIZE) return { error: 'File is too large' };

  const content = await fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8');
  app.addRecentDocument(filePath);      // appears in the OS "recent" lists
  return { name: path.basename(filePath), content };
});

ipcMain.handle('notes:confirm-delete', async (event, title) => {
  const { response } = await dialog.showMessageBox(BrowserWindow.fromWebContents(event.sender), {
    type: 'warning',
    buttons: ['Cancel', 'Delete'],
    defaultId: 0,                       // Enter = Cancel: the safe choice
    cancelId: 0,                        // Esc = Cancel
    message: `Delete the note "${String(title).slice(0, 80)}"?`,
    detail: 'This cannot be undone.',
  });
  return response === 1;
});
```

The important design point: the **user** chooses the path in a dialog shown by main, and the page only receives the result. Compare an IPC handler `fs:read(path)` that reads any path the page asks for: one XSS bug and the attacker reads the user's SSH keys.

**Where to store application data.** Files the user chooses go where the user chose. The app's own data (settings, caches, a local database, offline copies of books) goes under `app.getPath('userData')`, never next to the executable, which is read-only after installation on macOS and often on Windows.

```javascript
const settingsFile = path.join(app.getPath('userData'), 'settings.json');

async function saveSettings(settings) {
  const tmp = `${settingsFile}.tmp`;
  await fs.writeFile(tmp, JSON.stringify(settings, null, 2));
  await fs.rename(tmp, settingsFile);   // atomic replace: no half-written file after a crash
}
```

For larger structured data, use a local database such as SQLite (`better-sqlite3` is a native module, see 16.3) or IndexedDB in the renderer. For secrets such as an API token, use `safeStorage.encryptString()`, which encrypts with the operating system's key store (Keychain on macOS, DPAPI on Windows, the Secret Service or KWallet on Linux).

**Drag and drop.** Users expect to drop files onto the window. The renderer receives `File` objects through standard DOM drag events, and the preload can turn one into a real file system path with `webUtils.getPathForFile(file)` (the old non-standard `file.path` property was removed). The path is sent to main, which validates it before reading.

```javascript
// preload.js
const { contextBridge, ipcRenderer, webUtils } = require('electron');
contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('bookshelf', {
  importDroppedFile: (file) => ipcRenderer.invoke('books:import-path', webUtils.getPathForFile(file)),
});

// renderer
dropZone.addEventListener('drop', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  for (const file of e.dataTransfer.files) window.bookshelf.importDroppedFile(file);
});
```

Main should still check that the dropped path has an allowed extension and size, because the renderer could send any string.

**The `shell` module.** For actions handed to the operating system: `shell.showItemInFolder(p)` reveals a file in Explorer or Finder, `shell.openPath(p)` opens it with its default app, `shell.trashItem(p)` moves it to the trash (safer than deleting), and `shell.openExternal(url)` opens a URL in the user's browser. Validate URLs before `openExternal` (16.3).

**Key Takeaways**

- Use `dialog.showOpenDialog`, `showSaveDialog` and `showMessageBox` in main, modal to the requesting window.
- Let the user choose paths in dialogs shown by main; never expose "read or write any path" to the renderer.
- Store app data under `app.getPath('userData')`, write atomically, and protect secrets with `safeStorage`.
- For drag and drop, use `webUtils.getPathForFile` in the preload and validate the path in main.
- Use `shell` to reveal, open or trash files and to open external URLs (after validation).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement "Export Reading List" with a Save dialog that defaults to `reading-list.json` in the Documents folder, and a "Show in folder" button that calls `shell.showItemInFolder` after saving.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Store the bookshelf API token with `safeStorage` in `userData`, and add a confirmation dialog before logging out. Verify that the stored file does not contain the token in plain text.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is an IPC handler `readFile(path)` dangerous, and how would you design file access instead?" *Hint:* consider who controls the argument if the renderer is compromised, and how user-driven dialogs or an allow-list of directories change that.

#### Desktop Notifications

**Why notifications.** A desktop app often has news while the user is looking at something else: a sync finished, a book came back from loan, a reminder is due. Notifications are the operating system's standard way to report this. They appear in the corner of the screen, are collected in the notification center, respect Do Not Disturb and Focus modes, and bring the user back to the app with a click.

**Two APIs.** Electron offers two ways to show a notification, and both end up as native OS notifications:

| API | Process | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Web Notification API: `new Notification(title, { body })` | Renderer | Same as in browsers (6.4); no permission prompt in Electron by default (you can control it with a permission handler) |
| Electron `Notification` class | Main | More options: `silent`, `urgency` (Linux), `timeoutType`, `actions` and `hasReply` (macOS), `toastXml` (Windows), `close` events |

Use the main-process API when the notification is triggered by background work (sync, timers, the tray) that does not belong to any window, or when you need platform features.

```javascript
// main/notify.js
const { Notification, app } = require('electron');
const path = require('node:path');

function notifyBookReturned(book, showBook) {
  if (!Notification.isSupported()) return;          // e.g. some minimal Linux setups

  const n = new Notification({
    title: 'Book available',
    body: `"${book.title}" is back on the shelf.`,
    icon: path.join(__dirname, '..', 'assets', 'icon.png'), // Windows/Linux; macOS uses the app icon
    silent: false,
    actions: [{ type: 'button', text: 'Borrow' }],  // macOS only; ignored elsewhere
  });

  n.on('click', () => showBook(book.id));           // user clicked the notification body
  n.on('action', (_e, index) => { if (index === 0) borrowBook(book.id); });
  n.show();
}
```

**Platform requirements.**

- **Windows** shows notifications as "toasts" attributed to an **AppUserModelID**. Call `app.setAppUserModelId('com.example.bookshelf')` early, with the same ID as the installer's Start menu shortcut. Installers made with electron-builder or Squirrel create this shortcut. During development, notifications may appear under "electron.app.Electron".
- **macOS** attributes notifications to the signed app bundle. Users control them per app in System Settings > Notifications, and an unsigned development build may behave differently from the released app.
- **Linux** uses the freedesktop notification specification through D-Bus (libnotify). Features such as actions and images depend on the notification daemon.

**Designing good notifications.** The OS gives users an easy way to silence an app permanently, so treat notifications as limited:

- Notify about events the user cares about and cannot see, not about things happening in the focused window (check `BrowserWindow.getFocusedWindow()`).
- Group or summarize: "5 books synced" instead of five notifications.
- Make every notification actionable: clicking should open the relevant view.
- Offer in-app settings per category (reminders, sync results, availability).
- Never put sensitive data in notification text: it can appear on a locked screen.

**Key Takeaways**

- Notifications can come from the renderer (Web Notification API) or main (Electron `Notification`, with more options).
- Both become native OS notifications that respect Do Not Disturb and per-app settings.
- On Windows, set an AppUserModelID that matches the installed shortcut; on macOS, behavior depends on the signed bundle.
- Handle `click` (and `action` on macOS) to route the user to the relevant content.
- Notify rarely, group events, avoid notifying about the focused window and avoid sensitive content.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Show a notification from the renderer with the Web Notification API and one from main with the `Notification` class, and compare how they appear on your OS.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a reminder feature: the user sets "remind me to finish this book on Friday", main schedules it, shows a notification at the right time (even if the window is closed to the tray) and opens the book when it is clicked. Persist reminders across restarts.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your Electron app's notifications work in development but not after installation on Windows. What would you check?" *Hint:* think about how Windows associates toasts with an application identity and installed shortcut.

#### Global Shortcuts and Clipboard

**Why system-wide keys.** Normal keyboard shortcuts (menu accelerators, `keydown` listeners) work only while your window has focus. Some apps should react to keys from anywhere: a quick-capture window ("save this quote to my reading notes"), a launcher, push-to-talk in a voice app, media keys in a player. The **clipboard** is the other channel apps share with each other: the user copies in one app and pastes in another.

**Three kinds of shortcuts.**

| Kind | Mechanism | Active when |
|---|---|---|
| In-page | `keydown` listeners in the renderer | The page has focus |
| Application (local) | Menu item `accelerator`, or `webContents` `before-input-event` | One of the app's windows has focus |
| Global | `globalShortcut.register()` in main | Always, even when another app is focused |

Prefer the narrowest kind that does the job. Global shortcuts are a shared, limited resource: two apps cannot both own `Ctrl+Shift+N`, and taking a combination another app relies on annoys users.

**Registering a global shortcut.**

```javascript
// main.js
const { app, globalShortcut } = require('electron');

app.whenReady().then(() => {
  const accelerator = settings.quickCaptureShortcut ?? 'CommandOrControl+Shift+B';

  const ok = globalShortcut.register(accelerator, () => {
    showQuickCaptureWindow();          // a small always-on-top window for a note
  });

  if (!ok) {
    // Already taken by another app or the OS: tell the user and let them choose another
    console.warn(`Global shortcut ${accelerator} is unavailable`);
  }
});

app.on('will-quit', () => {
  globalShortcut.unregisterAll();      // release the keys for other applications
});
```

Notes:

- Registration only works after `ready`, and `register` returns `false` if the combination is unavailable.
- Make the shortcut **configurable** and off by default unless it is the app's core feature.
- On macOS, some global key handling requires the user to grant accessibility permission; on Linux under Wayland, global shortcuts depend on compositor and desktop portal support and may not work everywhere.

**Clipboard basics.** The system clipboard can hold the same content in several formats at once: plain text, HTML, RTF, images and app-specific formats. A paste target picks the richest format it understands. Copying a book citation as both HTML (with italics) and plain text lets a word processor keep the formatting while a terminal gets plain text.

In the **renderer**, use the standard asynchronous Clipboard API (`navigator.clipboard.writeText`, `readText`, `write` with `ClipboardItem`), as on the web. In the **main process** (for example from a tray menu or a global shortcut, where there is no focused page), use Electron's `clipboard` module:

```javascript
// main.js
const { clipboard, nativeImage } = require('electron');

function copyCitation(book) {
  const text = `${book.author}, ${book.title} (${book.year})`;
  clipboard.write({
    text,                                                           // for plain-text targets
    html: `${escapeHtml(book.author)}, <i>${escapeHtml(book.title)}</i> (${book.year})`, // for rich targets
  });
}

function captureFromClipboard() {
  const formats = clipboard.availableFormats();   // e.g. ['text/plain', 'text/html']
  if (formats.includes('text/plain')) return { kind: 'text', value: clipboard.readText() };
  const image = clipboard.readImage();            // a NativeImage; empty if no image
  if (!image.isEmpty()) return { kind: 'image', png: image.toPNG() };
  return null;
}

// Linux has a second clipboard: the "selection" (text highlighted with the mouse)
const selected = process.platform === 'linux' ? clipboard.readText('selection') : '';
```

**Putting them together: quick capture.** Pressing `Ctrl+Shift+B` anywhere reads the clipboard and saves it as a note:

```javascript
globalShortcut.register('CommandOrControl+Shift+B', async () => {
  const item = captureFromClipboard();
  if (!item || item.kind !== 'text') return;
  await notes.add({ text: item.value.slice(0, 10_000), createdAt: Date.now() }); // limit size
  new Notification({ title: 'Saved to Bookshelf', body: item.value.slice(0, 80) }).show();
});
```

**Privacy.** The clipboard often contains passwords and personal data. Read it only in response to a clear user action (a shortcut or a Paste command), never poll it in the background, and do not send its content anywhere without the user's consent.

**Key Takeaways**

- In-page and menu shortcuts need focus; `globalShortcut` works system-wide but competes with other apps.
- Register global shortcuts after `ready`, check the boolean result, make them configurable and unregister them on `will-quit`.
- Renderer code should use `navigator.clipboard`; main uses Electron's `clipboard` module.
- Write several formats (`text` and `html`) so each paste target gets the best one.
- Treat clipboard content as private and untrusted: read it only on user action and limit its size.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a "Copy citation" button to each book card that copies a plain-text citation with `navigator.clipboard.writeText`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the quick-capture global shortcut with a settings field where the user records a new combination. Handle the case where registration fails and restore the previous shortcut.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When should a desktop app register a global keyboard shortcut, and what problems can it cause?" *Hint:* consider conflicts with other apps and the OS, accessibility, user expectations, platform permissions and Wayland.

#### Protocol Handlers and Deep Linking

**Why custom URLs.** Links connect the web. A desktop app can join in by registering a **custom URL scheme** such as `bookshelf://`. A link `bookshelf://book/42` on the bookshelf website, in an email or in another app then opens the desktop app directly on book 42. This is **deep linking**. Common uses: "Open in desktop app" buttons, single sign-on (the browser finishes login and redirects to `bookshelf://auth/callback?code=...`), and links shared between users. A related feature, **file associations**, makes the app open `.bookshelf` files on double-click.

Electron uses the word "protocol" for two different things:

| Feature | API | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| Deep links: the OS opens your app for `bookshelf://` URLs | `app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient`, `open-url`, `second-instance` | Outside world -> your app |
| Custom schemes for loading your app's own content (`app://bookshelf/index.html`) | `protocol.handle` | Your renderer -> your main process |

**Registering the scheme.** At runtime, `app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient('bookshelf')` registers the app with the operating system. For installed apps, the scheme should also be declared in the package configuration so that the installer registers it (16.3): `CFBundleURLTypes` in `Info.plist` on macOS, registry keys on Windows, a `MimeType=x-scheme-handler/bookshelf` line in the `.desktop` file on Linux. electron-builder generates all three from one `protocols` entry.

**Receiving the link differs per platform.**

```text
 User clicks bookshelf://book/42
          |
          +-- macOS --------> the running app (or a newly launched one) receives
          |                   app 'open-url' event (event, url)
          |
          +-- Windows/Linux -> the OS starts a NEW process: electron.exe bookshelf://book/42
                              - app not running: URL is in process.argv of this process
                              - app running:     single-instance lock makes the new process
                                                 quit; the first one gets 'second-instance'
                                                 with the URL in its argv
```

```javascript
// main.js: deep-link handling for all platforms
const { app } = require('electron');
const path = require('node:path');

const SCHEME = 'bookshelf';

// Development: Electron is started as "electron path/to/app", so pass the app path explicitly
if (process.defaultApp && process.argv.length >= 2) {
  app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient(SCHEME, process.execPath, [path.resolve(process.argv[1])]);
} else {
  app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient(SCHEME);
}

let pendingUrl = null;   // a link that arrives before the window exists

// macOS
app.on('open-url', (event, url) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  mainWindow ? handleDeepLink(url) : (pendingUrl = url);
});

// Windows and Linux
const findLink = (argv) => argv.find((arg) => arg.startsWith(`${SCHEME}://`));

if (!app.requestSingleInstanceLock()) {
  app.quit();
} else {
  app.on('second-instance', (_event, argv) => {
    const url = findLink(argv);
    if (url) handleDeepLink(url);
    mainWindow?.show();
    mainWindow?.focus();
  });

  app.whenReady().then(() => {
    mainWindow = createMainWindow();
    const url = pendingUrl ?? findLink(process.argv); // link that launched the app
    if (url) mainWindow.webContents.once('did-finish-load', () => handleDeepLink(url));
  });
}
```

**Parse and validate every link.** A deep link is input from *anywhere*: any web page can contain `bookshelf://...` and trigger your app with one click. Treat it like an HTTP request from an anonymous user.

```javascript
// main/deeplink.js
function handleDeepLink(raw) {
  let url;
  try { url = new URL(raw); } catch { return; }          // malformed: ignore
  if (url.protocol !== 'bookshelf:') return;

  // bookshelf://book/42 -> host 'book', pathname '/42'
  switch (url.host) {
    case 'book': {
      const id = Number(url.pathname.slice(1));
      if (Number.isInteger(id) && id > 0) mainWindow.webContents.send('nav:book', id);
      break;
    }
    case 'auth': {
      const code = url.searchParams.get('code');
      const state = url.searchParams.get('state');
      if (url.pathname === '/callback' && code && state === expectedOAuthState) {
        completeLogin(code);                              // PKCE + state check (10.3)
      }
      break;
    }
    default:
      // Unknown routes are ignored. Never: shell.openExternal(url.searchParams.get('target')),
      // never pass link content to a shell command, never load it into a BrowserWindow.
  }
}
```

Real vulnerabilities have come from deep-link handlers that passed URL parameters to command-line arguments, loaded them into windows with privileges, or opened arbitrary files. Use an allow-list of routes, validate every parameter, and never perform destructive actions without asking the user to confirm.

**Serving your own content with a custom scheme.** Loading the UI from `file://` gives every page broad file-system read semantics and an unusual origin (`null`). The recommended alternative is a privileged custom scheme that serves only your bundled files:

```javascript
// main.js
const { protocol, net } = require('electron');
const { pathToFileURL } = require('node:url');

protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged([            // must run before 'ready'
  { scheme: 'app', privileges: { standard: true, secure: true, supportFetchAPI: true } },
]);

app.whenReady().then(() => {
  const root = path.join(__dirname, 'renderer');
  protocol.handle('app', (request) => {
    const { pathname } = new URL(request.url);       // app://bookshelf/index.html
    const filePath = path.normalize(path.join(root, decodeURIComponent(pathname)));
    if (!filePath.startsWith(root + path.sep)) {      // block ../ path traversal
      return new Response('Forbidden', { status: 403 });
    }
    return net.fetch(pathToFileURL(filePath).toString());
  });
  mainWindow.loadURL('app://bookshelf/index.html');  // origin is now app://bookshelf
});
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A custom scheme (`bookshelf://`) lets links on the web and in other apps open your app on specific content.
- Register with `setAsDefaultProtocolClient` and in the installer configuration (Info.plist, registry, `.desktop` file).
- macOS delivers links through `open-url`; Windows and Linux start a new process, so combine `process.argv` with the single-instance lock and `second-instance`.
- Deep links are untrusted input from any website: parse with `URL`, allow-list routes and validate every parameter.
- `protocol.handle` serves your own content from a custom origin; guard it against path traversal.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Register `bookshelf://` in development and open `bookshelf://book/7` from a browser's address bar. Log the URL that reaches the main process on your platform.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement `bookshelf://book/:id` and `bookshelf://search?q=...` routes, including the case where the app is not yet running. Write five malicious or malformed links and show that each is ignored.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is a custom URL scheme handler a security-sensitive part of a desktop app?" *Hint:* consider who can trigger it, with how little user interaction, and what the handler might do with the parameters.

#### Auto-Update Mechanisms

**Why updates must be automatic.** A web app is updated for everyone the moment you deploy. A desktop app is installed: whatever version the user downloaded stays on their machine until something replaces it. Electron makes this more pressing, because each app ships its own Chromium. A user who never updates keeps every browser vulnerability that has been fixed since, in an app that has access to the file system. Users rarely check for updates by hand, so the app must update itself: check for a new version, download it in the background, verify it and install it with minimal disruption.

**How it works.**

```text
 Bookshelf 1.4.0 (installed)                      Update server / GitHub Releases / S3
 ----------------------------                      ------------------------------------
 1. on start and every few hours:
    GET latest.yml (or the update feed) ---------> latest version: 1.5.0, file, sha512, size
 2. 1.5.0 > 1.4.0 ?  yes
 3. download installer/package in background <---- Bookshelf-1.5.0.exe / .zip / .AppImage
    (differential: only changed blocks, if supported)
 4. verify checksum and code signature
 5. tell the user "Restart to update" (or install on next quit)
 6. quitAndInstall(): app quits, updater replaces files, app restarts as 1.5.0
```

**The options.**

| Option | Platforms and formats | Server | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron's built-in `autoUpdater` | macOS (Squirrel.Mac, zip), Windows (Squirrel.Windows) | A feed URL you provide | Low-level; no Linux support |
| `update-electron-app` + update.electronjs.org | macOS, Windows | Free service for public GitHub repositories | One line of code; open-source apps on GitHub only |
| `electron-updater` (from electron-builder) | Windows (NSIS), macOS (dmg + zip), Linux (AppImage, deb, rpm) | GitHub Releases, S3, generic HTTPS server, others | Most widely used; staged rollouts, differential downloads, channels |
| Store updates | Microsoft Store, Mac App Store, Snap Store, Flathub | The store | The store handles updates; in-app updaters must be disabled |

**electron-updater in practice.** It reads a small metadata file (`latest.yml`, `latest-mac.yml`, `latest-linux.yml`) that electron-builder generates and publishes next to the installers:

```yaml
# latest.yml (generated; published with the release)
version: 1.5.0
files:
  - url: Bookshelf-Setup-1.5.0.exe
    sha512: 3q2+7w...                 # verified after download
    size: 98340211
path: Bookshelf-Setup-1.5.0.exe
releaseDate: '2026-09-28T10:12:00.000Z'
stagingPercentage: 20                 # optional: roll out to 20% of users first
```

```javascript
// main/updater.js
const { app, dialog, BrowserWindow } = require('electron');
const { autoUpdater } = require('electron-updater');
const log = require('electron-log');

autoUpdater.logger = log;               // write updater activity to the log file
autoUpdater.autoDownload = true;        // download in the background when found
autoUpdater.autoInstallOnAppQuit = true; // if the user ignores the prompt, install on next quit

function initUpdater() {
  if (!app.isPackaged) return;          // no updates in development

  autoUpdater.on('update-available', (info) => log.info('Update available', info.version));
  autoUpdater.on('download-progress', (p) =>
    BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()[0]?.setProgressBar(p.percent / 100));
  autoUpdater.on('error', (err) => log.error('Update failed', err)); // never crash on update errors

  autoUpdater.on('update-downloaded', async (info) => {
    BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()[0]?.setProgressBar(-1);
    const { response } = await dialog.showMessageBox({
      type: 'info',
      buttons: ['Restart now', 'Later'],
      defaultId: 0,
      cancelId: 1,
      message: `Bookshelf ${info.version} is ready to install.`,
      detail: 'The update will be installed automatically the next time you quit.',
    });
    if (response === 0) autoUpdater.quitAndInstall();  // quits, installs, relaunches
  });

  autoUpdater.checkForUpdates();
  setInterval(() => autoUpdater.checkForUpdates(), 4 * 60 * 60 * 1000); // every 4 hours
}

module.exports = { initUpdater };
```

**Release channels.** Publish beta builds with a prerelease version (`1.6.0-beta.1`) and let users opt in with `autoUpdater.channel = 'beta'` (or `allowPrerelease = true`). Testers get new features first, and everyone else stays on stable.

**Requirements and pitfalls.**

- **Code signing is required.** macOS refuses to apply updates to an unsigned app, and on Windows, unsigned updates trigger SmartScreen warnings (16.3). The update mechanism is also an attack vector: it downloads and runs code. It must use HTTPS, verify checksums, and ideally verify that the new version is signed by the same publisher (electron-updater checks the Windows publisher name).
- **Use the right formats.** macOS auto-updates need the `zip` target in addition to the `dmg` users download. AppImage is the only Linux format that updates itself in place; `deb` and `rpm` users usually update through a package repository.
- **Data migrations.** A new version may find data written by an older one. Version your settings and database files, and migrate on startup.
- **Roll out gradually.** Staged rollouts (`stagingPercentage`) limit the damage of a bad release; you can stop a rollout and publish a fix. Because a broken updater cannot fix itself, test the update path itself (install version N, update to N+1) before every release.
- **Respect the user.** Never force a restart while the user is working. Download silently, offer to restart, and fall back to installing on quit.

**Key Takeaways**

- Desktop apps must update themselves; for Electron apps this also delivers Chromium security fixes.
- The updater checks a feed, downloads in the background, verifies, and installs on restart or quit.
- `electron-updater` covers Windows, macOS and AppImage with GitHub, S3 or generic servers; `update-electron-app` suits public GitHub projects.
- Updates require code-signed builds, HTTPS and checksum verification; macOS needs the `zip` target.
- Use channels and staged rollouts, migrate data between versions, and never force a restart mid-work.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Read the update-related events of `electron-updater` and draw a state diagram (idle, checking, available, downloading, downloaded, error) for the Bookshelf updater.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Publish two signed or test builds (1.0.0 and 1.0.1) to a local static HTTPS server with the `generic` provider, install 1.0.0, and observe the full update cycle in the log file.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you design the update system of a desktop app so that one bad release cannot brick every installation?" *Hint:* think about staged rollouts, keeping the updater independent of app features that might break, testing the update path, and how users recover if the app crashes at startup.

<a id="163-building-securing-and-distributing"></a>
### 16.3 Building, Securing and Distributing

A folder with `main.js` and `npm start` is not a product. Users need a signed installer they can trust, an app that does not turn a web bug into a system compromise, and builds that start fast, use memory sensibly and report their crashes. This subchapter follows Bookshelf Desktop from source code to the user's machine, then compares Electron with its main alternatives.

#### Packaging with electron-builder and electron-forge

**Why packaging is a separate step.** During development, the `electron` npm package runs your source folder with a generic Electron binary. Users need something different: an executable named *Bookshelf* with its own icon and version information, containing only production code (no `devDependencies`, no tests), native modules compiled for the right architecture, built separately for each operating system and wrapped in an installer. Packaging tools automate this.

**What a packaged app looks like.**

```text
 Windows (unpacked)                         macOS
 Bookshelf/                                 Bookshelf.app/
   Bookshelf.exe        <- renamed           Contents/
                           Electron binary     Info.plist        <- bundle id, version, URL schemes
   resources/                                  MacOS/Bookshelf   <- renamed Electron binary
     app.asar           <- your code           Frameworks/       <- Electron Framework, helpers
     app.asar.unpacked/ <- native modules      Resources/
   locales/, *.pak, *.dll <- Chromium            app.asar
                                                 icon.icns
```

Your code lives in **`app.asar`**, an archive format similar to tar that Electron reads as if it were a folder (`fs.readFile(path.join(__dirname, 'index.html'))` works inside it). ASAR speeds up startup on Windows (one large file instead of thousands of small ones), avoids path-length problems and enables integrity checks. Native modules (`.node` files) cannot be loaded from inside an archive, so they are placed in `app.asar.unpacked`.

**The two main toolchains.**

| | Electron Forge | electron-builder |
|---|---|---|
| Maintained by | The Electron project (official) | Community |
| Philosophy | Complete pipeline using official `@electron/*` tools (packager, rebuild, osx-sign, notarize) | One highly configurable tool with its own implementations |
| Config | `forge.config.js` | `electron-builder.yml` or the `build` key of `package.json` |
| Project templates | Yes: Vite, webpack, TypeScript | No (use with any setup) |
| Installers ("makers"/"targets") | Squirrel.Windows, MSI (WiX), MSIX/AppX, DMG, zip, pkg, deb, rpm, Flatpak, Snap | NSIS, MSI, MSIX/AppX, portable, DMG, pkg, zip, AppImage, deb, rpm, Snap, Flatpak and more |
| Auto-update | Built-in `autoUpdater`, `update-electron-app` | `electron-updater` (16.2) |
| Publishing | Publishers: GitHub, S3, others | `publish` providers: GitHub, S3, generic, others |

Both are good choices. Forge follows the Electron team's recommendations and is the default for new projects; electron-builder is very common in existing apps, mainly for NSIS installers and `electron-updater`.

**Electron Forge.**

```bash
# Create a project from a template (Vite + TypeScript)
npm init electron-app@latest bookshelf-desktop -- --template=vite-typescript

npm run start     # electron-forge start: dev mode with hot reload of the renderer
npm run package   # electron-forge package: app folder for the current platform (out/)
npm run make      # electron-forge make: installers for the current platform (out/make/)
npm run publish   # electron-forge publish: make + upload to the configured publisher
```

```javascript
// forge.config.js
const { FusesPlugin } = require('@electron-forge/plugin-fuses');
const { FuseV1Options, FuseVersion } = require('@electron/fuses');

module.exports = {
  packagerConfig: {
    name: 'Bookshelf',
    appBundleId: 'com.example.bookshelf',
    icon: 'assets/icon',            // icon.ico / icon.icns chosen per platform
    asar: true,
    protocols: [{ name: 'Bookshelf', schemes: ['bookshelf'] }],
    osxSign: {},                    // sign on macOS with the identity found in the keychain
    osxNotarize: {                  // notarize (next topic); credentials from environment variables
      appleId: process.env.APPLE_ID,
      appleIdPassword: process.env.APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD,
      teamId: process.env.APPLE_TEAM_ID,
    },
  },
  makers: [
    { name: '@electron-forge/maker-squirrel', config: { name: 'bookshelf' } }, // Windows Setup.exe
    { name: '@electron-forge/maker-dmg', config: {} },                         // macOS disk image
    { name: '@electron-forge/maker-zip', platforms: ['darwin'] },              // needed for auto-update
    { name: '@electron-forge/maker-deb', config: { options: { categories: ['Office'] } } },
    { name: '@electron-forge/maker-rpm', config: {} },
  ],
  publishers: [
    { name: '@electron-forge/publisher-github',
      config: { repository: { owner: 'example', name: 'bookshelf-desktop' }, draft: true } },
  ],
  plugins: [
    new FusesPlugin({               // flip security-relevant switches in the binary (see the security checklist below)
      version: FuseVersion.V1,
      [FuseV1Options.RunAsNode]: false,
      [FuseV1Options.EnableNodeOptionsEnvironmentVariable]: false,
      [FuseV1Options.EnableNodeCliInspectArguments]: false,
      [FuseV1Options.EnableEmbeddedAsarIntegrityValidation]: true,
      [FuseV1Options.OnlyLoadAppFromAsar]: true,
    }),
  ],
};
```

**electron-builder.**

```yaml
# electron-builder.yml
appId: com.example.bookshelf
productName: Bookshelf
directories:
  output: release
files:                      # what goes into app.asar
  - dist/**/*               # compiled main, preload and renderer code
  - package.json
asarUnpack:
  - node_modules/better-sqlite3/**   # native module must live outside the archive
protocols:
  - name: Bookshelf
    schemes: [bookshelf]
fileAssociations:
  - ext: bookshelf
    name: Bookshelf Reading List
mac:
  category: public.app-category.productivity
  target: [dmg, zip]
  hardenedRuntime: true
  entitlements: build/entitlements.mac.plist
  notarize: true            # uses APPLE_ID / APPLE_TEAM_ID / ... environment variables
win:
  target: [nsis]
linux:
  target: [AppImage, deb]
  category: Office
publish:
  provider: github
  owner: example
  repo: bookshelf-desktop
```

```bash
npx electron-builder --mac --win --linux   # build for the listed platforms (where possible)
npx electron-builder --win --publish always # build and upload to GitHub Releases
```

**Native modules.** Packages with C/C++ code (`better-sqlite3`, `keytar`, `node-pty`) are compiled against a specific Node.js ABI. Electron's embedded Node.js has a different ABI from your system Node.js, so these modules must be **rebuilt for Electron** (`@electron/rebuild`; Forge and electron-builder do it automatically) for each target platform and architecture. A missed rebuild is the classic "NODE_MODULE_VERSION mismatch" error at startup.

**Building for every platform.** You can build Windows and Linux installers on several systems, but macOS apps must be signed and notarized on macOS, and native modules are easiest to build on their own platform. In practice, teams use a CI matrix (17.3) with one runner per operating system:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/release.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [windows-latest, macos-latest, ubuntu-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run make            # or: npx electron-builder --publish always
        env:                          # signing secrets come from the CI secret store
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Packaging produces a renamed, branded Electron binary with your production code in `app.asar`.
- Electron Forge is the official, template-based pipeline; electron-builder is a widely used, highly configurable alternative.
- Both declare icons, bundle ids, URL schemes, file associations, targets and publishing in one config file.
- Native modules must be rebuilt for Electron's Node.js ABI and unpacked from the ASAR archive.
- Build on each operating system in CI; macOS builds must be made and signed on macOS.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a Forge project with the Vite template, run `npm run make`, and inspect the output: find `app.asar` and list its contents with `npx @electron/asar list`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure electron-builder for Bookshelf Desktop with NSIS, DMG + zip and AppImage targets, a `bookshelf://` protocol and a `.bookshelf` file association. Add `better-sqlite3` and make sure the packaged app starts.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A packaged Electron app crashes at startup with `NODE_MODULE_VERSION` mismatch, but works with `npm start`. What happened?" *Hint:* compare the Node.js ABI the module was compiled against with the one embedded in Electron, and think about which step of the build pipeline should handle it.

#### Code Signing and Notarization

**Why sign.** When a user downloads `Bookshelf-Setup.exe`, how can the operating system know it really comes from you and was not modified on the way? **Code signing** answers this. You obtain a certificate from a trusted authority, which verifies your identity, and use its private key to sign your binaries. The OS verifies the signature at install and launch time, much as a browser verifies a TLS certificate (10.1).

Without signing, users get frightening warnings or are blocked outright, and auto-updates do not work on macOS (16.2). Signing also matters for security: if your download server is compromised, a modified binary will fail verification.

```text
 Build machine                                           User's machine
 -------------                                           --------------
 Bookshelf.exe --hash--> digest --sign with private key--> signature embedded in the file
                                                              |
                                  download                    v
                                  -------->  OS: recompute digest, verify signature with the
                                             certificate's public key, check certificate chain
                                             to a trusted root, check timestamp & revocation
                                                  |
                                     valid -------+------- invalid / unsigned
                                     install/run           warning or block
```

A **timestamp** from a trusted timestamp server is added to the signature, proving the code was signed while the certificate was valid. Thanks to it, the signature stays valid after the certificate expires.

**macOS: Developer ID, hardened runtime and notarization.**

1. **Developer ID certificate.** Join the Apple Developer Program, create a *Developer ID Application* certificate and install it in the build machine's keychain (in CI, import it from a base64-encoded `.p12` secret).
2. **Hardened runtime.** Apps distributed outside the App Store must enable the hardened runtime, which blocks code injection and similar techniques. Electron needs a few exceptions, declared as **entitlements**.
3. **Sign** every binary in the bundle (the app, Electron Framework, helper apps, native modules). `@electron/osx-sign` (Forge) and electron-builder do this in the right order.
4. **Notarize.** Upload the signed app to Apple's notary service, which scans it automatically for malware and returns a ticket. Gatekeeper (the macOS component that checks downloaded apps) blocks apps that are not notarized.
5. **Staple** the ticket to the app or DMG so that verification also works offline.

```xml
<!-- build/entitlements.mac.plist -->
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit</key>   <!-- V8's JIT compiler needs executable memory -->
  <true/>
  <key>com.apple.security.device.camera</key>  <!-- only if the app scans ISBN barcodes -->
  <true/>
</dict>
</plist>
```

```bash
# What the tools do under the hood (useful for debugging)
xcrun notarytool submit Bookshelf-1.5.0.dmg \
  --apple-id "$APPLE_ID" --team-id "$APPLE_TEAM_ID" \
  --password "$APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD" --wait    # upload and wait for the verdict
xcrun stapler staple Bookshelf-1.5.0.dmg               # attach the ticket

# Verify the result
codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=2 Bookshelf.app
spctl --assess --type execute --verbose Bookshelf.app  # "accepted, source=Notarized Developer ID"
```

Request only the entitlements you need: each one weakens the hardened runtime a little. Device access (camera, microphone) also requires a usage description in `Info.plist` (for example `NSCameraUsageDescription`), shown to the user in the permission prompt.

**Windows: Authenticode and SmartScreen.**

- Windows code signing uses **Authenticode** certificates from a certificate authority. Since 2023, industry rules require the private key to be kept in a hardware security module: a USB token, a cloud HSM or a cloud signing service such as Microsoft's Azure-based signing service. You can no longer export a key to a `.pfx` file on a build server.
- **SmartScreen** shows "Windows protected your PC" for downloads without established reputation. Reputation builds up as many users install files signed with the same certificate, so a newly signed app may still see warnings at first. Unsigned apps fare worst.
- Sign the installer *and* the executables inside it, with SHA-256 and a timestamp.

```bash
# Sign with a certificate in the local store or on a token (thumbprint identifies it)
signtool sign /fd sha256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td sha256 /sha1 <thumbprint> Bookshelf-Setup-1.5.0.exe
signtool verify /pa /v Bookshelf-Setup-1.5.0.exe   # check signature and timestamp
```

electron-builder and Forge call `signtool` for you (or a custom signing hook for cloud HSMs) when they are configured with the certificate or signing service.

**Linux.** There is no central code-signing check at launch. Trust comes from the distribution channel: packages in an APT or RPM repository are signed with the repository's GPG key, Snap Store and Flathub packages are signed by the store, and AppImages can carry an optional GPG signature. Publish checksums (`SHA256SUMS`) alongside downloads.

**Protecting the keys.** Signing keys are among the most valuable secrets a company has: a stolen key lets attackers distribute malware under your name. Keep them in HSMs or the CI secret store, sign only in release pipelines, restrict who can trigger those pipelines, and know how to revoke a certificate.

**Key Takeaways**

- Code signing proves who published a binary and that it was not modified; timestamps keep signatures valid after the certificate expires.
- macOS requires a Developer ID signature, the hardened runtime with minimal entitlements, notarization and stapling.
- Windows uses Authenticode with HSM-protected keys; SmartScreen reputation builds over time.
- Linux relies on signed repositories, stores and published checksums.
- Signing keys are critical secrets: keep them in hardware or managed services and sign only in controlled pipelines.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Download a signed app installer and inspect its signature: on Windows, open the file's Properties > Digital Signatures; on macOS, run `codesign -dv --verbose=4` and `spctl --assess` on an installed app.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write the macOS signing part of a CI release job for Bookshelf: import the certificate from a secret into a temporary keychain, build with hardened runtime and entitlements, notarize, staple and verify with `spctl`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "What is notarization and how is it different from code signing?" *Hint:* one proves identity and integrity; the other involves a third party scanning the build and issuing a ticket that the OS checks.

#### Installers for Windows, macOS and Linux

**Why the installer matters.** The installer is the user's first contact with your app. It decides where files go, whether administrator rights are needed, whether shortcuts, file associations and URL schemes are registered, how uninstallation works and whether auto-updates can replace the files later. Each operating system has its own conventions, and enterprise IT departments have their own requirements.

**Windows.**

| Format | Install scope | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| NSIS (`.exe`, electron-builder) | Per-user (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs`) or per-machine (`Program Files`) | Flexible: one-click or assisted wizard, custom pages; works with `electron-updater` | Not natively manageable by enterprise tools |
| Squirrel.Windows (`Setup.exe`, Forge) | Per-user only | Zero-prompt install, built-in delta updates | No install location choice, no per-machine install; extra startup events to handle |
| MSI (WiX) | Usually per-machine | Standard for enterprise deployment (Group Policy, Intune) | Complex; updates managed by IT, not the app |
| MSIX / AppX | Per-user, containerized | Clean install/uninstall, Microsoft Store, Windows-managed updates | Sandbox-like restrictions on file system and registry |
| Portable (`.exe`) | None | Runs without installation (USB stick) | No shortcuts, file associations or auto-update |

**Per-user versus per-machine.** Per-user installs need no administrator rights and let the app update itself silently, which is why most Electron apps use them. Per-machine installs (one copy for all users, in `Program Files`) need elevation for installation *and* for every update, so they are typically managed by IT with MSI.

Squirrel.Windows launches your app with special arguments during install, update and uninstall, so the app can create or remove shortcuts and then exit:

```javascript
// main.js (Forge + Squirrel.Windows): handle installer events before anything else
if (require('electron-squirrel-startup')) app.quit(); // creates/removes shortcuts, then exits
```

**macOS.**

| Format | Use |
|---|---|
| DMG | Standard download: a disk image with the app and an alias to `/Applications`; the user drags one onto the other |
| zip | Required by Squirrel.Mac auto-updates; also a simple download |
| pkg | Installer package for cases that need system-level steps or managed (MDM) deployment |
| Mac App Store (`mas` target) | Store distribution; requires the App Sandbox and store-specific signing; updates through the store |

**Architectures.** Macs use Apple Silicon (`arm64`) and older Intel (`x64`) processors. Ship either a **universal** binary (both architectures in one app, about twice the size) or separate downloads per architecture. Windows also has `arm64` devices; building `x64` and `arm64` separately gives the best performance on each.

**Linux.**

| Format | Install | Updates | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| AppImage | None: download, `chmod +x`, run | `electron-updater` replaces the file | Works on most distributions; desktop integration is limited unless a helper is used |
| `.deb` | `apt install ./bookshelf.deb` (Debian, Ubuntu) | Through your APT repository | Declare dependencies; integrates with the system |
| `.rpm` | `dnf install` (Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE) | Through your RPM repository | Same as deb for the Red Hat family |
| Snap | Snap Store | Automatic by the store | Confined; mainly Ubuntu |
| Flatpak | Flathub | Automatic by Flatpak | Sandboxed with portals; popular across distributions |

Linux packages also install a **`.desktop` file**, which provides the menu entry, icon, file associations and URL schemes:

```ini
# /usr/share/applications/bookshelf.desktop (generated by the packager)
[Desktop Entry]
Name=Bookshelf
Exec=/opt/Bookshelf/bookshelf %U
Icon=bookshelf
Type=Application
Categories=Office;
MimeType=x-scheme-handler/bookshelf;application/x-bookshelf;
```

**Choosing a set of targets.** A typical consumer app ships: Windows NSIS per-user (`x64` and `arm64`), macOS DMG + zip (universal or per-architecture), Linux AppImage + deb (+ rpm). Add MSI for enterprise customers and store packages if store presence matters.

**Uninstalling cleanly.** Uninstallers remove the program files but usually leave `userData` (settings and local data), so a reinstall keeps the user's data. Offer an option to remove data too, and document where it lives.

**Key Takeaways**

- Windows: NSIS or Squirrel for per-user installs with auto-update; MSI for enterprise; MSIX for the Store.
- macOS: DMG for downloads plus zip for updates; pkg for managed deployment; the `mas` target for the App Store; ship arm64 and x64 or universal.
- Linux: AppImage for a self-updating download; deb and rpm through repositories; Snap and Flatpak through stores.
