```text
       any alert -> route everything back to v1
```

**Database changes and zero downtime.** During rolling, blue-green and canary deployments, old and new code run at the same time against the same database. Schema changes must therefore be **backward compatible**, using the *expand and contract* pattern: first add the new field and write both (expand), deploy code that reads the new field, migrate old data, and only in a later release remove the old field (contract).

**Key Takeaways**

- CI builds and tests every change automatically; continuous delivery makes every green build releasable; continuous deployment releases it automatically.
- A pipeline verifies, builds an immutable artifact, deploys to staging, runs smoke tests and promotes the same artifact to production, often with an approval gate.
- Fail fast, protect branches, use least privilege and OIDC for credentials, pin actions and cache dependencies.
- Rolling, blue-green and canary deployments avoid downtime and limit risk; feature flags separate deployment from release.
- Old and new versions coexist during deployment, so database changes must be backward compatible.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a GitHub Actions workflow for the bookshelf API that runs lint, type check and tests on every pull request, and make it a required check on `main`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend the workflow to build and push a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, deploy it to a staging environment, run a Playwright smoke test, and require manual approval for production.
> 3. *(Interview)* "How would you rename a database field used by a running API without downtime?" *Hint:* consider that two versions of the code run at once during deployment; think in several releases (expand, migrate, contract).

#### Cloud and Serverless Deployment Models

**Why so many models.** Running an application requires hardware, an operating system, a runtime, scaling, patching, networking and monitoring. Cloud providers offer to take over different amounts of that work. The more they manage, the less you control and configure, and the more the pricing shifts from "rent a machine" to "pay per use". Choosing a model is choosing where to draw that line.

An analogy: transport. Owning a car (a VM) gives you full control and full maintenance. Leasing with service included (PaaS) removes maintenance but limits choice. A taxi (serverless) costs nothing when idle and is pricier per kilometre at high use.

**The models.**

```text
                 You manage                                       Provider manages
 IaaS (VMs)      app, runtime, OS, scaling, patching              hardware, network, virtualisation
 CaaS            app, container image, scaling rules              OS, cluster, orchestration
 PaaS            app code, config                                 runtime, OS, scaling, TLS, deploys
 FaaS            individual functions                             everything else, including scaling to zero
 Edge functions  small functions near users                       global distribution
 Static + CDN    built files                                      storage, global caching, TLS
```

| Model | Examples | Scaling | Billing | Strengths | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IaaS (virtual machines) | AWS EC2, Azure VMs, Google Compute Engine, Hetzner | Manual or autoscaling groups | Per hour while running | Full control, any software | You patch, secure and operate everything |
| PaaS | Heroku, Render, Fly.io, Azure App Service, Railway | Configured instance count | Per instance | `git push` deploys, little ops work | Less control, platform limits, cost at scale |
| Containers as a service | Google Cloud Run, AWS ECS/Fargate, Azure Container Apps | Automatic, can scale to zero (Cloud Run) | Per vCPU-second and memory | Any Docker image, portable | Some container and network knowledge needed |
| Kubernetes | EKS, GKE, AKS, self-managed | Horizontal pod autoscaler | Cluster nodes | Most flexible, portable, huge ecosystem | Steep learning curve, significant operations work |
| Functions as a service (serverless) | AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions | Per request, automatic, to zero | Per invocation and duration | No idle cost, no servers | Cold starts, time limits, statelessness |
| Edge functions | Cloudflare Workers, Vercel/Netlify Edge, Deno Deploy | Automatic, global | Per request | Runs close to users, very low latency | Restricted runtime (Web APIs, not full Node), limited CPU time |
| Static hosting + CDN | Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, S3 + CloudFront | Automatic | Bandwidth | Cheapest and fastest for SPAs and static sites | Needs a separate API for dynamic data |

**A typical split for the bookshelf app.** The React build goes to a static host/CDN. The Express API runs as a container on Cloud Run or a PaaS. MongoDB and Redis use managed services (MongoDB Atlas, a managed Redis), so nobody operates databases by hand. Image thumbnails are generated by a serverless function triggered on upload.

**A serverless function.** In FaaS you deploy a *handler* function; the platform invokes it for each event (an HTTP request, a queue message, a file upload) and runs as many copies in parallel as needed:

```javascript
// AWS Lambda behind an HTTP endpoint (API Gateway / Function URL), Node.js runtime
import { MongoClient } from 'mongodb';

// Created OUTSIDE the handler: reused across invocations while the instance stays warm
const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI, { maxPoolSize: 2 });

export async function handler(event) {
  const isbn = event.pathParameters?.isbn;
  if (!isbn) return { statusCode: 400, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'isbn required' }) };

  const book = await client.db('bookshelf').collection('books').findOne({ isbn });
  return {
    statusCode: book ? 200 : 404,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(book ?? { error: 'not found' }),
  };
}
```

An edge function uses the standard Fetch API `Request`/`Response` instead:

```javascript
// Cloudflare Worker: runs in data centres worldwide
export default {
  async fetch(request, env) {
    const url = new URL(request.url);
    if (url.pathname === '/api/featured') {
      const cached = await env.CACHE.get('featured');              // edge key-value store
      if (cached) return new Response(cached, { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
    }
    return fetch(request);                                         // otherwise pass through to the origin
  },
};
```

**Serverless characteristics to design for.**

| Characteristic | Consequence | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Cold starts | The first request on a new instance loads the runtime and your code (100 ms to seconds) | Small bundles, few dependencies, provisioned concurrency for critical paths |
| Statelessness | Memory and local disk do not persist between invocations | Store state in databases, caches, object storage |
| Massive parallelism | 1,000 concurrent invocations can open 1,000 database connections | Connection reuse outside the handler, small pools, data proxies or HTTP-based databases |
| Time and size limits | Maximum execution time (e.g. 15 minutes on Lambda), payload limits | Move long work to queues and background jobs |
| Vendor-specific APIs | Handlers and triggers differ per provider | Keep business logic in plain modules; thin adapters per platform |

**Infrastructure as code.** Clicking resources together in a console cannot be reviewed, repeated or rolled back. **Infrastructure as code** (Terraform/OpenTofu, Pulumi, AWS CDK) describes servers, databases, DNS and permissions in files that live in Git and go through the same review and CI process as application code.

**Shared responsibility.** In every model, the provider secures what it manages and you secure what you manage. Even with serverless, your code, dependencies, configuration, access policies and data remain your responsibility.

**Key Takeaways**

- Deployment models range from VMs (most control, most work) through PaaS and containers to serverless and edge functions (least work, least control).
- Static front ends belong on a CDN; APIs commonly run as containers or on a PaaS; managed databases remove most operational burden.
- Serverless functions scale to zero and bill per use, but require stateless design and attention to cold starts and connection counts.
- Describe infrastructure as code, and remember that security of code, configuration and data stays with you.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Deploy the bookshelf React build to a static host and the API container to a PaaS or Cloud Run free tier, using a managed MongoDB. Note which steps the platform handled for you.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement `GET /books/:isbn` as a Lambda (or Cloud Function) handler and as an Express route, sharing the same `findBookByIsbn` module. Measure cold and warm response times.
> 3. *(Interview)* "When would you choose serverless functions over a container platform for an API, and when not?" *Hint:* consider traffic patterns (spiky versus steady), latency requirements, execution duration, database connections, cost at high volume and team experience.

#### Logging, Monitoring and Observability

**Why observe production.** Tests show that the code behaved correctly in the situations you imagined. Production produces situations you did not imagine: an unusual browser, a slow third-party API, a data shape from 2019, a traffic spike. When users report "the site is slow" or, worse, do not report anything and leave, you need to answer *what* is wrong, *where* and *since when*, without attaching a debugger to a production server. **Observability** is the ability to understand a system's internal state from the data it emits.

An analogy: a car's dashboard and its maintenance log. The dashboard (metrics) shows speed and warnings at a glance; the log (logs) records what happened; a mechanic's diagnostic trace of one journey (traces) shows exactly where time and fuel went.

**The three signals.**

| Signal | What it is | Answers | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logs | Timestamped records of discrete events | What happened in this request? | `{"level":"error","reqId":"a1","msg":"payment failed","provider":"stripe"}` |
| Metrics | Numeric measurements aggregated over time | How much, how fast, how often? | `http_requests_total{route="/books",status="500"}` per second |
| Traces | The path of one request through all services, as timed spans | Where did this slow request spend its time? | Gateway 5 ms -> API 20 ms -> MongoDB 480 ms |

**Logs: structured, correlated, safe.** As in 11.6, log JSON objects rather than free text, so log platforms can filter and aggregate by field. Every log line for one request should carry the same **request ID**, which is also returned to the client so a support ticket can be traced:

```javascript
import pino from 'pino';
import pinoHttp from 'pino-http';
import crypto from 'node:crypto';

export const logger = pino({
  level: config.LOG_LEVEL,
  redact: ['req.headers.authorization', 'req.headers.cookie', '*.password', '*.token'],   // never log secrets
});

app.use(pinoHttp({
  logger,
  genReqId: (req, res) => {
    const id = req.get('X-Request-Id') ?? crypto.randomUUID();   // reuse the proxy's ID if present
    res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', id);
    return id;
  },
  customLogLevel: (req, res, err) => (err || res.statusCode >= 500 ? 'error' : res.statusCode >= 400 ? 'warn' : 'info'),
}));

// In a route: req.log already carries reqId
req.log.info({ bookId, userId: req.user.id }, 'book borrowed');
```

| Level | Use for |
|---|---|
| `fatal` | The process cannot continue |
| `error` | A request or job failed and someone may need to act |
| `warn` | Unexpected but handled (retry succeeded, deprecated API used) |
| `info` | Significant business and lifecycle events (started, user registered) |
| `debug` / `trace` | Detailed diagnostics, normally off in production |

Containers write logs to stdout; the platform collects them and ships them to a log store such as Grafana Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Datadog or a cloud logging service.

**Metrics: measure what users feel.** Two simple frameworks tell you what to measure. **RED** for request-driven services: *Rate* (requests per second), *Errors* (failed requests per second), *Duration* (latency distribution). **USE** for resources: *Utilisation*, *Saturation*, *Errors* of CPU, memory, connection pools. Prometheus is the common open-source metrics system; it **scrapes** a `/metrics` endpoint on each instance:

```javascript
import client from 'prom-client';

client.collectDefaultMetrics();                       // event loop lag, heap, GC, CPU

const httpDuration = new client.Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'HTTP request duration',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'],
  buckets: [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5],      // seconds; histograms allow percentile queries
});

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const end = httpDuration.startTimer();
  res.on('finish', () => end({
    method: req.method,
    route: req.route?.path ?? 'unmatched',             // the route PATTERN, not the URL: keeps label count bounded
    status: res.statusCode,
  }));
  next();
});

app.get('/metrics', async (req, res) => {             // restrict to the internal network in production
  res.type(client.register.contentType).send(await client.register.metrics());
});
```

Report latency as **percentiles** (p50, p95, p99), not averages: an average of 100 ms can hide the 1% of users who wait 5 seconds.

**Traces with OpenTelemetry.** **OpenTelemetry** (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for generating traces, metrics and logs. Its Node.js auto-instrumentation patches `http`, Express, MongoDB, Redis and `fetch`, so each request produces a trace without code changes. The trace context travels to other services in the W3C `traceparent` header:

```javascript
// src/tracing.js: load before anything else: node --import ./dist/tracing.js dist/server/server.js
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node';
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http';

new NodeSDK({
  serviceName: 'bookshelf-api',
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter(),            // sends to OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT (Jaeger, Tempo, a vendor)
  instrumentations: [getNodeAutoInstrumentations()],
}).start();
```

```text
Trace 4bf92f... GET /api/v1/lists/42                           total 612 ms
|- express middleware: authenticate                        8 ms
|- express handler: getList                              598 ms
|   |- redis GET list:42 (miss)                            2 ms
|   |- mongodb find lists                                 31 ms
|   |- mongodb find books {_id: {$in: [...]}}            540 ms   <- missing index
```

**Health checks.** Orchestrators and load balancers need two different questions answered:

```javascript
app.get('/healthz', (req, res) => res.json({ status: 'ok' }));            // liveness: is the process alive?

app.get('/readyz', async (req, res) => {                                  // readiness: can it serve traffic now?
  if (!app.locals.ready) return res.status(503).json({ status: 'shutting down' });
  try {
    await Promise.all([mongoClient.db().command({ ping: 1 }), redis.ping()]);
    res.json({ status: 'ready' });
  } catch {
    res.status(503).json({ status: 'dependencies unavailable' });
  }
});
```

A failing liveness check causes a restart; a failing readiness check only removes the instance from the load balancer. Do not check databases in liveness, or a database outage will restart every instance in a loop.

**Alerting on what matters.** Alert on *symptoms users feel*, not on every cause. Define **SLIs** (service level indicators, such as "fraction of requests answered successfully in under 500 ms"), set **SLOs** (objectives, such as 99.5% over 30 days) and alert when the error budget (the 0.5%) is being used up too fast. An **SLA** is the contractual promise to customers, usually looser than the SLO. Every alert should be actionable, with a link to a runbook; alerts that fire constantly get ignored.

**Errors and real users.** Error trackers (Sentry, Rollbar, or OTel-based tools) group exceptions from servers and browsers, attach stack traces mapped through source maps, and show which release introduced them. **Real User Monitoring** (RUM) collects performance and errors from actual browsers (next section).

**Key Takeaways**

- Observability combines logs (events), metrics (aggregates) and traces (request paths) to explain production behaviour.
- Log structured JSON with request IDs and redaction; use levels consistently and ship logs from stdout.
- Measure RED metrics with histograms and percentiles; keep metric labels bounded.
- Use OpenTelemetry for vendor-neutral tracing across services.
- Separate liveness from readiness, and alert on SLO-based symptoms with runbooks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add `pino-http` with request IDs and redaction to the bookshelf API. Make a request with an `Authorization` header and verify that the token does not appear in the logs, while the `X-Request-Id` does.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Expose Prometheus metrics, run Prometheus and Grafana with Docker Compose, and build a dashboard with request rate, error rate and p95 latency per route. Add OpenTelemetry tracing with Jaeger and find the slowest span of `GET /lists/:id`.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Users say the app is slow, but average latency looks fine. How do you investigate?" *Hint:* look at percentiles instead of averages, break down by route and region, then follow slow traces to the span that dominates.

#### Performance Optimization and Web Vitals

**Why performance is a feature.** Users notice delays of a few hundred milliseconds. Slow pages lose visitors, conversions and search ranking, and slow interactions feel broken. Performance problems are also hard to see from a developer's fast laptop on office Wi-Fi: the real audience includes mid-range phones on mobile networks. Optimisation therefore starts with *measuring what real users experience*, then fixing the largest bottleneck first.

**Core Web Vitals.** Google's **Web Vitals** initiative defines a few user-centred metrics. Three of them, the **Core Web Vitals**, cover loading, interactivity and visual stability, and are used as a search ranking signal:

| Metric | Measures | Good | Needs improvement | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint) | Time until the largest image or text block in the viewport is rendered: "has the main content appeared?" | <= 2.5 s | <= 4.0 s | > 4.0 s |
| **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint) | Delay from a user interaction (click, tap, key) to the next frame painted, worst-case over the visit: "does the page respond?" | <= 200 ms | <= 500 ms | > 500 ms |
| **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift) | How much visible content unexpectedly moves: "does the page jump around?" | <= 0.1 | <= 0.25 | > 0.25 |

INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) in March 2024, because FID only measured the *first* interaction's input delay. Supporting metrics help diagnose the core ones: **TTFB** (Time to First Byte, server and network; good <= 0.8 s) and **FCP** (First Contentful Paint; good <= 1.8 s). A page passes when the **75th percentile** of real visits meets the "good" threshold, separately for mobile and desktop.

```text
 navigation start
 |--TTFB--|                                                     (server + network)
          |----FCP----|                                         (first text/image)
          |---------------LCP---------------|                   (main content)
                                    user clicks |--INP--| next paint
 layout shifts while loading:    ^  ^       ^                   (summed into CLS)
```

**Lab data vs field data.**

| | Lab (synthetic) | Field (real users, RUM) |
|---|---|---|
| Tools | Lighthouse (15.2), Chrome DevTools Performance panel, WebPageTest | `web-vitals` library, Chrome UX Report (CrUX), PageSpeed Insights field section |
| Conditions | One simulated device and network, repeatable | Every real device, network and behaviour |
| Good for | Debugging, CI regression checks, before release | Knowing what users actually experience |
| Limits | Cannot measure INP well (no real interactions) | Needs traffic; slower feedback |

Measure field data with the `web-vitals` library and send it to your own endpoint:

```javascript
// client/src/vitals.js
import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS, onTTFB } from 'web-vitals/attribution';   // attribution build explains WHY

function send(metric) {
  const body = JSON.stringify({
    name: metric.name,                      // 'LCP' | 'INP' | 'CLS' | 'TTFB'
    value: metric.value,
    rating: metric.rating,                  // 'good' | 'needs-improvement' | 'poor'
    page: location.pathname,
    target: metric.attribution?.interactionTarget ?? metric.attribution?.target,   // the slow element
  });
  navigator.sendBeacon('/api/vitals', body);   // survives page unload, unlike fetch
}

onLCP(send);
onINP(send);
onCLS(send);
onTTFB(send);
```

**Improving LCP.** LCP breaks down into server response, resource load delay, resource load time and render delay.

```html
<!-- Discoverable, prioritised hero image; never lazy-load the LCP element -->
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/covers/featured-640.avif" fetchpriority="high">

<img src="/covers/featured-640.avif"
     srcset="/covers/featured-320.avif 320w, /covers/featured-640.avif 640w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 640px"
     width="640" height="960"
     fetchpriority="high"
     alt="Cover of this week's featured book">

<!-- Below-the-fold images can wait -->
<img src="/covers/related-1.avif" loading="lazy" width="200" height="300" alt="...">
```

Other LCP levers: reduce TTFB (caching, CDN, server-side rendering or static generation for content pages, 14.5), compress with Brotli, serve modern image formats (AVIF, WebP), avoid render-blocking scripts and large CSS, and `preconnect` to required third-party origins.

**Improving INP.** INP is poor when the main thread is busy when the user interacts, or when the handler itself does too much work before the browser can paint. Any task over 50 ms is a **long task**. Break work into chunks and yield to the browser so it can handle input and paint:

```javascript
// Filtering 20,000 books on every keystroke blocks the main thread
async function filterBooks(books, query) {
  const results = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < books.length; i++) {
    if (books[i].title.toLowerCase().includes(query)) results.push(books[i]);
    if (i % 1000 === 0) await yieldToMain();       // give the browser a chance to paint and handle input
  }
  return results;
}

function yieldToMain() {
  return globalThis.scheduler?.yield?.() ?? new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}
```

Other INP levers: give immediate visual feedback before heavy work, debounce input handlers, use React's `useTransition` or `useDeferredValue` for non-urgent updates (14.2), virtualise long lists, move heavy computation to a Web Worker, avoid layout thrashing (alternating DOM reads and writes, 6.2), and reduce third-party scripts.

**Improving CLS.** Always set `width` and `height` (or CSS `aspect-ratio`) on images and videos; reserve space for ads, embeds and late-loading banners; avoid inserting content above existing content except in response to a user action; animate with `transform` rather than properties that change layout; and use `font-display: optional` or size-adjusted fallback fonts to limit shifts from web fonts.

**Back-end performance.** Front-end metrics often trace back to the server:

| Problem | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| N+1 queries | One query per list item | Batch with `$in` or joins |
| Missing index | Slow queries as data grows (trace above) | Add indexes; check `explain()` (13.2) |
| Repeated expensive reads | Same data computed for every request | Cache in Redis (13.3) or with HTTP caching and ETags (10.1) |
| Large responses | Slow on mobile networks | Pagination, field selection, compression |
| Blocking the event loop | All requests slow at once | Streams, worker threads, async APIs (11.3) |

**Performance budgets.** A budget turns performance into a pass/fail check, so regressions are caught in CI rather than by users. Lighthouse CI (15.2) can assert thresholds on every pull request:

```json
{
  "ci": {
    "assert": {
      "assertions": {
        "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 2500 }],
        "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 0.1 }],
        "total-blocking-time": ["warn", { "maxNumericValue": 200 }],
        "resource-summary:script:size": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 250000 }]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Core Web Vitals measure loading (LCP <= 2.5 s), responsiveness (INP <= 200 ms) and visual stability (CLS <= 0.1) at the 75th percentile of real users.
- Use lab tools to debug and gate regressions, and field data (RUM, CrUX) to know real experience.
- LCP: fast TTFB, discoverable and prioritised hero resources, modern images. INP: short tasks, yielding, less JavaScript. CLS: reserved space and explicit dimensions.
- Many front-end problems originate on the server: queries, indexes, caching and payload size.
- Enforce performance budgets in CI.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights on the bookshelf home page. Identify the LCP element and fix two issues they report, such as missing image dimensions or a lazy-loaded hero image.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add the `web-vitals` library with attribution, store the results through a `/api/vitals` endpoint, and compute the p75 of each metric per page. Then use the Performance panel with 4x CPU throttling to find and split a long task in the search page.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Our Lighthouse score is 98 but CrUX shows poor INP. How is that possible?" *Hint:* compare lab and field conditions: real devices, real interactions after load, third-party scripts and pages that Lighthouse never tested.

#### Scalability and Load Balancing

**Why scalability.** An application that serves 100 users comfortably may collapse at 10,000: the CPU saturates, the database runs out of connections, latency climbs until requests time out. **Scalability** is the ability to handle more load by adding resources, ideally with cost growing roughly in proportion to load. Designing for it early mostly means avoiding choices that make scaling impossible later, such as keeping user state in one server's memory.

An analogy: a supermarket at rush hour. You can hire a faster cashier (vertical scaling) only up to a point; opening more checkout lanes (horizontal scaling) works much further, but needs someone directing customers to free lanes (the load balancer), and every lane must be able to serve any customer (stateless servers).

**Vertical vs horizontal scaling.**

| | Vertical (scale up) | Horizontal (scale out) |
|---|---|---|
| How | Bigger machine: more CPU, RAM | More machines or instances |
| Limit | The largest available machine | Practically very high |
| Availability | Single point of failure | Survives instance failures |
| Code changes | None | Instances must be stateless or share state externally |
| Cost curve | Rises steeply at the top end | Roughly linear; can scale down when quiet |

Node.js adds a twist: one process uses one core for JavaScript, so even on one machine you scale horizontally with the cluster module, PM2 (earlier in this subchapter) or several containers.

**Statelessness: the prerequisite.** If instance A stores a session in memory and the next request goes to instance B, the user is logged out. Every piece of shared state must move out of the process:

| State | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| Sessions | Redis session store (13.3) or stateless tokens (10.3) |
| Uploaded files | Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), not the local disk |
| Caches | Redis instead of in-process `Map`s (or accept per-instance caches that may differ) |
| Rate-limit counters | Redis-backed store (12.2) |
| WebSocket broadcast | Redis pub/sub adapter so a message reaches clients on all instances (10.5) |
| Scheduled jobs | A single scheduler or a queue with locking, so jobs do not run once per instance |

**Load balancers.** A load balancer distributes incoming requests across healthy instances.

| Type | Operates on | Can route by | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layer 4 (transport) | TCP/UDP connections | IP and port | AWS NLB, HAProxy in TCP mode |
| Layer 7 (application) | HTTP requests | Path, host, headers, cookies | nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, AWS ALB, Google Cloud Load Balancing |

| Algorithm | Behaviour | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Round robin | Each instance in turn | Similar instances, similar requests |
| Weighted round robin | Proportional to configured weights | Mixed instance sizes, canary releases (see CI/CD above) |
| Least connections | Instance with fewest active connections | Requests of varying duration, WebSockets |
| IP hash / consistent hashing | Same client or key goes to the same instance | Cache locality, sticky behaviour without cookies |

Load balancers run **health checks** (the `/readyz` endpoint) and stop sending traffic to failing instances. **Sticky sessions** (pinning a client to one instance) are a workaround for stateful servers; they hurt balancing and fail when the instance dies, so prefer stateless instances.

```nginx
upstream bookshelf_api {
    least_conn;                                        # algorithm
    server 10.0.1.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    server 10.0.1.12:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    server 10.0.1.13:3000 weight=2;                    # a bigger instance gets twice the share
}
```

**A scalable architecture for the bookshelf app.**

```text
                               +-------------+
   Users ----> DNS ----------> |     CDN     |  static assets, cached public API responses
                               +------+------+
                                      |
                               +------v------+
                               | L7 load     |  TLS, health checks, routing
                               | balancer    |
                               +--+---+---+--+
                                  |   |   |
                        +---------+   |   +---------+
                        v             v             v
                    API inst.     API inst.     API inst.     stateless, autoscaled on CPU / latency
                        \             |             /
          +--------------+------------+------------+-------------+
          v                           v                          v
     Redis (sessions,           MongoDB replica set         Job queue (BullMQ) --> worker instances
     cache, rate limits)        primary + read replicas      e-mails, thumbnails, imports
```

**Scaling the data layer.** Stateless API instances are easy to multiply; the database usually becomes the bottleneck next. In order of increasing complexity:

1. **Indexes and query fixes**: often the cheapest large win (13.2).
2. **Caching**: Redis or HTTP/CDN caching for frequently read, rarely changed data (13.3, 10.1).
3. **Connection pooling**: each instance keeps a bounded pool; total connections = instances x pool size must stay below the database limit.
4. **Read replicas**: send reads that tolerate slight staleness to secondaries.
5. **Asynchronous work**: move slow tasks (e-mail, image processing, imports) to a queue processed by workers, so requests return quickly and spikes are absorbed.
6. **Sharding / partitioning**: split data across several database servers by a key (13.2); powerful but operationally complex.

**Autoscaling.** Cloud platforms add and remove instances based on metrics such as CPU utilisation, request rate or queue length. Set minimum instances for availability and to avoid cold starts, and maximum instances to protect the database and budget.

**Load testing.** Do not guess capacity: measure it before users do. **k6** runs load scenarios written in JavaScript; **autocannon** is a quick Node-based HTTP benchmarker:

```javascript
// load/browse.js: run with `k6 run load/browse.js`
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: '1m', target: 50 },      // ramp up to 50 virtual users
    { duration: '3m', target: 200 },     // hold a higher load
    { duration: '1m', target: 0 },       // ramp down
  ],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],      // fewer than 1% errors
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'],    // 95% of requests under 500 ms
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/v1/books?page=1&limit=20`);
  check(res, { 'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);                              // think time between user actions
}
```

Run load tests against a production-like environment, watch the metrics and traces from the previous sections while they run, and find which resource saturates first. That resource is the next thing to scale or optimise.

**Key Takeaways**

- Vertical scaling is simple but limited; horizontal scaling goes further and improves availability, but requires stateless instances.
- Move sessions, files, caches, counters and broadcasts out of process memory into shared services.
- Load balancers spread traffic (round robin, least connections, hashing) and remove unhealthy instances; prefer statelessness to sticky sessions.
- The database is usually the next bottleneck: index, cache, pool, replicate, queue, and shard only when needed.
- Load test with clear thresholds to find the real bottleneck, and autoscale within safe limits.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run three bookshelf API containers behind nginx with round robin. Log the instance hostname in each response and verify the distribution. Then stop one container and check that requests keep succeeding.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Move sessions and rate-limit counters to Redis so login works across all instances. Write a k6 test with p95 and error-rate thresholds, run it with one and with three instances, and report which resource saturates first.
> 3. *(Interview)* "Your API runs on three instances behind a load balancer. After a marketing campaign it becomes slow even though the API servers' CPU is at 30%. What do you look at?" *Hint:* follow the request path beyond the app servers: database connections and slow queries, cache hit rate, external APIs, connection pool waits and event-loop lag.
